- **D827** — **Two of the hand-written checks standing in for gates could not return a hit, and one of them *confirmed* the thing it was written to falsify.** In GNU grep's ERE a backslash before a backtick matches nothing, and two of `CLAUDE.md`'s commands escape it. **Instance 1**, the re-check standing in for §15 **D319**'s blind spot — `git diff <base>..HEAD -- crates/ | grep -E '^\+ *(///|//!).*\[\`'`, credited with **a catch per session for six sessions running** — returns **0 matches / exit 1** against a fixture the unescaped pattern matches. 🚨 **Instance 2 is worse and is why this is one entry**: `review/`'s census defends against a count reading *high* by extracting `^\| \`\[` as a **second reading and comparing**, and an inert second reading does not merely fail to falsify the census — it comes back empty, reads as *"no fix-log row names a finding in its body"*, and **corroborates** the high count. *A check that goes quiet wastes a reading; a check that answers in the shape of a corroboration is worth less than no check, because it is spent as evidence.* 🚨 **Both were found by *running* them, neither by reading**, which is §15 **D732**'s advice failing on its own terms: `'.*\[\`'` reads as a careful author escaping everything, so the defect is invisible to the attention that catches a wrong anchor. **The advice needs its second half — a command you cannot falsify by reading, control.** ⚠️ **The correct spelling was already in the tree, inside D319 itself**, whose `find … grep -nE '^ *//[/!].*\[`'` uses a bare backtick: one check written twice, once correctly and once incapably, with the incapable copy in the file everybody reads. *(Both commands fixed 2026-09-22; **Keep** — resolved as to the two commands, **open as to the class**. 🚨 ***Fix:* no sweep has been run.** What was checked is the commands this session had reason to touch plus the `review/` one; `CLAUDE.md`'s other greps, `awk` programs and `comm` pipelines are **uncontrolled**, and every clean reading ever taken from one is worth what that command was capable of. Run each against a fixture that must match and one that must not. ⚠️ **The six-session record is a tell nobody read**: either those catches came from elsewhere or the command was typed differently each time, and **which is not recoverable** — a run record is evidence about the command only if the command is what was run. ⚠️ **A third command misreads its output the opposite way**: the citation census run wide from the repository root reports `D00` and `D000` out of `target/`'s generated `unicode-general-category` tables, false positives that read exactly like a dangling citation — run it from `crates/` or with `--exclude-dir=target`. **All three outputs were plausible and none is falsifiable by looking at what it printed.** Fixing the commands buys no gate: `cargo doc` still cannot see a `#[cfg(test)]` module, and the corrected doc grep still asks only half its question, a `#[cfg(test)]` **item** at module level sitting outside every check that looks for a `mod tests`. Record-only, no production line changed; **the citation is planted by hand** on `app::CLIPBOARD_OFF`, the one doc that narrates a doc-gate catch and the neighbour of D798's note on the D319 convention)*

---

## 15. Deviations from the original design

Recorded so the rest of this document can be read as fact. Each is a live decision, not an
oversight: either fix it or keep it deliberately.

**D110 — An arriving font face did not wake the UI thread. *Resolved.*** `FontService` held no
`egui::Context`; its threads only `send`, and the one `request_repaint` sat in `app.rs` *after*
`fonts.poll()`, inside a frame that had to happen for some other reason. eframe here is reactive, so a
message nobody wakes for is a font that arrives on the next mouse move. It survived hand-testing twice
because pointer motion generates frames continuously and `FontPoll::any` self-sustains once any frame
picks a message up; the stranded case is the **first** arrival after the UI goes quiet — sitting still
and reading a list.

`FontService::new` now takes `&egui::Context` and clones it into every background thread, each calling
`request_repaint()` after a successful send. All four send sites are covered — the `fontdb` scan, the
catalog's disk read, its network fetch, and the six face workers **including their `Failed` message**,
which is what clears `FamilyState::outstanding` and so what the field's "loading" state reads; a face
that fails with nobody awake leaves a spinner up indefinitely. `impl Default for FontService` is gone,
being unable to supply a context.

*The rule this leaves: a thread that hands work back to this UI owes it a `request_repaint`, and the
absence is invisible for as long as the pointer is moving.*

**D111 — The Google Fonts catalog was refetched on every launch. *Resolved.*** `fetch_catalog` ran
unconditionally after the disk read, so every start made two Fontsource API calls. The network half is
now gated on mtime — `fonts::is_fresh(path, max_age)` against a `CATALOG_MAX_AGE` of seven days.

Two decisions in the gate are load-bearing. **Freshness is asked of the copy that could actually be
read** (`disk.is_some() && is_fresh(…)`), because a corrupt or empty `catalog.json` has a good mtime and
no catalog in it. And **every uncertain answer is "not fresh"** — missing file, unavailable mtime, a
stamp in the future — since one wasted refresh costs two requests where a wrongly skipped one never
updates again. `a_just_written_catalog_is_fresh_and_a_missing_one_never_is` pins it, and the
absent-file case is the one that matters: read the comparison the other way round and a first run never
fetches at all. D83's open question is untouched — the gap is still first launch with no network.

**D112 — SVG dropped three of a decoration's four properties. *Resolved, with offset a stated limit.***
The writer emitted `text-decoration="underline line-through"` alone, so colour, thickness, offset and
line style were honoured on the canvas and in PNG and silently lost in SVG. Three are now written, and
four things about how are not guessable from the attributes:

- **Each is written only when every decoration on the element agrees** (`svg::agreed`) — CSS gives an
  element one colour, one thickness and one style, and a run can carry both an underline and a
  strikethrough. The property is dropped rather than one picked, leaving both on the text's own ink and
  the font's metrics. **D81's `<tspan>` conversion did not change this**: the disagreement is between
  two decorations on *one* run. `agreed` moved to each run's own style (`svg::run_attrs`) and otherwise
  means what it did.
- **The three longhands are written *after* the shorthand, and the order is load-bearing** — a
  shorthand's omitted parts reset to their initial values, so written last it would undo all three.
  `a_decorations_colour_thickness_and_style_are_exported` asserts the order, not just the presence.
- **Thickness carries an explicit `px`** where `letter-spacing` beside it is unitless: the latter is an
  SVG property permitting a bare number, the former CSS's, where a unitless length voids the
  declaration. A CSS `px` in SVG is the user unit, so the number is unchanged. An `Em` resolves against
  the font size.
- **Colour puts its alpha in the hex** (CSS Color 4's eight-digit form, only when not opaque);
  `text-decoration-color` has no `-opacity` companion.

`LineStyle` maps to CSS keywords verbatim (`svg::line_style_css`), which is the only reason style is
expressible; `Solid` is skipped as CSS's initial value, on the mitre limit's grounds (§7). Five tests in
`ondin-export/tests/svg.rs` cover it.

**Offset stays lost only where it must be.** `text-underline-offset` is underline-only with no
strikethrough counterpart, so a run carrying both decorations has no attribute two offsets could share —
a real limit. A run with an underline alone now writes it, negated, CSS measuring downward from the
baseline where we measure up (D159).

**D113 — The key layer is an explicit designation, not "the last one selected". *Keep.*** A
multi-selection can now name one member the **key**: the layer align aligns *to*, and the base operand
`build::boolean` places at the bottom. `Selection` (§9.3) carries it as a private `key: Option<NodeId>`
behind `key()` and `set_key()`, `Alt`+`Shift`+click designates it (§9.4), and `canvas::draw_key_outline`
marks it.

The plan that asked for the feature said "key = last selected", derived from `Selection.ids` order — a
`Vec` that `toggle` and `add` push to, so the answer was already there for free. It was dropped for two
reasons that are the whole design. Deriving it takes the **union** away from every align that already
worked: "align these to each other" is the common case and it is `align_target`'s `_ =>` arm, so with a
key always present align would silently start measuring against whichever layer happened to be clicked
last. And the canvas mark would then be drawn on one member of *every* multi-selection — permanent noise
that reads as a bug rather than as an answer to a question the user asked. `None` is therefore the
ordinary state and means "no key": today's behaviour, unchanged, until someone asks for something else.

The rules live on `Selection` rather than at the three consumers, and `session.rs`'s `mod tests` pins
each of them. `set_key` refuses an id that is not selected, since a key sitting outside the set would
align the others to a layer the user cannot see is involved. Designating the same layer twice **clears**
the designation — the way back to union alignment without deselecting everything. `key()` answers `None`
below two selected layers whatever is stored, because a key says "this one, not the others" and has
nothing to contrast against on its own; answering that once is what stops align, the boolean builder and
the canvas mark disagreeing about when a key means anything, and the stored value survives the shrink so
that dropping to one layer and growing back does not silently lose it. `toggle` drops the designation
when the key itself is deselected, `clear`/`set_one`/`set` clear it, and `retain_existing` prunes a
deleted one. Both consumers additionally require the key to survive `build::outermost`: one nested inside
another selected layer is not an operand of the operation at all, and aligning a set to a box *inside* one
of its own members reads as the ancestor jumping for no reason.

**Align needed no geometry.** "The key must not move" is not code — aligning a layer to its own edge lands
it where it is — so only `inspector::align_target` changed and `align()` and `build::align` are untouched.
**Booleans needed a parameter and a correction.** `build::boolean` gained `key: Option<NodeId>` and moves
that member to index 0 for `Subtract`; §9.4 has the rest. The correction is that the plan, and
`boolean.rs`'s own module doc on `evaluate`, both said Subtract *and* Exclude are non-commutative. Exclude
is not: symmetric difference is commutative and associative, so the left fold gives one answer per
permutation. Measured rather than reasoned — `exclude_gives_the_same_answer_in_any_operand_order` uses
**three** operands, because two would pass on the pairwise symmetry alone, and it was checked to fail when
pointed at `Subtract`. The comment is fixed; this document already had it right (§9.4: "only the first
operand is order-sensitive — Subtract's tail is a union and the other three are commutative"), which is
the useful lesson about which of the two to trust. The consequence is that the key is inert for three of
the four operations rather than two.

**The chord is `Alt`+`Shift`, and its safety is that it starts no drag.** Alt alone turns a move into a
drag-a-copy, armed on *press* (D40), and `finish_drag` commits the copy on any release that moved more
than `1e-4` world units — so a designation whose click slipped past egui's drag threshold would silently
leave a duplicate behind. `begin_select_drag` is therefore gated on `!(alt && shift)`, which turns the
slip into a no-op instead: the failure that can be seen and repeated rather than the one found three edits
later. *Keep that gate if the chord is ever moved; it is the whole reason Alt is safe to build on.*

**The mark is a deliberate second chrome hue, in tension with D13.** `draw_key_outline` traces the key with
`stroke_outlines` at 3px in a new `theme::color::KEY` (magenta, `0xd264c8`), matching the hover outline's
weight and exact-shape trace, and suppressed during a gesture where the box, the ghosts and the snap guides
are already competing for those pixels. D13 reserves `color::SELECT` for "the app is talking about the
selection" and directs anything wanting it faded to be *derived* — but a shade of `SELECT` cannot work here,
because every other member of the selection is already wearing `SELECT` and the mark's whole job is to
separate one of them from the rest. So it is a different hue at the same weight and the same trace, which
reads as the same kind of statement in a different register. The hover outline needed no change: it already
returns early for anything in the selection and the key always is, so two outlines never land on the same
path.

**It is drawn *over* the selection boxes, and that is not a z-order preference.** Under them — where it went
first — it was all but invisible, and the reason is that the selection outline is drawn **per node** rather
than as one box round the union: a rectangular key therefore gets a 1.2px `SELECT` hairline laid along its
3px `KEY` trace for the entire perimeter, leaving under a pixel of magenta either side. Reported from the
screen, not caught in review, because in the source the two are hundreds of lines apart and neither mentions
the other. *A mark whose only job is to tell one selected layer from the others cannot be the one that gets
painted over.* The key's own box is covered in exchange, which is the right trade: it is still plainly
selected, and heavier than anything beside it.

An **inside** stroke was the other candidate and was declined: it would dodge the collision by sitting within
the shape rather than on its boundary, but `epaint`'s `StrokeKind` is `RectShape`-only, so on a traced
`PathShape` it means offsetting the flattened screen polyline by hand — real geometry, with winding and
self-intersection to get right on concave shapes — to buy what a one-line reorder already bought. Centred is
fine once the mark is on top. *Measured rather than assumed: a 2px `closed_line` stroke on a 100..200 square
tessellates to 99..201 with feathering off, i.e. exactly half either side.*

**Scope, not gaps.** Numeric distribute spacing ("24 apart, starting from this one") is where the key
would pay next and was not built when this was written — plain `distribute` equalises gaps between the
two extremes, so it has no use for a key. It was built on 2026-08-19 and its record is **D243**. The
other sentence this paragraph used to carry — that a *multi*-selection still cannot ask for the
container, and that the key covers the case people actually ask for — was closed as a **decided
non-goal** on 2026-08-23, and its second half was wrong: **D309** has both.

**D309 — A multi-selection will not be able to align to its container. *Decided by the maintainer;
nothing built, and the record `roadmap.md`'s §0 points at.*** The roadmap carried this as open work —
three candidate targets, only two of them reachable with several layers picked, the third waiting on a
control `design/` does not draw. The blocker was never the control, and the gap is smaller and less
well-defined than the entry made it sound.

**The capability is already there, spelled differently.** `align_target`'s `1 =>` arm returns the
*parent's* world bounds, so one selected layer already means "align to my container". Aligning several
layers to their container is therefore *select them one at a time* — exact, no new concept, and the
case people actually have ("centre this in the frame") is one selection anyway. A three-way control
would save keystrokes while turning a silent working default into a mode that has to be read before the
eight buttons can be trusted.

**"The container" is not well-defined for a set.** Members of a multi-selection need not share a
parent, so the candidates are the nearest common ancestor — usually the root, which makes this "align
to the page", a different feature — or each member's own parent, which makes *Align Left* send each
layer to a *different* left edge. That is per-member alignment, also a different feature, and one that
should be asked for by name rather than arrive as a setting on a target picker.

**And even when the parents agree there are two readings.** `build::align` moves each id independently
toward the target box, so "align these three to the frame" stacks all three on the frame's left edge.
That is standard — Illustrator's *Align to Artboard* does exactly that — but it is not what "align this
group to the frame's left edge" sounds like, which is the set moving as a unit. The eight buttons can
only mean one of the two, and nothing decides which.

**The control was the easy half all along.** There is a precedent to copy: Illustrator's *Align To*
three-way (Selection / Key Object / Artboard), the same lineage the key layer came from (D113). "Needs
a panel design `design/` does not carry" was true and was never the reason.

⚠️ **The reason D113 and the roadmap both gave for the delay was wrong**, and that is the part worth
keeping. "The key covers the case people actually ask for" does not cover *this* case at all:
`align_target` runs `build::outermost` over the selection first, so selecting a frame **and** its
children collapses to the frame alone — `ids.len()` is 1, the `_ =>` arm that consults the key never
runs, and the target becomes the frame's *parent*. A frame can never be the key of a selection that
also contains its own contents. The bullet was right that this is not urgent and wrong about why.

**The contrast with the transform origin is the useful part.** Both questions are *does a
multi-selection mean one body or* n *layers*, and they were answered differently on the same day. The
origin one is **parked** (`roadmap.md`, *Later*) because neither reading is better and picking one is
assuming; this one is **closed** because the *n*-layers reading is already reachable a selection at a
time, and the one-body reading is not what these buttons do to begin with. *A question with two good
answers parks; a question whose answers are "already built" and "a different feature" closes.*

*Keep the non-goal.* **Revisit if** a real case turns up for aligning many layers each to its own
parent — that is the per-member reading above, and it wants its own verb, not a third entry in a target
picker.

**D310 — The Align card vanished where it had no target, in the one panel whose own comment says a
control dims instead. *Resolved.*** `inspector_align` opened with an early `return` when `align_target()`
answered `None`, which happens when the selection collapses through `build::outermost` to one layer whose
parent is the root: there is no container to align to and no second layer to make a union with. So the
whole card — eight buttons, two rules and the spacing row under them — was absent for a rect on the page
and present for the same rect inside a frame.

⚠️ **That is not only the one-layer case, and the brief and the new comment both said it was.** The
panel routes on `selection.len()` while `align_target` measures after `outermost`, so a **top-level frame
selected together with its own children** is `len() >= 2` — the multi-selection panel — and still
collapses to the frame alone with the root for a parent. D309 records exactly that collapse for a
different reason. The card therefore vanished under a genuine multi-selection too, which makes the
reported "the panel jumps when you select a second" reachable from the other side as well. The fix covers
it either way, since `can_align` is now the same `is_some()` for every route.

**Two faults in one line, and the second is the sharper.** Reported as "it leaves the user wondering: a
single layer in a frame shows it, but a top-level one doesn't", which is the panel reading as
inconsistent rather than as the buttons having nothing to do; and "the panel jumps when you select a
second, which is visually not great" — a card arriving under the pointer as the selection grows, moving
everything below it.

**The card already carried the argument against itself, twice.** The spacing row inside it is kept
*dimmed* below two members rather than hidden on exactly this ground (D243: "no point in hiding them for
single layers since it will make the panels jump when selecting multiple"), and a comment sixteen lines
above the `return` said "with fewer, the buttons dim rather than vanish, as everywhere else in this
panel". What argued the other way was the function's own doc comment — "that last case is why the panel
is skipped for a top-level layer" — and the `return` it described, which was the part that ran. **D134
is the rule, and this was it broken in the file that states it**, with a whole card rather than a button:
the mechanism D134 names is horizontal, a control that vanishes widening the fields beside it, and this is
the vertical one. *A rule written in a comment beside the code that breaks it is not a rule. Grep for the
behaviour, not for the sentence.*

**The fix is the `return` deleted and `can_align` becoming `self.align_target().is_some()`.** Everything
in the card was already parameterised on `can_align` / `can_distribute` / `can_space`, so nothing else
moved — which is the tell that the early return never carried a design, only a case nobody had looked at.
The dimmed buttons gained the tooltip an absent card cannot have: *"Nothing to align to — select another
layer, or put this one in a frame"*, naming **both** ways out, because what is wrong is that neither
candidate target exists and either one would fix it.

**Two tests in `inspector::align_card_tests`, both driving the real panel on a headless app (D303).**
`a_lone_top_level_layer_gets_the_same_card_as_a_nested_one` measures the card twice — one rect at the top
level, the same rect inside a group — and asserts the heights are **equal** rather than merely non-zero,
because the symptom is that one selection draws a different panel from another: a stub card, or one that
dropped its second row when the buttons went dim, passes "greater than zero" and still jumps. Flipped by
putting the `return` back, where the top-level card measures 0 against the nested one's full height.
`align_moves_a_nested_layer_and_leaves_a_top_level_one_alone` pins the other half — `OndinApp::align`
returns before building a transaction when there is no target, so the guard holds however the row is
drawn. ⚠️ **That second test deliberately does not flip on this entry**: with the `return` back it stays
green, because the guard it pins lives in `align` rather than in the card. It was written anyway and that
is the load-bearing part — dimming a control is only safe if the verb behind it refuses on its own, and
the card is no longer the thing standing between a press and the model. Its nested half is the control,
since "a layer did not move" is also what a wholly broken align produces.

**The fixture puts two rects side by side and selects the right-hand one**, which is not decoration: a
group holding a single child has that child's own bounds, so aligning to it lands the layer exactly where
it already is, and neither test could then tell an inert card from a live one.

**D114 — A pen anchor carries two handles, not one mirrored vector. *Keep.*** `preview::PenAnchor` was
`{ at, out }` and `arriving()` returned the mirror `at - out`, which made every anchor smooth by
construction. It is now `{ at, out, back }` with `arriving()` returning `at + back`, so the two sides of
one anchor can disagree. The shape that bought the field is a segment that **arrives straight and leaves
on a curve** — the join between a polyline and a curve, which one mirrored vector cannot express at all,
not merely express awkwardly. `PenAnchor::smooth(at, out)` builds the mirrored case and `corner` the flat
one, so the two ordinary anchors are still one call each. `PenAnchor::pull_side(side, to, break_pair)` is
the whole of what a drag does to an anchor and lives on the type rather than inline in `canvas::pen_input`,
because the canvas cannot be tested without a window: a mirror computed at the call site would be a
second statement of the rule, and the one that drifted would be the one nothing runs. (`pull` was that
function fixed to the outgoing side; both tools go through `pull_within` now, which adds the retract snap —
D120 has why the pen came to need it.) **`Alt` while
dragging breaks the pair**, read live every frame rather than latched at the press, so pressing and
releasing it mid-drag puts the handles back together — the same live-modifier rule `sync_alt_clone`
follows for a duplicate drag (D40).

`is_corner()` requires **both** handles to be zero, which is what keeps an anchor with only an incoming
handle from reading as a corner. It is no longer what decides line-or-cubic, though: that question is
per *segment*, and D117 moved it to `PenAnchor::straight_to`. Three tests in `tools::tests` pin the set —
`an_anchor_can_break_its_handles_and_bend_only_one_side` asserts that the segment into a broken anchor is
a straight `LineTo` while the one out of it curves along `out`, with a mirrored A/B beside it so the
assertion cannot pass for the wrong reason; `an_anchor_with_only_an_incoming_handle_is_not_a_corner`
guards the predicate directly; and `pulling_a_handle_mirrors_unless_the_pair_is_broken` covers both
branches of `pull_within` *and* the release, since re-mirroring is the half a latched modifier would lose.

**Backspace takes back the last anchor mid-draw** (`canvas::pen_backspace`), cancelling the path when the
first one goes. Undo cannot do this job — nothing is committed until the path is finished (§4), so a
mis-clicked anchor is not in the history at all, and without this the only way out of one was to abandon
the whole path. It is intercepted in `app::dispatch` as `Action::Delete if self.pen.is_some()`, which
looks like a special case and is the only place early enough: Backspace and Delete already resolve to the
same `Action::Delete`, and keyboard actions are dispatched *before* `pen_input` runs, so a plain
`Action::Delete` would have deleted a layer before the pen ever saw the key. It also clears `shaping`,
because the flag refers to the anchor that has just gone and leaving it set would let the next pointer
move drag the handles of the anchor *before* it — which reads as the pen having grabbed the wrong one.

**`PEN_PICK_PX` replaces an inline `10.0`.** One named number for "close enough to a pen anchor or a
handle". It had one caller — the close-the-path test in `pen_press` — and now has two, since resuming an
open path grabs its endpoint at the same distance (D117); dragging an anchor will be the third. Left as a
literal each would have invented its own, and the pen
grabbing at three different distances is the kind of inconsistency nobody reports and everybody feels.
It was 9 here, matching a corner handle rather than `PICK_SLOP_PX`'s 4: an anchor is chrome the user is
deliberately aiming at, where the 4 exists for a `Line` that sits among other artwork and must not reach
past it. It also had to beat the 10 it replaces being wrong the other way, where closing the path was
easier than placing an anchor next to the start. It is **7** now — D116 has why the argument for a
generous radius weakened once the radius became visible.

**Two decisions that were open are now closed.** First, **`BezPath`, not a vector network.** Points shared
by more than two segments and independently fillable regions are Figma's differentiator and its
complexity; `NodeKind::Path` holds a `BezPath` and the scene walk, the boolean engine, the SVG writer and
the save format all read it as one (§5.3). A network is a model change with no half-step, and nothing in
the roadmap needs it — recorded here so the codebase does not *drift* into one a feature at a time.
Second, **point type stays inferred from the handles, and the loss is accepted**: a smooth point whose
handles are dragged flat is indistinguishable from a corner. The reason a stored flag was rejected is the
interesting part. It would have to live in the **model** to survive being committed, because the node
holds a `BezPath` and nothing else — so an app-side flag would be a fact that existed only until the path
was deselected, which is worse than not having it, since it works right up to the moment someone relies
on it. `PenAnchor::is_corner`'s own doc says the same, so the next reader meets it at the predicate.

**Scope, not gaps.** Resuming an existing path needed the inverse of `tools::pen_outline`, and both are
now built — D117. The rest of the editing half followed from that reader: the node tool, point selection
and the anchor drag in D118, add and remove point in D120.

**D115 — The picking allowance now reaches every kind, not only an open shape. *Resolved.*** Reported as
"selecting a shape is a bit tricky, as I need to move the mouse within the stroke of the shape." D222
gave `geometry::contains_local` a `slop` and spent it on the `Line` arm alone, on the reasoning that a
filled shape has an interior to aim at. That missed the shape with a stroke and **no fill** — most of
what the pen draws — where the ink you can see is the outline, so landing a pixel past it hit nothing.

Every arm spends it now, as a band of `stroke_expansion + slop` reaching **outward** from the ink on top
of whatever interior the shape has. `Rect` and `Artboard` grow the box by `tol`; `Ellipse` grows its
radii, approximate at the diagonals by a fraction of `tol` nobody can feel; `Polygon`, `Star` and `Path`
test `contains || near_outline`; **`Text` inflates its layout box**. The private `geometry::near_outline`
flattens and measures distance per segment, a cubic having no closed-form point distance, with its
flattening tolerance tied to `tol`.

⚠️ **`Text` is in that list because D483 put it there, and its absence is the whole of what went
wrong.** This entry's enumeration ran `Rect`/`Artboard`, `Ellipse`, `Polygon`/`Star`/`Path` and stopped,
because the sweep did — the `Text` arm went on testing the bare box, so the kind users click most spent
nothing, and a text node with a 40pt outside stroke reported world bounds 40 units wider on every side
than a click could reach. **A sweep is only as complete as its own list**, and this list is what every
later reader, and D483's own investigation, checked the code against.

⚠️ **And a landed summary of it sat in `roadmap.md` for two months, saying the opposite.** *"Every kind
now gets the picking allowance … Nothing outstanding, recorded so the exemption is not restored"* —
false for `Text` the whole time it stood there. The entry that existed *so the exemption could not be
restored* is precisely the one that failed to notice it had never been removed. Deleted at D483's fix,
and recorded here rather than there, which is the point: `roadmap.md` holds **open work**, and a
finished item copied into it is a claim nobody re-checks outliving the thing it summarised.
`CLAUDE.md`'s rule is one sentence — *a decided non-goal is never an open item* — and this is its
corollary: neither is a finished one.

**An open `Path` changed most.** `BezPath::contains` closes the path implicitly and asks for a winding
number, so a pen squiggle was selectable by the empty air inside its imaginary closure and hardly at all
by its ink — the second limit D222 deferred to editable paths, fixed here instead. The band is strictly
a superset of the old test; what it costs is that a shape now shadows the few units outside its edge.

**A pre-existing test failed and was rewritten rather than deleted**, which is the part to read if this
ever looks like a regression. `a_picking_allowance_widens_a_line_and_nothing_else` asserted that 3 units
outside a rect is still outside. It is now `a_picking_allowance_widens_every_kind_by_a_bounded_band`,
and the half worth guarding moved from *exemption* to **bound**: 3 units hits, 9 does not, and a zero
allowance still means the exact interior. Two unit tests in `geometry.rs` say it from below —
`a_shape_is_grabbable_just_outside_its_edge_not_far_outside` and `an_open_path_is_grabbed_by_its_ink`.
*A new kind owes the band; an assertion that something a few units outside a shape is unreachable is the
old rule coming back.*

**D116 — Closing a path announces itself, and swallows the press that does it. *Resolved.*** Two changes
at the same moment of the same gesture.

The affordance: within `PEN_PICK_PX` of the first anchor the pending segment stops dead **on** it and
the anchor takes a ring. **One radius answers both the snap and the click, deliberately** — the snap is
a promise that the next press will close, and two radii is that promise broken whichever way they
differ. So `tools::pen_close_snap` is one function returning one `Option`, asked by `canvas::pen_press`
and by the pen overlay alike. Only the **first** anchor is a target. The radius is screen pt over zoom,
pinned by `the_pen_snaps_closed_within_a_screen_radius_not_a_world_one` at three zoom levels — a version
comparing world distance passes every other assertion and feels wrong only at magnifications nobody
tests at. `PEN_PICK_PX` was tuned on screen, 9 → 5 → 7. D114 argued 9 from a corner handle, but that was
for an *invisible* target; a radius that announces itself need not be discovered by clicking and
missing. The value is feel; the *pairing* is the rule.

**The second is a real bug.** Reported as the path losing selection and the inspector flashing on close,
but not on Enter or Escape. Closing happens on the **press**, and `finish_pen` switches to
`Tool::Select`, so the release arrives as an ordinary `clicked()` with Select active and picks whatever
is under the pointer — the path's own thin stroke, which is why it hit sometimes and missed sometimes.
`pen_press` sets `gesture_cancelled = true` after `finish_pen(true)`, reusing the flag rather than
inventing a second: it already means "the pointer is still down and the rest of this press is not ours".

*The general rule: any gesture that completes on the press and changes what the release will mean owes
the same swallow.*

**D117 — A stored path reads back into anchors, and the pen resumes one. *Resolved.*** D114 recorded the
reader as owed and larger than it looks. `tools::pen_anchors` is where the general case is decided,
once. Four decisions in it.

**A quad is elevated, not flattened or dropped** — `kurbo`'s own `QuadBez::raise` arithmetic, asserted
against `QuadBez::raise` itself so the two cannot drift. This is the one place the round trip is not
byte-identical: read and write a quad and it is a cubic afterwards.

**A `ClosePath` whose last point is already the first folds.** `pen_outline` draws the closing segment
*and* emits `ClosePath`, so read naively every trip adds an anchor.
`reading_a_pen_path_back_gives_the_anchors_that_drew_it` asserts the **count**, because that is the
assertion the bug fails.

⚠️ **That closes the read side and leaves the write side asymmetric, which D583 is about.** A closed
subpath whose last point is *not* already the first — the ordinary SVG spelling, and what
`BezPath::from_svg` gives for any `d` ending in `Z` — comes back out of `pen_path` with the closing
`LineTo` written in. So the round trip has a third movement and it **adds** rather than removes, which
is why the no-op comparison two paragraphs down had to start canonicalising both sides.

**Line-or-cubic is a property of the segment, not of its two anchors.** A `LineTo` arriving at an anchor
that then curves away came back as a cubic with both control points on its endpoints — same curve, three
times the data, and the path grew every trip. `pen_outline` asked `is_corner()` on both anchors, but an
anchor that arrives straight and leaves on a curve is not a corner; it is what D114 added the second
handle **for**. The test is now `PenAnchor::straight_to(next)`. `is_corner` stays, still requiring both
handles zero, and is still what the overlay asks; D114's claim that it decides line-or-cubic is
corrected there. `an_anchor_can_break_its_handles_and_bend_only_one_side` moved with the rule rather
than being deleted.

**Resuming appends, so the path is reversed and then un-reversed.** The pen only appends, so a grab at
the *start* reverses a working copy; `PenEdit::subpaths` keeps the original orientation and `finish_pen`
reverses back. Two things fall out: extending the start **prepends** rather than flipping the whole
path's direction, which a fill rule and a dash pattern can both see; and `tools::rewrite_path` can
recognise a gesture that changed nothing by **comparing the finished path against the stored one**, so
resuming and pressing Escape is not an empty undo step. Counting anchors would not have done it — a
backspace and a click leave the count where it was. The endpoint is ringed on hover by the same
`pen_resume_target` query the press uses (D116's pairing). ⚠️ **That comparison was raw until
2026-09-08 and therefore held only for paths already in `pen_path`'s own output shape** (D583): both
sides go through `pen_anchors` first now, because a path read from SVG differs from its own round trip
by a closing segment and by radii that trim to nothing.

`rewrite_path` commits `GeometryPatch::Path` and **does not touch the node's transform**, which is the
whole difference from `create_path`. `PenEdit` carries **every** subpath with an `active` index, so a
multi-subpath path cannot lose the ones nobody touched. And the resumed endpoint keeps its handles —
`shaping` stays off, the press having landed up to `PEN_PICK_PX` *away* from the anchor.

**D118 — The node tool: points are a third subject, and the selection box gets out of their way.
*Resolved.*** `Tool::Node`, `A`, on the rail beside the pen. Five decisions.

**The layer selection *is* the subject**, rather than a second "which path" field. `canvas::edited_path`
asks the one question; a separate field would be a second answer, and the interesting bugs live in the
frames where two answers disagree.

**Double-click enters it, and that is the same gesture as the other two.** `double_click_pick` already
opened a text node and stepped into a group; all three mean *one level in*, and what that level is
depends on what you are on — children, characters, points. Safe to add because of the tool switch: an
invisible "vector mode" entered by double-click is the failure the mode principle is written against; a
rail button with a letter and its own chrome is not.

**Points are a `PointSet` beside `Selection`, not inside it.** `Selection` is layers-or-guides and its
exclusivity is structural. Two things make the set safe: every read goes **through the node id**, so a
set left behind by another path is invisible rather than wrong; and `retain_valid` is a *truncation*,
not a remap. A `PointRef` is a position in a list — the cost `BezPath` charges for having no per-anchor
identity (D114) — so an index surviving an edit and pointing at a *different* anchor is the silent
failure. Two unit tests in `preview.rs` pin both.

**One suppression question, not five conditions.** `canvas::chrome_hidden` hides the selection outline,
its handles, the size badge, the pivot marker, the key trace and the hover outline. Three reasons ask it
— a pen gesture in flight, a path under point edit, and the inspector's edit-time hide (D128), which
went in as a third *term* and not a third set of conditions. It matters because a resize box around a
path whose points are being dragged offers two contradictory gestures over the same pixels, and the
box's corners land near enough to a path's corners to be grabbed by mistake. *A box over the selected
**points** is a different thing and is drawn — D120 has why that is not this rule being walked back.*

**Handles outrank anchors, and only a handle you can *see* is grabbable.** `canvas::node_grab` returns
what the pointer would take, at `PEN_PICK_PX`. Handles first because a handle can be dragged back on top
of its own anchor. But the grab has to match what `draw_points` draws: only a **selected** anchor's
handles, and only **non-zero** ones. The second was missing and was reported — a corner's two handles
both sit *on* the anchor, so a second click grabbed an invisible zero-length handle and pulled a curve
out of it. `HANDLE_DRAWN` is the one threshold both sides ask. Pulling a handle out of a corner is
**`Ctrl`+drag** on the anchor, `Alt` breaking the pair — a modifier rather than a second click, because
the click version is the one you reach by accident.

*That fixed what `Ctrl` means in this tool: **plain moves, `Ctrl` shapes the curvature** (built in
D120). A third gesture giving `Ctrl` a third meaning is what would break the tool's legibility.*

**The cursor stays the plain arrow, and that is a correction.** It was `Grab`/`Grabbing` over a point, by
analogy with a line's endpoints — where the cursor is right, because those endpoints are invisible. A
path draws a marker on every anchor, so a hand flickering across a dozen marks is noise. *Announce a
grab with the cursor only when nothing on screen already does.*

**A marquee over points reuses `Drag::Marquee`** — no second variant, no branch in the layer path. It
selects **anchors only**: a handle is a property of its point, and a set holding one would have to answer
what Delete means for it. A plain press on empty canvas is a zero-area marquee, which clears the set.

**`Enter` is a toggle; `Escape` is a ladder.** Enter steps into point editing and straight back out, one
press each way. Escape unwinds one rung per press — points, then the tool, then the selection, with the
pen bias above the points since D125. Making Enter an Escape alias was the request and would have been
worse twice over: two presses to leave a path with points selected, and Enter closing the colour picker.
`Action::Enter` is a keymap entry so `input::resolve`'s focus guard covers it, and `dispatch` hands it
to the pen when one is in flight.

**A click on a point was leaving an empty undo step.** A press starts a `Drag::Points` whether or not
the pointer moves, so a zero delta committed a `SetGeometry` identical to what it replaced. `points_tx`
and `handle_tx` now pass the stored path to `rewrite_path` — the second caller D117's no-op comparison
predicted. ⚠️ **The remedy inherited that comparison's limit and so held only for paths the pen
itself wrote** (D583): an imported outline came back from the round trip carrying a closing `LineTo`
the stored path did not have, so the guard could not fire and a bare click committed a `SetGeometry`
after all — the same symptom this paragraph is about, at a door nobody had checked.

**Retracting a handle onto its anchor makes it a corner.** `is_corner` wants both handles at zero to
better than 1e-9, which no hand can drag to. Within `PEN_PICK_PX` of the anchor `tools::pull_handle`
substitutes the anchor for the pointer — a substitution, not a branch, so the mirror zeroes the other
side for free and `Alt` still buys a one-sided retract. The marker flipping circle-to-square comes free:
the overlay reads the preview.

**The inspector changes subject with the tool** (`inspector_points`), as it does for a guide. The
identity card reads **Edit Path** with every action dead, via `add_enabled_ui(false)` around the live
boolean row rather than a parallel dead copy, so the two cannot drift. Transform keeps **X and Y only**,
reading the box the selected points occupy and moving the set by the difference. Appearance keeps
**opacity**, drawn rather than skipped so D119's corner radius arrives in a card that already exists.
Fill and Stroke stay pointed at the node.

**Align and distribute act on points, on the same eight buttons** — not a second row of the same glyphs.
Two points enable align, three distribute; below that they dim. The target needs no deciding, which is
the real difference: for layers it is a genuine three-way question (`align_target` weighs key, union and
container), while a set of points has no key and no container but the path, whose box is derived from
those very points. Distribution is simpler by one term too — `build::distribute` subtracts each layer's
width to leave equal *gaps*, and a point has no width.

**Two reads of a path, and conflating them broke the X/Y fields twice at once.** `edited_subpaths` reads
the **committed** document; `preview_subpaths` reads through the render override. Reported as "X/Y
doesn't update while moving" and a slide-drag "stuck around ±2 points" — one cause. The field read the
committed path, so a *canvas* drag reported the pre-gesture position, and a *scrub* was handed the same
number every frame (egui's `DragValue` adds the frame's movement to the value it is given, so the delta
was always one frame's worth).

The rule is about what the caller's `delta` **means**, not which read is fresher. A canvas drag hands
over the *total* since the press and must measure from the committed path or it compounds — the rule
`move_line_end` and `resize_tx` already state. A scrubbed field hands over an *increment* and must
measure from the preview or it never accumulates. Hence `points_tx` and `nudge_points_tx`. Anything that
merely *shows* a point uses the preview read, through the same accessor so they cannot disagree.

The chain this depends on is worth naming, the fix being invisible without it:
`SetGeometry`/`GeometryPatch::Path` → `renderer`'s override projection → `over.kind` →
`DisplayNode::kind` → `preview_subpaths`. If a geometry patch stops landing in the override's kind, the
field goes back to sticking.

**Arrow keys move the selected points**, intercepted in `dispatch` beside Delete. The arrows are the one
way to move a point by an exact amount, so moving the layer instead answers the wrong question.

**D119 — A path's corner radius lives in the model, not in the geometry. *Resolved.***

**Stored, not baked, and that was the whole decision.** Baking fails the first thing anyone does with a
field: scrub 8 → 12 and there are no corners left to round, so it reads 0 again and the second drag does
nothing — a command wearing a field's clothes. `NodeKind::Path` gains `corner_radii: Vec<f64>`, resolved
into geometry at read time exactly as `Rect`'s are (§5.3).

**One resolution point, and it already existed.** `geometry::local_path` is where every consumer that
draws, measures, exports or hit-tests gets its outline, with `Resolved::local_path` layered over it for
booleans. Three readers were bypassing it and were redirected: `contains_local`'s `Path` arm (a fillet
cuts the corner away, so the raw path kept dead shape clickable), the SVG writer, and the MCP snapshot —
the AI-handoff surface, where a shape described wrong is worse than one drawn wrong. `local_path`
returns the path untouched when there are no radii.

**Both indexings are core's now.** A radius is stored per *anchor*, so `geometry::anchor_runs` is the
canonical numbering and `tools::pen_anchors` has to agree with it. Nothing in the type system ties them,
so `the_app_and_core_number_a_paths_anchors_alike` does — two walks of the same `BezPath` compared over
closed runs, folded closing points, quads, several subpaths and an empty path. Its failure mode is a
radius on the wrong corner, which reads as a rendering bug.

**The parallel list is the cost of `BezPath` over a vector network** (D114), paid in one place: the
radius rides **on** `PenAnchor`, so `move_points`, `remove_points`, `align_points`, `distribute_points`
and `PenSubpath::reverse` needed no change, and the flattening happens once at the model boundary
(`tools::pen_radii`). The one place it had to be said is `PenAnchor::pull_side`, whose mirrored arms
rebuild the anchor from a constructor and so save and restore the radius — exactly how a per-anchor
value gets dropped by an edit that has nothing to do with it.

**"Lines only" was the first cut, and it was wrong twice over.** Reported from one drawing:
a quadrilateral with three corners and one curved side, radius 50, one corner rounded and the smooth
point turned into a corner.

The worse defect: `AnchorRun` carried `points` and a `straight` flag and threw the control points away,
so rounding **rebuilt the path from its vertices** — every curve flattened the moment any corner had a
radius. It now carries the real `PathSeg`s. *A derived representation that keeps less than its source
will be asked to reproduce the source.*

The other is a design correction. **A corner is a corner** — what its neighbours do is not the question
the radius is asking. Legs are trimmed back **by arc length** (`PathSeg::inv_arclen`), so a curved leg
is shortened rather than replaced. What the fillet *is* still depends on the legs: between two straight
legs it is an exact circular arc, so a path and a `Rect` at the same radius agree; against a curve there
is generally no circle tangent to both, so the bridge is the cubic leaving each side along its own
tangent with control points at the fraction a circular arc's would sit at — the straight case comes out
the familiar 0.5523, so it is one construction generalised.

A radius on a **smooth** anchor draws nothing and needs no rule: the tangents are collinear, so there is
no turn to cut. An endpoint of an open subpath is never rounded. Each radius is clamped to half of each
adjoining segment; the test is that an absurd radius on a square gives the inscribed *circle* rather
than an inverted contour.

**The test that covered this passed while both bugs were live.** It asserted the vertex beside a curve
survived — it did, as a polyline vertex — and that the area shrank — it did, because flattening a bulge
shrinks it. Neither could distinguish "left alone" from "flattened". The replacement asserts the
**segment kinds**: every original vertex gone, and a cubic still bowing past its chord.

**The save format did not need a version bump.** `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if =
"Vec::is_empty")]`, and `pen_radii` trims trailing zeros so one shape has one canonical form — which
byte-stable output requires (invariant 9) and the no-op comparison depends on.
`path_corner_radii_survive_a_save_and_an_old_file_still_loads` asserts all three **per path node**
rather than by grepping the file, `Rect` having a `corner_radii` of its own. That caught a bug on the
first run.

`GeometryPatch::Path` now carries the outline **and** the radii, being one fact. The Scale tool
multiplies a path's radii where resize leaves them alone (§5.6, as `Rect`'s four already do).

Three smaller things. An anchor drag is a **delta** from where the press landed (absolute tracking would
snatch it up to `PEN_PICK_PX` on frame one) while a handle drag is **absolute**, matching
`PenAnchor::pull_side`. `Delete` **heals** — dropping an anchor leaves its neighbours adjacent and the
curve running through the handles they already have, which falls out of the representation; removing the
*segment* is the edit that needs machinery, and got it in D120, which is why the two are separate verbs
on one key rather than one verb with a modifier. And Delete had to be intercepted in `app::dispatch`,
not in the canvas — keyboard actions dispatch before the canvas runs, so by the time `node_input` saw
the key the whole layer would be gone. The trap D116 recorded, arriving as predicted.

**D125 — The pen is reachable from inside a path edit, and a run can be turned round afterwards.
*Resolved.*** Joining two open ends already worked, but only by leaving the edit first. `P` is an
ordinary tool switch and dropping the edit is what a tool switch means, so the answer had to be neither
a tool switch nor a mode.

**`app::pen_bias` is a bool, and it changes exactly one thing** — what a press on the canvas means.
`input::resolve` never sees it, no key is rerouted, nothing is added to `input::Mode`. It is not the
mode `Tool::Node`'s doc argues against because it borrows the pen's letter, cursor and rail slot, so
what announces it already meets all four of D118's criteria. It is intercepted in **`choose_tool`**, not
`dispatch`, because the rail's pen button issues the same request and two answers to one question is
what that would be.

**The pointer target picks the verb** — `canvas::pen_verb`, three variants. An open end of the edited
path means *continue*, tried first as the smallest and most deliberate target; the path's ink means
*insert an anchor*; bare canvas means *begin a fresh run in this same node*. A handle, a middle anchor
and the point box answer `None`, and so does **another layer**, because `node_press`'s "press another
path to switch subject" rule is the only way to change which path you are editing without a trip out
through Select. The edited path's own fill does not count as occupied.

**The design under-counted the conflicts, which is the part worth recording.** The plan said three of
the four verbs needed nothing but a cursor. In fact two more presses change meaning: an endpoint press
already selected and dragged that anchor, and a segment press already selected and dragged the segment —
both worth keeping. So all three verbs live behind the bias, one keystroke deep either way. `pen_verb`
is asked by **the press and by the cursor**, same query, same pixel (D116's pairing). The cursor is
`Bitmap::Pen` exactly where a verb is armed, and never mid-drag.

**`Shift` under the bias is the pen's constraint, not the node tool's extend**, at the price of
`Shift`+click to extend the *segment* selection. One rule Escape turns off beats two rules told apart by
a key nothing on screen reports.

**The bias reaches one node, and that is where "join is within one path" is enforced.**
`canvas::pen_scope` is `pen_bias.then(edited_path).flatten()`, and `pen_resume_target` was split into
`pen_resume_target_in(world, only)` so both halves of the confinement ask one question. Reaching out to
another layer would be a node merge, whose answer is not the one the pen tool's own join reaches (D123:
the node being drawn *into* survives). Two joins with two rules, told apart by which tool was in hand,
is how a verb becomes unpredictable. **The pen tool's own cross-layer join is unchanged.**

**A new subpath joins the same node, and its consequence is winding.** `PenVerb::NewSubpath` appends an
empty placeholder run and points `PenEdit::active` at it. `PenEdit` needed `minted: bool` and
`endpoint()` had to become `Option<Point>`, because a minted run left with fewer than two anchors is
**pruned** by `finish_pen`: `pen_path` would otherwise emit its lone `MoveTo` into the model. Pruning
*every* short run would reach a **stored** one — an import can hold one — and a resume that changed
nothing would then compare unequal and commit an edit, defeating `rewrite_path`'s no-op test. The first
anchor is snapped **after** the pen is holding the node, because `pen_point` can only exclude the node
being edited once `editing` is set.

**We do not auto-reverse a contained run.** It is magic, and it breaks the moment two runs partly
overlap where neither answer is "inside". The honest substitute is a status line at the moment the
choice is made: the `info` on `NewSubpath` says drawing it the other way round cuts a hole, and names
the verb that fixes it after the fact.

**That verb is `Shift+D`** — `D` for direction, in the plain-plus-`Shift` shape `Shift+R` established; a
*plain* letter is reserved for switching tool. `tools::reverse_subpaths` drives `PenSubpath::reverse`
over the runs `tools::subpaths_touched` names, and the subject is those runs or **every** run when
nothing is selected — D119's corner-radius rule, and it works on a selected path outside point editing
for the same reason.

**It is keyboard-only, with no inspector button, and that is a decision.** Every structural verb in the
tool is keyboard-only, and the align row it would join is width-exact by measurement: eight 24×22
buttons with 3px between them and two hairlines come to the card's content width exactly
(`inspector.rs`), so a ninth cell would break a measured layout.

**`PointSet::reverse_within` remaps the selection instead of dropping it** — the only structural edit in
the tool that does, because reversing is a *permutation*, so there is a right answer. Anchors mirror as
`n − 1 − a`; segments as `n − 2 − a`, a segment being named by the anchor it *leaves*, wrapping on a
closed run. Leaving the indices unchanged is the failure this prevents: they stay in range and light the
**mirrored** points.

Three consequences elsewhere. **Escape grew a rung** — present → picker → text → pen path → gesture →
**pen bias** → points → pivot → group → tool → selection — with the bias above the points, being the
more transient; it is also the way out to the *standalone* pen, since `choose_tool` will not switch
while an edit is live. `normal_mode_input`'s pen gate is now `self.tool == Tool::Pen ||
self.pen.is_some()`, a path in flight owning the pointer whichever tool armed it. And `finish_pen` and
`pen_join` both end through `end_pen_gesture`, which returns to the **node tool** when the node tool
armed the gesture and drops to Select otherwise — the tool is the test, since the bias never changed it.
That last is the complaint itself: the edit you were in used to be gone.

`draw_points` **stands down entirely while a pen gesture is in flight**, not for tidiness: the pen draws
a circle on every anchor and `draw_points` a *square* on every corner, so overlaid they would put a
circle on top of a square — a mark nothing in the app means.

Tests worth naming: `reversing_a_subpath_flips_its_winding_and_leaves_the_others_alone` asserts on
**signed area**, the reported symptom rather than the mechanism, and pins that the magnitude survives,
that unnamed runs are untouched, and that a corner radius rides to the index it now occupies;
`reversing_a_subpath_carries_the_selection_to_the_same_points`;
`a_freshly_minted_run_has_no_endpoint_and_does_not_panic_for_one`, which pins the `usize` underflow the
placeholder run is one `len() - 1` away from; plus
`the_subpaths_a_selection_touches_are_listed_once_each` and
`shift_d_reverses_a_path_and_ctrl_d_still_duplicates`.

*One gap, stated rather than papered over: `pen_verb`'s routing has no unit test. It is a method on
`OndinApp`, which needs a wgpu `RenderState`, so no `OndinApp` is constructible headlessly. Revisit if a
verb ever fires on the wrong target: lift the choice out of `&self` into a free function over the
`pen_scope`/`node_grab`/`pick_leaf` answers, at the first bug rather than before one.*

✅ **Discharged on 2026-08-22 (D303), and *without* the refactor prescribed above.**
`canvas::headless_app_tests::the_pen_bias_routes_a_press_by_what_is_under_it` pins all four answers by
driving the method on a headless app, so the choice stayed on `&self` and the test came to it instead.
Worth keeping as the one case that qualifies D303's own rule: lifting a decision into a free function is
still the better shape, but it is a preference rather than the only door, and here the door was cheaper
than the lift.

**D124 — The two tools read against each other, and four ways they disagreed. *Resolved.*** None was
reported: they came out of reading the pen and the node tool side by side once both were finished, which
is a different exercise from using either. One turned out to be a live bug.

**The pen constrains with `Shift`**, to an eighth of a turn from the anchor before it — every other
drawing gesture has that key, and `pen_input` did not read it at all. It is `canvas::axial_corner`
against the **previous anchor** rather than the path's origin, and does nothing on the *first* anchor.
**Shift replaces the snap rather than composing with it**, the rule `line_end_tx` already states: a
point pulled onto a guide and then forced to 45° is on neither. `axial_corner` still rounds *along* the
constrained direction when the grid is on. The rubber band asks the same function, or it would promise
an angle the press does not commit.

**The pen's shaping drag gets the tangent snap**, which the node tool had since D123 — and the pen is
where a handle is first *aimed*. **Wiring it up exposed a real defect in the snap.** `tangent_snap`
offers the direction collinear with the anchor's *other* handle, read from the anchor as it stands —
**last frame's**. On a mirrored anchor the other handle is the negation of this one, so the "smooth"
candidate is the direction this handle is already pointing: the snap pulls it back and a slow drag
sticks then jumps. Every unmodified pen *and node tool* drag is that case, so the defect was shipped and
merely unexercised. The guard is one clause — offer the collinear candidate only when the pair is
**already broken** — which is not a special case but a statement of what the candidate is for. The test
grew the mirrored case and fails without it.

**`Alt`+click no longer removes a point.** Built in D120 as Delete without the keyboard; gone on the
judgement that a destructive edit on a *single click* is one slipped modifier from happening by
accident, over a target this tool puts a dozen of within a few pixels of each other. Delete is one key
and already covers a point and a segment alike — a symmetry `Alt` could not have had without a second
arm for segments.

**And the marks are one family again.** `POINT_PX` went 7 → 9 and the secondary marks did not follow. A
handle's dot goes 2.5 → 3. The **pen's in-progress anchors** now wear the marker the node tool will give
them (`paint_anchor`), because they were a plain 3pt dot before and a path therefore changed appearance
at the instant it committed. **Always circles**, though, where the node tool draws a square for a
corner: that distinction reads a *finished* anchor, and mid-draw whether the anchor is a corner depends
on a drag still happening. A marker flipping shape under the pointer would report a decision the user
has not made.

The snap ring went the other way from the obvious one. It was a flat 5pt radius chosen when the marker
was a 3pt dot, so the first move was to keep the daylight by deriving marker + gap, 6.5. Wrong: at 9pt
the mark carries the statement itself and a ring standing off it reads as a *second object* orbiting the
point. It is 5 again, **on** the marker's own 4.5pt edge at 2pt of weight. *The lesson is not "express
the derivation" — it is that the old value encoded a look rather than a measurement, and once the dot
was no longer small the look itself was the thing to re-decide.*

**D122 — One segment, two parameterisations, and the affordance drifted. *Resolved.*** Reported as the
half-opacity point drifting away from the pointer. Measured before it was theorised about: **28 units
out of 300 at the quarter point of a straight segment, zero at the middle**.

That signature is the whole diagnosis. `geometry::nearest_segment` measures against the real `PathSeg`,
so a straight segment gives the *linear* parameter; `tools::segment_cubic` expressed the same segment as
the cubic with its **control points on its own endpoints**, whose `B(0.25)` is 15.6% along. Same line,
different parameterisation — worst at the quarters, exact at the middle, which is what `(1−t)³ +
3(1−t)²t` does against `1 − t`.

**The fix is the degree-elevated line — control points at the thirds — and it is exact rather than
close.** `B(t)` for that cubic is `p₀ + d·t[(1−t) + t]²`, which is `lerp(t)` identically, so the two
modules agree by algebra instead of by luck.
`a_segments_parameter_means_the_same_to_the_hit_test_and_to_the_app` walks a pointer along a line and a
curve and asserts core's reported point and the app's are the same point.

Three things followed. `insert_point` keeps its own straight-line branch, because a *split* must still
write **zero** handles — subdividing the elevated cubic leaves the halves' control points at their own
thirds, the same line at three times the size (D117's "a path grew every trip"). `bend_segment` elevates
a straight segment before applying the pull. And because elevating changes the *representation* without
changing the shape, a bend of zero returns early, or a `Ctrl`-press that never travelled would rewrite
the path and land on the undo stack.

*The rule worth keeping: a derived representation of a segment owes the original's parameterisation, not
just its shape. `segment_is_straight` exists because `segment_cubic` can no longer be asked.*

**D121 — A resize about the box's minimum side mirrored it, and had since `resize_factors` was written.
*Resolved.*** Reported against the box over a path's selected points — "resizing multiple points
sometimes sends the shape completely off" — but the cause is older and belongs to two other gestures.

`resize_factors` computes the scale as *the pointer's distance from the anchor* over *the box's extent*.
The first is signed; the second is not, and needed to be. A handle on the box's **minimum** side starts
at −extent from the corner it holds, so dividing by +extent made the factor −1 before the hand moved:
grabbing the top-left handle of a **group** or a **multi-selection** mirrored it instantly. The fix is
one term — the signed distance from anchor to dragged corner, `(2u−1)·extent` anchored and `(u−½)·extent`
under Alt.

**It hid behind the one caller that does not use it.** `resize_layer` routes a `Rect` and its relatives
to `resized_box`, which takes `.abs()`, so every ordinary shape resize was correct. It hid behind the
tests too: every existing test used `Handle::BottomRight`, the single handle whose sign comes out right
either way. *A test suite that exercises one member of a symmetric set will miss exactly this.*
`a_handle_dropped_where_it_was_grabbed_scales_by_one` now loops all eight, with and without Alt, and
`a_min_side_handle_scales_rather_than_mirroring` pins the direction, including that a handle dragged
*past* its anchor still mirrors.

**D120 — Points snap, segments are a subject, and a burst of edits is one undo step. *Resolved.***
Five things the roadmap listed as what was left of path editing; they share three decisions.

**Both tools snap, and what snaps is the *point*.** The pen took the raw pointer and the node tool
consulted `snap.rs` not at all — the only gestures in the app that did not snap, and the ones where it
matters most. `snap::snap_point` needed nothing new. What each gesture had to decide is **which** point
it is aiming, and the answer is never the box:

- an anchor drag snaps the anchor the *press took* and moves the whole set by the adjustment it earns.
  Snapping the box over a multi-point selection would pull the set by whichever edge caught, and that
  edge can belong to a point on the other side of the shape from the hand;
- a segment move snaps the point *on the segment* the press grabbed, not either bounding anchor;
- a `Ctrl` bend snaps **nothing** — it moves two control points, and a control point rounded to a whole
  unit says nothing about where the curve goes;
- the point box scales its **pointer**, as a resize does.

Two consequences worth more than the feature. **A snap on a gesture that has not travelled edits the
document on a click**: `node_input` runs its drag arms on the press and release frames of a plain click,
where a snap pulls a point off its coordinate and leaves an undo step behind a press that was only ever
a selection. `rewrite_path`'s no-op comparison cannot catch it — the snapped path really is different.
`canvas::gesture_travelled` gates every snap on `MIN_CREATE_PX`, a *threshold* rather than an exact zero
because a click with a pixel of wobble is still a click.

**The pen's own handle drag had to learn the retract snap.** A press plants its anchor on the snapped
point and then shapes it from the raw pointer, so every plain click would otherwise leave a handle
exactly as long as the snap adjustment — a corner that is not quite a corner, on every click. The
substitution moved onto the type as `PenAnchor::pull_within`; `PenAnchor::pull` is gone, being that
function with the radius left out. `pulling_a_handle_mirrors_unless_the_pair_is_broken` covers the
radius as well as the mirror now.

**The close snap and the press are still one question**: the pointer is snapped *before*
`pen_close_snap` is asked, and the rubber band asks with the same snapped point (D116's pairing).

**A segment is a named thing, and core owns the name.** `geometry::anchor_runs` already carried the real
`PathSeg`s indexed by the anchor each one **leaves** (D119), so `geometry::nearest_segment` answers a
pointer in that numbering and every verb acts on it: `tools::insert_point`, `remove_segments`,
`bend_segment`, and `segment_ends`, where the subtlety lives — the closing segment of a closed run and
the missing segment of an open one sit at the same index, so the answer is an `Option` rather than
arithmetic at five call sites. `the_app_and_core_number_a_paths_anchors_alike` now compares segments
too, a disagreement there putting an inserted point on the wrong side of a corner.

Four smaller decisions inside that:

- **Inserting splits the curve rather than rebuilding it** (`CubicBez::subsegment`), and a **straight**
  segment is its own case, for D117's reason. `splitting_a_line_leaves_two_lines_and_a_corner` caught
  it, and failed before the fix.
- **The inserted point becomes the selection** — an insert renumbers every anchor after it, so the old
  set is stale by `retain_valid`'s own rule, and it is what the gesture is asking for anyway.
- **Removing a segment is structural where removing a point is not.** A closed run opens, starting after
  the cut; an open one becomes two. The handles at the new ends are zeroed, which is not tidiness:
  `pen_path` writes neither of them, so leaving them set would be a value only the app knew about — and
  it would reappear the moment the run was closed again, bending a segment nobody drew.
- **A bend puts the grabbed point exactly under the pointer.** `u = 3(1−t)²t` and `v = 3(1−t)t²`, so
  `u·δ₁ + v·δ₂ = delta` is one equation in two unknowns and the minimum-norm solution splits it. The
  anchors' *other* handles are left alone, so bending beside a smooth point breaks its pair — the honest
  reading of "bend this segment".

**Plain moves, `Ctrl` shapes the curvature** — D118's rule, now built. The modifier is re-read every
frame rather than latched, both readings measuring the same total from the same press (D40's
live-modifier rule).

**The gestures competing for one press are ordered, and the order is the tool.** `NodeGrab` runs from
the smallest, most deliberate target outward — handle, anchor, point-box corner, segment, then a
marquee. A **handle** beats its own anchor (D118); an **anchor** beats a box corner, because the box's
corners *are* the extreme selected points whenever two are diagonal, and the other order would make the
points that define the box the only ones you could not drag. `PEN_PICK_PX` is the segment radius too,
read as "the pointer is on this path".

**Insertion is a double-click, because both modifiers were already spoken for** and because "one level
finer" is what a double-click means everywhere else here. It arrives on the second release, by which
time the second press has armed a segment drag, so it cancels that drag rather than living beside it.

**A selected segment is a subject, so it answers every question a selected pair of points does.**
`PointSet` holds anchors **or** segments — `Selection`'s exclusivity argument one level down, since
Delete needs a single subject — and `canvas::subject_points` derives the pair a segment covers, which is
what makes X/Y read it, the arrow keys move it, align straighten it and the radius field round it, all
from one accessor. **Delete is the one verb that reads the segment itself**, removing a segment and
removing its two points being genuinely different edits. The hover trace is the affordance a segment has
instead of a marker.

**A scalable box over the points, and it is not the selection box coming back.** `chrome_hidden` takes
the *layer's* box away (D118); this box is derived from the selected points themselves, so it never
surrounds anything the tool is not already acting on, and where it lands on a point the point wins. A
**flat** box is suppressed entirely — not because the arithmetic minds, but because its four corners all
land *on* the extreme points, where the point wins the press, so the chrome would promise four handles
none of which could be grabbed. The box the *arithmetic* uses is captured at the press
(`Drag::PointBox::box_`); the box that is **drawn** is read live, or the handles hang behind while the
shape moves out from under them.

**Coalescing lives in `history.rs`, and the split is mechanism from policy.** Nudging a point four times
was four undos. `History::commit_into_run` folds a commit into the step before it by **keeping the older
inverse and discarding the new one**: two consecutive absolute overwrites of the same field compose, so
a single undo of the pair is exactly the first one's inverse. That needs both edits to have overwritten
the same fields of the same nodes, which the private `Shape` check enforces — refused outright for
anything structural, because the inverse of a create is a delete and folding two leaves a node in the
document with nothing on the stack that removes it. ⚠️ **`Shape` was built from `Operation::overwrites`
and is built from `Operation::shape_key` since D482**: an operation's discriminant is its *variant*
rather than the fields it writes, which is the same thing for 22 of the 23 overwriting operations and
not for `SetGeometry`, and `overwrites` answered `None` for every guide operation and so kept a guide
nudge out of a run altogether. `shape_key` enumerates rather than defaulting, so a new operation still
has to choose — and now has two things to choose.

Core can say when a merge is *sound*; only the app knows when two edits are one **decision**. So
`EditorSession::commit_run` holds the policy: the same verb, nothing else committed in between, no
pointer press between them (`end_edit_run`, which is also how the subject changes), and close enough in
time to read as one burst. The window is feel, not correctness. Both nudges use it under their own verbs
so a point nudge and a layer nudge can never merge; align and distribute deliberately do not, being one
decision each however often repeated.

**Five corrections from living with it, all in the same shape: chrome that promised more than the
gesture did, or less.**

- **One selected segment gets no box.** The segment already has a complete gesture, and a box adds four
  handles and a rectangle to say nothing new. Two or more is where a box earns its place.
  `point_box` asks `PointSet::segment_count` and refuses at one.
- **The box grew side handles.** Four squares of which only the diagonals did anything reads as three
  broken edges. The argument against sides was real but it is *the user's* trade to make, and every
  other editor makes it the other way. The bands are invisible and 6pt, as a layer box's are, and they
  beat a segment.
- **The box is drawn from the live extent, not the captured one.**
- **A ghost point on the hovered segment**, at half opacity, at the parameter `insert_point` would
  actually split at — a promise rather than a hint, taking the square-or-circle of the marker the insert
  will produce. Only while hovered: an affordance always on screen is furniture.
- **`Alt`+click removes a point.** *Reversed in D124.*

**And segments select as a set**, which was recorded as a limit and did not survive contact. The
argument for the single slot survives intact, because the *exclusivity* was the load-bearing half.
`subject_points` is the **deduplicated** union of the selected segments' ends, so a chain moves as one
piece; `tools::remove_segments` takes the whole set, rotating a closed run so it starts just after its
first cut, which turns the wrap-around into the open case. A **bend** stays single: the pointer names a
parameter on the segment under it.

**D123 — The rest of the path-editing list, and one recorded decision that did not survive being
checked. *Resolved.*** Six items; what they share is that each had already been decided in the roadmap.

**`Tab` steps the point selection along the path**, `Shift`+`Tab` back — one flat order over the whole
path, the numbering `pen_anchors` already produces. It steps from the **last** point of the current
subject and replaces the selection rather than extending it. Resolved in the keymap rather than the
canvas: `Tab` is egui's own focus key, so it has to pass `input::resolve`'s focus guard, and `dispatch`
drops the action unless the node tool has a path.

**And then it worked exactly once.** `egui_wants_keyboard_input` is `focused().is_some()` — *anything*
focused — and `Tab` is what egui drives its focus ring with. The first press found nothing focused and
stepped a point; the pass that followed put focus on some chrome button, and every press after was
dropped. Measured before it was theorised about: four synthetic `Tab`s through a two-button pass,
printing the guard each frame — open, shut, shut, open again as the ring wrapped, which is why it looked
intermittent. It cannot be fixed by consuming the key, egui reading focus movement out of `RawInput`
before the app runs. So `<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui` **gives the focus back at the end of a frame
in which it claimed a `Tab`**, which scopes the workaround exactly (the method name was `update` here
until D698).
`a_focused_widget_silences_the_keymap_and_tab_is_what_focuses_one` pins the egui behaviour rather than
our handling of it, so a future version that narrows `wants_keyboard_input` shows up as a failing test.

**Numeric handle editing, X/Y** (`inspector::point_handle_rows`): a handle is a point like any other and
the inspector speaks X/Y about every one. Two rows, **`←X`/`←Y` and `→X`/`→Y`**. They began as
`IX`/`OX` and were reported as obscure, for a reason worth keeping: two letters cannot say "incoming",
and *those* two misparse into a Roman numeral and an animal. An arrow does not misparse, and it states
the geometry — a path arrives along one handle and leaves along the other. **Two glyphs and no more**,
because `value_field` reserves the prefix's width *beside* the digits and a field whose digits do not
fit grows, taking the card and the inspector's width with it. Measured at the prefix size: `←X` is
20.8px against `OX`'s 18.4 and `OutX`'s 30.8, where a six-digit coordinate needs 40. They also fix an
alignment flaw nobody had reported, `I` being 12.3px where `O` is 18.4. Shown for a single selected
anchor and **dimmed** otherwise. Two rules it does not share with the drag: it uses `nudge_handle_tx`,
the *increment* form (D118); and **it preserves the mirror rather than imposing one** — a field has no
key to hold, so it asks `PenAnchor::is_smooth` and a broken anchor stays broken.

**Tangent-continuity snapping** (`tools::tangent_snap`), by the substitution the retract snap uses. The
direction that matters is the one that makes the anchor **smooth** — `Alt` breaks a pair in a moment and
"nearly smooth" is exactly what a curve shows and a hand cannot fix — plus the eight axis and diagonal
directions. **A perpendicular distance, not an angle**: an angular tolerance is a different-sized target
at each end of a handle, forgiving on a short one and a hair's breadth on a long one, and the long ones
are where the aim matters. The length is kept; a candidate the pointer is *behind* is skipped, since
