projecting onto the far side would flip the handle through its own anchor. `TANGENT_SNAP_PX` is 4 —
smaller than the layout tolerance, because this one competes with free aim.

**A rounded corner wore a ring, and it is gone again.** The argument was that the field reports the
*largest* radius of the set. The answer from using it: the fillet is right there on the ink, at the very
corner the marker sits on. *Reported and removed the same day it was added, which is the shortest
possible version of the rule that an affordance must answer a question the screen has not already
answered.*

**A hovered point is heavier, not tinted** — two pixels of outline where there was one. The first cut
filled it with the selection colour at 30% and was reported as looking bad, for a reason that
generalises: **the fill is what this marker uses to say selected-or-not**, so a third fill reads as a
third selection state. Drawn from `node_grab`, the one question the *press* asks, so the highlight
cannot promise a grab the press will not make.

**The stroke is laid inside the marker's edge, and the circle needed measuring.** A heavier stroke
centred on the edge puts half outside, so every marker would swell as the pointer neared it. A rect can
be asked for `StrokeKind::Inside`; a circle has only its radius, and the obvious correction — pull in by
half the extra weight — is **wrong**: measured through the tessellator, a stroked circle reaches `r +
w`, not `r + w/2`. `the_hover_weight_does_not_change_a_markers_silhouette` asserts both shapes
tessellate to the same bounds at both weights, and fails against the half-weight version.

**Joining two paths with the pen** — which node's paint, name and transform survive falls out of the
gesture rather than the model: **the one being drawn into**. What survives is what the hand was already
holding; the other node is absorbed and deleted. Drawing a fresh run and joining it onto an existing
path is the case with no node to hold, and there the target survives. **Every subpath of the absorbed
node comes across**, or deleting the node deletes artwork nobody touched (D117's reason for `PenEdit`
carrying the whole list). Two details easy to get backwards, and got backwards: the target's run is
turned so its grabbed endpoint comes **first**, the opposite of `PenEdit::working`; and **a run's own
far end is not a join but a close**, since joining a run to itself would append a duplicate of every
anchor. `pen_join_target` is one query asked by the press and by the ring that promises it.

**And `local_bounds` now reports a rounded path's real box** — the one place a recorded decision was
wrong rather than superseded. D119 kept the *unrounded* box "as `Rect` does", but they were never
disagreeing: a rectangle's fillets cut in from corners that are not on any extreme, so its box is
unchanged by a radius and the unrounded box was **exact** for that kind and a superset only for this
one. Only the path was paying, with the inspector's W/H reading generous on anything heavily rounded.

**The point box turns, too**, on the ring just outside a corner — the same band a layer's box has, same
cursor, same 15° steps under Shift. It was left out on the grounds that the band is where a marquee
starts; that is equally true of a layer selection, where the ring wins anyway. One rule, not two. The
pivot is the box's own centre and there is no other candidate. `tools::rotate_points` carries the
handles through the same `Affine` as their anchors, via the control points they describe rather than the
linear part, so a zero-length handle stays at zero rather than at a rounding error.

*One item is deliberately not built: every point edit is still a whole-path `GeometryPatch::Path`. That
is right for undo granularity and coarse only for MCP, where "move anchor 3" would rather be an op —
and MCP is parked until the editor is finished (§8). It stays in the roadmap as a decision rather than a
gap.* ⚠️ **It moved within that file on 2026-09-22**, from *Now · Path editing* — which it was the last
item in — to *Later · Parked decisions*. **That is this sentence being honoured rather than overridden**:
it is still in the roadmap, and a **Now** heading means *open work on live code*, which is the one
reading this note exists to refuse. The trigger is unchanged and is stated there — revisited *with*
MCP, not before.

**D126 — Three stroke features are declined, and one stored field is deliberately not offered.
*Intentional.*** Carried in the todo as settled and moved here so the answer stops being re-argued from
the options popover, which is where all three look like the obvious next row. They share one answer:
`Stroke` describes ink laid along an outline at a single width, and each of these asks it to describe
something else.

**Arrowheads and line endings** are markers hung on a path's ends rather than a property of the ink —
their own geometry, their own scale rule, and their own export (`<marker>`, which §7's writer does not
emit and has no other use for). **A variable-width profile** replaces `width: f64` with a function along
the path, and every reader of a stroke takes that scalar as the whole story: `geometry::stroke_expansion`
(D68), the `kurbo::Stroke` both backends build (§6.3), and `stroke-width`. **Separate start and end caps**
is the small one and is still a model change — `cap` is one `kurbo::Cap` and `stroke-linecap` is one
attribute, so a split cap would be ours to draw and ours to lose at the SVG boundary. None of the three is
hard; all three are a model change wearing a control's clothes, which is the distinction being drawn.
Outlining a stroke into a filled path is declined on the same grounds, and is recorded next to the
boolean's refusal of text because that is where a reader meets the question (§5.7a).

**`dash_offset` is the exception, because it is already in the model.** It is stored, saved, multiplied by
`tools::scale_scalars` with the rest of the pattern (D70), and honoured by both backends and the SVG
writer — and nothing in the inspector writes it. That is the decision, not an omission: a *static* phase
offset is a setting nobody reaches for, while an animated one is marching ants, and the field is being
kept for that. It costs nothing to leave in place, and removing it would cost a schema change to put back.

*Do not add any of the four to the dash/cap/join popover to "finish" it (§9.4), and do not delete
`dash_offset` as dead state — a `pub` field in core has no compiler pressure behind it and will look
unused for as long as it is reserved.*

**D127 — Generated layer names are numbered, and the numbering is a courtesy rather than an
invariant. *Resolved; two non-goals recorded, and one inference about invariant 3 marked as such.***
Every create site passed `name: None` and `op_create` turned that into `NodeKind::default_name()`, so
ten rectangles were all literally "Rectangle". That costs more here than in Figma, whose plugin API
addresses nodes by id: `snapshot.rs` emits `node.name()` into the AI-handoff projection (§7) and Command
Mode addresses layers by name as a fallback (§13). §5.7b states the rules; this is the reasoning.

**The name is resolved in `Document::op_create`, not by the callers, and that is the design.** Every
production create site passes `None` except the two `build::flatten` sites §5.7b names, so a tool added
later is numbered without knowing numbering exists — where a name computed by each builder would be a
rule every future create site had to remember, failing silently. The cost is that an op's *result* now
depends on the document it lands in, so two clients replaying from diverged states would name the node
differently. Invariant 3's determinism is explicitly about **ids**, which still ride inside the op; a
name is not structural, and a rename conflict is something §12 has to resolve for typed names anyway.
*That is an inference about the spirit of invariant 3 rather than something this document ever stated,
and should be read as one.* What is not an inference is that redo must land on the same string the
create landed on first —`redoing_a_create_resolves_the_same_name_it_did_the_first_time` pins it.

**Three choices inside the numbering.** **Every generated name carries a number, the first included.**
It landed the other way round first, with the first of a kind left bare, and what the asymmetry cost was
reported straight back: one name in the series is shaped differently from all the others for no reason a
user could name. *The corollary is that an unnumbered generated name now means something* — an older
document, or somebody imitating our stems — and `copy_name` puts its copy at the bottom of the series.
The number taken is the **first free** one rather than the next after the highest (Figma's
reset-on-delete), which needs no stored state; a persisted per-kind counter would reset silently on
reload. That a reused name refers to a different object is mild: a file's identity is the string node
id. And numbering is **per parent** — "Rectangle 137" is no benefit, and names repeating across parents
was already accepted (§9.2's ancestor rows exist so a repeat can be located).

**Two non-goals, recorded so they are not re-argued.** *Uniqueness must never become load-bearing* —
nothing resolves a node by name, and §13 already said a name lookup is a disambiguated fallback. *And
uniqueness is never re-established afterwards* — recomputing names on a move would rename layers behind
the user's back. `reparenting_into_a_collision_leaves_both_names_alone` asserts both.

**Two things numbering broke that were correct before it.** `build::set_boolean_op` compared the name
against the four `BoolOp` labels *exactly*, which was right while the first boolean was called plainly
"Union" and wrong once they are all numbered — switching an operation left a row reading "Union 1" over
an intersection. It asks `naming::is_boolean_label` now, which strips a number first, and remains the
**strict** question deliberately: `copy_name` increments anything that looks numbered, while this asks
whether the string is one we would have written, because getting it wrong renames a layer the user
named. *Do not unify the two tests* — `only_our_own_boolean_names_may_be_overwritten` pins both sides.
And `build::flatten`'s union arm emits its `CreateNode` **before** its deletes, so numbering counted the
layers being replaced; it names the result itself now, against `child_names(parent, except)`.

**Two smaller load-bearing details.** `build::CopyNames` is an accumulator, not a function, because
several copies in one transaction cannot see each other in the document; neutering it made three pasted
"Rectangle 1"s come back `["Rectangle 1", "Rectangle 2", "Rectangle 2", "Rectangle 2"]`, held by
`three_copies_in_one_transaction_get_three_different_numbers`. And `GENERATED_NAMES` is a hand-written
list rather than a walk over the variants, the question asked of it being the inverse one — "would we
have written this string" cannot be answered by a `match` on a kind. A kind missing from that list
compiles, saves and loads perfectly and simply never gets numbered, so
`every_default_name_is_listed_as_generated` goes through a **wildcard-free** `match` helper that stops
compiling when a `NodeKind` is added — the `matches!`-over-a-list trap of D87–D88. *Keep the list, keep
the exhaustive match.*

*While there:* `layers::layer_rename_field` trims and refuses empty (D54); the inspector's identity-card
field did neither, so selecting all and pressing Delete there committed `""`. The inspector shares the
layers panel's rule now — "the user owns the names they typed" needs one definition of a typed name.

**D128 — The selection chrome gets out of the way while an inspector edit is looked at. *Resolved at the
third attempt: the first classification asked about the widget, the second asked only what the edit does,
and it takes both questions.*** Scrubbing a width put the number under the hand and the result under a
blue box, its handles, the size badge and the pivot marker.

**The list of what hides was already in one place, so this is a third *term*.** `canvas::chrome_hidden`
(D118) gains `chrome_hold.holding()`, and everything the request named is inside that gate already —
`draw_key_outline` included, which asks the predicate itself. `app::ChromeHold` owns only *when*.

**Two clocks, because the two gestures are shaped differently.** `Free`, `Scrubbing`, `Until(f64)`, with
`CHROME_HOLD_SECS = 1.5`. A scrub's count starts at the **release**, so ten seconds of dragging cannot
bring the box back mid-gesture. A keystroke has no duration, so each restarts the count. The end of a
scrub cannot come from the field — a `DragValue` reports nothing on the frame the button lifts — so
`pointer_down` is what ends it; a machine waiting for the field to fall silent would hold for ever.

**The chrome comes back on whichever comes first, the timeout or the pointer moving over the canvas**,
and the motion rule is the better half. It is *canvas* motion and not pointer motion — travelling from
one field to the next must not bring the box back, and "the pointer moved" is the version written by
accident. **But canvas motion never cancels a scrub in flight**, which the design did not say and the
mechanism demands: a long drag wraps the pointer round the screen edge (`ui::wrap_scrub`, D66) and
crosses the canvas on the way. And `cancel_gesture` goes straight to `Free` with no courtesy, a
cancelled scrub having no result.

**`ChromeHold::advance` is a pure function, and that placement is the point.** `OndinApp` cannot be
constructed headlessly, so a decision left inside `fold_chrome_hold` is one no test can reach; this is
the lift D125's closing note said to make at the first bug, made up front. The clock is seconds off
`InputState::time` rather than an `Instant`, that being what `request_repaint_after` is measured against
and what a probe can drive. `app.canvas_rect` is deliberately **last frame's**: the canvas is drawn
before the inspector, so it is the only rect that exists when the question is asked.
`app::chrome_hold_tests` is the machine as a table, and three rules were checked by neutering — sending
the release straight to `Free` failed the first (`left: Free, right: Until(11.5)`), dropping the
canvas-motion term failed the third, letting motion cancel a scrub failed the fourth.

**A timer in a reactive app has nothing to wake it**, so an `Until` frame asks `request_repaint_after` —
the same stranded-first-wake shape as D110. Asked on **every** held frame rather than the one that
starts the count: egui keeps the earliest request, so repeating it is free and cannot be forgotten.

**The first seam asked about the widget, and could not see most of the edits it existed for.**
`note_value_edit` had one call site inside `value_field_f64`, so a `field_button` or a `ui::segmented`
cell was silent. Seven controls were reported changing the artwork with the box still over it: rotate
90° either way, flip horizontal/vertical, a colour set on the saturation plane or hue bar, that colour's
opacity, and a stroke's position. **What the seven have in common with the two the design excluded is
not their shape but their effect: they change what is drawn.** The proportion lock commits
`SetProportionsLocked`, which draws nothing; opening the per-corner dialog commits nothing at all.

**So the question is asked of the transaction.** `Operation::changes_ink` and `Transaction::changes_ink`
(§5.7) — wildcard-free, so a new operation stops the build and has to be classified, and **any** rather
than all, because a transaction that moves a layer *and* renames it has a visible result.
`OndinApp::note_edit(resp, tx)` early-returns unless the transaction changes ink and then or-s
`resp.dragged()` into `pending_edit`; or-ed rather than overwritten, so a drag in flight wins over a
keystroke landing in another field. `resp` is `None` for a discrete edit, and `edit_valve` passes one
**every frame**, which is what makes a drag's count start at its release.

**The committer is the seam, so the hide is not a roll-call.** The panels commit through `commit_edit`
or `edit_valve` and **never through `session.commit` directly**: 22 sites in `inspector.rs` and 5 in
`typography.rs` were converted, and the only `session.commit` left under `panels/` is in `layers.rs`. A
control added later inherits the behaviour. Two paths had to be said by hand. The hand-rolled valves
`multi_valve` and `char_valve` call `note_edit` themselves every frame — a valve that noted only on its
committing frame would leave the box up for the whole drag and hide it *afterwards*. And `char_valve`'s
**partial** branch, where a live text session owns the range, commits nothing until the session ends
(§9.3), so `note_live_edit` arms it there and skips the question, the edit being a `SetText`.

🚨 **That grep sentence was false from the day it was written, and D679 is the correction.**
`inspector::remove_selected_guides` — the guide card's Trash button — committed through
`session.commit` directly, under `panels/`, in a file this entry names as converted. The difference
from the two *stated* exceptions matters: the identity row's *Group* and *Ungroup* (D562) reach
`session.commit` through an `OndinApp` method in `app.rs`, so the grep passes over them honestly and
`commit_edit`'s doc says so; this one the grep would have caught, had anyone re-run it. It is routed
through `commit_edit` now — behaviourally identical, `RemoveGuide` being one of the eleven ops
`changes_ink` answers `false` for — and the grep is a test,
`app::tests::only_the_layers_panel_commits_without_the_committer`, so the sentence above is enforced
rather than asserted.

**The per-field opt-out has an instance after all, and it is box trim.** Under the transaction test its
`SetBlockStyle` changes ink as far as the op can tell, so it *would* arm the hide, and must not: D78
guarantees that trimming never moves the ink, so what it moves is the box the selection outline draws,
and hiding that box takes away the only thing there was to see. The sharp test — **opt out where the
edit changes the box without changing the ink** — is unchanged, and `OndinApp::commit_chrome_edit` is
now the thing it documents: **a named committer rather than the `Scrub` flag the design proposed**. One
caller, `typography::commit_trim`. Nothing else qualifies — max lines removes lines, so the ink moves.

**"Discrete choices do not count" was wrong and is withdrawn.** Rotate, flip and stroke position are all
discrete and all must hide. The discrete/continuous distinction was never the right axis; what a
discrete edit lacks is only a *duration*, which is why it gets `Until` at once where a drag gets
`Scrubbing`. The exclusions survive for a different reason: the proportion lock draws nothing, and
opening a dialog commits nothing.

**The hide lands one frame after the keystroke, and that is a latency rather than a disagreement.** The
canvas is drawn before the inspector, so the earliest the chrome can go is the following frame. It is
the *next* frame only because the end of `OndinApp::ui` asks for one whenever a note is pending —
nothing on the edit path requests a repaint by itself. A scrub rides its own pointer motion and a
keystroke usually rides the key release, which reads as a guarantee until the one case without it turns
up; the same class as D110.

**What is tested is the two pure halves, and the chain between them is read rather than run.**
`only_the_chrome_operations_change_no_ink` pins the exact set as a list — the wildcard-free `match`
stops the build for a new operation but does not stop its author choosing the wrong arm — and
`a_transaction_is_visible_if_any_of_its_operations_is` holds the `any`. What has no test is the **join**:
`edit_note` → `pending_edit` → `advance` runs inside `OndinApp`. That the seven controls each reach a
committer is verified by reading and by the grep for a stray `session.commit` under `panels/`, which is
the only thing holding that rule. *Re-run it after adding a panel.*

**Moving the question to the transaction dropped the other half of it, and the drop shipped.** The
transaction says what an edit *does*; it cannot say whether an edit *happened*. `edit_valve` is called
every frame and its transaction is built every frame — `inspector::place_at` returns a `SetTransform`
whether or not the number moved. So with any layer selected the resting X field noted an edit every
frame, `advance` restarted its 1.5 s every frame, and canvas motion was the one rule left that could
clear it: *"once I select a layer, the layer chrome always hides unless I move the mouse."*

The first seam had this half and it was easy to miss losing: the guard was a property of *where the call
was* rather than anything the call said. **So the decision is now one free function that asks both
questions** — `app::edit_note(resp, tx)`: `changes_ink` for what the edit does, and for a live control
`dragged()` then `changed()` for whether anything happened, `changed()` being exactly `nudged || value
!= before` and therefore the thing that leaves the arrow keys, Home, `lost_focus` and a click-to-focus
alone.

*The general lesson: a guard that lives at a call site rather than in the thing being called survives
exactly as long as the call site does.* `app::edit_note_tests` is aimed at the reported end rather than
the mechanism — a real `value_field` driven through ten idle frames, a hover, a drag, a release and a
typed digit. Restoring the buggy arm fails four of five, the first on frame 0.

**D129 — A press on the picker's plane or strips changed nothing until the pointer moved. *Resolved.***
`picker::pointer_slot` had two branches: `resp.clicked()` committed, everything else went to `valve_slot`
and so to `edit_valve`, which previews on `dragged()` and commits on `drag_stopped() || lost_focus() ||
changed()`. **A press sets none of those.** Read out of the vendored `egui-0.35.0/src/context.rs`:
`Flags::DRAGGED` waits until the gesture has travelled, and `Flags::CLICKED` is set only on the release.

**The colour was already computed on the press frame and thrown away.** `interact_pointer_pos` is `Some`
whenever `is_pointer_button_down_on || long_touched || clicked || drag_stopped`. The fix is one middle
branch — `resp.is_pointer_button_down_on() && !resp.dragged()` → preview, and return.
`is_pointer_button_down_on` is true from press to release, so the two conditions carve the gesture
cleanly. *Both terms are load-bearing — without `!resp.dragged()` this branch would shadow the valve for
the whole of a drag.*

**Why it belongs in the picker and not in the shared `edit_valve`: a plane or a strip is
position-valued, where a `DragValue` is delta-valued.** Where the button went down names a colour on its
own; a press on a numeric field carries nothing and must stay silent. Extending `edit_valve` would have
made a bare press on every field preview an unchanged value, and leave that preview *uncleared*, a press
and release with no travel satisfying none of the valve's commit conditions.

**`OndinApp::preview_slot` is the third slot verb**, beside `write_slot` and `valve_slot`. It returns
whether it had anything to preview — `false` for a `PaintSlot::TextDecoration`, which previews through
the live text session and has its own valve (`char_valve`). **A decoration colour picked on the plane
therefore keeps the old press-does-nothing behaviour.** A recorded narrow gap, not an oversight: closing
it means touching `char_valve`'s preview/commit pairing, which is the code D109 was written about.
*Revisit if a decoration colour is reported as dead on press.*

**The press has to arm the chrome hide itself (D128), because nothing downstream would.** A raw
`allocate_exact_size` region sets neither `dragged()` nor `changed()` on the press frame, so the branch
calls `note_live_edit(true)` — `true` because the button is down, so the 1.5 s must not start counting
until it lifts. Both its callers sit behind a guard of their own, which is the only reason it may be
unconditional where `edit_note` may not. Move either and D128's every-frame hold comes back.

**There is no test, and the reason is worth recording.** The three controls are `&mut self` methods on
`OndinApp`, and unlike D128 there is no pure decision to lift out: the fix *is* the branch, and what it
turns on is egui's own flag timing. Reading that timing out of the vendored source is what was done
instead. *If a version bump changes either fact, this branch is where it lands.*

**D130 — Mixed is the word "Mixed" everywhere there is room for it, and a dash only where there is not.
*Resolved; this entry once said the opposite and was reversed on review.*** This entry first resolved
the two live conventions by value type — the word for a text-valued control, the dash for digits. **That
was the right diagnosis of an inconsistency and the wrong end to fix it from.** Reviewed on screen, the
word won and the dash retreated to where the word does not fit.

**The rule, stated once.** A control says **"Mixed"**. If it is too small to hold five letters it says a
dash, and there are exactly two: `ui::segment_mixed`, a segmented cell, and `ui::Swatch::Mixed`, a 16px
chip — where the dash also has to stand in for a colour, and any *plausible* colour is the one thing it
must not show, since whichever it picked would read as a claim the next click would make true of every
layer. There is no value-type threshold to remember, only a size one.

**One cost, accepted rather than worked around.** The paint row reads "Mixed … Mixed" whenever the
opacities differ, an alpha only disagreeing if the brushes holding it do. The alternative is one field
spelling the state differently from the three beside it.

**And the word is not enough on its own, because a suffix outlives the formatter that wrote it.** The
paint row's percentage read **"Mixed%"**, having put its `%` on the `DragValue` as a `suffix`, and egui
appends a suffix *after* the custom formatter. The suffix has to come **off** in the mixed branch, and
taking it off takes egui's own suffix-stripping parser with it, so the field needs a `%`-trimming
`custom_parser` — otherwise typing "50%" fails silently on the one field not showing the sign. *Any new
mixed field: put the unit in the formatter, or drop it and the parser together.*

**And a mixed *numeric* field owes one thing more than a display rule, which D465 is the cost of
learning.** The word is painted over a real number — one member of the disagreeing set, since the
control has to have something live to operate from — so the field must not write that number back
until the user has moved it. The hex field beside it is safe without a guard only because its "Mixed"
is the buffer's own text and `parse_hex` refuses it; **a word drawn by a formatter is not a value the
code can refuse.**

*Do not re-derive the dash from "digits should not carry words". It was tried, it is recorded here, and
what settled it is that "Mixed" is what the state **is**, while a dash is a glyph the reader has to have
been taught.*

**D131 — A very wide stroke left a hole in the middle of its own ink. *Resolved; the SVG path is
knowingly left behind.*** Reported with a 309pt centred stroke on a 200×120 shape. Measured headlessly
through the CPU backend on a bare stroke with **no fill at all**, so it is a gap in the stroke's own
coverage: a 200×120 **ellipse** draws correctly to 200pt and holes from 202pt, the hole's half-width
being `width/2 − 100` — the *larger* semi-axis — while the same **rect** draws to 320pt and holes from
330pt at `width/2 − 160`, half the width plus half the height.

**The roadmap's diagnosis was half right, and the half that was wrong was the threshold.** The mechanism
is confirmed: offsetting a closed contour inward by more than it has room for sends the inner contour
out through the far side, the region it encloses nets to winding **zero**, and a non-zero fill leaves it
empty — measured on `kurbo::stroke`'s expansion of the ellipse, winding 2 at the centre at 120pt, 1 at
200pt, 0 from 220pt. But the predicted *inradius* threshold is not where either shape fails, so a fix
gated on it would have been tuned against a number the bug does not use. The suggested fix does not work
either: `path_remove_interior_points` left the inverted contour standing at some widths, and a flo_curves
union had thrown away nearly all the ink by 1000pt.

**What works is expand, drop the inner contours, add the outline, wind alike, fill** —
`scene::lay_stroke`, which every alignment arm of `paint_stroke` goes through. The proof is two
sentences: an inner offset is the outline pushed inward, so anything it encloses lies inside the
outline; and the outline's interior is wholly covered by ink once the gate has fired, the gate being
"the ink is at least as wide as the shape is thin". So the outline's own path goes in beside the
expansion and every subpath is wound the same way (`wound_alike`), turning a non-zero fill into a plain
union. Dropping the inner contours (`outermost_subpaths`, by bounding-box containment) is separately
load-bearing and not an optimisation: pushed far enough in, an inner offset becomes a figure-eight with
both windings inside one contour, which `wound_alike` cannot correct because a subpath has one signed
area — measured, a 200×120 rect kept a 59pt ring void from 500 to 950pt until they were dropped.

**Three gates, each with a failure behind it.** `width >= min(bbox)` is deliberately conservative,
firing at 120pt on the ellipse where the bug starts at 202, and it *cannot* fire late because a shape's
inradius is never more than half its narrowest dimension. **Closed** is read off the path's last element
rather than the node's kind, because a per-side stroke runs along an open edge of a closed rect and its
bounding box can be flat. **Solid only**, because a dashed stroke is a row of open segments with no
interior to lose and the outline plug would fill the shape solid.

**A second, older bug was found on the way: `geometry::local_path` did not close the ellipse.**
`kurbo::Ellipse::to_path` emits four cubics whose last point is the first and no `ClosePath`, so the
backend capped its two ends instead of joining them; `Rect`, `RoundedRect` and `star_path` all close
their own. A fill cannot tell the difference, which is why it survived.

`a_very_wide_stroke_buries_the_middle_of_the_shape` (`ondin-export/tests/png.rs`) is the regression, at
five widths on both shapes, asserting no hole in the centre scanline **and** that the ink still reaches
as far as it should — otherwise a fix that drew something smaller and solid would pass. *Record
honestly: the SVG writer still emits `stroke-width` (§7), so the PNG/canvas path and the SVG can now
disagree. Fix that by building the same expansion in the writer if it is ever reported.*

**D132 — The chrome keyed by a paint's index follows the paint now, instead of being dropped or
silently left behind. *Resolved; no per-paint identity was needed.*** The roadmap said a stable
per-paint identity would fix the stroke options popup closing on a reorder. Nothing needs one: a reorder
and a removal **renumber** the list rather than replacing it. `paint::reordered_index(n, from, to, i)`
and `removed_index(gone, i)` answer "where did the paint at this index go", derived from
`paint::reordered` by construction, and `inspector::remap_paint_indices` carries the detached picker,
the hex buffer and — for strokes — the options popup, the open sides rows and the dash buffer over the
map. `forget_stroke_chrome` survives for the one case with nowhere to follow *to*, a change of subject.

**The removal was the reported half and the reorder was the worse half.** `drop_picker_on` closed the
picker when its paint was removed; through a *reorder* it did nothing, so the picker stayed on index 0
and went on editing under the same swatch while the paint underneath it changed. Closing a panel is
visible and editing the wrong paint is not. `drop_picker_on` is deleted.

The two pure functions are pinned **against `reordered` itself** rather than a table of expected
indices, which is where an off-by-one hides:
`a_reorder_renumbers_the_chrome_the_way_it_renumbers_the_list` moves labelled items over every from/to
pair of a four-item list and asserts that following the map lands on the same item, and
`a_removal_brings_the_chrome_above_it_down_one` is the twin. Both verified to fail on an off-by-one.
*Keep them stated as a property against `reordered`; a table would pass while the mapping drifted.*

**D133 — Nothing caps a paint list, and nothing should. *Intentional.*** Carried in the todo as an open
decision — "two-ish is the design ambition and the `Vec` will hold more; a soft cap is a decision, not a
bug" — and decided here so it stops being re-opened from the `+` button, where a limit looks like the
obvious missing guard. There is no cap, hard or soft.

A **hard** cap would be a UI-only rule with nothing behind it: `Paint` holds a `Vec`, the scene walk and
the SVG writer both walk all of it (§6.3, §7), the save format round-trips any length, and every tool
this panel is modelled on lets the list grow — so the app would be refusing a document it can still
open, draw and export. A **soft** cap is worse, because it has to explain itself: a warning affordance
on a panel whose whole job is to stay compact, spent on a state the user chose on purpose. And the panel
already discourages long lists in the only way that costs nothing — each paint is a row, a stroke two or
more (§9.4), so the price of a fifth fill is paid in the space it takes. *If long lists are ever
reported as a performance problem, that is the perf item about clip pushes per aligned stroke, not this.*

**D134 — A control that does not apply is shown and disabled, never removed. *Keep — this is a rule about
every panel in the inspector, not about the five that prompted it.*** Asked for after living with the
multi-selection panels: "let's keep the panels consistent. Otherwise when you jump from a single select to
a multi, you notice things moving around in the panel and it makes the feel cheap. Let's keep showing
things but have them disabled when not relevant for the current action."

**The mechanism is that a control which vanishes takes its space with it.** Every row in this inspector
divides the width it is given between its fields and its buttons, so removing a 28pt button does not
leave a 28pt hole — it widens the fields beside it and moves the edge between them. Clicking a second
layer therefore slid every number in the row sideways, and the drift is worst exactly where the panels
should agree most: the same properties, the same order, one layer versus several. It is also cheap to get
wrong in the honest direction, because "this cannot apply here" reads as a reason to omit the control,
and omitting it is what produces the shift. **There is a vertical form of the same mechanism and it took
until 2026-08-23 to find one — D310**, a whole *card* returning early for the one selection it had nothing
to align to, sixteen lines below a comment stating this rule.

**The vocabulary already existed, and one piece was added.** `ui::FieldButton::Disabled` is D72's enum
doing the work it was built for; `ui::HeadAction::inert` is new, beside `new` and `toggle`, for a header
action that must be present and take no press; and a `HeadAction::toggle(.., active: false, enabled:
false, ..)` is the dimmed pivot crosshair. In all three the **tooltip carries the reason**, which is the
part not to skip: a dimmed control can say "not for this selection" by itself but cannot say why, and the
why is usually a real fact about the model — the per-corner radii are per-node flags, a selection has no
shared transform origin, a stroke's dash pattern and side set are keyed by list index. ⚠️ **One of those
reasons was not a fact about the model but a rule nobody had looked up**: `proportions_locked` is also a
per-node flag, and D50 had long since decided what a *set* of them reads as, so the chain button sat
dimmed against a decided answer for as long as the card existed (D347). *A tooltip that explains a dimmed control is also the
claim most worth checking, because nothing about a control that does nothing ever gets reported.*

**Four applications landed with the rule.** The multi **Transform** panel was the worst offender and was
pre-existing rather than new: it put the two mirrors *beside* rotation and left skew alone underneath,
where the single-layer panel pairs rotation with skew and puts four buttons below — the code said so in a
comment and deferred it, on the grounds that nobody had decided what a quarter turn should sweep over a
set. The rows match now, the chain button sits in the slot it occupies on one layer — inert when this
landed, live since D347 — and W/H use the single-layer split so the edge down the middle of the card
lands in the same place in both. The multi **Appearance** panel gained
the per-corner button and the arithmetic that leaves room for it — both of its fields were wider than
their single-layer twins. The mixed **stroke** row got its dash/cap/join and per-side buttons back,
dimmed; dropping them had widened the position and weight fields. And the Fill and Stroke **headers** keep
their `+` as `HeadAction::inert` over a mixed panel, where it was absent: the reasoning for why there is
nothing for it to do is unchanged (D53), and what changed is that the panel says so in place.

**The rule is about the spacing as much as the controls**, which the fifth application made plain: the
mixed stroke's properties row "goes down a few px when the value is mixed". The per-stroke loop wraps a
stroke's colour row and its properties row in a scope setting `item_spacing.y = 6.0` — the unit's tighter
pitch, so the pair reads as one stroke against the card's own 9px between strokes — and the mixed branch
was outside that scope, so it took 9 and sat **3px** lower than the single-layer row. It is in the same
scope now. Three pixels is the smallest thing this entry covers and it was still reported, which is the
argument: a panel is consistent when nothing in it moves, and *presented in the same place* includes the
gap above the row. Like the field arithmetic, it is invisible in the source — the two branches differ in
nothing but the spacing they inherit. *The scope is now a function both branches call
(`inspector::paint_unit`) and the 6 is `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP`, because the pitch itself was reported wrong
later — D196. What stands here is that a shared scope is not shared enough.*

**The colour picker's kind tabs are the application that *reversed* a standing exception**, which is worth
recording because the old arrangement had an argument behind it: a slot that cannot hold a gradient got no
tabs at all, on the grounds that three tabs where two collapse back to the first is worse than none (D18).
What that actually left was a header holding nothing but a close button, reported as looking empty — and
it made the guide's picker read as a *different, smaller* panel rather than as the same one with two
choices unavailable. Disabled says which it is, and the row keeps the height it has everywhere else, which
is this entry's own mechanism. `ui::segmented_enabled` takes a per-cell `enabled` predicate (a disabled
cell keeps its place and its label, takes no hover ground and returns no click) and
`ui::segment_label_disabled` paints in `text::FAINT` — a **third** tier rather than the resting one,
because the resting label is what an *available* choice looks like and two readings of one colour is how a
disabled control comes to look merely unselected. `ui::segmented` delegates, so its eighteen call sites
are untouched. *The alpha slider is still absent where it cannot be honoured, and that is not an
inconsistency: a missing slider leaves no header empty.*

**And it is about consistency between *panels*, not only between selection states.** The layers panel's
search field was the one text input outside the inspector, and it was also the only one not built from
`ui::field_row` — so its text started hard against its own border and it sat shorter than every field it
is read alongside, egui's own `TextEdit` frame having a different height and no horizontal padding to
speak of. It is a `field_row` now, with the `TextEdit` framed `Frame::NONE` inside it (a second frame
inside the row draws a box in a box), which brings the 28pt height, the 9pt gutter and the 5pt radius with
it and leaves no second set of numbers to keep in step. *A new input anywhere in the chrome goes in a
`field_row`; that is where these numbers live.*

**What the rule does not license is dimming a control that has a real answer.** Deciding the meaning is
the better fix where one exists, and the quarter turns are the case in point: over a selection they turn
each layer about its **own** origin (`inspector::rotate_selection_quarter`), which is the reading the
rotation field beside them already takes, so they are **live** — and live even over a mixed rotation,
because a quarter turn is relative and needs no shared value to start from. Deciding that cost less than
the layout shifting under anyone who clicks a second layer. *So the order of preference is: make it work
over the selection, and only dim it where the model genuinely has nothing for it to act on. Dimming is
the fallback, not the goal.*

*And the button being present is only half of it — the fields beside it have to use the arithmetic that
reserves its slot, or the panel still shifts with every control in place. That is what both Appearance
fields and the mixed stroke row got wrong, and it is invisible in the source: it shows up as a number
moving a few points when the selection changes.*

**D135 — Group Colors lists gradients, and a row is keyed by *where* the paint is rather than by what it
is. *Resolved; the "not editable" half of this entry was wrong and is reversed.*** Reported as "Group
colors panel only shows solid colors, no gradients". The old reasoning was that a gradient is not one
colour, so no row could stand for it — **true of the *edit*, and the wrong conclusion about the row.**
Half of what a census row does is D71's count-and-reticle: is this in here, and where. That half works
for a ramp exactly as for a colour, and it was simply absent.

`build::colors_in` and the new `gradients_in` are two thin wrappers over one private `census(doc, ids,
key)` (§5.7a) — one walk with a key function rather than one function per key, because the two answers
have to agree about which paints and which layers they found and in what order; the layer-dedupe rule (a
shape whose fill and stroke share a paint is one layer using it twice) is the fiddly part.
`gradients_in` keys by the whole `Brush`: two ramps of the same colours at different angles are two
gradients, and merging them would print a count no selection could match.
`the_census_counts_gradients_separately_from_colours` pins the answer **and** that `colors_in` is
unchanged.

**The first version shipped the rows as countable and selectable but *not* editable, and that was
wrong.** The blocker this entry named was misread rather than imaginary. `PaintSlot` is `Copy + Eq` and
a gradient's identity is its stops **and** its geometry, so it will not fit in a slot the way four bytes
of RGBA do — which rules out a key that *is* the paint, and says nothing about a key that names **where
the paint is**. `build::PaintAt { node, target, index }` is `Copy + Eq` and small, a frame's background
answering to **fill 0**, the same stand-in `fills_seen_as` already makes of it. `census` carries the
**first** place each entry was met (deliberately not updated on later hits: first is what is stable to
name). `build::paint_at` reads the brush there and `build::repaint` changes every use of a whole brush.
**`repaint` is not a generalisation of `recolor`**: that one matches the exact RGBA *bytes* the colour
census keys by, this matches brushes with `==`, and folding them together would make one kind of row
disagree with its own edit. `slot_transaction` reads `from` back from the **committed** place before
repainting — mid-drag the preview already holds the new gradient, so a `from` read through the preview
would be the brush the drag is replacing *with*.

**The general lesson is that a location key is the *better* key, not merely the one that fits.** A value
key names something the document stops having the instant the edit commits, which is the whole reason
`GroupColor` needs `retarget_group_color` — D53's machinery, written for the trap where the picker found
nothing to edit and shut in the user's hand. A place still holds the paint afterwards, so
`GroupGradient` needs **no retargeting at all**.
`a_gradient_is_keyed_by_where_it_was_found_and_the_key_survives_the_edit` is the pin, and its fixture is
the point: the ramp sits at **fill index 1** of one layer and on a **stroke** of another, so a location
that assumed the obvious place would miss both. *If the solid rows are ever revisited, that is the
direction — and the retargeting is what it would buy back.*

`RowCtx::slot` briefly became `Option<PaintSlot>` for the uneditable version and is a plain `PaintSlot`
again. §9.4 has the rest of the row.

**D136 — Present mode hid the rulers and left the guides drawn over the artwork. *Resolved; the fix is
read rather than tested, and that is stated here rather than papered over.*** `rulers_on()` gated the
**bars**, and the loop over `doc.guides()` below it was gated by nothing at all — against present mode's
own promise to hide "every piece of chrome at once" (§9.4), a guide being chrome by `rulers.rs`'s own
definition since it never enters the scene.

Fixed as **one more predicate rather than a second test beside the bars'**: `guides_on()` is
`show_guides && !present`, and `guides_pickable()` is that plus `!lock_guides` so the lock needs only
`guide_at`'s single early return — still the only place it is asked, though the measure overlay now goes
*round* it on purpose (D202). `guide_lines()` returns an empty `GuideLines` when the guides are off for
the same reason the hit test does — the paint and the pick must mean the same thing (D35's class of
bug), and a shape jumping to an invisible line reads as a bug rather than a snap. Both predicates fold
present mode in, so leaving it restores whatever the user had.

**What is honest to say about the evidence: `guides_on`, `guides_pickable` and the gating of the guide
loop rest on reading rather than on a test.** `OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly — D35's constraint,
the same seam `canvas::autopan` and `resize_tx` sit behind. The predicates are trivial (`a && !b`) and
single-sourced, which is most of why this is acceptable, but nothing pins the loop. Everything that
*could* go behind a free function is tested — `upright`, `guide_ink`, `snap_across_axis`,
`extension_ends`, `in_view`, `GuideLine::distance_to` and `chip_along`, core's `guide_span`, and
`Selection::clear_guides`, whose `clearing_guides_leaves_a_layer_selection_alone` holds the layer
selection *and* the key layer through a lock. *Anything further added to the guide chrome should go the
same way: the arithmetic into a free function, the wiring read.*

**D137 — A user-draggable ruler origin is a non-goal. *Intentional.*** Illustrator and Photoshop both let
you drag 0,0 out of the corner box and double-click it to reset, so people will look for it and its
absence will be read as a gap. It is not: `ruler_origin`'s own doc already contains the argument that
rules it out, and only the conclusion was unwritten. The inspector shows X/Y in **world** space by
decision (D5, "world in, local out"), so an origin the user could move would put the ruler and the panel
in disagreement about where the same shape is — which is precisely why re-origining on a *shape inside* a
frame was declined in D36. Re-origining on a lone selected **frame** survives because there is no clash
there: 0-to-width is the `W` the inspector is already showing.

So the reason is not "it is work we have not done" but "the two readouts would contradict each other", and
the way in is the same as D36's: *adopting it means changing the inspector's coordinate space first, not
just the ruler's.* Carried in the todo as "worth recording in §15 rather than leaving implicit" until
2026-08-03, and struck from there when this was written — a decided non-goal is exactly what belongs here
and not in that file.

**One thing here reads as a contradiction and is not, so the line is worth drawing.** §9.3 records a
single exception to the world-space rule: a frame-scoped guide's position field shows its offset from its
frame. This entry rules out a movable **lattice**, which is the space *every* subject is measured against,
compared with the panel's number for the *same* subject — a node's position, given twice, differing by an
offset the user set and can then forget, with neither number the authority. The guide field changes
neither of those: the subject is not a node, the offset is the value the model stores (§5.5) and the
ruler's own readout of it, the **chip**, quotes exactly the field's number — so there is no second number
for one thing. And for a guide in a rotated frame world is not a rival choice, it does not exist, which is
a rule failing to apply rather than an exception carved for convenience. *If a movable origin is ever
argued for again, the test is the one above and not this precedent: does it create two numbers for one
subject's position?*

**D138 — A guide's pixel-grid parity was measured in points, and both obvious repairs were worse.
*Resolved.*** `rulers::snap_across_axis` puts a guide's coordinate on the device grid, centring an **odd**
device width on a pixel centre and an even one on a pixel edge. Getting the parity wrong turns a 1px line
into a 2px grey smear, which at 100% zoom is the entire appearance of a guide. A throwaway probe over
100/125/150/175% `pixels_per_point` overturned two plausible answers — the class of bug §15 already
collects (D9, D32, D44, D67).

The original test was `width as i32 % 2` — the **point** width, i.e. the assumption that one point is one
device pixel. At 150% and 175% a 2pt line is 3 and 3.5 device pixels (*odd*) and was being edge-centred:
3 device pixels of ink spread over 4 as `[0.5, 1, 1, 0.5]` instead of landing on 3 as `[1, 1, 1]`.

`round` was the obvious repair and is **worse than either**: it rounds 1.5 up to 2, calls a 1pt line
even, edge-centres it, and leaves the *resting* guide with no fully covered pixel at all — `[0.75,
0.75]`. A fractional device width cannot put both edges on the grid, so what there is to preserve is the
**core**, and `floor(width × ppp)` keeps one: 1.5 floors to 1, odd, pixel-centred, `[0.25, 1, 0.25]`.
`the_two_guide_weights_keep_a_solid_core_at_every_scale` pins the property at five scales and asserts
the selected weight covers *more* solid pixels than the resting one — the failure being a "fix" that
rounds back to a no-op at 150%, i.e. on the user's actual machine. The assertion is about the core
rather than crispness on purpose: demanding both edges on the grid is demanding what 125% and 175%
cannot give. `flooring_the_device_width_is_what_keeps_the_resting_guide_solid` asserts the two rejected
rules still fail. *Do not "simplify" the floor to a cast or a round; each has already been tried and is
a different regression.*

**D139 — A selected guide takes the selection blue, and that silently killed the discard fade.
*Resolved; the earlier decision is deliberately reversed.*** `draw_guide` used to argue the opposite,
and it was a real decision: a selected guide was drawn twice as thick and *not* recoloured, because a
per-guide colour is the one thing about a guide the user authors. What changed is the reading — a
selected guide is canvas chrome and has to make the same statement as the box round a layer, so it takes
`color::SELECT` (D13). Three states, and only the selected one moves the ink: resting 1px in the guide's
colour, hover the same plus the chip and dotted extension, selected 2px blue plus the chip. Intended,
and written here so it is not later filed as a bug.

**The reversal then broke something a hundred lines away, which is the part worth keeping.** The guide
in flight is drawn *as selected*, so once selection meant "another colour" rather than "the same colour,
thicker", `draw_guide` resolved the ink to `color::SELECT` and threw away the faded colour the caller
had prepared. A guide held over its own ruler looked identical to one held over the canvas, and the only
signal that letting go would **delete** it was gone. Fixed by resolving the ink in one place —
`rulers::guide_ink`, with the fade applied **after** the state's colour choice.
`a_discarding_guide_is_faded_even_though_it_is_drawn_as_selected` is the pin, and
`a_selected_guide_takes_the_selection_blue_over_its_own_colour` the other half. The drawn `Discard`
cursor is a second, independent signal for the same moment; both were later narrowed from `discarding`
to `GuideDrag::announces_discard()` (D140). *The general shape: a state that replaces a value silently
discards everything computed from the value it replaced — so compose the two in one function and pin the
composition, rather than trusting two call sites to stay in order.*

**D140 — A guide pulled out of the ruler announced its own deletion from the press. *Resolved.***
`discarding` is a pure geometric test — is the pointer over this guide's own ruler — and a new guide is
dragged *out of* a bar, so it was true from the moment the button went down.

**The distinction the fix records is that *not yet placed* and *about to be deleted* are different
states, and only the second is worth a cursor.** `GuideDrag::left_ruler` latches once the pointer is off
**both** bars rather than off the guide's own one: the other bar and the corner square (which `ruler_at`
gives to the left ruler) still count as being on the rulers. `announces_discard()` is `discarding &&
left_ruler`, one conjunction in one place so the fade and the cursor cannot disagree. `discarding`
itself is untouched and still drives the commit. An existing guide is grabbed on the canvas —
`guide_at` never answers over a bar — so it announces immediately, which is right.
`a_new_guide_does_not_announce_a_discard_until_it_has_left_the_ruler` walks the three frames.

**One consequence looks like an omission and is not: an Alt-copy released over the ruler *does* still
announce.** The announcement is always about **the line in flight**, and for a copy that line is the
copy. `an_alt_copy_over_the_ruler_still_announces_the_discard` exists so it cannot be "fixed" by
suppressing it. *Do not fold `announces_discard()` back into `discarding` — they are two questions, and
the geometric one is the one the commit needs.*

**D141 — The guide colour picker's *press* did nothing, and the symptom named the wrong culprit.
*Resolved.*** Reported as the guide's picker being "an older version". **There is only one picker and it
never diverged**, which is worth stating plainly: two components is the reasonable inference from that
symptom, and it would have sent the next reader looking for a second file that does not exist.

The cause is D129's press preview meeting the one piece of document state the renderer cannot carry.
`preview_slot` previewed *only* through `session.set_preview` — i.e. `RenderOverrides` — and a guide is
egui chrome rather than scene content, so the `SetGuideColor` was absorbed as a no-op (§6.2).
`edit_valve` has always forked to `preview_guide` for exactly that reason, so the **drag** worked and
only the press was dead. `preview_slot` calls `preview_guide` too now.

**The general shape is the one D129 and D109 share: a second path added for a state the first path
cannot express, with only one of the two entry points taught about it.** *Every entry point that calls
`set_preview` owes `preview_guide` next to it. There are two today, and a third would owe it as well.*

**D142 — The multi-guide position field flickered between the value and `Mixed` and committed nothing on
release. *Resolved; and the absolute reading is intentional.*** Two independent causes, both textbook.

**`guide_preview` was one `Option<Guide>` and `preview_guide` assigned to it per operation**, so a
transaction touching two guides previewed only whichever came last. The other went on reading its
committed position, the pair disagreed, and the field reports `Mixed` exactly when they disagree. It is
`guide_previews: Vec<Guide>` now, built on the pending entry so several ops in one transaction compose.

**And the field had no held drag target, which is D51 verbatim.** The layout runs against the committed
document every frame, so a field knowing only this frame's step commits the last step and loses the rest
— and on the release frame the pointer has not moved, so that step is zero and the gesture commits
nothing. `OndinApp::guide_position_drag` holds it, keyed by **axis** because a mixed-axis selection lays
two fields side by side.

**The decision inside the repair: the guide position field is *absolute*.** A drag sets every guide on
that axis to the value shown, exactly as typing does, so a drag over a disagreeing pair *ends* the
disagreement. That is the **opposite** of `multi_number`'s relative nudge for layers, and the difference
is deliberate: a layer's X is one property of a spatial arrangement worth preserving, whereas a guide's
position is the whole of the guide. The relative reading is the **arrow keys**' (`nudge_guides`), so
both are reachable and neither control has two meanings. *If the two fields are ever unified, this is
the difference that has to survive it.*

Small and the kind of thing that bites: the cancel path uses `continue`, not `multi_number`'s `return`,
because this loop lays out *both* axes and returning would skip the second field for that frame.

**D143 — The icon catalogue's atlas test could not fail, and covered a quarter of the icons.
*Resolved.*** `every_named_icon_has_a_glyph_behind_it` laid each named glyph out, read its coverage out
of the font atlas and asserted `ink > 8`, on the stated premise that a wrong Phosphor codepoint "lays
out perfectly and comes back blank". **The premise is false on this stack**: egui falls back and lays out
a `.notdef` box, and a 16pt box is far more than eight texels. Demonstrated by breaking one constant
twice — `WAVE_SINE` at `\u{ea9b}` (a *different* real icon) passed, and at `\u{efff}` (undefined
anywhere) passed as well.

**Its coverage was the second defect and an independent one.** The list of names lived inside the test,
hand-written, and had reached **28 of 117** — among them not one of the typography glyphs, the newest
and least verified. The test's own comment had predicted this and was not heeded, which is what a second
copy of a catalogue always earns.

- **`icon::ALL` lists every constant, beside the constants**, and the test reads it.
- **`the_catalogue_lists_every_icon_it_declares` counts `pub const` in the module** — `include_str!` on
  its own source, bounded by `pub mod icon {` — and compares with `ALL.len()`. Rust cannot reflect over
  consts, so the count cannot be derived; what it can be is one list with a guard. ⚠️ **A count is
  narrower than the rule in the bullet above it, and it was replaced at §15 D551** — see the paragraph
  after the flips.
- **The atlas test fingerprints the fallback.** It rasterizes a known-undefined codepoint once and
  asserts no icon's coverage equals it, keeping `ink > 8` as a cheap first check, and asserts the
  sentinel itself draws *something*, so an egui that renders nothing for a missing glyph reports "this
  test needs a new sentinel" instead of going inert again.

Both guards were confirmed by breaking them: an undefined codepoint now fails with "came back as the
*missing-glyph box*, not as an icon", and dropping one entry from `ALL` fails with "the module declares
117 icons and ALL lists 116". **All 117 codepoints are correct**, typography included.

⚠️ **The second of those two flips proved nothing, and the membership rule stated above went
unenforced from here until §15 D551, which corrects both.** A count cannot see a
**count-preserving** corruption: one entry in `ALL` replaced by a duplicate of another leaves the
length unchanged, all four tests in the module green, and one constant covered by nothing.
**Dropping** an entry changes the count, so this entry's own flip exercised precisely the case the
count answered — `CLAUDE.md`'s second vacuity shape, *"it asserted a consequence the wrong version
also produces"*, in this codebase's flagship anti-drift test. D551 replaces the flip with four,
parses the constants out of the module's source, and asserts the two name **sets** and the
name-to-glyph **pairing**; the rule in the first bullet is unchanged and is now the thing the test
actually checks. *A flip has to break the rule the test names, not the assertion the test happens to
make.*

**What this still does not prove, stated so it is not over-claimed.** It shows every name maps to a real
Phosphor glyph, not to the *intended* one: a transposed digit landing on another valid glyph passes.
Identifying a glyph by its picture is the by-eye atlas dump, and there is no substitute. **The
typography set has since been read that way, and all of it is right** — all 29 glyphs dumped as ASCII
art at 28pt, `TEXT_INDENT`/`TEXT_OUTDENT` not swapped, `ARROW_UP` pointing up (which is what lets it
carry the decoration offset's sign, D151). This says nothing about the other 88 icons.

*The general shape, twice over: a test whose coverage is a second copy of the thing it tests will drift
behind it; and a threshold has to be checked against the failure it claims to catch, never against the
success it happens to observe.*

**D144 — Frames stroke, over their contents and outside their own clip. *Resolved — D68's held-open
widening is taken.*** D68 excluded `Artboard` from `stroke_sides_apply` because the scene walk painted a
frame's background and *returned*. Its verdict was *build it*. Built.

**Two placements, and both are the feature.** `scene::paint_node` paints a frame's strokes **after** its
children and **outside** its clip layer. Over the contents, because that is where a border belongs —
under them it is covered by the very layers it encloses. Outside the clip, because a frame's clip is its
own box: a centred stroke drawn inside it loses its outer half and an outside stroke is erased outright.

**The opacity moves to an outer group when a frame has both.** Contents in the clip layer and the border
beside it are two composited groups, so a translucent border would blend against its own contents rather
than with them. One extra layer, paid only by a frame with a stroke *and* an opacity, which
`a_translucent_frame_with_a_border_composites_as_one_group` asserts in both directions.

**`takes_stroke` is a second predicate, not a wider `takes_paint`.** A frame is the one kind where the
two differ: its fill is `NodeKind::Artboard::background` — one brush, its own field, no visibility flag
— and its stroke is an ordinary stroke list. Widening `takes_paint` would have given a frame a Fill
panel beside its Background and let a `SetFills` write a list nothing paints.
`a_frame_takes_a_stroke_where_its_fill_is_its_background` pins both directions, and the inspector draws
Background *above* Stroke because Background is the fill and the panel order is the paint order.

**`geometry::local_path` answers for `Artboard`, and three gates follow from that alone.** A frame's
outline is square-cornered, out of the same `Rect::to_path` a square-cornered rect takes, so the two
cannot drift. Once it is there, `stroke_align_applies` measures it closed, `stroke_join_applies` sees
four corners, `stroke_sides_apply` widens, and `side_path` needs one arm. Two duplicate constructions of
that rect were deleted: the walk's clip path and `boolean::operand_of`'s frame arm. The one place this
changed behaviour and should not have is `canvas::stroke_outlines`, where a frame is still traced by its
selection quad — the quad and the outline being the same rectangle, and routing through `local_path`
would be one mark drawn two ways.

**The SVG writer mirrors the placement, and only when it has to.** A frame with both a clip and a stroke
becomes two `<g>`s — outer with the transform and opacity, inner with only the `clip-path` — and the
border's `<rect>` sits between. Gated on both being present, so no document that never put a stroke on a
frame changes by a byte. `a_frames_border_is_written_outside_the_group_that_clips_it` asserts the
ordering by byte offset, the only way to say "after the clip group closes" about a string.

**One divergence next door was found and closed with it.** The walk draws a text node with no ink at all
in black; this writer emitted `fill="none"`, so an unpainted text node was in the file, in the viewBox
and invisible. The condition is what D145 changed.

**D145 — Type strokes, which is what makes outlined type expressible. *Resolved.*** The model could
always put a stroke on a text node and neither the walk nor the writer drew it. §5.3's
`StrokeAlign::Outside` on text — the outlined-type case the two-stack paint order exists for — was ink
the document could describe and nothing painted.

**The mechanism is a path, not a glyph-stroking backend call.** `ondin_core::text::outline(&TextLayout)`
returns the filled outline of the node's glyphs in text-local space, and `scene::paint_strokes` takes it
as the shape. Both backends *can* stroke glyphs and neither is used, because a centred glyph stroke is
the only thing they buy: alignment needs a clip built from the glyph outlines, and once the outlines
exist the whole existing construction — doubled width, complement clip, dash resolution, D131's
wide-stroke fill — applies verbatim. `ScenePainter` is unchanged, and canvas and export clip against the
same path by construction.

**Outlining is not shaping.** The glyph ids and positions come from the cached `TextLayout`, so §5.9 is
untouched. It is built at the render boundary and **gated on there being a visible stroke**.

**The y-flip is the trap and it is stated in the code.** Font outlines are y-up, text-local space is
y-down, so each point is `(g.x + x, g.y − y)`. Backwards, every glyph reflects about its *own* baseline —
the letters stay in reading order, so it reads as a font bug rather than a sign error.
`a_text_outline_sits_above_its_baseline_and_closes` is aimed at exactly that: "Inter" has no descender,
so its ink must sit above the baseline bar the **optical overshoot** of its round letters, 0.47 units at
40pt (1.2% of the em, against a 2% allowance). Flipped, the lowest ink lands at 67 against a baseline at
38.

**Every contour comes back closed**, forced if the face did not say so — the invariant
`stroke_align_applies` leans on when it answers yes for `Text` without measuring.
`stroke_join_applies` widens too; `stroke_sides_apply` does not, five letters having no top edge between
them.

**The black fallback is for a text node with no ink at all, not for one with no fill.** An unpainted
text node still draws in black, but outlined type *is* a stroke and no fill, and the old test would have
filled every hollow letter solid black. `outlined_type_gets_no_black_stand_in_fill` pins all three
cases. The decoration bands fall back to black for the same reason, and are deliberately **not** stroked
with the glyphs, which would put a second, differently-shaped rule under every one.

In the SVG the stroke rides the `<text>` element, so the output stays re-shapeable, and an aligned one
sits inside a `clipPath` built from the glyph outlines.
`text_carries_its_stroke_and_an_outside_one_gets_a_glyph_clip` checks the clip is curves and not the
node's box.

**D146 — One alignment clip per *run* of same-aligned strokes, and the stroke costs are now measured.
*Resolved.*** `roadmap.md` carried two perf bullets and said "nothing measured yet" on both. Each
aligned stroke pushed its own clip layer and rebuilt its own complement path, per stroke per frame.

**A clip is a geometric mask, so applying the same one twice is applying it once.** `paint_strokes`
pushes one layer per maximal run of consecutive strokes that agree about alignment. **Runs rather than a
sort**, because the list order *is* the z-order (§5.3): grouping across a differently aligned stroke
would move paint, and `a_differently_aligned_stroke_breaks_the_run_rather_than_being_reordered` asserts
the break. The run's ring is padded for the widest reach in it, sound because the ring only has to
*enclose* the ink — too large clips nothing, too small takes rectangular bites out of a wide stroke.

**Measured, on 400 rounded rects in one frame at 1600×1200, scene build only, release.** Left column
with the sharing, right without:

| | shared | per stroke |
|---|---|---|
| 1 centred stroke | 0.39 ms | 0.43 ms |
| 1 outside stroke | 0.55 ms | 0.55 ms |
| **2 outside strokes** | **0.68 ms** | **0.92 ms** |
| **4 outside strokes** | **0.90 ms** | **1.36 ms** |
| 2 inside strokes | 0.54 ms | 0.58 ms |
| 1 `Custom` outside stroke, 4 sides | 0.99 ms | 1.00 ms |

The sharing removes the part that scaled with the stroke count — a third off four outside strokes — and
the answer to the bullets is that **the clip push/pop was never the dominant cost**. The per-side row is
the most expensive shape measured and the sharing does not touch it (one stroke is one run either way):
its extra ~0.45 ms is four `side_path` builds and four stroke calls per shape, about 1.2 µs a shape.
None of this is near a frame budget. *No further work; the numbers are the record.*

**The one cost worth watching is the new one.** Text outlines run about **1 µs a glyph**: 100 text nodes
of "Hamburgefonstiv" at 24pt build in 0.017 ms with fills alone and **1.43 ms** with an outside stroke.
The gate is doing very heavy lifting; realistic counts are single-digit nodes at ~0.014 ms each. *If it
ever bites, cache the outline in `Resolved` beside the layout; do not remove the gate.*

**D147 — A fitted dash pattern is fitted per subpath. *Resolved — D69's approximation is closed.***
A fit *scale* is a property of one closed run, and one `dashes` array cannot say two things, so two
subpaths of different lengths shared a scale and neither landed on its own corners.

`geometry::dash_fit_pieces` splits the path when — and only when — there is a fit to disagree about: a
fitted, non-empty pattern on a path with more than one subpath. It hands back one piece per subpath with
that subpath's own pattern, and `None` otherwise, so a solid stroke, an unfitted one and every
single-subpath shape clone no path and measure no perimeter twice. The SVG writer emits one `<path>` per
piece, an element carrying one pattern — which is also why its `plain` fast path now demands
`dash_fit_pieces(..).is_none()`.

`a_fitted_dash_is_fitted_to_each_subpath_it_is_laid_along` is the assertion the old behaviour fails: two
rings of perimeter 100 and 40 against a period of 7 must come back as *two different* patterns fitting
14 and 6 times, where the whole-path answer is one pattern fitting 20 times into 140. Confirmed by
putting the old measurement back. `geometry::subpaths` is now shared rather than spelled per consumer.

**D148 — A resize gesture can now produce auto-height, and a group scale stopped collapsing one to a
1px sliver. *Resolved.*** Every resize of a text layer wrote `TextSizing::Fixed`, so auto-height was
unreachable by dragging.

The rule that replaced it belongs to the *handle*, not to the gesture. A side handle owns one axis and
says nothing about `y` — exactly what `Handle::anchored` already returns — so it leaves the height as it
found it, while a corner or a top/bottom handle authors the height. Read with
`TextSizing::height_is_authored`: `Auto` → `AutoHeight` on a side drag, `AutoHeight` → itself, `Fixed` →
`Fixed`.

The same edit closed a bug of the same shape one axis over. `resizable_size` reports `Size::ZERO` for
`Auto` and `(w, 0)` for `AutoHeight`; `scale_geometry` guarded only against the first, so an auto-height
child of a scaled group walked into the `max(1.0)` floor and came out `Fixed(w × 2, 1)` — a wrapping
paragraph turned into a 1px sliver by a gesture that only widened its group. The guard is now
`scaled_text_sizing`. Confirmed by flipping it back: the probe reports `Fixed(120.0W×1.0H)`.

The other half — an `Auto` layer's handles drawn on its *measured* box while `resizable_size` reports a
zero one — is fixed in **D158**.

**D149 — The variant dropdown read one face's `fvar`, so italic Inter had no control anywhere in the
app. *Resolved.*** `family_named_instances` read `family`'s **default** face. A variable family very
often ships as two files, upright and italic, and the italic file's `fvar` is where its italic cuts are
named. That is worse than it sounds: the panel replaces its bold/italic button pair with the variant
list as soon as the list has two entries, so for the one family the app always has there was **no**
italic control on any tab.

`with_family_fonts` walks every face, default first; `family_named_instances` unions their instances,
deduplicated by name and slope. Neither Inter face carries an `ital` axis, so nothing in the coordinates
could tell the two apart — which is why `NamedInstance` now carries an `italic` read from fontique's
`FontInfo::style` (i.e. `OS/2`), and `family_variants` ORs it with the `ital` and `slnt` terms.
`inters_variant_list_offers_both_slopes` pins it and reports the symptom on failure.

`family_axes` and `family_features` **deliberately still read the default face.** The right answer for
them is the face that will actually shape the run; unioning would draw an axis row, or offer a feature
switch, that the shaping face does not have. Both Inter faces carry the same `opsz`/`wght`, so nothing
observable turns on it today; if a family turns up whose faces disagree, thread the style through rather
than widening the union.

**D150 — A decoration inheriting a gradient text fill showed a flat black chip. *Resolved.***
`scene.rs` gives an uncoloured decoration `inks.first()`, the whole brush, so the canvas draws that
underline with the node's gradient. `TypeSubject::text_color` flattened any non-solid fill to
`Color::BLACK`.

`TypeSubject` now carries `text_paint: Option<Brush>` — the first *visible* fill, matching the
renderer's choice — and the two readouts derive from it. `text_ramp` gives the swatch the gradient's
stops through `picker::ramp`; `text_color` is the collapse the controls that need one colour ask for,
and is now the **first stop** rather than black. Both halves match something that already existed: the
first stop is `write_char_slot`'s stated collapse for this slot, so the hex the row shows is the colour
that adopting the gradient produces, and black survives only for a node with no visible fill.
`a_gradient_text_fill_is_inherited_as_a_ramp_not_as_black` covers all three cases.

**D151 — The two sign traps in the Character tab, hinted in the two different places they belong.
*Resolved.*** `fvar` measures slant *counter-clockwise*, so the right-leaning oblique everybody means by
"oblique 10°" is `slnt −10`; a decoration's offset is positive-*up*, so pushing an underline clear of
the descenders means typing a negative number.

They are hinted differently on purpose, being different kinds of fact. `slnt` is a fact about the
**format**, applying to exactly one of the axes the rows are generated from, so a permanent mark would
be noise on every other axis; it goes in the hover the row already carries, through `axis_sign_hint`,
which returns `None` for everything else. The offset is a fact about **this field**, so it is on the
field: `Prefix::Icon(ARROW_UP)` in place of the symmetric `ARROWS_VERTICAL` — one glyph that points the
way the positive numbers go, which also takes the prefix out of a collision with line height two fields
away. The tooltip carries the consequence the picture cannot.

*The general shape: a hint about the file format belongs on hover, a hint about a control belongs in the
control's own ink — and the cheapest at-a-glance sign hint a numeric field can have is a prefix that
points.*

**D152 — The typography popup's spacing is one axis compressed and one axis matched, not one number
split in two. *Deviation from the mock, deliberate — recorded because it came back as a question.***
`design/Editor.dc.html` does not use one gap. It draws the **popup** at 6 across and 5 down and the
**Type card** the popup hangs from at 7 across and 9 down. The app takes 5 down (`LABEL_GAP`, covering
both of the vertical jobs the mock's sections cover with it — label-to-controls and control-to-control)
and 7 across (`COL_GAP`, which is `GAP`, the card's).

So the popup keeps the mock's whole **vertical** compression — 5 against the card's 9, the same bargain
`CELL`'s 26 makes against `ROW_H`'s 28, and for the same reason: a card of three rows against a popup of
seven sections. And it matches the card exactly **across**, which is the axis on which the two are read
side by side at the same width, where a one-point difference is not a distinction but a wobble. The
mock's 6 was never a decision — the card behind it in the same file is 7. `SECTION_GAP` is the third
number and the only one raised outright: 15, not the mock's 10, because at 10 against an in-section 5 the
2:1 ratio was not enough to group by and the card read as one long list (reported as "a bit too tight",
with 5 more asked for by name).

*Two gaps that differ by axis are a rule, not a drift. The thing to check when one of them looks wrong
is whether the source ever had a single number to disagree with — this one never did, and the question
was asked twice on the assumption that it had.*

**The four numbers that were still a first draft are settled as of 2026-08-04**, reviewed on screen and
accepted: `LIST_MAX_H` (104, the design's own), `FEATURE_ROW_H` (22), the 9pt gap between axis rows, and
`Bounds`. Three of those are visual and were confirmed by eye; **`Bounds` is the odd one out and worth
naming as such** — it caps what a spacing or line-height field can be scrubbed or typed to (−50%…200%
tracking, 0…1000% line height), which is a limit you only meet by driving a field to its end, so what
stands behind it is judgement about where a number stops describing type rather than use. Not provisional
any more either way; a value that turns out to be wrong is now a change with a reason, not a draft being
finished. The six geometry tests stay as they were — they pin what the arithmetic may not break, which is
a different question from whether the numbers are the right ones.

**D167 — The text session's input path never had the guards the normal one has. *Resolved.*** Two
defects with one shape behind them: `Mode::TextInsert` routes to `canvas::text_mode_input`, a **second**
input path, so everything `normal_mode_input` and `input::resolve` do for the canvas either had to be
built there again or was simply absent — and nothing in the compiler asks for any of it.

**The middle button panned nothing and selected text instead.** Panning lives entirely in
`normal_mode_input`, so while a session was live there was no pan at all — in the mode you are *most*
likely to need to scroll in. Worse, `Response::drag_started`/`dragged` are button-agnostic, so the middle
button was arming `Drag::TextSelect`. The middle button now arms `Drag::Pan` and only the **primary**
button starts a selection, both through `drag_started_by`. **Space is deliberately not a pan modifier
here**: in a text session Space is a character, so the middle button is the one of the three that cannot
