mean anything else. The two-line camera pan is now `canvas::pan_by_drag`, called from both paths, so the
two modes cannot drift into panning at different speeds.

**Typing a value into the Type panel also typed it into the document.** `text_mode_input` reads raw
events rather than going through `input::resolve`, so it never had that function's opening guard: a size
typed into the panel while a session was live went to the field *and* inserted those digits at the
caret. The events are dropped now when `ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()` — **deliberately the
over-approximating predicate**, "anything is focused", where `text_edit_focused` is the narrow one, which
is the same trade `input::resolve` already makes (§9.3; D123 records what that guard costs). It is the
right way round: failing to type is one click from recovery, where typing into the document is a
corruption the user has to notice before they can undo it.

*The rule: a second input path owes every guard the first one has, and every one of them goes missing
silently. Read `normal_mode_input` and `input::resolve` alongside `text_mode_input` before adding to
either.*

**D168 — Right-click cancel asked egui a question egui had already forgotten, so a fast click did
nothing at all. *Resolved.*** Reported as: click-drag a value, right-click to reset, and it *almost
always* works — with no pattern in where the click landed or how far the drag had gone.

`cancel_gesture`'s gate for a field scrub was `ctx.dragged_id().is_some()`, and **that is the wrong
question to ask on the one frame it is asked.** egui clears `dragged` on the release of *any* button —
`interaction.rs`'s `PointerEvent::Released` arm takes `button: _` — and the handler runs on
`input.pointer.button_pressed(Secondary)`. So a right-click whose press and release fall in the **same
rendered frame** reads a snapshot that has already been cleared. At 60fps that is any click under ~16ms,
which is exactly "random".

**Confirmed by probe rather than by reading, and the probe is now the keeper test** —
`a_right_click_short_enough_to_fit_one_frame_takes_the_drag_away`. It drives a headless `Context` through
`RawInput` (hover, primary down, three moves to reach a *decided* drag, then the secondary events) and
asserts the fixture reached a real drag first, so it cannot pass by never having dragged at all.

The gate asks two further questions now, both ours and neither of which blinks:
`EditorSession::has_gesture_preview()`, since the valve installs one on every frame of a scrub, and
`session_scrub.is_some()`, armed for the one kind of scrub that previews through the *session* instead.
Both are absent when nothing is in flight, which keeps the whole thing a strict no-op and leaves the
right-click that removes a gradient stop alone.

**The second exists because a session-scoped scrub has no preview to drop.** A field scrubbed while a
live session owns the range writes into the **editor** (§9.2, §9.3), so the cancel had nothing to unwind
— the same right-click reported as "the value resets on the text, but on the field it stays".
`OndinApp::session_scrub` snapshots both span lists on `drag_started`, armed from `char_valve` **and**
`valve_paragraph` so the Character tab's identical hole closed with the Paragraph tab's, and
`cancel_gesture` winds them back. It is cleared when no pointer is down rather than on `drag_stopped`,
the session-scoped valves being reached only on a frame the field actually changed.

**The gate itself rests on reading**, `OndinApp` not being constructible headlessly (D35). *Do not
simplify the gate back to `dragged_id` alone. It is the bug, and it comes back as an intermittent one —
which is the hardest kind to believe a report of.*

**D171 — Two cursors for two gestures, and the caret blinks. *Resolved — both reported from use after
D170, and both accepted on use afterwards.*** The two numbers with a feel to them — the **500ms**
half-cycle and the crosshair/I-beam split — were used and accepted, so they are settled here; the rate is
one constant (`CaretBlink::HALF`).

**The pointer.** `Tool::Text` showed an I-beam everywhere, right when a click could only plant a caret
and a half-truth the moment a drag drew a box. It now asks `text_layer_at` — the same question
`draw_hover_outline` asks, so the cursor and the outline cannot promise different things — and shows the
I-beam over a text layer a click would *enter*, the drawn crosshair everywhere else. **Not while a drag
is in flight**, so dragging a box across existing text does not flicker. The live-session branch still
wins over both.

**The caret.** It was drawn every frame and never blinked. Reported as "an affordance we're so used to
that it feels wrong", which is the right diagnosis: nothing was *incorrect*, and a static caret still
reads as a frozen application.

`preview::CaretBlink` is 500ms on, 500ms off — the middle of what platforms use, and not read from the
OS because neither winit nor egui exposes it. It lives in the app and **not on `TextEdit`**: the caret
model is about bytes and geometry, and a timestamp there would be a value the save format and both
exporters had to ignore.

**The phase restarts on activity, and activity is *observed* rather than announced.** A caret in its dark
half on the frame you clicked is exactly the failure this is fixing, so every mover and every edit owes a
restart — and `text_mode_input` has a dozen. Rather than a call at each, `phase` compares a `BlinkState`
and restarts when it changed. *A call site cannot forget to do something it does not do*, and the drag
case comes free. Asking is what notices the move, which is why `phase` takes `&mut self` and why the draw
site calls it *unconditionally*.

**Three things are in that state, each because comparing the obvious one alone misses a case.** The
selected range; the **content length**, so a forward `Delete` — which does not move the offset — still
counts; and **window focus**, in the same comparison rather than a branch of its own. An unfocused window
hides the caret, and *coming back is activity in exactly the sense a keystroke is*: with focus in a
branch, returning would show a caret resuming halfway through the phase it left.

**And the blink pays for the repaint it needs rather than one per frame.** `phase` returns a deadline
beside the answer, and `draw_canvas` schedules `request_repaint_after` instead of the unconditional
`request_repaint` a live session used to ask for every frame — so an idle session costs two frames a
second rather than sixty, and an unfocused one none at all.

Only the caret blinks; the selection highlight is drawn either way. Five tests pin the type, each
confirmed to fail against the plausible wrong version. **One only discriminated after being rewritten**:
the deadline test first asserted that "adding the deadline changes the answer", and a deadline of a whole
`HALF` passes that from anywhere inside the phase, since adding exactly half a cycle always flips it.
Sampling a hair *either side* is what pins it to the **next** flip rather than to *a* flip.

**D170 — The Text tool draws a box, and it is the one create tool that is also a click tool.
*Resolved.*** It planted `TextSizing::Auto` at a point and had no drag path, so the only way to a
fixed-width column was to make one, type into it, and set the width in the Box tab.

**`Tool::Text` joins `drags_a_box`, and the sizing mode is what the two gestures differ by.** A click
plants `Auto`; a drag commits `tools::create_text`, an empty node at the drawn box with
`TextSizing::Fixed`. Everything else on the create path was already general.

**The vertical extent is honoured rather than dropped for `AutoHeight`.** The user dragged a height, and
a gesture whose second axis silently does nothing is the "inert is indistinguishable from forgotten" trap
this document refuses for `indent_end` (D163). `TextOverflow::Visible` is the default, so text typed past
the box hangs out instead of clipping. **`AutoHeight` was offered as the alternative and declined**, the
report having said "fixed *width*". *Do not "correct" it on the strength of the report's wording.*

**Two edges, and both are the drag being a *text* drag rather than a shape drag.** The release opens the
editor instead of switching to Select. And a drag that finds no box plants a caret rather than abandoning
the gesture — a shape is right to abandon it, but for text that would leave the tool doing nothing at
all, *which is the reported complaint arriving from the other side.*

**The reason first given for that second arm was wrong, and measuring it is what caught it.** It was
written as a gap between two thresholds. There is no such gap: a sweep through `RawInput` puts egui's
drag threshold at **6 screen px** — 6.0 is still a click, 6.5 is a drag — while `MIN_CREATE_PX` is 3 on
the same scale, so every gesture egui calls a drag has already moved far enough to create, at any zoom.
What is actually reachable is a drag that goes out past 6px and comes **back** to within 3px of its
origin, and a caret is right for that because a gesture ending where it began is indistinguishable in
intent from a click. `egui_starts_a_drag_only_past_the_distance_a_create_needs` asserts the
*relationship* rather than the number, so raising `MIN_CREATE_PX` above egui's threshold fails the test
instead of quietly creating a gesture that does nothing.

**A thin drag is floored at one line box**, taken from a shaped layout rather than from `font_size`
because `line_height: None` means "the font decides" (D162). The width has no floor: a narrow column is a
real thing to want. The floor is a commit-time clamp, so the chrome outline of a deliberately-degenerate
drag is a couple of units shorter than what lands — accepted rather than special-cased into geometry five
other tools share.

**`open_text_session` is `begin_text`'s second half, split rather than copied.** A session is four fields
and `original` is the one a copy gets wrong: a node created empty must record an *empty* original, or
closing it reads as a change and commits a second undo step over the create. It takes the parts off the
**node** rather than off `self.fonts`, so the editor measures what was committed.

**Pinned where it can be, and read where it cannot.** `create_text` is a free function, so the drawn box,
the parent transform, the one-line floor and *that the text wraps to the box* are all tested.
`Tool::drags_a_box` is a `matches!` list, so its membership is pinned as a list. The **routing** is not
(D35), so "a press starts a create and the release opens a session" rests on reading `normal_mode_input`
against egui's rule that a press is reported as a click *or* a drag and never both.

**D169 — Lists are ink without bytes, and the route the plan named is unusable. *Resolved — stage 3 of
paragraph layout.*** `roadmap.md` asked for the marker to be a parley **inline box** with a hanging
measure, and to check that first. Checking it settled the design by ruling the route out.

**`InlineBoxKind::OutOfFlow` is honoured by parley's drawing and ignored by its caret.** Out-of-flow is
the only kind that reserves no space in the line, and only `Line::items()`, the *positioning* iterator,
tests the kind before advancing its offset. `Cluster::visual_offset`, `Cluster::from_point_impl` and
`Selection::geometry` each do `offset += inline_box.width` unconditionally. Measured with a throwaway
probe: a 30px out-of-flow box at byte 0 leaves the first glyph at x 0 and puts the caret at x **30** —
D165's failure shape mirrored, and it would have arrived as "the caret sits one marker to the right of
the text". `InFlow` is consistent across all four and is `list-style-position: inside`, where wrapped
lines align under the marker and every item's text starts at a different x.

**So the marker is neither in the content nor in parley.** `ParagraphStyle::marker` is a spannable
`Option<ListMarker>`; `None` is a value like any other, and a span carrying it is how one paragraph opts
out of a node-level marker. Keeping the marker out of `content` is what makes the whole feature cheap:
byte indices are the currency of the span lists, the caret, the hit test and the case transform, and ink
without bytes cannot be selected, typed into, or move a span. `ListMarker` is CSS's core
`list-style-type` and deliberately not a free string.

**The gutter was already built.** It is the paragraph's own `indent_start` (D163), which every line
honours — *that is the hanging measure the plan wanted* — and the marker is right-aligned on it, which
keeps `1.` and `10.` putting their text in one column. **There is no gap constant**: the right edge lands
on the start edge and the sidebearings are the gap. Turning a marker on writes a 24px default *only* when
the indent is still zero, where the marker would otherwise draw at a negative x.

**Numbering has no markup to read, so the model supplies the only thing it can**: a list is a run of
consecutive paragraphs asking for the **same** marker. A paragraph with no marker ends the run, and so
does one asking for a different marker, and each run counts from one. Unordered markers are counted too
and ignore the number, which keeps it one rule.

**Two consumers, one decision.** `ListMarkers::at` answers per paragraph and both passes ask it, the ink
taking two forms: a `GlyphRun` appended to the cached `TextLayout` for the canvas, and an `ExportLine` of
its own for SVG — a `<text>` rather than a `<tspan>`, since tspans flow and a marker sharing the line's
element would sit against the first word (D81). The render path needed **nothing** else,
`TextLayout::runs` being per-run already. `a_list_marker_exports_as_its_own_text_element` guards against
the second path drifting.

**Three things reading would not have settled.** The bundled Inter carries U+2022, U+25E6 and U+25AA —
checked before they were offered, and to the same advance, so switching between them moves no text —
while the tempting U+25FE and U+2219 come back as `.notdef`; *a marker set is a claim about the font, not
about CSS*. `trim_insets` was expected to want work and does not: it folds the *face metrics* of the
first and last line's runs, and a marker is set in the same face at the same size — a consequence of the
marker leaving parley, and the guess would have been right under the inline-box design.
`a_marker_shares_its_paragraphs_baseline_through_the_y_map` pins why spacing, trim and vertical alignment
each need no term, confirmed to fail against a marker placed at the raw layout baseline.

**And two tests that passed for the wrong reason first.** `numbering_restarts_…` asserted only the
*no-marker* boundary and passed against an implementation that never restarted on a **changed** marker,
a marker-less paragraph resetting the run through the other arm; it now states both. The SVG test
numbered all five items twice over — first because its span covered a byte *inside* a paragraph rather
than its first byte, then because it applied `SetText` before `SetParagraphStyle`, so a `Marker(None)`
span was normalized away against a default that was still `None`. *The op order `para_attrs_tx` uses is
load-bearing for anything that installs a span list* (D164).

**Nested lists were deferred here, and the deferral was itself a decision.** Nesting wants a level, and
the obvious place to read one from is `indent_start`. Rejected because `indent_start` is a `Length` a
user drags: nudging one item's indent by a hair would silently renumber the list. That is D172.

**The four decisions with a look to them were reviewed on a rendered export the same day and accepted**:
the marker right-aligned on the gutter, the gutter being `indent_start` with no gap constant, the marker
taking the item's own face and colour, and the eight-marker set. *Do not re-derive them from CSS; they
were looked at.*

**D172 — Nesting is a level of its own, and one function places both the text and the marker. *Resolved
— stage 4 of paragraph layout, and D169's deferral.*** `ParagraphStyle::level: u8` is the rejection of
reading a level from `indent_start`. `ParaAttr::Level` and `ParaAttrKind::Level` are **appended** to
their enums, because that order *is* the `(attribute, start)` sort a file is written in (§5.11, invariant
9), and the field is `skip_serializing_if`, so no existing document changes byte-for-byte.
`MAX_LIST_LEVEL` is 8, enforced in `ParagraphStyle::set` — the one door every edit comes through.

**The step is `indent_start`**, measured from the level-1 edge, the amount being the gutter the marker
already sits in; CSS's default stylesheet says the same with one number. A second length would be a
second number to keep in step for no gain. `ParagraphStyle::start_edge(font_size)` is `indent_start ×
(level + 1)`, with a `saturating_add(1)` so a hand-edited `u8::MAX` cannot wrap the multiplier to zero.
It also means the **scale tool leaves the level alone** — a level is a count of gutters and the gutter is
what scaled — pinned by `the_scale_tool_leaves_the_nesting_level_alone` at three gutters of 60 rather
than six of 30, and `a_levels_bound_is_enforced_where_it_is_written_and_survives_a_wild_file`.

**One function, because two readers have to agree.** `text::line_geometry` hands parley a `line_x` and
`ListMarkers::at` answers with the marker's right edge, and both call `start_edge`. Two copies of the
multiplication is how a marker ends up on a gutter its own text is not using — the class of bug D163 was
— and the flip proved it: with the multiply in `line_geometry` alone, the nested marker draws at x 48.7
while its own text sits at 30. *Do not inline it back into either caller.*

**A level on a paragraph with no marker still indents it**, which is how a continuation paragraph sits
under the item it belongs to. It does **not** keep that paragraph inside the list: a paragraph with no
marker still ends every open run, so a continuation between two items restarts the numbering after it. A
real limitation of a model with no container, stated in `ParagraphStyle::level`'s own doc rather than
fudged. *Revisit only with a container, which would be a format change and not a control.*

**The numbering rule generalises rather than changes**: consecutive paragraphs belong to one list only if
they ask for the same marker **at the same level**. `ListMarkers::ordinals` is a stack of counters, one
per open level — going back *out* truncates the deeper levels, so `1, (a, b), 2, (a, b)` numbers both
sublists from `a` while the outer run counts through. With every level 0 the behaviour is identical to
before, and `numbering_restarts_where_the_marker_changes_or_stops` passed untouched.

**Two details in that stack are load-bearing, and both were flipped.** It holds `Option<(ListMarker,
usize)>` and the `None` is the point: a level skipped on the way in has no count of its own and must not
lend one to a level-1 item arriving later — the tidier `resize(level + 1, Some((marker, 1)))` numbers the
*first* item of every sublist `2.`. And a marker-less paragraph clears the **whole** stack rather than
its own level and deeper; `truncate(1)` fails both the new test and the pre-existing level-0 one.

**Nesting does not rotate the marker glyph.** In HTML the marker is a default over markup that names none
of its own; here every paragraph stores the marker it asked for, so deriving one from the level would
draw something other than the value in the model. Recorded on `ListMarker`'s own doc.

**Neither paint path needed anything, and the export one is tested as one anyway.**
`a_nested_item_exports_on_its_own_gutter` asserts **positionally**: a run carries its own hard break, so
`<tspan>two\n</tspan>` puts a literal newline in the file and the element's own `x` is on the output line
above its text, which is why it cannot match on content.

**The panel is a `Level` field under the marker dropdown, drawn only where there is a list** — full
width, `Scrub::whole(0.05)` over `0..=MAX_LIST_LEVEL`, through `valve_paragraph` for D108's reason. A
**text** prefix rather than a glyph: Phosphor's nesting glyphs are trees and file hierarchies, which is
the layers panel's language. **The keyboard route was left to a keymap decision, and that reading of the
cost was wrong** (D173).

**The field shows mixed as a dash, and that is D130's rule broken once more.** `mixed_text` formats a
mixed value as `–` and is what the panel's numeric fields all go through, where D130 says the dash
belongs only to a control with no room for the word, and this field is 250pt wide. Inherited from the
call sites rather than introduced here. *Fix `mixed_text` itself, or record the Type panel's fields as
D130's third exception; fixing this one field alone would leave the card inconsistent with itself.*

**`level` is invisible to the MCP snapshot**, joining the run colour and the marker itself — parked with
MCP (§8) rather than open. Same emitter, same trip.

**D173 — `Tab` nests a list item, and it turned out not to be a keymap change. *Resolved — D172's one
declined decision, taken.*** D172 shipped nesting with no keyboard, on the reasoning that `Tab` was
spoken for. What that missed is that the two claimants are in different modes and cannot meet —
`input::resolve` resolves no **bare** key in `Mode::TextInsert` — and the user's own answer to the rest:
point editing is a different section and a different workflow. (It returned nothing *whatever* there
until D211 admitted the styling chords; `Tab` carries no modifier, so the argument is untouched and is
now the rule rather than a consequence of the mode being empty.)

**`TextEdit::step_list_level(delta: i32) -> bool` is per paragraph and relative, where `style_paragraph`
is one absolute value over the whole range**, and that difference *is* the feature. Select an item and
the sublist under it, press `Tab`, and they must become levels 1 and 2 — a uniform write flattens exactly
the structure the gesture builds. The flip proved it: `[0, 1, 1]` came out `[3, 3, 3]`. Each paragraph is
clamped **separately**, so a selection with one item at the floor still moves the rest, and the `bool` is
"did anything move", which lets the caller leave the undo stack alone on a no-op.

**Only paragraphs with a marker move**, a narrowing of D172's fourth decision rather than a contradiction
of it: `indent_start` is zero until something opens a gutter, so nesting a plain paragraph would usually
do nothing visible, and the panel's Level field is reachable only through an item.

**`paragraphs_touched` is `paragraph_bounds`' rule read in index space, and it has to be indices.** The
empty paragraph a trailing break leaves owns no bytes, so the only range a span can be set on for it is
the break byte *before* it — the same byte the paragraph above ends on. Two paragraphs sharing a byte
cannot be told apart by that byte. The write still goes through `paragraph_bounds(start..start)`, which
is what makes the reach-back happen: flipping it to `start..next_start` leaves the empty paragraph
unnestable, and **that is the paragraph a user is most likely to press `Tab` on**.
`the_paragraphs_touched_are_the_ones_paragraph_bounds_spans` sweeps all 120 selections of a fourteen-byte
string and asserts they agree, **except** for a caret in the empty tail, where it asserts the divergence
explicitly and that it is the only one. That case was found by the test failing, not by being written
for.

**The app wiring is two lines and one is interesting.** `text_mode_input` gets a `Key::Tab` arm gated
plain-or-`Shift`. The other is that **`<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui`'s `took_tab` now fires for a live
session too, and unconditionally** (the method name was `update` here until D698):
point editing claims `Tab` only when there is a path to step, but a session claims
it whether or not anything moved, because *nothing* still has to mean "not the focus ring" — otherwise
the **next keystroke of the session would be swallowed**, D123's reported failure in a second place. The
ordering that makes it work is D123's too: egui applies the ring move for the *following* pass.

**It is deliberately not an `Action`**, recorded at both ends because either read alone would look like
an omission. Six core tests plus the tripwire, and three flips against the plausible wrong versions. The
wiring is not tested and cannot be, but the egui behaviour the focus give-back rests on *is* pinned by
D123's own test — the same mechanism, so it needs no second.

**D109 — A valved edit was compared against its own preview, so the release never committed.
*Resolved.*** Reported as the controls becoming unresponsive after setting a decoration colour — "I can
slide a slider and it resets immediately to the value it had".

`char_attrs_tx` returned `Option<Transaction>`, `None` meaning "this changes nothing", and `char_valve`
read that as "nothing to do". But it compares the new style against **`subject`**, read through
`display_node` — which applies the render override. During a drag that override *is* the preview, so:

- frame N: the value moves, the new style differs from the committed one, `set_preview`;
- frame N+1: `subject` reports the previewed value, so the field starts from it and moves on again;
- the **release** frame: nothing moved, the new style equals the previewed one, `None` came back, and
  `edit_valve` was never called. No commit.

The edit lived only in the preview — which looks exactly like a working control until anything else
commits and clears it, at which point every "set" value snaps back at once.

- **`char_attrs_tx` always returns its transaction**, with the equality reported beside it. The two
  callers want different answers to the same comparison: `apply_char_attrs` is for clicks with no preview
  in play, where a no-op must not leave an undo step; `char_valve` must hand the release over regardless.
  It being an `Option` made one answer look like the only one.
- **`EditorSession::try_commit` clears the preview**, rather than each caller remembering to. A preview
  that survives its own drag is easy to arrange: `edit_valve` previews on `dragged()` and clears on
  `drag_stopped()`, and a widget that stops existing mid-drag never delivers the second. **A live text
  session's preview is the exception** and is marked as such (`set_session_preview`), standing for
  uncommitted content for the length of the session (§9.3). **That exemption is spelled once, as
  `EditorSession::clear_gesture_preview`**, whose second caller is `cancel_gesture` — which was calling
  plain `clear_preview` and so arrived at the same bug from the other direction, a right-click cancelling
  an inspector scrub dropping a session's uncommitted text (D168). Three arrivals of one rule: read
  D155's *a preview is not one thing* beside this, and add no third spelling.

*The rule this leaves: a control that previews must not decide whether to commit by comparing against
what it is showing.*

**D174 — That rule had a fourth arrival, in the *field* in front of the valve. *Resolved.*** The four
paragraph `Length` fields do not reach the valve directly: they go through `paragraph_length`, which
returns early unless `LengthEdit::next` is `Some` — and `length_field` filled that in only when the
number moved. So the guard D109 removed from the valve was still sitting one call up, on exactly the same
frame. The `Level` field beside them had it too.

`roadmap.md` carried this as a *reading* of egui 0.35 rather than a sighting, and the reading was right
in its mechanism and wrong about the cost of the fix. Both halves were measured by driving pointer events
through `length_field` with `RawInput`:

- **A four-step scrub scored `commits=false` on every frame.** The release frame comes back `next=None,
  drag_stopped=true`: `value_field` settles the number to whole units on every dragged frame, so by the
  time the button comes up there is nothing left to round. The valve's committing frame is the one frame
  a changed-only field is silent on.
- **A bare click never reports `drag_stopped` at all.** A stationary press-release is a click in egui and
  never a drag, so the junk undo entry the fix was priced at does not exist. That was the reason the
  obvious fix had been left as an open question, and it was not a real cost.

A scrub now reports its value on the frame it changes it **and** on the frame it ends, pinned by
`a_scrub_reports_its_value_on_the_release_frame_and_a_click_reports_nothing`, which fails against both
plausible wrong versions.

**The user could not have caught this by using the panel, and said it worked.** Asked to scrub a
paragraph indent, they did it three or four times and reported that every one landed — which is exactly
what a preview looks like, because the panel reads its own subject back through it. *A "does this work?"
question cannot distinguish a commit from a preview, and asking a person to check one is asking the wrong
instrument.*

**The same pass found the two decoration fields had never been moved onto the valve at all.**
`optional_length_field` discarded its response and its callers wrote through `apply_char_attrs`, so a
drag committed on every changed frame, one undo step each, and said nothing on the release: D108 and D109
both, on the two fields that were missed. It now returns an `OptionalLengthEdit` and writes through
`char_valve`. It stays silent while the field shows "auto", the scrub being clamped to a zero-width range
there.

**D108 — The paragraph length fields were the only numeric controls that did not preview, and scrubbing
them did nothing. *Resolved.*** `length_field` returned a bare `Option<Length>` and its two callers
committed it on the spot — one history entry per frame of a drag, each built from a snapshot taken before
the frame started. Every other numeric field in the panel goes through the valve. `LengthEdit` now
carries the response back, plus an `immediate` flag for the unit toggle: that is a click, and a valve
waits for a drag that will never come.

Worth recording how much of this was *not* diagnosed from the outside: driven headlessly, `length_field`
responded to a synthetic drag correctly. What the probes settled was what it was **not** —
`bare_drag_value` does not report a spurious `changed()` when its value fails to round-trip through
`max_decimals`, and the field's own arithmetic is sound. The cause was upstream in D109.

**D107 — The inspector's popovers hung over the inspector, and the two surfaces are the same colour.
*Resolved — a design change, and the design file does not cover it.*** `design/Editor.dc.html` draws the
popovers floating over the canvas, well clear of the cards, and says nothing about the case where they
are not. Both were anchored right-aligned *under* the button that opened them, which on a 284pt column
puts a 272pt card almost exactly over the panel behind it — same fill, same hairline, same corner radius.
The detached colour picker had already solved this by sitting to the **left**, so the popovers now do
what it does (`OndinApp::popover_anchor`), `constrain_to` the window so a low row does not push a tall
popover off the bottom.

The alternative was to give a popover its own ground — a second surface colour invented to work around an
overlap that need not happen, and one that would then have to be justified against every other card.

**Two knock-ons, and the second is worth remembering.** The popovers are now the same width
(`app::POPOVER_W`, the design's 272), because the clearance below is computed from it and a clearance
derived from a width that might be the other popover's is sometimes wrong. And **the popovers now share
the picker's side of the screen**: a picker opened from a Fill chip is placed relative to its row, which
put it straight on top of an open popover — and the popover is `Foreground` where the picker is `Middle`.
`OndinApp::picker_lane_right` reserves the lane. A picker opened from *inside* a popover needs no special
case.

*Any third floating surface owes the same question: which lane is it in, and what is already there.*
⚠️ **It was not asked of the two the Export card added** (§15 D533): the Export card's row settings and the
Export panel's own menu were both hung in this lane at `POPOVER_W` and neither was added to
`picker_lane_right`, so a picker opened after one of them landed underneath it — the failure this
paragraph describes, by the route this sentence predicted, two popovers later.

**D105 — A field's unit was subtracted from its width and never allocated, so the field painted short
and the unit landed outside it. *Resolved.*** Reported as three separate complaints in one message, and
they were one bug seen from three angles.

`value_field_suffixed` measures the unit's galley, subtracts a strip from the number's `interact_size`,
and then *paints* the unit into that strip. Nothing ever allocated it. `field_frame` shrink-wraps its
content, so the frame came out exactly the strip's width narrower than the `size` its caller asked for —
while the unit's *placement* still came from `ui.max_rect()`. Measured: a field given 130.5pt painted
110.5, and its `%` spanned 108.8–119.8 across a border at 110.5.

- **The strip is allocated** (`Sense::empty()` — the chip below claims the clicks; two claimants over one
  region is the trap `icon_button_padded` describes).
- **`item_spacing.x` is zeroed in the row.** Every gap here is measured by hand, and the moment the strip
  became a real allocation egui inserted one of its own before it — the same bug with the sign flipped.
- **The chip hangs `SUFFIX_BLEED` past the content box** into the field's own padding, the design's
  `margin-right:-4px`. That was the actual complaint; the two above are what made it satisfiable.

`a_field_with_a_unit_fills_its_width_and_keeps_the_unit_inside` asserts both halves, each checked to fail
without its own change. *The general shape: in egui, space you reserve by arithmetic and fill by painting
is not space the layout knows about.*

**D106 — The typography popup's height ratcheted downwards and never recovered. *Resolved.*** A feedback
loop, not a cache. A `ScrollArea` takes its outer size from `available_rect_before_wrap()`; inside an
`Area` that is the area's size **from the previous frame**; and the area's size is whatever the scroll
area produced. Each short tab teaches the loop a smaller number and nothing teaches it a larger one. The
fix is an explicit `max_rect` on a `scope_builder` around the scroll area — the cap is then the same
number every frame — with `auto_shrink` on y free to do the part that *is* wanted. The same trap
`inspector_ui` documents one panel over, and the same fix.

`a_short_tab_does_not_shorten_the_card_for_the_next_tall_one` drives tall → short → tall, two frames a
phase (the first frame of any `Area` has no previous size and is always right), and asserts the fix *and*
the bug: the unpinned form is asserted to still ratchet, so the day egui changes and it stops, the test
says so rather than passing for the wrong reason.

**D103 — `ParagraphStyle::each_line` is gone, and the indent always reaches every paragraph.
*Resolved.*** With the flag off the indent reached only the first line of the whole **layout**, so typing
an indent into a three-paragraph node moved one line and left the other two flush — which reads as a bug,
not a setting. For a single paragraph the two states are identical: they differ *only* where there are
hard breaks, and there per-paragraph is what is meant every time. `text::layout` passes `each_line: true`
unconditionally.

The **field** went, not only the control — it is `pub` in core, where `dead_code` never fires — and
dropping it is save-compatible because serde ignores unknown keys. It also left one button in that row,
which is what made the two-button first-line/hanging pair possible.

**The revisit condition has since been met, and the answer does not change.** `ParaSpans` (D163) makes
"just the opening paragraph" sayable — an `indent` override on the first paragraph's byte range says
exactly that — so the case the flag existed for is now expressible without a boolean whose off state was
a puzzle. What expired is the clause about paragraph attributes being unable to target one paragraph; the
reasoning for removing the *control* stands. *Keep the field gone.*

**D104 — The typography popup can be taller than the window, so it scrolls. *Deviation from the
design, kept.*** `design/Editor.dc.html` draws the Character tab as one long card and says nothing
about what happens when it does not fit. Measured, the tab reaches a little over 700pt with a variable
font, a decoration expanded and `opsz` on Manual — taller than the anchor leaves below a Type panel
sitting anywhere but the top of the inspector. The body is therefore a `ScrollArea` capped at the
content rect's height less the margins, and the `Area` is `constrain_to` the same rect so the card
cannot hang off the bottom either.

Two things about the shape. The **tab strip stays outside the scroll**, because it is how you leave a
tab and a tab scrolled to its end is exactly where you want it. And the scrollbar **overlays** the
right edge of the content rather than taking a gutter, unlike the axis and feature lists inside the
tab, which give one up (`LIST_GUTTER`): those two always scroll, so a permanent gutter costs nothing;
the card scrolls rarely, and a permanent 10pt of dead space on every tab to serve the rare case is the
wrong trade. *If the overlay reads badly in practice the fix is `scroll_bar_inner_margin` on this one
`ScrollArea`, not a gutter on the card.*

**D1 — Preview was a document clone, not `RenderOverrides`. *Resolved.*** The app cloned the
`Document`, applied the pending transaction and re-resolved, every frame of a gesture — correct,
but O(nodes) per frame including re-shaping every text node. `RenderOverrides` (§6.2) now carries
per-node patches plus ghosts for in-flight creates, and `EditorSession` has no preview document at
all. The differential tests in `ondin-render/tests/overrides.rs` pin the property that made the
clone tempting in the first place: preview and commit produce identical draw calls.

**D2 — `trait Renderer` / `RenderTarget` deleted. *Resolved.*** Neither was ever implemented; the
two backends' entry points genuinely differ (device + queue + texture view vs. a returned pixel
buffer) and no useful abstraction unified them. `trait ScenePainter` is the real boundary and
always was, so invariant 11 now names it. *Do not reintroduce a trait without a second caller.*

**D3 — No `TransactionBuilder` type. *Resolved.*** §5.7 sketched a builder holding
`&mut IdSource`. The composites landed as free functions in `build.rs` taking
`&Document`/`&Resolved` explicitly, which compose better and are far easier to test.

**D4 — `ondin serve` and `ondin mcp-proxy` are unimplemented.** M6, deliberately deferred. The
seams they need exist: `EditorSession` is GPU-free, `build.rs` holds the world-space adapters MCP
tools want, and the snapshot carries what an agent needs to read. *Intentional.*

**D5 — The inspector edited local, not world, coordinates. *Resolved.*** X/Y and rotation are now
world-space (Figma semantics), projected back through `build::place_at_world`. W/H remain geometry
edits, which is correct: resize changes the shape, not a scale factor (§5.6).

**D6 — Multi-layer copy took only the first selection. *Resolved.*** The clipboard holds one
captured subtree per copied layer, and `build::insert_subtrees` places them all in a single
transaction — one undo step, with indices advanced as earlier inserts land so relative order
survives. Duplicate uses the same path. That advancing used to assume the placements ascend, which held
while they all appended and stopped holding once a copy named its original's slot — see D100 for how it
counts now.

**D7 — Controls in `design/Editor.dc.html` that are not built. *Intentional.*** The design is the
source of truth for the *screen*, and these would each be a lie in the current build:

- **The picker's eyedropper.** Screen sampling needs a capture path the app does not have, and the
  tool rail already lists the eyedropper as unbuilt. Leaving the glyph in the hex field as decoration
  would promise otherwise. *Fix with the eyedropper tool.*
- **`Share`.** Drawn in the top bar, wired to nothing — there is no sharing to wire it to. Predates
  this pass; called out here so the next reader does not assume a handler went missing. The design's
  page-breadcrumb caret next to it was never built at all, for the same reason: there are no pages.

Design details deliberately *diverged from* rather than skipped: the pane-coloured ground behind the
inspector is gone (§9.2 — pure floating panels was the explicit intent); the kind pill in the panel
title (`Rectangle` + `Rect`) is gone, because every node is named after its kind and the header
already carries the kind icon; and the top bar's breadcrumb is the document name alone rather than
the design's `file / page`, which is the same call as the missing page caret above — there is one
canvas per document, so a second crumb named nothing reachable. ⚠️ **That last one stopped being true
on 2026-08-26 and the reasoning was satisfied rather than overturned**: the crumb is now `Project /
Document` (§15 D363, D365), because a *project* is somewhere to go — the segment is a link into the
library — where a page was not. A document in no project still draws its name alone, since a segment
that navigates nowhere is exactly what this paragraph was refusing. The **page** crumb and its caret
remain unbuilt, and for the original reason. The Transform panel's proportion lock
is one more: the design draws a solid chain in the resting state and the build breaks the chain when
the lock is off, for the reason §9.4 gives.

Inside a paint row, two of the design's borders are gone as well. The colour chip has none — on a
14px square an inset hairline is a visible fraction of the chip, darkening every light colour's
edge and reading as a frame rather than as the colour; it is 16px now to carry the same weight
without one. And the opacity `DragValue` has no ground, border or hover border (`bare_drag_value`),
because the row *is* the field: a second bordered box inside it read as a control bolted on, and
the hover state was the loudest of the three.

*Additions* to it: the **Appearance** panel shown when nothing is selected, which is where the
canvas ground lives (D18). The **Clip content** checkbox joins Appearance on a frame (§5.3).

There was a third, the **Order** panel, and it is gone again. It was added when z-order had
operations and no reachable control at all; `Ctrl`+`[`/`]` (with `Shift` for all the way) and
dragging a row in the layers tree have both landed since, which is where a designer reaches for
restacking anyway, so the panel was four buttons restating them and a card's worth of inspector
height on every selection. `build::z_order` is untouched — this removed a view, not a capability.

The top bar's zoom cluster is *no longer* an addition. The build had in/out, zoom-to-fit and
actual-size as four buttons beside the readout, because the shortcuts alone left zoom
undiscoverable; the design now answers that with a readout, a caret, and a menu carrying the same
four (with their icons), which is the better trade — discoverable without spending four slots of top
bar. Distribute likewise moved *into* the design's Align row rather than sitting in a second row of
its own.

**D8 — Stroke alignment was missing from the model, and the inspector showed `join` in its slot.
*Resolved.*** `Stroke::align` exists, both backends and the SVG writer honour it, and bounds and
hit-testing expand by the aligned amount rather than assuming centred. §6.3 has the construction and
why it is a clip rather than a path offset. Join moved to its own row in the Stroke panel.

**D9 — Most canvas cursors are bitmaps, not `CursorIcon`. *Resolved.*** The canvas cursor says what the
armed gesture or active tool will do: hands for panning, crosshair for the shape tools, a nib for the
pen, that same crosshair with a count badge on it for the Image tool's *loaded* pointer (D236), and —
for the Text tool — an I-beam over text a click would *enter*, against the same drawn
crosshair the shape tools use (§15 D171). Only the I-beam survives as a stock cursor. Windows ships no
hand, so winit maps `Grab`, `Grabbing`, `Move` and `AllScroll` all onto `IDC_SIZEALL` and both pan
states came out as one four-headed arrow; `CursorIcon` has no pen at all, on any platform; and
`IDC_CROSS` is 32 texels across, roughly twice what a design tool uses. So `cursor.rs` rasterizes the
tool rail's own `hand` / `hand-grabbing` / `pen-nib` Phosphor glyphs out of egui's font atlas — which
makes a tool's cursor and its rail button the same drawing — and draws the crosshair and the rotate
arc outright. Both
paths meet at `compose`, so the set shares one white-core, dark-rim treatment. They reach the OS through
`Context::set_cursor_image` rather than being painted into the scene, a painted cursor lagging the
pointer by a frame and clipping at the window edge. `CursorIcon` is still set underneath as a fallback.

**The rotate cursor is one cursor per 15° of heading**, drawn rather than taken from a glyph:
`Bitmap::Rotate(Turn)` and `Turn::toward(screen_direction)` pick the step facing the handle, and
`cursor::rotate_arc` draws it. One arrow held at a fixed angle read as a decoration that happened to
mean "rotate". It was four quarter turns of Phosphor's `arrow-clockwise` until 2026-08-19, which was
exact but illegible — **D232** has why, and why the drawing being the fix collapsed two pieces of work
into one. Mid-gesture the arrow follows the **pointer** rather than the corner it was grabbed from. One
cached slot per step, the caching being what keeps egui from uploading a cursor to the OS every frame.

**The pen, by contrast, is mirrored — and a mirror is not a rotation at all.** Phosphor draws
`pen-nib` with the tip at the bottom-left, which reads as a pen leaning the wrong way. `rasterize`
reflects the glyph in the horizontal axis when the hotspot is `Hotspot::Nib`; a 180° turn — the closest
a turn of the whole bitmap gets — would put the tip top-*right*, a third wrong answer. `nib()` searches
for the tip from
the **top**-left now; the reflection and the search have to move together, and
`the_pen_points_from_its_nib_not_its_middle` says so, asserting the hotspot is near the top where it
used to assert the bottom. Which way round the glyph came out was settled by dumping the bitmap as ASCII
before and after, not by reasoning about the icon.

Two things are load-bearing and easy to undo by accident. *Do not "simplify" the hands back to
`CursorIcon::Grab`* — a test fails if the two bitmaps ever come out identical. And the canvas sets
**both** cursor channels on every frame, including to nothing: egui resets neither (`PlatformOutput`
carries both across frames deliberately), so a cursor claimed and not withdrawn follows the pointer out
over the panels and stays there.

**D10 — The locked-layer glyph is drawn, not set in type. *Keep.*** `design/Editor.dc.html` marks a
locked row with Phosphor's **Fill** weight (`ph-fill ph-lock-simple`), permanently, where every other
glyph in the app is Regular. Phosphor ships Fill as a separate font file and we bundle only
`Phosphor.ttf` (Regular), so `ui::paint_lock_filled` reproduces `lock-simple-fill` from its own
geometry instead — a rounded body plus a stroked half-circle shackle, in Phosphor's 256-unit design
space so it lines up with the outline lock it replaces. Bundling a second 480 KB font for one glyph
was the alternative and is not worth it. `the_filled_lock_has_a_body_and_a_shackle_with_a_hole`
rasterizes it and checks the shackle still has a hole in it, because "solid lock" is one careless
edit away from a blob. *Revisit if a second Fill-weight glyph is ever needed — at two, ship the font.*

**D11 — Per-corner radius, and what it cost. *Resolved.*** The design's Appearance panel has a
"per corner" disclosure, which the model could not express: `Rect` carried one `f64`. It now carries
four (§5.3). Three consequences worth knowing: the save format went to v2 with a real migration
(§5.11); `<rect rx>` can only state one radius, so the SVG writer emits a `<path>` from
`geometry::local_path` when the four differ — the same outline the canvas draws, not a second
construction; and `snapshot::Geometry::Rect` reports `corner_radii` rather than `corner_radius`,
which is a breaking change to the agent-facing schema that costs nothing today only because M6 is
parked (D4).

*While there:* `svg.rs` now formats every `d` attribute through `path_d` rather than
`BezPath::to_svg`, which prints full `f64` precision. A flattened rounded rect turned that into
tangent points like `-0.0000000000000008881784197001252`; hand-drawn paths were merely verbose.

**D12 — `Polygon` and `Star` are new `NodeKind`s, not `Path`s. *Keep.*** They could have been baked
down to a `Path` at create time, which would have cost nothing in core. But then "5 points" would
exist only in the moment the shape was drawn, and the Appearance panel's sides/ratio fields — the
whole reason they were asked for — could not exist at all. Keeping them parametric is what makes
them editable. The cost is one match arm per kind in nine places, which the compiler enumerates.
Adding *variants* to `NodeKind` is purely additive on disk (an old file never contains one), so no
schema bump; the migration policy in §5.11 is about changing fields, not adding cases.

**D13 — The canvas selection colour is not the chrome accent. *Keep.*** `color::SELECT`
(`#63b3f5`) is the one hue nothing else in the app uses. The panels are steel blue and so is a great
deal of real artwork; an outline in that family disappears into both, which is how the old
accent-blue bounding box behaved over a blue hero image. Everything that is *the app talking*
shares it: bounding box, hover outline, handles, marquee, pen anchors, the size badge's ground, a
selected frame's name tag (D22), and — since it is the same statement — the selected row in the
layers tree, its lit guide leg (D331), and that tree's two drop affordances, which were `ACCENT` until
they were pulled onto this hue in D345's follow-ups: a drop hint is the panel talking about a layer in
exactly this sense.

Two consequences of the badge taking the selection colour: `BADGE` is now a *light* ground, so its
ink is `BADGE_INK` (near-black) rather than the near-white tier the rest of the chrome uses; and
`SELECT_FILL`, the dark core the handles used to be filled with, is gone with the fill (D14).

The hue was retuned once (from `#6fc9f2`), which is the reason `SELECT_DIM` and `SELECT_ROW` are now
`select_a(alpha)` — `SELECT` at an alpha, const-evaluated — rather than the hand-premultiplied
constants they were. Those two had been mixed against the *old* blue by hand, so a one-line hue
change left the marquee fill and the selected layer row behind on it, in a way that reads as a
slightly wrong tint rather than as a bug. *Derive anything else that wants the selection colour
faded; do not paste a fourth literal.* There are exactly two sanctioned further hues, `color::KEY` and
`color::MEASURE`, and D113 and D198 have why a shade of `SELECT` could not have done either one's job.

**D14 — There is no rotation handle, and no mid-edge squares — but the sides do resize. *Resolved.***
Rotation is armed by hovering the band just outside a corner, with a drawn cursor (D9's machinery) to
announce it. The stalk-and-knob was chrome on every selection for one verb, and it collided with the
size badge under the box.

Three things changed after the first pass, all because the zones were unusable in practice rather than
wrong on paper:

- **The rotate band is outside the shape only.** It used to be a plain annulus around each corner, which
  armed rotation over the *inside* of every selection near its corners, where the gesture anyone expects
  is a move. `Handles::contains` (a convex quad test, so it is right on a rotated layer) excludes the box.
- **The band is half again as wide** — 10px to 15px. At 10 it was a sliver between the corner's own 9px
  grab radius and open canvas, and missing it resized instead, silently.
- **The four sides are grabbable**, at 6px, even though nothing is drawn on them. Eight squares around a
  small shape really is a wall of chrome, so the *squares* stay gone; what came back is single-axis
  dragging. `Handle` gained `Top`/`Right`/`Bottom`/`Left`, and `Handle::anchored` states the whole
  corner-vs-side difference once: which coordinate each axis holds still, and `None` for an axis the
  handle does not touch. `resize_to_handle`'s pinned-axis branch is back as `resized_box`, pure and
  tested.

`Handles::armed` is the single statement of the priority — corner, then side, then rotate — so the
cursor, the gesture and the hover outline cannot disagree about what the pointer is over. One function
is only half of that guarantee: they also have to ask it about the same point, which they did not until
D29.

**D15 — The selection box is the node's own rotated box. *Resolved.*** It used to be the axis-aligned
world bounds. On a rotated layer that rectangle is not one the shape has: its handles move screen axes
rather than the shape's width and height, so a resize leans the shape instead of scaling it — a lean the
model can now express (§5.6) but that a plain resize has no business producing unasked.
`query::local_box` mapped through the node's world transform gives the real thing, the outline becomes a
quad, and the `W × H` badge quotes the same numbers as the inspector.

`resize_icon` snaps a direction to octants — the handle's local direction turned through the node's
rotation (`Handles::screen_direction`), not measured from the box centre, which on a wide box would call
a corner horizontal.

**D16 — The size badge turns with the layer. *Resolved.*** D15 left it under the *screen footprint* of
the rotated quad and upright, on the grounds that a tilted pill is hard to read. In use the trade goes
the other way: an upright badge drifts away from the edge it belongs to as the shape turns, and past 90°
the number stops looking like it is measuring *that* box. It is laid out in the layer's own frame
(`ui::Frame2`), centred under the box's own bottom edge at the box's own angle.

**That rule now holds only within a quarter turn of upright.** Following the shape all the way round was
right for the first 45° and wrong after it. The angle is reduced into ±45° and the pill hops to the next
edge at each diagonal; D49 has the mechanism. **The angle no longer comes from the layer at all**: since
D327 the pill hangs off a chosen *edge* of the outline and since D329 it is laid **along** that edge,
reduced by half turns rather than quarters. For a turned rectangle that is the same answer — such an edge
is never more than 45° off horizontal — so what is written above still describes what happens; a
*sheared* shape is where it stops.

The cost is that egui can only rotate text: `TextShape::with_angle` handles the label, and the pill and
the locked-layer glyph had to become geometry (`Frame2::rounded_rect`, and `lock_filled_shapes` taking a
rotation) because `RectShape` is axis-aligned. `badge_frame` is tested at five angles, including that
the pill clears the box rather than covering the edge it measures — the test passes its own gap, so it
pins the geometry and not the number.

The gap is `HANDLE_PICK_PX` (9.0) rather than a free 11.0: the badge wants to be as close to the bottom
edge as it can get, and the floor is where the pill starts covering the grab area beneath it. Tying it
to the pick radius says that out loud, so widening the handles cannot quietly swallow the badge. Not yet
seen on screen.

**D17 — The clipboard trio is read from events, not keys. *Resolved.*** `Ctrl`+`C`/`X`/`V` did nothing.
`input.rs` watched for `key_pressed(Key::C)` and friends, which reads correctly and fires never:
`egui_winit` intercepts those chords (and their `Insert` synonyms) *before* the `Key` event is built,
pushes `Event::Cut`/`Copy`/`Paste`, and returns. The keymap reads the events now, which picks up the
platform clipboard keys for free. The unit test that "covered" this synthesized `Key` events directly
and so passed against a keymap that could not work. *The same vacuous test shape came back one chord
along and stayed green for months — the boolean `Ctrl+Alt+X`, D204.* Reading this loop from events
rather than keys is also why D207's Alt guard, swept across the keymap's `on(…)` calls, passed it by.

One consequence: `egui_winit` only emits `Event::Paste` when the **system** clipboard is non-empty, so a
copy that touches only the in-app clipboard cannot be pasted. `copy_selection` therefore also puts the
copied layers' names on the system clipboard. ~~The real payload is still the captured subtrees in
`OndinApp::clipboard`. *Fix properly by giving core a serializable subtree — that would also buy paste
between two Ondin windows.*~~ **Done 2026-09-22 — D823**, and exactly as prescribed:
`ondin_core::io::clip` is that subtree, the payload follows the names past a fence, and a copy made in
one `ondin` window pastes as layers in another. **The names stay on the first line**, for this
paragraph's reason and because they are what someone pasting an Ondin copy into a note wants to read —
so the stand-in was extended rather than replaced.

**D18 — The canvas ground is editable. *Superseded in part by D28 — it is saved now.*** Clicking
empty canvas opens an Appearance panel holding one colour field for the ground behind and around
the frames, plus a reset that is dead while it is already the default. Above it sits a heading card
reading **Canvas** — the root's kind icon and a fixed name, the same shape as a layer's identity
card but with **no eye and no lock**, because the canvas is not a layer and neither operation means
anything on it, and nothing to rename. Without it the empty inspector was the one state whose first
panel had no title, which read as a panel that had lost its header rather than as the canvas. Not
yet seen on screen. The colour lived on `EditorSession`, not in the `Document`, as a working-surface
preference like the camera, and reset when a file was reopened; the three things persisting it would
have cost — a document-level field, an operation to carry it through history, and a schema bump —
are what this entry traded away. Its revisit trigger fired. The first two were then paid and the
third turned out not to be owed: **D28**.

It rides on `PaintSlot::Canvas` — a slot with no node behind it — so the swatch, the picker and the
hex field are the ones every other paint uses rather than a second parallel panel for one colour.
The slot answers `takes_gradients()` and `takes_alpha()` with `false`, because the backdrop is a
single clear colour with nothing behind it, and the picker offers neither rather than building a value it
would quietly flatten. **The tabs half of that is reversed as of 2026-08-03**: the alpha slider is still
absent, but Linear and Radial are **shown disabled** rather than dropped, because dropping them left the
picker's header holding nothing but a close button — D134 has the reasoning and §9.2 the widgets.

**D19 — Dragging a layer row did nothing. *Resolved.*** The reorder/reparent gesture in the layers tree
was fully built — drop targets, the between-rows line, the into-container highlight,
`reparent_preserving_world` — and completely dead, because it asked `resp.hovered()` to find the row
under the pointer. egui documents the opposite: "If currently dragging, only that and nothing else is
hovered." It tests `rect.contains(pointer)` now, and the target is re-derived from scratch each frame so
dragging off the tree and releasing drops nothing rather than acting on a stale one.

**D20 — A layer's frame follows the artwork. *Resolved.*** Dragging a shape more than half out of its
frame moves it to the canvas, and dragging a canvas layer more than half into a frame attaches it — one
rule in both directions, evaluated in `canvas::frame_covering`. It is **area**, not the centre point: a
centre test flips membership the instant the midpoint crosses an edge, which for a layer larger than the
frame happens while it is still mostly outside, and along an edge it flickers.

This is what the §5.3 relaxation is for. Three limits, all deliberate: only layers whose parent is the
root or a frame can hop (something inside a group was put there on purpose); artboards never do; and the
reparent lands in the same transaction as the translation, so a move-and-adopt is one undo step — which
is why `move_tx` is hand-built rather than going through `build::move_by_world`. The preview during the
drag is still the plain move: `RenderOverrides` cannot represent a reparent (§6.2), and a preview that
disagrees with the commit is worse than none.

**The destination is chrome instead.** `canvas::draw_frame_drop_outline` outlines the frame a release
would drop the selection into, in the hover outline's 2px `SELECT` (§9.4) — the canvas answering the
question the layers tree has answered since D19, *beside* the artwork preview rather than as part of it.
What makes the outline safe is that the adoption rule was **extracted** rather than read a second time:
`OndinApp::move_destination`, split out of `move_tx`, is asked by the outline and by the commit, with
the same snapped delta. Only frames are outlined, the root not being a box that can be. *Anyone adding a
second reading of the rule has put back the disagreement this avoided — call `move_destination`.*

**D21 — The type is `Artboard`; every word the user reads is "frame". *Keep.*** The two names have
run alongside each other since M0 — the tool rail says frame, the model says `Artboard`, and neither
this document nor the code ever said which governed where. Settled now, in the only place it can be
settled cheaply: **user-facing text is frame, the wire format and the type name stay artboard.**
`NodeKind::default_name` returns `"Frame"`, so the starter document's frame comes out as **"Frame 1"** and
its text layer as "Text 1" — both pass `name: None` and are numbered like anything the tools make
(D127, §5.7b). The number is not this entry's business and never was: what this entry objected to is the
*word*, and what "Frame 1" replaced is `Artboard 1`. `OpError::ArtboardPlacement` reads "a frame belongs to the
canvas or to another frame, not to a group" (it was `ArtboardNesting`, "frames may not nest", until D62
made them nest).
Deliberately unchanged:
the `NodeKind::Artboard` variant, the `"Artboard"` serde tag, the snapshot's `"artboard"` kind
string, and internal identifiers such as `target_artboard` and `create_artboard`.

The reason it is a split rather than a clean rename is the save format. The tag *is* the on-disk
discriminant, so renaming the variant means a schema bump and a migration to change a word (§5.11),
and the snapshot string is agent-facing schema on top of that — D11 records what breaking it costs,
which is nothing today only because M6 is parked (D4). The cost of keeping the split is that a
reader must know the two words name one thing; §5.3 carries that bullet so nobody has to infer it.
*Revisit only if the schema is being bumped for something else — then rename the variant in that
migration and delete this entry.*

**D22 — A frame that holds anything is not directly clickable. *Keep — unverified on screen.*** Its
background used to take the press and select the frame, which made it impossible to drag a marquee
around the shapes *inside* a frame — the one gesture the whole of that surface area invites, and the
reason a frame exists at all. `canvas::pick_leaf` is the fix: `hit_test` minus any frame with
children, so the press falls through to the marquee. Core is untouched, deliberately — this is a
picking policy, not a hit test, and a query about what covers a point must still answer honestly
(§5.10). Figma resolves it the same way and offers the same two exceptions, which we take as well:
an **empty** frame is still clickable anywhere, because there is nothing inside it to prefer, and
the frame's **name tag** on the canvas is clickable (§9.4) — which is most of why the tag was drawn,
since without a handle an occupied frame would be reachable only from the layers tree. A frame that
is already the selection also stays draggable from anywhere inside it (`selected_frame_at`);
without that, picking one by its name and then reaching for it rubber-bands the selection away and
reads as the click not having taken.

**A hidden frame has no tag.** The tag is the one piece of a frame drawn *outside* it, so it was the one
piece the renderer's own visibility check never reached: switching a frame off emptied its box and left
its name floating above nothing. `canvas::frame_label` now answers `None` for it, which also takes the
tag out of `frame_label_at` — a frame nobody can see is not something the pointer can pick either, which
is how every other hidden layer behaves. The whole ancestor chain is checked (a frame inside a hidden
frame is hidden too) and read through `display_node`, so the eye in the layer tree previews rather than
leaving the tag for the length of the gesture. `locked` is deliberately *not* consulted, unlike
`query::is_effectively_interactable`: a locked frame is one you can see and cannot move, and its name is
how you find it in the tree to unlock it.

One consequence had to be handled explicitly, and was a regression until it was. A click on an
occupied frame's background now resolves to *nothing*, and the code that dropped `entered_group`
lived in `pick_for_click` — which a click on nothing never reaches. So clicking empty canvas had
quietly stopped leaving an entered group, the one gesture everyone uses to get out of one. The
`None` arm of the click clears the scope itself now (§9.4).

Load-bearing: `pick_leaf` replaced the raw `hit_test(..).first()` at **all three** sites — the
click, the hover outline and the drag start. Leaving one behind is worse than not having the policy,
because the outline would then promise a frame the click refuses to select. Frames, the tag and the
policy are all as-built and compile-and-test green, but none of it has been seen on screen yet.
*Revisit once it has been used: the tag's offsets — the gap above the frame has already come down
from 10px to 5 — and the empty-frame exception are the parts most likely to feel wrong in practice.*

**D23 — The hover outline left every rectangle's left edge undrawn. *Resolved.*** §9.4 promised the
**exact** shape a click would select, and it delivered it minus one edge on every closed path.
`flatten_to_screen` returned a flat `Vec<Pos2>` and dropped `PathEl::ClosePath` on the floor, while
`egui::Shape::line` does not join the last point back to the first — on a rect from
`geometry::local_path` that missing join is the entire left side. It returns `Vec<Polyline>` now,
one per subpath, each carrying whether it closed; closed ones go through `Shape::closed_line`. The
flag has to travel *with* the points, because the caller cannot recover it: a closed triangle and an
open three-point polyline are the same three positions. Pinned by
`canvas::tests::a_rect_outline_closes`.

**D24 — The colour picker does not remember where it was left. *Keep.*** §9.3 said the opposite one
revision ago: `OndinApp::picker_pos` outlived the `Picker`, was read back out of the window's rect
every frame, and was what a reopen spawned at. That is not wanted. The picker belongs to the field
it edits and opens beside it every time; dragging it is how you clear a view of the artwork
underneath, which is something you do to see the canvas once, not a standing preference about where
pickers live. `picker_pos` is deleted.

*Not* remembering is the part that takes work, which is what makes this worth an entry. egui keeps
an area's position under its id for the life of the process, so `default_pos` is honoured on the
first show and ignored on every one after it — offer a spawn point and a picker that had been
dragged would still reopen where the user left it, with nothing in our code saying so. `Picker`
therefore carries `spawn` and a `placed: bool`, and the window is pinned with `current_pos(spawn)`
on its first frame only, leaving egui to own the drag from the second frame on. *Do not "simplify"
that to `default_pos`: it is a no-op after the first open.* Retargeting an already-open picker
deliberately does keep its position — clicking through several fills on one layer should read as one
panel following the selection, not as a window hopping between rows.

That override was then silently defeated on the *first* opening in a process, and only that one,
which is what made it read as a mystery rather than a bug. On the frame an `Area` first appears it
has no stored size, so it lays out once invisibly to measure itself — and for that pass `Area::begin`
fills `state.size` from `Style::spacing::default_area_size`, **600×400**. egui constrains that
imaginary box to the screen, which shoves `pivot_pos` up by the overhang of a window that does not
exist (and left as well, on a screen narrower than `spawn.x + 600`); the shoved position is what gets
stored, and by the next frame the picker is already `placed`, so `current_pos` never comes back to
correct it. Measured, and identical at `pixels_per_point` 1.0, 1.25, 1.5 and 2.0: **60px up at
1600×900, 160px up and 20px left at 1280×800.** Nothing later fixes it — the sizing pass is invisible
(`Area::content_ui` does `ui_builder.sizing_pass().invisible()`) and nothing calls `request_discard`.
Every *later* opening was fine, because `AreaState.size` outlives the window being closed, so the
estimate is never consulted again under that id.

The fix is `.default_size(vec2(WIDTH, 0.0))` on the window: an estimate of zero cannot overhang, so
it cannot be clamped, and the real height is still measured on that same pass. *An estimate larger
than the true height brings the bug back in proportion, so the honest 294 is exactly the wrong
answer* — this is a place where the obviously-correct-looking value is the bug. The builder was
extracted into `picker::picker_window()` so the test drives the real one rather than a copy of it
that would keep passing after someone deleted the line;
`the_picker_opens_where_it_was_spawned_on_the_very_first_frame` sweeps two screen sizes against four
scaling factors, and was checked to fail by 100px in x and 60px in y with the line removed.

The attempt before that is worth recording, because it looks obviously right and is a trap: keep
offering `default_pos` as a fallback and only set `placed` once the window's reported `rect.min` came
within a pixel of `spawn`. It settles at 1600×900 and **never** settles at 1280×800, because a spawn
near the bottom is *legitimately* clamped by the screen edge and so never equals the position asked
for. And a window that never settles is not merely untidy — with `current_pos` forced on every pass
it is completely immovable, since `Area::begin` overwrites `state.pivot_pos` from `new_pos` before
the drag branch runs and the delta is discarded on the pass that produces it. Measured as zero
movement across a press, three moves and a release, with no snap-back. *Anyone tightening this
placement rule needs to know that forcing the position every frame silently disables dragging.*

**D25 — A layer drawn outside every frame is standalone. *Resolved.*** `canvas::target_artboard` used to
fall back to *the first frame in the document* whenever the point was inside none of them, so a shape
drawn in open space was adopted by a frame it was nowhere near, and thereafter moved with that frame and
was clipped to it — with nothing on the canvas to say so. It now returns only a frame that actually
**contains** the point (topmost wins), and `canvas::draw_target` falls back to the document root;
`begin_create`, `begin_text` and `pen_press` all go through it. The three refusals that went with the
old rule are gone, drawing outside a frame now being legitimate rather than a mistake to report.

This is creation catching up with the model rather than a new permission: §5.3 has allowed a layer at
the root since D20. Frames stay pinned to the root wherever they are drawn, since they may not nest. One
dependency: a layer drawn clear of all existing artwork hangs its ghost off the root, which the renderer
was culling — D27.

**D26 — The wheel pans; only `Ctrl` zooms. *Resolved.*** Plain scroll used to zoom, and `Shift`+scroll
and `Ctrl`+scroll did nothing. `canvas::wheel_input` splits it three ways now: scroll pans vertically,
`Shift`+scroll horizontally, `Ctrl`/`Cmd`+scroll zooms at the cursor.

It reads the raw `Event::MouseWheel` events rather than `smooth_scroll_delta` / `zoom_delta`, and that
is the half not to undo. egui spreads one notch across several frames (`WheelState::smooth_wheel_delta`;
`zoom_factor_delta` derives from the same value). On a pan that is pleasant; on a zoom it reads as a
tween, which is what was reported as zoom feeling "synthetic". For the record, since it was the first
suspect: **there has never been a zoom animation in `Camera`**, and there is none now. Line-unit events
are converted with egui's own `line_scroll_speed` and page units with the viewport height; the zoom
factor is `exp(px / 200)` — egui's `scroll_zoom_speed` — clamped to 0.2..5.0 per event, because a
trackpad can deliver a whole gesture's travel in a single frame. The whole thing is gated on the canvas
being hovered: `Context::input` is global, so without the gate a wheel meant for the inspector pans the
artwork behind it.

**D822 — `Event::Zoom` and touchscreen pinch are *Later* with a stated trigger, not open work.
*Ruled by the maintainer 2026-09-19; Resolved — filed *Later*, and no production line changed.***

`roadmap.md`'s *Now · Canvas* carried these as the section's last two items. Both are real and
neither is work anybody here can do, which is the distinction that moves them.

**`Event::Zoom` would be dead code in this app.** egui only ever *consumes* that event —
`input_state/mod.rs` is its one reader — its sole producer is `egui-winit`'s
`WindowEvent::PinchGesture` arm, and winit raises `PinchGesture` from its **iOS and macOS** backends
alone; `platform_impl/windows` has no path to it at all. So handling it is a **macOS portability
item** rather than a defect, and on this machine the handler could be written and never entered.

**Multi-touch is the reachable half**: winit does deliver `WindowEvent::Touch` on Windows, so egui's
`multi_touch()` would see a touchscreen pinch. It needs a touchscreen to develop against, which is a
different kind of blocker and a smaller one.

🚨 **Neither can be built *or tested* on the machine this is developed on, and that is the whole
ruling.** An item nobody can write or check is not open work; leaving it in a *Now* section reads as
cheap work somebody keeps not doing, which is the misreading `roadmap.md`'s own bullet warned about
in its last line. **The trigger is stated rather than implied: a Mac, or a touch device.** Until one
of those exists there is nothing to attempt and nothing to re-derive.

⚠️ **Re-derived rather than inherited.** The analysis was last checked against the vendored sources
on 2026-08-19 — one consumer, one producer, iOS and macOS only, `Touch` present on Windows — and
re-reading it for this ruling changed nothing. This is the class of item that closes with *no change
to this repository at all*, so the date it was last asked is the useful record.

**Record-only, so the citation is planted by hand** on `canvas::wheel_input`, the function carrying
the `Ctrl`+wheel path these two would join and the place the question is met.

**D27 — A node holding a ghost was culled. *Resolved.*** `scene.rs` skips a node whose cached world
bounds miss the viewport, and skips its whole subtree when those bounds cover it (§6.3) — which they are
taken to do for `Root`, unconditionally. But a ghost is a layer that does not exist yet (§6.2), so no
cached bounds can account for it. Dragging out a frame clear of the existing artwork showed **nothing at
all** until release. The cull now also requires `ov.ghosts_of(id).next().is_none()`.

The chrome outline the create tools draw around their box (§9.4) was added for the same symptom and is
kept regardless: it states where the layer will land in the app's own hue, which is a different job from
previewing what the layer looks like.

**D28 — The canvas ground is document state, saved with the file. *Resolved — this reverses D18.***
D18 kept the ground on `EditorSession` as a working-surface preference and named its own trigger:
revisit if people set it per document rather than per session. That is what happened. `Document` gains
`canvas_background: Color` — **the first piece of document state that is not a node**, and no longer the
only one: ruler guides (§5.5) are the second, and were argued onto this entry's precedent.
`DEFAULT_CANVAS_BACKGROUND` (the design's near-black `#171718`) moved into `ondin_core::document`.

`Operation::SetCanvasBackground { background: Color }` was, when it landed, **the only operation with no
`NodeId`** — the five guide ops (§5.7) are the others now — and everything odd about it follows:
`op_set_canvas_background` is infallible, there being no id to miss and no kind to be wrong, and it
dirties nothing, `Resolved` holding transforms and bounds and neither depending on the colour behind the
frames. It takes a `Color` and not a `Brush` because there is nothing behind the canvas — a gradient
would have nowhere to go and an alpha nothing to blend with, the same reason `PaintSlot::Canvas` already
answered `takes_gradients()` and `takes_alpha()` with `false` (D18).

**No schema-version bump.** `DocumentDto` gains `#[serde(default = "default_ground")]` at the top level
rather than per node, the purely-additive case §5.11 allows: a file written while the ground was session
state was drawn on exactly that near-black, so the default is what such a file already meant. The loader
forces `.with_alpha(1.0)`. Pinned by `a_saved_file_without_a_canvas_ground_loads_with_the_default` and
`the_canvas_ground_round_trips_and_undoes`.

Two things this does **not** change. The line between document and view data (§9.2/§9.3 — camera,
selection, hover) is untouched for everything else: this is one deliberate reclassification, not a
loosening, and the reason is narrow — people set the ground for the artwork, not for the sitting. Guides
were later admitted on exactly that test and no wider one; *anything else proposed for the `Document`
has to pass the same sentence.* And the ground is not exported: SVG and PNG paint frame backgrounds
only, the ground being the surface behind and *around* the frames.

The payoff is that `PaintSlot::Canvas` stops being a special case: `slot_transaction` returns a real
transaction for it, `write_slot` and `valve_slot` lost their branches,
`EditorSession::set_canvas_background` is deleted, and the ground gets proper undo. Keeping the picker's
drag preview live cost one field, `RenderOverrides::canvas_background` (§6.2). Green, and not yet seen
on screen.

**D29 — Resize and rotate armed from the wrong point. *Resolved.*** `begin_select_drag` decided what had
been grabbed from the pointer position at `drag_started`, but egui does not call a press a drag until
the pointer has passed its drag threshold — so by then it can sit several pixels from what the user
aimed at. Several pixels is the whole budget: enough to leave a side's 6px band (`EDGE_PICK_PX`), or to
leave a corner's 9px grab (`HANDLE_PICK_PX`) and land in the rotate ring beyond it. Reported as "the
