cursor says resize but it rotates". `Handles::armed` exists precisely so the cursor and the gesture
cannot disagree (D14), and it was being asked two different questions.

Everything that decides **what was grabbed** now reads `i.pointer.press_origin()`: the handle arming,
the frame name tag, `pick_leaf`, `selected_frame_at`, and the marquee's origin, which otherwise pins its
corner where the gesture was recognised. The rulers and their guides joined that list later, having been
written the old way first — D35. The gesture maths still runs from the live pointer, so nothing jumps by
the threshold when a drag begins. *That split is the load-bearing part — press origin for "what", live
pointer for "how far"; collapsing it either way brings back one of the two bugs.* A diagnosis from
reading, not from watching it happen.

**D30 — The `+` on a Fill or Stroke header opened the picker against the panel. *Resolved.*** Every
other way in has a row to sit beside: `paint_row` takes `ui.cursor().min` before it draws and
`open_picker` puts the card immediately to that row's left (§9.3). The `+` has none, because it
*creates* the paint the picker is for and the row is not laid out until the next frame.

The request is parked now rather than answered early: `OndinApp::pending_picker: Option<(NodeId,
PaintSlot)>` records which slot was asked for, and `paint_row` claims it on the next frame with the same
anchor a click on that row's swatch would have used, so the two ways in cannot drift apart. `inspector_ui`
drops a parked request whose layer is no longer selected — the panel that would claim it is not being
drawn, so it would otherwise ambush whoever selected that layer next. Verified by reading the layout
order, not by looking.

**D31 — Right-click abandons the gesture in flight. *Resolved — not yet seen on screen.*** Nothing in
the design said what the secondary button does mid-drag; it now cancels, the CAD/3D convention rather
than the drawing-tool one. The reasoning is worth keeping: the alternative is finishing an edit you
already know is wrong and then undoing it, which leaves a step in the history for something that should
never have been an edit.

`OndinApp::cancel_gesture` is the whole of it, extracted from the arm of `escape()` that used to do
this, so Escape and right-click share one rung and cannot drift apart. It covers all three kinds of
gesture, because the user does not distinguish them: ours on the canvas (`Drag`), ours in the layers
tree (`LayerDrag` — which Escape did *not* clear before, and which has to be dropped here rather than
left to `finish_layer_drag`, since that runs on a release still to come), and egui's on a value field.
That last asked `ctx.dragged_id().is_some()` and nothing else until D168. It runs from `eframe::App::ui`
before any of the UI, and returns false having changed nothing when there is no gesture — which is what
leaves the right-click that removes a gradient stop working.

The load-bearing half is `OndinApp::gesture_cancelled`. **Cancelling cannot end the press** — the
pointer belongs to the user — so the release that eventually arrives would otherwise be an ordinary
`drag_stopped` and commit the edit after all; `ctx.stop_dragging()` is not sufficient on its own. Every
path that turns a release into an edit checks the flag: `edit_valve`, `picker::pointer_slot`, and
`canvas::normal_mode_input`, which sits out the *whole* rest of the press rather than only the commit —
a cancelled drag too short to beat egui's drag threshold would otherwise come back as a `clicked()`. The
flag is cleared at the **end** of the frame, once `!i.pointer.any_down()`: the release and the
suppression it needs happen in the same frame. *Do not move that reset earlier, and do not narrow the
canvas check back to the commit.*

**D32 — The picker's palette chips are one rounded rect, and the checkerboard was what stained them.
*Resolved — confirmed on screen.*** Three passes. They were first drawn the way every other rounded
thing in the picker is — square fill, corners carved out by `mask_corners` — and that mask emits a
`Mesh`, which epaint rasterizes without feathering, so the corners came out hard-stepped. Masking a
board and laying a rounded fill over it fixed the corners and left three subtler faults:

- **`ui::paint_checkerboard` lays down a solid white base** before its grey cells, so a rounded fill
  drawn over it anti-aliases against *white* rather than the card — a pale halo on all four edges,
  present even for a fully opaque colour that has no business drawing a board at all. The board is now
  painted only when `col.components[3] < 1.0`. *That white base is the trap for anyone else reaching for
  `paint_checkerboard`: it is only safe under a hard edge.*
- **A `Mesh` beneath a snapped fill will not line up.** epaint's tessellator snaps every `RectShape` to
  the physical pixel grid (`TessellationOptions::round_rects_to_pixels`, on by default) and does *not*
  snap meshes, so `mask_corners` sat at fractional coordinates under a fill that had been moved. A pixel
  probe across 48 combinations of chip index, fractional width and scaling factor found the fill's own
  edges crisp either way, so **do not credit `round_to_pixels` with this fix**. It stays for the honest
  reason: it makes the mask mesh and `ui.interact`'s rect derive from the same snapped rectangle.
- **The translucent chip's inset was one point, not one pixel.** `rect.shrink(1.0)` is 1.5 device pixels
  at 150%, and epaint rounds the near and far edges the same way, so the ring came out 2px on the left
  and top against 1px on the right and bottom. It is `rect.shrink(1.0 / ui.pixels_per_point())` now,
  with the mask radius `SWATCH_RADIUS - inset` to match, measuring a uniform 1px at 100%, 125%, 150%
  and 200%. `the_translucent_chip_board_is_inset_one_device_pixel_all_round` pins it, checked to fail on
  the old spelling.

Rejected, because it is the obvious next idea: give the board a rounded white base so there is no gap.
It **reintroduces the halo, worse than before** — the white base and a translucent fill are feathered on
the same arc, and a 40%-alpha fill cannot hide an opaque white beneath it at partial coverage. The only
halo-free way to close the ring is a single rounded shape with a checkerboard texture brush.

What is left is a single `rect_filled` at `SWATCH_RADIUS` (5.0), with the in-use chip's 1.5px accent
ring sharing that radius, and `mask_corners` touching only the board. (D231 later put a 1px hairline on
that same radius, under the ring.) The inspector's own paint-row chip
(`ui::swatch`) is untouched here and still boards-then-fills-then-masks at 4.0, unconditionally: this changed
one call site, not the technique. That chip gets away with the white base only because its fill is a
hard-edged `CornerRadius::ZERO` rect — *round that fill and the halo comes back on all four sides,
exactly as it did here.*

**D33 — The ruler bars are opaque, and their tick step is chosen rather than fixed. *Keep.***
`design/Editor.dc.html` gives the two bars no background at all — tick marks and a hairline, with
the canvas showing through — and it freezes one zoom, 100 world units every 51.94px at 51.94%. Both
are artefacts of a mock being one static picture, and the build departs from both.

The ground first. A ruler's ticks and type are near-white chrome, and the canvas ground is document
state the user may set to anything (D28), so a transparent bar over a light ground — or over busy
artwork panned beneath it — leaves the numbers unreadable exactly when the canvas is busiest. The
bars are filled in `color::BG` instead. The mock has nothing under its rulers but the default
near-black, so the two are indistinguishable there; the divergence only appears once someone changes
the ground, which is the case the mock could not show.

The step follows from the same limitation. `rulers::nice_step` picks the smallest 1/2/5×10ⁿ step
whose labels stay at least `MIN_LABEL_PX` (50pt) apart, which reproduces the design's 100 at the
design's zoom — `the_step_matches_the_design_at_the_designs_zoom` pins that, so the mock is still a
reachable state of the real ruler — and stays readable either side of it. Zoomed in past whole
units the labels grow decimals (`label_decimals`), and `-0` is spelled `0`, because a minus sign in
front of the origin reads as a bug. A chip's number is deliberately *not* held to the ruler's
precision: a tick labels a whole band and can afford to be round, while a chip quotes one exact
coordinate — the same number the inspector's field holds — so rounding 12.5 to `13` in the one place
that claims to say where a guide is would be a readout that lies.

A geometry probe then found the hole in all of that, which is again a case the mock could not show.
A left-ruler label has `THICKNESS - LABEL_INSET` = 17.0pt to read across, and the design's own
widest number, `-100`, clears it by 1.03pt — but `1000` is 17.25pt at 7.5pt Inter and `20000` is
23.5pt, and the canvas painter's clip rect is the whole canvas, so the overhang was painted in ruler
grey over the user's artwork. That starts at any zoom of 50% or less, and at the design's own zoom
as soon as the view pans past a thousand units. The fix has three parts, and the middle one is the
reasoning: **a truncated number is a different number** — `20000` sliced at the hairline reads as
`2000` — and being read is the ruler's entire job. `rulers::tick_number` tries the plain form, falls
back to a thousands form (`20000` → `20k`, `-1100` → `-1.1k`, via `tick_label_thousands`), and if
neither fits draws **no label at all**: a tick standing on its own says "one step further" and
cannot be misread, and its neighbours say how far a step is. Under that, each bar's labels are
painted through `painter.with_clip_rect(bar)` as a hard backstop, so nothing can escape onto the
artwork whatever the number, and the same `room` test drops the number on the top bar's last tick
rather than slicing it at the canvas edge. Pinned by
`a_long_tick_number_has_a_short_form_that_fits_the_left_bar`, which asserts the measurements as well
as the short forms. *The clip and the fallback are not redundant — the clip is what guarantees
nothing reaches the artwork, the fallback is what keeps a readable number on screen; deleting either
because the other looks sufficient brings back one half of the bug.*

⚠️ **The ladder has a second caller since 2026-09-08, and this entry's scope is why it took that
long.** Everything above is written for **ticks** and enumerates only them, so the selection band's
two end numbers (§9.4, D36) — the third readout in the same bar — were laid plain and dropped when
they did not fit, inheriting the least useful half of this reasoning and none of the fallback. On the
left bar that made a 1920×1080 frame's band read `0` and then nothing at all, while the lattice
beside it printed `1k` and `1.2k`. `rulers::draw_extent_number` takes the same three rungs now,
through `chip_label_thousands`; **D547** has the split between the width test and the end test, why
D34's grow-rather-than-drop rule does not extend to the band, and the one case the ladder still
deliberately refuses.

**D34 — A guide's position chip is transient, and guides outlive the rulers. *Keep.*** The design
draws one guide, with its position chip sitting in the ruler, which reads as "the chip is always
there". It is not: the chip is drawn only for the guide being dragged, hovered or selected. Four
guides on a page would otherwise be four blocks filling the ruler end to end with no ruler left
between them — the chip would have eaten the thing it is annotating. Figma shows it on the same
terms.

The same probe behind D33 caught the chip's own geometry. It was fixed at 20pt across, and only a
*vertical* guide's chip grew, so `chip_label(-1024.75)` — 33.03pt of type — overhung a horizontal
guide's chip by 6.5pt each side. Both orientations grow along their reading direction now, and a
horizontal guide's chip grows **out of the left bar into the canvas**, anchored at the canvas edge
rather than centred on the bar's midline, so it reads as a tab pulled out of the ruler. The contrast
with D33's dropped labels is the point rather than an inconsistency: a tick's number may be dropped
when it will not fit, because the tick still means "one step further" without it, but a chip's may
not, because the chip *is* the readout for a thing the user is holding.

`CHIP_PAD_X` is 2.5 rather than a round number, and that is load-bearing rather than fussy. `332` at
`CHIP_TEXT` measures 14.75pt, and 14.75 + 5 = 19.75, which the clamp to `THICKNESS` lifts to exactly
the design's 20 — so a three-digit chip **is** the design's 20×13 chip, and only a number too big
for that grows the block. That is what keeps D33's "the mock is still a reachable state of the real
ruler" true for the chip as well, so *rounding the padding up to 3 quietly costs that property*.
Pinned by `a_guide_chip_contains_its_own_number`.

The design also only ever draws the bars and the guides together, so it has no opinion on `Shift`+`R`
with guides on the page. Hiding the rulers hides **only** the bars; the guides stay exactly where
they are, and the chip — the one part that needs a ruler to live in — is what goes with them. That
is the Figma split as well, and the reason to take it is that the two toggles answer different
questions: the rulers are about measuring, the guides are about the artwork, and someone clearing
chrome to look at their work has not asked to lose their alignment. The one consequence to know is
that `guide_at` refuses any pointer over a ruler band while the bars are shown and stops refusing
when they are hidden, so a guide underneath a hidden bar becomes grabbable — correct, since there is
nothing there any more to grab instead. The split held: *Show guides* (`Ctrl+;`) is the separate switch
for the other question, added later and never folded into this one (§9.4, D136).

**D35 — A guide was nearly impossible to pick up, and the cursor lied about it. *Resolved.***
`guide_input` claimed the gesture at `resp.drag_started()` and hit-tested at
`resp.interact_pointer_pos()`, and the two are wrong *together*. `drag_started` fires only once egui has
decided the press is a drag, which takes several points of travel; by then `interact_pointer_pos`
reports where the pointer is **now** — off the 6pt guide band, and off the ruler bar whenever the drag
went the natural way. So the press fell through to a marquee, while `ruler_cursor`, which hit-tests on
**hover**, went on saying a drag was armed. It made the ruler read as intermittent rather than broken,
which is the worst way for it to fail.

This is D29 again in a new file, and the general form is worth stating once: *a hover hit-test and a
press hit-test that consult different positions will disagree, and the cursor will lie.* The fix is
D29's: claim the gesture on `i.pointer.primary_pressed()` and hit-test at `i.pointer.press_origin()`. Two
consequences follow. The gesture is armed *before* egui calls it a drag, so it has to be ended by the
button coming up (`!primary_down`) rather than by `drag_stopped`, which never fires for a press that did
not travel — leaving that alone would glue the guide to the pointer for the rest of the session. And a
guide is selected on the press rather than the release, which is right independently: the press is also
what starts the move.

`GUIDE_PICK_PT` went 4pt → 6pt in the same pass, matching `canvas::EDGE_PICK_PX`. The two are the same
affordance — an invisible strip along a line you drag sideways.

**And that pick band is why the press then had to stop *teleporting* the line.** Clicking a guide to
select it moved it a few points and committed that as an edit, because the press put the line at the
**pointer's** coordinate and the pointer is within `GUIDE_PICK_PT` of the line rather than on it. A dead
zone is the wrong shape — a threshold released at the far end would jump by exactly the offset the moment
it was crossed. What it needed was for the guide to be **grabbed** rather than moved to the hand:
`GuideDrag::grab` is the gap between where the pointer went down and where the guide already was, on the
guide's axis, added to the pointer's coordinate for the whole gesture, and zero for a guide pulled out of
a ruler. `guide_coord` adds it **before** the snap, deliberately: snapping is a statement about where the
*line* will sit, or a guide grabbed 3pt off centre snaps when the pointer reaches an edge and settles 3pt
past it.

Worth recording why the existing guard did not catch it: `finish_guide_drag` already refuses to commit an
unmoved guide, but it compares against `d.position` — which the press had already moved. *A no-op guard
that measures against state the gesture has already written is not a guard.*

*Not directly covered by a test.* `OndinApp` needs a wgpu render state, so the reasoning above and the
code's own comments are what hold it; the claim that `position = under + (g.position − under)` is
`g.position` is algebra rather than a measurement. The snapping work shipped alongside is tested
(`a_box_snaps_to_a_ruler_guide`, `snapping_to_a_ruler_guide_draws_no_extra_line`,
`a_ruler_guide_takes_ties_but_not_a_closer_node`, `a_box_centres_on_a_ruler_guide`), `snap.rs` being pure
geometry. *Anyone who finds a way to construct an `OndinApp` headlessly should pin this first.*

✅ **That way was found on 2026-08-22 (§15 D303) and this instruction is discharged the same day.**
`rulers::guide_grab_tests::pressing_a_guide_inside_its_pick_band_does_not_move_it` is the test this
entry asked for: it sweeps the press across the whole `GUIDE_PICK_PT` band, both sides of the line and
both axes, and demands the drag open at the coordinate the guide already had. **Swept rather than
sampled, and that is the point** — the error is proportional to the offset, so a press *on* the line
passes against the broken version, and that is the press nobody makes. Flipped by forcing
`grab = Vec2::ZERO`, which is the code as it stood before this entry: *"pressed -6pt off its line opened
the drag at 194"*, the reported symptom to the point. Its sibling pins the other half — a guide pulled
from a ruler has no grab and lands under the pointer — because a fix that made guides stop following
the mouse would pass the first test perfectly.

**The pointer is placed through `to_screen`**, so neither test says anything about the camera: whatever
zoom or pan is in force, the round trip has to come back to the number the guide already had.

✅ **The *commit* half followed on 2026-09-07 (§15 D474), and until then this entry read as though it
had not.** Both tests above stop one call short of the release: they assert what the press *opens*,
which is the teleport bug, and neither of them ever called `finish_guide_drag`. So the paragraph
beginning *"worth recording why the existing guard did not catch it"* — the whole no-op-guard rule —
was still held up by nothing but the comment at the site, and so were the five other arms of that
`match`. `the_guide_commit_table_answers_each_of_its_arms` closes that, and it turned up two things
this entry could not have known: **the guard's stated consequence is now D428's rather than its own**
(a `SetGuideScope` writing back the values already stored is dropped at `commit_inner`, so `let moved
= true;` costs no undo step), and **one arm still has no caller** — the Alt-drag released over the
canvas. D474 has both.

⚠️ **This entry is also the citation 38 doc comments across nine files reach for when they say
`OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly** — every one of those sentences is now false in its reason,
whatever is still true of its conclusion. D303 has the count and the rule.

**D36 — The rulers re-origin on a lone selected frame, and no further than that. *Keep.*** Figma's
behaviour, asked for with a screenshot, and taken in two parts. The tinted band across each ruler
(§9.4) is Figma's outright. The origin is only half of it: with a **single frame** selected
`ruler_origin` returns `world * Point::ZERO` for that frame — an artboard's local box is
`Rect::new(0, 0, w, h)` (`geometry.rs`), so its local origin *is* its top-left — and the whole tick
lattice is anchored there, not merely relabelled, so `0` lands on the leading edge and the band reads
`0` to the frame's width, which is the `W` the inspector is already showing.

Figma **also** re-origins for a shape *inside* a frame, and this stops short of that on purpose,
because of a decision already recorded here: `panels::inspector` shows X/Y in **world** space (D5 —
"world in, local out"), on the grounds that a number relative to whichever container a layer happens
to sit in is not a number anyone asked for. A ruler counting from the frame while the panel counts
from the world origin would have the two disagreeing about where the same shape is, and of that pair
the ruler is the weaker authority. With the frame *itself* selected there is no clash at all —
0-to-width agrees with the inspector's W. So the rule is: re-origin for a lone selected frame, never
for its contents. *Adopting Figma's fuller behaviour means changing the inspector's coordinate space
first, not just the ruler's.*

One known rough edge: on a **rotated** frame the origin is a corner while the band is axis-aligned
world bounds, so the band does not read 0 to the width. Honest, and not useful —
but rotated frames are unusual and it was not worth special-casing. The band's own arithmetic is
pinned by `the_selection_band_spans_its_axis_and_clips_to_the_bar`, and ⚠️ **the origin is pinned
too as of 2026-09-19 — D797**, which spends the *"writable now and unwritten"* this paragraph used
to end on. 🚨 **The figures it used to give — *"-50 to 480"* — were an illustration and read like a
measurement.** Measured, on a 480×320 frame at 30°: **−160 to 415.7**, a band 575.7 wide for a frame
of 480, the far end coming out **short** of the width rather than past it because the two ends are
two different corners. **D797 has the numbers and the reason.**

⚠️ **The band's *numbers* were a separate defect and this entry did not cover them either.** The
`0`-to-width reading above is the whole point of the band, and on the left bar the second of those
two numbers went missing for every frame over about a thousand units — D33's fallback being scoped to
ticks and nothing having given the band one. **D547** has it.

**D797 — The ruler origin is pinned, and D36's rough edge is a measurement now rather than an
illustration. *Tested 2026-09-19; Keep — the rough edge is a decided one, and the test pins its size
rather than demanding the useful answer.***

D36 has said since it was written that *"the band's own arithmetic is pinned by
`the_selection_band_spans_its_axis_and_clips_to_the_bar`; the origin is not — writable now and
unwritten, D303 having retired the reason this used to give."* `rulers::origin_tests` is that, two
tests, and the second pins a behaviour the same entry calls *"honest, and not useful"*.

`an_upright_frame_puts_the_origin_on_its_corner` is the positive control and the half that is
actually useful: a 480×320 frame translated to (100, 60) puts the origin on its mapped local (0,0),
and the bands then read 0 to the width and 0 to the height — the `W` the inspector is already
showing, which is D36's whole argument for moving the origin at all.

🚨 **The rotated case is worse than D36's own illustration, and that entry is amended rather than
left standing.** It says the band *"can read -50 to 480 rather than 0 to the width"*. Measured on a
480×320 frame at 30°: **−160 to 415.7**, a band **575.7** wide for a frame of 480. D36's figures are
the right shape and were never offered as a measurement; these are.

⚠️ **The upper end goes *down*, not up, and the first draft of the test asserted it the other way** —
575.7, on the reasoning that a band wider than the frame must end further out. It does not. The
width is `480·cos30 + 320·sin30`, only the first term is on the `to` side, and the second is what
pushes `from` negative. **The two ends come from two different corners**, which is exactly why the
number is unhelpful, and asserting the width alone would have hidden it.

**A test demanding the useful answer would be asserting a decision nobody has taken**, which is why
`a_rotated_frames_band_does_not_start_at_zero` pins the disagreement's *size* instead. The rough
edge is decided: the origin is a mapped corner, the band is `selection_extent`'s axis-aligned world
bounds, they answer different questions, and D36 judged rotated frames unusual enough not to
special-case. What the assertion buys is that whoever does special-case it has the number they are
changing written down beside the reason it is what it is.

⚠️ **The first flip tried was a no-op, and it is recorded as one because it looks like a flip.**
Taking the origin from the affine's `translation()` rather than from `w * Point::ZERO` leaves both
tests green — for *any* affine those are the same point by definition. *A mutation that cannot
change the answer is not a weak flip, it is not a flip.*

⚠️ **The flip that works** takes the origin from `preview_world_bounds(id).origin()`, the
axis-aligned top-left, which is what somebody reaching for the useful answer writes first: **red on
the rotated origin assertion, the predicted site, and green on the upright test beside it.** That
pair is the finding — the two implementations agree *exactly* while a frame is upright, which is why
this has never been noticed from inside the app, and why the upright test cannot stand in for the
rotated one. ⚠️ **And that flip does not close the rough edge either**, which the next person to
take this on should know before starting: it moves `from` to 0 and leaves `to` at 575.7, so the band
still does not read the frame's width. Making the bars read 0-to-480 on a rotated frame needs the
**band** to stop being axis-aligned world bounds — a change to what a ruler means, not to where its
zero is.

A third arm rides on the rotated test rather than taking a test of its own: with nothing selected
`ruler_origin` answers `Point::ZERO`, which is why the bars show *document* coordinates most of the
time and is one `matches!` away from being silently lost. ⚠️ The same function answers `ZERO` for a
single selection that is **not** a frame, and that arm is stated in the test's doc and asserted by
nothing.

**D37 — The View menu outgrew the design's three rows, and Open/Save stayed in the top bar. *Keep,
both.*** The
regenerated `design/Editor.dc.html` grew the right-hand cluster: a **View** dropdown and a **Snap**
dropdown between undo/redo and the zoom readout. The build follows it in shape and in metrics — 160pt
wide, **24pt** rows, a 13pt tick column that holds its place whether the tick is showing or not (§9.4) —
and departs from it twice, both agreed with the user.

⚠️ **Two of this entry's numbers rotted while its verdict stayed live, and both were found by the
2026-09-07 sweep rather than by anything failing.** The rows were **26** here until D262 took the
dropdowns to 22 and gave the menus that allocate their rows exactly a constant of their own,
`ui::MENU_ITEM_H` at 24 — so half of this entry was superseded by a later one and neither cross-
referenced the other. And the headline said **five rows**, which was true of the build of 2026-08 and
is not true now: `input::ViewSwitch::VIEW_MENU` is `[Self; 8]`, *Show guides* and *Lock guides* having
been added under D136 (§9.4) and *Show layout grid* under D755, without this entry being amended
either time — ⚠️ **this clause itself said `[Self; 7]` between 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-15**, which is
the paragraph's own lesson happening to the paragraph. The other two metrics in the sentence
above still hold, which is why this is a stale clause rather than a stale paragraph — `MENU_W` is 160
and `ui::menu_check`'s `TICK_W` is 13. **The durable claim is the shape, not the count**: *the build's
View menu carries switches the design's does not, and Open/Save stay in the top bar*. A count in a
headline is the part that rots, and this is the same defect class as D355, whose sweep of six stale
Snap-menu counts looked only at `crates/` and so could not reach this one.

The design's View menu lists *Show toolbar*, *Show grid* and *Show layers*. The build adds **Show
rulers** and **Present mode**, and later the two guide switches (D136).
Rulers were already a toggle with a shortcut (`Shift`+`R`), and a
switch reachable only by a keystroke nobody has been told about is barely a switch; present mode is
new scope (§1) and is the row that most *needs* a menu, because once it is on there is no chrome left
to turn it off from — which is why Escape unwinds it first of all (§9.4).

The other is a subtraction the design makes and the build refuses: it **replaces** the Open and Save
icons with the undo/redo pair. The build keeps all four. Following the design there would leave
`Ctrl`+`O` and `Ctrl`+`S` as the only way to open or save a file, and those are the two operations a
user is least willing to guess at — a keyboard-only path to them is worse than a crowded cluster.
*Revisit when there is somewhere else for file actions to live*: a File menu in the same cluster,
built out of the `ui::menu_check` row and `OndinApp::dropdown` that now exist, would settle it, and
then the design's cluster is the right one.

**D38 — `Ctrl`+`Shift`+bracket was a chord that could not happen. *Resolved.*** Bring-to-front and
send-to-back were written and never fired. `Shift`+`[` is `{`, and egui gives that its **own**
`Key::OpenCurlyBracket` rather than reporting a shifted `OpenBracket`, so `key_pressed(Key::OpenBracket)`
guarded by `m.shift` is a condition that cannot be true. `input.rs` accepts both spellings per direction
now, and the curly form always means "all the way", since it cannot be produced without Shift. Pinned by
`the_shifted_brackets_arrive_as_curly_keys`, which also keeps an unmodified `{` inert.

This is D17's failure mode in a new place, and the shared lesson is worth stating once: *a keymap written
in the letters a human would name can be unreachable, and it reads correctly while firing never.* The
rule that follows: **any chord whose base key changes glyph under a modifier needs both glyphs**, which
is brackets and braces today and waits on every other piece of shifted punctuation.

Nothing changed about what the chords do once they arrive, and that is worth a clause so nobody "fixes"
it twice. Both spellings route through `Action::Restack` → `OndinApp::restack` → `build::ZMove`, so the
group-awareness §9.2 records was theirs from the start.

**D39 — A card's ids came from its position in the column, and the inspector flashed for it.
*Resolved.*** Reported as a border appearing round the Appearance panel's title when switching subject.
It was egui's own diagnostic: `Context::check_for_id_clash` paints a red rectangle round the offender for
one frame when two widgets share an `Id` with different rects. A card's `Ui` id came from its **index
among its parent's children**, and the inspector's panel list changes with the subject, so "Appearance"
inherits the index another panel used.

`OndinApp::panel` now wraps its card in `ui.push_id(title, …)`, so every id inside derives from *which
panel it is*. The four first-position cards go through an `identity_card` helper giving all four **one
shared salt**: exactly one is ever drawn and always first, so a shared salt is what makes their ids
stable across a change of subject.

The rule to keep: **an id derived from layout position is a latent clash in any panel whose contents
vary**, and the symptom is a one-frame red rectangle that reads as a stray border rather than a warning.
Honest limit: the clash could not be observed directly (D35), so the fix removes the *class* of cause
rather than having pinpointed the colliding pair. *Revisit if the flash is ever seen again.*

**D40 — An Alt-drag drags the copy and leaves the original. *Resolved — this reverses the verdict this
entry used to carry.*** This entry used to record the opposite and keep it deliberately, and the reason
was never taste. A preview must agree with its commit (§9.3); the gesture previews the thing being
dragged; and `render::Ghost` could carry only a **single childless leaf**, so a moving *copy* of a group
was not something the render layer could draw. `GhostNode` carries children now (§6.2), so the copy
previews as the artwork it will become — clip, contents and all. Pinned by
`a_dropped_subtree_previews_as_the_artwork_it_will_become` and
`a_dropped_frame_previews_with_its_clip_and_its_contents`.

**Ids are minted once**, on the frame Alt goes down, and this is the load-bearing part.
`OndinApp::alt_clone` holds an `AltClone` of one `ClonedSubtree` per selected layer, prepared and
discarded on the *edge* by `canvas::sync_alt_clone`, so Alt can be pressed and released mid-drag
repeatedly. `clone_tx` is asked for a transaction every frame to preview it and once more to commit, and
per-frame minting would mean committing a different set of nodes from the one shown. *Do not move the
minting into `clone_tx`.*

The copy is adopted by whatever frame it is dropped over, by the same rule and code as a plain move
(`move_destination`, D20). It lands **immediately above the original**, and **appends only when the copy
has crossed into a different frame**, where the original is not a sibling. This entry used to argue that
the index cannot always be named — right about the case and wrong to generalise from it: that is an
argument for a fallback, not for always appending (D42 for the preview half). `clone_tx` keeps a
per-parent count of what the transaction has already added, for the same reason `move_tx` does.

The chrome follows the copy: `alt_clone_offset` measures the original-to-copy vector by projecting one
point twice rather than scaling the world delta by the zoom. The badge takes that offset on its **box**
rather than the finished pill, so it stays under the copy's own bottom edge (D16, D49). The `SELECT_DIM`
outline survives with its meaning reversed — it marks the original that is staying.

`alt_clone` is cleared in three places and all three are needed: `finish_drag` on both paths,
`cancel_gesture` (a stale one is what the *next* Alt-drag would silently insert), and
`reset_transient_state`, because it holds ids minted from the old document's stream. *Do not drop any of
the three.*

**D41 — The proportion lock is a constraint on the layer, and it was not saved. *Resolved.*** The
chain-link button used to govern the W/H fields only, which is what let it be filed as view state.
Confining it to those two fields is what made it a **numeric convenience** rather than a property of the
layer. Once it governed the handles as well (`canvas::keep_ratio`, lock XOR Shift) it became a
**constraint the user has put on the layer**, and a `HashSet<NodeId>` on `OndinApp` was the wrong home:
the user locks a layer's proportions, saves, reopens, drags a corner and distorts it, with nothing
warning them. That is the argument `keep_ratio`'s doc comment cites this entry for; *do not delete it
from either place.*

The lock lives on the node: `Node::proportions_locked` (§5.3), set by `Operation::SetProportionsLocked`
(§5.7), on disk as a bare `#[serde(default)]` field with **no schema bump and no migration**, `false`
being exactly what every existing file meant. Four details are deliberate and each is a way to get it
wrong again. `op_set_proportions_locked` dirties **only the node**, mirroring `op_set_locked` and not
`op_set_clip`: nothing derived depends on the flag. There is no `OpError` variant, a bool having nothing
to validate. There is no kind gate, unlike `clip` — the flag is inert on anything unresizable rather than
illegal on it. And `RenderOverrides::absorb` treats it as a **silent no-op**, in the `SetName`/`SetLocked`
arm rather than the refusing one: the flag changes what a *future* gesture does and nothing about what is
on screen, so refusing it would blank the preview of everything committed alongside it (§6.2).
`NodeSnapshot::proportions_locked` is populated but `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` stays at 2 — additive field (§7).

`set_proportions_locked_applies_and_reverses` pins the op and its inverse, and it is worth saying that
`SetClip` never had an equivalent: an op's inverse can go unchecked for a whole milestone if nobody
writes the four lines, and a bool's inverse looks too obvious to test right up until someone returns the
*new* value.

One cost went the wrong way and is recorded rather than hidden: `Node::from_parts` took **eleven**
parameters as of this deviation and thirteen by D60, three of them consecutive bare `bool`s. *Give
`from_parts` a parts struct before adding another bool, not after.* That instruction was taken up
elsewhere first — the resize run is `tools::Resize { keep_ratio, symmetric, scaling }` now and both
`#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]`s are gone (§9.4, D70) — and **`from_parts` itself was answered on
2026-08-19 by deleting it** (D240): every site writes the named-field literal the crate already used in
two other places, so the parts struct is the literal. The paragraph this one used to end with, that "both
live call sites pass named struct fields, so a transposition would not be silent *there*", counted two
callers of four and was wrong about the other two — see D240.

**D42 — A ghost does not honour its `InsertSubtree` index. *Resolved — this is the revisit the entry
asked for.*** It used to read as a kept gap: ghosts drew after their parent's real children, and
`absorb` discarded the `index` rather than pretending otherwise. That was right for the only caller there
was — an Alt-drag copy did land on top, because `clone_tx` appended — with the instruction to revisit the
moment anything previewed an insert lower down, such a preview being wrong rather than merely coarse.

Something did. A copy now lands immediately above its original (D40), so a ghost drawing last showed it
over siblings it was going to end up *under*. `Ghost` carries `index`, `absorb` fills it from the op, and
`scene::paint_node` **interleaves ghosts among the real children by it**. The walk runs
`0..=children.len()`, so an appending caller still draws at the end — which is why this went unnoticed
for as long as every caller appended. `a_ghost_draws_at_its_index_not_on_top` is differential *and*
asserts the draw order outright, because preview-equals-commit alone would pass if both were wrong in the
same way.

**D43 — `snap::targets` excluded the frames its own comment said it kept. *Resolved.*** The doc comment
claimed "artboards themselves stay in". It was not merely stale, it was inverted: the function excluded
the moving node's **ancestors**, and since `Root` and `Group` are not in the spatial index at all (§5.9),
the only ancestor kind that exclusion could ever reach was an artboard. The rationale it came from — a
node is always flush with some feature of its own container — is true of a group, whose bounds *are* its
children's union, and false of a frame, whose rect is its own declared size. Because a layer joins a
frame as soon as it is more than half inside one (D20), that was very nearly every shape on the page.
The rule is now **the gesture's own subtree and nothing else** (`is_inside_any`).

The reason it survived is worth more than the fix: **`targets` had no test at all.** Every snap test
exercised `snap_rect`/`snap_point`/`snap_guide` downstream of it with hand-written `Rect` literals, so
*which* rects reach the comparison went unasked. `a_shape_snaps_to_the_frame_it_lives_in` and
`a_gesture_never_snaps_to_what_it_is_carrying` build a real `Document` — the first tests in that module
to do so. *A pure-geometry module with a document-shaped input needs one test that speaks documents.*

**D44 — The top bar's right cluster has one gap, a rule gets 3pt more, and equal gaps were still not
equal spacing. *Resolved — this reverses a decision the code stated in a comment.*** The View, Snap and
zoom heads passed `1.0` where the zoom readout passed 5, defended by the argument that a mark and its
caret are *one* control. Reversed at the user's direction: those three heads are the only place two
carets sit close enough to compare, and against the zoom readout's 5pt, 1pt read as a mistake. All three
pass `TOP_GAP` (5.0).

The rules are the exception, because a rule is 1px of ink where every other control is a 26px box:
the gap that separates two boxes leaves a hairline looking stuck to whichever icon is nearer.
`TOP_RULE_GAP` (3.0) is added on both sides by the free `top_rule(ui)` helper rather than at the call
sites — the cluster is laid out `right_to_left`, so padding one by hand puts the space on the wrong side
of one of the two. *Keep the padding in the helper.*

**Both of those were true and the cluster still read as unevenly spaced, which is the part worth
keeping.** The gaps were already equal; the **ink** was not. `ui::icon_button` draws a 16pt glyph centred
in a 26pt box, while `ui::menu_head` allocated its two galleys and nothing else. At the *same*
`item_spacing`, a mark's ink sat five points nearer whatever was beside it, and in a row that alternates
the two kinds no amount of tuning the gaps can fix that. `HEAD_PAD: f32 = 5.0` is `(HEAD_H - 16) / 2` —
exactly the slack an icon button already had. Measured after the change, every control's glyph box is
**13.000** from a rule's column on both sides and **15.000** from the next control's, identical at 100%,
125%, 150% and 200%. `a_head_and_an_icon_button_inset_their_glyphs_alike` pins the two insets together.

**Equal gaps are not equal spacing when the things being spaced carry different amounts of built-in
padding.** `TOP_GAP` describes the distance between *allocations*; the eye reads the distance between
*ink*. Any new control that joins this cluster owes it the same 5pt of slack.

**D45 — A field row painted two pixels taller than it asked for. *Resolved.*** Two reported bugs, one
cause: **egui counts a `Frame`'s stroke width as margin**, so `field_frame()`'s 1px hairline made
`field_row`'s `set_min_height(size.y)` paint `size.y + 2`. In isolation that looks right, and it only
goes wrong in company, which is how it survived. A `ui.horizontal` asks for `interact_size.y` (24); the
first over-tall row grows the row's `max_rect` to 30; egui clamps the *first* widget to the row top but
`Align::Center`s every later one in that 30, landing it 1px low. Measured, the three grounds of an X/Y
row came out 30/30/28 tall at y 0.0/1.0/1.5 — which is what put **Y below X, H below W and border-radius
below opacity**.

`FIELD_BORDER_H` (2.0) names that margin, and the contract is the part to keep: **`size.y` is the height
of the painted ground, hairline included.** Three rules follow, each a way to put the bug back. Anything
a `field_row` closure allocates uses `size.y - FIELD_BORDER_H`, never `size.y` — asking for the full row
height pushes the frame back out **from the inside**. A control that has to line up beside a field
(`field_button`) takes `size.y` directly. And the test measures the **painted grounds**, not the response
rects — the response is the frame's *content* box, which is exactly where the missing 2px hid, so an
assertion on response rects passes while the bug is on screen.

Both halves were invisible in code review and settled only by measurement. One scaling detail matters:
the offset is **1 physical pixel at 100% and 125% and 2 at 150% and 200%**, because epaint snaps the
already-wrong odd origin to the device grid. *Check a fix here at 150%, not only at 100%.*

A third widget joined the disagreement later, over the same 2px. The Stroke panel's position `ComboBox`
came out **26** against the 28px weight field beside it: a combo sizes its own height from
`interact_size.y` plus `button_padding.y`, and `ComboBox::width` is the only dimension it accepts. It
wants the **full 28**, *not* the `size.y - FIELD_BORDER_H` a `field_row` closure wants, because a combo
strokes its border **inside** the rect it fills where a `Frame` counts its hairline outside.

**And the same convention in the other direction**, which cost another round. `ComboBox::width` is what
the combo *paints*, so the full-width sides combo given `available_width() - FIELD_BORDER_H` came out
**266px against a 268px card** — a 2px notch down the right edge. It takes the full width. *A combo
paints exactly the width and height it is handed; a `Frame` paints its hairline outside whatever its
contents asked for. Both conventions live in one row of the Stroke panel, and the 2px between them has
now been the bug three times.*

**D46 — `ui::rule` snapped its hairline in point space, and point space is device space only at 100%.
*Resolved.*** `rule` placed its line at `rect.center().x.round() + 0.5` — a round to whole *points*. A
rule's neighbours are galleys, so its 1pt column starts at a fractional x, and rounding that centre
**up** put the ink as much as 0.7pt right of centre and, at 100%, mostly outside its own column. Both
top-bar dividers took the bias in the same direction — the second contributor to D44's unevenly spaced
cluster. At 125% and 150% the same expression snapped to a point boundary that is *not* a pixel boundary,
rasterising the hairline across two physical pixels as a soft grey. The fix is `((rect.center().x *
ppp).floor() + 0.5) / ppp` — the **device** grid, and downward so the ink stays over its own column.
`a_rules_hairline_lands_on_a_pixel_inside_its_own_column` pins it at four scales; the two spaces agree
only at 100%, which is exactly what hid this.

The residual is a genuine limit rather than a shortfall: a *point*-wide stroke on a column whose edges
fall between pixels must overhang slightly, and a centre snapped to the grid can be up to half a device
pixel from the column's true centre. That is why the test asserts the **centre line** and not the ink,
and why the drift bound is `0.5 / ppp` rather than zero.

⚠️ **That formula asks for a pixel *centre* unconditionally, and it was copied into two more files with
the fault in all three** (2026-09-07, D479). A line whose *device* width is **even** wants a pixel
**edge**, so at 200% — a 1pt rule being 2 device pixels — it spread `[0.5, 1.0, 0.5]` across three,
which is the smear the paragraph above is about. The reasoning here is unchanged and the expression is
now `ui::hairline_in_column`, whose odd arm is this one; the parity is `ui::hairline_on_pixel_centre`.
The test named above asserted the odd answer unconditionally too, and D479 has why that made it worse
than no test at all.

**D47 — Shift meant two unrelated things, and now means one. *Resolved.*** The key used to switch
snapping off during a move, off during a resize (on top of keep-ratio) and off while a shape was being
drawn. It is now a **constraint everywhere and a snap-disable nowhere**: it locks the axis of a move
(`snap::move_axes`), keeps the aspect ratio of a resize, holds a rotation *or a skew* (D52) to 15° steps,
and constrains a shape being drawn. Snapping is switched off from the Snap menu and nowhere else — D48
is the last gesture to come into line.

Of the two meanings, only one genuinely needed the key. An axis lock has to be something the hand presses
and releases *mid-drag*, while snapping already had three switches in a menu. The old reading also cost
something real: axis-locked dragging is the convention in every design tool, and its absence was reported
as a bug.

Two details are load-bearing. `snap_rect` gained the `axes: (bool, bool)` parameter `snap_point` always
took, and the constraint is enforced **inside** the snap rather than by zeroing its result afterwards,
because a snap on the locked axis would slide the layer off the line the user is holding it to and the
guide explaining it would take credit for an adjustment then discarded. And `move_axes` re-reads the
dominant axis from the **live** delta every frame rather than fixing it when the key went down; the tie,
and so the first frame of every Shift-drag, goes to x, an undefined answer there being a layer that
refuses to move until the pointer breaks the tie.

Two consequences are better stated than discovered. A Shift-resize now snaps its pointer and applies the
ratio to the snapped result, so the dragged corner lands *near* the feature it caught — the constraint
wins over the snap. And `Snapping::none` is now `#[cfg(test)]`: left `pub` and ungated it would be a
constructor that reads as production API and is reachable only from tests, the decoy D2 warns about.

The way this survived is worth as much as the change. `canvas::snapping`'s `disabled` parameter was
**already dead** — all three call sites passed `false` — while its doc comment went on explaining it.
*A parameter no caller exercises stops being checked, and its comment then outlives the mechanism it
describes.*

*The named gap is closed, and as angle steps rather than equal extents.* `create_corner` dispatches on
the shape: a box takes `squared_corner`'s equal extents, a line takes `canvas::axial_corner`, and the
**pen** takes nothing — its exclusion is permanent, placing anchors one click at a time. `axial_corner`
snaps to eighths of a turn and not to `ROTATE_SNAP`'s 15°: rotating an existing shape is a fine
adjustment wanting many stops, whereas a constrained line asks for one of the few directions a designer
names.

One detail carries the whole feature and would be lost by a rewrite that looked equivalent. **The
direction is kept as an integer step, not as an angle**: at a multiple of 45° the unit vector rounds to
one of the eight, so a whole-numbered *length* along it puts the endpoint on the pixel grid while it
stays exactly on the angle. The obvious alternative — go through `cos`/`sin`, round per axis — buys the
same grid alignment by taking the angle away again, and a constraint only approximately the angle it
promises is worse than none, the designer being unable to tell by eye. The length is a projection of the
pointer onto the direction, so the endpoint follows the hand along the line. *Keep the integer step; do
not reintroduce `cos`/`sin` on the endpoint.* `a_constrained_line_lands_on_an_exact_eighth_of_a_turn`
asserts whole `dx`/`dy` **and** equal-or-one-zero in all eight directions — the two together because the
grid and the angle are precisely where they could be traded against each other — and covers the no-drag
case a careless `atan2` turns into a `NaN`.

`shift_locks_the_axis_the_drag_is_mostly_travelling_along`,
`a_locked_axis_neither_snaps_nor_explains_itself` (a box 2 units from an alignment on *both* axes, so a
leak in either direction shows) and `a_constrained_draw_is_square_in_every_direction` are the rest.

**D48 — A dragged ruler guide kept reading Shift as a snap-disable. *Resolved.*** The one gesture that
did not honour D47's rule. **Shift is now inert on a guide drag** — a guide has one axis and therefore
nothing to constrain, so inert is the consistent outcome rather than a compromise.

The flag was **removed rather than passed and ignored**, which is the part to keep. `update_guide_drag`
lost its `shift` parameter and there is no live read of the key left in `rulers.rs`. That is D47's fifth
paragraph applied straight away. `guide_coord` keeps its `snap: bool`, which is not the same hazard —
both call sites exercise it, `false` at the press and `true` from the first move.

**D49 — The size badge follows the shape for a quarter turn and then hops to the next edge. *Resolved —
a refinement of D16, not a reversal of it.*** Past the diagonal the label leans further than is
comfortable to read, and past 90° it is upside down. A badge is a *number*, and a number the user has to
tilt their head for has stopped doing its job. It now follows the shape only within a quarter turn of
upright and hops at 45/135/225/315°.

The whole mechanism was one free function — `canvas::badge_angle`, `angle - (angle /
FRAC_PI_2).round() * FRAC_PI_2` — and **`badge_frame` was unchanged**. What made that enough is that a
frame a whole quarter turn off the shape's own still sees the shape **square-on**: `Frame2::bounds_of`
measures it tightly and its bottom edge there is a real edge of the box. The label still reads W × H **of
the layer**, not of the edge the pill landed on.

**That mechanism is gone, and `badge_angle` with it (D329).** A quarter turn is exactly the difference
between a label lying *along* an edge and lying *across* it, which was harmless while the input was a
shape's angle and became the bug the moment D327 hung the pill off a specific edge. The reduction is by
**half** turns now, in `badge_text_angle`. **The rule this entry decided survives untouched for a turned
rectangle** — the chosen edge is never more than 45° off horizontal there, so mod-180 and mod-90 agree,
which is why the sweep below needed no new expectations — and it is a *sheared* shape that can now be
given a steep label. The measured facts below are unchanged and live on `badge_edge` (D327), except that
the ±45° tie is now `badge_edge`'s and not the reduction's.

Three measured facts, each nearly got wrong the other way. First, **the edge it picks is the one whose
outward normal points most steeply down, not the one whose midpoint is lowest on screen.** Those coincide
only for a square: the normal switches at 45° whatever the aspect ratio, while the lowest midpoint
switches at `atan(h/w)`, 31° for a 200×120 box — so a non-square layer has four bands of `45° −
atan(h/w)` per turn, measured 14° each, up to 16px of difference. The normal is correct because what is
protected is the *angle* of the label. Recorded as the drift it was: the midpoint reading had been
written into two comments as fact, and measurement caught it. Second, **the badge is not below every
corner of a rotated box** — it hangs off an edge *midpoint*, and at 135° the badge origin sits 59px above
the lowest corner. It never overlaps the shape. *Do not "fix" it.* Third, **the tie at exactly ±45° is
deterministic but not decided alike at all four boundaries**: `315f32.to_radians() / FRAC_PI_2` evaluates
to 3.4999998, so that boundary rounds down where the other three round up. Written down only so that a
test asserting the four boundaries agree never gets written.

`the_size_badge_stays_legible_and_hops_edges_as_the_shape_turns` sweeps a whole turn in 5° steps — a
sweep rather than spot checks, the interesting values being the four boundaries. Two details in the test
are load-bearing. The steepest-edge assertion compares **steepness rather than index**, because on a
diagonal two edges tie. And the outward normal of a clockwise screen quad is `(e.y, -e.x)`, not `(-e.y,
e.x)`; the wrong handedness picks the *top* edge for an unrotated box, which is how it was first written
and what the test caught.

The pre-existing `the_size_badge_stays_under_the_boxs_own_bottom_edge_at_any_angle` was unchanged here: it
pins `badge_frame`'s placement arithmetic in whatever frame it is handed, a separate rule from the choice
of frame. *Keep the two apart* — a single test over both would not say which rule had broken. **D327
renamed it `the_size_badge_hangs_off_a_real_edge_at_any_angle_or_lean`** and folded the choice into it,
because the two became one call there: `badge_frame` can no longer be handed a frame that disagrees with
the quad. What stayed separable, and separate, is the legibility sweep.

**D50 — Three rules a multi-selection transform needs and the design never stated. *Intentional, all
three — each could have gone the other way; the fourth item, the inexactness they inherited, is now
resolved.*** One box with handles over two or more layers (§9.4) had
to settle a pivot for rotation, a reading of the proportion lock over a set, and where
`build::outermost` applies. The document was silent on all three, so the reasoning is recorded here
rather than left to be reconstructed from the code by whoever next disagrees with the behaviour.

**The rotation pivots on the union box's centre**, shared by every member, so the set holds its
arrangement and sweeps round as one thing. `tools::rotate_selection` is per-member `rotate_node` about
that one pivot, which composes because the rotation is applied in world space before being projected
back through each node's own parent. The alternative — every layer turning about its own centre — is a
different verb: it changes each shape's orientation without changing where any of them is, which is not
what a box drawn over all of them promises. Figma does it this way too. *Keep.*

**A multi-selection is proportion-locked only when *every* member is.** The lock is a property of a
layer (D41), and a set is only as constrained as its least constrained member: taking *any* locked
layer as locking the whole box would let one member silently constrain a drag the others never asked to
have constrained, with no way for the user to see which one did it. All-or-nothing can surprise nobody.
`canvas::keep_ratio` therefore reads it as `all` over the selection, and Shift still XORs it either way
(D47). *Keep.*

⚠️ **The rule was right and went unapplied by two of the doors it is about, which is the part worth
carrying away.** It was decided for the *handles* and written inline where the handles needed it, so for
as long as they were its only reader it read as one expression inside `keep_ratio` — and when the
numeric doors onto the same box arrived, the multi card's W and H fields and then `Ctrl`+arrows (D346),
neither consulted it. Dragging a corner over a set of locked layers kept their proportions; typing a
number into the field beside that corner did not. The visible symptom sat on the card the whole time:
its chain button was **inert**, excused by *"`proportions_locked` is a flag on a node, so a selection has
no shared one"* — which is the premise this entry answers, argued from the shape of the data against a
rule already decided. Since 2026-08-25 the reading is `tools::proportions_locked`, shared by the
handles, both numeric doors and that button, and the button is live (D347). *A rule spelled inline in
the place that first needed it is a rule the next door has to notice in order to obey; when one acquires
a second reader, move it before the third arrives.*

**The box and the ops disagree about `outermost` on purpose.** The *box* is the union over the whole
selection: a covered descendant sits inside its ancestor and so cannot widen the union, which makes the
filter pointless there. The *ops* route through `build::outermost` as §5.7a requires, or a layer inside
a selected group would be scaled twice, once on its own and once by its container. Both readings are
correct for their own job. *Keep — do not "tidy" the two into agreement; making the box filter costs a
walk for no change, and making the ops skip it corrupts every selection that contains a group and one
of its children.*

**The fourth thing here was not a free choice, and it is now closed.** §5.6 used to approximate one
case: a member rotated off-axis under a non-uniform drag would need a shear, so the scale reaching it
was evened to the geometric mean of the two factors and it kept its shape while drifting out of step
with the box. That reached a selection through the same `child_scale` — a helper that no longer
exists, so do not go looking for it — and a selection is exactly
where unrelated, differently-turned layers meet, so the fudge sat on the common path here rather than
the rare one. This entry used to end *"revisit only with a model that can store a shear, which is a
much larger change than this one"* — and that estimate was wrong, in a way worth recording. **The
storage was already there**: `Node::transform` was always a full `kurbo::Affine`, six coefficients on
disk included. What blocked a shear was not the model but everything that *read a basis back*:
`Orientation::of` → `to_affine` assumed the form `R(θ)·flip`, so any shear present was silently
destroyed on the next nudge of the inspector's rotation field. Replacing that decomposition with the
RQ split (`build::Basis::of`, §5.7a) was the whole of it. `tools::split_geometry_scale` now carries
each member bodily through the intended scale and splits the result — rotation, skew and flip to the
transform, the residual diagonal to the geometry — which between them reproduce the intended matrix
exactly at every angle. No approximation is left on either path, and no save-format change was
needed. *Resolved; D52 has the decomposition and the gesture that came with it.*

Four tests pin the pair of paths against each other rather than each against itself.
`resizing_a_selection_scales_its_members_and_the_gaps_between_them` puts two sibling squares in the
same 100×20 union the group tests use and asserts the identical output numbers, so the two mechanisms
cannot drift apart; `resizing_a_selection_holds_the_opposite_corner_still` covers the anchor.
`rotating_a_selection_turns_it_about_the_shared_centre` takes a quarter turn and checks that the box's
extents swap, the centre holds and each member keeps its size — and, the assertion that separates this
from the alternative above, that the members end up spread along the *new* long axis rather than landing
on each other, which is where rotating each about its own centre would have put them.
`a_selection_member_at_an_odd_angle_leans_instead_of_evening_out` replaces the test that used to pin
the approximation: it turns one square 30°, drags the union 3× wider, and asserts the turned member's
world bounds land *exactly* where the box put them, that its world basis really did come out sheared
rather than merely stretched, and that the axis-aligned sibling took the full non-uniform scale — the
last so it cannot pass by the scale having come out uniform after all. It asserts on world bounds, not
on any one node's fields, because the split is free to divide a given result between transform and
geometry however it likes; what must not move is the picture.

**D51 — Preview-equals-commit is structural for the renderer and unenforced for chrome. *Resolved for
the create outline; the class is open.*** Reported with a screenshot: holding Shift while drawing gave a
correctly *square* shape with a **rectangle** drawn around it. The outline the create tools paint took
the **raw pointer** for the far corner, so it honoured neither Shift nor the pixel grid, while the
transaction went through `create_corner` — exactly the §9.3 failure the preview-agrees-with-commit rule
exists to prevent, arriving in *chrome* instead of in a `RenderOverrides` preview, which is presumably
why the rule never caught it. The outline calls `create_corner` too now, and `create_corner` reads the
**gesture's own** `shape` out of `Drag::Create` rather than `self.tool`, so switching tools cannot change
the constraint under a drag already in flight.

The instance is small and the class is not. `RenderOverrides::from_transaction` makes it structurally
impossible for a *rendered* preview to drift from its transaction (§6.2), but an overlay painted with
egui reads whatever it likes: the marquee, the frame-drop outline, the Alt-drag chrome and this create
outline are all hand-drawn from gesture state. **Anything drawn as chrome that claims to show where an
edit will land must derive from the same function the transaction does** — and nothing checks that.
*Fix by derivation, never by duplication: when an overlay needs geometry a gesture is computing, factor
the arithmetic out and call it from both sides. A second copy that "matches" is the bug, one edit later.*

**D52 — The model could always shear; what could not was the way it read a basis back. *Resolved.***
This document asserted in three places that a skew was something the model had no room for, and D50
priced admitting one as "a much larger change than this one". The premise was wrong. `Node::transform`
was always a full `kurbo::Affine`, so the storage had been there since M0. What blocked it was
everything that *read a basis back*: `build::Orientation::of` → `to_affine` assumed the form `R(θ)·flip`,
which cannot express a shear, so any shear a transform happened to carry was destroyed the next time the
rotation field round-tripped it — silently, one nudge later. *A limit that lives in one function reads
like a limit in the model until someone goes and looks.*

**The decomposition is now RQ, by Gram–Schmidt** (`build::Basis::of`, §5.7a). Every invertible 2×2
factors *uniquely* as `R(θ) · skewX(k) · mirror · diag(sx, sy)` — four degrees of freedom for four
coefficients, so it is exact for any matrix whatsoever rather than only the well-behaved ones. That
exactness is the load-bearing property: it is what lets a world-space edit be pushed onto a node whatever
its ancestors have done to it. `Orientation` gained `skew` (radians, SVG/CSS `skewX` semantics) and
`Basis` keeps the residual scale. The mirror rule is undisturbed.

**§5.6's rule survives unchanged in substance.** The transform still never carries **scale**, because
that is what keeps a layer's size one number in one place and keeps a stroke from thickening when its
group is resized. Skew is admitted for the reason scale is not: it has no geometry field it could live in
instead. So the rule reads "translation, rotation, skew and flip — never scale".

Two consequences are traps, both invisible when got wrong. First: **the split must be done on the node's
LOCAL transform, after projecting back through the parent — never on the world matrix.** Splitting in
world space leaves the parent's basis wrapped round the outside of the split, which is scale back in the
transform by another route, and it passes every test whose nodes happen to sit at the root.
`tools::split_geometry_scale` says so and `resize_selection` projects before splitting; *do not
"simplify" the two lines into one.* The second is its mirror: a node's own transform never holds scale,
but a **world** basis can, a sheared parent with a turned child multiplying out to one. The inspector
therefore multiplies the residual back on when it rebuilds from an edited rotation or skew, instead of
rebuilding from the angle alone — which would resize the layer every time its angle was nudged.

**The gesture is `Ctrl` on a side band** (§9.4), and every choice in it is a choice. *Sides only*: a
corner has no side facing it to hold still. Ctrl was free because it is otherwise the deep-select
modifier and handle bands are dispatched first, and it is read at the **press**, for D29's reason — and
so, since D322, is the point the lean is measured from. ⚠️ *This entry said "there is no start reference
— the dragged side tracks the pointer absolutely", and that was the bug written down as a rule*: measured
from the box's **centre**, an off-centre grab leant the shape before the pointer moved. **Nothing snaps to the
pointer**, because the pointer stands for an *angle* and a lean that catches on a guide is a lean whose
number came from somewhere the designer cannot see. Shift snaps to 15° steps. The lean clamps at ±89°, a
degree short of where the matrix stops being invertible, and clamps rather than refuses so a wild drag
pins at the extreme. The cursor points **along** the side, the only thing telling it apart from the
resize cursor on the same band; `Handles::screen_tangent` takes the tangent in the box's own frame rather
than turning the screen direction 90°, and on an already-leaning box those differ. A single node leans in
its own frame on its own local box, needing no recursion; a multi-selection takes a world-axis lean about
the shared upright union.

**No migration and no schema bump.** `transform` was already six coefficients, and the SVG writer emits
`matrix(a b c d e f)` anyway. The `skewX` sign convention was picked for that: the coefficient is
`tan(skew)`, so a 25° lean comes out as `matrix(1 0 0.4663 1 …)` with nothing to fix up.

Nine tests hold it. `orientation_round_trips_every_mirror_and_lean` asserts the *basis* survives `of` →
`to_affine`, not the three fields, since `of` is free to name a reflection either way.
`a_basis_splits_into_a_storable_orientation_and_a_scale` is the exactness claim — *that test is the
licence for everything above; if it is ever relaxed, the resize path is approximate again and nothing
else will say so.* `a_collapsed_basis_decomposes_to_numbers_not_nan` covers the one case exactness is not
on offer for and pins what matters instead: a NaN here would go into a transform and take every
descendant's world transform, the bounds and the culling with it. Plus
`a_selection_member_at_an_odd_angle_leans_instead_of_evening_out` (replacing D50's geometric-mean test),
`skewing_a_side_holds_the_one_facing_it` (the whole feel of it — a skew that slides the shape sideways
reads as a broken move), `a_leaning_selection_carries_a_turned_member_exactly`,
`a_lean_does_not_change_how_much_shape_there_is` (area, which a wrong pivot or a doubled shear quietly
destroys), `ctrl_turns_a_side_into_a_skew_and_leaves_corners_alone`, and
`the_skew_cursor_runs_along_the_side_a_resize_pushes`.

**D53 — "Mixed" is a panel, not a label — qualified: it is a panel *and* one non-destructive row.
*Intentional; the five traps inside it are resolved.*** The
canvas has handled a multi-selection completely since D50, and its skew since D52 — one box over
several layers, resize, rotate, lean, an all-or-nothing proportion lock — while `inspector_multi`
carried "N layers selected", Group/Ungroup and Align. Everything else about several layers had to be
done one layer at a time, so setting one fill across eight of them — a daily gesture — could not be
done at all. The panels now exist
(§9.4) over the bulk builders in `build.rs` (§5.7a), and the decision worth recording is what the
Fill panel does when the layers disagree.

**Not a "Mixed" label** — as first built. Told that a fill is mixed, the only move a designer had left
was to overwrite it and lose whatever was there: the word reported a problem and offered exactly one
destructive answer to it. So the disagreement was enumerated instead. **Group Colors** lists every
distinct solid colour in the selection as its own editable row, and editing a row recolours every use
of that colour — fills, strokes and frame backgrounds alike — in one transaction and so one undo step.
The Fill panel above it keeps the other intention, *whatever these are now, make them all this*.

⚠️ **That sentence is written in the present tense and two thirds of it have since moved.** It is left
as it was because the *decision* it records — enumerate the disagreement rather than label it — is
unchanged and is what this entry is for; what has moved is the panel it describes. **D135** put
gradients in the list, so *"solid"* is no longer the whole of it. **D400** made a frame's ground an
ordinary fill and **D401** took the container's own paint out of its own census, so *"frame
backgrounds alike"* is now exactly backwards for the one case it names: a selected frame's ground is
the Fill card's business and this panel reports what is inside it. The pairing in the last line — this
panel against the Fill panel — is the half that survived all three intact.

**The objection was never to the word, and that is the qualification.** It was to a word with one
destructive answer behind it. A mixed row that edits **one property** and leaves each layer its own
list has a non-destructive answer, so both halves can exist and each carries the intention it always
had: Group Colors is *whatever these are, keep them different and change that one*, and the Fill panel
is *whatever these are now, make them all this*. The panels therefore say mixed now, on terms §9.4
states — one stand-in row over `PaintSlot::SelectionAll`, values agreed property by property, writes
through `build::edit_fills_all` / `edit_strokes_all` in place, a header `+` left **inert** rather than
taken away (D134), and the `x` as the single
deliberate destruction because it is also the way back to the empty state. What the row must never
become is a row that *replaces* the lists: that is the label this entry refused, wearing a chip. Three
core tests hold the shape of it —
`a_shared_fill_list_means_the_whole_list_agrees` (which also pins the empty state as the
nothing-is-painted case, below),
`a_mixed_row_states_what_the_paints_agree_on_and_edits_one_property` and
`a_mixed_stroke_row_agrees_per_property_too`. `inspector_group_colors`'s doc comment used to open "this
is what a 'Mixed' label should have been"; it and this entry were rewritten together, and *they have to
keep saying the same thing.*

**An unpainted layer among painted ones is mixed, and getting that backwards was reported.** The first
build required *every* target to have a paint before it would draw a stand-in, on the reading that a row
standing for nothing is a row with nothing behind it, and fell back to the empty state otherwise. That
is the commonest disagreement there is, and the report says why it is the wrong answer: "when selecting a
layer that has a stroke and another that doesn't, the stroke panel doesn't report any stroke … since
reporting there's no stroke would be a lie." It is mixed in every property at once — colour, position and
weight — which `build::shared_over_fills` / `shared_over_strokes` deliver by treating **absence as a value
that agrees with nothing**, so the lone stroke's weight is not reported as shared. `paint_shown` needed no
second pass to make the panel-level half of this true: empty lists are all equal to each other, so
reaching a disagreement at all proves something is painted (§5.7a). *The only empty panel is one where
nothing in scope is painted; do not restore the "all of them must have one" test, because the panel it
produces denies ink that is on the screen.*

**The third trap is that the mixed row's own numbers cannot be read from the committed tree.** The stroke
weight could be typed into and not dragged — reported exactly that way — because the row read
`build::shared_over_strokes` against the committed document, and a scrubbed field re-reads its own value
each frame and adds that frame's delta to it. Fed the pre-gesture number every frame, it never
accumulated. `OndinApp::shown_over_fills` / `shown_over_strokes` ask the same question of `display_node`
instead, which is the `shared_opacity` / `shared_opacity_shown` split this file already had, while the
*transaction* is still built against the committed tree — the invariant-5 split every valve here follows
(§9.3). `build::fills_seen_as` became `pub` and took `(&NodeKind, &Paint)` for it, so the app's
`DisplayNode` can call the one definition of "a frame's ground is a fill" rather than a second copy
of it.

**The fourth trap is the general lesson, and it is not about paint: what a control may *say* and what it
*operates from* are two questions.** Live was only half of the third trap; the other half is that the
base has to be **real**, and the row was handing its controls the *absence* of an agreement as though
that were a value to start from — the weight from `unwrap_or(0.0)`, the picker from a placeholder grey.
A scrubbed control adds this frame's delta to the base it is given, so where the agreement is `None`
**permanently** — which is exactly the reported case, since a bare target agrees with nothing however far
the drag travels — the field was handed 0 back every frame and oscillated 0 → 0.5 → 0, committing whatever
fraction happened to be in flight. Reported as "slide dragging the weight or color opacity doesn't work.
I can see the stroke resize or change opacity, but it flickers on and off, and it doesn't show when I let
go", and in the same breath as a picker whose plane, tabs and alpha slider all snapped back within the
frame. **The user's own observation is what pinned it**, and it is the kind worth keeping: only the hue
slider appeared to respond, because `paint::new_solid()` is achromatic, so `picker::hsv_of` substitutes
`Picker::hue` for an s=0 colour's hue — and `Picker::hue` is the one value the picker remembers for itself
instead of reading back off the brush. The single control that worked was the single control not reading
the dead brush.

`inspector::Spread<T> { values, bare }` is the split: `agreed()` is what a control may say (`None` when
the values differ *or* when a target is bare), `base()` is what it operates from (the **first** value,
whatever the rest say), and `map()` asks a second property off the same walk so the alpha and the brushes
cannot disagree about what they found. `shown_over_fills` / `shown_over_strokes` return one, `shown_brushes`
is the entry point the chip, the hex and the picker share, and the stroke weight is
`shared_width.or_else(|| widths.base())`. *First*, not largest or mean: any real member does and the first
is the one a reader can predict — the single-layer corner-radius field picks the largest for the same job,
and the difference between those two choices is not what makes either work. Two tests in
`inspector::spread_tests`, both verified to fail if `base` stops being live:
`a_bare_target_removes_the_agreement_and_not_the_base` is the reported case — no agreed weight, and still
a 4 to drag from — and `mapping_a_spread_carries_the_bare_flag`. *Do not "simplify" the pair back to one
`Option`. The `None` is the report; the row still has to be operating on something.*

**The fifth is the price of a base that is real: it is a real *brush*, so it can be a gradient.** Once
`base()` hands back the first paint in scope rather than a solid stand-in, a mixed row can be holding a
`Brush::Gradient` — and the ordinary row would then print "Linear" where a solid row prints a hex, which is
precisely the claim a mixed row must not make about a set that is not all linear. So a mixed row takes
the **hex field whatever kind its base brush is**, and the hex says "Mixed", which is true of both cases.
The comment asserting the opposite — that a row whose colour is unknown always lands in the Solid arm,
because the brush it was handed is the solid stand-in — was true when it was written and is gone.

**That panel is not a second panel.** Fill and Stroke take a `PaintScope` — `Node(NodeId)` or
`Selection` — rather than a `NodeId`, because a single shape and a whole selection want the identical
control, a list of paints with rows to add, edit and remove, and differ only in who the list is
written to. Threading the difference through as a scope is what got the selection add-and-remove for
free and is why there is no second implementation to drift from the first; `PaintScope::Selection`
borrows the document root as its slot anchor, the placeholder the canvas-ground and guide rows
already use. **What is shared is the whole list, not the first brush.** `build::shared_fills` /
`shared_strokes` return the `Vec` every target agrees on, so two layers that both start red
but differ in their second fill do not share a fill list — a panel claiming they did would delete one
of them on the next edit. Whenever they differ at all the panel draws the stand-in row above
(`build::PaintShown`, §5.7a); the empty state means nothing in scope is painted, and adding from there
gives every target that one fill.
**The empty chip this entry used to describe is gone**, and with it any bespoke "layers differ"
affordance: the stand-in row says it in the panel's own vocabulary and Group Colors says what it
consists of. `set_fills_all` /
`set_strokes_all` write every target *exactly* the list, which is the property that keeps the panel
believable — what it shows is then true of all of them — and `PaintSlot::Selection(PaintTarget,
usize)` carries an index because it names one row of that list. Stroke width, join, cap, dash, mitre
limit, alignment and sides came along for free once the scope carried a whole `Vec<Stroke>`, so the
