bespoke multi-only stroke-width field is gone too; alignment and sides are the two offered over a
selection only when **every** target qualifies — one open path among them would draw centred, and one
ellipse would draw its whole outline, while the field claimed otherwise (D68).

**A group is organisation; a frame is a thing.** This is the load-bearing distinction and it is worth
stating plainly, because it decides three separate things. A group has no paint of its own and exists
to hold layers together, so a paint edit passes straight through it to the shapes inside — which is
why a single selected **Group** now gets Fill and Stroke in `PaintScope::Selection`, exactly what a
multi-selection gets, where this entry previously said "Group Colors only" for both containers. A
frame is rendered: its background, stroke and other properties are its own and its contents are *its*
contents, so a single selected **Frame** keeps its own single-node inspector and gains only Group
Colors — two different fills in one inspector is a trap of its own. And `build::paint_targets` is the
walk that encodes it: outermost, passing *through* groups and the root, stopping **at** a frame, the
frame being the target and its contents not. That is deliberately **not** `subtree_nodes`, which is
still right for the census — "what colours are in here" does mean everything inside a frame, while
"paint these" does not. Frames cannot nest inside groups (`can_parent`), so no frame is reached by
passing through one.

**A frame's background is its fill**, which is what makes "make all of these red" work over frames
and shapes in one gesture: `fills_seen_as` presents the background as a one-entry fill list,
`set_fills_all` writes `fills.first()` back to it, and clearing the list clears it. The limitation is
stated in the code and worth repeating — a frame holds one background rather than a list, so on a
shared list of two the frame takes the first while the shapes get both. **Frames take no part in
strokes**: `local_path` returns `None` for an Artboard, so the renderer has no outline to stroke, and
a frame therefore neither contributes to `shared_strokes` nor is written to by `set_strokes_all`.
`build::any_strokeable_in` hides the Stroke panel outright for a selection of nothing but frames.

**The two Transform angle fields say `Mixed` and can be *dragged* while they do, which the paint row
cannot.** Nothing enumerates rotations the way Group Colors enumerates colours, and unlike a colour an
angle has a meaningful *relative* edit — dragging nudges every layer by the same amount and their
differences survive, typing lands them all on one number. A colour has no such middle reading: there is
nothing between "they differ" and "make them the same" for a hand to drag toward, which is why a mixed
paint row's every control is absolute. §9.4 has the rest of that
panel, including why position and size describe the union box while rotation and skew describe the
layers.

**The first trap is that a multi field cannot accumulate the way a single-layer field does.**
`OndinApp::multi_transform_drag: Option<(MultiField, f64)>` holds the in-flight drag total, and the
single-layer panel needs nothing like it because it reads its number back through the render
override — the preview *is* the running total, and each frame's edit is an absolute `SetTransform`
computed from it, which works only because that op is absolute and is always emitted. (The Rotation
field is the exception added by D206, and reading the number back through the preview is precisely what
made it necessary. These fields are immune for the reason the *first* half of this paragraph gives:
their base is the committed tree, which does not move under the drag.) Neither half
holds over a selection: `multi_transform_tx` builds from the **committed** document every frame, so
a field that only knew this frame's *step* would commit the last step alone and lose the rest of the
drag — and on the release frame the pointer has not moved since the last, so that step is zero. On
the angle fields it is worse than losing the tail: `multi_angle_tx` drops the layers a nudge leaves
alone, so a zero step is an **empty** transaction, `EditorSession::try_commit` takes an empty
transaction as a no-op success, and `edit_valve` then clears the preview — the whole gesture
disappears at the moment the button comes up. Holding the total means every frame of the drag — the
last included — builds the same transaction from the same committed base, so preview and commit are
the same edit by construction rather than by agreement
(D51). *Do not "simplify" `multi_valve` back into `edit_valve`, and do not read `multi_union`
through the preview: the first drops the total on release, and the second measures each frame's drag
against a box the drag has already moved, so the gesture runs away under the pointer.*
⚠️ **That temptation is stronger since D519**, which gave this valve the shared valve's engagement
latch as well: the two now differ in the total and in nothing else, which is exactly the difference
that cannot be given up. The cost of the duplication is what D519 is about — the *condition* was
copied once and then fixed in one of the two copies only.

**The second is that a Group Colors row is keyed by a colour it is about to destroy.**
`PaintSlot::GroupColor([u8; 4])` holds the **committed** RGBA, which is what keeps the recolour
transaction well defined for the whole of a drag — the document does not change until release. But
the instant the edit commits, that key names a colour the document no longer has, and the picker
sitting on the row finds nothing to edit on the next frame and closes itself in the user's hand. So
`valve_slot` retargets the row and the picker onto the colour it became. ⚠️ **That named one of the
two slot verbs and the code agreed with it, which is D580**: the click door is `write_slot`, it had
only the mixed row's retarget, and a *click* on the hue strip over one of these rows therefore did
exactly what this paragraph says must not happen. Both verbs go through `retarget_after` now. The
swatch has the mirror
problem and is solved the other way round: `group_color_shown` uses the committed tree to find
*where* the colour lives and the override to read *what it has become*, so the chip follows a live
drag while the key stays fixed. Both new slots are orphaned by the **selection** emptying rather than
by a particular node leaving it, which is what lets layers be added to the set while the picker is
still up. *All of that machinery is the price of keying a row by a value*, and D135 is the same panel's
gradient row keyed by a **place** instead — which needs no retargeting and no `_shown` reader, because
the place still holds the paint after the edit. If these rows are ever revisited, that is the direction.

Three smaller things are load-bearing. `subtree_nodes` is the apply-once rule for properties and is
*not* `outermost` — §5.7a has why, and `set_opacity_all` is the one edit that takes `outermost`
anyway because opacity composes down the tree. Every bulk builder skips no-op writes, because a field
that loses focus without having been edited would otherwise push an undo step made entirely of writes
that change nothing, and the six multi Transform fields skip building their transaction at all unless
the control is mid-edit — a W or H edit runs `resize_selection`, which recurses into every
descendant's geometry, and six of them are laid out every frame.
⚠️ **Both halves of that sentence were false when it was written, and D520 is where they became
true.** The mid-edit test is `inspector::interacting`, which contains `lost_focus()`, so the field
built on the one frame the sentence is about — the defocus frame — and two of the four box builders
then wrote unconditionally: `build::move_by_world` and `tools::resize_selection` emit one op per
member whatever the delta, so a click through X and then Y was two undo steps of N no-op writes. Only
`multi_angle_tx` had the filter, one arm away, with a comment naming this exact case. The X/Y and W/H
arms have it now. Nothing else in this paragraph moves — the apply-once rule and the cost argument
for the early return are unaffected. *While there:*
`picker::document_palette` had been an undocumented second colour census; it is now a call to
`build::colors_in` with the root as its scope, so the palette chips and the Group Colors rows cannot
learn about a new place a colour hides at different times.

Twenty-five tests in `crates/ondin-core/tests/bulk.rs` hold the core half.
`a_selection_holding_a_group_and_its_child_visits_each_node_once` is the apply-once claim;
`setting_opacity_over_a_group_does_not_also_set_its_children` is its deliberate exception, and
`corner_radius_reaches_into_a_selected_group` the other side of the same coin. The census is pinned
from three directions — `the_color_census_counts_uses_and_leads_with_the_commonest`,
`the_color_census_leaves_gradients_out` and
`the_color_census_counts_paints_that_are_switched_off` — because each of the three is a rule someone
would plausibly "tidy" away. (The second is a rule about **`colors_in`**, not about the panel: gradients
*are* listed now, by a census of their own that cannot recolour them — D135.) `recoloring_changes_every_use_and_nothing_else` and
`recoloring_reaches_a_frame_background` pin the reach;
`recoloring_leaves_untouched_layers_out_of_the_transaction` and
`setting_a_property_to_what_it_already_is_produces_no_operations` pin the emptiness of a no-op. Six
more pin the list-shaped paint, replacing the two that covered the removed
`set_paint_color`/`shared_paint_color`: `a_shared_fill_list_means_the_whole_list_agrees` and
`setting_the_fill_list_replaces_it_everywhere` are the whole-list rule from both directions;
`paint_reaches_through_a_group_and_stops_at_a_frame` is the walk;
`a_fill_over_a_frame_and_a_shape_colours_both` and
`clearing_the_fill_list_clears_a_frame_background` are the background-as-fill reading; and
`frames_take_no_part_in_strokes` is the exception to it. **No save-format change**: every one of
these builders emits operations that already existed.

**D54 — The layers panel became a place to work, not a list to read. *Resolved; one standing drift risk
flagged below.*** The tree could reorder one row at a time: a drag carried a single `NodeId`, `Shift`
toggled a row while `Ctrl` did nothing, rename lived only in the inspector, and a drag could not reach
past one screenful. Five changes close that: `LayerDrag` holds `ids: Vec<NodeId>`, already reduced
through `build::outermost` so a selection holding both a group and something inside it does not move the
inner node twice (§5.7a); a double-click renames in place; `Shift` takes a range and `Ctrl`/`Cmd`
toggles; the tree follows a selection made elsewhere; and a drag near either edge auto-scrolls. Dragging
a row that is part of the selection carries the set, dragging a row outside it selects that row first —
exactly what the canvas does, because the rule should not depend on where the gesture starts. Both the
self-drop rejection and the `can_parent` check now have to hold for *every* carried row.

**The load-bearing part is that every index is computed against the child list the previous operations
leave behind**, not against the document as it stands — the care `build::z_order` takes and for the same
reason (§9.2): three rows dropped at one index with three indices read off the original list arrive
reversed or past the end, and nothing about the result looks wrong until you count. So `plan_layer_move`
simulates the affected child lists and plans each operation against the simulation — and lifting a row
out of the destination list ahead of the drop slot shifts that slot down by one. It is a free function
returning `MovePlan` rather than a method because it is the whole of the tricky part and none of the UI.
`several_rows_dropped_together_keep_their_order` and
`a_drop_after_the_moved_rows_accounts_for_their_removal` are the two failures above;
`rows_gathered_from_two_parents_land_in_order` is the case where the destination grows while a source
shrinks; `a_drop_that_moves_nothing_plans_nothing` keeps a drag released where it started out of
history; and `a_reparented_row_does_not_move_on_screen` pins the `reparent_preserving_world` promise.

**`Shift` for a range and `Ctrl`/`Cmd` for a toggle is the split every file manager and design tool
has.** It does not conflict with D47: that entry governs `Shift` during a transform or a draw and says
nothing about selection clicks. **It is deliberately not the canvas's `Shift`**, which still adds and
removes one layer at a time — on canvas there is no order to take a range *along*. The anchor is the last
row clicked *without* `Shift` and a `Shift`-click does not move it, so a range can be stretched and
pulled back from one end. With no anchor it falls back to toggling rather than doing nothing.

**The range runs along the rows as displayed**, which is what `visible_rows` / `collect_visible_rows`
are for and the one thing here that can rot. A collapsed subtree is not in the range and, while a name
filter is up, neither is anything filtered out. That walk **must match `layers_row` exactly** — same
filter, same forced-open branches, same reversed children — and the two are separate only because one
paints and one does not, so nothing but review keeps them in step. *Change one and change the other in
the same edit; if a third caller ever wants the row list, that is the moment to make `layers_row` read it
rather than mirror it.*

**A selection made on the canvas opens the tree to itself and scrolls to it, once.** Only a *change* of
selection re-opens anything — collapsing a frame the selection sits inside is the user closing something
deliberately — and the scroll happens **only when the row is actually off screen**, recentring a row
already in view moving the whole tree under the pointer for no reason. A click made in the panel updates
`layers_synced_selection` itself. The ancestor walk has no early exit, unlike `matching_rows`: collapse
state is per node and independent, so meeting an ancestor that is already open says nothing about the
ones above it.

The rename is buffered rather than committed per keystroke, so one rename is one undo step. `Enter` and
clicking away keep it, `Escape` discards it, and a name typed empty is discarded too. *Two defects in
the first cut of that field are fixed and neither should come back.* It asked for focus from **inside
itself**, guarded on "does not have focus and nothing else does" — a condition that also holds on the
very frame `Enter` or `Escape` takes focus away, so the field grabbed it straight back and the rename
could never be committed or dismissed; focus is now requested once, at the double-click. And it was
inset by 3px with `TextEdit`'s own default margin on top of that, so the name visibly jumped up and left;
it now uses `rename_field_rect` with the margin zeroed and `vertical_align(Center)`, pinned by
`the_rename_field_sits_where_the_painted_name_sits`, which measures against a real `Align2::LEFT_CENTER`
galley rather than reasoning about the offsets that got it wrong. A press anywhere outside the field also
ends the rename now, because most of this app's surface is hand-painted and senses clicks without ever
taking focus. Auto-scroll ramps its speed with how far into the 28px edge margin the pointer has pushed.
The collapse control is one button that reads the tree's state and does the other thing, rather than two
of which one is always a no-op. **No save-format change and no new operations.**

**D55 — The pivot is baked by the gesture that reads it, never composed into the world transform.
*Resolved.*** Every transform gesture used the centre of the node's box, that being the only point the
model could name. So a shape could not be rigged to swing from a corner, and — the part that was a live
bug — the inspector's rotation and skew fields turned the layer about its **local origin** while the
canvas drag turned it about the box centre, so typing 30° and dragging to 30° put the same shape in two
different places. The old comment claimed it rotated about "the same pivot the canvas handle uses", drift
of exactly the kind this section exists for.

**The decision worth the entry is that the pivot never enters the world-transform pipeline.** A gesture
*reads* it and produces a transform; nothing composes it. `Resolved`, the scene walk, both backends, the
SVG writer, hit-testing and the `Basis`/`Orientation` split are untouched, and `absorb` takes `SetPivot`
as a silent no-op (§6.2). The alternative — a stored origin the world transform is composed *about* —
would have reached into the §6.2 render boundary and the SVG writer for a feature a handful of gestures
read and nothing draws. What baking costs is honest and worth stating: the pivot is not recoverable from
the matrix afterwards, so **every consumer has to remember to ask**, and one that forgets does not fail
loudly — it quietly uses the centre. Animation interpolating about a stored pivot is the seam where
composing would start to pay; *revisit then, and not before.*

**`build::flip` asks whether a pivot has been *placed*, not where one resolves to.** For a shape the two
are the same point — but a rotated group's box is the union of its children's axis-aligned bounds, which
is not the bounding box of their rotated union, so resolving an untouched pivot would move an untouched
flip by a pixel. A feature nobody has used must not change an existing gesture's answer.
`flipping_a_layer_with_a_moved_pivot_mirrors_about_the_pivot` and
`an_unset_pivot_flips_a_rotated_group_exactly_as_before` are the two halves. The same rule of "no change
until asked" is the one Alt-resize broke: scaling about the pivot with the pivot on the centre is
*arithmetically* the old rule, which was read as licence to generalise the gesture — and it is only the
same gesture at that one point. **D60 reverses that half.** `op_set_pivot` dirties only the node, the
`SetProportionsLocked` reading rather than the `SetClip` one (D41).

**Skew is one gesture the pivot deliberately does not generalise — and after D60, resize is the other.**
`Ctrl`-dragging a side holds the side *facing* the dragged one, and that fixed line is the gesture's own
bargain, not a stand-in for a transform origin. The inspector's Skew *field* does turn about the pivot,
because it rebuilds a whole transform rather than tracking an edge. *Keep the two apart.*

**No schema bump, and this one changed no bytes at all.** `NodeDto::pivot` is `#[serde(default,
skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]`, so unlike `proportions_locked` and `clip` the field is absent
from every document nobody has moved a pivot in — additive in the strongest form §5.11 allows. One cost
went the wrong way again: `Node::from_parts` is up to **thirteen** arguments; D41's request for a parts
struct stands. *(It was met on 2026-08-19 by deleting the constructor — D240.)*

The core half is pinned. The inspector rebuild is **not**, for D35's reason. What stands in for a test is
that the rebuild is exact for the identity edit — writing back the angle already showing reproduces the
world transform coefficient for coefficient, because `Basis::of` is an RQ decomposition (D52) and the
pivot is held by construction. *That exactness is the licence for rebuilding the whole transform from two
numbers every frame; if it ever stops holding, the fields start walking the layer as they are scrubbed.*

**The predicted symptom arrived, by a route the prediction did not name — D206.** The exactness never
stopped holding; what broke was the *other* side of the subtraction, the field re-reading its base from a
preview §5.7a relabels by 180° as a mirrored layer crosses ±90°. The Rotation field now composes a delta
onto the matrix from a latched reference instead of rebuilding at all, and the skew field is the only
rebuild left. **Search here first for a scrubbing field that walks its layer, and then read D206.**

**D56 — The Fill and Stroke `+` added paints that were never painted. *Resolved.*** The model held
`Vec<Fill>` and `Vec<Stroke>` from M0, the panels could add rows to both, and
`geometry::stroke_expansion` already maxed over **all** visible strokes — so a second stroke widened the
world bounds `Resolved` caches, and with them the snap targets, zoom-to-fit and the export viewBox, while
contributing not one pixel of ink. `scene::paint_shape` took `.find(|p| p.visible)`. That the bounds knew
about paint the canvas did not draw is the tell worth remembering — *a feature can be half-built in a way
where the maths agrees and only the pixels disagree.* Both lists are now walked in full (§6.3), text
draws one pass per visible fill over the same shaped runs, and §5.3 states the z-order the document had
never committed to: all fills, then all strokes, each in `Vec` order. Two stacks rather than one
interleaved appearance list, affordable only because `StrokeAlign::Outside` covers the outlined-text case
that would otherwise need a stroke *under* a fill; *an appearance list is the change to make if that
stops being true, and it is a model change, not a renderer one.*

The SVG writer was restructured around keeping the ordinary case ordinary. **At most one fill and one
centred stroke still exports as one plain element** — the overwhelming majority of every document —
while several fills, several strokes, or an aligned stroke go to `emit_stacked` (§7). `write_element` is
the single per-kind writer both paths share, and `align_clip` is §6.3's clipped-double-width construction
applied **per stroke**. Gradient slot names carry the paint's index now (`grad-<node>-fill-0`), including
when there is only one: a slot has to name *which* paint, and half-indexing would leave two spellings of
the same thing. `stacked_paints_export_one_element_each_in_paint_order` and
`an_ordinary_shape_still_exports_as_one_element` pin the two paths against each other.

One piece of drift outlived the fix and has since been closed too. `Paint`'s own doc comment read "v1
uses 0..=1 of each; `Vec` is forward-compat", false in both directions — v1 uses as many as you like, and
the `Vec` is load-bearing rather than headroom. It now opens with what the field means and keeps the old
sentence in a closing parenthesis pointing here: the claim is *history of the bug*, not a rule, and a
comment that records what it used to promise is harder to reinstate by accident than one simply deleted.

**D57 — A hidden paint row is faded and its swatch is not. *Keep.*** The eye on a paint row dims the
row to `HIDDEN_OPACITY` (60%, §9.2), and the colour chip is deliberately left out of that: it is
painted at `set_opacity(1.0)` in a nested scope. Fading it too is the obvious reading and it breaks the chip. `Ui::multiply_opacity`
fades everything drawn inside the scope, and `ui::swatch` rounds its corners by painting the leftover
slivers in the **ground** colour (`mask_corners`) — so a translucent mask lets the chip show through it
and the square corners partly reappear. That is the "four visible notches" artifact `mask_corners`
exists to prevent, arriving by a route it cannot defend against, and it would read as a tessellation
bug rather than as an opacity one, since the cause is a scope several lines above the drawing. This is
D32's family, and the general form is the part to keep: *anything whose rounding is done by
overpainting in the ground colour is unsafe inside a faded scope* — `swatch` today, and whatever else
reaches for `mask_corners` tomorrow. `a_dimmed_row_fades_everything_but_the_swatch` holds it as an A/B,
the faded mask under 255 and the escaped one exactly 255, because "the mask is opaque" would also pass
if the dim had silently stopped working — the assertion that proves nothing.

**D58 — `Visuals::selection.stroke` has two jobs, and zeroing it made selected text invisible.
*Resolved.*** `ui::value_field` suppresses the focus outline a focused `TextEdit` frames itself with, and
did so with `Stroke::NONE`. But `selection.stroke.color` is *also* the colour egui repaints **selected
glyphs** in: `paint_text_selection` writes it straight into the galley's own vertices. `Stroke::NONE` is
transparent, so every selected digit became invisible and a field being typed into showed an opaque
`selection.bg_fill` block with nothing legible in it. The picker's hex field was not affected, being a
plain `TextEdit` outside `value_field`, which is why this reported as "the number fields" rather than as
a theme fault. The fix is to zero the **width** and keep the **colour** (`Stroke::new(0.0,
selected_ink)`): a zero-width stroke is skipped by the tessellator.

**The general form is the entry, and it rhymes with D57:** *a `Visuals` field that serves two purposes
cannot be neutralised, only redirected.* `selected_digits_are_never_painted_transparent` is the
regression test, and it has to work the way it does: the selection lives **inside the text mesh** rather
than as a separate shape, so there is nothing to look at but the galley's own vertex alphas. It drives
real pointer and key events to make the selection instead of asserting on the visuals it is testing, and
fails against the old code with exactly the reported symptom.

**The same line was one helper over, and the first fix missed it.** `ui::bare_drag_value` carried the
identical `Stroke::NONE`. It was missed because the report named the number fields, and the review that
caught it was reading the code rather than the report. The test is a two-row table over both rather than
one case each: *a fix to a helper that has a twin is not done until the twin is in the same test*,
because the next reader will find the fixed one and conclude the pattern is safe.

**D59 — A reordering paint row moved nothing but an insertion line. *Resolved.*** The gesture drew a line
where the paint would land and left every row where it was, so nothing said *which* entry was in the air.
The line itself survived this fix and not the next one: **D61** replaces it with a live reorder.
`inspector::carried_unit` draws the dragged entry into an `Order::Tooltip` layer and translates that
layer's shapes with `Context::transform_layer_shapes`, which is egui's own drag-and-drop recipe: the
**visuals** move and the **layout** does not. Vertically only, the list being a column.

**The untouched layout is load-bearing, not a happy side effect.** `paint::Slots` measures the drop
against the rects the rows were actually laid out at, so a slot that collapsed when the drag began would
shift every boundary under the pointer mid-gesture and the paint would land somewhere it was never shown
going. `carrying_a_unit_does_not_reflow_the_list` pins it against the resting layout.

**What it costs is the grip's `Response`.** Everything drawn in one of those layers gets an empty one —
egui's rule rather than a bug: a widget can only be interacted with where it was laid out — so the grip
stops reporting the instant its row starts moving and `drag_stopped` would never arrive. Only the drag's
*start* is read from the grip; the release is read from `pointer.primary_down()` being false, a *state*
rather than an event, so it also cannot be missed by a frame the panel did not draw on.

Two consequences follow from what travels. **The whole entry does**, which for a stroke is both of its
rows: a colour without its weight is not a stroke. And the stroke options menu is closed when a drag
starts, an `Area` being its own layer that would otherwise sit over the slot the row has just left.
`a_carried_units_ink_follows_the_pointer` checks the **difference** between the carried and resting paint
rather than "something was painted near the pointer" — the latter would pass if the row had simply been
laid out there, which is precisely what this mechanism does not do.

**D60 — Alt-resize about the pivot was arithmetically exact and unusable. *Resolved — resize holds the
box's centre, and always will.*** D55 called the generalisation free because the degenerate case was the
old rule coefficient for coefficient. It is free only *at* that case. Reported after living with it: with
the pivot near the dragged edge the far side moved at a huge multiple of the pointer, and with the pivot
*exactly* on a corner Alt-resize did nothing at all.

**The reason is a genuine impossibility, and that is the entry.** Three constraints, any two of which can
be satisfied:

1. the dragged edge tracks the pointer — non-negotiable for a handle;
2. the pivot is the fixed point — what "about the pivot" means;
3. the gain is bounded — usability.

Constraints 1 and 2 together *force* the scale factor to be `|pointer − pivot| / |draggedEdge₀ − pivot|`,
whose denominator goes to zero as the pivot approaches the edge being dragged, so 3 cannot also hold. The
old code's `lever` was exactly that denominator, and its `MIN_EXTENT` guard is what turned the corner
case into a no-op rather than an infinity — the guard was doing its job; the formula was the problem.
Clamping the lever was considered and rejected: it would make the pivot only *approximately* fixed, which
is the geometric-mean fudge D50 already threw out, with a magic constant on top.

So `symmetric` is the box's own centre again, unconditionally. What the pivot still governs is rotation —
the canvas drag, the inspector's rotation *and* skew fields, and the quarter turns — and mirroring.
Resize therefore joins **skew** as the second canvas gesture it deliberately leaves alone, for the reason
D55 gives for the first: both already have a fixed point that is part of their own bargain.

**The wider lesson is about what the tests could and could not say.** *A generalisation that is exact at
the degenerate case can still be wrong everywhere else, and only using it finds that out.* Three unit
tests asserted the new behaviour and all three passed; what a test of that shape cannot report is that
the gain was unusable. `a_moved_pivot_does_not_change_an_alt_resize` now pins the reversal, comparing
whole **transactions** across four pivot placements including both corners — whole transactions rather
than `resized_box`'s output, because the point is that no *caller* consults the pivot either. *Do not
generalise this one again; read the three constraints above first.*

**D61 — Paint-row reordering is live: the rows change places under the pointer. *Resolved.*** D59 gave
the carried row a floating copy but kept the insertion line, and the line was the wrong instrument —
dragging *upward* it is drawn beneath the carried row and therefore invisible. It is gone. The whole list
is drawn in the order it would end up in, so what is on screen during the gesture *is* the result of
dropping.

Three things make that work and each is a trap avoided. **The slot geometry is stable, so it can be
reused across frames.** The target has to be known *before* the rows can be laid out in it, so
`paint::Slots` is carried on `PaintDrag` from the previous frame — exact rather than stale, because
reordering the *contents* of the slots does not move the slots. `Slots` stores real spans rather than a
pitch, so a list whose entries differ in height needs no special case.

**The landing is a pure function of where the pointer is and where the entry is *shown*, which is what
makes it settle instead of oscillate.** `paint::landing(n, shown_at, gap)` carries both off-by-ones: the
entry is already in the list at `shown_at`, so a gap counted against the list *as displayed* is one too
many for anything below it; and slots count from the top of the panel while the model counts from the
bottom of the stack. `PaintDrag::to` is consequently both "where it will land" and "where it is being
shown".

**Widget ids have to follow the paint, not the slot**, and this is the one that bit. egui derives a
widget's id from its position among its parent's children, so reordering the draw order renumbers every
id under the gesture: a hex field being edited loses focus the instant its row moves. `carried_unit`
therefore uses **`UiBuilder::id`, not `id_salt`**, and the distinction is the whole point — a salted
child still folds the parent's running widget counter into its *unique* id (`unique_id =
stable_id.with(next_auto_id_salt)`), and that counter is exactly the positional number being escaped.
`id_salt` was tried first, and `a_units_widget_ids_survive_the_rows_changing_places` failed against it.

`paint::display_order`, `Slots`, `landing` and `reordered` are **list-generic**, and so is
`carried_unit` — but the layers tree will not be taking the same treatment, and **D306 is why**. Five
tests cover them, including `the_shown_order_and_the_committed_order_agree`, which runs every pointer
gap and asserts that the order the panel *shows* is the order a release would *commit* — the two are
computed by different functions, and them agreeing is the property that matters. *Keep that test
regardless; it is about this panel, not about a second caller that is not coming.*

**D306 — The layers tree keeps its insertion line, and unifying the two drags is a decided non-goal.
*Keep.*** D61 above closed by saying the tree "can take the same treatment", and `roadmap.md` carried
that as open work. It is not work. A flat list and a tree are being asked different questions, so the
two drops differing is the shape of the answer rather than an omission. The maintainer raised it from
the panel and settled it there: "the rows stay in place while reordering, showing a blue line between
them. That line is important to know exactly where the row sits."

**A gap cannot name a parent.** `layers::DropTarget` was `{ parent, index, into }` when this was
decided; it is `{ parent, index }` now, and D345 says why the third field went. A gap between two
rows expresses an *index* within one list; it cannot say **which** list that index belongs to, and it
had no way at all to say `into`. So the "inside this frame" case would still need the outline
`drop_hint` draws today, and the panel would be left holding two *unlike* affordances where it
now holds two matched ones. `DROP_LINE_PT` was 1.0 for exactly that reason when this was written; **it
is 2.0 again since D345's follow-ups**, and the outline is still 1pt, so the two are matched by *hue*
rather than by weight — both `color::SELECT`, which is the stronger half of the pairing anyway and the
half this ground actually rests on.

**There is not one row to carry.** `LayerDrag.ids` is a `Vec<NodeId>` — dragging a row that is part of
the selection takes the whole selection, already reduced through `build::outermost` — so "show the
result" has no single carried row once rows from two parents are in flight. `plan_layer_move` has to
*simulate* the affected child lists to plan the operations at all, every index computed against the
list the previous ops leave behind; that is the arithmetic a live reorder would have to run and then
paint on every frame of the gesture, rather than once on release.

**And a live reparent would have to re-indent rows mid-drag**, and open a collapsed frame to show a
landing slot inside it. `drop_spot` offers `into` on a collapsed container as readily as on an
open one, which is only honest because nothing is claiming to show the result. **Spring-loading (D345)
does now open a collapsed frame mid-drag, and it is not this**: it opens on a deliberate one-second
dwell, because the hand asked, and what appears inside is the branch's ordinary rows rather than a
landing slot showing where the carried layer would sit. The paint lists are flat
and always fully visible, so none of this arises there.

**D345 answers the first ground for the *static* case, and reverses none of this.** A gap now names a
*set* of parents — one per level its two rows share — and the pointer's x picks between them, so "a gap
cannot name a parent" no longer holds of a line that is drawn once and moves nothing. That is the
indent gesture, not a live reorder: the rows stay where they are, nothing re-indents, and there is
still exactly one static line, which is the sentence this entry was decided
on. The other two grounds are untouched — a multi-row drag still has no single carried row, and a live
reparent would still have to show a landing slot inside a branch that is not on screen. ⚠️ **A collapsed
frame does open now**, on D345's one-second spring, which is the one clause of this paragraph that has
moved; it is a dwell the hand asks for and it shows the branch rather than the result, so the ground
above survives it intact.

Two facts from the struck `roadmap.md` entry are worth keeping as **evidence rather than as work**.
`inspector::carried_unit`'s salt is `(&'static str, usize)` — an index — where a tree row's identity is
a `NodeId`; that was the entry's stated blocker, and it is real, but it is now moot rather than
pending. And the reparent half was *further along* than the entry claimed: `drop_is_legal` →
`build::can_parent` already refuses an illegal parent, so the depth the entry wanted `paint::landing`
to grow was already computed on the drag side. Also moot.

The paint side stands exactly as it is. `paint::Slots`, `display_order`, `landing`, `reordered` and
`carried_unit` stay where they live; nothing moves out of `paint.rs` or `inspector.rs` for a caller
that is not coming.

⚠️ **The scope is narrow and this entry must not be read wider than it is.** What is decided is *do not
port the paint panels' live-reorder idiom to the layers drag*. It is **not** "the layers panel is
finished", and it does not freeze the drop affordance: the panel is due to become more tree-like under
a spec of its own, and nothing here is an argument against that spec or against changing how a drop is
drawn. *Keep the non-goal, not the drawing. Revisit only if a layers-panel spec asks for a live reorder
by name — in which case the three obstacles above are its brief, not its refusal.*

**D62 — Frames nest. *Resolved.*** `can_parent` allowed an `Artboard` only under the `Root`, so "put this
frame in that one" was inexpressible. A frame is a page, and a page inside a page is how a card, a
component or a state gets expressed — the same shape of mistake as the old "the root parents nothing but
artboards" rule D25 relaxed, and relaxed the same way. A `Group` is still refused, having no box of its
own for a clipping page to be clipped by and because §5.7a's `paint_targets` relies on no frame being
reachable through one. `OpError::ArtboardNesting` became `ArtboardPlacement`.

Four app-side readings of the old rule had to go with it, each the ban leaking somewhere it did not
belong. **`begin_create` forced a frame to the root** whatever it was drawn over, so `create_artboard`
took no `parent_world`; it takes one now, or a nested frame under a moved parent would land offset.
**`move_destination` excluded artboards from hopping** — it may hop now, filtered by `is_within` so a
frame cannot land in itself or in anything it contains (`Reparent` would bounce that as a cycle *after*
the drop outline had promised it). **`artboards()` looked only at the root's children** and now walks the
tree depth-first in child order, which is paint order — load-bearing, because every reader takes the
*last* match and the last of two nested frames is the inner one. And `marquee_candidates` keeps the old
"one level in from the canvas" meaning through a new `root_artboards()`. The layers tree needed nothing —
it asks `can_parent` — and neither did the snapshot.

**D63 — Four chrome corrections from living with the inspector. *Resolved.*** Each is the same kind of
finding: ink that looks interactive and is not.

**The header `+` and the reorder grip were smaller targets than they looked.** Both now sense more than
they paint (`ui::HEAD_ACTION_PAD`, `ui::grip`'s band), and in both cases the neighbour gives up exactly
the band the control takes, overlapping targets not sharing a press. The grip deliberately stops short of
the gap before the colour swatch: taking it would trade a grip that is hard to grab for a swatch that is
hard to click, and the swatch is used on every paint where the grip is used only on a list of two or
more.

**A value field's prefix was inert.** It was a widget laid out ahead of the number, so the leftmost
15–20pt of every field did nothing — and that is where the hand goes, the label being what names the
number. The number's box took over the whole field and the prefix became a galley painted over its left
inset. *Narrowed by D73, then restored by D75*: the inset is reserved space rather than the number's own
padding now, because as padding it made the field grow with its contents.

**`Prefix::Text` is 13pt, not the design's 10.5.** The two kinds of prefix share a column in one panel,
so they are read against each other, and against each other the design's sizes do not match. Measured off
the font atlas: a capital at 10.5 inks 8pt tall where a 15pt Phosphor glyph inks 11. A full match would
want about 14.5, which is *larger* than the number the prefix labels; 13 inks 10pt. The design's own
value is a first draft here, as it was for `HIDDEN_OPACITY` (D57). *Revisit if the two ever stop sharing
a panel.*

**Nothing in the chrome sets `CursorIcon::PointingHand` any more.** Nine call sites. A web page uses the
hand to mean "this is a link"; a panel is all controls, so a cursor that changed on everything said
nothing and flickered constantly. §9.2 records the policy and the two exceptions that survive.

**D64 — An emptied paint panel stayed shut over the next layer's fill. *Resolved.*** The collapse rule
fired only on the transition *into* empty, which meant it could only ever close: walk from a painted
layer to an unpainted one and back, and the collapse the empty layer earned was inherited by the next
layer's fill. `sync_paint_collapse` takes a `fresh` flag now and asserts the resting state outright in
both directions when the subject has moved, keeping the transition rule for the frames in between — so a
hand-collapse holds for as long as you stay on the layer that earned it, and is forgotten on the next
one, because whether *that* layer has a fill is a fact about it rather than a state to inherit.

**D65 — egui's "this rect changed id" warning is off. *Keep.*** It paints a 2px red outline, with no
text, for one frame — and in a debug build it fired every time a Fill or Stroke list got *shorter*,
around the top row of the panel. Reported as a red border flashing on the first stroke.

Not a bug being silenced. The paint panels are drawn top-of-the-stack first, so a list of n shows
`n-1 .. 0` down the column and each row is salted with the index of the paint it shows — which is
deliberate and is what lets a hex field survive a live reorder (D61). Delete a paint and the rect at the
top of the panel keeps its position while the id inside it drops by one, and the id that was there is
gone from the pass entirely: exactly the shape `warn_if_rect_changes_id` looks for. It is right about the
mechanism and wrong about the conclusion — the row at the top *is* a different paint now, and its state
should not carry over. Any index-keyed list that shrinks trips it.

`DebugOptions` is per-context, so there is no narrower switch: the choice is the false positive on every
paint delete or losing the diagnostic. The false positive reads as a rendering fault in the chrome, which
is the more expensive of the two. **`warn_on_id_clash` stays on** — that one catches genuine duplicate
ids, the trap `inspector::panel` documents and the reason every card is salted by title (D39).
`shrinking_a_paint_list_paints_no_warning_outline` guards it as the thing the user sees rather than as
the flag, and shrinks the list rather than growing it, since growth leaves every previous id in the pass
and would have passed with the warning fully armed. *Revisit if egui's heuristic learns about
deliberately renumbered lists.*

**D66 — Scrubbing is half as sensitive, and no longer runs out of screen. *Resolved — the wrap is
unverified on screen.*** Two reports about the same gesture.

**Sensitivity is one scale, not twenty-two literals.** `ui::SCRUB_SCALE` is 0.5 today and is meant to be
turned; §9.2 has why the per-field rates are scaled together rather than re-chosen. Nothing about 0.5 is
principled — it is the starting point the report asked for.

**The drag now wraps the pointer at the window's edge**, which is what Figma, Blender and Photoshop's
scrubby sliders all do: how far a field can be pushed should depend on how long you are willing to drag,
not on how wide the monitor is.

The plumbing was already there — `ViewportCommand::CursorPosition` reaches
`winit::Window::set_cursor_position` through egui-winit — and the real problem is the one pass each
teleport costs. `drag_delta` is the difference between successive pointer positions, so a teleport and a
very fast flick are the same event as far as egui is concerned. **There is no supported way to correct
egui's pointer state after the fact**, so the artefact is not removed: `ui::scrub_speed_for` gives the
field a speed of zero for that one pass, and egui's own `if delta_value != 0.0` guard means nothing is
written and its precision accumulator is untouched. A zero speed rather than a disabled widget, because a
`DragValue` at zero speed is still *dragged* and the gesture survives.

**Which pass that is cannot be predicted, and assuming it could was this feature's one real bug.** The
first version keyed off `cumulative_pass_nr`, zeroing the speed on the pass after the request. Reported
from the Rotation field: the value did a full turn on reaching the edge, flashed a wild `X`/`Y`, then
settled somewhere else entirely — a jump that *stayed*, because a single-layer transform field commits an
absolute `SetTransform` every pass (D51), and the angle it committed was the spike reduced mod 360. The
cause is that the request only reaches the backend after `update` returns, winit then calls
`set_cursor_position`, and the OS posts the move whenever it gets round to it — several passes later,
with the hand's own events interleaved. Size is the signal that does not depend on timing: `Wrap` records
how far the pointer was asked to jump and more than half of that is the teleport, which no hand produces
in one pass. Measured on the way in — the same simulated jump moves the value by ~1120 with the detection
disabled and by exactly zero with it on.

**And the swallowed pass had a second, subtler cost: the field's *precision*.** For exactly the frame the
pointer teleported on, Transform read `411.672736201535258`. Nothing was wrong with the number: a
`DragValue` guesses how many decimals to show from its **speed**, and the pass whose speed had been
borrowed guessed at the ceiling of that formula, fifteen. So the fix is not in the wrap at all — every
scrubbable field pins its own precision (§9.2), worth doing on its own account since a coordinate never
wanted three decimals either. `ui::number` trims trailing zeros, so `160` stays `160` where a bare
`max_decimals` would have left `160.00` on the swallow pass and `160.0` on every other.

Two smaller things fell out. **Only the x axis wraps**; that was caught by a test on the first attempt,
because the field under test sits within a trigger band of the window's *top*, so a purely horizontal
drag teleported vertically the moment it began. And **an unanswered request gives up** after
`WRAP_GIVE_UP` passes: a platform that refuses to move the cursor reports nothing back, and without a
deadline one such request would block every later wrap.

Load-bearing, and it cost ten seconds a test to find: **never nest two `Context` accessors.**
`ctx.data_mut(|d| d.insert_temp(id, ctx.cumulative_pass_nr()))` deadlocks — both take the context's own
lock, and epaint's debug build panics with "Failed to acquire RwLock read after 10s" where a release
build would simply hang. Read first, then write.

*Five tests cover it, each checked to fail without the thing it defends — the last reports "showed 15
decimals", which is the screenshot. The OS actually moving the pointer is the backend's half and cannot
be seen headlessly. Revisit `WRAP_EDGE` (24pt) and whether the teleport should hide the cursor, once it
has been used.*

**D67 — A drop between layers drew a line on every sibling. *Resolved.*** The layer tree has two drop
affordances meaning opposite things: a line *between* rows says the layer lands beside them, an outline
*round* a row says it lands inside it. `paint_drop_hint` ran once per row, and the rule it used to pick
an edge was `target_index > row_index ? top : bottom` — which never asked whether the boundary was this
row's. On a list of two that meant an edge above *and* below the row under the pointer, which reads as an
outline. Reported as the tree offering to put a layer inside an ordinary layer, which has no inside.

`layers::drop_line` was the rule as an `Option<RowEdge>`, extracted so
`every_drop_position_draws_exactly_one_line` could exercise it, an `OndinApp` being unbuildable in a
test at the time (D35, a reason D303 has since retired). Against the old rule it reported four
boundaries where one was wanted. **Both are gone and the rule is structural now** (D345): the hint is painted once,
after the walk, and a boundary is named by its position *on screen*, so no row evaluates anything and
the same boundary cannot be reached from two child lists at all.

**The first fix let both rows either side of a boundary name it**, on the reasoning that a row's bottom
edge *is* the next row's top edge. Both halves of that were wrong, and each was reported in turn.

It is not one line: two strokes composite their antialiased fringes into a heavier one, and where the two
coordinates fall either side of a device pixel the band doubles outright — a line that changed weight as
it moved down the list. So each boundary has exactly one owner and the test asserts a count of one.

And a row's bottom edge is **not** the next row's top edge, because `item_spacing.y` is 1: they are a gap
apart. Between siblings the single owner hid that, but the boundary a frame shares with its topmost child
belongs to two different lists at once — the top of the frame's own, and beside the frame in its parent's
— so it has an owner in each, and the two drew a pixel apart. `drop_line_y` centres it in the gap, where
both readings agree by construction; `both_sides_of_a_boundary_put_the_line_in_the_same_place` reports
"66 from above, 67 from below" against the edge-based version.

Twice in one feature, then, the same lesson as D32 and D44: "the same place" in points is not the same
place in pixels, and adjacent boxes in a layout do not share an edge unless they were built to.
`snap_across` handles the pixel half, with the parity case spelled out because a 1pt line is an odd
number of device pixels at 100% and an even number at 200% (D9). The line was taken to 1pt rather than 2
here so it weighed the same as the "inside" outline; **it is 2pt again since D345's follow-ups**, that
pairing argument having turned out to be weaker than it looked — it compared two strokes of equal
length, where a 1pt outline runs the whole way round a 26pt row and a 2pt line is one short horizontal
run. The parity note stands whichever the width is, and is the half of this entry that was never about
the pairing.

**D68 — A rectangle's stroke can sit on one side, and a side is an open path. *Resolved.*** The design's
Stroke card carries a sides selector and the model had nothing to put in it. `Stroke::sides` is that
field (§5.3); the two decisions worth keeping are how narrow it is and what a "side" actually is.

**The boxes only, and narrower than it looks.** An ellipse, a polygon, a star, a path and a line have no
nameable top edge, so `geometry::stroke_sides_apply` answers for `Rect` and — since D144 — `Artboard`,
and nothing else. As with alignment the stored value is never rewritten to suit the kind —
`geometry::effective_sides(kind, stroke)` is the question every consumer asks, so a `sides` that cannot
be honoured draws the closed outline while the number the user set survives. `All` is deliberately *not*
four full-width sides: it is the one case that keeps the closed outline, so its corners still join, and a
caller that treated the two as equivalent would lose every join.

**A side owns half of each corner it touches.** `geometry::side_path` splits each corner arc at its 45°
midpoint, which is what CSS does with `border-top` against `border-radius` and the only cut on which two
sides of different widths meet cleanly; cutting at the straight edge leaves a rounded rect's corners
bare, which reads as four gaps rather than a border. The radii come back off
`RoundedRect::from_rect(…).radii()` rather than being clamped a second time locally.
`the_four_sides_of_a_square_rect_tile_its_outline` and
`a_rounded_corner_is_split_between_the_two_sides_that_share_it` pin it by arithmetic rather than by eye —
four lengths summing to the perimeter, and the top side *starting inside* the corner — because four lines
round a rectangle is exactly the drawing where an overlap reads as a tessellation bug rather than a wrong
number.

Two consequences are load-bearing. `scene::paint_stroke` takes **`path` and `shape` separately** — what
gets stroked and what the alignment clip is built from — because "inside" is a question about the rect
and not about the edge. For the same reason `closed` is asked of the **kind** rather than measured off
`path`: a side path is open and the shape it belongs to is not. The SVG writer mirrors the split exactly,
which is why its `plain` fast path now also demands `effective_sides(…).is_all()` (§7).
`a_per_side_stroke_inks_only_that_side` closes the loop through the CPU raster.

**Bounds pay for it with one scalar, deliberately.** `stroke_expansion` asks
`effective_sides(kind, s).max_width(s.width)`, so the thickest side is what the box allows for and a
stroke that is 0 on every side no longer inflates it at all. It is still **one number for all four
sides** rather than per-side insets, because the callers inflate a rect uniformly and bounds may be
generous but must never be tight.

**It takes the kind, and that is not tidiness.** `stroke_expansion` is the only bounds consumer that
reads `sides`, so it is the only one that can *disagree with what gets painted* — and its first version,
taking `&Paint` alone, did: on a kind with no nameable sides an all-zero `Custom` reported **no reach at
all** while the walk stroked the whole outline at full width. Ink outside its own reported bounds is
precisely the clipped-by-its-own-frame and culled-a-frame-early failure. Only a hand-edited file can set
that up today — but two functions that must agree should be unable to disagree rather than merely
unlikely to, and passing the kind is what makes it structural rather than a load-time normalisation a
later operation could bypass. `bounds_allow_for_a_stroke_the_walk_will_actually_draw` pins both halves,
because either one alone passes with the bug in place.

**One measured trap, and it is a kurbo reading.** `BezPath::is_empty()` means "contains no *segments*",
so a path holding a lone `MoveTo` is empty by it. `side_path` shipped its first version asking that
question and produced sides made of two `MoveTo`s that drew nothing; what `append_arc` needs to know is
whether the pen has been put down, which is `elements().is_empty()`. Caught by measuring, not by review:
the tiling test reported a perimeter of `-0`. *Do not "simplify" that back.*

**Join is now the third of these gates.** `geometry::stroke_join_applies` answers true for `Rect`,
`Polygon`, `Star` and `Path`, false for an `Ellipse` — four cubics meeting tangentially — and false for a
`Line`. It is gated on the **kind and not on the geometry**, which is the part to defend: a fully rounded
rect has no sharp corner either, but gating on the radii would make the control appear and disappear
while the radius field was being scrubbed. `a_join_is_offered_only_where_there_is_a_corner_to_shape`
asserts that the rounded rect *keeps* the control and says why, so the next reader tightening this finds
the argument rather than a hole. The residual is one field: `miter_limit` is not gated, so a stored
`Miter` on an ellipse still draws the mitre angle, dimmed with the Join row it sits inside. *Hide it with
the row.*

One thing was deliberately still missing when this was written: **frames drew no strokes at all**, which
was the reason above for excluding `Artboard` here, and the verdict was *build it*. Built — D144.
`stroke_join_applies` gained `Artboard` and `Text` at the same time.

**D69 — The dash mode is classified from the pattern, never stored beside it. *Keep.*** The panel's four
cells (Solid / Dotted / Dashed / Custom) need to know which mode a stroke is in, and the classifier that
existed compared `dashes.first()` against `width * 1.5`. That worked only while the numbers were derived
from the width, which they stopped being the moment they could be typed: a 12-long dash on a 9px stroke
came back as *dotted* and lit the wrong cell. The obvious repair is to store the mode — and it buys a
second source of truth, a label that can disagree with the pattern it names, which is the same bug in a
better hiding place.

So nothing is stored. `Stroke::dash_style` reads `[]` as Solid, `[len, _]` with `len <= 0` as Dotted,
any other pair as Dashed and anything longer as Custom — the *shape* of the value and never its size,
so it is **invariant under width**. `the_dash_style_does_not_depend_on_the_stroke_width` asserts that at
four widths from 0.5 to 40, and reports the original symptom when it fails. `DashStyle` lives in core
with `ALL` and `label()` because it is what the panel iterates, but it is a projection of `dashes` and
holds nothing.

A dot is therefore a **zero-length dash**, `[0, s]`, which is what makes `s` unambiguously
centre-to-centre spacing rather than a gap. Two consequences follow that a model cannot answer, and
both are resolved at the render boundary instead of written back into the field (§6.3). A zero-length
dash draws nothing under `Cap::Butt` or `Cap::Square`, so those two get a square dot one width long with
the gap shortened to match: the **period** is preserved, so the spacing field means one thing under all
three caps. The alternative on the table was to leave the gap alone, which makes `spacing` mean the gap
under two caps and the period under the third — a field with two meanings is worse than a substitution.
`a_dotted_stroke_survives_a_cap_that_cannot_draw_a_zero_length_dash` pins the period, not just the
numbers. And **fit to corners is a flag honoured at render time**, neither a one-off write-back into
`dashes` nor a recompute on every resize. Write it back and the toggle reads as on while being true only
until the shape next changes size; recompute it and the fields stop showing what was typed. A flag costs
the path's `perimeter` at render and export time and fits against the whole path rather than per subpath
— exact for a rect, which is the shape the control exists for, approximate for a multi-subpath path.
`fitting_a_dash_pattern_divides_the_outline_a_whole_number_of_times` asserts that the same stroke fits
two different rects to two different patterns, which is precisely the assertion a write-back fails.

*Do not add a `dash_mode` field.* The moment one exists it can disagree with `dashes`, and that is the
bug this replaced wearing a different hat.

**D70 — The Scale tool is built, and it does not multiply the transform. *Resolved — §5.6's sentence
saying it would is replaced.*** The model permits a transform-multiplying scale and the tool must not use
it: §5.6's own opening rule is that a layer's size lives in one place, and a scale carried in the
transform is a stroke that thickens when its group is resized. So Scale is a second *verb* on the
existing geometry recursion rather than second arithmetic. `tools::Scaling` is `Geometry` or
`Photographic`, and `tools::scale_scalars` is the one extra step, multiplying what a resize deliberately
leaves alone: stroke widths, dash patterns, `dash_offset`, `Custom` per-side widths, corner radii and font
size. A gesture rather than a preference, because you resize a card for layout and scale an icon
photographically in the same session.

Four details are each a way to get it wrong. The factor is the **geometric mean** `sqrt(|sx·sy|)`, a
stroke width having no non-uniform reading, and the mean is the choice that degenerates to exactly `s`
under a uniform scale; it is absolute, so a mirror scales the numbers instead of negating them.
`Scaling::scalar` returns `None` within `SCALE_NOOP` (1e-9) of 1, and not `f64::EPSILON`, because the
factors come out of a square root: a tighter test makes every plain move and every lean drag a phantom
stroke rewrite into the undo stack. **Corner radii scale from the stored radius**, never re-derived from
the new box — `local_path` clamps to half the shorter side and the stored number can legitimately exceed
it, so re-deriving would silently square off a clamped corner — and a square corner emits no operation at
all. And **auto-sized text takes the font size but never a box**: `scale_geometry`'s early return is
about its *box*, which does not exist, so `scale_scalars` runs ahead of that return.

The chrome is Select's, on purpose. `Tool::Scale` sits in rail slot three with Select and Hand rather
than among the shape tools, keyed `K`; `Tool::selects()` is the one statement of what the two tools share
(§9.4); the drag is proportional by default because `canvas::keep_ratio` treats the tool as "locked", so
Shift releases it exactly as on a proportion-locked layer; and `Bitmap::Scale` is the **rest** cursor
only, since over a handle the directional arrow says which way the box grows. This is also what finally
retired the resize argument run D41 asked about — `tools::Resize` carries the three terms of a handle
drag, and `scaling` would have been the ninth positional argument.

**D71 — A Group Colors row counts layers, not uses, and its button selects them. *Resolved.*** The panel
listed a colour and let you edit it but never let you *find* it. Each row now shows a match count and a
`scan` reticle that selects those layers (§9.2). The load-bearing part is which number that is:
`ColorUse::uses` counts paint slots and `ColorUse::nodes` the distinct layers, and **they differ** — a
shape whose fill and stroke are the same colour is two uses and one layer. The count beside the button
and the selection the button makes come from the same field, so they cannot report different things;
`uses` is still what orders the census. *Do not "tidy" the label back onto `uses`.* `nodes` is carried
out of the one census walk rather than re-derived, which is what cost `ColorUse` its `Copy`; the
alternative was walking the tree once per row per frame. *A **gradient** row is the same row over a
different key — D135.*

Two decisions the design left open are made in `inspector::select_by_color`. The selection is
**replaced**, and `entered_group` cleared with it: a selection that also kept the frame the census was
taken inside would put that frame's bounds round the result and make the next drag move everything, and
the new members can be anywhere in the tree. And ~~**locked layers are included** — they carry the
colour, so the census counted them, and a button whose selection came out smaller than the number
printed beside it would be reporting one thing and doing another. What a lock refuses is dragging, not
selecting.~~

🚨 **Reversed by the maintainer on 2026-09-10 — the objection was right and the cure was not**
(D748). The ruling is *"a locked layer shouldn't be selected in any way except clicking on the layers
panel"*, and this is a panel but not **the** panel: unlike a row click it is not deliberate about the
layer, one click on a colour swatch putting locked layers into a selection `delete_selection` reads
no lock over. **The button was reporting one thing and doing another either way**, because the thing
it silently did was arm `Delete` — so the paragraph above diagnosed a real failure and prescribed the
larger half of it. What answers the objection without the selection is the **message**: *"Selected 2
of 3 layers with this colour — 1 locked"*, which says more than the honest-by-omission version ever
did. The census row's own count is untouched and must stay so — it is still `ColorUse::nodes`, the
**layers carrying the colour**, which is a fact about the document rather than a claim about what a
click will take; narrowing it would answer *"where is this colour"* with a lie in the other
direction, and the *"do not tidy the label back onto `uses`"* rule above is untouched by any of this.
D748 has the predicate
(`may_select_in_bulk`, D746's renamed) and the flips; the two paragraphs above are otherwise
unchanged and still decide what the button does to the selection it *does* make.

**D72 — A control that can be collapsed while it holds a value needs a third button state. *Resolved —
§9.4's "shown, not merely opened" rule is replaced.*** The stroke panel's sides row was shown whenever
the button was on *or* `sides != All`, on the reasoning that a control carrying a value the user set must
not be hideable. What that misses is that the button is then left with nothing to do: it sat lit beside a
row it could not close. The version that *did* close the row put the stroke back on the whole outline,
throwing the setting away. Both are what two `bool`s force — `(active, enabled)` cannot say *off while
holding a value*.

So `ui::FieldButton` is an enum — `Off | On | Set | Disabled` — replacing the pair at all eighteen call
sites. **`Set` is `On`'s border over `Off`'s fill**: the ordinary field ground and a muted glyph with the
accent hairline round it, so a collapsed control can say "there is a setting in here, and it is not open"
without lying about either half. The border is the whole of the signal and the ground reading as *off* is
the whole of the point, so *do not give `Set` a wash*, and do not fold it back into a `bool`.

`inspector::sides_button_state(applies, open, sides)` is the rule, a free function so it can be tested:
`Set` is reachable in exactly one combination — closed, and not on every side — and
`a_collapsed_sides_selector_still_says_it_is_set` pins it. The tooltip in that state names the setting,
since the row that would otherwise say so is shut.

The cost is real and recorded in §9.4: `OndinApp::stroke_sides_open` is **no longer pure chrome**. Losing
it collapses a row that has a value in it, where before the value forced the row open. Acceptable rather
than incidental, because the button's border still declares the setting from the collapsed state.
`forget_stroke_chrome`'s guarantee is unchanged: it can close a panel and it cannot lose a setting.

**D73 — The stroke weight field grew with its contents, and its prefix's padding was why. *Resolved.***
Two symptoms with one cause. The prefix's inset was applied as `ui.spacing_mut().button_padding.x`, and
`button_padding` is a `Vec2` egui applies to **both** sides. The wanted left inset therefore arrived with
an identical 22px of dead space on the right: **44 of the stroke weight field's 68px content box was
padding, and the digits had 24.** Past four of them the resting face of a `DragValue` — a `Button` with
`TextWrapMode::Extend` — simply grew, and the frame, the card and the inspector's width grew with it. The
same family as D45: an egui spacing field means something slightly other than what the caller wanted.

The fix makes the inset **reserved space rather than padding** — `ui.add_space(inset)`, a `DragValue`
allocated at `full - inset` with `button_padding.x` at zero, and the prefix galley painted back into the
strip. The digits get ~46px instead of 24, measured rather than assumed:
`a_value_field_holds_its_width_up_to_the_largest_value_it_accepts` sweeps 1 → `MAX_STROKE_WIDTH` at both
widths the Stroke panel uses, and fails at exactly 1000 with the old padding put back.

**The attempt that failed is the part to keep**, because it is the obvious fix and egui offers the API
for it. `DragValue::prefix` takes atoms, so the widget would size around its own prefix. But atoms are
laid out by the **resting `Button` only** — the keyboard face is a bare `TextEdit` that never sees them —
so the glyph vanished and the digits jumped left the moment the field took focus.
`a_value_fields_prefix_survives_being_typed_into` catches the glyph going missing where the jump test
would not. *Painting the galley ourselves is what makes the prefix survive both faces of a `DragValue`.*

One cost was given up knowingly and has since been bought back: **the reserved strip is not part of the
`DragValue`, so it does not scrub for free.** For one round a drag had to start on the number — a
narrower version of D63's own finding — and D75 restores the gesture with a second claimant. *The strip
being outside the `DragValue` is still what forces that plumbing; do not read D75 as making the padding
safe again.*

And a cap: **`ui::MAX_STROKE_WIDTH` (10 000)** bounds the stroke weight, the four per-side widths and the
dash lengths. It is a cap on the *field, not on the model* — any positive width is a legal
`Stroke::width` — and explicitly **not** a layout allowance, since `value_field` no longer grows at any
magnitude. `tools::scale_scalars` can still multiply a width past it and deliberately does: clamping in
the Scale tool would silently distort a photographic scale (D70).

**D74 — Choosing an end cap closed the popover the combo was sitting in. *Resolved.*** The cap
`ComboBox`'s list is its own `Area`, below the stroke options popover, so a click on one of its items
missed `menu.contains_pointer()` and the dismiss read that as "clicked outside". You pick a cap in order
to look at it.

The dismiss asks about **layer order** instead of containment: `ctx.pointer_interact_pos()` →
`ctx.layer_id_at(p)` → `l.order >= egui::Order::Foreground`. The popover and the combo's list are both
`Foreground` while the panels and the canvas are `Middle` and below, so "the click landed on something
floating above the page" covers the combo's list, any list the popover grows later, and nothing in the
inspector — which makes it the right question rather than merely the working one. Asking egui whether a
popup is open **cannot** work: `Memory::any_popup_open` is `pub(crate)`, and the combo closes itself in
the same frame the item is clicked, so the answer afterwards is the same `false` that caused the bug.
*Do not "simplify" this into naming the combo's id.*

Escape still closes both at once, deliberately — what Escape means everywhere else in the app
(`input::escape`'s ladder) rather than a stack unwound one layer at a time.

**D75 — The prefix scrubs again, and a drag lands on a whole number. *Resolved.*** D73 gave up the
prefix's share of the scrub as the price of a field that stops growing; the request was to have it back,
a field where the number scrubs and its own label does not meaning having to remember which apps start
the drag on the icon (Figma) and which on the digits (most others).

**`value_field` therefore owns its number** — `value: &mut N` and a `Scrub` in place of a finished
`DragValue`. It has to: the reserved strip is outside the `DragValue`'s box, which is exactly why the
padding is no longer doubled, so the only way that strip can scrub is a **second claimant** sensing the
drag there. Generic over egui's `Numeric` so the `f32` opacity fields and the `f64` rest read alike, all
`f64` inside, written back only on a real change so an `f32` field is not rewritten every frame with the
round trip's error. §9.2 has the rest of the seam, including the strip's response `union`ed into the
number's so neither a caller nor the edit valve can tell the two halves apart.

**Two egui routes are closed, and both look tidier than the one taken.** Re-registering the number's id
over a wider rect is the obvious trick, and egui would cooperate as far as its bookkeeping goes. But
`Context::create_widget` is `pub(crate)`, and `Ui::interact` sets `rect` as well, which trips the clash
warning and paints D76's overlay over every field. *The second-claimant design is not a preference;
neither door is open.*

**Whole units under the hand, any number from the keyboard**, at the user's request and applied to X, Y,
W, H, rotation and skew: a coordinate dragged to 109.25 is precision the number does not mean, it reaches
the saved file, and it shows in the panel. Typing is untouched, and the rounding is keyed on the drag
rather than on focus — "round it unless it is being typed into" would round a typed 1.5 away the moment
the field lost focus. The same rule went to everything else integral by nature. Line height stayed
fractional at `Scrub::fine(0.02, 2)`, where whole units would give 1, 2, 3 and nothing usable between.

`Scrub` carries the speed and the rounding rule **together** because `value_field` needs both, and it
collected six hand-written copies of `if resp.dragged() || resp.drag_stopped() { v = v.round() }` from
the call sites. *Do not fold it back into a bare speed: the rule has to reach the place the prefix drag
is applied, which is inside `value_field`.*

**Why `decimals` is stated rather than inferred** is the subtle half. A `DragValue` rounds its *own* drag
to a precision derived from the speed, while the prefix strip's drag is applied by `value_field` and
would keep every digit the pointer produced — a 37px drag came out `109` on the digits and `109.25` on
the label. One stated number settles both paths.
`a_scrub_starting_on_the_prefix_moves_the_value_the_same_way` runs the same drag from both halves, and
`a_whole_field_still_accepts_a_typed_fraction` pins that the clamp comes *after* the rounding.

**One field did not fit the rule, and that is where the rule stops.** The star's inner-ratio percentage
took `Scrub::whole(0.25)` with the rest, and the comment above it says why that is wrong: fractions of a
percent are the point, the default sits at the golden section 38.2%, and rounding this field to integers
had *already* made that value unreachable by dragging once before — measured, a drag from 38.2 went to
38.0 on its first step. It is `Scrub::fine(0.25, 1)`.

**A ratio is not an integer by nature**, and that is the boundary of "everything integral by nature": a
count, a coordinate, a length and an angle are quantities you say in whole units; a *ratio between two
lengths* is not. `a_fine_field_keeps_the_tenths_a_whole_one_destroys` pins it as the contrast rather than
as one assertion, because `fine` behaving correctly proves nothing about which rule the field was given.

**D76 — The prefix strip's id was the row's, not the field's, and two fields shared it. *Resolved.***
The strip's first id was `ui.id().with("prefix-scrub")`, and **`Ui::id` is the *containing* Ui's** —
which every field in a `horizontal` row shares. egui lit the whole Transform and Stroke panels with its
clash overlay and the strips were inert behind it. `ui.auto_id_with("prefix-scrub")` is the fix —
`next_auto_id` is positional within the Ui, so it distinguishes what the container's id cannot.

**The overlay was hiding a live bug rather than being it**, which is the part worth recording. Writing
the negative check turned up a second symptom: with the shared id, dragging the *second* field's prefix
moved the *first* field's number. X/Y and W/H were genuinely cross-wired, not merely complaining.

Two guards, each checked to fail with the old id restored. `a_row_of_value_fields_has_no_id_clash`
asserts through the **overlay** rather than by comparing two ids, because the overlay is what the user
saw; it first asserts `warn_on_id_clash` is *enabled*, so it cannot pass because the diagnostic was off
(D65). `each_fields_prefix_scrubs_only_its_own_number` drags the second field's prefix and asserts the
first does not move, which a clash test alone would miss, two ids being able to be distinct and still
plumbed to the wrong value.

*Any second widget put inside a `field_row` wants `auto_id_with`: `ui.id().with(…)` reads like the
widget's own id and is the container's.* This is the fourth egui surprise to cost a round on this one
panel — after D45's `Frame`-versus-`ComboBox` hairline, `ComboBox::width` being the painted width, and
`button_padding` being symmetric (D73) — and the first in a register other than spacing.

**D77 — Five paragraph attributes are spanned and the rest are node-level; the character defaults are
boxed. *Deviation from `typography-plan.md`, since resolved in the plan's favour — its stated reason for
declining was too strong, and D163 has what the investigation that overturned it also got wrong.***
*(`typography-plan.md` is deleted, as `images.md` and `per-run-color.md` are: it was the live scope
document until the work landed, and the entries citing it here are its whole surviving record.)* The
plan asked for paragraph attributes to use the same span mechanism as character ones — "One mechanism,
not two" — with setters snapping the range outward to `\n` boundaries. For a long time they did not, and
this entry recorded that as the deviation; `ParaSpans` is now built (§5.4) and carries the spacing, the
first-line indent, `hanging` and the two block indents. **The class really is split across two
mechanisms**, which is the cost the plan wanted to avoid and which is paid deliberately: three of the
node-level survivors (`TextWrapMode`, `WordBreak`, `OverflowWrap`) *are* per-range parley properties and
could be spanned, but nobody sets those per paragraph, and the three that are genuinely one value per
layout — named two paragraphs down — cannot be spanned at all. What keeps the split honest rather than
arbitrary is that `ParaAttr`'s membership states it in the type.

**The reason recorded here until 2026-08-04 was that parley lays a node out as one `Layout` and
`Alignment`, `IndentOptions` and the base direction are "one value per layout", so a paragraph span would
be a value the renderer had to ignore. Read against parley 0.11 that is half wrong, and the half that is
wrong is most of the feature.** `Layout::break_lines` hands back a `BreakLines` driver whose
`BreakerState` carries **per-line** `line_x`, `line_max_advance`, `line_y` and `line_max_height`, settable
before each `break_next()`. Those are not cosmetic: `line_x` becomes the line's
`metrics.inline_min_coord` and `line_x + line_max_advance` its `inline_max_coord`, which is the coordinate
space `align_impl` aligns *within*, and the same metrics `Selection::from_point`, word selection and
selection geometry all read. So a per-paragraph **measure** — a start indent, an end
indent, a hanging first line — is expressible on one `Layout` rather than needing a cursor model rebuilt
across N layouts. **"And the caret follows it for free", recorded here until 2026-08-04, was true of
three of parley's four x-readers and false of the fourth**: `Cursor::geometry` reads `metrics.offset`
alone, so `TextEdit` corrects the caret itself (D165).

`text::break_lines` **already drove the breaker one line at a time**, for the line-limit and
height-limit case, so the hook this needed was already in the file. What each line has to know is which
paragraph it starts in — and the answer recorded here, "the previous line's `text_range().end`", is not
available from a breaker mid-break. See D163, where it is an index instead.

What is genuinely one value per layout, and therefore still cannot be spanned: the **`Alignment`**
passed to `Layout::align` (and with it `Justify`, which works by adjusting cluster advances), and the
**bidi base direction**. Note that Figma does not offer per-paragraph alignment either, so this is not
the gap it sounds like.
