*The standing instruction, honoured by what was built and still the rule for anything added: `ParaSpans`
may carry only what a single `Layout` can honour — the indents and the spacing — and must **not** carry
alignment or direction. The original hazard is what makes the set's membership the whole design: a span
type holding a value the renderer must ignore is worse than not being able to say it, because then the
model lies about what is on screen.*

Separately, `NodeKind::Text::style` is **boxed**. Measured: `TextStyle` is 288 bytes where the whole of
`NodeKind`'s next-largest variant is 176, and a Rust enum is as large as its largest variant — so
unboxed it made *every* node in the document, a line and a rect included, 288 bytes bigger than it needs
to be (`Node` went 344 → 624). One pointer indirection on read, paid only by text nodes, buys that back,
and `Box<T>` serializes as `T` so nothing on disk changed. This is what `clippy::large_enum_variant`
was reporting, and the honest fix rather than an `#[allow]`.

**D163 — Per-paragraph attributes are built, and the route the investigation was surest of does not
exist. *Resolved — stage 1 of paragraph layout; stage 2 is D164 and stage 3, lists, is in
`roadmap.md`.*** Two of D77's claims about parley were wrong outright — the one this heading names, and
its account of how `line_x` reaches the ink — and a third mistake was made here rather than there, in the
reading of `\r\n`.

`ParaSpans` sits on `NodeKind::Text`, `ParaAttr` carries exactly the five attributes D77 said would be
the whole design, `ParagraphStyle` gained `indent_start`/`indent_end`, and the span machinery is one
generic `Spans<A>` over a `SpanAttr` — so every invariant, the boundary rule, `edited`, `normalize`,
`clamped`, `scaled` and `values_in`/`shared_in` are written once for both scopes. The serde output is
byte-identical to before, a newtype over a type parameter serializing exactly as one over a concrete
type. The model and the renderer went first and the panel later, which is the safe half of that
asymmetry: a value a file can hold and the canvas honours, rather than a control writing into nothing.

**The ops.** `SetText` gained a `para_spans` field for the identical reason it carries `spans` — a
`ParaSpans` entry is a byte range too, so one character typed anywhere before a paragraph moves the byte
its override is keyed to. `SetParagraphSpans` is the twin of `SetTextSpans`. `TextSession::original` is a
3-tuple so a session that changed only paragraph overrides is not thrown away on close. The renderer's
text-op helper is six arms now rather than five, which keeps a field added to the kind from being
preserved by five of them and reset by the sixth.

**A line cannot learn its paragraph from the previous line's `text_range().end`.** D77 and the roadmap
entry both said it could. `BreakLines` exposes no committed line while it is breaking — `self.lines` is
private, and `layout.lines()` only reads back after `Drop` has swapped them in — and
`YieldData::LineBreak` carries no range at all. So a line learns its paragraph by **index**:
`break_lines` counts `BreakReason::Explicit` exactly as `y_map` already did, into a table
`text::Paragraphs` builds by scanning the content for hard-break characters. That is deliberately two
mechanisms on one edge, the thing D77 warned about, and what makes it payable is that the seam is one
integer wide with a tripwire across it — `paragraph_starts_agree_with_parleys_hard_breaks` shapes eleven
strings and asserts the scan and parley agree. *Do not replace the scan with something that reads a range
off the breaker; there is none to read.*

**`\r\n` is two hard breaks in parley, with an empty paragraph between them**, and that test failed the
first time it ran because the scanner had coalesced it. CRLF is one grapheme cluster under UAX #29, so
one cluster and one break was the obvious reading, and it is not parley's. Reading it the "correct" way
puts every paragraph of a CRLF document on its neighbour's indent.

**`line_x` reaches the ink through `inline_min_coord`, not through `metrics.offset`.** `align_impl`
assigns `line.metrics.offset = line.indent` and a glyph's x is `run offset + inline_min_coord +
metrics.offset`, so the indent arrives by the coordinate space and not by the offset. **That distinction
is exactly what cost the caret**, which reads the offset and not the space — D165. It works out
identically under alignment because parley computes `free_space = (inline_max − inline_min) − indent −
advance + trailing_whitespace`.

**The `break_next` assertion is switched off, not clamped around, and that is required rather than
tidy.** `break_lines` hands parley `set_layout_max_advance(f32::INFINITY)`, which is the assertion's own
escape hatch. An outdenting first line needs a measure **wider** than the box in order to keep its right
edge at the box's; clamping the measure to the wrap width would drag the wrap point left along with the
ink. `an_outdenting_first_line_keeps_the_right_edge` was confirmed to **panic** inside parley when the
value is the wrap width. *That line looks like an oversight and is the feature.*

**The double-count trap is resolved by deleting the other mechanism.** `Layout::set_text_indent` is no
longer called at all: the first-line indent, `hanging` and both block indents are one piece of arithmetic
in `text::line_geometry`. The `break_all_lines` fast path went with it, per-paragraph geometry having to
be set before each `break_next`.

**`TextSizing::Auto` was decided rather than left to fall out of the arithmetic.** A start indent there
is a plain x offset and the emergent box grows by it; an end indent is **inert**, there being no wrap
width for it to narrow. `an_auto_width_node_grows_by_a_start_indent_and_ignores_an_end_one` pins both
halves, and the second is the one worth having: "inert" is indistinguishable from "forgotten" without an
assertion.

**`spacing` is now space-*before*, resolved from the paragraph *below* the break**, which reproduces the
old node-level meaning exactly while letting one paragraph ask for its own.

**One defect found in passing and left open at the time, in *both* scopes — now fixed.**
`op_set_paragraph_style` re-states the paragraph spans against the new defaults, mirroring
`op_set_text_style`, and neither inverse carried the span list — so the re-statement was one-way. Node
default `indent_start` 0, a span puts one paragraph at 10, the user sets the node default to 10: the span
is dropped, correctly and invisibly; undo restored the default to 0 and that paragraph sprang back to 0
rather than to its own 10.

**`SetTextStyle` and `SetParagraphStyle` now carry `spans: Option<…>`, and the inverse always carries
`Some`.** `None` means "re-state", which is what every forward caller means and the only thing any could
compute. `Some` installs exactly that list, clamped to the content, so a hand-assembled op cannot point
past the string. The pair round-trips indefinitely: redo is the undo's own inverse and carries the
dropped-empty list explicitly. `undo_restores_a_span_the_defaults_made_redundant` states both scopes in
one test, each half confirmed to fail on its own.

**Two things fell out of doing it.** The re-statement is now `Spans::restated`, a method rather than
three lines at each of four call sites in two crates — the two style ops and the **render preview** of
each. `RenderOverrides::absorb` used to set the style and leave the list alone, so a preview's *kind*
disagreed with its own commit's on any node with spans.

**And a claim made while fixing that was wrong, which is worth recording because it is the tempting
one.** `assert_preview_matches_commit` would *not* have caught it, and was checked: the re-statement only
drops spans that have become **echoes** of the new defaults, so the resolved style of every byte is
identical either way and nothing about the drawing can differ — by construction, not by luck. The
divergence is in the model alone, and the model is read: `TypeSubject::read` goes through `display_node`,
so a stale list there is a value the panel's next write builds on.
`a_restyle_preview_restates_the_spans_like_its_commit` therefore asserts on the override's **kind**
rather than on a recording of the scene. *A preview may diverge from its commit in ways no picture
shows.*

**D164 — A paragraph write is not a character write with a wider range, and the whole-node path is shut
while a session is open. *Resolved — stage 2 of paragraph layout.*** The Paragraph tab's "Spacing &
indent" section is now five paragraph-scoped controls that can all read mixed, and
`text::paragraph_bounds` is the range they act on: the selection snapped outward to hard breaks, `pub` so
the panel and `TextEdit::paragraph_range` ask one function, the hard-break set being parley's.

**Two rules inside that snap are places the obvious formula gives an answer a user would call a bug.** A
selection ending exactly on a boundary does not reach the paragraph after it: selecting a whole paragraph
*including* its newline puts `end` on the next paragraph's first byte, and taking that literally styles a
paragraph the user can see is unselected. A bare caret in that same position *does* belong to the
paragraph after it, which is why the empty case is answered separately rather than by one formula. And a
paragraph with no bytes of its own reaches back over its own break — the one after a trailing newline
owns nothing, so its range would be empty, `Spans::set` would no-op and the control would be dead on
exactly the paragraph somebody had just made with Enter; the byte it reaches back over is the same byte
`text::Paragraphs` clamps that paragraph's lookup to, so the two clamps are one rule read from either
end.

**So the scope question is answered three ways differently from the character one**: the range is snapped
rather than the selection; **a bare caret is partial**, where for a character attribute it is not, since
a caret has no characters to restyle but is unambiguously inside one paragraph; and **any open session is
partial, a select-all included**. `style_paragraph` has no `pending` counterpart for the same reason. The
cost is that the node's paragraph *defaults* are reachable only with the layer selected and no session
running — while you are editing, you are editing paragraphs.

**That third rule was built the other way first, and the reversal is what this entry is for.** A snapped
range covering the whole node counted as *not* partial, so select-all-and-set wrote the defaults and
dropped the overrides — better model hygiene by some distance. It was reversed because it walks into a
hazard that already exists in the character scope: `text_session_restyled` deliberately lets the live
editor's own span lists win over the document's, so the *clearing* half of a whole-node write is put
straight back on the very next frame. Reachable as "select every paragraph, set the indent to 0, and one
of them does not move". Mirroring the character scope's rule keeps the non-partial path from ever running
while a session is open, so the whole class is avoided rather than guarded against. *Do not "tidy"
`TypeSubject::read`'s `partial = !range.is_empty()` into a test for the whole node; that is the bug,
restored.*

**The same hazard was live in the character scope, and stage 2 did not touch it. It is fixed now.**
`apply_char_attrs`'s non-partial branch runs when a session has a bare caret; it commits
`char_attrs_tx`, which clears that attribute's spans over the whole node, and then called
`text_session_restyled`, which puts the editor's uncleared lists back.

**`text_session_restyled_after(&tx)` is the per-caller distinction, and the transaction is the witness
rather than a flag.** A boolean at each call site can be passed wrongly; a `SetTextSpans` sitting in the
transaction cannot, and it answers **per scope** — a character write must not make the editor adopt the
document's *paragraph* list, which may hold uncommitted session work of its own. The three entry points
share one body, so "who wins about the spans" is asked in exactly one place.

**It adopts the list from the op, not from the document.** A live session's content is a commit ahead of
the document's, so what `SetTextSpans` actually installed was clamped to the shorter committed string;
the list *in* the transaction was computed from the editor's own and is keyed to the editor's bytes.

**One thing reading the fix found that the original report did not contain.** Both character sites commit
first, and `Session::try_commit` clears a *gesture's* preview while a valved control's drag frames have
already replaced the session's preview with a gesture one — so after the commit the canvas could be left
reading the document. `text_session_restyled_after` therefore ends with `preview_session`. That is safe
only *because* its callers have just committed: folding the refresh into the shared body breaks
`valve_paragraph`, which reaches the plain re-style **mid-drag** — D109's shape from a new direction.

**Still not reproduced by hand** (D35), so the wiring rests on reading. What is pinned is the decision:
`stated_spans` is a free function and `a_transaction_states_only_the_scopes_it_carries` covers the
per-scope rule, the says-nothing case, and the other-node case — confirmed to fail against a
one-flag-for-both implementation, which is the way this would most plausibly have been written.

**`para_attrs_tx` is `char_attrs_tx`'s twin down to the order of its two operations**, and that order is
load-bearing: `op_set_paragraph_style` re-states the span list against the new defaults, and the spans op
then installs the list computed here, normalized against those same defaults. Reversing them would
install a list and then have the style op recompute it against the old ones.

**The hanging pair needed a fourth reader, not three.** `shown_paragraph` resolves at the range's *start*
— over a non-partial range the **first** paragraph. So with a hanging override on the second paragraph
and none on the first, the pair drew "first-line" lit, the click's value comparison saw no change and
wrote nothing while that paragraph plainly hung. `para_ragged` is the question the guard needed, arriving
through the same door `ragged` did in the other scope: `mixed` is about what a control may *say*,
`ragged` about whether there is anything to flatten.
`the_hanging_pair_has_something_to_do_when_the_paragraphs_disagree` pins the two apart, because they
agree in every case except the broken one.

**The two block-indent icons were read out of the font atlas before they were trusted, and the reading
can go the other way.** Each glyph is a bar against one edge with the arrow pointing **at** that bar, so
the bar is the margin the number is measured from and swapping the two constants would put each number on
the opposite margin with nothing on screen to show it. The first version of
`the_block_indent_arrows_bar_the_edge_they_measure_from` asserted one glyph reversed equals the other and
failed on a pair that is perfectly correct: the outlines are mirrored but the antialiasing is not
(27/167/12 against 35/180/16 on the same row). **Column ink is the property the claim is about**, and the
test asserts that plus the two names not pointing at one codepoint — which
`every_named_icon_has_a_glyph_behind_it` would happily pass.

**D165 — The caret drew where the text used to be, because parley measures a caret in a frame with no
line indent. *Resolved — a regression of D163's stage 1, and it corrects a claim made there.***
**Three of parley's four x-readers add the line's start edge and the fourth does not.**
`Cursor::from_point` opens with `metrics.offset + metrics.inline_min_coord`, so the hit test followed the
indent; `Selection::geometry_with` opens with the same sum; a glyph run is positioned at `run offset +
inline_min_coord + metrics.offset`. But `Cursor::geometry` goes through `cursor_rect`, which measures
from `Cluster::visual_offset` — the sum of `line.metrics.offset` and the cluster advances, never
`inline_min_coord`. The caret alone drew in an un-indented frame.

**A regression rather than a gap in a new feature**, which is why the user found it and no gate did: the
first-line indent went in through `Layout::set_text_indent`, which lands in `metrics.offset` — which
`visual_offset` *does* include. So the caret followed a first-line indent for nothing until D163 moved
the amount to `line_x`. `TextEdit::caret_rect` now adds the caret line's `inline_min_coord`.

**The same omission breaks vertical movement, and worse — nobody reported that one.**
`Selection::move_lines` seeds its sticky column from the frame *without* the start edge and then lands
the caret with `Cursor::from_point`, which reads it. The two frames differ by exactly `inline_min_coord`,
so the landing point came out one indent left of where the caret visually was — down from x=115 in a
60px-indented paragraph landed at x=60. So `move_up`/`move_down` no longer call parley's
`previous_line`/`next_line`: a private `move_line` measures the column with `caret_x`, finds the target
line and lands with `Cursor::from_point`, falling back to `line_start`/`line_end` past either end. **The
sticky column had to become ours**: `Selection::h_pos` is private *and* seeded from the wrong frame.
`sticky_x` is invalidated in one place, a new `caret_moved()` that also clears `pending`.

**`caret_line_index` was a containment search first, and it returned the line above.** The first line
whose `block_min_coord..block_max_coord` contains the caret's y is what parley's own `line_for_offset`
does, and that range spans ascent to descent, so the line boxes **overlap** whenever the line height is
tighter than the two together — Inter at 20pt being 24.4 of type in a 20pt box, the ordinary case rather
than a corner. An existing test caught it at once. It now asks one monotonic question instead: the
**last** line whose `block_min_coord` is at or above the caret's y.

*Do not "simplify" `caret_rect` back onto parley's rectangle, and do not apply the same correction to
`selection_rects`.* `Selection::geometry` was already right — correcting both would push the highlight
one indent past the ink. `the_selection_highlight_already_follows_an_indent` turns that from a claim
about parley's source into a claim about behaviour; `the_caret_sits_inside_a_paragraph_indent` covers the
block indent *and* the first-line indent, and reads 0 with the correction removed.
`a_short_line_does_not_pull_the_column_in` **asserts on the byte offset rather than on x** for a reason
worth keeping: twelve `c`s measure 133.2 where twelve `a`s measure 131.25, so an x comparison needs a
tolerance wide enough to hide the bug it is testing for — its first version had exactly that and failed
on correct behaviour.

**D166 — The caret drew one whole gap too high in every spaced paragraph, because a shift belongs to a
line and not to a y. *Resolved — this one is ours, not parley's, and it is older than D163.*** Found
immediately after D165, by writing the test that was only meant to de-risk it. `YMap::breaks` is keyed on
the line-**box** top — the running sum of `line_height`, which D79 chose over `block_min_coord` — and
`YMap::to_local` decided a point's paragraph spacing by comparing the point against those keys. But
`caret_rect` and `selection_rects` both mapped *parley rectangles* through it, and a rectangle's `y0` is
`block_min_coord`: the line's **ink** top, which sits *above* the box top whenever the leading is
negative. The ink top therefore fell short of its own break and picked up the *previous* paragraph's
shift. Measured before the fix, three 20pt paragraphs 40pt apart put the caret's top at local y −2.0,
18.0, 78.0: steps of 20 and 60 where every step should be 60. The highlight is the second face of the
same fault, one rectangle carrying two different shifts. **Glyph drawing was never affected**, which is
why neither the export nor the scene walk ever showed it: `extract` maps *baselines*, and a baseline
always sits below its own line-box top.

**A scalar boundary cannot fix this**, and re-keying `breaks` on `block_min_coord` is what D79 already
rejected. The deeper reason is that consecutive lines' ink ranges *overlap*: there is no y that separates
one line's descender from the next line's ascender — the same overlap that made a containment search
return the wrong line in D165. The line **index** does distinguish them, so `breaks` is now `Vec<(f64,
usize, f64)>`. *The standing rule: `to_local` decides from a coordinate and must not be handed the top or
bottom of a box. `to_local_on_line` is for those, and both callers already know their line.*
`vertical_motion_survives_paragraph_spacing` covers both faces and was confirmed to fail with the numbers
above. **Do not delete it as redundant with the click tests**: paragraph spacing is the only thing that
makes layout y and local y differ at all.

**The asymmetry this fix exposed is closed too, and the 2.2pt this entry first claimed for it was the
tail of a 40pt fault.** Sweeping the whole band with a throwaway probe showed the arithmetic putting
local y 22.5 through 40 on the paragraph's first line while the pointer was in empty space 20pt above it,
and 42.5 through 57.5 on its **second**. The deeper reason is not the ink at all: a paragraph gap is
space that exists in local y and **does not exist in layout y**, where the two lines it separates are
adjacent. So the points inside one have no layout y to be given. *An inverse by subtraction was the wrong
shape of function, not a mis-tuned one.*

`YMap` is one direction now. `Shaped::layout_y` is the way back: line **boxes** tile local space, so
which box a point is in or nearest to is exact, and the hit test becomes the tiling's own inverse. A
point in a gap takes the nearer of the two lines bounding it, ties going to the line above. What stays
approximate is only the y handed back, and it is parley's. Nothing above is reversed — re-keying `breaks`
on `block_min_coord` is still wrong — but *"not a re-keying, in either direction"* was one conclusion too
many: the resolution moved out of the map rather than into a different key.
`a_click_in_a_paragraph_gap_lands_on_a_line_that_bounds_it` asserts the whole band with the measured
numbers in its failure messages, and no existing click test disagreed with the change.

**D78 — Box trim tightens the box and never moves the ink; `Fixed` keeps meaning the typed box.
*Resolved — the plan's two open decisions, decided.***

*Where is the node?* Trimming does **not** move the local origin. `TextLayout::origin` is an offset from
the node's local origin to the top-left of its box; `local_bounds` returns `Rect::from_origin_size(origin,
size)` and every consumer — align, distribute, snapping, the size badge, the selection quad, the W/H
fields, the export viewBox — reads that one function. The glyphs keep their own coordinates, so
**toggling trim tightens the box around ink that does not move**, which is what makes trim useful for
aligning one label's cap height to another's. Moving the origin instead would have shifted every text
node in every saved file. **That default has not moved and must not**, so a reader who finds `#[default]
None` and concludes the feature is off is half right: new text *is* trimmed, and D199 has where that is
authored.

*What does `TextSizing::Fixed(size)` mean?* The box the user typed, full stop. What trim changes under
`Fixed` is the **datum vertical alignment measures**: the cap-height extent rather than the line box.
That keeps the sizing control and the trim control, which sit next to each other, from having a hidden
interaction. `trimming_tightens_the_box_without_moving_the_ink` was checked to fail both ways.

**D79 — Paragraph spacing, box trim and vertical alignment are one y map, applied at both boundaries.
*Resolved, after getting it wrong once.*** All three move text *after* parley has broken the lines.
`text::YMap` is a table of cumulative offsets keyed by hard break, plus a constant shift.

It was built split, and the split was a bug. The constant half was computed inside `extract` on a *local
clone* of the map, so the drawing was right and the hit test silently kept a zero shift: a click in a
bottom-aligned box landed a line out. Computing the whole map in `shape` and storing it on the shaped
layout is the fix.

A second bug came out of the same test. The spacing table was keyed on `LineMetrics::block_min_coord`,
which reads like the line box's top and is the line's **ink** extent: for a 10px line box it measured −1
to 11. Keying on it put each paragraph's shift one baseline early. A running sum of `line_height` is the
line box's top.

**Both guards had to be rewritten before they caught anything**, which is the part worth recording. The
first pair aimed each click at the *last* line, and passed with the inverse map removed entirely, because
a y below the layout's own height clamps to the final line anyway. Aiming at the **middle** paragraph,
and at the **first** of two bottom-aligned lines, is what discriminates. *A caret test that targets the
end of the text proves nothing; parley clamps.*

**The key is right; what it does not survive is being handed an *ink* coordinate** (D166). Nothing above
is reversed: re-keying on `block_min_coord` is still wrong, and is now known to be *unfixable* that way.

**"One function used twice, in opposite directions" is no longer literally true, and that is the
correction rather than a loss.** `YMap` is the *forward* direction only, because a paragraph gap is space
that exists in local y and not in layout y at all; `Shaped::layout_y` resolves which line's box a point
is in and then asks `YMap` for that line's shift. What the original requirement was protecting is intact
and in fact stronger: there is still exactly one statement of *how far* the text moved, and both
boundaries read it.

**D80 — The case transform is length-preserving only. *Deviation, kept with a stated limit.***
`typography-plan.md` calls text case "small: transform the string before shaping". It is small only
because of this restriction: byte indices are the currency of the span list, the caret and every hit
test, so a transform that changed them would need a full offset map threaded through all three — its
own project, and one with a caret bug in it for every case it got wrong. `text::case_char` therefore
declines any character whose cased form is a different number of UTF-8 bytes: `ß` stays `ß` under
UPPERCASE, `İ` stays `İ` under lowercase. That covers the whole of Latin, Greek and Cyrillic bar a
handful of characters, and `a_case_transform_that_would_change_the_byte_count_is_declined` pins the
behaviour so it is a known limit rather than a surprise. *The fix, when it is wanted, is a
shaped-byte → content-byte table built alongside the transformed string — not a wider `case_char`.*

**D81 — One `<text>` per line, one `<tspan>` per run. *Resolved.*** This entry recorded the writer's
single unwrapped `<text>` as a deviation for as long as the attribute model existed; it is now built, and
the paragraphs below are kept because the *mechanism* this entry proposed was wrong.

`text::export_lines` is the seam, returning one `ExportLine` per line — its `x`, its baseline, and its
`ExportRun`s. The writer emits one `<text>` per line carrying the node's ink and one `<tspan>` per run
carrying the face, the spacing and the decorations (`run_attrs`). Two things improved beyond the stated
goal: the baseline is now the **shaped** one where it used to be a `y = font_size` guess, and
`text-anchor` is gone — alignment, indent and justification are all in the line's own `x`, so the writer
no longer asks a viewer to re-align text it re-shaped itself.

**Three claims in the original entry were wrong, each found by reading rather than assuming.** "The
shaped layout is already in `Resolved`" is true and not sufficient: `TextLayout.runs` holds glyph
**ids**, which do not map back to characters through ligatures and reordering, and it has no line
structure at all. parley has no per-`GlyphRun` byte range either — only `Run::text_range`, which covers
the whole run across every line it was broken over. What works is `Line::text_range` intersected with the
style-run boundaries, which is fully determined and needs nothing from the brush; comparing those ranges
against the laid-out string is sound because `cased_text` preserves byte length by construction. And
re-shaping beats widening `GlyphRun`: a `String` per run on every relayout would serve a consumer that
runs once (§5.9 permits it outside a hot path).

`a_wrapped_text_node_exports_one_text_element_per_line` and `a_styled_span_exports_as_its_own_tspan` are
the two assertions the old writer fails. The `agreed` collapse came along unchanged in kind: it resolves
an underline disagreeing with a strikethrough on the **same** run, which a `<tspan>` per run does not
separate.

**D162 — The last two Text deferrals: a trimmed label's handles, and a line height that could not say
what Auto was worth. *Resolved.***

**The trim mismatch is an *auto* box's alone, and D158's note about it was half wrong.** `text::box_of`
gives an `Auto` or `AutoHeight` node `(0, trim_top)` as its origin — the box *is* the visible extent, so
tightening it moves no ink (D78) — while `Fixed(size)` is the authored box at the local origin. So a
fixed node's handles already sat exactly on the box the gesture edits, and only the auto case was
measuring from a datum the handles never drew.

`anchored_size` is now `anchored_box` and returns a **`Rect`** — the box the handles were drawn on,
origin included. `resize_to_handle` shifts the pointer into that box's space, and adds the same inset
back to the translate on the way out, because the box being *written* starts at the local origin even
when the box being *measured* did not. Both halves are load-bearing and each fails the test on its own:
dropping the shift leaves the dragged edge 3.4px off the pointer, dropping the inset moves the held edge
by the same amount. Zero for every other kind and for fixed text, so this is one code path rather than a
text branch. `dragging_the_top_of_a_trimmed_label_holds_the_bottom_the_handles_drew` asserts the
**held** edge. **Since D199 this path is the ordinary case rather than a rare one** — trim was off by
default when it was written, and every newly created text node is now `Auto` + `CapToBaseline` — so it is
where a resize regression would show up first.

**Line height's Auto state showed the word "Auto" over an unscrubbable zero**, which said the state twice
and the value never. Worse, leaving Auto seeded a round `120%`, so clicking the unit chip to *look* at
the number in percent re-spaced the lines of any face whose leading was not 1.2. Both halves were the
same missing fact: what Auto resolves to is the face's own metrics (`LineHeight::MetricsRelative(1.0)`),
knowable only from a shaped layout.

`TextLayout` now carries `line_height`, the **first line's** box height from `LineMetrics::line_height` —
the one number a single field can honestly show, since a node whose runs differ in size has a different
height per line. Not the block coordinates, which measure the line's ink and read smaller (D147).
`TypeSubject` snapshots it from the *preview* layout, so the readout tracks a live edit, and
`next_line_height` is the cycle's decision as a free function because `OndinApp` cannot be built
headlessly.

`a_layout_reports_the_line_height_its_first_line_actually_got` pins the read, and its own first version
was wrong in a way worth recording: the fixture's `style()` sets `Em(1.0)`, so reading 20.0 back off a
20px font looked like Inter's leading and was the em. The assertion needs `line_height: None` spelled
out.

**The same question does not arise for tracking, and that is why only one field got this.** Letter and
word spacing have the same two units and the same absence-is-a-state shape, but their absent value is a
face's own spacing, which is zero in effectively every family. Leading was the odd one out because
`MetricsRelative(1.0)` is a *number the font chose* and nothing on the row could name it.

**D187 — Every pasted image became a layer called "Pasted image". *Resolved.*** A label describing how
the layer got here rather than what it is, and not even a unique one. `LoadedImage::name` is
`Option<String>` now, `Some(filename)` for a file placed or dropped and `None` for a paste.
`canvas::image_layer_name(doc, parent, given)` answers the given name or the next free `"Image N"`,
through `ondin_core::free_name`, and both creation paths call it. Asked **here rather than at the load,
because this is where the siblings are**: `free_name` takes the lowest free number among them, so
pasting after deleting "Image 2" fills that hole, and the question cannot be put before the parent is
chosen. It is a **free function over the `Document`** rather than a method, which is what makes it
testable at all.

**`CreateNode { name: None }` was the wrong answer even though it numbers for free.** It would have
called the layer "Rectangle 4": an image is a *fill* on a Rect rather than a kind of its own, and
`created_name` can see only the kind. So this is the one generated name core does not resolve, which
§5.7b now says outright.

**`"Image"` is deliberately *not* added to `GENERATED_NAMES`.** That list is pinned as the inverse of
`NodeKind::default_name` — "would we have written this string" — so a stem no kind produces would make it
a lie in the one direction it is ever asked in. Nothing needs it there: duplicating "Image 2" reads the
number off the *name* through `naming::numbered`. The only thing `is_generated` decides alone is
`copy_name`'s **unnumbered** arm, and a bare "Image" is a name the user typed.

`LoadedImage::label()` is the separate thing a status message uses — "Replaced with hero.png", falling
back to "the pasted image" — because a one-line message has no business naming a layer that does not
exist yet. `canvas::image_name_tests` asserts the **stem** rather than the shape of the name: flipping it
to "Rectangle" — the naive fix — fails outright.

**D188 — The image popover closed itself whenever the colour picker beside it was touched.
*Resolved 2026-08-16, reviewed on the machine and accepted.*** The dismissal read only where the pointer
is *now*, and **a click away is a press away *and* a release away, with only the second half asked**. A
scrub begun on one of the card's own rows routinely ends out over the canvas.
`press_began_away(ctx, id, card, head)` is the missing term, a free function both `image_menu_popup` and
`stroke_menu_popup` call.

Two details are load-bearing. It is hoisted **outside** the `&&` chain, because it records as well as
answers and short-circuiting it would mean it never saw the press frame. And it has to *remember* the
press at all: egui clears `press_origin` on the very frame the button comes up, which is the only frame
this is ever asked, so a version reading `press_origin` directly answers "away" for every release there
has ever been — the term present, compiling, and doing nothing. That version fails the first assertion of
`a_drag_that_began_on_the_card_is_never_a_click_away`. Nothing recorded — the first press of a session —
counts as away, or a fresh popover would be undismissable. It asks the **rects** rather than
`contains_pointer`, since where a press *was* is not something a later layer can change.

**And that term was not the reported bug — `on_picker` was.** Four hypotheses died to measurement before
an instrumented run named it, which is the part worth keeping. egui stops calling a press-release a click
at exactly **6.0pt** of travel (binary-searched), so a scrub leaving the card is never a click;
`ctx.dragged_id()` is already `None` on the frame a drag ends; and none of the other five writers of
`image_menu` fires on a scrub release. The log answered it in one run: the press was at **(412, 500)**
with the card at `[[622, 237] - [896, 788]]` — *left* of the card, in the lane `picker_lane_right` shoves
the detached colour picker into while this popover is open. The picker is an `egui::Window` at
`Order::Middle`: below this `Area`, so `over_overlay` says no, and a separate layer, so `on_menu` says
no. Every term was satisfied by a click made *in the picker*.

**The exemption already existed and this card was not using it.** `on_picker` is documented in
`dismissed_by_click` against this exact symptom, and the image and stroke popovers had hand-rolled three
of that rule's terms rather than calling it. The rule moved to `panels/mod.rs` and all three cards share
it, `press_began_away` joining as its sixth term. The stroke popover had the identical hole, unreported.
**The general lesson: a fourth hand-rolled copy of a rule with six exemptions gets three of them, and the
term that was missing had already been paid for by a report against another card.**

*One thing is verified by reading rather than by test:* the three lines computing `on_picker` at each
call site. Flipping them to `false` leaves the whole suite green — only the decision function is
reachable, and it is tested at seven cases.

The typography popup answers the same shape of question a different way, through a gesture term (§9.2)
rather than the press origin, and both now sit on one function, so there is no longer a second mechanism
for a fourth popover to copy.

**D189 — Thumbnails, and the entry point a chip must not share with the canvas. *Built and tested
2026-08-16; reviewed on the machine and accepted the same day, with the three changes recorded
below.*** The last build item of `images.md`'s v1 scope, and the two
call sites had been carrying notes saying so — the paint row's 16pt chip, whose comment already read
"it is where the thumbnail goes when there is one to draw", and the layers row, where an image layer
is a `Rect` and therefore drew `icon::SQUARE` like any other rectangle.

**The open question was ownership, and the answer is the split `fonts::FontPreviews` already makes
(D160): `ondin-render` owns the pixels and `ondin-app` owns the texture.** The store gains
`ImageStore::thumbnail(&ImageRef, edge) -> Option<ImageData>`, plus `ThumbKey` and `THUMB_BASE` on
the crate's re-exports and the two free functions `square_of` / `un_orient` kept private to the
module; the app gains `thumbs::ImageThumbs`, a field on `OndinApp` beside `previews`, and nothing
frees anything because a `TextureHandle` frees on drop. It is **not**
on `CanvasRenderer`: `CanvasRenderer::images()` is deliberately a `&self` handle, and a mutable
texture cache behind it would put every panel on `images_mut()`, which exists for one caller for a
stated reason.

**The load-bearing decision is that a thumbnail does not go through `ImageStore::pixels`, and it is a
correction to a premise `images.md` recorded.** That file said `pixels` "now returns adjusted pixels,
so a thumbnail gets the adjustment for free". Free is wrong and the direction is the point: `pixels`
calls `note_ask`, and the same ask on two consecutive frames promotes the entry to a
**full-resolution** pass (`SETTLED_FRAMES`, D186). A sixteen-point chip asking that question would
spend a twelve-megapixel pass on a picture nothing is drawing at size — including one on a hidden
layer or scrolled off the canvas — and would hold `wants_frame()` true on a row's behalf, so the app
would go on repainting for it. `thumbnail` touches neither clock, so a panel may ask as often as it
likes and change nothing. The second premise was wrong the same way: the *buffer* `small` holds is
not "close to what a thumbnail wants" — it is at `PREVIEW_EDGE = 1024`, about 4 MB for a 16-point
chip, and `evict_derived` drops it whenever no derived entry references the picture, which a
thumbnail deliberately never creates. What is reusable is `reduced(src, edge)`, the *function*,
already parameterized by edge.

**`THUMB_BASE = 128`, cut once per `ImageId`** into `Adjusted::thumb_base`, a third map beside
`entries` and `small` under the same `Mutex`. `reduced` is O(width × height) whatever its target, so
per-thumbnail reduction would put a full-size box filter in the layers panel on every frame of a
scrub — a scrub walks a new `ThumbKey` each frame. Per picture, the per-frame work is a 128×128 read
instead. **The base is evicted with the *picture*** (`sources.contains_key(id)`), not with the last
adjustment of it, which is one step further out than `small`'s rule: applying `small`'s rule here
would discard it every `prepare` and re-cut it the next frame for ever, since a thumbnail leaves no
derived entry to keep it alive. `a_thumbnail_base_goes_when_its_picture_does_and_not_before` pins
that.

**Reduce, then adjust — the opposite order to the canvas, and they do not commute**, the transfer
table being nonlinear. Deliberate: at sixteen points the difference is invisible, and it runs the
adjustment over a few hundred pixels instead of over twelve million. **Orientation and the crop
are applied and the framing mode is not** — two layers sharing an `ImageId` with different crops are
two different thumbnails, which is why `ThumbKey` is not the id, while Fill/Fit/Crop/Tile are
statements about the shape's box and a chip has no box. The crop is read in the *oriented* picture's
space, per §5.5a's normalization rule. What a chip does instead of a mode is **centre-crop, not
fit**: fitting 16:9 into the square draws a sliver with ground above and below, and a column of those
reads as a list of slivers rather than as pictures.

**`ThumbKey` collapses the neutral adjustment to one key**, which is the corner `AdjustKey`'s doc
comment says it is safe from *because the neutral value never reaches it* — in a thumbnail key it
does. `-0.0` and `0.0` are equal with different bits, so keying on the raw bits would give one
drawing two textures and neither would ever hit.

**`ImageThumbs` sweeps where `FontPreviews` does not.** Families are bounded; a thumb key holds seven
scrubbable floats, so one exposure drag walks hundreds of keys, each one texture uploaded and never
asked for again. `KEEP_PASSES = 3`, swept at the top of a pass, so the steady state during a scrub is
four textures — three carried in plus the pass's own. The rest is D160's: `FRAME_BUDGET = 2 ms`, the
one-upload-a-pass progress guarantee, and `request_repaint` on a deferral.

**A missing picture and a thumbnail are mutually exclusive by construction, not by a rule anyone
maintains**: `thumbnail` answers `None` for a picture the store cannot draw, and the row falls back
to the kind glyph D179 has already coloured amber. `layers::picture_of` is narrower than
`picture_missing` beside it on purpose — first visible *fill* only, no strokes and no artboard
background — because that function asks whether the layer is broken, where a stroke counts, and this
one asks what it looks like, where a stroke is nothing in a 16-point square.

Four numbers are load-bearing and none of them is guessable from the source. `THUMB = 16.0` points in
a `ROW_H = 26.0` row — **20 first, and 16 after the tree was seen on the machine**: the argument for
the larger number was that a thumbnail wants to be recognisable and 20 is roughly the row's height,
and in a real tree it simply read as too heavy. 16 is also the size of the 15pt glyph it replaces, so
an image row no longer sits taller than every other row in the column. The caret is centred 19pt left
of `icon_x` with an 11pt glyph and the name starts at `icon_x + 15`, so 16 clears the caret by 5.5 and
the name by 7, against 3.5 and 5 at 20 — nothing in the column forced either. What is worth keeping is
the ceiling, and it is unchanged: at 26, the row's own height, the square would come within half a
point of the caret, so "as tall as the row" was never available here whatever it looks like elsewhere.
The device edge is in the key, so a display-scale change invalidates by
*missing* rather than through a `ppp` field — unlike `FontPreviews`, which clears on a scale change.
**The layers thumbnail is rounded to `THUMB_RADIUS = 3`, which reverses what this entry said.** It
recorded the thumbnail as square, on the grounds that `mask_corners` works by painting the leftover
corner in the ground colour and a row's ground is three colours (resting, hovered, selected), so the
same treatment would show notches in the wrong grey on two rows out of three. Every word of that is
true of `mask_corners` and none of it binds here: `epaint::RectShape` carries its own `corner_radius`
through tessellation and takes its texture through `with_texture`, so a rounded textured rect needs to
know nothing about what is behind it — `Painter::image` is that same shape with a radius of zero. *A
stated impossibility that was a property of the first tool reached for rather than of the row.* 3
where the inspector's chip is masked to 4, and deliberately not shared: the chip's radius belongs to
`ui::swatch` and every colour in the app wears it, so matching them would mean restyling every swatch
or special-casing the one that holds a picture. And the new `ui::Swatch::Picture(TextureId)` draws
over the checkerboard
**untinted** — `Color32::WHITE` is `image`'s identity multiplier, not a colour — while the layers row
tints to `from_white_alpha(102)` for a dimmed layer, matching the 40% its glyph and name take.

Eleven new tests. Three on the render side were flipped against the implementation somebody would
actually have written and each failed with the right message: `un_orient` written as the forward map
rather than its inverse — invisible without an asymmetric fixture, because the forward map for one
quarter turn *is* the inverse for three; an origin-crop instead of a centre-crop; and a `thumbnail`
that reuses `pixels()`, caught by counting what it left in the adjustment cache. The app-side sweep
test was flipped both ways, against no sweep (ten textures) and against a `clear()` (one), where the
correct answer is four.

*What acceptance covers, and it covers the drawing.* The tree and the paint row were reviewed on
the machine the same day and accepted with **three changes, all of them above**: `THUMB` from 20 to
16, the 3px radius in place of the square, and the chip's tooltip shortened from "This paint is an
image" to **"Image paint"** — the chip draws the picture now, so the old sentence was explaining a
grey square that no longer exists. The author then went over the result of those three, so the 16pt
rounded thumbnail in the layers row and the picture in the paint row's chip are **seen and accepted**
rather than argued from painter calls. What is still only *read* is the arithmetic, and that is a
limit on the suite and not on the review: the clearances above come off the painter calls rather than
off a measurement. **Writable now and unwritten** — this said `paint_row` and the layers row *cannot*
be driven, which stopped being true on 2026-08-22 (D303); nothing about the review's verdict depends
on it either way.
*Keep.* The one number the review did not touch is the decision to draw the picture in the glyph's
column rather than beside it, which is where to look first if a row ever reads wrong again.

**D190 — The image row's card became two, and the adjustment fields got a meter that grows from the
centre. *Built and tested 2026-08-16; revised the same day after a review on the machine, then run and
reviewed in full and accepted — the split, both buttons, both cards, the row gap, the centre-origin
meter and the right-aligned value. The zero tick and the strip's 28px height were built after that look
and have since been confirmed on the machine too, so nothing here is outstanding.
**Partly superseded by D268 (2026-08-20):** the two cards became two *tabs* of one card, the two
buttons and the mode strip left the row entirely, and the 28px height went with them — `TRACK_CELL`
is the card's version of the same `segmented` trap. The reason for the split survives the move
unchanged, which is why it is worth reading here; the placement does not. **Three names below no
longer exist** and are left in place as the record of what was measured: `image_fit_strip` is
`image_card_anchor` and draws no strip, `IMAGE_STRIP_CELL` is gone, and
`an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges` is replaced by
`the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height`.***
The regenerated `design/Editor.dc.html` no
longer has one card with three sections. It has two `sc-if` blocks — `framePopOpen` and `adjPopOpen` — and a second
line of `1fr 28px 28px`. Framing and colour are two jobs done at two different times, and stacking
them made a card tall enough that the section you wanted was usually below the one you did not, which
is the height `images.md` had already flagged as reasoned about rather than lived with.

**`panels::inspector::ImageCard { Framing, Adjustments }` is part of `OndinApp::image_menu`'s key
rather than a second `Option` field**, so the key is `Option<(NodeId, PaintSlot, ImageCard)>` and
**opening one closes the other** is the type's business instead of a rule two call sites keep. That
behaviour is wanted rather than tolerated: both cards are `POPOVER_W` wide and land at the same
anchor, so both open is one card hidden behind the other. The `Area`'s own `Id` gained the card too —
one id across both would carry the first card's remembered size and position into the second.

**One function branching on the card, not two copies.** `image_menu_popup` takes the card and branches
at two `if`s; the `Area`, the anchor, the header and the six-term click-away rule are shared. A second
hand-rolled copy of a rule with six exemptions is precisely the mistake D188 is about, and this is the
card that paid for that lesson.

**Framing first, adjustments second, which is the order of the work rather than of the cards.** How a
picture sits in its frame is decided once, when it is placed; what its colours do is returned to. Left
to right is earliest to latest, and it also puts the more-often-reached button nearest the eye's
column, where the hand already is. The cost falls on the strip: its track is `available − (28 + 6) *
2`, so the second line now ends **34** short of the field above it, and the right edge the two lines
share is the *row's*, carried by the last button, which still sits exactly in the eye's column.
`an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges` asserts that 34 exactly rather than "less than the field",
because the version somebody would otherwise write — leaving the track at one button's width and
letting the second push off the end — also ends short, and ragged. Its fixture is hand-built rather
than driven through `image_fit_strip`, `OndinApp` not being constructible headlessly, so it had gone
on passing while describing a one-button row; it was rewritten with the code.

**The two section eyebrows are gone, and the *Asset* one with them.** A heading repeating its card's
title one line above it divides nothing, so `ImageCard::title` says the word once. Asset is the one
that is a decision rather than a tidy: splitting the card left that heading standing over a single
entry, so *Replace…* joined Framing's action list, which is where D179's repair now lives. The heading
comes back with the rest of what Asset was planned to hold — *Replace and reset*, *Embed*/*Link*,
*Relink…*, *Export original…* — under a third card if there is no room by then.
*Two of those four landed on 2026-08-19 and **the eyebrow is back**, over three of five entries with
*Replace…* moved under it (D225). Framing had room, so the third card stays in reserve for
*Embed*/*Link* and *Relink…*, which need the linked source nothing in the app can author.*

**`ui::value_field_metered` is a `value_field` with a proportional bar across its ground**
(`METER_ALPHA = 41`, 16% of `color::ACCENT_400`), for values whose *size and direction* are what a
column of seven rows is read by. Four things about it are load-bearing. It is threaded **through** the field
rather than drawn by the caller, because the bar has to sit between the ground and the content: the
ground is opaque, so a bar drawn before it is hidden and one drawn after it tints the digits. The
shape is reserved with `Shape::Noop` at the one point in the frame that is after the background and
before the content, and filled once the row's ink box is known. That ink box is **neither the size
asked for nor the content box** — the cursor sits one `FIELD_PAD_X` inside the frame, so the rect is
pushed back by a padding at the left and grown by two across, which is what lands the bar inside the
hairline rather than under it. And the parameter is `signed`, **a signed offset growing from the
middle of the field, which reverses what this entry recorded**. It was a magnitude first — `|pct| /
100`, −40 and +40 drawing the same bar — on the argument that the sign is in the digits where it is
exact and that a two-sided bar spends half the field's width encoding what one character already
carries. The author reversed it on the machine the same day and called the omission theirs. *The
argument was true and the conclusion was wrong*, and the correction is a rule rather than a
preference: these seven are **offsets from a neutral zero, not quantities**, so a bar that draws −40
and +40 identically is not compressing the sign, it is contradicting it. A single-direction bar can
only be right for a value that has a bottom, and none of these has one — their bottom is the middle.
So `signed` is clamped to `-1..=1`, zero is the middle of the field, negative fills left from it and
positive right, and each half's travel is `ink.width() / 2.0` so that ±1 reaches an edge. It is still
the fraction of the *reachable range* rather than of the scrub's clamp — `pct / 100` where it was
`pct.abs() / 100` — so the bar is full exactly when the slider is, which is the property that has to
survive the ranges being retuned (D186 records them as first-draft numbers). **The corner rule
generalised with it: each pair rounds only when the bar reaches that end**, where it was left corners
always and right corners only at full width. Rounding a pair unconditionally is a capsule floating in
a field and rounding neither paints accent slivers into the corners the ground leaves for the popover
behind it — and a centre-anchored bar has two ends in play where a left-anchored one only ever had its
right, so the old rule left in place would draw a rounded left edge in the middle of the field on
every negative value. **The value is right-aligned in a metered field**, which is an exception to what
every other `value_field` does: they put the number beside the prefix at `Align::Min`, and
`value_field_f64`'s own comment says why, so this branches to `Align::Max` on `meter.is_some()`. Two
reasons and the second decided it — a number in the middle of a field the bar is also crossing reads
as a label *on* the bar rather than as the field's value, and since these prefixes are words of the
model's rather than glyphs it would land in a different place in all seven rows, so the card would
have no column of numbers to read down at all. `inspector::signed_number` is
the formatter beside it — `+12`, `-8`, `0` — because these are offsets from a neutral zero, and
unsigned the positives read as amounts while only the negatives read as directions; zero keeps neither
sign.

**A row at zero drew nothing at all, and that reads as an empty box rather than as a control at its
neutral value.** Reported on the machine against the accepted version above, and answered with
`ui::METER_TICK_W = 1.0`: a 1pt square rect at the middle of the field's **ink**, the full height of
that ink — which is already the field less its two hairlines, so the tick stops short of the border
rather than meeting it. It is **the same blue as the bar**, which is why `ui::meter_wash()` exists as
one function rather than two literals: being the same colour is the point of it, not a coincidence,
and a second literal is how the two would drift apart. A 1pt line at 16% is legible here rather than
assumed not to be — over `color::FIELD` the wash resolves to about `rgb(62,66,76)` where the field's
own hairline border is `rgb(53,53,54)` on that same ground, so the tick is the **higher-contrast** of
the two lines the field draws. **Always drawn, not only at rest**: it is the origin the bar grows
from, so a row that hid it as soon as it had a value would take the reference away exactly when there
is something to read against it. It is painted *under* the bar, so at a non-zero value the two overlap
by half a point at the origin instead of the tick cutting a line through the fill. The reservation is
therefore **two `Shape::Noop` slots rather than one `Shape::Vec`**, and that is a constraint rather
than a style choice: a `Vec` arrives in `FullOutput::shapes` as a single nested `ClippedShape`, so
every probe that walks that list for a `Shape::Rect` stops finding *either* shape. Flat is what keeps
the bar measurable.

Five tests in `ui.rs`'s `meter_tests`, rewritten for the centre origin, and the helper under them is
the part worth keeping. The first version measured the bar against the field's `Response`, which is
the **content** box, and reported a
correct bar escaping its field by nine points at each end; `parts()` takes the ground, the tick and
the bar out of `.shapes` instead. The ground is found **by colour**, a flattened shape list carrying
nothing else to tell two round rects at almost the same place apart; the tick and the bar **cannot
be**, since sharing the bar's colour is the whole point of the tick, so those two are taken in **paint
order** — a real property rather than a convenience, the tick being reserved first precisely so the
bar covers it. For the same reason the corners test reads the **second** wash rect: the tick is square
by construction, so reading it there would make every case pass for free. Flipped against the
plausible wrong version: the ink rect without the
`FIELD_PAD_X` push-back reports a bar starting at 10 where the field's ink starts at 1, and the row
fixture left at one button's reservation ends 0 short where it must end 34 short.

Three are written the way they are because the obvious version would have been about
nothing. `the_meter_grows_from_the_middle_and_mirrors_across_it` asserts the **pair** of signs rather
than one of them: a single positive bar a quarter of the field wide is also what a left-anchored bar
at 0.5 paints, so either sign alone passes against the implementation being replaced and only the two
together pin where the origin is. And `the_meter_is_empty_at_zero_and_fills_one_half_at_each_extreme`
checks that the extremes reach **half** the field, because scaling the full width by the signed
fraction — the likeliest slip on the way to a centre origin — makes ±1 reach twice as far as the field
has while everything under about 0.5 still looks right. Flipped against the previous implementation
(left-anchored, `frac.abs()`), those two fail with the symptom in the message: "the bars must meet at
the field's middle (90): + starts at 1 and − ends at 90", and "a bar at +1 is 178 wide where half the
field's ink is 89". The corner test **passes** under that flip and is meant to — it is about the
corner rule given correct geometry, and the geometry tests are what catch the origin. Flipping the
alignment back to `Align::Min` fails
`a_metered_fields_value_sits_at_the_far_end_where_a_plain_ones_sits_by_its_label` with "the metered
field's number is at 70 and the plain one's at 70". And
`the_zero_tick_is_a_hairline_at_the_middle_whatever_the_value` checks a **non-zero** value as well as
zero, which is the half that would otherwise rot: "draw a tick when the value is zero" is the obvious
spelling of the request, and it takes the origin away exactly when the bar gives it something to be
read against.

**The mode strip is 28 painted, and so is everything else on the row — decided 2026-08-16, and it
reverses what this entry left open.** `IMAGE_STRIP_CELL` is 24 and `ui::segmented` pads two either
side, so the track paints 28, and the two popover buttons are sized from it at `CELL + 4` and are 28
with it. The rule is worth more than the number: **the yardstick is the row's own neighbours, not a
distinction drawn inside the row.** The eye beside the field is 28, every button in the Appearance and
Stroke panels is 28, and a strip four short of all of them reads as a control that failed to line up
rather than as one holding itself back. That answers both halves of D180's argument for 20 painting
24 — that a strip flush with its 28px field is "the one thing a mode strip must not look like", and
that the picker's kind tabs were the closest thing in the app to copy. The tabs were the wrong
comparison; the neighbour is what the eye compares against, which is the same correction the row gap
took the same day (D180). **It deliberately does not land on the design's numbers either**, and this
entry framed the disagreement as design-versus-build with the design implicitly the target, which was
wrong: the regenerated file has the strip at 26 and the buttons at 28, mismatched by two, where the
author's rule gives one height throughout. The build follows the rule rather than the file.

`IMAGE_STRIP_CELL` moved out of `image_fit_strip` to module scope for this, so
`an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges` reads the constant instead of carrying a copy of its
value — and that is not tidiness. The test builds its own fixture, `OndinApp` not being constructible
headlessly, so a literal leaves it green while the row changes underneath it, which is exactly how it
went on describing a one-button row for a whole revision. **This is the second time that hole has been
found in this one test.** The height assertion is likewise against the **eye** rather than against a
pair of literal 28s, so a version that moved the strip and left the row's other controls behind fails
it: flipped back to 20 it reports "the strip paints 24 beside a 28 eye". The flip case for reading the
constant as the height rather than as the cell moved with the number, from 22→26 to **28→32**, since
that is the mistake this row has now made in both directions.

*Reviewed on the machine and accepted, 2026-08-16.* This entry said "not seen on screen" until the
author ran the app and went over all of it — the row split, both buttons, both cards, the 6pt row gap,
the centre-origin meter and the right-aligned value are all seen and accepted, so none of them is an
open question and none of them is to be re-argued from the painted-shape probes. The whole of this
entry came out of looking at the row: the earlier pass asked for the two buttons, the two popovers and
the slider style, and produced the row gap recorded in D180 above; this one asked for the **zero
tick** and the **strip's height**, both specified by the author and built *after* they looked, which
left them the only two parts of this entry nobody had seen. **They have since been run and accepted
as well, 2026-08-16**, so every number in this entry has now been looked at on the machine and none of
it is an open question. *Keep.*

**D191 — What images deliberately do not do. *Intentional; none of these is a todo item — except
masks, whose verdict the user reversed on 2026-08-21 (D282).***
`images.md` kept an *Out of v1, deliberately* list beside its build list, on the argument that the out
list was worth as much as the in one. That file has been folded into this document and deleted
(§5.5a), so the list is here — which is where it belonged anyway, §15 being the thing that stops a
non-goal being re-argued from first principles by the next session.

**Masks. *This bullet's verdict was reversed on 2026-08-21; its reasoning stands.*** The user asked
for masks and they are built — D282 has the feature, D283 its bounds, D284 its hit test and D285 its
chrome. What is *not* superseded is the argument for why they could wait, which is the only reason
this bullet was ever worth writing: the **fill model covers what masks are mostly used for**. An image
is a fill, so any shape, path or boolean carries one and "image in a circle" worked on day one without
a mask existing at all. What it did not cover is a picture masked by **text**, or by a **group** — and
those two cases are now, exactly and only, the two arms `Resolved::mask_path` grows past what
`boolean::operand_of` already answered. The scoping was right about the shape of the work and wrong
about its size, for the reason `roadmap.md` records: the parts arrived for other reasons while nobody
was looking. *Read the rest of this entry as still live; this bullet is history.*

**PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF — and a GIF is its first frame** (§5.5a). Naming a closed list is the point:
"why not TIFF" then has an answer that is a decision — one dependency, not worth it — rather than an
omission somebody quietly reopens by adding a decoder. **Animated GIF and video are out** on the same
line. Figma treats video as a fill and it is a stretch there too, and a still document has nowhere to
say *when*. **Multi-frame and layered formats — PSD, TIFF layers — go with them**: a layered file is a
document rather than a picture, so reading one is an import feature and not a format.

**No colour management and no profiles. Everything is sRGB**, which invariant 7 states for the
document's colours and §6.3's `color.rs` bullet for the backends, and the adjustments are in sRGB
too — deliberately and *visibly*, since the exported filter has to carry
`color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"` or a viewer works in linear RGB and draws a different exposure
with nothing in the file looking wrong (D186).
Saying so out loud is the whole of this bullet: it is what makes the first wide-gamut photograph
landing flat a **known limitation** rather than a bug nobody can reproduce.

**No tiling controls beyond `Extend`** — no per-axis repeat count, no offset. Tile stores one scale
and anchors at the frame's top-left (§5.5a), which is the whole of what `peniko::Extend::Repeat` can
be asked for; everything past that is a pattern editor.

**No background removal, no vector trace, no content-aware anything.** None of them is a larger
version of the adjustment pipeline — each is its own feature with its own model — and the same
sentence answers the case that looks closest. **Blur, sharpen and noise are the ones worth reading
twice**, because adjustments landing reads like a door opening and is not: D186's closing note has it,
that a colour matrix and a tone curve are both per-pixel where a convolution is a third stage with a
real kernel and a real edge-handling question. **Blend modes** are the same shape — already deferred
in §1, and images do not change that.

*Intentional. Each of these is a decision with a stated reason, so reopening one costs an argument
against that reason rather than a fresh look at the feature — and none of them belongs in `roadmap.md`.*

**D186 — Image adjustments, shaped by the writer that cannot invent arithmetic. *Resolved; the scrub was
reviewed on the machine and accepted 2026-08-16, after the two rounds below.*** `ImageAdjust` puts seven
`f32`s on `ImageRef` — exposure, contrast, saturation, temperature, tint, highlights, shadows — each
`0.0` at rest and held in `-1.0..=1.0`, with a `skip_serializing_if` per slider as well as one for the
struct, so an untouched picture's line is byte-for-byte what it was: no schema bump, no migration
(§5.11). It sits on the **fill** rather than on the entry, because the bytes are deduplicated by content
hash and what is done to them is not.

**The pipeline's shape was not chosen, it was dictated.** Three writers have to produce the same picture
and one of them cannot invent arithmetic: SVG can only name primitives a viewer already has. So
`ImageAdjust::pipeline()` resolves to exactly the two that can say this — a 4×5 colour matrix
(`feColorMatrix type="matrix"`) and a per-channel transfer table (`feComponentTransfer type="table"`,
`TONE_STEPS = 33`) — and the two pixel backends evaluate the very same numbers, with
`ondin_core::transfer` spelling out SVG's own interpolation rule. The export is therefore the same
description read by a different reader rather than an approximation of the canvas, which is what
`the_filters_numbers_paint_the_picture_the_canvas_paints` asserts. That test carries a temperature and a
tint together on purpose, because a grey-preserving matrix transposes to something very close to itself
and a saturation-only probe would pass against a column-major write.

Which slider lands in which stage follows: exposure, contrast, saturation, temperature and tint are
linear in the channels and collapse into one matrix, where highlights and shadows are a curve. Three
details there read as arbitrary and are load-bearing. Saturation uses **SVG's own** luminance
coefficients (0.213/0.715/0.072) rather than Rec.601's. Contrast pivots on mid-grey through the matrix's
fifth column, and `contrast_holds_mid_grey_still` exists because the plausible wrong version — a bare
diagonal scale — spreads the tones exactly as this one does and merely darkens the picture, so only the
fixed point catches it. And the tone curve's ±0.4 strength is **the largest that keeps it monotonic** at
both ends (the derivative of `v + a(1−v)²` at `v = 0` is `1 − 2a`); a curve that doubled back would
invert one end of the picture at a strong setting. `the_tone_curve_is_monotonic_at_every_extreme` was
checked by raising it to 0.55, where the shadow arm fails. The matrix runs **before** the curve, pinned
on a pixel the matrix pushes past white, where the two orders answer 0.6 and 1.0.

**The cache grew a second kind of thing, and where it is filled is the interesting part.** `ImageStore`
now holds derived pixels beside decoded ones, keyed by `(ImageId, AdjustKey)` — the seven values' bit
patterns, an `f32` struct being neither `Eq` nor `Hash`, and safe bitwise only because the neutral value
resolves to no pipeline and so never reaches a key, which is what stops `-0.0` and `0.0` splitting one.
They live behind a `Mutex` because they are filled **where they are read rather than where the table is
prepared**: an adjustment belongs to a fill, and only the scene walk knows the fills — including a
previewed one a walk of the document would never see. `ImageStore::pixels(&ImageRef)` is what a backend
paints with now; `get(&ImageId)` remains the decode and the right question for `ScenePainter::has_image`,
an adjustment being able to fail at nothing, so D179's placeholder path is untouched.

**Preview while scrubbing, promoted on stillness rather than on commit.** A fresh adjustment is answered
with the picture reduced towards `PREVIEW_EDGE = 1024` — a **floor**, not a ceiling — box-averaged in
premultiplied space, and rebuilt at full resolution once the same value has been asked for on two
consecutive frames. *On commit* was rejected because the cache has no way to know when a commit happened.
**Two frames rather than one**, because one frame of stillness spends a full-resolution pass on every
value a drag passes through, one frame late and thrown away. That is the test that had to be rewritten:
asserting the *width* handed back passed against the one-frame rule too, and only `derived_full_len()`
can see the work the eager one throws away.

Three things around that are easy to undo. `Pixels` carries `to_source`, the map from the answered
buffer's grid onto the source's, because `ImageRef::framing` maps *source*-pixel space and a reduced
buffer under the raw framing draws the picture at a fraction of its size — a bug that appears only while
a slider is moving. `cpu.rs`'s per-render `ImageSource` memo is keyed by `(id, adjustment bits)` rather
than the id alone, or two exposures of one photograph paint with the first's pixels. `ImageStore::new()`
**never** previews and `interactive()` is `CanvasRenderer`'s alone — an export that quietly wrote a
downsampled photograph is the one defect here no visual check would find. And `wants_frame()` owes a
`ctx.request_repaint()`: the promotion happens in a *later* frame's `prepare` and the frame that releases
a slider is routinely the last one egui draws. Eviction is two rules for two kinds of waste — a preview
goes as soon as it is stale, where a full buffer goes only under `ADJUSTED_BYTES`, least recently asked
first and never while it is still on screen. That budget bounds a genuinely different thing from
`DECODED_BYTES`: every derived buffer is recomputable, so it is a working-set bound where the decode
budget bounds waste. ⚠️ **Both halves of that last rule were amended on 2026-09-08 by D596**: the
budget is enforced where a buffer is *inserted* and not only from `prepare` — being only there, it
bounded nothing at all on a path that prepares once and then reads, which is every export — and it
takes a live buffer when there is no stale one, because on such a path everything is live.

**Two reports the same day, and the measurement is what separated them.** They read as one complaint
about the preview and were a debug-build arithmetic cost and an inverted reduction rule, sharing nothing.
One adjustment pass over an 800×500 photograph, both stages:

| | debug | release |
|---|---|---|
| one `AdjustPipeline::apply` per pixel | 101.5 ms | 11.5 ms |
| compiled to tables (`AdjustLut`) | 51.7 ms | 1.9 ms |
| tables + `opt-level = 3` on `ondin-render` | **2.1 ms** | — |

**Two independent fixes, both needed, and their factors do not multiply** — worth the table, because
written as two multipliers it comes out wrong and did: the tables are worth 6× where the optimiser is
already running and only 2× where it is not, so quoting "6× and 25×" claims 150 where the end-to-end
figure is 48. `AdjustLut` compiles the pipeline to a fixed-point contribution table per *input* channel
(`Contributions`, `FIXED_ONE`, 16 bits of fraction) plus the matrix's fifth column as an offset, and a
256-entry `u8` tone curve; `[profile.dev.package.ondin-render] opt-level = 3` is the other, `opt-level`
only, so symbols and debug assertions still name a panic's line. **The input-first indexing is a
measurement rather than a preference**: written output-first one pixel is nine scattered loads, where
input-first it is three loads of twelve adjacent bytes — a third on its own.

**The table is a memoization of core's function, not a second copy of it**, which is the whole of why it
is safe: every number in it is read out of the `AdjustPipeline` or produced by calling
`ondin_core::transfer`. `the_table_agrees_with_the_function_it_compiles` sweeps the two over seven
settings and the colour cube to a tolerance of one level — the tables round twice where `apply` rounds
once. Checked against the plausible wrong version by transposing the matrix indices in `build`. The
strongest evidence is outside the suite: an `ondin export --png` of an adjusted document is
byte-identical before and after.

**`PREVIEW_EDGE` is a floor and was being read as a ceiling**, which is the second report and a real bug.
The factor was `long_edge.div_ceil(edge).max(2)`, so a 1200-pixel photograph reduced by 2, to 600 — half
its resolution thrown away to get 17% under a line, and the `.max(2)` meant *every* picture over the
threshold paid at least half. It is `long_edge / edge` rounded down now, `None` when that is under 2, so
**a picture under twice `edge` is not reduced at all**. The trade is stated: such a picture pays the full
pass while a slider moves, 2–13 ms, affordable only because of the tables. 1024 stays, but chosen from
the sharpness end now. `a_picture_just_over_the_floor_keeps_all_of_itself` pins both arms and catches the
round-up spelling; `a_reduced_picture_maps_onto_the_source_box_corner_to_corner` gained an explicit
`assert!(px.data.width < n)` first — a size that is not reduced makes everything after it trivially true.
*Revisit if the jump is still visible on a genuinely large photograph: what would remove it is sizing the
preview to the picture's on-screen size, which needs the zoom plumbed to the store.*

**In the markup**, the filter is a def named by the `<image>` *inside* the pattern and never by the
pattern, which would colour whatever the pattern fills. Two attributes are load-bearing and look like
decoration: `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"`, without which a viewer works in linear RGB and draws a
visibly different exposure with nothing in the file looking wrong; and a filter region pinned to the
element's own box, since the default region is 10% larger on each side and inside a `<pattern>` would let
a tile's output bleed into its neighbours. Each stage is emitted only where it is not the identity, there
is **no `feFuncA`** — a shadow lift on alpha would turn a soft edge opaque — and an unadjusted picture
emits no filter at all. `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` goes 4 → 5 on D185's precedent.

**In the panel**, Adjustments sits *between* Framing and Asset. Seven rows off `Adjustment::ALL`, so the
panel cannot list six or call one something the snapshot calls something else; each is one `value_field`
whose **prefix is the word** — no icon set has seven tone-adjustment glyphs anyone can tell apart.
Percent under the hand, `-1..=1` in the file, written through `valve_slot` so a scrub is one undo step.
The per-slider reset is **dimmed rather than absent** at rest, because a control that came and went would
move the six rows under it every time a value crossed zero, and it re-checks the state after `.clicked()`
exactly as the undo and redo buttons do: `ui::icon_button`'s `enabled` still senses a click, so without
the re-check a dimmed reset writes a zero over a zero and pushes an undo step for it.

*Deliberately not done, and not roadmap items: there is no GPU-side adjustment — vello has no
colour-filter hook on an image brush — and no convolutional effects, the pipeline being per-pixel only.
A thumbnail does read the adjustment (D189) but through an entry point of its own, precisely so a chip
cannot promote a full-resolution pass.*

*What acceptance covered.* Two rounds settled the **performance**, the **preview** and the popover's
dismissal (D188). The card's **height** has since been answered structurally (D190). What is left is the
*feel* of the seven ranges — ±0.3 on the white-balance channels, ±0.4 on the tone curve, `2^±1` for
exposure, `1±1` for contrast and saturation, scrub speed 0.25 — first-draft numbers the author has now
scrubbed and called "alright", wanting more time. **Provisionally accepted future polish, not an open v1
item.** *Revisit after living with them; do not retune on reading alone.*

One cost is **unmeasured rather than known-and-unfixed**, and it is the one to suspect next if a scrub is
reported slow after the two fixes above. Every value a slider passes through produces a *different*
derived buffer, and the GPU backend hands vello the picture's `ImageData` inline — so a scrub implies a
**texture upload per frame** by construction. It cannot be reached headlessly. *Measure before optimising
— the two fixes above were separated by measurement and would have been mis-attributed without it.*

**D185 — An image resolves to a `<pattern>`, and that made it `paint_attr`'s business after all.
*Resolved.*** `images.md` predicted this would be "a change to the element writer, not to `paint_attr`".
Right in its premise and wrong in its conclusion: an image is indeed not a `fill` attribute's *value*,
but a `<pattern>` is a **paint server** exactly as a gradient is, and a paint server is what a `fill`
names. So images went through the `Defs` machinery gradients already used, and `write_element` learnt
nothing at all.

`image_def` writes a `<pattern patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse">` round an `<image
preserveAspectRatio="none">`, where W×H is the source's **intrinsic pixel box** — the space
