`ImageRef::framing`'s transform maps *from*, so the whole framing is the one `patternTransform` and the
element never learns which of the four modes it is in. **`ImageEntry::href` is new and it is in core**,
not in the writer: one encoder is what keeps a document and its export saying the same thing about the
same file. The *encoded original* goes out, never a re-encode: it is what the content hash names.

**A pattern always tiles, and three of the four modes want `Extend::Pad`.** Not a divergence in anything
the app can author — Fill and Crop cover the frame, and Fit's letterbox is cut by `with_image_clip`. What
*would* diverge is a crop rectangle reaching outside `0..1`, where the canvas smears an edge pixel and
SVG repeats the whole picture. The gesture cannot produce one (D181); a hand-edited file can.

**A letterboxing image is as much a reason to stack as an aligned stroke is**, so `emit_shape`'s `plain`
gate now also fails when any visible paint's framing asks for a clip. On a stroke the image clip sits
**outside** the alignment clip, because the two cut different things.

**`paint_frame` mirrors `scene.rs`'s three cases**: an artboard's own box, a text node's **layout
bounds**, and otherwise the outline's bounding box. Text is the one that bites — this writer reaches for
glyph outlines everywhere else, and taking them here would frame a picture to the ink instead of to the
box the words sit in. **An image the table cannot answer for gets no def**, never a `url(#…)` naming one
that is not in the file: SVG treats that as an error.

**A formatting wart that predates images came out of this and is fixed**: `fmt` never writes `-0`. A
rounded rect's outline has a bounding box whose top is `-8.88e-16`, so a picture *fitted* into that box
came out translated by `-0`. Found by a test asserting the clip rect, not by review.

**And its twin, reported off a real export: an identity written out longhand.** An 800×600 photograph in
an 800×600 frame exported as `patternTransform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)"`. `transform_attr` is now one caller
of `matrix_attr(name, affine)` and the pattern is the other. **The rule tests the *printed* form rather
than the `Affine`**, and the two genuinely part company here: an element's transform comes from the
model, where the identity is exact, while a pattern's is computed against a bounding box — so the same
`-8.88e-16` makes a picture sitting perfectly still an affine a hair off the identity and a matrix of `1
0 0 1 0 0` on paper. Pinned by `a_picture_at_its_frames_own_size_writes_no_pattern_transform`, whose
fixture is a *rounded* rect precisely because that is the arm an `Affine::IDENTITY` comparison would
miss.

**The Export scope of `images.md` closes here**, `PaintSummary::Image` becoming `{ id, fit, alpha }`: a
snapshot saying a photograph is there but not *which* cannot answer the first question anyone asks.
`SNAPSHOT_VERSION` goes 3 → 4.

**Three of the five SVG tests were checked failing against the version somebody would plausibly have
written**, rather than against the feature's absence: no clip at all, no `Defs::has` gate, and the glyph
outline as the text frame (`an_image_filled_text_node_is_framed_by_its_layout_box`, whose failure message
reports that what it got was exactly the ink's transform, and which asserts the fixture's ink and layout
box actually differ first). The other two fail only against the feature being absent, which proves less
and is worth knowing before either is edited.

⚠️ **One thing here has been extended: the `<image>` inside the pattern is a `<use>` of a shared one
now** (§15 D595). Keying every def per node *per slot* meant thirty shapes on one photograph carried
thirty base64 copies of it, and the payload is written once per `ImageId` since 2026-09-08. Nothing
above changes — the pattern is still per node, because the `patternTransform` this entry is mostly
about is the thing that genuinely differs per node.

**D184 — The drop announces itself, and announcing it honestly found that Windows never sends a drop
point. *Resolved — the indicator and the bug it exposed; the cursor recovery below is an open option and
not a plan.*** D183 left one gap: `hovered_files` was unread in the whole workspace, so a drop worked and
nothing said it would. `canvas::draw_drop_indicator` is now that field's only reader, **under
`draw_rulers_and_guides` like every other overlay** — it went over them first and that was reported the
day it landed. It draws a 3px `color::SELECT` line round the frame that will take the picture, or a 2px
border inside `canvas_inner` where there is no such frame; and a pill by `paint_drop_label` in the size
badge's treatment, kept inside the canvas by a hand-written clamp. **Not `egui::Rect::clamp`**, which
panics on a rect narrower than the pill. `drop_label`'s words are the future tense of `drop_images_at`'s
own messages, so the promise and the receipt read as one sentence.

**It asks the release's own two questions**, `drop_point` and `image_drop_target`, rather than a
hover-shaped copy of them; that is the one thing stopping it promising something the drop does not do.
**The count is of *files*, not of images**: the bytes are what decide whether a file is a picture and
they are not read until the drop, so a drag of two files one of which is a spreadsheet says "Place 2
images" and then places one. Nothing here asks for a repaint: `InputState::wants_repaint_after` returns
`Duration::ZERO` while `raw.hovered_files` is non-empty.

**And D183's drop point is wrong in a way this found: on Windows there is never one, so the fallback is
not the near-miss case, it is the case.** Read out of winit's `drop_handler.rs`: `DragEnter` emits one
`HoveredFile(path)` per file and carries no position, **`DragOver` is handed the cursor point as `_pt`,
discards it and emits no event at all**, and `Drop` discards its `_pt` too. No ordinary pointer event
fills the gap either: the drag source holds the mouse capture, and the cursor left this window before the
drag began, which egui-winit turned into `Event::PointerGone`. This half was read from library source,
and **the indicator was its own instrument for it**: if that label ever read "Replace image in …" on
Windows, `drop_point` answered after all. **It has since been run on the machine, and the label reads
*Place image*** — so the paragraph above is measured as well as read.

**That exposed a live bug, now fixed.** `drop_images_at` asked `self.image_drop_target(at)` with `at` —
`None` on every Windows drop, which is `image_drop_target`'s *paste* arm: the selection alone, with no
bounds check. So a single dropped file replaced the selected shape's picture wherever it was released,
and that is not an edge case, because `create_image_at` selects what it places — **the second picture
dropped into a document replaced the first**. The gate is now `n == 1 && let Some(p) = at && …`. A paste
keeps the selection-only arm deliberately: the asymmetry is *intent* rather than platform, since pressing
the paste keys with a shape selected is the act of aim.

Stated plainly because it was what a user met between 2026-08-13 and 2026-08-19: **on Windows a drop
could not replace at all**, and every drop landed at `viewport_centre()`. Replacing was reached by
pasting, or by *Replace…* (D179). The open option this entry left — recovering the real cursor position
through `GetCursorPos` plus `ViewportInfo::inner_rect` — **has since been taken, and it is D241**; read
that one for what the recovery costs and where it is asked. **What is tested here is the pill's clamp and
nothing else**, both assertions checked failing against the version somebody would actually have written:
the pill stays inside the canvas with its anchor three screens away, and a canvas too small to hold it
centres the pill instead of panicking — without the `max(Vec2::ZERO)` floor that is `f32::clamp` with
`min > max`, which is why the clamp is written by hand.

**One change was asked for after living with it: the border goes round the frame, not round the window.**
Inside `canvas_rect` it crossed the rulers, so chrome about the window cut across chrome about the
document. The mark goes round the box that will really take the picture, drawn as
`draw_frame_drop_outline`'s 3px line, because it is the same sentence that outline says during a move.
The canvas edge survives as the fallback in exactly two cases: no frame under the landing point, and a
frame whose screen quad is not wholly inside the canvas, where the only mark would land where nobody can
see it. **The rulers are answered three times over** — the indicator moved under them, the fallback
border is inset to `canvas_inner`, and the frame test and the pill's clamp are against that same inner
rectangle. Reviewed and accepted.

**D183 — The other two ways an image gets in, and the paste that arrives as a key *release*. *Resolved;
the paste confirmed on the machine.*** Drag-and-drop and paste both reuse the place path.
`load_image_file` split into `load_image_bytes(bytes, ext, name)` plus a read, and that seam is what all
three ways in share — keeping it one function is what stops the three disagreeing about the hash, the
format sniffing or the intrinsic size. `image_format_of` takes an `Option<&str>` rather than a `&Path`
for the same reason.

**The drop** reads `ctx.input(|i| i.raw.dropped_files)`. Each `DroppedFile` gives `bytes` or a `path`,
tried in that order. The drop point is `pointer_interact_pos` falling back to `pointer_latest_pos`, a
drop's release not being an egui interaction. A point outside `canvas_rect` becomes the viewport centre
rather than a refusal, which would throw the files away for a near miss (D184: on Windows that is every
case). **SVG is refused and never rasterized** (`looks_like_svg`, the leading 512 bytes sniffed) — from
the *bytes* rather than the name, because a browser drag often has neither a usable extension nor a
filename — and counted separately from unreadable files, so "not an image" and "could not read" stay two
messages.

**The cascade lives in `drop_images_at` and nowhere else**, at 24 world units per file. A drop is where
it is genuinely owed, because N files arrive at *one* point and without it they stack exactly.
Deliberately **not** scaled by zoom: at 400% a screen-constant step would put the second one a quarter of
the way across the document.

**A drop places from a list of its own, and the first spelling borrowed the tool's.** `drop_images_at`
used to assign the dropped files to `OndinApp::pending_images` — the Image tool's loaded cursor — and
then clear it, so a drop arriving while the tool was armed left the tool armed over an empty queue: the
"cursor whose clicks do nothing" §5.5a says arming must never produce. **A field that is one gesture's
scratch space is not scratch space for another gesture**, and *that* was the tell — the new path never
called `placed_one_image`, the function that maintains the invariant. `create_image_at` now takes a
`&LoadedImage` and the queue is the caller's business.

**Dropping or pasting onto a shape replaces its picture**, and the **selection** in that rule is
load-bearing: a drop can address a shape by landing on it, but a paste has no pointer, so the selection
is the only thing the two gestures can share. It also makes the destructive reading opt-in. Only ever for
a *single* dropped file. `replace_image_fill` **keeps the framing**, rewriting only `ImageRef::id`. The
fill acted on is the first **visible image** fill, falling back to `paint.fills.len().checked_sub(1)` —
the **last** fill, which is also the emptiness guard. **Last and not index 0, and the first spelling was
index 0**: §5 fixes list order as paint order, so element 0 is the *bottom* of the stack, and a
photograph written there on a shape carrying two opaque fills reads as the drop having done nothing.
Invisible in the one-fill case, which is every case anyone tests with.

**Paste** returns whether it took the paste so `Action::Paste` falls through to the layer paste when the
clipboard holds no picture. **`arboard` is now a direct dependency**, already in the lock through
`egui-winit`, so this declared an edge and compiled no new crates; it is needed directly because
`egui::Event::Paste` carries a `String` and there is no image variant. And **what comes back is *decoded*
RGBA, so it is re-encoded to PNG before hashing** — the whole format rests on storing the encoded
original and hashing *that*, and a clipboard image has no original. PNG because it is lossless and one of
the four formats v1 accepts. The consequence, stated rather than discovered later: a pasted image's id is
the hash of *our* encoding, so the same screenshot pasted twice dedupes, while the same picture pasted
and then placed from a file does not.

**`images.md`'s trap understates the problem: there is nothing to detect.** Read against
`egui-winit-0.35.0/src/lib.rs` around line 1007, the three clipboard guards sit inside `if pressed`, each
`return`s unconditionally, and `Event::Paste` is pushed only when the clipboard yields non-empty
**text** — so `Key { V }` is never pushed on the press *and* no `Paste` is either. `Ctrl+V` over a
clipboard holding a picture produces **no event whatsoever**, and no eframe hook sees the raw winit
event. **The adjacent shape is the release**, which falls past those guards and arrives as an ordinary
`Key { key: V, pressed: false }`. `input::normal_mode` takes a paste from either signal, guarded by a
`pasted` flag so a text paste does not paste twice.
`a_paste_is_taken_from_the_release_as_well_as_the_event` pins **our** half, and its doc says which half
is unverified: this is the backend→egui direction, where `ctx.run_ui` shows only egui→backend.

Two things follow. **The release arm examines Alt now** — `cmd_only && key_released(V)`, changed with
D204 — and `docs/shortcuts.md` §7 plans `Ctrl+Shift+V` and `Ctrl+Alt+V`, so Alt will want that guard
**widened into a branch** rather than removed. And **this early return was exactly the root cause of
§L2's `Ctrl+Alt+X` bug** — one root cause, two symptoms. *Both* fixes were taken: the `Event::Cut` arm is
gated on `!m.alt` and Exclude is read off the release. **D204.**

**D182 — The image row's framing popover, and a picture that flips and turns inside its frame.
*Resolved; the card moved into image editing by D268 (2026-08-20).*** The controls below are all still
built and still say what they say; what changed is where they live and how they are reached — one card
with two tabs, owned by the mode, with no button and no click-away rule. The *fourth way into the crop
tool* this entry added is gone with the tool it opened.
Everything an image still wanted is a control rather than a mode — about twenty of them
against a row whose first line is already a grip, a chip, a label, an opacity and a cross inside 28px. So
they go in one card (**two since D190**), following `stroke_menu_popup` exactly. The button that opens it
sits in the **eye's column**, the only free 28px on either line and free *because* the mode strip
measures itself to the field rather than to the row (D180). It is asked for `CELL + 4` and not `CELL`,
`ui::segmented` taking the cell height and padding two either side.

**`ImageOrient` is a mirror and a quarter-turn count, and each of the eight states has exactly one
spelling.** `flip_x`/`flip_y`/`turns` would spell the rectangle's eight symmetries sixteen ways — a
horizontal flip *and* a vertical flip together **are** a half turn — so a file could carry a state the
buttons can never produce. It is deliberately not `build::Orientation`, which carries a real angle.
**The controls are actions and not toggles, and that is forced by the maths rather than preferred by the
design**: once a quarter turn is involved "is it flipped horizontally?" has no answer. So `OrientOp`
*composes* through `ImageOrient::applying` and neither button ever lights up. The composition rule is the
load-bearing line: **a mirror conjugates a rotation into its inverse** (`M∘Rᵏ = R⁻ᵏ∘M`), so `FlipH`
reverses the turn count as well as the mirror. Written as two independent flags it is wrong for six of
the eight states and right for the two anybody tests with, which is why
`a_flip_or_a_turn_composes_in_the_frames_axes_from_every_orientation` asserts the matrix for all eight
against all three ops instead of sampling.

**The two mirror buttons carry words rather than glyphs, and a measurement is why.** They shipped with
the Transform panel's exact strings over its exact glyphs and were reported as redundant. Measured end to
end through the CPU renderer, they are not: on a **symmetric** shape the two are the same drawing,
because `build::flip` mirrors about the box's own centre; on an **asymmetric** outline they part — a
triangle's layer flip turns the *outline* over as well (top-half ink 1246 px → 2109) where the popover's
leaves it alone. So the defect was never redundancy but **naming**, and in the common case nothing on
screen distinguishes them, so only the words can. *A future editor must not "simplify" the glyphs back
in.*

Different glyphs were tried first, and Phosphor has no second flip pair — **its own two are not even a
matched pair**: `flip-horizontal` is two upward triangles about a *dashed* vertical axis, while
`flip-vertical` hangs right-triangles off a *solid* bar, so side by side the second reads as a flag. That
is recorded on `theme::icon::FLIP_HORIZONTAL`, being the Transform panel's problem too. Words won on
measurement again: the buttons are 122px wide and the labels ink 55.6px and 41.0px. An eyebrow **Mirror**
carries the verb, *Horizontal* first. **`ui::label_button` is `field_button_sized` with a word in it**,
and the two share a new private `ui::button_face` rather than a copy, so they cannot disagree about any
of the four `FieldButton` states. *Keep them one function.*

**The quarter turn is gone from the popover, on usefulness and not on redundancy.** It was the one of the
three that measurably is *not* redundant — the popover's turn leaves a 200×100 box at 200×100 where the
Transform panel's makes it 100×200 — and it was removed anyway, by the author's call: a photograph that
came in sideways lands in a shape cut to its own aspect, where turning the **layer** is the right answer.
**`OrientOp::Turn` therefore stays in core with nothing writing it**, said on the variant so the next
reader does not take it for an oversight. It is not spare: `applying` resolves `FlipV` to `quarters: 2`.
*Revisit if an import arrives carrying an EXIF orientation.*

**`ImageOrient::affine` writes the three turn matrices out by hand, and that is not a drawing concern.**
`Affine::rotate(π/2)` returns a cosine of about `6.1e-17`, so a composed spelling leaves a shear of that
size in every turned picture's brush transform. Invisible on screen; not invisible in the file, because a
brush transform differing in its last bits is a `SetFills` no equality guard catches.
`every_orientation_maps_the_source_box_exactly_onto_the_oriented_box` rejects the composed spelling.

**`ImageRef::crop` is normalized to the picture *as oriented*, not to the raw source.** The crop gesture
drags in frame-aligned axes, so putting the rectangle in that space leaves `crop_panned` and `crop_zoomed`
knowing nothing about orientation. The price: changing the orientation has to carry the rectangle with
it, or you turn a portrait to find yourself looking at its shoulder. `OrientOp::crop_carried` is that map,
and `ImageRef::reoriented` is the **only** way to reach `orient`.
`reorienting_a_cropped_picture_keeps_the_same_pixels_in_the_frame` asserts on the source pixels that
reach the frame; the version that writes the orientation and leaves `crop` alone passes every other test
in the file. `ImageRef::framing` composes rather than branches. On disk it is additive again — no bump,
no migration.

**The tile-scale field is dimmed rather than hidden when the mode is not Tile, which departs from
`stroke_menu_popup` on purpose.** That card *hides* its mitre field, a mitre limit on a round join being
a number that cannot exist; a tile scale is a real stored value three of the four modes are simply not
reading. The mode strip is also *outside* this card, so a section that changed height when something out
there was clicked would read as a glitch. The valve is guarded on `tiling` rather than left to the dead
response a disabled `Ui` returns: a control that cannot be used has no business arming the chrome hide.

*Edit crop…* enters `Tool::Crop`, answering a gap the mode strip leaves. It is enabled only where this
row really is what the tool would act on. *Reset crop* restores `whole_crop()`, the sentinel, and **not**
a computed cover rectangle — which would look identical and quietly mean the picture had been cropped to
exactly what it was already showing. *Original size* is the one entry here that is not a paint edit: it
resizes the **node**, to `ImageRef::oriented_size`. **That sentence is why it left the card on
2026-08-23** (D305): a verb aimed at the layer belongs where the layer is right-clicked, not inside a
mode entered to work on the paint, and the row it left behind in `context-menus.md` §5.7 is the one
that dims on a lock — this one never did.

**`OndinApp::image_menu` is keyed by node *and* slot where `stroke_menu` is a bare index**, an image row
being able to be a fill, a stroke, a frame's background or a selection row. The `Area`'s own egui id is
the node alone — `PaintSlot` is not `Hash` — sound only because at most one card is open. It is dropped
on a grip's `drag_started` and in `forget_stroke_chrome`: a stale card never *draws*, but it would keep
`picker_lane_right` reserving a lane for a card nobody can see.

**A dimmed row needs a second claimant to explain itself, and that took three responses to find out.**
The tooltip matters most in exactly the state where it is hardest to fire: a widget inside a
`disable()`d `Ui` reports no hover at all. The obvious alternative — hang it on the wrapping `ui.scope`'s
response — is **silently dead in both states**, `Ui::scope` handing back a placeholder over the rect
rather than a registered widget, and that is the spelling `menu_action` had first. What works is an
explicit `ui.interact(rect, id, Sense::hover())` beside the disabled scope, salted by the row's label.
`ui::menu_item` returns an `egui::Response` rather than a `bool` for this — a `bool` cannot carry a
tooltip. `a_dimmed_control_can_be_hovered_only_through_a_claimant_of_its_own` pins all three responses
with real pointer events over several frames (D96's rule); its assertion that the **scope** is not
hovered even with the row inert is the one that failed first and corrected the function.

**And what that test cannot see is worth knowing: a tooltip's own galley never reaches `ctx.run_ui`'s
`.shapes`.** Checked by pumping eight frames with time advancing past the 0.5s `tooltip_delay`, the
pointer still and the row reporting `hovered()` throughout — only the row's own two galleys appear. So
the test asserts on the `Response` the tooltip hangs from, one step back from the ink.

**The tile-scale field had the dead spelling too, and that is the finding worth keeping.** Extracting
`menu_action` fixed the three rows and left the field immediately above them hanging its dimmed tooltip
on `scoped.response` — with a comment asserting the falsified rule as fact. *A mechanism corrected in one
place is not corrected in the place it was extracted from*: the fix has to be swept for. The test now
runs over **both** shapes the card uses rather than one with a reading across to the other. The same
spelling predates this change at seven other sites — four in `panels/inspector.rs`, three in
`panels/typography.rs` — every one a control explaining why it is unavailable, so each is a real loss of
information. Tracked separately.

Two tests are worth naming for what they do **not** prove.
`four_quarter_turns_come_back_to_exactly_where_they_started` reads as the strongest of the set and is the
weakest: `quarters` is recomputed rather than accumulated, so the fourth turn lands on the identity arm
whatever the other arms are made of. Its doc comment now says so — and the finding came from putting the
`Affine::rotate` spelling in and seeing which three tests failed. And
`an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges` is a check on the arithmetic and not on the wiring. What
covers the whole path instead is `each_of_the_eight_orientations_permutes_the_pixels_on_screen`, which
goes end to end for all eight: the 2×2 fixture makes a flip or a turn *permute the colours on screen*, so
the eight expected grids are hand-derived rather than computed from the code under test — and it asserts
those eight grids are distinct from one another, which is the failure a version that dropped the mirror
would otherwise slip past.

**D181 — The crop gesture: a tool rather than a mode, and it starts from the picture already on screen.
*Superseded by D268 (2026-08-20); the seeding argument below survives, the tool does not. **Its
"reviewed on screen and accepted" was false about the chrome** — see D269: the box and handles this
entry describes were never drawn once.*** The rail
slot, the letter `C` and the "a tool rather than a mode" reasoning were all reversed after the feature
was lived with — read D268 first. What still holds, and is why this entry is not struck: `cover_crop`,
the sentinel, and the rule that everything entering cropping seeds from the rectangle already on
screen. `crop_zoomed` and `crop_zoom_factor` are gone with the zoom gesture; `crop_reframed` and
`ImageRef::picture_box` took their place.
Four pure functions in `image.rs` carried the
arithmetic — `cover_crop`, `crop_panned`, `crop_zoomed`, `crop_clamped` — and the app supplied only the
pointer. `cover_crop` is the one to read first: it returns the rectangle `ImageFit::Fill` is *already*
showing, so choosing the mode changes nothing on screen. Without it the gesture began at the whole source
stretched onto the frame. It is also the widest the gesture can zoom back out to, because a larger
rectangle at that aspect would have to leave the source, where `Extend::Pad` smears the edge row.

**A tool and not a mode, for the reason `Tool::Node` is one** (D118): a rail slot, the letter `C`, and
chrome of its own. Crop needs those more than point editing does, because cropping is otherwise
indistinguishable from resizing. It is **subject-conditional exactly as the node tool is**, and
`canvas::cropped_fill` is the single question "are we cropping", derived from `tools::croppable_fill` —
in turn the single question *what counts as a croppable picture*, asked by both entry arms rather than
restated in each. **No app state field was added at all**, which is what makes it impossible for a stored
subject to disagree with the tool. `C` is the letter a comment tool would want; comments are unbuilt and
inert on the rail, so the built thing takes the mnemonic.

**Where the tool lives was an open question, and the author closed it: crop stays on the rail.**
*Decided 2026-08-11.* Taking it off the rail would have cost D118's test — a rail button, a letter and
chrome of its own — so the rule would have had to be *answered another way*. The popover's *Edit crop…*
makes four ways in rather than three. *The reason to keep the rail slot is written down here rather than
assumed, so the next person who wants the panel button can have it as well and not instead.*

**Corners zoom, anywhere else pans, and there are deliberately no side handles.** With the frame held
still a crop has three degrees of freedom, and a side handle could only add a fourth by stretching, which
is the one thing "scale the image within the frame" rules out. `Drag::CropPan` and `Drag::CropZoom` each
capture the crop rectangle **at the press** and re-derive from it every frame, the rule `resize_tx`
already follows. It is routed **inside** `normal_mode_input` rather than beside it — D167's lesson.

Three details a later editor would simplify and thereby break. `crop_clamped` **slides rather than
clamping each edge**: clamping edges independently silently changes the crop's size, so a pan that ran
into the edge would zoom as well as stop —
`panning_into_the_edge_slides_rather_than_resizing_the_crop` asserts the *size* surviving. **Two
inversions live in `tools::crop_zoom_factor` and nowhere else**: dragging a corner out makes the picture
bigger, and a bigger picture is a *smaller* crop rectangle, so the factor is the reciprocal of the
pointer's travel. And the factor is **projected onto the diagonal the drag started on**, without which a
sideways wobble during a corner drag zooms. `panning_moves_the_picture_with_the_pointer` asserts where a
*source pixel lands* rather than which way the numbers went.

**The chrome is a fourth term, not a parallel check.** `chrome_hidden` gains `cropped_fill().is_some()`,
and `draw_crop_box` draws the frame in `SELECT_DIM` with **filled** corners where the selection's are
hollow. The two boxes are the same rectangle in the same place, so the shape of the corner is the only
thing saying which gesture you are in. The cursor is grab/grabbing over the picture and **nothing over a
resting corner** — D118's rule applied rather than repeated. *Reviewed on screen and accepted,
2026-08-11.* **The filled corner is not to be re-derived from D14 by a later reader tidying the two boxes
into one handle rule**: D14 is about not painting over a corner being *aimed at*; a crop corner scales
the picture *under* it.

**An honest limit: `crop_input` itself is read, not tested.** The decisions were pulled out into
`crop_zoom_factor` and `croppable_fill`, which are unit-tested, and what is left is plumbing.

**`whole_crop` and `cover_crop` are two steps of one rule, not two candidates for the same job.**
`whole_crop` means *never cropped*, and it is the `skip_serializing_if` value for exactly that reason;
mapped onto a frame of a different aspect it stretches. Everything that *enters* cropping replaces it
with `cover_crop`.

**Settling that exposed a gap, and it was reachable from the panel.** Choosing *Crop* from the mode strip
left the sentinel in place, so a square photograph in a 2:1 frame stretched to twice its width on the
click. `panels::paint::with_fit` now takes the frame and seeds when it sees the sentinel, and
`inspector::crop_seed` supplies it from the same box `framing` is given. It answers `None` in three
cases: two are simply not knowing which frame is meant, and the third is a **slot that spans a
selection**, which is the whole of why the slot is a parameter — a seed is a rectangle computed *for one
frame*, while a selection write sends one brush to every node in scope.
`choosing_crop_from_the_panel_seeds_the_picture_already_on_screen` asserts against **`Fill`'s own
framing** rather than a rectangle, so it stays true if `cover_crop` is re-derived; with the seed disabled
it reports `Affine([2.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0, …])`, which is the stretch itself.

**The cost of declining, stated rather than hidden: choosing *Crop* for a multi-node selection does not
seed, so those pictures do jump.** *Fix with `write_slot` carrying a function rather than a brush*; not
done here because `write_slot` is the path every other paint control writes through.

**D180 — An image fill has a row, and the two controls it already had were quietly destroying the
picture. *Resolved.*** An image classified as `PaintKind::Solid`, so its row drew a grey swatch and a hex
field, and typing in that field replaced the photograph with a colour. Closing it needed the variant
first, and the variant is where the one real design decision is — **`PaintKind::Image` is deliberately
not in `PaintKind::ALL`**, the picker's tab strip. The other three convert to one another; an image does
not. `an_image_is_its_own_kind_and_stays_out_of_the_pickers_tabs` pins both halves, the variant existing
and the tab strip not offering it being separate claims.

**The row keeps its shape and changes what each part does.** The chip stays a chip but opens nothing; the
hex field becomes a plain "Image" label; and a four-cell **Fill / Fit / Crop / Tile** strip is drawn as a
second line *inside the scope the grip carries*, so it travels with the row and `out.rect` spans both
lines. `picker_body` returns early for an image rather than painting a hue wheel over a photograph.

**Two bugs it fixed, and they were one bug.** Every control on a paint row is written against the stop
list, and an image has none — so `paint::stops_of` invents a placeholder grey and `with_stops` used to
hand that grey *back* as a `Brush::Solid`. One nudge of an image row's opacity replaced the photograph
with a grey rectangle. `with_stops` now returns an image unchanged, and the opacity is read and written
where it actually lives — peniko's `ImageSampler::alpha`.

**Two measured numbers, both invisible in the source.** `ui::segmented` takes the **cell** height and
paints two pixels of padding either side, so the track is four taller than the number written down — this
row has now got that wrong in both directions. It was 20, painting 24; **both halves were reversed on
2026-08-16 (D190): it is `IMAGE_STRIP_CELL = 24`, painting 28**, because the yardstick is the row's own
neighbours and not the picker's tabs. And the paint lists space their rows 6 apart while a vertical
layout inserts that spacing before every item, so a plain `add_space(4)` put the strip **10** below its
own field; the gap was pulled back with a negative `add_space`. **That 4 is gone as of 2026-08-16 and the
gap is the layout's own**, which reverses the argument this entry made for it. Seen on the machine and
reported as the opposite: the *stroke* row is also two lines to one feature and takes the plain spacing,
so the pull-back made the image row the one thing in the panel whose two lines sat closer together than
its neighbour's. A rule that holds for one row and not for the row beside it is not a rule.

***The 6 in the paragraph above was never the number this row painted.*** A paint list is a card body,
and `ui::card_at` spaces that at 9 — so an image fill's two lines took **9** in the Fill list and only
the *stroke* pair's own scope was ever at 6. The yardstick argument survives the correction and the
measurement did not; fixed under D196, where the number becomes `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` **stated** by
`paint_row`. And the reason this went unnoticed is in the test: the fixture supplied the number the gap
assertion checked — and, underneath that, it set its own `item_spacing.y` *after* laying the field row
out, too late to be the gap beneath it (D195), so what the assertion measured was the theme's default.
Both halves were fixed, and the second was found by fixing the first.

**D179 — A dangling image reference drew nothing where the design says a placeholder. *Resolved.***
§5.5a asserted it in the present tense until this entry first recorded the gap. Recording it rather than
rewording the design was the right way round — the code was short of the design, not the design short of
the code.

**What survives is real, and it is what a repair aims at.** A fill naming an id the table does not carry
loads, saves and comes back with the reference intact, and bytes that will not decode are skipped rather
than taking the renderer down. Refusing either at load would turn a repairable picture into an unopenable
document.

**The three states stay merged, and a later editor should not split them.** An unknown id, a link nothing
has read off disk, and bytes that will not decode are one condition on purpose: one drawing to build
rather than three, and one thing for the user to do about it. `scene::missing_picture` asks the painter
one question — `ScenePainter::has_image` — and that is the only split that keeps one drawing.

**The drawing is described in core and painted by the walk.** `ondin_core::missing_placeholder(bounds)`
answers a `Missing { ground, ink, width, cross }` — grey `#E4E4E6`, ink `#A0A0A8`, the box's two
diagonals as one path, width `min(w, h)/40` clamped to `0.5..=4.0` — and sits beside `ImageRef::framing`
for that function's stated reason: three copies of a drawing are three drawings. Grey and a cross because
a walk with no font cannot draw words. **Light rather than mid-grey deliberately**: a placeholder should
read as an *absence*. `scene::paint_missing` fills the shape with the ground, then pushes a layer clipped
to the **shape's own path**, so an image fill in a circle stays a circle.

**Fills only, in both writers, on purpose.** A stroke or a text run painted with a missing picture still
draws nothing: the placeholder is a statement about an *area*. A deliberate asymmetry, which is why it is
written down.

**The SVG writer draws the same picture off the same description**, and its unresolvable set is **smaller
by construction**: only a dangling id reaches it. **A frame's background reached that rule a step late,
and reading the two writers against each other is what found it** — the walk sent it through
`fill_or_placeholder` while `emit_node` wrote it through `paint_attr` alone, so a frame whose picture had
gone drew the cross on canvas and exported a hole. *"One drawing" is a claim about every call site of it,
and the two writers each have their own list of them.*

**Two PNG tests changed sides, which is the honest signal.** They asserted the very behaviour this entry
called a defect, and now assert the ground **against `missing_placeholder`'s own colour** — an end-to-end
check — plus a pixel on the diagonal being darker. All three were flip-checked against "just fill it
grey". **The first sample point was wrong and is worth recording**: (25,75) sits exactly on the
anti-diagonal and read the cross as the ground, so the sample is (25,40) with a comment saying why.

**The repair is *Replace…*, not *Relink*.** It picks one file, hashes and embeds it, and **keeps the
framing**, with the `AddImage` prepended to the *same* transaction so one undo restores both. It is the
better half of the trade twice over: it repairs **all three** merged states where Relink repairs one, and
Relink additionally needs linked-image loading, which is unbuilt.

**The layers panel marks it.** `picture_missing(store, node)` is a **free function over the store** so it
can be tested at all, and it asks the *decode cache*, the same question the walk asks, so the row and the
canvas cannot disagree. It covers visible fills, visible strokes and a frame's background — **wider than
the canvas placeholder**, because the row is a statement about the *layer*. The mark is the row's
**existing kind glyph tinted** `theme::color::WARN`: the icon is the one part of a row that cannot be
renamed away. Amber rather than red, because the usual cause is a file that moved.
`a_layer_is_marked_for_any_visible_paint_whose_picture_is_gone` was flip-checked by dropping strokes from
the predicate.

**D178 — peniko has no transparent extend, so a fitted picture needs a clip and not just a brush
transform. *Resolved.*** `images.md` priced the four scale modes as *"a brush transform plus
`peniko::Extend`; none needs pixel work."* The second half held; the first was one short. `Extend` is
pad, repeat or reflect and there is **no transparent option**, so the band beside a contained picture
samples the picture's own edge row: a square photograph fitted into a 200×100 shape drew `[252,0,3,255]`
at x=5 — a solid red column down the letterbox.

So `Framing` carries three things and not two, and `scene::clipped` pushes a layer around the **one**
draw that asked for it rather than around a whole shape. **The clip is the only part of framing that
costs anything**, which is why it is emitted only where the aspects genuinely differ (a tolerance rather
than an exact comparison, so a rounding bit does not buy a layer). `a_fitted_image_leaves_its_letterbox_empty`
pins the pixels by asserting **alpha 0** in the bands — the assertion the smear fails and that no reading
of the middle would notice. `a_tiled_image_repeats_across_its_shape` reads at **odd** coordinates on
purpose, because an untransformed 2-unit tiling lands on the right colour at every even one.

Two details a later editor would simplify and thereby break. **Fill and Fit read nothing**, so cover and
contain re-derive against whatever the frame currently is; a baked-in affine would come apart on the
first resize. And **the extend belongs to the fit, not to the model's sampler** — `color::framed_sampler`
puts it in force at the render boundary and never writes it back.

**The parameters moved out of the variants, and that is the half of this entry to read before touching
the shape.** `ImageFit` was `Fill | Fit | Crop(Rect) | Tile { scale }` and is now a plain four-variant
enum with `crop` and `tile_scale` beside it on `ImageRef`. The payloads made the panel's mode strip
**destructive**: a payload has nowhere to live while its mode is not selected, so clicking *Fit* to look
at the whole picture and clicking back handed you a fresh identity crop. A mode switch has to be a change
of view, not a reset. It is the shape Figma's `scaleMode`/`imageTransform`/`scalingFactor` has. It was
changed **before** the crop gesture was built rather than after, which is the only cheap time to do it.

What it costs is real and is paid for by a test rather than by the type. The enum used to make it
physically impossible for one mode to read another's number; now it is merely wrong, so the isolation is
asserted — `a_mode_ignores_the_parameters_it_does_not_use` checks that each mode really is reading its
*own* number rather than both falling back to a default. On disk it is still additive, so an image that
has been cropped and set back to Fill writes its rectangle — it is still the user's — while one never
cropped writes nothing at all.

**D177 — Images: the model, the decode cache and placing. *Reviewed on screen and accepted.***
Built 2026-08-10 in three passes, and confirmed by the user placing an image and seeing it land on the
canvas. The rules are in §5.5a; what follows is the part that is **settled rather than provisional**, so
that a later session extends it instead of re-deriving it:

- **An image is a fill over a document-level table, keyed by a content hash of the encoded bytes**, and
  the model's brush is peniko's over an `ImageRef` (D176). Undo restores the bytes because `AddImage`
  carries the whole entry; nothing garbage-collects the table.
- **The decode cache's budget bounds waste, not the working set.** Eviction never drops an image the
  document still carries. That is a decision with a stated cost — a document larger than the budget
  keeps all of it decoded — taken against the thrash alternative, not an oversight to be tightened.
- **Placing: a click fits and centres, a drag draws its own box.** Fit is shrink-to-fit and
  **never scale up**, against the frame under the pointer or the viewport on bare canvas. The tool
  disarms itself when the last loaded image is placed, and `choose_tool` putting the load down is what
  makes Escape and every rail button agree.
- **`sha256:<hex>` of the encoded bytes, through `ring`.** A standard digest was chosen over a faster
  non-cryptographic one *because the id goes in the file*: `sha256sum` on an exported original
  reproduces it. Do not swap it for speed without changing that argument first.
- **The alternative that was offered and not taken**: a cascade offset for multi-file placement.
  `images.md` asked for one, it was written, and it turned out to have no caller — a loaded cursor
  places each file at its own click, so nothing stacks. It was deleted rather than kept, and the drop
  path is the thing that will actually need it.

What is left is in §5.5a — linked-image loading — and what is deliberately never coming is D191.
`images.md` was the live scope document until its build list closed; it is folded in here and deleted.

**D176 — The image work's stated prerequisite was a brush enum of our own, and it was not needed.
*Deviation from `images.md`, deliberate.*** The plan named one blocker before any of the feature could
be built — *"an image reference cannot live in `peniko::Brush`, which holds pixels. So the model needs
its own brush — `Solid | Gradient | Image(ImageRef)` — resolved to peniko's at the render boundary"* —
and priced everything else behind it.

The premise is not true of peniko 0.6. Both `Brush<I, G>` and `ImageBrush<D>` are generic over their
storage, and peniko's own doc comment gives the reason: *"different renderers can use different types
here, such as a pre-registered id."* So the model's brush is `peniko::Brush<ImageBrush<ImageRef>>` — the
same enum, with our reference substituted for the pixels — and the prerequisite dissolves into a type
alias. **The whole switch cost three `use` lines inside core** and one per downstream module.

What that buys is not brevity but the two things a hand-rolled enum would have had to earn back:

- **No migration.** `Solid` and `Gradient` keep their exact serde shape, so every existing document
  loads byte-for-byte. Re-declaring the enum would have re-spelled two variants that were already
  right, in order to add a third, and needed a schema bump to do it. ⚠️ **`Gradient`'s payload
  stopped being the same *type* on 2026-09-03 and the property still holds** — it is
  `GradientBrush`, wire-compatible by `#[serde(flatten)]` rather than by being `peniko::Gradient`,
  and **the second generic parameter is what made that a one-line change**: the same door this entry
  came through, used again for a reason nobody had in mind when it was chosen (D412).
- **`images.md`'s own trap answered by construction.** It warns *"`peniko::Image` carries `alpha` and
  `extend` already — do not add parallel fields for them"*. Keeping `ImageBrush` keeps its
  `ImageSampler`, so there is nothing to duplicate and nothing to remember.

**One claim of the plan's did survive, and one was already false.** The render seam was exactly where it
said (`brush_to_backend`, until now `brush.clone()`), and taking the model's serde off a rendering
crate's shape is *not* something this achieves — `peniko::Color` is written directly into the DTO
regardless, so that dependency was never Brush's alone to break.

**And the compiler found something the plan had wrong in the other direction**: "resolve to peniko's at
the render boundary" is one step short. `vello_cpu` paints images through `vello_cpu::ImageSource`, so
`brush_to_backend` cannot hand it a `peniko` image directly and the CPU backend converts one step
further.

**That was first written here as "there is no single conversion", which is too strong, and the decode
cache is where it was corrected.** `ImageSource::from_peniko_image_data` exists, so the conversion is
available and the three brushes are the *same* generic enum over three image slots — the model's
`ImageRef`, vello's `ImageData`, vello_cpu's `ImageSource`. What is true is narrower and is the part
that shaped the cache: the CPU step **premultiplies a whole buffer** rather than cloning a handle, so it
cannot sit on the per-fill path. `cpu.rs` memoizes it per render, and does so by taking the image arm off
the *model's* brush — the backend brush has dropped the id the memo is keyed on. §5.5a carries the
resulting shape.

**A dependency note the plan also had stale**: it lists `image` and `arboard` as "not a dependency yet …
three new pieces of plumbing before a single pixel is drawn". Both are already in the workspace lock —
`arboard` through `egui-winit`, `image` through `arboard` and `eframe` — so the app-side cost is
declaring a direct edge at a version already compiled, not adding a tree.

**D192 — A web face is a *subset*, so its OpenType list is a fraction of the font's.
*Intentional; the shortfall is the file's, not the panel's.*** D157 said the three SIL faces that
declare n-way `cvXX` "arrive through the app's own web-font cache and need no install". That was tried
on the machine and it is false: Andika picked out of the font list offers **four** rows. The cause is
the download URL and not the list. `static_face` and `vf_face` build
`{FONTSOURCE_CDN}/{id}@latest/{subset}-{weight}-{style}`, where `subset` is the family's own
`defSubset` from the Fontsource list API — `latin` for every Latin family, and the only subset name the
parsed `Item` carries at all. So the cached `andika-latin-400-normal.ttf` is **38 KB** against the
**654 KB** of the `Andika-Regular.ttf` SIL ships, and its entire `GSUB` feature list is `ccmp` and
`liga`; with `GPOS`'s `mark` and `mkmk` that is exactly the four rows on screen. The full face declares
**43** `cvXX`, three of them n-way — Gentium Plus 33 and 3, Charis SIL 30 and 3.

**The mechanism is not arbitrary, which is why this generalises past the `cvXX` row.** Subsetting drops
glyphs, and a feature whose glyphs are gone goes with it: Andika's character variants act on IPA and
African-orthography letters — rams horn, Capital Eng, V hook — that a Latin subset does not carry. So
*any* list derived from the face's tables is bounded by the subset, and the OpenType list is simply the
one where a user can count the difference. The axis rows survive because `fvar` is not per-glyph;
nothing else should be assumed to.

**The list is honest about the face it has, and the face it has is not the one the foundry shipped —
and nothing on screen says which.** That is the whole of the defect, and it is recorded rather than
fixed: a wider subset is a bigger download for every family the picker previews, which is exactly what
D160's byte budget is sized against, and the catalog entry we parse does not even list a family's other
subsets. *Intentional. Verify anything about a face's tables against an **installed** copy of it, and
restart afterwards — `FontService::new` runs the `fontdb` scan once, so a font installed mid-session
does not exist until the next launch.*

**D193 — *Show fewer features* vanished under the hand. *Resolved — reported from use.*** "Sometimes
the *Show fewer features* just disappears — not sure which toggle does that, since on one font it was
the last one, on another the second one." Both reports are the same bug, and the differing ordinal is
the tell: what differs between those faces is a count, not a behaviour.

`features_section` gated the reveal on `withheld`, a count of the features not currently shown — and
`shown` is `offered || the document's set already mentions this tag`, which is D157's rule that a
withheld feature the document has an opinion about is shown anyway. That makes the count a property of
the **document**, not of the face. Touching a withheld feature writes it into the set *even when
switching it off* — the explicit-`0`-rather-than-removed rule, also D157 — which makes it shown, which
takes it out of the count. Switch the last hidden feature while the list was expanded and the way back
went with it.

The fix is `features_reveal(show_all, hidden) -> Option<String>`, a free function because the whole of
the bug is one decision and `OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly. **The two states ask different
questions, and that is the part to keep.** Expanded, the way back is **unconditional**: a user in a mode
must be able to leave it whether or not the mode still has anything left to hide. Collapsed, the offer is
only real when something is actually hidden.
`the_way_back_from_show_all_survives_the_last_hidden_feature_being_switched` pins it, and its first
assertion is the reported symptom.

**D194 — The search field inside the font picker dismissed the font picker. *Resolved — reported from
use.*** The cause is egui's own default rather than anything of ours: a `ComboBox` popup gets
`PopupCloseBehavior::CloseOnClick`, and egui's documentation for that variant says the popup "will be
closed on click anywhere, **inside or outside** the popup". So the field the list exists to be filtered
by dismissed it on the way in — pre-existing, and nothing the recent typography work introduced.

The `font-family` combo alone asks for `.close_behavior(PopupCloseBehavior::CloseOnClickOutside)`. **The
cost is that nothing inside the popup closes it any more**, picking a family included, which is what the
explicit `ui.close()` at the family row's click site is for — and the two halves are one fix: delete
either and the list either dies on the search field again or never closes at all. The popup's own `Area`
is `closable()`, so `ui.close()` reaches it from inside the `ScrollArea`. Every other combo in the app is
a plain list of rows and keeps the default, which is right for one: a pick *is* a click inside.

`a_combo_survives_a_click_in_its_search_field_but_not_a_pick` drives real pointer events through the
shape — the call site itself is still only read — and asserts three states: the symptom under egui's
default, the fix under `CloseOnClickOutside`, and that picking a row still dismisses the list. **The
default-behaviour case is the test's own flip**, so it fails against the unfixed version by construction.
It builds the popup with its `ScrollArea` in place deliberately: without one it would be proving
`ui.close()` for a shape the code does not have.

**D195 — A widget's trailing `item_spacing` is banked when the widget is placed, so it cannot be
changed after the fact — and it is invisible until something is allocated after it. *Keep — it is
egui's rule; the answer is to allocate rather than to fight it.*** Recorded on its own because it is
not about the row that found it (D157) and it will catch the next person laying out a two-line row. A
vertical layout advances its cursor past a widget by the `item_spacing` **in effect when that widget is
placed**, not by the one in effect when the next thing lands, so restoring the spacing at the end of a
scope changes nothing: the advance has already happened.

**The half this entry first got wrong is where the banked advance goes.** It claimed a scope that
tightens the spacing pays it after its last widget too, so the gap to whatever follows the scope moves
with the gaps inside it — and that is false, because a `Ui`'s `min_rect` covers **allocated rects
only**. The banked advance is not in it. Measured on 2026-08-16: a card at 9 containing two scopes that
each set 6 and allocate two rows gives gaps of **6, 9, 6** — the inner spacing does not reach the
boundary between the scopes, and a scope really can be tighter inside than outside.

**What makes it appear is allocating anything after the last widget, and then it appears in full.** The
same structure with a tail allocated under the second row — spacing zeroed immediately before the tail,
which is too late — measures **27** between units: the 9 banked when the second row was placed, plus
the 9 of the tail, plus the card's own 9. That is what produced D157's sweep, which stands as evidence
and now has the right explanation: with the tail under the dropdown held at 6, sweeping the row's
`item_spacing.y` through 2, 5 and 10 moved the gap *below* the dropdown to 13, 16 and 21. So the rule
bites exactly where a two-line row in a list needs it to — a hand-allocated gap is added to a banked
one, never substituted for it.

**The practical shape is unchanged and is the thing to keep loud: zero `item_spacing` for the whole
scope and allocate every gap**, after which the gaps are exactly the numbers written and are
independent — sweeping D157's label gap from 2 to 10 now moves the inside gap alone.

**It bites in test fixtures exactly as it does in panels, and there it is worse.** A fixture that
hand-builds a row and sets its pitch *after* the first line has set it too late to be the gap under
that line, so what the assertion measures is the theme's default 6 while the fixture appears to state
its own number — and it goes green. That is what kept a false 6 in
`an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges`'s assertion message across a whole revision, describing a
row that painted 9 (D180, D196): the tautology was the visible half, and the stale default underneath
it is what made the tautology look deliberate. Setting the pitch to `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` in place,
without moving the assignment, is what found the second layer — the test failed at 6 against 9 — and
moving the assignment above the first row is the fix. *A fixture that states a pitch is measuring
itself only if the statement precedes the first widget; otherwise it is measuring the theme.*

**`a_choice_row_groups_its_label_with_its_control` does not pin it**, and that is worth knowing about
that test rather than about this rule: it asserts a *ratio* between the two measured gaps, and the
double-payment version satisfies it, so a future editor folding those two `allocate_space` calls back
into an `item_spacing` gets a row whose outer gap is silently its inner one plus the tail and a green
run. What does pin it is `two_rows_of_one_stroke_sit_half_as_far_apart_as_two_strokes` (D196), which
asserts the measured gaps as exact numbers rather than as a ratio: the banked version of that layout
adds the spacing to both allocations, so it cannot reach 9 within and 18 between. The comment in
`feature_choice_row` is still the guard for the row that found this, and it carries the sweep so the
claim is checkable. *Revisit if egui gains a spacing that applies at the cursor rather than at the
widget.*

**D196 — A stroke's two rows were tighter than an image fill's two lines, and one stroke sat only 1.5×
that from the next. *Resolved, sides rows included — but their pitch moved with them and has not been
seen on the machine.*** Reported against the row that is the yardstick: the spacing between a stroke's two
rows should equal the image's, and between two stroke groups twice that, "so it creates a proper visual
group".

**Three numbers where there should have been one, and only one of them was written down.** `ui::card_at`
sets the card body's `item_spacing.y` to 9. An image fill's second line is drawn inside `paint_row`'s own
scope, which only ever set `item_spacing.x`, so the image's two lines **inherited** that 9. The stroke
unit's scope overrode it to 6, and the card's 9 was the only thing between one stroke and the next — which
also retires D180's claim that the two two-line features matched at 6: they never did.

`ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` (9.0) is now named and is the one number all three read. `paint_row` **states** it
inside its own scope rather than inheriting it — until it did, the same image row drew two different ways
depending on which list it was in — and `inspector::paint_unit` owns the whole layout of a two-row entry:
`item_spacing` zeroed, one `CARD_ROW_GAP` between the rows and a second after the pair **unless it is the
last entry**. Entry-to-entry is therefore 18. Both stroke call sites go through it — **one function
because they have already drifted once**: the mixed branch missed the tighter pitch and the properties row
sat 3px lower on a mixed selection (D134).

**`last` is a display position, not an identity**, which is what a live reorder needs: the number of tails
is `len − 1` whichever entry is at the bottom, so the slot spans do not change shape as the carried entry
moves through them (D61).

**The drop bands grew by the tail, and it is a real shift rather than a harmless one — just a small one.**
`Slots::gap` claims a slot once the pointer passes its **middle**, so for a non-last entry that middle is
now half a gap (4.5) below the entry's visual centre, and swapping downward asks for 4.5 more travel than
swapping upward. Nothing downstream is off by one: `paint::landing` is still a pure function of the
pointer and `shown_at`. *Fix by having `paint_unit` hand back its pre-tail bottom if the asymmetry is ever
felt; do not "fix" it by dropping the tail.*

**What this broke, and the fix moved that number a second time.** `paint_unit` zeroes `item_spacing` for
the whole unit, and `stroke_sides_row` took its vertical gaps from the ambient spacing and set none of its
own. Rows that sat 6 apart sat at **0**, so a stroke with its sides showing was three or five 28pt rows
touching; `paint_unit`'s own test uses stand-in rows and cannot see it. Fixed by `stroke_sides_row`
**stating** `item_spacing.y = ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` at the top of its own scope, rather than by giving the
unit its spacing back — the pair's numbers depend on the zero. **The pitch is therefore not what it was
before this entry either**: those rows took 6 and take 9 now, so a stroke with its sides showing is taller
than it has ever been. Deliberate, but a visible change to a control the report was not about and not yet
looked at on the machine. *Revisit if an expanded stroke reads loose there — the answer would be a
decision about `CARD_ROW_GAP`'s scope, not a literal in `stroke_sides_row`.*

`two_rows_of_one_stroke_sit_half_as_far_apart_as_two_strokes` drives `paint_unit` directly with stand-in
rows, so it tests the layout rather than a replica of it. It asserts the *measured* gaps down a list of
three — the rhythm repeats, the inner gap is `CARD_ROW_GAP`, the outer is exactly twice it — which is what
makes it the pin D195 lacked. Two flips confirmed failing.

**D197 — Two shapes sharing an edge drew a lighter line down the join, and no antialiasing setting touches
it. *Resolved for axis-aligned boxes; rotated pairs and curves still conflate — reviewed and accepted on
the machine 2026-08-16.*** Reported against the simplest scene there is: an 800×100 rect above an 800×500
rect, both the same grey, showing a **lighter** line along `y = 100`. Not a geometry bug — the rects abut
exactly.

It is vello's **conflation artefact** (its open issue #49, listed as an alpha-state limitation): coverage
is computed per path and each path is alpha-blended independently, so where the shared edge falls at
fraction `f` across a device pixel what is *behind both* leaks through the gap. The composite works out to
`C + f(1−f)·(behind − C)`, peaking at a quarter of the fill→backdrop contrast at `f = 0.5`. Measured
through the CPU backend: on a pixel boundary 102, a quarter pixel off 130 against a predicted 130.7, half
a pixel off **140** against 140.25.

**Three things were ruled out with measurements before anything was built.** A GPU probe under
`AaConfig::Area`, `Msaa8` and `Msaa16` read exactly 140 for all three, because vello's MSAA sharpens
*coverage* and then collapses it to a scalar `area` before blending — AA configuration is a dead end
rather than a knob left untuned. Supersampling attenuates and never removes: 1× = 140, 2× = 121, 4× =
111.5, 8× = 106.8, halving per doubling for 4×, 16× and 64× the fragment work. And no peer app has solved
it — Graphite renders through vello with `Msaa16` and shows the same seam on a much newer rev.

**So the fix removes the fraction rather than sampling it better.** `scene::snapped_box_world` rounds an
axis-aligned box's device edges to whole pixels and returns an adjusted world transform. The property that
makes it work is that everything rounds to *one* global grid: two shapes that abutted round the shared
edge to the same integer and still abut, and the edge they now meet on carries no antialiasing to
conflate. **`device_base` must stay in step with `cpu::CpuPainter::base` and `gpu::GpuScenePainter::base`**
— three copies of one formula, and if they disagree the walk snaps to a grid nothing rasterizes on,
silently and only at fractional zooms.

**Children keep the unsnapped transform and snap on their own terms**, which is load-bearing rather than
tidy: the rounding adjusts scale as well as translation, so passing it down would compound. Snapping is
**only `Rect` and `Artboard`**, deliberately not `Ellipse`, `Polygon` or `Star`, whose box edges are
tangent points rather than ink.

**Two guards, each with a test pinned to it.** A box already on the grid returns `world` untouched — not
an optimisation, because `build` promises world transforms bit-identical to `Resolved`'s (§6.2) and the
`base.inverse()` round trip perturbs an untouched one in the fourteenth decimal: invisible on screen and
very visible to `assert_preview_matches_commit`. And a non-empty box cannot round away to nothing: at 25%
zoom a 2-unit bar is half a device pixel and both edges round to the same place, so without a floor
snapping *deletes* hairlines. Each flipped against the plausible wrong version rather than against
nothing.

**Ghosts snap too, and the existing suite is what said so.** They were left unsnapped at first, on the
reasoning that a preview glides during a drag. Three `tests/overrides.rs` cases failed: an unsnapped
preview draws in a different place from what release commits, so a shape would **twitch at the instant you
let go of it**. The preview-equals-commit invariant caught a decision rather than a slip.

**Export.** The SVG writer does not go through this walk, so an SVG carries the seam to whatever renders
it; this is the canvas's and the PNG path's mitigation only. PNG shares the walk and so snaps, a no-op
wherever the frame is 1:1 on whole-number bounds.

**The residual is real and is not softened.** Two rotated rects sharing an edge still conflate, as do
abutting ellipses, polygons and paths. That case reads as a diagonal fringe and is far less visible, but
it is a genuine gap, and supersampling is the only avenue that would close it.

**An "at rest" gate was designed, offered and proved unnecessary.** The predicted cost was that snapping
would make motion steppy. The user tested a 45-node scene and reported "I don't see any weirdness", so
snapping is unconditional. *Revisit only if motion is reported as steppy: the at-rest gate is the first
rung and supersampling at rest the second, and neither is built.*

**D198 — The Alt-hover measure, and the four questions `roadmap.md` held open for it. *Resolved.***
"Figure out distances" was three missing pieces; this one landed first and alone, the other two in D200.

**`measure.rs` is `snap.rs`'s sibling and deliberately not part of it.** The two compute the same kind of
thing for opposite purposes: snapping nudges a live gesture and draws a line to explain the nudge,
measuring changes nothing and draws a *number*. Keeping them apart is what stops a tolerance leaking into
a measurement, and nothing in `measure.rs` has one, because a measure is never "close enough". `Measure`
reuses `snap::Axis` with the same meaning — the direction of the *line* — which is not duplication to be
collapsed but the shape a drawn line in world space has.

**The four questions, answered.** *Measure to `pick_preview`'s answer rather than the raw leaf* came out
stronger than asked: it is the **same call**, `canvas::hover_target`, lifted verbatim out of
`draw_hover_outline`. Two resolutions written the same way would still let `Ctrl`+`Alt` split them, and
the overlay would then ring one layer and measure to another. *Suppress during any drag* is
`canvas::hover_chrome_live`, which the hover outline and the key trace each spelled out separately and now
share. *Shift does not drop the measures*: the key layer is always designated *through* a measure overlay,
and not flickering it while the hand reaches for a chord is worth more than "the click is armed now".
**The fourth was whether `Alt` going down with the pointer stationary wakes a frame, and it does** — the
user confirmed it on the machine, 2026-08-18. It had to be answered from the chair, being the
backend→egui direction (D110's class). Nothing in the implementation ever depended on the answer.

**Four load-bearing choices in the geometry, each flipped against the plausible wrong version.** `spans`'
disjointness tests are `>=`, so **flush counts as apart**: two touching boxes report a gap of zero, which
is dropped, rather than an "overlap" whose near-edge distance is a whole box width. The **L-corner
asymmetry** — the horizontal on the selection's near edge, the vertical on the target's — is what makes a
diagonal pair *meet* at the third point of the L; the symmetric-looking spelling fails both L tests. `EPS
= 0.005` is half the last digit `label` shows, so no measure can say `0`. And a line sits on the **middle
of what the two boxes share**, so both its ends land on a real edge of a real box. `to_guide`'s boundary
is strict where `between`'s is not, which looks like an inconsistency and is the decision: a guide lying
on an edge takes the *across* branch, because a point has no gap reading to protect where two flush boxes
do.

**`label` is two decimals with trailing zeros trimmed, and deliberately not `round()`, which is what
`draw_size_badge` does.** A badge summarises the thing you are looking at; a measure answers "exactly how
far", asked by someone who has already decided the eye is not enough, so `7.5` reported as `8` would be
this overlay's only possible failure. It measures **world bounding boxes**, which is Figma's rule and the
only one available.

**`color::MEASURE` (`f26d6d`) is a third chrome hue in a scheme D13 otherwise reserves for `SELECT`**, and
it argues its case the way D113 argues `KEY`'s. Red is what a distance annotation looks like in every tool
that has one; and a shade of `SELECT` would attach the measure to one of the two boxes when it is a
statement about the *gap*. Light rather than the guides' dark red, and that separation has to hold,
because measures are frequently drawn *to* a guide.

**The ticks across each end are not decoration, and the pill is centred on the line as Figma's is.** A
measure is frequently a few pixels long, where a red line with a pill over it is indistinguishable from a
stray mark. Centring is only tolerable if the pill is narrow, which is a number rather than an opinion, so
`the_label_pill_is_narrow_enough_to_centre_on_its_own_line` measures it with the app's own fonts installed
— at 9.5pt, `8` → 13.9px, `1200` → 29.7px, `40.25` → 34.1px. **The guess it replaced was 26px for a
two-digit label**, a third too wide, which would have argued for offsetting the label instead. Raising the
font to 12pt fails it, so it bites.

`rulers::measure_guide` answers the guide half and lives in that module because both halves are its
private business: `shown_guide`, so a guide mid-drag is measured to where it *looks like* it is, and
`guide_world_coord`. Its two `None`s are `guide_lines`' two.

**Nothing tests the `Alt` gate or the drawing, and nothing in this crate can** — the same seam that leaves
`canvas::autopan`, `resize_tx` and `pen_verb`'s routing read rather than pinned.

**D199 — New text is trimmed to cap height, and the line box it gave up is drawn. *Resolved — new text
only, by decision.*** Asked for after using D198's measure overlay, and against a peer: Graphite draws
**two** boxes on a text node and the tight one is what its transforms use; Figma has the same as *Vertical
trim*. The ask here was for it **on by default**. The mechanism already existed — `BoxTrim` and D78 — so
the change is two things: author the trim, and draw the box it takes away.

**D78's byte-identical guarantee is preserved rather than falsified, and that was decided rather than
assumed.** `BlockStyle.trim` serializes with `skip_serializing_if`, so every text node in every existing
file *omits* the field: moving `BoxTrim`'s `#[default]` would have silently re-measured all of them.
Three options were put to the user and **new text only** was chosen. So `BoxTrim::None` remains
`#[default]` while `FontService::default_text_parts` **authors** `CapToBaseline`. *The app authors a trim;
the format assumes none* — that sentence is the whole compatibility story. The cost is recorded because it
will otherwise read as a bug: **text in a file written before this keeps the full line box until someone
toggles it**, `stress.ondin` included.

`CapToBaseline` rather than `AscentToDescent`: cap height to baseline is what Figma's Vertical trim and
Graphite's tight box both mean. The consequence is that **descenders fall outside the box**, which is not
a defect but the reason the untrimmed box is *drawn* rather than discarded.

**Core grew a second box that nothing measures with.** `text::box_of` returns a private `NodeBox { origin,
size, untrimmed }` — a struct because two of the three are a `Size`, and a call site that swapped them
would produce a box that is right on every *untrimmed* node, which is almost everywhere. `Fixed(size)`
answers `size`, because `Fixed` is the authored box and trim does not reinterpret it (D78).
`TextLayout::untrimmed_bounds()` is the reader, and **nothing measures with it**. The API property that
matters is that `untrimmed_bounds() == bounds()` **exactly** when trim changed nothing, so a consumer
tests equality instead of asking what the trim setting is.

`FontService::default_text_parts` **lost its receiver** and is now an associated function. It took `&self`
and used none of it, which is the spelling that made the app's most consequential authoring decision
reachable only by standing up a `FontService` — threads, a cache directory, a system-font enumeration — so
nothing tested it. *If it ever needs session state, it becomes a method again and the test follows it.*

`canvas::draw_text_line_boxes` draws the line box dashed. Two details are load-bearing: it is drawn
**before** the selection outlines so the trimmed box that carries the handles reads on top, and the quad
is closed by **repeating its first corner**, because `Shape::dashed_line` takes a polyline and four points
leave the fourth side undrawn.

**D162's trimmed-auto resize path went from rare to universal in this change**, which is the risk worth
naming: `resized_box`'s special case was written against a configuration almost nobody had, and every
newly created text node is now in it. And this is one story with **D198** rather than two: measuring
**to** a text node now quotes its tight box, so the number is the distance to the letters.

Three tests, each flipped against the plausible wrong version.
`the_line_box_contains_the_trimmed_box_and_is_taller_by_the_trim` asserts the line box equals the height
the *same content laid out untrimmed* reports — measured against a real untrimmed node rather than
arithmetic on itself. **Note its flip's symptom**: forgetting to add the insets back makes
`untrimmed_bounds() == bounds()`, so the canvas draws nothing, which looks exactly like "the feature is
off". `a_node_whose_box_trim_did_not_change_reports_no_line_box`'s `Fixed` fixture is deliberately
*smaller* than the line box, so a leak shows up as a larger rectangle instead of being hidden by a
coincidental match. `a_new_text_node_gets_the_tight_box_and_keeps_its_line_box` checks the field too,
which is the easy half; the geometry is there because a `trim` that reached the node and not `box_of`
would pass a field check and produce the old behaviour. **Its baseline assertion is not a duplicate of
`a_cap_trimmed_box_ends_on_the_baseline`, and neither should be deleted as redundant**: the core one
proves the arithmetic at 40pt on the font's own leading, this one for the configuration every user gets,
24pt at a stated 1.2em — a stated line height being exactly the thing that could put the baseline
somewhere else.

**D200 — Equal-gap spacing snapping, and the distance labels that explain it. *Resolved — "figure out
distances" is closed.*** The two were one job and were built as one. Labels with no snap behind them would
be noise on every drag, and a spacing snap with no numbers would be the app moving a layer for a reason it
declines to state.

**`Axis` moved from `snap.rs` to `measure.rs`, and that is what keeps the dependency one-way.** `snap` now
produces `Measure`s, so it reads `measure`; had `measure` gone on reaching back the two would be mutually
dependent over a two-variant enum. *The direction is the point: `measure` knows nothing about snapping,
which is what D198 bought by keeping tolerance out of it.*

**`measure::gap(a, b, axis)` is `between`'s single most useful answer, by name.** The spacing snap has
already decided which two boxes and which axis; `between` would hand it the perpendicular edge offsets as
well, which during a drag is three lines where the gesture means one.

**Two candidates per axis**: **centre between the two nearest neighbours**, where the delta that equalizes
the gaps is half their difference, and **match the rhythm** past the end of a run — so a row spaces itself
as it is *built* rather than only once it is finished and distributed. Three filters keep it honest: a
strict shared band, nothing against a neighbour the box overlaps on the axis, and nothing under `MIN_GAP`.

**`Matched::Spacing` stores the *neighbours*, not finished measures.** The gaps a candidate produces are
only true at the position it would move the box to, so `snap_rect` calls `spacing_marks(snapped, ..)`
after applying the delta. Building them at candidate time would have the labels quoting the **unsnapped**
gaps — wrong by exactly the delta the snap is about, which is the one error that makes numbers worse than
no numbers.

**Precedence: whichever is nearer claims the axis, and alignment takes ties.** An alignment lands a
feature on a coordinate, an exact statement about two visible things, where a spacing snap **invents** a
position; so where the two are equally near the alignment is the more predictable answer.

**The payoff of D198 having produced a reusable `Measure`**: the gaps go through `canvas::draw_measure`
unchanged, so a labelled distance looks identical whether the app is *reporting* one under `Alt` or has
just *created* one.

Seven tests, each flipped. Measuring the gaps at the pointer instead of after the snap fails three,
reading `left: [76.0, 84.0] right: [80.0, 80.0]`: the label wrong by exactly the delta that makes it
interesting.

**The `MIN_GAP` test was vacuous first, and that is the part worth reading.** Its first fixture was a row
of **flush** boxes, and it passed with the floor removed: a zero-length gap is dropped by `measure::gap`'s
own epsilon, so `marks.gaps` came back empty either way. It now tests just *above* zero, where the floor
is the only thing deciding — gaps of 0.4 and 0.5 put the spacing delta at 0.05, so without the floor
spacing wins a contest it should not be in. It carries a control asserting the same geometry *widened*
does fire, so it cannot become a test about a fixture that never reaches the state.

**One fixture trap, recorded because it will be made again: a box has three features per axis.** The
precedence test's third box was 100 wide, and its **centre** landed 4 from the moving box's right edge —
so the test compared an alignment against an alignment and dutifully reported that spacing had lost. *Any
test about which snap won has to prove the loser was the snap it meant.*

**D201 — The measure overlay reads the other way round: a selected *guide* measures to the layer under the
pointer. *Resolved.*** Small to build, because the geometry was already symmetric — which is the
interesting part of the entry.

**`measure::to_guide`'s first parameter is now `box_`, not `selection`.** The distance between a box and a
line does not depend on which of the two was clicked first, so one function answers both directions and
they cannot disagree about a number they both quote. Renaming the parameter is how that is stated where a
reader will meet it: `selection` was a claim about the *caller* sitting in a module that deliberately
knows nothing about selection, and it would have invited a second function for the reverse direction.

**`rulers::measurable_guide(GuideId)` is `measure_guide`'s by-id half**, split out so both directions meet
in one place. What they have to agree about is where a guide *is*, and the interesting half of that is the
`None`s, which are easy to get right once and easy to forget the second time.

**A near-bug found while writing it, and now the reason for a guard.** `measurable_guide` asks
