`guides_on()` itself rather than inheriting the check, because the by-id path cannot inherit anything:
*View ▸ Hide guides* does **not** clear the guide selection — only *Lock guides* does — so a selected
guide can be invisible, and without the check this feature would have measured from a line nobody can see.
The hover direction never had the problem, `guide_at` declining on `guides_pickable`, which is precisely
why the *by-id* path was the one able to go wrong. *A predicate that arrived free on one path is the first
thing to re-check when a second path is added.*

**The branch is an `else`, not a precedence rule, and `Selection`'s exclusivity invariant is what makes
that sound.** Every way of selecting a guide clears the layers and vice versa (§9.3), so the two branches
cannot both apply and there is nothing to rank. Writing it as a precedence would have been inventing an
answer to a question the model does not allow to be asked. **Every** selected guide measures, not just
one: a vertical and a horizontal together read as a cross through the hovered layer.

**No new tests, and this one is genuinely not a gap.** The geometry is `to_guide`, already covered. What
is new is *routing* — which selection, which hover, and the `guides_on` guard — which lives on `OndinApp`,
so **the routing is read rather than pinned**, including the guard, which is the piece a regression would
be silent about.

**D202 — A locked guide is measured to, because it is already snapped to. *Resolved — decided on an
inconsistency, not on a preference.*** Reported as a genuine open question rather than a complaint.

**What settled it was an inconsistency already in the code.** `guide_lines` gates snapping on `guides_on()`
and never on the lock, so a locked guide *already* pulls a dragged shape onto itself. One that attracts a
layer and then declines to say how far away it was is a single predicate answered two ways. Locking exists
to stop a guide being **changed**; measuring is the one thing in this app that changes nothing at all, so
it is the last thing a lock should reach. The rule is statable in one line: **what may be measured is what
may be snapped to, not what may be picked up.**

`rulers::guide_under` is the nearest-guide search with **no** question about what may be done with the
result, split out of `guide_at`, which keeps its `guides_pickable()` check above the call — so hover, the
cursor, the press, the drag and the discard are untouched. Both keep refusing the **ruler band**, for a
reason neither can drop: that band is the ruler's, and a guide's grab region overlapping it would take
presses meant for pulling out a new guide.

**A property worth having falls out.** The cursor over a locked guide does not change — so the chrome says
"no grab on offer here" and the overlay says "but here is the distance", which are exactly the two true
statements about a locked, visible guide. *Neither half is a special case; they are one predicate each,
asked of the right question.*

**No tests, and it is D201's gap with more at stake** — unlike D201 this is a *behaviour change* guarded
by nothing, whose failure mode is silent in **both** directions: a lock that quietly starts suppressing
measures again, or a `guide_under` that stops refusing the ruler band. *If either half ever needs pinning,
the seam is `guides_on`/`guides_pickable`/`guide_under` over a small state struct, not the overlay.*

**D203 — Guide to guide, the fourth pairing, and the line it is drawn on is *chosen* rather than derived.
*Resolved — the overlay is complete.*** Hovering another **guide** with a guide selected did nothing,
because that branch resolved the hover through `hover_target`, which only ever answers with a layer.

**The one real decision is where to put the line, and it was the user's to make.** Every other pairing
derives its perpendicular coordinate from the geometry, but **two parallel guides share nothing**, both
being infinite. The two candidates were the pointer's position latched at `Alt`-down and the centre of the
screen, and the recommendation was the centre, because **the pointer is the worst available source for
that coordinate**: to hover a vertical guide you must be within `GUIDE_PICK_PT` of it in x, so the
coordinate you are free to sweep is exactly the y the measure needs — the label would slide under the hand
while the number never changed. Three supporting reasons: a latch needs **state**, where the snap overlay
deliberately recomputes its marks every frame; a latch is **wrong for the gesture order**, `Alt` going
down *before* the hand moves to choose a target; and padding to keep the cursor off the label stops being
a concern. So it is `canvas_inner(rect).center()`, `canvas_inner` rather than `rect` so the line does not
sit under a ruler bar — the precedent being the drop-target overlay (D184).

**A refinement deliberately not built, and available rather than missing.** Frame-scoped guides draw as
*finite* segments, so two scoped to the same frame do share a drawn extent, and `shared_middle` would be
the better answer there. *Add it if scoped guides start being measured against each other in earnest; do
not replace the fallback.*

**Two `None`s that are statements rather than guards.** Perpendicular guides *cross*: the distance between
two lines that meet is zero everywhere along one axis and undefined along the other. Coincident guides
come back `None` through `EPS`, which is also what makes hovering a guide that is **itself** selected
quietly draw nothing.

**`Axis::across()` is the flip from "the axis a guide pins" to "the axis a line quoting it runs along",
spelled once.** `to_guide` was rewritten to use it, which is what makes the flip properly guarded: making
`across` the identity now fails **five** tests, because routing `to_guide` through it put that function's
three pre-existing guide tests to work on the flip as well.

**The geometry is pinned and the routing is still read** — which selection, which hover, and now which of
two hovers. *It is the largest untested surface in the feature.*

**D204 — `Ctrl+Alt+X` cut the selection instead of excluding it. *Resolved — one root cause, two symptoms,
both fixed.*** Destructive and silent, which is the pairing that makes it the worst bug the keymap has
had: a cut looks exactly like a boolean that consumed its operands. Found by reading `egui_winit` against
the keymap rather than by using either.

`is_cut_command` is `keycode == Key::Cut || (modifiers.command && keycode == Key::X) || …` — **it never
looks at Alt** — and on a press its caller pushes `Event::Cut` and **returns**. One early return, both
halves of the bug.

**The cut** happened because the clipboard event loop read `Event::Cut` unconditionally. The whole loop is
gated on `!m.alt` now, which is the `cmd_only` rule every `on(…)` call already states for itself (D207)
and which this loop had simply been missed by, D17 having built it before there were any `Ctrl+Alt` chords
to collide with. **The consequence was deliberate**: `Ctrl+Alt+C` and `Ctrl+Alt+V` were inert rather than
clipboard operations — so when `docs/shortcuts.md` §7's copy- and paste-properties rows land, that guard
has to become a *branch* rather than be lifted. They landed 2026-08-20 and it did (D257); the `Event::Cut`
arm is the one Alt still only silences, this bug being what it silences it for.

**Exclude** had no keyboard route at all, because `key_pressed(Key::X)` can never fire however right it
reads. It comes off `i.key_released(egui::Key::X)` now, the other three booleans still reading the press:
the release falls past the guard because the guard sits inside `if pressed`, the same seam `Ctrl+V` is
already read at (D183).

**The test was encoding the bug**, which is the part to carry away. `the_four_boolean_chords_resolve` fed
a synthetic `Event::Key` press for `X` — the one signal the real app never produces for C, X or V — so it
was green for the whole time Exclude was unreachable: D17's own vacuous shape, one chord along. It drives
the release now, and `ctrl_alt_x_excludes_and_does_not_cut` is the new pin, each half confirmed to fail
alone.

*Any keymap test for a `Ctrl`+letter chord where the letter is C, X or V must drive the event or the
release, never the press.*

**D205 — `Shift+1` had never once zoomed to fit. *Resolved.*** `Shift`+`1` reaches egui as
`Key::Exclamationmark`, and `InputState::num_presses` matches only on `Event::Key`'s logical `key` and
never consults `physical_key`. So `plain && m.shift && key_pressed(Num1)` read perfectly and fired never,
from the day it was written.

Both spellings are accepted now, the precedent the bracket restack had already set (D38) — the third time
the workspace has met this. `Num1` stays in the pair rather than being swapped out, because it is the
spelling a layout that passes the unshifted digit through would send.

**`Ctrl+1` was never broken, and that is why the dead line survived review** — it carries no Shift, so the
digit arrives as itself, and the pair reads as one binding written twice rather than as one binding and
one dead line.

**D206 — The Rotation field spun a mirrored layer half a turn per frame past ±90°, and the fix is a latch
rather than the composed write. *Resolved — and this is the case D55's closing note predicted.***
Reported as a top-only stroke "flipping from top to bottom, basically flashing" while the Rotation value
was dragged, and narrowed by the reporter to the field: the canvas rotate ring was immune.

**`roadmap.md`'s recorded diagnosis was right and its recorded fix was incomplete**, which goes first
because the incomplete fix is the obvious one. The roadmap asked for the field to apply a delta about the
pivot instead of rebuilding; that was implemented first and measured **not** to fix the bug. The mechanism
has four parts and the write is none of them. `world` in `inspector_transform` is the **previewed**
transform, so the field reads back its own preview and `Basis::of` re-reports it every frame. That report
jumps 180° as a mirrored layer crosses ±90°, by §5.7a's "whichever axis leaves the smaller angle" rule —
which is correct and untouched. egui's `DragValue`, meanwhile, keeps its **own** accumulator in `ui.data`,
seeded on the frame the drag starts and driven by the pointer alone thereafter. So on the frame the report
jumps, the accumulator says 92 while the re-read base says −89, and `typed − base` is 181° instead of 1°.
**The subtraction was wrong**, and composing the delta does not help, because it faithfully applies a 181°
delta. Measured with a throwaway probe stepping the arithmetic 1° at a time across the threshold.

**So the fix is `AngleScrub { base, world, shown }`**, held in egui temp data for the length of the
gesture. `AngleScrub::reference(latch, at_rest, world)` returns the `(base, world)` a frame measures from
— the latch while a gesture is in flight, the document's own reading otherwise, which is also right for
the **first** frame of a drag (`drag_started` is only knowable after the widget has run) and for the frame
the drag **stops**. Holding `shown` as well is what keeps the field's *other* claimant honest: the prefix
strip scrubs by adding this frame's pointer delta to the value it is handed, a **relative** step where the
`DragValue` is absolute. One visible consequence, and it is the rule rather than a symptom: the readout no
longer flicks to the far side mid-drag — it does so once, on release.

**A real deviation from the stateless-rebuild pattern, and the inspector's only latch of gesture-*start*
state.** The nearest neighbours hold a running *total* rather than a reference to measure from — and the
multi-selection angle fields are immune to this bug for a related reason: their base is read from the
**committed** tree, which does not move under the drag. D55 closed by predicting that if the identity
edit's exactness ever stopped holding "the fields start walking the layer as they are scrubbed". The
symptom arrived and the exactness never stopped holding; it was the other side of the subtraction that
broke.

**`turned_about(world, pivot, delta)` also landed, and is explicitly not the fix.** Measured both ways
round: keeping the latch and restoring the old rebuilt-basis write leaves the field correct, and dropping
the latch while keeping `turned_about` leaves it jumping. It is kept because it is the simpler and safer
spelling: exact by construction rather than by an argument about the decomposition. *Do not let a later
reading credit composition with the fix.*

**The skew field is unchanged and must stay that way.** It replaces `skew` alone and keeps `angle` and
`mirror` together, so the entangled pair is never split.

**The report's one open question is closed.** It asked whether two flips could have netted to a mirror.
They cannot: `flip` composes `translate(c) · FLIP · translate(−c)`, whose 2×2 part is exactly `FLIP_X` or
`FLIP_Y`, and each flip contributes −1 to a determinant that is multiplicative. Two flips are exactly a
half turn.

Four tests. `a_mirrored_layer_turns_by_the_drag_and_not_half_a_circle` models the whole per-frame loop
headlessly — the accumulator and the preview feedback included — having first asserted that the fixture is
really mirrored and really starts below 90°. **`OndinApp` still cannot be built headlessly, so the wiring
between these and the widget is still only read** — D35's seam, and the pattern that keeps working.

**D207 — The first `Ctrl+Alt` chords exposed that every other `Ctrl` chord was ignoring Alt. *Resolved —
and D204 is its sequel.*** `Ctrl+Alt+S` fired `Save` **and** `Subtract`, so every subtract also wrote the
file. Silent in the worst way — the save succeeds, so nothing looks wrong until the artwork is.

The fix is one line applied at every chord: `cmd_only = cmd && !m.alt`, with `plain = !m.command &&
!m.alt` beside it for the single-key tool switches. **`cmd_only` is not a verbose spelling of `cmd`** —
collapsing it back is how the collision returns, destructively and without a symptom.
`save_and_cut_are_not_booleans` asserts both directions, because either half alone passes against a keymap
that is wrong the other way.

**The gap it left is the part to carry away.** The sweep visited the `on(…)` calls and stopped there; the
clipboard event loop reads events rather than keys and so was not one of the sites, which is what let
`Ctrl+Alt+X` keep cutting for months until D204. *A rule swept across "every call site" misses the sites
that are not calls.*

**And it missed one site that *is* in the same function, found 2026-09-08 (D545).** The z-order
bracket loop opens `if !cmd { continue; }` and then tests the keys, so it was never an `on(…)` call
either — eight `Ctrl+Alt` bracket spellings restacked the selection and spent an undo step, for
chords `docs/shortcuts.md` binds to nothing. Nothing collided, which is exactly what the paragraph
above this one predicts and is why it survived every reading since: **the harm from a missing `!alt`
is not visible until a second chord claims the spelling.**

**D208 — The View and Snap rows were keyed by their own labels, and a chord is a second caller that never
sees a row. *Resolved.*** The string keying held a row and the state it drives in step only for as long as
nobody typed a different string, and `docs/shortcuts.md` §6 was about to add seven more chords. The
failure mode is a switch that silently does nothing while its tick goes on painting.

So the key became a type. `input::ViewSwitch` has one variant per switch, a `label()`, and
`VIEW_MENU`/`SNAP_MENU` arrays that *are* the menus' row order; `Action::ToggleView(ViewSwitch)` replaces
the three old variants. A row's label, its position and the state it drives now come out of one place.
`VIEW_MENU` is Illustrator's reading order, so reordering the array reorders the menu — the point, and
also the thing to know before "tidying" it.

**The toast moved into the setter, and that is a decision rather than a tidy-up.** A menu row shows its own
tick as it is clicked; a chord toggling snap-to-grid is otherwise completely silent. Two switches opt out
because their own paths already speak.

Seven chords land on the enum, and two of them need both spellings of a shifted punctuation key, because
`:` and `|` have `egui::Key` variants and win over the physical key while `"` has none (D205).

**D209 — `ZoomFit` fitted the selection whenever there was one, so "fit everything" was unreachable.
*Resolved.*** With any layer picked there was no key, no menu row and no gesture that framed the document:
the only way to it was to deselect first — a capability lost to a convenience nobody chose. Carried in
`roadmap.md` as *zoom-to-selection needs a distinct action, not just a binding*, and that phrasing is the
right one.

`content_bounds` is split into `document_bounds` and `selection_bounds`. `ZoomFit` fits everything
unconditionally and the new `Action::ZoomSelection` fits the selection. **`ZoomSelection` is a no-op with
nothing selected**, deliberately: falling through to the document is exactly the behaviour the split
removed.

Two things fell out that the binding did not ask for. `reveal_selection` shared `content_bounds` and so
scrolled the *whole document* into view on an empty selection — inert in practice but not what the name
says. And the zoom dropdown gained a **Fit selection** row, because *Fit to page* had quietly been doing
that job and splitting the actions without splitting the menu would have taken a capability away from the
mouse.

**D210 — Two opacity digits are one edit, so the first one previews. *Resolved.*** `4` is 40%, and `4`,`5`
inside 600 ms is 45%. Read as two keystrokes that is two edits, and the history reads 40% and then 45% — a
step the user never asked for sitting in front of the one they did.

`Action::OpacityDigit(u8)` therefore carries **the digit and not the percentage**: what a key means cannot
be decided without knowing the key before it, and `input::resolve` is deliberately a pure function of one
frame's input. The first digit is a **preview** — live on screen, absent from history — and the commit
happens when the window shuts, whichever way it shuts.

⚠️ **There are three ways it shuts and this entry named two of them until 2026-09-08** (D535). A
second digit and the deadline both commit; **`Escape` and the right-click cancel shut it without
committing**, because a cancelled gesture owes zero transactions (§9.3) and the pending digit is a
gesture preview — `set_opacity_pct_on` goes through `EditorSession::set_preview`, so
`has_gesture_preview()` is true and `cancel_gesture` is the rung `escape` stops on. It was not on
that function's clearing list, so the cancel reverted the preview on screen and the deadline
committed 40% six hundred milliseconds later anyway. **The sentence above is what made this look
covered**: *"whichever way it shuts"* reads as exhaustive and the enumeration below it was not.

**The deadline needs `request_repaint_after` and would otherwise never arrive.** Nothing wakes a reactive
frame loop after the last keypress, so a lone `4` would sit previewed at 40% for ever and then vanish on
the next unrelated repaint. Same stranded-first-wake shape as D110 and `fold_chrome_hold`'s timer, and
re-asked on every pending frame for the same reason.

**`opacity_window_open` is shared by both readers on purpose.** Written as two `now - at` comparisons they
are one edit away from an instant at which a digit is folded into a pair that has already been committed
on its own — one keystroke, two history steps, and the second a number nobody typed.
`the_pairing_rule_and_the_commit_deadline_agree_everywhere` sweeps the boundary a thousand times finer
than the window, because *which* side of `<` the exact boundary falls on is a float artefact rather than a
decision anyone made. `two_digits_inside_the_window_are_one_exact_value` fails against the plausible wrong
version, which commits the first digit instead of previewing it — a version any test checking only the
final number would pass.

⚠️ **The pending entry carries its *subject* as well as its digit, and this entry did not say so until
2026-09-07** (D470). The window is 600 ms wide and the selection is free to move inside it, so a commit
that re-read the live selection at deadline time put the typed value on a layer the user had merely
clicked; the same field is what stops two digits typed against two different layers pairing into one
value. Everything above is unchanged — this was a gap in it rather than a violation.

Plain digits only, which is what keeps them off `Shift+0/1/2` (zoom) and off `Shift`+`3`…`9`, reserved for
blend modes and required to stay *unclaimed* rather than fall through to an opacity nobody meant to set.

**D211 — `Mode::TextInsert` stopped being exclusive: modified chords resolve, bare keys stay the
buffer's. *Intentional.*** `resolve` returned an empty `Vec` for everything in `TextInsert`, so the
canvas editor owned every key and the buffer could not drift from the document behind its back.
`shortcuts.md` §10's styling set needed that relaxed, and the rule taken is the narrowest one that
keeps the original argument intact: **a bare key in a session is a character; a modified chord is
not.** `Ctrl+U` does not touch the buffer. `input::text_insert_mode` resolves the chords and nothing
else, and `no_bare_key_is_a_command_in_a_text_session` states that as the invariant rather than as a
list of cases.

The chords are `Action::TextStyle(TextChord)` — underline, font size ∓2, tracking, leading and the four
paragraph alignments — handled by `OndinApp::text_chord`, which routes through the **same**
`apply_char_attrs` / `commit_paragraph` the Type panel's own controls use. So a chord and a click are
the same edit, including the scope rule where a selection styles the selection and a bare caret sets
the node's defaults; duplicating that here is how the two would come to disagree about a mixed run.
Underline is exclusive with strikethrough per the 2026-07-31 redesign and **carries the decoration's
colour and thickness over**, because switching which line is drawn is not a reset of how it is drawn.
Line height seeds from what Auto is currently worth rather than from a round number (D162's rule), and
`step_length` steps a `Length` **in whatever unit it already carries** — a tracking of 2% nudged up
stays a percentage — since converting would make one key mean different things depending on a unit chip
the user set deliberately.

**This is the first time `Mode` carries load rather than merely swallowing keys.** Three chords now
mean two things and nothing but the mode tells them apart: `Ctrl+U` is snap-to-shapes in Normal and
underline here, `Ctrl+Shift+L` is lock and align-left, `Alt`+arrows are the nudge and
tracking/leading. Each therefore has a **paired** test — the chord in Normal and the same chord in
TextInsert — in `the_colliding_chords_mean_one_thing_per_mode`, and the rest of the new chords keep an
inertness sweep. D173's "`input::resolve` returns nothing at all in `Mode::TextInsert`" is narrowed to
"no *bare* key" by this and its argument is untouched: `Tab` carries no modifier, and it stays in the
editor's own loop because what it changes is the paragraph the caret is in rather than its styling.

**D212 — `Ctrl+Shift+C` never arrives as a press either, so centre-align is read from the release.
*Resolved — D204's bug one letter over.*** `egui_winit`'s `is_copy_command` tests `modifiers.command &&
Key::C` and **never looks at Shift**, exactly as `is_cut_command` never looks at Alt: the press is
swallowed, `Event::Copy` is pushed, and the caller returns. So `cmd_only && m.shift &&
key_pressed(Key::C)` — the obvious spelling of §10's centre-align chord — reads perfectly and fires
never. Caught before it shipped, by writing the test to the rule D204 left behind rather than by using
the binding.

The fix is the same seam: `i.key_released(egui::Key::C)`, which falls past the guard because the guard
sits inside `if pressed`. `L`, `R` and `J` keep the press, so the alignment loop is three keys and an
odd one out — the shape the boolean loop already has for `X`.
`the_alignment_chords_resolve_and_centre_comes_off_the_release` drives the press *and* the release for
`C` and asserts only the release resolves; it was confirmed to fail against the press spelling.

*D204's rule stands and is now general: any binding on `C`, `X` or `V` with `command` held must come
from the event or from the release whatever else is in the chord, and any test for one must drive that
signal.*

**Reading the release was only half of it, and the other half took until 2026-09-08 (D545).** The
press that gets swallowed still becomes an `Event::Copy`, and `canvas::text_mode_input` was reading
that event with no Shift term — so `Ctrl+Shift+C` centred the paragraph **and** overwrote the system
clipboard, one keystroke doing both, with the *"Copied text"* toast the only thing on screen naming
what the key had done. This entry and D217 were each right about their own half and neither
enumerated the pair. *Where a chord is read from a release because its press was stolen, ask what the
thief did with it.*

**D213 — `Ctrl+Alt+←` was claimed by nobody at all. *Resolved — found by a test before it shipped.***
An arrow key in a live text session has two claimants: the editor's own loop moves the caret, and the
keymap's `Alt`+arrows are tracking and leading (D211). The editor yielded on `!modifiers.alt` while the
keymap's binding is `alt_only` (`!command && alt`), so the two conditions were not complements — with
Ctrl *and* Alt down the editor handed the key over and the keymap refused it, and `Ctrl+Alt+←` did
**nothing whatever**. Dead rather than doubled, which is the quieter of the two failures and the one
that survives review, since the chord nobody uses is the chord nobody reports.

The yield is `!(alt && !command)` now, so the editor gives away exactly what the keymap takes and
`Ctrl+Alt+←` stays the by-word caret move `Ctrl+←` already is. It was extracted as
`canvas::arrow_moves_caret` **specifically so a headless test could hold one half of the pair**:
`the_two_claimants_of_an_arrow_key_never_both_fire` sweeps all eight modifier combinations × four
arrows and asserts the two conditions *partition* the modifier space. That sweep is what found the
hole — a test asserting only the case someone thought of (plain arrows move the caret, `Alt`+arrows do
not) passes against the broken version. **The wiring between the predicate and the loop was only read
until 2026-08-22** — the loop sits inside `&mut self` on an `OndinApp` — and D303 closed that:
`an_arrow_key_reaches_the_caret_or_the_keymap_but_never_both` drives real `Key::ArrowLeft` events through
`text_mode_input` on a headless app and measures the **caret**, which is the observable the user has. So
the pair is pinned twice over: the partition as a property of two functions, and the loop actually
consulting it.

*Where two claimants share a key, assert that they partition the modifier space rather than that they
differ on one case.*

**D214 — Right-click had one meaning and now has two, and four rules are what keep them apart.
*Built; the four rules were unpinned and named as such until 2026-09-19 — D795 has one test
each.*** `roadmap.md` carried "no context menus
anywhere, `grep context_menu` → 0" from the beginning, and what kept it there was a real collision:
the right button was already spent on abandoning a gesture (D31, D168), so a menu on that button
either takes the click away from the cancel or shares it. `context-menus.md` §0 is where that was
decided and that file stays the source of truth for the row set, the way `shortcuts.md` does for the
keymap. The four rules are recorded here because they are about this app's frame rather than about
which rows a menu should hold.

**R1 — the press cancels, the release opens, and both halves of one click are accounted for.** The
cancel could not move to the release: D168 established that a fast right-click's press and release
land in the same frame and that egui has forgotten the drag by the time anything asks, which is why
the cancel is bound to `button_pressed(Secondary)` and has to stay there. The menu could not stay on
the press, because a menu drawn then has the release that follows land *inside itself* and activate
whatever row it opened under the pointer. So the press cancels and the release opens, and
`gesture_cancelled` — which already means "the rest of this press is not ours" — is what stops one
click paying out twice. No second flag, which matters because a second flag is a second thing to
clear. The cost is one field, `OndinApp::secondary_press`: egui delivers `secondary_clicked` on the
release having forgotten where the press was, and the menu has to open at the press or a click that
jitters a few pixels shifts the card out from under the hand.

**R2 — six targets and no global handler.** Every menu is claimed by a region's own
`Response::secondary_clicked()`, so nothing opens over a control that has its own use for the button
— `picker::stop_bar` still removes a gradient stop, untouched. Three responses do the claiming (the
canvas, a layers row, the layers panel's background) and the canvas's resolves five of the six
targets in one stated order (§9.4). The alternative — one handler in `update` asking what is under
the pointer — is what would have made the picker's stop bar a special case in a file that knows
nothing about pickers.

**R3 — an open menu is Escape's first rung and it *consumes* the press.** `app::update` handles the
key itself rather than calling `escape`, and that is the load-bearing part: `escape` is a ladder that
pays out one rung per press, so a version that closed the menu and then fell through would deselect,
leave the group or drop back to Select in the same keystroke that dismissed a menu opened by accident
— eating the very state the menu was aimed at. Returning rather than calling is what makes that
structural; there is no path from the arm to the ladder. `input::resolve` does not run at all while a
menu is open, for the same reason it already stands down for `egui_wants_keyboard_input`: `Delete`
with a menu up would remove the layer the menu is pointing at. `self.present` keeps the top of
`escape`'s ladder regardless, ~~because `open_context_menu` refuses in present mode and the two can
therefore never contend~~. ⚠️ **That refusal is gone and the two *do* contend now — and R3 wins**
(D756). A menu opens in present mode, `update` answers Escape off `context_menu.is_some()` and never
calls `input::resolve`, so `escape` is not entered and its first arm is not reached: the first press
closes the menu and the second leaves the mode. `self.present` is still first *inside* `escape`,
which is all this sentence ever needed to say; what was wrong was the reason given for it, which a
later reader would have reinstated the refusal from.

**R4 — one slot, and the two things that fall out of it.** `OndinApp::context_menu` is an `Option`,
so a right-click elsewhere *overwrites* it and opening the next menu is what closes the last — the
shape `TopMenu` already had, and a dismissal rule that happens to fire first would have been the
fragile spelling of the same guarantee. It is one slot across every floating thing rather than only
across menus: opening clears `open_menu`, `picker`, `stroke_menu`, `image_menu` and `type_menu`, all
five of which draw over the canvas the menu was aimed at. Then **D82 exactly**, one door further on:
the release that opens a menu is a click outside every menu that existed when it was pressed, and
both of `dropdown`'s exemptions miss it — `any_click()` counts the secondary button, and a context
menu has no head to forgive. The menu showed for a single frame. `ContextMenu::just_opened` is the
answer, a flag on the menu rather than a fifth term in the shared test, because the fact is about
*this* menu's age and not about where the pointer is. The second consequence is the one that reads as
a bug rather than as a design: **a click that dismisses a menu is spent doing so**, so the canvas
skips its mode input and a layers row skips its click while a menu is open. Without it, getting rid
of a menu retargets the selection and dismissal becomes an edit.

**Four of the rules had no test, and now have one each — D795.** R1's spent click, R4's replacement,
R3's single rung and "no document action fires while a menu is open" each need `RawInput` driven
through the whole app, which read as impossible until D303 built `OndinApp::headless` — and then
went unwritten for the four weeks after that reason expired. `app::context_menu_rule_tests` is the
four, driven through `canvas_context_menu`'s own door, which **no test in the workspace had ever
been through**: every earlier context-menu test either called `open_context_menu` by hand or built a
`menu::Context` directly. `context-menus.md` §10 listed them with the plausible wrong implementation
each would fail against and every one of those flips was run; ⚠️ **what survives of that list is the
Escape bullet's wider fixture**, which also asks for `entered_group` and the tool to be untouched.
What *is* pinned is placement, projection and chrome, and two of those were vacuous until they were
flipped: "the menu is on screen" passes against a placement with **no flip in it at all**, because
the clamp alone shoves the card back inside, so the assertion had to become *the card lies wholly on
one side of the press on each axis*; and "the groups come out in order" became a tautology the moment
`build` bucketed rows by their registry group, so what is asserted now is the primitive menu's
sixteen labels in sequence — which is what would have caught the View switches sitting in
`Group::State` and pushing *Zoom to fit* below them.

**D215 — One registry with a canonical order, and the four places `context-menus.md` did not survive
the model. *Built; all four deliberate.*** `menu.rs` holds one enum of verbs and one `spec()` per
verb — label, glyph, accelerator, group, and whether it destroys something — and `menu::build`
buckets whatever rows a menu asks for into that group order, dropping an empty group with its
separator. The shape is not tidiness: a *Flatten* that is fourth in one door and seventh in the other
is worse than no menu at all, and a menu function that cannot choose *where* a row goes cannot get
that wrong. `Row::promote()` is the single exception, for §3's rule that a verb a kind lifts into its
head is moved and not duplicated — an override on the row rather than a second group on the spec, so
the default stays the answer for every other menu the same row appears in. Most rows dispatch
straight to an existing `input::Action`, which is what stops a row and its chord coming to mean
different things; the ones that do not are exactly the ones a keyboard cannot express — paste at the
pointer, the key-layer and base-operand designations, the guide verbs.

Eight `OndinApp` methods, one free function and two `panels` modules went from private to
`pub(crate)` for this (`dispatch`, `select_all`, `paste_at`, `pick_for_click`, `pick_leaf`,
`designate_key`, `image_pixels`, `resize_to_original`; `panels::layers::rename_field_id`, which
D216's focus request reaches from `app.rs`; `panels::layers` and `panels::paint`). That is the
registry *calling* what already existed rather than restating it, which is the whole reason a row and
a chord cannot diverge — but it is also nine more things a later edit can reach, and the table test
that demands every row of every menu the app can open be present in `Item::ALL` is what keeps the
reach answerable.

`sync_tree_to_selection` was a tenth for one day and is private again, because the row that reached it
is gone. *Reveal in layers panel* was built, tried and removed the same day on the user's call —
"redundant, useless 99% of the time" — and `context-menus.md` §7 now carries it as a **decided
non-goal** rather than leaving it sitting in §4 as an unbuilt row. Selecting on canvas already scrolls
the tree to the row and opens its ancestors, on every frame the layers panel draws, so by the time the
menu is up the panel is already showing what the row promises to reveal; it earns its line only when
the panel is shut, and a row worth having in one configuration out of two, for a panel a chord
toggles, does not pay for itself in a menu whose ceiling is a scrollbar (§3). *If it ever returns it
should return as* Show the layers panel, *which is a different row with a different name.* Two counts
moved with it: the invariant tail is 17 rows rather than 18 (Navigate 1, not 2), and a primitive's
menu is 16
(`a_primitives_menu_is_sixteen_rows_in_canonical_group_order`). `menu::Door` is left deciding exactly
one thing — whether *Paste* means "here, at the pointer" or "as a sibling above this row", which today
is the row's label alone; the placement half of it is the third deviation below.

Then the four deviations:

- **§6.5 asked for two Delete rows and gets one that renames itself.** *Delete points* and *Delete
  segment* were to be where the two verbs `Del` carries (D120) are finally told apart — but
  `PointSet` holds anchors **or** segments and never both, so one of the pair would be dim on every
  open, which §3 itself calls indistinguishable from broken. The row takes whichever name the
  selection has armed. The distinction shows where the spec wanted it shown, and the unreachable half
  is never offered.
- **A checkable row has no tick column; its own glyph goes accent.** §5.3 wanted `menu_check`'s tick
  *and* `layers::op_glyph`'s boolean mark on one row, and 210pt does not hold both columns. So a
  checked row paints its own glyph in `ACCENT` — where `menu_check` puts its tick — and keeps the
  second signal too, the label full strength on and muted off. Two channels for one bit, exactly as
  the View menu has. The glyph is the half worth keeping, because a checkable row here is also the
  row whose picture the inspector's dropdown already shows.
- **The panel's *Paste* is not yet "as a sibling above the clicked row"** (§1's table). It pastes by
  the ordinary rule, back where it came from and just above the original. The row is live and
  correct; only the placement refinement is missing. *Fix with the placement, not with a second row.*
- **§3's nine groups are eight in the code, and the eighth is new.** Properties and Export have no
  built rows to hold — *Copy/Paste properties* and both *Export* rows are absent rather than
  present-and-dead — and the four workspace switches the canvas and guide menus carry are not one of
  §3's nine at all, since §3 is a *layer*'s menu. They have a `Group::View` of their own, last, which
  is where §6.1 already put them.

*`context-menus.md` §9.6 lists the same four beside the ledger they came out of — with a fifth item
that is D216's bug rather than a deviation; they are recorded here because they are decisions about
the code rather than about the row set.*

**D216 — *Rename* opened the field without the caret in it, and the bug was never the menu's.
*Resolved.*** The context menu's *Rename* row is only the newest of three doors onto one function:
`Ctrl+R`, `F2` and the row all dispatch to `OndinApp::rename_selection`, which set `show_layers` and
`renaming_layer` and asked for **no focus at all**. Only the layers panel's own double-click ever
requested it. So the field opened, the panel looked ready to type into, and the first keystroke went to
the canvas — for as long as the chord had existed. The menu row did not introduce it; it made it easy to
find, being the more discoverable door.

⚠️ **The mechanism below is superseded by D332 and the reasoning is what survives.** `rename_selection`
took `&egui::Context` and requested focus on `rename_field_id(id)` at the moment the rename opened, and
that spelling **crashed the app** — a focus request naming a widget the frame does not draw hands
AccessKit a focused id with no node. The field asks on its own first draw now. What was right here and
stays right is *why* the obvious version of that was rejected: any "re-request while it does not have
focus" spelling also fires on the frame Enter or Escape takes focus away, so the field grabs it straight
back and can never be left. A one-shot on the field's first *existence* is not that test.

The fix rested on an assumption about **egui**, not about this app: that a focus request survives until
the widget it names first appears, which here is a frame later, because the layers panel is drawn earlier
in the frame than the context menu that dispatched the row. That was pinned rather than trusted, by
`a_focus_request_survives_until_the_rename_field_exists` — frame 0 builds no `TextEdit` at all and
requests focus, frame 1 builds it and asserts `has_focus()`. Flip-checked by deleting the request. **The
assumption was correct and fatal anyway** (D332), and the test has been replaced by two that assert the
caret arrives *and* that no frame ends holding focus for a widget it did not draw. *The
shape is worth suspecting anywhere else: two doors onto one function where only one door did the setup.
The setup belongs in the function, not at whichever door was written first.*

**D217 — Text could be pasted into a session and never copied out of it, and the menu row that looked
like the fix pasted layers. *Resolved.*** `Ctrl`+`C` and `Ctrl`+`X` inside a live session did **nothing
at all**, and the reason is two claimants neither of which was reading them. `input::resolve` resolves
nothing in `Mode::TextInsert` for anything without a modifier and nothing clipboard-shaped at all (D211),
by design; the session's own event loop handled `Event::Paste` and had no `Copy` or `Cut` arm. So the
clipboard was one-way into the document's text for as long as in-canvas editing had existed.

**The model half is core's, and it is two functions.** `TextEdit::selected_text` is the slice a copy
takes, empty for a bare caret; `TextEdit::cut` removes the selection and hands it back, `None` for a bare
caret. The `None` earns a test: it is what lets the *Cut* row be dimmed rather than offered dead, and
what stops a cut with no selection putting an **empty string** on the system clipboard — a keystroke that
looks inert and silently destroys whatever was on it. `cut` is `replace`, not `insert("")`, and the
difference is exactly one thing: `insert` consumes `TextEdit::pending`, because a pending style is
waiting for *the next thing typed*, and a cut is not that. The state is reachable — `drag_to` is the only
mover that does not call `caret_moved` — so `a_cut_keeps_a_pending_style_where_an_insert_would_eat_it`
is flip-checked against the shorter spelling somebody would actually have written.

**The two arms go in the session's own loop, and the trio is gated on `!alt` there too.** That is D204's
rule reaching a second loop: the three events carry no modifiers of their own, so the frame's are the
only place to read one, and the reason to read it is `AltGr` — which on Windows *is* `Ctrl`+`Alt`, and
which `is_cut_command` does not examine. `AltGr`+`C` on a layout that spells a character with it arrives
as `Event::Copy` with the character already discarded upstream; a silent copy — or a silent **cut** — is
not the better of the two outcomes. `Event::Paste` was ungated and is now gated with them.

**The removal stays in event order; only the clipboard write is deferred.** A frame holding both a `Cut`
and a `Text` event is barely reachable, and deferring the *mutation* past the insert would be wrong in
the one case that is.

**Text is a third kind of copy with no field of its own, so it clears both the others.**
`OndinApp::clipboard` and `guide_clipboard` are the "one clipboard, two typed fields" pair every other
copy path clears the other half of; a text copy's payload *is* the system clipboard, so
`put_text_on_clipboard` drops both. Without that, copying a word in a session and then pressing `Ctrl`+`V`
on the canvas pastes layers the OS clipboard no longer describes.

**And §6.4's *Paste* was reading the wrong clipboard, which is worse than the missing rows.** The row
dimmed on `Context::clipboard_full` — the in-app clipboard of captured *subtrees* — and dispatched
`Item::PasteHere`. So copying text in a browser and right-clicking in a session offered a dead *Paste*,
and copying a layer first offered a live one that pasted **layers onto the canvas** from inside a text
session. Both halves are now `ContextMenu::system_text`: `app::system_clipboard_text` read once **at
open**, which is the one piece of a menu that is a snapshot rather than rebuilt per frame, because it
means opening an OS clipboard handle and doing that sixty times a second fights other applications for
the clipboard lock. A clipboard that changes while a context menu is open is not a case worth serving
live.

**The four rows share their `Item` with the layer verbs of the same name and route by target.** Guarded
arms first in `perform_menu_item`, the rule `Item::Delete` has always rested on: what a verb acts on is
the *target's* question, not the row's. Sharing the item keeps one label, one glyph and one accelerator
per verb.

**One of `docs/context-menus.md` §9.5's claims was simply wrong, and is worth recording as wrong**:
*Select all* was scored as needing an entry point that "takes the whole buffer". `TextEdit::select_all`
existed and the session's own loop had been calling it from `Ctrl`+`A` all along. The ledger was written
from the menu outwards and did not check the editor.

**What is tested and what is not.** The two core tests above, and
`a_text_sessions_paste_reads_the_system_clipboard_and_not_the_layer_one`, which asserts §6.4's four rows
and their order *before* asserting availability — a projection test over the one-row menu this replaced
would have passed three of its four assertions by finding nothing. Flip-checked by putting
`!cx.clipboard_full` back. The routing itself cannot be unit-tested. Read-verified, and the two things to
try on the machine are *Paste* in a session with a layer on the in-app clipboard (it must insert text or
do nothing, never place a layer) and `Ctrl`+`X` over a selection.

**D218 — Text on the clipboard pastes as a text layer, and *Paste* stopped asking the wrong
question to decide whether it can. *Built.*** Requested against the session clipboard D217 had just
finished: with a sentence on the clipboard, `Ctrl`+`V` on the canvas should make a text layer holding
it and select it, the way Figma does. The verb is `canvas::paste_text_as_layer`, and it is the last
arm of `OndinApp::paste` — a picture, then the app's own payload, then text.

**Placement is the selection's question, not the pointer's**, which is the one place this differs from
every other creating gesture on the canvas: **the centre of the frame the selection is in, or the
middle of the view.** A chord has no pointer to ask, and the tuning over Figma's unconditional
view-centre is worth having because a frame is where the text is going to belong. The parent is that
frame rather than `draw_target`'s answer for its centre, which would be a **nested** frame if one
happens to cover the middle. The menu's *Paste here* passes its pointer instead and skips all of it.

*This shipped as "exactly one selected `Artboard`" and that was too narrow to be reachable — see
**D221**, which is the correction and the reason to prefer a rule that does not depend on what a click
on a frame selects.*

**The box is centred on that point, so the layer has to be measured before it is created.** Shaped
through a `TextEdit` rather than measured some other way, and that buys two answers from one object:
`insert` is what normalizes the clipboard's line endings (D220) and `text_layout` is the box the
centring needs, so the content committed and the size it was centred at cannot disagree.

**And what gets centred is the *box*, which is not the node's origin.** `TextLayout::origin` is the
offset between them and it is **non-zero for this app's default text**: `default_text_parts` trims
`CapToBaseline`, so a 24pt line measures 17.46 high inside a 28.8 line box and the box starts 4.54
below the origin the transform places. Probed rather than reasoned about, and centring on `size` alone
put every pasted layer that much low — a **constant**, so it does not scale away at a larger paste and
it is exactly what shows when a paste lands beside something else. `centred_paste_origin` carries the
term and is a free function for the same reason `wrapped_paste_sizing` is: arithmetic worth pinning in
a method that cannot be built headlessly. Its test asserts the untrimmed case as the fixture and the
trimmed one as the claim, so the flip — dropping the term, which is the naive spelling and reads
perfectly — fails by exactly 4.54 on the second assertion alone.

**And it wraps rather than running off the page** — `create_image_at`'s rule, for the reason that
entry already gives: a frame is a page and on bare canvas the visible world is the only bounded thing
there is, so an auto-width paste of a long paragraph would land one line wide, mostly off screen, with
nothing visible to grab. `wrapped_paste_sizing` is a free function so the rule is testable without an
`OndinApp` (D35's habit), and it is **`AutoHeight`, never `Fixed`**: the width becomes the page's and
the height stays the content's, where `Fixed` would clip at a height nobody chose. Exactly-fits stays
auto, which is the boundary the test is aimed at — `>=` reads as well as `>` and converts a paste that
fits perfectly into a wrapped one.

**The layer is selected and not opened for editing.** Figma's behaviour, and the right one: the text
already says what it says, and a session would mean the next Escape is spent leaving it.

**The half that made the feature possible at all is a staleness check.** Every in-app copy puts a text
stand-in on the system clipboard — layer names, or a guide's axis and number — because `egui_winit`
emits `Event::Paste` only for a non-empty clipboard (D17). **That stand-in doubles as a receipt.**
`OndinApp::clipboard_stamp` keeps what was written and `owns_the_clipboard` reads it back: if the
system clipboard no longer says it, something else has copied since and the in-app payload is a stale
answer to `Ctrl`+`V`. Without it the text arm is unreachable in the commonest case there is — copy a
layer, then copy a sentence in a browser, then paste, and the **layer** arrives. It is the same
staleness the "picture wins over the layers" rule already reasoned about, one payload over, and the
stamp is written by `stamp_clipboard` at the same moment as the payload so a copy cannot set one and
forget the other. A `debug_assert` says so.

**So `Context::clipboard_full` was the wrong question and is now `can_paste`.** It asked "is the
in-app clipboard full", which is wrong in both directions: a payload the OS clipboard no longer
describes must not be offered, and text copied elsewhere is pasteable with the app holding nothing.
`(payload && payload_current) || system_text`, computed once per menu open beside `system_text` —
which is now read for **every** target rather than only the text session, since every *Paste* row bar
that one can now end in a text layer. The text session's *Paste* keeps asking `system_text` alone,
because it inserts at a caret and has no use for a captured subtree.

*One honest asymmetry, older than this change, **closed 2026-08-19 by D224**: the menu's *Paste here*
had no image arm, so a clipboard holding a picture was reachable from the chord and not from the row.
It was recorded rather than half-fixed, and the fix was the point `paste_image` did not take — plus a
term in `can_paste` this entry did not spot, since a picture-only clipboard answers no to both of the
two payloads above.*

**Tested**: three, each flip-checked — `wrapped_paste_sizing`'s two (`>=` fails the exactly-fits
assertion alone) and `centred_paste_origin`'s. `paste_text_as_layer` itself is on an `OndinApp` and
cannot be built headlessly, so
the placement is read-verified — the things to try on the machine are a paste with a frame selected, a
paste with a shape inside a frame selected, and a long paragraph pasted onto bare canvas at a high
zoom. *The first of those came back wrong: D221.* ⚠️ **And the placement is no longer read-verified**
(D731): it is `canvas::paste_placement` now, a `&self` decision function shared with `paste_svg` and
pinned over all four arms through `OndinApp::headless` (D303). What still cannot be driven is the
*verb*, which opens with a clipboard read — and a rule reachable only behind a clipboard read is a
rule whose paragraph can go false without anything disagreeing, which is what happened here.

**D219 — One text paste resolved *twice*, a frame apart, for as long as the release has been read.
*Resolved.*** Found while building D218. D183 reads a paste from `Event::Paste` **or** from the
`Ctrl`-without-Alt `V` **release**, because an image-only clipboard emits no event. A text paste produces
*both*: the event on the press frame and the release a frame or more later. The guard was `let mut pasted
= false` — a **local**, so it could only ever see the two landing in the *same* frame, which is not the
case that happens. Its own test asserted that same-frame case while its doc comment claimed the two "one
frame apart", so the test read as covering the bug it did not cover.

A two-frame probe said **`press=[Paste] release=[Paste]`**. Two pastes, two undo steps, and the second
copy lands *exactly* on the first, so it is invisible on the canvas and shows only as a doubled row in the
layers panel. **Intermittent rather than constant**, because `cmd_only` has to still hold when V comes up:
release Ctrl first and the second paste never fires, which is why it reads as "I must have pressed it
twice".

**It cannot be fixed in `input::resolve`.** That function is a pure function of the keymap and the mode,
and there is nothing to key a window on: `egui_winit` swallows the V *press* outright, so `key_down(V)` is
**false** on the frame the event arrives. So the release becomes its own action, `Action::PasteRelease`,
and the discrimination moves to the one place that can make it. `egui_winit` pushes `Event::Paste` when
and only when the clipboard yields non-empty text, so **"the clipboard has no text" is the exact
complement of "the event fired"**, not a heuristic. `dispatch` tests it and all six cases come out right:
text only, image only, image *and* text, layers, an empty clipboard, and `Shift`+`Insert` — which emits
the event and no V release, and would have been the casualty of the other obvious fix.

**A second variant rather than a payload on `Paste`**, because the two are not the same intent: one is a
witness, the other a *weaker* witness that must stand down when the stronger one spoke. Worth knowing when
the cheatsheet lands: this is one keymap row and two `Action`s.

**Tested**: `the_press_and_the_release_of_one_paste_are_two_different_actions`, which pumps **two frames of
one `Context`** — two `actions` calls would prove nothing about frame-to-frame state. Flip-checked by
restoring the `pasted` local.

**D220 — A `\r\n` pair was two line breaks, so every line of pasted Windows text came out double-spaced.
*Resolved.*** parley maps `\r` and `\n` each to `Whitespace::Newline` on their own, and a newline cluster
is what raises `BreakReason::Explicit`. Measured rather than reasoned about: `"a\r\nb"` shaped **72 high,
the same as `"a\nb\nc"`**.

Fixed at the one door: `TextEdit::insert` normalizes through `normalized_newlines`, which returns `None`
when there is no `\r` at all so the common case allocates nothing. A lone `\r` becomes a newline rather
than being dropped, because it *is* a break and parley already treats it as one. **`insert` and not
`TextEdit::new`**: this is the *input* door, where a clipboard, a drop or a keystroke arrives; `new` is
handed the **document's** content and rewriting that would silently put the editor and the document out of
step.

`a_crlf_pair_is_one_line_break_not_two` asserts heights against the two-line answer, so the flip fails on
the CRLF case alone and leaves the lone-CR and three-line cases green — which is what says the
normalization did not simply swallow every `\r`.

**D221 — A pasted text layer ignored the selected frame, and a paste with no frames at all refused to
happen. *Resolved.*** Two reports against D218, and they are the same shape twice: **a rule that answers
"no" too easily, falling through to a default that then looks like the answer.**

**"It always goes in the first frame" was really "it never used the selection".** `paste_frame` was
`single_selected_frame` — *exactly one* selected `Artboard` — and answered `None` for every selection that
was not precisely that. `None` falls through to the middle of the view, and the frame under the middle of
the view is whichever one the camera happens to be over. **The symptom named the fallback and the bug was
in the guard**, which is why "no matter what I try" was the accurate description.

It is now **the frame the selection *is, or is inside***, taking the first of a multi-selection.
`enclosing_artboard` walks **self first, then ancestors**, and that first step is the whole fix. Widening
this way also makes the rule independent of what a click on a frame actually selects — the frame or
something in it, both give the same answer — which is the property the narrow rule lacked. The
consequence: a shape selected inside a frame now pastes into **that frame**, which D218 had recorded as a
deliberate choice and was the wrong half of it.

**And "Nowhere to paste — create a frame first" was enforcing a rule the rest of the app does not have.**
A layer does not need a frame: every tool that draws on bare canvas creates a root child through
`draw_target`, and frames are root children themselves. So the fallback is **the root** and the failure is
gone. The "first frame" was arbitrary in the same way the view-centre fallback was.

**Read the two together as one lesson.** Neither bug was in the code that does the work; both were in the
*last resort* the work falls back to, and in both cases the fallback was plausible enough that the symptom
pointed at it instead of at the guard. When a placement rule has a default, the default is where to look
first — and it should be somewhere the user can *see* rather than somewhere the document happens to list
first.

**Tested**: `the_frame_a_paste_is_aimed_at_is_the_one_the_selection_is_or_is_inside`.
`enclosing_artboard` is a free function over the `Document` precisely so this walk is testable without an
`OndinApp` — which is where the rule it replaces was able to hide. **Flip-checked by seeding the walk from
`parent()` instead of `id`**, one word, and the spelling that reads equally right out loud: the frame case
then answers the frame's parent and every other assertion still passes, which is what makes the first one
the assertion worth having.

**D223 — Three rules a menu's keyboard navigation needs and `context-menus.md` §8 never stated.
*Built 2026-08-19.*** The spec named four keys — `↑`/`↓`, `Home`/`End`, `Enter`, with `Escape` already
R3's — and one constraint, that none of them may go through `input::resolve`. That was enough to start
and not enough to finish. Recorded the way D50 records the three rules a multi-selection transform
needed: the design was silent, so the code decided, and the decision has to be visible as one.

**1. The highlight is a *verb*, not an index.** A context menu is rebuilt from live app state on every
frame it is open — that is what lets a checkable row tick under the pointer without the menu closing —
so an index into the row list silently comes to mean a *different row* the moment a row appears or goes
away, and rows do: *Reset crop* and *Reset origin* are omitted rather than dimmed and arrive when the
state changes under them. `ContextMenu::highlight` is therefore an `Option<Item>`, and `menu::navigate`
finds it by identity each frame. This works only because **no menu offers the same verb twice**, which
is §3's "a promoted row is *moved*, not duplicated" seen from a new angle — so it now has a test of its
own, `no_menu_offers_the_same_verb_twice`, over every menu the app can build rather than over the one
kind that promotes.

**2. Only rows a press could *run* are reachable.** A dimmed row explains itself through a tooltip and a
keyboard cannot hover, so a highlight that stopped on one would offer a dead end with no way to read why
it is dead — the `Enter` does nothing and nothing says so. `navigate` filters on `enabled`, and
`Home`/`End` and the wrap all agree with it: `End` is the last **live** row, not the last row. The
consequence worth stating is that a locked layer's menu — sixteen rows, three of them live — walks three
rows, and the three it walks are the three that get you out.

**3. The keyboard and the pointer share *one* highlight channel.** `ui::MenuRow::highlight` is an
`Option<bool>` passed to **every** row rather than a `bool` set on one, and that shape is the whole
mechanism: a row told `Some(false)` does not read `resp.hovered()` at all, so with the pointer resting
on row 0 and `↓` walked to row 2 there is still exactly one ground painted. The version that reads
naturally — `highlight == Some(true) || hovered()` — paints two, and a menu with two highlights cannot
say what `Enter` will do. The first `Event::PointerMoved` clears the keyboard's and hands the channel
back, so the two never have to arbitrate for longer than a frame.

**And holding the keyboard has a second half the spec did not name.** R3 says `input::resolve` must not
run while a menu is open, which stops `Delete` deleting the layer whose menu is offering the row. It does
not stop **egui's own widgets** reading an `↑` the menu is using. So `read_nav` *consumes* the five keys,
and it does it in R3's own gate at the top of the frame — before any panel is drawn — rather than at the
draw site, which runs after every door has had its say and would be too late by a whole panel tree. The
press then travels down to `context_menu_ui` as a value, because the row a `↓` lands on does not exist
until `build` has run.

`Enter` with nothing highlighted is deliberately a **no-op** rather than "take the first row": a menu
opened by accident is dismissed with `Escape`, and a stray `Enter` must not commit an edit nobody aimed
at. No type-ahead, which §8 scoped out and the accelerator column partly answers anyway.

**Tested four ways, none of which needs an `OndinApp`** — `navigate` takes a built menu and returns the
next verb, so the walk is a pure function over the fixture that already existed. The flips are in
`context-menus.md` §10; the one worth repeating is that dropping `.filter(enabled)` is the obvious
spelling and lands the first `↓` on a *Cut* the locked layer cannot run.

**D224 — *Paste here* could not reach a picture, and the row was dim over one as well as dead.
*Resolved.*** D218 recorded the first half as "one honest asymmetry, older than this change" and
scoped the fix correctly — `paste_image` took no point to place at, and `create_image_at` already
does. Building it found the second half, which that entry did not spot: the row was not merely
*inert* over a picture, it was **dimmed**. `can_paste` is `(payload && payload_current) ||
system_text`, and a clipboard holding only a screenshot answers **no to both** — so the payload
`Ctrl+V` handles first was the one payload the menu would not offer at all. Two gaps wearing one
symptom, which is why the recorded scope was half of it.

**The interesting decision is which gesture *Paste here* is aimed like, and it is the drop, not the
chord.** `image_drop_target` takes an `Option<Point>` and its doc comment already argues the
asymmetry: a drop must pass `Some(p)` because a drop addresses a shape by *landing* on it, while a
paste passes `None` because "pressing the paste keys with a shape selected **is** the act of aim,
where a drag is aimed by the pointer and has none". *Paste here* is a third gesture and it has
**both** — a pointer *and* a selection — so the question is live rather than settled by that
sentence. It passes `Some(p)`, which means the fill it replaces has to be a selected shape *under the
point*: the two aims must agree before anything is overwritten. Right-clicking bare canvas and
choosing *paste **here*** cannot sensibly mean "replace the picture over there", and the chord in that
same state *does* mean exactly that — so the row and the chord deliberately differ here, in the one
direction where differing is conservative. The same `Some(p)` also places a new layer at the pointer
instead of at the view centre, which is the whole point of the row.

**Asking whether the clipboard holds a picture costs something, and that shapes the fix.** `arboard`
has no "which formats are on the clipboard" query, so the only way to ask is `get_image`, which
*decodes* a bitmap. Two consequences:

- **It is a snapshot per open**, beside `system_text` and for a sharper version of that field's
  reason (D218): once per right-click is the most a bitmap conversion can be asked for, and sixty
  times a second is out of the question.
- **The answer is a `bool`, not the picture.** Keeping the decoded image would make activation free
  and would park a clipboard-sized RGBA buffer on `ContextMenu` for as long as a menu is open — 96 MB
  for a 24-megapixel photo. So `paste_image` reads it again if the row is taken, and that second
  conversion is small beside the PNG re-encode that arm already does (D183: a clipboard image has no
  encoded original, so one is made).

What makes it affordable at all is that arboard's Windows path calls
`clipboard_win::is_format_avail(CF_DIBV5)` *before* it reads, so a clipboard with no picture on it —
which is nearly every open — costs the handle and nothing else. **That is an implementation detail
rather than a contract**, and it is the thing to re-check if right-click ever starts to feel slow.

`menu_context` now takes the `&ContextMenu` snapshot rather than a row of `bool`s. Three positional
bools was already at the limit and a fourth is a swap waiting to happen; the snapshot *is* the thing
being passed, so passing it whole is both shorter and harder to get wrong.

**Read-verified (D35)** — every function on this path hangs off `OndinApp`. The one invariant that
*is* pinned is the one widening `can_paste` could break:
`a_text_sessions_paste_reads_the_system_clipboard_and_not_the_layer_one` already asserts a live
`can_paste` with no `system_text` leaves §6.4's *Paste* dim, and it holds for a picture by
construction rather than by naming one — `can_paste` is the only channel by which any payload reaches
the registry. On the machine: paste a screenshot over a selected shape by right-clicking **on** it
(replaces), by right-clicking beside it (new layer at the pointer, where the chord would have
replaced), and with nothing selected at all.

**D225 — Two of the Asset section's four entries, and the eyebrow comes back with them.
*Built 2026-08-19; half of it withdrawn 2026-08-23.*** *Export original…* and *Replace and reset*, the
two `roadmap.md` scored cheap.
D190 promised the *Asset* heading returns once Asset has more than one entry to name; three of five is
enough, so it has, and *Replace…* moves under it out of Framing's action list. Framing had the room,
so **the third card D190 held in reserve stays in reserve** — for *Embed*/*Link* and *Relink…*, both
of which need the linked source nothing in the app can currently author.

⚠️ **This entry built two features and only one of them survives, which is the trap in reading it.**
***Export original…* was removed on 2026-08-23** — from this card and from `context-menus.md` §5.7
together, so no spelling of the verb is left anywhere (D305). ***Replace and reset* is untouched** and
is still the Settings tab's row, with the asymmetry two paragraphs below still the decision it
records. Everything here about the export row is history from that date; everything about the reset
row, the eyebrow and the two glyphs is live. The eyebrow now stands over **two** of five rather than
three, which is still more than one and so still earns the heading.

**`ImageFormat::extension` finally has the caller its own doc comment named.** It has been `pub` in a
library since images landed, which is the case `CLAUDE.md` warns about specifically: `dead_code` never
fires on a `pub` item however many callers it has lost, so the comment was the only thing saying who
it was for. *Export original…* writes `ImageEntry`'s stored bytes straight out — the encoded original,
the very bytes that were hashed to make the id (§5.5a) — so the file that comes back is
**byte-identical** to the one that went in. That is the payoff of a format that keeps originals rather
than decoded buffers, and it is why the extension has to be the *stored* format's rather than
anything chosen at the dialog. ⚠️ **And it has lost that caller again**, on 2026-08-23 with the row
(D305), so the function is back in exactly the state this paragraph was written to celebrate the end
of — `pub` in a library, reached from nothing, with a comment as the only witness. The scoring
premise and the rot are one fact seen twice: a verb that exists to give a lone `pub` helper a caller
is a verb nobody was asking for.

**Nothing is asked of the framing, and saying so is the point.** A crop is a way of *showing* a
picture; this writes the picture. Someone who wants the cropped result wants `ondin export`, which
renders. A **pasted** picture is the honest exception and needs no arm: its stored bytes are our own
PNG re-encode, because a clipboard image arrives decoded with no original to keep (D183) — so
*original* means "what this document holds", which is what it means for every other row in the table
too.

**The reset resets the framing and *keeps the adjustments*, and that asymmetry is the decision.**
`roadmap.md` scored *Replace and reset* as "*Replace…* without the framing carried", which leaves open
what counts. `ImageRef` holds six fields: the id, four framing ones — fit, crop, tile scale,
orientation — and `adjust`, which is per-pixel. The reset takes the four. The adjustments survive
because they are **the other card** since D190, because a row in the Framing card silently clearing a
slider in the Adjustments card is exactly the surprise that split was made to prevent, and because
the reason anyone reaches for this row is geometric in the first place: a crop is normalized, so it
*transfers* to a picture of different dimensions rather than breaking, and a region chosen on one
photograph is arbitrary on the next. The sampler survives with the adjustments, not being framing
either. Written as `ImageRef { adjust, ..ImageRef::new(id) }` rather than by clearing four fields, so
a fifth framing field added later is reset without anyone remembering to come back.

**Two new Phosphor glyphs, and both were picked by *atlas dump* rather than by name** — the technique
`CLAUDE.md` describes and D143's test cannot answer for, since a transposed digit landing on a
neighbouring *valid* icon passes every assertion:

- **`export` over `download` and `download-simple`.** All three are a tray with an arrow, and the two
  downloads point *into* it — which makes them a vertical stem with a chevron and a bar at the
  bottom, i.e. `ARROW_LINE_DOWN` with side walls added. At 15pt the walls are the
  whole difference. (⚠️ **This read *"`ARROW_LINE_DOWN` (*Send to back*)"* until 2026-09-09 and the
  gloss was wrong** — *Send to back* draws `STACK`, and `ARROW_LINE_DOWN` is drawn nowhere at all;
  `theme.rs`'s `EXPORT` doc carried the identical parenthetical and both are corrected. §15 D672. The
  *shape* argument is untouched, which is why the name stays and only the gloss goes.
  🚨 **And the gloss became *true* on 2026-09-15**, §15 D761 having given *Send to back* that very
  constant — so a sentence was corrected, and six days later the thing it had been corrected away
  from was the fact. The correction was still right: it was wrong when it was written, and a
  parenthetical that happens to come true is not a parenthetical anybody checked. The *shape*
  argument was never affected in either direction, which is why the gloss is simply not restored.) `export` points **up and out**, contrasting by direction rather than by detail,
  and is the glyph Phosphor named for this verb. `download` additionally carries a mark inside the
  tray that is noise at icon size.
- **`broom` for *Replace and reset*, because every ring was taken and they all look alike.** The
  obvious pick for "and reset" is a circular arrow, and this app has three already meaning three
  other things: `ARROW_COUNTER_CLOCKWISE` is *Reset crop* two rows above, `ARROWS_CLOCKWISE` is
  *reverse* in two places, `ARROW_CLOCKWISE` prefixes the Transform panel's rotation field and its
  rotate-90° button (and was the rotate *cursor* too until D232 drew that as an arc, for this very
  reason: at cursor size a ring says nothing a second ring does not) — and `arrows-counter-clockwise` is
  the *mirror image* of the second. A fourth ring would be one picture for two verbs, which is
  `context-menus.md` §8's glyph rule failing in the direction nobody checks for. A broom is
  unmistakable at 15pt and unmistakably not a rotation.

**The dump caught a live drift on the way past.** The inspector's *Replace…* drew `IMAGE` while the
context-menu registry gives `Item::ReplaceImage` the glyph `SWAP` — one verb with two pictures in two
doors, which is the exact failure §8's "name them in the registry rather than at the call site" rule
exists to prevent, and it had been sitting there since the row was written. Now `SWAP` in both.
*Anything drawn in both a panel and a menu owes this check; the registry is the authority and the
panel is the copy.*

**And the feature reached its second door for four lines.** *Export original…* is a `context-menus.md`
§5.7 row that entry scored *cheap* on the grounds that it would be "a second consumer" for
`extension`; with `export_image_action` written, the menu row is a registry entry and one arm. It is
**the only row in the picture head a locked layer keeps live**, and that is a rule rather than an
omission: a lock protects a layer from being *changed*, and writing its own picture out to a file
changes nothing — dimming it would be the lock claiming a reach it does not have, over precisely the
state someone recovering an original is likely to be in. *Replace and reset* is deliberately **not** a
menu row: §5.7's table does not name it, and a menu is not the place to offer two spellings of one
verb. **"The only row" stopped being true on 2026-08-22**, when *Edit image* landed undimmed as well
(D268) — for the opposite reason, that reason being about the mode's other doors and not about what
locking means; and it became true again on 2026-08-23, when that row started dimming because the mode
began refusing (D320). The rule in this paragraph is unchanged and is still the only one of the two that is a
statement about locking. **It has no instance left in the app since 2026-08-23** (D305): the row that
carried it is gone, and *Original size* — the one row beside *Edit image* now — dims, because it
writes the node's geometry. Keep the rule; it is the thing to reach for the next time a read-only
verb lands on a locked layer's menu.

**Tested** by the descendant of this test, now `a_lock_dims_both_of_the_picture_rows` — the name in
this paragraph until 2026-08-23 was
`a_lock_dims_the_three_picture_rows_that_write_from_the_menu_and_neither_of_the_other_two`, which had
already been stale since D305 renamed it, and it has since been renamed once more (D320). It asserts
every picture row is present as its fixture, then the live rows and the dimmed ones with
their reason. **Flipped against `.dim_if(locked, LOCKED)` on the export row** — the plausible mistake
exactly, since the rows above it take it and that is what a hand types next — and it fails on the
`enabled` assertion alone. It was written as
`a_locked_picture_can_still_be_exported_and_nothing_else_about_it_can_be_touched` over five rows, one
live and four dimmed; D268 took *Edit crop…* out and put *Edit image* back, and the name went with the
second change because "nothing else can be touched" had become false. The two actions themselves are on `OndinApp` and open modal
dialogs, so they are read-verified (D35); on the machine, export a placed picture and diff it against
the file, export a *pasted* one and check the PNG opens, and replace-and-reset a cropped picture with
a differently-shaped one and check the adjustments are still on it.

**D226 — The panel's *Paste* lands as a sibling above the clicked row, and the door was being read
off the wrong field. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** `context-menus.md` §1's table has four lines and this was
the last one unbuilt; §9.6.3 recorded it as *live and correct but pasting by the ordinary rule*, which
is the mildest form this class of gap takes and the reason it sat there.

**Why the ordinary rule is wrong here rather than merely different.** It is *back where it came from,
just above the original* — the right answer for a chord, which was aimed at nothing and can only
consult the payload. A panel right-click **was** aimed: it is the one gesture in the app whose whole
subject is *where in the tree*, and answering it with the source subtree's own slot ignores the only
thing the user said. Same shape as D221, one door over: a placement rule with a plausible default,
where the default is what the symptom points at.

**The bug underneath was that the door was inferred from `world`.** `perform_menu_item` matched
`Item::PasteHere` on `Option<Point>` — `Some(p)` the canvas, `None` the chord — and a panel row has no
world point *by construction*, so it fell into the chord's arm and could never have done anything else.
The fix is to match on the **target**, which is the thing that actually knows which door opened
(`Target::Layer { door: Door::Panel }`). *Worth generalising: `world` is a fact about the pointer and
`Door` is a fact about the menu, and any row whose behaviour the door changes has to read the second.
`Item`'s own doc comment names `PasteHere` as the one row in that position.*

**`+ 1` is *above*, and that is the whole arithmetic.** `Node::children` ascends in z-order and the
layers panel draws it reversed, so the slot *after* the clicked row's is the one that paints over it.
Dropping the term reads perfectly out loud — "insert at the clicked row's index" — and pastes
*underneath* the thing that was aimed at, which on two opaque shapes is indistinguishable from the
paste having gone missing. It is the same term, and the same trap, that `paste_clipboard_at` already
carries against the row a subtree was *copied* from.

**Three payloads, and only one of them has a slot.** *Paste* means a picture, then the app's own
subtrees, then text, in that order at every door (D218, D224) — but a picture replaces a fill or lands
on the canvas and a pasted text layer belongs to the frame the selection is in. Those two keep their
own rules rather than being bent to a row that is about *ordering*; bending them would be this door
inventing a second placement rule for payloads that already have one.

**Two cases have no answer and fall back rather than refusing**: the root, which has no siblings, and
a row whose parent has gone. The fallback is `paste_clipboard_at`, i.e. exactly what the chord would
have done — the honest approximation, where the alternative is a menu row that silently does nothing.
D221 is the record of what a placement rule answering "no" too easily costs.
