**Tested**: `a_panel_paste_lands_in_the_slot_above_the_clicked_row`. `sibling_slot_above` is a free
function over the `Document` for `enclosing_artboard`'s reason, which is the same reason twice — that
is where the rule it replaces was able to hide — so the arithmetic and both `None` arms are assertable
without an `OndinApp`. The fixture is asserted first, because every number below it is an index into
one. **Flipped by dropping the `+ 1`**, which fails all four slot assertions; a blunt flip, and the
right one here, since there is no arm of the rule the wrong version gets right.

**D795 — The four context-menu rules that had no test have one each, and the first of them is the
first synthetic right-click driven through the whole app. *Tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — D214's
"writable now and unwritten" clause is spent, and writing these is what found D796.***

D214 closed on *"Four of the rules have no test: writable now and unwritten"* — R1's spent click,
R4's replacement, R3's single rung and *"no document action fires while a menu is open"* — and
`context-menus.md` §10 carried the same four, each with the plausible wrong implementation it would
fail against. `app::context_menu_rule_tests` is those four.

**What thirty-odd green tests in `menu.rs` could not reach.** Every context-menu test written before
these either called `open_context_menu` by hand or built a `menu::Context` directly, so **nothing in
the workspace had ever driven a synthetic secondary button through the whole app** and
`canvas::canvas_context_menu`'s door had no test through it at all. ⚠️ The one earlier synthetic
secondary press — `typography::a_right_click_short_enough_to_fit_one_frame_takes_the_drag_away` —
goes into a bare egui `Context` and a `DragValue`, not through `OndinApp`, so it is not a
counter-example to that sentence and should not be read as one. **The gap was not an accident of
coverage**: each of the four rules is about something that exists only *between* frames or *between*
subsystems — which of a press and a release opens the menu, whether the dismissal beats the open, and
whether `input::resolve` runs at all — and a `menu::Context` built by hand cannot be wrong about any
of them.

**R1 — `a_right_click_opens_its_menu_on_the_release_and_not_on_the_press`.** It asserts the menu is
**absent** after the press frame and present after the release, which is the half a unit test cannot
see. Flipped by giving `canvas_context_menu` the press —
`ctx.input(|i| i.pointer.button_pressed(Secondary))` in place of `resp.secondary_clicked()`, the
plausible wrong spelling rather than a deletion: **red on the press assertion, the predicted site**,
and the release assertion stays green under it. That is the point. A test asking only *"is there a
menu at the end"* passes against the bug §10 describes, where the release lands inside the menu and
runs the row under the pointer.

**R4 — `a_second_right_click_replaces_the_open_menu_rather_than_closing_it`.** Right-click at one
position, then far away, and assert one menu at the *second* position. Flipped with an early
`if self.context_menu.is_some() { return; }` in `open_context_menu` — the plausible wrong reading of
R4 — which is **red on the `expect`, with `None`**: §10's predicted *zero menus, not two*, arriving
by a route worth naming. The refusal leaves the **first** menu in the slot with `just_opened` now
false, so the same click that was refused an open is read as a click-away and dismisses it. **One
click, two rules, and the two answers cancel.** ⚠️ **The obvious flip here is too broad to isolate
anything**: removing `context_menu_ui`'s `!just_opened` guard fails **all four** tests at their
fixture assertions, because without it no menu survives the release that opened it. `just_opened`
holds up every rule in the module, not one of them.

**R3 — `escape_over_a_menu_closes_the_menu_and_keeps_the_selection`**, with a **selection**
underneath rather than present mode, and opened by a right-click rather than by a call to
`open_context_menu` — the rule asserted through the door a user comes in by, which
`escape_in_present_mode_closes_the_menu_first_and_the_mode_second` does not use. Flipped by running
`input::resolve` right after `self.context_menu = None`, the *closed it and then fell through*
version the arm's own comment warns about: **red on the selection assertion** with `[]` against the
fixture's two group ids, and **green on the menu assertion**, since the menu closes either way.

🚨 **That test's own argument for existing was wrong and is corrected at the site.** It read
*"present mode is a `bool` that `escape` clears on a later rung; a selection is cleared on the same
rung the menu is"*, which is backwards about `escape`: `self.present` is that function's **first**
arm and the selection clear is its **last**, the fall-through `else` under everything. And it went
on to claim the present-mode test does *not* bite on this flip — **asserted from a read and never
run**, with that test's own flip note recording the neighbouring mutation failing at *"and left
present mode alone"*. The verdict was right and the argument was not: what this test adds is the
door and the state at the bottom of the ladder. ⚠️ ~~***Fix:* re-run this flip against
`escape_in_present_mode_…` before relying on either test as the only cover for a fall-through**;
the comment now says so rather than answering it.~~ **Discharged 2026-09-22 — D824**, by running it
over the whole `escape_` filter rather than against that one neighbour: **three of twelve go red** —
`escape_in_present_mode_…` at *"and left present mode alone"*, this entry's R3 test on the selection,
and D824's on `entered_group` — and the other **nine stay green**. So no one of the three is the only
cover, which is what the ask was about; and the nine greens are the other half of the answer, saying
where the cover is *not*. **The read this entry distrusted was right and it was still right to
distrust it** — what makes the claim usable is that it is a measurement now.

**And `a_keystroke_does_not_reach_the_document_while_a_menu_is_open`**, which is §10's own wording —
open a menu over a layer, press `Delete`, assert the document is unchanged. ⚠️ **"Byte-identical" is
asserted as the reachable node count plus `is_dirty()`**, because `Document` has no cheap
serialization reachable from a test; the flag covers the one case the count cannot, an edit undone
before the assertion. Flipped by running `input::resolve` in the menu arm's `else`: **red on the
node-count assertion, the predicted site, at 4 against 7** — a group and both its children, not the
single node the prediction said. ⚠️ **The dirty assertion is not "also red", it is never reached**,
the count assertion panicking first, and that order is deliberate — the *loss before the mechanism*
(D453). ⚠️ **That citation read D614 until this entry was written**, which is the balanced-tree
union and carries no such rule; both numbers resolve, so nothing in this project could have seen it.
*A citation that resolves is not a citation that agrees.*

⚠️ **§10's Escape bullet is wider than the test written for it.** That bullet asks for the menu
opened with a layer selected inside an entered group and the node tool active, and for
`entered_group` and the tool to be untouched as well as the selection; what is asserted is the menu
and the selection. **That clause is what survives of the queue**, and §10 says so rather than
reading as closed. *Closed 2026-09-22 by **D824**, and not by widening this test — which turned out
to be the one repair that would have made it assert nothing.*

**Two helpers were widened to `pub(super)` rather than copied** — `library_wiring_tests::whole_frame`
and `ungroup_tests::app_with_two_groups`. A second copy of `whole_frame` would be a second statement
of the egui warm-up-frame rule its doc comment carries, and that rule is the part worth having once:
egui resolves a press against the widget rects it knew *last* frame, so a press on the frame a widget
first appears is assigned to nothing and the whole test passes while asserting nothing.

**D824 — The Escape context-menu rule gets its wider fixture, and the finding is that it had to be a
second test. *Tested 2026-09-22; Resolved — §10's queue is empty, and D795's own *Fix* is not this
one.***

D795 above closed on the one clause of `context-menus.md` §10 it could not write. That file's Escape
bullet words it exactly: *"Open one with a layer selected inside an entered group and the node tool
active, press Escape once, and assert the menu is gone while the selection, `entered_group` and the
tool are all untouched."* `escape_over_a_menu_closes_the_menu_and_keeps_the_selection` asserts the
first and the last of those.
`app::context_menu_rule_tests::escape_over_a_menu_keeps_the_entered_group_and_the_tool_as_well` is
the rest.

🚨 **It is a second test rather than a widening of that one, and §10 asked for the widening.**
`OndinApp::escape` pays out **one** rung per press, and its chain reaches `entered_group` *before*
the tool and before the selection clear that is its final `else`. So in the narrow fixture the
fall-through's one extra rung is the **selection** — which is exactly why that test's selection
assertion bites — and in the wide one it is `entered_group`, leaving the selection *and* the tool
untouched **under the very flip the test exists for**. **Widening the original would have taken the
teeth out of it and left the suite looking one test richer.** Both fixtures are needed, because the
ladder has two different rungs directly under the menu depending on what is set.

**Flipped the same way its neighbour is** — the *"closed it and then fell through"* mutation in the
menu-holds-the-keyboard arm, the dispatch loop
(`for action in input::resolve(&ctx, self.mode, self.prefs.nudge)`) run right after
`self.context_menu = None`, which is what that arm's own comment warns about and is D795's flip for
the test above. The new test is **red on the `entered_group` assertion**, the predicted site, with
`None` against the entered group, and **green on the selection and the tool**; the old one is red on
the selection with `[]` against its two group ids. Both at the sites predicted, which is the
paragraph above happening rather than being argued.

🚨 **That flip was first run in a spelling that is not this one, and the two are not one edit.** The
first run called `self.escape(&ctx)` directly in that arm — the ladder invoked, skipping the routing
— which comes back red at the same assertion with the same value and **proves less**, because it
reaches the ladder whatever `input::resolve` decides about the key. The documented mutation puts the
*dispatch* back, so a version in which the keymap refuses to produce the action at all would show.
Both spellings were run and both are recorded on the test. **The rule this is an instance of is the
one this project already has** — *name the mutation by its function, not by a description two edits
fit* (D803) — and here the looser description was the *safer*-sounding one, which is the direction
that does not announce itself: a flip that reaches further than the production path does cannot
distinguish a live route from a dead one.

**D795's closing *Fix* is discharged, and the measurement is what discharges it.** That entry asked
for the R3 flip to be re-run against `escape_in_present_mode_closes_the_menu_first_and_the_mode_second`
before either test was relied on as the only cover for a fall-through, its own argument for existing
having been *"asserted from a read and never run"*. Run over the whole `escape_` filter on
2026-09-22, **three of twelve go red** — `escape_in_present_mode_…` at *"and left present mode
alone"*, `escape_over_a_menu_closes_the_menu_and_keeps_the_selection` on the selection, and this test
on `entered_group` — and the other **nine stay green**. So **no one of the three is the only cover**,
which is exactly what the ask was about, and the nine greens are the other half of the answer: they
say where the cover is *not*, the fall-through being invisible to every `escape_` test whose fixture
leaves the rungs above the menu empty. D795's *Fix* is struck there.

*(The fixture enters the group through `enter_container` and chooses `Tool::Node`, and asserts all
three of those states **before** the right-click — a fixture that never reached the state is a test
about nothing. 🚨 **§10's bullet carried the same error D795 corrected at the test site, and it is
amended here too**: it read *"the selection is the sharper of the three anyway — it is cleared on the
same rung, where present mode and an entered group are further **down** the ladder"*, which is
backwards about `escape`. `self.present` is that function's **first** arm, `entered_group` its
second-to-last, and the selection clear the fall-through `else` under everything — so the selection
is the **bottom** of the ladder and the other two are above it, which is the whole reason this test
exists. **The `roadmap.md` clause is struck**, and with D823 that section has nothing open.)*

**D796 — Two threads opening the OS clipboard corrupt the heap, and the whole suite had been passing
on scheduler luck. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Keep — and two consequences were deliberately not
fixed, which is half of what this entry is for; **one of the two has since been closed by D798**.***

🚨 **Found by writing D795's four tests, and it is a real defect rather than a test artefact.** Each
of those four opens a context menu; `ContextMenu` snapshots the clipboard on every open
(`system_text`, `system_image`); and running just those four failed **four runs in five** with
`STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION`, exit `0xc0000374` — the whole test binary down, **no test named**.

**Attributed by bisection, and the final probe has no app in it at all.** Four `#[test]`s doing
nothing but calling `system_clipboard_text` and `system_clipboard_has_image` in a loop — no
`OndinApp`, no egui, no document — corrupt the heap **four runs in four**, while each of them alone
is green. `arboard`'s Windows path opens the **global** clipboard, which is a per-process resource
with no interior locking, so a second `Clipboard::new()` while the first is live is not a race this
app is entitled to lose gracefully.

**Three intermediate probes came back clean, and they are recorded because they are what a reader
suspects first**: four concurrent tests pumping `whole_frame` over a document with content; four
pumping `whole_frame` over an empty app; and the pre-existing whole-app tests, `close_card`'s three,
over six runs. It is not the renderer, not the document and not `eframe`.

**The fix is one lock at one seam.** Every `arboard` handle in the process is now opened inside
`app::with_clipboard`, behind a `static GATE: Mutex<()>`, and all four call sites go through it —
`system_clipboard_text`, `system_clipboard_has_image`, `copy_as_png`'s `set_image` and
`paste_image`. ⚠️ **In `paste_image` the whole read is inside the gate, not just the open**:
`get_image` is what touches the global clipboard, so taking the handle under the lock and reading
outside it would have left the race exactly where it was. **Poisoning is ignored on purpose**
(`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`) — a panic under the lock says nothing about the OS
clipboard's state, and refusing every later paste because one earlier one panicked turns a transient
failure into a permanent one.

⚠️ **The app has one UI thread, so no user can reach this today.** What it was reaching is the test
suite. 🚨 **And that is the larger half: the whole `ondin-app` suite was passing on scheduler luck.**
The colliding tests existed before today — anything that opens a menu takes a clipboard snapshot — and
were simply spread thin enough to rarely meet. Four new ones in a single module made it
reproducible. *A suite that passes because its tests are spread out is passing by luck, and the luck
was already being spent.*

**`clipboard_gate_tests::eight_threads_can_read_the_clipboard_at_once`** is the assertion, and three
of its choices are load-bearing. ⚠️ **It spawns its own threads rather than leaning on the
harness**: `cargo test`'s parallelism is what *found* the fault and is exactly the wrong thing to
assert against, since the thread count is the machine's and the interleaving is the scheduler's, and
a suite that grows by one test changes both. ⚠️ **There is no `assert!` under it** — a corrupted
heap takes the binary down, which cargo reports as a hard failure of the whole target, the same
shape as D445's `panic = "abort"` guard, where the evidence is the process dying rather than a line
of `assert!`; the `join` is the assertion. ⚠️ **It reads and never writes**, because a test has no
business overwriting what the developer copied — which is the reason D303's own *Declined* paragraph
already gives for leaving `owns_the_clipboard` untested, and the reason `copy_as_png`'s own test
stops at `png_for_the_clipboard`. ⚠️ That comment named `png_for_clipboard`, which is not a function
in this workspace, and is corrected — **a name in plain backticks is a name no gate checks** (D319).
Flipped by taking the `GATE` lock out: the binary aborts with `STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION` and **no test
named**, which is the argument for the module doc carrying the story rather than an assertion
message.

🚨 **The clipboard was a fourth thing `OndinApp::headless` did not swap, and it was not on D303's
list.** That entry swaps a device, five background threads and a file so that a probe cannot touch
the developer's machine; a headless app nevertheless read the developer's **real** clipboard, and
`copy_as_png` would have written it. So §11's *"a test may not write outside the repository"* bullet
held on this path by test discipline and not by construction. **It was the per-machine index's shape
one step worse**: there (D619) a mitigation exists and no production path is routed through it; here
there was no mitigation to route to. **D303's swap paragraph and §11's bullet both say so now.**
**Stubbing it was left as a maintainer decision and the decision has been taken** — see **D798**,
which is this paragraph's sequel: `Prefs::ephemeral` was named here as the shape one module away, a
`#[serde(skip)]` flag `headless` sets and the writer reads on its first line, and that is very nearly
what was built. Until then it was queued in `roadmap.md` beside the per-machine index, the other
resource the suite reaches with no injection point; the per-machine index is still there and this is
not.

**D798 — A headless app can no longer reach the OS clipboard, and the flag is process-wide because
the clipboard is. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — D796's open half, and the fourth item on
D303's swap list with it.***

**The maintainer's ruling on the question D796 left open.** That entry put every `arboard` handle in
the process behind one `Mutex` and recorded — deliberately, so that fixing the race would not read as
having answered this too — that a headless app still *read* the developer's real clipboard and that
`copy_as_png` could *write* it. It is the fourth machine-touching resource beside the wgpu device,
`FontService`'s five background threads and the preferences file, and the only one of the four with
no inert twin. **The ruling is: stub it.**

`static CLIPBOARD_OFF: AtomicBool` in `app.rs`, set by `OndinApp::headless`, never cleared, read
through `clipboard_is_reachable()`.

**A process-wide flag rather than a field, and the argument is not convenience.** There is one OS
clipboard per *process*, so *"do not touch it"* is a fact about the process and not about an
`OndinApp`; the two readers are free functions with eleven call sites across three modules, none of
them a natural place to thread a field through; and D796's own lock is already a static for exactly
that reason. ⚠️ **It is deliberately one-way.** A test that could turn the flag back on could turn it
off for every other test in the binary, which is the property this exists to remove — the refusal has
to be something no later test can undo, or it is discipline again in a new spelling.

🚨 **Checked by the four callers and deliberately *not* inside `with_clipboard`.** That is the same
split `Prefs::save` uses for `ephemeral` — the flag is read by the seam that *decides to want* the
resource, not by the seam that *opens* it — and here it is load-bearing for a specific reason:
`clipboard_gate_tests::eight_threads_can_read_the_clipboard_at_once` has to keep reaching a real
`arboard` handle to prove D796's lock holds under eight threads, and a check one level down would
make that test return early and **assert nothing**. It calls `with_clipboard` directly for exactly
this. *A refusal placed at the lowest seam refuses the test that proves the seam works.*

⚠️ **`copy_as_png` refuses out loud.** On a headless app it puts *"Copying to the clipboard is off in
this build"* through `session.info` rather than silently doing nothing — a refusal a test can read,
on the one path that would have **overwritten** what the developer had copied.

**`clipboard_gate_tests::a_headless_app_cannot_reach_the_clipboard`** asserts the flag directly **and
then** the two readers' behaviour, in that order, and the order is the finding. Flipped by dropping
the `CLIPBOARD_OFF.store` from `headless`, it is **red on the first assertion** — the one that does
not depend on what the developer has copied. The two reader assertions are the behaviour that
matters, but on an empty clipboard they are *also* green under the flip, so on their own they would
be a test that passes whenever the machine happens to be quiet. ⚠️ **It is order-independent on
purpose**: the flag is one-way and every other test in the binary that builds a headless app sets it
too, so this one builds its own and asserts from there rather than pretending it can run first.

⚠️ **One doc link was written as a link and the doc gate caught it.** `CLIPBOARD_OFF`'s doc named
`OndinApp::headless` as an intra-doc link; `headless` is `#[cfg(test)]`, so `cargo doc` exited 101 —
**D319**'s mechanism arriving from the production side, where a *production* doc cannot name a
test-only item. Plain backticks now, with a sentence saying why, which is D319's own convention.

**D823 — A layer copied in one `ondin` window pastes as a layer in another, and the wire form is the
document schema. *Built and tested 2026-09-22; Resolved — D17's closing *Fix* is spent.***

D17 closed by saying what to do: *"Fix properly by giving core a serializable subtree — that would
also buy paste between two Ondin windows."* Until now a copy captured subtrees into
`OndinApp::clipboard` and put only the layer **names** on the OS clipboard, so a second window's
`Ctrl+V` saw text and pasted the names as a text layer. `ondin_core::io::clip` is that subtree.

**Text, because text is the only channel there is.** `arboard` offers the system clipboard as text or
as an image and nothing else, so a payload that is to survive leaving this process has to be a
string. It is the layer names, then `io::clip::FENCE` (`--- ondin clipboard ---`), then the JSON. The
names stay on the first line for both of D17's reasons — `egui_winit` emits `Event::Paste` only for a
non-empty clipboard, and someone pasting an Ondin copy into a note wants to read what they copied —
so the payload *follows* the stand-in rather than replacing it. ⚠️ **The fence is found with
`rsplit_once` and not `split_once`**, so a layer actually named `--- ondin clipboard ---` does not
truncate the heading and take the payload with it; a pathological name is not a reason for a paste to
fail, and `a_layer_named_like_the_fence_still_crosses` pins it.

**The payload is the document schema, and that is the decision this entry is really about.**
`NodeDto::from_node`/`into_node` and `ImageDto::from_entry`/`into_entry` were lifted out of
`DocumentDto::from_document`/`into_document`, which now call them; nothing about the file changed and
`save_load_roundtrips` and `save_is_byte_deterministic_through_load` say so. A second projection
beside `NodeDto` would have put D663's out-bound `clip` normalization, the opacity clamp, the
stored-versus-effective `fill_rule` and the unusable-export-spec drop in **two places that nothing
compares** — a field added to one and not the other compiles, saves and loads. So
`a_clipboard_payload_round_trips_every_node_kind` is not *"a clip round-trips"* but *"a clip
round-trips through the same DTO a file does"*, which is the claim worth having.

**The version is checked for equality, not migrated**, which is the one place this deliberately
differs from `io::load`. A file is an archive and has to open in a build written years later; a
clipboard is a handoff between two processes running right now, and the honest answer to *"this came
from a schema I do not know"* is to say so rather than to guess. The migration ladder stays where the
archives are.

🚨 **`io::clip::read` answers `Option<Result<Payload, IoError>>`, and the third answer is why it is
not a `bool`.** `None` is *no fence, somebody else's*, and the caller's other arms get it.
`Some(Err)` is *ours and unreadable*, which has to be **said** rather than fallen through on: falling
through hands the payload to `paste_text_as_layer`, so the user asks for their layers back and gets a
text layer holding several megabytes of their own JSON. `parse` also refuses an empty subtree, a
subtree with other than exactly one root, and a duplicate image id. ⚠️ **The root check is
deliberately here rather than left to `remap_subtree`**, which answers `None` for a malformed
template and whose caller then *skips* it — so a payload with one bad subtree in five would paste
four layers and report four, with nothing anywhere naming the one that vanished. A non-finite `from`
box is dropped rather than carried, since it would sit in every comparison `paste_aim` makes and
match none of them; the copy still pastes, at the fallback a copy with no box at all gets.

**App side**: `enum Clipboard { Layers, Foreign, Unreadable }`, `OndinApp::take_clipboard` — the
receipt asked first as a fast path, then the OS read, then adoption — and `OndinApp::adopt_clip_text`,
which is that decision with the OS read lifted off it. **Split for the reason D805 split
`pick_from_chain` off `pick_preview`**: `OndinApp::headless` sets `CLIPBOARD_OFF` (**D798**), so
`system_clipboard_text` answers `None` to every probe and the layer arm is unreachable from a test
through the outer door, while the decision is the half worth pinning. All four paste doors — `paste`,
`paste_in_place`, `paste_at` and `paste_beside` — call `take_clipboard` where they called
`owns_the_clipboard`, so the crossing is a property of the clipboard rather than of any one chord.
⚠️ **The rule that makes that worth stating is D224's and not D218's**, which `take_clipboard`'s doc
said until this entry was written: D218 *recorded* the opposite as an honest asymmetry — *Paste here*
having no image arm — and **D224** is what closed it. D224 also records the one place the row and the
chord **deliberately differ**, which is the *aim*: *Paste here* passes `Some(p)`, so the fill it
replaces must be under the pointer. What must not differ is what the clipboard is found to **hold**,
and that is what this change makes uniform.

🚨 **Two things `roadmap.md`'s cost estimate got wrong, both in the cheap direction.** It read:
*"what is missing is a serialization of it that is not `NodeDto`, which is `pub(crate)` to
`ondin-core`, **and the id minting on the way back in**."* The id minting **did not exist as work at
all** — `build::insert_subtrees` already remaps every captured subtree through
`document::remap_subtree`, which mints fresh ids, refuses a template with more than one root and
refuses one whose child is not in the set. And the serialization is **`NodeDto` itself**: the
visibility was never the obstacle once the module lives in `ondin-core::io`, so the sentence
prescribed the one shape the fix must not take. *A cost estimate that names a mechanism is a claim
about the code, and this one had never been read against it* — which is that file's own standing
warning arriving from the pleasant direction twice over.

**Placement across windows needed nothing written for it either.** `paste_clipboard_at` puts a
subtree back under the parent it was copied from *if this document has one*; ids are minted against a
per-process-random actor (`session.rs`), so `Document::contains` answers no for a foreign parent and
**D221**'s fallback — the canvas root, appended — is already the right behaviour. ⚠️ **The exception
looks like a bug and is not**: the *same document* open in two windows does resolve, and the paste
lands back in its own group, which is what someone doing that meant.

**The pictures cross too.** `Payload::images` carries the table entries the subtrees key into, base64
through `ImageDto`, because a node carries the key and the document carries the bytes — which is
**D280**'s lesson, where a picture copied into another *document* arrived as the missing-picture
placeholder and *Export original…* then blamed a link the app cannot author.

⚠️ **`menu.rs`'s `can_paste` needed no fourth term, and that is a coincidence rather than a design.**
A foreign copy arrives as *text*, so the `system_text` term already makes the *Paste* row live; what
it is live **for** is layers, which is `take_clipboard`'s business and not that predicate's — the row
says *Paste* either way. Said at the site as well as here, because if a payload ever crosses by a
channel that is not text, that is the line that goes wrong.

*(**Tests**: four in `ondin-core/tests/io.rs` —
`a_clipboard_payload_round_trips_every_node_kind`,
`a_clipboard_payload_carries_the_image_table_entries_it_keys_into`,
`clipboard_text_is_foreign_ours_or_refused` and `a_layer_named_like_the_fence_still_crosses` — and
three in `app::clipboard_crossing_tests`. Every one flip-checked, each test's doc naming its mutation
and the site it came back red at, and all seven predicted sites were correct. ⚠️ **That app module
states its own limit in as many words**: one process standing in for two, because no test here can
put anything on the real OS clipboard or read it back; what is *not* asserted is that the OS carries
the text between two processes, which is `arboard`'s job. ⚠️ **On a `write` failure `copy_selection`
falls back to the names alone**, which is the pre-D823 behaviour — the crossing is lost and the
in-app clipboard still works — and that arm is a fact about the function rather than about today's
model, nothing in a well-formed document being able to make `write` fail. **D17's closing *Fix* is
struck**; §5.11 gains the second reader and §9.4's clipboard paragraph the crossing. **The
`roadmap.md` bullet is struck**, which with D824 leaves *Now · Canvas and interaction* with nothing
open.)*

**D227 — The missing-font warning gets its UI half, and the third state it needed first.
*Built 2026-08-19.*** §5.4a carried this as a **gap rather than a decision** for as long as it was one,
and the reason it gave was correct: `text::is_family_available` answers *"not here yet"* and *"never
coming"* identically, so a warning built on it would have accused a font that was on its way. The
warning therefore existed in the MCP snapshot, where nothing is on its way, and in no panel.

**`fonts::FamilyStatus` is the distinction.** Three states — `Ready`, `Pending`, `Missing` — and the
only boundary that carries information is the last two. `Pending` deliberately folds together **three**
reasons that all mean *wait*: a face is in flight, a source that could still list the family has not
landed, or nothing has asked yet. One word for the three because the UI has one thing to say about
them, and because promoting any of them to a warning is the accusation the enum exists to avoid. The
rule is a free function over five named facts (`status_of`, `FamilyFacts`) rather than a chain of `if`s
inside a method that needs threads, a disk cache and a network to exist — so it is a truth table a test
can walk. **A struct rather than five positional `bool`s**, which is a swap waiting to happen.

**Two facts the service had and was not keeping.** Both are the same shape: the information existed and
was thrown away one line after arriving.

- **`FamilyState::failed`.** `FontMsg::Failed` already reached `poll` — the roadmap said so — and was
  read *only* to decide the variable-file retry (a family whose variable cut this build cannot decode
  still has its static cuts). The count is what lets `Missing` be said about a family the catalog
  **lists** and cannot actually deliver, which is otherwise indistinguishable from one nobody has asked
  for. Bytes core *declines to register* count too, because that is the same failure wearing a
  different message. A count rather than a flag, and only a verdict alongside `faces` being empty: an
  italic that never arrived beside an upright that did is not a missing family.
- **`catalog_done`, read off the channel *closing*.** Nothing could be concluded about an unresolvable
  family until the sources stopped arriving, and there was no signal for the catalog having finished.
  The one that covers every path is the sender being dropped: that thread sends up to two batches — the
  disk copy, then a refreshed fetch — and then returns on **all three** endings, including the fetch
  that failed. `try_recv` reports it as `Disconnected` for free. A "done" message would have had to be
  sent from three places and would be missing from whichever one somebody forgot.

**The UI half is D179's precedent applied unchanged**: `TEXT_AA` in `theme::color::WARN` on the family
row's own glyph, which is how a layers row whose picture cannot be drawn says the same thing. The
family's **name stays full strength**, because it is the identity the row exists to report and dimming
it would read as the pick not having taken — the same mistake the loading ellipsis was added to avoid.
The sentence hangs off the `ComboBox`'s own head response, the one place a tooltip on that row fires: a
tooltip on the wrapping `ui.scope` is silently dead, its response being a placeholder over the rect
rather than a registered widget.

**What did *not* close, and why it is not a defect.** The roadmap wanted "the snapshot's warning and
the panel's the same question asked twice". They cannot be yet: `snapshot.rs` is in `ondin-export`,
which has no `FontService` and asks core directly. That is **honest for a headless run** — `ondin
export` never fetches anything, so it has no "not here yet" state to confuse — so unifying them is
worth doing only if the snapshot ever reads a live service. Recorded so nobody re-derives the
three-state design for a consumer that does not need it.

**Tested twice, and the second one is the interesting one.**
`a_family_is_pending_until_its_sources_have_stopped_arriving` walks the table; the flips are dropping
`!sources_settled` (the term that reads as belt-and-braces, and which is the state a **cold start**
spends its first second in — getting it wrong flashes a warning over every font in a document that then
loads perfectly, and D175 is the record of that second being real) and dropping the `listed` arm. The
second test asserts the tint reaches the **painted galley's vertices**, because whether egui honours a
`LayoutJob`'s own colours inside `selected_text` or overrides them with its own text colour is egui's
business and not ours to assume — and if it overrode them the warning would simply be invisible, which
is the one failure mode a colour-only signal has. It also asserts the label is *not* tinted, and that
half was flip-checked by tinting both, which leaves exactly one colour in the galley.

**D228 — `Enter` steps into a text node, a group and a boolean, and the order it asks in is
`double_click_pick`'s. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** `roadmap.md` scored this as "an arm in `enter_action`
rather than a new key", which was right about the cost and silent about the interesting part.

**The order is the decision, and it is not a new one.** "One level in" means something different on
every kind — a text node's characters, a picture's framing, a path's points, a group's children — and
there are now *two* gestures that mean it: a double-click and `Enter`. They must not disagree about
which meaning applies to the same layer, so `enter_action`'s arms are `double_click_pick`'s arms in
`double_click_pick`'s order. **Text first**, so a text node with a photograph in it is still type;
picture ahead of the group step, because an image-filled shape is a leaf and has no group step to
steal. Two lists in the same order is a duplication worth naming as one: if a third gesture ever wants
it, the order should become a function rather than a third copy.

**The asymmetry with `Escape` is deliberate.** `shortcuts.md` calls `Enter` the ladder's counterpart,
and the counterpart is not a mirror: `Enter` **toggles** the two *tools* it can enter — the node tool
and Crop, which are modes you are either in or out of — and only ever goes **deeper** into a group,
because a group is a *depth* and `Enter` on a group inside a group has an obvious meaning. Coming back
out of a depth is the ladder's job, one rung per press, and always was (D125).

**Two supporting changes, each fixing something small that was already there.**

- **`begin_edit_text` takes `Option<Point>`.** It took a bare `Point`, so the one caller with no
  pointer — the context menu's *Edit text* through the panel door — invented one:
  `world.unwrap_or_default()`. `Point::ZERO` is a *position in the document*, not an absence of one,
  and it reads as "the caret goes to the start" only by accident of where a text node's local origin
  sits. With `None` the editor now **selects the whole string**, which is the useful one of the three
  available answers and what Figma and Illustrator both do: `Enter` on a text layer means "I am about
  to retype this", so the very next keystroke should replace it, where the other two answers insert
  somewhere the user did not choose. `select_all` on an empty buffer collapses to a bare caret, so an
  empty text node comes out exactly as it would have.
- **`enter_container` is the menu's own body, lifted out of its dispatch arm.** *Enter group* and
  *Enter boolean* worked; the key did not; and the reason is that the verb existed only as the arm.
  Both doors call it now, which is the rule the registry rests on — a row and its chord must not be
  able to come to mean different things. The pointer stays optional inside it for the same reason as
  above: the menu has one and uses it to choose *what* to land on, and a keypress falls back to the
  **last** child, the topmost in z, which is the one the eye is already on.

**Read-verified (D35).** `enter_action` and `enter_container` are both `&mut self` on `OndinApp`, and
the order they encode is a `match` over kinds rather than arithmetic worth extracting. On the machine:
`Enter` on a text layer then typing (the string should be replaced), `Enter` on a group then `Enter`
again on a group inside it (two levels deep), and `Escape` twice to come back out.

**D229 — A `Line` has a length field where every other kind has W and H.
*Resolved 2026-08-19.*** `roadmap.md` had this as a gap in its own words: a line's box is meaningless
— the axis-aligned rectangle round a diagonal is not a property of the diagonal — which is why `size0`
is `None` for one and why `selection_handles` suppresses its size badge (D98, D99). What a line
*has* is a length, and it is precisely the number the suppressed badge would have wanted.

**The field goes in W's slot rather than in a row of its own.** It is the same question — how big is
this — asked in the same place, so the card's rhythm does not change for one kind; and nothing follows
it on the row, because there is no second dimension to put there.

**Written through `tools::move_line_end`, which is the verb the endpoint handle already drags
through.** Same rule W and H follow with `resize_box_to` (D101's neighbour): a second way to say where
a line's end is would be a second *definition* of what a line is, and the two would drift.

**The start is the anchor, and that is a decision rather than an accident.** X and Y report a line's
**start** point and the Rotation field reads the start→end vector, so growing it from the far end — or
centring the growth, which is what a W field does to a rect — would move the numbers in two *other*
fields and read as the layer having jumped. This changes one of the three and leaves the other two
exactly where they were.

**The direction is kept by scaling the vector, not by going round through the angle.**
`start + v * (length / current)` is bit-exact for any angle; `atan2` out and `sin`/`cos` back is the
spelling that reads as equivalent and is off in the last few decimals at 45° — which matters here for
the reason `LENGTH_PLACES` exists in typography: a value that does not round-trip churns the saved file
on every edit. The identity write is therefore a true no-op, which is what lets the field write back
the value it is already showing on every frame of a scrub.

A degenerate line answers `None` rather than inventing a direction: zero length has none, and the
caller has no length to *show* in the same condition, so the field and the arithmetic agree about when
the question is unanswerable.

**Tested, and the first flip found a bad fixture** — worth recording, because it is the failure mode
`CLAUDE.md` warns about and it happened here in the mildest possible form.
`a_typed_length_moves_the_end_and_leaves_the_start_and_the_angle_alone` originally shortened a 30-unit
line to a **half**, and halving lands on the midpoint from *either* end — so flipping to
`end - v * k` (anchor the far end) left that assertion green and was caught two assertions later by
the angle. A **third** discriminates, and the assertion now names the wrong answer in its message. The
second flip drops the `/ current`, which is what somebody writes when the vector is already thought of
as a direction, and puts the end 190 units out.

**That the field *appears* was eye-only** — `size0` being `None` and `line_ends` being `Some` are both
read off an `OndinApp` — until D303 removed that seam and
`a_line_trades_w_and_h_for_one_l_and_a_point_gets_no_size_field_at_all` measured it, which is the
pattern D310 set for the Align card. It drives **`inspector_single`** on a headless app and collects
the galleys reading exactly `W`, `H` or `L`: a rect answers `["W", "H"]`, a line `["L"]`, and a line
whose end is on its own origin answers **nothing at all**. The caller is driven rather than
`inspector_transform` on purpose — the `size0` match that decides the W/H half lives in
`inspector_single`, so handing the card a hand-computed `size0` would assert a copy of the rule made in
the test and leave the panel's own free to disagree with it. Flipped both ways, and they fail in
different places: adding `NodeKind::Line { .. }` to `size0`'s derived-box arm — the `Path | Boolean |
Group` one, which a line fits as well as a path does — reports `["W", "H", "L"]`; dropping the `> 1e-9`
gate on `line_ends` reports `["L"]` for the point and leaves the other two green, so that assertion is
carrying the degenerate state on its own.

**D230 — *Outline shape* is allowed, and it is a second verb rather than a wider *Flatten*.
*Decided and built 2026-08-19.*** `roadmap.md` held this open as "**Flatten refuses a single
non-boolean** — and the reason has now expired… Decide it", and `context-menus.md` §4 held a row for
it marked *undecided*, with the note that the spec would not decide it. **Decided: allow it.**

**The reason it was refused expired rather than turning out to be wrong.** Converting a rect traded
its W/H and corner fields for a path nothing could edit — a strictly worse layer. Anchor editing and
per-anchor radii both exist now (D118, D119), so the trade is W/H **for anchors**, which is the trade
the operation *is*.

**It is `build::outline`, not a widened `build::flatten`, and that is the load-bearing part.**
*Flatten* means "throw the operands away and keep the answer"; its subject is a boolean or a set. This
means "stop describing this shape parametrically and start describing it as anchors"; its subject is
one shape. A *Flatten* that quietly did the second on a lone rect would be the row a user reached for
doing something the word does not say — so `flatten`'s answer to a lone non-boolean **stays no**, and
its doc comment now says that is *why* rather than that the conversion is unwanted. The two rows are
never offered together, by construction: `one` excludes a set and `Shape | Path` excludes a boolean.
That "by construction" is the kind of claim that stops being true when someone widens a condition, so
`outline_shape_appears_on_one_shape_and_never_beside_flatten` holds it, and dropping `one` — the exact
edit somebody makes wanting the row on a multi-selection — puts both rows in the same menu.

**It needs no `Resolved`.** `geometry::local_path` is a pure function of the node's own kind, so unlike
`flatten` there is no evaluated outline to look up and nothing about the tree to consult. That is the
whole difference in cost between the two.

**The two questions the scouting left open, decided here.**

- **A `Path` does get the row, and what it does there is bake the per-anchor radii into the
  geometry.** That makes `can_outline` a question about *state* on that one kind — `round_corners`
  returns the path untouched when every radius is `<= 0` — so the row is **present and dimmed** on a
  path with nothing to bake, which is §3's rule rather than absence: the kind can be outlined, this
  instance has nothing to gain. Flipping the arm to `Path => true` makes it a live row on every path
  in the document that then does nothing at all, which is the failure with no symptom until someone
  clicks.
- **A `Group` does not.** Its outline is the union of its contents — which is precisely what `flatten`
  gives two or more layers, and a *different verb* from outlining *this* shape. Offering it here would
  be one row meaning two things depending on the kind under it. `Artboard` is out because a page is
  not a shape that can be replaced by one, `Boolean` because that is `flatten`'s, and `Text` because
  it has no outline until its glyphs are converted — *Convert to path*, which is a **third verb** and
  has been built since 2026-08-20 (D260). Five refusals, one line and one reason each, in
  `can_outline` where a caller can read them.

**Sharing a body with `flatten` found a small loss in `flatten`.** The two differ only in the kind
gate and where the path comes from, so the tail is now `replace_with_path` — one definition of *what
survives being redrawn*, because that is a list and a list written twice drifts (D87 and D92 are the
record of one written three times). Its own comment claims "this **is** the same layer, so everything
about it that is not its geometry comes across", and it was **dropping a moved pivot** — silently
resetting the rotation centre of a layer the user had deliberately placed it on. Carried now, which is
the sentence being kept rather than a new feature. The two things still deliberately dropped say why
in place: *lock* is a property of the layer the user is holding rather than of the picture, and the
**proportion lock** is a constraint on resizing an *authored box* (D41) — and the whole of what this
operation does is stop the layer having one, so carrying it would preserve a rule about a field that
no longer exists.

**Unbound, and that is a third reason an `Item` is not an `Action`.** `Item`'s doc named two — a verb
about *where the menu was opened*, or about a target the keymap has no name for. This is neither: no
key was spent on it, which `shortcuts.md`'s *Deliberately unbound* list is for. A one-way structural
conversion is not a thing to make one keystroke away.

**The glyph is `POLYGON`, the layers tree's `Path` icon**, which is `context-menus.md` §8's rule read
the other way round: a verb whose whole *result* is a kind should wear that kind's picture. It had
exactly one meaning in the app before this and still has one.

**Tested four ways, every one flip-checked**: `outlining_a_rect_keeps_its_shape_its_paint_and_its_place`
(flipped by dropping the pivot), `can_outline_takes_the_five_shapes_and_asks_a_path_about_its_radii`
(flipped by `Path => true`), the menu test above (flipped by dropping `one`), and
`flatten_refuses_a_lone_shape_and_anything_with_no_outline`, which is unchanged and is now the
assertion that keeps the two verbs apart. The rect fixture is asserted to be *visibly rounded* before
the area comparison, or the outline assertion is one a square-cornered rect would also pass.

*A footnote worth keeping: the primitive menu is **17** rows now, which is what `context-menus.md` §10
said before it was corrected to 16 on this same day. The spec had been describing the menu with this
row in it all along; the correction was right about the code and the number is right again.*

**D231 — Every colour chip wears a hairline, and it is translucent white and always on.
*Resolved 2026-08-19.*** Reported 2026-07-31: a `2F2F2F` fill on a paint row is a `2F2F30` ground with
nothing whatever on it, so the chip reads as a hole in the row rather than as a colour. `ui::swatch`
now strokes `ui::SWATCH_HAIRLINE` — `Color32::from_white_alpha(76)`, written premultiplied because
that is the `const` constructor — over its rounded boundary, and the picker's document-palette chips
carry the same stroke because they do not go through `ui::swatch` (D32) and a border added in one
place would leave the inspector row and the palette below it disagreeing.

**Always on, never conditional.** A threshold pops — scrub a colour across it and the border flicks on
and off — and getting one right at all needs a *perceptual* metric, since RGB distance fires on
`2F2F2F` against `262626` and stays quiet for a saturated blue beside a saturated purple. None of that
is needed, because **the risk is one-sided**: the UI is dark, so only dark chips vanish, and a light
hairline at low alpha is either helping or invisible.

**White, not the picker's black**, which is the half of the old complaint that was real. A border
existed here before and was removed for painting badly; `picker::preview_chip` hairlines its gradient
thumbnail in `from_black_alpha(90)`, which is right over a bright ramp and exactly the wrong direction
here — black on a dark chip on a dark row is invisible twice over, and the old *inset black* darkened
every light colour's edge until it read as a frame around the swatch rather than as the swatch. White
self-cancels on exactly the colours that complained.

**The other half of that complaint was the mask's, not the border's, and it has expired.**
`mask_corners`' own note has the mechanism: a corner sliver is tangent to both edges it meets, so an
anti-aliased *fill* mitres that zero-degree vertex and throws spikes several pixels clear of the rect,
which on a 14px chip read as crop marks around the colour. The mask is one `Mesh` now, rasterized with
no feathering and no mitre, so the reason for removing the border no longer holds — and the same lack
of feathering is why the hairline is *wanted* rather than merely tolerated: a masked corner with no
stroke over it is a hard aliased step, and smoothing that arc is the second job `mask_corners` has
always described the hairline doing.

**76/255 is set by the black chip.** Composited over a chip, the hairline's value climbs from the
alpha itself (over black) to the chip's own colour (over white), so the *darkest* chip is the one that
has to clear the ground and every lighter one clears it by more. All three `ui::swatch` call sites
pass `color::FIELD` — the inspector's paint row and its guide-colour row, and the type panel's
character-colour row — so the number to beat is 47: grey 76 against 47 is a step of 29 levels, which
is what the constant is for. The palette chips sit on `color::CARD`, ten levels darker again, so the
same constant clears more there.

**Two traps, both of which a future editor will meet.** The stroke goes **after** the mask, or the mask
bites four pieces out of it; and it is `StrokeKind::Inside`, because a chip sits in a row of fixed
height and a stroke drawn `Outside` grows it by a point each side and pushes the label beside it —
which is the shape of the complaint that got the previous border removed. On a palette chip it goes
*under* the in-use `ACCENT_200` ring rather than instead of it: one says "this is a chip", the other
"this is the one you have".

**Tested at both ends, and both ends are load-bearing.**
`a_chip_the_colour_of_its_row_is_still_visible` composites the hairline over the reported `2F2F2F` and
over black, and asserts each edge is at least 25 8-bit levels from `color::FIELD`. Flipping the
constant to `from_black_alpha(76)` — the picker's direction — fails on the reported chip at 15 levels,
and trimming the alpha to 65 to be subtler fails on **black** at 18 while the reported chip still
passes, so neither chip in that fixture is spare.
`the_hairline_goes_over_the_mask_and_does_not_grow_the_chip` asserts the stroked rect's index in
`FullOutput::shapes` is past the mask's `Mesh` and that its `visual_bounding_rect` stays inside the
rect the chip allocated; painting it before the mask fails the first at index 4 against 5, and
`StrokeKind::Outside` fails the second by reaching `[-1,-1]..[17,17]` on a 16px chip.

*One claim arrived with this change and is false, so it should not become folklore:* `ui::swatch` was
**not** the only caller of `mask_corners` with no hairline over it. `picker::stop_bar`, `sv_plane`,
`hue_slider` and `alpha_slider` all mask and stop there; `preview_chip` was the only site pairing the
two, and the palette chips now join it. So this restores the pairing for chips and leaves four call
sites still unpaired — `stop_bar` most visibly, its 5px arc being as hard-stepped as the chip's was.
Their colour would not be this one: they are masked against `color::CARD` under a bright ramp or
plane, which is the case `preview_chip` chose black for. *Fix the sentence in `SWATCH_HAIRLINE`'s doc
comment that says chips were the only maskless caller, and decide the four separately.*

**D232 — The rotate cursor is a drawn two-headed arc at 15° steps, and the glyph was the problem
rather than the machinery. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** `roadmap.md` had the diagnosis right in its own
title, and it is worth restating because it is the half nobody re-solves: `cursor.rs` was already
angle-aware, and both call sites already handed it the correct **screen** vector — `pointer −
to_screen(pivot)` mid-drag, `h.screen_direction(handle)` on hover — so a turned box and a user-moved
pivot were honoured before any of this. What failed was the picture. Phosphor's `arrow-clockwise` is a
ring open down its right side, and at 19pt a ring turned by any amount is still a ring: the only moving
evidence was a few texels of gap and arrowhead, so the one thing this cursor exists to say — *which
handle you have* — never reached the eye. Nor was there anything to swap in. Phosphor has no two-headed
arc; `arrow-arc-right` is single-headed and `arrows-clockwise` is another ring.

So `rotate_arc` draws it: a band of radius 5.6pt and thickness 1.9pt sweeping ±0.40 rad, with a
tangential triangular head at each end — 2.3pt of half-base measured radially, 4.0pt long — for about
128° of figure in all. Coverage is a plain insideness test supersampled 4×4 per texel and precomputed
into a grid, because `compose` calls its coverage closure once per texel *and* once per texel of the
rim's dilation window, so sampling on demand would run the geometry nine times over. **Two heads, not
one**, because a rotate drag goes either way and a single head would be a claim about which.

**The roadmap called this two pieces of work and it is one.** It listed "draw the arc" and, separately,
"go continuous by putting `Affine::rotate` in the rasterization transform". Once the arc is drawn
rather than glyph-sourced there is no rasterized bitmap left to rotate: the angle goes straight into
the geometry, and continuity is free. `Quarter` became `Turn(u8)` with `STEPS = 24`, `Turn::toward` an
`atan2` quantized to a step, and `turn`/`turn_size` are gone along with `rasterize`'s `turns`
parameter. Step 0 is +x, due right, where `Quarter::Zero` faced up-right.

**Quarters were exact, and that reasoning is now beside the point rather than overcome.** A
whole-quarter rotation of a coverage field is a permutation of its texels, where an arbitrary angle
would have had to resample a finished 20-texel bitmap and come back soft — which was true, and is why
the old cursor was an enum. With the arc drawn there is no finished bitmap to resample, so the
objection stopped applying instead of being answered. Worth knowing which of those two it was: nothing
here got better at resampling.

**The footprint-and-hotspot trap is dissolved, not handled.** The roadmap warned that a square drawing
needs √2 the extent at 45°, with the rotation taken about the hotspot, or it clips at exactly the odd
angles — the last place anyone looks. `rotate_arc` sizes from the **circumscribed circle**, `RADIUS +
HEAD_W`, so the figure is a disc about its own hotspot by construction and its reach is the same at
every angle: nothing has to grow and nothing can clip. Be honest about how strong that is, though. For
this near-circular figure the √2 is mild. The outermost ink is a head's base corner, which sits at
exactly `RADIUS + HEAD_W` = 7.9pt from the hotspot but only 7.3pt out along x when the arc is upright,
and 5.9pt is the whole of its upright half-height — so a buffer sized angle-blind from the upright
extent would have fallen about 8% short and clipped slightly, not spectacularly. The test's border arm
is cheap insurance, and what it actually bites on is the padding being trimmed.

One detail underneath that is load-bearing and reads as incidental: `n` is **odd**, and `compose` adds
the same rim on both sides, so the hotspot it computes — `[w / 2, h / 2]` — lands on the very texel
`centre` puts the arc's own centre of rotation in. Make the buffer even and the two sit half a texel
apart, which shows as the drawing wobbling about the pointer as it turns; at that size the offset is
worth roughly 0.09 rad of centroid angle against `the_arc_faces_the_direction_it_was_given`'s 0.13
tolerance, so do not expect the test to catch it for you.

**Caching is not optional, and 15° is what it costs.** egui dedupes cursor uploads by `Arc` pointer
identity, so an unquantized angle would push a new cursor to the OS on every frame of every rotate
drag. 24 steps is fine enough that the cursor reads as a heading rather than as a set of discrete
states — the quarter version changed four times in a revolution, which is what made it read as four
states — and the images are built on demand, so a session that never rotates anything builds none.

Four tests, each flipped against the version somebody would plausibly have written.
`every_rotate_step_is_its_own_drawing` generalises the old four-cursor assertion to all 24, which is
the assertion that catches a `Turn` plumbed all the way through and never reaching the pixels.
`the_arc_faces_the_direction_it_was_given` measures the alpha-weighted ink centroid — the arc is
symmetric about its facing direction and lies entirely to one side of its own centre, so the centroid
sits on that ray — and asserts its angle is within 0.13 rad of `Turn::radians()`. Two details there are
load-bearing: it measures from the **hotspot** rather than the middle of the buffer, those two being
the same point being half of what is under test; and it wraps into (−π, π] the long way round rather
than through `sin().asin()`, which folds 180° onto 0 and would pass a cursor pointing at the opposite
handle. `the_arc_has_an_open_side` asserts no ink at all behind the hotspot, which is the "it is an
arc, not a ring" statement. `no_angle_clips_the_arc` asserts no ink on the buffer's own border and the
alpha-weighted **mass** within 4% across the 24 steps — mass rather than texel count, because counting
puts the antialiased fringe on one side of a threshold and swings 6% on rasterizer phase alone where
the mass moves 3%. Hardcoding the rotation to identity fails three of the four; a near-closed ring
(`BAND = 2.90`) fails two; trimming a texel off the buffer fails the border arm at step 0.

`a_quarter_turn_walks_the_arrows_gap_clockwise` is **deleted** rather than generalised: it asserted
where the *glyph's* gap sat, and there is no glyph. `each_screen_diagonal_picks_the_quarter_facing_it`
became `a_screen_direction_picks_the_step_facing_it` and gained an assertion that each 45° diagonal
lands *on* a 15° step rather than between two — which is what keeps an unrotated box's corner cursor
exact rather than 7.5° out, and would otherwise be a silent regression the moment `STEPS` changed to
something 45 does not divide.

**D233 — Modifier badges on the cursor are declined: the compositing is cheap, and the base underneath
it is what is missing. *Intentional — decided 2026-08-19.*** Asked for 2026-08-03 — Figma's small glyph
at the bottom-left of the arrow, an unobtrusive statement of intent — and carried in `roadmap.md` as
cheap work on the strength of the machinery already being there. That half is true and should not be
re-litigated: `cursor::compose` takes an arbitrary `coverage: impl Fn(i32, i32) -> u32`, so a compound
is one closure — `|x, y| base(x, y).max(badge(x - dx, y - dy))` — and because the rim is a *dilation*
of whatever that closure returns, the badge picks up the same white-core/dark-rim treatment, including
the outline between it and the arrow, for nothing. Any Phosphor glyph is available, the hands and the
pen being rasterized out of the tool rail's own font.

**What is missing is the base, and that is what settled it.** `cursor.rs` draws only the cursors no OS
provides a usable one for — its own opening sentence — and every one of the seven modifiers the
roadmap entry enumerated lands on a stock `CursorIcon` with `None` beside it. Deep select,
Alt-duplicate on a body drag, the key layer and Alt-hover's measure all fall through `select_cursor` to
`canvas::rest_cursor`, which is `(CursorIcon::Default, None)` for every tool except Scale. The node
tool's two — `Alt` breaking a handle pair, `Ctrl` shaping curvature — are on the plain arrow because
**D118 deliberately put them back there**, a drag being mid-gesture and therefore never armed for the
pen. A guide drag, Alt-copying or not, is `rulers::ruler_cursor`'s `axis_cursor` — stock
`ResizeHorizontal`/`ResizeVertical`, `None` again. So six of the seven are the arrow and the seventh is
the axis-resize pair, and `compose` composites a badge *onto a base*. Shipping badges means **drawing
our own arrow first**, plus a move cursor and two axis-resize ones.

That is not a cheap prerequisite, it is a different decision, and it goes the other way. There is no
reason to override the system's cursor: the arrow is the pointer a user looks at all day, and replacing
it is a visual decision in its own right rather than an enabling step for a glyph in its corner. It
also forfeits what a stock cursor gets from the OS free — the roadmap's own last bullet suspected,
without confirming, that custom cursor images do not follow the pointer-size accessibility setting,
which costs little on a rotate arc seen during one gesture and a great deal on the arrow. And the
footprint-and-hotspot trap comes back: **D232 dissolved** it for the arc by sizing from the
circumscribed circle, so the figure is a disc about its own hotspot and cannot clip at an odd angle. A
badge hangs off one corner, so the canvas would have to grow asymmetrically while the hotspot stayed on
the arrow's tip — handled rather than avoided, which is the more expensive of the two.

**The drawn cursors are untouched.** This is a decision against *adding* badges over stock cursors, not
against `cursor.rs`: the hands, the pen, the crosshair, the rotate arc and the discard bin all stay,
and the maintainer's note alongside this one was that a few of them want tweaking, which is work on
that set rather than on this.

**One badge survived, and it survived for exactly the reason the rest died.** The Image tool's
remaining-count badge sits on `Bitmap::Crosshair`, which this app draws, so it is the one badge with a
base under it and overrides nothing the OS supplied. It landed the same day as **D236**, which is also
where to read what the footprint-and-hotspot paragraph above was worth: the prediction that a compound
is one closure held exactly, and the trap bit precisely where this entry said it would.

*Revisit only if a drawn arrow is wanted for its own sake.* The badges would then follow cheaply, in
that order and not the reverse — the mistake this entry exists to prevent is reading "the machinery is
there" as "the feature is small".

**D234 — Six dimmed controls: three tooltips that never fired, two strings nothing could reach, and
one row at two dim levels. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** D182 counted the damage and left it — "the same
spelling predates this change at seven other sites… every one a control explaining why it is
unavailable, so each is a real loss of information. Tracked separately." This is that sweep, over
every `Ui::disable` and `add_enabled_ui` in the app, and it turned up one more kind of defect than it
went looking for.

**It was prompted by a false alarm, and that is worth a paragraph so it is not rediscovered.** I
measured, and reported, that `Ui::disable` fades grounds but leaves explicitly-coloured text at full
strength, and wrote a test asserting it. **Both were wrong.** A galley carries its colour in two
places and only one of them paints: `galley.job.sections[..].format.color` is the layout *input*,
which nothing mutates, while `galley.rows[..].row.visuals.mesh.vertices[..].color` is the output,
baked from that same format at layout time, and is what the tessellator draws. egui disables with
`painter.multiply_opacity(disabled_alpha)`, and `epaint::adjust_colors` takes `Arc::make_mut` on the
galley to recolour those **vertices** — and `fallback_color` besides, which is what a `PLACEHOLDER`
vertex defers to, so that path fades too. A probe reading the *section* therefore reports
"explicitly-coloured text does not fade": confidently, reproducibly, and wrongly. Measured properly,
an explicit `theme::text::MUTED` glyph goes `#9090929E` → `#4848494F`, exactly halved, the same as a
plain label. `ui::dim_tests::disabling_a_scope_fades_everything_including_explicitly_coloured_text`
asserts the opposite of the test it replaces, and reading the section instead of the vertex
reproduces the original wrong answer — so the trap is pinned rather than described. The sweep was
worth running anyway; the six below are what it found.

**One consequence, because the suspicion was mine:** `stroke_menu_popup`'s comment justifying
`Ui::disable` over a flag threaded through `segmented` — that it "blocks the interaction *and* fades
the painter", `segmented` painting its cells straight onto `ui.painter()` — is true in both halves.
It was the prime suspect while the false finding stood, and it was correct all along.

**Three "why" tooltips hung on a `Ui::scope`'s response, and each was dead twice over.**
`inspector::stroke_menu_popup`'s "Only a shape with corners takes a join",
`typography::type_alignment_row`'s "Only a fixed-height box has room to align in" and
`typography::wrap_section`'s "Nothing to break: the lines do not wrap" — every one guarded by the
same condition that disables the scope, so the state where the sentence carries information is the
only state it was ever asked in. Dead for two independent reasons: a scope's response is a
placeholder over the rect rather than a registered widget, so it never reports a hover; and
`on_hover_text` is `Tooltip::for_enabled`, gated on `Response::enabled()`, which is false for
everything inside a disabled scope. Each is now an explicit `ui.interact(rect, id, Sense::hover())`
claimant, the spelling `inspector::menu_action` and `image_menu_popup` already use, and which
`a_dimmed_control_can_be_hovered_only_through_a_claimant_of_its_own` already pins — so no new test
was written for these three. The behaviour was never in doubt; the sweep was.

**This is the trap `CLAUDE.md` already documents**, in the words "worth suspecting anywhere a tooltip
hangs off a `scope`'s response" — and it was live at three sites while the note sat there. That is
the argument for repeating the sweep rather than trusting the note: a written trap catches only the
person reading the document at the moment they need it. *Sweep the `disable()` sites after adding
one, rather than assuming the note did the work.*

**Two strings were unreachable rather than merely unfired**, which is worse, because dead code shaped
like a working affordance reads as done. `inspector::point_handle_rows` ("Select one point to edit
its handles") and `inspector::points_appearance` ("No corner point selected — a smooth point has no
corner to round") each chose the sentence with `match enabled { true => …, false => … }` and passed
the result to `on_hover_text` on a widget inside `add_enabled_ui(enabled, …)`: the `false` arm cannot
run, by the same `for_enabled` gate. Both are split now — `on_hover_text` for the live string,
`on_disabled_hover_text` for the unavailable one. **The split is not cosmetic**:
`Tooltip::for_disabled` asks `ctx.rect_contains_pointer(layer, rect)` where the enabled path asks
`Response::hovered()`, and hit-testing the rectangle is exactly what survives a disabled scope.

**One row carried two dim levels, and `ui::disable_unless` is the answer to it.** `Ui::disable`
**multiplies** the painter's opacity by `Visuals::disabled_alpha` — 0.5 — rather than setting it, and
`add_enabled_ui` does not guard on the ambient state: its doc promises that a call inside a disabled
`Ui` is disabled regardless, and the way it keeps that promise is by disabling a second time. So a
gate inside a gate lands at 0.25. `inspector::points_header` wraps the whole identity row in
`add_enabled_ui(false)` to show the design's second row inert, and `identity_boolean_row`'s four
controls each gate themselves again — so in point-edit mode the boolean dropdown, *Mask* and
*Ungroup* sat at 0.25 while *Group* beside them sat at 0.5. **Group is the odd one out because it is
the only one of the four whose own gate is open there**: point editing implies exactly one selected
`Path` (`edited_path`), which `build::group` accepts, while `selected_boolean`,
`booleanable_selection` and the container test behind `can_ungroup` all say no to it. One row, two
greys, which reads as a rendering fault rather than as a gate — the kind of thing that is invisible
in the source and obvious on screen. All four now go through `disable_unless`, which passes `enabled
|| !ui.is_enabled()` so that an already-disabled parent's state simply stands.

**`Ui::add_enabled` — the *widget* form — already guards this way** (`if self.is_enabled() &&
!enabled`), and that is why the scope form's not doing it is easy to miss: the two read as one thing
spelt twice. `ui::dim_tests::nesting_a_disabled_gate_does_not_double_fade` is an A/B against a single
gate; flipped by dropping the guard it reports **64 against 128**, the 0.25-vs-0.5 doubling exactly.
Its third assertion **fails** if egui ever guards `add_enabled_ui` itself, and its message says the
helper can then be deleted — the cheapest way to stop a workaround outliving its cause. That fixed the
*opacity* channel only; a second axis on the **colour** channel survived it, and D235 is that one.

**D235 — "Unavailable" gets a grey of its own, and the two dim channels stop compounding. *Resolved
2026-08-19.*** The roadmap carried this as one item — *dimmed because off* and *dimmed because
disabled* being the same grey app-wide, so dim alone read as "inert, don't bother" on a control that
was merely switched off. It turned out to be two, and the second was only visible once the first was
fixed.

**The numbers I first reported were wrong, and the way they were wrong is D234's trap.** I described a
four-way pileup at 79/95/97/102 in which disabled was *dimmer* than off at some sites and brighter at
others, so the ordering encoded nothing — which would have made this a re-derivation of the whole
ladder. It was an artefact of reading a galley's layout *section* instead of its mesh vertices, the
same bad measurement D234 records at length. Measured as painted: live text is `MUTED` at 158; off is
95 (a hidden paint row, `HIDDEN_OPACITY`'s 0.6 over `MUTED`) or 102 (a hidden or locked layer row,
absolute); disabled was 97 (`FAINT`, explicit), 79 (a `Ui::disable` scope halving a `MUTED` glyph) or
49 (both at once). **Nothing was inverted** — every disabled route sat at or below 97 and both off
routes at 95–102 — so the real collision was narrow and single: `FAINT`-as-disabled at 97 against off
at 95 and 102, two and five levels, which is no distance. The scope-disabled tiers were already clear.
*A wrong measurement does not just get a number wrong; it invents a shape of problem.*

**`theme::text::DISABLED` is `text_a(79)`, and 79 is matched rather than chosen.** `Ui::disable` fades
a `MUTED` glyph to exactly that whatever any constant says, so the app was reaching one meaning by two
routes and landing on two inks; this moves the *colour* route onto the *scope* route rather than
picking a third value. It is applied at the four places a grey meant unavailable rather than quiet —
`ui::icon_button_padded`'s disabled glyph, `ui::button_face`'s `FieldButton::Disabled`,
`ui::segment_label_disabled`, and `ui::menu_row`'s disabled arm. For `menu_row` the **whole triple**
moved, (97, 80, 60) becoming (79, 65, 49) for glyph, label and accelerator: dropping only the glyph to
79 while the label stayed at 80 would have collapsed the top two tiers of that row into one.

**`FAINT` keeps 97 and keeps its meaning** — eyebrows, hints, placeholders, prefix icons,
`segment_mixed`'s dash, a menu row's accelerator: text that is faint because it is not the point, not
because it is unavailable. That is 26 uses in shipping code (11 in `ui.rs`, 7 in `inspector.rs`, 3 in
`typography.rs`, 2 each in `layers.rs` and `picker.rs`, 1 in `app.rs`), so this split moved four sites
out of twenty-six rather than renaming a constant. `FAINT` is explicitly *allowed* to sit where the off
tiers do, and `unavailable_and_switched_off_are_different_greys` asserts nothing about it. **Both off
tiers are deliberately untouched**: `HIDDEN_OPACITY` was set by eye against the real panel, and
`layers.rs` argues its own case for locked and hidden sharing one grey — that argument is about
locked-vs-hidden and this does not bear on it.

**The second axis: `ui::resting_ink`, which is `disable_unless` on the colour channel.** With the two
disabled routes agreeing, a control that took *both* was dimmed twice — `DISABLED`'s 79 painted inside
a scope already faded by `disabled_alpha` gives **40**. `resting_ink(ui, enabled)` returns `MUTED`
while the control is usable and `DISABLED` when it is not, **except where the surrounding `Ui` is
already disabled**, where it returns `MUTED` and lets the scope's fade supply the rest. Deferring is
not an approximation but an identity: `MUTED` faded by a disabled scope *is* `DISABLED`, which is where
the constant's value came from. It lives inside `icon_button_padded` and `button_face`, so every caller
of `icon_button`, `icon_button_sized`, `field_button` and `label_button` is fixed at once.

**It was never only point-edit mode, and that is what justifies fixing the helper rather than the call
sites.** D234 framed the compound fade as an artefact of `points_header`'s outer gate, true of the
opacity channel. On the colour channel the same shape is in *ordinary* selection: `identity_boolean_row`
spells Group as `disable_unless(ui, can_group, …)` wrapped around `icon_button(…, can_group)` — the
same condition on the scope and on the flag — so a disabled Group button was at 40 with nothing
nesting above it, and Ungroup and the permanently-disabled Mask beside it likewise. **Any** `icon_button`
inside a scope gated on its own condition was a tier below the app's disabled grey.

Both tests were flipped. `ui::dim_tests::unavailable_and_switched_off_are_different_greys` asserts the
two halves of the first change — that a scope-faded glyph and the constant are the same ink, and that
the result clears both off tiers by at least 15 levels; putting the constant back to 97 fails it with
"a faded scope gives 79, the constant 97". `a_control_disabled_twice_over_is_no_darker_than_one_disabled_once`
asserts that the three spellings — flag alone, scope alone, both — agree, **and asserts no particular
value**, which is the point: it survives the ladder being retuned and fails the moment the channels
start composing again. Dropping the ambient deferral fails it with 40 against 79.

*Keep.* The load-bearing detail is that 79 is not a taste number: it is `disabled_alpha` applied to
`MUTED`, so an editor who changes either `MUTED` or `Visuals::disabled_alpha` owes `DISABLED` the same
move, and the first test is what will say so. The second trap is `resting_ink`'s `|| !ui.is_enabled()`
guard, which reads like a redundant condition and is the whole fix — the same simplification
`disable_unless` exists to resist.

**D236 — The loaded Image cursor gets its count badge, and the digits are knocked out of the chip
rather than drawn. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** The last badge D233 left standing, and the reason it was
worth building is not the one the roadmap gave. The count *is* real information — how many pictures
are still to place — but the sharper fact is that `Tool::Image` and the six drawing tools were handing
the OS the same bitmap while a click on one plants a picture and a click on the other starts a box.
The badge is the only thing on screen that says the cursor is loaded, which is why it is drawn for a
**single** remaining image too, where the number alone tells the user nothing they do not know.
`Bitmap::Loaded(Remaining)` is the arm, `canvas.rs`'s cursor match answers it, and the tools above it
keep `Bitmap::Crosshair` untouched.

`Remaining::of(n)` is `None` at zero rather than a badge reading `0`: an armed tool over an empty
queue exists only if something failed to disarm it — `canvas::placed_one_image` hands back to Select
as the last picture goes down — and the plain crosshair is the honest drawing for that, where a `0`
would be the cursor claiming to be loaded. Exact to 99 and `99+` beyond, and **the clamp is what
bounds the cache**: egui dedupes cursor uploads by `Arc` pointer identity (D9, D232), so every
distinct badge is a bitmap that has to be kept, and an unclamped count would build one per file in a
two-hundred-file drop. The store is a `HashMap<Remaining, Slot>` on `Cursors` rather than an array,
since a session touches a handful of the hundred values and counts down through them; it is dropped
with the rest when the display scale changes.

**The digits are knocked *out* of a solid chip, not drawn as ink, and that is the decision to keep.**
Both were dumped as ASCII art before anything was written, and drawn ink loses at the size that
matters: `compose` gives every shape a white core and a dark rim, and a nine-point digit at 1x is a
one-texel stroke, so *drawing* it puts a white hairline inside a black outline — a blob. Knocked out,
the same treatment paints the chip white and the digits' holes fall inside the rim's dilation and come
