out dark, which is a black number on a white badge at every scale. Note what this does *not* need: the
badge asks nothing of `compose` the other cursors do not, which is exactly what D233 predicted when it
said a compound is one closure.

**The trap D233 and D232 named was footprint and hotspot, and it bit precisely there.** The buffer
grows down and right to make room for the chip, so the middle of it is no longer the middle of the
cross, and `Hotspot::Middle` — which every other drawn cursor uses — would have put the click a few
texels off wherever the user aimed. `Hotspot::At(i32, i32)` names a texel of the **coverage** field
instead, `compose` adding the rim to it. The plain crosshair was moved onto the same spelling through
a new `Cross` geometry struct whose `aim()` is `near + thick / 2`, so the two cursors are provably the
same point under the pointer rather than coincidentally so. Do not put either back on `Middle`;
`the_badge_does_not_move_the_aiming_point` asserts the loaded hotspot *equals* the plain crosshair's,
over 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0/3.0, and that the aiming point is still transparent — a hotspot landing on the
gap but painting over it would satisfy the first half and lose the point of a crosshair.

`Cross::ink` also had to become **bounds-checked**, and this is the live defect the refactor found.
The closure it came out of was handed a buffer exactly its own size, so anything outside was
unreachable; called over a buffer the badge has widened, an unbounded `on_arm` reads true for every
`x` past the end and runs the horizontal arm off to the badge and beyond. The guard reads like
redundant defensiveness and is not.

Two numbers a picture settled and arithmetic did not. The chip stands off by one **rim width** past
the arm's gap (`Cross::badge_at`), because lining it up with where the arm's *coverage* ends leaves
the two dark rims sharing the column between them and the badge reads as welded to the arm rather than
hung beside it. And the chip is **never narrower than it is tall**: Inter's `1` is three texels of ink
at 1x where a `4` is six, so padding alone gives a one-digit badge a chip half the width of a
two-digit one — a white bar rather than a badge. The square floor is what makes every count read as
the same object, and the digits centre in whatever room it leaves.

`digits()` lifts a short string's coverage out of the font atlas the way `rasterize` lifts a single
glyph, with one difference worth recording because it is invisible where it is wrong: a glyph's `pos`
and its `uv_rect.offset` come back in **points** while the atlas is in texels, so they are scaled.
Getting that wrong looks perfect at 1x and shears the digits apart at 1.5x — a Windows norm.

Four tests, plus the new cursor joining `every_bitmap_cursor_rasterizes_legibly`.
`the_badge_draws_the_count_it_was_given` gives every count its own bitmap — a `Remaining` plumbed
through and never reaching the pixels would leave nine images and one looking identical — and asserts
the clamp from both sides, 99 differing from 100 and 100 matching 4000.
`an_unloaded_cursor_has_no_badge` pins the zero case. **The two worth knowing about are in
`the_count_reads_dark_on_a_light_chip`, and both drafts of it failed the same way: they eyeballed a
region of the finished cursor and guessed which texels were which.** The first measured a rectangle
and counted anything dark, and passed against a chip with **nothing knocked out at all**, because the
chip's own dark *rim* is inside that region. The second asked a gap to be enclosed on four sides,
which classifies the whole of a one-texel-wide `1` as outside, found no digits and reported there was
nothing to check — green for the same reason, one step further along. The version that bites takes the
classification from the badge's own **coverage** and finds the rounded corners by filling in from the
chip's border. Of its two arms only **transparency** is a live catch: at 40pt instead of nine the
strokes outrun the rim, `rim == 0` inside a stroke and the digits come out as see-through slots. The
darkness arm restates the coverage — inside a chip the dilation always finds white, so `lum` comes
back equal to what the closure returned — and is there as the visible outcome rather than as a second
catch. *A test that samples a region of a finished drawing is measuring whatever else is in that
region.*

*Keep.* The load-bearing details, in the order an editor would undo them: the square floor on the
chip, which looks like arbitrary padding; `Cross::ink`'s bounds check, which looks like a redundant
guard; and `Hotspot::At`, which looks like a long way to say `Middle`. ~~`Bitmap::hotspot`'s `Loaded`
arm is read by nothing and says so — the real hotspot comes from `loaded_crosshair`, not from
there.~~ ⚠️ **That note held for one arm and then for four** (D682): `Rotate` and `TextOnPath` grew
the same dead arm, and `Crosshair`'s carried a *reason* for a value nothing read, which is the
version a reader spends an afternoon on. `glyph()` and `hotspot()` are one
`glyph_and_hotspot() -> Option<(&'static str, Hotspot)>` now, so a variant with no glyph has nowhere
to put a hotspot and the routing in `Cursors::image` is the only place that decides. **A note saying
"this is dead" is a claim about today's routing**, and the routing is what grew.

**D237 — The downloaded-font cache is bounded on disk, and the stamp it evicts by had to be made to mean
"last wanted". *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** The roadmap carried this as a parked decision for as long as it
was one: every family a picker row previews leaves a file in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\fonts` and nothing
ever removed one, so scrolling the whole Latin catalog left ~85 MB there **permanently** and a browse
through CJK families a few hundred MB. Permanence is what this ends, and the distinction is worth
holding on to, because what was built deliberately does not do more than that.

`FONT_CACHE_BYTES` is 256 MB, chosen so the case that is *not* a problem is never touched: the whole
Latin catalog previewed end to end is about 85 MB (§14's own estimate, now in the roadmap's parked list),
and someone who has browsed it should not have to fetch it again next launch. What the budget is *for* is
the browse through CJK families, where twenty rows can be a couple of hundred megabytes on their own.
Bytes rather than a count of files, for D160's reason on the other side of the same cache — a Latin
subset is tens of KB and a CJK face is megabytes, so a count bounds nothing. A pruned file costs one
re-download and nothing else, the cache being derived data, which is what makes a bound safe to apply
without asking anybody.

**No floor, unlike its in-memory twin, and the difference is the part to keep.** `PREVIEW_FLOOR` exists
because evicting what the picker is drawing *this frame* makes it re-fetch and re-evict forever. The disk
sweep runs once at startup, with nothing on screen and nothing in flight, so there is nothing to thrash
against — and a floor there would be exactly the "second, weaker cap in disguise" that `PREVIEW_FLOOR`'s
own doc warns about. `files_over_budget` is split out of `trim_font_cache` for `families_over_budget`'s
stated reason: it is the whole of the rule and none of the deleting, and the alternative is a policy that
can only be checked by filling a real directory. Its `budget` is a **parameter** rather than the constant
read directly, so exercising the sweep does not mean writing 256 MB.

**What makes "least recently used" true is one new call in `load_face`**: a cache *hit* now touches the
file, so the mtime means last wanted rather than first downloaded. Without it a family opened in every
document is evicted ahead of one glanced at once, purely for having been fetched earlier. **And `touch`
has to open the file for writing**, which is the trap and it fails silently: `File::set_modified` needs a
handle with write access, so `File::open` — the obvious spelling for a function that writes nothing —
returns an error `touch` discards and leaves every file wearing its download time, with no test of the
*rule* noticing. Checked by putting the bug back:
`touching_a_cached_face_moves_its_stamp_forward` fails with "the stamp did not move". `write(true)` alone
does not truncate, so nothing is written through the handle.

**The sweep runs once, at startup, and that is a kept limitation rather than an oversight.** A single
session that browses an enormous number of families can exceed the budget until the next launch. Sweeping
again mid-session is the case that has rows on screen and faces in flight, which is precisely what the
missing floor assumes cannot happen.

`the_font_cache_drops_its_stalest_files_and_stops_at_the_budget` pins the rule, and its fixture is built
so the sizes and the stamps **disagree** — which is what separates it from the plausible wrong version,
since a rule sorting on bytes deletes the 40 MB file and leaves the 200 MB one, confirmed by flipping the
sort key. It also asserts that being over budget is not a reason to empty the cache: two 200 MB files are
144 over and dropping one answers it. `the_sweep_deletes_the_stalest_faces_off_the_disk` covers the real
directory — sizes read, non-files skipped, files actually deleted — and its subdirectory arm is
**insurance rather than a live catch, and says so in its own doc**: deleting the `is_file` guard leaves it
green, because a directory's `len()` is zero and `remove_file` refuses one anyway.

*Keep.* The load-bearing detail is `touch`'s `write(true)`, which reads like a mistake in a function that
writes nothing and is the whole of what makes the mtime an LRU stamp. ~~What is **not** built is the other
half of the parked item — "Font cache — 180 MB · Clear" — and it is blocked on something that has nothing
to do with the cache: there is no preferences panel in the app at all (`panels/` is inspector, layers,
paint, picker and typography, and nothing greps as settings or preferences). It survives in the roadmap
against that blocker rather than against this.~~ **Built 2026-08-24 — D330**, and the blocker was named
correctly: what it took was a surface, not a cache change. `fonts::dir_bytes` and
`FontService::clear_cache` are fifteen lines between them over the same `read_dir` this sweep already
walked; the row lives in `settings.rs`.

**D238 — A lone line's chrome rule is lifted out to where a test can reach it, and it was quietly failing
open. *Resolved 2026-08-19.*** D99 built the suppression and stated its own gap: the rule lived in an
`OndinApp` method, `OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState` and cannot be built in a test, so nothing pinned
the single answer that takes away the box, the four side bands, the skew, the rotate ring and the size
badge at once. `canvas::lone_line(session) -> Option<(NodeId, Point)>` is that answer as a free function —
exactly one selected node, and it is a `Line` — handing back the far end with it. `line_ends` and
`selection_handles` both read it, so the two cannot drift. This is the pattern the roadmap's *Now · Text*
section already names: lift the decision into a free function or a plain type, pin that, and say plainly
which wiring is still only read.

**The lift found a small fail-open.** `selection_handles` used to refuse the box on
`self.line_ends(rect, ppp).is_some()` — the same question with a transform lookup in front of it — so a
line whose world transform did not resolve fell through to the *box* arm, where only the `?` on the next
lookup happened to stop it. The rule is about the kind alone, so it should not be able to fail open, and
it now asks about the kind alone.

`only_a_line_on_its_own_trades_its_box_for_endpoint_handles` gives each half its own arm and both were
checked against the plausible wrong version. Dropping the `[id]` pattern would take the union box away
from any multi-selection containing a line — the only thing giving the set a size — and dropping the kind
test takes the box away from everything. Both flips fail the test.

*Resolved for the rule, and since 2026-08-22 for most of the **drawing**.* This said the drawing was
eye-only and that `canvas::autopan` and `resize_tx` sat behind the same `OndinApp` seam; D303 removed
the seam and the other two are pinned — `autopan_tests` plus
`reaching_the_canvas_edge_scrolls_the_view_toward_the_pointer` and
`cancelling_a_drag_that_auto_scrolled_puts_the_view_back` for the autopan, and
`dragging_a_corner_of_a_multi_selection_scales_the_whole_box`, which calls `resize_tx` directly.
`headless_app_tests::a_lone_line_gets_no_selection_chrome_but_a_line_in_a_set_does` covers the chrome
`selection_handles` owns — the corner handles, the side bands, the skew and the rotate ring — in three
cases, and `a_lone_line_gets_no_size_badge_and_a_rect_does` covers the badge, which asks its own guard.
**The box outline is the one reader with nothing on it, and it is unobservable rather than unwritten** —
D266 has why. The load-bearing detail is that `selection_handles`
refuses on `lone_line` and not on `line_ends`: the two read as interchangeable and only one of them is
about the kind.

**D239 — Booleans are measured: three of the four cost nothing worth caching, and the measurement found a
live flo_curves panic. *Resolved for the cost; the panic was contained here and then **fixed upstream** in
flo_curves 0.8.1 — Keep the guard, whose meaning has changed. Amended 2026-08-31.*** The roadmap carried
"Performance is unmeasured" with its own instruction attached: measure before optimising, and the first
lever is caching per operand rather than per container. Both halves of that are now answered, and the
second one is answered by something other than a number — there is nothing to optimise, and there is
something much worse than a slow boolean.

Release profile, best of three, one whole `evaluate` over a ring of circles of radius 90 spaced round a
circle of radius 120, so every operand overlaps several of its neighbours (`boolean::tests::ring`).
Milliseconds:

| operands | Union | Subtract | Intersect | Exclude |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.01 |
| 5 | 0.08 | 0.03 | 0.01 | 0.26 |
| 10 | 0.21 | 0.09 | 0.03 | 2.06 |
| 20 | 0.60 | 0.21 | 0.07 | 19.9 |
| 40 | 1.94 | 0.41 | 0.16 | *(panics)* |
| 64 | 3.64 | 0.68 | 0.29 | 1111 |

**Three of the four are a non-problem, so the caching is a decided non-goal rather than a deferred
optimisation.** Union, Subtract and Intersect grow about linearly and are all still inside a frame's budget
at sixty-four operands, which is far past what anyone selects on a canvas. Caching per operand means a
cache keyed on every operand's geometry, invalidated by every edit of one, to save a millisecond nobody was
waiting on — and the entry that proposed it said to measure first, so the measurement is entitled to close
it. **A boolean of booleans costs nothing extra** either, which was the other open question: four unions of
five and then a union of those four results is 0.58 ms against 0.60 ms for the same twenty flat. Nesting
splits the work rather than multiplying it, so the shape of the tree is not the thing to look at.

**`Exclude` is the outlier and part of its cost is honest.** It genuinely produces far more geometry — 680
path elements at twenty operands where Union produces 60, and 6,784 at sixty-four. But the growth outruns
even that: twenty to sixty-four is 3.2× the operands and 10× the output for **56×** the time. Nothing is
proposed for it, because at the counts where it would hurt it is likelier to trip the panic below than to be
slow.

**The panic is the part that matters.** Some operand sets make flo_curves 0.8.0 panic with *"user-provided
comparison function does not correctly implement a total order"*, out of `GraphPath::exterior_paths`
(`graph_path/mod.rs:1051`), reached in the reproduction through `path_full_intersect`
(`full_intersect.rs:56`). It reproduces in debug and in release.

**The cause is exact and it is not a NaN.** That sort's comparator treats two points as equal in x when
they are within 0.01 and compares their y instead, and otherwise compares x. That is not transitive: three
points 0.008 apart in x give `a ≈ b`, `b ≈ c` and `a < c`. Rust's sort has detected inconsistent
comparators since 1.81 and panics rather than sorting to nonsense — so **the fault is older than the
panic**, and what changed is that it became loud instead of silently producing a wrong path.

**It is not `Exclude`'s alone**, and that is the detail an obvious fix would get wrong. `add.rs`, `sub.rs`,
`intersect.rs` and `full_intersect.rs` all call `exterior_paths`, so no operation is exempt and recomposing
`Exclude` (D91) would only make it rarer. What makes `Exclude` the one that shows is volume:
`path_full_intersect` calls `exterior_paths` three times per operation where the others call it once, and
its accumulator is an order of magnitude larger, so it has far more points to cluster. Sweeping the same
ring from 2 to 64 operands, `Union` never panicked and `Exclude` panicked at 40, 42, 44, 47, 49, 59, 60 and
63. **The gaps are the tell**: the real variable is the geometry, not the count, so no count that passes
rules anything out, and a much smaller selection with the wrong coincidence is not excluded.

The workspace sets no `panic = "abort"`, so it unwinds — and until 2026-08-19 that unwind went up the UI
thread and took the editor with it, document open.

**Of the three options this entry left open, the one taken is catching the unwind at the `evaluate` seam.**
The others were a patched fork of flo_curves, in which the comparator is made transitive by bucketing x and
comparing the bucket as an integer — small, but ours to carry upstream from then on — and living with it.
`evaluate` is now a guard around a private `fold_operands` holding its old body verbatim: `catch_unwind`
around the fold, `Ok(path) => path`, `Err(_) => None`.

**The seam is the reason it is one guard and not four.** Every call into flo_curves in the workspace —
`path_add`, `path_sub`, `path_intersect`, `path_full_intersect` — is inside `fold_operands`, including the
union `operand_of` runs over a group's contents, which reaches it through `evaluate` like everything else.
That is what "no operation is exempt" demanded and what a fix aimed at `Exclude` would not have given.

**`None` is not a new state.** It is what an intersection that came out empty already answers, and what a
boolean whose operands contribute nothing answers, so every caller handles it today. A boolean that trips the
defect draws nothing and undo brings the operands back. **The bug is not fixed and the shape is still wrong;
what changed is that a wrong shape is not a lost document.**

`AssertUnwindSafe` is argued rather than waved through: the arguments are borrowed read-only, every scrap of
state flo_curves builds is local to the call and is dropped by the unwind, and there is no shared mutable
state for a half-finished operation to leave torn.

**One `eprintln!`, once per process, behind an `AtomicBool`** — and both halves of that are load-bearing. The
default hook already prints on every unwind and a library must not replace it, since replacing it would
swallow the message of every *real* panic in the app; what this line adds is the one thing the hook's message
cannot carry, which is what the panic means and what was done about it. Once per process because the
renderer's preview path re-evaluates a boolean while an operand is being dragged, so an unguarded line would
be sixty a second.

**A panic inside a group operand is caught by that inner `evaluate` call, not by the outer one**, which is
worth stating rather than discovering: the group drops out of the boolean above it instead of failing the
whole thing — the same silent contributes-nothing a text operand already makes, and a wrong-looking shape
rather than none.

**It depends on unwinding.** Under `panic = "abort"` the guard is inert: `catch_unwind` never returns, the
process dies as before, and nothing in the code can detect the setting. The root `Cargo.toml` carries a note
beside its profiles saying not to set it without reading this entry, because **no test can fail if somebody
does** — that is the whole reason the note exists.

`boolean::tests::exclude_panics_on_forty_overlapping_circles` is gone and its `#[ignore]` with it;
`a_boolean_that_panics_comes_back_empty_rather_than_taking_the_process` asserts a panicking boolean comes
back `None`,
*and* that the guard is not eating ordinary answers on the way past — the same ring still unions to a real
shape. Flipped against the version somebody would actually write, the `catch_unwind` replaced by a plain
call, it fails. It takes the panic hook, silences it around its own call and restores it afterwards, so the
test's output is not a wall of backtrace and a missing hook does not hide the next failure in the run.

The numbers above are the only thing that expires if flo_curves is ever forked, patched or replaced; the
guard would outlive all three.

### Amended 2026-08-31 — fixed upstream, and the guard is kept anyway

**flo_curves 0.8.1 fixes it, and the fix is exactly the diagnosis above.** `exterior_paths` no longer sorts
through the epsilon comparator; it sorts on `f64::total_cmp` of x — a total order by construction — and then
walks the sorted array re-sorting *runs* of close-x points by y. The epsilon still exists and now segments
the array instead of living inside the comparison, which is the correct shape and not a workaround. Found by
re-running this roadmap's premise pass, where "has flo_curves released past 0.8.0" was one of two questions
the pass had recorded as unanswerable offline.

**Measured, not assumed.** On 0.8.1 every one of the eight counts this entry names — `Exclude` at 40, 42,
44, 47, 49, 59, 60 and 63 — returns a real path. So do NaN, infinite and 1e300 coordinates across three
operations, which is unsurprising once the sort is `total_cmp`, that being a total order over NaN too. The
bump was `cargo update -p flo_curves` alone: the requirement was already caret `"0.8.0"`, so only the lock
had pinned it.

**The guard, `failures`, the layers mark, the status message and both placeholders are all kept.** The
argument is this entry's own best finding turned around: *the variable was the geometry and not the count*,
so "nothing panics now" was never a claim a sweep could establish — only "none of the ones we tried". What
changes is what a caught unwind *means*. It was a workaround for a known defect; it is now a general refusal
to let an upstream panic take the document, and an unwind reaching it is **unknown and unreported**. The
stderr message says so in as many words, which is the one place a reader would otherwise be told the
opposite.

⚠️ **What the fix cost is the reproduction, and that is the part worth reading.** Six tests across three
crates — the two here, `resolve`'s mark and click-target pair, and the placeholder tests in the PNG and SVG
writers — all reached the abandoned state by evaluating the forty-circle ring, and on 0.8.1 not one of them
can. Three ways out were weighed: hunt a new panicking operand set (**declined** — proving a negative, and a
sweep of degenerate coordinates found nothing); retire the failure-marking feature (**declined** — the guard
is still right, so its consequences still need cover); or inject the panic. The third was taken, as
`boolean::poison_next`, a `#[doc(hidden)] pub` counter that makes the next *n* `evaluate` calls on the thread
unwind inside the guard. `pub` because four of the six callers are integration tests in other crates, which
cannot see a `cfg(test)` item — and CLAUDE.md's warning applies exactly here: `dead_code` will never report
it if the last caller goes, so its call count is a thing to grep rather than a thing a gate defends.

**The tests now make a strictly weaker claim, and they say so.** They assert the guard turns an unwind into
`None` and that every consequence downstream of that still lands on the right node; they no longer assert
that flo_curves can produce one. The old fixture asserted both at once, which is precisely why this entry
kept it rather than deleting it once the guard went in — so the loss is real and is recorded rather than
papered over. If a genuine panicking set is ever found again it belongs back in that first test in place of
the injection.

**One new test guards the injection itself**: `the_poison_is_spent_by_the_call_it_arms`. The arming is a
decrementing counter rather than a flag, and an off-by-one would be invisible — every test that arms it
asserts on the call *after* arming, so a poison outliving its call would surface as an unrelated test failing
somewhere downstream. Flipped against the version somebody would actually write — `p.set(n)` instead of
`p.set(n.saturating_sub(1))`, a poison that never spends — it fails, **and so does the control assertion in
`a_boolean_that_panics_comes_back_empty_rather_than_taking_the_process`**, which was not the predicted site:
"the same ring, unpoisoned, unions to a real shape" catches a leaking poison on its own. *Two assertions in
two tests, and only one of them was designed to.*

**The cost table above was re-measured the same day, and the upgrade costs nothing.** Every cell that existed
on 0.8.0 reproduces within noise — Union at 64 was 3.64 ms and is 3.40, `Exclude` at 20 was 19.9 and is
18.81 — so the comparator fix is not a trade. **`Exclude` at 40, the cell that used to panic, is 197.58 ms**
for 2,640 path elements, which lands exactly on the curve its neighbours describe (18.81 → 197.58 →
1087.24). *The row that could not be measured held no surprise*, and that is worth recording so the next
reader does not re-run it expecting one: the panic was never where the cost went.

⚠️ **The measurement did find something, and it is not about 40.** `Exclude` leaves a 60 Hz frame budget at
about **nineteen operands** — 18 is 13.34 ms, 20 is 18.81 — and the preview path re-evaluates a boolean on
*every frame of a drag*. So an `Exclude` of twenty circles is already dropping frames while an operand is
being moved, and one of forty spends a fifth of a second per frame; Union at the same counts is under 2 ms.
**This narrows the entry's own headline.** "Three of the four cost nothing worth caching" stands and was
always about those three; what this adds is that the fourth has a specific, low, *reachable* threshold rather
than a merely alarming number at 64, and that a drag is the case that meets it.

### Amended again the same day — the per-operand cache is built, and it is not what it sounds like

**This entry named per-operand caching as "the first lever" and then made it a decided non-goal on the
grounds that there was nothing measurable to win. Both halves were wrong, in opposite directions**, and the
correction is worth more than the cache is.

⚠️ **The obvious per-operand cache is *unsound*, and the measurement that says so is the most important
thing here.** During a drag one operand moves and the rest are static, so the fast design is to fold the
static ones once and combine the moving one **last** — a left fold in which "only the first operand is
order-sensitive, Subtract's tail being a union and the other three commuting", which is what both this
module and `RenderOverrides::operand_children` said in as many words. That would take a twenty-circle
`Exclude` drag from 18.81 ms to 2.57. **The commuting is a property of the mathematics and not of this
implementation.** Moving one operand of a twenty-circle `Exclude` to the end of the fold changes the result
by **2,482 area units of 85,850 — about 3% — at an unchanged element count**, and the error grows with the
count (0.009 at five operands, 1,654 at twelve). `Union` and `Subtract` move by float noise; `Exclude` does
not. A preview folding in a different order from the commit would draw a visibly different shape and jump on
release, which is the exact class of bug the preview layer exists to prevent.

**Nothing caught this because the test that looks like it would compares areas.**
`exclude_gives_the_same_answer_in_any_operand_order` uses **three** operands and a tolerance of 1.0; at
twelve the reordering error is three orders of magnitude past that tolerance. *A test whose fixture is too
small to reach the regime it certifies is worse than no test, because it is quoted as evidence* — this one
was, twice, by two modules.

**It had already caused a live defect.** `operand_children` appended a ghost operand rather than inserting
it at the index its `InsertSubtree` names, excused by exactly that commuting claim, with its own doc noting
that the test which would catch it did not exist. So an Alt-drag of a copy into a large `Exclude` previewed
a shape about 3% off the one it committed. Fixed the same day, with the differential test that doc asked
for: `a_ghost_operand_folds_in_the_slot_its_insert_names`, twelve operands and index 1, both load-bearing.

**What was built instead is an order-preserving prefix cache** (`boolean::fold_cached`): the fold's own
intermediate accumulators, per node, reused up to the first operand that differs from last time. It does not
reorder anything, so its answer is bit-identical; it is keyed on the operand paths themselves, so it has no
invalidation to get wrong; and it engages only at eight operands or more, so the two-operand boolean that is
99% of them stores nothing.

⚠️ **What it buys is narrow and an average is the wrong way to state it.** Cached against uncached, one drag
frame of `Exclude`: at twenty operands, dragging the **last** is 3.54 ms against 19.49 — over the frame
budget to well under it, the case this was built for — while dragging the **middle** is 16.53 against 18.92
and dragging the **first** is 19.60 against 19.51, which is to say nothing at all. At forty, the last operand
is 30.99 against 199.79. **Half the steps is nowhere near half the time**: the accumulator is largest at the
end, so the late steps carry most of the cost. An earlier note in the module doc said "about 22% on average",
which is arithmetically defensible and practically misleading — there is no typical case near 22%.

**So the non-goal is reversed on evidence and the headline claim is not.** There is something to win, it is
real, and it is confined to one gesture on one operation on one operand. The frame-budget problem at
nineteen operands is *not* solved for a drag of anything but the last operand or two, and no sound cache
solves it, because the reordering that would is the thing this entry now records as unsafe.

### Amended a third time — going after `Exclude`'s *cost* found that its *answer* is wrong

**The instruction was to attack `Exclude`'s cost directly, and the first honest measurement of it found
something that makes the cost the second problem.** ⚠️ **`Exclude` returns a materially wrong shape for some
operand geometries — up to 35% wrong — and does it silently.**

**Nothing had ever checked it against anything but itself.** Every test in `boolean.rs` compares one boolean
against another boolean, or against an area derived from the same arithmetic; the one that reads like an
independent check compares *permutations of the same call*. A fold wrong the same way every time was
therefore indistinguishable from a correct one, and had been since booleans landed. The referee this module
had never had is arithmetic-free: **the symmetric difference is exactly the set of points covered by an odd
number of operands**, so a grid sampler answers it with no path arithmetic at all. Measured on the same ring
the cost table uses, 4000² grid, areas:

| operands | true | `Exclude` says | error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 64,182.9 | 64,196.2 | 13 |
| 11 | 76,259.2 | 76,280.0 | 21 |
| 12 | 81,424.4 | 85,580.0 | **4,156** |
| 13 | 77,888.4 | 92,098.5 | **14,210** |
| 14 | 69,810.3 | 94,564.1 | **24,754 — 35%** |
| 15–18 | — | — | under 20 |
| 19 | 77,696.5 | 79,635.8 | **1,939** |
| 20 | 76,745.1 | 85,874.2 | **9,129** |

*(Those are the numbers as found. The spatial cull below halves each of them and is what ships; the module's
own table carries both columns.)*

**The pattern is this entry's own signature, read back to it.** Not monotonic in the count, accurate either
side of a bad run — *the variable is the geometry and not the number of operands*, which is the sentence
D239 already carries about the panic that started it. It is presumably the same fragility in
`path_full_intersect`, and the difference is the one that matters: **that fault was loud and this one is
silent.** The boolean draws, `failures` does not move, the layers row is unmarked, and the shape is simply
wrong. Every mechanism D298 built to tell the user about an abandoned boolean is blind to this, because
nothing was abandoned.

`boolean::tests::exclude_is_wrong_for_some_operand_geometries` is a **characterisation** test and not an
approval: the accurate counts guard against regression, and the inaccurate ones are pinned as they stand so
that a fix — or a further slide — is visible. It asserts the bad rows are *still bad*, which is the assertion
somebody will one day be pleased to see fail. The truth values are recorded constants with
`the_recorded_truth_matches_a_fresh_sampling` (`#[ignore]`d, 23 seconds in debug) as the instrument that
regenerates them, because a table nobody can regenerate is a table nobody can trust.

**A spatial cull was built, put to the maintainer because it changes rendered geometry, and merged.** A
subpath of the accumulator whose bounding box cannot meet the incoming operand's cannot interact with it, so
it is passed through untouched and only the rest handed to the arithmetic — exact set algebra, per operation,
with the one subtlety that a hole must travel with its outline (the accumulator is read even-odd, so an inner
subpath left behind would stop punching its hole). The decision was put rather than taken because this entry
had already rejected a *reorder* for moving `Exclude`'s answer, and consistency demanded the same question be
asked of a cull that moves it too.

**What it is worth, measured with it live:** `Exclude` 18.81 ms → **6.00** at twenty operands, 197.58 →
**49.06** at forty, 1087 → **258** at sixty-four. Nothing for the other three, which is exactly where the
cost never was. ⚠️ **The 60 Hz frame budget now holds to about twenty-nine operands, up from nineteen** — 28
is 16.01 ms and 30 is 22.37. A real gain and not a cure: forty operands is still twenty frames a second.

**And it halves the error in every failing row of the table above**, which is what made shipping a change to
the answer defensible rather than merely tempting: 12 operands 4,156 → 837, 13 14,210 → 7,104, 14 24,754 →
12,374, 19 1,939 → 1,133, 20 9,129 → 5,808. The characterisation test's bounds are set against the *culled*
numbers, so **turning the cull off now reddens it** — flipped and confirmed, failing at n=12 with 0.0510
against a bound of 0.015.

⚠️ **It preserves the shape and not the bytes, which the first version of its test got wrong.** That test
asserted `elements()` equality and failed on the `apart` fixture: a subpath the arithmetic never touches is
emitted as `to_flo` built it, while the uncalled fold re-traverses it through flo's graph and emits the same
ring **rotated to a different starting vertex** — same points, same order, same direction, different first
element. So the assertion is subpath count, element count and area, and the consequence worth recording is
that **an exported SVG's `d` attribute can differ for a boolean whose operands are disjoint**. The SVG and
JSON goldens were unaffected; nothing about the drawn result changes.

**The actual fix is probably neither.** XOR *is* even-odd fill: the symmetric difference of `n` shapes is the
concatenation of their outlines read even-odd, which is exact, free, and needs no boolean arithmetic
whatsoever. What stands in the way is that this model has no per-node fill rule — `from_flo`'s whole job is
converting flo's even-odd result into the non-zero winding the renderer, the SVG writer and the raster path
all assume. A fill rule would make `Exclude` exact and instant and is a change to the model, the three
writers and the schema. **That is the thing to cost next**, and it is a feature rather than a fix.

### Amended a fourth time — the fill rule is built, and `Exclude` is exact

**Built 2026-08-31 as `Node::fill_rule`, and it does what the paragraph above predicted**: `Exclude` now does
no path arithmetic at all. Its outline is its operands concatenated, the node reads even-odd, and against the
odd-coverage referee it agrees at **every sampled point at every count** — where the fold was out by up to
17.7% of the area.

**The premise was measured before the feature was costed**, which is the order this file's own rule asks for:
sampling winding *parity* over the concatenated operands matched the referee to within its own grid noise at
all eleven counts, while the fold was out by thousands. Nothing was built on the strength of the argument
alone.

**Where it lives, and why not on the paint.** SVG puts `fill-rule` on the fill; this puts it on the **node**,
because it is a property of the *geometry* rather than of one brush: the hit test asks it, a mask asks it
when the node clips, and a node with no fill at all still has an inside. A per-fill rule would let two fills
of one shape disagree about what the shape is, which is not a question anyone has.

⚠️ **The rule for a boolean is *derived*, not stored, and that is the whole migration story.** `Node::fill_rule`
answers `EvenOdd` for a `Boolean { op: Exclude }` whatever the field holds. So every `.ondin` written before
this existed — none of which carries the key — is correct without being touched, and **no bytes move**. Had
it been stored, `build::boolean` would have needed to write it, `set_boolean_op` would have needed to keep it
in step through undo, every directly-constructed fixture would have had to remember it, and every existing
file with an exclusion in it would have drawn a *union* until migrated. The `io` test asserts the absence
directly: an `Exclude` writes no `fill_rule` key. The DTO reads the **stored field** rather than the
accessor for the same reason — writing the derived answer would have rewritten every file with an exclusion
in it on the first save.

**Its shape as an authored feature**: `Operation::SetFillRule` with its inverse, an additive `NodeDto` field
skipped at `NonZero` (`mask_mode`'s discipline exactly), and an *Even-odd fill* row on the layer menu. The
row is offered on a `Path` **alone** — a rect, ellipse, star or polygon is a single non-crossing outline
where the two rules agree and a control would visibly do nothing; a boolean's rule is its operation's, so a
row appearing to toggle it would offer to make the shape wrong; and a multi-selection has no single answer
for the check mark. The preview layer refuses `SetFillRule` as it refuses `SetMaskMode` — a click, not a
drag — with the note that the fix is a `NodeOverride` field if anything ever scrubs it.

**Three things the tests caught that reading would not have.**

- **`fold_cached` implements the fold a second time**, so short-circuiting `Exclude` in `fold_operands` alone
  left `evaluate` concatenating and `evaluate_node` still folding — *the preview and the commit taking
  different answers*. Caught on the first run by
  `the_cache_returns_exactly_what_the_uncached_fold_returns`, which exists for exactly that class.
- **kurbo's `area()` and `contains()` are both winding**, so four tests were measuring an even-odd path with
  a non-zero instrument and reporting the union. Two were rewritten to assert *points* — exact, cheap, and a
  stronger claim than an area, since two shapes can share an area and differ — and the ring test now compares
  the path's even-odd reading against circle coverage at 400 sample points rather than by area at all.
- ⚠️ **The SVG flip did not bite.** With the rule plumbed and tested through the model, the canvas, the raster
  path and the hit test, deleting the writer's `fill-rule="evenodd"` left the entire suite green — so an
  exported exclusion would have filled solid in any browser, the canvas and the file showing **different
  pictures**, which is the one divergence §3 exists to prevent. `an_exclusion_exports_the_even_odd_rule`
  closes it and was confirmed to fail without the line. *A flip that does not bite is a finding about the
  tests, and this is the clearest instance this project has had.*

**What it retires.** The spatial cull and the prefix cache were both built to make `Exclude`'s fold cheaper,
and there is no longer a fold: `Exclude` short-circuits before either. They still serve the other three
operations, which never needed them — that is a simplification available to whoever wants it, and the reason
to take it is that two mechanisms now earn nothing.

**The cache is testable only through a counter.** `boolean::fold_steps` counts pairwise combinations, because
a prefix cache that never hits returns exactly the right answer — every correctness assertion passes against
a no-op. `the_cache_reuses_the_prefix_that_did_not_change` asserts nine steps cold, one after moving the last
operand and nine after moving the first. ⚠️ **Its second flip's predicted site was wrong and the correction
is the lesson**: dropping the check that the operands still match was predicted to fail the *first*-operand
assertion and instead fails the *last*-operand one with **0** steps rather than 9 — a wrong cache and an
inert one fail at the same assertion from opposite sides. Worse, `the_cache_returns_exactly_what_the_uncached_fold_returns`
was **green under that flip** until it was rewritten, because its cold and warm calls used the same operands,
so handing back the stored fold was handing back the right answer. *A cache's correctness is not testable
without changing the operands between the two calls*, which is the drag it exists for and was the one
sequence the first draft omitted.

⚠️ **This entry's "`None` is not a new state" is the sentence D298 had to undo.** It is true, and being
true is exactly what made the failure silent — see there.

### Amended a fifth time — the carry `flatten` needed, which the costing had booked as free

**A day after the rule landed, flattening an `Exclude` still drew its union.** `build::replace_with_path` —
the one body *Flatten*, *Outline shape* and *Convert to path* share — carries name, transform, paint,
opacity, visibility, pivot, mask and effects, and did not carry the fill rule. So the operation that throws
the `Boolean` away also threw away the *derivation*: the identical concatenated subpaths, sitting in a
`Path` under the default `NonZero`, fill solid. Every hole the exclusion cut filled in, on a one-click
**destructive** command, with all six gates green.

**The fix is one carry and it is the *effective* rule.** `node.fill_rule()` rather than `node.fill_rule`,
skipped at the default so no document grows an operation for the rule it already meant — which is the same
discipline as the pivot and the effects beside it. Reading the accessor is what makes one line serve two
cases: the rule a `Boolean` derives, and the rule a user stored on a `Path`.

**The second case is the one a user can reach.** *Even-odd fill* is offered on a single `Path` and nothing
else, so a compound path with a hole in it is the only even-odd shape the app can author — and *Outline
shape* is offered on it the moment one corner is rounded. It was losing the hole the same way, which makes
this a defect in two verbs rather than a wrinkle in `Exclude`.

**Two tests, and the pair is deliberate.** `flattening_an_exclude_carries_the_even_odd_rule_its_holes_depend_on`
and `outlining_a_path_keeps_the_fill_rule_the_user_set_on_it` (`ondin-core/tests/build.rs`) both sample each
path under **the rule its own node reports**, so the assertion is the picture and not the field — the
geometry survives either way, which is exactly why nothing caught this. ⚠️ **Only the first discriminates
the two plausible implementations**: carrying the stored *field* instead of the accessor fails it with the
identical `[true, true, true]` — an `Exclude`'s stored field is the untouched default — while the outline
test stays green, since for a `Path` the two values are the same. Both were confirmed red before the fix,
and each fails on its band assertion rather than its field one.

⚠️ **Where the costing went wrong, and it is not where a costing usually does.** Design B was priced as
*fixing* `flatten` — "because the converted `Path` can carry the rule". The sentence is true and describes
a capability; the code implemented none of it. *A costing's estimates are unfalsifiable until the work is
done, but its **predictions** are checkable the moment it is* — and this one was never re-read against the
function it named. The roadmap's own retrospective had already listed two costs the estimate missed; this
is a third of a different kind, a claim rather than an omission.

### Amended a sixth time — the cull and the cache are removed, on the same day they were built

**Both existed to make `Exclude`'s fold cheaper, and the fill rule deleted the fold.** An `Exclude` is
its operands concatenated now; `fold_operands` short-circuits before either mechanism can run. What was
left was a spatial cull and a per-node prefix cache serving `Union`, `Subtract` and `Intersect` — three
operations that were never the problem, all three inside a frame's budget at sixty-four operands
without help — and, worse, a **third implementation of the fold**: `fold_cached` folded a second time,
so `evaluate` and `evaluate_node` had to be kept agreeing by hand and had already diverged once (the
first bullet of the amendment above). **642 lines out**, and the module's purity claim comes back with
them.

**The retiring sentence was checked rather than repeated.** "They still serve the other three
operations" was written when the fold still existed and reads like a reason to keep them; measured
after removal, three runs, release, the same ring:

| operands | Union | Subtract | Intersect | Exclude |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | 0.58 | 0.19 | 0.06 | 0.00 |
| 40 | 1.63 | 0.39 | 0.14 | 0.00 |
| 64 | 3.32 | 0.61 | 0.24 | 0.00 |

⚠️ **The cull moved the other three by about a tenth of a millisecond, in *both* directions.**
`Subtract` at sixty-four went 0.48 → 0.61 without it, and `Union` went 3.47 → **3.32** — the cull was
costing more in bookkeeping than it saved on the operation it helped least, which no earlier
measurement could have said, because the cull was only ever measured against the operation it was
built for. *A mechanism justified by one case is not measured on the others until someone takes it
away.* Neither number is material; the argument for the removal is the third fold, not the
microsecond.

**What the tests lost, and it is worth naming.** Five went with the code —
`the_cache_returns_exactly_what_the_uncached_fold_returns`, `the_cache_reuses_the_prefix_that_did_not_change`,
`a_small_boolean_is_not_cached_at_all`, `culling_the_fold_changes_no_geometry` and the `fold_both`
harness — and with them the flip-check recorded above about a wrong cache and an inert one failing at
the same assertion. That finding is kept *here* precisely because its test is gone: it is about how to
test a cache, not about this one.

**Two consequences to know.** The cull's caveat that a passed-through subpath keeps its own start
point is spent — a disjoint boolean's exported SVG `d` goes back to what the plain fold emits, and the
goldens were unaffected in both directions. And `boolean::clear_cache` and `boolean::fold_steps` are
gone from core's API; neither had a caller outside the module's own tests.

**D298 — A boolean that draws nothing because the arithmetic gave up now says so. *Built and tested both
ways, both halves flip-checked; the row and the status line read.*** D239 caught the unwind and stopped
there, and the entry's own reasoning is what left the gap: `None` was chosen *because* every caller
already handles it. Handled means unremarkable — the scene walk and both exporters get an empty path and
draw nothing, which is what they do for a boolean that is legitimately empty. So a crash became a wrong
result with no signal anywhere except one `eprintln!` on a stderr nobody reads, and `Exclude` is the
likeliest door but no operation is exempt.

**The distinction the surface rests on is not "did it come out empty".** An intersection of two shapes
that do not overlap is `None`, and drawing nothing for it is *correct*. Marking that would call correct
work broken, which is worse than saying nothing — so the signal cannot be derived from the result at all,
and `boolean_path`'s `None` is not enough to build on.

**`boolean::failures()`: a thread-local count, read either side of a call.** No signature changes and no
caller is obliged to care, which matters because `evaluate` has callers in four crates. `Resolved`
brackets each `evaluate_node` and records the id in a `failed` set beside the outline cache;
`Resolved::boolean_failed` is what everything else asks.

**A count and not a flag, and that is the load-bearing detail.** A group operand is unioned by an *inner*
`evaluate` that catches its own unwind, so the outer call never sees a panic — a flag set by the inner
one would be cleared by the outer one on its way out. A number that only goes up composes: every bracket
asks whether it moved across its own span, and none can tread on another's answer. It also makes the
right attribution fall out for free, since what the user needs to know is *this boolean draws nothing*, at
whatever depth it happened. Thread-local for the matching reason: the renderer previews booleans off the
edit path.

**Two surfaces, one durable and one transient, and neither is a new visual.** The layers row tints its
kind glyph `theme::color::WARN` — the same mark, in the same slot, that §5.5a gives a layer whose picture
cannot be drawn, because it is the same fact about a layer: it is there and what it draws is not what it
says it is. One `if`, no new colour; a second warning vocabulary for a second cause would be two things to
learn about one symptom. And `commit_inner` — the one door every edit goes through — reads the counter
across its `Resolved::update` and calls `session.fail`.

**What the status line does *not* claim.** `Status` holds one message, so a caller that reports on its own
edit afterwards wins the slot, and undo/redo keep their own "Undo" rather than re-announcing a boolean
they merely arrived back at. Opening a file with a broken boolean already in it says nothing either, for
the same reason: `app::open` sets "Opened …" after `adopt_document`. All three are why the durable half is
the row and not the line, and the line is worth having anyway because it fires at the one moment the user
can connect it to something they did.

**Tested at both levels and in both directions, because one direction is vacuous.**
`boolean::tests::the_counter_moves_for_an_abandoned_boolean_and_not_for_an_empty_one` puts two circles 500
apart through `Intersect` and the forty-circle ring through `Exclude`: both answer `None`, and only the
second may move the counter.
`resolve::a_boolean_the_arithmetic_gave_up_on_is_marked_and_an_empty_one_is_not` is the same pair built
out of real `Ellipse` nodes, which is the part worth having — it proves the ring still trips the defect
through `operand_of`'s path construction rather than through a hand-built `kurbo::Circle`, and that the
mark lands on the boolean rather than on an operand. Flipped against the version somebody would actually
write — `failed` set from `result.is_none()`, since `None` is where the guard already lives — the disjoint
case fails in both tests: *"an empty result is an answer, not a failure"*.

**D299 — The canvas half: a failed boolean draws the missing-picture placeholder. *Built and tested on
real pixels and in markup; both gates flip-checked.*** D298 left this named and undone — the row and the
status line were the two surfaces, and the canvas, which is where the user is actually looking, still
showed a clean blank. Asked for directly.

**No new drawing, which is the whole of the design decision.** It is `image::missing_placeholder`, the
same grey ground, rim and cross §5.5a gives a picture that cannot be drawn, because it is the same fact
about a layer: it is there, and what it draws is not what it says it is. The layers row already made that
call with the same warning colour (D298), and a second placeholder vocabulary for a second cause would be
two things to learn about one symptom. What it costs is that the two causes are not distinguishable at a
glance — accepted, because the row, the status line and the inspector all name the layer, and the cause is
one click away.

**Over the operands' union, because that is the only extent the node has left.** Its own outline is what
failed, and unioning the operands to get a better shape means running the arithmetic that just gave up.
`query::boolean_placeholder` is that box — `local_box`'s existing child-union fallback with the failure
test in front of it — and it is asked by the scene walk, the hit test, `Resolved`'s own bounds and the SVG
writer, so the drawing, the click target and the box the canvas culls against are one rectangle by
construction rather than by agreement.

⚠️ **A failed boolean had no world bounds at all, and that was three bugs wearing one coat.**
`recompute_bounds` measured a boolean from its cached outline and answered `None` when there was none —
so it was absent from the R-tree and **unclickable on canvas**, had nothing for *zoom to selection* to
measure, and would have given the walk's own cull nothing to test the new drawing against. Ink you can
see and cannot select is worse than the blank it replaced, so the box had to come first and the drawing
second. `hit_test` needed its own arm for the same reason: it tests a boolean against `boolean_path`, and
a placeholder is not one.

**Only when it *failed*, at all four sites.** Giving every pathless boolean a box would put an invisible
click target — and, worse, a grey slab — over whatever sits behind a boolean whose operands correctly
cancel out. That is the exact bug this is meant to be the opposite of, and it is what the flip check
below produces.

**Not during a gesture, and the gate is `ov.boolean_path(id).is_none()` rather than a new flag.** A
preview that is re-evaluating a boolean always leaves an entry — the new outline, or an empty path when
the result vanished mid-drag — so "no entry" is exactly "no preview owns this node". Without the gate a
drag would paint the placeholder over the *last committed* operand positions while the operands are under
the pointer: a box lagging behind the thing it describes. Failing mid-gesture therefore looks the way it
always has, until the release that commits it — which is also the moment the user goes looking for the
shape. A **ghost** gets `placeholder: None` for the neighbouring reason: it has no id in the document to
ask about, and a copy being dragged is not the place to report a defect in the original.

**Tested where it is drawn rather than where it is decided.**
`png::a_boolean_the_arithmetic_gave_up_on_paints_the_placeholder` is the important one: `--png` shares
`scene.rs`'s walk with the GPU canvas, so it is the closest a test gets to what the user sees. **The ring
carries no fills and no strokes at all**, which is what makes it say something — a boolean with no paint
draws nothing however well its arithmetic went, so ink at all can only have come from the placeholder
branch. It samples world (100, 200), fifty units clear of *both* diagonals; the first draft sampled the
box's centre, measured the cross, and reported the ink colour as a missing ground.
`svg::a_boolean_the_arithmetic_gave_up_on_exports_as_the_placeholder` is the same claim in markup, where
the writer is a second implementation rather than the same one, and it counts **two** stroked paths in
the placeholder's ink rather than matching coordinates — the box comes off flattened ellipses and pinning
its digits would make it a test of kurbo's tolerance.
`resolve::a_failed_boolean_has_a_box_and_a_click_target_and_an_empty_one_has_neither` holds the bounds and
the hit test.

Every one of them asserts `boolean_failed` on its fixture **before** asserting anything about the output,
because a ring that quietly stopped tripping the upstream defect would leave all three green and about
nothing.

**Flipped against gating on "this boolean has no outline" instead of on `failed`** — the version somebody
would write, since that is the condition the drawing is really *for*. The disjoint-intersection control
fails in the PNG test (`left: 255, right: 0` — a placeholder over an empty intersection), and so does the
pre-existing `export::boolean::a_boolean_with_no_result_exports_nothing`, which is a better witness than
any of mine because nobody wrote it with this in mind.

**Still not done: the inspector says nothing**, and neither does `ondin export`'s exit code. Named here so
the next reader does not have to rediscover that the list was three surfaces and is now four.

**D300 — `Ctrl+V` is position-free on purpose, and paste-at-pointer is a non-goal. *Decided by the
maintainer 2026-08-22; the row struck, two doc comments corrected, no behaviour changed.*** The roadmap
carried this as an open decision with three sub-decisions attached, on the grounds that two of our own
documents disagreed: `shortcuts.md` §7 wanted `Ctrl+V` to paste at the pointer because Figma does, and
`paste_at`'s doc comment gave the fixed 20×20 offset as intended. Figma is this project's default for
interaction semantics, so it was a real disagreement rather than a stale line.

**Decided against, on the merits and not on cost.** A `Ctrl+V` that lands where the mouse happens to be
resting is *less* predictable than a fixed step — the pointer is wherever it was left, not where the user
is looking — and the pointer-aimed paste already exists one right-click away as *Paste here*. Nothing was
blocking it: it is one dispatch arm, `paste_at` already takes a world point and already covers all three
payloads in the chord's own order, and `canvas::drop_point` proves the pointer→world conversion off a
bare `&Context`. **Cheap and unblocked is not a reason to build something**, which is worth stating
because the entry that carried this had established both and read as momentum.

**Two of the three sub-decisions were not open.** *What the chord does off-canvas* is already written
twice: `Item::PasteHere`'s `None` arm falls through to `Action::Paste`, and `drop_point` filters on
`canvas_rect.contains` precisely to produce that `None` — so a pointer arm would have inherited an answer
rather than needed one. And *whether Paste here becomes redundant* was moot once the chord was left
alone. Only the third — reversing the rule in the two places that state it — was real, and it reversed the
other way.

⚠️ **The behaviour is right and the reason given for it was false**, which is the finding worth keeping.
`paste_at` and `menu.rs` both said "a key has no position to paste at". A key press arrives on a frame
like any other event and its pointer position is readable there; `drop_point` does exactly that from
`app.rs` with nothing but a context. Both comments now say the true thing — the chord is position-free by
*choice* — and cite the rule `image_drop_target` already stated from the other side: "pressing the paste
keys with a shape selected *is* the act of aim, where a drag is aimed by the pointer." **A justification
that is false protects a decision only until somebody checks it**, which is what happened here, and is why
the correction matters more than the row.

**And a second contradiction, found while checking the first and unrelated to the decision.** `paste`'s
doc comment described the picture asymmetry as open — "the menu's *Paste here* has no image arm … making
it symmetric means giving `paste_image` a point to place at, which it does not take; it is small, and it
is not this change" — and it *was* that change, under D224. `paste_image` takes an `Option<Point>`,
`paste_at` asks it first, and `paste_at`'s own comment recorded the fix the whole time. **Two doc comments
in one file disagreeing about one fact, with every gate green**, which is precisely the class D296's
`cargo doc` gate cannot reach: both names resolve, and only the prose is wrong.

**Three stale lines in `shortcuts.md` went with it**, all of the same kind — a deferral outliving its
members. The file header still said "what is still unbuilt is §7 in its entirety" while §7's own
heading said "nothing here is deferred any longer"; the ledger's *Still to build* list still named
`PasteInPlace`, `CopyProperties` and `PasteProperties`, built two days earlier under D248 and D257;
and the ledger's "not keymap work" bullet still described the whole of §7 as a group deferral. *A
section that is closed reads as open work for exactly as long as the sentence that deferred it
survives.*

**D301 — Every committed edit deep-copied every photograph in the document. *Fixed; measured both
sides, tested on allocation identity and flip-checked.*** `Document::apply` clones the whole document
to get a working copy it can fail out of — that is how atomicity is bought (§5.7) — and
`ImageSource::Embedded` was a bare `Vec<u8>`, so the clone was a memcpy of the entire image table.
Undo and redo go through the same `apply`, so they paid it too.

**Measured before touching it, because the roadmap entry that carried this said to and had not.**
Release, best of twenty, one `SetTransform` on a rect:

| photos | MB in the table | ms per commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0.000 |
| 1 | 2 | 0.332 |
| 5 | 10 | 1.712 |
| 10 | 20 | 3.496 |
| 10 | 60 | 10.166 |
| 30 | 60 | 10.780 |

**The cost is the byte count and not the entry count** — thirty 2 MB photos and ten 6 MB ones land
within 6% of each other — which is what makes it unbounded in the direction that matters: a document
does not have to be complicated to be slow, only to contain photographs. Roughly 0.17 ms per MB. **A
held arrow key commits per repeat**, so this was a stutter with no visible cause, and the same
per-commit cost sat behind every undo. After the change every row reads 0.001 ms.

**`Arc<[u8]>`, which is the surgical fix and not the staged-diff rewrite it was filed beside.** The
entry predicted that correctly. *What it got wrong was the reason*: it said the image table is
"append-only **by design**", and it is not — `RemoveImage` exists so that a purge can be undone, which
is D179's own requirement. What actually makes the sharing safe is that the bytes are **immutable**:
nothing anywhere mutates an embedded blob in place, because a *Replace…* writes a new entry under a new
content hash. That is a weaker claim and a more durable one, and it is the one now written on the
variant — no caller needs `Arc::make_mut`, so the sharing can never be observed.

**Two unused serde derives fell out, and finding them was an accident.** `Arc<[u8]>` has no
`Serialize` without serde's `rc` feature, so the derive on `ImageSource` failed to compile — and
removing it, and `ImageEntry`'s, broke **nothing**. The save format goes through `io::schema`'s DTOs,
which convert by hand; the derives had never had a caller. That is precisely the trap CLAUDE.md's
clippy note names — a `pub` item in a library keeps its trait impls however many users it has lost —
and it is why the alternative fix, enabling serde's `rc` feature workspace-wide, would have been the
worse one: it would have kept two dead impls alive and added an Rc/Arc serialization footgun to every
crate to do it.

⚠️ **The control in that test was itself wrong for a day**, and D302 is what found it — see there.

**Tested on identity, not on time.** `cloning_a_document_shares_its_image_bytes_rather_than_copying_them`
asserts that the bytes reachable from a clone are the *same allocation*, and again through `apply`
itself, which is where the clone actually happens. A stopwatch would be a flaky test of this machine;
the sharing is the fact and the milliseconds are the symptom. **The control is not a formality**:
`<[u8]>::as_ptr` on an empty slice answers a dangling constant, so two empty slices compare equal and
the whole test would hold against a deep copy — it asserts the fixture is non-empty and that a real
copy of the same bytes lands at a different address. Flipped by putting `Vec<u8>` back: *left:
0x2af0a7297d0, right: 0x2af0a7298e0*.

**D302 — The clippy gate had never linted a single test. *Done; the gate is green and `CLAUDE.md`
now matches `rust-verify`.*** Asked for after D301, where the observation was left at the end of a
report: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` reported four warnings the documented gate did not.
The cause is that a bare `cargo clippy --workspace` builds **lib and bin targets only** — so every
`#[cfg(test)]` module in the workspace, which is where most of this project's assertions live, and
every file under `tests/`, had gone unlinted since the gate was written.

⚠️ **One of the five was a test written the day before, and it was wrong rather than untidy.**
D301's control assertion read `original.to_vec().as_ptr()`, which drops the `Vec` at the end of the
statement and compares a **dangling** pointer — an address the allocator is free to hand straight
back. `dangling_pointers_from_temporaries` is a *rustc* lint, not a clippy one, and warn-by-default;
it had been printing into `cargo test`'s output the whole time, where it was scrolled past. So the
gate's real contribution here is not the lint but the **distillation**: a warning nobody reads is a
warning nobody has. The control now binds the copy to a name. *A test whose control can pass for the
wrong reason is worse than no control, because it reads as rigour.*

**The other four are `clippy::mixed_attributes_style`** in `canvas.rs` — four test modules written as
a `///` summary line above `#[cfg(test)] mod x { //! detail }`. Both texts are wanted, so the summary
moved *inside* as the first `//!` line rather than either being deleted; that is what the module docs
would have read as anyway.

**The lesson is not about clippy.** `rust-verify`'s agent definition has carried `--all-targets` since
it was written, and `CLAUDE.md`'s *Build / test* block had not — so which gate ran depended on whether
the work was delegated, and this session's was not. **A gate written down in two places is two gates**,
and the weaker one is the one that gets run by whoever is in a hurry. Both say the same thing now.

**D303 — `OndinApp` can be built headlessly, and could have been all along. *Built; three tests against
a real app, the multi-selection one flip-checked.*** Raised as debt with no obvious actionable: the line
chrome, `pen_verb` routing, the cursor decisions, autopan and `resize_tx` are all verified by reading,
two passes have gone wrong there, and the reason given everywhere is that `OndinApp` holds a wgpu
`RenderState`.

**The reason is true and the conclusion drawn from it was not.** `CanvasRenderer` held three GPU
members — `render_state`, the Vello renderer and the offscreen target — and they are touched in
**exactly two functions**, `render` and `ensure_target`, and nowhere else in the crate. That is not a
coupling, it is a field. Boxed into a `Gpu` struct behind an `Option`, the whole of a headless canvas is
one `let Some(gpu) = self.gpu.as_mut() else { return None };` in a function that already returned
`Option`. *This is the shape my own §15 entries keep recording: a "mechanical blocker" is a hypothesis
about one shape of solution, and the adjacent shape was one indirection away the whole time.*

**Three things are swapped by the constructor, and naming them is the design** — a fourth is refused
by a flag instead, which the 🚨 below has. A device, five background threads and a file:
`CanvasRenderer::headless`, `FontService::inert` and `Prefs::default`. ⚠️ **The third was only
half swapped until 2026-08-26** — the value was in memory but `Prefs::save` still wrote to
`dirs::config_dir()`, and a probe that reached any of the app's `prefs.save()` calls put its own temp
folder into the developer's real preferences file (§15 D370). `FontService::new` spawns a
cache sweep, a system-font enumeration, a catalog fetch that makes a **network call**, and `WORKERS`
face loaders — right for an app, and a test that paid an HTTP request per case would be worse than no
test. The inert one's receivers are live channels whose senders are already dropped, which is what makes
it inert rather than half-built: `poll` gets `Disconnected`, which is precisely the "that source has
stopped arriving" signal `catalog_done` is documented to read off a closed channel, so `status_of`
reaches its conclusions instead of waiting for ever. The three tests run in **0.01 s**, which is the
evidence that none of it started.

🚨 **There is a fourth machine-touching resource, and it went unswapped for as long as this entry
said there were three: the OS clipboard** (D796). `system_clipboard_text`,
`system_clipboard_has_image` and `paste_image` read the developer's real clipboard out of a headless
app, and `copy_as_png` would overwrite it — so "naming them is the design" named three of four, and
the one left out was the one with no inert twin. **The list is what is swapped, not what a probe can
reach**, and until it was closed what held on this path was test discipline — the *Declined* paragraph
below refuses a clipboard test for exactly this reason, and D796's own test reads and never writes —
where the other three held by construction. **Closed 2026-09-19 (D798)**: `OndinApp::headless` sets
a process-wide `CLIPBOARD_OFF` flag that the two readers and both writers check, so the list is four
long and every one of them holds by construction. ⚠️ **It is a static rather than a constructor
argument like the three above**, because the OS clipboard is one per *process* — D798 has why, and
why the check sits at the four callers rather than inside `with_clipboard`.

**`OndinApp::new` and `OndinApp::headless` share one field list** (`with`), so a new field still has one
place to be initialised and cannot mean different things in the two builds. That was the whole risk of a
second constructor and it is answered by construction rather than by discipline.

**What it does *not* change**, said plainly because the temptation is to overclaim: no test can still say
*where* a `&mut self` method is called from. `crop_chrome`'s module records that as the whole story of
D269 — a call in a place it could never run from — and a headless app makes the method callable without
making the call site observable. Lifting decisions into free functions therefore stays the better shape;
this is a door, not a licence.

**The proof is `resize_opts` and `resize_tx`**, chosen because `resize_tx`'s `Target::Selection` arm has
no free-function twin: it reads the *selection* off `self` before it can measure anything, so it was
unreachable in the strong sense rather than merely unlifted. Two facts fell out that nothing had ever
asserted — that **`Shift` inverts the proportion lock rather than setting it**, so a locked layer
resizes freely while it is held (all four combinations), and that a multi-selection drag scales members
about the *shared* box. The second is flipped by handing `resize_selection` the first member's bounds
instead of the union — the wrong-box error somebody would actually make — and the far rect lands at
1200 instead of 400. **The assertion is on the far rect's position, not its size**: a version that
resized each member in place produces the right width and leaves it where it was.

⚠️ **38 doc comments across nine files carried a false reason** — some form of "`OndinApp` needs a wgpu
render state, so this is read rather than tested": `app.rs` 8, `canvas.rs` 12, `inspector.rs` 10,
`export.rs` 3, `typography.rs` 4, and one each in `layers.rs`, `picker.rs`, `rulers.rs` and `text.rs`.
Four were corrected with the change — the `//!` module headers that *excuse missing coverage*, the ones
that would stop the next person writing the test — and **the other thirty-four were swept the same day**,
in one deliberate pass rather than opportunistically. Nothing fails while such a sweep is undone, which
is the only reason it was safe to separate and the exact reason it would have rotted if it had been
forgotten.

**The sweep found that most of them were arguing for the right thing badly.** A free function over a
`Document`, two `HashSet`s, a `Response` and a `Transaction` — the reason to lift those was never "the
owner cannot be built", it was that *the decision is addressable on its own terms* and a test of it
should not have to stand a panel up first. So the replacements say what the function is a function
**of**, which is a better argument and one that does not expire. Three sentences turned out to be about
something else entirely and now say so: `core::text.rs`'s is about a *crate* boundary (the panel is in
`ondin-app`, which core cannot reach), and two in `typography.rs` are claims about **egui's** own popup
and pointer behaviour, which are worth asserting against egui whatever the app can do.

**Where a comment genuinely excused missing coverage, it now says "writable now and unwritten"** rather
than being quietly reworded — five of them, in `canvas.rs`, `inspector.rs`, `typography.rs` and
`app.rs`. *A sweep that turns "impossible" into confident prose about why the current shape is fine is
how a gap stops being visible.*

**And D35's standing instruction was discharged the same day.** It ends "*anyone who finds a way to
construct an `OndinApp` headlessly should pin this first*" — the guide grab. `rulers::guide_grab_tests`
is that test; D35 has the detail.

**The four that were "verified by reading" are written, and all four flip-checked.** Line chrome,
`pen_verb` routing, autopan and the cursor ladder — the list this entry was raised against.

- **Line chrome is one assertion for the whole feature**, which is the design D238 chose: the corner
  handles, the side bands, the skew modifier, the rotate ring, the size badge and all their cursors
  hang off `selection_handles`, so `None` there removes every one. **Three cases, because the rule is
  "lone" and not "line"**: a rect keeps its handles (without which this passes against a function that
  had simply broken), and a line selected *with* something else keeps them too — the arm a
  `matches!(kind, Line)` in the obvious place gets wrong, leaving a two-layer selection unresizable
  because one member is a line.
- **`pen_verb`'s four answers in one test, because what matters is that they are distinct** — each arm
  asserted alone passes against a function answering the same thing everywhere. The fourth is the one
  an obvious implementation gets wrong: over *another layer* the answer is no verb at all, because a
  press there still switches subject. Flipped by making the empty-canvas arm unconditional, which is
  the natural way to write it.
- **Autopan needed a real frame, and the finding is the harness rather than the feature.** egui
  resolves a press against the widget rects it knew *last* frame, so a press on the frame the widget
  first appears is assigned to nothing — `interact_pointer_pos` stays `None`, `autopan` returns at its
  `let Some(p)`, and **the test passes while asserting nothing**. A probe printing
  `ipp=None dragged=false down=true` named it in one run; a warm-up frame fixes it. The assertion is
  the sign, flipped by removing the negation in `autopan_delta`.
- **The cursor ladder had the same trap one layer over.** `PlatformOutput` is drained each frame, so
  reading `ctx.output()` *after* `run_ui` returns reads the next frame's empty one and answers
  `Default` for every case — a tautology about egui's default cursor. It is read off the returned
  `FullOutput` instead. The case worth having is the reported one: **Space held part-way through
  drawing a shape must not show the open hand**, since `panning_armed` is consulted only on the frame a
  drag starts and nothing was ever going to pan. Flipped by dropping the `Drag::Create` guard — the
  version that shipped — and the first two cases pass against it.

**The five comments that said "writable now and unwritten" are answered — three written, two declined
with the reason recorded where the comment was.** *A queue that empties only by being written is a queue
that stays full; the useful outcome for two of these was a better sentence.*

- **`cancel_gesture`'s gate**, which fails in opposite directions and did both. Too narrow is the random
  one: `Context::dragged_id` is a per-frame snapshot egui clears on the release of **any** button, so a
  right-click short enough to fit inside one rendered frame reads a value that has gone. Too wide eats
  the right-click that removes a gradient stop. The test asserts each of *our* two witnesses arms it
  **with `dragged_id` empty** — precisely the case the snapshot loses — and that an idle app answers
  `false`. Flipped by reducing the gate to egui's witness alone, the version that shipped.
- **The autopan restore**, chained onto the autopan test's own setup rather than a hand-set accumulator:
  the only honest way to have a real `autopan_total` is to auto-scroll, and asserting against a value
  poked in would test the subtraction and nothing else.
- **The arrow router.** `arrow_claim_tests` proves the two predicates partition the modifier space —
  a claim about two functions. This is the claim about the **loop**, measured on the caret, which is
  the observable the user has. Flipped by dropping the guard from the `ArrowLeft` arm: the caret jumps
  from 11 to 0 on `Alt+←`.

**Declined, and the reasons are the finding.** Which caller passes a **zero guide step** reaches
`paste_guides` through `owns_the_clipboard`, which compares a receipt against the real **system**
clipboard — a test of that wiring would read, and could disturb, whatever the person running it had
copied. And **`paint_unit`'s two callers** and the **Rotation field's wiring** both wanted a
`DragValue`'s or a card's frame-by-frame interaction state reproduced, which two probes in this project
have already disagreed about (D96). What they got instead is one assertion that covers the wiring of
every field in the panel and is the shape of three reported bugs: **drawing the inspector commits
nothing and previews nothing.** Two frames, because the first is where egui hands out ids; a fixture
carrying two strokes and a fill, so `paint_unit`'s real callers are the ones being drawn; flipped by
making the W field commit unconditionally, which takes the revision from 2 to 4. *`paint_unit`'s `last`
flag is still read, and the comment says so rather than implying otherwise* — telling it apart needs the
card's absolute height rather than a difference, and the header makes that a measurement of the chrome.

**The slot verbs and the picker's call pattern close the list.** Both were on the character- and
paragraph-attribute bullet as things that "genuinely rest on reading", and both are the kind where
reading is weakest.

- **`preview_slot` shows exactly what `write_slot` will do**, asserted by committing after previewing
  and finding the same paint rather than by checking each verb does something. A preview that is not
  the commit means the colour under the hand is not the colour the release lands on — invisible in the
  source and obvious on screen.
- **A character-scoped slot is diverted onto the type's own colour**, by `write_slot` and
  `preview_slot` separately, since the diversion is written out once per verb.
