  ⚠️ **This asserted only "no fill appeared" at first and passed with the diversion deleted** —
  `slot_transaction` writes nothing for a `TextColor` slot either, so the fill list is empty both ways
  and the test was about nothing. The flip found it; the assertion is now on `TextStyle::color`, which
  is where a diverted write actually lands, and a probe was what said so. *A test of an absence is the
  easiest kind to write and the easiest to write vacuously.* **`valve_slot` is driven too**, through a
  real drag — a resting `Response` reaches `char_valve` and does nothing, so a test built on one would
  have passed with the diversion deleted, which is the same vacuum one arm over. The fixture asserts
  `dragged()` was reached before asserting anything about the colour.
- **The picker's `pointer_slot` routing**, driven through real frames — which is the point, because
  this is the code my own notes record as having burned **three code-reasoned fixes** for one frozen
  picker before a ten-line `eprintln!` named the cause in a single run. *"Who calls this and how often"
  is never in the text of the function.* Two cases: a **press previews before it travels** (it sets
  neither `dragged` nor `changed`, so the shared valve is cut for it and without the explicit arm the
  plane does nothing until the pointer moves — which is what "frozen" looked like), and a **cancelled
  gesture does not land as a click on release**, asserted at the release because that is where it would
  get through. Flipped by disabling the press arm and by deleting the cancel guard; both bite.

**And `paint_unit`'s `last` flag, on the real card.** The stand-in test pins the rhythm; what it cannot
see is whether `inspector_stroke` passes the flag correctly. **A difference between two card heights
cannot tell**: getting the flag wrong adds one gap and only one, however many strokes there are — `n`
trailing gaps instead of the `n − 1` between them — so every difference is identical in both worlds and
only the *absolute* height separates them. Hence the card's chrome is measured on its own, as the same
`panel` call with an empty body.

**No measured constants survive in the assertion**, so it outlives a redesign of the rows: the unit's
height is derived from the slope (two cards differ by one unit plus one gap) and the claim is that a
card holding *one* unit is exactly one unit tall past its chrome. The numbers found while writing it are
kept as the record rather than as the test — chrome 50, cards 124 / 207 / 290 at a 9pt gap, which is
`50 + 74n + 9(n − 1)` exactly. Flipped by forcing `last = false`: 83 against 74, the predicted single
gap.

⚠️ **Writing the autopan test found a doc comment arguing both ways**, which is the return this entry
was hoping for. `Drag::autopans`'s own comment listed "dragging a pivot **or a guide** across the
document" among the gestures that want more room, three lines above the paragraph explaining that a
guide is excluded — the phrase outlived the exclusion. Two smaller faults came with it: a **duplicate**
summary sentence had drifted into the middle of the comment, where it read as part of that list, and
the count said "two answer no" where the code has excluded three since the guide arm landed. *None of
the three is reachable by any gate; all three are reachable by writing the test the comment describes.*

**D304 — §11's byte-exact goldens: SVG and JSON are built and compared, PNG is not, because the CPU
renderer as originally called could not produce one portably — the stroked path is the only thing
that moves. *Measured, then pinned; two of the three formats are built and PNG is outstanding by
choice.*** The roadmap has carried, since 2026-08-21, the
sentence "whether the output is bit-identical across SIMD levels today is unknown — not known to be a
problem, not known not to be", with the note that the answer decides whether pinning the level is a
nicety or the whole feasibility question. It was the whole feasibility question, and the answer is
narrower than the sentence feared.

**One scene at three explicit levels through `RenderContext::new_with`**, 200×200 premultiplied RGBA8
= 160,000 bytes. Gradient ramp, antialiased circle, rotated stroked curve, a `Multiply` layer at 0.6
alpha and a glyph run, together. ⚠️ **Every figure in this table and the paragraph under it is a
*premultiplied* byte, which is not the byte a PNG golden compares** — the straight-alpha numbers are
below and they are larger:

| pair | bytes differing | worst channel delta |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Fallback` vs `Sse4_2` | 0 | — |
| `Fallback` vs `Avx2` | 14 (0.0088%) | 2 |
| `Sse4_2` vs `Avx2` | 14 (0.0088%) | 2 |

Drawn one primitive at a time against `Fallback`, **the stroked path is the only thing that moves** —
11 bytes, delta 1. Gradient, antialiased fill, blend layer and glyph run are byte-identical at every
level. Debug and release agree; the same level rendered twice in one process agrees exactly, which was
asserted rather than assumed. `Fallback ≡ Sse4_2` with `Avx2` as the lone outlier is *consistent with*
AVX2 bringing FMA into the float arithmetic of stroke expansion — offered as the shape of the cause,
not as a verified one — which would make AVX2 the **more** accurate of the two. That is why this is a
pin and not a bug report: the worst of it lands on pixels that are almost entirely transparent, so
nothing is visible and the only thing it breaks is a byte comparison.

**Two of the three machine-derived settings turned out not to be variables at all**, which is the part
that shrinks the work. `RenderMode` is inert in this build: `vello_cpu`'s default features are `std,
png, text, u8_pipeline`, the workspace pinned `vello_cpu = "=0.0.9"` with no feature list, and with
exactly one pipeline compiled in `dispatch::single_threaded` does `let _ = render_mode;` and takes the
u8 path unconditionally. (⚠️ **The pin is `=0.2.0` now and this finding was re-checked against it
rather than renumbered** — same feature set, same `cfg`-gated `match`, so `RenderMode` is still inert;
what changed is that it lives on a different struct, §15 D414.) So `OptimizeSpeed` is already pinned *by the feature set*, and reaching the
`OptimizeQuality` that `RenderMode`'s own doc comment recommends "for visual regression testing" means
enabling `f32_pipeline` — a larger decision, and one that changes the rasterization arithmetic under
every pixel assertion already in the suite. `num_threads` is the third such field and nothing had ever named it: `RenderSettings::default`
computes it from `available_parallelism` only under the `multithreading` feature, which is off (no
`rayon` in `Cargo.lock`), so it is 0 and the single-threaded dispatcher is chosen regardless. **Only
`Level` is live.**

⚠️ **The numbers above are one step upstream of the exported file, and the exported file is worse.**
`render_subtrees_to_rgba` puts the pixmap through `color::straight_rgba8_from_premul` before the PNG
encoder sees it, and that divides each channel by alpha — so a premultiplied delta of 1 on a pixel that
is barely covered comes out as a much larger straight-alpha delta, and an antialiased stroke edge is
made of exactly those pixels. Measured on the second pass, the stroked curve alone, `Fallback` against
`Avx2`:

| buffer | bytes differing | pixels differing | worst channel delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| premultiplied | 11 | 7 | 1 |
| straight alpha (what a golden compares) | 17 | 7 | **9** |

**The byte count grew and the pixel count did not** — the six extra bytes are further channels inside
pixels that already differed. The worst case is `(119,154)`, where two channels read 20 against 29 on a
pixel whose alpha is 25; the next is `(104,100)` at 32 against 34, alpha 16. So the amplification is
confined to the near-transparent edge, which is why the composited picture is still identical to the eye
and the verdict is unchanged. **The figure to quote at a PNG golden is 9, not 1 or 2.**

**Untested: aarch64/NEON.** The measurement is x86_64 only, so whether `Neon` agrees with `Fallback` is
still genuinely unknown rather than measured, and it is the question that decides whether a
second machine on Apple silicon can share goldens at all.

**The work that was left was a choice, not a discovery.** Pinning is mechanical — `new_with` already
exists — and had to stay **export-only**, because `cpu.rs`'s `rasterize_glyph_run` draws the font
picker's live preview strips and should keep the detected level. (Doubly safe now: glyph runs are
level-invariant, so those strips are the same pixels at any level.) Three ways forward were on the
table: `Level::baseline()`, which is cheapest but *target*-dependent — `Fallback` on default x86_64,
`Neon` on aarch64 — so goldens become per-architecture; `Level::fallback()`, which needs fearless_simd's
`force_support_fallback` feature that neither `vello_cpu` nor `vello_common` re-exports, reachable by
adding `fearless_simd` as a direct dependency of `ondin-render` and letting feature unification turn it
on (verified compiling, and how the probe named the three levels) at the price of scalar exports; or
keeping strokes out of the golden fixtures, which makes PNG as free as SVG and JSON at the price of a
coverage hole exactly where strokes live. ⚠️ **`Level::fallback()` is not the cross-architecture
guarantee its name suggests** — its own doc says the fallback branch may still contain SIMD, because
LLVM is free to auto-vectorise it against the ambient target — so it removes the *dispatch* variable
and not necessarily the last byte of it.

**`Level::baseline()` is what was written**, on 2026-08-22. `cpu.rs` grew a private
`export_settings()` returning `RenderSettings { level: Level::baseline(), ..Default::default() }`, and
`render_subtrees_to_rgba` builds its context with `new_with` instead of `new` — which covers the whole
export path, since `render_to_rgba` is one call of it and the only production callers of either are
`ondin-export/src/png.rs`. `rasterize_glyph_run` is unchanged and still detects. `render_mode` and
`num_threads` are left to `Default` deliberately: they are already constants in this build, as
measured above, and naming them in the literal would imply they were variables. The other two options
were declined on what they buy rather than on cost — `Level::fallback()` buys a cross-architecture
guarantee it does not actually give, at the price of a scalar path under every export; keeping strokes
out of the fixtures buys portability by deleting from the fixture the one primitive the measurement
says is fragile, which is a coverage hole in exactly the place the test exists to watch.
`export_pins_the_simd_level_rather_than_detecting_it` guards the pin, and the failure it guards is a
one-word revert — `new_with` back to `new` — that compiles and passes every pixel assertion in the
suite on the machine that made it. It compares `Debug` strings because `Level` is `#[non_exhaustive]`
and implements no `PartialEq`, and it **prints whether the machine running it can tell a pin from a
detect at all**: on a CPU whose detected level already is the baseline the assertion is vacuous, so a
green run there is not a proof and the note says which case ran.

**The SVG and JSON goldens landed in the same change** — `crates/ondin-export/tests/goldens.rs` with
`tests/goldens/every-kind.svg` and `every-kind.json` beside it, regenerated by
`ONDIN_UPDATE_GOLDENS=1 cargo test -p ondin-export --test goldens` and byte-compared otherwise, plus a
coverage check and a determinism check. The fixture holds **one node of every `NodeKind`**, all eleven
— deliberately not the shared `common::fixture()`, which covers eight and is the subject of two dozen
substring assertions that would have to move with it. `kind_name`'s exhaustive `match` is the
tripwire: adding a variant breaks this file's compile, which is the half of a `NodeKind` sweep the
compiler can do. It cannot force the *fixture* to grow the new node, and the comment beside
`EVERY_KIND` says so rather than leaving it to be discovered. A root `.gitattributes` marks the
directory `-text`, so a clone with `core.autocrlf=true` cannot fail a byte comparison for a reason
that has nothing to do with the exporter. Flip-checked against `svg::fmt` rounding to three decimals
instead of four — a plausible tidy-up rather than a deletion — which failed at line 12 with both sides
shown.

**Reading the first generated golden caught two defects in the fixture itself**, which is the argument
for goldens in miniature: neither is visible in the source, and a substring assertion would have
caught neither. An outside-aligned stroke on the `Line` did nothing, because
`geometry::stroke_align_applies` is `false` for a kind with no interior — it moved to the polygon,
where it emits the real markup (an `evenodd` `<clipPath>` and a doubled width of 6). And a `Boolean`
painted on an *operand* rather than on the container exported at `fill="none"`: the container carries
the paint, and an operand's fill is not inherited by the result.

**PNG stays unbuilt, and that is now a decision rather than a gap.** `Level::baseline()` is
target-derived, so a checked-in PNG would be a golden for x86_64 that fails on Apple silicon for
reasons having nothing to do with the change under review, and aarch64/NEON is still unmeasured. It is
one *measurement* away, not one line away, and `goldens.rs`'s module header states that where the next
person to want one will read it. ⚠️ **There is a second axis since 2026-09-03**: the `=0.2.0` bump
moved every pixel of one mitered outside stroke, so a raster golden is per-architecture *and*
per-`vello_cpu` (§15 D414).

*Revisit PNG when NEON has been measured on a real aarch64 machine* — that measurement, not another
line of code, decides whether one checked-in raster can serve both architectures or whether the
goldens directory grows a per-target subdirectory. The recommendation this entry carried was accepted
whole: build SVG and JSON now, pin PNG to `baseline()`, do not add `f32_pipeline`. **What is left of
the deviation is one format**, §11 specifying byte-exact PNG goldens where none exists, held open on
purpose rather than for want of the work.

The ⚠️ this entry used to end on has been carried out. `cpu.rs`'s module header called the backend
"byte-comparable everywhere", *everywhere* being the one word this measurement falsifies; it was fixed
with the pin in the same change, and now reads "across machines of one architecture, and only because
the SIMD level is pinned", dated and pointing here.

**D305 — Where a picture's verbs live: five menu rows down to two, one verb removed outright, and a
fourth door onto the mode. *Built and tested; the split is the maintainer's, decided row by row.***
`context-menus.md` §5.7's head had grown to five rows and the inspector's image-editing card offered
four of the same verbs, which is two standing lists of everything a picture can do rather than one
list of what a hand reaches for. The maintainer went through them one at a time and the answers do
not follow a rule, which is why they are recorded as answers: *Original size* "is something someone
may reach if they've played around with the image and want to revert it back — it can stay in the
menu, doesn't need to stay in the Settings tab"; *Export original…* "is irrelevant really, both in
the menu and the Settings tab — there's export options in several sizes and formats, no one will
reach for that"; *Replace…* "doesn't need to be in the context menu"; *Replace and reset* is "not
especially useful, but good to have — only in the Settings tab". So the menu keeps *Edit image* and
*Original size*, the tab keeps *Reset crop* and the two replaces, and *Export original…* keeps
neither door.

**The one general thing in it is the axis the answers fall on**, and it is worth naming because the
next picture verb will want it: a row goes to the **menu** when it is wanted *without* being in the
mode, and to the **tab** when it is only wanted while working on the picture. *Original size* is the
clear case in the first direction — it resizes the **node**, the one card entry that was never a
paint edit (D182), and it is what a hand reaches for after playing with a picture and wanting the
layer back — and the card could only offer it to somebody who had already entered a mode to do
something else. *Reset crop* and *Replace…* fall the other way: worth having, not worth a row in a
menu that opens on every layer.

**Removing *Export original…* is D264's argument one surface further in.** That row was a second door
onto a file the Export panel (D274) already writes better: the panel answers where, at what size and
in what format from the layer and remembers all three, where the row asked nothing and offered one
answer. Two rows have now been withdrawn for that reason within four days, which is what makes it a
pattern rather than a taste — a one-off export loses to a door that keeps settings.

**The *Original size* half closes a `roadmap.md` question by answering it.** That file asked "is
*original size* in the right place, given that there are two doors onto it?", corrected itself once
along the way — the mode-free door had been there since the context menus landed — and settled on
"the question is not *should it move out of the mode* but which of the two doors is the redundant
one". It got its answer, and the reason the entry itself named is the reason the menu door won: it is
the one entry in that card which resizes the node rather than editing the paint. The bullet is struck.

**The compiler walked the removal out and it did not stop at the rows.** `Item::ResetCrop`,
`Item::ReplaceImage` and `Item::ExportOriginal` went whole — variant, `Item::ALL` row, `spec()` arm,
push and dispatch arm, the five sites D268 counted — and `LayerState` lost `cropped` and
`picture_refusal`, which had no other readers. Then `OndinApp::export_image_action` was dead, then
`tools::original_refusal` was dead, and then **two `pub` items in `ondin-core` were left with no
caller in the workspace at all**: `ImageEntry::is_linked` and `ImageFormat::extension`. Neither
warns, because core is a library and `dead_code` never fires on a `pub` item (CLAUDE.md's rule), so
both were checked by grep and both carry a doc comment saying so. ⚠️ **`ImageFormat::extension` is
not `ExportFormat::extension`**, which has four live callers and is about a *rendered* file rather
than a stored one; the two names are one grep apart and only one of them is dead.

**D280's own finding has come undone, and that is the part to read before touching this.** That entry
records `is_linked` as having sat `pub` with zero callers while both doors hand-rolled
`bytes().is_some()` — a predicate equally false for a linked picture and for an id the table does not
hold, so a document that had merely *lost* a picture was told it used linking, a feature the app
cannot author. `original_refusal` was what gave the predicate its caller and the refusal its third
state. It is back to zero callers. **The three-state distinction is written down in two places rather
than left to be re-derived**: a comment where `original_refusal` stood in `tools/mod.rs`, and
`is_linked`'s own doc in core. *Rebuild from those the day linking is authored; re-deriving is what
produced the two-state version the first time.* A `refusal_tests` module was written mid-change to
keep D280's assertion alive when only the menu row was going, and deleted an hour later when the
inspector door went too — a test of a deleted function is not a test — with a comment marking where
it was.

**The fourth door: clicking a fill row's swatch or its *Image* label enters image editing.** The
maintainer's framing was "kind of emulates how you open the colour picker for a shape", and that is
exactly the shape it took — the gradient arm beside it already had `.sense(Sense::click())` and opens
the picker, so this is the same row aimed at a *mode* instead. Both halves were inert before, and
inert in two different ways: the chip carried `if chip.clicked() && !picture`, the click explicitly
suppressed for a picture, and the `PaintKind::Image` label was an `egui::Label` with no `Sense` at
all. Both now carry the tooltip *"Edit this picture — crop it, move it, scale it"*.

**Four doors saying one sentence is what finally earned the constant D268 asked for.**
`OndinApp::begin_image_edit(id)` is `selection.set_one(id)`, `choose_tool(Tool::ImageEdit)` and the
status line; the `Enter` arm, the double-click arm and the *Edit image* dispatch all route through it
now. D268's own note said the string was "duplicated on purpose… and if it ever earns a constant all
three want it at once" — the fourth door is what earned it. `set_one` is called even where the caller
has already selected the layer, the `Enter` door having found `id` *in* the selection: the redundant
write costs nothing where four doors each deciding selection differently is how they come to disagree.

**Which row is the door is a real decision and is lifted into a free function.**
`inspector::row_edits_the_mode_s_picture(doc, id, slot)` asks `tools::croppable_fill` — **not**
whether this row's own brush is an image. The two agree on every ordinary layer and come apart on one
with two image fills: `croppable_fill` answers the first *visible* image fill, so a click on the
second row would enter the mode and put the handles on the other photograph. It is inert there
instead, which is the answer the canvas already gives, the double-click going through the same
predicate. A stroke is refused by the `Fill(i)` pattern before the predicate is asked, `croppable_fill`
reading `fills` alone. It is a free function because it is the one line in a frame of egui that can
be wrong.

**Four tests in `inspector::fill_row_door_tests` pin it**, and the flip is the interesting part. ⚠️
Flipped against `paint::kind_of(brush) == PaintKind::Image` — the obvious spelling, and the one the
row computes a line above for its own label, so it is what a hand reaches for — which fails **two** of
the four rather than one: the predicate carries *which* picture and *visible*, and that spelling
drops both. The test comment said "one" until the flip was actually run.

⚠️ **The fourth door was also a second *live* door on a locked layer, which nothing said before.**
`begin_image_edit` read no lock, matching every other door — but the reachability argument D268
made, that `query::hit_test` filters the double-click out so `Enter` is the singular live door on a
locked picture, was a count and the count became two: the inspector's paint rows are deliberately
live on a locked layer (`select_by_color` — a lock stops a layer being dragged about, not
recoloured). The conclusion was unchanged, the doors still agreeing by all declining to check; what
changed is that "answer it in one place" had one more place to reach. **Both are shut as of
2026-08-23**: the funnel this entry built is where the lock is now answered, and the count stopped
mattering the moment there was one place to answer it in (D320).

**And a D261 disagreement was closed in passing, which is worth stating as a fix rather than as a
consequence.** The card's *Original size* was gated on `sized.is_some()` alone — **no lock check** —
while `Item::OriginalSize` carried `.dim_if(locked, LOCKED)`. Two doors, one verb, opposite answers:
on a locked layer the menu refused and the card committed the `SetGeometry` anyway. Removing the card
row leaves the door that dims. Note what kind of write it was: **geometry**, not a crop, which made
it a sharper case than the then-open "should a lock reach the crop at all?" question — this fix
deliberately did not prejudge it, and the answer came the same day and went the same way: a crop *is*
a geometry write, `crop_resize_tx` going through `tools::resize_layer` (D320).

*Keep. The split is a set of answers rather than a rule, so a future row wants asking rather than
deriving — but the axis above is the question to ask it. **Revisit if linking is ever authored**: the
refusal that was deleted has to come back somewhere, and the two comments named above are its spec.*

🚨 **Linking will not be authored in v1, decided 2026-09-19 (D819)**, so that *Revisit* has a date on
it now rather than an open question behind it.

**D819 — Linked images are a decided non-goal for v1, and `is_linked` stays with no production
caller. *Ruled by the maintainer 2026-09-19; Resolved — a decided non-goal, and no production line
changed.***

The three Asset entries `roadmap.md` carried — *Embed*/*Link*, *Relink…*, and the document-wide
*Embed all* for a file that arrives with dead links — all wait on **the same missing thing**: a
gesture that **authors** a linked source. That is one dependency holding three rows, not a
cheap-versus-expensive split, which is why they are decided together.

**The dependency is exact.** `ImageSource::Linked` is constructed in exactly one place,
`io/schema.rs`'s deserializer, and every app path onto a picture funnels through
`app::load_image_bytes`, which builds `Embedded` unconditionally. So a hand-written or foreign
`.ondin` **can** carry a link and the app will open it — the subject exists in the model and can be
put in front of the user — and **nothing can make one**. ⚠️ **"One place" is about the *constructor*
and not about the ways a link can reach you**: `build::missing_image_ops` copies an entry wholesale
out of the document a paste came from, so a `Linked` entry can enter a document this app never
deserialized. That does not change the verdict and it does change what the three rows would have to
cope with.

**D191** is the out-of-v1 image list this joins, and **D305** already withdrew *Export original…*
the same way — so this is the second time a linked-image verb has been decided out rather than built,
and the first one is where the reasoning is kept.

🚨 **`is_linked` and the preserved reasoning stay, which is the half a future editor would tidy
away.** `dead_code` cannot object — `ondin-core` is a library, so a `pub` item is API however many
callers it has lost — and that silence is exactly why this entry has to say the keeping is
deliberate. Three grounds: the subject exists in the model; a foreign document can put one in front
of the app; and `tools::original_refusal`'s **three-state** answer — fine, linked, or an id the table
does not hold — is kept as comments where that function stood. **Rebuild from those rather than
re-deriving them**, and in particular *do not infer "linked" from absent bytes*: that inference is the
bug **D280** is about, committed once already by two hand-rolled `bytes().is_some()` doors that told
a user who had merely lost a picture that they were using linking.

**Record-only, so the citation is planted by hand** on `ondin_core::image`'s `is_linked` — the place
a reader meets the question *why does nothing call this*, and the one question no gate in this
workspace can ask there.

**The three rows move into `roadmap.md` §0** and the *Now · Images* open bullet is struck, leaving
that section as the record of the v1 image build with nothing open.

**D240 — `Node::from_parts` is deleted rather than given a parts struct, because two of its callers were
already the parts struct. *Resolved.*** D41 recorded the constructor at eleven positional arguments and
asked for a parts struct "before adding another bool, not after"; D60 re-recorded it at **thirteen**, three
of them consecutive bare `bool`s, and said the request stood. It has been answered by removing the
constructor: every site now writes `Node { id, parent, … }` directly, which is a named-field literal and so
is the parts struct the request was for, with no new type to name, and `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]`
goes with it.

**What made deletion the right shape is that the crate already had the other door.** `Document::new` and
`Document::op_create` build a `Node` by struct literal — the fields are `pub(crate)` (invariant 2) and both
of those sites live in `ondin-core`, as do all four `from_parts` callers, so the constructor was never
reaching anywhere a literal could not. It was a second idiom for one job, and the second idiom was the one
that could be got wrong.

**D41's own scoring of the hazard was optimistic, and the two sites it did not count are the interesting
half.** It said "both live call sites pass named struct fields, so a transposition would not be silent
*there*", which is true of `capture`'s remap in `document.rs` and of `SchemaDto::into_document` — both pass
`n.visible, n.locked, n.proportions_locked` and `dto.…` respectively, where a swap reads wrong. It counted
only those two. The other two callers are **test fixtures** — `document::tests::node` and
`geometry::tests::bare` — and each passed `true, false, false, 1.0, false` as bare literals, which is
exactly the silent-transposition shape the deferral was meant to keep out. So the hazard was not latent
pending a fourth bool; it was already live in the fixtures the tree's own invariants are asserted against.

**`Document::from_parts` stays and is not the same problem.** Six arguments, every one a distinct type, one
caller — and `Document`'s fields are private to `document.rs` rather than `pub(crate)`, so `io::schema`
genuinely cannot write a literal. It is a door because there is no other way in, which is what the node's
was not.

Nothing here changes behaviour and no test asserts on it: the whole of the change is that thirteen
positions became thirteen names. What it buys is the property the constructor was kept for — a new field on
`Node` still fails to compile at every construction site — held by the compiler rather than by a signature
somebody has to remember to widen.

**D241 — The Windows drop position is bought back from the desktop cursor, and it is asked *before* the
event stream rather than after it. *Resolved; run on the machine and accepted.*** D184 left one
option open and this takes it. `canvas::drop_point` now begins with `os_cursor_screen_pos`, which is
`GetCursorPos` plus the viewport's `inner_rect`; on Windows a drop aims and replaces like a drop on any
other platform, where before this every one landed at `viewport_centre()` and *Replace…* or a paste were
the only ways to repaint a picture.

**The ordering is the decision, not the call.** The obvious spelling is a last-resort fallback — try
egui's pointer, then ask the OS — and it is wrong here. `drop_point` is only ever reached inside a file
drag (the `dropped_files` handler and `draw_drop_indicator`, which gates on `hovered_files`), and inside a
file drag egui's pointer is by construction not the pointer: the drag source holds the mouse capture, and
what is left is either `None` or, for exactly one frame, the spot the cursor left the window at —
`Event::PointerGone` clears `latest_pos` immediately but egui clears `interact_pos` a frame later, on
purpose, so a drag that leaves the window keeps working. A stale position that reads as live is worse than
no position, because the whole of `image_drop_target` is *which shape is under it*. So the OS is asked
first and the two egui readings stay as the fallback, which is also what keeps the function correct off
Windows: there `os_cursor_desktop_px` is a `None` and the function is what it was.

**One Win32 call, and it buys an existing edge rather than a tree.** `windows-sys` is already in the lock
at 0.52.0 through winit, whose own feature list already carries `Win32_Foundation` and
`Win32_UI_WindowsAndMessaging` — the two this needs — so the manifest change is one line in `Cargo.lock`
and no new package. It is `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]`, so nothing off Windows sees it at all.

**The DPI question is answered by both readings living in the same space, and that is the part to get
wrong.** `GetCursorPos` reports physical desktop pixels under per-monitor-v2 awareness, which is what
winit sets; `ViewportInfo::inner_rect` is `Window::inner_position` and `inner_size` — also physical — with
the *whole rect* divided by `pixels_per_point` (`egui-winit::inner_rect_in_points`). So the physical
reading is scaled first and the window origin subtracted after. Subtracting first and scaling after is
right at 100% and wrong by the scale factor everywhere else — the class of bug that is invisible on the
machine it is written on unless the machine happens to be scaled — and it is what
`screen_pos_of_desktop_px` is a separate function for.

**Two tests, and the flip was checked.** `the_desktop_cursor_lands_in_egui_space_at_a_scale_factor_that_is_not_one`
uses 1.5 with the window off the desktop origin, because a fixture at 1.0 passes against either ordering —
the wrong one answers 233.3 where the right one answers 200, and the failure message says both.
`the_client_areas_top_left_is_the_origin_of_egui_space` pins which corner is the origin. The FFI itself
was run once through a throwaway probe to confirm the symbol resolves and the call succeeds, and the
probe was deleted; note that a test binary is DPI-*un*aware, so a probe can prove the call works and
cannot prove the space it answers in.

**What is not tested is the thing a user sees**, and this entry says so rather than implying otherwise:
whether the recovered point lands where the pointer is. `drop_point` is an `OndinApp` method and
`OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState`, the same seam `canvas::autopan` and `resize_tx` sit behind — and
the position cannot be synthesized anyway, since the whole point of it is that it comes from outside the
process. **The instrument is `draw_drop_indicator`, exactly as it was for the original reading**: drag a
picture over a selected image layer and the pill should read *Replace image in …* with the hover outline
on that shape. If it lights the wrong shape, the mapping is off; if it still reads *Place image*, the
recovery is not firing.

**Run on the machine 2026-08-19 and accepted**: dropping on a selected image says *Replace image*. So the
same drawing that measured `drop_point` returning `None` on Windows has now measured it returning the
pointer — the whole of D184's open option is closed by the same instrument that opened it.

**A known and accepted approximation.** The position is read when the frame runs, not when the OS
delivered the drop, so a fast hand between the release and the next frame moves the landing point by a few
pixels. The alternative would be recording a position on the hover frames, which are *older* than the
drop and therefore worse. The indicator lags by the same frame, which is true of every aimed drop
anywhere.

**D242 — A `Group` was the one kind the canvas would resize and the panel would not name. *Resolved.***
The roadmap carried this as *Scale tool — still no numeric path*, and its premise had gone stale in three
directions before anyone re-read it. A `Path` and a `Boolean` got W and H from their derived box (D98); a
`Line` got an `L` in W's slot (D229); a multi-selection has had W and H over its union for as long as
`inspector_multi_transform` has existed. What was actually left was **one kind**: a single `Group`, whose
handles resize it on canvas and whose panel showed no size at all. So the fix is one arm of one `match` —
`NodeKind::Group` beside `Path` and `Boolean` in `inspector_single`'s `size0` — and not the percentage
field the entry proposed.

**Nothing else had to change, and that is the finding rather than a convenience.** `tools::resize_box_to`
routes through `resize_layer`, which has dispatched a node *with children* to `resize_group` since it was
written; `resizable_size` already answers `None` for a group, so the panel's `authored` test already sent
it down the derived path; `query::local_box`'s own doc comment already described itself as the box "the
inspector's W/H reports". Every piece was in place and pointed at each other. The kind was simply missing
from the list — which is the shape §15 D87 records for `is_paintable` and the memory of this project
records generally: *a `matches!` over kinds is a list the compiler does not check.*

**An empty group stays `None`.** `local_box` unions its children and there are none, so the row does not
appear. That is better than a 0 × 0 row: the field would clamp to 1 and write a transaction
`resize_geometry` has nothing to apply to, which is a control that looks live and is not.

**The test is on `resize_box_to` and a group, which had no coverage at all** —
`typing_a_width_on_a_group_resizes_it_from_its_own_top_left`. Its fixture is two rects whose union starts
at (10,5) rather than at the group's own origin, and it asserts the fixture measures 150 × 75 before it
asserts anything interesting, because a fixture in the wrong state tests nothing. Both the size *and* the
held corner are asserted: scaling the contents about (0,0) instead — the shape a hand-written answer
takes, a group having no `size` field to assign — produces exactly 300 × 150 as well and walks the corner
to (20,10), so the size alone would pass against it. Flipped against holding the wrong corner
(`Handle::TopLeft`) it fails on the size, 150 × 75 out of a 300 × 150 request.

**Not tested, and said plainly: that the row appears.** `size0` is computed inside an `OndinApp` method
and `OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState`, the same seam D229's length field and `canvas::autopan` sit
behind. What is pinned is the verb the field writes through.

*"And not the percentage field the entry proposed" was true of the gap this entry closed and is no
longer true of the field:* it was built on 2026-08-23 for a different reason entirely, and **D311** has
it.

**D311 — The Scale tool's verb had no numeric door, on one layer or on many. *Built and tested
2026-08-23.*** `roadmap.md` carried the last of D242's section as "does the Scale tool want a percentage
field of its own?", and answered its own question with "the one thing a set of layers cannot ask for as
a single number". **That clause was wrong.** The multi `W` field runs `tools::resize_selection` over the
union with `Handle::BottomRight`, so typing a width has scaled an arrangement by one number for as long
as `inspector_multi_transform` has existed — the same sentence D242 had already had to correct once.

**The gap is the verb, not the arithmetic.** `tools::Scaling` has two values: `Geometry`, where a 1px
border stays 1px, a 4px radius stays 4px and 16pt type stays 16pt, and `Photographic`, which takes all
three with the box. The canvas honours whichever tool is armed (`canvas`: `scaling: self.tool.scaling()`,
and `Tool::Scale => Scaling::Photographic`), while **every W/H path in the inspector passes
`Resize::geometry` as a literal and never asks which tool is up.** So the Scale tool — a whole rail slot,
its own cursor, its own keystroke — had no numeric door at all, and the same tool's handle drag and W
field disagreed about what a doubled box means. `inspector::scale_row` is that door, one percentage in
both the single-layer and the multi cards — *and in neither of them is it drawn unless the Scale tool
is held*, which **D312** decided the same day. The field is in both cards; both cards omit it while
another tool is armed.

**W and H still disagree with the armed tool, deliberately.** The obvious alternative — make the W/H
fields read `self.tool.scaling()`, so a typed width follows the tool the way a dragged handle does — was
considered and **rejected**: it makes one field mean two things with nothing *in the field* to say which,
and the cursor that would have said it is not visible while the pointer is in the inspector. A separate
control for a separate verb says *photographic* by existing, rather than by a mode the user has to
remember having armed. *Expect this to be re-proposed; it is the tidier-looking answer and it is the
wrong one.*

**It reads and acts, because a scale is not stored anywhere.** `Resize` writes geometry, so a rect
dragged to twice its size has an authored size of 200 and a basis still at 1.0 — there is nothing to
decompose and no percentage to show at rest. The field is therefore a verb with a live readout: it shows
what is being typed or scrubbed, applies it against the **committed** box every frame (so a scrub tracks
the pointer instead of compounding), and returns to 100 when the valve closes, because by then the box
*is* the new size. *And when the row goes away — but only since **D314**:* the commit was the one thing
that cleared the field, so a percentage typed and then abandoned was still there the next time the tool
was picked up.

**Over a selection it scales the union** — the same box X/Y/W/H move — so the arrangement scales as one
thing and the gaps go with it. Rotation and skew in the same card do the opposite, acting on each layer
about its own origin, and the difference is not an oversight: a set *has* one box and one size, where it
has no one rotation. This is the third time in one day the *one body or* n *layers* question came up —
D306 closed it for the layers tree, the transform origin is parked, D309 closed it for align — and it is
the one instance with an obvious answer.

**`inspector::scale_tx(&self, pct)` is a method rather than the body of the widget**, so the whole of
what the field decides — which box, which anchor, which verb — is reachable from a test; a `&mut self`
call site is not (D303 makes the app headless, not the call site observable). It anchors
`Handle::BottomRight` so the union's **top-left** is held: the corner X and Y report, and the corner the
one W and H already resize from. `selection_union` now returns the outermost members *and* their union,
and **`multi_union` calls it** instead of repeating the reduction beside it — "the Scale row resizes the
same box W and H move" made structural rather than left as two copies that happen to agree. An axis with
no extent scales by 1 rather than by nothing (`scale_along` returns `1.0` below `MIN_EXTENT`), so a
horizontal line takes the percentage on x and is left alone on y, which is the only reading it has.

**In W's slot, on a row of its own, with nothing beside it** — the shape a `Line`'s `L` already takes
(D229) and for the same reason: it is the row above's question asked as a ratio, and there is no second
dimension to put next to it, non-uniform scaling being exactly what W and H are. (*No second **number**
is the durable half of that:* D312 filled the space to its right the same day with three multiples,
which are the same verb rather than a second dimension.) ⚠️ **The maintainer is
not fond of a field taking a whole row at half width** and said so of the `L` row too, then parked it:
*"that's a polish item I can think of later. For now, that works."* Recorded as a known, deferred
objection covering **both rows together** rather than as a settled preference — whoever picks it up
should move the two at once, or the card gains a third rhythm.

**`Scrub::whole(0.5).range(1.0..=10_000.0)`, where the image crop scale beside it takes hundredths**
(D273). The contrast is worth keeping: that field is multiplicative *and* accumulates, so near its floor
a whole point is a sixth of the picture, where this one is 100 again after every commit and a step is
always one part in a hundred of what is on screen.

**Two tests in `inspector::scale_row_tests`, both on a headless app (D303).**
`scaling_takes_the_stroke_with_it_where_a_width_edit_does_not` asserts 200% doubles the authored box
*and* the stroke, and that the *inked* box goes 102 → 204 — the property the two halves only make
together. It is flip-checked against `Resize::geometry(false, false)`, which is what copying the W field
beside it would give, and fails with "and take the stroke with it — that is the whole difference from W",
2.0 against 4.0. That is the *plausible* wrong version rather than a deleted feature: it still scales, it
just scales the other way. `a_selection_scales_about_its_union_and_the_gap_grows_too` puts two rects 200
apart and pins the held corner staying while the far one moves 200 → 400 — two rather than one because a
single layer's union *is* its own box, so nothing about "which box" is observable until there are two. It
correctly stays green under the geometry flip, which is the isolation working rather than a gap.

⚠️ **`world_bounds` includes the stroke's ink**, half a width outside the geometry on each side, so the
first version of both tests asserted a fixture state that never existed: a 100pt rect with a 2pt stroke
measures 102 and starts at −1. The fixture takes the stroke as a parameter now, so the test about *which
box* has no stroke in it and the test about the stroke does. *A test whose fixture is not in the state it
claims is about nothing* — and what caught it was asserting the fixture before asserting anything
interesting, which is the habit rather than the luck.

⚠️ **A real bug in the reset, found by re-reading the code during the flip check rather than by a test.**
The first version reset the field on `drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()`. A `DragValue` reports
`changed()` on **every frame of a scrub**, so all three are true while the pointer is still down;
`edit_valve` never sees that because `dragged()` is the arm it tests first, and a reset written without
the same guard fires on the second frame of every drag — the number snapping back to 100 under the hand
while the layer keeps growing. The condition is `!resp.dragged() && !resp.has_focus() &&
!self.canvas_scaling()` now — the same three-part question the valve asks about engagement, plus the
canvas readout D315 added, and `changed()` is not in it at all. **No test covers it**: it needs
synthetic *pointer* events through `RawInput`, and D315's `drive_field` clicks and types rather than
scrubbing, so this is still said here rather than implied to be pinned. *Fix with a `RawInput` drag if
this row is ever touched again — and keep the `!dragged()` guard; it is the whole of what makes the
readout survive a scrub.*

*Keep.* **Revisit if** anyone proposes folding this back into W and H: the rejected alternative above is
the argument, and it does not improve with the second telling.

**D312 — D311's row, reviewed in use the same day: one defect and two changes. *Fixed and changed
2026-08-23; the defect's premise tested, the fix itself not; the `1x` button flagged, and answered the
same day by D313.*** This
is not a new feature — it is D311 put in front of the maintainer on the machine, which is where all
three of these came from.

**The defect: typing a percentage scaled the layer twice.** Reported as *"It works alright by
scrubbing… It doesn't work well when typing though. I think it's applying the scale on every keyboard
press, so if I want to scale it to 50%, I type 5: it scales to 5 percent, then 0 (for 50): it scales to
50%. Since the operation is accumulative, each press runs a scale on a different target."* **The
diagnosis in the report is right.** A `DragValue` being typed into reports `changed()` on every
keystroke, and `edit_valve`'s third arm commits on `changed()`. For every other field in the app that
is harmless — `W` typed as `4`, `48`, `480` commits three absolute widths and the last one wins — but
this transaction is **relative to the box it is about to write**, so each digit aimed at what the
previous digit had just built. Typing `50` left the layer at **2.5%** of its original size: 5% first,
then 50% of that.

**The fix was a second valve, and the reusable part was meant to be the rule for choosing it.**
`OndinApp::edit_valve_on_release` sat beside `edit_valve` in `app.rs` and was the same valve **without
the `changed()` arm**: it previewed while dragged and committed on `drag_stopped()` or `lost_focus()`,
which is what `Enter` does to a field. Its doc comment stated the general form — a field wants this
valve exactly when its transaction reads the document it is about to write — and the test for any new
control was to ask what typing its value one digit at a time would do. That is the family D51 names, at
a different surface: there an overlay drew from gesture state instead of from the function its
transaction used, here a transaction was built against a document its own previous commit had already
moved. *Derive the edit from the state it claims to be about, and commit it once.*

⚠️ **That reading was too narrow and the second valve lasted a day. *Superseded by D316.*** Committing
per keystroke was not a hazard peculiar to a *relative* field — it was wrong for every field in the
app, and an absolute one merely survives it (`W` typed as `1`, `10`, `100` ends at 100, leaving three
undo steps and the right shape on screen). The fault was in the shared valve all along; splitting the
row off from it hid that for a few hours. `edit_valve` now asks whether the control is **engaged**, the
two valves are one function again, and `edit_valve_on_release` is gone. *A fault that leaves the
visible state correct is invisible until somebody counts the invisible state* — read D316 before
reasoning from this paragraph.

What is pinned here is the premise, in
`scaling_compounds_which_is_why_a_commit_per_keystroke_was_wrong`: two commits of 5% then 50% leave the
box at 2.5 where one commit of 50% leaves it at 50 — the reported symptom written down as a number. The
valve itself went untested for a day and is now driven through real key events by D315's
`drive_field`; D311's `!dragged()` reset guard is the one behaviour on this row still carried by
reading, since that helper clicks rather than scrubs.

**Three multiples beside the field — `1x`, `2x`, `3x`.** *Superseded the same day by **D313**, which
made the set `0.5x` and `2x`; everything else in this paragraph still describes the row.*
`ui::label_button` at `FieldButton::Off`,
filling the width to the right of the field, three 7pt gaps, the split measured at the row's start the
way the multi W/H row measures its own. **Plain buttons, never a selected one**, and the maintainer
said so explicitly when sending a mock-up that showed one highlighted: *"The screenshot shows one of
the buttons highlighted. It won't be."* The reason is worth stating because it is the same fact the
field's spring-back to 100 rests on: **there is no state to be in.** A scale is applied and gone —
nothing stored says a layer is "at 2x" — so a highlighted cell would be claiming a state the model does
not have. They commit through `commit_edit` directly rather than through a valve, because a button has
no drag to preview and no focus to lose. They also, incidentally, fill the empty half-row D311 records
an objection to — *this* row is no longer a field alone at half width. Whether that answers the
objection is the maintainer's to say; the `L` row it was half about is untouched, so the note there
stands.

⚠️ **`1x` was a no-op, and recording it rather than quietly changing it is what got it fixed.** The
field is relative, so "scale to 1×" scales by 100% and does nothing at all. It was asked for as one of
three and built as asked; writing it down pointed the next reader at the *control* rather than at the
arithmetic, which is the tempting repair and the wrong one — there is no reading of a relative field
under which `1x` does something. The alternatives recorded here were a half (`0.5x`) or dropping to two
buttons; the maintainer took both at once the same day, and **D313** is the record.

**And the row appears only while the Scale tool is held**: *"Let's show the scale row only when the
scale tool is held. Otherwise it may confuse a user who may think this is a normal scale, and not one
that scales everything."* `scale_row` returns early unless `self.tool == Tool::Scale`. This is the same
reasoning that **rejected** D311's alternative, arriving at the opposite disposition, and the contrast
is the interesting part: a field that changes meaning with the armed tool is a hidden mode, whereas a
field that only *exists* while the tool is held announces its verb by being there. One is a mode you
have to remember arming, the other is a control you can see. *That is the rule for any future control
that wants to follow the tool: make it appear, do not make it mean something else.* It also narrows
D311's own claim — the field is in the single-layer card and in the multi card, which is still true,
but neither draws it under another tool — and D311 has been amended rather than left disagreeing.

⚠️ **The gate cost two things nobody costed at the time, and both were reported from the machine the
next day**: an optional row renumbers every row beneath it, so a typed percentage committed itself as a
*rotation*, and a field that is only cleared by its own commit keeps an abandoned number until the tool
is armed again. **D314** has both, and the rule it leaves behind — a row that comes and goes is
identified by name — is the price of this paragraph's "make it appear".

**Tested by `the_scale_row_is_offered_only_while_the_scale_tool_is_held`**, which runs the row on a
headless app (D303) under each tool and measures the height it adds: nothing under Select, something
under Scale. Flip-checked by dropping the tool test, where it fails with the row measuring the same
height under Select as under Scale.

*Keep* the valve and the gate. The multiples did not last the day: **D313** has the set that replaced
them, and the reason the first one was the wrong shape rather than one button short.

**D313 — `1x`/`2x`/`3x` became `0.5x` and `2x`, because a *relative* control has no rest position to
return to. *Changed 2026-08-23 on the maintainer's decision; the round trip tested, the anchor
deliberately not.*** D312 flagged `1x` as a known no-op and named two ways out — a half, or dropping to
two buttons. The maintainer took both at once: *"Just two buttons: 0.5x and 2x."*

**The mistake worth recording is the shape of it, not the fix.** `1x`, `2x`, `3x` is the shortcut set
for a control that *reports a state* — it offers the rest position and the two steps up from it. This
field reports nothing: a scale is applied and gone, nothing stored says a layer is "at 2x", and so
there is no 1× to return to. A relative control's obvious shortcuts are instead **the two ways out of
where it already is** — halve and double. Read that way the old set had two faults, a dead button at
one end and no button at all in the shrinking direction, and one change fixed both; *that they fell to
one change is the tell that they were one fault.*

Mechanically the row is D312's row with one cell fewer, and nothing else about the buttons moved —
`ui::label_button` at `FieldButton::Off`, plain and never selected because there is no state to be in,
straight to `commit_edit` rather than through a valve. Two cells now: `cell = (available − fw − 7 × 2)
/ 2`, committing `scale_tx(50.0)` and `scale_tx(200.0)`.

**Tested by `halving_then_doubling_puts_the_selection_back`** — two rects with strokes, `0.5x` then
`2x`, asserting every world box and every stroke width comes back identical. What it pins is that the
two are inverses **through a recomputed union**: the second call does not remember the first, it
measures the box the first one left — whose ink includes a stroke that has itself been halved — and
derives fresh factors from that. Nothing in `Scaling::Photographic`'s scalar (`sqrt(|sx·sy|)`, which is
exactly `s` under a uniform scale) or in `scale_along`'s clamp is lost on the way back.

⚠️ **What it does not pin is the anchor**, and it is said here rather than left for the test's name to
imply otherwise: *any* consistently held point round trips, so this cannot tell the union's top-left
from its bottom-right. `a_selection_scales_about_its_union_and_the_gap_grows_too` is what pins which
corner. Flipping `symmetric` *does* fail all four tests in that module — and for the wrong reason:
`resize_factors` halves the distance it divides by under `symmetric`, so the flip moves the **factor**
as well as the anchor and is not the anchor experiment it looks like. Both halves of the standing rule
are in that. The question of a green test is what would also pass it, and **a flip that bites is not
automatically a flip that bites for your reason.**

*Keep.* **Revisit if** a third multiple is ever proposed: the pair is halve and double because they are
each other's inverse, and a multiplier with no inverse in the row is `1x` in a different costume.

**D314 — A percentage typed into the Scale field committed itself as a rotation, because the row that
went away renumbered the rows beneath it. *Diagnosed with a probe and fixed 2026-08-23; the identity
tested with the wrong version inside the test, and the geometry tested beside it.*** Reported from the
machine as four screenshots in sequence: a rect with the Scale tool armed and the field at 100%; `50`
typed and nothing committed, as it should be; **`Escape` pressed instead of `Enter`**, the tool falling
back to Select — and the **rotation** field now reading 50°, the layer turned fifty degrees by a number
typed into a scale field. The fourth screenshot is the second half of it: picking the Scale tool up
again showed the field still stuck at 50%.

**egui derives a widget's id from its position among its parent's children.** D312 made the Scale row
appear only while the Scale tool is held, which made it the Transform card's first genuinely *optional*
row, and a `DragValue`'s half-typed text lives in `Context::data` under the widget's id. So `Escape`
switched the tool, took the row away, handed the rotation field the scale field's id, and the rotation
field committed the `50` it had inherited. One keystroke does all of that, which is why it is
reproducible and why nothing about it looks like a transform bug.

**Proved with a throwaway `eprintln!` of the two `Response::id`s rather than reasoned**, run under each
tool. With Scale armed the field printed `9930425302827968550` and rotation `18304658187782178510`; with
Select armed, **rotation printed `9930425302827968550`** — the scale field's id, on the field that
committed the number. The values mean nothing in themselves; the point is that *do these two widgets
share an identity* is answerable in one run, and was not guessed at.

**`inspector::transform_row(ui, name, body)` is the fix** — a row identified by name rather than by
position, wrapping the card's rows from the optional one downwards: the Scale row, the rotation/skew row
and the quarter-turn/mirror row, in **both** the single-layer and the multi-selection card. Rows *above*
the optional one were deliberately left alone, which keeps the change to the rows that need it instead
of restyling the card — X/Y is first in both cards and cannot move, and the W/H-or-`L` row above the
Scale row is the near-miss the last paragraph here is about.

**`UiBuilder::id`, not `id_salt`** — the same distinction `inspector::carried_unit` already documents,
and worth reading together with it. A salted child still folds the parent's running widget counter into
its unique id (`Ui::new`: `unique_id = stable_id.with(next_auto_id_salt)`), and that counter is exactly
the positional number being escaped, so `id_salt` alone would have left the ids inside the row moving
with it.

⚠️ **The first version of the fix was wrong in a way the id probe could not see, and this is the part
worth reading later.** Handing `UiBuilder` the row's layout directly — `UiBuilder::new().id(id)
.layout(left_to_right(Center))` — produced perfect ids and inflated every row to the height of the
panel: `Ui::horizontal` allocates a child sized to its content, where a `scope_builder` inherits the
parent's whole `max_rect`. **The card went from 235 points to 974**, and the id probe stayed green
through both. The shipped version nests instead — an identified scope wrapping a plain `ui.horizontal` —
and measures 235 again. *An identity fix wants a geometry test beside it; the two failures look nothing
alike, and only one of them shows up in the number anybody was already watching.*

**The other half of the report was the field's own memory.** `scale_pct` is now reset to 100 in
`scale_row`'s early return as well as when the valve closes. The field is a verb with a live readout
(D311) and **the commit was the only thing that ever cleared it**, so a percentage typed and then
abandoned was still sitting there the next time the tool was picked up. Nothing commits it and nothing
clears it — that is the whole of "stuck at 50%".

**Two tests, and the first one carries the wrong version inside it.**
`a_conditional_row_does_not_renumber_the_rows_below_it` draws the same two rows through
`transform_row` *and* through the plain `ui.horizontal` it replaced, asserting that the first is stable
across the row above being drawn or not and that **the second is not**. It therefore cannot pass for the
wrong reason, and cannot rot into a test of nothing if the helper is ever quietly reverted. That is
worth stating as a technique: where the old implementation is a few lines, putting it in the test beside
the new one beats describing a flip in a comment nobody re-runs.
`the_scale_row_costs_the_card_one_row` measures the card under each tool and asserts the difference is
exactly 37 points — a 28pt row and the 9 the card puts between rows — which is the assertion that caught
the 974-point version.

**The Scale row was the card's first optional row but not its only conditional block**, and saying so is
the point of this paragraph: a `Line` gets an `L` where every other kind gets W and H (D229). That pair
has never collided because the two arms are mutually exclusive — one row either way, so the count below
them does not change. ⚠️ *Not quite always:* both conditions can be false at once, since `line_ends` is
`None` for a degenerate line and `size0` is `None` for an empty group (D242 records that case), and then
the pair contributes no row at all. And being one slot, the `W` field and the `L` field are handed the
same id — harmless as far as anyone can tell, because reaching it needs the selected *kind* to change
while a field still holds uncommitted text, and taking the selection somewhere else takes the focus with
it; that is read off the code rather than pinned by a test. So the near-miss was luck twice over rather
than design.
`transform_row` makes it not matter for everything below, which is the reason to record it — the next
person adding a conditional row to this card will look at `L`, conclude the card tolerates them, and be
right only because of the helper.

*Keep.* **Fix with `transform_row`** if another optional row is ever added anywhere above the bottom of
this card, and add its name to the helper rather than reaching for `ui.horizontal`; the failure is
silent, lands in a *different* field, and reads as a transform bug rather than an identity one.

**D315 — The Scale row reviewed in use again: a valve that fired twice, an `Escape` that committed, a
field that would not read out the canvas, and a right-click that moved the selection. *Fixed
2026-08-23; three of the four tested on a headless app — the first two through real key events — and
the fourth read-verified and said so.*** Four reports from the machine, all from driving the row
D311–D314 built.

**The valve fired twice, and it was reproduced rather than reasoned.** Reported as Escape *"commits the
scale but doesn't reflect it in the canvas… the 200px rect stayed 200. But when I went back to scale and
did 50%, this time committing with Enter, the field became 50px wide. So the first scale was somehow
registered somewhere."* ⚠️ **The inference was wrong and the observation was exact**, which is worth
saying because the report is what made the test worth writing. The `Escape` did nothing at all — it
switches the tool, the row goes away (D312), and no valve runs. ⚠️ *How the key reaches that tool
switch was recorded here as unaccounted for, and **D317 accounted for it**:* the objection was that
`input::resolve` returns no actions at all while `ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()` — any focused
widget, a `DragValue` included — so a field holding the keyboard ought to swallow the press before
`OndinApp::escape`'s ladder ever sees it. It does not, because **egui surrenders focus while
processing input**: by the time `resolve` runs, the focus that would have gated it is already gone and
the `Escape` press is still in `input`. So the tool switch the machine showed here and in D314's four
screenshots was never mysterious, and the same one frame carries the key to `cancel_gesture` and to the
valve — which is the whole mechanism of D317. What produced the extra halving was the
**`Enter`** edit applying itself twice. `inspector::scale_row` returns its `Response` now so a test can
reach the real widget, and driving it through `RawInput` — click to focus, an `Event::Text` per
character, then a key — failed on the first run at **25 where 50 was expected**. A frame trace named
it: `lost_focus=true` → commit 50% → w 100→50, and then on the *next* frame `lost_focus=true` again →
commit 50% → w 50→25. **egui reports `lost_focus()` on two consecutive frames and hands the typed value
back on both.** That is the whole of the bug, it is not peculiar to this row, and **D316** is the same
fault found in the shared valve for every field in the app.

**`Escape` abandons the edit now, and the guard is explicit because egui's is not.** egui does **not**
revert a `DragValue`'s number on `Escape`: `ui.rs` builds every field with `update_while_editing(true)`,
so each keystroke has already been written through the `&mut`, and egui's own `!key_pressed(Escape)`
tests merely skip the re-*parse* at `lost_focus`. The value the valve is handed on that frame is
therefore the typed one, and without a guard the key that means *cancel* everywhere else in the app
would apply the edit. `edit_valve` refuses the commit while `Escape` is down, and
`escaping_the_field_abandons_the_edit` pins it. ⚠️ *Load-bearing:* the guard looks redundant if you
believe egui reverts, and that belief is the thing to check against `drag_value.rs` before deleting it
— the test's own doc comment argued exactly that when this was written, and if it still does, it is
wrong.

**The field reads out a canvas drag.** Asked for on the machine: *"When I scale with the bounding box in
the canvas, the scale field doesn't show the percentage it's scaling. In this case, it's just an
indicator and once I release the mouse, it can go back to 100%."* `canvas::live_scale_pct` compares the
**previewed** union against the **committed** one, which is the only reading available — no scale is
stored anywhere (D311), so "how much has this grown" is a comparison rather than a value to look up. One
number out of two factors by the **geometric mean**, `sqrt(|sx·sy|)`: the same reduction
`Scaling::scalar` already uses to give a stroke width one number from a squashed box, and exactly `s`
under a uniform scale. An axis with no extent contributes 1, which is the answer `scale_along` gives it
too. It is written into `scale_pct` from the `Drag::Resize` arm while `Tool::Scale` is armed, and
`scale_row`'s reset grew a third clause (`!canvas_scaling()`) or the readout would be blanked on the
frame after it was written. **It commits nothing**: the valve fires on the *field's* own engagement and
that never begins. `the_field_reads_out_a_scale_that_is_still_a_preview` drives it through a preview
rather than a commit, because that is the state the readout exists for and the only one in which the two
boxes differ.

**A cancelling right-click no longer moves the selection.** Reported as *"I select layer 1, then scrub
any field. I right click to cancel over layer 2. The change is rolled back, but now the 2nd layer is
selected."* `canvas_context_menu` sets the selection — the layer branch's `set_one`, the guide branch's
`set_guide` — **before** it calls `open_context_menu`, which is where the `gesture_cancelled` guard
lives. So no menu opened, correctly, and the click had already re-selected. The guard sits at the top of
`canvas_context_menu` now, where the click is claimed, which is what the comment above the call already
claimed was happening: *"a gesture the same button cancelled has already set the flag that **spends this
click**"*. R1 says spending the click, not spending the menu. ⚠️ **Read-verified, not tested** — driving
it needs a canvas response reporting `secondary_clicked`, and that is stated here rather than left to be
assumed.

**Reviewed and accepted on the machine, 2026-08-23**, all four: the canvas drag drives the field, the
right-click cancel no longer selects the layer under it, and `Escape` leaves the rect alone — though
the `Escape` half needed D317 before that was true, since the abandon was being undone a frame later.

*Keep.* **Revisit if** anything else on the canvas grows a claim on the right-click: the rule is that
the flag is asked once, at the top of whatever function claims the button, and never beside the last
thing that function does.

**D316 — Every keystroke was an undo step, in the one valve every inspector control routes through.
*Fixed and tested 2026-08-23, flip-checked against the old condition; the blast radius is every valved
field in the app and is being ridden on the machine.*** D315's doubled commit looked like a quirk of a
*relative* field. It was not. `edit_valve` — the §9.3 seam every inspector control puts a transaction
through — committed on `drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()`, and **a `DragValue` reports
`changed()` on every keystroke**.

**The maintainer tested it directly and photographed each step.** Typing `100` into the width of a 200pt
rect, pressing `Enter`, then pressing undo five times: `100`, `100`, `100`, `10`, `1`, `200`. Five
entries in the history for one edit — one per keystroke, plus two more from the doubled `lost_focus()`.
Their comment: *"So… yeah. It's kinda bad :D"*

**Why nobody had seen it for as long as the valve has existed**: every one of those commits writes the
same *final* number, so the shape on screen is right and only the history is wrong. An absolute field
survives being committed per keystroke — `W` typed as `1`, `10`, `100` ends at 100 — which is exactly
why D312 diagnosed this as a problem with *relative* fields and gave the Scale row a valve of its own.
That reading was too narrow, and D312 has been amended rather than left standing as the explanation.
*A fault that leaves the visible state correct is invisible until somebody counts the invisible state.*

**The fix is a question about engagement, and `edit_valve_on_release` is gone.** The valve asks whether
the control is **engaged** — `dragged() || has_focus()` — and commits on the frame that stops being
true; "ends" is a transition, not an event, however many times egui announces it. ⚠️ **Both halves of
that test are load-bearing**: a bare `Sense::click_and_drag` region is not a `Widget` and never reports
focus at all (the picker's wheel, the gradient strip), while a field being typed into is never dragged.
With that rule the two valves became the same function, so there is one again; D312's second valve
lasted a day. Keyed on the widget's own id in `Context::data`, through **one** accessor rather than two
nested — `data_mut` inside `data_mut` deadlocks (`CLAUDE.md`).

**It previews while engaged, which is what keeps typing live.** Committing per keystroke was also what
made a typed width appear on the canvas as it was typed; the preview does that now and the document
hears about it once. That is D51's rule — preview and commit are the same transaction, built from the
committed document — applied to the keyboard rather than only to the pointer.

⚠️ **This entry claimed `cancel_gesture` was *not* what abandons a typed edit, and D317 proved the
opposite by tracing it.** The claim rested on `input::resolve` returning no actions at all while
`ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()` — any focused widget, a `DragValue` included — and concluded that
`Action::Escape` is never dispatched from a field that owns the keyboard, so the whole ladder in
`OndinApp::escape` sits out the keystroke. It does not: **egui surrenders focus while processing
input**, so the focus that would have gated `resolve` is already gone when it runs and the press is
still in `input`. `Escape` therefore reaches `cancel_gesture`, which finds the preview this change
installs during typing and drops it — and that is what abandons the edit. The valve's own `Escape`
guard (D315) is still load-bearing and still tested, because it covers the frames where the ladder
stops at an earlier rung (an open picker, a live text session) and never reaches the cancel at all.
⚠️ *The in-flight preview turned out to have a cost as well as this benefit*: dropping it exposed a
latch the cancelled frame was not spending, which is D317 — read it beside this.

**Tested by `typing_a_value_leaves_exactly_one_step_in_the_history`**, which asserts the history grows
by exactly 1 and that one undo returns the layer, driven through real key events by D315's
`drive_field`. Flip-checked against the old three-way condition, where it fails on the first assertion.
It is driven on the **Scale** field because that is the widget the test module can reach, and the entry
says so rather than letting the name imply otherwise: the valve under test is the shared one and the
count is the whole point.

⚠️ **The blast radius is every valved control in the inspector**, not the Scale row: the colour picker,
the guides, the stroke widths, the export fields, typography. Their commit *timing* moved on this date.
**That warning was ridden and found good — reviewed and accepted on the machine on 2026-08-23**, with a
typed width landing one undo level, typing previewing live, and a right-click cancel of a scrub leaving
the history clean; it is a record now rather than an open risk. It still earns its place: the next
report about a control committing late, twice, or not at all is to be read against this change first —
and one such report arrived the same day, D317.

⚠️ **One inspector control was outside the valve's reach the whole time, and the blast-radius list
above could not say so, because it is a list of *categories*.** `inspector::paint_hex_field` commits
straight to `commit_edit` on `resp.lost_focus()`, so the engagement latch never reached it and a bare
click through the field committed **twice** — this entry's own symptom, at the one site this entry does
not name (§15 D517, 2026-09-07). It is guarded by a **comparison** rather than by the valve: nothing is
written unless the typed bytes differ from `hex_of` of the colour that is already there, which also
closes the quantisation D517 is mostly about and which the valve alone would not have. So "one edit,
one commit" holds at that field by a second mechanism, and D517 records the routing as still owed.
⚠️ **One clause of this valve did reach it in the end, and it took a defect to find out which**
(§15 D808, 2026-09-19): the field committed a typed colour on `Escape`, because `lost_focus()` alone
cannot tell a cancel from a confirm, and so did three other chrome text fields. The `Escape` refusal is
`ui::defocus_commits` now and all four call it. **The engagement latch still does not reach any of
them, and is not meant to** — a text field has no per-keystroke value to smooth out, and a half-typed
hex is a real colour, so the routing D517 left owing is answered with that sentence rather than with
the valve.

*Keep.* **Revisit if** a control ever genuinely wants a commit per keystroke; the answer is that it
wants a **preview** per keystroke, which is what it now gets.

**D317 — A cancelled frame did not spend the edit, so the cancel worked and the commit landed one frame
later. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-23, the test flip-checked after its first version turned out to be
vacuous; reviewed and accepted on the machine the same day.*** Reported as a flash: *"I set it to 50%
and pressed escape. It went like: 1) rect was 100px, 2) single frame of 200px, 3) rect was 100px again.
So there is a flash of the rect with the previous size in the canvas. That doesn't happen when pressing
enter. Only when pressing escape."*

**The follow-up is worth recording as a technique.** A single frame is unreadable in use — *"a 1 frame
flash was impossible for me to read"* — so the maintainer **video-recorded the app and scrubbed the
capture in DaVinci** to photograph the frame. Four screenshots on a 137pt rect showed the flash at 137
and, critically, the **final** state at **68.5**. So the scale had been *committed* and the flash was
the abandon working for exactly one frame before something re-applied it. My reading up to that point —
"Escape abandons, and the flash is cosmetic" — was wrong, and it was the screenshot of the *end state*
rather than of the symptom that overturned it.

**Three code-reasoned hypotheses, all wrong, and then one instrumented run.** A ten-line `eprintln!` in
`edit_valve` and `scale_row`, which the maintainer ran once, named it immediately:

```
ROW   pass=1479 pct=50 stored=50 focus=false ...      ← no valve line at all
ROW   pass=1480 pct=50 stored=100 focus=false ...
VALVE pass=1480 engaged=false was=true esc=false → COMMIT
```

The chain, in four steps. **`Escape` does reach `OndinApp::escape`** — egui surrenders focus while
processing input, so `ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()` is already false by the time `input::resolve`
runs and the action dispatches. That is the gap D315 flagged as unaccounted for, and D315 has been
amended rather than left holding the open question. `cancel_gesture` then finds the preview that
**typing** installs — new since D316 — and drops it, which is pass 1479 and the one frame of un-scaled
rect. It sets `gesture_cancelled`, and `edit_valve` returned on that flag **before** updating its
engagement latch, so the frame that cancelled never consumed the transition. The flag clears at the end
of a frame with nothing held down, which for a key press is the same frame; the next frame then sees
`was_engaged` without `engaged`, finds the `Escape` key gone from `input` so that D315's guard cannot
fire, and commits the edit the cancel had just thrown away. **The cancel worked, the guard worked, and
the latch simply survived the cancellation.**

**The fix is one reordering**: the latch is read and written *before* the `gesture_cancelled` bail, so a
cancelled frame **spends** the transition. That is the rule `context-menus.md` R1 already states for a
click — whatever calls the gesture off has used it up — applied to the edit instead of to the menu.

⚠️ **The scope is every cancelled valved edit, not `Escape` on this field.** Right-clicking to cancel a
scrub on any field in the inspector had the same deferred commit; it is invisible on an *absolute*
field, because the field re-reads the committed value and the late commit writes back the number that
is already there. That is exactly D316's shape — visible state correct, invisible state wrong — and it
is the **second** fault of that shape found in this one valve in two days. A third is worth suspecting
before it is worth ruling out.

**Tested by `inspector::scale_row_tests::a_cancelled_edit_does_not_commit_on_the_next_frame`**, driven
through real events. ⚠️ **Its first version was vacuous and passed against the unfixed code**: it set
`gesture_cancelled` on a pass where the field **still had focus**, and there is no transition for the
next frame to inherit unless the cancel and the loss of focus fall on the *same* pass — which is what
`Escape` does on the machine and what the test now reproduces. Flipped properly, by moving the latch
back below the bail, it fails at `50.0` where `100.0` was expected, which is the reported bug exactly.
*A cancellation test has to cancel the thing at the moment it would otherwise complete.* The flag is
still set by hand rather than driven from a secondary press, so the **right-click** half of the scope
above is reasoned from the shared valve and not pinned; D311's `!dragged()` reset guard is unpinned for
