the same reason, since `drive_field` only clicks and types.

*Keep.* **Revisit if** anything else grows an early return in `edit_valve`: the latch has to be spent
above every one of them, and the ordering looks like an accident of style until it costs a frame. The
instrumentation that found this is in history as commit `c7be738` if the trace is ever wanted again —
**when a question is "which frame does what", the function's text does not contain the answer**, so
reach for the trace on the first failed explanation rather than the third.

**D318 — D303's sweep was scoped to `crates/`, so the three documents went on stating the reason it had
just retired. *Fixed at fifteen live sites across all four documents; thirty dated §15 passages are named
below as a queue — Fix.*** D303 built `OndinApp::headless` and swept the 38 doc comments that had said
some form of "`OndinApp` needs a wgpu render state, so this is read rather than tested". **`docs/` was
not in that sweep.** Fifty-two lines in this file cite that reason over about forty-five passages, plus
five in `architecture.md`, three in `roadmap.md` and one in `context-menus.md`. **Eleven were audited as
live and present-tense; the audit found four more** — this file's D238 and D266 closings, and
`architecture.md`'s `mask_card_targets` and `crop_chrome` — and every one of the fifteen was false in
exactly the way D303's own ⚠️ at D35 predicted: *"every one of those sentences is now false in its
reason, whatever is still true of its conclusion."*

**This is the mirror image of the drift `CLAUDE.md` warns about, which is why it survived a whole day of
people reading these files.** The usual fault here is a document asserting a feature the code never had.
This is a document asserting a *limit* the code had just lost — and a limit is a reason **not** to write
a test, so every day it stood cost coverage rather than merely being wrong. `roadmap.md` had got as far
as contradicting itself on one page: the *Now · Text* section read "the reason that list was unreachable
is gone as of 2026-08-22 (§15 D303) … the line chrome, `pen_verb` routing, autopan and the cursor ladder
**written and flip-checked the same day**", while two sections above it a bullet still said the line
chrome could not be tested because `OndinApp` needs a wgpu render state. *A sweep is scoped by the
command that runs it — `grep -rn crates/` is not `grep -rn .` — and the change that made the code honest
is the one that left the record wrong.*

**A false *reason* is not a false *conclusion*, and each correction says which it was.** Three sites had
both die at once and are simple closures: `pen_verb`'s routing (D123's closing note, discharged), the
arrow-key loop's wiring (D213), and a lone line's chrome (D238) together with `canvas::autopan` and
`resize_tx`. Three had only the reason die and now read **"writable now and unwritten"**, which is the
phrasing D303's sweep adopted for exactly this and is a queue rather than an excuse: D36's ruler origin,
D189's thumbnail clearances, and D214's four context-menu rules — the last of which had `context-menus.md`
§10 saying they "cannot be" unit tests, when several tests in `canvas.rs` already pump `RawInput` through
a headless app. `architecture.md`'s lone-container group/ungroup refusal joins them. **Four
`architecture.md` passages kept their *practice* and lost only their reason**: `sync_paint_collapse`,
`extent_band`, `mask_card_targets` and `crop_chrome` are still free functions, but because the decision
is addressable on its own terms and a test of it should not have to stand a panel up first — the better
argument D303 already made, and the one that does not expire. `crop_chrome`'s passage keeps its *other*
half intact, because where a `&mut self` method is called from is the one thing `headless` genuinely does
not change.

⚠️ **Thirty passages in this file still state the retired reason and were deliberately left.** Each is a
dated record of what was true when it was written, and rewriting thirty §15 entries in one pass is a diff
nobody can review; this entry retires the reason for all of them at once. The rule that follows is the
useful part: **do not write a new one.** Anything reading "`OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly" in an
entry dated before 2026-08-22 is evidence; the same sentence in a newer one is a bug. The count is
`grep -cE 'headlessly|wgpu .RenderState.|wgpu render state|wgpu device|wgpu seam|.OndinApp. seam'
docs/decisions.md` → **52**, over about 45 distinct passages, of which eight were corrected here and
thirty remain live; stating the method is what makes the next re-check a comparison rather than a fresh
argument about what to count.

⚠️ **And checking the brief against the code found a green test whose doc comment overclaimed its own
coverage. The comment was the drift, not the test.**
`a_lone_line_gets_no_selection_chrome_but_a_line_in_a_set_does` drives `selection_handles` and asserted
exactly what it should; its comment said one assertion therefore covers the size badge too, which is
the one thing **D266 exists to deny** — three sites ask `lone_line`
separately, and the covered one is the reader that never had the bug. That is the sharper lesson of this
entry, because it is not the failure mode the suite can catch: a test that is right and a comment that
is wrong about it reads as coverage, and the next person to trust it deletes something. **D319 is the
mechanism** — the doc gate cannot see inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module either, so a test's prose is the
one text here that nothing at all checks.

**Both halves were answered rather than filed.** `a_lone_line_gets_no_size_badge_and_a_rect_does` now
pins the badge, flip-checked against its guard's deletion. The **box outline** turned out not to be a
missing test at all — `draw_canvas` matches `line_ends` first, so the arm the `!lone` guard protects
needs a selected node absent from `Resolved`, and a test of it would pass with the guard deleted. D266
records that as a named blind spot with a `*Keep.*`, which is why nothing went back into `roadmap.md`:
one half landed and the other is a decided non-goal, and neither is open work.

*Fix, and the fix is the queue above.* **Revisit if** a fourth document ever grows a testability claim:
the lesson is not about wgpu, it is that a reason recorded in two places rots in the one nobody swept,
which is the same shape as D302's "a gate written down in two places is two gates".

**D319 — The doc gate cannot see inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module, so no test's doc comment is checked —
and in this project that is most of the prose there is. *Measured, not reasoned; no flag closes it, so
the answer is a practice — Keep.*** D296 made `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` a gate and called it the
only one that reads the doc comments, which is true and reads as broader than it is. `cargo doc` builds
**without the `test` cfg**, so a `#[cfg(test)] mod` is simply absent from the crate rustdoc walks, and
the `#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links, rustdoc::invalid_html_tags)]` on all five crate roots
never gets the chance to fire there. **Measured 2026-08-23:** a deliberately broken
`[`totally_nonexistent_item_xyz`]` inserted into the doc comment of
`a_line_trades_w_and_h_for_one_l_and_a_point_gets_no_size_field_at_all` — in `inspector.rs`'s
`#[cfg(test)] mod line_length_tests` — survived a full run at **exit 0 with no warning**. Forcing the
cfg on does not rescue it: rustdoc excludes `#[test]`-attributed items from documentation under any
flags, so even `RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg test" cargo doc --document-private-items` gives such a function no
page and therefore no link check. That second half came from a subagent's isolated reproduction rather
than from this tree, and is the part to re-measure before anything is built on it.

🚨 **Every number in the two paragraphs below was stale by 2026-09-09 and they are corrected in
place** (§15 D622, `[A8-L6-01]`). *Eighteen* files is **23** and *nine* links is **18**; the entry
also missed a **third** target kind, `build.rs`, which the doc gate is equally blind to. The figure
did not rot by neglect — it rotted because suites landed, and no commit that adds a test file has any
reason to think about a count in a §15 entry. **One number had seven stale copies at two different
values**, across this entry, `CLAUDE.md`, `SKILL.md` and `rust-verify.md`; the copies outside here
now carry no number at all and say to count during the sweep, which is the only version of this that
cannot go stale. D622 has the argument.

**And `#[cfg(test)]` is only half of it — the other half was measured the same day, and it is clean.**
The **23** files under `crates/…/tests/` are separate test *targets* rather than gated modules, so
the `test` cfg is irrelevant to them. They are missed because `cargo doc` documents lib and bin targets,
and **the flag that would ask it for a test target does not exist**: `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps
--tests` → `error: unexpected argument '--tests' found`, exit 1. That is
where the analogy to D302 breaks down, at the one point that matters: the flag which closed the clippy
hole has no counterpart here, and that is most of the reason this entry cannot carry a `Fix`. **There are
two mechanisms, not one.** An integration test file is also **its own crate root**, so it carries none of
the five `#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links, …)]` — the only crate-level attribute anywhere in
the set is `#![allow(dead_code)]` in `tests/common/mod.rs`, and ⚠️ **that file is not a crate root
at all**, being reached through `mod common;`, so the set of test crate roots carries *no*
crate-level attribute — so even a rustdoc pointed at them would
warn rather than fail. "Add a doc step for the tests" is therefore not enough on its own.

🚨 **And there is a third target kind, which this entry did not know about: `build.rs`.**
`crates/ondin-app/build.rs` carries 22 lines of `//!` prose, and a `//! [` + a nonexistent item left
in it passes the doc gate at **exit 0** — while `cargo fmt --check` prints a diff for the same probe
and clippy warns under both spellings. So of the six gates, the doc gate alone is blind to it, and
links have lived there: two now-deleted `pub fn`s in that file carried D405 citations (D409's
paragraph records them).

**18 intra-doc links live there today and all 18 resolve** — re-counted 2026-09-09; the nine below
are the 2026-08-23 measurement and are kept as the record of what was checked then:
`build::group`, `build::outline`, `build::outermost` and `build::paint_targets`,
all in scope through the `use ondin_core::{… build}` in `tests/build.rs` and `tests/bulk.rs`; then
`kind_name` in `goldens.rs`, `image_doc` in `png.rs`, `image_fixture` in `svg.rs`,
`ondin_core::ImageRef`, and `fixture` in `tests/common/mod.rs`. The count is
`find crates -path "*/tests/*" -name "*.rs" | xargs grep -nE '^ *//[/!].*\[`'`, and **it must be the
`find` rather than a `crates/*/tests/*.rs` glob** — the glob reports 17 files and 8 links, because it
does not descend to `tests/common/mod.rs`, and a shared fixture module is exactly where a suite's
most-reused prose lives. So the honest state of this half is **clean today and guarded by nothing**: nine
resolving links whose only protection is somebody repeating that check.

**So every intra-doc link in a test's prose is decoration, and the convention was already in the source
ahead of the rule.** `CanvasRenderer`'s `gpu` field writes "`CanvasRenderer::headless` — not a link,
because it is `#[cfg(test)]` and rustdoc builds without that cfg": plain backticks and a sentence saying
why is the whole practice. Two smaller traps sit under it that would otherwise be blamed on the gate.
`Self::x` on a bare `#[test] fn` cannot resolve in any case — there is no enclosing `impl` for `Self` to
mean anything — and a bare `OndinApp::draw_size_badge` written from inside a nested test module does not
resolve either; it needs `super::` or `crate::`, which is why the test above reaches its own subject as
`use crate::app::OndinApp`. Neither is reachable by the gate, which is exactly why neither has ever been
reported.

**This is D302's lesson a second time, and worse in one specific way.** D302 was `cargo clippy` without
`--all-targets` never linting a single `#[cfg(test)]` module; this is the same hole in the other gate.
The difference is what stands behind it: a test's doc comment is where this project keeps its reasoning,
its flip-check notes and its ⚠️ traps — the sentences most worth trusting, and the only ones nothing
verifies. It is also the mechanism behind D318's closing ⚠️, where a green test carried a comment
claiming one `selection_handles` assertion covered the size badge and it did not. **No gate could have
caught that comment.** What caught it was somebody counting the call sites by hand, which is the only
check there is.

**It has bitten twice more since, both on 2026-08-24 and both with every gate green.** D322's insertion
reassigned thirteen lines of a doc comment onto the wrong item, and D329's deletion of `badge_angle` left
three `[`badge_angle`]` links resolving to nothing — all three inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules, so `cargo
doc` exited 0. Each was found by grepping the name after the edit. *That grep is the practice this entry
ends on, and it is now the thing with a track record: three finds, no gate.*

**Two counts were deliberately not taken, which is worth saying so the next reader does not go and get
them.** There is no census of the intra-doc links inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules: the number is large, it
moves with every test written, and unlike the nine above it has **no failure mode** — those links are
*known* to be unchecked and the convention writes them as plain backticks anyway. A number nobody can act
on and that rots weekly is the kind this project's own rules warn against.

🚨 **The second half of that paragraph said `--document-private-items` should stay *off*, and it was
false — measured, not argued** (§15 D622, `[A8-L6-05]`). It read:

> ~~And `--document-private-items` stays off the gate command: a broken link is reported whatever the
> item's visibility, which is the only thing this gate is for, so the flag would change what gets
> *rendered* and nothing about what gets *caught*.~~

**rustdoc does not read what it does not document.** A deliberately broken link on a *private*
method (`svg_in::Builder::pick_family`) leaves `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` at **exit 0**, and
adding the flag catches it. The claim was never measured; it was reasoned from what a gate is *for*.
The flag was then off for the nine days between this entry and 2026-09-01, over a body of code that
is almost entirely private — and the day it went on it surfaced **three** broken links plus **eight**
naming a struct with no `impl` block at all.

⚠️ **This is the worst shape a record can take, and it is worse than an ordinary stale sentence: a
live *Keep* entry that tells the next reader to remove a working gate.** The other holes on this
list are gates that do not cover what they claim; this one is a gate that existed, was argued away
in §15 on a false premise, and had to be re-discovered by probe. **When the record says a check is
unnecessary, check** — which is the mirror of D445's *"when the record says a check is impossible,
check"*, and the two now bracket this entry from both sides.

*Keep, with the consequence named rather than a `Fix`, because no flag closes this* — and there is
literally no flag: `--tests` does not exist and the test crates carry no deny. A `Fix` verdict
would imply a switch exists and send the next reader hunting for it. The practice that replaces it:
**when a test's doc comment makes a claim about what the test covers, that claim is checked by hand or
not at all**, so write it as a claim somebody *can* check — name the assertion and name the call sites,
as D318's correction had to. Note that D296's flip-check was real and still missed this, because a dead
link placed where the gate looks proves only that the gate looks there; the question to ask of a green
gate is the one to ask of a green test — *what would also pass this*. And the sentence to set beside
D302's: a gate written down in two places is two gates, and **a gate described more broadly than it runs
is a gate people stop checking behind**. `CLAUDE.md`'s doc-gate paragraph claimed `cargo doc` "resolves
every `[`link`]` in every doc comment"; it now reads "every doc comment it can *see*" and carries the
measurement.

**D827 — Two of the hand-written checks standing in for gates could not return a hit, and one of them
*confirmed* the thing it was written to falsify. *Both commands fixed 2026-09-22; Keep — resolved as
to the two commands, open as to the class, and no sweep has been run.***

This project keeps several checks that no gate performs, written down as shell commands in
`CLAUDE.md`. **Two were found incapable of reporting a hit on any input whatever**, by the same
mechanism, on the same day — and **both were found by *running* them, neither by reading them**,
which is the part that decides what this entry is about.

**The mechanism is one character.** In GNU grep's ERE a backslash before a backtick matches nothing:
a backtick is not a metacharacter, so escaping it produces a pattern that can never match. Both
commands escape it. Measured with controls rather than reasoned, GNU grep 3.0 in both cases.

**Instance 1 — the doc gate's re-check, which goes quiet.** D319 above ends on a practice rather than
a `Fix`, no flag closing the hole, and `CLAUDE.md` gave that practice a command: the diff-scoped grep
a session runs over its own changes, looking for a new intra-doc link written inside a `#[cfg(test)]`
module.

```
git diff <base>..HEAD -- crates/ | grep -E '^\+ *(///|//!).*\[\`'
```

Against the one-line fixture `+/// see [`Foo::bar`] for why`, **0 matches, exit 1** as written and
**1 match, exit 0** with the backslash removed. Found by running it during a session's own re-check,
getting nothing back from a diff known to contain new doc links, and then putting the two spellings
side by side. **The consequence is a false negative that looks like a clean result**: the reader
concludes *no new links to check*, which is what a healthy diff also produces.

🚨 **Instance 2 — `review/`'s second reading, which agrees with the count it was written to
contradict, and this is the one that costs.** That census has a trap that makes the closed-findings
count read too **high**: a finding id mentioned in the *body* of a fix-log row is extracted as closed.
The defence is a second extraction compared against the first — *"extract `^\| \`\[` as a second
reading and compare"*. Against the fixture ``| `[S8.2-L1-01]` | High | fixed |``, **0 matches, exit 1**
as written and **1 match, exit 0** unescaped.

**Set the two consequences side by side, because they are different failures.** The first returns
nothing and is *indistinguishable from* a tree with no defects. The second returns an empty **second
reading**, which is then compared against the first and reads as *"no fix-log row names a finding in
its body"* — so the inert command does not merely fail to falsify the census, it **confirms** it. A
check written specifically to catch a count reading high, silently agreeing with the high count. *A
broken check that goes quiet wastes a reading; a broken check that answers in the shape of a
corroboration is worth less than no check at all, because it is spent as evidence.*

**This is D732's shape twice**, and the advice that came out of that entry is the advice these two
were there to be caught by: *when a claim comes with a command, read the command against the claim,
not just its output.* 🚨 **Reading is exactly what failed here, twice — the patterns look right.**
`'^\+ *(///|//!).*\[\`'` reads as a careful author escaping everything that might be special, and
that is the reason it survived: the defect is invisible to the sort of attention that catches a wrong
anchor or a missing `-r`. **What found both was running them against a fixture that should match.**
So the advice needs its second half: *a command you cannot falsify by reading, control.* One line
each, and both took under a minute.

🚨 **One tell was on the page the whole time and was never read as one.** The doc-gate grep was
credited with **a catch per session for six sessions running**. Either those catches came from
somewhere else, or the command was typed differently each time it was run. **Which of the two is not
recoverable**, and this entry says so rather than guessing: the sessions are not at a resolvable sha
(the reset of 2026-09-16), and a grep leaves no trace of the spelling it was invoked with. What *is*
certain is that the **written** command has never been capable of the catches attributed to it — so
the claim and the command were two different things, and only the claim was ever checked. *A run
record is evidence about the command only if the command is what was run.*

⚠️ **The correct spelling was already in the tree, in D319 above.** That entry's own count of the
integration tests' links is `find crates -path "*/tests/*" -name "*.rs" | xargs grep -nE '^ *//[/!].*\[`'`
— `\[` and then a **bare** backtick, which works. So one check existed twice, once correctly and once
incapably, and the incapable copy was the one in the file everybody reads. *A gate written down in two
places is two gates*, which is D302's sentence and D319's closing one, arriving from the direction
where the two copies **disagree about whether the check runs at all**.

⚠️ **Fixing the commands buys no gate, which is why this is *Keep*.** `cargo doc` still cannot see a
`#[cfg(test)]` module (D319); `review/`'s census is still hand-run; both corrected greps are still
habits somebody has to remember; and D319's zero-dangling-links figure is an invariant kept by
reading. The corrected doc grep also asks only half its question: a `#[cfg(test)]` **item** at module
level — not inside a `mod tests` — is absent from rustdoc's crate by exactly D319's mechanism while
sitting outside every hand-rolled check that looks for the module. *Ask whether the item is
`cfg(test)`, not whether it is inside a test module.*

🚨 ***Fix:* no sweep has been run, and the honest state is two found out of an unknown population.**
What was checked is the commands this session had reason to touch, plus the `review/` one. `CLAUDE.md`
carries many more — greps, `awk` programs, `comm` pipelines, the citation census, the `///`-run length
ranking — and **not one of the rest has been controlled.** Every count and every clean reading this
project has ever taken from an uncontrolled command is worth exactly as much as the command was
capable of. **Run each of them against a fixture that must match, and against one that must not.**
Two of two checked came back dead; that is not a base rate, but it is not a reason to assume the rest
are alive either.

⚠️ **A third command was found misreading its output the same day, and it fails the opposite way** —
worth recording beside these because it completes the picture. The citation census run in its wide
form from the repository root over `.` picks up `target/debug/build/…/category.rs`, generated
`unicode-general-category` tables, and reports **`D00` and `D000`** in the unresolved half: two false
positives that read exactly like a citation with no entry behind it. Run it from `crates/`, or with
`--exclude-dir=target`. **So one command could not report a hit, one reported an absence as a
corroboration, and one reported hits that were not citations — and all three outputs were plausible.**
None of the three is falsifiable by looking at what it printed.

*(Record-only, no production line changed. **The citation is planted by hand** on
`app::CLIPBOARD_OFF`, the one doc in the tree that narrates a doc-gate catch and the neighbour of
D798's note on the D319 convention — which is where a reader meets the question *what catches the
other kind*. The answer, at that site and here, is **nothing does**, and until the sweep above is run
nobody knows how much of what stands in for it works.)*

**D320 — A crop is a resize, so the lock reaches it: image editing refuses on a locked layer, and the
row dims *because* the mode refuses. *Decided, built and tested both ways. Keep — read the ordering
paragraph before touching either half.*** D268 shipped *Edit image* deliberately undimmed and wrote the
reason down as "a match rather than an exemption": no door onto the mode read `Node::locked`, so a row
that refused would have been the only one that did, which is D261's two-doors-disagree failure arrived
at by tidying rather than by drift. That was honest, and it was also the shape of the problem —
*matching a gap is not agreement, and a comment that says "consistent with X" is only as good as X*.
The gap is closed now rather than matched.

**The argument that settled it is one verb.** `canvas.rs`'s `crop_resize_tx` writes through
`tools::resize_layer` — literally, before it appends the `SetFills` that records the new crop. That is
the same write *Original size* has been dimmed on a locked layer for since it was built, on grounds
the assertion beside it still states in as many words: "resizing the node is a write and the lock
reaches it". Those two rows are the whole of `context-menus.md` §5.7's head since D305, adjacent in
one `Group::Head`, and they disagreed about whether resizing a locked layer is a write.
`Item::EditPoints`, the other geometry-editing mode a menu row steps into, dims two rows below. The
maintainer's decision was three words — *"The lock should block it"* — and crop-is-a-resize is why
they are the right three.

**Refused in the mode rather than at a door, and the ordering is the load-bearing part.**
`OndinApp::begin_image_edit` is the one funnel all four doors pass through (D305 made it one), so a
single early return covers `Enter`'s arm, the canvas double-click, the *Edit image* row and the
inspector's fill-row click: it posts *"This layer is locked — unlock it to edit the picture"* and
returns before `set_one` and `choose_tool`. **Only then** does `Item::EditImage` take
`.dim_if(locked, LOCKED)`. The row dims *because* the mode refuses, never instead of it — D261's rule
is that a menu must not refuse where the chord allows, and it is kept by the mode changing first and
the row following. Dimming the row while the mode still allowed it would have been the defect even
though the resulting menu is identical, which is why the order is worth a paragraph rather than a
comma.

**And the test relationship is the thing a future reader would undo.** The pin is
`menu::tests::a_lock_dims_both_of_the_picture_rows` — its **fourth** name, renamed from
`a_lock_dims_original_size_and_leaves_edit_image_alone` with its `EditImage` assertions inverted — and
that test carried a warning that the plausible wrong version had become "a hand seeing a single dimmed
row beside a live one and making them agree". **That warning was right, and it was answered rather
than deleted**, mechanically: with the guard deleted from `begin_image_edit`, the menu test still
passes and only `app::image_edit_lock_tests::a_locked_picture_refuses_every_door` fails. So the menu
test alone genuinely would be asserting a tidy-up, and its guard is the app test — both doc comments
now say so, in both directions. The app test asserts its fixture carries a croppable picture *before*
the claim, drives the funnel directly and through `enter_action`, and was flipped both ways: deleting
the guard arms `ImageEdit` on the locked layer (`left: ImageEdit, right: Select`), and making the guard
unconditional fails the **control** (`left: Select, right: ImageEdit`) — the vacuous version, a mode
nobody can enter at all.

**The inspector's fill row stops advertising what it would refuse, and only that.** `paint_row`'s
`door` predicate now requires `!locked_layer` beside `picture` and `row_edits_the_mode_s_picture`, and
both `on_hover_text` chains — the chip's and the *Image* label's — gained a third state carrying the
same sentence. Without it a locked layer is told "editing works on the topmost picture", which is a
*different* refusal and sends the reader hunting for a second image fill that is not there. The click
itself still fires and still reaches the funnel; what changed is the promise, by the rule that row's
own comment already stated for the two-pictures case: a row promising "edit this picture" while doing
nothing is worse than a row that promises nothing. `row_edits_the_mode_s_picture` is deliberately
untouched — it answers *which* row is the mode's picture, and the lock is a separate question answered
in the funnel. The rest of the row stays live, because a lock stops a layer being dragged about rather
than recoloured, so a locked layer's colour rows still open the picker.

**Bounded on purpose, in two directions — and D321 removed both bounds the next day.** It read
`n.locked()`, the node's own flag, matching `menu::LayerState::locked` and every other lock refusal in
the panels, so **a picture inside a locked *group* was deliberately not decided here**: nothing in core
answered effective lock as a standalone query and *Original size* did not ask it either, so making image
editing stricter than its neighbour would have re-created the inconsistency this closes, in the other
direction. And the same fault was still live for text and for points, in its worse form —
`Item::EditText` and `Item::EditPoints` both dimmed while `canvas::begin_edit_text` read no lock and
`enter_action`'s `Path` arm called `choose_tool(Tool::Node)` with none either, so those two menus refused
where `Enter` allowed, which is D261's failure itself rather than an echo of the permissive-but-consistent
state this entry left.

**Both halves are D321**, decided by the maintainer on 2026-08-23 in one sentence about what a lock on a
container *means*. The bound is left standing here rather than rewritten, because the reason it was drawn
is what D321 had to answer: one row must not be stricter than the row beside it, so the fix could not be a
second reading of the lock at this call site — it had to be a query the whole tree asks. This guard and
*Original size*'s dim did move together, as the note below asked; what did not change is that *Original
size* has only the dim behind it, its dispatch arm writing with no gate of its own (D261, D305).

*Keep. The "revisit if effective lock ever becomes something core can be asked" this entry closed with
happened the next day — see D321.*

**D321 — A locked group locks everything inside it, and the lock became one query the whole tree asks:
text, points and the picture all refuse. *Decided by the maintainer, built and tested — four new tests,
seven flips. Keep, and read the `LayerState` paragraph before merging its two fields back into one.*** Two
things at once, and the maintainer's sentence carries both: *"we should block text editing on a locked
layer in any way. We should also block it in a locked group. A locked group means everything inside is
also locked, so it's an expected behavior, not a good to have."* The first half is what D320 left in
`roadmap.md`; the second reverses the bound D320 drew for itself, which said in as many words that a
picture inside a locked group was not decided there. **A lock on a container is not a convenience laid
over the contents** — a group is one thing to the hand that locked it, so nothing inside it is editable
while it holds.

**One rule had two spellings, and the weaker one always looks like it works.**
`query::is_effectively_interactable` — private, reached only through `hit_test` — held the **only**
ancestor-aware reading of the lock in the entire tree. So every refusal outside the canvas asked
`Node::locked` and stopped at the node's own flag: four of them, each defensible on its own and each
wrong one group deep. That is D266's shape — several sites answering one question and only one of them
asking the shared answer — and a lock is the worst place to repeat it, because the weaker reading
behaves correctly on every layer that is not nested. The walk is now
`query::is_effectively_locked(doc, id)`, `pub` and exported from `lib.rs`;
`is_effectively_interactable` calls it for the lock half and keeps its own walk for visibility.

**A missing node answers `true`.** That is a refusal rather than a licence: `false` would hand a caller
permission to edit something the document does not hold. The polarity is worth noticing next to its
neighbours — this predicate's `true` and `is_effectively_interactable`'s `false` are the *same* answer,
so a lookup failure returns the opposite constant in the two functions and means the same thing in both.
**Locked alone, deliberately not visibility.** Hiding says "do not draw",
locking says "do not change", and a text layer switched off is still a text layer whose words can be
fixed — `context-menus.md` §5.9 has recorded a hidden-but-unlocked layer as fully editable all along. The
two flags travel together only inside `is_effectively_interactable`, where a click needs both.

**Three mode doors refuse now**: `canvas::begin_edit_text`, `enter_action`'s `Path` arm, and
`begin_image_edit`, upgraded from the node's own flag. Text and points are **D261's failure itself
rather than an echo of it** — `Item::EditText` and `Item::EditPoints` have always dimmed, so the menu
refused where the chord allowed, which is the exact inversion of the permissive-but-consistent state
D320 inherited. The points guard is the one that is **not** in a shared funnel, and that is worth
knowing before it is tidied into one: nothing in `tools/` reads the lock at all, so a locked path's
anchors are draggable the moment the tool is armed, which makes *arming it* the thing to refuse.

**⚠️ The brief for this entry said `Enter` was the only door left onto point editing, and it was
wrong.** `A` and the rail's `BEZIER_CURVE` button both reach `choose_tool(Tool::Node)` with no lock
check, and `canvas::edited_path` derives its subject from the **layer selection**, which a locked layer
can join from the layers panel. So selecting a locked path in the panel and pressing `A` put its anchors
up and let them be dragged, bypassing the `Enter` guard entirely. `Item::EditPoints`' own dispatch arm
is the same three lines and is still shut only by the row being dimmed.

**The same commit shut it, and this entry then said otherwise for two days.** Of the two places a guard
could go — inside `choose_tool` or inside `edited_path` — the second was taken: a lock check in the
general tool switch would be a rule about one kind living in the code that knows about none, whereas
**arming onto nothing is an existing, understood state**, exactly what pressing `A` over a *rectangle*
already does. And `edited_path` is the one query every reader of "which path is being edited" passes
through — `node_press` opens with `match self.edited_path()` and its `None` arm only picks or clears the
selection, `draw_points` returns on it, and `pick_leaf`/`hit_test` already skipped a locked node at any
depth — so one guard covers all of them, and `Item::EditPoints`' undimmed three lines now arm a tool
that finds no subject. `app::image_edit_lock_tests::arming_the_node_tool_finds_no_subject_on_a_locked_path`
pins it, asserting on **`edited_path`** rather than on the tool for precisely that reason; its flip
removes the guard and the locked path comes back as `Some` with the tool armed, which is the state where
its anchors drag. ⚠️ ~~**There is no analogous second door on image editing** — `Tool::ImageEdit` is armed
from exactly one place, `app::begin_image_edit`, which already refuses on the effective lock — so
`edited_image` needs no guard of its own and the shape does not generalise.~~ **False, and found on
2026-09-07 — see D463.** The mode is armed from one place, but arming is not the only way to be *in* it:
the layers panel can lock the row while image editing is already armed, and it can move the selection
onto a different, locked picture without `choose_tool` being re-entered. Neither route passes
`begin_image_edit`, so `edited_image` needed exactly the guard `edited_path` has. **The enumeration
above is of the three *mode* doors this entry closed and is correct as that**; what it is not is a list
of every place the lock has to be asked, and D463 adds two more — `edited_image` and
`canvas::image_drop_target`, a locked layer's picture having been replaceable outright by a drop or
`Ctrl+V` all along.

⚠️ **And a *verb* has a door of its own, found on 2026-09-07 — see D514.** `canvas::reverse_subpaths`
asks `edited_path` first and so inherits the guard above, but it falls back to *a single selected
`Path` outside point editing* — the same latitude the corner radius has — and that arm asked
`canvas::is_path`, a test on the **kind**. So `Shift+D` on a locked path that was merely selected
reversed its geometry and spent an undo step while `edited_path()` was answering `None` in the same
call. The sentence at the head of this entry is about the three *mode* doors and remains exact as
that; **what it is not is a promise that every verb reaching a path passes through one of them**, and
this is the second time that reading has cost something.

⚠️ **The warning above was written from the brief rather than from the tree, in the same breath as the
fix**, and it propagated: **seven** passages across four documents — this entry, its index row,
`architecture.md` §9.4, `shortcuts.md`'s `A` row *and* its `Enter` section, `context-menus.md` §5.4 and
a `roadmap.md` bullet, five of them pointing at `roadmap.md` as the place holding the open question —
all said the door was open, and all seven were false the moment they were written. The seventh was not
in the list the sweep was given and was found by grepping the key rather than the concept. `CLAUDE.md`'s warning about a premise rotting is
usually about weeks; this was one commit. *A ⚠️ costs nothing to write and is trusted for as long as it
stands, so the last thing a fix should do is read its own claims back off the tree.*

**The marquee's lock half went effective; its visibility half deliberately did not.** `hit_test` refused
a locked node at any depth while `apply_marquee` asked the own flag, so a rubber band swept over a layer
inside a locked group picked it up where clicking it could not — a band and a click disagreeing about the
same layer. ⚠️ The asymmetry left behind is known and intentional: a layer inside a *hidden* group is
still marquee-selectable. What was decided here is the lock, and hiding already has an answer written
against it (§5.9's editable hidden layer), so widening the visibility half would have been a second
decision taken by tidying.

⚠️ **The filter moved on 2026-09-10 and the rule did not** (D746). It lives in
`OndinApp::marquee_candidates` now — the list both the band and `Ctrl+A` walk — behind
`canvas_may_select`, because a predicate written at each door is what let `select_all` go on
selecting, for the eighteen days between the two entries, what the band refused. **The enumeration of doors above does not include that
one**, which is the gap D746 closes rather than a claim this entry got wrong; a reader looking for
the lock in `apply_marquee` finds a comment naming where it went and this entry's own sentence
quoted beside it.

**`menu::LayerState` carries two facts and *derives* the third, which is the transferable part.**
`ToggleLocked`'s label reads the layer's **own** flag on purpose — a row offering *Unlock* on a layer
whose own flag is already clear would write nothing and read as a broken control — while every `dim_if`
reads the effective answer. Storing the combination was tried first and was wrong within a minute: the
struct derives `Default` and its fixtures are written `LayerState { locked: true, ..default() }`, which
the compiler accepts while silently meaning *locked but not effectively locked*, a state that cannot
exist. Four tests failed on it, and a fifth written later would not have failed at all. So the
field is `locked_by_ancestor` — the ancestors alone, asked of the **parent** so the node's own flag is
not folded in twice — and `locked_within()` derives the combination. *Do not merge them back: the
invariant is structural this way and remembered the other.*

**A dimmed row gives one of two reasons, because they send the hand to different places.** "This layer
is locked" points at a toggle that is already off when the lock is on an ancestor, so the second sentence
is *"A group containing this layer is locked"* — the reason a refusal states has to name the thing that
would have to change. Both `layer_menu` and `head_rows` compute the pair, which is a duplication in the
same shape as the `locked` binding beside it.

**And the rule had no test at all.** `hit_test_is_topmost_first_and_respects_visibility` locks the node
it then fails to click, so the *own flag* was covered and the ancestor walk was not — while
`context-menus.md` C4 has always claimed the filter works "directly or through an ancestor". Measured:
breaking the walk (`cursor = None` in place of `cursor = node.parent()`) left the whole of `ondin-core`
green. That is the reason the app drifted into four own-flag refusals, and it is the general form of it —
the case that separates a strong reading from a weak one is the case nobody wrote down.
`resolve.rs::a_locked_group_locks_its_contents_for_the_query_and_for_a_click` closes it, asserting the
query and the click separately because they can fail apart.

**The rest of the coverage, and what each flip bit.** `app::image_edit_lock_tests` gained
`a_locked_layer_refuses_text_and_point_editing_too` — which asserts on the **session** (`app.text`) for
the text arm, because that is what `begin_edit_text` opens and a tool assertion would pass against the
bug — and `a_locked_group_refuses_the_picture_inside_it`; `menu::tests` gained
`a_layer_inside_a_locked_group_dims_with_the_groups_reason`, flipped three ways, one of them
`ToggleLocked`'s label pointed at `locked_within()`. Both app fixtures lock the **group** and never the
child and assert the child's own flag is still clear before claiming anything, so neither can pass by
accident. Four flips bit four different assertions: the text guard leaves a live session, the points
guard arms `Tool::Node`, and the walk itself fails both app tests and the core one.

*Keep.* The `A` and rail doors onto point editing were shut by this entry's own commit, described above.
The one site left untouched on purpose was `canvas.rs`'s size badge, which showed its padlock on a
selected layer's **own** flag — a label rather than a refusal, which is why it was not swept with the
four. That reason turned out to be the wrong way round, and it was swept on 2026-08-25 under **D348**.

**D322 — A skew jumped on the first frame, because the lean was measured from the box's centre rather
than from the press. *Fixed and tested; reviewed and accepted on the machine 2026-08-23 — single shapes,
multi-selections, groups and already-skewed shapes, all four named. Keep.*** `tools::skew_about` computed a
side drag's lean as `atan(offset / span)` with the offset taken from the **box's centre**, so the first
frame of any drag leant the shape by whatever angle the *grab point* already implied — no pointer
movement required. Grabbing a side's exact midpoint was the only place it behaved, which is why it
survived so long, and it hit a single shape, a group and a multi-selection identically because there is
one function and one formula behind all three: *"same exact thing happens to groups and to multi
selection"*.

**The arithmetic was the diagnosis, and that is the transferable part.** The report came with photographs
and one number — a 200×120 rectangle, `Ctrl`-hovering the top edge near its right end, and *"the moment I
click and do a very small drag, it jumps to −26.76° skew"*. `−26.76°` is `atan(60.5 / −120)`: an offset of
60.5 from the centre of a 200-wide box, i.e. a grab **80.3% along the top edge**, which is exactly where
the cursor sits in the screenshot. The sign follows too — right of centre on `Handle::Top` is a negative
lean because `span = min_y − max_y` is negative. *Decoding the reported number named the line before any
code was read.* Same shape as the "it works if I move it 1px" rule: a number in a bug report is a
measurement, not a description.

**And the first diagnosis was wrong in a way worth keeping.** This read as *compounding* — the gesture
re-measuring against a box its own preview had already changed — and it is not.
`EditorSession::set_preview` writes only `overrides`; it touches neither `doc` nor `resolved`, so the
committed tree is frozen for the whole drag and `skew_tx` was already reading its box from a stable
source. A probe settled it: one frame of skew left the local box identical for a lone rect, for a group,
and for a group with a turned child, and moved only the **multi-selection's** union — 300 → 340 wide,
because shearing a rect widens its axis-aligned bounds. That growth is real and is not this bug; it is
chrome, and it is still open (below).

**`Drag::Skew` now carries `press: Point`**, captured at the arm site for the reason the code already gave
for reading `Ctrl` there: the gesture is decided by what the user aimed at when they pressed. The offset
became `p − press`, so the grabbed point follows the pointer. ⚠️ **The doc comment on that variant was the
bug stated out loud**: it read *"Carries no start reference, unlike `Drag::Rotate`. The dragged side tracks
the pointer absolutely, the way a resize handle does, so there is nothing to remember from where the press
landed."* True of a resize handle, because a resize handle **is** the thing you grabbed; false of a lean
measured from a centre. §9.4's and D52's copies of the same sentence went with it. This is the session's
recurring shape — a comment asserting the very rule that was wrong — and D319 is why nothing caught it.
D119 has the precedent in the pen, already decided the right way: an anchor drag is a **delta** from the
press because absolute tracking would snatch it up to `PEN_PICK_PX` on frame one.

**One consequence, confirmed rather than assumed**: a second skew on an already-leaning shape starts from
zero instead of re-adding the grab offset. Recorded as a consequence and not as a design choice, and the
maintainer's acceptance covers it by name.

**The two points travel as one value, which is the second trap in the same function.** Clippy's
`too_many_arguments` fired at 8, and it was pointing at something real: two adjacent `Point` parameters
where exchanging them silently negates the lean — a mistake that compiles, draws something plausible and
reads as a sign error rather than as a transposition. They are `tools::SideDrag { press, at }` now, with a
private `mapped(Affine)` so the local-space conversion cannot be applied to one and not the other:
`skew_to_handle` maps by `world.inverse()`, `skew_selection` maps neither, the union being in world
already. *Do not unpack them back into two parameters to save the struct.*

**The test is the reported fixture, in the reported numbers.**
`tools::tests::a_side_grabbed_off_centre_does_not_lean_until_the_pointer_moves` presses at 80.3% along the
top edge of a 200×120 rect and asserts three points, because the bug is entirely about the *first* frame:
pressed and not moved is a no-op; a 1-unit drag leans `atan(1/120)`, which pins the scale as well as the
origin; a 60.5-unit drag still reaches −26.76°, so the angle is not gone, it just takes a drag.
**Flip-checked by restoring `p.x − box_.center().x`: the stationary-pointer case leans −26.7557°, the
screenshot to two decimals.** Three existing tests — `skewing_a_side_holds_the_one_facing_it`, D52's
`a_leaning_selection_carries_a_turned_member_exactly` and `a_lean_does_not_change_how_much_shape_there_is`
— had the centre-based measurement baked into their pointer positions, and now state their press
explicitly at the side's midpoint for the same intended geometry.

⚠️ **The multi-selection's skew chrome was left open here and is now closed by D324.** A set's frame was
the upright union of world bounds (`canvas::selection_handles`, from `preview_world_bounds`) and could not
lean, so as the members sheared the frame *inflated* — the measured 300 → 340 in one frame — and its
handles crawled outward instead of following the shear. The maths was unaffected, which is what *"from
that point on it follows my cursor fine"* confirms, so it was a drawing question, and the answer was the
one predicted here: the start box sheared, i.e. a parallelogram. D324 has it, with D325–D329 for the turn,
the pill and the label.

**D323 — A lock guards against accidents on the canvas, not against deliberate edits through a panel.
*Decided by the maintainer; a non-goal, no code changed. Keep — this is the general rule the paint rows
were always an instance of.*** `roadmap.md` carried "a locked layer can still be moved and resized by
typing, and nobody has decided whether it should" — the Transform card's X / Y / W / H, rotation and skew
all commit straight through, so `X: 500` on a locked layer moves it where dragging it refuses — and put it
as two field groups wanting one decision each, the paint rows being settled (D71) and the geometry fields
not. Raised again after D321 and closed in one sentence: *"The panels are not an issue. They only show up
when you click on the layer anyway, since you can't click on the canvas. Which would be a deliberate
action by the user, not an accident. And at that point they're free to update the layer's properties."*

**The reasoning is worth more than the verdict, because it is general.** A lock is protection from the
hand, not permission machinery: what it stops is the stray drag, the shape that moves because it was
under a pointer aimed at something else. Reaching an inspector field costs a deliberate selection of the
locked layer, and a user who has done that has said what they mean. So the two field groups are not two
decisions — the paint rows and the geometry fields are the same answer for the same reason, and D71's
"a locked layer can be selected and recoloured; what the lock stops is dragging it about" turns out to
have been stating this rule rather than an exception to it.

**D321's marquee fix is what makes the premise sound**, and that is the load-bearing dependency here.
Before it, `apply_marquee` read the node's own flag while `hit_test` read the effective one, so a rubber
band could sweep up a layer inside a locked group without the user ever clicking it — "you had to select
it deliberately" was simply untrue, and this argument would have been wrong. *Revisit if any path back
into the selection stops being deliberate*: the rule is one step of reasoning away from a selection route
that can happen by accident, and the refusals it declines to add would be the only thing left standing
in front of a stray edit.

⚠️ **That condition was already met when this was written, by a door nobody counted** (D746).
`Ctrl+A` took every unfiltered candidate, locked layers included, and it is not a deliberate
selection of any *particular* layer — so *"the panels are only on screen because you clicked the
layer"* had a second exception beside the one D321 closed. The rule survives untouched, because it is
about what a panel may do to a layer you chose; what changed on 2026-09-10 is that the chord no
longer chooses one for you. **The last route was `inspector::select_by_color`** (D71), and **D748
shut it the same day**: the reticle filters through `may_select_in_bulk` and the button says what it
took — *"Selected 2 of 3 layers with this colour — 1 locked"* — so no door left in the app hands a
locked layer to the selection without the user having pointed at one. The condition this entry set
for itself is therefore met again rather than merely restated.

⚠️ **That last sentence read *"recorded as a question rather than shut"* for five days after it was
shut, and it is worth the space because it is this project's most reliable kind of rot.** D748
amended D71, D746, D709, §9.2 and §9.4 on the day it landed and did not reach here; `design-oracle`
found it on 2026-09-15 while answering a question about something else. **A closure leaves a fix-log
row and an entry of its own, and neither of those revisits the prose that described the problem** —
and prose that describes a defect *precisely* is the most convincing thing in the file once the
defect is gone, because its precision is what makes it read as freshly checked. It cost something
real the same week: `review/index.md` carried the identical claim through the very commit that closed
it, and the door was reported to the maintainer as open work off the strength of it. *Fix with a grep
for the mechanism, not for the entry number* — D748's own closing parenthetical names five sites and
that list was the sweep, where the sweep is the phrase (D754).

**D324 — A skewing multi-selection's frame leaned by inflating, and so moved even the side the gesture
was holding. *Fixed and tested; reviewed and accepted on the machine 2026-08-24 — the whole D324–D329
arc, after four rounds of the maintainer's review: "Working great". Keep.*** A set's box was the upright
union of its members' world bounds with `Handles.world` the identity, so it had nothing to lean *with*;
the only thing that could change from frame to frame was the union, and re-unioning the **previewed**
members grew it — 300 wide → **340** after one frame of skew — while the arithmetic went on measuring the
committed 300. That is worse than a frame which merely fails to lean: a shear widens an axis-aligned
union at **both** ends, so the edge the gesture is supposed to be pinning came loose too. The flip check
is what turned that up — drop the `Drag::Skew` arm and the test fails on `BottomLeft`, the *held* side,
not on the slide — and it is the sharper symptom, the one a user would describe as the box coming adrift.

The fix is to draw the frame on the box the arithmetic uses — the **committed** union — carried by the
lean. That is the single-layer shape exactly, a fixed box plus a transform, rather than a second
mechanism for sets. `tools::side_shear` is derived **once**, in `skew_tx`, and handed both to
`tools::skew_selection` (which no longer derives its own) and to the chrome through `Drag::Skew`'s
`lean`, written from the same computation that built the transaction. Deriving it twice is how the two
came to disagree in the first place — D266's shape — and `Shift`'s 15° snap is what makes that concrete:
two derivations would round one drag two ways. *Do not let `skew_selection` compute its own shear again
to save a parameter.*

`a_skewing_selections_frame_leans_rather_than_inflating` asserts on the **corners** rather than on a
width, because "it leans" is precisely the claim a width cannot make — a parallelogram's bounding width
grows too. What separates the two is that the bottom pair stays put while the top pair slides, by equal
amounts.

**D325 — The same fault for rotation, and the same fix. *Fixed and tested; part of the D324–D329 arc
reviewed and accepted on the machine 2026-08-24. Keep.*** A 300×100 upright frame measured **236.6 ×
309.8, still upright**, at 60° of turn: the axis-aligned bounding box of the turned set, which is a
*different rectangle* from the one the handles belong on, so every handle sat somewhere the gesture had
not put it. `tools::turn_about(pivot, angle)` was lifted out of `rotate_node` so the chrome and the
shapes share one expression, exactly as `side_shear` is shared for a lean.

**Both gestures go through one method, `Drag::selection_frame()`**, and that is the load-bearing part
rather than either arm inside it: a third gesture that reorients a set has one obvious place to declare
itself instead of quietly inheriting the upright box. `None` is the right answer for a resize or a move —
their frames *should* follow the re-unioned preview, the box genuinely changing size with no rotation to
carry.

`a_turning_selections_frame_turns_and_keeps_its_size` asserts the **side lengths**, which is what a
bounding box cannot keep, and the diagonals as well, so a frame that kept its sides and stopped being a
rectangle would still fail. Flip-checked by making `selection_frame` answer `None` for a rotation: 236.6
and 309.8 come straight back, which is the measurement above and the reported symptom.

**D326 — The orientation outlives the gesture, and the pill was reading a second answer. *Fixed and
tested; both halves found by the maintainer's review of D324 and D325 and accepted with the arc on
2026-08-24. Keep.*** Two things.

**(a)** `badge_placement` derived its own box by unioning `preview_world_bounds`, so the moment D324 made
the frame lean the pill stayed behind on the old upright one — D266's shape again, two derivations of a
single question. Both arms read `selection_frame_box` now, which also fixes what the pill *says*: the
set's own extent in its own axes, 300 × 100, rather than the 236.6 × 309.8 of an upright box drawn round
it. That is the convention the single-layer pill has always followed.

**(b)** A set has no frame stored anywhere, so the box could only come back upright the instant the
gesture's own transform went away: *"Once I release the mouse, the frame returns to the square one… It
only resets if I deselect and select again."* `Selection` carries it now, composed on commit —
`set_frame(lean * selection.frame())` — so a lean after a turn keeps both. It is a **session**
orientation and not a document one: a selection is still not a group, and nothing about the members'
own transforms changed.

Three details matter more than the feature itself.

⚠️ **Keying it to the ids alone resurrects the old orientation.** That was the first implementation, and
it looks like it invalidates on any change: `clear()` only makes the ids stop *matching*, the stored entry
survives, and selecting the same pair again matched it and brought the lean back. Hence
`Selection::forget_frame()` on every mutator of `ids`, with the id key kept as the guard against a future
mutator that forgets to call it. `deselecting_does_not_leave_an_orientation_to_come_back_to` covers that
path by name. **And which call is load-bearing is not the one it looks like**: a flip check written for
this entry claimed that removing `forget_frame()` from `clear` would fail the resurrection test, and it
does not — the reselect goes through `set`, which forgets anyway. **`set`'s call is the guard**; `clear`'s
is defence in depth. *Know which is which before deleting either.*

**`retain_existing` forgets only when it actually dropped something.** It runs after every commit and
every undo, so forgetting unconditionally would throw the orientation away on the very commit that set it.

**The box is built from the members' geometry quads, not from their ink bounds, and that is what makes it
exactly stable mid-gesture.** A quad transforms exactly: with `frame = G · F` the gesture cancels, since
`frame⁻¹ · (G · Wᵢ) = F⁻¹ · Wᵢ` whatever `G` is. An axis-aligned bounding box does not transform that way
— `AABB(G · ink) ≠ G · AABB(ink)` — so a box built from `world_bounds` would creep as the set turned,
which is D324's defect moved out of the frame and into the box rather than removed. It also agrees with
the single-layer arm, which always used `preview_local_box`. ⚠️ **The price, stated and then accepted**:
the resting frame hugs **geometry** where it used to hug **ink**, so it is half a stroke width tighter on
each side of a stroked member. That is the single-layer frame's own rule, so the two now match rather
than differing by a stroke.

⚠️ **One thing this left crooked, and it was not the chrome — closed two weeks later by D478.** A
multi-selection's **resize** was still measured on the upright union of world bounds (`resize_tx`'s
`Target::Selection` arm) and still travelled along world axes (`resize_axes` short-circuited to the
identity for a set) — nothing about a resize was in scope here. That was consistent while a set's box
could only be upright. It was not consistent with a box a turn or a lean has left oriented, so dragging a
corner of a turned set scaled it along axes its own frame was no longer on: **62.2243 units off the
pointer** on a 60°-turned pair, measured. The instruction this paragraph carried — *"fix by giving the
resize arm the frame the chrome reads: `selection_frame_box` is the one answer"* — is exactly what D478
did, `canvas::selection_resize_box` being that twin.

⚠️ **The paragraph above is left standing, in the past tense, because the way it sat here is the
finding.** This entry's heading says *Fixed and tested*, and for two weeks it carried inside it a defect
that was known, described, reproduced in prose and given its own fix — with **no verdict** on that half,
nothing in `roadmap.md` (`resize_axes`, `D326`, `selection_frame_box` and *world union* all returned
nothing there), and §9.4 repeating the warning rather than tracking it. So the only record of open work
was a ⚠️ filed under a heading that says the work is done, which is the one place nobody rereads. *An
entry that closes one half of a question and warns about the other owes the other half a place that is
read as open work* — a `roadmap.md` line, or its own entry with a `*Fix.*` verdict.

Two tests. `a_sets_frame_outlives_the_gesture_and_dies_with_the_selection` is driven through the real
`finish_drag`, so it pins the commit arm that stores the orientation rather than a stand-in for it, and
its three flips are three assertions — squaring up on release is the report, ignoring the stored ids
leaves an orientation on a *different* selection, composing with `IDENTITY` loses the first of two
gestures. `the_size_pill_measures_the_frame_the_handles_are_on` asserts the pill's box *is*
`selection_frame_box`'s, which says "the same" rather than "close enough today".

**D327 — The size pill hung off a bounding box, so a shear moved it off the shape. *Fixed and tested;
part of the D324–D329 arc accepted on 2026-08-24. Keep.*** The pill was placed against the bounding box
of the selection outline measured inside a **rotation-only** frame. No rotation holds a parallelogram
square-on, so that box is looser than the shape at every non-zero lean and its bottom edge can sit a long
way below any real one — reported on a group at −54.89° turned and −67.96° leaning, and on a single layer
and a multi-selection for the same reason, all three sharing the path. **It was pre-existing for single
layers**; D324 merely put sets onto it as well. `canvas::badge_edge` picks the edge whose **outward normal
points most steeply down the screen** and `badge_frame` pushes the pill out along it. An edge is an edge
at any shear.

It reproduces the old placement exactly for a pure rotation, which is why the rotation tests needed no new
expectations: in the reduced frame a turned rectangle *is* square-on, so the bounding box's bottom edge
and the lowest real edge are the same segment. D49's edge-choice reasoning — the normal rather than the
lowest midpoint, and the measured 14° bands where they disagree — is unchanged and now lives on
`badge_edge`, where it is still true.

`Frame2::to_local` and `Frame2::bounds_of` lost their last production caller and are `#[cfg(test)]` with
the reason written on them: projecting into a frame was precisely the step that could not survive a shear.

Two test-quality notes, both worth keeping.

⚠️ **The first version of the test was vacuous and its own flip caught it.** It asserted that the badge
hangs off *a real edge*, `GAP` outward, centred — every one of which is true of *any* edge, the top one
included. Flipping the choice to "take the first edge" passed the lot. It now also asserts that the badge
is below the centroid and that no edge faces further down.

**An existing assertion was measuring a proxy.** `the_size_badge_stays_legible_and_hops_edges_as_the_shape_turns`
checked the pill's clearance against the *bounding box's* bottom rather than against the chosen edge. At
exactly 225° two edges face equally down; `badge_edge` takes one and the box's bottom is the other, so a
correctly placed pill failed. **The proxy was fixed, not the tie-break** —
`the_badge_label_lies_along_its_edge_at_every_angle` records that the tie has no preferred side.

**D328 — The pill was pushed out along its edge's normal but still laid at the *reduced* angle, so at a
steep lean one end swung back over the artwork. *Superseded by D329 within the hour — this is not a live
rule. Kept for the coupling it leaves behind.*** D327 hung the pill off a real edge, but
`badge_text_angle` still reduced by quarter turns, which can leave the label up to 45° **across** its
edge — so half the pill's height was the wrong offset, and one end reached back inside the shape:
measured **5pt inside** at −54.89° turned / −67.96° leaning, which is the pill sitting on the drawing in
the report. The fix replaced half the pill's height with the pill's half-extent **projected** onto the
outward normal, which is correct at any angle under the quarter-turn rule.

D329 made it unreachable an hour later. A label parallel to its edge sends `u · out` to zero, so the
projection collapses to `pill.y * 0.5` at every angle: the general form was carried for one revision and
then removed as arithmetic nobody can get to. **What survives is the coupling, and it is written at
`badge_frame`** — half the pill's height is the whole offset *only because* the label is parallel to the
edge. Go back to quarter turns and the projection has to come back with it. Recorded rather than dropped
because a reader who reverses D329 will otherwise reintroduce this bug with no note saying it was once
fixed.

**D329 — The label lies along its edge, not across it. *Fixed and tested; accepted on the machine
2026-08-24 with the D324–D329 arc and with the cost named. Keep; it supersedes D49's mechanism, and D16
and D49 are amended to point here.*** Reported from one group at two skews **half a degree apart** —
−1.29° and −0.74° — where the pill flipped between lying along its edge and lying across it.
`badge_angle` reduced by **quarter** turns, which was right while its input was a *shape's* angle (D49's
rule: keep a label within 45° of upright) and wrong the moment the label hangs off a **specific edge**,
*because a quarter turn is exactly the difference between along and across*. The chosen edge sat near the
45° boundary and the reduction jumped the other side of it; in the small, the test's 44/46 pair returned
+44 and −44 — an 88° swing for 2° of input. `badge_text_angle` reduces by **half** turns now, which can
only ever flip the label end-for-end and leaves it parallel to the same edge.

**Unchanged for turned rectangles, structurally rather than by luck**: the lowest edge of a turned
rectangle is never more than 45° off horizontal, so mod-180 and mod-90 agree there and
`the_size_badge_stays_legible_and_hops_edges_as_the_shape_turns` keeps its ±45° guarantee unweakened. It
is only a *sheared* shape that can now be handed a steep label.

**The cost, in the maintainer's own framing:** *"There may be extreme angles where it's hard to set a pill
in a comfortable place"*, weighed against a pill perpendicular to the frame being "not right". Parallel
and steep beats upright and across. `badge_angle` is **deleted**; its edge-choice reasoning — the normal
versus the lowest midpoint, and the 14° band measured between them — moved to `badge_edge` under D327.

⚠️ **And D319 bit again, inside this very change.** Deleting `badge_angle` left three
`[`badge_angle`]` intra-doc links pointing at nothing, all three inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules — so
`cargo doc` reported **zero errors**. They were found by grepping the name after the delete, which is
`CLAUDE.md`'s own rule and the only check there is. That is the second time in one session: D322's work
reassigned thirteen lines of a doc comment onto the wrong item, also with every gate green.

**D330 — The Settings modal, and the web-font row the roadmap had nowhere to put. *Built and tested
2026-08-24; Keep. It closes the roadmap's *Now · Web fonts* items 1 and 3 and the §14 parked entry on the
font cache's size; item 2 — prefetching a popular set — followed as D352, and that section was retired
2026-08-25 with the rejected three-way and the API evidence behind it migrated into this entry.*** The design
regeneration of 2026-08-23 added a `sliders` button in the top bar and a 376pt modal behind it, and the
maintainer's reason for it was the web-font cache switch: *"so we can tackle that section that's been
living in the roadmap for a while now."*

**What the surface actually cost, against what the roadmap predicted it would.** That entry filed the
missing panel as the smaller half of the problem — "the panel is not the only thing standing between here
and *180 MB · Clear*", the other half being a size query and a clear verb. It had that the wrong way
round. `fonts::dir_bytes` and `FontService::clear_cache` are fifteen lines between them, over the same
`read_dir` the startup sweep (D237) already walked; what took months was having nowhere to put a row.
*A blocker named as one of two halves can still be the whole of it.*

**Three states for the cache row, not two, and this is the one thing in the change that no reading would
have found.** `cache_bytes` is `Option<u64>`, and `None` — a scan that has not landed — must not render
as `0 MB`: a directory holding two hundred megabytes would report itself clear for however many frames
the scan took, which is the exact opposite of what the row exists to say. So the row says *counting*,
`cache_row` is a pure function of the three cases, and `the_cache_row_tells_unknown_from_empty` flip-checks
by folding `None` into the `Some(0)` arm.

**The scan is off the UI thread and the delete is not, and the asymmetry is deliberate.** A `read_dir` with
a `metadata()` per entry over a few thousand files is a syscall per entry, and it is asked on the frame a
modal opens — the one frame that must not stall — so it goes to a thread and lands through its own channel
(not on `FontPoll`: that type is what the caller *acts* on, and a byte count changes neither the family
list nor the text cache). `clear_cache` is synchronous because it answers a button, and a deletion
reported on a later frame is a button that appears not to have worked.

**Off means no request, and that took closing two doors rather than one** — ⚠️ **three, since
2026-09-10** (§15 D720): the two below are about what a *new* request may start, and neither of them
reaches a catalog fetch that is already out. `FontService::set_web_fonts` cancels that thread now,
and D720 restates the whole promise as a rule rather than as a door count, because a count is what
went wrong here and in D352 both. `rebuild_families` leaving the
web names out of the picker's list is the visible half. The other is `faces_of`, and it is the half a
list-only filter would have missed: a family name reaches `ensure` from a **document** — one saved on a
machine where the switch was on — which never goes near the picker, so opening such a file would still
have queued a download. `web_fonts_off_hides_the_catalog_and_refuses_to_fetch_from_it` asserts both, and
each arm was flip-checked separately **because each flip passes the other assertion**. At startup the
switch is enforced a third way: `FontService::new` does not spawn the catalog thread at all, and drops the
sender on the spot — which is the same `Disconnected` signal `catalog_done` is documented (D227) to read
off a thread that has finished, so nothing downstream needed a second spelling of "there will be no
catalog". `set_web_fonts` moves it inside a session, and turning it back on is a rebuild rather than a
re-fetch whenever the catalog is still in memory.

**Why the switch has two positions and not three.** `Off | Popular | All` was the obvious middle way, and
it was rejected for three reasons that were argued in `roadmap.md` and migrated here when that section was
retired on 2026-08-25 — none of them is recoverable from the code:

- **List length stopped being the cost the day the list was virtualized (D84).** 1,900 names are as cheap
  to show as fifty. What costs is bytes per row *scrolled past*, and a curated subset does not change that
  rate: browsing fifty popular families fetches fifty files exactly as fast as browsing fifty out of
  1,900. A middle tier reduces what the user can *find*, not what the app downloads.
- **The traffic is already shaped.** The preview lane is LIFO and capped at `PREVIEW_BACKLOG`, so a flung
  scrollbar cannot bank thousands of stale fetches. What remains is someone steadily scrolling 200
  families — a user genuinely looking at 200 previews, which is fair traffic. The defect was never the
  volume but that none of it was ever deleted, and that is D237.
- **There is no ranking to build "popular" from — checked 2026-08-20 against the live endpoint rather than
  against our parsing of it.** The whole of `https://api.fontsource.org/v1/fonts` is 537 KB and carries
  exactly **eleven** distinct keys — `id`, `family`, `subsets`, `weights`, `styles`, `defSubset`,
  `variable`, `lastModified`, `category`, `license`, `type` — and **not one of them is a rank, a count or a
  trend**. Nor does the *order* carry one, which is the other way popularity could have arrived without a
  field: the list is alphabetical, opening *42dot Sans · ABeeZee · Abel · Abhaya Libre*. It is **1,976**
  Google-typed families of 2,096, `fetch_catalog` filtering on `kind == "google"` — the precise version of
  the 1,900 the first bullet rounds to. So a curated tier would be **hardcoded in the app**: an editorial
  judgement we own, going stale by itself, whose failure mode is *my font is not listed*, answered by a
  setting.

**The third of those is load-bearing and D352 rests on it** — it is why `fonts::POPULAR` is a prefetch
*set* rather than a filter, and why fifty family names are typed out in the source at all. *Re-check it
against the endpoint before anyone re-argues the middle tier*: a rank or a usage count appearing in the
API is the one change that would reopen this, and nothing in the build would notice it had. The nearest
thing to a door is D352's `every_prefetched_family_is_spelled_the_way_the_catalog_spells_it`, the one
test that touches the endpoint at all — `cargo test -p ondin-app -- --ignored`, since it is `#[ignore]`d.
⚠️ **It cannot surface a new key, and reading it as though it could is the trap**: it goes through
`fetch_catalog`, whose `Item` is a plain serde struct that silently drops every field it does not name —
which is exactly the parsing the 2026-08-20 check deliberately went around by reading the raw 537 KB. So
the re-check is a request and a pair of eyes; the test only says the endpoint is still answering.

**A form, not a switchboard — which is the opposite of the only preference rows that existed before.**
*Slashes in names make folders* and *Re-export on save* each call `prefs.save()` on the spot, in the export
panel's popover. This modal stages every row and writes on *Save changes*, because a popover beside a
button is an adjustment to work in progress where a modal over the whole editor is not — and because
turning web fonts off drops ~1,976 families out of the picker, which is not a thing to do on the way past.
*Clear* is the one exception and is not an inconsistency: a deletion cannot be staged honestly, so it acts,
says how much went in the status line, and the count beside it is the receipt. `Settings` mirrors `Prefs`
field for field so the *dirty* test is one `!=`, and `the_form_is_a_round_trip_through_the_preferences`
pins both directions — a field added to one and forgotten in the other makes the modal quietly unable to
save it, or quietly unable to keep it.

**The keymap is silenced while the modal is open, in the same guard the context menu uses.** `Escape`
belongs to `ModalResponse::should_close`, which consumes it at the *bottom* of the frame; every other key
would otherwise reach the document behind the backdrop — an arrow nudging the selection, `R` switching
tools — which is an edit the user cannot see being made. ⚠️ **This paragraph read *"Read-verified, not
tested: the guard is in `OndinApp::update`, which … is not reachable from a test even with
`OndinApp::headless` (D303, D269). The same hole exists in `close_confirmation` and is left alone
here"*, and every part of that was wrong — see D464, which closed it.** There is no
`OndinApp::update`; the method is `<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui`, it **is** reachable from a test by
`eframe::Frame::_new_kittest()` plus `ctx.run_ui`, and the hole was in the crash-recovery card as well
as in `close_confirmation`, which this sentence did not name. Both are guarded now and the four-row
test is `every_modal_owns_the_keyboard_not_only_settings`. *A verdict whose reason names a code fact
needs re-checking against the code* — the reason given here is what kept the test from being written.

**The nudge step became a parameter of `input::resolve` rather than a read inside it**, which is what keeps
that function what `shortcuts.md` §9 relies on it being — a pure resolution of one frame's events, one
frame in and one list out. `NudgeStep` is a struct and not two `f64`s because the pair crosses three seams
(the modal writes it, `Prefs` persists it, `resolve` reads it) and a swap of two same-typed fields
compiles; `the_arrow_step_is_the_one_the_preference_names` uses a deliberately lopsided `0.5`/`64` so the
wrong field is unmistakable, where the default `1`/`10` would leave two numbers either of which could have
come from either field.

**`#[serde(default)]` moved to the container.** The field-level spelling fills a missing key from
`Default` *of that field's type*, which is `false` for a `bool` and `0.0` for an `f64` — and three of the
new settings are not that: web fonts default on, and a nudge of zero is an arrow key that silently does
nothing. The container attribute reads `Prefs::default()` instead, so what an old `prefs.json` means is
the one place the app already states its defaults. The four redundant field attributes were removed rather
than left, since two spellings of one rule is two rules.

**Four numbers depart from the regenerated design, all four for consistency with the app the card sits
in**, which is the maintainer's own standing answer to a design/build disagreement — *as tall as the other
controls are, for consistency*, given once as a **rule** rather than as a pick between the two numbers on
offer:

- **The switch is `ui::paint_switch`'s rounded rectangle, where the design now draws a 32×19 pill.** That
  function's own doc already argues the case and it did not weaken: every other control in the chrome is a
  4–5px rounded box, and a capsule among them reads as borrowed. The design's *travel plus accent* is
  exactly what it paints.
- **Buttons are 28pt**, against the design's 30 in the footer and 26 for *Clear*. Two heights for the same
  class of control one card apart; 28 is the field height they sit among.
- **Section labels are `ui::eyebrow`** — 9.5pt at `text::FAINT` — against the design's 11px at 20% with
  letter-spacing. Every section label in the app is an `eyebrow` and this card is read against the panels.
  The design's *hairline out to the card edge* was kept, and it earns its place here where a panel does not
  need it: a panel's sections are bounded by card edges and this card has none, so three bare eyebrows down
  one column read as a list of three labels.
- **The nudge fields carry their label inside**, as `Prefix::Text("Step")` and `Prefix::Text("Shift")` with
  a `px` suffix, where the design puts a caption above each field. A caption over a field is a shape this
