  app does not otherwise use, and the eyebrow above already says *Nudge*.

**One layout finding worth keeping, because it is invisible in the source and reads as a mistake on
screen.** In the cache row the *Clear* button has to be allocated **before** the sentence beside it: a
`ui.horizontal` centres each item against the row height it knows at the moment that item is allocated, so
with the label written first it is centred in `interact_size.y` and the 28pt button then grows the row past
it — measured at y 581 against the button's centre of 583. Setting `interact_size.y` ahead of the label
does **not** fix it, which was the obvious guess and was tried. The nesting that does — the button in a
right-to-left scope, the label in a left-to-right scope inside it — is load-bearing and now says so;
`a_row_and_the_button_beside_it_share_one_centre` pins it, and it was flip-checked by rewriting the row the
tempting way. Same 2pt family as `ui::FIELD_BORDER_H`.

⚠️ **And one claimed flip-check that did not bite, corrected rather than left.** `every_row_fits_the_cards_own_column`
originally said squeezing `CARD_W` would push the web-fonts caption out of the card. It does not:
`ui.label` *wraps*, so a sentence in this card physically cannot overflow it, and at 300pt the caption
re-wrapped and the loop passed clean. The loop is a guard over the runs `painter.text` puts down — the
switch labels and the button words, which do not wrap and are clipped by nothing — and the caption is
asserted on its **height** instead, where a third line is the real failure and a longer sentence produces
39pt against the two lines' 26. Both halves bite separately now. *The question to ask of a green test is
what would also pass it.*

**What was deliberately left out, and it is the design's own row.** *Layers › Show tree guides* was not
built, because the tree guides were not built: the same regeneration introduced dotted per-ancestor guides
in the layers panel with hover highlighting the ancestor chain, and `layers.rs` drew nothing of the kind.
A switch for a feature that does not exist is precisely the drift `CLAUDE.md` opens with, so the row was
absent rather than inert. **Both arrived the next request — D331**, which is what that reasoning was for:
the answer to a switch with nothing behind it is to build the feature, not to wire the switch.

### D330's second round, 2026-08-24 — five things after living with the card

Reported the same day, and **four of the five are corrections to this entry rather than to the design**.
The pattern is the maintainer's usual one: every symptom exact, and the one stated *cause* a good guess.

- **`Ctrl+,` opens it.** Left unbound on the first pass and offered as an option; taken. `,` was
  completely unspent in every combination, so the chord cost nothing (`shortcuts.md` §8). It **opens and
  cannot close** — `resolve` is not called while a modal is up — which is why `Action::OpenSettings` is
  named for what it does.
- **Share is gone.** The first pass reported the design's removal and left the button standing, on the
  rule *implement what they named and report the rest*. The answer was one line: *"Remove the Share
  button. Not needed."* Reporting was right and keeping it was right; the button was a promise a local
  file editor has nothing behind.
- **The nudge fields take whole pixels.** They shipped as `Scrub::fine(_, 2)` over `0.01..=1000`, which
  this entry's own prose defended as "a fraction is the point". It is not: *"nudging by 0.1px is crazy"*.
  `Scrub::whole(0.5)` over `1..=1000`, plus an explicit `round()` in `nudge_field` — **both are needed**,
  because `Scrub::whole` settles a drag and deliberately leaves typing alone, which is right for a stroke
  width and wrong for an arrow key.
- **A right-click cancels those scrubs, and did nothing at all before.** `OndinApp::settings_scrub` is
  D168's `session_scrub` problem in a second place, for exactly the reason that field's doc
  gives: the modal writes into its own staged draft rather than through `RenderOverrides`, so
  `cancel_gesture` had no preview to drop and nothing held the pre-drag pair. It is also the term that
  keeps `cancel_gesture` from *blinking* on these fields — that function's `field` test leads on
  `ctx.dragged_id()`, which egui clears on the release of any button, so a right-click inside one frame
  would read an empty snapshot. Third instance of that pattern; the shape is now clearly reusable.
- **The section spacing was accumulating, and the guessed cause was the right one.** Reported as
  *"padding top/bottom in sections is unbalanced… if I have to guess, a section has both padding bottom
  and margin-top, so they accumulate"* — and it did, twice over: a 15pt `add_space` compensating for an
  11pt `item_spacing`, **plus** ~6pt of the eyebrow row's own box over its 12pt galley, which nothing in
  the source hinted at. 32 above each header against 20 below, where 26/11 was written down.

  The fix is not a smaller number but a different rule: `item_spacing.y` is **zero** for the whole card
  and every vertical gap is written out, the eyebrow row is allocated at exactly `EYEBROW_H`, and
  `SECTION_AIR` is *one* value used above and below a header — 18 each. **Equal rather than the design's
  2:1**, which the design has too and which is not what was asked for; a header can be centred in its air
  because it carries a hairline out to the card's edge, and a rule reads as *everything below me* however
  the space around it is divided. `a_section_header_has_equal_air_above_and_below_it` pins it on the
  **ink** rather than the boxes — the boxes are exactly 18/18, the ink is 18/21 because a `switch_row` is
  22pt around a 16pt track — with the 4pt of slack that costs stated, against the 15pt that was reported.
  ⚠️ Its own first version then failed on *Nudge*, whose neighbour above is the card's **title**: that gap
  is deliberately larger and now has an assertion of its own saying so.

  **Two accumulations, and finding the second is what the probe was for.** `TITLE_GAP` had to become a
  *total* — `TITLE_GAP - SECTION_AIR` at the call site — because `section` adds air of its own; unfixed,
  the title stood off by 44pt against the design's 26. *A gap that looks right on its own is not evidence
  about the gap next to it.*

**And the layers panel is 300 wide** (§9.4), which the first pass had reported as an unasked-for design
change and left alone: *"That was a deliberate change."* The resizing floated alongside it —
*"add resizing just for the layers panel. Probably the inspector panels too"* — was withdrawn in the same
breath (*"I'm rambling. Leave resizing out of this"*) and is filed in the roadmap under *Now · Inspector*,
where the note that matters is that it is **two jobs**: the tree is an `egui::Panel` and nearly free,
where the inspector is an `Area` of floating cards with no edge to put a handle on.

**D331 — The layers tree draws its structure, and D330's switch has something to switch. *Built and
tested 2026-08-24; Keep. Closes the "more tree-like layers panel" §9.2 left open beside D306, and the
row D330 filed as deliberately absent.*** The design regeneration added dashed per-ancestor guides to
the layers pane, lit under the pointer, and enabled them by default with *Layers › Show tree guides*
in the Settings modal. `layers::tree_guide_segments` is the whole rule and `paint_tree_guides` puts it
on the screen; `Prefs::tree_guides` is the switch, on by default.

**Three runs per row, and naming them is what makes the rest of this legible**: the **trunks**, one per
ancestor whose branch is still open, each crossing the row down the caret column of the level it
belongs to; the **connector**, the part of the *parent's* trunk above this row's elbow, which is what
makes the row hang off its parent rather than merely sit under it; and the **elbow**, a horizontal run
out of that column to the row's own leading glyph. Two greys — 8.5% of the text colour at rest, 34% on
the lit path — both under `theme::text`'s dimmest tier, because this is a hairline in the gutter of
*every* row and it must not compete with the names.

**They are worked out after the walk rather than during it, and that is the shape of the change.** Every
guide is a statement about rows *other than* the one being painted: the trunk crossing this row belongs
to an ancestor several rows up, whether it carries on depends on a row below, and whether it is lit
depends on which row the pointer is over — which a top-down walk only learns when it reaches it. So
`layers_row` collects a row record per row it draws and one pass over that list answers all three —
`GuideRow` then, `TreeRow` since D345 gave the drop hint the same treatment for the same reason.
The alternative was the usual one — read last frame's hover off the app — and it would have put the
guides one frame behind the row grounds that use `resp.hovered()` directly, which is a disagreement
between two things drawn in one row. *A single bad frame counts.*

It also buys two things for nothing. A **filtered** tree gets the guides of what is shown, because the
structure is read off the displayed order and `matching_rows` already keeps the ancestors that locate a
hit. And the rule is a **free function over a list of depths**, so all of it is testable without a
document: five of the seven tests are one line of fixture each. The other two go through the panel,
for the two things a segment list cannot say — that the walk feeds this at all and the preference
reaches the painter, and that the `hovered` a row hands over is the same `resp.hovered()` its own
ground is painted from, so the two cannot disagree for a frame.

**And the gutter was read as a picture before any of it was believed** — a throwaway probe rasterizing
the `LineSegment` shapes into ASCII, the technique `CLAUDE.md` describes. It showed the frame row bare,
the group hanging off x 11 with its trunk stopping at its own elbow because it is an only child, the two
rects off x 42 with one continuous trunk between them, and **no fragment at x 11 in the deep rows** —
the closed-branch rule visible rather than argued. Deleted afterwards, with what it proved kept as the
hover assertion.

**`caret_column` is a function for one reason.** The guide for level *n* is the trunk of an ancestor at
depth *n* and it is drawn in that ancestor's *descendants'* rows, so the line and the caret it hangs
off have to agree about where the column is from rows that never compute each other's geometry. The
row's own arithmetic now goes through it as well, and `a_row_hangs_off_the_column_its_parents_caret_is_on`
flip-checks against `caret_column(left, depth)` — the row's own column rather than its parent's, which
is the off-by-one anyone would write — reporting 42 where 11 belongs.

⚠️ **A trunk whose branch has already closed is not drawn at all, and this is the one place the drawing
departs from the design.** The design's markup gives every row a stub-height background for *every*
level, which is right for the fixture it was drawn against: no ancestor in it dies above a deeper row.
Read as a rule it leaves a fragment in mid-air — with `A → B → C` each an only child, A's trunk ends at
B's elbow, so a stub in A's column in C's row is a dash under a line that stopped a row earlier.
`a_trunk_that_already_ended_leaves_no_fragment_in_a_deeper_row` is flip-checked against exactly that
reading and is the only one of the six that bites for it. *Hand-drawn markup is a fixture, not a
formula, and the case it does not contain is the one to derive.*

**Hovering lights the path from the parent, not the whole ancestry** — the parent's trunk from the row
under the parent down to the hovered row's elbow, and below that elbow the same trunk goes back to
rest. It answers "which one is this inside" once, where a lit ladder down every ancestor answers "how
deep is this", which the indent already says. Four separate claims, and each is a different way to get
it wrong: the trunk lights over the rows *between* the two, the connector lights but the trunk under
the hovered row's own elbow does not, an intervening row's elbow stays dark, and no other level lights.

⚠️ **And a flip that did not bite, which is a finding about the test rather than a failed experiment.**
`hovering_a_row_lights_the_trunk_it_hangs_off` originally hovered the **last** child of its parent — so
there was no trunk under that row's elbow at all, and the claim about it iterated over an empty set. The
`start..=h` flip, which is the range anyone would write first, passed clean. The fixture now gives the
hovered row a sibling after it and asserts *that it has one* before asserting anything about it, and the
flip fails on the run it was always about. *Assert the fixture is in the state you think, or the test is
about nothing.*

**One number nobody would guess and a probe cannot see: the dash phase.** The pattern is 1.5pt of ink to
2.5pt of gap, phased from the top of each row as the design's per-row backgrounds are. That costs nothing
here because the tree's pitch is 27 — `ROW_H` 26 and `item_spacing.y` 1, which is exactly the row height
the regenerated design gives its rows with no gap — against a 4pt period, so the reset lands one join per
row 1.5pt where an ordinary gap is 2.5. But a trunk **broken at the elbow** is two runs from one row, and
phasing the second from its own start would put a dash where the half above it left a gap, at every elbow
in the panel. `dash_phase` carries the offset — 3.0, thirteen points into a four-point period — and
`a_trunk_broken_at_the_elbow_keeps_one_dash_pattern` pins it.

**The indent is the one item reported rather than implemented — and the report is what settled it.** The
same regeneration widened the pane's indents — 15 then 22 for the two levels it used to draw, a consistent
22 across the three it draws now — and the change was described on the machine as *"bigger idents"*.
`layers::INDENT` has been **31** since long before, which is *bigger than 22*, so following the design
here would tighten somebody's tree by 9pt a level in the name of widening it. Reported as two numbers
rather than implemented as one, and answered the same day: *"Indent is fine too, no need to change it."*
**31 is the settled number and this is not an open item** — the roadmap entry that carried it for a few
hours is struck. Two things are worth keeping
about it: the design's 22 is coherent as a **pair** with the guides — a guide says which container a row
is in, so the indent no longer has to carry that alone, which is precisely the argument `INDENT`'s own doc
comment gave for 31 in the first place — and **nothing in the guides turns on the number**, since they are
drawn from `caret_column` at whatever it says. *A design/build disagreement is reported as two numbers and
a rule, never as a number to be picked.*

**And the row D330 left out is built.** That entry's *"a switch for a feature that does not exist is
precisely the drift `CLAUDE.md` opens with, so the row is absent rather than inert"* was right, and the
answer to it was to build the feature. `Prefs::tree_guides` defaults **on** — the indent says how deep a
row is and nothing about which of the rows above it the row is inside, which is the question a nested
document raises — and off is for the reading the ink costs a shallow one. `#[serde(default)]` on the
container means an existing `prefs.json` reads it as on rather than as `false`, which is D330's own reason
for putting the attribute there; the count in that entry's prose goes from three settings to four.

### D331's second round, 2026-08-24 — a state the guides were missing, and a corner that did not meet

Reported after looking at the panel: *"Very little to polish."* Two items, and the second **reverses a
number this entry had just pinned with a test**. Both **reviewed and accepted on the machine** the same
day — *"It looks really good"* — which is also where the indent above was closed.

**A selected row lights its leg in `color::SELECT`.** Asked for as a *depth affordance* — the tree
saying where the selection lives, not just which row it is — in "the same blue we use on the shape next
to the name", and *"this goes both for selecting it in the layer panel or in the canvas"*, which came
free: `session.selection` is one selection for the whole app and the row already reads it for its own
ground and glyph. Full strength rather than a tier of it, on the reasoning that a dashed hairline inks
37% of its length, so the blue arrives as a tint without being mixed as one.

**The path shape is *shared* with the hover, and that is what makes the precedence expressible.** The
caveat arrived with the request and is the interesting half of it: *"hover takes precedence… a vertical
line completely blue from a selected layer becomes light gray when another layer is hovered — of course
only on the part that applies to that layer"*, and *"the currently selected layer doesn't apply a hover
anymore"*. Both fall out of one rule per run rather than a rule per row: `guide_path` is asked for the
hovered row and for every selected row, the runs each path covers are marked, and hover is resolved
last. Hovering a row *between* a selected row and their shared parent therefore greys the trunk down to
the hovered row's own elbow and leaves the rest of the leg blue — the colour changes exactly where the
two paths part. The exception is a `filter`: a hovered row that is itself selected yields no hover path
at all.

`lit: bool` became `GuideInk`, three variants **in precedence order**, because "which of two claims wins
this run" is the whole of the rule and a pair of booleans would have left it to be re-derived at each of
the four sites that ask. A selection is also a *set* — two selected siblings light two legs off one
trunk, and the union is what gets drawn — where a hover is at most one row.

⚠️ **And the dash phase was wrong on screen, having been right in the abstract.** *"There's also a slight
gap on the vertical lines where they meet the horizontal ones."* Three causes, in order of how much they
contributed:

- **The offset.** This entry pinned `dash_phase` with a test and a flip-check: the below-elbow run was
  phased to continue the lattice the row's top had started, so the trunk was "one dash pattern with a
  colour change in it". That is exactly what put the pattern's **2.5pt gap directly under every
  corner** — the one place on the line where an interruption reads as a break rather than as a dash.
  Every run now starts with a dash, which is what `Shape::dashed_line` does unasked, and the property
  that matters is the one that follows: *a run beginning at a junction inks it, whatever the arithmetic
  either side works out to*. The cost is one double-length dash per junction, which reads as the
  junction being marked.
- **The snap.** The elbow's y was snapped in the painter, for the horizontal run only, while the
  vertical was *split* at the unsnapped value — half a device pixel of disagreement at every corner,
  and the half that survives any dash arithmetic. It moved to `elbow_y`, which is now the one place the
  number comes from, the fixture in the tests included.
- **The clearance.** `ELBOW_CLEAR` was 1.0, which put the elbow's first dash half a point off the
  trunk's ink — a blot rather than a corner. It is `0.5 + GUIDE_GAP` = 3, one gap of the pattern past
  the trunk's own edge, which is the *"start a pixel or two more to the right"* the report asked for and
  makes the corner read as the pattern turning.

**The lesson is about the flip-check, not about the arithmetic.** `a_trunk_broken_at_the_elbow_keeps_one_dash_pattern`
bit correctly against `0.0` and proved the offset was *reaching the painter* — it could not say the
offset was the right thing to want, because nothing about a phase is visible in a list of runs. What
replaced it asserts on the **painted dashes** instead, and its own doc says which half of it bites: the
connector's last dash ended exactly at the elbow in the broken version too, so "there is ink at the
elbow's y" passes either way, and only what happens *below* it changed. *A test can pin a decision
without having any opinion about it.*

The ASCII probe came back for both items and was worth it again: hover grey down to the hovered row's
elbow, blue from there to the selected row's own, and a double dash straddling every junction.

**D345 — The drop follows the indent, both ways, and the hint had to move out of the walk to say so.
*Built and tested 2026-08-25, with five follow-ups the same day after it had been lived with on the
machine, and **reviewed and accepted** that day — "Works quite well."; Keep. Answers D306's first ground
for the static case without reversing its non-goal, and
makes D67's one-owner rule structural.*** Asked for as the gesture every tree tool
has: *"I can order a layer inside a group, or get it at the bottom of that group and shift it to the
left so it now indents out of the group and into the parent. Same way I can make a layer belong to a
group. That means that the drop indicator we show takes indents into account visually."*

**A gap between two rows is a *run* of insertion points, not one** — a level for each the two rows have
in common — and the pointer's horizontal travel is the only thing that picks between them.
`layers::depth_range` is the whole rule. The shallowest offer is the depth of the row **below** the
boundary, and it is a hard floor: anything shallower would have to close containers the rows below are
still inside. The deepest is the depth of the row **above**, or the floor where that is deeper. So the
boundary under a group's last child spans the group's level and its parent's, and moving left there
carries the layer out.

⚠️ **That second clause is the "first child of an open container" case, and it is why no row records
whether it is open.** A container's children are drawn immediately below it, so "the row below is
deeper than the row above" and "the row above is an expanded container" are the same statement about a
tree. A *collapsed* container has nothing of its own below it, so the range stops at its own level and
the only way in remains the middle-of-row outline (§9.4). The first draft carried an `expanded: bool`
on the row record and computed `above.depth + is_expanded`, which is the identical number on every
input — a field with nothing to say and one more thing that could come to disagree with the walk, so
it was removed. (A `closed` flag arrived later for spring-loading, and it is not the same question
asked the other way round — see below.)

⚠️ **The x is a displacement from the grab, never an absolute reading.** `depth_asked_for` is
`grab_depth + round((x − grab_x) / INDENT)`, floored at 1 and then clamped into the boundary's range.
Reading the depth straight off the pointer is the obvious spelling and it is unusable: a row is picked
up by its *name*, which at depth 1 already starts ~45pt in, so the drag would be asking for depth 2
before the pointer had moved. `LayerDrag.grab` is the pair it measures from — the pointer's x at
**`press_origin()`**, not the position at `drag_started()`, which is already a drag threshold's travel
away and would bake that slop in as a constant offset for the rest of the gesture — the same seam D35
found in `guide_input`, and the same answer — and the *grabbed* row's depth, since a drag carrying rows
from several levels has no one depth. The unit is `INDENT`, 31,
settled by D331. The line is then drawn at the chosen level's own column — `rect.left() +
indent_of(depth)` to the panel's right edge — which is the only thing on screen saying which of the
levels the drop means; the gap-centred y is D67's, unchanged.

**Then the hue and the width moved, both asked for on the machine.** The line and the "inside" outline
were `color::ACCENT` and are `color::SELECT`: `GuideInk::Selected` is `SELECT` (D331) and so is a
selected row's kind glyph, and a drop hint is the panel talking about a layer in exactly the sense D13
reserves that hue for — *"so we keep it consistent"*. And `DROP_LINE_PT` is 2.0 again, *"right now it's
a bit too thin"*: at one point the line is a hairline the eye has to hunt for, which is the wrong trade
for the single most important thing a drag has to say. ⚠️ **That partly reverses D67's pairing
argument, and the outline has *not* moved with it** — D67 took the line to 1pt *because* the outline
was 1pt, since at two "the pair read as belonging to different controls rather than as two answers to
the same question". That argument compared two strokes of equal length and is weaker than it looks
here: a 1pt outline runs the whole way round a 26pt row where a 2pt line is one short horizontal run,
so the outline is already the heavier mark of the two by area. Both doc comments carry it. *If the
outline is ever reported as looking thin beside the line, the outline is the thing to re-read — not
this constant.*

**The level is held with hysteresis, because plain rounding has no threshold at all.** Reported as
*"moving the line between indents is a bit twitchy"*, and the diagnosis is the whole entry: 0.5 of an
indent is not a threshold but the point where two levels are *equally close*, so a hand that is aiming
at neither — holding a drag still, or moving down the tree with a few points of sideways drift — sits
exactly on it and the line flips frame to frame. Anything above 0.5 turns that edge into a band.
`depth_asked_for` grew a fourth argument, `held`, the level the drag settled on last frame: the level
only changes once the pointer is more than `STICK` — 0.65 of an indent, 20pt of travel against the bare
15.5 — from the one being held, and then it re-rounds to the nearest, so the jump is never to a level
the hand has passed over. **It is real hysteresis rather than a wider dead zone because the band is
centred on the level being *held* and so travels with the answer**: leaving level 2 rightwards takes
2.65 and coming back from 3 takes 2.35, two different x for the same crossing.
`the_level_sticks_until_the_pointer_has_really_left_it` demonstrates one x — 2.55 indents from the grab
— reading as 2 or 3 depending only on where the drag already was.

⚠️ **The fed-back value is the *unclamped* one, and that is load-bearing.** `drop_spot` returns a
`DropRead { spot, level }`: `spot`'s depth has been clamped into what the boundary offers, `level` has
not, and `level` is what `LayerDrag.level` stores for next frame. Feeding the clamped one back would
let a boundary offering a single level quietly re-origin the gesture, so dragging *over* a one-level
gap would change what the hand's position meant on the far side of it. `LayerDrag.level` starts at the
grabbed row's depth, and the `Into` arm carries it through untouched for the same reason — the pointer
is not asking about indents in the middle of a container row, and zeroing it there would re-origin the
gesture on the way past a group.

**The restructure was forced rather than cosmetic.** `update_drop_target` ran from inside `layers_row`
for whichever row contained the pointer, `paint_drop_hint` ran per row, and the free function
`drop_line` decided whether *this* row owned the boundary; all three are gone. An indent-aware drop is
a claim about the row above a boundary and the row below it at once, and a row painting itself does not
know what follows it — the same argument D331 made for the guides, and the walk's `GuideRow` is now
`TreeRow`, with an `id` and a `container` flag added and two passes reading it. **The side effect is
worth as much as the feature**: a boundary is named by its position **on screen** (`boundary_y`,
`0..=rows.len()`), so D67's "exactly one row draws each boundary" is true by construction and the same
boundary can no longer be reached from two different child lists. That report is now unreachable rather
than fixed — which does not make `drop_line_y`'s arithmetic optional, since the day something reaches
for `rect.top()` again the line moves a pixel at *every* boundary instead of at one.

**Resolving a level to a parent and an index** is `resolve_drop`. One level in from the row above means
inside it, at `child_count` — the top of its list on screen and the end of it in the model, the walk
being reversed (§5.3). Otherwise the row above is walked up to the ancestor sitting at that depth
(`ancestor_at_depth`) and *that* node's own slot is the answer, which degenerates to the row itself
when the drop is at the row's own level, so there is one path rather than a special case. No row above
is the end of the root's list, guarded on `depth == 1`.

**`DropTarget` lost its third field to the same reading.** It was `{ parent, index, into }`, `into`
saying whether the drop landed inside a container rather than between siblings, and nothing outside a
test had ever read it: the affordance is chosen from `DropSpot`, which is what the pointer actually
landed on, and `plan_layer_move` only ever wanted the parent and the index. It had also stopped
meaning what it was called, which is the half worth keeping — a drop indented in as a container's
first child *is* a drop inside it and set `into: false`, because by then the field meant "which of the
two hints was drawn" rather than anything about the destination.

⚠️ **And no gate would have said so — the one that kept it quiet is the derived `PartialEq`, which
makes this a fact about most of the small records in the app crate rather than about this struct.**
Measured rather than reasoned about, on a private module holding one `pub` struct with one unread
field, built as a bin under `rustc --edition 2021`: bare, `dead_code` fires; with `Debug` it still
fires, rustc deliberately not counting that as a read; with `Clone, Copy` it still fires; add
`PartialEq, Eq` and it goes silent, `--test` or not, with the test module absent entirely. So the
tests were never part of the explanation — they made the field *look* alive to a reader, but plain
`cargo check` had already stopped seeing it, and **any struct here that derives `PartialEq` can carry
a field nothing reads with every gate green.** And it is **not** the `pub`, which is worth stating
because that is the reflex and the first draft of the source comment blamed it: `ondin-app` declares
only `[[bin]] name = "ondin"`, so a `pub` item inside one of its modules is not externally reachable
and the lint does analyse it — that exemption is `ondin-core`'s, one crate over. This one went because
the struct was read against `plan_layer_move`, not because anything failed. *Removed 2026-08-25; the
struct's own doc comment carries the measurement.*

⚠️ **The no-cycle check moved from the hovered row to the destination parent, and that is not a
simplification.** The old check refused a drop when the row *under the pointer* was a dragged node or a
descendant of one; during an outdent the pointer sits on a dragged row's own child the whole way, so
that reading refuses the gesture it is there to allow. What is actually illegal is a destination inside
what is being carried, so `parent` is what is asked. `build::can_parent` for every carried node against
the chosen parent is unchanged (D54).

**Two smaller decisions inside it, both about the pointer rather than the tree.** It is allowed to
**leave the panel to the left**: `drop_spot` bounds it with `pointer.x > row.rect.right()` only. The
whole row is the drag handle — `allocate_exact_size(available_width(), ROW_H)` with
`Sense::click_and_drag()` — so a row can be picked up in the empty gutter left of its glyphs, a few
points from the panel's edge, and one indent of leftward travel from there is off the panel altogether.
`rect.contains(pointer)` would leave the outdent reachable from some grab points and not from others,
which reads as it working intermittently. ⚠️ **The number to reason from is the grab, not the glyph**:
the code comment on `drop_spot` used to say "grabbed by its icon at depth 2 is roughly 20pt in", which
was wrong and made the case sound tighter than it is — `icon_x` at depth 2 is 47 or 61 depending on
whether the row keeps caret room, and an outdent from *there* stays on the panel comfortably. The
comment has been corrected and now carries those two numbers and the reason the *whole row* being the
handle is what matters. What actually needs the freedom is the gutter grab, which is what
`the_outdent_still_works_when_the_pointer_has_left_the_panel` uses (`grab_x = 18.0` on a depth-2 row,
asserted to be off the panel after one indent). To the right the rect still bounds it; past the panel
is the canvas. And **the gap between two rows is the boundary, not a dead
band**: the pointer picks the first row it has not passed the bottom of, rather than the row containing
it. The rows do not touch — `item_spacing.y` is 1 — so containment blanked the indicator for the frame
the pointer spent crossing each boundary, and a single bad frame counts.

**Spring-loading: rest a drag on a collapsed group for a second and the branch opens.** Asked for as
*"drag a layer, hover over a group for 1 second, it auto expands"* — the maintainer corrected the word
in the next message, having written *collapses*, so the record says expands. `SPRING_SECS` is 1.0,
`LayerDrag.spring` is an `Option<(NodeId, f64)>`, and `OndinApp::spring_load` does
`self.collapsed.remove(&id)` — the same set a caret click writes, so the tree is left open afterwards.
Without it a collapsed branch can only be dropped *onto*, never ordered within, and the way in is to
abandon the drag and click the caret. Two decisions inside it. **Only the "inside this one" zone
springs, not the whole row**: the row's edges mean "between", and opening a branch there would shift
every row below the pointer out from under a drop the hand had already aimed at, where aiming at the
middle is the one case in which opening is what was being asked for — and the group's own row does not
move when it does. And **passing `None` restarts the wait rather than pausing it**, so a drag that
crosses a group and comes back waits the full second again: two visits of 0.6s do not add up to one of
1.2.

⚠️ **`TreeRow` gained a `closed: bool` and it is *not* the negation of the `expanded` flag removed
above.** That is why one could go and the other had to come. An *open* container is exactly a row whose
successor is deeper, so the row list already said it and the field had nothing to add; a *closed* one
is invisible in the same list, because it has no rows below it and neither does a leaf. Nothing on
screen tells those two apart, and spring-loading is the one thing that has to.

**The timing is the `request_repaint_after`, not the clock read.** egui only lays out a frame when
something asks it to and a hand holding still asks for nothing, so without it `spring_load` would read
the clock once, on the frame the pointer arrived, and the group would open on whatever unrelated event
woke the panel next. The drag already requests a repaint every frame in `layers_tree`, which makes this
redundant today and correct on the day that changes.

**The line cannot say *which* container, so the container says it — in its own ink.** Two levels are
one 31pt step apart and the eye otherwise counts indent columns, which was the fifth thing asked for.
It was built first as a dim dashed outline round the destination row (`dotted_outline`,
`color::SELECT_DIM`, the tree guides' own dash rhythm) and **taken straight out again on the machine**:
*"let's remove the dotted outline, that doesn't sit right"*, then *"only highlight the text and icon of
the group to blue, should be enough affordance"*. Two boxes in a panel that already uses one to mean
"inside" is a second vocabulary — which is exactly what this entry's own non-goal said when it refused
a container outline on D67's reasoning, so that refusal was right about the mark and wrong only about
whether the *question* needed answering.

**What stands is `LayerDrag.lit`.** The destination parent's row paints its name and kind glyph
`color::SELECT` for as long as the drop points into it, read in `layers_row` as `drop_host`. ⚠️ **It is
the destination parent**, which during an outdent is several levels above the row under the pointer,
not the row above the line; nothing lights at the top level, where the parent is the root and has no
row. ⚠️ **And it is a frame behind, necessarily** — a row's ink is painted while the walk is passing
it, and an indent-aware target is not known until the walk is over, so the walk reads the answer the
*last* one reached. That is the same deal every hover in the panel already runs on, and the lag shows
only on the frames where the drop changes container. `layers_tree` copies `target` into `lit` at the
top of the frame, in the one place `target` is thrown away, so the two cannot drift: there is no second
assignment that could forget. ⚠️ **`lit` is for painting only.** `target` is still cleared every frame
so that releasing off the tree drops nothing (D19); this is that same staleness kept deliberately, and
it must never decide where a layer lands. **The drop host outranks both selection and dimming**, the
way a hover beats a selection in the guides (D331): a drag is a question being asked now where the
other two are states that persist, and a locked or hidden group still takes children, so a host left at
40% would be the panel declining to answer.

**This entry listed three things deliberately not built, and the day it was lived with settled all
three differently.** Spring-loading was simply wrong and is built. The middle 40% of a container row
**is still `into` whatever the x says**, and that one holds: the middle of a container row is where the
hand goes to say "inside", and an indent gesture there would be two meanings on one 10pt band. And the
container outline — refused because "a box means inside", per D67 — was asked for, built, looked at and
removed within the day for the reason it had been refused for. ⚠️ **So the non-goal was right about the
mark and wrong about the question**: naming the destination container was worth doing, and a box was
not the way. That is the shape to watch for in a non-goal reasoned from the implementation rather than
from use — it can be a correct objection to one drawing standing in for a decision about the need.

*Nine tests in `layers::drop_indent_tests`, each flip-checked against the plausible wrong version and
each flip run rather than argued.*
`one_gap_offers_a_level_per_indent_and_the_pointer_picks_it` drives a real drag through `layers_tree`
over a six-row fixture and asserts that one gap gives `{group, 0}` at depth 3 and `{frame, 1}` at depth
2, with the two lines drawn exactly `INDENT` apart; the flip is the old behaviour — the depth taken
from the hovered row — and every assertion fails on it, where asserting merely that *a* line is drawn
would have passed. Five more pin the middle of a container row against an indent-aware reading of it
(which is a claim rather than an absence now that every other part of the drag reads the x), the
boundary against `rect.y_range().contains`, the left-hand
freedom against `rect.contains(pointer)` (with the right-hand edge still refusing), `depth_range` over
the six boundaries of `[1,2,3,3,2,1]` plus a tree whose last row is nested, and the displacement
arithmetic. ⚠️ **The fixture's group holds *two* rects and its frame holds something besides the
group, and both are load-bearing**: with one rect the interesting drag is a drop beside itself, so
"stayed inside" and "went nowhere" are the same outcome, and without the extra row the boundary has no
shallower row below it and the range collapses to one level, leaving nothing to pick between.

**The three follow-up tests, and what each flip proved.**
`the_level_sticks_until_the_pointer_has_really_left_it` flips `STICK` to 0.5, which is *identical* to
plain rounding — ⚠️ and only the ±0.64 entries of its first loop fail on that, which the test's own doc
says rather than claiming the whole test bites: everything nearer the column agrees with plain rounding
by construction. `resting_a_drag_on_a_collapsed_group_opens_it` asserts four things — that it does not
open on arrival, does not open early, opens at the second, and that the wait restarts — against a flip
that starts the timer afresh every frame, which is the shape you get from writing the assignment before
the comparison, and on which it never opens at all.
`the_line_names_its_container_by_colouring_that_rows_ink` reads galleys rather than dashes — every
`Shape::Text` whose layout job carries `color::SELECT`, as `(text, y)` — and asserts three things: the
group's name and kind glyph light for a drop inside it, the frame's light instead and the group's goes
out one indent left, and nothing lights at the top level, where the parent is the root and has no row.
The two rows are identified by asking the document for the node's name and `node_icon`'s glyph rather
than writing either out.

⚠️ **Its first flip did not bite, and that is a fact about the code rather than a failed experiment.**
Lighting the row *above* the line — the reading that looks right and is only right at one level — leaves
every assertion green, because `lit` is derived in exactly one place, from `target.parent` at the moment
`target` is discarded, so a wrong answer written anywhere later is overwritten before any row reads it.
The error the test names is not reachable by a one-line slip. The flip that *does* bite is **clearing
`lit` at the top of the frame instead of carrying last frame's answer**, which is the mistake with a
comment three lines above it telling you to make it, since that is exactly what `target` beside it
wants: the row's ink never changes and the first assertion fails on `[]`. **Both halves are worth
keeping** — the flip that failed is the evidence that this has only one place to go wrong, which is why
it is written that way, and what would reintroduce the error is someone deriving `lit` from the rows
instead.

⚠️ **It is also the sharpest demonstration of the frame-lag from the test side**: it needs more than one
pass, and `pump`'s five are why it holds. A row's ink is painted while the walk passes it and the drop
is not resolved until the walk is over, so one pass shows nothing lit and would prove the opposite of
the truth. And ⚠️ **the colour is read off the layout job's section, not off a mesh** — `FullOutput::shapes`
is pre-tessellation, so there are no vertices yet, and the input is the only one of a galley's two
colours available there. `painter.text` puts it in the section and nothing in this panel overrides it
afterwards, so for these rows the two agree; that is a property of these rows rather than a general
licence to read a galley's colour off its job.

⚠️ **Measuring the tree can change the tree, and the fixture assertion is the only reason that did not
ship.** `row_rects` reads row boxes out of the paint by selecting rows and finding their `SELECT_ROW`
grounds — and `sync_tree_to_selection` opens *every ancestor* of anything selected, so measuring with a
blanket selection re-expands the very group the spring-loading test had just collapsed. It caught it at
six rows against the four expected. `row_rects` now takes the rows to light as an argument and
`open_rows` is the blanket case named as such; the trap is written on `open_rows`. The other new helper
is `pump_at`, which pins the frame clock through `RawInput::time` so the wait is explicit rather than a
race with the wall clock — all five of its settling passes see the same `t`, so a spring can only fire
on a later call. `pump` deliberately still runs on egui's own clock, because pinning it there would
change the conditions of every test that already goes through it.

**Reviewed on the machine 2026-08-25 and accepted: *"Works quite well."*** That verdict covers the
whole of it, follow-ups included — the `SELECT` hue on both affordances, the 2pt line, `STICK`'s
hysteresis, spring-loading, and the destination container's own ink standing in for the dashed outline
that was asked for and withdrawn. So none of the five is a provisional value waiting for a second look,
and **none of them is to be re-argued from the reasoning above** — the reasoning is why they are what
they are, not an open case. *Change one only against a fresh report from use.*

**D332 — Double-clicking a layer crashed the app, and the culprit was a focus request that had been
right for six months. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-24, and **verified on the machine at all three doors**
— "no crash on double click, ctrl + r, rename on the menu". Keep. Supersedes D216's mechanism and keeps
its reasoning.*** Reported verbatim: *"Double clicking on a layer in the layer panel crashes with a panic:
`accesskit_consumer-0.35.0\src\tree.rs:71: Focused ID #2077194978197920161 is not in the node list`"*.

**The mechanism, because it is a trap in egui's shape rather than a mistake in ours.** `Focus::end_pass`
carries a dead-man's switch — a focused widget the pass did not register is dropped — with one
deliberate exception, commented in egui as *"Allow calling `request_focus` one frame and not using it
until next frame"*: a **recently gained** focus survives it. The AccessKit update is assembled *after*
that, taking its nodes from what the pass registered and its `focus` from `Memory::focused()` regardless.
So a fresh `request_focus` naming a widget the frame does not draw is not the deferral it reads as; it is
a `TreeUpdate` whose focus is not in its own node list, and `accesskit_consumer` panics on that rather
than ignoring it.

**Which makes the invariant sharp, and narrower than "focus must always name a live widget":** a widget
that *disappears* is fine — the dead-man's switch clears it, and it runs before the AccessKit block — so
the only crash is the frame a request is made for a widget that frame will not draw. That is worth
knowing before hunting for other cases: closing the document under an open rename, hiding the panel, a
row scrolling away, all safe.

**Two of the four doors onto a rename were in exactly that state, and the third was safe by accident of
frame order.** The layers panel's double-click sets `renaming_layer` and the field is drawn a few lines
later — but gated on a `renaming` flag latched *above* the click handler, so not on that frame. The
context menu's *Rename* row dispatches from `context_menu_ui`, which is drawn **after** `layers_panel`,
so nothing could put the field in that frame at all. `Ctrl+R` and `F2` reach the same
`rename_selection` from the keymap, which runs *before* the panels — so the chord drew the field in the
same frame and never crashed. One function, three callers, and the frame position decided which of them
was a bug.

**The field asks for the caret itself now, on the frame it first draws** —
`read_response(fid).is_none()`, which is "this field did not exist last pass". That is the spelling D216
explicitly rejected, and D216 was right about *why*: the version it was rejecting is "re-request while
it does not have focus", which also fires on the frame `Enter` or `Escape` takes focus away, so the field
grabs it back and the rename can never be committed or cancelled. A one-shot on first **existence** is
not that test, and it is the only arrangement that works from all four doors. `rename_selection` no
longer takes a `&Context`: nothing about opening a rename is a question for egui.

**The rest of the app's focus requests were checked against the same rule and are safe**, which is the
part worth writing down because they look identical at the call site. The layer-search field requests
focus from the header button and is drawn — `if let Some(filter) = &mut self.layer_filter` — a few lines
later in the *same* frame. That is the difference, and it is the question to ask of any
`request_focus`: *does this frame still have the field in it?*

⚠️ **D216's test was the wrong kind of correct and has been replaced.**
`a_focus_request_survives_until_the_rename_field_exists` asserted that egui holds a request across the
gap. It does. Pinning a true fact about a library is not the same as pinning that the app is allowed to
rely on it, and this is the second time in two days a green test has guarded a decision it had no
opinion about (see D331's second round). The two that replace it assert what the app needs:
`the_rename_field_asks_for_the_caret_on_the_frame_it_first_draws`, whose second half flip-checks against
the re-request trap by surrendering focus with the field still open, and
`a_rename_opened_after_the_panel_has_drawn_leaves_no_dangling_focus`, which turns AccessKit on with
`Context::enable_accesskit` and asserts the invariant the consumer panics on — `update.focus` is among
`update.nodes` — in the menu's frame order. Flip-checked by putting the request back into the dispatch
arm: it reports the focus missing from a list of three nodes. **The crash is reproducible headlessly**,
which was not obvious: it needs no window, only the update egui would have sent one.

**D333 — Layer effects, and the two that were designed beside them and deliberately not built.
*Built and tested 2026-08-24; Keep. The inspector panel and the GPU canvas's passes are unbuilt and
sit in `roadmap.md`; that file's §0 line "effects (shadow/blur)" is struck and `architecture.md` §1's
*Deferred* bullet rewritten.*** Effects were a decided non-goal — §1 read *"Filters, blur, shadows, blend modes beyond
normal"* — until the maintainer reopened them: *"Something we marked for after v1, but the target has
changed"*, with `design/Editor.dc.html` regenerated to draw an Effects panel of **six** types.

**Four of the six, and the four are not an arbitrary subset**: they are the ones that can be made to
agree across the canvas, the raster export and the SVG writer. The other two were put to the
maintainer explicitly and declined, and the reasons are recorded here because they are exactly the
kind of thing a later reader re-argues from the mockup:

- **Background blur** blurs the *backdrop*, so it only means anything when the thing being exported
  contains the backdrop — export the frame and it is already baked in, export the blurred layer alone
  and there is nothing behind it to sample. SVG cannot express it at all: the `BackgroundImage` filter
  input was specified and never implemented by any renderer, which is why Figma's own SVG output
  substitutes a transparent flood named `BackgroundImageFix`.
- **Noise** would need the same generator written three times — a WGSL shader, the CPU rasterizer and
  `feTurbulence` — agreeing *to the pixel*, or the file stops matching the screen. And it is probably
  not an effect: Figma moved noise into the **fill** list, where it would inherit our `Brush`
  machinery and the SVG writer's existing embedded-raster fallback, which makes it exact for free.
  Filed as a brush question rather than as a deferred effect, so the next reader starts from `Brush`.

**Blend modes stay deferred, including the per-effect "Blend" dropdown the new mockup draws inside
both shadow popovers.** That was my call rather than the maintainer's, and it is here so it is not
mistaken for an omission: blend modes are their own non-goal with `Shift+3`…`Shift+9` reserved behind
them in `shortcuts.md` §2, and reversing that deserves its own decision rather than a ride-along on
this one. The cost when it comes is small — both backends' `push_layer` already takes a blend mode
and SVG has `feBlend`.

**A repeatable ordered `Vec`, not one slot per kind**, chosen by the maintainer against the
alternative. Two drop shadows at different distances is an ordinary thing to want, the list order is
the compositing order, and it makes an effect row the same shape of code as a fill row.
`an_effect_stack_round_trips_in_order_and_costs_nothing_when_empty` puts **two entries of the same
kind** in its fixture for that reason: a loader that deduped by kind still round-trips a one-entry
stack and still equals itself, and fails only there.

**Three controls were added to the design**, at the maintainer's invitation — *"if there's any
controls I forgot to add in the design (like color for shadows), please add it"*: a **colour** on both
shadows, **spread** on the inner shadow (the mockup had it on the drop shadow alone; it is the same
dilation of the same silhouette, and Figma offers both), and a **visibility toggle** per row. The
mockup drew only an `×`, and delete-to-hide is destructive over half a dozen tuned numbers — the same
argument `Fill::visible` already won, one step louder. The shadow's **opacity is the colour's alpha**
and is not a field of its own, which is the rule fills already follow (`paint::alpha_of` /
`with_alpha`); the mockup's Opacity field edits that alpha. A second spelling of alpha is what ends up
disagreeing with itself the first time an eyedropper writes one of the two.

**The model is a node field, not part of `Paint`** (§5.3a). A drop shadow on a group and a blur over a
whole frame are the commonest uses and neither has a fill to hang from, so `Operation::SetEffects` is
gated on **the root alone** where every other paint op asks `takes_paint()` — the root being the
document rather than a layer in it, the line `op_create` and `op_delete` already draw
(`effects_go_on_a_container_but_never_on_the_root`). The op writes the whole stack, so a reorder, a
removal, a visibility toggle and a tuned number are one operation with one inverse and the panel never
has to describe *which* of those it made. `changes_ink` answers **true**, and it is the one
paint-adjacent op that changes ink outside the layer it names. The save format is purely additive
(§5.11): no schema bump, and no existing file's bytes move.

**`Filters` is factors with 1.0 neutral and degrees for hue, and deliberately not `ImageAdjust`'s
`-1.0..=1.0` with zero neutral** (§5.5a). Two conventions for the same idea in one codebase is exactly
what drifts, so the difference is stated rather than carried quietly: `ImageAdjust` is a photographic
control surface authored against a picture, while these numbers go straight into `feColorMatrix` and
into the shader, and D186's lesson was that the writer which cannot invent arithmetic should choose
the units.

**A blur stores the radius the designer types, not the gaussian deviation**, with `BLUR_DEVIATION` as
the one place the two are related (CSS's `blur(12px)` means a deviation of 6; SVG and both vello
backends take the deviation). Storing the deviation would make every panel field divide on read and
multiply on write and would put a number in the file that no part of the UI ever shows.

**The render passes are one specification read by both backends** (§6.4), which is a dependency fact
rather than taste: `vello` 0.9 has no filter beyond `draw_blurred_rounded_rect`, and `vello_cpu` 0.0.9
implements only `GaussianBlur` and `DropShadow` over single-primitive graphs — no `ColorMatrix`, no
`Composite` — so neither colour filters nor an inner shadow can be expressed there at all. (⚠️ Still
true at the `=0.2.0` pin, **re-checked rather than renumbered**: 0.2.0's filter module grew `flood`,
`offset` and `shift` and neither missing kind is among them — §15 D414.) Taking the
library's two would mean two implementations of blur on the two backends §3 exists to keep identical.
`ScenePainter::push_effect_layer` **defaults to compositing plainly**, so a backend without the passes
draws the artwork unfiltered rather than dropping it, and the walk's push/pop pairing holds either way.
The walk emits it **outermost** — outside the clip, so a clipping frame's own shadow escapes the frame
instead of being cut off at the very edge it exists to escape, and outside the opacity, so the shadow
is cast from the layer as it actually appears. Those two orders agree for a plain fade and part
company the moment a `Filters` row is in the stack. Ghosts get their own in `paint_ghost`, measured
from the ghost's outline rather than from `Resolved`, which has never seen a ghost: without it an
Alt-drag copy of a shadowed layer draws flat for the whole drag and gains its shadow at the instant of
release.

**Both writers build the graph in two stages, not one fold** — appearance first (`Filters`,
`LayerBlur`, in list order), then every shadow cast from *that* and merged behind or in front. The
one-fold version is what anyone writes first and it makes an inner shadow following a drop shadow take
its silhouette from the layer **plus the shadow**, drawing a second inner edge along the shadow's
outside. Three SVG traps are recorded in §7 because the markup is well-formed in every wrong version:
the explicit filter region, the wrapper outside the clip, and a `<filter>` with no primitives
rendering its element as *nothing at all* rather than as a no-op.

**What is not built, said plainly so nobody re-discovers it as a bug**: the inspector's Effects card
is a stub reading "Shadows, blur and filters export but have no panel yet", so a stack can be authored
only through `Operation::SetEffects` today; the GPU canvas takes the painter's default and draws
effected layers unfiltered; and there is no drag-reorder in the UI, though the model has the order.
All three are in `roadmap.md`. *All three closed within a day: **D337** is the panel, and **D339** is
the GPU's passes — which also found **D338**, a panic this entry's own layer ordering had been setting
up since it was written. What is left of the three is the drag-reorder alone.*

⚠️ **A shape converted to a path loses its effects.** `build::replace_with_path` is what *Outline
shape*, *Convert to path* and a one-boolean *Flatten* all funnel through, and it states the rule this
breaks: "this **is** the same layer, so everything about it that is not its geometry comes across". It
carries the name, the opacity, the visibility, the pivot and the mask — the pivot having been added
after being lost silently once (D230) — and lists the two deliberate exclusions beside them, the lock
and the proportion lock. Effects are in neither list, so outlining a shadowed shape drops its shadow
with nothing on screen saying why. *Fix with a `SetEffects` beside the `SetMask`, on the mask's own
argument: the new path is the same layer in the same slot, so it decorates the same way.*

**D334 — The ink box, and the three readers that did not follow it. *The split is built, tested and
Keep; the three readers were fixed the same day.*** An effect draws outside the geometry it hangs on, which is the
first thing in this model to do so, and it forced a question the codebase had never had to answer:
*which* box does a caller mean. `Resolved` gained a second cache, `ink_bounds`, beside `world_bounds`
rather than widening it.

**`world_bounds` keeps meaning the box of the thing you are editing.** The selection outline, the
inspector's W and H, snapping, the rulers, the marquee and the R-tree all read it — **192 references
across `crates/` on 2026-08-24**, tests included, and **202** when that was re-run on 2026-09-07 — and
a shadow must not move any of them: softening a blur would grow
the reported height, and a snap would catch on a shadow's edge. `ink_bounds` is that box grown by
`effect::stack_escape` at every level of the subtree — measured from the children's *ink*, or a shadow
one level down would be forgotten by every ancestor — and it is the answer culling and export want.
It is a second **map** rather than a field on every entry because the two are equal for the
overwhelming majority of nodes: nothing carries an effect until someone adds one.

That count is **dated rather than updated**, and deliberately. It is load-bearing in this entry's own
argument — it is *why* `ink_bounds` was added beside `world_bounds` instead of widening it — so what
matters is the size of the sweep the decision declined to make, which is a fact about 2026-08-24. A
number silently refreshed to today's reads as though the decision were taken against it. **A §15 entry
is a record of a decision at a time**; where a figure argues for the decision, carry both readings and
say when each was taken.

**`escaped` splits a local escape into an offset and a radius rather than transforming four corners,
and my first implementation was the other one.** A blur's reach is a **disc**. Read as a local square
and rotated, its AABB is up to √2 bigger than it should be, so a rotated blurred layer would have
cached — and exported — a box **41% too wide**. Split, the offset is a vector the linear part maps
directly and the radius becomes the exact half-extents of the mapped ellipse, which is the row's
euclidean norm rather than its absolute row sum. The four-corner reading looks completely reasonable,
which is the whole reason this is written down; `a_rotated_blur_reaches_its_radius_and_not_its_diagonal`
answers 14.142 against it. Two more properties are pinned because each is a plausible wrong version:
`stack_escape` is the **union** and not the sum (two effects reaching 10px out reach 10, not 20), and
`escaped` **never shrinks** a box, since a shadow thrown entirely to one side leaves the geometry's own
edge needing coverage on the other.

⚠️ **That union sentence is right about the case it was written for and was not the whole rule**
(D473, 2026-09-07). It holds for two **shadows**, which are cast side by side from one silhouette; it
is false for anything §6.4 *composes*, and §6.4 composes two things — `Filters` and `LayerBlur` run
sequentially on the layer and every shadow is then cast from **that**. So two layer blurs convolve at
`σ = √(σ₁² + σ₂²)` and a drop shadow's reach starts one stage-1 blur further out, and the union is now
taken **per stage** rather than over the raw per-effect escapes. The union half is kept and never
became a sum; what changed is the quantities it is taken over.

⚠️ **Three readers were not swept when the split landed, and each was visible.** **Culling**
(`scene::paint_node`) still tested `world_bounds`, so a layer whose own box had left the viewport was
skipped while its shadow was still reaching into it — the shadow vanishing at the edge of the window.
**`plan::raster_size`** measured `world_bounds` where the render frames from `extent`'s `ink_bounds`,
so the Export row predicted a smaller image than the file it writes, and **`plan::raster_opts`** worked
out a `Width(512)` multiplier against a box the file is not framed on. All three were fixed the same
day, and the sweep is the lesson rather than the bug: **adding a second spelling of an existing
question does not move the callers of the first one**, and the compiler cannot say which of them meant
which — `world_bounds` has close to two hundred occurrences across `crates/` and every one of them
still compiled. Two comments of the author's own asserted the cull already followed the ink box while
it did not, which is how a wrong sweep survives review: the prose describes the intended state.

**D335 — The snapshot grew effects without a version bump. *Bumped to 8 the same day.*** `NodeSnapshot::effects`
reports a layer's visible entries in compositing order, with a string `kind` and the authored numbers
(a blur's radius, not the deviation), skipped when empty. Reporting them is right — the alternative is
a projection describing a layer with a drop shadow as a layer with no shadow, which is the exact
failure `snapshot.rs` is careful about everywhere else. What did not happen is `SNAPSHOT_VERSION`
moving off **7**, and that is against this list's own precedent rather than a judgement call: **5** was
bumped for `PaintSummary::Image::adjust`, which is likewise absent when neutral, on the grounds that a
reader who has never heard of adjustments describes an adjusted photograph as the file it came from.
A reader on 7 describes a shadowed layer as a flat one. Bumped to **8** with a paragraph in the
version's doc comment, and `every-kind.json` regenerated: the diff is **one line**, the version itself
— which is the byte-compared golden (D304) incidentally proving the other half of the claim, that
`skip_serializing_if` keeps the key out of a document carrying no effects.

**D336 — "Exactly nine operations change nothing drawn" was nine in the prose and ten in the `match`.
*Fixed 2026-08-24.*** `only_the_chrome_operations_change_no_ink` exists to catch a new operation being
filed in the wrong arm of `changes_ink`, and says so in its own doc comment: the `match` is
wildcard-free, so a new op stops the build, but nothing stops its author choosing the wrong arm. It
had missed one itself. `SetExports` arrived under D274 answering `false` — correctly, nothing drawn
reads it — and neither the count nor the fixture was recounted, so a test that lists the invisible ops
listed nine of the ten and passed.

Nothing failed, and nothing could have: a count in a doc comment and a list in a fixture are both
prose as far as every gate is concerned, which is the same lesson as D302's unlinted tests and D319's
unreadable ones. Ten in the test, in the test's doc and in §5.7 on the day, with the miss written into
the test's own comment so the next reader recounts rather than trusts.

⚠️ **A fourth copy of the number was missed by that fix**, in `Operation::changes_ink`'s own doc
comment, which read *"The same **nine** operations `RenderOverrides::absorb` treats as a no-op"* while
that arm of `absorb` held ten. It was corrected, and the set has since moved again: `SetLayoutGrids`
arrived answering `false`, so the answer is **eleven**.

🚨 **The sentence that stood here — *"and `absorb`'s no-op arm holds the same eleven. The two lists
have never disagreed. Only the sentences about them have."* — was itself wrong, and is corrected at
§15 D659.** `absorb` has a **second** no-op arm further down the same `match`, `AddImage |
RemoveImage`, so its no-ops are **thirteen** and `changes_ink`'s eleven are a *subset*. The two lists
have never disagreed in the sense that matters — nothing `changes_ink` calls invisible is refused a
preview — but *"the same eleven"* was never true, and every prose copy said it at once. **That is the
opposite failure to this entry's own**: a count going stale in five copies is found by recounting;
a **relationship** stated wrongly in every copy is not, and `[A7-L8-04]` certified it by hand-counting
the first arm and stopping short of the second. D659 has the mechanism and what it costs
`cancel_gesture`'s gate.

⚠️ **And they went stale a third time, which is what makes this entry a rule rather than an anecdote.**
On 2026-09-07 a sweep found *ten* still standing in two places — §5.7's second copy of the bullet, and
the opening paragraph of `only_the_chrome_operations_change_no_ink` itself, ten lines above a sentence
in the same comment that says eleven. Both corrected. **Five copies of one number, three of them wrong
at some point, and the only one any gate reads is the fixture's `assert_eq!(invisible.len(), 11)`.**
*The advice this entry closed with the first time is now an instruction: if it moves again, delete the
number rather than updating it and let the fixture be the record.* A count written in five places goes
stale five ways, and a recount only ever finds the copies the recounter thought to look at.

**D337 — The Effects panel. *Built and tested 2026-08-24; Keep. The GPU passes and the drag-reorder
stay in `roadmap.md`, and the panel does not appear over a multi-selection.*** D333 built the model,
the save format, the SVG writer and the CPU backend and left the inspector's Effects card a stub
saying so. This is the card: one row per effect, a popover behind each row, and the three controls
D333 added to the design on the maintainer's invitation — a **colour** on both shadows, **spread** on
the inner one, and a **visibility eye** per row.

**Model order, first at the top, and it is the opposite of what the Fill card does.** That was worth
deciding rather than copying. Paints are stacked in *space* and the renderer walks the list forward,
so the row on top of the Fill panel has to be the paint you see on top — hence its reversal. Effects
are a **pipeline**: §6.4 builds the appearance first, in list order, then casts every shadow from
that, so each entry takes what the one before it produced. A pipeline reads top-down like the sentence
it is, and reversing it would put the last thing that happens first.

**The popover's title is a kind combo, where the mockup draws a static heading.** A title is the one
thing about a popover already known from the row that opened it, so spending the line on it buys
nothing; a combo says the same word *and* makes the row's kind changeable, which a fill row has had
all along through the picker's tabs. It costs no new `Area` — the combo's list is egui's, and
`dismissed_by_click`'s `over_overlay` term already exempts exactly this, which is how the stroke
popover's cap combo works. The alternative considered was a four-row menu hung off the header `+`,
which is more faithful to the mockup's six separate trigger rows and needs the card's rect plumbed out
of `OndinApp::panel` to anchor on; it also leaves a mis-added row needing a delete.

**Retyping carries across what the two kinds share** (`EffectKind::retyped`), rather than starting the
new kind from its default. Two shadows share every field they have; a shadow and a blur share the blur
radius and nothing else; `Filters` shares nothing with any of them. `DEFAULT_BLUR_RADIUS` is what
makes the middle case exact — one number for a shadow's blur and a fresh layer blur, because it is one
quantity. The reset version throws half a dozen tuned numbers away to answer a question about *where*
the ink lands, which is the argument `Effect::visible` already won against the mockup's `×`, one step
quieter. `retyping_keeps_what_the_two_kinds_share` is written against the reset version specifically:
its fixture is a **tuned** shadow, because every assertion that only checks the kind came out right
passes against it.

**A shadow's colour is `PaintSlot::Effect(i)`** — the fifth slot naming something that is not a fill,
riding there for the fourth time for the third time's reason (D141, D154): the swatch, the hex field
and the detached picker are all written against a slot, so a shadow's colour gets the whole colour
panel instead of a hex box standing in for it. The row is the Fill row's row — a chip, a hex and a
percentage — because **the opacity is the alpha and there is no second field for the two to disagree
about**, which is D333's rule arriving at the control that implements it. `takes_gradients` answers
`false`: `Shadow::color` is one `Color` and all three writers cast the silhouette in a single ink.

**Percent for a factor, degrees for the angle, and `FilterChannel` owns which is which.** The model is
factors with 1.0 neutral because that is what `feColorMatrix` and the shader take (D333, D186); 100%
is how every app that has these shows it, and it is the same number with the point moved rather than a
second convention. The list is in core beside `Filters` for `Adjustment::ALL`'s reason — a panel
spelling its own list can offer three of the four — and
`every_channel_the_summary_counts_has_a_control` pins it against the literal **four** rather than
against `ALL.len()`, which is the version that reads better and tests nothing, since dropping a
channel shrinks both sides of the comparison together.

**Three departures from `design/Editor.dc.html`, reported rather than taken.** (1) The mockup's
popover fields carry a **label above the field**; the built inspector puts that word in the field's
own `Prefix`, which is what every numeric field in the app already does and what the stroke popover
did with the same mockup. (2) The mockup's two-column grid is `gap:9px`; this uses **6**, the stroke
popover's — and the mockup is not of one mind, its own two-column grids running 6, 7 and 9 across the
file with 9 used by the six `fx` cards alone. (3) The mockup anchors the popover `right:10px;
top:70px`, i.e. *over* the cards; the built app moved every popover to the lane left of the inspector
because the two grounds are the same colour and a 272pt card on a 284pt card read as one surface
(`popover_anchor`). Everything else agrees: 28pt rows at 9pt padding, a 272pt popover at 11pt padding
with 10pt between sections and 26pt fields. The one near-miss is the row glyph, which the mockup puts
at **55%** ink where the theme's nearest token is `text::MUTED` at 62%; inventing a sixth grey for one
glyph is the worse answer.

**The four row glyphs were read out of the font atlas before being trusted**, which corrected a
comment written above them: `DROP_HALF_BOTTOM` and `DROP_HALF` are one droplet with half of it filled
by Phosphor's zigzag hatch, split horizontally and **vertically** — not left-and-bottom as first
written. `CIRCLE_HALF` hatches the same way, so the blur row belongs to the set; it is also the
identity card's *mask* button, which is a reuse rather than a collision (a 15pt row glyph against a
30pt action button, never in one card).

**The card opens itself on a layer with effects and shuts on one without**, through a third
`*_synced_selection` field. That is not duplication: `paint_subject_changed` **consumes** its edge, so
the second caller in a frame gets `false` and never learns the subject moved — which is why Export
already keeps its own. The panel-collapse rule itself is Fill and Stroke's (`sync_paint_collapse`), and
its `fresh` arm is the half that cannot be derived: the transition rule only ever *closes* an emptying
panel, so without the edge, walking to an unpainted layer and back leaves the card shut on a layer that
has something to show.

**The popover is keyed by `(NodeId, usize)` where `stroke_menu` is a bare index.** A node in the key
answers "is this pointing at the layer we are drawing" without a fourth copy of the
consumed-edge machinery, and the panel drops a popover belonging to another layer outright rather than
merely ignoring it — a card that reappears when you walk back is a panel remembering something nobody
asked it to.

⚠️ **The card carried one temporary line for a day, and it was written after somebody met the gap.**
*Removed 2026-08-25 with D339.* The first
drop shadow authored in this panel was reported the same day as *"tried out a drop shadow but nothing
drawn on canvas"* — which is correct and is D333's third unbuilt thing, but a panel that takes an edit
and shows nothing on screen is indistinguishable from a broken one. So a faint *"Not drawn on the
canvas yet"* sits under the rows, with the whole answer in its tooltip. `roadmap.md` had recommended
saying so in the panel before the panel existed, and the report is what settled that it was worth a
line of chrome. **One `if`, over a non-empty stack only** — an empty one has nothing it is failing to
draw — so it comes out in one line the day the passes land.

The stack it reported was checked through the SVG writer rather than assumed: X 16, Y 13, blur 12,
black at 100% emits `feOffset dx="16" dy="13"`, `feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="6"` (the radius halved
by `BLUR_DEVIATION`, as the model intends) and a flood merged behind the graphic, with the viewBox
grown to hold it. So the panel writes a correct model and exactly one surface does not read it.

**The panel's headless tests drive real pointer events**, because everything worth pinning here is
about *where a press lands* and none of it is observable from what a row returns (D303). No count is
given, on D336's rule — a number in prose is the thing that goes stale. Two of them found something
while being written:

- **The row's click target had to exclude the `×`'s corner**, the shape `OndinApp::panel` uses for a
  collapsed card that still has to let its `+` through. The row's claimant is registered *after* the
  button and laid over the same field, so without the shrink egui hands it every press and the remove
  button silently opens the popover instead. Flip-checked: the whole-field version fails two tests.
- **Removing a row does not renumber an open popover, because the click has already dismissed it.**
  The first version of that test asserted the popover followed the renumbering and failed: pressing
  another row's `×` is a click on the page outside the popover. `remap_effect_slots` still covers it —
  covering it twice is the right way round, since the dismissal is a different rule that could be
  relaxed — but the **live** half is the detached picker, which nothing dismisses by clicking, and that
  is what the test asserts now.

⚠️ **And one claim in a doc comment was wrong until it was measured.** `effect_valve` said it reads the
*shown* stack rather than the committed one so that a drag accumulates. It does read the shown stack —
matching `stroke_valve` — but that is not where the accumulation comes from: the dragged number is the
`DragValue`'s own, seeded each frame from what the **panel** read through `display_node`, and this
rebuild only decides what the *other* entries look like. Swapping the valve's read for the committed
node changes nothing any test can see; swapping the panel's takes an 80-point drag from 20 units to 0.
Both were run rather than reasoned about.

**D340 — The Effects card over a multi-selection, and the ordering question that closed the
drag-reorder. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.*** The card was drawn from `inspector_single` alone,
which D337 recorded as the first pass being honest about its scope rather than a rule. The maintainer
asked for the selection case and named the model: *"Those will apply like the exports."*

**The Export panel's shape, not Fill's**, and the difference is about what an effect stack *is*. Fill
answers a disagreement per property — `PaintShown` plus a stand-in row that states the colour where
they agree and reads "Mixed" where they do not (D53) — because a fill has properties a set of layers
can partly share. An effect list has none: there is no honest "mixed offset" across two layers whose
stacks are different lengths. So there are two states, `shared_effects` returning the agreed `Vec` or
`None`, and the card either draws the rows or says *"These layers have different effects"*.

⚠️ **The `+` over a disagreement replaces every selected layer's stack**, which is the exact opposite
of the call D53 made for Fill — *"replacing their lists is the destruction this whole state exists to
avoid"*, which is why Fill's `+` goes **inert** there. Both are right for their own panel and the
difference will look like an inconsistency to the next reader, so: a fill row has a way out of the
mixed state (the row's own `×` clears them all), and an effect card has none — an inert `+` would
leave the disagreement permanent. The tooltip says what the press will do, and it is one undo step.
The maintainer's call.

**One slot, not a second one.** `PaintSlot::Effect(i)` writes a shadow's colour to **every selected
layer** rather than to the node it was opened on, which is what let the selection case arrive without
Fill's `PaintSlot::Selection` twin. It is sound because the card's subject *is* the selection in both
cases — `inspector_single` draws it for the one selected node, so `selection.ids()` is `[id]` there —
and because the rows are not drawn at all over a disagreement, so the anchor's stack is the shared
one. ⚠️ That premise is load-bearing: a panel that drew this card for a node which is not the
selection would silently recolour layers nobody was looking at.

**A flip that did not bite, and what it found.** The `+`'s replacement was written as
`if mixed { Vec::new() } else { effects.clone() }`, which reads as the intent; flipping it to a plain
append changed nothing any test could see, because `shared_effects` answers `None` over a
disagreement and `effects` is therefore *already* empty. The branch was a no-op dressed as a decision
and is gone; what carries the replacement is `write_effects` sending the one-element list to every
