subject. The rule this is an instance of: **when a flip does not bite, that is a finding about the
code.**

**And the drag-reorder, measured rather than argued.** The maintainer's instinct was that order does
not matter — *"A layer blur will apply to the whole layer, drop shadow included, no matter the
order"* — and the conclusion is right for a reason worth writing down, because the stated mechanism is
not quite it. Rendering every pair both ways round and counting the channels that differ:

| pair | differs? |
| --- | --- |
| layer blur ↔ drop shadow | **no** (0 channels) |
| layer blur ↔ inner shadow | **no** |
| filters ↔ drop shadow | **no** |
| filters ↔ layer blur | **yes** (1,080 channels, worst 255) |
| drop ↔ drop | **yes** (826 channels, worst 93) |
| inner ↔ inner | **yes** (72 channels) |
| drop ↔ inner | **no** |

The reason a blur and a shadow cannot reorder is **D333's two-stage design**, not that the blur covers
the shadow: stage one transforms the layer's appearance and stage two casts every shadow from *that*,
whatever order the list is in. What the shadow inherits is the blurred silhouette — measured, a hard
shadow's edge under a 10px layer blur goes from 255 to 194 — so it *looks* like the blur reaching the
shadow, while the shadow's own extent does not grow. And a drop and an inner do not reorder either,
which is not obvious: a drop always goes fully behind the accumulated result and an inner fully over
it, so either order stacks drop → layer → inner.

So ordering changes a pixel in exactly two places: **Filters against LayerBlur**, and **two shadows on
the same side**. That is narrow enough that the drag is not worth building now, and narrow enough that
it must not be forgotten either — it is a real difference a user can reach by adding two drop shadows.
`roadmap.md` carries it as a *narrowed* item with this table rather than as the general "the list has
an order and the panel cannot change it".

**D341 — An effect layer was sized from the committed document, so the effect being dragged was
clipped for the whole drag. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-25.*** Reported from the machine: *"When I add an
effect that expands (like drop shadow or layer blur), the effect is clipped while I add it. It applies
the proper effect once I release the mouse when scrubbing, or pressing enter on the field."* That is
the exact signature of a cache only the commit refreshes.

`scene::effect_bounds` read `Resolved::ink_bounds`, which is built from the committed document — so a
scrubbed blur drew into the buffer the *old* radius needed. Its own doc comment had the shape of the
problem and dismissed it: it said the cache was stale about a resize "for one frame of a drag" and
that fixing it was "not worth a second bounds computation on every frame of every gesture". **Both
halves were wrong.** It is stale for the whole drag, not a frame; and the live answer costs one call
to `geometry::world_bounds_of_parts`, a function `Resolved` already uses and which exists — its own
doc says so — precisely so a preview can call it.

**Every input is live now**: `painted.kind` and `painted.paint` under a geometry preview (so resizing
a shadowed shape sizes its buffer for the shape being dragged), `effects` under an effects preview,
`world` under a move. `world_bounds_of_parts` rather than `local_bounds` because it also adds the
**stroke expansion**, without which a stroked layer's buffer is short by half a stroke all round.

**`Resolved` grew a third bounds cache**, `inner_ink` — the subtree's ink *before* this node's own
escape. That is a third question rather than a convenience, and it is the only one of the three a
caller holding a **different** effect stack can use: `world_bounds` is what you are editing,
`ink_bounds` is what is drawn (D334), and this is what an effect layer must be big enough to hold
before its own padding. Only the `Group`/`Root` arm reads it — every other kind's ink is its own box,
where the walk has the live geometry.

⚠️ **One input is still the cache and stays that way**: a container's children, because the walk has
not reached them when the layer opens. A `Group`'s ink is its children's ink with the mask clipping
`Resolved` works out, and recomputing that in the walk would be a second copy of a rule with an edge
case in it. So a preview that moves a child *inside* a blurred group is a frame behind — narrower than
what it replaced, and stated where it happens.

**What made it findable was giving the recorder the number.** `overrides.rs`'s differential harness —
*"previewing `tx` must draw what committing `tx` draws"* — could not see this, because its `Recorder`
took `push_effect_layer`'s default and logged an effect layer as a plain `Push` with no bounds on it.
`Call::Effect` carries the box now, and two tests fail against the old code: one for the three numbers
that reach into `Effect::escape` (blur, offset, spread) and one for a resize under a shadow. A test
that drops the number cannot tell a right box from a wrong one.

**D342 — A layer scrolled out of the viewport lost its shadow, because the buffer that holds the
silhouette is the same buffer that gets clipped. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-25.*** Reported as something
wrong *"when panning and the shape is off screen"*.

An effect layer's buffer is clamped to the enclosing target so that an effect on a mostly-off-screen
layer costs the visible part — which is right, and which D333 recorded as a virtue. What it missed is
that the buffer is **also what the silhouette is read from**. Clipped at the target's edge, a layer
scrolled half off the top casts a shadow computed from the sliver still showing; scrolled fully off it
casts nothing at all, while its shadow should still be reaching into view. Measured: with the square
at world y 30…70 and its ink reaching y 90, panning the view to y 78 produced **no ink anywhere**.

`effect::buffer_box` is the fix and it lives in core because both backends call it: the target is
grown by the escape before the intersection, so any geometry within reach of the viewport survives to
cast into it. **The two sides swap** — ink landing at the target's right edge is cast from silhouette
`offset` to the *left* of it, a distance this module packs into `escape.x0`, the left inset — and the
grow is clamped at zero, because a large offset makes one inset negative and the arithmetic would
otherwise pull the target's own edge inwards, correct for a shadow and wrong for the layer, which is
drawn in the same buffer.

⚠️ **Both backends had the identical clamp, so every differential test agreed perfectly on the wrong
answer.** `gpu_effects::both_backends_draw_the_same_shadow` passes at every pan offset with the bug
present, and so does a GPU-versus-CPU sweep over fractional pans and zooms — because the mistake was
in the shared walk, not in either backend. What found it was **asking where the ink actually landed**:
an absolute assertion about which device rows carry alpha, against a number worked out from the
document. The lesson is D302's and D319's wearing another face — *a comparison between two things that
share a mistake is not a test of it* — and it is why the keeper lives on the CPU backend, in the
default suite, with the GPU one beside it for the surface it was reported on.

**D343 — The filter rows take the image card's metered field, and the ranges were narrowed to make
the bar honest. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.*** Asked for directly: *"Let's do the filter
controls like image adjustements. They have a different style of slider, one similar to image editing
apps. So we align them both."*

The four channels drew plain `value_field`s. They draw `value_field_metered` now — the same control
the seven image adjustments use, a bar painted across the field's ground **growing from the middle**,
so a card of four answers *which of these are doing anything, which way, and roughly how much* at a
glance rather than one row at a time. That is `value_field_metered`'s own argument for existing, and
it applies here for the same reason: these are offsets from a neutral, not quantities.

**The ranges went from `0…400%` to `0…200%`, and that is the price of the bar rather than a change of
mind about headroom.** A centre-growing bar tells the truth only if its two sides are the same scale.
Against a range that is not symmetric about the neutral, the left half is three times as sensitive as
the right — `40%` and `250%`, one step down and one step up as the number reads, would draw bars of
wildly different lengths. Symmetric, the meter is literally `factor − 1.0`, which is worth noticing:
the offset from neutral *is* the fraction of the reach, with no arithmetic between the model and the
picture. `MAX_HUE` was already symmetric at ±180 — every rotation there is.

What it costs is that brightness stops at 2× where CSS would keep going. First-draft numbers, like
every range in that file (D186), and one constant to turn.

**What did *not* change is the reading**, and that is deliberate: the numbers stay factors at 100%
neutral rather than becoming `ImageAdjust`'s signed offsets from zero. D333 chose those units because
they go straight into `feColorMatrix` and the shader, and stated the difference rather than carrying
it quietly; adopting the *control* while keeping the *units* is what "align them both" means without
undoing that. The `+` on positives that the adjustments' formatter adds stays off here for the same
reason — `+50` for 150% would be the other convention leaking in through the formatting.

⚠️ **The bar is a one-point tick at rest, not nothing.** The test asserted "no bar" first and failed
on it; the field marks its own neutral, and that mark is the only thing saying where the middle is.
The channel hints were rewritten to three points — bottom, neutral, top — to match, since the tooltip
is now describing a bar rather than a number.

⚠️ **And a flip that did not bite the first time.** The ratio assertion — the one carrying the test —
survives the whole meter being scaled by a third, because a uniform rescale leaves the ratio alone. It
fails at 2.571 against 0.857 under the mapping it is actually about, each side scaled to its own end.
Both are recorded on the test, because only one of the two is a mistake anybody would make.

**D344 — An image fill went blank whenever any layer on the page carried an effect. *Fixed and
tested on-device 2026-08-25.*** Reported as *"pasting an image into the canvas while there's an effect
on a layer makes the image empty — the bounding box still shows, the thumbnail on layers and Fill
still shows, but nothing on the canvas"*. Those three surfaces are the diagnosis: they read the image
**store**, and only the canvas reads vello's **atlas**.

**vello's image atlas evicts by resolve pass, and every effect layer added one.** `ImageCache` holds a
`last_used_generation` per resident image and drops anything not *drawn* for `EVICT_AFTER_GENERATIONS`
= 2 passes; a `Renderer::render_to_texture` is one pass. D339's design rendered each effect layer's
sub-scene on the page's own renderer, so a frame with one effect spent two passes there and a picture
drawn in only one of them fell out. First frame right, every frame after it empty — which is exactly
what the report describes, since a picture new to the atlas is uploaded whatever else is happening.

**The fix is one pass per renderer per frame, and it took two goes.** A second `Renderer` for the
sub-scenes fixes the reported case and *moves* the problem one level down: a picture **inside** an
effected layer, with any other effect layer beside it, blanks on the layers renderer for the same
reason — and a page of shadowed image cards is not an exotic document. So sibling layers of one
nesting *level* are packed into a single texture and rasterized in **one** `render_to_texture`
(`Scene::append` at each slot's origin), and each level gets a renderer of its own. Every renderer is
then back to the rhythm vello is tuned for. Levels are walked deepest-first, which the walk already
produces: `pop_layer` records a frame as it closes.

The passes read from the packed texture through `fx_gpu::Slice`, so no copy is needed on the way in —
only the layer with *nothing* to filter takes one (`copy_out`), and it cannot be handed the packed
texture because that holds every sibling.

⚠️ **Three hypotheses were wrong before this one, and each was killed by a measurement rather than by
argument.** That a fresh atlas slot per frame was leaking — reusing one slot per size changed nothing.
That `unregister_texture` was leaving a corrupt entry — never unregistering changed nothing. That it
was atlas *capacity* — a 200-frame warm-up made no difference, and neither did the picture's size.
What discriminated was the shape of the failure: **frame 0 right, frame 1 wrong, independent of
history**, which is a cache rhythm rather than a leak.

**Measured after**: a frame with **20** effect layers costs 1.06 ms against 1.08 for eight and 0.70 for
one — flat in the layer count, because the layer count no longer changes the pass count. 🚨 **That
last clause stopped being true when §15 D402 landed and nobody amended it here.** The page-area
budget splits a level whose layers outgrow the page, so above that line the count grows with the
sibling count again — measured at §15 **D776**, where 32 blurred squares at one level demand **11**
passes on a 100×100 page. The timing above stands: those 20 layers packed into one texture. A vello
`Renderer` costs 84 ms to build (49 with area-only antialiasing), which is why they are built on
demand: a document with no nesting builds exactly one, and most build none.

🚨 **That figure does not reproduce and is superseded by §15 D777, which is the only number of the
two to say what it was measured on.** Six consecutive `Renderer::new` calls on an RTX 4070 Ti,
vello 0.9.0, `--release`, run twice **on an otherwise-idle adapter**: **15 ms for the first in the
process and a 6–8 ms band for every one after it** — fifteen-fold below this sentence, and against
the *same* option set, since
`RendererOptions::default()` is `AaSupport::all()`, the arm priced at 84 here rather than the
area-only one priced at 49. ⚠️ **It is not a version drift**: D337 and D339 name `vello` 0.9 the day
before and the day of this entry, and the pin has been `=0.9.0` since. **This sentence records no
profile, no machine and no version**, which is why nothing could adjudicate it for three weeks while
`[S11.2-L4-05]`, D763 and D776 all quoted `~5.7 ms` a few thousand lines away. ⚠️ **Under adapter
contention the same build is 48–65 ms, so this sentence is only fifteen-fold out on an idle
machine** — which puts *machine load* on D777's candidate list beside profile and machine, though it
does not reconstruct the 84/49 **pair** and so explains nothing yet; **84 reproduces under neither
condition.** **The figure is kept
rather than deleted because the conclusion it carries is the load-bearing part** — renderers are
built on demand — and that conclusion survives a cheaper renderer untouched, as does the
**correctness** rule above it: one pass per renderer is about the atlas evicting a picture, not
about a saving.

**D338 — A shadow plus an opacity, or a shadow plus a clip, panicked the CPU backend. *Fixed and
tested 2026-08-25; found while porting the backend rather than by anything using it.*** The walk opens
an effect layer **outside** the clip and the opacity (§6.4, D333), which is the right order and is
recorded as such — so a layer with a shadow and `opacity < 1`, or a frame with a shadow and `clip`,
has an ordinary layer nested inside the effect one. `CpuPainter::pop_layer` closed whichever effect
frame was open, whatever kind of layer the walk meant, so the *inner* pop closed the effect layer and
the ordinary one was never closed at all. `vello_cpu` notices at `flush` and panics: *"some layers
haven't been popped yet"*.

**A panic, not a wrong picture**, which is why it is worth its own entry rather than a line in D333:
`render_to_rgba` never returned, so `ondin export --png` on such a file died and so did the headless
server. It was reachable from the Effects panel in two clicks — add a shadow, drag the opacity down.

**The fix is a count, not a second stack**: `FxFrame::depth`, incremented by `push_layer` and
`push_mask_layer` whenever an effect frame is open, decremented by `pop_layer` before it will
consider closing the frame. Two tests pin it,
`a_shadow_survives_the_layer_being_faded` and `a_shadow_survives_the_layer_clipping` — separately,
because `needs_layer` has two arms and a fix that counted one of them would pass the other's test.

**Nothing was drawing wrongly and no test was failing**, and that is the part worth keeping. Every
effects test used a plain opaque shape; the combination was reachable in the app and unreachable in
the suite. What found it was writing the GPU backend and having to *state* the pairing rule — the
same shape as D333's own note that a brief you can falsify is what catches a bug (`arch-scribe`), one
level down.

**D339 — The effect passes on the GPU, closing the last of D333's three. *Built and tested on-device
2026-08-25; Keep.*** The canvas took `ScenePainter::push_effect_layer`'s plain-composite default and
drew effected layers unfiltered — the honest failure while the passes were unwritten, and the one
surface that disagreed with the file. Reported as *"tried out a drop shadow but nothing drawn on
canvas"* the day the panel landed.

**The shape of it is forced by `vello::Scene` being a *recording*.** The CPU backend can rasterize an
effect layer the moment it pops, because its `RenderContext` is a surface; on the GPU there is no
point during the walk at which pixels exist to filter. So `GpuScenePainter::push_effect_layer`
redirects drawing into a **sub-scene** and `pop_layer` closes it into an `EffectJob`, putting a
`draw_image` of a fresh atlas slot into the enclosing scene; after the walk,
`VelloGpuRenderer::resolve_effects` rasterizes each job, runs the compute passes and points that slot
at the result through `Renderer::override_image`. Jobs come out **innermost first** because a frame is
recorded as it pops, so consuming them in order is already correct for nesting — no sort, no
dependency graph.

**The shaders are a port, and the port is checked rather than trusted.** `fx.wgsl` has one entry point
per step of `effects::run`, in the same order, over the same premultiplied 8-bit values. Two choices
make the two byte-comparable rather than merely similar: the gaussian kernel is built by
`effects::kernel` **on the host** and handed over as a buffer, so there is one implementation of the
formula and not two; and every store goes through an explicit `q` that rounds half-up to an 8-bit
level, because `rgba8unorm` quantisation rounds however the driver likes and the reference rounds
half-up. `tests/fx_gpu.rs` runs both over one buffer across seven stacks and allows **one** channel —
measured, that slack is used by at most 52 channels of 12,288, with no structure. Three flips were run
against it and each failed the right tests and only those: the silhouette offset reversed, the colour
matrix left on premultiplied data, and the drop/inner composite swapped.

⚠️ **vello's GPU output is straight alpha, where `vello_cpu`'s `Pixmap` is premultiplied.** Measured
on-device rather than assumed — a 50%-alpha white fill reads back `255,255,255,128` — and it is the
one place the two backends genuinely differ at the seam the passes sit on. Its image atlas takes
straight alpha too (`register_texture` says so and vello 0.9 carries a `TODO` for the premultiplied
variant), so `fx_gpu` brackets the stack with a `premul`/`unpremul` pair. That round trip is the whole
of the one-channel tolerance above.

**`gpu_effects::both_backends_draw_the_same_shadow` asserts *exact* equality**, which was not the
intention — the test was written with a tolerance and a comment estimating the disagreement, and the
measurement came back mean 0.000, worst 0. It holds because the fixture sits on integer pixel
boundaries, so neither rasterizer has anything to antialias and the effect arithmetic is the only
thing that *can* differ; the comment now says that rather than claiming the backends agree in general.
The estimate in the first version of it was invented, which is the habit that entry exists against.

**Cost, measured rather than guessed**: 0.60 ms/frame for a small shape with a 12px blur, 0.73 for an
800px layer with one, 2.22 for an 800px layer under a **60px** blur. So the resolve's per-frame texture
allocation — one vello target plus five scratch buffers per effect layer — is not worth pooling yet,
and `roadmap.md` says so rather than filing it as work.

**D243 — A named gap, which is the thing the key layer was built past align for. *Built and tested;
reviewed on screen and accepted, with the scrub fixed under D245.*** The roadmap carried this as "the real prize, and the reason the key was worth
building past align", and the reasoning it carried is what shaped the geometry: `build::distribute`
equalises the gaps inside a span the two extremes already fix, so **nothing in it can be chosen** and a
key has no work to do there. Naming the gap frees the whole run to slide, and *then* one member has to
hold still or the arrangement has no position at all. (⚠️ **"Equalises the gaps" is conditional since
D487**: once the layers overlap more than their own span, equal gaps and the set's left-to-right order
are incompatible and the *order* is what `distribute` keeps, spacing the leading edges evenly instead.
The extremes hold still either way, so the argument above — that nothing in `distribute` can be chosen
— is untouched.) That member is the key —
`build::distribute_spacing(.., anchor, gap)` packs everything before it on the axis backwards from it and
everything after it forwards, and gives the anchor no operation at all rather than one that happens to be
zero.

**Two layers is enough, and that is a property rather than a leniency.** `distribute` needs three because
with two there is no interior to place anything in; two layers have exactly one gap, and one gap is a
number worth typing. The pair is asserted in one test for that reason —
`two_layers_have_a_gap_to_name_even_though_they_have_none_to_spread` checks the even distribution still
declines at two in the same breath.

**With no key the first member on the axis holds**, which is the one fallback that cannot surprise:
"exactly 24 apart" leaves the leftmost or topmost where it was. A key that does not survive `outermost`
falls back the same way, for the reason `align_target` states — a key nested inside another selected
layer is not an operand of this arrangement at all.

**The readout deliberately does not answer the question the panel asks.** It returns *every* gap, in axis
order, negative where two layers overlap. How close two gaps have to be before a field calls them one
number is a question about **how that field prints**, and the fold that answers it —
`inspector::shown_gap` — lives in the panel with a tolerance of half the last digit `ui::number(2)`
writes. Core holding an opinion about that would be core holding an opinion about a formatter. (It
shipped as `build::spacings(doc, res, ids)`; **D245 replaced it with `build::gaps_along(boxes)`** the
next day, because that signature could only ever read the committed tree.)

**`shown_gap` is not `Spread`, and the reasons are worth stating because `Spread` is right there and
answers the same two questions.** `Spread::agreed` compares by `PartialEq`, which over gaps that came out
of a drag means *Mixed* for ever; `Spread::base` is the *first* value, on the argument that any real
member will do — true of a stroke weight and false of a gap, where taking the first shoves the whole run
by however far that one happened to be from the rest. So the base here is the **mean**, and a drag over a
mixed set equalises the layers near where they already are. Both halves are pinned by
`the_spacing_field_agrees_to_what_it_prints_and_drags_from_the_mean`, and each was flipped separately:
exact equality fails the first assertion, `gaps[0]` fails the second.

**The row follows the subject the row above it follows.** With the node tool up the same two fields space
the selected *points* (`tools::space_points`), because the align card's own rule is that align and
distribute are one idea and the subject changes while the control does not — a field that worked on layers
and went dead on points would be the panel saying so twice. Points take no anchor argument: a set of
points has no key to designate, the same reason `align_points` takes no target, so the first on the axis
is the only candidate rather than a fallback. `points_along` was lifted out so the two point arrangements
cannot disagree about which point is first, exactly as `sorted_along` does for layers. (⚠️ **This
entry's *"Built and tested"* was drift about the point arm until 2026-09-09**: `space_points` had one
production call site and **zero test callers**, so the very rule this paragraph states — which point
holds — was asserted nowhere, and the review's reversed-`order` flip was green across 972 tests.
**D617** has the test and the flip.)

**A gap is between *edges* for layers and between *positions* for points**, which is the same collapse
`distribute_points` already documents — a point has no width, so the two readings are one.

**The valve is guarded by `interacting`**, `multi_number`'s early return and owed here for the same
reason: each of the two fields builds an operation *per member of the selection*, and without the guard it
would build two whole transactions a frame whether or not the pointer is near the card.

**The row is *dimmed* below two members rather than hidden. Reviewed on screen and accepted, and the
reason given is better than the one it was built on.** It shipped on the align card's own written rule —
"the buttons dim rather than vanish, as everywhere else in this panel" — with the counter-argument
recorded, that with one layer there are no neighbours at all, so this is *not applicable* rather than
*not enough yet*. Offering to hide it was declined on 2026-08-19: **"no point in hiding them for single
layers since it will make the panels jump when selecting multiple."** That is a stronger argument than
the house rule and it is the one to keep — the objection is not about the dead row, it is about the
*transition*, and a card that changes height under the pointer as a second layer is picked costs more
than 28pt of grey. *Do not re-open this by re-deriving the "not applicable" reading.*

**One live defect came back from that same review and is D245**: the fields could not be scrubbed at all,
only typed. It is worth noting against this entry that the geometry below was right and every test above
passed — what was wrong was which tree the *readout* came from, which is the one thing none of these
tests touch.

**That the row appears was not tested** — the `OndinApp`/wgpu seam, until D303 removed it and **D310**
measured the whole card on a headless app, dimmed and live, and asserted the two heights are equal. What
was already pinned is the geometry, both fallbacks, the two-layer property, the fold the field displays
through, and — since D245 — that the readout follows a live preview.

**D244 — The base operand of a `Subtract` says so, in the slot the row already had. *Resolved; the mark
reviewed on screen and changed from a word to a glyph.*** The
roadmap had scoped this precisely and the scoping held: "the question is only whether the bottom row
should also *say* so under Subtract, not whether to store anything". Nothing is stored.
`layers::subtract_base` asks the *parent* — a `Boolean { op: Subtract }` whose `children[0]` is this node
— so being a base is not a property of the shape, and dragging it up one row stops it being one on the
next frame. That is the whole reason D113 refused a stored "primary" index, and a derived mark is the
only kind that cannot come to disagree with the order the user can see and drag.

**It reuses the badge rather than adding a mark.** The row already paints one string at its right-hand
end — an artboard's `800 × 600` — in `text::FAINT` at 10.5, in an `else if` chain *after* the eye and the
lock, so it yields to the controls on hover. The base mark is a second arm of that same `match` and
inherits all of it. The two cannot collide: a frame is never an operand of anything.

**It shipped as the word `base` and was changed to the `stack-simple` glyph on review**, same ink. A
pictogram is the right register for an annotation that repeats down a tree, and the row's other marks are
already glyphs. What that cost is a `RowBadge` enum, because a Phosphor glyph wants `theme::icon_font`
and not the proportional face — and then the size, which is the part that had to be **measured rather
than picked**. `uv_rect` off the galley is the *tight* glyph bitmap where the galley's own height is the
line box, so laying both out and reading it says what a word and a pictogram really ink: `800 × 600` at
10.5 and `stack-simple` at 11.0 agree at 100%, 125% and 150% display scaling and are half a point apart
at 200%, while 12 is taller at every scaling above 100%. `BADGE_ICON` is 11 and
`the_base_badge_inks_as_tall_as_the_worded_one` holds it there, across four scalings because the atlas
quantizes to whole texels and a size chosen at 100% is exactly the kind of thing this codebase has
already caught drifting at 150%. **It matches the word, not the eye and lock** that take the slot over on
hover: those are controls and this is an annotation, and the artboard badge has been the quieter of the
two in this exact slot since it was written.

**Only `Subtract`, and that is not conservatism.** Union, Intersect and Exclude all fold commutatively
(D113, and `exclude_gives_the_same_answer_in_any_operand_order` measures the one that reads as though it
should not), so marking an operand of one of those would be the panel asserting a significance the
arithmetic cannot see — the same argument that keeps `build::boolean`'s `key` inert for them.

**Four tests, and the discriminating one is about identity rather than position.** `children[0]` is the
base under every spelling of this function, so
`designating_the_key_moves_the_mark_with_it` asserts *which shape ended up there* — the layer that was
second in z-order before the key moved it, and that the one which would have been the base without a key
is not one now. `only_the_bottom_operand_of_a_subtract_is_the_base` asserts the operand *above* as well,
since "mark every operand" and "mark the last" both pass a test that only looks at `children[0]`. Flipped
to `.last()` — the plausible slip, the tree drawing bottom-last — two of the four fail.

**Not tested: that the badge paints.** `layers_row` is an `OndinApp` method, the wgpu seam. What is
pinned is the rule it draws from.

**D245 — The spacing field could not be scrubbed, because it re-read its base from the tree its own
preview was not in. *Resolved.*** Reported the day D243 landed, and reported exactly: "the value doesn't
change and the layers try to change distribution, but it's a flicker several times per second and always
ends up in the same position. Setting them by updating the value with the keyboard works." Every clause
of that is the same cause. A scrubbed field re-reads its base every frame and adds *that frame's* delta;
the base came from `build::spacings(&session.doc, &session.resolved, …)` — the **committed** tree — and
`edit_valve` only *previews* while the pointer is down. So the base reset to the original gap on every
frame: the number never moved, the layers were driven to original-plus-one-frame and back at frame rate,
and typing worked because a typed value commits.

**This is the third control to make the same mistake, and the second one where the fix is written in a
doc comment beside it.** `Spread::base` exists because a stroke weight, an opacity and the colour picker
all did it (D-nothing: it is in `inspector.rs`'s own prose); `canvas::preview_subpaths` exists because
the point X/Y fields did. The rule both state is one sentence — **anything that *shows* a value wants the
preview; anything that computes an edit from a fixed origin wants the committed tree** — and it now has a
third instance. The point half of this field had it too: `point_spacings` read `edited_subpaths` where it
wanted `preview_subpaths`, which is the pair of functions whose doc comment already says so.

**`build::spacings` is gone and `build::gaps_along` replaces it.** The old signature took `(doc, res,
ids)` and so could only ever read the committed tree, core having no preview — the bug was reachable
*through the API shape*. The new one takes the boxes, and which boxes is now the app's question, where it
belongs: `inspector::layer_spacings` walks `build::outermost` through `session::preview_world_bounds`.
That is the same division `align_target` already draws — geometry in core, *which box* in the app.

**`OndinApp::spacing_tx` still reads the committed tree and must keep doing so.** The two halves want
different trees and that is not an inconsistency: the readout has to move with the preview or the drag
has no purchase, and the write has to be anchored or an absolute target re-derived from its own preview
would compound. Both are stated on the functions.

**Pinned, and it took lifting the readout out of `OndinApp`.** `layer_spacings` is a free function over
`EditorSession` rather than a method, for the reason `session.rs`'s own test module gives — the session
is device-free where the app holds a wgpu `RenderState`. So
`the_spacing_readout_follows_a_live_preview_rather_than_the_committed_tree` can set the preview a scrub
would set and ask what the field would show next frame. Flipped back to `resolved.world_bounds` it fails
with the reported symptom in the message: *the field would read [20.0, 20.0] while previewing 40*.

**D246 — A layer row's controls had no hover state, and the reason is that a layer row is not three
widgets. *Resolved.*** Reported after living with the panel. The row is one `Sense::click_and_drag()`
region with everything painted into it by hand (`layers.rs`'s module note says why), so `Response::hovered`
answers *the row* — which is what makes the eye and lock appear at all — and there was nothing asking
whether the pointer was on any one of them. They appeared on hover and then said nothing about being
pressable.

**The fix is one answer where there were four hand-written comparisons.** `RowTargets { caret, eye, lock }`
holds each control's x as an `Option` — `None` where the row is not drawing it — and `RowTargets::at(x)`
resolves a point to a `RowHit`. The press and the mark both go through it, which is the property worth
having: *what lights up is what a click acts on*. Before this the press had three inline
`(x - c).abs() <= 9.0` tests and the hover would have needed three more, and two hand-written bands are
how a control comes to glow somewhere it cannot be pressed. `CONTROL_HIT` is the one number.

**One destination rather than one step per resting colour.** A hovered control paints `text::STRONG`
whatever it was resting at — and it rests at four different greys, since the eye has a visible and a
hidden ink and the lock an open and a filled one. "A tier up from wherever you were" would give four
different amounts of feedback for one gesture. **No ground behind it**, as asked: the row already has a
hover ground, and a second rectangle inside it would read as a button the rest of the panel does not
have.

`RowTargets::at` is pinned three ways — that a control the row is not drawing is not a target, that the
band reaches `CONTROL_HIT` and stops, and that two overlapping bands resolve in the press's order (a deep
row in a narrow panel can put the caret under the eye). **That the painting reads `under` is not tested**:
`layers_row` is an `OndinApp` method, the wgpu seam.

**The caret was left out for a day and then put in, and the reasoning that left it out was wrong.** Two
of the three were reported, and the argument for stopping there was that a caret is *structural* where
the eye and lock are toggles. It does not survive the shape of the fix: all three sit in one
`RowTargets`, all three are pressed through one band, and a row where two of three click targets answer
the pointer and one does not is an inconsistency inside a single row — which is a worse thing than the
distinction the argument was drawing. Asked for on 2026-08-20 and it is one more `lit(…)` call. What it
cost is that `lock_x`, `eye_x` and `targets` are now worked out **above** the caret rather than beside
the controls they name, because the caret is the first thing painted; nothing between the two points
bears on them.

**D247 — The transform origin got two numbers, and they are percentages so that the stored variant
stays stored. *Resolved; the percentage was reviewed and accepted, the placement was superseded the
next day by D252.*** ⚠️ **Read D252 before this entry**: the two numbers are on the *canvas* now, not in
the Transform card, so every sentence below that places them in a card is history. What survives whole
is the percentage and the reasons for it — which is the half that was re-decided on the machine rather
than inherited. The roadmap carried this as "there is no numeric X/Y for it — the marker is the only way to
place one", with the open question attached: "it needs deciding whether they read as a fraction or as
local units, **which is the stored variant leaking out**". That framing is the answer once it is taken
literally. `Pivot` is `Normalized` for a kind with an authored box and `Local` for one whose box is
emergent (D55), so a field that read out *whichever was stored* would be a control that changes
meaning with the kind under it — a percentage on a rect, a coordinate on a group, and nothing on
screen to say which. So the display is a **fraction for everything** and `pivot_for` goes on choosing
the storage. That is the division X/Y already draw: the panel says where the point is, core says how
it is kept.

**Three things fell out of picking the percentage rather than local units, and one argued against it.**
For it: the marker's snap set is exactly 0, 50 and 100 on each axis and `pivot_label` reads those nine
out in words, so the fields speak the vocabulary the gesture already does; and the `%` is what stops
the row being a second, differently-meaning `X`/`Y` pair in a card that already has one — local units
had no such disambiguator and the collision was the sharpest objection to them. Against it: **a
percentage of a degenerate axis is meaningless**, and a line is degenerate on one axis whenever it was
drawn with Shift held. That is answered per *axis* rather than per box — the dead half is dimmed with
a sentence saying why, the live half goes on working — which is the answer that keeps a flat line's
row useful. Testing the box instead is the plausible wrong version and is what
`a_flat_line_dims_one_field_and_keeps_the_other` is flipped against.

**Both at 50 clears the origin, and that rule is now core's.** `geometry::pivot_placed_at` answers
`None` for the box's own centre and `Some(pivot_for(…))` for anything else, and both doors go through
it: the marker dragged back to the middle, and the row typed to 50/50. They are not interchangeable
states — `None` is what `build::flip` reads, what the save format omits (§5.11) and what the canvas
stops drawing a badge for, while a stored half resolves to the same point and reads as *placed*
everywhere that asks. The row is therefore the first **field** that can un-say "not moved"; the menu's
*Reset origin* is no longer the only door, and it stays because it reaches a whole selection where the
row is one layer's and only while its handle is armed. Both code comments that called it the only one
were corrected.

**Hoisting that rule found a small bug older than the work.** `canvas::pivot_at` decided "centred" by
accumulating, per axis, whether the snap had landed on the *middle* of three candidates. A zero-extent
axis puts all three candidates on the same coordinate and the loop reports the first, which is labelled
`0.0` — so an axis-aligned line could never be dragged back to nothing at all. Asking whether the point
*is* the centre has no such gap, because the minimum of a zero extent is its centre:
`a_degenerate_axis_is_centred_by_itself` is flipped against the old reading and fails with
`Some(Local((50.0, 0.0)))` where `None` was wanted.

**The fields are present only while the header's crosshair is armed, and that is the whole answer to
"where do they go".** The toggle arms a *handle on the canvas*; a pair of fields that exists only while
an origin is being placed belongs to the same gesture, and they are two rows of dead weight in every
card where nobody has rigged one. It is also the cheapest form the addition could take — one branch, no
new panel state. They sit **above the two angle fields** rather than below W/H: X/Y/W/H are the rows
read constantly and must not shift when the toggle is clicked, and the fields immediately below turn
*about* the point named here, so the card reads "here is the origin, here is the rotation about it".
Unclamped, because the marker is — a pivot may sit outside the box it is measured against, and a field
that clamped would be the one door that cannot say what the canvas already stores.

**What actually cost the work is that the fields could not be scrubbed, and it is D245's shape in the
one place the overrides genuinely cannot help.** `RenderOverrides::from_transaction` absorbs `SetPivot`
as a no-op **by design** — the pivot is baked by the gesture that reads it rather than composed into a
transform (D55), so the renderer has nothing to do with one. But a scrubbed field re-reads its base
every frame and adds that frame's delta, and `edit_valve` only *previews* while the pointer is down: a
base taken from the committed node resets on every frame, so the number would never move, the marker
would never move, and typing would work. That is D245's report almost word for word, arrived at from
the other side — and the general rule both instances state is one sentence: **anything that shows a
value wants the preview; anything that computes an edit from a fixed origin wants the committed tree.**

`EditorSession::pivot_preview` is the fix, and where it lives is the part worth keeping. Guides have
the same problem — chrome the overrides cannot carry — and answered it with `OndinApp::preview_guide`,
a fork **every `set_preview` call site owes beside it**, which is a debt that has already been paid
wrong once. This is filled inside `set_preview` from the transaction itself, so no call site can
forget it, and it is read through `preview_pivot`, which all five readers already came through. A
second reader, `previewed_pivot`, hands back the pivot's own `Option` rather than a resolved point,
because the marker's *badge* names a placement and had been asking the committed node — so it stayed on
for the length of the edit that removed it, and off for the length of the one that made it.

**Pinned three ways, all of them flipped.** In core, the centre rule and its degenerate-axis
consequence (`the_centre_of_the_box_is_the_absence_of_a_pivot` fails against a centre taken from the
local origin rather than the box, which is why its fixture box is offset). In `session.rs`, which is
device-free, that the readout follows a live preview — flipped, it reports the box centre while a
placement at the corner is being previewed, which is the field scrubbing against a base that never
moves. And in `inspector.rs`, the two free functions the row's decisions were lifted into
(`origin_percent`, `origin_pivot`) and the property that they are inverses, since the identity edit has
to be a true no-op or a scrub walks the value. **The row itself is read rather than reproduced**:
`origin_row` is an `OndinApp` method and `OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState` (D35). What is *not*
pinned, and is said plainly here rather than implied: that the dimmed field's tooltip has a claimant to
hang on. It is spelled the way `menu_action` is (an explicit `ui::interact` beside the disabled scope)
because a widget inside a `disable()`d `Ui` reports no hover and `Ui::scope`'s own response is never
hovered — but a tooltip's ink never reaches `.shapes`, so that is a thing to check by eye.

**D248 — Paste in place is one constant swapped for zero, and it was never behind the blocker that
deferred it. *Resolved.*** `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`V` and a canvas-menu row under *Paste here*
(`shortcuts.md` §7, `context-menus.md` §6.1). Both files had scored the work as *cheap* and both were
right about the cost; what neither had was why it was still not built.

**`paste_clipboard_at` already measured its delta from where the copy came from**, because *Paste
here* needed that — it aims a paste by taking the source bounds' centre to the pointer. So "back where
it came from" is that same function with `Vec2::ZERO`, and the whole layer half of this is one
argument. The three payloads are asked in [`paste`]'s order and for its reason — a picture, the app's
own subtrees, then text — because two paste chords that ask different questions of one clipboard are
two features wearing one name (D218, D224). The picture arm is where "in place" has nothing to say: a
pasted image replaces a fill or lands in the middle of the view, and neither has a position to
restore, so the modifier is ignored rather than made to mean something.

**Guides are the half that needed a change, and it is the one place the feature could have quietly
become two.** `paste_clipboard_at` hands its guide arm the fixed `GUIDE_PASTE_OFFSET`, so a paste in
place would have moved a guide 20 units along while every layer stayed put. `pasted_guide` takes the
step as a parameter now — every other caller passes the constant, which is the rule its doc comment
already stated — and `paste_in_place` takes the guide arm itself before delegating, rather than
threading a second offset through a signature that would then carry two. *A guide's axis is the only
coordinate it has, so "same position" is exactly a step of zero*, which is what
`a_guide_pasted_in_place_keeps_its_own_number` pins. The tempting wrong version is a small nudge so
the copy is visible, and that is the ordinary paste wearing a second name.

**What the build actually settled is a *grouping*, and it is the part worth reading.** `shortcuts.md`
§7 deferred four rows together on one stated blocker: the `!m.alt` guard on the clipboard event loop
"has to be widened into a branch, and doing that for two rows while the other two stay inert leaves
the event loop half-converted". That argument is sound and it binds the two `Ctrl`+`Alt` property
rows. It does not bind this one at all: *paste in place* is **`Shift`**, read as one arm on
`Event::Paste` *inside* the existing guard, and it wants the Alt branch neither widened nor touched.
*Paste at the pointer* is the same shape. So two of the four were standing behind a blocker that was
never theirs, and the section has been corrected rather than just struck. **A shared blocker is a
claim about each member**, and it is the same failure mode as a premise that is a list — nothing
recompiles when one member stops being covered.

Why an `Action` of its own rather than a flag on `Action::Paste`: the discrimination can only be made
where the event is read. `egui_winit`'s `is_paste_command` tests `command && Key::V` and never
examines Shift, so the press is swallowed exactly as a plain one is and `Event::Paste` — which carries
no modifiers — is the whole signal (`shortcuts.md` §0). `dispatch` runs later and has no frame to
re-derive the modifier from. The **release** path is unaffected and had to be checked rather than
assumed: `Action::PasteRelease` acts only when the system clipboard holds no text, which is the exact
complement of "the event fired" (D183, D219), so `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`V` over a picture is an ordinary
image paste and over anything else the release does nothing.

**Pinned at the seam, and flipped three ways.** `shift_makes_the_paste_event_a_paste_in_place` asserts
the new arm, that the plain chord is untouched, that **Alt still excludes the trio however it is
combined**, and that copy and cut are given no Shift reading of their own — `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`C` is the
text session's centre-align (`shortcuts.md` §L2) and a second meaning here would collide with it the
moment no session is open. The flips: dropping the arm (which reads as working, because a paste still
happens); hoisting it above the `!m.alt` guard, which makes `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`Shift`+`V` paste and is the
shape of §L2's live bug; and inverting the condition. **`paste_in_place` itself is read rather than
reproduced** — it is an `OndinApp` method and `OndinApp` needs a wgpu render state (D35) — so what is
asserted is the resolution and the guide placement, and the wiring between them is stated here as
read.

**D249 — Frame selection is `group`'s sibling and not a flag on it, because a frame has a box. *Built
and tested; the row is placed as specced, not yet reviewed on screen.*** `context-menus.md` §9.3 had
this in *Features* rather than in *New but cheap*, and that was the right bucket for the right reason,
which the build confirmed from the other side: **the row is four lines and the builder is a hundred.**

**One statement, two opposite amounts of work.** Both verbs promise the same thing — *nothing moves* —
and `build::group` keeps it by touching nothing at all: the group is created with the identity
transform in the shared parent's space, so every member's local transform is already correct.
`build::frame` cannot, because the frame is created *at the union's corner*, so every member has to be
moved back by exactly that corner. The correction is a pure translation and needs no `Resolved` lookup
of its own — the frame and its members-to-be are siblings for the length of the arithmetic, so
`translate(−origin) · local` is expressed in the one space both already share. `Resolved` is still
needed to *measure*, a text node's box coming from its shaped layout and a container's from its
children. **This is the half the test is aimed at**, and the flip is the spelling somebody arrives at
by copying `group`: drop the `SetTransform` and both members jump by the union's corner. The fixture's
artboard is translated by (50, 30) precisely so that a correction applied in the wrong space lands 50
units out rather than looking right.

**Two rules differ from `group`'s, and each is the frame having a box:**

- **The parent has to accept a frame.** §5.3 lets an `Artboard` hang off the root or another
  `Artboard` and nowhere else, so a selection inside a `Group` cannot be framed where it stands. That
  is the one refusal a user can *act on* — move the layers out and it works — so it dims the row with
  a sentence rather than failing after the click, which is §3's rule. The predicate is
  **`build::can_frame`, the builder's own**, for `can_outline`'s reason (D230): a row that restates a
  rule is a row that can come to disagree with the verb behind it.
- **Frames may be members**, where `group` refuses them outright. A frame nests in a frame, so a
  selection of frames has an honest answer here and none there. *That is what makes this a second row
  rather than a rename* — a pair of rows agreeing about every kind would be one row — and it is what
  `frame_selection_is_offered_where_group_is_and_on_the_frames_group_refuses` is named for. The flip
  is pushing the row inside the `!cx.kinds.contains(&Kind::Frame)` arm, which is exactly what copying
  the line above it produces, and it is wrong in the one case that makes the verb worth having.

**Three smaller decisions, each stated because the alternative is defensible.** The frame is created
with **no background**: framing must not change what is drawn, and a fill behind the selection would
hide whatever it was sitting on — the inspector's *Fill* card is one click away (it was headed *Frame
background* until D397). **One layer
is enough**, where grouping wants two: a group of one is a container that does nothing, but a frame of
one is how a single piece of artwork gets a page to sit on. And the new frame is left **open** in the
layers tree where `finish_grouping` leaves a group shut — grouping is tidying, so collapsing the rows
is the point, while framing is making a page and the artwork on it is what you are about to work on.

**No accelerator, and that is a statement rather than an omission.** Figma's `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`G` is free
here — nothing in `input::normal_mode` claims it — but `shortcuts.md` is the keymap's source of truth
and does not bind this. A chord invented at a menu row is a chord that file does not know about, which
is the drift the row/`Action` split exists to prevent (D215). `frame_selection` is an `OndinApp`
method rather than an `Action` for the same reason; if `shortcuts.md` ever binds one, it becomes a
`dispatch` like its sibling and nothing else moves.

**The primitive menu is 18 rows and the test is renamed with the count**
(`a_primitives_menu_is_eighteen_rows_in_canonical_group_order`). Worth noting because the count in
`context-menus.md` §5.5 has now been wrong twice in two days in opposite directions; the *name*
carrying the number is what stops a stale one sitting in a green suite.

**D250 — Make corner / Make smooth, and the smooth pair has to be exactly mirrored rather than well
shaped. *Built and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** `context-menus.md` §6.5 scored this *cheap*
on the grounds that "`PenAnchor::corner` and `::smooth` are the constructors; a builder over the
selected anchors is missing". The builder is indeed small. The scoring misses that
`PenAnchor::smooth(at, out)` **needs an `out`**, and the whole point of a corner is that it has none —
so one of the two directions has to invent a handle, and inventing it is the entire decision.

**Two cases, and only the second invents anything.** An anchor that already carries a handle — a pair
broken with `Alt`, or one that arrives straight and leaves on a curve — is *mirrored*, keeping the
**longer** handle, because that is the one that was aimed on purpose and keeping the shorter one reads
as a reset. An anchor with no handle takes its tangent from the neighbours: the chord `next − prev`,
which is the direction a curve through all three actually travels, rather than either leg. Deriving it
from one leg is the obvious reading of "point along the path" and makes the curve leave flat and then
turn twice; it is one of the three flips on the test.

**The length is the part that reading would have got wrong, and running it is what found it.** The
good curve gives each handle a third of *its own* leg — that is what a Catmull-Rom spline through the
same points reduces to, and it is what Illustrator draws. It is wrong here, because this app's
*definition* of a smooth anchor is `back == −out` **exactly**: `PenAnchor::pull_side` builds one that
way, `is_smooth` reads it that way, and a drag consults `!is_smooth()` to decide whether to break the
pair. An anchor with collinear handles of unequal length is therefore **not smooth**, and the very next
handle drag would take the `break_pair` arm and pull it apart — a *Make smooth* that comes unsmoothed
the moment it is touched. So both handles get one length, from the **shorter** leg, since a handle
longer than a third of its own leg starts to loop and only the short side can be overshot. *The first
version of the test asserted `is_smooth()` and failed, which is how this was found; the constructor
reads as if either would do.*

**An endpoint of an open subpath gets one handle, not two**, and does not report `is_smooth()`
afterwards. Mirroring would put a draggable handle off the end of the path controlling a curve that
does not exist. That is not a gap: an endpoint is not a joint between two segments, and smoothness is
a property of a joint. Closing the subpath gives the same index two neighbours and it takes the
two-handle path, which is what
`an_open_subpaths_endpoint_smooths_on_the_side_it_has` asserts so the rule is about *ends* rather than
about first and last indices.

**The corner radius is untouched in both directions.** A radius on a smooth anchor already draws
nothing — `geometry::fillet` returns `None` for collinear tangents and its comment says exactly why —
so clearing it would discard a number the user typed in exchange for nothing, and it comes back the
moment the anchor is a corner again.

**Two rows, where *Delete points* is one that renames itself.** The two look like the same problem and
are not: `Del`'s pair cannot both be offered because `PointSet` holds anchors *or* segments and never
both (D120), where a point selection can perfectly well hold a corner and a smooth point at once. Both
rows are then live and both mean something. Neither dims on a selection that already agrees, because
§3's rule is about a verb having nothing to do and over a *set* it almost always has — four points of
which three are corners is the ordinary case, and a row that went dark only when all four agreed would
be dark exactly when asking is least interesting. It is idempotent besides.

**No accelerator, and the row dispatches to the canvas verb rather than through an `Action`** —
D215's rule, and D249's reasoning: nothing in `shortcuts.md` binds these, so there is no keyboard
intent for `dispatch` to resolve.

**A side finding, and it is the shape CLAUDE.md warns about.** `PenAnchor`'s struct-level doc comment
said "the incoming one is its mirror, which is what makes an anchor *smooth*" — describing a one-vector
anchor that has not existed since `back` was added, while the doc comment on `back` three lines below
described the real thing correctly. *The stale sentence was the one that would have been read first.*
Corrected in place.

**D251 — *Paste here* stopped aiming after a cut, and the reason it looked deliberate is that a
comment said so. *Resolved.*** Reported after testing the four paste doors against each other, and
reported exactly: "if I cut a layer, then Paste here, it will be pasted to its original position. If I
continue doing Paste here without copying anything else in the meantime, all copies will land in the
original spot. Acting basically like a Paste in place." Three clauses, one cause, and the third clause
is the one that names it.

`paste_at` measured its offset from the **source layers' bounds**, looked up by id through
`preview_world_bounds`. A cut deletes those layers, so the lookup answered `None` and the aim fell
back to the fixed 20×20 step — the original position plus a nudge, which is what "pasted to its
original position" is. And it kept falling there: a captured subtree keeps the *original* ids until
`insert_subtrees` remaps them on the way in, so the clipboard never comes to name anything that
exists, and the tenth paste aims exactly as badly as the first. Copy-then-paste-here worked throughout
— the originals are still in the tree — which is why the door looked fine and why the report
singles the other one out.

**The box is recorded at copy time now** (`OndinApp::clipboard_from`), which needs no new information
at all: `cut_selection` copies and *then* deletes, so the last moment either gesture can answer "where
did this come from" is a moment both gestures already pass through. It is stamped with the payload and
cleared with it, because a payload frozen at copy time whose provenance is read live is a pair that
disagrees the moment the original is moved — the same bug one step milder, and now unreachable too.

**What makes this worth an entry is the comment.** The behaviour was not unnoticed: `paste_at`'s doc
said *"Cut, then paste here, falls back to the fixed offset, **and deliberately**: the alternative is
inventing a rectangle for something the document no longer holds, which would land the paste somewhere
confidently wrong rather than somewhere honestly approximate."* That is a real argument against a
different design — guessing a box — and it was answering a question nobody had to ask, because nothing
needed inventing. *A justification attached to a defect is worse than no comment at all: it is what
stops the next reader looking.* The sentence is corrected in place rather than deleted, so the wrong
reasoning is visible beside the right one.

**The fix that makes it unreachable is the signature, not the field.** `paste_aim(from: Option<Rect>,
world: Point)` takes the box; it cannot consult a document that no longer holds the source, so there
is nowhere for the failure to happen. That is `build::gaps_along` replacing `build::spacings(doc, res,
ids)` for the identical reason (D245) — **second instance of one lesson: when a bug is reachable
through an API shape, change the shape.** `paste_aim` is a free function, so the aim is pinned without
an `OndinApp` (D35): a recorded box lands the payload's centre exactly on the pointer, a pointer
*inside* the source box aims backwards, and an absent box falls to the chord's step. The old shape
cannot be flipped against here at all, which is the point — reproducing it needs a document and some
ids — so the flip is the sign, where `centre − world` puts the paste as far the wrong side of the
original as the pointer was the right side.

**D252 — The origin's two numbers moved out of the Transform card onto the canvas, into the size
badge's slot. *Resolved; run on the machine and accepted*** — "working quite well" on the first pass,
with the two defects D253 records, and accepted outright once those were fixed. **The percentage was
reviewed and kept at the same time**, which settles D247's open half: it was chosen there for a reason
that stopped applying the moment the fields left the card, and it was re-decided on its own merits
rather than inherited. D247
put them in the card and they lasted a day. Reported with the replacement attached: *"the pivot X and Y
in the transform panel I'm not a fan of. They are another pair of X/Y and make the panel feel too busy.
It's already busy. So I thought, the moment pivot editing is enabled, show 2 fields below the bounding
box of the layer, taking the place of the size badge."*

**The objection is the one D247 answered and then under-weighted.** That entry chose a *percentage*
partly so the `%` would keep the row from reading as a second, differently-meaning `X`/`Y` pair in a
card that already had one. That is disambiguation doing a job the layout should not have needed — the
pair was one pair too many whatever suffix it wore. Moving them off the card removes the collision
instead of labelling around it.

**The percentage survives the move, and for a better reason than it arrived with.** With the card's
`X`/`Y` no longer beside them the `%` carries no disambiguation, so the choice had to be re-made on the
merits, and it was, by the person who types into them: *"percentage makes more sense to me, since I know
0 means left, 50% means exact center, and 100% means absolute right. Absolute positioning I'd have to do
mental math to position it exactly, and for a pivot, you usually want it snapped on one side or one edge
most of the time."* That is D247's own argument arrived at independently, and it is stronger here —
those three numbers are exactly the marker's snap set, so the fields and the handle speak one
vocabulary. **The design's own placeholder values are absolute** (`336` / `214`); values in `design/`
are a first draft and the rule stated above is what was implemented.

**They take the size badge's place rather than sitting beside it**, which is the design's structure:
`pivotActive` swaps the two pills in, `pivotInactive` swaps the `W × H` badge back, both at one offset
under the box. Both are a readout hanging under the selection, there is room for one, and W × H is not
what anyone is reading while placing an origin. `badge_placement` is shared by the two so the swap
cannot move — arming the crosshair must look like one readout being replaced, not like the canvas
shifting.

**Two differences from the badge, both deliberate.** The fields are **upright** where the badge turns
with the shape (`badge_frame`, and `badge_text_angle` since D329 deleted `badge_angle`): an egui widget
cannot be rotated at all, and a tilted
text field would be a poor one if it could — so they take the badge's *position* and not its angle,
which on an unrotated layer is the same placement. And they are offered for a **lone line**, where the
badge suppresses itself: a line's `W × H` is a rectangle nobody drew, but a percentage *along* a line is
perfectly meaningful, and the axis that is not gets dimmed by the same per-axis rule every other
degenerate box gets.

**This is the first live widget the canvas has ever hosted**, which the report named as the cost — *"this
is a new pattern we don't have. Means we render small text fields in the canvas that still support
scrubbing, manual entry, arithmetic functions, like any other field."* Correct: nothing in `canvas.rs`
had put an egui widget on the canvas before; it is painter plus hand-rolled hit testing throughout. What
made it small is that three of the four pieces existed — `Scrub` for the drag rule, `expr::eval` for the
arithmetic, and `pivot_preview` (D247) so that a scrub previews at all. `ui::badge_field` is the fourth:
the size badge's pill — same ground, same ink, same height, same radius, same padding — with
`value_field`'s plumbing inside it, including the second-claimant trick that makes the label scrub as
well as the digits. Its width is the **caller's** rather than shrink-wrapped, because a pill that resized
as its value was scrubbed would slide out from under the pointer mid-drag, and two of them would stop
being the same width the moment one read `100`.

**The pointer question was measured, and the answer is not the one the code looks like it rests on.** A
press on a field must not also start a marquee.
`an_overlay_takes_the_press_from_the_canvas_beneath` pins it, and flipping it three ways found that
*any* `egui::Area` shields the layer beneath — `Order::Background` shields, an area whose content senses
`empty()` shields, an area created *before* the canvas response shields. What does **not** shield is the
same rect interacted in the canvas's own `Ui`, which is the obvious way to write this and is the flip
that fails. **So the `Foreground` order is about painting above the chrome, not about the press**, and
both the test and `origin_fields`' doc comment say so — a comment crediting the order would be D251's
mistake committed in a new place a day later. The test asserts from both sides, because "the canvas saw
nothing" is also what a harness that dropped the press would report.

**What is still read rather than reproduced**: that the fields render where `badge_placement` puts them,
and the swap with the badge. `OndinApp` needs a wgpu render state (D35). The two decisions the fields
are made of — `origin_percent` and `origin_pivot` — moved from `inspector.rs` to `canvas.rs` with their
three tests, since a file whose contents no longer match its subject is the drift this project's own
rule exists to stop. *(Both of those "read rather than reproduced" halves were reported wrong the same
day and are measured now — D253.)*

**D253 — The origin pills sat two points low and clipped their own value, and a dragged marker lands on
a whole percent now. *Resolved; run on the machine and accepted.*** Two reports after living with D252
for an hour, and between them they
took out both of the things that entry had left as read-rather-than-measured. *Both were arithmetic, so
both are pinned by measurement now.*

**The gap: "the size pill sits approximately 8px from the layer, the pivot X/Y fields sit 11px, so they
need to be nudged up by 3px."** The symptom was exact and the cause was not the constant — both readouts
already went through `badge_placement` and both asked for `HANDLE_PICK_PX` (9), so on paper they hung in
the same place. `theme::install` sets `interact_size` to 24×24 for the panel's controls; a `horizontal`
takes that as a **minimum row height** and then *centres* its content in it, so a 20pt pill came out
2pt low inside a 24pt row. Measured with a throwaway probe that read the settled row back: `ROW rect
… 124.0` against an area placed at `100.0`, pills at `102.0`. **So the nudge is 2, not 3** — the
requested 3 was measured against an "approximately 8" that is really the 9 the constant says, and
taking it literally would have overshot by one and left the two readouts still unequal, just the other
way. Fixed by making the row exactly as tall as a pill rather than by subtracting a compensating
number, which is what makes the two equal *by construction* instead of by a second constant that can
drift. `the_pill_row_is_exactly_as_tall_as_a_pill` asserts the row, not the constant, and flips back to
24/+2.

**One number is left disagreeing on purpose, and it is the badge's, not the fields'.** The 2026-08-20
export moved the badge's own gap below the box from 11 to **14**; the build uses 9, and that 9 has a
reason older than either — it also has to clear `HANDLE_PICK_PX`, or the pill covers the grab area of
the nearest handle on a shape narrow enough for the two to overlap, and that handle stops being
reachable. 14 would clear it too, so this is a free choice now rather than a constraint. **Not changed,
because it was not what was reported**: the ask was for the two readouts to agree with *each other*,
which they now do at 9. Recorded so the next person to notice the export saying 14 finds out why the
code says 9 instead of re-deriving it.

**The clip: a fractional pivot overflowed its pill.** Reported with both fixes offered — "we could make
the fields wider. Or maybe approximate the pivot's movement to the nearest integer? Since having a
X: 29.75% and Y: 42.33% pivot isn't really that helpful." **Both, and the second is the real one.**
`31.25%` lays out at 36.72pt where a 62pt pill left 35.84 — a miss of less than a point, invisible in
the source and obvious on screen. But the deeper fault is that the *marker* stored whatever fraction
the pointer was over while the *field's* own scrub had settled to whole units since the day it was
written: one control, two classes of value. `pivot_at` now runs its result through `origin_percent` and
`origin_pivot` — the fields' own two functions — with each axis rounded, so the two doors cannot
produce different values for the same placement. It happens **after** the nine-point snap rather than
instead of it: that snap is in *screen* pixels and is what makes a corner easy to hit at any zoom, and
0 / 50 / 100 survive rounding untouched.

The width is measured too, and against the widest string the fields can be made to show rather than the
widest a drag produces: `-31.25%` at 41.44pt, since a typed value keeps its decimals and the fields are
deliberately unclamped (a pivot may sit outside its own box). 42 for the number, 69 for the pill.
`badge_field_chrome_w` exists so that the room `badge_field` leaves and the room a caller sizes against
are **one statement** — they were two, which is how a pill came to be a point too narrow — and
`the_number_has_room_for_the_widest_value_the_fields_can_show` asserts the relationship rather than the
number, so widening the label or the padding without widening the pill fails here instead of on screen.

**What rounding costs, stated because it is the one thing not visible in the tests.** A whole percent of
a big frame is a coarse step: 1% of a 1440-wide artboard is 14.4px, so the marker will visibly notch on
one. That is the trade the report asked for and it is the right one — the nine positions are exact, a
typed value is unrestricted, and the alternative is a number nobody meant sitting in the file. Worth
re-reading if anyone ever rigs a pivot on something very large.

**D254 — The origin fields swallowed the wheel, because shielding the press is indiscriminate.
*Resolved; the middle-button pan is the same cause and is a decided non-goal, tested on the
machine.*** Reported with the detail that
makes it worth an entry: *"it's more trouble than it sounds, because I hit the issue several times
while testing it."* A 69×20 pill is a small target, but scroll and `Ctrl`+wheel are gestures the hand
makes without looking at where the pointer is — so a dead zone that size gets hit constantly, where the
same zone would be unnoticeable for a rare verb. *Frequency of the gesture, not size of the target, is
what decides whether an exemption is worth building.*

**It is D252's own mechanism, taken further than intended.** An `egui::Area` takes the pointer away from
the layer beneath it **wholesale** — that is what stops a click on a field also starting a marquee, and
it was measured and written up as a virtue. It is also why `wheel_input`'s `resp.hover_pos()` returned
`None`: the canvas is not hovered while the pointer is over an area, for any purpose whatever. Nothing
was consuming the wheel; the canvas had simply stopped believing the pointer was on it. *A shield with
no opt-out is a shield against things you did not think of.*

The canvas takes the event back by asking `Context::layer_id_at` whether the topmost layer under the
pointer is **its own fields'**. By layer rather than by rectangle, deliberately: the pills move with the
shape, so a rect kept on this side of the seam would be a frame stale exactly during the gesture that
moves it — a zoom. `origin_fields_layer` is one function so the id the area is created with and the id
the exemption compares against cannot come apart; two literals is how an exemption silently stops
matching the thing it is about. Narrow on purpose — every other overlay keeps the wheel, since the
panels scroll and a menu should be dismissed rather than scrolled through.

`the_layer_under_the_pointer_is_nameable` pins the egui half, and flips against having no area at all
(the point answers with the background layer instead). The exemption's own wiring is inside
`wheel_input`, which needs an `OndinApp` (D35), and is read.

**The middle-button pan is the same collision and is a decided non-goal.** `Drag::Pan` starts on
`resp.drag_started_by(Middle)` and that is blocked over the pills for the identical reason. It was
raised here as open and answered the same day, **from the machine rather than from the argument**:
*"panning with the middle mouse click is fine. It's very hard to hit the fields while panning; I tried.
Not worth the trouble."* So the exemption is not built, and this is the record that stops it being
re-argued.

Worth keeping the reasoning that agrees with the test, since it is the general shape: the fix is not
the same as the wheel's — a wheel event can be handed over by asking who is under the pointer, where a
*drag* would need the canvas to reconstruct a gesture egui has already given to another layer, which is
drag tracking written twice. And the collision is far rarer, for the reason the wheel's was common: a
middle-drag begins wherever the hand happens to be and then leaves, while a wheel is turned with the
pointer parked. Space+drag and the Hand tool are unaffected either way, so there is always a way to
pan. *Two dead zones of one size, one worth an exemption and one not — the difference is entirely how
often the gesture starts where the zone is.*

**D308 — Nudging the transform origin from the keyboard is a decided non-goal. *Decided by the
maintainer; nothing built, and the record §0 of `roadmap.md` points at.*** The roadmap carried this as
the untouched half of the numeric-pair bullet — "there is no chord that nudges an origin, and
`shortcuts.md` reserves nothing for one" — and the statement is true: the only pivot in that file is in
the list of properties *Paste properties* leaves alone. What was wrong is the filing, because the
absence is not a gap: *"No one needs to nudge the pivot by 2 px. And if they do, they can type it in the
text field we added below the layer in the canvas."*

**The typed door is a real one, and that is what makes a chord redundant rather than merely unbuilt.**
`canvas::origin_fields` gates its `edit_valve` on `lost_focus()` and `changed()` alongside `dragged()`
and `drag_stopped()`, so a value typed into a pill commits without the pointer ever going down — the
fields are not scrub-only, which is the reading under which "type it in" would be an answer to a
question nobody asked. And because the pair is a **percentage of the box** (D247, re-decided on its own
merits when the fields left the card — D252), `0`, `50` and `100` name an edge or the centre exactly,
with no arithmetic and without reading a coordinate off the box first. Those three are the marker's own
snap set, so the keyboard already reaches every placement the *gesture* snaps to, and the ones in
between as well.

**What a chord would add is one more door onto a control that already has four** — the dragged marker,
the two pills and the menu's *Reset origin* — serving the one case the others do not: moving an origin
by a couple of pixels without looking at it. Nobody has that case. *Do not file it as a gap again*; §0
carries the one-line version and this entry the reason. *Revisit only under an accessibility pass that
needs every canvas control reachable without a pointer* — that is the one argument this does not answer,
and it is an argument about the whole canvas rather than about the pivot.

**D346 — The selection's size has a keyboard door, and it implements almost nothing. *Built and tested
2026-08-25; Keep.*** Asked for in one sentence: *"We're missing ctrl+left/right arrow keys change the
width of the selected shape on canvas. Ctrl+left makes it narrower, ctrl+right makes it wider. Figma
does something similar."* This is **undesigned territory**, and worth saying so before the reasoning:
no `Ctrl`/`Cmd`+arrow row exists anywhere in `shortcuts.md`, nothing reserved the chord, and neither
§5.6 nor §9.4 specified a keyboard-driven resize at all — so there was no step, no anchor, no
multi-selection rule, no rotated-node rule and no answer for a shape with no extent on an axis to
inherit. Every one of those below is a decision rather than a reading.

**It was built width-only and grew the other pair the same day**, which is the one part of this entry
that is a process note. The vertical arrows were left unbound deliberately and filed on the roadmap as a
question, with the three things a guess would have answered silently written beside it; the answer came
back as soon as the question was visible — *"Yes let's do height too. I was too focused on left/right, I
forgot to mention that."* So `→` widens, `←` narrows, `↓` makes it taller and `↑` shorter. *A guess would
have been cheap to write and expensive to notice was wrong. Writing the question down cost one roadmap
bullet and was answered in a sentence.*

**The chord was free because the nudge is gated on `!cmd`**, so `Ctrl`+arrow had always fallen
through to nothing. `Action::SizeStep(Vec2)` is a signed per-axis delta in points, resolved in
`input::normal_mode` on `cmd_only` — `Ctrl` *without* `Alt`. That last part is deliberate and is the
keymap's own habit since D207, whose test `save_and_cut_are_not_booleans` pins it: `Alt`+arrow is
already the nudge, the nudge block not being gated on `!alt`, so `Ctrl`+`Alt`+arrow is a chord one of
whose halves is spoken for and it stays unclaimed rather than quietly acquiring a second meaning.

⚠️ **The two arrow blocks are one, and that is a structural claim rather than a tidy-up.** The nudge and
the resize want the *same four signed pairs*: a nudge moves the box in the direction of the arrow, and a
