resize that holds the box's top-left moves the opposite edge, so it **also** grows in the direction of
the arrow. Written as two loops the shared signs would be two tables that happen to agree, and a later
edit to one of them would be silent — nothing would fail, and the two chords would simply start
disagreeing about what `↑` means. So there is one table and one arm, `if !cmd { Nudge(delta) } else if
cmd_only { SizeStep(delta) }`, and the keymap test asserts each `Ctrl`+arrow against **the nudge's own
vector for that key** rather than against written-out numbers, because what has to hold is that the two
agree. A `Vec2` rather than an axis and a scalar for the same reason it is one table: a box takes both
deltas in one edit, and only the keymap's own resolution makes it one axis at a time.

**The step is the nudge's, out of the same `NudgeStep`** (D330), so plain is 1, `Shift` is 10, and a
user who has retuned *Settings › Nudge* has retuned this too. A second "how far does an arrow key act"
preference would be one more thing to set and one more thing for the two to disagree about, and nothing
about a size makes 1 and 10 the wrong pair when they are the right one for a nudge.

⚠️ **Neither half of the arithmetic is written in `size_step`, and that is the whole design.** A width
already has exactly one definition per shape — the bottom-right handle's — and both of the inspector's W
fields are spelled as that drag with the pointer put where the number asks (§9.4). So the chord asks for
the same box the panel would: one selected layer through `tools::resize_box_to`, which works on the
**local** box and therefore grows a rotated shape along its own axes, and several through
`tools::resize_selection` over the world union, which is the only box differently-turned layers agree on.
**That split is the panel's own, not a new one** — a single selection shows the single-layer card — and
keeping it is what stops "make it 200 wide" typed and "make it a point wider" pressed from meaning two
different things about one shape. *The way to keep two doors agreeing is to have one of them not
implement the verb.*

**Held by its top-left corner**, which is the one X and Y report and the one the reader holds still. It
is also what makes a *held* key usable: the shape grows away from a fixed point instead of walking, which
is why — unlike `nudge` — it does not call `reveal_selection`, and why §9.4's list of edits that
deliberately do not scroll the view has gained it. And it is **load-bearing a third time**, as the
paragraph above says: the anchor is why the arrow names the edge that moves, which is what lets one table
serve both verbs. Undo coalesces a burst of taps through `commit_run`, under its **own**
verb, `resize-layers`, so a nudge and a resize can never merge into one step. Guides are inert: a guide
selection reads as empty through `Selection::is_empty` (§9.3), which is exactly what this wants. And
`dispatch` drops the action mid-create-drag for the reason it drops the nudge, in its sharper form — a
shape whose size the pointer is drawing must not also be taking one from the keyboard. ⚠️ **There is no
point-editing arm, unlike the nudge**: the arrows move path points because a point selection is what the
node tool is about, but a size is a fact about the whole layer whichever anchors happen to be picked.

⚠️ **The 1pt floor is not the floor it looks like, and this is the part worth reading twice.** The first
draft of the doc comment said it stops the width reaching zero. Traced press by press with the `max(1.0)`
removed, that is not what it does. Narrowing an 80-wide rect by 10: it goes cleanly down to 10, the next
press asks for 0 and something further down the resize stack floors *that* at 1, and the following press
asks for **−9** — at which point the rect **reflects across its own left edge**, coming out 9 wide
sitting to the *left* of where it had been anchored, and walking left from there. Which is not a bug in
the stack but §5.6 working as designed: a handle dragged past what it is anchored to flips the shape, and
the flip *is* the sign of the scale factor (D102). So the floor stops the **ask** going negative. The
failure it prevents is invisible in the width — the number stays positive throughout and lands back on 1
by coincidence — so a test asserting only the width would have been green for a shape that had turned
inside out and moved. That is why
`size_step_tests::narrowing_stops_at_a_point_rather_than_passing_through_zero` asserts `min_x`, and *any
future simplification of that assertion should be read as removing the test's only teeth.* The floor is
one closure, `want(extent, d)`, applied to both axes on both arms, so it cannot end up on three of the
four directions and not the fourth — which is exactly the shape a per-axis spelling would have taken when
the height pair was added to a function written for width.

⚠️ **The degenerate case is measured, not reasoned, and the doc comment had to be corrected.** A vertical
`Line` has a zero-wide local box. The comment claimed it would be left alone and named `tools::scale_along`
as the guard; the measurement agrees with the *outcome* — the line comes out exactly untouched, its width
still zero rather than floored up to a point it never had — and not with the explanation, since what
happens to a degenerate box is a claim about several layers of resize rather than about a guard this code
can point at. The comment now says it was measured and asserted. *A named helper in a "this cannot
happen" sentence is the tell that the sentence was reasoned rather than run.*

**A locked layer scales both axes, and the arrow says which one drives.** That was the last question this
entry left open, and it came back the same way the height pair had — *"Yes, ctrl+arrows on a
proportionally locked layer should resize it proportionally."* It makes the keyboard the **third** door
onto a rule the app already had, the other two being a corner drag (`canvas::keep_ratio`, §9.4) and the W
and H fields, which is the same argument the rest of this entry makes about not owning the verb. So the
pairing is spelled the panel's way, both of its guards included and in its order: `aspect = height /
width`, falling back to 1.0 where the width is not positive, and a height-driven press requiring
`aspect > 0.0` before it touches the width. The lock is read off the **committed document**, not off a
`DisplayNode`. The other two questions a width-only version would have had to guess at were answered by
building it — a height step anchors the **top** edge, the same corner, and `Shift` is the coarse step on
whichever single axis the arrow names, the keymap never emitting both at once.

⚠️ **It is paired by hand and *not* by asking `Resize::geometry` for its `keep_ratio` flag, and that is
counter-intuitive enough to have been run rather than reasoned.** The flag takes the **larger** of the
two factors, and this only ever drives one of them — so on a shrink it compares the step's factor against
the untouched axis's 1.0 and takes the 1.0. Measured on the several-selected arm: `Resize::geometry(true,
false)` asking for 40 points **off** a 100 × 60 union left it at exactly 100 × 60, no change whatever. The
flag would have made a locked layer un-shrinkable from the keyboard — silently, and in one direction
only, which is the kind of half-working that gets reported as "it feels sticky" rather than as a bug.
`resize_box_to`'s own doc says the same thing from the other side: the panel pairs *before* calling it,
and asking for the flag as well would apply the ratio twice.

⚠️ **The pairing was single-layer for a few hours, following the panel, and the premise it followed was
one D50 had already answered.** It was built as one because the multi W/H fields resized the union
through `Resize::geometry(false, false)` and consulted no lock at all, and the chain button on that card
was present and inert *"because `proportions_locked` is a flag on a node and a selection has no shared
one"* (§9.4) — so the keyboard inherited the panel's answer. But *"a multi-selection is proportion-locked
only when **every** member is"* is a decided rule with a *Keep*, and `canvas::keep_ratio` had been
reading it as `all` since, so a handle drag over a set of locked layers kept their proportions while the
two numeric doors onto the same box did not. That was not three doors agreeing to sit it out; it was
**two numeric doors not consulting a rule the pointer's door applies**, which is this entry's own
failure mode arrived at from the other end. **Closed the same day and in both doors at once** — *"Let's
do both doors then, keyboard and the multi W/H fields"* — so `size_step` pairs on its several-selected
arm as well, through `tools::proportions_locked` and `tools::paired_size`. D347 has that change, the
latent `max_y()` trap it walked through, and the chain button that had to come alive with it.

⚠️ **The lock is asked of `session.selection.ids()`, not of the `build::outermost` reduction this
function resizes through**, because that is the list `canvas::keep_ratio` asks. A shorter one would let a
handle drag and an arrow key disagree about a nested selection — a group whose child is also selected —
and about nothing else, which is the kind of disagreement that gets found years later.

*Ten tests, all flip-checked with the flip run.*
`input::tests::ctrl_arrows_size_the_selection_and_leave_the_nudge_alone` covers all four directions, the
`Shift` step, that a bare arrow is *still only* a nudge, that `Ctrl`+arrow does not also nudge, and that
`Ctrl`+`Alt`+`→` stays free; it flips twice — gating on `cmd` instead of `cmd_only`, which only the last
assertion catches, and swapping the two arms so a bare arrow resizes, which the nudge assertion catches
and which is the failure the merged table makes possible. The nine in `app::size_step_tests` are the
ones about a *shape*, which is the distinction its module doc makes — a keymap test proves a chord
resolves and says nothing about whether anything moved. The anchor test flips against asking for the size
*without* the delta, the shape a refactor leaves behind; the floor against dropping the `max`; the rotated
case pins **both** crossings, a point of local width landing on the world height and a point of local
height on the world width, which is what says the whole box is read in local space rather than one axis
being special-cased. The lock has a pair — `a_locked_layer_keeps_its_proportions_under_either_arrow`
against `an_unlocked_layer_moves_only_the_axis_the_arrow_names`, which is the control and asserts its
fixture starts unlocked. ⚠️ **That fixture is 80 × 60 and deliberately not a square**: the aspect is 0.75,
so every paired number is checkable by hand, where on a square a bug that swapped the two axes would be
invisible. Width drives 80 → 84 and carries the height to 63, height then drives 63 → 66 and carries the
width to 88, the ratio survives both — and **the top-left is asserted again**, because pairing is the one
change here that could have moved the anchor unnoticed: a shape growing on both axes from the wrong
corner reads far more plausibly than one growing on one. The flip is dropping the `locked` test, caught
by the second assertion. `a_set_pairs_only_when_every_member_is_locked` is the same pair over *two*
layers, added when the several-selected arm learnt to pair (D347): a 100 × 60 union so the aspect is 0.6
and 150 wide carries the height to 90, then the **mixed** half, one of the two locked, where the height
must stay at 60. Its flip is `any` for `all` inside `tools::proportions_locked` — the mixed half fails
and the all-locked half passes, which is exactly how that bug would reach the machine. The last three
are the degenerate line, the several-selected arm below, and an empty selection changing nothing *and
adding no undo entry*.

⚠️ **The flip that did not bite is the one worth carrying away: `Handle::TopLeft` in place of
`BottomRight` passed every test in the module.** That constant is only on the several-selected path, and
every test held a single selection — which takes the `resize_box_to` route, where the handle is fixed
inside the helper and the flip is inert. So **a whole arm of the split this entry is built around was
uncovered while the suite looked complete**, and the flip was the only thing that said so.
`several_selected_resize_as_one_box_from_the_unions_corner` is what closes it: two rects in a 100 × 60
union, asserting that the layer on the union's own corner stays put, that it is *scaled* rather than
translated, and that the far layer's outer edge lands on the box's new one. The flip bites there — the
corner layer jumps to x 140. *A flip that changes nothing is not a passed check; it is a question about
which paths the tests actually take.*

**D347 — A typed number and a dragged handle disagreed about a locked set, for as long as both existed.
*Fixed and tested 2026-08-25; Resolved.*** D50 settled how a multi-selection reads the proportion lock —
all-or-nothing, a set being only as constrained as its least constrained member — and `canvas::keep_ratio`
applied it from the day it was decided, so dragging a corner over two locked layers kept their
proportions. Typing 150 into the W field beside that corner did not, and neither did `Ctrl`+arrows once
they existed (D346). One box, two answers, depending on which door you came in by — which is precisely
what §9.4's "a width has exactly one definition per shape" argument exists to prevent, and it was living
in the panel the whole time. It was found from the other end, while the keyboard door was being built,
and closed in one sentence: *"Let's do both doors then, keyboard and the multi W/H fields"*.

⚠️ **Both doors excused themselves in comments that were *true*, which is why neither read as a
mistake.** `size_step` said the pairing was "only for a single layer, which is where the lock lives";
the chain button said `proportions_locked` is a flag on a node, so a selection has no shared one. Each
names a real property of the model — and each was answering a question D50 had already answered. *It
read as a scope decision because it named a real property of the model; what it actually was, was a rule
nobody had thought to look up.* Both comments are gone; D134 carries the same lesson from the tooltip
end, where the reason a control is dimmed is exactly the claim nobody checks.

⚠️ **The rule is one expression now, and the reason it was not before is the reason it had one reader.**
`tools::proportions_locked(doc, ids)` is `!ids.is_empty() && ids.iter().all(…)` — D50 verbatim, with the
empty case spelled out so that an empty selection cannot read as "every member is locked" through a
vacuous `all`. It came out of `canvas::keep_ratio` *because* a third reader had arrived; while the
handles were its only reader, inline was the obvious place for it, and inline is exactly what stopped
the next door noticing there was a rule to obey. `keep_ratio` calls it on both arms, `Target::Layer(id)`
passing `&[id]`, which is the same `all` over one element rather than a second spelling of it. Every
caller passes the **whole selection**, never `build::outermost`'s reduction: the question is what the
user picked, so a group whose child is also selected is a set of two.

**`tools::paired_size(now, want, drove_x)` is the arithmetic, once.** ⚠️ **`drove_x` is passed in rather
than inferred, and that is the load-bearing part**: "which axis differs from the current box" is the
tempting way to compute it and is wrong on any press whose paired value happens to land on the other
axis's current number, and wrong again once the 1pt floor has clamped the driven axis to something it
was already at. Both guards inside it are the single-layer card's, in the card's order — a box with no
width has no ratio and falls back to 1, and a height-driven edit needs `aspect > 0.0` before it can
divide — because the panel is where the pairing was first written and the two doors must not come out
with different boxes for the same ask. ⚠️ **The single card was routed through it rather than left beside
it**: it had two callers on the day it was written, its own source not among them, and identical
arithmetic sitting beside a copy of itself is precisely the state in which neither copy looks wrong.
Three callers now — `app.rs`'s `size_step`, `multi_transform_tx` and the single card's W and H — so a
change to the rule is one edit rather than three that have to be found.

⚠️ **Both call sites were passing the union's far edge for the axis they were not driving, and it had
been harmless.** `union.max_y()` for a width edit is the same number as `min_y + height` exactly while
the height is untouched — so it read as equivalent and was, until pairing made the height move. Both now
take *both* coordinates off the union's `min`. Nothing ever fired here; it is recorded because it is the
shape of the thing that gets "simplified" back, an expression that is provably equal under the
assumption the change is about to remove.

**The multi card's chain button had to come alive with it, and that was not scope creep.** It was inert,
excused by *"`proportions_locked` is a flag on a node, so a selection has no shared one to show and
nowhere to put the answer"*, with a tooltip saying "One layer at a time" — ⚠️ **both halves of which are
what D50 answers.** It survived because a control that does nothing is never reported as wrong; it was
arguing from the shape of the data against a rule that had already been decided. And it had to become
**live** rather than merely truthful, which is this change's own doing: now that the fields beside it
pair, a set of locked layers cannot be resized freely from that card at all, and unlike a handle drag —
where Shift releases the ratio (D47) — a typed number has no release, `Ctrl`+arrow's Shift being spent
on the coarse step. Reporting the state without offering the toggle would have been a door with no
handle on the inside. A press drives the whole set to one state, `!all_locked` for every member in one
transaction, rather than toggling each: flipping a mixed selection member by member leaves it mixed,
which is the one outcome no press of that button can be asking for.

*Four tests, all flip-checked with the flip run.*
`app::size_step_tests::a_set_pairs_only_when_every_member_is_locked` is described under D346.
`panels::inspector::multi_lock_tests::a_typed_width_over_a_locked_set_carries_the_height` makes the same
two claims against the field, and is ⚠️ **deliberately a duplicate rather than a shared helper**: what is
being asserted is that two doors agree while being asked *separately*, which a shared fixture would
quietly stop testing. Its flip is dropping the `proportions_locked` call — i.e. the field's behaviour up
to the day this landed — and the mixed half of the keyboard's twin flips on `any` for `all`.
`a_typed_height_over_a_locked_set_carries_the_width` is its own test rather than a third assertion on the
one above, because H is the arm where the `max_x()` above would have *moved* the box instead of resizing
it, and it asserts the union's top-left as well as its two extents.
`the_chain_button_drives_a_mixed_set_to_one_state_in_one_step` covers the button: a mixed set reads as
unlocked, one press locks **every** member including the one that already was, in **one** undo step, and
a second press from all-locked releases the set. The decision moved into `inspector::lock_all_tx`, a
free function, to make it reachable at all — a `&mut self` widget call site cannot be reached from a
test, which is why `scale_tx` is a method rather than the body of its own row.
⚠️ **Its flip is the toggle spelling, `locked: !was_locked(id)` per member, and it fails on the *first*
assertion rather than the undo-depth one**: the toggle *swaps* the two members instead of agreeing them,
so the set is still mixed long before the step count is reached. Recorded because the prediction was
written as "second" and corrected by running it — *a flip has a predicted failure as well as a predicted
colour, and only running it says which assertion is the load-bearing one.*

**D348 — The size badge's padlock read the node's own flag, so a layer inside a locked group had a box
that would not drag and nothing saying why. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.*** The `W × H` pill
under the selection is the **only** place on the canvas that says why the handles refuse to move, and
`draw_size_badge` decided its padlock with `doc.get(id).is_some_and(|n| n.locked())` — the weaker of the
two spellings D321 spent a whole entry collapsing. Every *refusal* on the canvas has asked
`query::is_effectively_locked` since that day; the label on those refusals had not, and D321 said why in
as many words: it is "a label rather than a refusal, which is why it was not swept with the four".
**That reason is the wrong way round.** A label on a refusal has to ask the same question the refusal
did, or the one state the padlock exists to explain — a nested layer whose box will not move — is
exactly the state it is silent in. `any` and not `all`, deliberately unchanged: the pill is one label
over a set, so if any member refuses to move the set does.

*Keep.*
`canvas::size_badge_lock_tests::the_padlock_follows_the_effective_lock_not_the_nodes_own_flag` pins it
on three fixtures over one grouped 120 × 80 rect — free, own flag set, group locked — measured as **the
width of the pill's ground polygon**. `paint_size_pill` reserves `LOCK_PT + LOCK_GAP` for the glyph and
moves nothing else, so the width *is* the padlock's presence stated as a number, and it stays a fair
test if the lock is ever redrawn. ⚠️ The three readings are compared against **each other**, never
against a literal: the label is `120 × 80`, whose galley width is a font fact this test has no business
asserting; what it asserts is that the two locked readings agree and that both are exactly
`LOCK_PT + LOCK_GAP` clear of the free one. ⚠️ **That last pair is `10.0 + 5.0` written out, not read**,
and the test says so where it is spelled: both constants are local to `paint_size_pill`, where they sit
in one documented group with `GAP` and `PAD` and are better off staying, so retuning either fails the
test rather than following it. That is the honest cost of leaving them local, and the assertion message
names them so a grep for `LOCK_PT` finds the site. *A first draft of this paragraph claimed the opposite
— "spelled from the constants so retuning either retunes the test" — which is the shape of comment this
whole file exists to catch, written while the code it described was being corrected.* ⚠️ **The flip is
putting `n.locked()` back, and it leaves the first two assertions green** — the
own-flag reading is right about a free layer and about a directly locked one — failing on the **third**,
the grouped one, at 53.15625 against 68.15625, the 10 + 5 the glyph and its gap are worth. Predicted
there and observed there, and worth recording as it stands: the two cheap assertions have no teeth
against the defect this entry is about and exist only to give the third a scale to be measured against.

**D349 — The layers panel is resizable, and getting there found a cursor bug it did not introduce.
*Built and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.*** The roadmap asked for it on 2026-08-24 in the same breath as
the width bump that answered half of it: *"in fact it wouldn't be a bad idea to leave it at 300px by
default, and add resizing just for the layers panel. Probably the inspector panels too. Both with some
minimum width."* D330 landed the 300; this makes it a **default the user can drag off** —
`Panel::default_size(prefs.layers_width).size_range(layers::MIN_W ..= MAX_W).resizable(true)`, with
`prefs::Prefs::layers_width` remembering the answer. **The inspector column is deliberately not in
this change**, and D351 closed it as a non-goal the day after: it is an `egui::Area` of floating
cards with no edge to hang a handle on, and `inspector_panel` re-establishes its column rect
explicitly (§9.2), so a user-set width would have to become an *input* to that rather than something
the layout discovers.

**`MIN_W` is 210 because it was derived, and that is the part worth recording.** Two independent
readings meet there. A **top-level** row keeps 96.5pt of name while hovered, against `Rectangle 12`
laying out at 75.06pt and `Button primary hover` at 124.34 — so the common case fits and the long case
is the one that clips, which is the trade the minimum makes, stated as the two numbers either side of
it. And a **four-deep** row's hovered name room stops being negative: it crosses zero at 206.5 and 210
is the next ten-point step clear. Four levels is not an arbitrary depth — it is the depth D330 itself
argued the 300 from ("a layer four deep had about 90pt at 250"), so this reuses that decision's own
reference rather than inventing one. The formula is `w − 2·PAD_X − icon_offset(depth, true) −
NAME_GAP − (LOCK_INSET + EYE_PITCH + ICON_PT/2)`, and it is **hovered** deliberately: at rest a
visible, unlocked, unbadged row draws nothing on its right at all and has the whole width, so a
minimum argued from the roomy state is one that breaks the moment the pointer arrives. Every term is
a constant the row walk itself draws with — `PAD_X` moved into `panels::layers` out of the `Margin`
literal in `app.rs`, the seven row-walk literals were named, and `icon_offset(depth, caret_room)` was
lifted out of the walk — so retuning any of them moves the assertions rather than silently
invalidating them. `MAX_W` is twice the default: a cap at all because a panel dragged over the whole
window has no signpost out of it, and *twice* because at 600 a row eight deep still has 269.5pt of
name, so the cap binds only on someone starving the canvas. That `MIN_W < DEFAULT_W < MAX_W` is a
`const _: () = assert!(…)` beside the three rather than a test assertion — clippy's
`assertions_on_constants` named it and was right, and the compiler refusing the build beats a test
that has to be run. ⚠️ **That number said 310 until the arithmetic was read back out of the constants,
and 310 is a real reading of the same row — the wrong one.** 269.5 is what the row has *hovered*: 576
of content, less 247 of indent and glyph, less the 15pt name gap and the 44.5 the eye-and-lock cluster
takes. 310 is the at-rest reading, where
the right-hand cluster is not drawn and only a badge's 4pt inset is owed. The sentence is about the
hovered formula the minimum is derived from, so it wanted the hovered figure; **nothing caught the
substitution because the test asserts `> 200.0` and both figures clear it**, and a bound loose enough
to be about the right thing is loose enough not to notice which number is in the prose beside it.
⚠️ **Every width figure in this paragraph was then found to be 12pt pessimistic and is superseded by
D444** — 96.5 is 108.5, the four-deep crossing is 194.5 and not 206.5, 269.5 is 281.5, 314 is 326 and
310 is 322 — because the derivation subtracted the *header*'s `2 * PAD_X` where a row is narrowed by
the tree's own `TREE_PAD_X`, half of it. They are left as written here, this entry being the record of
what was argued at the time; **read D444 for the numbers**. What it costs is the second reading above:
210 no longer sits where two readings meet, which is open work in `roadmap.md`.

**Three traps hold the mechanism up, all of them egui's and none of them visible in our source** — a
fourth, about where the drag edge reads its colours, is the paragraph after next. First, ⚠️ **a
`Panel` takes its width from what its *content* occupied**, so a resizable one whose content does not
fill does not merely fail to grow — it **collapses to `size_range`'s minimum**, because
`panel_axis_min` is the only floor `Frame::show` is given. egui says "you also need to make the ui use
the available space" in `resizable`'s own doc and that sentence badly undersells it. Hence
`ui.set_min_width(ui.available_width())` inside the closure. Nothing here had noticed because a
`Rangef::point` range — which is all `exact_size` leaves — cannot move.
`app::layers_width_tests::a_resizable_panel_collapses_to_its_minimum_unless_the_content_fills_it`
asserts **both** branches, and is deliberately written about egui with a bare label for content rather
than about the layers panel: the day it changes, every panel test would still pass while the drag
silently stopped holding. Second, ⚠️ **`default_size` must be called before `size_range`, and swapping
them breaks the clamp silently**: `default_size` widens the range to admit whatever it is handed
(`at_most`/`at_least`), and `size_range` replaces the range and clamps the stored default into it.
`prefs.json` is a plain file that can be hand-edited, copied between machines or written by a future
version, so this is untrusted input — with the calls swapped a stored 5000 comes straight through and
the panel opens over the window. Both spellings read as "a default and a range", which is the only
reason this is a test (`a_stored_width_from_outside_the_bounds_is_clamped`) rather than a comment.

Third, ⚠️ **the change found a live cursor bug, and the comment excusing that bug was wrong about
egui.** The panel's drag edge claims `ResizeHorizontal` while `layers_panel` draws; the canvas draws
*after* it, and `canvas_cursor`'s off-canvas arm answered "not me" by writing `CursorIcon::Default`
and `set_cursor_image(None)` — erasing the claim in the frame it was made, so the splitter would have
had no cursor at all. The arm was excused by a comment reading "egui never resets either one —
`PlatformOutput` carries both across frames on purpose". **That is false for egui 0.35 on this
route**: `Context::end_pass` takes the viewport's whole `PlatformOutput` with a plain
`std::mem::take`, so both channels start every frame at their `Default`. There *is* a sticky path —
`PlatformOutput::take`, whose body literally says "sticky between frames" against those two fields —
and nothing on `end_pass`'s route calls it. A true sentence about the wrong function, which is why
`a_cursor_does_not_survive_a_frame_and_the_last_writer_wins` is a test and not a correction: reading
egui twice would have given the same wrong answer twice, and the test failed on its first run because
it had been written from the comment. So the reset was never needed and was pure harm, and deleting it
is the whole fix. **The inspector's reorder grip kept its `Grab` only by being drawn after the
canvas**, which is why nothing had ever reported this. §9.2's rule that chrome changes the cursor only
where it means something still holds — a splitter means something — but ⚠️ **the count that passage
carried was wrong before this change and no longer exists.** It said "the two places" and there were
already four claim sites, for a mechanical reason rather than a careless one: a cursor is claimed
through **two** APIs, `Context::set_cursor_icon` and `Response::on_hover_cursor`, and a grep for the
first finds neither of `value_field`'s scrub strips. §9.2 now states the rule, names the trap and
carries the grep instead of a number, and `ui.rs`'s copy of the sentence says the same.

**The drag edge's two lit states are retuned, because egui picks them off the *parent* ui's style.**
`active.fg_stroke` while dragging and `hovered.fg_stroke` under the pointer are the **text** strokes —
`TEXT` and `ACCENT_100`, both effectively white — and a full-height near-white hairline against a
divider at 9% alpha is a jump this theme makes nowhere else, so the pair is set to the colours every
other control's border already uses for those two states (`ACCENT_700` hovered, `ACCENT` active). The
splitter says "interactive" in the vocabulary on screen rather than inventing a louder one; the
resting hairline is `noninteractive.bg_stroke` and is untouched. ⚠️ **The hovered half of that no
longer fires on hover.** Since the same day it waits out `EDGE_DWELL` first, and `hovered.fg_stroke`
holds the resting divider colour until then (§15 D350). The colour decision here is unchanged and the
mechanism is the one this paragraph describes; only *when* the accent is handed over moved.

**⚠️ The override is put back twice, and the two restores are for two different readers.** The outer
one, after the panel, is because that `ui` is the frame's central one and the tool rail, the canvas
and the inspector are all still to be drawn into it — `hovered.fg_stroke` is what a hovered button's
*label* uses, so without it every hovered label below that call goes accent-blue. The inner one is the
first line of the content closure, and is the scoping the retune needs to be honest: egui draws the
separator on the **parent** after the closure returns, but the content is a child that would otherwise
inherit the override, and `WidgetVisuals::text_color()` *is* `fg_stroke.color` — so the layers search
field's own text would have gone accent-blue on hover. A child `Ui` holds its own `Arc<Style>`, which
is what makes putting the theme's back there scope the override to the one line it was for.
`app::layers_width_tests::the_panel_puts_the_style_back_after_retuning_the_drag_edge` pins the outer
one, and **how it is written is the part worth recording**: it calls the real `layers_panel` through
`OndinApp::headless` (D303) rather than round-tripping `set_style` on a bare `Ui`, because the failure
worth catching is not "restore does not work" — it is *someone adding an early return between the
retune and the restore*, which only a test that calls the method itself can see. It also asserts the
two states the retune does **not** touch, `hovered.bg_stroke` and `noninteractive.bg_stroke`, so a
restore that overreached — putting back a snapshot taken too early — fails rather than passing.
⚠️ Its flip is deleting the outer `ui.set_style(style)`: it fails on the `hovered.fg_stroke`
assertion, reporting `#445C9A` where `#E9E9ED` is due. Predicted there and observed there.

**Persisting is three gates and no `Response`.** `Prefs::save` rewrites the whole file, so the width
is written on the frame the drag *ends*, never during it: `width_to_store(width, room, stored, down)`
answers `Some` only when `!down` (one write per gesture rather than a hundred into a synced config
directory), when `width < room - 0.5` (egui clamps a panel to its parent's space with
`.at_most(available_rect…)`, so a window too narrow to hold the panel shrinks the *reported* width
with no drag involved, and storing that would let a moment of a small window outlive it), and when it
differs from `stored` by half a point. ⚠️ **The two 0.5s are one thing** — egui `round_ui`s the panel
rect, so both comparisons are against a number that has been through rounding. **None of the three
reads egui's resize `Response`**, which is the obvious spelling and is unreachable: the handle's id is
`id.with("__resize")`, a private salt `Panel::show` does not hand back, and a guard built on it would
fail *silently* the day egui renamed it — it would simply stop persisting. ⚠️ **The decision was
lifted into a free function for a reason worth generalising**: `Prefs::save` writes into
`dirs::config_dir()`, so a test that could reach the write would rewrite the real `prefs.json` of
whoever ran the suite. That is a different argument from the usual one — D269's "no test can say where
a `&mut self` method is called from" — and it applies to every other preference.

*Flip-checks, with the site predicted and then corrected to what happened.* Each of `width_to_store`'s
three terms deleted in turn: `room` fails on the `window shrank` case, `!down` on `mid-drag`, the
deadband on `a hair of rounding` — three terms, three cases, no case answered by more than one term.
`MIN_W` at 180 fails on the **first** assertion of the top-level test, 66.50pt against 75.06, and on
the four-deep test at −26.50pt. `MIN_W` at 300 fails the top-level test's *second* assertion — the
"not a floor" one, which is the half worth having, since a minimum that is merely generous stops the
user doing something reasonable and nothing on screen would say so — ⚠️ **and took the other two tests
with it, which was not predicted**: the band test's lower bound (83.50pt of room ten points under a
300 minimum) and the ordering invariant, because a minimum equal to the default leaves the panel
opening at a width it cannot be dragged back to. Three tests, three different reasons, which is what
says the ordering check is not the formality it looks like. `DEFAULT_W` at 900 fails the **build**,
`error[E0080]: evaluation panicked`, pointing at the `const` assertion. ⚠️ **And that last move
invalidated the flip-check above it, which is a way for flip prose to rot that has nothing to do with
the code under test.** Promoting the ordering assertion out of `the_maximum_still_holds_a_deep_tree`
into a `const` means a reader reproducing the `MIN_W = 300` flip now gets a compile error and never
sees the three failures the paragraph describes — the finding is still true, but only of the tree as
it was that morning. The test's ⚠️ is in the past tense for that reason. *A flip-check is written
against a particular arrangement of assertions, so moving one is a documentation change as well as a
refactor.* ⚠️ **And one honest note about
`panels::layers::panel_width_tests`**: it composes the name-room formula itself. Every *term* is the
constant or function the row walk draws with, but the order they are added in is spelled twice. It
could only be shared by giving the row walk a "how much room has the name" question it never asks — it
paints from the left and lets the clip rect end the name, which is exactly why a panel dragged too
narrow is silent on screen.

**Deliberately not built: no double-click-to-collapse and no collapsed state.** `Panel::show_collapsible`
exists and is not used. Hiding the layers panel is already `show_layers`, a separate switch with a menu
row of its own, and a second way to make it go away would be two answers to one question.

**D350 — The drag edge lit on travel, because a splitter is on everybody's way somewhere else.
*Fixed and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.*** Reported from the machine within the hour of D349 being
accepted: *"The resize indicator lights up to blue the moment I hover over it. That's also true when
just moving the mouse back and forth the layer panel. Let's add a 200ms delay on the highlight, so
that it doesn't light up when not planning to resize."* So D349's **colour** was right and its
**timing** was wrong. The tree is a column you scan and the splitter sits between it and the canvas,
so a highlight that fires on hover fires on travel, and reports a gesture nobody is making.
`EDGE_DWELL` is 0.2s — the shortest delay that reads as *intent* rather than as lag: a pointer
crossing the band on its way somewhere is inside it for a couple of frames, and a hand that has
stopped to grab the edge has stopped for longer than that before the button goes down.

**Scope: the highlight only, never the cursor.** `ResizeHorizontal` still arrives on hover with no
delay. It is cheap to look at, it is the affordance that says the edge is grabbable at all, and it was
not what was reported; it also comes off egui's own resize response, which this does not touch.

**How the delay is applied is the part that is not obvious.** egui decides the separator's state
itself and hands nothing back, so there is no hover here to suppress. What *is* reachable from the
call site is what `hovered.fg_stroke` **contains** — so it holds `color::DIVIDER`, the resting
hairline's own colour, until the dwell is up and `ACCENT_700` after. The line is drawn in both states
and is simply indistinguishable from the rest state in the first one. D349's paragraph on the colour
retune is the mechanism this rides on, unchanged. ⚠️ **"Indistinguishable" is an identity and not a
resemblance**: `color::DIVIDER` is the very value `theme::install` puts in `noninteractive.bg_stroke`,
which is what the resting edge draws. Naming the same constant is what makes the delay invisible
rather than *nearly* invisible — retune one of the two and the wait acquires a visible first state,
which is a different feature nobody asked for.

**`EdgeDwell` is a three-state machine** — `Off`, `Waiting(f64)`, `Lit` — with `advance(now, in_band,
pressed, down) -> Self`, `lit()` and `due()`. Deliberately `ChromeHold`'s shape and for its stated
reason: the part that can be wrong is the machine, so it is driven through its own states rather than
through the frames that would produce them — and here that is the only way to reach two of the four
transitions at all, since "a press landed on the edge" and "the pointer left the band with a button
still down" both need a pointer history one `run_ui` cannot express. `OndinApp::fold_layers_edge`
gathers the inputs and does nothing else, `fold_chrome_hold`'s split. Seconds from `InputState::time`,
for `ChromeHold::Until`'s reason: it is the clock `request_repaint_after` is measured against and the
one a headless probe can drive.

Four things the machine has to get right, each with a test of its own:

- **The wait itself.** A pointer that crosses the band and leaves inside the dwell never lights it.
- **`pressed`, not `down`, for the shortcut.** A press landing in the band lights the edge at once,
  because a drag must never be the one gesture with no feedback. The press **edge** rather than the
  button state, since `down` is also true of a drag begun elsewhere and carried over the band.
- **`down` does two opposite jobs, and they are two arms rather than one.** It **holds** a lit edge
  once the pointer has left the band, which it does on every drag that reaches `MIN_W` or `MAX_W`,
  because egui stops the edge at the clamp and the hand keeps going — without that the highlight
  drops out exactly when the user is pushing hardest against a limit. And it **blocks** the dwell, so
  a gesture already in flight when it reaches the band can never light the edge by resting there.
  ⚠️ **The second job was missing when this first landed, and the omission was
  invisible**: the obvious bad case, a drag crossing the band, crosses in a few frames and never
  reaches the deadline. What reaches it is a drag that *hesitates* — a layer row carried out to the
  canvas and held over the splitter, a marquee paused there — and then the edge lights under a hand
  plainly doing something else, which is the reported complaint in its rarer form. The arm is
  `Waiting(t) if pressed || (!down && now - t >= EDGE_DWELL)` now. Found by reading the arm against
  the sentence documenting it, not by the test, which sampled the crossing case only to 100ms and so
  pinned the *shortcut* rather than the rule: **a test that stops short of the boundary is a test of
  the shortcut, not of the rule**, and its sample list has a fourth point past the deadline for that
  reason.
- **`due()` wakes the frame** through `request_repaint_after`. The case the whole machine exists for
  is a hand that has *stopped*, and a stopped hand generates no events — without the wake-up the
  highlight arrives on whatever happens next, which may be the press itself, i.e. never visibly. It is
  `None` in both settled states, or a lit edge would ask for a repaint every frame the pointer rests
  on it.

**Where the band comes from, and the refusal it repeats.** `fold_layers_edge` derives the grab band
itself rather than reading egui's resize `Response` — the same refusal `width_to_store` makes and for
the same reason, the handle's id being a private `__resize` salt that a hover built on it would follow
into silence. What it uses instead is public: `egui::PanelState::load` for the panel's outer rect,
`Interaction::resize_grab_radius_side` for the reach egui itself expands the handle by, plus half a
point so the band is never thinner than what egui will claim — 3.5 either side against egui's own 3,
a 7pt band over a 6pt handle. ⚠️ **`PanelState` is last frame's**, so mid-drag the band trails the
edge by one frame; that is the same staleness egui's own resize interaction runs on — it resolves
against `read_response`, also last frame's — and it cannot matter here, because by then the state is
already `Lit` and held by `down`. ⚠️ **On the very first frame, before the panel has stored a rect,
the edge is `f32::NAN`**: every comparison against it is false, so the band is *empty* rather than
everywhere. That is the one arm a reader would not predict from the arithmetic, and it is stated at
the line rather than left to be rediscovered.

**Both ends of `down` ask the *primary* button** — `button_down(Primary)` at the fold, matching the
`button_pressed(Primary)` beside it, rather than `any_down()`. The two ends are one question, "is a
gesture in flight on this edge", and asking it of a different button at each end is the shape a later
reader tidies in the wrong direction; concretely, `any_down` let a middle-button pan begun over a lit
edge hold it lit off the band, and let a right-drag block the dwell. ⚠️ **A fifth test exists because
that flip did not bite.** Putting `any_down` back left all four state-machine tests green, which is a
finding about the coverage rather than about the change: every one of them calls `advance` directly,
so the machine was pinned and the *gathering* of its inputs was not — which button the fold asks
about was reachable only by reading. `the_fold_blocks_the_dwell_on_the_primary_button_only` drives
the real `layers_panel` through `OndinApp::headless` (D303) over two `RawInput` frames, and its
discriminating case is a middle-button pan resting on the band past the dwell: under `any_down` it
blocks the dwell and the edge stays dark, under `button_down(Primary)` it is not a resize gesture,
does not block, and the edge lights like any resting pointer. One assertion tells the two spellings
apart, and with it in place the flip fails, `Waiting(1.0)` against `Lit`.

*Flip-checks, all six run, with the site predicted and then corrected to what happened.* Returning
`Lit` from the `Off if in_band` arm — the no-delay version, which is what shipped and was reported —
fails on the **first** assertion of the crossing case, "lit on the frame the pointer arrived", rather
than on the boundary pair it was predicted at. That is the more useful failure: the bug was never
about *when* the light arrived, it was that it arrived at all. ⚠️ **It also takes two of the three
other `advance` tests with it, which was not predicted** — with `Waiting` never reached, the
lingering-drag case lights at `t=0` and `due` has nothing to return. So the whole module hangs off
that one arm, and the rest are the ones that say where the teeth actually are: `down` substituted for
`pressed` fails the lingering-drag case at `t=0`, and the press-on-the-edge case still passes under
it, which is the cheap half kept only to give the other something to be read against; dropping
`!down` from the dwell arm leaves the first three samples of that same case green and fails on the
**fourth**, at `t = 0.25` — the one past the deadline, and the flip that would have caught the
original omission; dropping `|| down` from the `Lit` arm fails on the **second** assertion of the
clamp test, the state falling to `Off` the frame the pointer passes the clamp; `due()` returning
`None` unconditionally fails on the first assertion of the wake-up test; and `any_down()` back at the
fold is the one that did not bite until a test was written for it, above. ⚠️ **The dwell test samples
a hair either side of the deadline rather than at it**, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s caret-blink trap in
another form: asserting only "lit at `t + 0.2`" passes against a machine that lights the moment it is
touched, since that is also lit at `t + 0.2`. The pair `0.199 → not lit`, `0.201 → lit` is what pins
the deadline to *this* deadline.

**D351 — A resizable inspector column is a non-goal, because its width is a function of the design
where the layers panel's is a function of the document. *Decided by the maintainer 2026-08-25; a
non-goal. Keep — the principle is general, and the only code change is the defect the check turned
up.*** D349 landed the layers panel's drag and left *"the inspector column is still its own change"*
beside it. That was the hedged half of the original ask — *"add resizing just for the layers panel.
Probably the inspector panels too. Both with some minimum width."* — and it is answered the day
after: *"I'm not sure if the inspector panels are even worth doing. They're a compact size and we've
cared to have them look well. Letting people resize them feels like a waste over something
irrelevant."*, then *"No, leave it as non-goal."* once the reasoning below was put back. D349's quote
stands as written; what changes is that its closing sentence no longer means "a change still to come".

**One principle, two opposite answers.** The layers panel's width is a function of the **document**;
the inspector's is a function of the **design**. A tree four levels deep with long names genuinely
needs more room than a flat one, and only the person holding that document knows which theirs is —
which is exactly why D330 had to *pick* 300 and why D349 letting them override it earns its keep. The
inspector shows a fixed set of controls whose room requirement was known when they were drawn:
widening it makes fields wider, not more informative. No document makes the Transform card need more
space.

⚠️ **The check that decides this was rewritten around the site that falsified it, and the first
version of this entry would have been false.** The brief asserted that nothing a user types or names
is cut off in the inspector, on two named sites — a variable font's axis name and an action button's
label — neither of them the user's. Read against the code, one of the two *is* the user's:
`panels::export`'s button prints `Export {name}` off the selected layer, `ui::action_button` elides
it (D276), and `ui.rs`'s `a_long_action_button_label_is_elided_inside_the_button` says so in its own
first line, both of its fixtures being layer names off a screenshot. Its width is
`available_width()`, so it is exactly the control a wider column would help. **A decided non-goal
whose stated reason is wrong is worse than an open question**, because §15 is the thing that stops it
being re-argued.

So the check as it now stands, which is the weaker argument and the true one. The inspector shows
document-supplied text in exactly **one** place, that button — and the tooltip beside it gave only the
file count, so the elided name was recoverable nowhere. That half was a defect on its own terms and
is fixed: the single-layer arm of `export_buttons`'s `on_hover_text` carries the full label now, and
only that arm, the other label being `Export 3 layers`, which the module wrote and which cannot
elide. **The answer is still no**, because one elided button label is not worth a resize handle when
the affordance that recovers it was already there and now names what it acts on.

Everything else that clips in the panel is text a **font** supplies. There is exactly one truncating
label — the variable-font axis name in `typography::axis_row`, which carries the full name, the tag
and a sign hint on `.on_hover_text` immediately beside it. Production `opsz_row` draws no label at
all, the section's own heading naming the axis; and the layer name in `inspector_header` is a
`TextEdit` on a fixed `desired_width(140.0)`, which scrolls rather than clips and which a wider
column would not touch without editing that constant.

**The cost side, which the roadmap had recorded honestly and which should not go with the bullet.**
The inspector is not a panel: it is an `egui::Area` of independent floating cards drawn *after* the
canvas, deliberately (§9.2), so there is **no edge for a handle to live on**. And
`app::inspector_panel` re-establishes the column rect explicitly rather than inheriting it — the
`max_rect`-against-`ScrollArea` trap §9.2 documents — so a user-set width would have to become an
*input* to that rather than something the layout discovers. Several hard-coded field splits would
then meet a number they have never seen: `POPOVER_W` at 272 across seven call sites, and the 74/1fr
rows (`export::SCALE_W`, `typography::AXIS_FIELD_W`). Expensive half, smaller benefit.

⚠️ **What would reopen it, stated so the next reader can test the premise rather than re-argue the
conclusion.** The asymmetry holds only while the inspector shows no *document*-supplied text — and
that is now one live instance rather than none. If a card ever displays a long layer name, a path's
data or a shared-style name, then for **that card** the width does become a function of the document
and the answer changes for it, though not necessarily for the column.

**D352 — The popular set is prefetched, on a lane of its own, because neither existing lane's rule
fits speculation. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; reviewed and accepted on the machine the same day —
"Both landed."; Keep.*** This is `roadmap.md`'s *"Prefetch the popular set, do not filter by it"*,
the last open item under *Web fonts and the font cache*, and it is what the rejected `Off | Popular |
All` middle setting was actually reaching for: `fonts::POPULAR`, fifty families, warmed once per
session so the picker is worth opening on a machine with no network. Nothing is hidden from anyone —
all 1,976 families are still listed — this only decides what is on disk early. **It narrows D83's
offline gap rather than closing it**, and D83 says by how much: every offline session after one
successful online one, never the genuinely first run, which has no catalog to warm from.

**The third lane is the decision; the list is the easy part.** `queue::Queue` grew a `prefetch` lane
and `push_prefetch`, and neither existing lane could have carried this. `urgent` would put a guess
about a session that has not happened ahead of a face the user is waiting on, which is the one thing
that must never happen. `preview` fails three separate ways and all three are worth writing down: it
is **LIFO**, so the editorial order of the list comes out backwards and the least-wanted of the
fifty arrives first; it is capped at `PREVIEW_BACKLOG` (48), so **two of the fifty are dropped
before a worker ever wakes**; and the rest are evicted by the first flung scrollbar, silently turning
the feature off for precisely the user who is browsing fonts. So the new lane is **FIFO, because the
order *is* the editorial judgement**, uncapped because the list is a fixed fifty pushed once, and
served after both others. `a_prefetch_is_served_last_and_in_the_order_it_was_listed` and
`a_burst_of_previews_does_not_evict_the_prefetch` are those two properties, and both fail if the
prefetch is routed through `push_preview` — which is the tempting way to avoid a third lane.

**`Lane` had to be separated from `Want`, which it used to be derived from.** `Want` says *how much
of a family* to fetch; `Lane` says *how badly it is wanted*. The prefetch is the case that pulls them
apart: it asks for `Want::Preview`'s single face exactly as a picker row does, and must be served
after every picker row. Deriving one from the other was correct only while there were two of each.
`FamilyState::lane` stores it so the variable-file retry in `poll` goes back down the same lane —
without that a prefetch's retry would be *promoted* into the picker's bounded LIFO, where it can
evict a row the user is looking at.

⚠️ **`Lane`'s `Default` is the weakest variant, and it has to be**, because it is the identity for the
`min` that promotes `FamilyState::lane`: a fresh state must not out-rank the request that created it.
It was `Preview` for its first few minutes, on the reasonable argument that it should match `Want`'s
default — and every prefetch then came out as `Preview`, since `Preview.min(Prefetch)` is `Preview`.
Caught by `a_warmed_family_takes_the_prefetch_lane_and_the_switch_refuses_it` on its first run and by
nothing else: the family is warmed either way, and the only symptom on a real machine is a picker
stuttering while fifty speculative downloads elbow into its bounded queue. Declaration order is
priority order and `Ord` is derived, so reordering the variants silently reverses the promotion.

**The list is editorial and there is no alternative to one.** The Fontsource endpoint carries eleven
keys, not one of them a rank, a count or a trend, and the order is alphabetical — checked against the
live endpoint rather than assumed, and recorded in full under **D330**, where it is the third reason
the `Off | Popular | All` middle tier was rejected and the reason this is a set and not a filter. So
"popular" is a judgement the app owns and it will go stale by itself. ⚠️ **A misspelling fails
completely silently**: `faces_of` finds no catalog entry, returns no specs, and that family is simply
never warmed. All fifty were checked against a real catalog of 1,976 Google families rather than
typed from memory, and `every_prefetched_family_is_spelled_the_way_the_catalog_spells_it` re-checks
them against the live endpoint — `#[ignore]`d beside the existing network test, and run. Re-run it
after editing the list: Fontsource does rename families, `Source Sans Pro` having become `Source Sans
3`. `Inter` is deliberately absent, core registering it itself.

**Two things it deliberately does not warm.** Families this machine already has installed: `faces_of`
resolves a system family to its local file first (§5.4a's resolution order), so warming one would
register a face the picker was never going to ask the network for, and the filter is on
`FaceSource::Web`. And anything at all while D330's switch is off — `prefetch_popular` fires from
`poll` on the frame `catalog_done` turns true, which is *also* true from the first frame of a session
launched with web fonts off, so the `web_fonts` guard rather than the timing is what refuses. It runs
after the catalog loop, because a web family's `FaceSpec` is built out of its `CatalogEntry` and
before the catalog lands this would be fifty no-ops.

⚠️ **One hole, stated rather than fixed.** Turning the switch off does not cancel warms already
queued, so up to fifty requests can still go out after the user has said no. Bounded and brief, but
it is a hole in D330's *off means no request leaves the machine*, and it is called out here rather
than closed because the fix wants `queue` to grow a drain operation nothing else needs.

🚨 **It was not *one*, and the count is what was wrong rather than the hole** (§15 D720). The catalog
thread was a second and the more visible one — talking to `api.fontsource.org` rather than to the
CDN, and writing `catalog.json` to the user's disk on the way back — and it is closed now, which
makes the paragraph above true again *by arithmetic*. So the claim is stated as a **rule** wherever
it is made: the hole is *requests already queued or already in flight when the switch is turned off*,
this warm is the queued case, and it is the only one left. **A count in prose is a gate nobody
built**; `grep -n 'agent' crates/ondin-app/src/fonts/mod.rs` is the enumeration.

*Flip-checks.* The lane flip — `Lane::Preview` in `prefetch_popular` — fails the lane assertion and
nothing else: the family is still warmed, still registered, still evictable. **The wrong lane is
invisible in every observable except that one**, which is this change's whole hazard in a sentence.
⚠️ **Two flips did not bite at first and both were coverage findings.** `FontService::inert`
pre-sets `prefetched: true`, so the once-only assertion was testing the constructor; the fixture
starts it at `false` now and asserts the *transition*. And the "installed family" fixture used an
**empty** `fontdb`, so `faces_of` answered nothing and the `FaceSource::Web` filter was never reached
— deleting the filter left the test green. It loads a real face off disk now and asserts the fixture
resolves to a `FaceSource::File` before testing the skip. ⚠️ `load_font_file`, **not**
`load_font_data`: the latter registers a `Source::Binary` and `system_faces` skips anything that is
not a `Source::File`, which is exactly what made the first version vacuous. `warm` takes the list as
an argument rather than reading `POPULAR` so that fixture is expressible at all.

**Declined, and it is recorded so it is not re-argued.** A second, complementary prefetch was offered
— the *first screenful alphabetically*, which needs no editorial list and can never go stale — and
the maintainer declined it on its merits: *"For the 'first screen alphabetically' prefetch that's not
necessary. The first screen loads very fast, even in a moderate connection. The first list of fonts
is usually not the ones most people do anyway."* Two reasons, both good: the load it optimises is not
slow, and the alphabetical head — *42dot Sans, ABeeZee, Abel* — is not what anyone wants. ⚠️ That
also **corrects the benefit the roadmap item claimed for itself**, which was "top of the list
populated instantly": the picker's list is a `BTreeSet` built in `rebuild_families`, so it is
strictly alphabetical and fifty popular families populate none of the visible top. The benefit that
survives, and the whole point of the feature, is *useful offline* and *the family you search for is
already there*.

**D353 — A pulsing dot says a picker row is still arriving. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; reviewed
and accepted on the machine the same day — "Dot loading indicator looks solid."; Keep.*** Reported
from the machine, and this is the ask in full: *"What we could do on the font dropdown, is show a
simple pulsating blue dot next to the font name while it's loading. So it's transparent. Right now
you load the font list, and you're not sure if the font you're seeing is loaded yet or not."* The
picker already said it and said it badly: a row whose face has not arrived draws its name in the UI
font at `theme::text::MUTED` (§9.2's *the preview declines rather than falling back*), which is a
real signal and an unreadable one — plenty of families resemble the UI font, and a *failed* row looks
identical to a *pending* one. The dot is drawn at the row's right edge whenever
`FontService::is_loading` is true, which is the second half of the same sentence: the fallback says
*we cannot draw this yet*, the dot says *and something is being done about it*.

**Five small decisions, each of which is a visible defect if taken the other way.** The room is
reserved on **every** row, lit or not (`LOADING_DOT_SLOT`, 14pt): taking it only while loading
reflows the name at the exact moment its face arrives, so a list of 1,976 rows settling after a
scroll twitches once per row. It is a **pulse rather than a spinner**, because up to twenty are on
screen at once during a scroll and twenty spinners is a fairground. It is a **raised cosine rather
than `sin`**, so every dot starts at the trough — `t` is wall-clock rather than per-row, so a shape
that does not start at zero would have each row appear at a different brightness as it scrolls in.
It is **never fully dark** (alpha floors at 90/255), or twenty rows blink in and out and the list
strobes. And `paint_loading_dot` calls `request_repaint`, because the app repaints reactively and
without it the dot freezes at whatever phase the last input left — a static dot saying the opposite
of what it is for.

**`loading_dot_phase(t)` is split out from the painting**, `tools::resized_box`'s division, because
*the pulse is the one part of a drawing a still frame cannot show*: what has to be right is that it
moves and moves smoothly, which is a claim about a function of time rather than about any frame's
shapes. Placement and ink are one `circle_filled` and are checked by eye.

*Flip-checks, and the correction is the useful part.* Plain `sin` was predicted to fail the "starts
dark" assertion and fails the **crest** one instead — `sin(0)` really is 0, so both shapes start dark
and it is the peak, a quarter of the way through rather than at the half, that separates them.
`sin().abs()`, the fix somebody reaches for next to stop the phase going negative, passes both and
fails the *seam* test at 0.0872 per frame, folding the negative half doubling the rate. **Three
spellings, three different assertions; no single test pins the shape**, which is worth knowing before
deleting one of them. ⚠️ The seam bound is **derived, not picked**: `phase = (1 − cos(2πt/P))/2`
differentiates to `(π/P)·sin(…)`, so by the mean value theorem no 1/60s step can exceed `(π/P)/60`.
It was written as a round `3.0/P` first and **failed against correct code** at t=0.267 — 0.0426
against a bound of 0.0417 — which is worth knowing before reading a failure there as a flicker.

**D354 — A preview the backlog dropped was claimed for ever. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-25;
Resolved.*** A live bug, older than D352 and D353 both, and found only because D353 drew the value.
`queue::Queue::push_preview` has always dropped from `preview`'s oldest end once the backlog exceeds
`PREVIEW_BACKLOG` — deliberately, and the lane's own module doc explains why. What nobody accounted
for is that **a dropped job never reports**, so its key stayed in `FontService::claimed` and its
family's `outstanding` stayed at 1 for the rest of the session. Two consequences and the second is
the bad one: the family reads as permanently loading, and because `ensure` filters out specs already
in `claimed`, **its face can never be requested again** — one flung scrollbar left those rows
unpreviewable until the app was restarted. `push_preview` returns what it pushed out and `ensure`
hands it to the new `FontService::release`.

⚠️ **Released, not failed, and the difference decides what the picker says.** `FamilyState::failed`
is what `status_of` reads to call a family `Missing`; a job that was never attempted is not a missing
font, and counting it would put §5.4a's warning glyph on a family that is perfectly fine — the exact
conclusion §15 D227 exists to prevent. The two spellings are one line apart in `poll`, so
`a_preview_dropped_by_the_backlog_can_be_asked_for_again` asserts `failed == 0` explicitly alongside
the re-request. Flipping it — discarding `push_preview`'s return value — fails on the first
assertion, the family still claimed and still loading.

**The lesson worth keeping** is not about the queue. The bug was invisible for as long as nothing
displayed the value, and adding a visible state to a value nothing was drawing is what exposed it:
*a bound that discards work has to tell the bookkeeping it did.*

**D355 — Text baselines are snap targets, and are drawn. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; Keep.***
Closes `roadmap.md`'s *Baselines as first-class snap targets*, and the first thing to say about it is
that **the roadmap entry's central premise was wrong**. It read: *"`Glyph.y` already sits on the
baseline (its own doc says so), so the data is in the layout cache and nothing has to be re-shaped to
read it."* The doc comment does say that, and `text.rs`'s own layout builder contradicts it — a run
carrying a `baseline_shift` has its glyphs deliberately placed **off** the line's baseline, because
the shift is *"a draw offset, not a metric, so the line box does not grow and neighbouring baselines
stay aligned"*. So deriving baselines from the glyphs invents one per superscript. Measured rather
than argued: the flip-check fills `baselines` from `runs.flat_map(|r| r.glyphs).map(|g| g.y)`, sorted
and deduplicated, exactly as the roadmap described, and for a two-line node returns
**`[17.0, 29.0, 37.0]`** — 17 and 37 real, **29 the superscript `2` lifted eight points off the
second line**, reported with precisely the confidence of the other two. A snap target there pulls a
shape onto a line that does not exist. `text::tests::every_line_has_one_baseline_and_a_shifted_run_does_not_add_another`
pins it, and ⚠️ its fixture puts the shift on the **second** line of two on purpose, so the phantom
lands *between* the real baselines rather than at an end, where a `len()` check alone might still
look right.

The true value was being computed in `extract` and thrown away. `TextLayout::baselines` is a
`Vec<f64>`, text-local, top to bottom, filled in that function's **existing** per-line loop from the
same `ymap.to_local(line.metrics().baseline)` the list-marker walk already computed — asked one level
finer rather than by a second walk, which is what makes the whole feature cost nothing. ⚠️ **Not
`text::export_lines`**, the door that looks more convenient: it also reports a per-line baseline, and
it takes a `TextRef` rather than a layout, re-shapes through parley and allocates a
`Vec<ExportLine>` with every run and its `String` — on every frame of a drag. Its own doc says it is
for the exporters. Obeying the roadmap's own warning about that trap is the one part of the entry
that survived intact. On the app side: `canvas::baseline_lines` gathers them in world space off the
cached layout, `snap::Snapping::baselines` is a new y-only source, `snap::Matched::Baseline(f64)`
carries the matched coordinate, `canvas::draw_text_baselines` is the overlay, and
`ViewSwitch::SnapBaselines` with `OndinApp::snap_baselines` is the switch.

**Its own switch, not a refinement of *Snap to shapes*.** Every line of every text node in view is a
candidate, so on a page of copy this is an order of magnitude more magnetism than the other three
sources together, and someone who wants edges and centres without it needs a way to say so. On by
default — the feature is pointless off, and the switch is how we find out whether it is noise.
**Deliberately unbound**: no app has this, so there is no convention to match and no chord worth
spending, where the other three earned theirs by being Illustrator's. Fourth in `SNAP_MENU`, so it
reads as the addition it is rather than displacing a row whose position someone already knows.

**A y-only source rather than more `guides.y`**, though the shape is identical, because the two part
company downstream. A ruler guide is *already a drawn line*, so a match on one deliberately draws no
mark; a baseline is invisible unless its own node is selected, and the node being snapped to is by
definition not the one being dragged. So `Matched::Baseline` draws a mark where `Matched::RulerGuide`
does not, spanning the moving box alone — there is no target rect to reach towards, and a mark
stretched to the text node's bounds would point at the wrong edge of it. It carries the matched `f64`
rather than re-deriving the feature the way `Matched::Node` does with `nearest_of`: a rect has three
features per axis and the winner has to be recovered, where a baseline *is* the coordinate.

⚠️ **A deliberate asymmetry: a rotated text node shows its baselines and cannot be snapped to them.**
`draw_text_baselines` transforms two points and draws the segment between them, which stays true at
any angle. `baseline_lines` refuses anything whose world transform has non-zero off-diagonal terms,
because a snap target has to be one axis-aligned coordinate and a slanted baseline has no honest one
— offering the transformed y would snap a box to a number that lies on the baseline at exactly one
point and nowhere the user is looking. It is the argument `rulers::upright` makes about a guide in a
rotated frame, spelled differently — an off-diagonal test on `Affine::as_coeffs` rather than an
orientation decomposition, which means it also admits a **half-turn**, whose baselines really are
still horizontal. Visible-but-unsnappable is the better way round for a gap; the real fix
is a slanted snap target, which nothing in `snap.rs` can express. **The gathering half is pinned** —
`a_rotated_or_hidden_text_node_offers_no_baselines_but_a_half_turn_does` asserts the 45° refusal, the
half-turn *acceptance* and the hidden-node skip, and
`the_moving_node_is_excluded_from_its_own_baselines` asserts the exclusion without which a text node
snaps to itself and never moves; dropping the rotation guard fails on the 45° case and dropping the
visibility guard on the hidden one. Making the half-turn an assertion rather than a comment is what
stops the predicate being "simplified" into `rulers::upright`, which would refuse it. ⚠️ **The
gathering half was pinned and the exclusion was still half a rule** — the rotation and visibility test
passes `&[]` throughout and the one test that passes a non-empty `moving` passes the *node itself*, so
nothing here exercised a **containing** node, and a group went on being offered the baselines of the
text inside it until 2026-09-07 (D468). ⚠️ Two things
in this paragraph are still held up by reading alone: the `SNAP_TARGET_LIMIT` cap, and the *drawing*
half of the asymmetry — that a rotated node goes on **showing** its baselines is a claim about the
overlay rather than about the gatherer, and no test makes it.

**Drawn solid where the untrimmed line box beside it is dashed.** The dash means *notional* — a box
that was taken away, carried on past where it stops mattering — and a baseline is the opposite: the
line the type actually sits on. Same `SELECT_DIM`, so neither competes with the tight box the handles
are on; drawn after the line box and before the outline, so the hairlines sit on top of the dashed
box they are inside and under the box that carries the handles. The overlay is gated on the same
switch as the snapping — one switch, one feature — and it matters more here than in `snap.rs`,
because a forty-line paragraph draws forty lines and whoever finds that noisy will reach for the
switch named after it.

⚠️ **The precedence flip-checks are the part most worth recording, and two of them did not bite.**
The rule is that a ruler guide the user placed wins a dead heat against a baseline they did not. That
was documented as enforced by the baseline block sitting *before* the guide block in `snap_rect`; it
is not. Moving the block below the guide one changes no test, and neither does flipping the
baseline's tie flag on its own. The dead heat is settled by the **pair** — guides tie (`true`),
baselines do not (`false`) — and that combination holds in *either* order: baselines first and the
guide equals and takes it; guides first and the baseline cannot beat, so the guide keeps it. **Only
both changes together** hand the tie to the baseline, and then
`a_ruler_guide_takes_a_tie_against_a_baseline` fails on its first assertion at `y: 3.0` where `-3.0`
is due. So the property is over-determined: robust, and with neither mechanism individually pinned.
The call-site comment now says the flag is the rule and the position is convention. That search did
find where the flag alone is load-bearing — **against node edges**, where nodes are always considered
first and also do not tie, so there is no second mechanism propping it up. There is an assertion for
that case now, and flipping the flag alone bites there and nowhere else.

The other flips all bit at the predicted assertion, which is worth saying because they so often do
not. Drawing the mark at `snapped.min_y()` instead of the matched baseline fails the **centre** case
at 475 against 500 — the edge case passes, which is exactly why the centre one is in the test.
Offering baselines to `best_x` fails `a_baseline_never_claims_the_horizontal_axis`. Dropping the
overlay's switch guard fails the third assertion of
`a_selected_text_node_draws_one_hairline_per_baseline`. And drawing the overlay at the box top
collapses three hairlines onto one y and fails the **distinct** count, which is why that is asserted
rather than the length.

⚠️ **A count in a doc comment is a fact that goes stale on the next row with nothing failing**, and
one row here staled six of them. Four across `canvas.rs` and `snap.rs` asserted the Snap menu has
"three switches" or "three toggles" as plain fact and went off by one; they say "its own switches"
without a number now. Two more were found only by reading the neighbourhood a second time —
`canvas.rs`'s `snapping`, which opened *"Three switches and no fourth"* and now says **"the menu is
the only way to switch snapping off, and no modifier is a second one"** (the "no fourth" was about
there being no *modifier* route, never about the row count, so de-numbering it kept the whole
point), and `snap::Snapping::none`'s *"all-three-off state … three empty sources"*, now
"everything-off state … empty sources". `architecture.md` carried the same sentence with **three**
counts in it and was rewritten the same way. The sixth is the one that generalises the lesson past
this menu: §9.4's *"eight of the nine switches default on"* counts `ViewSwitch` variants rather than
Snap rows, in another file and another unit, and a sweep grepping for the word "three" would never
have reached it. **`input.rs`'s *"the three snapping switches"* is the exemption** and must not be
swept with them — it is specifically about the chord-bound set, still three because baselines is
unbound.

**D356 — Skip-ink is built, and it is an interval in the layout rather than a boolean at the render
boundary. *Built and tested 2026-08-25; not yet reviewed on screen.*** Closes `roadmap.md`'s
*Decoration skip-ink*, and reverses the half of D281 that was waiting for exactly this. An underline
now breaks around the glyph ink it crosses — CSS's `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto`, which is what
every browser draws and what the canvas said out loud that it did not do. `DecorationInk::gaps` is a
sorted, merged list of `x0..x1` pairs inside the band; `text::skip_ink` fills it in `extract`, after
the run walk, from the glyph outlines; `scene::decoration_path` subtracts them.

**The roadmap entry asked one question and this is the answer to it.** It said the cost was not the
issue and *"what is unanswered is not the cost, it is where the subtracted band is computed and
cached"*, and it proposed `boolean::evaluate(Subtract, &[band, glyphs])` sitting in a new resolved
product beside the boolean cache. That mechanism **subtracts from the wrong shape.** The four line
styles are built at the render boundary (§6.3), so the only band that exists in core is the plain
rectangle: a path handed up from the layout is unstyled, and a path cut down there would be cutting one
whose dash phase and wave crests are already baked — which puts a `flo_curves` fold inside a
`catch_unwind` on the frame path, per underlined node, where nothing else in the codebase runs one
uncached (`Resolved::boolean`, `renderer::reevaluate_booleans`). An **interval** has neither problem.
"The ink is here along the band" is true of a solid rule, a dotted one and a ribbon alike, so it can be
computed once, in the layout, and still leave the pattern to be built where §6.3 says it belongs. And
it needs no new cache and no new invalidation: a `TextLayout` *is* the dirty-set-invalidated product
the work wanted, which is the whole of what the entry thought was a larger piece of work.

**Underlines only, which is css-text-decor-4's rule and not a simplification.** A `line-through` is
meant to cross the letters, so a strikethrough's gaps stay empty. The geometry cannot tell the two
apart — a strikethrough over a superscript sits exactly where an underline over the run below it would
— so `skip_ink` is handed the *indices* of the bands that skip, which only `extract`'s two calls know.
⚠️ Flipped by pushing the strikethrough's index in beside the underline's: six gaps over five letters,
the `s` alone breaking its band twice, which is what that "improvement" would draw.

**The clearance is horizontal and the vertical test is the ink as drawn**, which is the one judgement
call here. Padding the band vertically as well is the obvious spelling, and what it spends is the clear
air between the underline and the *overshoot* of a round letter. Measured on Inter and proportional, so
the type size drops out: that air is **1.31 thicknesses**. So a whole thickness of padding survives
this face and 1.4 of it breaks the rule under every `o` and `a`
