(`[(6.4, 15.5), (82.6, 89.9)]` for `onmax`) — and a face whose `underlinePosition` is half as deep has
half the air. ⚠️ **The flip at 1.0 does not bite, and that is why the margin is asserted rather than the
rule**: `an_underline_with_nothing_in_its_way_is_one_unbroken_bar` pins 1.31, so the next reader who
reaches for vertical padding is told what it costs instead of being told not to.

**A wavy underline is measured against its crests, not its band** — the one number in core that belongs
to the render boundary. `scene::wave` swings a thickness either side of the band's middle and is half a
thickness thick, so its ink reaches `1.5t` where the band reaches `0.5t`; gaps cut for the band alone
would let a crest run straight through the descender they were cut for. It is stated in both places and
`scene::tests::a_wavy_ribbon_stays_inside_the_reach_core_assumes` asserts the ribbon's bounds **tight in
both directions**, so neither side can drift: reaching less makes core's gaps too wide, reaching more
makes them too narrow.

⚠️ **The first version cost six times the rest of the layout, and the fix was structural both times.**
Measured on an 816-glyph paragraph, release, whole `layout()` calls, milliseconds — the same text on one
line (1 band) and wrapped to 300 (24 bands):

| | 1 band | 24 bands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no underline at all | 0.25 | 0.26 |
| outline per glyph *occurrence* | 1.87 | 1.77 |
| memoized, no per-glyph box reject | 0.32 | 0.72 |
| as built | 0.32 | 0.36 |

It was not the flattening; it was the same work done over and over, twice over. Eight hundred letters
are about thirty *different* ones, so the ink is memoized per (face, instance, size, glyph) and placed
by adding the pen position — which is why `GlyphInk` is glyph-local, and worth 1.87 → 0.32. And a band
rejects a glyph on its bounding box before reading an edge, which is worth nothing on one band and
0.72 → 0.36 on twenty-four: without it the per-band pass multiplies by the node, and a fully underlined
page is the case that hurts. `text::outline`'s per-run setup came out into `RunFace` so both callers
share one face, one instance and one closing rule. **"It rides the relayout" was an assumption until it
was measured**, and the naive version was the version the roadmap entry described.

**The three debts the roadmap predicted all came due, and the third is the one that mattered.** The SVG
writer now says **nothing** about skip-ink: CSS's initial value is the behaviour, so the silence D281
called a lie is the accurate statement, and writing anything would be the noise `text-decoration-style`'s
`solid` is. `an_exported_underline_says_it_does_not_skip_ink` went red exactly as designed and is now
`an_exported_underline_leaves_skip_ink_to_its_initial_value`, three arms inverted, each still asserting
its fixture reached the decoration path — an absence is also what a misspelled attribute looks like.
⚠️ **The two implementations agree in kind, not in pixels**: ours breaks where a contour really crosses,
widened by a thickness; a browser's `auto` is its own geometry. That is a fraction of a letter where
`none` was the whole gap. If it ever has to be exact, the answer is writing the band as a `<path>` from
`gaps` and losing the `text-decoration-*` family with it (D112's trade, one level up). D281's
⚠️ note about the family being one question for all four is kept, minus the fourth.

⚠️ **Two flip-checks did not bite and both are findings.** Taking each edge's *whole* x range instead of
only the part inside the band's rows — the correctness `crossings` spends four lines on — moves `g` from
0.03 to 0.00 and `y` from 0.353 to 0.347 and changes nothing else, because flattening at an eighth of a
unit leaves edges too short for the clip to have much to remove; what it buys is that the answer does
not depend on the tolerance, which is worth keeping and is *not* what the test proves. And dropping the
`ClosePath` arm that emits a contour's closing edge changes not one number: of the seven contours in
`gypsy` exactly one leaves a non-degenerate closing edge, and its x range is inside a gap other edges
had already opened. Inter is a `glyf` face and TrueType contours are cyclic, so **no bundled font can
test that arm** — it is there for a CFF face, where the close really is implicit.

⚠️ **And a third: the two vertical rejects are redundant for correctness.** Dropping the box reject's
`y` half leaves `each_line_of_a_wrapped_paragraph_breaks_on_its_own_descenders` green, because the
per-edge test catches the other lines one level down; disabling the per-edge test alone leaves it green
too, because the box reject caught the glyph before its edges were read. Only both together lose the
first band its whole width — `293.8 of 293.8`. So that property is over-determined, like D355's tie
rule, and only one of the pair is redundant for *speed*.

**A bar shorter than the band is thick is not a bar, and is dropped** — asked for the same day, once the
edge was reported. A gap clamps to the band, so a word that *opens* with a descender leaves a sliver of
rule before it and two adjacent descenders leave one between them: `gypsy` at 40px came to five bars
`0.18, 0.51, 7.23, 32.39, 7.50` units wide against a thickness of 2.73, and the first two read as dirt.
`scene::kept_spans` now drops any fragment shorter than the band's own thickness, which is the same
decision as **merging the two gaps either side of it** — the two readings the report offered turned out
to be one operation, so there was nothing to choose. The threshold is the thickness rather than a tuned
number, so it holds at every type size and zoom, and it is applied to skip-ink's fragments and not to
the finished bars, so a dotted band — whose dots are exactly one thickness wide — is untouched. The
end-to-end test asserts **every bar clears the thickness** rather than the count, because the count is
what a differently-tuned clearance would move and the rule is not. ⚠️ Both flips bite: without the
`retain`, `gypsy` is four bars with an extra `(18.0, 19.5)`; at twice the thickness the legitimate
3-wide bar goes too.

**And then the order was wrong, which took three goes to see.** The slivers fix had a measured cost: at
40px `ggg`, `jjj` and `gg` came back with **no bars at all**, and a lone `j` had been blank since the day
skip-ink landed. The ask was "cut the clearance for narrow bands"; the answer went through three shapes
before it stopped popping.

⚠️ **First shape — three tiers, and the stated cause was right without being the whole of it.** Clearance
and speck rule as normal, then no clearance, then keep-the-widest-anyway, each conditioned on *the band
would otherwise show nothing*. Cutting the clearance alone does **not** save a lone `j`: at zero
clearance its bearings measure `2.04` and `2.60` and both are under the thickness, so the speck rule
erases them next — hence a third tier. It worked, and it still popped: `g` lost one of its two marks at
15 and 16pt as a bearing crossed the threshold.

⚠️ **Second shape — move the threshold off the coincidence, which moved the pop instead of removing it.**
An underlined `g`'s side bearing in Inter is **1.02–1.06 thicknesses** at most sizes, so a threshold of
one thickness sat exactly on top of the commonest case. The measured distribution at 40px falls in two
clumps — dirt at `0.07t` and `0.19t`, real bearings from `0.75t` to `1.23t` — so the threshold went to
half a thickness, and a *second* rule closed the fragments that a half could no longer reach: **a
fragment inside one letter's own ink box is a hole in the letter**, not a piece of underline, whatever
its width (the band showing through the loop of a `g`). Both rules are worth keeping. Neither fixed the
pop: it moved to **24pt**.

**Third shape, and the one that holds: decide the structure first, give the air second.** The bug was
never the threshold's value, it was that a bar's width was `bearing − clearance` — so *any* minimum has a
type size where a bar crosses it. `crossings` now settles which fragments are rules with **no clearance
at all**, and `give_air` then grows each gap by up to a thickness a side, **taking only what the bar
beside it can spare above a floor of one thickness**. Nothing that exists can be taken away by air.
An underlined `g` keeps two marks of `1.00t` at every size from 6pt to 400; a lone `j` keeps one of
`0.95t`; `page` keeps `0.90t, 12.86t, 8.07t`, the long bars untouched because a long bar can spare the
whole clearance. **The user's own sentence survives, one level in:** "a bar shorter than the band is
thick is not a bar" is now the limit on what air may take, not a veto on what exists.

⚠️ **A bar already narrower than the floor gets no air rather than being padded out to it** — `page`'s
leading `0.90t` and the `j`'s `0.95t` are their own raw bearings, untouched. The floor limits
subtraction; it does not add.

⚠️ **The speck rule moved from `scene::kept_spans` into core with this**, one commit after it was written
there. A back-off that has to know whether a rule two crates away would empty the band is the gate
written down twice this project keeps paying for (D302's lesson in a third shape), so `DecorationInk::gaps`
is now the *final* answer about where a band is interrupted and `kept_spans` is a plain complement. The
scene test that held the rule became `a_sliver_is_drawn_because_the_judgement_is_cores`, which asserts
the boundary instead — a sliver handed in is drawn, and flipping the `retain` back in is the symptom to
look for if a narrow band ever loses its rule again.

⚠️ **A stem's crossing was never measured, and the clearance was hiding it.** Chasing the pop turned up a
real defect underneath: crossings were the union of each *edge's* x-extent inside the band, and a `p`'s
descender is bounded by two **vertical** edges whose x-extent is zero — so the ink between them was never
measured at all. It looked right only because dilating each edge by a thickness made the two zero-width
spans overlap and cover the stem by accident. The moment the structure began to be decided at zero
clearance, every `p` in the document stopped breaking its underline. `raw_crossings` now takes **three
scanlines** through the band and pairs the crossings, which is the filled ink, and keeps the edge extents
on top to catch a thin feature that slips between the rows. The other half of the old bug — a stem
*wider* than twice the clearance, which would have had the rule drawn through its middle — **is not
reachable with Inter at any weight** (22.1 units of stem against a 50.8-unit dilation at 200px, weight
900), so it is recorded rather than tested. Cost: 0.02–0.04ms on the table above, because the per-glyph
box reject means almost no glyph reaches the scanlines.

⚠️ **Scale-invariance was claimed three times and is only now true, for a different reason than argued.**
The first two claims reasoned that every quantity compared is linear in the type size; parley rounds
glyph advances *and* Inter's `opsz` axis changes the letterform outright — a lone `j`'s raw bearing runs
from about 2.0 thicknesses at 6pt to 1.07 at 400. What makes the *drawing* steady is not the geometry but
the **floor**: air stops being taken at one thickness, so the mark measures 1.00t from 6pt to 24pt and
0.94–0.95t above, the second range being where the raw bearing has itself fallen below the floor. A width
steady *because a rule holds it there* is a different claim from one steady because the inputs are
proportional, and it survives a face whose bearings behave nothing like Inter's.

⚠️ **`jjj`'s bar count has been wrong in a comment twice, in both directions** — one under
keep-the-widest, three now that air cannot erase a fragment. Both were guesses from symmetry with `ggg`.

⚠️ **Strict containment of the solid gaps by the wavy ones stopped being true**, and the reason is worth
more than the assertion was: air is now rationed by the bar it eats into, and a wavy band's crossings are
taller and therefore wider, so its bars are narrower and can spare *less* air. The wavy gap answering the
solid `23.62..35.59` starts at `23.99`. The test asserts overlap and a bigger total instead.

⚠️ **A predicted flip site was wrong three times running, always the same way.** Each time the
*interesting* word was going to catch a change to the air and the **plain** one caught it first: `page`
fails before `gypsy` under no-clearance, and `page` fails before `g` under no-floor, because losing air
widens every surviving bar before it changes any count. Filed rather than re-learnt — *put the boring
fixture first and expect it to be the one that fails.*

**One stale sentence found on the way**, in `architecture.md`'s *Deferred* list: it named "lists,
hyphenation, and decoration skip-ink" as the paragraph-layout dependants not built, and lists have been
built since D169 and D172. Hyphenation is the only one of the three left, and it still needs a
dictionary crate — ⚠️ **re-derived 2026-09-01: it does not, and that clause was the stale sentence's
own successor.** The crate exists on crates.io, parley already breaks at `U+00AD`, and the real price
is an offset map and a two-pass line break; see **D399**, which is where that price was taken to the
maintainer the same day and declined, making hyphenation a non-goal rather than open work. *The finding above stands
as what was believed on 2026-08-25* — what is worth noticing is that a sweep for a stale sentence
replaced it with a sentence that went stale the same way. `DecorationInk` also lost its `Copy` to the new `Vec`; nothing outside `text.rs` ever
held one by value, so the whole price was two derives.

**D357 — Skip-ink is a setting, not a law, and the toggle is one icon button beside the line style.
*Built and tested 2026-08-25; not yet reviewed on screen.*** Asked for the day after D356 landed:
*"let's make the skip-ink feature a toggle into the Typography popup, Character panel. An icon button
next to the underline stroke type."* `Decoration::skip_ink` is a `bool` defaulting to **on**, which is
CSS's initial value and what D356 built; the panel's Decoration section grows a `field_button` on the
line-style row, and `text::skip_ink` never sees a band that has opted out.

**The flag is applied by not listing the band.** D356's own design already handed `skip_ink` the
*indices* of the bands that skip — because the geometry cannot tell an underline from a strikethrough —
so the toggle needed no new mechanism at all: `extract` pushes the index only when the run's resolved
underline says so, and a band that never reaches the list keeps the empty `gaps` every band is built
with. Nothing downstream reads a second flag, and the outlining pass is **skipped along with it**, so a
node asking for a continuous rule pays none of the cost measured in that entry.

**It is read for underlines only, so the button is absent on a strikethrough rather than disabled.** A
`line-through` is meant to cross the letters (css-text-decor-4) and `skip_ink` is not consulted for one;
a control whose state changed nothing would be worse than no control, so the dropdown takes the whole
card width back and the model field sits there unread. The toggle is **lit in its default state**, which
is unusual in this chrome and is the honest reading — the button reports what the line is doing, the way
`TEXT_BOLD` does, and the alternative lights a button beside a *continuous* rule and darkens it beside a
broken one, which is the state backwards.

**`Decoration` loses its derived `Default` to this**, since `skip_ink`'s default is not the zero value
and every `..Decoration::default()` in the workspace had to keep meaning what it meant; `serde`'s
`default = "skips_ink"` plus `skip_serializing_if` keeps the field out of the file in the ordinary case
and gives every document written before today the drawing it was saved with.

**D281's attribute is back, conditionally**, which is the third state of that sentence in five days:
written unconditionally from 2026-08-21 because the canvas did not skip, deleted at D356 because it did,
and now written for exactly the runs that have asked for a continuous bar. It is taken off the
underline alone and **not** through `agreed` — skip-ink is not one of the three element-scoped
`text-decoration-*` properties, and a strikethrough sharing the element has no opinion to disagree with.
⚠️ **`none` is the value that round-trips exactly.** Two `auto` implementations gap in nearly the same
places; a continuous band is a continuous band in every renderer, so the setting nobody will reach for
is the one the SVG reproduces perfectly.

⚠️ **The icon was read out of the font atlas before it was named**, against five alternatives, because
Phosphor draws nothing that means "a rule stepping around a descender". `LINK_SIMPLE_HORIZONTAL_BREAK`
(U+E2EC) is two chain ends facing each other across a gap on one horizontal axis — the only *horizontal*
break in the set, and unclaimed, where the diagonal `LINK_SIMPLE_BREAK` already means the Transform
panel's proportion lock. `theme.rs`'s catalogue test then proves the codepoint carries ink; what it
cannot prove is that it is the *right* picture, which is why the reading is recorded beside it.

⚠️ **The per-node fixture cannot tell the two implementations apart and the per-span one can.** Reading
the flag off `parts.style` instead of the run's resolved style — the slip the call site invites, both
being in scope on that line — leaves the whole-node test green, because that test sets the flag *on the
node's own default*. It fails only on the arm where a span over `gy` opts out while the node default
skips. The second flip site was predicted wrongly first, as the control.

⚠️ **A ground read on the frame the click lands on is last frame's state.** The panel test compares the
button's ground lit against dark to prove the toggle is visible at all, and its first version read both
on the click frames: `#212C46` twice, with the document already changed underneath. `TypeSubject` is
read before the UI runs, so the state is sampled on the frame *after* each click, with the pointer
resting in the same place both times so the hover treatment is not the difference. This is §15 D96's
lesson in a second shape — *pump a frame past the change before believing what was painted.*

**D255 — *Add point here*, and the group it is filed under decides a hairline rather than the order.
*Built and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** `context-menus.md` §6.5's first row, which §9.1
scored as *wiring only* — and that was right. The verb is `insert_point`, the same one the pen bias's
`PenVerb::Insert` and the node tool's double-click already reach; what a menu adds is nothing about
the edit and everything about *which* point on the ink, which is why the row carries no accelerator
and never will (D215).

**The gate and the verb ask one query.** `OndinApp::segment_at` is new and is four lines: it wraps
`node_grab` and answers `Some` only for `NodeGrab::Segment`. That is **D116's pairing rule reaching a
menu instead of a cursor** — one function behind both halves, so the row is dim exactly when taking it
would insert nothing, rather than dim when a second approximation of that says so. The *refusals* come
with it: `node_grab` tries handles, anchors and the point box **before** the ink, so a right-click on
an existing anchor answers `None` and the row declines to stack a second point on top of the first.

**Filled from `open.world`, not from this frame's pointer.** A menu is rebuilt every frame it is up,
so a live read would let the row go dark under the hand as it travelled down the list — and the
position the verb acts on is the one the menu was aimed with. It dims rather than vanishing when the
click missed, which is §3's presence/availability split: kind decides presence and *state* decides
enabled, and where the right-click landed is state. The sentence is "Right-click on the path's outline
to add a point to it", and what that guards against is a menu changing length under the hand because
the aim was two pixels off the stroke.

**The part worth recording was found by flipping the test and not by reading it.** Filing the row
under `Group::Clipboard` beside *Delete points* — the obvious place, since both act on points —
**still** puts it first in the rendered menu, because `points_menu` emits it first and `build` keeps
the emitted order within a group. So the group choice decides only whether a **hairline** separates it
from *Delete points*, and `Group::Head` — a group of one, which is the shape §6.5's table asks for —
is what puts one there. The first assertion in
`add_point_here_leads_the_point_menu_and_dims_off_the_ink` had to be rewritten from `first() ==
AddPointHere`, which passes under both spellings and was a test about nothing, into an assertion on
the first *group*.

**D358 — Ondin has one unit and it is px. *Decided 2026-08-26; Keep.*** Closes `roadmap.md`'s *Next ·
Units* whole, and closes it as an **answer** rather than as a deferral, which is the only reason it is
safe to strike: the entry named mm/cm/in/pt as work not yet done, and they are work that will not be
done. Asked as a question rather than a task — *"does Ondin need units? This is a UI app, target is
desktop (web, native apps, etc), so what would units really solve here?"* — and the honest answer is
nothing this app has a use for.

**Three things a unit system buys, and none of the three lands here.** *Physical fidelity* is what
mm and in are for, and it needs a px-per-inch mapping the document does not carry — the entry's own
first question, and there is **no `dpi`, `ppi` or `pixels_per_inch` anywhere in `crates/`**, the three
matches for the word being winit's display scaling and unrelated. Nothing downstream would read one:
`--png` writes a pixel grid and `--svg` writes `width`/`height`/`viewBox` as bare numbers, which *is*
px by the SVG spec (`svg.rs`'s root element). *Platform vocabulary* is the one that sounds like it
applies — iOS pt, Android dp, CSS px — and it is a mirage, because at 1x all three are the same
number: switching a chip from `px` to `dp` would relabel the field and change nothing else, which is
a suffix rather than a unit. *Density* is the conversion a screen tool genuinely needs, and it belongs
to the **export** (@1x/@2x/@3x) rather than to any field.

**The tree had already half-decided this and nobody had written it down.** `expr.rs` says it outright
— *"a unit is noise, not a conversion"* — and its `UNITS` is a drop-list, built on the assumption that
there is nothing to convert. `Length` is `Px | Em` and `LengthUnit::Em`'s label is **`"%"`**, so even
the one non-px unit in the app is not spelled as a unit. And the reference for interaction has no unit
system at all: Figma does not, nor Sketch; mm, in and pt live in Illustrator, Affinity and InDesign,
which are the print-facing tools. This entry is therefore mostly a *record* of a decision the code was
already making — the state `roadmap.md`'s own §0 exists to prevent, and the same shape as D279.

**What the entry was actually complaining about is a label, not a unit**, and its own first sentence
says so: *"nothing anywhere that says what the numbers are."* That collapses the ten-readout, eight-path
list it had rotted through twice. The ruler ticks, the size badge, `measure::label`, the layers frame
badge and `copy_guides` need **nothing** — a ruler reading `0 100 200` is unambiguous once the app has
said px once, which is what Figma's does. The inspector fields would take a static `px` at most, and
the argument against even that is that it is the same word forty times for something learnt once. The
**dash pair**, singled out in that entry as the one consumer that would have to be decided twice
because it has a parser of its own, needs deciding zero times: its existing behaviour *is* px-only
behaviour.

**`context-menus.md` §6.6 is struck rather than filled.** It reserved the ruler as a right-click
target with nothing to put in it, explicitly *"blocked on units existing"* — and both Adobe apps do
put the unit menu there. With one unit there is no menu: a list whose only row is the unit you already
have is worse than no list, so the reservation goes and the ruler claims no region. Whoever wanted
that menu was getting it "almost free" only because the rows were going to be somebody else's work.

⚠️ **One thing reopens this, and it is not a UI feature: PDF or print output.** That makes a document
resolution real, and units follow it rather than lead it — and the reopening is much narrower than
"units", being `mm`/`in` for the *page* rather than a variant on every coordinate. The entry's own
third question is what keeps that cheap and stands whatever happens: geometry arithmetic is `f64` px
and a unit is a presentation choice at the edge, never a variant stored per coordinate. `Length::Em`
is the legitimate exception and stays one, because an em is relative to a font size that changes under
it where a millimetre is a fixed multiple of a px.

⚠️ **`50%` is not closed by this and never was a unit question.** It needs a *referent* — of the
parent, or of the current value — before it can mean anything, and until it has one the parser goes on
treating `%` as the noise a percentage field's own formatter writes. It survives in `vm.md`'s open
questions, where the same question is asked of `.width = 50%` and should be answered once for both.
The line in that file pointing at this section was rewritten to point here.

⚠️ **Export is still a consumer, and what it consumes is not this.** The entry closed with *"SVG can
carry real units and currently does not"* — correct, and now deliberate. And the density multiplier
this entry names as the conversion a screen tool actually needs is **already built**: `ExportScale` is
`Times(f32) | Width(u32) | Height(u32)`, the Export panel offers Figma's exact ladder
(0.5/0.75/1/1.5/2/3/4×) per row, `raster_of` takes it through `png::viewport_at`, and a second row
writes `Close@2x.png`. What is missing is only the **CLI**: `ondin export` calls `viewport_over`, which
is 1×, and has no flag to ask for anything else. That is a gap in one binary's argument parsing rather
than a feature, and it is raised separately.

**D359 — A unit a `Length` field is not showing is refused, rather than read as the other one. *Fixed
and tested 2026-08-26; Resolved.*** `expr::eval` drops a trailing `%`, `°`, `px`, `pt` or `em` and
lets the number through, which is right wherever there is only one unit the value could have been
written in — and the typography `Length` fields are the one place in the app where there are two.
`12px` typed into a field showing `%` read as **twelve percent**, silently, and `150%` typed into a
`px` field as a hundred and fifty px. Found while answering D358 and independent of it: the px/em pair
is inside typography and survives the px-only decision untouched.

**`expr::eval_in(text, Unit)` beside `eval`, and `Tok::Unit` now carries which unit was written.** A
`Written` tag (`Px | Pt | Em | Pct | Deg`) comes off the lexer, and `evaluate` rejects the whole
expression if any tag disagrees with the field. `eval` passes `None` and behaves exactly as it did, so
every geometry field is unchanged. The check runs **before the parse rather than inside `atom`**,
where the word has already been dropped: `12px * 2` in a `%` field has to fail as a whole rather than
as its first operand.

**`Pct` refuses `em`, which is the counter-intuitive half and the one that matters.** A percent field
*is* an em field, so letting `em` through looks obviously right — and it is wrong, because the digits
are percent-scaled: `1.5em` would land as 1.5%, a hundredth of what was typed. Taking it correctly
would mean multiplying by a hundred, and that is the conversion the unit chip exists for. `pt` and
`deg` are refused by both for the same reason, and go on being ignored by `eval` where there is no
second unit to confuse them with.

⚠️ **Four call sites, not the two the fields are named for.** `length_field` and
`optional_length_field` are the obvious pair; `OndinApp::length_char_field` and the character
line-height field build their `value_field_suffixed` inline and needed the same parser. ⚠️ **That
first name read `OndinApp::char_length` until 2026-09-15 and there has never been such a method**
(§15 D765) — the same phantom that carried `optional_length_field`'s whole argument for diverging on
the release frame. Found by grepping the *phrase* rather than the sites already corrected. All four rely on
`value_field_f64` setting `expr::eval` **before** calling the caller's `build` closure — documented
there as the thing that lets a field take its parser back — and on `DragValue::custom_parser` being
last-write-wins, which was read in egui 0.35's source rather than assumed.

⚠️ **The parser is tested and the wiring is read.** `a_unit_a_field_is_not_showing_is_refused_rather_
than_read_as_the_other` pins `eval_in` from both sides; that the four fields actually reach it is a
claim about four `build` closures, and driving text into a `DragValue` headlessly would prove it for
one of them at best. Stated rather than implied.

⚠️ **Both flips bit where they were predicted to, which is worth recording because that has not been
the pattern.** Letting `Pct` accept `Written::Em` — the version somebody would actually have written —
fails on the third assertion and nothing else, so that assertion carries the whole distinction;
`accepts` returning a bare `true` collapses `eval_in` into `eval` and fails on the first. The
"auto" faces of both optional fields parse in `Px` and are unreachable — zero-width scrub range, and
the write gated on `current` being `Some` — which is commented at each rather than papered over with a
third variant.

**D360 — `ondin export` takes `--scale`, which is the one export route that could not ask for a
density. *Built and tested 2026-08-26; Keep.*** The third thing to come out of D358 and the smallest.
D358 leans on the claim that the conversion a screen tool actually needs is the export multiplier
rather than a unit — and that multiplier has been built for as long as the Export panel has:
`ExportScale` is `Times(f32) | Width(u32) | Height(u32)`, `COMMON` is Figma's exact ladder
(0.5/0.75/1/1.5/2/3/4×), every panel row has its own combo, `raster_of` carries it through
`png::viewport_at`, and a second row writes `Close@2x.png`. `ondin export --all` has always honoured
it, because it runs the document's own specs through `plan`. **Only the ad-hoc `--png` path was
pinned**, at a `viewport_over(view)` call whose comment said *"frame the whole document at 1:1"* and
meant it.

⚠️ **This was raised as "there is no `--scale` and a PNG comes out at 1×", which was true and misleading
in the same sentence** — it reads as a missing feature and is a missing *flag*, on one binary's
argument parser, over machinery that was already there and already tested. Recorded because the shape
is this file's recurring one: a gap named from the outside of a subsystem tends to be scored as
absent when it is unreachable, and the fix was `viewport_over` → `viewport_at` plus a parse arm.

**Three rules, and each is a rule this command already had.** It is **refused rather than ignored**
where it cannot apply — on `--svg` and `--json`, and on `--all`, where every layer already carries its
own and accepting one would silently overrule the file. The message names the *rule* rather than the
flag (*"--scale is a pixel density, so it applies only to --png"*), because the commonest way to hit it
is to type no format at all and inherit the SVG default, and a message about `--svg` would then name a
flag the person never typed. The multiplier is **`Times` only**: pinning an axis earns its keep across
a *set* of differently-shaped layers, which is what `--all` runs, and this command renders one box. And
the derived output name is **not** decorated — `plan`'s `@2x` marker separates files written in one go,
and letting a flag rename this command's single output would make `-o` the only way to know where the
bytes went.

**A clamp is now reported.** `viewport_at` caps the *multiplier* rather than each side — the same
picture smaller beats the same picture squashed — and `plan` says what it clamped where this path said
nothing; a build script asking 8× on a poster and getting 3.4× had no way to notice. `clamp_note` is a
free function returning the sentence rather than one that prints it, so the decision is assertable
without capturing stderr.

⚠️ **`--scale 0` is rejected in the parser rather than left to `viewport_at`'s floor**, which exists to
keep the renderer safe and would have turned it into a one-pixel file nobody asked for. `nan`, `-2` and
anything unparseable go the same way.

⚠️ **The predicted flip site was wrong again, and wrong in the useful direction.** Pinning `run_export`
back to `viewport_over` was expected to fail on the 2× file being too small; it fails on `(32, 24)`
against `(64, 48)` with **both files identical**, which says the flag did nothing rather than that one
number was off — a strictly better failure, and one that would still bite if the 1× path broke too.
The refusal's flip bit as predicted and prints the wrong outcome verbatim: an `Export` command carrying
`format: Svg, scale: 2.0`.

⚠️ **A third flip did not bite at all, and that is the finding.** `clamp_note` compares on `>=` rather
than `==` to say that a result *bigger* than the arithmetic is not a clamp — `px` floors every side at
one pixel. Flipping it to `==` changed nothing: `px` takes `ceil` of the same positive product, and the
ceiling of a positive is never below 1, so `got` can never exceed `asked` and **no input can tell the
two spellings apart**. The `>=` is kept as the honest statement of intent and is now documented as an
unreachable branch rather than a tested one. The sub-pixel case in the test still pins something real —
that 0.01× is *silent* — just not the distinction it was written for.

⚠️ **And one assertion in that test was simply wrong when written**: `h * 2 == w` on a clamped 100×50
box fails at 65536 against 65535, because both sides are `ceil`ed independently after the single
multiplier is applied, so a half-pixel on the short side rounds up alone. Proportions are kept to
within a pixel, not exactly. Caught by running it, which is the argument for asserting the number
rather than describing it. ⚠️ **The two numbers in that sentence are past tense**: `MAX_RASTER_SIDE`
was `u16::MAX` when this was written and is `65408` since **D434**, so the live assertion now reads
`(65408, 32705)` and its bound is 2 rather than 1 — each side lands a hair over an exact integer
where one of the old pair landed on it. The *reason* is unchanged and is the whole of what this
paragraph is for; the pair of integers is evidence about a tree that has moved.

**D361 — The other two size questions reach the CLI, and `--all` gets an override instead of them.
*Built and tested 2026-08-26; Keep.*** D360 shipped `--scale` and named two things it had deliberately
left out; both were asked for the same day — *"let's do the width/height flags too. Also the
--scale-override."* So `ondin export --png` now takes **`--scale <n>` | `--width <px>` | `--height
<px>`**, which is `ExportScale`'s three variants and the panel's three questions, and `ondin export
--all` takes **`--scale-override <2x|512w|512h>`**, which forces every spec in the file to one size.

**D360's argument for leaving width and height out was right about the one-off and wrong about the
set.** It said pinning an axis earns its keep across a *set* of differently-shaped layers, which is what
`--all` runs, and this command renders one box — true as far as it goes, and it misses that `--width
512` on a single document is a perfectly ordinary thing to want from a build step that feeds a fixed
slot. The reasoning survives as the *shape* of this entry rather than as the exclusion it was: the
one-off spends three flags because it answers one question, and `--all` spends one because it answers
it for a whole set.

**`--scale-override` is a separate flag rather than `--all --scale`, because it does not mean what
`--scale` means anywhere else.** There, the flag *is* the size; here it **overrules** a size the
document already carries, and the file goes on deciding which layers export and at what formats. The
refusal for `--all --scale` therefore now names the flag that would have worked, which is the shape a
refusal should have when the thing wanted is coherent: *"--all takes its sizes from the document; use
--scale-override to force them all"*.

**It takes the export row's own vocabulary, read backwards.** `ExportScale::from_label` is the inverse
of `label()` — `2x`, `512w`, `512h` — so what a designer reads off a row is what a script types, and
one argument covers all three questions where the one-off spends three flags. A bare number means `x`,
the one spelling it adds, matching `--scale` next door. Placed beside `label` in core rather than in
the CLI so the two cannot drift, and the round trip over `COMMON` is the assertion that holds them
together: a hand-written table of strings would go on passing while `trim_zeros` changed under it.

**The override lives in `PlanOptions`, not in the caller, and it is where the interesting decision
is.** A scale is not only a size — it is half the *filename* through `ExportScale::marker` — so a
caller that forced the multiplier after planning would render at 1× under names still saying `@2x`.
One interpreter, which is `plan`'s whole premise.

**And overriding makes two rows the same row, so specs that become identical collapse to one file.** A
layer set up at 1×/2×/3× forced to 1× is one asset three times: without the collapse the de-collision
turns that into `Close.png`, `Close (2).png`, `Close (3).png` — slower than the fast pass being asked
for, and two files of junk. The dedupe runs **only** under an override, so an unforced plan is
byte-for-byte what it was. Forced first and deduplicated second, since the override is what makes the
specs equal; the other order would collapse a set that is still distinct.

⚠️ **The collapse is flip-checked and bites exactly where predicted** — dropping the dedupe leaves
`["Close (2).png", "Close.png", "Close.svg"]`, naming the junk file in the failure message. **The
pinned-axis assertion is flip-checked against `factor`'s `Width`/`Height` arms being exchanged** and
bites at `(128, 96)` against `(96, 72)`. That one only bites because the fixture is 32×24: on a square
fixture both spellings agree and the test would have been about nothing, which is worth stating because
a square icon is the obvious thing to reach for. And **`from_label`'s bare-number arm is flip-checked
separately**, because the `COMMON` round trip has no teeth for it — `label` never writes a bare number,
so only the explicit line beside it is load-bearing.

⚠️ **An SVG spec is overridden too, and it costs nothing**: `effective_suffix` already returns empty
for a non-raster format, so the scale is inert in both the name and the bytes. The one visible effect
is that two SVG rows differing only in scale — a degenerate spec `plan` used to de-collide — now
collapse, which is the same improvement as the raster case.

⚠️ **`clamp_note` reports in the spec's vocabulary rather than the multiplier it resolved to.** A
`--width 200000` reduced by the raster cap is a sentence about `200000w`, not about `655.350×`, which
is a number nobody typed. That is why it takes the `ExportScale` and resolves the factor itself.

⚠️ **The same size flag twice is refused rather than last-wins.** `--png --svg` takes the last one and
that is fine — formats have an obvious ordering — but two sizes do not, so `--scale 2 --scale 3` goes
through the same "two answers to one question" guard as `--scale` with `--width`. The test walks all
six unordered pairs, because a guard that only fired one way round would pass a test written in
whichever order the author thought of first.

**D362 — The library: one configurable folder, no dialogs, and the identity that travels inside the
file. *Built and tested 2026-08-26; Keep.*** The *Next · Files, library and storage* section is closed
by this and the four entries after it. Documents live in a base folder that defaults to `~/.ondin` and
is user-settable; nothing asks where to save, where to open, or what to call a file on disk. A typed
name — "My cool design" — is slugged to `my-cool-design.ondin`, collisions take `-1`, `-2`, and the
typed name is stored because the slug cannot give it back.

**Where that name is stored is the whole decision, and it went against a recorded rule.** The roadmap
said *"sidecars in the app cache dir — thumbnails, journal, index — never beside the document"*, which
is right for anything derived and wrong for this: the base folder is meant to be a Drive, Dropbox or
OneDrive directory, so a fact that does not travel inside something syncable is a fact the user's
second machine does not have. A library arriving there with every document named by its slug and no
project assignments is not the same library. So `DocumentMeta` — `id`, `name`, `project`, `created` —
is a top-level block **in the `.ondin` itself**.

**Which collides with invariant 9, and the collision is resolved by volatility rather than by kind.**
Byte-identical re-saves are what make the format diff well, and the roadmap was explicit that *"a
modified-at stamp or view state in `DocumentDto` kills all of it"*. Every field in the block changes
only when the **user** changes it — a rename, a move, a creation — so a save that changed no drawing
changes no bytes. The rule the module states is the one that keeps it true: *if a field would be
written by a clock, it does not belong here*. An edit time is read off the directory entry, where it
already is, for free, and where every sync client in the world already carries it.

**Additive in the strongest form, so no schema bump.** Every field is `Option` and
`skip_serializing_if`, and the whole block is skipped when empty — `DocumentMeta::is_empty` — so a
document that has never been through the library is written byte-for-byte as it was before the field
existed. `Node::pivot`'s shape (§5.11), reached at the top level.

⚠️ **`io::load` does not mint a missing id, deliberately.** A loader that filled one in would make
loading non-deterministic: reading the same bytes twice would give two documents that disagree about
who they are. A pre-library file loads unfiled and the *app* gives it an identity the first time it
files it — `a_pre_library_file_loads_unfiled_and_is_not_given_an_identity` pins both halves.

⚠️ **The block sits at the *top* of the DTO, beside `schema_version`, and the first draft had it at the
bottom.** The argument for the bottom was the one that keeps `images` there — a large, still table
whose lines should not move — and it is worth nothing for four short lines whose entire purpose is to
be read *without* the rest of the file. The dashboard lists a folder by reading each document's name,
project and date; reaching them past the node array and a megabyte of base64 is a multi-second scan of
data nothing on screen uses. Worse on the setup this is all designed for: on a synced folder an
unhydrated file is a *placeholder*, so a scan that reads whole documents downloads the entire library
to draw a list of names. `io::probe::meta_in_prefix` reads a fixed 4 KB and the placeholder hydrates
that much and stops.

⚠️ **The probe is hand-rolled rather than `serde_json`, for one reason: serde must parse a complete
value and a prefix is by construction incomplete.** It walks the top-level object far enough to find
one key, and answers three ways — `Found`, `Absent`, `Inconclusive` — because "there is none" and "I
could not tell" lead to different work, and because a zero-byte read from a placeholder that failed to
hydrate must never be cached as "this document has no name". `Absent` is the one place key *order* is
trusted: reaching `root` first means there was none, which is a claim about files this crate wrote, and
a hand-reordered file costs the dashboard a filename instead of a typed name and self-heals on the next
save.

⚠️ **That hand-reordered file is the only wrong answer `Absent` is allowed to give, and from the day
this was written it gave three more** (D485). A file that is not a JSON object at all, a stray byte where a key belongs and
a second `meta` key all came back `Absent`, so a renamed PNG was reported as a healthy pre-library
document — `read_meta` maps `Absent` to default metadata *without opening the file*, and only the
`Inconclusive` arm reads the rest and can report it unreadable. All three are `Inconclusive` now. The
paragraph above is still the rule; what it did not say, and what D485 had to establish, is that the
**cost of a wrong `Inconclusive` is a slow scan and the cost of a wrong `Absent` is a lie**, so
everything the probe cannot definitely account for belongs on the slow side.

⚠️ **The test that ties the probe to the writer is over a *real* save, not a fixture.** `probe`'s own
unit tests are written against a literal and would all stay green if the key moved back down the DTO
while every folder scan silently fell back to reading whole documents. `the_first_four_kilobytes_of_a_real_save_carry_the_library_block` is the one that fails, and its
fixture is deliberately fat — a document with an embedded image — so that "fits in 4 KB" is a claim
about *where the block is* rather than about the document being small. Flip confirmed.

⚠️ **Windows device names go through the collision path.** `nul.ondin` opens the null device rather
than a file, and the error a create returns for it does not say so — the one filename rule that cannot
be discovered by trying it. `unique_stem` treats a reserved stem as taken, so `NUL` becomes `nul-1` and
needs no new vocabulary. `slug` is lossy and public; `unique_stem` is the only function allowed to name
a file, and anything that writes a path from `slug` alone is a silent overwrite.

⚠️ **The stem cap was checked after the write and let a 61-character stem out of a 60-character
limit** — caught by the first run of `a_long_name_is_capped_and_never_ends_in_a_dash`, which is also
why that test now carries two fixtures: a many-word one to catch going over, and a single-word one to
pin the boundary to exactly the cap rather than to somewhere near it.

⚠️ **`projects.json`'s read has three outcomes, and the third is the point.** A missing file is an
empty library and safe to write into; a file that exists and does not parse is `Unreadable`, and a
caller that treated the two alike would overwrite a half-synced project list with an empty one.
`Library::may_write_projects` latches every writer on it.

**D363 — A project is an id in each file's metadata, and its folder is optional. *Built and tested
2026-08-26; Keep. This reverses a recorded recommendation.*** The roadmap asked *"Is a project a
directory? Recommended yes, so nothing about grouping is virtual"* and the answer is no: a project is a
row in `projects.json` with an id, a name and a colour, and each document points at it through
`DocumentMeta::project`. A matching folder on disk is offered when the project is created and is the
user's choice; renaming the project renames the folder, and that is the only thing the folder does.

**The recommendation's premise was that a virtual grouping is a grouping nothing outside the app
respects — and the reversal is that a *derived* one is worse.** If the project came from the path, then
the first time somebody dragged a file between folders in Explorer the app would silently reassign it,
and a document dragged *out* of the library would forget what it belonged to. Metadata wins over
location everywhere here, and the two are allowed to disagree: a file sitting in `kestrel/` whose block
says `project: atlas` is in Atlas.

**Which makes "may or may not create a folder" invisible to every writer.** `Project::dir` is the
project's folder or the root, so filing, moving and restoring are one code path — and moving a document
into a folderless project rewrites its block and moves no file at all, which is the assertion that pins
the whole design (`moving_to_a_folderless_project_moves_no_file`).

⚠️ **A document naming a project nothing knows about is unfiled, not hidden.** That is the state a
half-synced library is in — the documents arrived and `projects.json` has not — and treating it as
unfiled means the file is listed, nothing is lost, and it joins its project the moment the list
catches up.

⚠️ **Deleting a project is the one action in the library with no trash**, because the project was never
anything but a row. So its modal has to answer the *files* question before it closes — transfer to
another project, leave them unfiled, or send them to Trash — and the files are settled before the row
is removed.

⚠️ **The latch check moved above the file loop, and a flip that did not bite is what found it.**
Removing `may_write_projects` from `delete_project` left the test green, because `save_projects`
latches on its own and `projects.json` was never at risk. What *was* at risk was the files: the check
sat below the loop that moves them, so a refused delete would have moved every document out of a
project that then stayed exactly where it was. The test now asserts the thing that was actually broken,
and the re-run flip fails on the file assertions while the bytes assertion stays green — the reverse of
what the first draft measured.

**D364 — `Ctrl+S` pins a version, autosave is silent, and *Save As* is gone. *Built and tested
2026-08-26; Keep.*** With a document written every thirty seconds by an interval nobody sees, "save" on
its own stops meaning anything a person can feel — so the chord's job changed rather than shrank. It
writes the file **and** copies it into `.versions/<document id>/<unix seconds>.ondin`, which is the
thing a designer actually wants a key for.

**Keyed on the document id rather than the stem, which is the whole reason `DocumentMeta::id`
exists.** A rename changes the filename, and history a rename orphans is history nobody will trust.
`pinned_versions_survive_a_rename` is that assertion. Two pins inside the same second take a suffix
rather than overwriting, because `Ctrl+S` twice is a thing people do.

**`Save As` asked where to put a file and nothing asks that any more.** What it was used for —
branching a copy — is *Duplicate* in the dashboard's file menu, which mints a **new** id: a copy that
kept the original's would share its version history and its cover, so pinning a version of the copy
would turn up in the original's history. `Ctrl+Shift+S` is now **unbound** rather than an alias for
Save, and the `!m.shift` guard stays in `resolve` to keep it that way — a chord that quietly became a
second Save would do so invisibly, and only for the user whose fingers still reach for it.
`save_takes_the_bare_chord_and_the_shifted_one_is_free` asserts the empty result.

⚠️ **Autosave is gated on `is_dirty`, and the reason is not the write.** A document left open overnight
would rewrite its own bytes every thirty seconds — invisible locally, and a file change every sync
client in the world will pick up and upload.

⚠️ **And it never creates a file.** A document that has never been filed is not autosaved into
existence: putting something in somebody's library on a timer, for a canvas they were doodling on, is
not ours to do. The first save of a new document is theirs to make.

⚠️ **The flip that found three vacuous tests.** Making `autosave_tick` pin a version left all eight
wiring tests green, because three of them set `autosave_secs = 0` meaning "fire immediately" — it means
**off**, so the function returned on its first line and the tests were asserting that nothing had
happened after nothing was asked. An `arm_autosave` helper now owns what "armed" means, and each of the
three carries an assertion that the fixture *did* autosave; the flip fails at three sites.

⚠️ **Renaming or deleting the open document moves the session with it.** A rename that left
`session.path` behind would have the editor saving to a file that no longer exists, and the next
autosave would recreate the document under its old name — two copies, one of which the user has never
seen. A delete that left it clears the path, or the next autosave writes the document straight back out
of the trash, undoing the delete thirty seconds later. The rename's flip failure site was **not** where
predicted: the library assertion passes either way, because the rename does happen on disk; it is only
the editor that is left pointing at nothing.

**D365 — The dashboard is a whole window, not a panel. *Built 2026-08-26; the screen itself is the one
thing here worth a look on the machine.*** `OndinApp::ui` calls `dashboard_ui` and **returns** — before
the font poll, before `input::resolve`. While the library is up there is
no tool, no selection to nudge and no canvas to autopan, and putting the boundary at the top of the
frame is what makes that a property of the frame rather than a rule thirty call sites have to remember.

⚠️ **This sentence read *"before `handle_close_request`"* until 2026-09-08 and that third term was a
defect rather than a design** (D526). The argument above it is *no tool, no selection, no canvas* — an
argument about the **editor's own machinery**, which the window's close is not — so intercepting the ✕
was below the return on the library screen and did not happen there at all. The close is above the
return now; everything else in the ordering is unchanged, and the boundary means what this paragraph
always said it meant.

**Three doors onto it and that is not redundancy.** The brand mark is where a person looks for "home",
the folder button is where they look for "open", and `Ctrl+O` is the habit; they are now the same
place. The mark was `Sense::hover()` and is now `click`, which is the whole change — a mark that does
nothing and a mark that navigates look identical at rest, so the cursor, the hover lift and the tooltip
are owed together. ⚠️ **Two of those three, since 2026-08-26**: the `PointingHand` is gone with the
other three the app was setting (§15 D371), on the rule that chrome shows the arrow and the cursor
changes only where the change means something. It was the loudest of the three and said nothing the
brightening did not.

**Two Settings modals, not one.** The editor's answers questions about editing — the nudge step, the
tree guides, web fonts — none of which mean anything on a screen with no document open. Joining them
would put six sections behind one button, of which four are about a document that is not there.

**The library's is the only modal in the app that edits a *draft* and applies on Save**, and it has to
be: two of its fields together are an **operation**, not a setting. A base folder plus *Move my
existing files there* moves every document the user owns, and an apply-as-you-type version would start
doing that while they were halfway through typing the path. Cancel throws the draft away; the
Cancel/Save pair is load-bearing rather than convention.

⚠️ **The draft's base-folder field is seeded from the *resolved* root, not the raw preference.** They
differ for every user who has never set one — the preference is `None` and the root is `~/.ondin` — and
an empty field there would be honest about the setting and useless about the library.

⚠️ **Relocation merges and never overwrites.** A document whose slug is taken at the destination
arrives beside it; a version file present at both ends is skipped, because the same id at the same
second is the same version; `projects.json` merges by id with the destination winning. A run twice
leaves duplicates rather than being idempotent — the right way round, since the other failure silently
eats work. Flip on `unique_stem` confirmed, and the useful half is that the *moved count* stays green
while the second document vanishes: a test asserting only the return value would have passed a
migration that ate a file.

⚠️ **Import copies rather than moves, and mints a fresh id.** The originals are somebody else's files
in somebody else's folder; taking them away is not what "import" means anywhere. Importing the same
file twice gives two independent documents rather than one silently overwritten. A document arriving
without a block takes its name from its filename — the *same* guess the list makes, or importing one
would rename it. Files already inside the library are skipped, because the dialog opens on the
last-used folder and that may well *be* the base folder.

⚠️ **The dashboard is drawn headlessly in a test and checked for egui's own complaints** — five navs ×
two views through `run_ui`, asserting no red stroked rectangle (`warn_on_id_clash`, D65). Flip
confirmed: collapsing the file-menu id from `("file-menu", path)` to a bare `"file-menu"` draws 4
warning rectangles. It fails on the *All* pass rather than the first, because a machine that has opened
nothing has an empty Recent and therefore no rows to clash — so this test's coverage depends on the
fixture having listed documents, not merely created them. **It says nothing about whether the screen
looks right**; that is still the maintainer's eye.

**D366 — What does not travel: Recent, stars and covers. *Built and tested 2026-08-26; Keep, reviewed
and accepted.*** D362 put every fact the user would expect on their second machine inside the document.
This is the other half of that line, and it is drawn at *"would you expect this on your other
laptop"*. Three things answer no and live in `dirs::cache_dir()/ondin`:

- **Last opened.** "Recent" means recent *here*. A file somebody else touched on another machine
  appearing at the top of this one's Recent list would be a bug rather than a feature — so a library
  synced onto a new machine has a full *All files* and an empty *Recent*, which is the honest answer.
- **Stars.** ⚠️ **The uncomfortable one, and the maintainer was offered the alternative and declined
  it.** A star reads as a fact about the *document*, so a synced library will reasonably be expected to
  carry it. It is local anyway because the alternative is a field in `DocumentMeta`, which makes
  starring rewrite the whole `.ondin` — a 12 MB write and a sync upload for one click.
- **Covers.** A picture that can be rebuilt in a second is not worth uploading.

⚠️ **The local index is swept against the live document ids, and the starred set is the half that would
rot silently.** An `opened` entry for a deleted document is invisible — nothing draws it. A `starred`
one is invisible *and comes back*: restore the document from the trash and it is mysteriously starred
again, months later.

**Covers are rendered by the same headless path `ondin export --png` uses**, so a cover *is* the
document rather than an impression of it. Two caches with different jobs: on disk keyed by document id
**and modification time** — the mtime is what makes it correct rather than merely fast, since a
document edited on another machine and synced in has a new stamp and therefore a new key — and in
memory as textures with a per-pass budget. Eight milliseconds rather than `ImageThumbs`' two, because
that one decodes a picture already in memory and this one runs the whole document → pixels path.

⚠️ **One render a pass whatever the budget says**, which is the progress guarantee: a document big
enough to spend the whole budget on its own would otherwise never be drawn at all. Flip confirmed —
without it a zero budget draws nothing, ever.

⚠️ **An empty document gets no cover, and that is a decision rather than a gap.** Returning a blank
raster would draw an identical grey rectangle on every card of a fresh library — worse than the plate,
because it looks like a preview. The card cannot tell "no cover", "will not load" and "not rendered
yet" apart, and neither does the code: all three draw the plate, which is what the grid drew before
covers existed.

⚠️ **The cover sweep is by key, so it also removes the superseded covers of documents that are still
here.** Without that the folder grows by one PNG per save, forever — the failure a cache keyed on a
changing value always has, and the one nothing on screen would ever show. It runs once per *visit* to
the dashboard rather than per refresh, since the refreshes inside the screen happen after every rename
and delete.

**D367 — The dashboard's controls are the app's controls. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-26; the screen is
still worth a look on the machine.*** Eight defects were reported on D365's library screen and they
were one defect. It had been built in a single pass from `design/Dashboard.dc.html`, and towards the end
of that pass it stopped reaching for `ui.rs` and began spelling controls out of egui's defaults — which
is invisible in a diff and obvious on screen. *"New project and settings use checkboxes instead of
toggles"*, *"all textboxes have no padding… we don't use the blue outline on focus anywhere and the
design doesn't tell that"*, the sort button and the grid/list switch matching neither the design nor the
editor. The fix is not eight fixes; it is the screen being held to §9.4's rule that a control the app
already has is the control it uses.

**The grid/list switch is one `ui::segmented` track of two cells, not two `icon_button`s.** Two separate
buttons say *two independent toggles*, which this is not — one of them is always on — and the design
draws the recessed group the inspector's tabs and the type panel's mode strips already are.
`VIEW_TRACK_W` adds the parts up (two 26pt cells, the 2pt gap, 2pt of track padding each end) because
`segmented` takes the **outer** width, and `VIEW_CELL_H` is `HEADER_CONTROL_H - 4` because the caller
passes the **cell** height and the track pads itself around it.

**The sort control is `ui::action_button` with a leading `icon::ARROWS_DOWN_UP`**, and it is sized by
the new `ui::action_button_w` to the widest of `Sort::ALL`'s four labels. ⚠️ **The widest, not the one
showing**: the button cycles its own word on every press, so measuring the current label would shove it
— and the track left of it — sideways by the difference between *Name* and *Date created* on each click.
`action_button_w` is measured off the same four constants `action_button` lays itself out with, for
`badge_field_chrome_w`'s reason: a caller re-deriving `PAD * 2 + GLYPH + GAP` from reading `ui.rs` is a
caller that disagrees silently the day one of them moves.

**`HEADER_CONTROL_H = 28` is shared by all three of the body header's controls** — sort, view track and
*Delete project* — and is `settings::FIELD_H`. The height matters less than the **centre**: a
`ui.horizontal` centres each item against the row height it knows *when that item is allocated*, so a
cluster whose members disagree by two points lands them on different baselines.

**A starred document's grid card carries a star, top-right of the cover**, in a new `theme::color::STAR`
(`#e0a93c`, the design's `starColor`) over a one-point black pass standing in for the design's
`drop-shadow` — a cover is arbitrary artwork and a gold outline on a pale drawing has nothing to sit
against. Its own constant rather than `color::WARN`, which is two points away and would have done: they
are near-identical because this palette has one warm hue, not because *you marked this* and *this cannot
be drawn* are the same idea. ⚠️ **An outline star, not the design's filled `ph-fill ph-star`** — the
bundled `assets/fonts/Phosphor.ttf` is Regular weight only, and a second font for one mark is not worth
it. The design's resting dark outline on *unstarred* cards was deliberately not adopted, which is also
what stops the outline being ambiguous: nothing else draws a star there.

⚠️ **The outline was reversed on 2026-08-28 and the reasoning above is why it took a third option to do
it (§15 D380).** Asked "is there a filled variant", the answer is still no — the fill weight is a
separate font file — but that was never the only way to get a filled star. `dashboard::star_shape` draws
one as a ten-vertex `convex_polygon`, no asset at all. The premise the paragraph rests on ("a second font
for one mark is not worth it") was true and was doing the work of a conclusion it does not support: it
rules out *bundling*, not *filling*. What made the outline wrong is what it looks like at 15pt over a
thumbnail — a gold ring whose hole is most of it.

⚠️ **`ui::text_field` exists for a trap, and this is the sentence to keep.** Passing
`.frame(egui::Frame::NONE)` is what suppresses egui's focus ring — egui paints `Visuals::selection.stroke`
in place of `bg_stroke` when a text edit has focus, and skips the frame entirely when the caller supplied
one — **and the same line silently kills `TextEdit::margin`**, because egui reads that builder only via
`let frame = frame.unwrap_or_else(|| Frame::new().inner_margin(margin))`. So `.frame(NONE).margin(m)`
drops `m`. Any caller wanting its own inset must put it in the frame, which is what
`OndinApp::rename_field` now does (`Frame::NONE.inner_margin(Margin::symmetric(4, 0))`, 4 because both
its callers reserve a box 4pt left of where they paint the name, and any other number makes the word
jump sideways the moment the field appears). **This was found by a flip that did *not* bite**: the
plausible wrong version of the search fix was egui's default `Margin::symmetric(4, 2)`, and putting it
back moved nothing — at which point `rename_field`'s 4pt inset turned out to have been doing nothing
either, since the hour it was written.

**The search field's placeholder no longer moves when the field takes focus** (*"text in search box
isn't aligned when it takes focus"*). `Ui::put` lays its widget out **justified**, so a `TextEdit`
handed the whole 28pt field is stretched to it and draws its galley at the top; the live placeholder
therefore sat higher than the painted one it replaces. It is now put into a rect exactly one text row
tall and centred by hand, and both spellings read one `SEARCH_TEXT_X = 30` and one `SEARCH_PT = 11.5` —
anything that paints a string beside a widget showing the same string owes a shared origin. Pinned by
`the_search_placeholder_does_not_move_when_the_field_takes_focus`; the flip that bites is restoring the
full-height rect, which fails the y assertion at 16.0 against 23.0 and leaves the **x** one green,
because the horizontal position never came from the margin at all.

**Fields lose focus now** (*"text boxes don't seem to lose focus"*). `NewProject::name_focused` is a
latch, so the name field asks for the caret on the frame the modal opens rather than on every frame — a
field that re-requests focus every pass is a field the switch below it and the footer buttons cannot
take focus away from. The search overlay is the other half: it closes on a pointer **press** outside the
field and outside its own results panel, read as a press so the dismissal lands on the same frame the
pointer goes down rather than after whatever is underneath acts on the release. `search_panel` returns
the rect it drew into, which is what lets the two be told apart. Requesting focus every frame is still
right *there*, and it is the dismissal that makes it safe.

Also pinned by `the_header_controls_share_a_height_and_a_centre` — flipping `VIEW_CELL_H` to
`HEADER_CONTROL_H` (the obvious wrong version: forgetting the track pads itself) fails the height
assertion at 32 against 28 and leaves the centre assertion green, since the row simply grows around
both. So the height is the load-bearing half and the centre is the guard against the next change.

⚠️ **Two departures from `design/Dashboard.dc.html` are deliberate and neither is a gap.** New project
keeps the app's own *Add a matching folder on disk* wording and the app-standard **right-hand** switch,
rather than the design's *Create folder* with the toggle on the left; and its colour swatches stay 16pt
circles rather than becoming 26×26 rounded squares with a check. The design's project **filter**
dropdown in the body header (`showFilter` / `filterOptions`) is a different thing — unbuilt rather than
declined — and was built the same day, in D369.

**D368 — One settings card, and every modal in the app stands on it. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-26;
Keep.*** The other half of D367's report, and the loudest line in it: *"Settings is a mess that looks
nothing like the layout in design/"*. The dashboard's Settings had been built as a second, independent
answer to a question the editor's Settings card had already answered — egui's default modal frame and
backdrop, `ui.checkbox`es, bare `ComboBox`es, `section_label`, a 420pt card — and two spellings of one
object is exactly how they end up looking nothing like each other. `crate::settings` is now that one
object: `CARD_W`, `PAD`, `SECTION_AIR`, `TITLE_GAP`, `FOOTER_GAP`, `ROW_GAP`, `SWITCH_H`, `FIELD_H`,
`COL_GAP`, `LABEL_PT`, `CAPTION_PT`, `section`, `caption`, `text_button` and `Decision` are
`pub(crate)`, and three helpers are new beside them — `card_modal` (the ground, the hairline, the 10pt
corner, the shadow, `PAD` of inner margin and the design's `rgba(0,0,0,.5)` backdrop), `modal_title`
(name plus ✕, returning whether the ✕ was pressed) and `modal_footer` (Cancel / Save changes, the
commit lit only when the draft differs from what is saved).

**The footer is shared for the reason it is the one row a user reads twice**: it is where they look to
find out whether the form has taken anything, so two cards whose commits light on different rules are
two cards that disagree about what *edited* means.

`OndinApp::library_settings_modal` was rebuilt on it — 376 wide against the 420 it shipped at,
`settings::section` eyebrows with their hairlines in place of `section_label`, `ui::switch_row` for the
three booleans, `ui::text_field` for the base folder, and two half-width `ui::value_field_suffixed`
columns for autosave and trash retention with the label **inside** the field, which is
`settings::nudge_field`'s shape and stops the card looking assembled from two kits. The three pickers go
through a `picker_row` carrying the two corrections every dropdown in this app owes: `ui::combo_chevron`
in place of egui's white triangle, and `interact_size.y` forced to `FIELD_H`, without which they paint
26 beside 28s. The redundant `Currently: <path>` line is gone — the field is seeded from the resolved
root (D365), so it restated the field exactly.

**The other four dashboard modals moved onto the same card** — New project, Delete project, Move to
project, Delete file — and all five now dismiss through `egui::Modal::should_close()` rather than a
hand-rolled Escape check, so Escape and a backdrop click mean the same thing on every one of them. It is
read *after* the body, because `should_close` consumes the Escape press.

⚠️ **The dismissal convention is wider than this card and one modal was outside both** (D525). The
editor's *Unsaved changes* card is a bare `egui::Modal` — three buttons, no `modal_title` ✕ — so it
never joined the eight drawn here, and it was also not reading its `ModalResponse` at all, which left
`Escape` over it unhandled until 2026-09-08. Nine dismiss through `should_close()` now and eight are
drawn on this card; **the two counts are not the same claim**, and §9.5 keeps them apart.

⚠️ **`LibrarySettings` gained `Clone, PartialEq, Eq` so the dirty test is one `!=`** rather than nine
per-field comparisons somebody has to remember to extend — and a derived `PartialEq` **silences
`dead_code` on a field nothing reads**, anywhere in the workspace, `pub` or not. So the compiler will no
longer say when a row is dropped from the card and its field left behind: read the struct against the
modal after removing a row.

Pinned by `every_settings_row_fits_the_card_and_the_commit_starts_dim`, which the shrink from 420 to 376
is what made necessary — every row had been laid out against 44 points it no longer has. ⚠️ **Its flip
result is worth recording because the first flip does *not* bite**: widening `PICKER_W` to 240 leaves it
green, since a `picker_row`'s label is a `ui.label` and a `ui.label` wraps — the row absorbs the squeeze
instead of overflowing, so the probe sees an escaping row and not a crowded one. What it does see is
*painted* text, which cannot wrap and is not clipped: lengthening a `ui::switch_row` label fails it at
23.8pt over. ⚠️ The probe also has to find the card by the rect **containing its first eyebrow**,
descending into `Shape::Vec` — a `Frame` with a shadow paints `Vec([shadow, rect])`, so the card's own
fill never appears in a flat scan, and `CARD_W` is an outer number no rect in the frame is.

**D369 — The body header's project filter, and one predicate behind it. *Built and tested 2026-08-26;
the screen is worth a look on the machine.*** D367 closed by recording the design's project filter as
unbuilt rather than declined and raising it in `roadmap.md`; this is that entry answered, plus two small
things reported beside it. `OndinApp::project_filter` draws the design's *All projects ⌄* — a colour
dot, an elided name and a caret — and `OndinApp::project_filter_menu` drops an `Area` listing *All
projects* and then every project, each with its swatch and a tick on the one in force. `FILTER_MENU_W`
is the design's 190; `FILTER_ROW_H` is its 26 **plus two**, so a row of this menu is not tighter than a
row of the ⋮ menu a card away on the same screen; `DOT` is its 7.

**A button and an `Area`, not a `ComboBox`**, because a `ComboBox`'s `selected_text` is one
`WidgetText` and the closed state here carries a colour chip beside the word. It is the shape
`OndinApp::file_menu_popup` already uses on this screen, so the dropdown that opens is the same object
in both places.

⚠️ **`ui::button_face` is `pub` for this.** The filter's content is neither a glyph nor a word, so
neither `action_button` nor `label_button` fits it — but it sits in one right-to-left row *with* both of
those and owes the same four `FieldButton` states, and a hairline half a shade off reads as two
different kinds of control rather than as one control being different. `FieldButton::Set` is the accent
border: the design lights it while the menu is open, and this also lights it while a filter is **in
force**, which is the state that matters once the menu has closed again.

⚠️ **The load-bearing part is `OndinApp::filter_applies`, one predicate read from two places.** It gates
the control *and* the `retain` in `OndinApp::visible_entries`, which is what the design does with its
`showFilter` — that flag guards both the markup and the `base.filter(…)`. Split, a filter set on *All
files* goes on selecting on *Recent*, where there is nothing on screen to unset it with: a list silently
missing most of itself and no explanation anywhere. It is false on *Recent* (a landing page rather than
a list), inside a project (the question is already answered), **and** when there are no projects at all
— which is this file's addition rather than the design's, on the grounds that a dropdown holding one row
cannot change anything.

⚠️ **The stale-id degrade runs above that early return, and that is deliberate.** A filter naming a
project that no longer exists is cleared; the case where an id stops resolving *because the last project
was deleted* is exactly the case where `filter_applies` is false, so a degrade written after the return
would never run on the nav that needs it. The header is drawn on every nav (`dashboard_body`), so above
the return is reached everywhere. Same reasoning as `Nav::Project` carrying an id rather than an index.

Pinned by `the_filter_selects_only_where_it_is_offered`. The flip is dropping `self.filter_applies() &&`
from the retain, and it fails the *Recent* assertion at 1 against 2 — the predicted site, for once.
⚠️ **Worth recording that the probe's fixture was wrong first**: *Recent* is what this machine has
**opened**, not what exists, so both documents have to go through `mark_opened` or that arm reads 0
either way and discriminates nothing. It failed at 0 against 2 on the first run, which is the fixture
being wrong rather than the code.

⚠️ **The sidebar's *New file* button was drawing an empty box where its plus should be.** It read
`"＋  New file"` in `FontId::proportional`, and U+FF0B is a **fullwidth** plus that the bundled Inter has
no glyph for, so the one accent button on the screen showed egui's fallback rectangle. It is `icon::PLUS`
in `theme::icon_font` painted as a separate run now, measured and placed so the pair is centred as one
thing — `ui::action_button`'s arithmetic, which cannot simply be borrowed here because that paints
`button_face`'s recessed ground and this button is the exception. The general rule is worth stating
because the mistake is a one-character one: **an icon is the icon font's business, and nothing in this
app should be spelling one as a character in a prose font.** A grep confirmed this was the only instance.

The New project modal's name placeholder went from `Kestrel` — the design's fixture, carried over
literally — to *Your awesome project*. A placeholder that reads as a real name is one a user has to look
twice at to see the field is empty.

**D370 — A headless app cannot write the preferences file. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-26; Resolved.***
⚠️ **This is not a deviation from the design; it is a harness fault that reached the maintainer's own
machine**, and it is recorded here because nothing else in the project would have caught it. Reported as
*"my base folder is some random directory: `C:\Users\jonid\AppData\Local\Temp\ondin-wiring-crumb-25960`.
I'm doing `cargo run`."*

`OndinApp::headless` had always pointed `Prefs::base_folder` somewhere harmless — **in memory**. But
`Prefs::save` wrote to `dirs::config_dir()` unconditionally, so any probe that reached one of the app's
nine `prefs.save()` call sites persisted its own `temp_root` into the real `%APPDATA%\ondin\prefs.json`,
and the folder it named was deleted by the very test that made it. Both `base_folder` and
`last_document` were poisoned; the file has been repaired to `null`/`null`. D303's "three things are
swapped" was therefore half true from the day it was written: the third was a *value*, not a write path.

The fix is a `#[serde(skip)] pub ephemeral: bool` on `Prefs`, defaulting `false`, set `true` by
`headless` and checked on the first line of `save`. **A flag on the value rather than a guard at each
call site**, because the call sites are the whole app — the export popover writes on every row, the
dashboard on every nav change — and one of them forgetting is the bug coming back. `headless` is already
the one place that decides what a test's app does differently (`OndinApp::with` takes a device, a font
service and this), so it is the one place that knows. `#[serde(skip)]` is the other half: a preferences
file that somehow contained the flag could never make a real install stop saving.

Two probes, and they are not equal. `prefs::tests::an_ephemeral_prefs_never_reaches_the_disk` asserts
the guard and the round trip, and ⚠️ **deliberately does not call `save()` on a real value** — a probe
proving that negative by writing would *be* the bug. The one that matters is
`app::…::a_headless_app_can_never_write_the_preferences_file`, flip-checked by removing `ephemeral:
true` from `headless`: it fails immediately, and it is **the only gate in the workspace that does**,
which is the whole point, since the damage this prevents is invisible to every other.

**D371 — The arrow is the cursor over chrome, everywhere. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-26; Keep.***
Reported as *"on the Editor, hovering on the logo mark (that sends you back to the dashboard) it's a
pointer cursor. We only use arrow cursor everywhere."* ⚠️ **This is §9.2's existing rule being applied,
