not a new one.** `ui::value_field` states it at length: a design tool's panels are all controls, so a
cursor that changes on every one of them says nothing and flickers, and the cursor changes only where
the change *means* something — `Grab` on a reorder grip, `ResizeHorizontal` on the layers panel's drag
edge and on a scrub strip, `Text` on the dashboard's search field, and the drawn bitmaps on the canvas.

Four production `PointingHand`s are gone: the editor's brand mark, the editor breadcrumb's project name,
the dashboard's project card and the typography panel's *Show all features* reveal. Nothing else in
`crates/ondin-app/src` sets one.

⚠️ **The design says otherwise, explicitly and repeatedly, and it is being overridden on purpose.**
`design/Dashboard.dc.html` puts `cursor:pointer` on the filter trigger, on every one of its menu rows
and on a good deal else besides — so this is not the design being silent about cursors, and a session
reading that file beside the code will otherwise read the arrow as a miss and "fix" it back. The rule
that wins is the maintainer's own, in their words after living with the shipped screen — *"we only use
arrow cursor everywhere"* — which puts it on the same footing as every other reported-after-use reversal
in this ledger. **It is that file's *values* being a first draft while its structure is not:** D369
followed the filter's markup, geometry and row content closely, and `cursor:pointer` alone is declined.

⚠️ **The brand mark had an argument for it in a comment** — "the only things telling the user it is a
control are the cursor, the lift on hover and the tooltip; all three are owed together" (D365). Two of
the three remain and that comment now says so. The hand was the loudest of the three and said nothing
the brightening did not.

⚠️ **The typography row is the interesting one, because its hand was itself a fix.** The reveal is an
`egui::Label`, and a selectable label claims an I-beam. Measured when the row was written and
re-asserted now: `selectable(true)` reports `CursorIcon::Text`, `selectable(false)` alone reports
`Default`. So `selectable(false)` was always sufficient for the reported symptom, and the hand it also
acquired was the part that broke the rule. The test is renamed
`the_features_reveal_asks_for_an_arrow_and_a_bare_label_asks_for_an_i_beam` and **keeps** the third case,
asserting that `on_hover_cursor` works and outranks the label's own — the alternative was available, it
was measured, and it was declined, which is what stops the arrow reading as an accident of egui to the
next person here. That case aims the pointer at the response's own rect from the frame before, for D96's
reason.

The census command in `ui::value_field`'s comment still holds and is still the right way to check this:

    grep -rn "set_cursor_icon\|on_hover_cursor" crates/ondin-app/src

**D372 — A single click picks a document out. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
Reported after asking what was left on the library screen: single-clicking a card or a row did
**nothing**. `OndinApp::file_card` and `OndinApp::file_row` both sensed `Sense::click()` and then read
only `resp.double_clicked()`, so a card lit under the pointer and swallowed the press — the one state no
file browser has and the design does not have either. Nothing in this ledger had declined it; it simply
was not built. `design/Dashboard.dc.html` carries selection throughout, keyed on its `sel`: `border: sel
? 'var(--color-accent)' : dim(8)` on a card and `rowBg: sel ? accent 12% : transparent` on a row.

`DashboardState::selected: Option<PathBuf>` holds the answer and `OndinApp::pick_or_open` is the rule,
called from the card and the row alike so the grid and the list cannot come apart about what a click
means.

⚠️ **It *sets* rather than toggles, and that is a deliberate departure from the design's own handler.**
egui reports `clicked()` on the release that also completes a `double_clicked()`, so a toggle — which is
what the design does, `select: () => this.setState({ selected: sel ? null : f.name })` — would deselect
a card on the way to opening it, and the picked state would flicker off under the second click of every
open. Setting is idempotent, so both clicks of a double land on the same answer. The design can afford
the toggle because it has no double click at all and opens from the ⋮; the app has a second gesture to
protect and pays for it here.

**Three tiers on a card, two on a row**, which is the design's own split rather than an inconsistency. A
picked card is a full `color::ACCENT` border where hover is the muted `ACCENT_700`: two tiers would make
a hovered card and a picked one the same picture, and telling those apart is the whole job of the border
while a pointer moves across a grid. A picked row takes the design's `rowBg` as a `color::ACCENT_900`
wash instead, because a hairline drawn around a 38pt row that is flush with its neighbours reads as the
row having *grown*, where a ground reads as the row being picked. The card gets the border because a
card already has one to change.

⚠️ **The body's background is `ui.interact`ed over `ui.max_rect()` *before* any card is drawn, and the
order of registration is the mechanism.** egui's hit test takes the **last** widget registered at a
point, so this claims the whole body, every card then claims a piece on top of it, and what is left over
is the empty space a click has to land on to mean *nothing, thanks*. This is `ui::icon_button_padded`'s
trap seen from the useful side. Flip-checked by moving the `ui.interact` below the `ScrollArea`: the
*first* assertion fails with `selected` still `None`, because the background swallows every click on the
grid and nothing is ever selectable — the predicted site, and a louder failure than the one being
guarded against.

⚠️ **A selection is a path, and it can name a file that is no longer there.** Every action on this screen
writes to disk and re-scans, so a delete, a move and a rename all strand it. `OndinApp::dashboard_body`
clears it against the **visible** entries rather than against `library.entries`, because a selection
filtered off screen is one the user can neither see nor dismiss.

Pinned by `a_click_picks_a_document_and_the_background_puts_it_back`, which drives real pointer events
through three frames per click and asserts all three states: nothing picked, the card picked, and the
background putting it back.

**Nothing acted on a selection when this landed**, and that was not a promise made here. Enter-to-open
and Delete-to-trash were the obvious pair, and they arrived later the same day with the rest of the
library's keymap — D374, which this entry is what made worth writing down.

**D373 — A document dropped on the library is filed in it. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
⚠️ **The dashboard had no drop handling at all.** `OndinApp::ui` returns to its caller as soon as
`view == View::Dashboard` (D365), several lines *above* `take_dropped_images`, so the whole drop path was
editor-only: a `.ondin` file dragged onto the library went nowhere and said nothing about it. Importing
was the sidebar's *Import files* row and a native dialog, which is the one thing a file screen should not
be the only way to do.

`OndinApp::take_dropped_documents` is called first in `dashboard_ui`. It filters `raw.dropped_files` to a
case-insensitive `.ondin` extension and hands what is left to the existing `import_paths`, which already
announces its own outcome — the count, the failures and the already-in-the-library skip — so nothing is
said twice.

🚨 **Amended 2026-09-09 (§15 D693): the last clause of that sentence was false when it was written and
stayed false for twelve days.** `import_counting` dropped an already-in-the-library file with a bare
`continue`, so nothing downstream had been told and the only place in `import_summary` that could
mention such a file was the `(0, 0)` arm — which did not *report* the reason, it **asserted** it. An
import of three documents two of which were already under the base folder said *"Imported 1 file(s)"*
and nothing whatever about the other two. **It is true now** rather than aspirational: the count
arrives, and the signatures below are the post-D693 ones.

**Two handlers, not one dispatcher, and that is deliberate.** An image dropped on the canvas becomes a
layer at a point; a document dropped on the library becomes a file in a folder. Different verbs,
different targets, and nothing shared beyond the `Vec` egui hands over — a single dispatcher would have
to know which screen is up in order to decide, which is exactly the fact the early return has already
established.

⚠️ **Only files with a `path`.** egui's `DroppedFile` carries either a path (a file-manager drop) or
`bytes` (a drag out of a browser), and `import_paths` is path-taking all the way down: it reads the file,
parses it, mints a fresh id and derives a name from the file **stem**, then skips anything already under
the base folder. A bytes-only drop has no stem and nothing to skip against, so it is counted and reported
rather than half-handled. The canvas makes the opposite choice for images and can afford to — a pasted
picture needs no name.

**Everything that is not a document is one message, not one per file.** A folder of forty PNGs would
otherwise be forty failures, where what the user needs to know is that this screen takes `.ondin` files,
said once.

⚠️ **The first version of that gated the message on `docs.is_empty()`, and it was a defect rather than a
decision.** A drop of one document and forty pictures reported *Imported 1 file(s)* and said nothing
whatever about the forty — a silent partial failure, and a partial refusal that says nothing is
indistinguishable to the user from files that never arrived at all. ⚠️ **It could not be fixed by adding
a second `session.fail`, and that constraint is what shaped the code**: `EditorSession`'s status is a
**single slot**, `info` and `fail` assign rather than append, so a second call does not add a sentence —
it erases the count the first one just gave. So the work and the announcement are separate functions.
`OndinApp::import_counting` imports and returns `(ok, failed, already)` without saying anything;
`import_paths` is
a thin announcing wrapper over it for the dialog path, passing `skipped: 0` because `rfd`'s extension
filter has already excluded everything else; and `take_dropped_documents` calls `import_counting` and
announces for itself. The free function `import_summary(ok, failed, skipped, already)` builds the whole
sentence, and its `skipped` clause — ` — {n} other file(s) were not Ondin documents` — is appended to
**every** arm, the happy ones included, which is precisely the half the bug got wrong. The `already`
clause is D693's and is appended the same way, for the same reason found in the arm next door. Only a drop with no document
in it at all still short-circuits, to the one refusal.

`OndinApp::library_drop_hint` draws a `theme::color::SELECT` outline and *Drop to import* — or *Drop to
import into {project}* inside one — while `hovered_files` is non-empty. The canvas's
`draw_drop_indicator` makes the same statement in the same colour, because a drop target that gives no
sign it is one is a feature nobody finds. ⚠️ It is named `library_drop_hint` rather than `drop_hint`
because `panels::layers` already has a `drop_hint` on `OndinApp`, and two inherent methods of one name is
a compile error rather than a shadowing — the useful kind of collision.

Pinned by `a_dropped_document_is_imported_and_a_dropped_image_is_not`; the flip removes the
`take_dropped_documents` call — the state this screen shipped in — and fails the first assertion at 0
imported against 1. ⚠️ **The probe's fixture is a document *outside* the library**, because
`import_paths` deliberately skips files already under the base folder: dropping one of the library's own
would assert that nothing happened and pass for the wrong reason. That test gained a **mixed-drop** arm
with the fix — a document and a PNG in one pile — asserting both that the document lands and that the
sentence names the file it ignored; and the mapping itself is pinned separately by
`an_import_says_what_it_took_and_what_it_left`, five cases against a free function that needs no app, no
library and no filesystem. One flip serves both: move `rest` into `import_summary`'s `(0, 0)` arm, and
the free-function test fails its second and fourth assertions while the drop test fails reporting
`"Imported 1 file(s)"` — the bug's own words, which is the failure message worth having.

**D374 — The library's own keymap, and the two bugs it put on screen. *Built and tested 2026-08-28;
Keep.*** D372 ended by saying that nothing acted on a selection yet and that Enter-to-open and
Delete-to-trash were the obvious pair. This is that pair, plus the arrows that make a selection worth
having without a pointer: before it the whole of the library's keymap was `Ctrl+K`/`Ctrl+P` to open
search, Escape to close it and Enter to take the first match. `OndinApp::dashboard_keys` runs at the top
of `dashboard_body`, before anything draws, and `shortcuts.md` §8a is the table.

⚠️ **Read straight off `egui::Context`, and it cannot be otherwise.** `input::resolve` is the *editor's*
keymap and is not called at all while the library is up — `OndinApp::ui` returns above it (D365) — which
is the same reason `Ctrl+K` already read the context for itself. So the guard that `resolve` would have
provided is written out by hand: the two confirmations, the ⋮ menu, the *Move to project* sheet, *New
project*, the library's Settings card, the rename field, the search overlay, and
`egui_wants_keyboard_input` for anything holding a caret. ⚠️ **This enumeration is scoped to
`dashboard_keys` and there are two context-reading sites on the screen, which is how D542 got in**:
`search_field` reads `Ctrl+K`/`Ctrl+P` for itself and had no guard at all. Everything but the last is
`dashboard::library_keys_are_free` now, read from both. That last one is about *focus* rather than
about text, and the menu, the sheet and the confirmations hold no caret at all, so they are named rather
than assumed. `modifiers.is_none()` closes the list, which is what keeps `Ctrl+K` from also stepping the
selection and leaves every chord on this screen free to be bound later without coming back through here
to be excluded.

⚠️ **The ⋮ file menu is the one guard that does not merely block: `Escape` shuts it, and it had no way
to be shut by the keyboard at all before this function existed.** Every card on this screen is a
`settings::card_modal` and gets Escape and the backdrop free through `should_close` (D368); the ⋮ is a
bare `Area` and took only an outside click. The hole was invisible while nothing on the screen read the
keyboard and is a hole the moment something does — the guard is what made it visible. It is handled
*above* the guard list with an early return rather than inside it, because the menu owning the keyboard
and the menu **ignoring** it are two different things. `shortcuts.md` §8a's `Escape` row is the
statement; this is why it reads that way. ⚠️ **"The one guard" was two floating things and only one
of them was named** (D578): the *All projects ⌄* dropdown is the same shape — `project_filter_menu`'s
doc says so in as many words — and was in neither half of this function, so `Escape` cleared the card
cursor behind it and `Delete` opened a confirmation underneath it. The early return asks
`library_menu_open()` now, the predicate D558's pointer-side doors already share, so the two twins
cannot drift apart again.

⚠️ **One of those guards is measurably redundant, and it stays.** Flip-checked: with `search.is_some()`
removed the keymap is still silent under the overlay, because the search field is drawn in the *top bar*
— before this runs — and `request_focus` makes `egui_wants_keyboard_input` true inside the same pass,
which is D317's fact and the opposite of what was predicted. A guard that holds only because of the draw
order of two functions is not a guard, so the explicit flag is kept as the belt. Removing **both** is
what fails `the_keyboard_moves_the_selection_opens_it_and_asks_before_deleting`, at the picked path
against `None`.

⚠️ **That measurement is true of a *steady-state* frame and of no other, and the sentence beside it
turned out to be a prediction** (D543). On the frame the overlay **closes**, `search_field` returns
before its field is drawn: `search` is already `None` here, egui has surrendered focus during
`begin_pass`, and both guards are false together — so one `Escape` closed the overlay *and* cleared
`dash.selected`, throwing away the keyboard cursor. The flip is kept above as it was run, because it
was run correctly; what it could not see is the one frame in which the field does not exist.

**The arithmetic is the free function `arrow_target(current, key, list_view, len)`**, which is D269's
standing answer applied deliberately: a decision inside `&mut self` cannot be tested, so the interesting
half is lifted out and the method is left as guards and a path lookup. The grid steps in **reading
order**, so `→` off the end of a row is the start of the next — the alternative, a `→` that stops at the
right-hand column, makes the fourth card a wall the keyboard cannot get past — and the list view is one
column whose horizontals are dead, a full-width row having nothing beside it. ⚠️ **Out of range clamps
rather than refusing**: `↓` from a column the short last row does not reach lands on the last card, which
is Explorer's behaviour and the one that never leaves a press doing nothing on a grid that plainly has
more below. The cost is that `↓` on the last row returns `Some` of the index it already had, which is why
the caller must **set** the selection rather than toggle it. With nothing selected, `↓`/`→` enter at the
top and `↑`/`←` at the bottom, so the first press enters the list from the end it came from.

⚠️ **The index is found by path every frame rather than stored.** Every action on this screen writes to
disk and re-scans, so a document's position in `entries` is not stable across a rename, a star, or
anything a sync client does to the folder; an index kept in `DashboardState` would step from where the
selection *used* to be.

**A key step scrolls the card into view and a click does not.** `DashboardState::scroll_to_selected` is
the message from the keymap, which knows an index, to `OndinApp::follow_selection`, called from the card,
which has the rect — and the rect exists only once the row it is on has been laid out. Setting the flag
on the keyboard path alone is what stops a pointer click near the viewport edge jerking the grid. ⚠️ It
scrolls with `ScrollAnimation::none()` where `scroll_to_rect` would take the style's 0.1–0.3s: a key step
is under one card, so an animated one leaves the highlight and the viewport disagreeing for a third of a
second on *every* press, and a held arrow re-targets the animation before it has finished. The duration
is also how the probe was found — the first version of it failed with the card still at y=822,
mid-animation.

**Two bugs that were already there, and that giving the screen a keyboard put on the screen.** ⚠️ **A
double click opened a document out of the trash.** `OndinApp::file_menu_popup` has said since the trash
was built that a trashed document gets two rows and neither is *Open* — opening one puts the editor on a
file inside `.trash` that the next autosave keeps writing to and the purge eventually deletes out from
under the person editing it — and `pick_or_open`'s double click ignored it, twenty lines away. There is
one predicate now, `OndinApp::can_open`, read by the double click and by `Enter`. ⚠️ **And the delete
confirmation said "moves to Trash" over a permanent delete.** `Act::Trash` means *move to trash*
everywhere except in the trash, where `trash_or_purge` deletes the file outright; the card had never been
on screen in that state because the ⋮'s own *Delete permanently* skips the modal and purges. `Delete`
does not skip it — deliberately, since a menu row was aimed at where a key can be the tail of a chord the
user thought they were typing into something else — which is what made the wrong sentence reachable. It
reads *Delete permanently* and "… is deleted for good. This cannot be undone." in `Nav::Trash`. Its name
lookup needed a fallback in the same breath: `Library::entry_at` searches the library and a trashed
document is not in it, so the name falls back to the file stem through `scan::display_name` — that
function rather than its `de_slug` half directly, so a stem becomes a name in exactly one place, and
because nothing may re-scan the trash from inside a layout.

Four tests. `the_arrows_step_in_reading_order_and_clamp_at_the_ends` is the free function on its own;
⚠️ its flip — the range test that returns `None` off the end, which is the first implementation anyone
writes — was predicted to bite on `↑` from index 0 and bites **four assertions earlier**, on the
short-last-row `↓`, which is the case the feature is actually about. Both assertions stay: the first says
the grid has no dead press at the bottom, the second that it has none at the top either.
`the_keyboard_moves_the_selection_opens_it_and_asks_before_deleting` drives real key events through the
app for all four keys, the overlay guard, and the ⋮ menu — which blocks the arrows and then takes the
`Escape`; that arm is flip-checked and fails at *and Escape shuts it*.
`arrowing_off_the_bottom_of_the_grid_scrolls_the_card_into_view` is the one that makes this a feature
rather than a state change — without `follow_selection` the label comes back at **y=970** against a
window 820 tall, a row and a half below the fold. ⚠️ **Its fixture is twenty documents and not a round
number**: rows are 172 apart (a 158 card and a 14 gap), so a sixteen-document version would have put the
fourth row's caption at y≈798 against a fold at 800 — a test that passes with no scrolling at all.
`nothing_opens_a_document_out_of_the_trash` covers the first bug ⚠️ **on the key rather than on the double
click**, since two press/release pairs inside egui's double-click window is wall-clock rather than
frame-counted; what pins the click is that it calls the same `can_open` one line away.

**Still unbound here, and listed in `shortcuts.md` §8a rather than in this ledger**: `F2`, `Ctrl+D`,
`Home`/`End`, `Ctrl+A`, and anything that would need a **multiple** selection —
`DashboardState::selected` is one path and every verb on this screen takes one document.

**D375 — A sync client's conflict copy is marked. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
⚠️ **The fact that makes this worth building is §5.11a's own consequence: a conflict copy is a copy of
the *file*, so it carries the metadata block** — the same typed name, the same project, the same id. Two
cards, one name, one project dot, one cover, and the only thing that differs is a filename the dashboard
never shows. `a_suspected_conflict_needs_its_original_and_a_stated_one_does_not` asserts exactly that,
with three entries all reporting `display_name() == "Landing v4"`. The mark is not decoration; it is the
only signal there is.

`scan::conflict_marker(stem) -> Option<(Conflict, String)>` reads one filename and answers in two tiers.
**`Conflict::Stated`** is a phrase no `naming::slug` can emit — Dropbox's `(… conflicted copy …)`,
Nextcloud's `(conflicted copy …)`, and Syncthing's `.sync-conflict-` followed by eight digits — and
stands on its own even when the document it copied is gone. ⚠️ Dropbox needs **two spellings and not
one**, because it puts a person's name inside the parenthetical, so a search for `(conflicted` misses it
and a search for ` conflicted copy` misses Nextcloud's. The eight digits are what make Syncthing's
stated rather than suspected: `sync-conflict-notes` is a name somebody can type. **`Conflict::Suspected`** is
`<base> (N)` and `<base> - Copy [(N)]` — the shapes a person also makes — and is only a conflict when the
document it claims to copy is beside it.

**The load-bearing fact is that every pattern here is one `slug` cannot produce**, which is what makes
the false-positive rate against this app's *own* files exactly zero rather than merely low: `slug` emits
lowercase alphanumerics and `-`, and collisions take `-1`, `-2`. A space, a `(` or a run of eight digits
is therefore proof the name came from somewhere else. That is why `document-2.ondin` — which the app
writes all the time — is not on the list, and why `roadmap.md`'s own illustration `document-conflict-2`
was Suspected at best: "Document conflict 2" is a name a person can type and it slugs to exactly that.

⚠️ **The other side of that argument is that the mark lives *only* in the filename, so any operation
that re-derives a stem deletes it** (§15 D509). `library::relocate` did, for every document in the
library, which turned `landing-v4 (1).ondin` into `landing-v4-1.ondin` — unmarked, and sharing the
original's `meta.id`, because a conflict copy carries the original's block. **Re-slugging is the one
operation this heuristic cannot survive**, and there is nowhere else for it to look.

⚠️ **But the `slug` argument protects this app's own files and does *not* protect a hand-made filename,
and that is where a loose arm does its damage.** A `.ondin` named in Explorer or arriving from
somebody else is the one class of file that can carry a parenthesis without being a conflict, and it is
precisely the class `slug` says nothing about. The stated tier carried a third, broader `(conflict` arm
for a day, to catch a parenthetical that does not spell out "copy"; **no client is known to write that
shape**, while `Notes (conflict resolution).ondin` — which can only have been typed by hand, since `slug`
emits no parentheses — matched it and was told it was a sync artefact. It is gone. **A pattern has to be
paid for by a client that actually writes it**, or it is a warning charged to somebody's real document,
which is the same trade OneDrive is refused on below.

⚠️ **OneDrive's shape is deliberately absent, and that is a stated non-goal rather than an oversight.**
It appends the machine name — `landing-v4-DESKTOP-8H2K1` — which is a hyphen and a word, i.e. precisely
what a typed name slugs to. There is no pattern that matches it without also matching "Landing v4 desktop
8h2k1", so this reports nothing rather than guessing, and the gap is recorded here instead of in a
heuristic that fires on somebody's real document.

⚠️ **The scan cannot finish the job, so `Library::conflict` does.** `conflict_marker` sees one filename,
and half its answers are about the *list*: `landing-v4 (1).ondin` next to `landing-v4.ondin` is a sync
artefact, while on its own it is somebody's file, and marking it would be the app telling a user their
document is broken because of a bracket. ⚠️ **Same directory, not merely the same stem** — a project is a
folder, so `landing-v4.ondin` at the root and `landing-v4 (1).ondin` inside *Kestrel* are two unrelated
documents that a stem comparison alone would pair; compared case-insensitively, because the filesystem
this most often runs on is. The lookup is linear and affordable only because the marker is checked first,
so it runs for a filename that already carries a suspected marker and nearly none do.

**A drawn pill rather than a tooltip, deliberately.** `conflict_chip` paints an amber `CONFLICT` mark —
bottom-left of the cover on a card, opposite the star, since the two are unrelated facts and a document
can wear both; beside the name in a list row. The thing it says has to be visible while the eye is
*scanning*, because the whole failure it marks is two cards that look identical, and a tooltip is by
definition invisible until one of the two has already been picked. Amber because `theme::color::WARN`
already means "a thing to fix rather than a mistake in the document"; red would read as *this click
removes it*, which is what the ⋮'s *Delete* means two inches away. ⚠️ **On a card it is two passes, and
the first is black**, because a cover is arbitrary artwork and a 26%-alpha amber over somebody's pale
mockup is an amber word on a white ground — the same problem the star solves one corner away with its
drop shadow. ⚠️ **In the list it takes its width out of the *Name* column before the name is elided**,
rather than being drawn over the end of it: the design's grid is `1fr 170px 120px 120px 90px` and has no
spare width, so the two genuinely compete and the name is the one that can shorten. `conflict_chip_size`
measures rather than guessing, since a fixed guess that came out short would put the chip on top of the
last letters of a long name, which is the one failure this mark cannot afford.

Four tests. `conflict_markers_catch_the_clients_and_never_this_app` covers both tiers, and ⚠️ **its
second block generates the negatives through `slug` rather than typing them**, so it asserts the property
the design rests on instead of a list of strings. **Its third block is the other class, written raw** —
`Notes (conflict resolution)`, `Palette (draft)`, `Landing v4 (final)` — because a hand-made name has by
definition not been through `slug` and the second block cannot reach it; restoring the `(conflict` arm
fails on the first of the three, at `Some((Stated, "Notes"))`. ⚠️ **The predicted failure site for its
flip was wrong
and where it actually failed is the more useful fact**: against a bare `contains("conflict")` arm — what
"surface the roadmap's two examples" looks like written directly — the prediction was
`conflict-resolution-flow` in the second block, and it fails four assertions earlier on
`landing-v4.sync-conflict-notes`, a *positive* case asserting that Syncthing's marker without a date is
nothing. The loose arm is caught by the tier boundary before it is ever caught by a false positive.
`a_suspected_conflict_needs_its_original_and_a_stated_one_does_not` and
`a_conflict_is_matched_inside_one_folder_only` pin `Library::conflict`; the flip that makes `Suspected`
answer without consulting `entries` fails the former at the lone `orphan (1)` — somebody's document being
told it is broken — and the latter at its only assertion. ⚠️ **Those fixtures are written by hand rather
than through `store`**, because nothing in this app can produce these filenames, which is the property
the whole feature leans on; and they are made with `std::fs::copy` of a real document, which is what
reproduces the shared metadata. `a_conflict_copy_is_the_one_of_the_two_that_is_marked` covers the chip in
both views, which draw it from different call sites.

**D376 — The *New file in {project}* card, and an empty project that is not a dead end. *Built and
tested 2026-08-28; Keep.*** `design/Dashboard.dc.html` puts a dashed card at the end of a project's grid
(`New file in {{ heading }}`, gated on its `inProject`) and a plain *New file* row at the end of its
list; neither was built. `OndinApp::new_file_card` and `OndinApp::new_file_row` are those, gated by
`OndinApp::new_file_into`.

**A shortcut, not a capability.** `Act::NewFile` still has exactly one meaning, and the sidebar's *New
file* button already filed into the project being viewed — `new_library_document` reads `Nav::Project`.
This is the same act offered where the eye already is. Which is also why there is no card on *Recent*,
*All files*, *Starred* or *Trash*: a document created from one of those has no project to land in, and a
card promising a destination the screen cannot name is worse than no card. **The row says only *New
file*** where the card says *New file in X*, which is the design's split and is right — a list has one
row per file and no picture, so the row reads in the context of the heading above it, while a card is one
of four in a grid a person scans rather than reads.

⚠️ **Gated on the project *resolving*, not merely on the nav being `Nav::Project`.**
`new_library_document` files into the project it can look up, so a nav holding an id `projects.json` no
longer has would leave the new document unfiled while the card named a project — the one state a shortcut
like this must not reach. Nothing else on the screen notices a dangling id, because everything else only
*filters* by it. A dangling project therefore shows the ordinary empty state and no card.

⚠️ **`file_grid` counts slots rather than using `entries.chunks(GRID_COLS)`.** The card is a *cell*, so
it has to be able to finish a short last row; a chunks loop can only put it on a row of its own, which is
wrong exactly when it matters — a project holding one file would show its card and then a whole empty row
with the *New file* card alone at the left of it. The `unwrap_or_default` on the one slot past the end is
unreachable rather than a fallback with a meaning: that slot exists only when `new_file` is `Some`.

**A departure from the code that was there**: an *empty* project now shows the card **instead of**
`empty_state`. The empty state's sentence and the base-folder path it prints are about the *library* — a
base folder pointing somewhere else — which is not the question a project with no files asks; the dashed
card says "nothing here, make one" and offers the verb in the same breath. The empty state is still what
a dangling project id gets, and still what an empty library gets.

Pinned by `a_project_grid_ends_in_a_new_file_card_and_nothing_else_does`, which asserts that *All files*
has no card, that the card sits in the next cell of the last row rather than under it, and that clicking
it files a second document into the project; and by
`an_empty_project_offers_the_card_and_a_dangling_one_does_not` for the two gates. ⚠️ **Both assertions of
the first bite, and the prediction that only one would was wrong.** The flip is `file_grid` back to
`chunks(GRID_COLS)` plus a trailing card, the shape this was written against: the x fails unambiguously
(the label lands at 359, centred in the *first* column, against 298 for the file's name beside it), and
the y was expected to pass vacuously and does not — the labels come out 138pt apart against a threshold
of `CARD_THUMB_H` at 116. ⚠️ **The margin is 22pt, and that is the finding**: had the threshold been the
card's full height of 158, which is the number a reader reaches for first when writing "the same row",
the assertion would have been green for exactly the layout it rules out. It is the thumbnail's height
that gives it teeth, and only by accident, so the x is the one to keep if these ever have to be cut to
one.

**D377 — Crash recovery is a snapshot, not a journal. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
`roadmap.md` carried "a journal is the answer and nothing writes one" for as long as there was no
crash recovery at all, and the answer that was built is the other one. **`ondin_core::Operation`
derives no `Serialize`**, so an op journal means putting a second versioned on-disk format over the
whole op tree — a change to the format's own guarantees, owed a schema version and a migration path
of its own, in exchange for the last ten seconds of somebody's work. A whole-document snapshot goes
through `ondin_core::io::save` and adds **no format at all**. The fork was put to the maintainer and
the snapshot was chosen explicitly; this is a decided replacement for the journal rather than a
shortcut to it, and is recorded here so the journal is not re-argued from the ambition.

`library::recovery` writes `<root>/.recovery/<key>.ondin`, one file per open document, keyed on the
document id when it has one and on a minted key when it does not.

⚠️ **Which puts it on the wrong side of D366's own line, and that is deliberate.** Nothing in a
snapshot is a fact about a document: it is in-flight work belonging to one machine and one run, and by
"would you expect this on your other laptop" it should be in the cache directory beside Recent, stars
and covers — where the roadmap's old rule, *"sidecars in the app cache dir — thumbnails, journal,
index — never beside the document"*, would also have put it (D362 quotes that rule going the other way
for the metadata block). It lives in the base folder anyway, beside `.versions` and `.trash`, so that
the whole library stays **one directory** to back up, move or point a sync client at; `relocate`
carries it along for the same reason.

**Three gates in `OndinApp::recovery_tick`, and each one is a different mistake.** `is_dirty` is
"there is work the file does not have"; `recovery::SNAPSHOT_SECS = 10` is "not more often than that";
and `recovery.at == session.revision()` is "something was actually committed since the last one".
⚠️ **Without the third, a document edited once and then left alone rewrites identical bytes every ten
seconds forever** — `is_dirty` stays true from the first edit until the next save, so a user who edits
and then reads their email for five minutes produces thirty identical writes into a folder a sync
client is watching. That is the thrash `roadmap.md`'s own *Technical, and still binding* list warns
about and that `autosave_tick`'s `is_dirty` gate avoids one level up (D364).
`an_idle_dirty_document_is_snapshotted_once_rather_than_every_interval` is that gate, and ⚠️ **it
watches `recovery.last` rather than the file's mtime**, since a second write inside the same second
would not move one; dropping the `recovery.at` comparison fails it on a second, identical write.

⚠️ **A write that fails says so exactly once, and the clock is stamped anyway.**
`RecoveryState::warned` latches the first `session.fail("Crash recovery is not running: …")`, because
the alternative is that status line every ten seconds; and `recovery.last` is set before the write
rather than after a success, so a folder that cannot be written to is a back-off rather than a retry
every frame — a permissions problem must not become a stutter. The failure is worth saying at all, and
worth saying once: crash recovery that silently does not work is the kind of thing a person only
discovers at the worst possible moment.

⚠️ **There is no `path.is_none()` gate, which is the one place this deliberately parts company with
autosave — and the most valuable thing the feature does.** `autosave_tick` refuses to file a
never-saved document because that puts something in the user's library they did not ask for, and that
rule is right. A snapshot is not a document: `.recovery` is a dot-directory `scan` skips, so nothing
it writes can appear in the library, be opened by accident or be counted by a heading. So it can
cover the one case where a crash costs *everything* rather than an interval — an hour of drawing on a
document that has never been saved. `a_snapshot_covers_the_unfiled_document_and_stops_at_the_save`
asserts that `scan` still sees an **empty library** afterwards, which is the assertion that fails if
the two features are ever collapsed into one. Its flip is the version somebody writes by copying
`autosave_tick`: the `expect` on `recovery.key` fires before the file assertion does, which is the
more informative failure, since a missing file could also mean a write that failed.

⚠️ **`SNAPSHOT_SECS` is a constant rather than a preference, and deliberately not
`prefs.autosave_secs`.** Autosave's interval is the user's to choose because autosave writes *their*
file; this writes a scratch file they never see, so the only thing a setting could buy is the chance
to switch off the thing that saves them. And `autosave_secs = 0` means **off** (D364) — which is
exactly when a crash costs the most.

⚠️ **The write is a temp file and a rename** — `<key>.writing`, then `std::fs::rename` over the
target — because this file exists to survive a process dying, and a process that dies *during* a
`fs::write` leaves a truncated file, which is a recovery offer that fails when accepted, at the one
moment the user is already unhappy. **`store::write_document` had the same exposure for the real
document and was deliberately not changed here**: making every save in the app atomic is a decision
about every save in the app, not about this file, so it was recorded as an open question rather than
left as a silent inconsistency between two writers of the same bytes. It was answered the same day —
*make every save atomic* — and this file's write is now `crate::atomic::write` like every other
record's (D378); what survives of the argument above is only that this one got there first.
`a_snapshot_replaces_itself_and_leaves_no_temp_file` pins the mechanism, flip-checked with `fs::copy`
in place of the rename — the assertion fails with the temp file still sitting in the folder.

**Recovering does not write the user's document.** `OndinApp::recover` loads the snapshot into the
session with the *original's* path and calls the new `EditorSession::mark_unsaved`, so the file on
disk is untouched and the next move is the user's: save it, or undo their way out of it and close. A
recovery that overwrote the file would be this feature destroying work in the name of protecting it —
the snapshot is up to ten seconds *behind*, and behind is not better. ⚠️ **The snapshot is kept, not
deleted, on recovery**: the session is dirty the moment it loads, so the tick adopts the same key and
keeps it current, where deleting it here would leave the recovered work protected by nothing for the
first ten seconds of its second life. ⚠️ **That is about the snapshot being recovered *from*, which
is the only one it ever contemplated** — see the next paragraph for the other key in play.

⚠️ **There is a second key, and *Discard* is no longer the only thing that deletes** (D681 → D768).
`recover` adopts the pending snapshot's key **over** whatever key this session already held, so the
**outgoing** session's snapshot used to be stranded in `.recovery/` with nothing naming it, offered
at every launch for ever. It is dropped now, at `open_path`'s position, and the count below is
**five**. 🚨 **The one-line repair on its own was written and then reverted**, because
`recovery::pending` is a queue: on the second press of *Recover* the key it drops names the snapshot
the user recovered a press ago and has not saved, so the drop alone deletes work where the leak
merely re-offers it. **What makes it safe is `may_replace_current_document` in front of it** —
`open_path`'s save-then-confirm pair, lifted into a predicate and asked by both doors — so past that
line the work has been saved or the user has been asked. **The two are one change and must not be
separated.**
🚨 **This paragraph and the count below were amended to five once before, in session 18, and reverted
inside the same day** when that repair was backed out; `CLAUDE.md` records it as the case of a
passage made false by a fix that does not survive. **This time the guard is at `HEAD` and the drop is
behind it**, which is the difference — a reader meeting the history should check `recover` for the
`may_replace_current_document` call rather than the `drop_recovery` line alone.

**`EditorSession::mark_unsaved` replaces the `#[cfg(test)] mark_dirty_for_test`.** It sets `dirty`
*and* clears `saved_at`, or the top bar's pill would read "Saved · just now" over a document that
matches nothing on disk — the one sentence that pill must never be able to say. Two callers now,
making the same claim from opposite ends: recovery, and the autosave tests, whose rules are all of
the form "given a dirty document, does the interval do X" and which would otherwise have to drag a
whole fixture document into a test that is about a timer.

**Where the snapshot is dropped, and why it is five places rather than one.** The tick's clean branch
handles the ordinary case — the document on disk *is* the document, so a snapshot would be a claim
about work that no longer exists anywhere else. But ⚠️ **the tick only runs on an *editor* frame**, so
**four** other functions have to say so themselves, at five call sites: `close_confirmation`'s *Save*
and
*Discard* arms, both of which end the process and therefore have no next frame; `open_path`, before
`adopt_document`, because past that line the app holds a different document and cannot name the old
session's key; `go_to_dashboard`, since `OndinApp::ui` returns at the library and a snapshot would
otherwise survive untouched for as long as the user stayed on that screen; and **`recover`, the
second door that replaces the session's document** (D768), at `open_path`'s position and for
`open_path`'s reason. ⚠️ **`recover`'s drop is safe only because
`may_replace_current_document` runs first** — it is the fifth site and the one with a precondition,
and removing that call leaves a drop that deletes the user's work on the queue route.
⚠️ **`go_to_dashboard`'s
drop is gated on `!is_dirty()`, and that gate is load-bearing**: the save above declines to write a
document with no path, so an unconditional drop would take the snapshot away from the one document whose
entire existence *is* that snapshot, at the moment its owner walked away from it.

**A rule that changed because a test found a hole in it.** `recovery::pending` drops a snapshot the
document already contains, which is what keeps a clean quit quiet. It was a timestamp comparison alone
— `entry.modified >= written` — and ⚠️ **`Entry::modified` is whole seconds**, so *save, edit, crash*
inside one second had its recovery silently discarded. **That is not a test artefact**; one second is
long enough for all three in real use. The tie is now decided on the files themselves: the snapshot is
dropped when the document is **strictly newer**, or when the two are **byte-identical**. ⚠️ The byte
comparison is reached whenever the document is *not older* — `entry.modified >= written` guards it, so
it is read in the strictly-newer case too and only skipped for a snapshot that post-dates its
document, which after a crash is the common shape and the one there is nothing to compare for.
⚠️ **Worth recording where that rule's coverage actually lives**:
`a_snapshot_older_than_its_document_is_dropped_rather_than_offered`
stays green under the flip that deletes the byte comparison, because the tie is dropped either way, and
only the app-level `work_lost_to_a_crash_comes_back_and_the_file_waits_for_the_user` catches it.

**`RECOVERY_DIR` joins `VERSIONS_DIR` and `TRASH_DIR` in `relocate`'s tree loop.** ⚠️ **It is the one
of the three whose absence would be silent.** A stranded version or a stranded trashed file is visible
— the history is short, the trash is empty, and the user can go and look in the old folder — while a
stranded snapshot is a question that is simply never asked again: the next launch reads the *new* root,
finds nothing, and says nothing. `an_unanswered_crash_snapshot_moves_with_the_library` is that
assertion, flip-checked by dropping `RECOVERY_DIR` back out of the loop; the `documents` count in the
first assertion stays green either way, because a snapshot is not a document and `merge_tree` does not
count into that field.

**The modal.** `OndinApp::recovery_modal` is drawn **above** the `View::Dashboard` return in
`eframe::App::ui`, so it appears over whichever screen the launch landed on; it is a
`settings::card_modal`, i.e. an `egui::Modal` and so an `Area` above every panel, which is why being
first in the frame costs it nothing. A snapshot with no document behind it gets an extra line saying it
comes back untitled, which beats a person recovering, seeing *Unsaved* and concluding the recovery
failed. `panels::dashboard::dashboard_keys` gained a guard on `recovery.pending`, because that keymap
reads `egui::Context` directly (D374) and no modal can intercept that.

⚠️ **Three answers behind two buttons, and the third is the whole of it.** `RecoverChoice` is
`Recover`, `Discard` and `Later`, where `Later` is what the ✕, `Escape` and the backdrop all mean: the
snapshot is popped from `pending` so the card closes, and **is not deleted**, so the next launch offers
it again. Those two free dismissals are the ones a hand reaches for without reading the card, and this
is the only modal in the app where that reflex could destroy an hour of somebody's only copy — which is
why this is an enum rather than the `bool` it was, and why `escape_defers_a_recovery_and_never_deletes_it`
flips it against `should_close()` mapping to `Discard`, the answer `delete_modal` gives one screen away.
The snapshot-still-exists assertion is the one that fails.

⚠️ **The card nearly had no ✕ at all, and the reason that was wrong is worth keeping.** The first
version argued that leaving the question unanswered is not a *nothing* answer — the file stays and the
prompt returns — so the two buttons were the two answers. What that missed is that the same omission
swallowed `Escape` and the backdrop with the ✕: a modal that ignores the key does not read as a question
insisting on an answer, it reads as the app having hung, and consistency of interaction outranks a local
argument about one card (D368: all seven dismiss through `Modal::should_close()`). The fix was in the
code rather than in the rule; what survives of the original argument is that a dismissal here means
*Later* rather than *Discard*. ⚠️ **The trap that cost the test a failure**: `ModalResponse::should_close`
gates Escape on `is_top_modal`, which egui derives from the modal stack the **previous** pass built, so a
single-pass probe delivers the key to a modal egui does not yet consider topmost and reports nothing.
The test pumps a frame before the key and says so. It is driven through `eframe::App::ui` rather than by
calling `recovery_modal`, which also pins that the card is reachable from a launch landing on the
dashboard — the screen `ui` returns at.

**`open_at_launch` collects `recovery::pending` *before* `reopen_last` runs**, and ⚠️ **the two are not
independent — they are usually about the same document**, since the one you were editing when the
process died is the one `last_document` names. So the question has to be asked *over* whatever the
launch opens rather than instead of it: a launch that reopened the file and then found nothing to ask
about would drop the work in exactly the case the feature exists for, and drop it **silently**, because
the document opens and looks fine. `reopening_the_last_document_does_not_swallow_its_own_recovery`
asserts both halves: the file reopened, and the snapshot still queued.

⚠️ **What that test pins is the outcome, not the statement order, and the order is currently not
observable at all** — measured, not assumed: moving the collect to the *end* of `open_at_launch`
leaves both assertions green, because nothing on the reopen path touches `library.entries` or the
document's mtime, which are the only two things `pending` reads. **The order earns its place against
the shape rather than against a symptom.** The reopen here is hand-rolled precisely because
`open_path` does more than load — including `drop_recovery`, which would **delete** the snapshot this
function is collecting. The day somebody simplifies those twenty lines into an `open_path` call the
order stops being cosmetic, and this test is what fails.

**One thing still asserted by reading rather than by a test.** `recover` deliberately skips three of
`open_path`'s steps: `local.mark_opened` (the *Recent* list), `prefs.last_document`, and
`collapse_groups_on_open`. A recovery is not the user reaching for a document, so it should not reorder
*Recent*, change what the next launch reopens, or fold the layer tree of work somebody is about to
inspect.

**D378 — Every record the app keeps is written atomically. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
D377 argued that a file whose whole purpose is surviving a crash cannot be written in a way a crash
can corrupt, gave the snapshot a temp file and a rename, and then had to record that
`store::write_document` — the *user's actual document* — was still a plain `fs::write` and had been
deliberately left that way. That inconsistency lasted about an hour. It was put to the maintainer as
an open question rather than left standing, the answer was *make every save atomic*, and the new
`crate::atomic` is that answer.

**A top-level module rather than one under `library/`, because five modules reach it from two
subtrees** — `library::store`, `library::project`, `library::cache`, `library::recovery` and `prefs`
— and because it is a filesystem primitive, not a library concept. `atomic::write(path, bytes)`
creates the parent directory (which every caller wanted and two of them used to do by hand), writes
`<path>.writing` — `<path>.<pid>-<counter>.writing` since D548 — `sync_all`s it and renames it over
the target; on a rename failure the temp is
removed, since the most likely reason to be there at all is a full disk and the debris would compound
it.

⚠️ **The window this closes is neither small nor rare.** Every one of these files is read back and
*believed*, and every one was a bare `fs::write` — or, for a pinned version, an `fs::copy`, which is
the same three steps with the bytes coming off a disk instead of out of memory. `write_document`
truncates the user's document *before* it writes a byte, so the exposure is the whole of every save,
the autosave firing every thirty seconds included.

**What it gives and what it does not**, which is worth stating precisely because it is the kind of
claim that rots into "saves are safe now". `rename` is atomic on POSIX and on Windows alike
(`MoveFileEx` with `REPLACE_EXISTING`), so once the call returns, `path` holds either the complete new
contents or the complete old ones. The `sync_all` before it extends that from *process death* to
*power loss*: without it the rename can land while the data behind it is still in the page cache,
which is a zero-length or garbage file after a hard cut. ⚠️ **The directory entry itself is not
synced**, which POSIX asks for and Rust does not portably expose — so a cut in the microseconds after
the rename can still leave the *old* name pointing at the old data. That is the pre-write state, and
therefore the safe end of the failure: nothing here can produce a torn file, and the residual risk is
losing the new version rather than corrupting the old one.

⚠️ **The temp name is derived from the target rather than randomised, and that is what bounds the
debris.** A crash between `create` and `rename` leaves exactly one `<name>.writing` per file ever
written, and the *next* successful save of that same file consumes it — `File::create` truncates it
and the rename takes it away — so the litter self-clears instead of accumulating one file per crash.
A randomised name would be safer against two writers racing, which this app does not have, and would
strictly grow. 🚨 **Both halves of that last sentence were wrong, and D548 reversed them.** *"Which
this app does not have"* is a claim about the **process**, and the file is addressed by an absolute
path: nothing prevents a second Ondin — no lock file, no named mutex, no single-instance check — and
two instances saving one document tore the destination outright, `BBBB` + twelve NULs + `AAAA` after
both saves reported success. The name carries a pid and a per-process counter now, and the
self-clearing this paragraph is about is replaced by a **sweep**: legacy debris cleared by name from
the target being written, stamped debris cleared once per directory per process, both age-gated by an
hour. *Read D548 before restoring anything here.* ⚠️ The extension becomes `writing`, which is what
keeps these out of the library:
`library::scan` matches an extension of exactly `ondin`, so `landing-v4.ondin.writing` is not listed,
is not counted by a heading and cannot be opened by accident, and `recovery::pending` filters the same
way. **Appending rather than replacing the extension is deliberate** — `landing-v4.writing` would
collide with a second document actually named that.

**Six call sites, and the boundary between them is what a torn file costs.** `store::write_document`
is the document. `Projects::write` is ⚠️ **the file with the most to lose from not being atomic**:
`Library::may_write_projects` exists because an *unreadable* `projects.json` must never be overwritten
by the empty list that failure produced, and a save killed halfway is precisely how a readable one
becomes unreadable — the latch guarded the second write and nothing guarded the first. `Prefs::save`
is written from more places than any other record in the app — every view switch, every open, every
settings commit — so it has the most chances to be the one a crash lands in the middle of.
⚠️ `LocalIndex::save` is **a cache and deliberately not exempt**: the covers and the font data are
exempt because they are *derived* and regenerate, and this is not — nothing can reconstruct which
documents this machine has opened, so a torn index silently loses *Recent* and every star. And
`recovery::write` was already this shape by hand (D377) and now shares the function.

⚠️ **`store::pin_version` is the sixth, and the near-miss is the useful part of it.** It was a
`fs::copy` and was very nearly left alone on the grounds that it cannot destroy anything: the target
is a fresh `<stamp>.ondin` that never collides, so a torn copy is a bad *new* file rather than a lost
old one. That reasoning is right and the conclusion does not follow from it — `store::versions` lists
that directory by the `ondin` extension, so a half-copied pin is **listed as a version**, offered for
restore, and fails when taken, and a history with an entry that cannot be opened is worse than one
with a gap because only the second is honest about itself. `Ctrl+S` is documented as *save and pin a
version* (§9.5), so a pin is a save and the maintainer's rule covers it. It reads the document's bytes
and writes them now, and the `create_dir_all` that used to stand above the collision loop is gone:
`atomic::write` makes the directory, and `exists()` on a directory that is not there is `false`, which
is the answer the loop wants.

**What is deliberately not converted, and the rule that decides it.** The cover PNGs
(`library::cover`) and the font cache: a torn one fails to parse and is regenerated from the document
it came from or re-fetched, and both are written in bulk where a `sync_all` each would be felt. **The
rule is that a file worth an fsync is one nothing else can reconstruct** — which is exactly why the
local index sits on the other side of the line despite also being a cache. The **export paths, CLI and
panel alike** — `main.rs` and `panels::export`'s three write sites — are not converted either: an
export is an output the user re-runs, not a record the app keeps, and in the CLI's case the process
exits immediately after writing one. So the un-converted set is exactly the two derived caches and the
exports.

⚠️ **`recovery::remove` also calls `atomic::forget`, and no other caller does.** Elsewhere a
`.writing` left by a dead process is consumed by the next save of the same file; after *Discard*
there may never *be* a next save, because the whole point of that button is that the key is never
written again — and a snapshot the user threw away must not leave a readable copy of itself in the
folder. (Since D548 the *elsewhere* is a sweep rather than the next save, and it is age-gated by an
hour, which **sharpens** this caller's reason rather than removing it: a discarded snapshot must not
sit readable in the folder for an hour either. `forget` clears every temp for the path,
unconditionally, which is exactly what this caller means.)

**One trap worth recording for the next reader who names something after a prelude macro.**
`atomic.rs` writes its own function as ``[`fn@write`]`` throughout, because a bare ``[`write`]`` is
ambiguous with `std::write!`; the crate roots `deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links)`, so that
ambiguity is a **build failure** rather than a warning nobody reads. The doc gate caught it, which is
the gate earning its keep on the day the module was written.

**Tests**: `atomic::tests::{a_write_replaces_the_file_and_leaves_no_temp_behind,
a_temp_file_left_by_a_dead_process_is_not_a_document}`. ⚠️ The second asserts through `library::scan`
rather than by inspecting the filename, because the property that matters is "the scan does not list
it" and not "the extension is `writing`" — those are the same fact only for as long as `scan` matches
on the extension it matches on today. Flip-checked by replacing the `rename` with an `fs::copy`: both
tests fail at their temp-file assertions while every content assertion stays green, which is exactly
the shape of the bug a leftover temp means — a save that reports success and left the old bytes in
place. ⚠️ **`sync_all` has no flip and cannot have one**: it is the difference between surviving a
process death and surviving a power cut, and a test can stage the first but not the second. That is a
**stated gap rather than a covered line** — the paragraph above says exactly what the call buys, and
it is the one thing in the module no assertion is watching.

⚠️ **`library::store::tests::a_pin_holds_the_documents_bytes` is new, and what it does *not* cover is
why.** Nothing asserted a pin's contents before this: the two tests around it count files in
`.versions` and never open one, so a pin that wrote the wrong document or an empty one would have
passed both and surfaced months later at a restore — counting is what a test writes while the
interesting part still looks like `fs::copy`'s problem. It does not assert atomicity either, and
cannot: flipping `pin_version` back to `fs::copy` leaves **every** test in `library::store::tests`
green, because both spellings produce the right file and the difference is only visible to a process
that dies between the halves. `atomic`'s own tests cover the mechanism; this one covers that a pin
goes through it with the right bytes.

⚠️ **One test elsewhere was nearly made vacuous by this, and the general form matters more than the
instance.** `recovery::tests::a_snapshot_replaces_itself_and_leaves_no_temp_file` asserted that
`<key>.writing` did not exist; once the temp name became `<key>.ondin.writing`, that assertion would
have gone on passing forever while checking for a file that could no longer exist under any
circumstances. It asks `atomic::temp_path` for the name now, which is the only reason that helper is
`#[cfg(test)] pub`. **A test asserting a file is absent must derive the name from the code under test,
or a rename turns it into an assertion about nothing.** ⚠️ **The scheme changed a second time at
D548, and that helper is `atomic::leftover_temps` now** — every temp for a path rather than one name,
because the question became *"is there any"*. The same test was saved by the same habit twice, which
is what makes the rule worth keeping rather than merely worth having written down once.

**D379 — *Edit project*, and archiving as a flag on the project. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***
`design/Dashboard.dc.html` grew an *Edit project* button on a project's page and the idea of archiving:
an *Archive project* switch in that card, and a collapsible *Archived projects* group in the sidebar
once there is one to hold. Both are built. `Project` gains `archived: bool`, written to
`projects.json` **only when it is true** — so a library that has never archived anything produces
exactly the file it produced before the field existed, and an older build ignores a key it does not
know. Additive, as `Projects::version`'s own note says such a field should be; the version is not
bumped.

**The rename is the part that was not free.** *Edit project* is the first thing in the app that
renames a project, and `library::project`'s module doc had promised for two days that renaming a
project renames its folder — a claim about a feature that did not exist. `project::rename_folder` is
that promise: it slugs the new name through `naming::unique_stem` with the project's **own** folder
excluded from the collision test (without which "Kestrel" → "Kestrel " walks to `kestrel-1`, the same
correction `store::free_stem` makes for a document), renames the directory, and returns **the stem the
move actually produced**. ⚠️ **The caller records that rather than the one it asked for**, which is the
whole of the second flip below: the recorded stem and the directory holding the files are two separate
things, and a library that files new documents into a directory the old ones are not in is a bug no
single assertion about either one would catch. A folder the user has since deleted in Explorer is
*adopted* rather than recreated — `atomic::write` creates the parent on the way past — because failing
there would make a project whose folder had gone permanently unrenameable. The open document follows
its folder exactly as it follows its file through a move.

**Archiving is a flag and nothing else, and what it costs is stated as a rule.** It moves no file,
touches no document's metadata and does not remove the project. What it takes away is every *list* a
project appears in: the sidebar's *Projects* group, *Recent*'s project cards, the header's filter and
*Move to project*. `Projects::active` is that predicate, read from all four; ⚠️ **`Projects::get` is
deliberately unfiltered**, because a list is a set of things to choose between and a lookup is "what is
this id" — a document filed in an archived project must still resolve to its name and its colour, or
archiving would silently unfile everything in it. **The maintainer chose this rule over the design's**,
which filtered only the sidebar and the cards and left the filter and *Move to project* untouched; the
cost, stated when it was chosen, is that a document cannot be filed into an archived project without
unarchiving it first.

⚠️ **Two exceptions, both because the thing being asked for is not a choice among projects.** Search
still matches an archived project by name: the name has already been typed, so the only thing hiding
the match could achieve is making the project unreachable while its group is collapsed. And the *Move
to project* sheet still lists the archived project a document is **already in** — a destination list
that omitted it would draw the sheet with nothing selected, i.e. would tell the user the document was
unfiled, and the row is the only place that sheet says otherwise.

**Departures from the design, all three deliberate.** The card's **Description** field is dropped: the
design writes `desc` and nothing anywhere reads it back, *Add project* has no such field, and the
maintainer confirmed it was a mock artefact rather than add a write-only key to a synced file. The
group is **collapsed on every launch** — the design's mock defaults it open, the maintainer's brief
says collapsed, and it is deliberately not a preference: remembering that it was left open would put
archived projects back in the sidebar on the next launch, which is the state archiving was asked for to
avoid. And *Create folder* is **not** in the Edit card: the folder is a decision made at creation, and
the honest way to offer it later would be to make it, move every one of the project's files into it and
say so — a different card.

⚠️ **Archiving the project a filter names clears the filter** (`forget_archived_filter`). Otherwise it
stays in force with no way to see or unset it: its dropdown lists only active projects, so the row that
would clear it is gone — and `filter_applies` hides the whole control once no active project is left,
at which point *All files* is silently showing a subset with nothing on screen saying so. That
predicate reads `active()` for the same reason: archiving is a second way to reach an empty dropdown.

**Two buttons rather than the ⋮ the files have**, which the design draws and is now a choice rather
than the absence of one — the note on that button said in as many words that it would become a ⋮ the
day a rename arrived. It does not: an overflow menu earns its place by hiding a *list*, and two items
are not one. `roadmap.md`'s *Projects have no rename* is struck. ⚠️ **The new button is gated on the
project *resolving* and the old one is not**, which is D376's rule applied where it belongs: a card
seeded from a failed lookup would be an empty form over no project, while deleting a nav that names a
project `projects.json` no longer has is still something a user may want to do.

**And *Delete project* became the design's icon button, which was raised as a divergence and answered.**
It had been a 104pt labelled button since D365 — a departure nobody had recorded, invisible while it was
the only control there and wrong the moment a second one arrived beside it: two labelled buttons read as
two ordinary actions, and one of these removes something with no trash to come back from. It is 32×28
with `icon::TRASH` now, on `ui::button_face` like the rest of the cluster, and the **hovered state is
repainted** — the design's red wash and red border, ⚠️ painted *between* the face and the glyph or the
wash covers what it is tinting, and rounded to the new `ui::BUTTON_R` rather than to a 5 written at the
call site, or the overlay leaves a hairline of the ground at each corner. ⚠️ **The design's `#e0645c` and
`#e0857e` are deliberately not used**: `theme::color::DANGER` already means *this click removes it*, and
its own note asks for exactly this — a second destructive control must be able to be the same red
without anyone going to find the first. ⚠️ **The words now exist only in a tooltip**, which is what the
label was carrying: *project* rather than *file*, on a screen with a *Trash* nav two inches away. The
tooltip is hung inside the function so a call site cannot drop it, and **no probe can see it** — a
tooltip's galley never reaches `.shapes` — so both tests moved from asserting the string to asserting
`icon::TRASH`, which the sidebar's *Trash* row cannot satisfy because that draws `TRASH_SIMPLE`. The
loop over the four non-project navs asserts the glyph *absent*, which is the only thing giving the
positive assertion teeth; flip-checked by hoisting the button out of the `Nav::Project` arm, which fails
there.

**Flip-checks, and two of them are the entry's own lesson.** Forcing the archived group open, and
listing every project in the sidebar instead of `active()`, **fail at the same assertion with the same
numbers** — two unrelated bugs, one failure message; the position assertion further down does not
rescue that, because the run aborts before reaching it. And discarding `rename_folder`'s answer fails
at the **recorded stem**, not at the moved file below it, which was predicted the wrong way round: the
files are already at their new path when that assertion fires, so a test asserting only the file's new
location would have been green for a library whose record and disk had come apart. On the model side,
dropping the self-exclusion from the collision test bites only the "rename that does not change the
slug" case — ⚠️ **the collision test stays green under it**, because its slug always changes, so a whole
arm is covered by one test alone.

**D380 — The library after a walk-through: nine reports, one of them a feature that did not work at
all. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.*** The maintainer lived with D365's screen and came back with a
list. Most of it is polish; the first item is not.

**Renaming a file was impossible, by three faults in one function.** Reported as *"it doesn't save if I
press enter. Doesn't lose focus if I press anywhere on the page. The only option is pressing escape,
which dismissed the name. There's no way I can rename the file."* — and that is the whole of it, not an
exaggeration. `rename_field` asked for focus on **every frame it drew**, so the pass that surrendered the
caret took it straight back and `lost_focus()`, the only thing that commits, was never true. Enter did
nothing, a click elsewhere did nothing and did not even leave the field, and Escape — which returns
before any of that — discarded. ⚠️ **This is D367's own lesson, in the one field that was left behind
when it was learned**: `NewProject::name_focused` is a latch for exactly this reason, and
`panels::layers` has had `the_rename_field_asks_for_the_caret_on_the_frame_it_first_draws` since its own
rename landed. `rename_entry` is now a three-tuple carrying the latch. The two other faults were on top
of it: the field was **justified into a 20pt box**, so its galley sat at the top and the word jumped two
and a half points up at the moment of the click (`Ui::put` lays out `centered_and_justified`; it gets a
one-row rect now, which is D367's search-field fix on the other axis) — and it was placed with
**`Ui::put`**, which ends in `advance_cursor_after_rect`, and since the name box is well *behind* the
grid row's cursor the next card was laid out **34 points to the left, on top of it**. `Ui::new_child`
places at an absolute rect and never touches the parent's placer. ⚠️ And the blue ring the report
mentions was the app's own: an `ACCENT_700` stroke, not egui's — a field only ever on screen *while*
focused has nothing to distinguish with it, so it is `ui::field_frame`'s `FIELD_BORDER` like every other
text box.

**Three things about *Recent*, which is the app's landing page and was quietly not one.** The header's
sort control did nothing there — an exemption with an argument (`recent()` is already ordered by when
this machine opened each document, so re-sorting makes it a second *All files*) that mistakes the *set*
for the *order*. The set is what makes Recent recent; a visible control that does nothing is worse than a
page ordered by name, and the exemption is gone. ⚠️ **Stated cost**: `Sort` has no *Last opened* to cycle
to, so "in the order I opened them" is no longer reachable — `Sort::Edited` is the default and is close
enough that the page reads right unopened. Projects with **no files** no longer get a card there
(`recent_projects`, which is `Projects::active` and a `file_count`): the sidebar must list an empty
project or it could never be filled, but a card carries a count and a *last touched*, and "0 files ·
Empty" is a picture of nothing to pick up. And ⚠️ **`Duplicate` now stamps its copy as opened here**,
because a duplicate made from *Recent* landed in the library and appeared nowhere the user was looking.
The alternative offered was dropping *Duplicate* from the ⋮ on that one nav; stamping is the better half
because `new_library_document` has never had this problem — it *opens* what it creates — so this is one
rule, spelled for the single action that creates a document without opening it.

**The star is filled now, and the entry above it was right about the wrong thing.** D365 recorded "an
outline star, because the bundled Phosphor is Regular weight only and a second font for one mark is not
worth it". Both halves are still true and the conclusion did not follow: bundling was never the only way
to fill a star. `star_shape` draws a ten-vertex `convex_polygon`, no asset. ⚠️ **A star is not convex and
that is fine** — `epaint` fans from the first vertex, and alternating radii keep every fan triangle
inside the outline. What made the outline wrong is the picture at 15pt over a thumbnail: a gold ring
whose hole is most of it.

**The *Delete project* card was busy and its confirm was grey.** The switch read "Delete its *n* file(s)
too — they move to Trash"; the reassurance is now cut, because *Delete* on a document already means the
trash everywhere on this screen and spelling it out made the loudest control on the card read as the
mildest. The folder line — "The folder “x” stays on disk — Ondin only removes the project" — is gone
entirely: true, an answer to a question nobody had asked yet, and the fourth block of prose on a card
whose job is one question and one switch; the folder surviving is the *harmless* outcome and a
confirmation should spend its words on what it is about to destroy. And the confirm is
**`FieldButton::Danger`**, a new fifth state: *Create project* and *Save changes* are filled blue, so the
button that removes a project with no trash to come back from is filled red, on a `DANGER_900`/`_700`/
`_200` ramp computed from `color::DANGER` by the accent ramp's own ratios rather than picked by eye. Two
grey buttons side by side, one of which deletes, is what this was.

**And four smaller ones.** The *New file in {project}* card's dashed outline was four straight lines
through the rect's corner *points* over a fill rounded to 9, so the ground curved away under a square
outline — `rounded_rect_path` samples the corners, and ⚠️ it works only because `Shape::dashed_line`
carries its dash phase across the whole polyline rather than restarting per segment (read out of
`epaint`'s `dashes_from_line`; a restart would put a dash at each of the twenty-eight points and draw a
solid line). The Settings card's *Base folder* row gained a folder icon button beside the field, same
row, same 28 — `panels::show_in_file_browser`, lifted out of `export.rs` where it started since two
panels now ask the same question, and **disabled while the typed path is not a folder that exists**,
which is the honest state for a control that opens one. The drop-import outline was drawn on
`ui.max_rect()` *inside* the central panel, i.e. the panel less its 20pt margin, so it sat in among the
headings and buttons; it takes the rect `CentralPanel::show` returns and is square, because a rounded
corner on a region boundary leaves four gaps against the sidebar and the window.

**Flip-checks: six run, and one of them corrected a test rather than confirming it.** Restoring the
every-frame `request_focus` fails at *"Enter closed the field"* — the honest site, since nothing was
renamed because nothing was committed. `Ui::put` fails the neighbour at 521 against 555. Justifying into
the full box fails at 255.5 against 258, which is the reported "few px" measured. Showing every active
project fails the card count at 2 against 1; dropping the duplicate's `mark_opened` fails with the list
the copy is missing from. ⚠️ **Exempting *Recent* from the sort failed at the wrong assertion** — the
`assert_ne!` rather than the `Sort::Name` one above it — because three documents stamped by
`mark_opened` land in the same second and `recent()` breaks that tie on the stem, so its order was
*already* alphabetical and the interesting assertion was vacuous. The fixture sets the opened times
backwards by hand now, and asserts that it did.

**D381 — Seven more from the same walk-through, and two of them undo decisions three days old. *Fixed
and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.***

**A click opens a document now, and D372 is mostly reversed.** *"The single click selection of files is
meaningless. That was copied from the design, but no need for it."* — and it was: nothing on the screen
ever *acted* on a pointer-made selection. Every action a card offers lives on its own ⋮ menu, so the
selection was a state the user could enter, could see and could do nothing with, and opening needed a
second click on top of it. `pick_or_open` opens; ⚠️ **`Response::double_clicked` is now read nowhere on
this screen**, because the first click of a double has already put the editor up. ⚠️ **D374's keymap
survives, and that was put to the maintainer rather than assumed** — the arrows, `Enter`, `Delete` and
`Escape` all had that same selection as their only subject, and "no selection outline" read literally
would have deleted them. The answer was *keep it as a keyboard-only cursor*: `DashboardState::selected`
is written **only** by `dashboard_keys` now, the accent outline draws for it, and the pointer never
touches it. Which makes the three border tiers *more* coherent than they were — the pointer can be
anywhere while the cursor sits where the keyboard left it, so hover and cursor genuinely coexist rather
than being two names for one click.

**And the sort on *Recent* went back the way it came, one turn later.** D380 made it *work* there
because a visible control that does nothing is a bug; the maintainer's answer was *"hide the sort control
