in Recent. That was my oversight."* — the control is the thing that does not belong. ⚠️ **The lesson is
the pairing, not the direction**: `sort_applies` is now one predicate read by the header and by
`visible_entries`, which is the shape `filter_applies` has had since D369 and the reason the *filter*
never had this bug. What made this reachable at all was that the sort's exemption lived in
`visible_entries` alone, with nothing stopping the button being drawn over it.

**A project card on *Recent* is a mosaic now.** The design draws one, the app drew a name and a count
under a band of the project's colour. Up to five covers, newest by `Entry::modified` first; the layout is
one rule — first cell takes a column at full height, the rest fill the columns after it two at a time,
⚠️ **and a column that ends up holding only one runs full height as well** — which reproduces all four of
`MOSAICS`' hand-authored layouts (one, two, three and five cells) and answers the four-cell case the
design has no entry for. One departure, stated: the design's first column is `1.25fr` in the three-cell
case and `1fr` in the other three; every column here is equal, because an exception for a single count is
a hand-tune rather than a rule. The arithmetic is the free `mosaic_cells` (D269), so the rule is asserted
without a frame — ⚠️ and the flip that matters is dropping the full-height-if-alone arm, which leaves the
one- and three-file cases green and fails at **two**, the layout that arm exists for. **The coloured band
is gone with it**: it was this file's own addition, argued as "the dot alone is 8px of signal on a 170px
card", which was true of a card that was a name and a count and is not true of one carrying five
pictures.

**The filled buttons had no hover at all.** `FieldButton::On` and the new `Danger` matched on `(state,
_)` and ignored `hovered` outright — deliberately, so a filled button would not fall through to the
neutral grey arm and go colourless under the pointer, and the cost was not noticed: *Create project*,
*Save changes* and *Delete project* were inert to the pointer in every modal on the screen. One step up
their own ramp each (`ACCENT_900` → `ACCENT_800`, and the new `DANGER_800`), **ground only** — the ink
stays put, because the danger ramp has no twin of `ACCENT_100` and a hover that brightens the text on one
button and not the other is the unevenness `button_face` exists to prevent.

**The star was reported as not looking great, and the fix is two constants.** The first drawn version was
a plain ten-vertex polygon: at 15pt that is thin-armed and needle-pointed, and the icon-font star it
stands in for is neither. `STAR_INNER` fattens the arms (0.42 → 0.5, away from the compass-drawn 0.382),
and ⚠️ **`STAR_ROUND` fillets every corner, points and valleys alike** — which is the one an icon font
gives for free and a polygon does not, and the thing the eye reads before it reads the proportions. The
fillet is capped at half the shorter edge, or a valley rounds past the corner beside it and
`convex_polygon`'s fan turns the self-crossing into a visible wedge.

**Three lines of prose and a colour.** *Delete file*'s confirm is `FieldButton::Danger`, so the two cards
that destroy something agree — which is the argument for that being a *state* rather than a colour
written at one call site. And the Settings card's *"Point this at a Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive folder and
the library syncs"* is gone: true, and an advertisement rather than an explanation — the field is
labelled and the button beside it opens what it names. That the base folder is syncable is why the whole
library is shaped as it is, and that belongs in `library::project` rather than over a text box.

**D382 — The keyboard's three blind spots. *Built and tested 2026-08-28; Keep.*** Three reports, and two
of them are the same complaint from opposite ends: a keyboard that can reach something it cannot see, and
a list it cannot reach at all.

**The search dropdown had no keyboard navigation.** *"I can't scroll up and down through results and
press enter."* The arrows move `DashboardState::search_row` and `Enter` takes the row it names — **every**
row, not only a document: a recent query refills the field and a project navigates, exactly as clicking
them does, because a list you can arrow through and then cannot act on is worse than no list.
⚠️ **The arrows are `consume_key`'d above the `TextEdit` rather than read after it.** The field holds
the caret the whole time the overlay is up, so an arrow it can still see is an arrow that moves the caret
to the start or end of the query — the text jumping about under the highlight the same key is supposed
to be moving. `consume_key` reads *and* removes, and it has to run before the widget is added.
⚠️ **`search_row` is an `Option` and `None` is not row zero.** Unsteered, the highlight sits on the first
*document* match, which is the rule `Enter` has followed since the field was built — *"opening a file is
the thing the field is for, and a project row is one click away with the answer visible"* — and the
recents and project groups above it change length with the query, so that default is recomputed rather
than remembered. It is cleared when the query changes, when a recent refills it, and when the overlay
opens.

**Modals had no focus-visible state.** *"I think tab works in modal forms. I just can't see where I'm
tabbing at."* — and it did: ⚠️ **`Sense::click()` is `CLICK | FOCUSABLE` in egui**, so every
`allocate_exact_size(.., Sense::click())` in this app — `button_face`, `switch_row`, the colour swatches
— has been in the tab order all along, whether or not anyone meant it to be. Read out of `egui::Sense`
rather than assumed, and it is why this needed no call-site changes. `ui::focus_ring` paints an accent
hairline `StrokeKind::Outside` whatever `Memory::focused` names, gated on a flag that `Tab` turns on and
any pointer press turns off — CSS's `:focus-visible`, and the gate is the whole feature: a ring on
whatever is focused would light every field the moment it was clicked, which is the thing browsers
stopped doing and which this app already suppresses by hand. **`settings::card` is a new wrapper over
`card_modal(id).show(..)` for one reason**: the ring has to be the *last* thing in the body, which makes
it exactly the call a new modal leaves out. The rect comes from `Context::read_response`, so it is last
frame's — one frame of lag on a ring nobody is watching move, against every caller having to report its
own rect.

**And the empty states no longer print the base folder.** The line was argued in D365 as the one empty
state about the *folder* rather than a filter — true of the cause and wrong about where the answer
belongs. A raw `C:\Users\…\.ondin` is the least readable thing on the screen, it is already in the
Settings card where it can also be *changed*, and it sat under a sentence that is usually right: most
empty lists are empty because the library is new.

⚠️ **Two findings from the probe, both about reading colours out of a modal.** The ring is drawn into a
`Modal`, which is an `Area`, and **an `Area` fades in** — the ring came out `#293451` at alpha 95 against
the `#6D8CD9` it was asked for, so an exact colour comparison on a single frame matched nothing at all.
The test pumps sixteen frames per measurement. ⚠️ **Eight was not enough and looked like it was**: the
"no ring before Tab" assertion passed against a build with the gate removed entirely, because the ring
was drawn and merely still tinted — found by the flip, not by the run, which is the argument for flipping
the case you believe is already covered. And ⚠️ **colour alone does not identify the ring**: the
sidebar's *New file* button is an accent hairline on a transparent rect at the same corner radius, and
counting by colour reported a ring on a card nobody had tabbed into. `StrokeKind::Outside` is what
separates them, and neither half is sufficient alone — `RectShape::filled` leaves `stroke_kind` at
`Outside` too, so every filled rect in the frame matches that half by itself.

**D383 — Four chords that had been waiting on a screen that already existed. *Built and tested
2026-08-28; Keep.*** `shortcuts.md` §8 carried `Ctrl+N` and `Ctrl+W` as *"wait on the dashboard"* from
before there was a dashboard, and §8a's own foot listed `F2` and `Ctrl+D` as the library's gap. The
dashboard landed on 2026-08-26 and nothing between the two dates said the premise had expired, which is
the failure mode `roadmap.md`'s own preamble describes — **an entry's premise rots faster than its ask,
and nothing recompiles when it does**. None of the four needed a mechanism that was not already there.

**`Ctrl+N` is one verb whose destination is computed at the door.** `new_library_document` no longer
reads anything ambient: the project is an argument, and the two doors compute it from what each of them
can see — `nav_project` from the nav being viewed, `open_document_project` from the open document's own
project. One rule, *the project in front of you*, spelled twice because "in front of you" is a
different fact on the two screens. ⚠️ **The alternative fails invisibly**: an editor that read the nav
would file into whichever nav the dashboard was left on, which may be a project the user has not
looked at this session and which nothing on the editor's screen names — a destination nobody can see
is the one wrong answer a file manager cannot fix by looking, since the file is not where it was made.

⚠️ **And neither door reads `OndinApp::view`, which was the first shape this took and is a trap.** That
field is exact in production — `OndinApp::ui` returns at the dashboard, so each screen's doors can only
fire on their own screen — and it is *not* exact under test: `OndinApp::headless` starts in
`View::Editor` and every probe in `panels::dashboard` draws the library without changing it. A branch on
it is therefore right in the app and answering for the wrong screen in every test that exercises it,
which is the worse of the two orders to get this wrong in. The version written first did exactly that
and the new test failed on its first assertion — the file landing at the root rather than in the
project the nav named. Passing the destination in makes the call site the witness, which is D269's
lesson again: **lift the decision to where the fact is, rather than reading ambient state and hoping
about the caller.**

**`Ctrl+W` is the walk back, not the window**, and that was put to the maintainer rather than assumed.
The app has one window and the library is what is behind a document, so it lands on
`go_to_dashboard` — autosave, drop the crash snapshot, re-scan — which is Figma's meaning of the chord.
⚠️ **The stated cost is that it is a fourth door onto the screen `Ctrl+O` already opens**: the two
differ in what the user is thinking, "take me to my files" against "I am done with this", and not in
where they arrive. The declined reading was the *window*, reusing `handle_close_request`'s unsaved-work
modal — which is what §8's "close is already guarded" had pointed at, and which is why the note was
worth reading before implementing rather than after. Recorded so the guard's existence is not mistaken
for a decision about the chord.

**`F2` and `Ctrl+D` are the ⋮ menu's *Rename* and *Duplicate* on the keys those verbs already have** —
`F2` renames a layer in §4 and `Ctrl+D` duplicates one, so this is one chord, one verb, two nouns.
`F2` fills the field from `Entry::display_name` rather than from the path, which is where the ⋮ reads
it: the display name is the stem with a sync client's conflict suffix taken off, and a field pre-filled
with the raw stem would hand the user that suffix back to save (D375).

**`Ctrl+R` was added the next day, because §4 binds *both* keys to renaming a layer and the library
had taken only one.** Reported as the last item on this change's own "noticed and left alone" list and
answered with *"bind ctrl+r too"* — the point being consistency between the two screens rather than
either key being unique, which is the same argument §4's own note makes for spending `Ctrl+R` on
rename instead of on Illustrator's rulers. ⚠️ **The two keys are read on opposite sides of the
`modifiers.is_none()` gate** — `F2` bare, `Ctrl+R` as a chord — and that is why the verb became a
function (`start_rename`) rather than a second arm: the trash refusal and the read of the display name
both live in it now, where two sites would have meant a rule one spelling obeyed and the other did
not. ⚠️ **Which then made the earlier flip-check stale, and it was re-run rather than re-read**: the
trash flip recorded here was against the arm the guard used to live on, and a flip is a claim about
the code as it stands. Re-run against `start_rename`, it fails at the **`F2`** assertion — the first
of the pair to reach the shared guard — rather than at the one the guard now sits closest to.

**Both are refused in the trash, through a new `in_trash` predicate that `can_open` now reads too.**
One fact, three rules: opening a trashed document puts the editor on a file the purge will delete
(D374), renaming one renames that same doomed file, and duplicating one is *Restore* without its
bookkeeping. ⚠️ **The flip on the duplicate half did not bite, and the finding is better than the
assertion would have been**: `Act::Duplicate` looks its subject up in `library.entries`, which does not
hold the trash, so a trashed duplicate was *already* inert by way of another module's scan. The guard
stays, because that silence is a coincidence of where the trash is kept rather than a decision about
what a trashed document may do. The asymmetry it exposed is the part worth keeping: `F2` reaches its
subject through the `entries` the keymap is **handed**, which in the trash *is* the trashed list, so
the same one-line omission is harmless in one verb and live in the other.

**The `modifiers.is_none()` guard was written to leave every chord on this screen free, and two of
them now are.** They are read *above* that gate rather than exempted inside it, so everything not
named is still refused by one line and a third chord costs one arm. In the editor's keymap both new
arms are `cmd_only && !m.shift`, like `Save` and `OpenSettings` — ⚠️ and the `!alt` half of `cmd_only`
is load-bearing rather than decorative for `W`, because **`Alt+W` is *align top*** one block below it.
`ctrl_n_makes_a_document_and_ctrl_w_closes_one` flips both: dropping `!m.shift` from `N` fails at
*"Ctrl+Shift+N is unspent and stays unspent"*, and weakening `W` to a bare `cmd` fails at *"Ctrl+Alt+W
belongs to neither row"* — while leaving the `Alt+W` assertion above it **green**, since align-top
needs `!cmd` and is untouched by a chord that has gained Ctrl. A test asserting only that align still
worked would have passed the broken build.

**Multiple selection is a decided non-goal as of today**, which is what takes `Ctrl+A` off §8a's gap
list rather than leaving it as work: *"we don't have multi-selection and I don't think we will"*. So
the four library verbs each take one document by design. `Home`/`End` are what is left there.

**D384 — The library's two parked questions, and what each of them was wrong about. *Built and tested
2026-08-28; Keep.*** `roadmap.md`'s *Files, library and storage* section carried exactly two open
items after the dashboard landed. Both are closed here, and **neither was the size the entry it came
from said it was**, which is the reason this is one entry rather than two.

**"A missing file is not marked missing" was asking about the wrong unit.** Its own premise says why:
documents cannot live outside the base folder, so there is no such thing as one file going missing on
its own — the thing that goes missing is **the library**, all of it, and the app could not tell that
from a library with nothing in it. A scan of an unplugged drive, a sync folder that has not mounted
and a folder renamed in Explorer all come back as an empty `Vec`, which is also what a fresh install
comes back as.

⚠️ **And the app did something with that emptiness, which is the part that makes this a bug rather
than a missing label.** `Library::refresh` calls `LocalIndex::retain_known` with the ids the scan
found, and that function drops every id it did not see — correct after a delete, and catastrophic
after a scan that could not look: one launch with the library offline takes every star on the machine,
permanently, the moment anything saves the index afterwards. The sweep is gated on the folder having
been *read* now, which is a second `read_dir` beside the walk (`scan::readable`) rather than a result
type threaded through it — every other error that walk meets is one it is right to drop, and this is
the only one that costs the whole list.

**`root_unavailable` is that reading **and** a witness**, because unreadable on its own is the
ordinary state of a fresh install: `~/.ondin` is created by the first write, not at launch. The
witness is `LocalIndex::is_empty` — a per-machine index with anything in it is this computer saying it
has opened or starred something here, so an empty scan is a *disagreement* rather than an answer. Both
of its sets count: a user who starred a document and never re-opened it has an empty `opened`, and one
whose stars were all on documents since deleted has an empty `starred`.

**Three consequences on screen, and the third is the one reading would not have predicted.** The empty
state answers before the nav does, in `WARN` rather than `FAINT`, because the four sentences under it
are each about a *filter* ("nothing starred", "the trash is empty") and each is a lie in this state.
The three doors that create a file — *New file*, *New project*, an import — refuse out loud
(`library_writable`), and ⚠️ **that guard is not belt-and-braces**: `store::file_document` begins with
a `create_dir_all`, so without it `Ctrl+N` on an offline library *succeeds*, into a brand-new empty
folder wearing the missing one's name, and the sync client that brings the real one back then has two
libraries to reconcile. The flip fails exactly there. And the dashed *New file in {project}* card is
not drawn (`new_file_into`), which matters because D376 had taken the empty state away from a project's
nav altogether — so without that gate the one nav that most needed the sentence would have shown a
promise instead. That flip fails at the **sentence**, not at the card, since the card takes the whole
branch.

⚠️ **And the witness has a hole that the guard turned into a dead end, found by reading the settings
path rather than by any test.** The per-machine index is keyed by document *id*, not by folder — so
"this machine has documents recorded" is true of the machine and not of the root being looked at, and a
user who points the base folder at a folder that does not exist **yet** gets a library that opens
unavailable and refuses every write, including the one that would have created the folder. Reachable
by typing a path, and permanent. `apply_library_settings` now creates the folder it is pointed at,
which is the honest reading of naming one as your library — `relocate` already did this for itself,
which is why only the non-migrating branch needed it. The flip fails at `may_write` and leaves the
`root` assertion above it green: the library does move, it simply cannot be used.

**"The `Created` column is UTC" priced one of its two options and parked on the other.** The entry was
right that correct local time needs the zone's *history* — a July stamp sits at a different offset
from a January one, and the rule itself changes by year — and right that this is "a dependency or a
platform call". What it did not notice is that the platform call was already paid for: `windows-sys`
has been a dependency since D241 for `GetCursorPos`, so this is one added feature flag
(`Win32_System_Time`), no new crate, and no second copy of the tz database.

`clock::local_offset` builds a `SYSTEMTIME` from the stamp, asks `GetDynamicTimeZoneInformation` for
the zone *including its registry key name*, and converts with `SystemTimeToTzSpecificLocalTimeEx` —
the `Ex` being the point, since it is the key name that the year-by-year rules hang off.
`days_from_civil` is new beside `civil_from_unix` to bring the answer back down to seconds. ⚠️
**`TIME_ZONE_ID_INVALID` is `u32::MAX` and every other return is a success**, `TIME_ZONE_ID_UNKNOWN`
included — a zone with no daylight saving is an answer, not an error. Off Windows the offset is zero,
i.e. exactly what the file did before.

⚠️ **The old test had to be moved off midnight, and that is the trap worth recording.**
`date_label(1_774_483_200) == "26 Mar 2026"` was exact while the label was UTC and became *a test of
the machine's timezone* the moment it was not — green in Europe, red in New York, for a function that
is right in both. It reads noon now, and `date_label` **clamps at the epoch** so `date_label(0)` is "1
Jan 1970" everywhere rather than 31 December 1969 west of Greenwich.

**What replaces it is written to be true in any zone, and was written from a measurement.** A probe
printed **3600** for 15 January 2026, **7200** for 15 July 2026 and 7200 again for July *2006* on the
machine this landed on — so the January/July difference is what a "current bias" implementation gets
wrong, and it is the assertion. The midnight test reads the offset and asserts what it *implies*, with
a probe either side of midnight so that one arm fires in any zone that is not UTC; ⚠️ **the flip that
proves it — making `date_label` ignore the offset — fails at the 23:30 arm and leaves the 00:30 arm
green**, because a positive offset never moves a stamp back a day. Both arms are there for that
reason, and the `else` names the zone it saw rather than passing quietly. The calendar round trip
(`civil_from_unix` ↔ `days_from_civil`, every day for sixty years) is the one part of this that needs
no machine at all.

**D385 — Frame size presets and layout grids, from a one-line entry. *Built and tested 2026-08-29;
Keep.*** `roadmap.md`'s canvas section carried *"No frame size presets, no layout grids (columns/rows
overlay)"* — the file's only one-line entry, and the whole specification there ever was. Both are
built; what follows is the design that line did not contain.

**A layout grid is chrome, and that decides almost everything else.** It is drawn over a frame and is
never in the artwork: no scene node, nothing in any export writer, nothing in the snapshot. So
`Operation::SetLayoutGrids` answers **false** to `changes_ink`, filed with the guide operations under
the sentence that list already had — *a guide is a line over the artwork rather than part of it* — and
`RenderOverrides::absorb` treats it as a no-op. ⚠️ **That took the pair from ten to eleven**, and the
doc comment on the test which pins them has been wrong about its own count once before (it said nine
while the `match` held ten). The fixture now **asserts its own length**, which is the only way a
number in prose becomes something a gate can read.

**The field is on the node; the offer is on the frame.** `Node::grids` sits beside `exports`: empty on
every layer until somebody adds one, skipped by the save format, ignored by every walk. That is
`clip`'s arrangement, and `clip`'s own note is the argument — a property of the *layer*, inert on
kinds nobody offers it for, rather than buried in one kind's payload where it would have to move out
again the first time a second kind wanted it. ⚠️ **What confines the offer is that a grid is measured
against an *authored* size**: `NodeKind::Artboard` has one, and a group's box is derived from its
contents, so a grid on a group would move whenever a child did. That is a reason to gate the panel and
not the field. **It is also the cheaper shape by an order of magnitude**, which is worth recording
because it did not decide the question and could have: a third field on the `Artboard` *variant* is a
sweep of some fifty construction sites, where a node field is seven.

**Nothing in the model is a mode with a payload.** `GridAlign` chooses which of the numbers are read —
*Stretch* derives the track size and reads both margins, *Start*/*End* keep the size and pin to one
edge, *Center* keeps the size and reads no margin at all — and every one of those numbers is a field
beside the mode rather than inside it. That is `mask_mode`'s rule: a value with nowhere to live while
its mode is unselected makes the switch quietly destructive, and a designer who sets a track size,
tries *Stretch* and comes back should find what they typed. The panel **dims** the fields an alignment
does not read rather than hiding them, which is `segmented_enabled`'s bargain one control over.

**The arithmetic is a free function and the clip is not.** `layout::tracks` reports what the grid
*says*, including a fixed run longer than the frame it is on; the overlay intersects each band with
the frame's own box — in **local** space, so a rotated frame's bands turn with it rather than being
cut by a screen-aligned clip. ⚠️ **Empty rather than clamped when the numbers do not fit**: a count of
zero, a NaN out of a half-typed field, or margins wider than the frame draw *nothing*, because a track
of negative width is not a thin track, it is a grid whose numbers do not fit the page.

⚠️ **The scrub is the third in this app that cannot preview, and the first whose value is on the
canvas.** `RenderOverrides` absorbs the operation, so `edit_valve` has nothing to preview and the
fields would re-read the committed number every frame; committing every frame instead makes the drag
uncancellable, since `cancel_gesture` undoes a scrub by dropping a preview. Both halves of that were
shipped and reported for the export panel's JPEG quality, and the answer here is the same one:
`OndinApp::grid_scrub` holds the in-flight grid, the panel reads it so the number moves, **the overlay
reads it so the bands move**, the release commits once, and `cancel_gesture` drops it by name — from
the cancel itself rather than from the panel's own check, because the canvas draws *before* the panels
and leaving it would put one frame of the cancelled grid on screen. One decision covers all four
numeric fields, so a scrub that crosses from Count into Gutter is still one undo step.

**Presets are the W and H fields filled in for you, and they read as well as write.** A frame matching
one shows its name; anything else reads *Custom*, in the dimmer ink because *Custom* is the absence of
a choice rather than one of them. ⚠️ **The match is exact and orientation-sensitive** — a phone on its
side is *Custom* — because matching either order would name a preset that applying would then silently
rotate. Print sizes are **points at 72/inch** (A4 = 595×842), which is the unit the fields already
show, this format having no notion of millimetres. Picking one writes `GeometryPatch::Size`, the same
patch the two fields write, so it cannot become a second definition of how big a frame is.

**Two things deliberately not built.** There is **no colour control** for a grid: the model carries
`color` and round-trips it, but every colour in that panel goes through `open_picker`, which is keyed
on a `PaintSlot` — a *paint* slot on a node — and a grid is not paint, so offering one means either a
slot naming something the document does not call paint or a second picker door. A gap rather than a
decision, and stated as one. And there is ~~**no global "show layout grids" toggle**: present mode is
the app's existing "show me the artwork" switch and already suppresses every overlay, so a second one
would be a second answer to one question.~~

⚠️ **That premise is false and is recorded as false here rather than quietly repaired, because the
repair is a ruling nobody has taken (read 2026-09-09).** Present mode hides the panels (`app::ui`'s
two `!self.present` blocks), the ruler bars and the guide lines (`rulers::rulers_on` / `guides_on`)
and these grids — and nothing else. `canvas_ui` runs under it in full, so the selection outline, the
handles, the size badge, the hover outline, the frame **name tags** and the snap guides are all still
drawn over the artwork: `chrome_hidden`, the one place the list of things that hide lives, has no
`present` term in it at all. `[S12.5-L2-01]` measured it as two overlays of a dozen. **The
suppression this paragraph decides is still right and only its *reason* is wrong** — a second toggle
would still be a second answer — but the sentence a later reader leans on is not true, and it is
repeated verbatim by `draw_layout_grids`' own comment and, in its strongest form, by `guides_on`'s
(*"present mode promises to hide every piece of chrome at once"*). **Record and code corroborate each
other and both are wrong**, which is the shape that survives longest.

🚨 **The ruling arrived on 2026-09-10 and it went the other way, so the suppression is gone and the
toggle question is *reopened* rather than answered** (D750). Present mode *"only hides the UI. The
canvas works as usual"*, so the grids stay on screen and `draw_layout_grids`' `if self.present {
return; }` is deleted. **There is now no global switch that takes a grid away at all**, which is a
different starting point from the one the struck sentence argued from: a per-frame *Show grid* was
declined **because** something else already answered the question, and nothing does. Whether the
feature wants a toggle of its own was genuinely open and was not decided by D750, which decided what
present mode is *for* and nothing about grids in particular.

🚨 **The maintainer answered it on 2026-09-15 and the struck clause above is now *closed* rather than
merely struck** (D755). *View ▸ Show layout grid* is the eighth row of the View menu, backed by
`OndinApp::show_layout_grids` and read by `draw_layout_grids` as an early `return` — the global
toggle this paragraph refused, built for the reason the refusal had rested on nothing since
`[S12.5-L2-01]`. ⚠️ **It is an outer gate and not a write over `LayoutGrid::visible`**, so the
per-grid eye the Layout grid card shows (D387) stays exactly as the designer left it and the switch
costs no undo step. The *other* thing this paragraph records as not built — the colour control — is
not reopened here and was closed by D387 the same day.

⚠️ **The flip-check paragraph below is
one suppression short since**: *"removing the present-mode guard fails at its own assertion while
leaving the other two green — which is why the three suppressions are one test rather than three"*
now describes **two suppressions and an inversion**. The test is
`a_hidden_grid_and_a_hidden_frame_draw_nothing_and_present_mode_draws_anyway`, and its present-mode
case is kept and turned over rather than deleted: the assertion that a grid *still draws* is what
fails if somebody reinstates the guard on the strength of the struck sentence. **Deleting the case
would leave the reinstatement ungated.**

⚠️ **And the one-line fix is not the drawing-only change it looks like, which is why this is the
maintainer's.** Nothing on the *input* path reads `chrome_hidden`: `frame_label` gates its tag on
`shown_visible`, and `chrome_claims` asks `on_pivot`, `line_ends`, `grab_rail_handle` and
`Handles::armed`. So folding `present` into `chrome_hidden` hides the box and the handles and leaves
them **armed** — invisible and still clickable — and does not touch the name tag at all, which
`draw_frame_labels` paints ahead of that gate. The shape that works is `rulers_on`'s: one predicate
both the paint and the hit test go through, which is D136's own arrangement and the reason its
comment says the bars being absent must mean the same thing to both. *Fix with* the ruling on whether
Present mode makes the canvas **inert** as well as clean, not with the folded term.

**Flip-checks, and one of them corrected the prose rather than confirming it.** In `tracks`,
subtracting one margin instead of two was predicted to fail at the *last edge* — the run overshooting
the far margin — and fails one assertion earlier, at the **width**, because a division handed more
room to share is wrong at every track and not only at the end of the run. Both assertions bite; what
was wrong was which one a reader should treat as load-bearing. In the overlay, dropping the buffer
read fails at *"the in-flight count is what is drawn"* with the committed 4 against 7, and removing
the present-mode guard fails at its own assertion while leaving the other two green — which is why the
three suppressions are one test rather than three.

**D386 — The chrome's hairline was resolved against the wrong ground, and its rhythm was seven
numbers. *Fixed and tested 2026-08-29; the outline is reviewed and accepted.*** Two audits in one
session, both of them started from a report that turned out to be about something other than what it
named, and both settled by measurement rather than by reading.

**The first report was "the fields have no border", and every field had one.** The ask was to compare
`design/` against the app and add the hairline everywhere it was missing. What answered it was a
throwaway probe that dumped every rounded `RectShape` the chrome paints with a ground and **no stroke
over it** — the inspector with a rect and with text, the colour picker, Settings, the dashboard, and
the *New project* and *Library settings* modals. Six naked grounds in the whole app, five of them
switches. Every field, every button, the filter, the search field and every modal input already had
the stroke. ⚠️ **The probe's first version found six that were not there**, because `rect_filled`
followed by `rect_stroke` is *two* `RectShape`s and a fill with no stroke on it is the normal case; it
has to pair them by rect before a bare ground means anything.

**What was actually wrong is the colour, and it is a CSS reading.** The design writes the hairline as
`border: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-text) 8%, transparent)` on a box whose `background`
is already `text 5%`, and CSS paints a background *under* the border area — `background-clip:
border-box` is the default — so a translucent border composites over the element's **own** ground
rather than over what the element sits on. `theme::color::FIELD_BORDER` resolved that 8% against the
card: `0.08·233 + 0.92·37 = 52.7`, which is **six levels** above the 47 it outlines. Read as the
design draws it, `0.08·233 + 0.92·47 = 61.9`, and blue `0.08·237 + 0.92·48 = 63.1`. The reported
symptom was *"so dim I thought it wasn't even there"*, which is exactly what six levels of separation
on a 1px line looks like. **`CARD_BORDER` keeps the old 53** for the three strokes that enclose a
*card* ground — the project and file cards and the *New file* slot's dashed outline — because the
design's own rule makes a translucent border brighter the brighter its ground, so those two numbers
are the rule rather than a disagreement; folding them together would give a resting card a lit edge,
which is what hover already means.

**The one control class genuinely missing its border was the segmented track**, and `design/` is
inconsistent about it: of twenty-two segmented controls in the Editor mock, **twenty are bare** and
the two with a hairline are the Type panel's align strips — the two that sit in a row beside a
bordered 28pt button. The app now draws it on all of them, translucent (`text_a(20)` over the track's
own `text_a(13)` ground, which composites to the same 62) so it works on a card, in a popover and in
the dashboard header alike. The cells give up the border's width on both sides, which makes a 28pt
control the design's `1 + 2 + 22 + 2 + 1` rather than `2 + 24 + 2`. ⚠️ **A track paints two shapes on
one rect now**, and two existing tests were counting shapes: `the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height`
read the tab strip's ground and its hairline as two controls and reported *"the fixture is not a
column"*. **Sliders, switches and the Align row's buttons stay bare**, which is what the design draws
and what the app already did.

**The second report was about spacing, and explicitly not to be checked against `design/`.** The
Transform card is the baseline: X beside Y is `7`, X/Y above W/H is `9`. The same probe, re-aimed at
gaps between adjacent controls, found the inspector's own cards clean at 7 and 9 throughout — and
four other rhythms around them. **The Fill, Stroke, Effects and image-edit rows ran at 6 across**,
directly under Transform in the same column. **The type and stroke popovers stacked two controls of
one section 5 apart**, against the card's 9. **Image editing's card had a pitch of 10.** And
`POPOVER_SECTION_GAP` was a tenth number at 10, invisible where an eyebrow stands between two sections
and not invisible in the stroke popover's dash block, where there is no eyebrow and it *is* the gap
between two controls.

**`ui::CARD_COL_GAP` is the horizontal twin of `CARD_ROW_GAP`, and naming it is half the fix.** ⚠️ The
gap is spelled **twice per row** — once as `item_spacing.x` and again inside the row's own width
arithmetic, `(available_width() - GAP) / 2.0` — so changing only the spacing pushes the last control a
point past the card and `Ui::horizontal` wraps it onto a line of its own. Fifteen rows had been
written at 6 and twenty-four at 7; all thirty-nine read the constant now, `BOOL_ROW_GAP` and
typography's `GAP` included.
⚠️ **That count was two rows short.** `stroke_properties` and `mixed_stroke_properties` both kept a
literal `6.0` in the weight field's width — in the very row this entry singles out above as having
run at 6 — and were found by `[S14.3-L3-06]` and fixed under **D637**, with a test pinning the two
rows of a stroke unit against each other. The sweep was right about the rule and wrong about the
count.

**The popover's vertical compression is reversed, and that was a decision with its reasoning written
down.** `typography::COL_GAP` carried a paragraph arguing that the popup takes the mock's vertical
compression whole — 5 down against the card's 9 — while matching the card exactly across, and called
*one axis compressed and one matched* the rule. Its only support was the mock, and the instruction
that replaced it was explicitly not the mock. `ui::labelled` is what makes the two gaps two numbers: a
section's eyebrow sits `SECTION_LABEL_GAP` (5) above what it names, and two controls of one section
sit `CARD_ROW_GAP` apart. `CELL`'s 26 against `ROW_H`'s 28 is the compression that survives, being a
height rather than a gap.

**Flip-checks.** The segmented hairline: removing the stroke fails at the hairline lookup; leaving the
cells at `shrink(PAD)` fails on the cell **height**, 24 against 22, and not on its position — a test
checking only that the cell starts inside the track would have passed the version that lays it on the
border. The rhythm test: putting the paint row back to 6 was predicted to fail on the stroke's
four-control line and reports **four** gaps, none of them that line — the fill and stroke rows, which
share one helper and are drawn first. ⚠️ **And one flip failed to bite, which is the finding of the
two.** Putting `IMAGE_CARD_GAP` back to 10 fails **nothing in the workspace**. Its doc named
`the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height` as the guard, and that test *reads* the constant —
deliberately, so the fixture follows the card. A fixture that reads the number it is checking cannot
check the number: it is green for every value. The image card needs a decoded texture before it draws
at all, so no probe here can measure it either, and what stands in is an equality against
`CARD_ROW_GAP` — a statement rather than a measurement, and labelled as one.

**Then two things the same audit had reported and left alone, taken up on the maintainer's word.**
**Popover controls are 28**, like everything else. Three constants in three files carried the same
argument — *shorter than the card's 28px fields, which is what keeps a popup of nine sections from
towering over the panel it belongs to* — and the mock draws it that way; the picker was a fourth at 26.
Overruled, because a popover hangs *beside* the card it opened from at the same width, so a control two
points shorter than the one that opened it is a difference nothing on screen explains. `ui::CONTROL_H`
is the one number, `SEGMENT_CELL_H` is what a `segmented` track is handed to paint that tall, and the
short controls left are the ones that are not fields: a swatch chip, a badge, the layers tree's rows.

⚠️ **And the stroke's per-side rows had no vertical pitch at all, for a reason worth stating: a scope
cannot supply the gap before its own first item.** `stroke_sides_row` states `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` on a
scope, which is correct and covers nothing — the scope holds one item, the sides combo, and what sits
between that scope and the align/width line above it is `paint_unit`'s deliberate zero. The two rows of
per-side widths are drawn *outside* that scope again, so they inherited the zero twice over. Three
flush joins from one missing idea. The fix is two `add_space` calls and a second scope.

**Flip-checks, one of which found a hole in the test rather than in the code — after three tries.**
Removing the per-side pitch left the rhythm test green, and the reason was in the test: the failure is
two rows *flush*, a gap of exactly zero, and its guard read `g > 0.0`, written to skip the negative gaps
two overlapping surfaces produce and skipping the one case it existed for along with them. Fixing that
surfaced two more cross-surface artefacts in the same run — a popover control and a panel control at one
y read as a **pair 551 points apart**, and two rows a point apart in y read as **stacked** when they are
two surfaces passing each other. Both settle on x: same row only if adjacent, stacked only if the two
rows overlap in their columns. With those in, the flips land where they should — the per-side pitch
reports three joins at 0.0, its leading gap one more, and `typography::CELL` back to 26 reports fourteen
controls at 26.0 across the three tabs. ⚠️ **One test went stale rather than failing usefully**: the
effects meter fixture picked its bar by the literal band `20.0..26.0`, right for a 26pt field's content
box and off the top of it at 28, so it failed at `expect` claiming the row draws no meter at all. It
reads `ui::CONTROL_H - ui::FIELD_BORDER_H` now.

⚠️ **`design/` regenerated mid-session**, at 03:16, between the first read and the audit built on it.
It gained the frame-preset and layout-grid cards D385 had just built and dropped the *Edit project*
description field; no border or spacing rule moved. The audit was re-run against the new files. The
lesson is the one already recorded about that folder — read the content, and re-read it, because a
number reasoned from an earlier read is a number about a file that no longer exists.

**D387 — The presets became a panel, and the grid got the colour control D385 recorded as a gap.
*Built and tested 2026-08-29; Keep.*** Four asks off the back of D385 and D386, and the one that
looks smallest — "make the spacing consistent with the other panels" — is the one D386's sweep had
missed, because the Layout grid panel had landed hours after the sweep ran.

**A dropdown of eighteen sizes is a list you have to already know the contents of.** `frame_preset_row`
was a `ComboBox` under W and H; `inspector_frame_templates` is a card of pictures, two across, five
eyebrow groups in a scroll box. The same eighteen entries laid out as shapes is a list you can *choose
from*, and choosing is what the control is for. What it costs is a card in the column, which is why it
collapses like every other and why the box is capped at `TEMPLATE_LIST_H` (184) rather than letting
five groups push Transform below the fold — landing between two rows deliberately, since a cut-off cell
is what says there is more under it. ⚠️ **A cell is painted rather than assembled from
`ui::button_face`, and the difference is exactly one state**: a resting cell has *no ground at all*
where every field button in the app has `color::FIELD`, because eighteen grounds in a scroll box is a
wall of buttons. The other three states are `button_face`'s own inks, so a lit cell and a lit button
stay the same mark, and anyone folding the two together should know that the resting state is the whole
reason they are apart. The name is elided against the galley that will actually be painted — the column
leaves about 86 points and *"iPhone 16 Pro Max"* needs 92, so **exactly one entry in the table elides**,
measured rather than guessed, and the tooltip is where it can be read whole.

**The table went from fourteen entries to eighteen, and the fourth new one is a decision.** Two across
means an odd group leaves a hole, so every group has an even count. The design's own list would have
made nineteen and carried a **duplicate box** — a *Wide 1920* under Desktop and a *Slide 16:9* under
Social, both 1920×1080 — and only one of the two is in the table, because `preset_named` answers with
the first match: a duplicate is a cell that can never be lit, and applying the loser lights the winner.
`frame_grid_tests::every_preset_names_itself_and_anything_else_is_custom` had walked the whole table for
exactly this since D385, which is why the entry was caught while it was being typed rather than seen on
screen.

**Templates and Layout grid are now the second and third panels, above Align and Transform**, which is
where the design puts them and the order the work is done in: what kind of page this is, then what it is
divided into, then where things sit on it. Layout grid used to sit under *Frame background*, between it
and Stroke. ⚠️ **Templates above Transform, though a template writes W and H** — that is the argument
for the old arrangement, and what it cost was a panel of visual sizes buried four rows into a card about
position and rotation. The read-back is what makes the separation safe: the panel says which template
the frame *is*, so the two cannot silently disagree.

**"Make the spacing consistent with the other panels" was one bug and one near miss.** `grid_rows` added
`ui.add_space(4.0)` *on top of* the card's nine between every row, so a five-row grid ran at 13 in a
column of panels running at 9 — the defect as reported, in a panel D386's sweep never saw. And
`GRID_ROW_GAP` was a literal 10, putting 19 between two grids where the stroke list puts 18. Both read
`ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` now, so two grids sit at twice the pitch like two strokes.

**The eye had the accent wash on the *ordinary* state.** It was `FieldButton::on_if(grid.visible)`, so a
panel of two grids drew its loudest mark on the thing that is true of every grid by default and said
nothing at all about the one that had been switched off. It is `FieldButton::Off` in both states now,
with the glyph carrying the state (`EYE` / `EYE_SLASH`) — which is what the Fill, Stroke and Effects rows
already spell. ⚠️ **The consequence is `ui::disable_unless`, not the `multiply_opacity` fade those rows
use, and that is a deliberate departure with a stated cost**: the maintainer asked for "disabled and
dimmed", so a hidden grid's axis, colour, numbers and alignment do not answer the pointer at all. The
eye and the ✕ stay live — everything that *describes* the grid goes out together, and the two controls
that decide whether there is a grid at all do not, or the eye would be a switch with no way back. If the
paint rows are ever brought into line, this is the half to move, not the other one.

**A grid's colour is `PaintSlot::Grid(usize)`, and D385's note about why it could not be was half
right.** That note argued that `open_picker` is keyed on a *paint* slot and a grid is not paint, so a
control would need either a slot naming something the document does not call paint or a second picker
door. The slot turned out to be the ordinary answer rather than an invention — `PaintSlot` already
carried five members naming things that are not fills, and a shadow's colour is the same shape of thing
exactly. What the note got right is that a grid is **chrome**, and that is what the feature actually
cost: a preview fork, not a slot. The row is `slot_color_row`, which is `effect_color_row` given a slot,
a size and a tooltip — one row, two callers, nothing between them to drift. `takes_gradients` is false
(`LayoutGrid::color` is one `Color` and the bands are flat convex polygons), and the alpha in the slot
**is** the wash's strength, exactly as D333 has a shadow's opacity be its alpha; there is no second
field for the two to disagree about.

⚠️ **This is `preview_guide`'s situation a second time, and the second buffer is deliberate.**
`RenderOverrides` absorbs `SetLayoutGrids` as a no-op, so `edit_valve` and `preview_slot` both fork to
`OndinApp::preview_grid`, which fills `grid_paint` — `Option<(NodeId, usize, Color)>` as written here,
and a `Vec<NodeId>` since **D389** took the panel to a selection of frames; the canvas applies
it **after** `grid_scrub`, `cancel_gesture` drops it, and `write_slot` clears it on commit. It is a
second buffer over the same grid on purpose: `grid_scrub` is the numeric fields' own, and a colour
dropped there would be read on the next frame by `grid_step` as a finished field edit and committed once
a frame. So `preview_grid` takes **only a colour change** out of the transaction — found by comparing
the list against the committed one, since `SetLayoutGrids` has no per-entry shape — and skips a list
whose length has changed, the indices no longer lining up. The two buffers must not write into each
other, and that rule is the one a simplification would break first.

**`remap_effect_slots` is now `remap_slots(anchor, mapper)` with two callers**, the second being
`remap_grid_slots`, called when a grid's ✕ removes a row. The failure it prevents is the silent one: a
picker open on `Grid(1)` after grid **0** is removed stays in range and quietly edits a different grid,
which is the one way an index-keyed slot goes wrong without closing.

**Flip-checks, and two of them are worth carrying.** Restoring a single `ui.add_space(4.0)` after
`grid_rows`' first `horizontal` was predicted to fail four gaps at 13.0 and fails **three** — one row in
each block, since one call moves one row and not the set; the failures name the row, so a partial
regression is legible rather than reading as a wholesale one. Making `preset_named`'s comparison
order-insensitive fails `the_templates_panel_lights_the_frames_own_size_and_nothing_else` at *"a landscape
phone lit a portrait template"* as predicted, and **also** fails the table's own walk with *"Story does
not answer to its own size"* — unordered, *Full HD* (1920×1080) and *Story* (1080×1920) are one entry
and *Full HD* is in the earlier group. Order-insensitivity is not merely a wrong answer for landscape
frames; it collides two entries that are distinct today. The colour's two flips both bit where
predicted: dropping `preview_grid`'s colour condition fails at *"a field edit wrote into the picker's
preview buffer"*, and widening `slot_transaction`'s `Grid` arm to every entry — the widening the
`Effect` arm above it really does make — fails at *"the write reached the other grid too"* and nowhere
else. The visibility test is measured against the **empty card** rather than a literal, so it stays true
if the header grows a third control; dimming instead of disabling reports *"answers on 15 controls of
its own, out of the 17 a visible one has"*.

**D388 — A new grid steps the hue, and the ramp's order is not the wheel's. *Built and tested
2026-08-30; Keep.*** The first item on D387's own noticed-and-left-alone list: a second grid got the
same default red, so two grids on one frame started indistinguishable and the colour control D387 had
just built was what a designer had to reach for before either grid said anything about itself. What
held it back was that it changes what *add a grid* looks like — a default that varies with what is
already there is a default somebody has to notice — and the maintainer picked it off the list.

**Six hues of one colour, not six colours.** `layout::GRID_COLORS` is `DEFAULT_GRID_COLOR` rotated
round the wheel by multiples of 60° at its own saturation (0.724), its own value (0.639) and its own
alpha (`0x26`), so a frame carrying four grids carries four washes of one weight rather than a red one
and three louder ones. **Entry 0 *is* the constant, bit for bit**, which is what keeps the ordinary
single-grid frame unchanged and keeps the family resemblance with the guides that constant's own note
argues for — the hue is the thing that says a guide and a grid are one kind of thing, and it still is
everywhere it was ever visible. Six because that is where 60° runs out; both the array and the rule
below are re-exported from `ondin_core`'s root beside the constant.

⚠️ **The order is not the wheel's, and that is the whole design.** Laid out by hue the ramp would go
red, olive, green, cyan, blue, magenta, and the **second** grid — a column grid beside a row grid,
which is the ordinary reason to have two at all — would be an olive 60° from the first. So it visits
the thirds first (red 3°, green 123°, blue 243°) and the halfway points only after them (olive 63°,
cyan 183°, magenta 303°): two grids are 120° apart, three are 120° apart, and the step narrows only
once there are more grids than anybody puts on a page. The count that matters is two, and it is the
one a wheel-ordered ramp serves worst. *Sorting those six literals into wheel order is the tidy-up
this entry exists to stop.*

**`next_grid_color(existing)` answers with the first entry nobody is using, not the entry at the new
grid's index.** Indexing by position is the obvious spelling and it fails a flow a designer walks on
the way to getting a grid right: add two grids, delete the first, add another, and both on the frame
are entry 1 — a duplicate wash, which is the one outcome the feature exists to prevent. Asking what is
*in use* answers that, and it does the right thing for a file the app did not author as well: a grid
whose colour is nobody's entry blocks nothing, so the ramp still starts at the top. ⚠️ **Past six it
repeats rather than refusing**, stepping by `existing.len() % 6` so two added in a row past the sixth
still differ. A frame with every hue in use has more grids than a 15%-alpha band can tell apart, and
the honest answer there is a duplicate colour on a control the user can change — not an error, and not
a seventh wash that only looks distinct in the panel.

**Only the panel's `+` steps.** `inspector_layout_grids` pushes `LayoutGrid { color:
ondin_core::next_grid_color(&grids), ..LayoutGrid::new(axis) }`, directly under the axis guess it now
matches in shape — *Columns for the first, rows for the second* — and for the same argument one step
over: the reason to add a second grid is to read it against the first. `LayoutGrid::new` still carries
the plain `DEFAULT_GRID_COLOR`, which is what a grid built anywhere else — a loaded file, a test
fixture — should get, and is why this is a rule about one panel rather than a change to the model.

**Two tests, and the assertion with teeth is not the one about hues.**
`the_grid_ramp_is_one_wash_at_six_angles_and_starts_with_the_thirds` checks entry 0 against the
constant, the two 120° separations and that every pair is at least 60° apart — but the load-bearing
assertion is that every entry shares the base's saturation, value and alpha, because six *distinct*
hues is what any six colours somebody liked would give, and what makes this a ramp is that they are
one wash at six angles. A hand-picked palette passes a distinctness check and fails that one. It
carries a local `hsv` helper, core having no colour model beyond `peniko::Color`'s components. ⚠️ **The
flip is the tidy-up**: swapping entries 1 and 3 toward wheel order fails at *"two grids are 60° apart"*
and **nothing else in the workspace notices** — the cost of that edit lands on the second grid a
designer adds and nowhere a compiler looks. In `a_new_grid_takes_the_first_colour_the_frame_is_not_using`
the case the rule exists for is delete-then-add: two grids, the first removed, a third added, where an
index by list length hands back the entry still on the frame. ⚠️ **It is not the only assertion that
catches that spelling, and the test's own doc comment says it is** — the hand-picked-colour case fails
an index too, from the other side (one grid, length 1, and the ramp should still start at the top),
while the three straightforward cases and both repeat-past-six cases pass under one. *Fix the comment,
not the test*: the second case is the one that protects a file somebody else made.

**D389 — The Layout grid panel finds its own subject, opens when it fills, and takes a selection of
frames. *Built and tested 2026-08-30; Keep.*** Three asks, and the first of them is the shape of the
other two. Clicking the `+` on a collapsed Layout grid card added a grid and left the card shut, so
the button did nothing anybody could see — every other panel here rests closed while it is empty, and
this one had taken half that rule: it closed and never reopened. The `+` adds **and** opens now, and
deleting the last grid closes it again. The empty card's words went from *"No grid"* to *"No layout
grid"*, which is the phrase the card's own title uses.

**Self-collapsing costs a fourth latch field, and the count is the finding rather than the field.**
It goes through the existing `sync_paint_collapse`, with `grids_synced_selection` and
`grids_subject_changed` beside Fill/Stroke's, Export's and Effects'. Each panel needs its own because
the edge is **consumed** by whoever asks first, so two callers in one frame lose it for one of them —
which of them would depend on the order they happen to be drawn in. Four is not yet worth folding into
a map keyed by panel title; a fifth would be, and the field's own doc says so rather than leaving the
next author to re-derive it. ⚠️ **A disagreement counts as *not* empty**, so a mixed selection opens
the card. The sentence in it is the whole point of the state, and a message nobody can see explains
nothing.

**The panel asks the selection what it is acting on, where every other frame panel is handed a node.**
`inspector_layout_grids(ui)` takes no id at all; `grid_subjects` — renamed `frame_subjects` the same
day, when *Frame templates* became its second caller (D390) — is the selected **artboards** in
document order, and empty for everything else, which is what draws nothing. That is `inspector_export`'s
shape and it is what lets **one call serve both** `inspector_single` — under *Frame templates*, which
is still the kind-gated one — and `inspector_multi`, where it is the second panel, directly under the
identity card. ⚠️ **The subject list is *filtered*, not all-or-nothing**: a selection that caught a
rectangle on its way round three frames still means the three frames, and a panel that vanished
instead would leave the user hunting for what disqualified it. Nothing that could have taken a grid is
silently skipped — a rectangle has no authored box to measure one against, which is §5.3b's own rule.
**There was deliberately no *Frame templates* panel for a multi-selection**: resizing *n* frames to one
template is a coherent thing to want and nobody had asked for it, so the panel that writes W and H
stayed a single frame's. ⚠️ **That clause survived the same day and is now D390's**, which is where the
argument for the panel is — the reasoning here was sound and the fact under it moved the moment
somebody asked, and what the measurement then found is that Transform's W and H over a selection are
not the same operation at all.

**Over several frames it is the Export panel's pattern, and it is the second instance rather than a
new rule.** No frame has a grid: the card rests closed, says *No layout grid* when opened, and adding
writes one grid to all of them. Every frame holds the same list: the card shows it, and changing,
deleting or adding reaches all of them in one transaction and one undo step. Any frame differs: the
card is shown **open**, says *Mixed layout grids. Add to override.*, draws no rows, and the `+`
replaces every frame's list with the single grid it seeds. Appending to each frame's own list is the
careful-looking answer and it is a dead end — the frames still disagree, so the card repeats the same
sentence with one more grid behind it and nothing reachable from inside the card resolves the state,
which is exactly the argument D274 made for exports. The `+`'s tooltip is three-way for the same
reason, so the destructive click says what it is before it happens.

`shared_grids(&subjects)` is `shared_exports` in shape and reads the **committed** document, which
here is not a preference: `Operation::SetLayoutGrids` is a no-op in `RenderOverrides`, so there is no
preview tree to read a list out of and `DisplayNode` does not even offer a `grids` accessor. The two
writes are `write_grids` — one list to every subject, one transaction, one undo step, because giving
four frames a twelve-column grid is one act — and `append_grid`, which reads each subject separately
even though the selection agrees, that being the honest spelling of an append and costing nothing when
the lists match.

⚠️ **The `+`'s decision is the free function `grid_add(shared: Option<&[LayoutGrid]>) -> GridAdd`, and
the extraction was earned by a flip-check that *passed*.** `GridAdd` is `Append(LayoutGrid)` or
`Write(LayoutGrid)` — two verbs rather than a bool and a grid, because they are not one act done to
different lists: one adds to what is there and the other throws it away, and a caller holding a bool
has to remember which way round it goes. The rule first lived inside the button's `if` and the test
spelled the seed and the choice out for itself, so making the disagreeing case append — the exact
mistake the rule exists to prevent — left every assertion green. A rule a test restates is a rule
nothing checks. `None` is the disagreement, and the seed is then guessed against *nothing*, which
comes out `Columns` at the head of the ramp and is right because the click is about to make it the
only grid on every frame.

**D387's colour write widened to the selection, and its own comment had said in as many words that it
deliberately did not.** That comment argued the effect arm's widening was safe because an effects
card's subject *is* the selection where this card's was one frame — and the premise stopped being true
the day the panel took a multi-selection. `slot_transaction`'s `PaintSlot::Grid` arm now emits one
`SetLayoutGrids` per grid subject. **The reasoning survived and the fact underneath it moved**, which
is the only reason a comment like that is worth writing at all; it has been rewritten in place to say
so rather than deleted. ⚠️ The load-bearing half is still the premise: the rows are drawn only where
the frames **agree**, so `subjects[0]` is a safe anchor for `PaintSlot::Grid(i)` and the anchor's list
is every subject's list. A panel that drew a row over a disagreement would silently recolour a grid
nobody was looking at, which is why the mixed state has a sentence and no rows.

⚠️ **Both preview buffers were re-keyed from one node to a list of frames**: `grid_scrub: Option<(Vec<NodeId>,
usize, LayoutGrid)>` and `grid_paint: Option<(Vec<NodeId>, usize, Color)>`. Without that a drag over
five frames previews on one and commits to five — the bands under the hand moving while the rest jump
on release — which is the failure a selection-wide write makes possible and a single-frame panel never
could. The canvas asks membership (`contains`) rather than equality, so a frame is previewed if it is
one of the subjects. `preview_grid` **gathers** the transaction's ops rather than letting the last one
win, a colour write being one op per frame; ops that disagree with the first about the index or the
colour are dropped, because the panel only draws rows where the frames already agree, so a
disagreement there means this is not the transaction it looks like. The rule D387 set — that only a
*colour* change is taken out of the transaction, found by comparison, and a list whose length changed
is skipped — is unchanged, and is still the thing that keeps the picker's buffer and the fields' out
of each other.

**Tests, and one of them would have passed while comparing two different things.** The new fixture is
`frames_with_lists` — three frames **and a rectangle**, all selected — which is what makes the
`frame_subjects` filter observable at all rather than assumed away, and `grid_panel_pass` draws the
panel four times and reports what the card said and whether it is collapsed; it drives the `+`
**through `grid_add`**, not through a copy of it, which is the whole of the flip above.
`a_multi_selection_of_frames_agrees_disagrees_or_has_nothing` walks the three states, and its doc
carries three flips. `grid_add`'s `None` arm returning `Append` fails at *"the + over a disagreement
appended instead of overriding"* — and passed before the extraction. `frame_subjects` dropping its
`Artboard` filter fails at *"the rectangle is a subject"*, the **third** assertion, where the closing
*"a layer with no authored box was given a layout grid"* was predicted: that one would have caught it
too, and the subject list is compared first and names the rule rather than the symptom. And
`sync_paint_collapse` handed a constant `false` fails at *"an empty panel should rest closed"*.
⚠️ The pre-existing `switching_a_grid_off_leaves_only_its_eye_and_its_x_live` needed an explicit
`collapsed_panels.remove` in its loop, and **would have gone on passing without one**: its empty
baseline is now a *collapsed* card measured against two open ones, and a collapsed card's whole
surface is one target beside its `+`, so it still counts 2. Green for the right number and the wrong
comparison is the shape this project's flip-checks exist to catch.

**D390 — *Frame templates* over a multi-selection, and the measurement that reversed D389's last
clause. *Built and tested 2026-08-30; Keep.*** D389 closed with the panel left out on the grounds that
resizing *n* frames to one template is coherent and nobody had asked for it; the maintainer read that
and asked. What settled it was not the ask, though, but a measurement, because the assumption under
"coherent and unasked" was that the capability already existed through Transform's W and H and that a
templates panel would merely be a nicer door onto it. It does not exist. Over a multi-selection
`inspector_multi_transform`'s W and H report the **union** box and go through `tools::resize_selection`
with `Handle::BottomRight`, which scales the selection as a **rigid body** and takes every frame's
contents with it — so typing `393` into W with four phone frames selected squashes the whole
arrangement into a 393-wide box rather than making four iPhones. `GeometryPatch::Size`, which is what a
template writes, sets the frame's own `size` field and leaves its children alone. **There was no way in
the app to say "make each of these four frames 393×852."** So the panel is not a convenience over an
existing capability; it is the only door onto a missing one, and that is what turned the answer from
"coherent but unasked" into "yes, and it is the interesting half".

**The shape is D389's, one panel over.** `inspector_frame_templates(ui)` takes no node and no size, asks
`frame_subjects()` like the grid card, and draws nothing where the selection holds no frame. It is
drawn from `inspector_single` — where it is no longer gated on `artboard_bg`, both frame panels
self-gating now — and from `inspector_multi`, second and third under the identity card in both.
**`grid_subjects` became `frame_subjects`**: two panels want the same rule, "which frames is this card
about" is one question, and two spellings of it would drift the first time one of them learned about a
new kind. `shared_frame_size(&subjects)` is `shared_grids`' twin and reads the **committed** document
for a reason of its own rather than by imitation — a frame being dragged by a handle previews through
`RenderOverrides`, and a template lighting up mid-drag would be the panel reporting a size the user has
not let go of yet. Four frames at 393×852 light *iPhone 16*; one dragged off it lights nothing.

⚠️ **The disagreement state needs no message here where the grid panel's needs one, and that asymmetry
is the entry's one general claim.** A template list is a set of *alternatives*, so "none of the above"
is a state it can already show: a custom size on a single frame has lit nothing since the day the panel
was written, and a reader meets no new vocabulary. A grid list is *content*, where an empty list and a
disagreeing one are different facts that look identical unless one of them says so. That is the whole
of why one panel needs three states and this one needs two. *Do not add a "Mixed sizes" sentence here
for symmetry with the card below it.*

Applying goes through `apply_frame_template(&subjects, size)` — one `SetGeometry`/`GeometryPatch::Size`
per frame, one transaction, one undo step, because making four artboards iPhones is one act — extracted
for the reason `grid_add` was extracted a few hours earlier, so that the test drives the same write the
cell does rather than restating it. The existing "nothing written where the frame is already that size"
guard now reads the **shared** size.

⚠️ **The test's load-bearing assertion is that the union has *grown*, because the wrong implementation
here is not "nothing happens".** `a_template_over_several_frames_sets_each_of_their_own_boxes`
(`rhythm_tests`) asserts each frame's own box *and* that `multi_union` came back wider than one
template, which is the only thing that tells this apart from the rigid-body resize: that one leaves the
union at exactly the template's width, and this leaves it wider, four iPads side by side being wider
than one. ⚠️ **And the shared `frames_with_lists` fixture had to lay its frames out side by side before
that assertion meant anything** — it created all three at the origin, where three coincident frames have
a union exactly one frame wide, so the assertion was true of both implementations and therefore vacuous
until a per-frame `Affine::translate` was added. The flip is `apply_frame_template` writing to
`subjects[0]` alone, which is the shape the panel had while it was a single frame's, and it fails at
*"frame 1 kept its old size"*.

**D389's own last sentence is amended in place rather than left standing.** It said there was
deliberately no templates card for a multi-selection, and the *reasoning* was sound — nobody had asked —
while the fact under it moved the moment somebody did. That is exactly the shape D389 itself recorded
for D387's colour-write comment, which makes it twice in three days: a comment whose premise is "nobody
has asked" is a dated fact wearing an argument's clothes, and is still worth writing, because it is what
makes the reversal one edit instead of a re-derivation.

**D391 — The grid overlay previewed the frame's size and not its transform. *Fixed and tested
2026-08-30; Keep.*** Reported as the layout grid "only applying when the action is finished — so it
lags behind while the transformation is happening", with a screenshot that shows the fault whole: a
white frame dragged to the right carrying its bands inside it, and a second, dark set of bands left
standing at the position it started from. The frame had slid out from under its own grid, and the two
met again only on release.

**One line, and the shape of it is worth more than the fix.** `CanvasRenderer::draw_layout_grids`
read the frame twice in adjacent lines and the two reads were not the same kind of read: the **size**
came off `session.display_node(id)`, which is the `RenderOverrides` tree and therefore previews,
while the **transform** came off `session.resolved.world_transform(id)`, which is the committed
resolve and does not. `session.preview_world_transform(id)` in place of the second is the whole
change.

⚠️ **The symptom of a half-previewing overlay is never "nothing previews", it is "half of it does",**
which is how this survived the feature landing (D385), a colour control (D387), a hue ramp (D388) and
a multi-selection rewrite (D389, D390) without anybody noticing. A **resize** is the gesture the
*size* read answers, so the bands re-flowed under the pointer and looked right the whole time; a
move, a rotation or a skew is what the transform read answers, and none of the three had ever been
exercised by a test or by a session. *Two reads of one node in adjacent lines, one previewing and one
not, is the shape to distrust* — the working half is what hides the broken one.

**The comment above the line was wrong in the same place, and that is not a coincidence.** It opened
*"The committed kind, not the display node's"* and then gave as its reason the exact opposite — a
frame being resized previews its size through `RenderOverrides`, and the grid has to re-flow against
the box the user is dragging rather than against the one on disk. It reads "The display node's kind,
not the committed one" now, with a note beside it saying that a comment naming the wrong source is
how the read beside it came to be the wrong source. **Third time in three days**: D387's colour-write
comment was reversed by D389, and D390 found D389's own closing clause backwards rather than merely
stale. Not a rule yet, but the same failure each time — prose that outlived the code it described,
and each time the prose was what the next reader trusted.

**The other seven reads of `resolved.world_transform` in `canvas.rs` were swept and none is this
bug.** `baseline_lines` offers snap targets and `continue`s on every node in the moving set, so
committed is the *correct* read there; `target_artboard` picks the frame under a point for creation;
`pen_resume_target_in` and `begin_pen_edit` are taken at the press, the latter off the **parent**;
`crop_frame` and `edited_subpaths` belong to gestures during which the layer is not simultaneously
being transformed, and `edited_subpaths` has a preview twin right below it for the caller that needs
one. The seventh is `quad_of`'s `false` arm, which is deliberately the committed half of a documented
preview/committed pair and is what an Alt-drag's left-behind copy is drawn from. ⚠️ *The sweep is
worth re-running rather than trusting, because what makes a site safe here is a fact about the
gesture — "the layer is not being moved while this is read" — and not anything a compiler or a grep
can see.*

**The test is `canvas::layout_grid_tests::the_bands_follow_a_frame_that_is_still_being_dragged`,** and
its three cautions are the reason it is one test rather than a coordinate check. It installs a
preview — `set_preview` with a `SetTransform` of `Affine::translate((137, 42)) * Affine::rotate(0.4)`
— and asserts one invariant, *the bands span the frame's `selection_quad`*, committed and
mid-gesture both. ⚠️ **Asserted against `selection_quad` rather than against numbers** because that
quad previews too, so one invariant covers both states, where a pair of expected coordinates would be
a second copy of the transform arithmetic and would pass for a version that previewed the outline and
not the bands. ⚠️ **A rotation and not just a translation**, since a translate-only preview is
satisfied by any implementation that adds an offset somewhere, including one that never composes the
matrix. ⚠️ **Two anti-vacuity guards, and one of them fired while the test was being written**: the
frame's quad must have actually moved from where it rested — first written as an absolute `> 5.0`,
which is wrong for whatever camera `headless` starts with and had to become a comparison against the
committed value — and `session.revision()` must be unchanged, or the fixture committed the gesture
and the test is not about a preview at all. The flip, run: `resolved.world_transform` put back fails
at *"mid-gesture: the run spans the frame"* with `-399.5..0.5 against -340.38..105.92`, the bands at
the committed x while the frame is elsewhere, and **leaves the committed half green** — which is
exactly the half that never looked broken.

**D392 — The crash snapshot serialises on a worker thread. *Built and tested 2026-08-30; Keep.***
`roadmap.md`'s *Technical, and still binding* list had carried the measurement and the fix in the same
item: `OndinApp::recovery_tick` called `recovery::write` → `ondin_core::io::save` →
`serde_json::to_vec_pretty` straight from the frame that noticed the interval had elapsed. Measured at
four sizes of embedded image rather than estimated — 1 MB costs 1.3 ms in release and 20 ms in debug,
20 MB costs 25 ms and 387 ms, and 60 MB costs 72 ms and **1.15 s**, before the disk write — which made
the feature that exists to protect work the most expensive thing in a photo-carrying frame, once every
ten seconds, in the build anyone develops in.

**What makes moving it cheap is `Document` being cheap to clone.** `ImageSource::Embedded` has held an
`Arc<[u8]>` since D301, so the copy handed to the worker is a refcount bump per picture and not the
pictures. The frame keeps the clone and gives away the serialise, which is the right way round:
`a_snapshot_of_a_photo_document_does_not_serialise_on_the_frame` measures **313 µs** where the same
tick with its old body back in it measures **402 ms**, and most of the 313 is the *first* tick starting
the thread rather than the clone. (That 402 also agrees with the table's 387 for the same size, which
is the only cross-check the numbers get.)

`recovery::Writer` is one long-lived thread with an `mpsc` job queue in and an `mpsc` result channel
back: `Job::Write { root, key, doc, at }` and `Job::Forget { root, key }` in, `Done::Wrote(at)`,
`Done::Failed(String)` and `Done::Forgot` out. The worker calls the same free `recovery::write` and
`recovery::remove` the frame used to, unchanged, so the module's own tests still exercise them
directly. `RecoveryState` gained `writer: Option<Writer>`, **`None` until the first snapshot** — which
is what keeps `#[derive(Default)]` honest and means no session that never dirties a document starts a
thread. The tick keeps every *decision* it had: the three gates, the key minting and the clock stamp.
⚠️ **All of that moved hours later, when autosave joined the same queue (D393)**, and the names in
this entry are the old ones: the type is `library::writer::Writer` in a module of its own, `Job::Write`
is `Job::Snapshot` beside a third `Job::Document`, `Done::Wrote` and `Done::Failed` are
`Done::Snapshotted` and `Done::SnapshotFailed` beside `Done::Saved` and `Done::SaveFailed`, and the
handle is `OndinApp::writer` rather than `RecoveryState`'s — because *the two cannot race for a path*
is a fact about the app rather than about either feature.

⚠️ **One worker rather than a thread per snapshot, and the ordering is the whole reason.** A removal
goes down the same queue as a write, so *Discard* and `OndinApp::drop_recovery` cannot be overtaken by
a write already in flight and resurrect the file they just deleted — which at the next launch is a
question about work the user already dealt with. `OndinApp::forget_snapshot` is the one door for a
removal; it routes through the queue when a writer exists and calls `recovery::remove` directly when
one does not, and ⚠️ **that second arm is not a shortcut**: no writer provably means this session has
never written a snapshot, so there is nothing to be ordered against. The case that reaches it is a
recovered session, whose key came from the previous process. A future editor tidying the two arms into
one unconditional `remove` is the regression this is written for.

⚠️ **`recovery.at` is written from the worker's answer and nowhere else**, which is what keeps the
