field's own doc ("the revision the last snapshot captured") literally true rather than aspirational.
Nothing re-queues the same revision in the meantime, because the clock is stamped at *queue* time and
holds the next tick off for `SNAPSHOT_SECS`, ten times the worst serialise ever measured. And a
`Done::Wrote` is **dropped** when `recovery.key` is `None`: that is a write finishing after
`drop_recovery`, and since `at` gates the next write, a stale one could silence the first snapshot of
whatever document replaced this one — `revision` is a per-session counter, so "a revision already
written" is not the same claim after an adopt. `OndinApp::recovery_results` drains at the *top* of the
tick, ahead of every gate, because the clean branch queues a removal behind that write and would
otherwise leave `at` claiming a snapshot on its way to being deleted. (It is `disk_results` and it
drains at the top of the *frame* since D393, ahead of both ticks rather than inside one of them, for
the same reason widened: two features now gate on state a result changes.)

**Three flush points, because a queued job must not outlive the process — and the order among them is
not the one it looks like.** (Four, with the relocation below; five since D393 added `save_file`.) `eframe::App::on_exit` is new and is the **primary**: it is reached on
every way out, through `save_and_destroy`, from `WinitAppWrapper::exiting` and from the
`!run_and_return` branch alike. Both arms of `close_confirmation` that end the process settle after
their drop, which is the case that has already decided. `Drop for Writer` joins, as the **backstop**
for whatever neither of those ran. ⚠️ **The brief this entry was written from had it the other way
round — `Drop` as the reliable one and `on_exit` as insurance — and eframe's own source says
otherwise.** A destructor is the *most* skippable of the three, by two paths rather than one: with
`NativeOptions::run_and_return` off, eframe calls `std::process::exit(0)` and nothing in the process
is dropped at all; and with it on — 0.35's default, which `main::run_gui` takes by
`..Default::default()` — eframe's own note on `exiting` in `native/run.rs` records that a macOS
`Cmd-Q` exits the loop and then `run_app_on_demand` *never returns*, so the app is never dropped
either. Read against the vendored eframe 0.35 source rather than assumed, which is the only reason the
ordering was caught; both code comments now say which is which.

⚠️ **A dead worker used to be silent, and `Done::Failed` (`Done::SnapshotFailed` since D393) is the
only thing that is not.**
`RecoveryState::warned` latches one status line off a `Failed` (D377), so a worker that panicked
inside a job would have taken crash recovery down without a word — the exact failure that latch exists
for. The first draft of `send` shrugged at a failed `tx.send`, on the argument that the next `settle`
would say so by finding the queue empty; that was false, since `settle` finds it empty and says
nothing to anybody. `Writer` now carries `reports: Vec<Done>` — answers this side makes up, drained
ahead of the worker's — and two places push into it. `send` reports when `tx.send` errors, ⚠️ **as a
*write* failure rather than as a queue detail**, because that is what it is: not one snapshot lost but
every snapshot this session will ever take, the worker being unrestartable. And `settle`'s `Err(_)`
arm reports when the channel hangs up mid-job, which is the one place a death *during* a job is
noticed — `send` only notices on the next attempt, and after a close there may not be one.
⚠️ **Neither arm has a test**: making the worker panic on demand needs a fault injected into
`recovery::write`, and none was added, so this is reasoned and unwritten rather than pinned.
🚨 ***"The one place"* was a defect rather than a design, and D549 is where that was found.** `settle`
runs from `save_file`, `on_exit` and `relocate`, none of which happen on their own — so on the frame
path a death mid-job was noticed **nowhere**: `drain` was `while let Ok(msg) = try_recv()`, which
leaves on `Disconnected` as readily as on `Empty` and therefore read a hung-up channel as an idle
one, turning autosave off for the rest of the session in silence. `drain` carries the same arm now.
D549 also supplies the fault this paragraph records as never injected — `writer::poison_document`,
keyed on a path rather than a one-shot flag — so both arms are pinned.

**A fourth wait, and it is this change's own race rather than an old one.**
`panels::dashboard::apply_library_settings` settles before `library::relocate` runs, because relocate
carries `.recovery/` to the new base folder on the UI thread: a write still aimed at the old root
either lands in a folder that has just been emptied, or is copied across and then deleted from under
the copy. The wait costs one document's serialise at the start of an operation that is about to move
every file the user owns.

**Two new tests, both in `app::library_wiring_tests` over a shared `app_with_a_photo` fixture** (20 MB
of embedded picture; the bytes are never decoded, since `AddImage` stores the intrinsic size, so a
pattern is as good as a photograph and what is under test is the base64 either way).
`a_snapshot_of_a_photo_document_does_not_serialise_on_the_frame` is a duration assertion, ⚠️ **paired
with two that are not** — the key was minted and the file on disk is over 20 MB — so a tick that
returned early cannot pass it vacuously; its flip puts the synchronous write back and fails at the
duration with both file assertions green.
`discarding_a_snapshot_beats_the_write_that_is_still_in_flight` ticks, calls `drop_recovery` with no
settle in between, settles, and asserts the file is gone; its flip makes `forget_snapshot`
unconditional and ⚠️ **fails there alone** — the other eight recovery tests stay green, including the
two that assert a snapshot is gone, because their documents are one rect and the worker wins the race
every time. *The 20 MB fixture is what gives the race a wrong answer to give*, and is the load-bearing
part of both tests. Four existing tests gained a `recovery_settle()` — `disk_settle()` since D393,
which also gave five autosave tests the same call — where they assert on a file; ⚠️
`work_lost_to_a_crash_comes_back_and_the_file_waits_for_the_user` deliberately did **not**, because it
relies on `drop(app)` flushing through `Drop for Writer`, which is now part of what it proves and is
the only one of the three flushes a test can reach.

**Autosave is the same call and was left on the frame on purpose**, which is what the roadmap entry
still holds. `OndinApp::save_file` calls `library::store::write_document` from the frame on the user's
`autosave_secs` interval, and moving it is not the same mechanical move: a save has user-visible
consequences a snapshot does not. It calls `session.mark_saved(path)` — the pill goes to *Saved · just
now* and the session goes clean — and then, conditionally, `pin_version`, which copies the file on
disk, and `export_all`. Deferring the write means deciding what the pill says while one is in flight
and what happens when a queued save fails after the session has already been marked clean; and
`go_to_dashboard`, `open_path` and the close-and-save arm all call it synchronously and need the write
to have happened before they proceed. That is a design question for the maintainer, not a refactor.
⚠️ **Answered the same day by D393, and the answer was "not all of it".** Autosave queues onto this
worker; the pill takes a third *label* and no third state; the session goes clean from the worker's
answer rather than at queue time; and `Ctrl+S`, the dashboard walk, an open and the close-and-save arm
stay synchronous **by decision** rather than by omission — a pin copies the file off the disk, so
deferring it moves the cost rather than removing it, and the three transitions each read the result on
the next line. This paragraph's "reusable mechanism" was right; its list of blockers was three
questions, of which two had answers and one was a non-goal.

**D393 — Autosave follows the snapshot off the UI thread, and the session goes clean from the
worker's answer. *Built and tested 2026-08-30; Keep.*** D392 moved the crash snapshot and left
autosave where it was, naming three blockers: what the pill says while a write is in flight, what
happens when a queued save fails after the session has been told it is clean, and the three
transitions that call `save_file` and read the result on the next line. The first two are answered
here and the third is a decided non-goal. `roadmap.md`'s *Autosave serialises the whole document on
the UI thread* item is struck, and this entry is where its three keepable parts live.

**The measurement, which now describes both features.** Four sizes of embedded image, measured rather
than estimated: 1 MB of pictures costs **1.3 ms** in release and **20 ms** in debug, 20 MB costs
**25 ms** and **387 ms**, and 60 MB costs **72 ms** and **1.15 s**, producing 1.4 / 28 / 84 MB of
JSON, before the disk write — about 1.2 ms per MB in release and fifteen times that in debug. So a
photo-carrying document stalled the frame for a second or more every thirty seconds, in the build
anyone develops in. The table lives in `library/writer.rs`'s module note as well, beside the code it
is about. The same 20 MB fixture now costs an `autosave_tick` well under the 50 ms its test asserts,
against ~400 ms for the synchronous write it replaced.

**The writer is a module of its own, and it has a third kind of job.** `recovery::Writer` and its
`Job` and `Done` are `library::writer`, whose module note carries the reasoning; `recovery.rs` keeps
only its free functions (`write`, `remove`, `pending`, `mint_key`), `Pending` and a `RecoveryState`
that no longer owns a `writer` field. The handle is `OndinApp::writer`, because *the two cannot race
for a path* is a fact about the app rather than about either feature. `Job` is `Snapshot`, `Forget`
and `Document`; `Done` is `Snapshotted(u64)`, `SnapshotFailed(String)`, `Forgot`, `Saved { path, at }`
and `SaveFailed(String)`. ⚠️ **Five variants rather than a `Result` per job, because one failure
latches and the other must not.** A snapshot failing is a standing condition worth saying once, which
is what `RecoveryState::warned` is (D377); a save failing is an event the next interval will repeat.
Collapsing them would put a save's error behind crash recovery's one-shot warning, where the user sees
it once and never again.

⚠️ **One worker rather than a second thread, and that is not tidiness — it is what keeps
`crate::atomic`'s temp-file scheme true.** `atomic::temp_for` derives the temp filename from the
target instead of randomising it, and its doc says in as many words that a randomised name "would be
safer against two writers racing, which this app does not have". A second background thread would have
made that sentence false the day it was added. 🚨 **It was *already* false, for a reason no amount of
care in this module could reach, and D548 fixed it at the write layer instead**: nothing stops a
second Ondin *process*, and two instances saving one document tore the destination outright.
`temp_for` carries a pid and a counter now, so the write layer no longer depends on how many writers
this app has — which is why this paragraph is **amended rather than struck**: the FIFO below still
matters, for the snapshot's ordering, and that is the reason the queue is still the shape it is.
One queue keeps it true by construction — exactly one
background writer of anything, in FIFO order — and the only other writer is the frame, which is why
`save_file` settles before doing its own synchronous write. That is a **fifth** wait beside D392's
four: `on_exit`, both closing arms of `close_confirmation`, `Drop for Writer`, and
`apply_library_settings` before `relocate`, all unchanged.

**The results drain moved out of `recovery_tick` and became the frame's.** One `disk_results()` at the
top of `eframe::App::ui`'s tick sequence, ahead of *both* ticks, because both gate on state a result
changes — the snapshot on `recovery.at`, the autosave on the session being dirty — so a drain owned by
one of them would decide the other's frame by accident. `recovery_results`, `recovery_settle` and
`apply_recovery` are `disk_results`, `disk_settle` and `apply_disk`; `apply_disk` is the one reader of
a `Done`, so no caller above it can come to mean something different by a result.

**What `autosave_tick` keeps is every decision and none of the work.** It takes an `&egui::Context`
(the worker clones it to `request_repaint`, or the pill's move from *Saving…* to *Saved · just now*
waits for a mouse), keeps its gates and its clock, and hands the worker a `Document::clone` — a
refcount bump per picture, `ImageSource::Embedded` being an `Arc<[u8]>` since D301. What left it is
the write, the `mark_saved` and the export, all of which now happen on the *result* in `apply_disk`.
⚠️ **A fourth gate, `session.is_saving()`, and it is not redundant with the interval.** The clock is
stamped at queue time, so a second queue is normally thirty seconds away — but `autosave_secs` is the
user's and can be set to 1, which is shorter than a 60 MB serialise, and two writes of one path in
flight would share `atomic`'s one temp file.

**The pill takes a third label and deliberately not a third state.** `save_label` was
`Option<Duration>` and is now `(saving: bool, ago: Option<Duration>)`. While a write is in flight the
document still differs from its file, so `dirty` stays true, `saved_ago()` is still `None`, and ⚠️ **the
dot stays amber**: it answers *does the file match*, which has not changed, and a third colour would
be claiming otherwise. Only the sentence moves — *Saving…* rather than *Unsaved*, which are the same
fact and very different news. The maintainer asked for it in those words.

⚠️ **`EditorSession::finish_save` has three guards and each answers a different way of being stale**,
and the middle one is the whole reason `saving` holds a revision rather than a `bool`. `saving ==
Some(at)` or return, because a `take()` here would let an older result end the *Saving…* of a newer
write still in flight. `revision == at`, because an edit committed while the serialise was in the
worker's hands means the file holds a document the session has already moved past — marking it clean
would put *Saved · just now* over work that is on disk nowhere, and do it **silently**, the pill being
the only thing that would have said otherwise. And the `path` matches, so the document has not been
swapped underneath; that one should be unreachable, `open_path` and `recover` settling first, and the
consequence if it ever is would be marking a *new* document clean because the *old* one was written.
It returns whether the session went clean, which is what `export_on_save` keys on: a superseded write
is not a save and does not re-export.

⚠️ **And the third state was entered in one place and left in only one of two, which is the bug a
third state invites.** `begin_save` sets `saving`, `finish_save` clears it on the way out — and the
*failure* path did not, for as long as it took to write the test below. The cost is not a lost write:
the session stays dirty, which is correct. It is the pill sticking on *Saving…* for the rest of the
session and `autosave_tick`'s `is_saving` gate never opening again, so **one failed write turns
autosave off silently** — the failure this whole feature exists to prevent, arrived at from the other
side. `EditorSession::save_failed()` is the missing exit, called from `apply_disk`'s `SaveFailed` arm
before the status message. *Any state with two ways out wants both of them found by grep before it is
believed.*

**`Ctrl+S` and the three transitions stay synchronous, and that is a decision rather than a
remainder.** A pin is a *copy of the file* — `pin_version` reads the bytes back off the disk — so
deferring the write only moves `Ctrl+S`'s cost rather than removing it. And `go_to_dashboard`,
`open_path` and the close-and-save arm each read the result on the next line: they leave the editor,
replace the document, or close the window, and every one of them is wrong if the bytes are not down.
Autosave is the one that fires unbidden while somebody is drawing, which is the whole of why it is the
one that moved. *Not open work — a future editor "finishing the job" by queueing the other four is the
regression this paragraph is written against.*

**Four new tests and five amended.** `app::tests::a_queued_write_says_saving_whatever_else_is_true`
is two assertions on the pure `save_label`; ⚠️ the second pins **precedence** — `saving` and a live
`ago` cannot both happen in the app, but the function does not know that, and *Saving…* is the newer
fact. Its flip moves the `saving` branch below the `ago` one, which is how somebody appends a case: the
first assertion stays green and the second fails with "Saved · just now".
`library_wiring_tests::an_autosave_of_a_photo_document_does_not_serialise_on_the_frame` is the
duration assertion bracketed by three that are not — `is_saving` and `is_dirty` right after the tick,
and both again after the settle. ⚠️ **Its flip's predicted site was wrong and the miss is the useful
part**: putting `self.save_file(false)` back as the body fails one line *earlier* than predicted, on
`is_saving`, because a synchronous save marks the session clean and never enters the third state at
all. The first assertion a wrong implementation trips is not always the one the test is named for, and
here the earlier failure is the more informative.
`library_wiring_tests::an_edit_during_a_save_leaves_the_session_dirty` queues an autosave, commits a
rect while the 20 MB serialise is in flight, settles, and asserts the session is still dirty,
*Saving…* has ended, and ⚠️ **the file on disk really is the older document** — that third assertion
is what makes the test about staleness rather than about a failed write. Its flip drops the `revision
== at` guard, fails at `is_dirty` and **leaves the file assertion green**: nothing about the disk is
wrong in the broken version, only what the app believes about it.
`library_wiring_tests::a_failed_save_stops_saying_saving_and_leaves_autosave_armed` is the one that
found the stuck state above, and ⚠️ **it exists because the failure arm turned out to be reachable
without a fault injected**: the session's path is pointed at a **directory**, so `atomic::write`
writes its temp file happily and then cannot rename over it. It asserts `is_saving` after the tick,
then after the settle that `is_saving` is false, the session is still dirty and the status line says
*Save failed* — and then arms and ticks again, because *the next interval still fires* is the
consequence the other three assertions are really about. Its flip removes the `save_failed()` call and
fails at the `is_saving` assertion after the settle, as predicted, with the last pair catching it too.
**Which is the counterpart to D392's two untested arms**: same class of failure, and this one is
pinned, because a directory is a fault the filesystem supplies for free where a panicking worker is
not. D392's note that its arms are reasoned and unwritten still stands. The five amended tests gained a
`disk_settle()`; worth one clause, because `only_a_manual_save_pins_a_version` and
`autosave_does_not_touch_a_clean_document` carry their own anti-vacuity controls (`assert!(!is_dirty)`)
and without the settle those fail saying the fixture never autosaved — the right failure for the wrong
reason.

**One drift found and corrected in passing, and it is not a decision.** `prefs::Prefs::export_on_save`
said the export happens "as a side effect of Ctrl+S"; `save_file` has always run it at the end without
asking which kind of save it was, so autosave, the dashboard walk and an open have each been
re-exporting all along. The summary line above it was right and the paragraph under it was narrower
than the code. The comment now says "a save" and states the new consequence: the export runs off the
*result*, so with the switch on and a thirty-second interval a photo-carrying document re-exports every
thirty seconds from a background thread.

⚠️ **Found while chasing a freeze and *not* the cause of it**, carried here from the roadmap entry
because it is the part of it worth someone reading. A picker's hue strip was reported as freezing the
app for a few seconds and swallowing the click; this cost has the right shape and the wrong subject —
the file was new and held one rectangle, which serialises in well under a millisecond, and the freeze
never recurred. The numbers above are a measured cost with **no attribution**, so the next person to
meet a stall inherits them and not the wrong suspect.

**D394 — SVG comes in, as layers, through the paste path. *Built and tested 2026-08-31; Keep, with
`<text>` and four other things named as the remainder.***

**Asked for by the maintainer in the terms that decided the design**: *"pasting a copied SVG"* is
what was missed while using the app, so the entry point is `Ctrl+V` and not a file dialog. D259 had
already written that down from the other side — with SVG on the clipboard `Ctrl+V` made a **text
layer**, and "closing the round trip is a change to the paste path rather than to this row".

⚠️ **The roadmap's premise was "a parser plus a mapping onto our node kinds", and it had never been
read.** Two of the three grammars were already in core's own crates: `kurbo::BezPath::from_svg` is the
whole `d` grammar including arcs, and `peniko::color::parse_color` is the whole CSS colour grammar
including the 148 named colours. The dependency the feature actually cost is **one** — `roxmltree`,
which was already in the lock through `fontdb` → `fontconfig-parser`, though only on Linux, so on
Windows it buys a compile rather than an edge. *This is the third time an entry priced as a feature
turned out to be wiring* — the others are *Convert to path*, costed on glyph outlines that had been
in the tree since D145, and text-on-path, whose every dependency has arrived.

**Where it lives, and the cost of that.** `ondin_core::svg_in`, not beside the writer in
`ondin-export`: reading is model construction and wants no renderer, so the importer is testable
without a graphics context and is shaped like every builder in `build` — a string in, one
`Transaction` out, ids minted, committed by the caller exactly as a group is. ⚠️ **The price is that
the writer and the reader are inverse functions in two crates and nothing binds them**; no gate
notices when one grows an attribute the other does not know, and neither crate's own tests can — the
writer's assert on substrings and the reader's on hand-written fixtures. `ondin-export/tests/svg_roundtrip.rs`
is the whole of what stops the drift, which is the reason to keep it green rather than to relax it.

**What it reads**: `svg`, `g`, `a`, `rect`, `circle`, `ellipse`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`,
`path`; `transform` in all six spellings; the inherited half of the presentation attributes with an
inline `style` beating them, CSS's own precedence; solid paint and `<linearGradient>`/`<radialGradient>`
in both `gradientUnits`; `fill-rule`; `opacity`, `display`, `visibility`; `viewBox` fitted onto the
declared `width`/`height`; and `id` as the layer's name.

⚠️ **That fit has one guard and it was in only one of the two readers** (§15 D511). A `width`/`height`
pair is a declaration only when both are positive: `declared_size` said so and fell through to the
`viewBox`, while `view_transform` ten lines below read the same attributes through the same parser and
divided by them unchecked, so `width="24" height="0" viewBox="0 0 48 48"` reported a size of 48×48 and
gave the pasted subtree the **singular** transform `[0, 0, 0, 0, 12, 0]`. One guarded reader,
`declared_pair`, answers both now, and a non-positive declaration means *no box to fit into* — the arm
`view_transform` already had for a missing pair.

⚠️ **`fill-rule` is why this could not have been built a day earlier.** The model gained a per-node
rule that morning (D239's fourth amendment); without it every compound icon — which is most of them —
would have pasted as a silhouette. The feature that closed a boolean's defect turned out to be the
one an importer could not do without.

**What it refuses, and the split is the decision.** Only two errors, and neither is about the
drawing: not XML, and a root that is not `<svg>`. Everything else it cannot read is **skipped and
counted**, and the paste says so: *"Pasted SVG — 12 layers, skipped filter"*. Refusing a whole icon
over one unsupported element is the wrong trade; losing half a drawing silently is worse than both.
*(The first cut's skip list was `<text>`, `<image>`, `<use>`, `<clipPath>`, `<mask>` and CSS blocks;
all six were built the same day — see the amendment below.)*

**Two asymmetries with the writer, both deliberate.** A `<polygon>` comes back as a `Path`, because
`NodeKind::Polygon` is a regular *n*-gon with a radius and reading every point list back as one would
turn an arbitrary outline into a hexagon — the geometry round-trips and the kind does not. And
`<text>` is skipped: the writer emits one `<text>` per *line* at a baseline the canvas computed
(D81), so reading it back is a paragraph-layout question rather than a parsing one.
`text_is_the_one_thing_the_round_trip_still_loses` records that gap where the gap is, and is a test to
**delete** when text import lands rather than to remember.

**Placed by measuring rather than by guessing.** An import's own transform is its `viewBox`, so where
the drawing lands is not known until the nodes exist — the transaction is applied to a **clone** of
the document, the group's bounds are read off that, and the root's transform is corrected before the
real commit. One transaction, one undo step, and the clone is the cost `Document::apply` already pays
to stage one (D301).

⚠️ **The bug the tests could not have found, and how it was found.** Nine hand-written fixtures were
green against a reader that ignored the root `<svg>`'s **own** presentation attributes. Every Figma
export opens `<svg … fill="none">` and lets each shape state its own paint, so starting the walk from
SVG's initial values gives **black** to every child that states none — a dashed rule arrives as a
filled bar, an outline icon as a silhouette. It took importing a *real* export to see it: a fixture
author who is thinking about fills puts them on the shapes. `the_root_element_is_styled_too` is the
assertion, and the same probe is what added the skipped-*attribute* count, since a real export hangs
`clip-path` on the group that holds everything.

**Flips, four of them, and each bit exactly one test.** The composition order in `parse_transform`
reversed → (6.7e-16, 11.0) where (10, 1) is wanted; `.to_radians()` dropped → **(9.55, 0.89)**, and
that value was *predicted wrong* as "very nearly nowhere", because 90 radians is 5156° and wraps to
60.7° — ⚠️ *a wrong unit does not read as a small error, it reads as a plausible one.* Element
`transform`s ignored → the round-trip arrangement test fails at shape 0 and the other three stay
green. `fill-rule` ignored → the exclusion test alone. **Neither of the last two is caught by the
group-opacity test**, which asserts opacity and no placement at all: four round-trip tests overlap
much less than the phrase suggests.

~~**What is left**, in the order it is worth doing: `<text>`, `<image>`, `<use>`, `clipPath` onto
`Node::mask` — which the model can now express — and CSS `<style>` blocks, which need a cascade
rather than a lookup.~~

### Amended the same day — all five remaining blocks, and a second report beside the first

**Asked for as "the remaining blocks, starting with clipPath and mask", hours after the paste was
tried on a real Lucide icon and worked.** All five are built; what is left of SVG is a list of things
nobody is missing.

⚠️ **The most useful thing here is the *second* list.** `Import::approximated` is new beside
`skipped`, and the distinction is one a user can act on: *skipped* means missing and *approximated*
means there and slightly wrong. Telling someone their mask was "skipped", over a drawing that is
visibly masked, sends them looking for the wrong bug. The paste says both, in two clauses.

**`clip-path` and `mask` are mask nodes**, which cost no new model concept: ours clips the run of
siblings *above* it (D282–D286), so a group holding `[clip, content]` is SVG's `clip-path` exactly.
⚠️ **A clipped *container* clips itself rather than gaining a wrapper** — a Figma export hangs
`clip-path` on its outermost `<g>`, so a wrapper would be a permanent extra level on every paste —
**except when the element carries both a clip and a mask**, because two mask nodes in one parent are
two *runs*, and the first would clip only the empty stretch before the second. ⚠️ **The transform
goes on the clip, not on the wrapper**, `userSpaceOnUse` resolving in the *referencing* element's
space; the flip that moves it was predicted to leave the clip behind and instead leaves the clip
**correct** and transforms the content twice — *the assertion that bites is the one about the thing
the change was not about*. SVG's `<mask>` is a **luminance** mask and ours reads alpha, which agree on
opaque white and are opposites on black, so a mask that is not opaque white is reported.

**`<use>` is a deep copy** placed by `x`/`y`, capped at sixteen deep so a reference cycle stops; a
`<symbol>` contributes its contents and is never drawn where it stands. **CSS `<style>` is** ~~**a
lookup, not a cascade engine**~~: type, class and id selectors with real specificity and the
document-order tiebreak, which is what an Illustrator export needs. ⚠️ **A class beats a presentation
attribute and loses to inline** — the one piece of precedence that is not obvious, and getting it
backwards leaves an Illustrator file looking exactly as it did before the stylesheet existed. A
selector needing a combinator is reported **once for the sheet**, not once per element it should have
matched. ⚠️ **It is a small cascade engine since 2026-09-19** (D806): compounds and the descendant and
child combinators are read too, and the line is drawn at what needs something other than an ancestor
walk — sibling order, a pseudo-class, an attribute. The reporting rule in the sentence above is
unchanged and the set it covers is narrower.

**`<image>` needed a host callback and that is the finding.** Core can do neither half of a picture:
the intrinsic size comes from *decoding* (`ondin-render`) and the id from a content hash (`ring`,
app-side) — and the bytes have to reach the decode cache anyway or the picture is a placeholder. So
`ImageSink` is a trait the app implements over the three steps `load_image_bytes` already takes, and
it is passed as a trait object rather than `&mut self` because the importer already holds
`self.session.ids`. Data URIs only; an external `href` is a **skip, not a fetch**. ⚠️ **SVG's default
is contain and ours is cover**, so the fit is set explicitly rather than left at the field's default.

**`<text>` is placed by its baseline**, which is the arithmetic the markup cannot give: SVG positions
text by the baseline and this model by the box, so the text is shaped (`text::layout`, headless, the
bundled family) to learn the ascent — and that is why an importer in core can do this at all.
⚠️ **A `<tspan>` carrying its own `x` or `y` starts a new layer and a bare one joins the text**, which
is the rule that tells two exporters apart: *this app* emits one `<text>` per line with a `<tspan>` per
**style run** (D81), and *Illustrator* emits one `<text>` with a `<tspan x y>` per **line**. Reading
the position rather than the element is the whole of it. `text-anchor` is folded into the placement
because the model has no anchor — an auto-width box *is* its text.

⚠️ **The structural loss is the paragraph, not the text, and it is asserted rather than left to be
found.** A two-line text layer of ours comes back as two layers in the right places; nothing in the
markup says they were one node, and rejoining them means inventing the line height that decides where
every line after the first sits.

**`text_is_the_one_thing_the_round_trip_still_loses` failed the day text import landed**, which is the
whole return on writing a test for something that does not work yet: it recorded the gap where the gap
was, so closing it was a red test rather than an act of memory. It now asserts the opposite.

**Two flips worth keeping.** Dropping `- ascent` — putting the box's *top* at `y`, the obvious wrong
version — lands the text a whole line low and leaves the anchor test green; the two tests are about
the two axes and neither covers the other. And a `?` on the `style` attribute inside `property`
returned `None` for the *whole property* on every element without one, which reads as "nothing has any
paint" — nine tests caught it at once, which is the shape of a mistake in a lookup everything goes
through.

### Amended a second time the same day — two bugs the fixtures could not have found

**Both came from running the importer over Wikipedia's own test card**, which the maintainer had
pasted and reported as *"almost pixel perfect"* except for one wrong element. Forty green tests said
nothing about either, and the reason is the same for both: **a fixture is written by someone who
already knows what they are testing.**

⚠️ **A `<!DOCTYPE>` was a whole-file refusal.** `roxmltree` rejects a DTD unless told otherwise, and
every SVG 1.1 file written by Inkscape, Illustrator or anything of that era opens with one. The
symptom is not a missing element: `import` answers `NotXml`, the paste falls through, and the user
gets their markup as a **text layer** with nothing saying why. *No fixture written by hand has a
doctype in it*, so nothing here could have caught it — and the maintainer's own paste worked, because
a browser's "copy SVG" hands over the rendered markup without the preamble. **Only opening the file
finds this.** `allow_dtd: true` with a `nodes_limit`, which is safe for the reason roxmltree's own
documentation gives: it carries billion-laughs checks regardless and never resolves an *external*
entity, so the parser cannot reach the network or the disk from a pasted string.

⚠️ **The font properties are inherited and were not.** They were read off the `<text>` element alone,
which is wrong twice: a `font-family` on an enclosing `<g>` — how every Inkscape file states it —
never reached the text, and a `font-size` on a **`<tspan>`** was ignored. The test card puts the size
on the `<text>` for one "TEST" and on the `<tspan>` for the other, so one rendered perfectly at 180pt
and its drop shadow rendered at the default 16 off to one side. *One file, both spellings* — which is
what made the report so precise. Now they live on `Style` and resolve down the tree like the paint,
and a positioned `<tspan>` is the source of its own run's font, id and opacity. ⚠️ **The `<text>`'s
transform has to be passed in rather than read from that element**, since a `<tspan>` cannot carry one
and reading it would silently drop the outer. ⚠️ **And so do its `opacity`, `display`/`visibility` and
`filter`, which took until 2026-09-08** (§15 D573): *"the source of its own run's opacity"* was never
the whole rule — the outer element's multiplies into it — and the three chrome properties were not
moved when the transform was, so every run after the first imported unfaded and visible.

⚠️ **The first draft of the regression test was vacuous and its own flip said so.** It used the test
card's two spellings and nothing else, so reverting `font_size` to a per-element read left it
**green**: a positioned `<tspan>` *is* the element by then, and it states the size itself. The flip
could not tell the two halves of the fix apart. A third `<text>` stating no size inside a
`<g font-size="90">` is what discriminates them, and with it the same flip fails. *A flip that does
not bite is a finding about the fixture as often as about the code.*

### Amended a third time, 2026-09-01 — seven defects behind one symptom

**The maintainer pasted `AJ_Digital_Camera.svg`** — an Inkscape drawing from the SVG-Web samples —
**and every gradient in it was gone.** Sixty-seven of its eighty-two shapes arrived unpainted; what
remained was fifteen flat colours and a handful of strokes, which reads as a wireframe of a camera.
The geometry was never wrong: the drawing landed in its declared 406×206 to the pixel, and the
scattered look was the *absence* of the shapes that fill the gaps between the strokes.

**Seven separate causes, and the first four each independently sufficed.** That is the shape worth
recording — a symptom that looks like one bug ("gradients do not work") and decomposes into a stack of
them, where fixing any three still leaves an unpainted drawing:

- ⚠️ **`xlink:href` inheritance between gradients was not read at all.** A gradient inherits its
  stops *and* its position attributes from whatever it references, and **Inkscape writes every
  gradient that way** — one stop-holding element in `<defs>`, one positioned element per use. That
  file declares 175 gradients and 21 stops: reading only the referencing element found stops on
  **nine** of them and dropped the other 166. The entry above says "both gradient kinds in both
  `gradientUnits`", which was true of the elements and false of every real file.
- ⚠️ **`gradientTransform` was not read at all** — 150 uses in that one file.
- ⚠️ **`userSpaceOnUse` coordinates were never mapped into the shape's own space.** The
  `objectBoundingBox` half had its mapping and its test from the first day; the other half had
  neither, so a user-space gradient sat wherever the shape's `x`/`y` had put it.
- ⚠️ **`reference` closed the `url(` at the *last* paren.** SVG allows a fallback colour after a
  paint reference, and Inkscape writes one on every filled shape: `fill: url(#g) rgb(0, 0, 0)`.
  Reading to the last `)` — which belongs to `rgb(` — yields an "id" of `g) rgb(0, 0, 0`. **The
  failure is in the ordinary path, not the fallback one**: a gradient that exists, is spelled
  correctly and is reachable resolves to nothing. This is the one of the seven that nothing in the
  code or the tests hinted at, because the fallback syntax never appears in a hand-written fixture.

**With those four the picture came back, and the remaining three are what the eye then found** —
each caught by rendering the import back out through `ondin-export::svg` and diffing it against the
original in a browser, which took the mean per-channel error from **20.6** to **3.0** out of 255:

- ⚠️ **A radial gradient's radius scaled by the average of the matrix *diagonal*, which a rotation
  zeroes.** For `matrix(0, -1.33, -1.33, 0, …)` — a quarter turn at 4/3, which is how a highlight
  gets rotated into a corner — `a` and `d` are both 0, so the radius collapsed and the gradient
  painted its last stop over the whole shape. The four corner highlights on that camera are
  white-fading-to-*transparent*, so **nothing was exactly the wrong answer to be invisible as a wrong
  answer**: the corners simply went dark and nothing said why. It is `sqrt(|determinant|)`, which is
  exact for any rotation with a uniform scale.
- ⚠️ **A linear gradient's bands are perpendicular to its vector *in the gradient's own space*, and
  mapping the two endpoints does not keep them there.** Only a similarity preserves right angles, so
  under `matrix(2.33, 0, 0, 0.51, …)` the bands tilt — the flash window's sheen is 0.4° off
  horizontal in a browser and came out at 8°. **An affine of a linear gradient is still a linear
  gradient**, so this is exact rather than approximate: what has to be carried is the *covector*
  `Tₗᵢₙ⁻ᵀ·d/|d|²`, read back as `u/|u|²` laid off from the mapped start. ⚠️ **This is not a
  `gradientTransform` corner** — the `objectBoundingBox` mapping of any rect that is not square is
  non-uniform too, so it was wrong for SVG's *default* units on most shapes, and the test that had
  covered that mapping since day one stays green under the naive version because its gradient is
  axis-aligned and the correction is a no-op on an axis.
- **`spreadMethod` was dropped going in and coming out.** A *reflected* gradient is how a
  brushed-metal sheen is written — one ramp, mirrored — and padding it leaves the outer half flat at
  the last stop, which reads as a white band. Thirty-four of that file's gradients reflect. The model
  had held the field all along (`peniko::Gradient::extend`, so it saves and renders); only the reader
  and the writer were dropping it, which is the two-inverse-functions price this entry named on day
  one, collected.

**And one that is not a gradient at all: `rx` ≠ `ry` was read as the smaller.** The entry above called
the alternative "a fidelity nobody asked for". Somebody asked. SVG's corner is an *ellipse* and clamps
each radius to half its own side, so `rx="7.5" ry="65"` on a 15×130 rect is Inkscape's spelling of an
**ellipse** — and the old reading drew a stadium, straight-sided where the drawing had a point. ⚠️
**The large disagreements live at the clamp, not near it**: `min(rx, ry)` is a small error while both
radii are small and becomes a different *shape* the moment one reaches half its side. It is now three
kinds — a `Rect` when the radii agree, an `Ellipse` when both reach half, a `Path` otherwise — so the
shape stays editable wherever the model can hold it exactly. ⚠️ **The test asserts the `NodeKind` and
not the outline**, because a stadium and an ellipse have the *same bounding box*: a `world_bounds`
assertion would have been green for the whole bug.

**What is left is one thing and it is reported.** A radial gradient under a non-uniform transform is
an *ellipse*, and `peniko::RadialGradientPosition` is two circles — fourteen of that file's gradients
are squashed, up to 10:1, and the badge strap is visibly round where the drawing wanted a long soft
streak. It now goes into **`Import::approximated`** rather than being drawn silently, which is what
that second list is for. Holding it exactly would need a per-fill brush transform on the model — a
save-format and inspector change, not a paste fix.

⚠️ **Three flips, three predicted sites, and all three predictions right for once** — worth recording
only because the entry above records two sessions where they were not. The diagonal-average radius
gives **0** at a quarter turn, the naive endpoint mapping gives exactly `(40, 10)` against a correct
`(4.71, 18.82)`, and `min(rx, ry)` gives a `Rect` where an `Ellipse` belongs. **The finding is in what
*else* the flips left green**: the naive endpoint mapping fails in exactly one test, the new one, and
the eleven-month-old `a_bounding_box_gradient_is_mapped_onto_the_shape` never had teeth against the
one error a gradient's geometry can make while still looking plausible.

*The method is the transferable part.* None of the seven is visible by reading `svg_in.rs`, and the
round-trip test that binds the reader to the writer passes with all seven present, because both sides
of a fixture written by hand agree about what SVG looks like. What found them was **importing the real
file and rendering the result back to SVG beside the original** — a counted probe for the first four
(67 unpainted of 82), then a canvas pixel-diff for the rest, which named the regions rather than the
causes and was right about every one. It is the same lesson as the `<!DOCTYPE>` and the inherited
font size one amendment above, met a third time: *a fixture is written by someone who already knows
what they are testing.*

### Amended a fourth time, 2026-09-01 — the blur, and the spelling a property is read in

**The maintainer pasted `car.svg`** — 7,415 lines, 417 paths, the largest thing this has been given —
**and reported it as very close except that the blurs were missing.** They were: 70 shapes that should
have been soft came through sharp, which on that drawing is the ground shadow, every headlamp glow and
every panel reflection.

⚠️ **Two bugs wearing one coat, and the second is the one worth the entry.** The reader tested
`el.has_attribute("filter")`, and **Inkscape writes the whole presentation block into `style=""`** —
so the filters were not read *and were not reported either*. `Import::skipped` came back **empty** on
a drawing that had just lost seventy effects. A silent loss is the one thing that list exists to
prevent, so *the spelling a property is read in is part of the feature*, not an implementation
detail: anything consulted through `property` is safe, and anything reached with `attribute` is a
claim that no file will ever use `style`. Grepping every attribute read in the module against the
list of presentation properties found `clip-path` and `mask` making the same claim — latent, since
nothing had reported them wrong yet, and fixed because the live one showed the price. *The sweep is
the return on the bug; the bug alone was one line.*

**The blur itself cost almost nothing, which is the shape this entry keeps meeting.** All 56 of that
file's filters are a lone `<feGaussianBlur>` — what Inkscape's *Blur* slider writes — and
`EffectKind::LayerBlur` is exactly that, held on a node so it composites on a `<g>` as readily as on a
shape. The conversion is one constant: `BLUR_DEVIATION` is a half, so the radius is twice the
deviation. And **the writer already emitted `<feGaussianBlur>`**, so the round trip closed the moment
the reader could read one — the two-inverse-functions price this entry named on day one, refunded for
once.

Everything else a `<filter>` can be is still skipped and counted: ~~a graph of primitives,~~ a
primitive that is not a blur, a reference to nothing, and ⚠️ `primitiveUnits="objectBoundingBox"`,
where `stdDeviation` is a **fraction of the bounding box** and reading it as a length turns half a
shape into half a pixel. Two unequal deviations are averaged and reported, since the model's blur is
isotropic. **A graph of primitives left that list on 2026-09-03** — the shadow idiom and
`<feDropShadow>` are read now, so what this amendment scoped as "a lone blur is all Inkscape writes"
turned out to be the reason every effect *this app* exported came back as nothing (D411).

⚠️ **The filter *region* is deliberately not modelled and deliberately not reported**, and the second
half of that was a decision reversed by its own measurement. A `<filter>` clips its output to a region
— `-10% -10% 120% 120%` of the bounding box by default — and a layer blur has none. The first pass
compared each region against the default and called **14 of that file's 22** tighter, which is what a
user would have been told. **Not one is a clip.** Inkscape fits the region to the blur *per axis*, so a
wide flat shape gets a smaller fraction in `x` and a larger one in `y` for the same absolute reach —
the fractions are not comparable across axes, and comparing them is the whole of the false positives.
What it fits to is 2.4 σ against `BLUR_CUTOFF`'s 3 σ, so the model paints an extra 0.6 σ of tail
carrying about 1.6% of the kernel. *A warning that fires on the common case teaches a reader to ignore
the list*, which costs more than the thing it warns about. The check is named in the source as a
`const _FILTER_REGION_IS_NOT_MODELLED` with its reasoning, because **a check that was written,
measured and removed is worth more to the next reader than one that was never considered.**

**The numbers, against the browser and by the same round-trip-and-diff method as the amendment
above**: mean per-channel error **6.07 → 1.14** out of 255, and pixels differing by more than 32/255
**6.19% → 0.13%**. ⚠️ **And the residual was *attributed* rather than assumed**, which is the method
worth copying: every shape in the source whose fill resolves to a squashed radial gradient was
repainted magenta, that file rendered beside the diff, and the two grids overlaid. Every error cell
above the noise floor sits on magenta coverage. Two cells in the 1–4/255 band do not, which is
rasterizer difference rather than anything named — *and saying so is the point*, since a report that
accounts for 100% of a residual is usually a report that stopped looking.

So the outstanding list for this feature is now one item, and it is the same one: an **elliptical
radial gradient**, ~~which `peniko::RadialGradientPosition` cannot hold~~. Everything else in two real
Inkscape drawings reads. ⚠️ **That reason is wrong and was re-scoped on 2026-09-03** (D411): an
elliptical radial gradient is a circular one under a non-uniform **brush transform**, and both
backends already have that mechanism — what is missing is a gradient transform on the model's `Fill`,
which is a model change rather than an upstream wall.

**D806 — The SVG reader's CSS is a small cascade engine, and the line is drawn at the ancestor walk.
*Built and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — D394's "a lookup, not a cascade engine" is the rule that
changed.***

`roadmap.md`'s *Now · SVG import* carried this as *"a CSS selector needing a combinator, which is a
cascade engine rather than a lookup"*, and the framing was the thing that was wrong: a cascade engine
of the kind an SVG file wants is a compound parser and an ancestor walk, and what makes a real one
large is everything this still refuses. `Css` reads **compounds** — one optional element name or `*`,
any number of `.class`, at most one `#id`, all of which must match the same element — joined by the
**descendant** (whitespace) and **child** (`>`) combinators in any chain, so `.outer .inner` and
`#a > rect.b > .c` both resolve. **The contract is unchanged and the refused set is narrower**: `+`
and `~` need sibling order, `:pseudo` needs state, `[attr]` needs attribute matching, and each still
comes back as `"style (complex selector)"`, counted **once for the sheet** on D394's own argument.

🚨 **Matching is right-to-left and `chain` is stored that way** — `chain[0]` is the compound
immediately left of the subject. That is not a detail of the walk, it is the reason the walk is
cheap: the subject is the filter most rules fail on before an ancestor is ever looked at, which is
why real engines match in this direction too. `Sel::matches` is
`subject.matches(el) && match_chain(&self.chain, el)`, and `Css::declaration` tests the specificity
and the declaration's *presence* before it calls `matches` at all, so the tree is walked only for a
rule that could win. **Storing `chain` left-to-right is the obvious simplification and it costs the whole
ordering.**

⚠️ **`match_chain` is recursive because the descendant combinator backtracks.** `.a .b .c` against a
tree where the nearest `.b` above a `.c` has no `.a` above *it* has to keep looking further up; a
greedy walk that takes the first matching ancestor and commits answers `false`. The case is not
exotic — it is any repeated class in a nested group, which is exactly what a hand-written sheet
produces.

🚨 **A malformed selector is refused, not repaired**, which is this module's *"nothing is lost
silently"* contract pointed at its own parser. `.a > > .b` read leniently becomes `.a > .b`, a
**wider** rule than the one written, so it answers `None` and is reported — as do a leading or
trailing `>`, two ids on one compound, and an empty class name. Half-understanding a selector paints
the wrong shapes and says nothing, which is the one outcome this reader exists to avoid.
⚠️ **`parse_compound` refuses an *empty* compound rather than reading it as `*`** for the same
reason, and that is the line a later simplification will reach for.

⚠️ **Specificity is summed as `100·ids + 10·classes + 1·types` across the whole selector**, which
generalises the single-component 1/10/100 the old code used — **and a selector with more than nine
classes on one side would carry into the next place.** Named as a known bound rather than left as an
assumption: a real SVG stylesheet does not reach it, and comparing the triple instead is a different
ordering to write and test for no case anybody has. *Revisit if a generated sheet ever produces one.*

⚠️ **`skipped` rather than `approximated`, unchanged and right on the record's own rule.** D394's
amendment draws that pair as *missing* against *there and slightly wrong*, and a rule that does not
apply is D493's case exactly — the shape takes whatever it inherits, which is not the declaration in
some other form. ⚠️ **The "D477 rule" both code comments cite for this was carried by D493's
prose and by `svg_in.rs` alone until 2026-09-19, D477 having had no body entry**. It has one now — a
reconstruction written from its citation sites — but it states the rule by pointing rather than by
restating it, so **D493 is still where the bucket is worked through** and re-deciding it from D477's
citation alone would still be re-deciding it from very little.

*(Built and tested 2026-09-19; **Resolved.** Two tests, one amended.
`a_selector_reads_combinators_and_compounds` builds a `<g class="outer">` over a `.a`, a direct-child
`.kid`, a nested `<g>` holding a grandchild `.kid`, and a `rect.both`. ⚠️ **The child combinator is
asserted against the grandchild that must *not* match**, without which a `>` implemented as a
descendant walk passes. ⚠️ **Specificity is asserted by the rules *losing*, not by arithmetic**:
`.outer .a` is written **first** and still beats the bare `.a` after it, so the later-wins tiebreak
cannot explain the result. 🚨 **Both flips land on the grandchild assertion** — making `Child` walk
every ancestor, and dropping the `chain` check from `Sel::matches` entirely — which says that one
shape is carrying the test and that nothing else there would notice either mutation; whether the
assertions after it stay green is **reasoned, not measured**, since it panics before them.
`a_selector_this_cannot_read_is_refused_rather_than_guessed` is a table over nine refused selectors
and eight accepted, the four malformed ones among them.
⚠️ **`a_selector_that_needs_a_cascade_is_reported_once` went red and was amended**, its unreadable
example having been `g > rect`: **a test that goes red because a feature landed is the test doing its
job**, and the repair is to move the example — `rect + rect` now — rather than to weaken the
assertion. D394's *"a lookup, not a cascade engine"* sentence is amended in place, and §7's two
copies of that phrase with it; the `!important` half of one survives on its other leg, there being no
important-vs-normal tier here either way. Three prose sites in `svg_in.rs` are corrected by the
change and a fourth was found here —
`Css::declaration`'s doc closed *"every selector here has exactly one"*, a claim about components
that this entry makes false. **The *Now · SVG import* bullet is struck from `roadmap.md`** and the
*CSS combinators* clause in that section's table row with it; `<foreignObject>` and the rejoined
paragraph are what the row has left — **and `<foreignObject>` left it the same day as a decided
non-goal, D813**, so the rejoined paragraph is the whole of what remains)*

**D813 — `<foreignObject>` is a decided non-goal, and the words are said at last. *Ruled by the
maintainer 2026-09-19; Resolved — a decided non-goal, and no production line changed.***

`roadmap.md` carried this as an open SVG-import item whose own text said it should not be one: it
*"sits here rather than in §0 only because no one has said the words"*, a state it was audited into
on 2026-09-03 (**D411**) and then left in for sixteen days.

**The words are said.** `<foreignObject>` is HTML inside an SVG, nothing in this model draws HTML,
and there is no version of it to build — not a smaller one, not a partial one. It is not a feature
held up by a dependency, which is the state most of that section's remaining items are in.

It is **reported like any other unread element**, so `svg_in`'s *"nothing is lost silently"* contract
already covers it and always did. That is worth stating, because the contract is the reason this can
be a non-goal rather than a gap: a file carrying one is not quietly mangled, it is told about.

**Record-only, so the citation is planted by hand** on `svg_in`'s module head, in the
`Import::skipped` list — the one place a reader meets the question *why does this element not come
in*. ⚠️ **It moves into `roadmap.md` §0 as well as being struck from *Now · SVG import***, which is
what §0 is for: an item that sat for sixteen days one sentence short of a decision is exactly the
thing that ledger exists to stop being re-argued. With this and D806 gone, that section has the
rejoined paragraph and nothing else. *That went three days later — **D826**, below — and the section
is empty.*

**D826 — Rejoining a multi-line paragraph on SVG import is a decided non-goal for v1. *Ruled by the
maintainer 2026-09-22; Resolved — a decided non-goal, and the last item in its section.***

A multi-line text layer of ours exports as one `<text>` per line (D81) and comes back as one layer
per line, because nothing in the markup says they were one node. `svg_in`'s `text_node` has argued
for as long as it has existed that this is **a real loss rather than an oversight** — the writer put
each line at a baseline the canvas computed, and rejoining them means **inventing the line height**
that decides where every line after the first sits.

🚨 **The refusal is about what the only available signal actually identifies.** Same `x`, a constant
`y` step and a matching resolved style is not evidence of a paragraph: it is *also* exactly what a
stack of separate labels in a foreign file looks like — a legend, a table column, a set of axis
ticks. So the heuristic welds unrelated layers into one text node, and the user has no way to say
which reading was meant. *An importer that guesses wrong here destroys structure the file did have,
to recover structure it never recorded*, which is the wrong side of `svg_in`'s standing bargain.

⚠️ **And the case it would have been worth most for is answered elsewhere.** The paragraph a user
most wants back whole is one of *their own*, and since **D823** a copy crossing between two `ondin`
windows carries real nodes — paragraph and all — through `io::clip` rather than through markup. What
is left here is the foreign file, which never had the structure to lose. *The round trip closes for
the picture and not for the paragraph, and that sentence is now the end of an argument rather than
the start of one.*

Nothing else about the element is open: a positioned `<tspan x y>` already starts a new layer and a
bare one joins the text, pinned by `a_positioned_tspan_starts_a_new_layer_and_a_bare_one_does_not`,
and a `<tspan>`'s own style is read as character spans (D396, D398). The loss is reported like every
other, so `svg_in`'s *"nothing is lost silently"* contract covers this as it covers `<foreignObject>`
above — which is the reason both can be non-goals rather than gaps.

*(Record-only, no production line changed; **the citation is planted by hand** on `svg_in`'s
`text_node`, in the run that already argued the loss was real, because that paragraph is where a
reader meets the question. **It moves into `roadmap.md` §0** and is struck from *Now · SVG import* —
which D813 had already reduced to this one item, so **that section now has nothing open**.)*

**D395 — A blur is rasterized coarser the further in you zoom, because its cost is otherwise
unbounded. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-01; Keep, with a second timeout recorded and not fixed.***

**The maintainer zoomed to about 800% on the pasted car drawing and the app died**, with

```
wgpu error: Validation Error
  In Texture::create_view
    Texture with 'ondin-fx-batch' label is invalid
```

⚠️ **Neither of the two obvious readings is right, and both were checked before anything was
changed.** Nothing had run out of memory, and nothing exceeded `max_texture_dimension_2d` — the shelf
packer already clamps to it, the app's device (via `egui-wgpu`) reports exactly 8192, and at the frame
that actually failed the packed chunk was 7520×2170. A texture is "invalid" in wgpu when its
*creation* failed, and here creation failed because **the device was gone**.

**A separable gaussian is `O(w · h · σ)`, and σ in device pixels is the authored deviation times the
zoom.** So the cost of a fixed drawing grows without bound as someone zooms in, and that file's
largest blur — 55.5 units, from `stdDeviation="27.8"` — asked for:

| zoom | σ (device px) | kernel | blur work, whole frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1× | 27.8 | 169 taps | 0.2 G texel fetches |
| 4× | 111 | 669 taps | 5 G |
| 7× | 194 | 1,169 taps | **25 G** |
| 8× | 222 | 1,335 taps | **32 G** |
| 12× | 333 | 2,001 taps | **72 G** |

Windows resets a GPU that has not finished in two seconds. ⚠️ **Every resource on a lost device
reports invalid at once, so the panic lands wherever the *next* frame happens to touch the device
first** — which is why the reported label and the one the reproduction hit are different: a
`Texture::create_view` on `ondin-fx-batch` for the maintainer, a `get_mapped_range` on
`ondin-fx-params` (a buffer of a few bytes) in the sweep. *A tiny allocation failing is the tell that
it is not about size at all.* The second panic in the report — a swapchain semaphore destroyed while
in use — is the unwind running over the same dead device, not a second bug.

**The fix is that the resolution was never needed.** A gaussian of deviation σ carries nothing finer
than σ, so a layer whose output is blurred by 222 device pixels is fully described by a buffer nine
times coarser — and the blur *that* buffer needs is nine times narrower, which is the same picture for
an eightieth of the convolution. `effect::buffer_downscale` returns the factor, both
`push_effect_layer`s divide the buffer and the pass scale by it, and both `pop_layer`s scale the
result back up. **Past the budget the cost stops growing with the zoom and starts falling**, because
the kernel is pinned and the buffer keeps shrinking: 32 G → 2 G at 8×, 72 G → **1 G** at 12×, kernel
pinned at 145 taps everywhere.

⚠️ **Only a `LayerBlur` may buy the downscale, and this is the one way the optimisation could be
*wrong* rather than merely ineffective.** A blur on the layer softens everything the layer produces,
so the output has no detail left for a coarser buffer to lose. A **drop shadow blurs a silhouette**
and composites it behind artwork that stays sharp — so reading its deviation as the layer's would
license a downscale that visibly softens the drawing. `layer_blur_deviation` is the function that says
so, and `a_shadows_blur_does_not_buy_a_downscale` is the test; its flip — letting a shadow count —
returns 66.7 where 1.0 belongs.

⚠️ **Factors under 2× are declined, and the deadband is a measurement rather than caution.** Rendering
the drawing through the CPU backend at 1×, 4× and 8×, with the cap and without it, came back
**byte-identical at 4× and 8×** — where the factors are 4.6 and 9.3 — and differed at 1×, where the
largest factor is 1.157: mean 0.007/255, worst channel 13, on 0.000% of pixels. That is the shape to
expect, and it is the opposite of the intuition that a *smaller* change is safer — a shallow downscale
resamples without the blur being wide enough to hide it, while saving a quarter of a convolution that
was never the problem. With the deadband all three views are byte-identical and three layers are still
downscaled, so the check is not vacuous. **The whole benefit is in the large factors.**

Both backends compute the factor from the one function in `ondin-core`, for D342's reason from the
other direction: two backends that chose different buffer *resolutions* would blur the same drawing by
different amounts, and would agree with each other about nothing.

⚠️ **A second timeout remains and is deliberately not fixed here.** Sweeping viewport, zoom and origin
on device found one more frame over the watchdog — 3840×2100 at 1600%, **2,118 ms**, and the next
frame found the device dead. Its blur work is 2 G, so it is **not** this bug: it is the cost of
rasterizing 417 paths at sixteen times magnification, in the main scene and in the effect batch. It
needs its own answer (culling at extreme zoom, or a ceiling on the fx pass) and its own entry. Naming
it is what stops the next reader concluding that the crash class is closed because this one is.

*Two things about the method, both of which cost time to learn.* **The sweep was the instrument**: a
single render at the reported zoom passed, and so did 600 repeats of one frame — the failure only
appears when a genuinely expensive frame is followed by another, so a reproduction has to vary the
parameters rather than repeat one. And ⚠️ **`pack`'s doc comment asserted the thing that needed
checking** — *"a layer larger than that cannot exist — the walk clamps every buffer to the target"* —
which is true, and which quietly framed the whole investigation as being about sizes. It was about
time.

**D396 — A `<tspan>`'s own colour comes back as a character span, so a two-colour line survives the
round trip. *Built and tested 2026-09-01; Keep — the per-run **font** properties were still lost, and
lost silently, when this was written; **D398 closed that the same day**.***

D394's amendment read an unpositioned `<tspan>` as text and threw its style away with a
`text (per-run style)` report. That was honest and it was avoidable for the colour: `CharSpans` **is**
a per-run colour over a byte range (D154), and one `<tspan>` per style run **is** what this app's own
writer emits (D81) — so the one file this reader was most certain to be handed was the one it
flattened. A two-colour line went out as markup and came back monochrome with a note.

`Import::text` now collects `(start, end, Color)` against the **untrimmed** `pending` string and
clears them with it, a range meaning nothing once the string it indexes has gone; `Import::text_node`
takes them as *ranges rather than as spans* because it owns the trim, and a range shifted by anyone
else is a span over the wrong letters. ⚠️ **Only the back end of that trim can bite, and nothing here
should be read as saying the front one runs**: `push_collapsed` starts with `space = out.is_empty()`,
so leading whitespace never enters the string, `lead` is `0` for every input this module can build,
and the `saturating_sub` is defensive against a change to *collapsing* quietly becoming a change to
*which letters are coloured*. The `min` is the half that does run — dropping it leaves a run ending on
a trailing space spanning `4..8` of a seven-byte string, the predicted site and the one the flip hits.

`paint_differs` is gone, and the pair that replaced it carries the reasoning. `solid_fill` is the
run's colour with `fill-opacity` folded in — folded *there*, or two runs differing only in opacity
compare equal — and `None` for a gradient, the one fill a character span cannot hold. `ink` is that
colour at `to_rgba8` precision. ⚠️ **The comparison that decides "does this run differ" has to ask the
question `Spans` will ask, and that question is in `u8`**: `Spans::set` canonicalizes every value
through the scope's own setter and `Spans::normalize` then drops any span equal to the node default,
so comparing at `f32` can call a run different, mint a span for it, and have the span silently vanish.

**One of the three flips did not bite, and it corrected a comment rather than the code.** The node's
own colour is now stored through `TextStyle::set` instead of assigned to the field, so `fill-opacity`
is quantized to the 1/255 `typography::canonical_color` keeps and the hex field and the opacity
control can express — an `f32` alpha of exactly 0.5 is a value *the user cannot reproduce or clear*.
The comment above that line said it was what stopped an invisible span, and putting the raw assignment
back left every test **green**: `ink` has already compared the two runs one function up and never
pushed the range, so `normalize` is never reached. The comment now says what the line is for, and the
assertion that does bite is a new one on the *stored* alpha, `fill-opacity="0.5"` reading back as
128/255. *A comment justifying a line can name a mechanism that is real and is not the one doing the
work* — which is this project's own standing lesson, met on a line written the same hour.

**The second flip was read wrong, and the correction is the more useful half of this entry.**
Deleting `text`'s `if positioned { continue; }` left every test green, and this entry's first draft
recorded it as an inert **shortcut** on the strength of that. It is not: the colour and stroke arms
below it are indeed comparisons with themselves, a positioned `<tspan>` having just *become*
`run_style`, but the **gradient** arm is not a comparison at all, so without the `continue` a
positioned `<tspan fill="url(#g)">` reports `text (per-run style)` there *and* `text (gradient fill)`
again from `text_node`, which sees it as the node it becomes. The flip was green for want of a
**fixture with that input**, not for want of a mechanism; with the fixture written it bites,
`["text (per-run style)", "text (gradient fill)"]` against one. *A flip that does not bite is a
finding about coverage*, and reading it as a finding about the code is how a live line comes to be
documented as decoration — which is the same lesson as the paragraph above it, arriving from the
opposite direction on the very next line of the same function.

⚠️ **A gradient the text node itself cannot hold was dropped in silence, and that is now closed.** A
gradient *stated on a run* was already reported, and must be read through `property` so the `style=""`
spelling counts (D394's fourth amendment) — but a gradient on the `<text>` itself, or on a positioned
`<tspan>`, which becomes a node of its own, reached **no report at all**, and
`a_per_run_gradient_is_reported_where_a_per_run_colour_is_carried`'s second case asserted `approximated`
was *empty* over exactly that markup, so the test pinned the wrong side of the gap. `text_node` now
carries an `else if style.fill.is_some()` arm calling `approximate("text (gradient fill)")` — **there
rather than in `text`, because it is the only place that sees a whole node's fill**, and a positioned
`<tspan>` arrives there as its own node, which is what makes the `continue` above the honest way to
report one gradient once. That second case now asserts `["text (gradient fill)"]` and that no span is
minted; a **third** case covers the positioned `<tspan x y fill="url(#g)">` that had no fixture at all,
asserting two layers and exactly one report. ⚠️ **Nothing green found this**: it was a brief read
against the code, and the assertion that would have had to fail was the assertion that had been
written to agree with it. Per-run **font** properties (`font-size`, `font-weight`, `font-family`, italic) are
lost the same silent way, and `CharAttr` holds all four, so that one is the next step colour just
took rather than a wall; it was this module's one standing breach of its own "nothing is lost
silently" contract, and ⚠️ **D398 took that step the same day** — so this paragraph is the state of
the module for a few hours only, and is kept because it is what made the next change obvious.

`a_runs_colour_survives_the_round_trip_where_its_paragraph_does_not` is the only thing binding the
writer's per-run `<tspan>` to the reader, the two living in different crates and neither suite seeing
the seam. ⚠️ **Its fixture says `Hi <there>` and the angle brackets are the point**: the writer escapes
them, so byte 3 of the content and byte 3 of the markup are different characters and a reader counting
markup bytes would colour `t;there` and still pass every assertion about a span existing. The range is
asserted exactly and the decoded content is asserted first. Removing the `inks.push` fails it with
`left: 0`. The name is the other half of the report: the colour closes, the **paragraph** still does
not, for D394's reason.

**D397 — A frame's paint card is headed *Fill*, like every other layer's, and the old name made the
header depend on how many things were selected. *Built and tested 2026-09-01; Keep — but the second
half of that verdict lasted hours. It read "the name matches the rest of the app now and the capability
still does not, which is a model question nobody has asked"; somebody asked the same day, and D400 is
the answer. Read every "still" below as history.***

Reported as a wording inconsistency: a frame's paint card said *Frame background* where every other
layer's says *Fill*. Reading it made the inconsistency sharper than a word. `build::paint_targets`
counts an `Artboard` and `build::fills_seen_as` presents a frame's background as a one-entry fill
list, so a **multi-selection containing frames has always drawn their backgrounds under a panel headed
*Fill*** — only `inspector_artboard`, the single-frame path, renamed it. The same paint, the same row,
two names decided by how many things were selected.

The title `inspector_artboard` hands `self.panel` is now `"Fill"`. ⚠️ **That title is the collapse key
and the widget-id salt as well as the header** (`OndinApp::panel`), so the rename is not only a
string: a frame inherits the same collapsed-or-not state as every other layer's Fill, which is the
half of the unification you can feel rather than read. It is why the panel joins the collapse
machinery at all — `sync_paint_collapse("Fill", bg.is_none(), fresh)` for the resting state, and the
`+` that adds a ground calls `open_paint_panel("Fill")`, or the ground is added, the picker opens over
a collapsed card, and closing the picker leaves no sign anything happened.

**Getting `fresh` there safely moved the read up a level.** `inspector_paint_panels` no longer asks
`paint_subject_changed` itself; it takes `fresh: bool`, and each of its four call sites asks once.
That extends a rule `paint_subject_changed`'s own doc already stated for Fill and Stroke — read once
and handed to both — to *three* panels, and it is load-bearing rather than tidy: the background panel
draws **before** the paint panels, so letting it ask would have consumed the edge and left Stroke told
that nothing had happened.

**`NodeKind::takes_paint()` stays false for an `Artboard`, and that is not the contradiction it looks
like.** It answers "are this kind's fills in `Paint`", which is a question about the model, and a
frame's background is in its own field because a frame has exactly one. The panel is a question about
what the user is looking at. Worth stating outright, because it is the thing the next reader would
"fix" for consistency — and a frame that answered true would then be drawn *two* Fill cards, the
background one and the ordinary one, with nothing to say which is which. ⚠️ **It answers `true` since
the same day** (D400): a frame's fills genuinely are in `Paint` now, so the question this paragraph
splits in two has one answer again. The warning was right about the mechanism and wrong about which
way it would be resolved — what stopped the two Fill cards was **deleting the background card**, not
keeping the predicate narrow.

**The capability did not change and is not an oversight.** A frame still holds one background rather
than a list, so the card has one row, no reorder grip, no eye, and its `+` goes away once filled — the
known limitation `architecture.md` §5.7a already records. The **name** now matches the rest of the
app; the *capability* still does not, and giving a frame a real fill list is a model change nobody has
asked for. Recorded plainly so it is not re-argued as an oversight. ⚠️ **Asked for hours later and
built the same day** (D400) — a frame's fills are a real list, this card is gone, and the paragraph
above is a record of the state that made the rename worth doing rather than a description of anything
still true. *Recording a decision plainly is what made the next one one sentence long;* the ask came
back as "there's no reason for frames to be treated different", which is this paragraph read from the
other side.

`panels::inspector::frame_fill_tests` runs `inspector_single` headlessly over a `Rect` and an
`Artboard` and reads the panel headers back out of `FullOutput::shapes`. ⚠️ **The probe filters on
`"FILL"`, not `"Fill"`, because `section_head` uppercases the title** — in `ui::eyebrow`, which is
where a reader grepping `section_head` for a `to_uppercase` will not find it. The string handed to
`panel` is the collapse key, the id salt *and* the source of the header, and only the last of the
three is upper case. The first run filtered on the mixed-case spelling and collected nothing at all, **control
included**, which is the only reason the mistake was caught rather than shipped as a green test about
nothing. The assertions are on the **count** of Fill headers and on the `["FILL", "STROKE"]` order
rather than on Fill being present, because the failure this really guards against is *two* Fill
panels, which is what a frame gets the day `takes_paint()` starts answering true for an `Artboard`.
⚠️ **That day was the same day** (D400), and the test survived it green: `takes_paint` answers true,
and what kept the count at one was the background card going. An assertion that outlives the change it
was written against is the only kind worth keeping, which is why the module's own doc now says so.
Flip: `"Frame background"` put back fails the "old title is gone" assertion, reporting
`["FRAME BACKGROUND", "STROKE"]` — a picture of the state this change was about.

**D398 — A `<tspan>`'s font scope comes back as character spans too, which closes the importer's last
silent loss. *Built and tested 2026-09-01; Keep — with one known non-fixed-point in the round trip,
recorded below and read rather than measured.***

D396 carried a `<tspan>`'s colour into `CharSpans` and named what it left behind: `font-size`,
`font-weight`, `font-style` and `font-family` were read into `Style`, compared nowhere below it, and
dropped with **no report at all**. That was this module's one standing breach of its own "nothing is
lost silently" contract, and it is the shape `text`'s own doc now warns about by name — *a field read
into `Style` and compared nowhere below is exactly how the font scope came to be dropped in silence*.
`Import::text`'s per-run carrier is `Vec<(usize, usize, CharAttr)>` where it was
`Vec<(usize, usize, Color)>`, and `Import::text_node`'s last parameter with it.

**One entry per attribute rather than a style per range.** The four properties are decided
independently — a `<tspan>` may state a size and inherit its weight — and that is also the shape
`Spans::set` takes, so a run that states two of them owes two spans over the same bytes rather than one
style. `a_tspans_font_scope_becomes_spans_rather_than_being_dropped_in_silence` therefore asserts the
exact **set** of kinds, which is what gives the flip teeth: dropping the `Weight` push fails it with
`[(4, 7, Size)]` against `[(4, 7, Size), (4, 7, Weight)]`, where an assertion that merely counted spans
or looked one up by kind would have passed.

⚠️ **Size, weight and italic are plain comparisons against `run_style`; the family is not, and the
difference is why there is a new function.** A `font-family` is a preference *order*, so the run's list
goes through `Import::pick_family` — the first name in it this machine actually has — which is the same
helper the node's own default now uses. That extraction is the point rather than tidiness: two copies
of that choice are how a node and its runs would come to substitute differently, i.e. how one line of
text would come to be shaped in two faces the file never named. A run naming only families this machine
lacks gets **no span and a report**; `approximate` dedupes by name, so a file whose every run names the
