same missing font reports once. Making the picker take the list's head regardless fails the new family
case **and two older tests with it** — `an_unavailable_family_is_substituted_and_said_out_loud` and
`font_properties_inherit_and_reach_a_positioned_tspan` — which is the return on one shared picker
instead of two copies, collected by a flip.

⚠️ **A value equal to the node's own is pushed anyway and dropped by `Spans::normalize`**, rather than
filtered out here. Two families resolving to the same face is the case that makes this worth stating:
`"Foo, Arial"` and `"Arial"` differ as lists and agree as spans, so a pre-filter here would be a second
answer to a question the model already answers, and the two would drift.

**The node's own defaults are built through `TextStyle::with`/`set` now instead of a struct literal**,
so a size is clamped into `MIN_FONT_SIZE..=MAX_FONT_SIZE` and a weight into `1..=1000` **on the node
exactly as `Spans::set` clamps them on a span**. A default assigned raw is a default a span can never
equal once the file states something out of range, and `normalize` keeps an override of a value
identical to the one under it — an invisible span that no rendering and no eye can find.
⚠️ **The predicted failure site was wrong here and the test's comment now says so**: reverting to
`font_size: style.font_size` was predicted to fail on the *span* and fails one assertion earlier,
`left: 0.1, right: 1.0`, on the node's own size. The stranded span is real and simply never witnessed,
which is the whole reason this project writes the predicted site down and then corrects it.

**A span covering every byte is hoisted onto the node default, and that came out of a failing test
rather than out of taste.** ⚠️ `svg_roundtrip`'s
`a_runs_colour_survives_the_round_trip_where_its_paragraph_does_not` began reporting **two** spans
where it expects one: `[Span { 0..10, Weight(500) }, Span { 3..10, Color(…) }]`. The cause is this
app's own writer — D81 emits one `<tspan>` per style run and puts every font property **on the tspan**,
stating none of them on the `<text>` — so re-importing our own single-weight line produced a node
saying SVG's initial 400 with a `Weight(500)` lying over the whole string. **It renders identically,
which is exactly why nothing would ever have surfaced it**; only a test counting spans could.
`text_node` now `set`s any span whose range is `0..content.len()` onto the `TextStyle` and then
`clear`s it. Two runs that *agree* land here too, `normalize` having merged them into one span over
everything before this sees them. The loop works in **kinds, not values**, so clearing one attribute
leaves another's spans alone; dropping the `clear` and keeping the `set` fails `spans.is_empty()`, and
dropping the whole block fails one line earlier, on the node's weight reading 400.

⚠️ **A line of two *different* weights is a known non-fixed-point, and this paragraph is a reading of
the two functions rather than a measurement.** What is measured is the one-cycle case, which is what
the round-trip test asserts. The rest follows from the writer stating no font property on the `<text>`
at all: on re-import `run_style` is SVG's initial 400, so every run whose weight differs from 400 mints
a span, and a node whose own weight is not 400 gives it up — "node 500, `Weight(700)` over the tail"
comes back as "node 400, `Weight(500)` over the head and `Weight(700)` over the tail", neither span
covering the whole content and so neither hoisted. It renders identically at every step, and it is a
fixed point from there on, because the two documents produce the *same markup*: the run styles the
writer reads are unchanged, only where they are written down has moved. *Revisit if the writer ever
starts stating a font property on the `<text>` element*, which would make the first cycle an identity
and this paragraph wrong in both directions.

What a `<tspan>` still loses is a **gradient** fill, which a `CharAttr` cannot hold, and a **stroke**
where only one of the two states has one, strokes being node-level here — both **reported**, which is
the whole of the difference this entry closes.

**D399 — Hyphenation is not being built for v1, and the reason is its price rather than any wall.
*Decided 2026-09-01; Keep — re-take it if D80's offset map is ever built for another reason.***
Asked and answered in one line — *"agreed, file it and don't build it"* — against a recommendation to
file the price accurately rather than pay it.

⚠️ **What this entry exists to protect is the correction, not the decision.** The position it replaces
was that hyphenation was *blocked*: the roadmap carried *"still wants a dictionary crate, and there is
none in the lock"*, which measured the lock file and read as if it had measured the world.
`cargo search` finds `hyphenation 0.8.4` (Knuth–Liang, many languages) with `kl-hyphenate` beside it,
and no step of a re-derivation against `crates/` would ever have said so. Everything below was
measured on 2026-09-01 and every part of it says the feature is **buildable**. If this entry is ever
summarised as "hyphenation is blocked", the summary is wrong, and the error it re-inherits is the one
the correction cost a day to find.

**Two of the three pieces are already here.** parley breaks at `U+00AD` without being asked:
`"hy\u{ad}phen\u{ad}ation"` at a 60pt wrap width lays out as `hy` / `phen` / `ation`, where the same
word without soft hyphens does not break at all and runs to ~112pt. Nothing in parley 0.11.0 mentions
hyphens — it segments with `icu_segmenter`'s `LineSegmenter`, and UAX #14 puts the soft hyphen in
class BA. **And the glyph is inkless**: with the bundled family it shapes to a real glyph id of zero
advance and zero ink, so the laid-out ink box of the soft-hyphenated string, unbroken, is *identical*
to the plain one — `x0: 1.4375, x1: 112.119140625` for both, thirteen glyphs against eleven. Mid-line
soft hyphens cannot smear, which is what makes putting them into the shaped string safe at all, and a
line that breaks at one simply shows no hyphen until we draw one in `text::extract`.

⚠️ **The break decision reserves no room for that hyphen, and it is *not* justify-all's wall.** A
hyphen's advance is 8.99 at 20pt and the fixture's widest line measures 46.34, so parley breaks there
for any wrap width ≥ 47, and at a wrap width of 50 the line plus the hyphen we owe comes to 55.33 —
over the box by more than five points. Justify-all is stuck because the cluster advances it would
re-space are `pub(crate)` and parley exposes no setter for them; **line breaking has to change a
line's measure, for which it does**. `BreakLines::state_mut`, `BreakerState::set_line_max_advance`,
`BreakLines::revert` and `BreakLines::revert_to` are all `pub` in parley 0.11.0, and
`text::break_lines` already calls the first three — `set_line_max_advance` per line for the paragraph
indent, `revert()` for the height limit. So charging the hyphen to the line it ends is a **retry in
that loop**: break the line, and if it ended on a soft hyphen and overflows, revert and re-break it at
`measure − hyphen`. Two details a future reader would otherwise rediscover the hard way —
`break_next` saves `prev_state` at its top, so `revert()` is exactly **one line deep** and the retry
has to happen immediately rather than at the end; and `revert_to` assigns the whole `BreakerState`
back, `line_max_advance` included, so the narrower measure has to be set *after* the revert, which
this loop's top already does for its own reasons.

The piece that genuinely is missing on parley's side is *which byte the line ended at*.
`LineBreakData` is `reason`, `advance`, a line height and two y coordinates, with no range;
`BreakReason` is `None`/`Regular`/`Explicit`/`Emergency`, with no hyphen variant; and
`LineData::text_range` is `pub(crate)` — which is the same fact `Paragraphs`' own doc comment records
from the other side, that a committed line's range is unreadable while the breaker is still running.
So the retry needs a second source for "did this line break at a `U+00AD`": a pass over
`layout.lines()` after `finish()`, which is where `export_lines` already reads `Line::text_range`.
That is a **second layout pass**, and it is a cost rather than an obstacle. The paragraph table is
untouched by any of it — `paragraph_starts` scans `content` and `break_lines`/`y_map` count `Explicit`
breaks by index, and a soft hyphen raises none.

**The price, then, and it is the whole of the decision.** A dictionary crate; that second pass; and
the offset map **D80** already specifies, which is the expensive one. The soft hyphens have to reach
the shaper without entering `content`, and `content` is what `CharSpans`, `ParaSpans`, the caret and
every hit test are indexed on — so this is precisely the wall D80 declined to climb for the case
transform, *"a full offset map threaded through all three — its own project"*, and D80's stated fix, a
shaped-byte → content-byte table, is the same table this needs. That refusal is load-bearing rather
than historical: `cased_text` is length-preserving **by `debug_assert!`**, and D81's byte comparisons
against the laid-out string are sound only because it is. The crossings were counted rather than
estimated: four `Selection::from_byte_index` and one `Cursor::from_byte_index`, the `Cursor::index()`
family that feeds `replace` in `backspace`, `delete_forward` and `delete_word_back` plus the
anchor/focus pair `reshape_keeping_selection` re-derives, `selected_range`, and the style-run ranges
`shape` hands the builder. ⚠️ **The crossings are not confined to
`text.rs`, which a first reading suggests they are**: `selected_range` and `paragraph_range` are `pub`
and read from four sites in `ondin-app` — `preview.rs`, `canvas.rs` and two in `panels/typography.rs`
— every one of them treating the answer as a `content` offset, so the map has to be applied *inside*
those accessors rather than left to their callers. That is a property to preserve, not a fact to lean
on.

*Revisit if the offset map ever arrives for another reason* — D80's case transform is the obvious one,
since it wants the same table — because what is left after that is a dictionary and a retry loop, and
the decision is then worth re-taking rather than inheriting. `roadmap.md` §0 carries the decision and
`text::break_lines` carries a pointer here, on the loop the retry would go in.

**D825 — Tab stops, columns and widow/orphan control are decided non-goals for v1, and justify-all is
emphatically not one. *Ruled by the maintainer 2026-09-22; Resolved — three non-goals and one parked
item, out of what had been one word over four different situations.***

`roadmap.md`'s *Now · Text* carried these as *"the four deferred features"*, which is exactly the
shape D399 above had to spend a day correcting one item at a time. **What the three share is the
opposite of a wall: not one of them is short of a dependency.** Widow/orphan control is a second pass
over the lines `text::break_lines` yields. Tab stops are a layer over `Whitespace::Tab`, which parley
classifies and does not lay out. Columns are a change to what a paragraph's box *is*, above that
function entirely. Each is a build of our own that nobody has asked for, and each was being carried
as though something outside the project were holding it up.

⚠️ **Justify-all is the exception and is not on the list.** It is blocked **upstream**: parley's
`align_impl` hard-codes skipping `BreakReason::None | Explicit`, and `align`, `LayoutData` and
`ClusterData::advance` are every one of them `pub(crate)` — the measurement D399 made from the other
side while pricing the hyphen's retry, and the reason that entry could say *"line breaking has to
change a line's measure, for which it does"* while justify-all cannot. Its trigger is therefore a
**patch upstream**, not a decision here, and it goes to *Later · Parked decisions* rather than to §0.
`roadmap.md` already files it *"beside the flo_curves comparator rather than beside hyphenation"*,
and this entry is what stops the distinction being lost the next time the four are summarised
together.

🚨 **That is the whole point of splitting them, and the file's own history says so.** One word —
*deferred* — stood over a price, a build nobody wants, and an upstream wall, and a sentence like that
gets re-derived as a blocker: *"all six dependencies are still genuinely absent"* covered six
different situations and was true of **none** of them, which is what D399 found and what took a day.
A decided non-goal and a parked upstream gap have different triggers and belong in different lists;
filing them together is what lets one inherit the other's excuse.

*(Record-only, no production line changed; **the citation is planted by hand** on
`text::break_lines`, beside D399's hyphenation note, which is where a reader meets the question of
what this loop is not being asked to do. **The three move into `roadmap.md` §0** and justify-all to
*Later · Parked decisions*, leaving that section with the MCP snapshot's paragraph scope — parked
with MCP — and D171's watch-note, which is a note rather than work.)*

**D400 — A frame's fill is its fill list, exactly like every other painted layer's. *Built and tested
2026-09-01; Keep.***

Asked for in the maintainer's own words: *"Right now frame's fill behaves differently from shapes. It
should be synced. The fill panel should behave on frames exactly as on other layers. Adding fills,
removing, reordering, the whole cast. There's no reason for frames to be treated different."* This is
the model change **D397 predicted and declined**, in as many words — *"giving a frame a real fill list
is a model change nobody has asked for. Recorded plainly so it is not re-argued as an oversight"* —
and the ask arrived hours later. Recording it plainly is what made this one sentence long.

`NodeKind::Artboard { size, background: Option<Brush> }` is `NodeKind::Artboard { size }`. A frame's
fills are `Node::paint().fills` and its strokes are `Node::paint().strokes`, which they already were
(D144). `NodeKind::takes_paint()` answers **true** for an `Artboard`, and `NodeKind::takes_stroke()` is
**deleted**: it existed for exactly one disagreement — a frame could be stroked and not filled — and
there is none left, so `document::op_set_strokes` gates on `is_paintable` where it gated on
`takes_stroke`. `Operation::SetArtboardBackground` is deleted; `SetFills` targets a frame.

⚠️ **`NodeKind::can_mask()` had to be rewritten, and that is the trap this change had in it.** It was
`takes_paint() || matches!(Group)`, which was only ever correct because `takes_paint` said `false` for
a frame. Widening that predicate would silently have handed every frame a mask switch beside its clip
— a real behaviour change with **nothing failing**, since a frame would simply have grown a second
clip control. It is `!Artboard && (takes_paint() || Group)` now, written out rather than inherited,
which is what a predicate defined in terms of another one owes the day the base moves. A frame still
may not mask.

**What core's bulk verbs got is not shorter code; it is answers they were getting wrong.** Every one of
them had a frame-shaped branch, and the branch is where the defect lived.

- `build::fills_seen_as` is **gone**. Its whole body was the frame case — one `background` presented as
  a one-entry stand-in list — and every other kind fell through to `paint.fills.clone()`, which is what
  the function now *is*, so its six callers read the field. The app's `DisplayNode` needed it because it
  is not a `Node`; it needs nothing now, the two pieces having become one.
- `build::any_strokeable_in` and the private `strokeable_targets` are **gone**. The fill scope and the
  stroke scope are the same set of targets (`paint_targets`), and the Stroke panel asks `any_paint_in`.
- `build::set_fills_all` gave a frame `fills.first()` and **dropped the rest** — the "known limitation"
  `architecture.md` §5.7a recorded, where a shared list of two left the frame with one and the shapes
  with both, so the panel's list stopped being the truth for part of what it was showing. It takes the
  whole list.
- `build::edit_fills_all` pulled only the *brush* back out of the stand-in, which carried no `visible`
  flag. **"Hide every fill in the selection" silently skipped the frames in it.** That works.
- `build::recolor`, `build::repaint` and `build::colors_in` each had a third branch beside the fill loop
  and the stroke loop that could only ever see **one** paint on a frame; a frame with two fills now has
  both recoloured and both counted. `build::properties_of` was `!takes_paint() && !matches!(Artboard)`
  and is one predicate, so *Copy properties* off a two-fill frame carries both.
- `build::paint_targets`' `Artboard` arm went as **redundant, not as a change of behaviour**: the
  `takes_paint` arm does the same thing. ⚠️ The *fact* it stated is load-bearing and is the reason this
  walk exists at all, so it is written in the doc comment instead — **a frame is a target, never a
  container to pass through.** A match arm that cannot be reached is a claim the compiler has stopped
  checking, which is worse than prose.

⚠️ **A frame still cannot fall through `scene::paint_shape`'s generic tail, and the duplication is
deliberate.** The tail fills *and then* strokes in one place; a frame's fills go behind its children
while its strokes go over them and outside its own clip (D144), which are two different depths of the
walk. So the frame arm carries the tail's own fill loop and the stroke call stays in `paint_node`, and
the two loops sit side by side on purpose: a rule added to one is owed to the other.

**The SVG writer emits one `<rect>` per visible fill**, in list order, before the children.
⚠️ **The def slot name went from the literal `"bg"` to `fill-{i}`, and that is load-bearing rather than
cosmetic**: it is the id `collect_defs` registers a gradient, pattern or filter under and the one
`emit_node` references it by, so the two have to spell it the same way — `visible_fills` hands both of
them the index now. Two export tests asserted the old literal. A frame's **missing** picture also draws
the placeholder through the same `emit_missing` a shape's fill goes through, which closes the one place
§7 recorded the two writers disagreeing (D179); it was written `fill="none"` first and caught by
reading the emitter against the walk, `scene::fill_or_placeholder` taking a frame's fills and a
shape's alike.

**`plan::frame_background` had to decide something it never had to before: what one colour means over a
*list*.** The rule is deliberately strict, matching the strictness already there — the topmost visible
fill if it is an **opaque** solid; or the only visible fill if it is a solid of any alpha; `None`
otherwise. That second clause is exactly what a v3 frame could hold, so **no document that existed
before the list did changes its export.** Compositing a stack down to one colour would be the silent
substitution §7's model-completeness gate forbids, and the honest failure — the layer on transparency —
is visible in the file.

**The save format moves: `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` 3 → 4, with a real `migrate_3_to_4`.**
`{"Artboard": {"size":…, "background": <brush>}}` becomes `{"Artboard": {"size":…}}` with the brush
moved into that node's `fills` as `{"brush": …, "visible": true}`; a `null` background contributes no
fill, which is exactly what it meant. ⚠️ **Prepended rather than appended, and it matters on exactly
one shape of file.** The list is the z-order, bottom first, and a frame's background painted behind
everything — but a v3 frame could not hold a fill at all, `SetFills` having refused an `Artboard`, so
today the list is always empty and the two are the same operation. The rule is written the strict way
so a file some future reader hands this step does not get its ground painted on top of its own artwork.
⚠️ **One of the two migration tests carries the flip worth knowing**: removing the fill-write while
still removing the key leaves the *kind* assertion green and fails only the colour assertion, with
`left: []`. That is the shape of a migration that silently never ran, and nothing else would say so —
there is no `deny_unknown_fields` here, so a `background` key simply ignored would load, pass every
integrity check and draw a frame with no ground.

**`SNAPSHOT_VERSION` goes 8 → 9.** `snapshot::Geometry::Artboard` lost its `background` field — a
frame's paint arrives in `NodeSnapshot::fills` with everyone else's, and repeating it under the
geometry would report one paint twice and leave a writer two places to send it, which is the model's
own old problem surviving in the snapshot after it had gone from the document. By §7.3's own precedent
that is **two** reasons to move the number at once: a reader on 8 looks for a frame's ground where the
schema says it is, finds nothing, and describes a filled frame as an empty one, which is 5's argument;
and an untouched document's snapshot changes bytes, which is what 6 moved for, a consumer diffing
snapshots reading the version first. ⚠️ **It was missed on the first pass and caught by `arch-scribe`
reading this entry against `snapshot.rs`** — the fourth time that agent has found what no gate can, and
the fifth if the stale `docs/architecture.md` §7.3 it corrected on the way counts: that section still
said the current version was **7** and carried a live *"fix by bumping to 8"* instruction, four bumps
after the code had done it.

`every-kind.json` was regenerated twice, and the two diffs are worth reading together. The first is the
paint moving out of `geometry.background` and into `fills`; the second is the version line alone. ⚠️
**The SVG golden is byte-identical through both**, which is the useful corroboration in the other
direction: a frame with one solid fill renders the markup it always did, so the whole of this change is
in what the model *says* rather than in what it draws.

**In the app a frame is simply a layer.** `inspector_artboard` — the *Frame background* card, and after
D397 the one-row *Fill* card — is deleted. A frame is `PaintScope::Node` like anything else and gets
the shared Fill and Stroke panels: the `+`, the per-row eye, the reorder grip, the ✕, the
mixed-selection row, the lot. Every control that card had was a smaller version of something
`inspector_fill` already did properly. `PaintSlot::Background` goes with it — the only node slot with
no index on it — a frame's fills being `PaintSlot::Fill(i)`, which is also what lets a frame's row carry
a grip and its picture open crop mode.

⚠️ **One user-visible thing was given up, and it is recorded rather than glossed.** A frame with no
fill said *Transparent*, which is truer of a frame than the shared *No fill*. The argument for the
change is that an empty shape is exactly as transparent as an empty frame, so the distinction was never
about frames — and one empty state that reads the same on every layer is worth more than a truer word
on one of them. *Revisit if the maintainer disagrees; it is a one-line revert.*

⚠️ **Two behaviour changes fell out rather than being designed, and both match what a rectangle does
and what Figma does.** A frame filled with a **photograph** now shows that photograph as its
layers-panel thumbnail (`picture_of` reads `fills`) and can be **double-clicked into crop mode**
(`croppable_fill` reads `fills`). Neither was possible while a frame's ground was not in `fills`, and
neither was ever decided against — the doc comment excusing the omission ("a frame is a container
rather than a picture") was written after the fact. And a frame's fill now **previews live** through
`RenderOverrides` on the ordinary `SetFills` path, where `SetArtboardBackground` had a bespoke arm in
`renderer.rs` that rebuilt the whole `NodeKind`.

`tools::create_artboard` emits `CreateNode` + `SetFills`, two ops, exactly as `create_rect` already
did, and the starter document's white frame ground moved into the same `SetFills` transaction as the
rect's and the ellipse's colours — it used to be the one paint in a fresh document not written there.
**`build::frame`, the Frame-selection verb, still emits no `SetFills`**: framing must not paint over
what was behind the selection, which is the rule the existing test pins and which is unchanged.

**Four new tests, every flip verified at the predicted assertion.**
`render::a_frames_fill_stack_paints_in_order_behind_its_children` needed a **brush-capturing recorder**,
because the existing `Sequence` throws the paint away and the test would have been vacuous without one;
dropping the visibility filter fails on the length and reversing the iterator fails on the order.
`svg::a_frames_fill_stack_is_written_in_order_before_its_children` asserts **positions in the string**
rather than `contains`, since every `contains` passes against a writer that emits the rects either way
round. `inspector::frame_fill_tests::a_frames_fill_card_draws_one_row_per_fill_just_as_a_rects_does`
compares a frame's hex fields against a **rect's carrying the same fills**, so the claim is parity
rather than agreement with itself — ⚠️ and its first draft failed with four hexes instead of two,
because a frame also has a *Group Colors* card that counted the frame's own paint. That predated this
change (the census had an `Artboard` branch for exactly that) and was asserted explicitly as a
remainder rather than trimmed away. ⚠️ **That sentence is history within hours**: **D401** stops the
census at a single selected container, so the surplus is gone and the test now asserts the frame's
hexes equal the rect's **outright**, with no remainder to excuse, plus that an empty frame gets no
Group Colors card. This change surfaced that defect rather than causing it — D397 predicted D400 and
D400 made D401 visible, three entries in one day each exposing the next one's.
`io::migration_moves_a_v3_frame_background_into_its_fill_list` and its
null-background sibling are above. Five tests were rewritten in the opposite direction —
`bulk::recoloring_reaches_every_one_of_a_frames_fills`,
`bulk::a_fill_over_a_frame_and_a_shape_colours_both`, the new
`bulk::a_frames_fill_list_reorders_hides_and_removes_like_any_other`,
`bulk::a_frame_is_counted_in_a_shared_stroke` and `ops::set_fills_reaches_a_frame`, which used to commit
a `SetArtboardBackground` and assert the opposite fact.

⚠️ **The number was very nearly wrong.** This entry was written as D399 first and collided with the
hyphenation non-goal decided the same day; sixty-three citations across twenty files had to be
renumbered. That is precisely the failure `CLAUDE.md`'s census paragraph already warns about — *a
citation written against a number nobody has reserved is how two entries come to share one* — and the
only thing that caught it was re-running the count.

**D800 — A frame's *Background…* row is a decided non-goal, because D400 removed the thing it was a
door to. *Ruling by the maintainer; recorded 2026-09-19; Resolved — record-only, and a decided
non-goal rather than a deferral.***

`context-menus.md` §5.1 specifies a *Background…* row on a frame's context menu. It was never built —
`menu::head_rows`' `Kind::Frame` arm pushes *Clip content* alone — and the operation it was scored as
wiring for, `Operation::SetArtboardBackground`, was **deleted by D400** above, the change that made a
frame's fill `Node::paint`'s list like every other painted layer's and took a frame-shaped special
case out of every fill verb in the workspace.

**The ruling is D400's own reason.** The inspector's Fill row already does this job for a frame
exactly as it does for anything else — `+`, the per-row eye, the grip, the ✕, the picker — so a
second, frame-only door is precisely the special case D400 deliberately removed. 🚨 **A row would
need no new operation**: it could open the picker through the ordinary paint path, the way every
other layer's fill is reached. **That is what makes it tempting and is also exactly why it is
redundant** — cheap to build is not the same as worth having, and the cheapness here comes from the
verb already being general, which is the argument against a second door rather than for one.

⚠️ **The same argument is already made once in that file**, at §6.1: *Canvas background…* is *"a
candidate rather than a row"* because the inspector shows it when nothing is selected, *"so this
would be a second door to a control that has one"*. A frame's row is that sentence with the frame's
name in it.

*(No production line changed and none is proposed. This closes a state §5.1 described as one its
ledger has no bucket for — the row was neither landed nor struck nor blocked, the op having gone
without the menu ever being mentioned — and answers that section's own instruction, **"a row this
file specified cannot leave without one"**. `context-menus.md` §5.1's row is **struck in place** with
the reason rather than deleted, which is the treatment §9.1 already gives *Reset crop* and
*Replace…*; §9.1's *wiring only* bucket and §9.5's *"all of §9.1 except a frame's Background…"*
sentence follow it. ⚠️ **Not §9.6** — that ledger is for where the *code* differs from the file, and
after this the file and the code agree; a row struck from the spec is not a divergence. **The
citation is planted by hand** on `head_rows`' `Some(Kind::Frame)` arm, since a record-only entry is
invisible to the citation census until somebody does (D741's fix for D735's shape) and that arm is
the one place a reader meets the question *why is there no Background row here*. The *Background…*
sub-bullet and the clause in the *Now · Canvas* table row that named it are **struck from
`roadmap.md`**; ⚠️ C5's edge clause beside it **stays**, D469 having left that half open in its own
text rather than closing it.)*

**D401 — Group Colors stops at a single selected container: it lists what is *inside* it, not the
container's own paint. *Built and tested 2026-09-01; Keep.***

The prompt was cosmetic. After D400 a selected frame's ground appeared as a swatch in the *Fill* card
and again as a row in *Group Colors* directly below it, which reads worse now that the two cards are
adjacent, and the maintainer said do it. **But the documents already said the code was wrong**, and had
for longer than D400 has existed. §9.4: *"a second panel called Fill meaning 'everything inside' beside
it is two different fills in one inspector, and Group Colors is the only way to reach the contents
without picking them apart"* — and `inspector_single`'s own comment gave exactly that as the reason a
frame gets this card and not a second Fill card. The census walked `subtree_nodes` **from the
container**, so the container's own paint was in its own census. **Nobody could see it while a frame's
ground was not a fill** — it was one swatch in one card — and D400 put the same swatch in the card
above. So this is drift the documents already described, surfaced by D400 rather than created by it.

⚠️ **There is a concrete defect and not only a redundancy, and that is the argument to lead with.**
`select_by_color`'s own doc comment says why the reticle replaces the selection and drops
`entered_group`: *"a selection that kept the frame as well would put the frame's own bounds round the
result and make the next drag move everything. Asking the question is accepting the answer."* Yet a
census row keyed on the **selected frame's own colour** had `ColorUse::nodes == [that frame]`, so its
button selected exactly the frame — the state that comment exists to prevent, produced by the panel
itself. That row's button either did nothing visible or re-selected its own subject.

`OndinApp::group_color_scope` is the whole rule: a single selected `Group` or `Artboard` contributes
its `children()`, and every other selection contributes itself.

⚠️ **It is a function rather than a filter at the call site because the scope is read in four places,
and they must agree or the panel lies about itself.** The listing (`colors_in` / `gradients_in`),
`slot_transaction`'s `GroupColor` arm (`build::recolor`), its `GroupGradient` arm (`build::repaint`)
and `group_color_shown`'s live-preview read were four separate spellings of `selection.ids()`.
Narrowing only the listing would have produced **a row that prints `1 match` and recolours two
layers** — the count is `ColorUse::nodes.len()` (D71), so the census's answer is literally what the row
states, and an edit taken over a wider set makes the row's own number false. The invariant is that the
count and the edit are taken over the same set.

**A group is unaffected, and that is what makes this one rule rather than a frame exception.** A group
has no paint, so excluding the selected container from its own census removes nothing — the scope
function returns a genuinely *different* set for a group (`children()` rather than `[group]`) and
`subtree_nodes` produces the same answer from it. **A multi-selection is unaffected too, and
deliberately**: `inspector_multi` is reached only above one selected node, so the `[only]` arm never
matches there, and over a selection this card and the Fill card above it are two intentions about the
same paints on purpose (D53 — *keep them different and change that one* against *make them all this*).
The rule is only about a container being the box the question is asked **about** rather than part of
the answer. A **nested** frame is therefore still content: select an outer frame holding an inner one
and the inner one's ground is in the census, only the subject being excluded. The picker's
document-palette chips call `colors_in(doc, [root])` and are untouched.

Two consequences, stated so they are not read later as bugs. **An empty frame now shows no Group Colors
card at all** — the census is empty and the panel returns early — where a childless frame with a ground
used to show a one-row card; an empty frame has nothing inside it, which is the better answer. And
where a frame's ground and a child carried the same colour, the row read `2 matches` and recoloured
both; it reads `1 match` and recolours the child, the Fill card above being where the ground is
changed.

Two new tests in `frame_fill_tests`.
`group_colors_on_a_frame_lists_its_contents_and_not_its_own_fill` puts a rect filled `070809` inside a
frame filled `010203` and asserts the card is drawn at all (the control), that only the child's hex
appears below the *GROUP COLORS* header, that the frame's own is still on the page *above* it in the
Fill card, and that the row prints `1 match`. ⚠️ **That last assertion is the one with teeth**: the hex
list alone would pass against a narrowed listing over an unnarrowed edit, and `1 match` is the census's
own node count read back off the drawn row. Flip verified — returning `ids.to_vec()` unconditionally
fails at the hex assertion with `["010203", "070809"]` against `["070809"]`.
`group_colors_inside_a_group_are_unchanged_by_the_narrowing` is the group half, and ⚠️ **its flip
deliberately does *not* bite**, which is written into the test as a finding rather than left looking
like a weak assertion: there is no paint on a group for the two scopes to disagree about, so it guards
a non-regression and the frame test is the one that proves the feature.

⚠️ **A third test was added after the first two, and the measurement that produced it is the one worth
keeping.** Both of the above read galleys, so both see the *listing* — and the failure this entry is
most about is a listing that narrows while an edit does not, which draws a row saying `1 match` and
changes two layers. Asking *what would also pass this* of the pair gave the answer directly: that
change would. So `the_group_colors_edit_reaches_exactly_the_layers_the_row_counted` builds the one
fixture that can tell them apart — a frame and the rect inside it carrying **the same** colour — and
asserts on the `Transaction` `slot_transaction` returns rather than on the document after a commit,
because the transaction is where the scope is visible: one `SetFills` naming the child, and no
operation naming the frame. ⚠️ **Run the whole module against that flip and not just the new test**:
putting `selection.ids()` back in the `GroupColor` arm leaves **all four** of the others green while
the panel is lying about its own count. That is the measurement that says the third test earns its
place rather than restating the first two, and it is why *"the count and the edit are taken over the
same set"* is written as an invariant above rather than left as a property of how the code happens to
read.

⚠️ **The `galleys` test helper was fixed on the way past, and the fault is worth naming.** It emitted
`SetFills` unconditionally, which is `WrongKindForOp` on a `Group` — so the helper could be pointed at
every kind *except* the one whose census is the control here. The paint is a separate, conditional
transaction now, and the helper gained a `galleys_holding(kind, fills, inside)` form that puts a filled
rect inside the subject, a child being what makes the Group Colors card appear at all.

**D402 — The effect batch is bounded by the page, in two places, and neither of them is the zoom.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-01; Keep, with a third term measured and left growing.***

The roadmap's last open canvas defect — the second timeout **D395** recorded, named there as *"the
cost of rasterizing 417 paths at sixteen times magnification, in the main scene and in the effect
batch"*. ⚠️ **Every clause of that sentence is wrong except the crash**, and a sweep says so in one
run: with the effects stripped, the same drawing renders at 3840×2160 in **2.0 ms** at 32× zoom, and
a fixture of **20,000** paths renders in 30 ms. The page's own scene is nowhere near any limit. All
of the cost, and both of the hangs, are in the effect pass.

**And the 2,118 ms in D395 was never a measurement of work.** A frame that trips the watchdog returns
just after two seconds however long it would have taken, so *every* hung frame reports ≈2,1xx ms —
reproduced at 2,065, 2,080, 2,096, 2,109 and 2,126 on five different configurations. The number to
read is not the duration but whether the device is alive afterwards: a 256×256 frame rendered after
each, and the ones that came back `DEVICE GONE` are the hangs. **Twenty-first-century GPU timing has
exactly one honest reading at the top end, and it is a boolean.**

**Two mechanisms, found in that order.**

⚠️ **One: a level of sibling layers was packed into a single scene bigger than the page.** Three
viewport-sized layers side by side make one 8332×2069 target — 17 MP against a 7 MP page — carrying
the same paths. vello's intermediate buffers are hand-picked fixed sizes, and **vello 0.9 cannot
report an overflow**: `render_to_texture` neither reads the bump allocators back nor returns an error,
so past capacity the fine shader loops on garbage, Windows resets the GPU at two seconds, and the app
panics in whatever the *next* frame touches first. The cliff is sharp and it moves with **both** terms:
8332×1968 with 417 paths is 12 ms and 8332×2069 with the same paths is gone, while 8562×1968 with
2,500 paths is gone too. So `pack` takes a **budget** — the page's own pixel count — and starts a new
chunk rather than exceed it. *A scene of at most the page's pixels carrying at most the page's paths
is a load the page itself is measured to survive*, which is the whole argument for that number and the
reason it is not a tuned constant.

⚠️ **That change had to move D344's rule or it would have put D344's bug back.** One vello pass per
nesting *level* was the rule because a level was one pass; a level is now deliberately several. The
renderers are handed out **per pass** instead — the same rule stated against what it was always
about, since what evicts an atlas image is a renderer doing two passes in a frame, not a level.

⚠️ **Two: a shadow's buffer grows with the zoom without any bound at all, and this is D395's own
mechanism at one remove.** D395 bounded a blur's *kernel* by rasterizing the layer coarser, and only a
`LayerBlur` may buy that — a drop shadow blurs a silhouette behind artwork that stays sharp. But the
**escape** is in device pixels: an 18-unit shadow blur reaches 27 units, which at 32× is 864 pixels on
every side, so a viewport-sized layer's buffer went to 5248×3708 — **19.5 MP for a 7 MP page**, over
the cliff on its own, where no amount of splitting helps. `effect::buffer_box_within` gives up escape
rather than the GPU: it bisects the escape down to whatever fits the budget, and `t = 0` is the target
itself, so **the visible part of the layer is never what gets clipped**.

**What that costs, measured rather than argued.** Against an unclamped CPU render of the same
fixture: **worst channel error 1/255, on 0.28% of bytes**, at 4×, 16× and 64×, and the same 1/255 with
the shadow blur raised to 55.5 units. ⚠️ **It bites at every zoom, not only the extreme one** — a
layer covering the viewport is at the budget before any escape is added — and the first draft of the
comment on it claimed the opposite, in the shape this file keeps warning about: a prediction written
in the tense of a measurement. What is given up is the faint tail of a gaussian cast from off-screen.
*The case that would show more is a wide shadow falling from off-screen onto empty canvas, and it has
not been measured.*

**Both backends call `buffer_box_within`**, for D342's reason and D395's from the other direction: two
backends choosing different buffer *boxes* would blur one drawing differently and would agree about
nothing. The CPU budget is the export target's own area, which an export at its own scale never
reaches.

**Result.** Every configuration that killed the device renders: 3520×1980 at 1× went from a lost
device to **21 ms**, and 3840×2160 now renders at 8×, 16×, 32×, 64× and 128×. The app's own
`MAX_ZOOM` is 256.

⚠️ **Reproduced afterwards on the actual drawing, and the reproduction is the part worth keeping.**
The maintainer supplied the file — `dev.w3.org/SVG/tools/svgweb/samples/svg-files/car.svg`, 417
`<path>`s and **112** `<feGaussianBlur>`s, which is where D395's "417 paths" came from — and it
imports with nothing skipped and one approximation (the elliptical radial gradient this file already
knows about). ⚠️ **It does not crash at the obvious places**: 3840×2100 at 16× is 23 ms at the centre
of the drawing, and the whole of a 7-zoom × 3-origin sweep passes. Standing on a **9×9 grid of
origins** at 8× and 16× finds it — one frame of 162, at **0.8/0.4, 2,129 ms**, which is D395's
2,118 ms to within the noise of a watchdog. With the budget in place that same frame is **16 ms**.
*So the synthetic fixture this was developed against was the harsher instrument of the two* — it hangs
at three origins out of three — and the real file needed 162 frames to show the defect once. Neither
would have been enough alone: the synthetic one made the mechanism reproducible in a second, and only
the real one says the fix reaches the reported bug.

⚠️ **A third term is still linear in the zoom and is deliberately not fixed here: a drop shadow's
kernel.** It is the one thing D395's downscale may not touch, so σ in device pixels is still the
authored blur times the zoom — 65 ms at 32×, 130 at 64×, 263 at 128× with an 18-unit blur, and with
the blur at 55.5 units, **1,557 ms at 256×**, which is a real 1.5-second frame rather than a hang (the
device is alive afterwards) and is 20% short of the watchdog. A wider shadow, or a larger monitor,
crosses it. The fix is D395's insight applied one level in — the shadow *pass* convolving a
downscaled silhouette, which softens nothing that was sharp, since its output is a blurred alpha — and
it is a feature on both backends rather than a bound, so it is filed in the roadmap rather than built
here. **The CPU backend is worse off than the GPU on this term**: an unclamped 64× render with that
shadow did not finish in ten minutes.

**The instrument is `ondin-render/tests/zoom_sweep.rs`**, `#[ignore]`d beside `gpu_device.rs`, and it
is kept rather than deleted because nothing else in the tree can re-check a GPU timing claim. It
sweeps viewport, zoom and origin on a synthetic drawing of the same order as the one that crashed
(`ONDIN_SWEEP_DOC` points it at a real file), and it **stops at 1,200 ms rather than tripping the
watchdog** — resetting the display driver is not a thing to do to the machine someone is working on,
and the curve either side of the budget is the measurement anyway. What it pins in the ordinary suite
is four `pack` tests and three `buffer_box_within` tests; the flips bite where they were predicted to,
the packing ones on the chunk *count* and the clamp ones on the *area* — the latter by a hair, 6,969,609
against a budget of 6,969,600, which is what returning a bisection's `hi` rather than its `lo` looks
like.

⚠️ **`pack`'s doc comment was wrong again, in the same place D395 caught it before.** It said *"a
layer larger than that cannot exist — the walk clamps every buffer to the target, which is the
viewport"*; the walk clamps to the target **grown by the escape**, so a blurred layer's buffer is
routinely larger than the viewport — measured at 2069 device pixels tall against a 1980-pixel one.
Nothing depended on the false half, which is exactly why it survived a second reading.

**D403 — A shadow's silhouette is resampled, which is the one place D395's downscale was allowed to
go and nobody had taken it. *Built and tested 2026-09-01; Keep.***

D402's closing note, taken the same day: the last term still linear in the zoom. **D395's rule stands
and this is not an exception to it** — a drop shadow may not coarsen the *layer's buffer*, because the
artwork composited over the shadow stays sharp, which is what `layer_blur_deviation` exists to say.
But the silhouette a shadow is blurred *from* is not artwork. It is an alpha field on its way to
becoming a gaussian of deviation σ, and by D395's own argument that output carries nothing finer than
σ. So the resample happens **inside the shadow pass**, over the mask, and nothing that was ever sharp
is touched.

`effect::shadow_downscale(σ)` picks a **whole number** — a mask is resampled on a grid, so `ceil(σ/24)`
rather than a ratio, and the same *"nothing between 1 and 2"* deadband `buffer_downscale` carries, for
the same measured reason. Then `effects::blur_coarse` is three steps: box-average into `k`×`k` blocks,
blur at σ/k, read back bilinearly. Cost stops depending on the zoom in both terms at once — the
convolution runs over `w·h/k²` pixels with a kernel that no longer grows.

**What it is worth**, on 3840×2160 with a 55.5-unit shadow blur — the largest in the car drawing:

| zoom | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 64× | 409 ms | 8.9 ms |
| 128× | 792 ms | 10.6 ms |
| 256× (`MAX_ZOOM`) | **1,557 ms** | **20.5 ms** |

The curve was doubling with every zoom step and is flat now. ⚠️ **The CPU backend was the worse half
and nobody would have noticed**: the same frame at 64× took **19.6 s** through `VelloCpuRenderer` and
takes **0.1 s**, so this was an `ondin export --scale` hazard as much as a canvas one — and an export
has no watchdog to make it fail loudly, it just never comes back.

**What it costs, measured three ways.** A whole rendered frame at 64× is **byte-identical** to the
unresampled one. A disc blurred at σ = 60 (so `k` = 3) differs by **1/255 worst, mean 0.032** — the
curved edge and nowhere else. And the GPU port agrees with the CPU reference within the same ±1 the
rest of `tests/fx_gpu.rs` allows, on a resampled shadow with and without a spread.

⚠️ **Three things about the port that are easy to get wrong and invisible when you do.** The coarse
grid lives in the **top-left corner of a full-size scratch texture** rather than in a buffer of its
own, so every slot in `fx_gpu` stays one size; what makes that work is a `dom` on the dispatch — the
grid a pass is *for*, which is now what sizes the workgroups and what `inside()` reads, and which was
`(w, h)` everywhere before. `coarsen` is dispatched over the coarse grid, one thread per block, so the
total work is one read per source pixel however large `k` is — the full-size spelling reads `k²` texels
per thread and is `k²` times the work, which is the version that writes itself. 🚨 **That sentence has
a precondition it did not carry, and this shader shipped as the spelling it rejects** (§15 D743): it
holds only while `k ≤ min(w, h)`, and past that the grid is 1 × 1 and one thread walks `k²` taps over
a buffer of `w·h`. Both backends bound the loop by the **source** since 2026-09-10. And `src_size` went in
at the **end** of the `Params` struct rather than beside `size` where it belongs by meaning, because
those offsets are a hand-written contract with the shader and inserting a field in the middle moves
every one of them, compiles on both sides and draws nonsense.

⚠️ **The half-block is the whole of `upsample`.** A coarse sample stands at the *centre* of the block
it averaged, `(k-1)/2` pixels in; dropping that term shifts every shadow by half a block, and a block
is large exactly when the shadow is soft enough to hide it. It is the flip this entry's GPU test was
checked against — worst channel goes to 13 — and the failure it produces on screen is a shadow that
creeps sideways as the zoom changes rather than anything that looks broken.

**The other flip is the one the scheme invites**: blurring the coarse grid at the *full* σ rather than
σ/k, i.e. dividing in one place and not the other. It gives 45/255 worst, mean 3.65 — and *still looks
like a shadow*, which is why the assertion is a number rather than an eye.

**D404 — An effect layer inside an effect layer crashed the app, and had since effects existed.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-01; Keep.***

**Not a regression from D402 or D403** — the sources from before either panic identically, which was
checked before anything was changed. It survived because **nothing in the tree could produce the
state**: `tests/gpu_effects.rs` had no nested fixture, and SVG import does not make one either — the
car drawing carries **70** effect-bearing nodes and *none* of them sits inside another effect layer,
so a 648-frame sweep over it never came near this. What produces it is a person: group a shadowed
group and put a blur on the wrapper.

**The mechanism is one line's worth of scope.** An effect layer's result is drawn by the scene it
popped back into — the page's for a layer at level 0, and the **parent layer's own sub-scene** for
anything deeper. Since D344 every pass has a renderer of its own, and an atlas of its own with it;
`override_image` was called on `self.renderer`, the page's, for every job at every level. So a nested
layer's slot was registered where nobody would draw it, and vello refuses that outright:

```
Tried to draw an invalid empty image (id: 2). Maybe it was registered to a
different renderer, or unregistered before this render was submitted.
```

⚠️ **A panic rather than a missing picture, which is the lucky half.** The slot's blob is deliberately
empty — an identity with no pixels behind it (`EffectJob::image`) — so vello can tell the difference
between "nothing to draw" and "you never gave me this". A backend that quietly drew transparent would
have left this as an intermittently blank layer nobody could reproduce.

**The fix is that `resolve_effects` plans its passes before running any of them.** A job at level L is
drawn by level L−1's passes, which run *after* it, so their renderers have to be named while they are
still in the future; `passes[level]` is each level's stretch of pass indices, worked out from `pack`
up front. Every job is then registered on the renderers that will draw it — the page for level 0, and
**all** of level L−1's passes otherwise, since which chunk holds the parent is not recorded and an
extra atlas entry is cheaper than a search. `Holder` says which renderer each slot went to, so the
end-of-frame unregister goes to the same place; leaving that as the page's would have leaked one
texture per nested layer per frame.

**The test is in `tests/gpu_effects.rs`**, comparing against the CPU backend, which composites layers
directly and has no atlas at all and so cannot share the failure. Four fixtures: a shadow alone, a
blur alone, a blur inside a shadow, and a blur inside a shadow inside a blur. ⚠️ **The first two are
the control and they passed the whole time** — the bug needs one layer to *contain* another, so a
test asserting only the nested case would not say which of the three had broken.

⚠️ **Three deep is not byte-exact and finding that out is what the fourth fixture is for**: it allows
one channel level. Every effect layer the GPU path opens is bracketed by a
straight→premultiplied→straight round trip, which at eight bits is not the identity on a partly
transparent pixel — the same ±1 `tests/fx_gpu.rs` allows for the same reason, and the CPU backend has
no such boundary because it stays premultiplied throughout. Two layers move nothing in this fixture;
three move one.

⚠️ **The flip failed somewhere else than predicted, for the third time in this project.** Putting the
registration back on the page renderer was expected to fail the pixel comparison; it panics inside
`render` instead, before a single pixel is compared. So *the comparison is not what catches this bug*
— it catches a slot registered on the **wrong** renderer, where the panic catches one registered on
none, and the test needs both halves for reasons that are now written on it.

**D405 — Type on a path: the rail belongs to the text node, and the layout is bent onto it as a pass
over the finished flat one.
*Built and tested 2026-09-01; **reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-09-02** with
D406–D410 — "pretty good, let's call it closed". Keep.***

Picked off `docs/roadmap.md`, which had carried it since scaffold time behind the sentence *"all six
dependencies are still genuinely absent"* — a claim the 2026-08-31 pass had already reduced to zero
items. **Re-derived before starting, and the dependency half was right while the price was not.**
`kurbo 0.13.1` implements `ParamCurveArclen::inv_arclen` **for `PathSeg`**, which is the segment type
`BezPath::segments()` yields, with no feature flag and in a crate core has depended on since scaffold;
glyph outlines arrived with D145. But *"a design, not a feature"* was wrong in one clause that decided
the shape of the work: **`text::Glyph` was `{id, x, y}` — a translation with no rotation** — and both
backends draw a run in a single `draw_glyphs` call under one `Affine`, which is all either backend's
glyph API offers.

**Where the rail lives was the decision, and it was taken by the maintainer from three.** A container
kind holding the path and the text as children, the `Boolean` shape; an `Option<NodeId>` at a sibling,
SVG's `<textPath href>` shape; or a field. The field won: a container puts itself between every
existing text feature and the node it edits, and an id would be **the first cross-node reference in
this model** — nothing here references anything — so it would have to invent dangling, delete,
duplicate and cross-document-paste semantics no other field needs. Applying consumes the layer the
rail came from and *Detach from path* gives it back, which is what Illustrator and Affinity both do.

**`Option<Box<BezPath>>`, and the boxing is measured rather than assumed.** `NodeKind::Text` *is* the
largest variant — its payload is **200** bytes, which is `NodeKind`'s whole size — and unboxed the
rail takes it to **216**, i.e. 16 bytes on every node in the document to serve the few on a curve.
The neighbouring doc comment on `style` said it was "the only field here that is [boxed]" and is
fixed; that sentence had been true for a day.

**`TextRef` carries the rail, and that is what keeps one drawing.** `TextRef::of` is the single place
a `NodeKind` is taken apart, so the renderer, the hit test, `geometry::local_bounds`, the SVG writer
and the live `TextEdit` session all bend without being told to. A second argument to `text::layout`
would have been how the caret comes to sit where the text used to be.

**`bend` is a pass over the finished flat layout, and the ordering is the whole economy of it.**
parley shapes and breaks exactly as before; `decoration_ink` and `skip_ink` compute in flat space,
where a band is a rect and its skip-ink gaps are plain intervals; only then is the plane mapped.
⚠️ **It maps the plane and not the line**, which is why a second line needs no special case at all:
flat `y` is distance *across* the rail, so a line one `line_height` down comes out running parallel
one `line_height` off the curve, and a marker, a superscript and a descender all land where the same
arithmetic puts them. Glyphs are carried **rigidly** — placed and rotated, never distorted, because a
bent `e` is a font bug — via a new `Glyph::rot`; continuous geometry that runs *along* the line is
**warped** point by point, which today is `DecorationInk` and nothing else. ⚠️ **A flattener is not
enough for that**: a band's long edges are straight, so a curvature-driven subdivider returns each as
one `LineTo` and the ribbon comes out straight across a curved rail. `PathWarp::warp` resamples by
*length*.

**Each glyph is placed by its own midpoint**, SVG's rule, because rotating about the left edge fans
wide glyphs outward exactly where the feature is most visible. ⚠️ **An advance is read from the next
glyph on the same line**, since `GlyphRun` carries positions and no advances — parley's own run
advance spans every line the run was broken over, the trap `export_lines` already documents. ⚠️ **This
paragraph read *"the last glyph of a run borrows its predecessor's advance"* until 2026-09-07, and
that was the bug** (§15 D489): the scan ran per run, so a run of **one** glyph had no predecessor and
took the seed `0.0`, which places it by its left edge — the very thing the sentence above rejects. It
scans the flattened sequence now, across run boundaries, and only a glyph with no successor at all
borrows.

**The box is the ribbon the *whole rail* sweeps, and the obvious alternative is wrong twice.**
Measuring over the stretch the glyphs occupy makes the layer's box — and its handles, its snap targets
and its W/H fields — **move as the string is typed**, which is the instability the roadmap's own
"don't use ink bounds for alignment" rule is about; and it leaves a resize handle with nothing to say,
since a drawn rail is usually longer than the words on it. Measured: on a 150-long rail under a
78-wide word, doubling the rail took a glyph-stretch box from **78.0 to 73.4** — the wrong direction,
and small enough to read as a dead control.

⚠️ **Two real defects were found by flipping, and neither was visible to a green suite.** The
alignment measure was `layout.size.width`, which on an auto-height or fixed node is the width the
*user* authored rather than the shaped content width — a 300-wide box on a 600-long rail centred at
150 instead of 272.6. And the box was swept from flat `x = 0` rather than from where the glyphs are,
so an indented or truncated line got a rectangle adrift from its own text. Both fixed; the second
became moot when the box became the rail's.

⚠️ **The sign of the normal was unpinned, and two drafts of the test that was meant to pin it were
wrong in opposite directions.** The first sorted the distances of two lines from an arc's centre and
asserted a gap — *symmetric*, so it passed with the normal negated, and so did every other test in
the section. The second demanded the second line be **outside** the arc, which is the wrong side, and
passed only against the flipped build. Both read as careful. What settles it is a straight rail, where
"the side a descender goes" is just larger `y` and there is no geometry to argue about; the curved
case then only has to agree. **Assert the sign where it cannot be reasoned about, then make the
interesting case agree with that.**

⚠️ **The alignment gate in `shape` is redundant today and says so.** Removing it alone changes nothing
any test can see, because the wrap gate beside it leaves parley with no measure to align *within*.
Removing **both** produces the double-count: 395.2 against 272.6, the two offsets summed. Kept because
the two are one decision — "the box is inert on a rail" — and stated as redundant so nobody reads it
as load-bearing.

⚠️ **A per-glyph transform drags the brush with the glyph, so a bent run under anything but a solid is
filled as an outline.** A gradient and an image are authored in the node's local space; a glyph drawn
under its own transform carries that space with it, and every letter restarts the gradient at its own
origin. The flip is not subtle — the whole word comes out in the *first stop*, flat red — which is why
`ondin-export/tests/png.rs` asserts it at the pixels rather than at the scene. `text::run_outline` is
the door; a solid has no position to lose and keeps the cheaper arm.

**Nothing in the two backends changed.** `ScenePainter::draw_text` already took a transform per call,
so the walk had the whole vocabulary it needed: `scene::draw_run` splits a bent run into one call per
glyph, and a run whose rotations are all zero takes the single-call path it always took.

**The SVG writer hands *placement* back to the viewer, which is a deliberate exception to D81.**
Everything else there is built on "we place, they shape" — one `<text>` per line at a baseline we
computed. The exact spelling for a rail would be one `<text>` per glyph under its own rotation, and
that is unreachable for a reason already written down rather than an unexplored one: `export_lines`'
own doc records that **glyph ids do not map back to characters** through ligatures and reordering, so
this writer cannot say which characters a rotated glyph is. `<textPath>` over a rail in `<defs>` is
what is left that keeps text as text; the alternative that *is* exact — filling the glyph outlines as
a `<path>` — gives up selectable text, searchable content and re-shaping in another family, which is
most of what an SVG of type is for. Alignment survives as `startOffset` in **percent** plus a matching
`text-anchor`, the one spelling that does not also depend on our measure of the text. ⚠️ **Checked
against a real browser** and overlaid at 50% on our own CPU render of the same node: the rail's start
point, its tangent and every rotation agree; the per-glyph *advances* drift toward the end of the
word, because the viewer re-shapes, with a font it may not even have. That drift is the cost the
choice was made for.

**A resize handle on a railed node scales the rail, and the factor is solved rather than computed.**
It has to edit *something* — `TextSizing` is inert on a rail, so the ordinary arm hands back a patch
the layout ignores and the handle drags with nothing moving, a dead control on a selected layer. And
it is the right thing rather than the available one: §5.6's rule is that this gesture edits geometry
and never scale, and on a railed node the geometry *is* the rail. ⚠️ **The naive factor — the ratio of
the two boxes — is wrong on both counts**, because the box is a swept ribbon and a unit normal does
not scale with the curve under it: asking for 317.2 landed 304.7, and **the top-left corner the drag
was holding still moved 9.8 units to the right**. The drift is the one that could not stand; a corner
drag is a promise about the opposite corner. `tools::railed_resize` therefore *shapes* — twice, plus
once more for the placement — which no other arm of `resize_to_handle` does, and the note on it says
why. Placement comes out exact, extent comes out close, which is the right way round.

⚠️ **This paragraph was about the resize *handle* alone, and the other doors did not carry it until
2026-09-07** (D472). `tools::scale_geometry` — which is where a **group** resize, a **selection**
resize and a **skew** all reach a child — had no rail arm, so a railed child came out of a group drag
as `scale_scalars` plus a bare `SetTransform` and did not move at all, while its ribbon went on pinning
the group's width: 47% short of the drag, on the first frame, silently. D472 has the measurement and
what the arm shares with this one.

**What is not built, stated rather than left to be discovered.** ~~There is no *flip to the other
side* control — reversing the rail is the workaround, and the model has room for the field.~~
~~And the SVG *reader* does not read `<textPath>` back, so the round trip loses the rail.~~ **Both
were asked for the same day and are D406**, which is the return on writing this paragraph at all:
two of its four items were picked off it within hours, and the field it predicted room for is the
field D406 added. `Justify` falls
in with `Start`, because justification needs a measure to stretch to and the rail's length is not one
the line was broken against. The MCP snapshot does not carry `on_path`, which joins the twelve
paragraph fields already parked with §8 — and now `on_path_flip` and `on_path_offset` with it.

**Closed 2026-09-02, and this is the list of things not to re-argue.** Six entries over two days —
D405 to D410 — accepted on screen with *"pretty good, let's call it closed"*. Every option that was
offered and turned down, so a later reader finds the answer rather than the question:

- **The rail's home.** A `Boolean`-shaped container and an `Option<NodeId>` at a sibling were both put
  to the maintainer and both declined in favour of a field (top of this entry). Not revisitable
  cheaply: it is the model.
- **Anchor points on the drawn rail.** Offered explicitly when D408 drew the curve — Affinity shows
  them — and not taken. The rail is a field rather than a layer and nothing edits it in place, so
  points would advertise an edit that does not exist. *Detach from path* is the way to real handles.
- **Auto-flipping when the type would read upside down.** Considered at D409 and declined: right for a
  triangle's base, wrong for type round the bottom of a circle, which is the commoner case. The flip
  is a control, not a heuristic.
- **Folding the offset into an absolute `startOffset` with `text-anchor="start"`.** Declined at D409;
  the anchor and the offset say different things, and the percentage is what survives a viewer whose
  shaping differs from ours.
- **Carrying the press's offset in the drag.** Written, then removed at D410 — the committed value
  stands still for the gesture, so a carried copy is one invariant with nothing to buy it.

⚠️ **What is genuinely still open is short and is not an oversight**: `Justify` on a rail, the MCP
snapshot's three fields, and an elliptical radial gradient's cousin — a `startOffset` given in **user
units** by a foreign file, which is reported and dropped because converting it means measuring the
curve. Nothing else about this feature is waiting on a decision.

**D767 — A gradient's opacity is a field, not a rewrite of its stops. *Decided by the maintainer;
fixed and tested 2026-09-15; Resolved. The chips it broke are D773; what is left open is the image
arm, which is older than this entry.***

`[S23.2-L1-01]`, on the maintainer's *"do the model change"*. `GradientBrush` gains `opacity: f32`;
`panels::paint::with_alpha` writes it and leaves the stops alone, and `alpha_of` reads it.

🚨 **A rewrite could not have worked, because scaling is not invertible through zero.** The old body
multiplied every stop by `alpha / peak`. Taking a ramp to 0% made `peak` zero, and the only thing the
next call could do was fall back to writing one flat alpha across the whole ramp — so `[1.0, 0.0]`,
the shape **every** gradient this app authors starts as, since `convert` fades a solid out, came back
`[1.0, 1.0]`: flat, opaque, the fade gone, and no undo step to blame. The maintainer's *"0 alpha means
fully invisible"* rules out the floors that would have kept `peak` away from zero, and a *hidden*
clamp is the same thing with the field lying about it.

🚨 **The old test asserted the defect.** `opacity_scales_a_ramp_rather_than_flattening_it` drove
`with_alpha(_, 0.5)` and checked the stops **had been** scaled. It passed. It had **no round trip in
it at all** — 1.0 → 0.5 keeps a ratio and 0.5 → 0.0 → 1.0 does not — so the finding was filed against
code a green test was endorsing. It is replaced by
`a_ramps_opacity_is_stored_and_survives_a_round_trip_through_zero`, whose round trip is the whole
assertion. ⚠️ **Its flip bit three assertions earlier than predicted, and that is worth keeping**:
restoring the scale-the-stops body in `with_alpha` alone fails at *"the field reads back"*, because
with the writer scaling stops and the reader returning the field, nothing writes the field at all.
**The reader and the writer are one mechanism now and cannot be flipped apart** — which is exactly
why the defect was hard to see before, when the "field" was a derived `max` over data the writer was
free to rewrite underneath it.

**The argument for the shape is not in the finding: the image brush has had it all along.**
`peniko::ImageSampler::alpha` is a multiplier beside the pixels, so `with_alpha` on a picture assigns
a number and touches nothing — already lossless, already invertible. **The gradient arm was the only
one of the three that destroyed its subject, and that asymmetry *was* the defect.**

⚠️ **The cost came in well under what session 23 stated to the maintainer**, which said *"a
save-format version bump"*. There is none. `#[serde(flatten)]` was already load-bearing on this
struct — D412's `transform` arrived the same way — so `default` plus `skip_serializing_if` means **no
`CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and no `migrate` arm**: every gradient ever saved loads unchanged and
**re-saves byte-identical** (invariant 9), which
`a_gradient_written_before_the_transform_existed_still_reads` now asserts for both fields. Render is
**one line** — `peniko::Gradient::multiply_alpha`, on a clone that was already being made, in
`color.rs`, the single conversion site both backends share. SVG expresses it **natively**:
`fill-opacity`/`stroke-opacity` on the shape multiplies the paint server's alpha, so `gradient_def`
is untouched and the stops keep their `stop-opacity`. Only `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` moved, **9 → 10**,
because a half-faded gradient and an opaque one described identically before — the same hole the
image arm's `alpha` was added to close in D185.

⚠️ **Guarded in three places, deliberately.** `build::brush_is_finite` gained `valid_opacity` — the
same predicate a layer's opacity uses, per `schema.rs`'s *"one answer rather than two spellings of
it"* — `alpha_of` clamps on the way out, and `picker`'s out-clamp stays. **A `#[serde(default)]`
float the loader does not validate is D713's shape one field later**: a non-finite one dies at serde,
so what had to be refused here is the **finite out-of-range** one, `-5` subtracting alpha and `1e30`
saturating every stop opaque, both silently and both surviving a round trip.

🚨 **And `picker.rs` carried a safety argument this change made false**, which is D713's lesson
arriving in D713's own neighbourhood. It read *"an alpha **is** 0..1 by construction
(`paint::alpha_of`, `Color::components[3]`), so `pct` cannot arrive outside `0..=100` and this clamp
cannot fire … dead weight rather than a defect."* It gained a producer. **A safety argument that
enumerates its producers is false the day a second one appears**, and that one enumerated two by
name; it is corrected in the same commit and the clamp is load-bearing now.

⚠️ **The repair is forward-only, and this entry says so rather than letting a reader assume documents
heal.** A ramp already flattened to `[1.0, 1.0]` in a saved file stays flat: the ratio is gone from
the file and no migration can invent it.

🚨 **The gradient *chips* did not show the new opacity, which is D564's door being missed a second
time. *Fixed by D773, the same day; the image arm it left open is closed by D784.*** Found reading
§5.5a's *"it is asked at four doors"* paragraph
against this change rather than from any finding. `picker::ramp` is `paint::stops_of` mapped to egui
colours and folds **nothing**, so a gradient fill dropped to 30% draws its inspector row chip and the
picker's 34×34 preview chip at **full** alpha over a canvas that draws it faint — *one document drawn
two ways in one frame*, which is D564's sentence for the mirrored swatch. **It was right for free
before this entry**, the opacity having *been* the stops; the field is multiplied in at `color.rs` for
both backends and written as `fill-opacity` by the SVG writer, and the chrome was the door nobody
added a third multiplication to. ⚠️ **The stop bar must stay raw** — it is the editing surface for
the stops and sits directly under the opacity slider, so dimming it would fight the control beside
it — so fold the multiplier where a chip means *"this paint"*, not where it means *"these stops"*.
🚨 **This paragraph went on to call that *"a caller-side fix rather than a change to `ramp`"* and
D773 did the opposite, which is corrected here and in the code** (§15 D784): `ramp` folds the
multiplier and `stop_colours` is the **named opt-out**, so the common case is the default and the one
surface editing the stops opts out by name — which is the better shape, because a chip written next
year is then right by doing nothing. *A sentence proposing the design that was not taken outlives the
decision to reject it*, and the copy of it on `ramp`'s own doc stood for four days saying the function
folded nothing while it folded.
⚠️ **The image arm had the identical gap since D185 and was why this read smaller than it is**:
`Swatch::Picture` drew untinted, so a half-faded photograph had always had an opaque thumbnail, and
the gradient arm **joined** a standing gap rather than opening a new one. ⚠️ **This paragraph asked
for both arms to be fixed together and they were not** — D773 took the gradient alone, because that
is the one this entry broke, and gave the image arm a verdict of its own so the survivor would not
read as a decision. **D784 closes it**, on the maintainer's ruling and on the strength of that
verdict, and found the arm was **two** surfaces rather than the one D773 names.

⚠️ **The importer bakes its alpha into the stops and leaves `opacity` at 1.0, which is load-bearing
and reads like an omission.** SVG's `opacity` on a gradient-filled shape is a *shape* property, and
`svg_in` has already multiplied it through the stop list by the time the brush is built — so carrying
it into the new field as well would apply it **twice**. A future editor tidying that `opacity: 1.0`
into the value beside it would halve every imported faded gradient.

⚠️ **Two D692 tests changed meaning and were rewritten rather than deleted.** `alpha_of` no longer
folds the stops for a gradient, so an out-of-range *stop* alpha cannot reach the opacity field by any
route — D692's first harm is **unreachable** rather than mitigated, and its second, a bare click
rescaling the ramp, is gone with the division. **What is genuinely lost is an accidental repair**:
clicking the field used to *normalise* a stored out-of-range stop, a side effect of dividing by the
peak rather than a designed behaviour. It no longer does, so a hand-written `stop-opacity="5"` stays
5.0 in the document — a **stop-validation gap, which it always was**, `brush_is_finite` checking
finiteness and not range and the raster clamping it. **Recorded, not fixed**; the opacity field was
never the right place for it.

*(D692 amended, and the `alpha_of` doc it is quoted from corrected — the summary line still said
*"for a gradient, the alpha of its most opaque stop"* three lines above the arm that returns the
field. §5.5a's stop-alpha paragraph amended for the same sentence, §5.7's shadow-opacity bullet for
the rule it cites, §5.9's `Resolved` listing being unrelated and fixed for its own reason below, and
invariant 8 gains this as its **fifth** instance. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.
Closes `[S23.2-L1-01]`.)*

**D768 — *Recover* saves or asks before it replaces the document. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed
and tested 2026-09-15; Resolved — this is D681's ruling.***

`[S16.3-L2-06]`. `open_path`'s opening four lines are `OndinApp::may_replace_current_document(what)`
now, asked by **both** doors that replace the in-memory document; `recover` calls it, then drops the
outgoing session's snapshot at `open_path`'s position, then adopts.

**Lifting the pair into a predicate is what makes *"a door that replaces the document"* a thing with
one implementation rather than a thing two functions each remember.** Only one of the two ever did.

🚨 **The drop and the guard are one change and must never be separated.** The one line was written,
tested, flip-checked and **reverted** in session 18, because on its own it makes the reachable case
worse. The finding's own route — editing the document behind the card — was closed by D464. What is
live is the **queue**: `recovery_modal` prints *"N more after this one"*, so *Recover* is clickable
twice **with no keyboard**, and the second press finds `recovery.key` naming the snapshot the user
recovered one press ago and has not saved. Dropping it there deletes the last copy, where leaking it
merely offers it again. Past `may_replace_current_document` the work has been saved or the user has
been asked, so there is nothing left that exists only in `.recovery/` — which is exactly `open_path`'s
own argument, *"the two branches above are a save and a confirmed discard, and there is no third way
to reach here"*, now true of the second door.

⚠️ **The guards run before the pop, and that ordering is load-bearing.** `recovery_modal` popped
`pending` and *then* called `recover`, so a declined discard would have consumed the card and the
snapshot would have gone unoffered for that launch. **A *Recover* the user backed out of is not a
*Later*.**

**The tripwire test is inverted**, which is unusual enough to say out loud:
`recovering_leaks_the_outgoing_snapshot_until_someone_rules_on_the_guards` becomes
`recovering_drops_the_outgoing_snapshot_now_that_the_guards_are_there`. It sets `recovery.key` by
hand, so it depends on neither route, and it is **structurally unable to see the queue** — which is
why `a_second_recover_asks_before_it_spends_the_first` exists and why each names the other.
⚠️ **That second test's limit is stated in its own doc rather than glossed.** `confirm_discard` raises
a blocking `rfd` dialog, so the decline path cannot be driven headlessly; it asserts the *state* that
forces the ask — dirty, unfiled, the key naming the first recovery, a card still offering the second
press — and says plainly that **removing the guard call leaves it green**. Naming what a test does not
cover is the point; the pair is what covers it.

⚠️ **A doc-comment theft was found at this change's own insertion site and repaired.**
`confirm_discard`'s two-line doc — *"A blocking yes/no dialog. Used for the destructive paths
only…"* — was sitting at the **head** of `may_replace_current_document`'s doc run, with
`confirm_discard` left with none. The merged run is about 27 lines against `CLAUDE.md`'s 52-line
floor, and nothing lost a `fn`, so **neither recorded detector could see it**; what found it was
reading the function against its own doc while checking this entry. Its enumeration was corrected
while it was moved back: the window-close path raises an in-app `egui::Modal` and does **not** go
through this dialog, and `may_replace_current_document` is its only caller.

*(D681 is **resolved** by this and points here. **D377's drop-site enumeration goes four → five and
its *"Discard is the only thing that deletes"* is amended** — 🚨 both were amended to five and
**reverted inside one day** in session 18 on the strength of the repair that was then backed out,
