answerable — and the sibling half is D776.***

That finding is open because its own confidence line says so: the per-renderer cost is measured —
about 5.7 ms of vello pipeline build — and **`K` is not**. (⚠️ **That cost has since been measured
here too, and it is a 6–8 ms *band* on an idle adapter, not a figure: §15 D777.** The finding's number is the right
order; what D777 settles is that **D344's 84 ms**, the other half of a fifteen-fold disagreement
this entry quoted one side of, does not reproduce.) It was reasoned from `pack`'s budget rule
and never observed, which is `[S4.1-L4-08]`'s shape exactly, a finding ranking itself on a quantity
its own evidence had not counted. `VelloGpuRenderer` records a `pass_high_water` and exposes it, and
`gpu_effects.rs`'s `how_many_effect_passes_a_nested_document_demands` prints it for three fixtures.

🚨 **Measured on an RTX 4070 Ti, and it substantially de-ranks the finding: `K` is the nesting
*depth*, not a function of how many effect layers a document has.** One blur → **1** pass; a blur
inside a shadow → **2**; three deep → **3**. So a realistically nested drawing pays `3 × ~5.7 ms` ≈
**17 ms of pipeline build once in the life of the process** and holds three vello `Renderer`s —
against the unbounded `K` the finding feared. (**About 21 ms at D777's measured band**, which does
not change the reading.)

⚠️ **The case this does *not* answer is the sibling one, and it is the one the budget rule is
actually about**: many effect layers at *one* level whose combined area exceeds the page, which is
where `pack` starts a second chunk. **Depth is bounded by how deeply a designer nests groups; area is
not.** The test says in as many words which case its number is for, because ***a number measured for
the wrong case reads exactly like a number measured for the right one*** — and this one would read
as closing the finding. 🚨 **It was measured the same day and it is the unbounded half — §15 D776.**
32 siblings on a 100×100 page demand **11** passes, and the count is a ratio of total effect-buffer
area to page area with nothing capping it. **The de-ranking above holds only for the nested case**,
and this paragraph's distinction is the reason the two numbers can be told apart at all.

🚨 **Two corrections to how the finding reads, and the second is the larger.** The 5.7 ms is **per
pass index, once ever**, not per frame: the frame that first demands `K` pays
`(K − high-water) × 5.7` and every frame after it pays nothing, because `layers` only ever grows.
And **§15 D402's page budget does not cap the count — it drives it.** `budget` is the page's own
pixel area and `pack` starts a new chunk whenever the accumulating texture passes it, so bounding
each pass's *area* makes the *count* grow with total-effect-area ÷ page-area;
`MAX_EFFECT_BUFFER_SIDE` (§15 D744) bounds one layer's **side**, not how many layers there are.
**Nothing anywhere caps `total`.**

⚠️ **Nothing in the suite substituted for this, which is why it had to be written.**
`tests/render.rs`'s `layers.len()` assertions are the `RecordingPainter`'s CPU-side layer **stack**,
a different quantity wearing the same name; `tests/gpu_device.rs` never reaches an effect pass; and
`zoom_sweep.rs` prints frame times without touching either the pass count or `Renderer::new`.

⚠️ **`pass_high_water` is deliberately not `layers.len()` read back**, though the two are equal
today. The vector is what is *held* and this is what was *asked for*, and the bound-and-reuse scheme
the finding suggests is precisely what makes them diverge — at which point the number worth knowing
is still this one.

**The test asserts only a floor** — a document with effect layers demands at least one pass — because
the interesting figure is the printed one and a hard upper bound here would be asserting `pack`'s
arithmetic against itself. It is `#[ignore]`d and needs a GPU adapter.

*(No production line changed beyond the counter and its accessor. **Any future bound-and-reuse scheme
must be argued against §15 D344 directly**: that entry is why there is one renderer per pass, it is a
**correctness** rule rather than a saving, and the symptom it was written for was a pasted image
going blank from the second frame onwards. §6.3's pass bullet gains the measurement; nothing struck
from `roadmap.md`, whose effect-pass rows are struck already. **`[S11.2-L4-05]` stays open.**)*

**D762 — One predicate for *"is this affine safe to invert"*, and two of the four spellings it
replaced were the same test written backwards. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-15; Keep — and the loader's
half is now decided, against normalising.***

§15 D713 counted four guards asking one question and deliberately left them, on the argument that a
fifth number would have been a fifth number to defend. All four call `build::affine_is_invertible`
now:

- `svg_in`'s gradient mapper — `t.determinant().abs() > 1e-12`
- `svg_in`'s `transform=` fold — `det == 0.0 || !finite`
- `svg::effect_region` — `world.determinant().abs() < f64::EPSILON`
- `svg::sweep_radius` — `!det.is_finite() || det == 0.0`

⚠️ **D713's *"no two alike"* overstates by one, and the overstatement was the reassuring direction.**
The second and the fourth are the same test with the operands reversed, in two crates. Four
independent opinions is a problem you can see; **one opinion nobody knew was shared** is worse,
because neither site can be corrected by reading the other and a fix to either leaves the tree still
holding two answers.

🚨 **`f64::EPSILON` was the least defensible of the four and deserves the sharpest sentence.** It is
≈2.22e-16 and it is a **relative** quantity — the gap between 1.0 and the next representable double —
where a determinant is in **squared world units**. On a node at millimetre scale the test is
effectively `== 0.0`; on one at `1e8` units it can never fire, so the guard silently stopped guarding
at exactly the coordinates where a filter region is most expensive to get wrong. Its refusal point
has no relation to the thing it measures at all. **It is a number chosen because it is spelled like a
small number**, and that is a different failure from an epsilon somebody picked badly: there was
never a value of it that would have been right.

🚨 **And D713's own revisit trigger had already fired on the day D713 was written.** That entry says
*revisit when a second reader wants an inverse*. `svg::sweep_radius` is a **third** inverting reader
of `GradientBrush::transform`, it predates the entry, and **it is one of the four guards the entry
counted** — so the enumeration offered as the reason to wait contained the condition for not waiting,
four paragraphs above the trigger. Nothing in this project can see that: every number resolves, every
guard is real, and the two facts are in one entry that nobody re-reads end to end. **An enumeration
written to argue a deferral is worth reading against the deferral's own trigger.** D713 is amended to
say so.

**The loader's half is decided and the answer is not to normalise.** The maintainer's ruling is to
unify the guard instead, and the argument is `io`'s existing house rule rather than an exception to
it: a **structural** error is refused, a **recoverable value** is repaired, **decoration** is dropped,
and **geometry with no defensible rewrite is carried as written and guarded at the reader** — a
degenerate text rail is already carried untouched and refused at layout by `PathWarp::of` on exactly
that ground. ⚠️ **And normalising would be worse than D713 supposed.** D713 worries that it *"silently
rewrites the content of the user's file"*; the sharper objection is what the rewrite *paints*. A
singular brush transform paints a **degenerate** gradient, where the identity paints the ramp across
the whole shape — so normalising does not substitute one invisible thing for another, it makes an
**invisible paint visible**, in artwork nobody authored. The *"draws nothing either way"* argument
D713 borrows from `svg_in`'s `transform=` fold is about a matrix applied to *geometry* and does not
transfer to a stored brush transform.

**Test** `affine_is_invertible_asks_one_question_and_the_old_spellings_disagreed`, in
`crates/ondin-core/tests/build.rs`. ⚠️ **Its flip bit at a different row than predicted, and the
correction is the useful half**: `< f64::EPSILON` only starts refusing below a ~1.5e-8 scale, so the
millimetre-scale row — determinant `1e-6`, four hundred million times the threshold — was never at
risk. The old guard's fault is therefore **not** that it refused ordinary small shapes; it is that it
is calibrated against nothing, and the `small` row stays in the test as the row that says so.

⚠️ **One thing this did not fix and it is worth expecting.** `svg::sweep_radius` returns `None` for a
transform this predicate refuses, and its caller writes `.unwrap_or(50.0)` — which silently reinstates
§15 D647's own fixed defect, a literal `r="50"` whatever the shape's size, for any sweep gradient
carrying a singular brush transform. D647 removed that literal because *"it is the one number in this
writer that does not survive a change of scale"*; the fallback arm keeps it. **Recorded rather than
repaired**, because what the right fallback is — the frame's own diagonal, or dropping the paint —
is the same question D647 answered for the ordinary path and has to be answered again for the
degenerate one.

*(§5.11's invariant 8 bullet amended — the predicate is the workspace's only spelling now, and the
loader's open half is closed there as a **fourth** thing the loader does rather than as an exception
to the three; §7's `effect_region` bullet gains the predicate it was missing, having described a
guard against *singular* transforms that was written as a relative epsilon; §9.2's `paint.rs`
paragraph gains the same clause. **D713 amended** in three places — its verdict line, its four-guard
paragraph and its open-half paragraph. `affine_is_invertible`'s own doc claimed in the **present
tense** that the tree carries four spellings *"no two alike"*, which this change made false the
moment it shipped, and is corrected. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row on
determinant guards. Closes D713's open half.)*

**D761 — The z-order rows get the arrow-to-a-bar pair, and the design export's own answer would have
moved the duplication rather than removed it. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested
2026-09-15; Resolved.***

The maintainer's ruling on §15 D672. *Bring to front* and *Send to back* both drew `icon::STACK` —
one picture for two verbs, which is D225's failure direction — and they are the **first and last**
rows of one four-row group `restack_rows` emits unconditionally, so the two are on screen together
every time either is. The four Order rows are `ARROW_LINE_UP` / `ARROW_UP` / `ARROW_DOWN` /
`ARROW_LINE_DOWN` now: the *all the way* halves against the *one step* halves, which is the family
`theme.rs`'s own `// Z-order: one step vs all the way` comment already groups them as. It needs no new
constant, it spends two that were already in the registry, and **it is the only one of the three
candidate schemes with no picture used twice.**

🚨 **D672's *"no document settles it"* is wrong, and correcting it is worth more than the ruling.**
`design/Editor.dc.html` gives *Bring to front* `ph-stack` and *Send to back* `ph-stack-simple`, and
`context-menus.md` §8 makes that export **normative for what a row looks like**. D672's census asked
`context-menus.md`'s tables, `architecture.md`, `shortcuts.md` and this file, and the design export is
a document none of those four is — so the sentence was a true report of a search that had not looked
in the one place that answers. **A document you did not think to ask is not a document that does not
exist.**

**So this is a recorded deviation rather than a free choice, and the reason it is taken is that the
export's answer does not remove the duplication — it moves it.** `ph-stack-simple` is also *Flatten*
in the same export; `restack_rows` emits the Order four unconditionally and *Flatten* is pushed on any
2+ selection, so those two co-occur. Following §8 literally would trade a collision inside the Order
group for a collision across it, at the cost of the arrow family's own reading, which is why the
ruling goes the other way and §8 gains the ⚠️ naming the departure.

**Both stale `#[allow(dead_code)]` are removed, and that was not optional.** A shield left over a
constant that has just become live is precisely the accident D672 was written to fix, and nothing
anywhere would have reported it. `STACK` keeps one, with its reason stated: it is the export's answer,
so it is the constant a reversal of this entry reaches for — one line away rather than a codepoint
somebody has to recover from `Phosphor.codepoints.txt` again. That is D672's own shape for
`CARET_UP` and `ARROWS_HORIZONTAL`.

🚨 **Measured while removing them, and it corrects D672 a second time.** That entry says *"under
`--all-targets` it is live again and shields everything, so the gate that catches the next dead icon
is the plain build"*. Removing the attribute warns under **both** spellings: `icon::ALL` being
`#[cfg(test)]` shields the *test* target, while the **bin** target is compiled without that cfg
either way and is what reports the dead constant. **The gate is better than D672 claims** — and the
claim is the sort a reader trims a command on, which is why it is corrected rather than left as a
harmless pessimism.

⚠️ **`theme.rs`'s `EXPORT` doc claimed *"§15 D225 **still carries** the same parenthetical"* and D225
had been amended in the very change that wrote the sentence**, so it was false the moment it shipped —
D672's own subject arriving inside D672's receipt. 🚨 **And the parenthetical it was corrected away
from is now *true***, this entry having given *Send to back* that very constant. The correction stands:
it was wrong on the day it was written, and a claim that happens to come true is not a claim anybody
checked. The *shape* argument the parenthetical sat inside was never affected in either direction,
which is why the gloss is simply not restored.

*(**D672 amended** — its *"no document settles it"* paragraph, its `--all-targets` paragraph, and the
ruling recorded against it; **D225 amended**, its 2026-09-09 ⚠️ gaining the clause that says the gloss
came true. `context-menus.md` §8 gains the ⚠️ recording the deviation from its own normativity rule;
§4's *Order* table lists no icons and is untouched, and nothing in `architecture.md` assigns a glyph
to these rows. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row on icon assignment.)*

**D760 — A point rotation turns about a fixed pivot, so it does not auto-pan. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-15; Keep.***

`[S19.2-L1-05]`. `Drag::PointRotate` auto-panned — 42.23px of drift, measured — **on the exact
argument `Drag::autopans`' own doc gives for exempting `Drag::Rotate`**. Worse, `PointRotate`'s own
doc cites `Drag::Rotate` while establishing two of the three clauses that earn the exemption: a pivot
fixed at the press, and a gesture that measures a *change* so it never chases the pointer. The third
is that its reachable set is a circle bounded by the box's circumradius and does not grow with pointer
travel — which is the *"is this gesture reaching for somewhere"* test failing three ways at once.

**The doc states a rule now rather than a list of names**, and carries no count. It said *"three"*,
and there is already a ⚠️ in the same comment (§15 D303) recording that number going stale once
before — it read *"two"* while the code excluded three. **A count in prose is a gate nobody built**,
and here it is worse than that: it is the thing that made the fourth turning gesture look like a
different subject. *"Every gesture that turns about a fixed pivot"* covers the next one without
anybody editing the sentence.

🚨 **The test was one exemption short of the code before `PointRotate` was even considered.**
`canvas::autopan_tests::panning_and_rotating_do_not_autopan` never asserted `Drag::Guide`, which has
been exempt since §15 D303 and has **eleven lines** of `autopans`' doc devoted to it — and which is
the one exemption with a *reported symptom* behind it (*"much less than before, but still there"*,
after suppressing the ruler bar alone). So the suite was green for a version that auto-panned a guide
drag out of the bar it was born in. Both are asserted now and both were flip-checked at their
predicted sites: dropping `PointRotate` from the `matches!` fails at the point-rotation case,
dropping `Guide` at the case that had been missing.

⚠️ **The test's name and doc no longer state the count either**, for the reason the paragraph above
gives: this test is where a stale number in `autopans`' doc would be found the third time, so it must
not carry its own copy of one.

⚠️ **A doc-comment theft was found in the same enum while reading `PointRotate` and is repaired here.**
`Drag::PointBox`'s six-line doc — *"Dragging a corner of the box over the selected points"* and the
*box is carried, not re-derived* rule — was sitting on `PointRotate`, which had been inserted between
`PointBox` and its own comment; `PointBox` had none at all. **Neither detector in `CLAUDE.md` can see
it**: the merged run is sixteen lines against the length ranking's 52-line floor, and the neighbour
grep asks *"did the item below lose its comment"*, which answers no for a `fn` and was never run on
an enum variant here. The check that finds it is the **enum-variant sweep** — does a variant's first
doc line name a sibling? — and `PointRotate`'s opened by describing `PointBox`.

*(§9.5's auto-pan passage amended: it read *"`Drag::autopans` names the three exemptions"* and named
`Rotate` alone, which is the document having the same shape as the bug. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, whose autopan row is struck already. Closes `[S19.2-L1-05]`.)*

**D759 — A modal owns the pointer too, and a dropped file is the pointer. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-15; Keep.***

In no finding: this is §15 D464's other half, and nobody had asked it. D464 found that `Delete` and
`Ctrl+A` reached the document behind a modal backdrop and guarded the keyboard. **`raw.dropped_files`
is filled from winit before any widget runs**, so the `egui::Modal` backdrop that refuses every click
does not touch a drop — and `OndinApp::take_dropped_images` sat outside the guard chain, called
unconditionally from `update`, **committing ops to the document behind the card**. A picture dragged
onto the window while Settings, the *Unsaved changes* confirmation or the recovery prompt was up
became a layer the user could not see arrive.

⚠️ **Worst on the recovery card, for D464's own reason.** It is drawn above the view branch (§15
D377), so it can be up over a freshly reopened document while asking about a **different** one's
snapshot — and a drop there also marks the session dirty, which mints a second snapshot key. 🚨 **That
is the route §15 D681 is about, and D681's premise sentence said it could not happen**: *"the card
blocks the pointer, so nothing behind it can be edited and no second key can be minted that way."*
The backdrop blocks a click; it does not block a drop. **D681 is amended** — the sentence was written
the day the keyboard hole closed and generalised from *the keyboard* to *the pointer* without
anybody asking the pointer.

**The condition is a predicate now.** `OndinApp::modal_is_up` is `settings.is_some() ||
confirming_close || !recovery.pending.is_empty()`, asked by the keyboard arm and by the drop. D464's
own comment had already noted that *"a modal is up"* was written out twice — the other copy being
`dashboard_keys`' guard list, §9.5 — and this wanted it a third time; *a rule with one statement and
several implementations* is the shape this codebase keeps finding broken. ⚠️ **`edited_image` is
deliberately not a member**: image editing is a *mode* the canvas is in rather than a card drawn over
it, and a drop while cropping is an ordinary drop. ⚠️ **And it is not
`ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()` and must not become it** — D464 measured that **false** for a modal
holding three buttons and no text field.

**Test** `app::library_wiring_tests::a_file_dropped_on_a_modal_does_not_reach_the_document_behind_it`.
🚨 **Its control is the whole test.** An assertion that a drop behind a modal changes nothing is
satisfied by a drop that never works at all — a PNG the loader rejects, a fixture with no document, a
`RawInput` field egui ignores — so the first case drives the same bytes into the same app one frame
earlier and asserts they **land**. ⚠️ **It measures `session.revision()` and not a child count**,
because the defect is *"ops reach the document"* and the revision is that question exactly, where a
child count also has to be right about **which** parent a picture lands under: `drop_images_at`
decides that four ways, and a first draft counting the root's children **failed its own control**.
⚠️ **All three cards are asserted rather than the one that motivated it**, the guard being one
predicate, so a test naming only the recovery card would be green for a version that guarded only the
recovery card. Flip: the bare `take_dropped_images(&ctx)` takes the revision 0 → 1 behind the Settings
card, failing at the first card asserted.

⚠️ **One drop path was not in this and was an un-enumerated remainder rather than a decision.**
`OndinApp::take_dropped_documents` runs first in `dashboard_ui`, above every card that screen draws,
and had no modal guard — so a `.ondin` dragged onto the library while a confirmation, *Move to
project*, *New project*, Settings, the search overlay or the recovery card was up was filed, and
reported itself into a status line behind the backdrop. Read off the call graph while writing this
entry, not measured on the machine. It is a *file into a folder* rather than an edit to an open
document, so it does not carry D681's key-minting consequence. 🚨 **Closed by §15 D772, and the
prediction this paragraph closed with was wrong in both halves**: it said *"expect the answer to want
a third list or a second predicate — which is the argument for the maintainer rather than for a
fix"*, and the answer wanted neither. The second predicate **already existed** —
`library_keys_are_free`, this screen's own enumeration since D542 — and had exactly one caller, the
keyboard. It has two now. *An un-enumerated remainder usually closes by asking the list the screen
already keeps.*

*(§9.3's input-routing bullet gains the pointer half of the modal rule; §9.4's picture-arrives
paragraph names the guard; §9.5's *"two hand-maintained lists of one fact"* ⚠️ records that the
editor's side is a predicate now and that this list is still by hand. **D681 amended** — its false
premise sentence, kept quoted. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row on drop
routing.)*

**D758 — Present mode dims *Show rulers* in the canvas menu, and only that row. *Decided by the
maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-15. Resolved.***

The maintainer: *"For 'Show rulers' in present mode, make the field disabled so it's not confusing."*
The row writes a flag present mode overrides — `rulers_on()` is `show_rulers && !self.present` — so a
click there moved the tick and left the bars where they were. `menu::Context` gains a `present: bool`
and `view_rows` closes with `.dim_if(sw == ViewSwitch::Rulers && cx.present, "Present mode hides the
rulers")`. Two lines; no other production change.

**The confusion is new, and D756 is why.** `open_context_menu` refused in present mode until
2026-09-14, so this row was unreachable there and nobody could have clicked it. That is the shape to
expect from D750's ruling generally: taking a refusal out does not create a bug so much as *expose*
every state the refusal had been standing in front of, and this is the first one that surfaced.

🚨 **One row, not the group, and the asymmetry is the whole content of the entry.** Present mode
overrides exactly **one** of the five View rows: `guides_on()` is `show_guides` alone,
`grid_visible()` reads no present flag at all — both by D750's ruling — and *Lock guides* is a
property of the guides rather than a visibility, so nothing about present mode touches it. The other
four are fully live in present mode and dimming them would be the app claiming a reach D750 took away
from it. **A test that only looked at *Show rulers* would pass the wrong version**, which is what the
second flip says: widening the predicate to `cx.present` alone fails at *"present mode overrides only
the rulers"* and **not** at the rulers assertion, which is still satisfied.
`menu::tests::the_canvas_menu_carries_every_view_row_and_present_dims_only_the_rulers` asserts both
halves, and the live set is derived by subtraction from the expected set rather than typed out.

**Dimmed rather than absent**, which is `context-menus.md` §6 rather than a choice made here: *"Kind
decides presence … State decides enabled. A row that belongs to the kind but cannot run now is dimmed
and says why."* The kind is the canvas and the canvas has rulers; what it cannot do is *now*. The
test asserts the row is still **present** under present mode for exactly that reason — a repair that
filtered it out would satisfy every other assertion here.

**The reason names the thing that would have to change**, which is §5.9's rule for a `why` string,
written for `LayerState::locked_within()`'s two sentences: *"a layer inside a locked group is not
itself locked, so the first sentence would point the hand at a toggle that is already off"*. *"Present
mode hides the rulers"* names present mode, which is the state the user would have to leave, and says
what it is doing — where *"The rulers are hidden"* would name the symptom and point at nothing.

⚠️ **`present` is deliberately not a sixth `ViewState` field, though *Present mode* is a `ViewSwitch`
like the other five.** That struct answers one question — *"what is this switch's state, for the tick
beside its row"* — and §6.1 keeps *Present mode* out of the canvas menu, so it has no row and no tick.
Putting it there would make `ViewState::get` answer `Some` for a switch nothing draws, which is
precisely the confusion D675 removed. `Context::present` asks a different question: *"is another
switch's row worth offering"*. **Two fields that both hold a `bool` off the same flag are not the same
field**, and the argument for keeping them apart is the one D675's repair paid for.

⚠️ **The canvas menu is the only surface this dim could live on, which is why there is no pattern to
follow.** Present mode hides the top bar, the layers pane, the tool rail, the inspector and the picker,
so the View menu's own *Show rulers* row cannot be reached in present mode at all — and of the two
things `update` draws outside its `!present` guard, `settings_ui`'s only door is a button present mode
has already hidden (D756). So this is the first control in the app dimmed because present mode
overrides it, and it is first because until D756 there was nowhere for it to be.

*(In no finding — the maintainer's report. §9.4's present-mode paragraph gains the consequence; its
*"It reads three of the other seven View rows"* sentence is untouched and is what this dim follows
from. `context-menus.md` §6.1's *Show rulers* row says so. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which
carries no row on present mode or on the View switches.)*

**D757 — *Show layout grid* is in the canvas menu too, and the question D755 wrote down was answered
in a sentence. *Decided by the maintainer; built and tested 2026-09-15. Resolved.***

The maintainer: *"Canvas right click menu should show 'Show layout grid' to keep it consistent."*
D755 built the switch, gave it a View-menu row and then **recorded the asymmetry rather than
resolving it** — `menu::ViewState` had four fields, `context-menus.md` §6.1 listed four View rows, and
*Show grid* was therefore in both menus while *Show layout grid* was in one. `menu::ViewState` gains a
fifth field, `layout_grid`; `ViewState::get`'s `LayoutGrid` arm moves **up** out of the `None` group to
answer `Some(self.layout_grid)`; `view_rows` lists it fifth, after `Grid`; `menu_context` fills the
field; `Item::ALL` gains the row. No other production line changed.

🚨 **Nothing pinned the canvas menu's View rows at all, and D755 is the proof rather than the
hypothesis.** `the_canvas_menu_ignores_the_selection` asserts *Lock guides* is on the menu — it has to,
since a guide cannot be reached while guides are locked and that row is the only way back — and **no
test asked what else was there.** So D755 could add a `ViewSwitch` to one menu, leave the other short,
and keep the whole suite green for a session. That is this codebase's *"a rule stated in one place and
broken in the two beside it"* shape with the statement in a **spec table** and the breakage in a
`Vec`. `the_canvas_menu_carries_every_view_row_and_present_dims_only_the_rulers` **derives** its
expectation from `ViewSwitch::VIEW_MENU` less §6.1's three deliberate excludes (`Layers`, `Toolbar`,
`Present`) rather than typing the set out, so the next row added to that array either appears in the
canvas menu or fails here. ⚠️ **Deriving it is the whole of the repair** — a typed-out list of five is
a count in prose, which is a gate nobody built (D754), and it would have been green for D755 too.

**The glyph is a decision and not a pick.** `icon::COLUMNS`, moved out of the `SLIDERS_HORIZONTAL`
placeholder arm that holds the seven switches no menu draws, because this one is now drawn.
`inspector::axis_glyph` already gives `GridAxis::Columns` that same constant in the Layout grid card,
so the menu row and the panel it is about are **one picture** — which is `context-menus.md` §8's
direction (*"name them in the registry … so the same verb cannot be two pictures in two menus"*) and
the converse of D225's fourth ring, *"one picture for two verbs, which is §8's glyph rule failing in
the direction nobody checks for"*. D225's closing rule is the one that applies literally: *anything
drawn in both a panel and a menu owes this check; the registry is the authority and the panel is the
copy.* `GRID_FOUR` is spent on *Show grid*, the row directly above, and `SQUARE_SPLIT_HORIZONTAL` —
the other candidate — is the stroke-alignment glyph.

⚠️ **The accepted cost is that the glyph reads as the *columns* axis while the row is about both
axes**, and it is recorded rather than discovered later: the label says *Show layout grid* and the
alternative was a picture with no tie to the feature at all. ⚠️ **`icon::COLUMNS` is unique in the
menu registry and is not unique in the app** — the inspector also draws it for *Distribute
horizontally* and for the horizontal gap field, both of which are about an X axis rather than about a
grid. Those are panel controls and can never share a menu with this row, which is the argument
`context-menus.md`'s deviation 8 makes for `icon::EXPORT` (D274) — and that same passage says the
collision there was *"never decided, only twice made moot"*. **The day a second grid-flavoured verb
wants this glyph, the argument has to be made again rather than inherited.**

⚠️ **A second test exists for a silent failure the fifth field makes newly possible.**
`ViewState::get`'s new arm returning `self.grid` is a plausible copy-paste and is exactly what D675's
wildcard used to do for seven switches; it draws a *Show layout grid* row wearing the **pixel grid's**
tick, and nothing renders differently enough to notice.
`view_state_answers_only_for_the_switches_it_holds` asks only whether the answer is `Some`, so it is
green for that version. `every_view_row_ticks_from_its_own_field` builds a `ViewState` whose fields
disagree with their neighbours — `grid` off against `layout_grid` on is the pair a copy-paste
collapses — and the flip fails naming *Show layout grid*, `true` against `false`, as predicted.

*(In no finding — the maintainer's decision, taken on D755's own recorded question. **D755 amended**:
its *"Not in the canvas context menu, and that is an open question rather than a decision"* paragraph
says it was answered the same day, in the body and in the §15.0 index row. `context-menus.md` §6.1's
table gains the fifth row and its ⚠️ is **struck and replaced by the row itself**, which is the
cheapest possible outcome for a question recorded in a spec table; §6.1's *"the four View rows a
canvas right-click plausibly wants"* and the deviation ledger's *"the four View switches §6.1 and §6.3
carry"* are both five now. §9.4's D675 ⚠️ gains the field count. 🚨 **A comment this change shipped was
already wrong and is corrected**: `ViewState::get`'s *"`view_rows` and `guide_menu` between them ask
only the four this holds"* survived the fifth field being added directly above it — the paragraph two
above it keeps D675's counts in the **past** tense on purpose and this one is present tense, so the
two read alike and only one of them was safe. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose context-menu
bullet is *Background…*, C5's edge clause and the four untested rules, none of which this touches.)*

**D756 — Present mode refused a context menu, on two arguments that were both wrong. *Decided by the
maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-15. Resolved.***

The maintainer's report is the whole of it: *"Present mode hides the context menus. It shouldn't."*
`menu::open_context_menu` opened `if self.gesture_cancelled || self.present { return; }` and the
second disjunct is gone. One deleted term; no other production line changed. It is the second
consequence of D750's ruling — present mode hides the app's **chrome** and the canvas goes on working
normally — and a context menu is the canvas answering a click, not a piece of the app around it.

🚨 **The bullet that justified the refusal carried two arguments and they failed in different ways,
which is why both are written down here rather than deleted with the code.** The first read *"it
hides the very chrome a menu would sit over — which is also why Present mode is not a row in the
canvas menu"*. **The row rule stands**: `context-menus.md` §6.1 keeps *Show layers*, *Show toolbar*
and *Present mode* out of the canvas menu because *"they are chrome-wide switches, the View menu is
one click away, and Present mode hides the very chrome the canvas menu sits over"* — a fact about
that **row**, and never a reason to refuse the whole **menu**. One sentence carried both, so striking
the refusal reads as striking the row rule too. *It does not.* The second read *"it is what lets
`self.present` stay first in `escape`'s ladder without ever contending with R3"*, and that was never
load-bearing.

🚨 **A stated rule this change breaks, in two documents, and it is amended rather than left
standing.** `architecture.md` §9.4 read *"`self.present` stays first inside `escape` regardless:
`open_context_menu` refuses in present mode, so the two can never contend"*, and `context-menus.md`
§0 R3 said *"One thing stays above the menu, and it is the arm that is already first:
`self.present`"*. **They can contend now, and the menu wins.** Measured rather than reasoned:
`<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui` answers Escape off `context_menu.is_some()` at the top of the frame
and that arm never calls `input::resolve`, so `escape` is not entered at all and `self.present` being
its first arm is simply not reached. The effective order is **menu → present**, which is what R3 says
for every other state and is the order to want — had present won, the first Escape would have
restored the whole chrome *underneath a menu that stayed open*, which is the user pressing Escape at
a menu and getting the top bar back instead. **It cost no code**: it falls out of R3's arm already
being a `return`. `self.present` is still first *inside* `escape`, which is all that arm ever said.

**The test asserts both halves of the deleted disjunction, and that is not belt and braces.** The fix
is a deletion inside an `||`, which is the edit most likely to take its neighbour with it:
`if self.gesture_cancelled || self.present` and `if self.present` differ by three tokens, and a test
that only opened a menu in present mode would be **green for either**.
`menu::tests::present_mode_opens_a_menu_and_a_cancelled_gesture_still_does_not` opens in present
mode, refuses after a cancelled gesture (R1, D168 — unchanged and not what this is about), and
refuses with both flags up. **Flips:** restoring `|| self.present` fails at the present assertion —
the predicted site — and deleting the whole condition fails at the R1 assertion, which exists for
exactly that slip. The Escape order is pinned separately, by
`app::library_wiring_tests::escape_in_present_mode_closes_the_menu_first_and_the_mode_second`, which
drives two real Escape frames through `eframe::App::ui`; **both presses, because a ladder is about
what the second one does**, and its fixture assertion (*"D756's deletion is what lets a menu exist
here at all"*) is what caught the first flip.

⚠️ **`context_menu_ui` is called outside `update`'s `!present` guard and always was, which is what
made this a deletion at one site instead of a repair at two.** Had the draw been inside that guard,
lifting the refusal would have opened a menu that never painted — a `context_menu` slot filled, every
gate green, and nothing on screen. The comment above that call argued the old position (*"no menu can
be open in present mode, since `open_context_menu` refuses there, so the guard would only hide the
fact"*) and now argues the reverse; the call is load-bearing rather than merely honest.

*(In no finding — the maintainer's report. §9.4's ladder sentence and `context-menus.md` §0 R3
amended, and **D214's copy of the same claim** with them — that entry states R3 in full and ended
*"`self.present` keeps the top of `escape`'s ladder regardless, because `open_context_menu` refuses
in present mode and the two can therefore never contend"*, which is the sentence a later reader would
reinstate the refusal from. Three `crates/` comments corrected: the one above `context_menu_ui`,
`settings_ui`'s beside it — which cross-referenced *"the context menu's reason"* and now carries its
own, the two having come apart, the menu's being that it genuinely opens in present mode and the
card's that nothing can open it — and `escape`'s *"nothing may take the key ahead of it"*, which is
true of the ladder and is now said that way. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row
on present mode.)*

**D755 — The layout grids got the global switch D385 declined, because the argument for declining it
had been measured false. *Decided by the maintainer; built and tested 2026-09-15. Resolved.***

*View ▸ Show layout grid* — `input::ViewSwitch::LayoutGrid`, the eighth row of `VIEW_MENU` and
directly after *Show grid*, backed by `OndinApp::show_layout_grids` (on by default, per session) and
read by `canvas::draw_layout_grids` as an early `return`. D385's *"Two things deliberately not
built"* refused it: *"no global «show layout grids» toggle: present mode is the app's existing 'show
me the artwork' switch and already suppresses every overlay, so a second one would be a second answer
to one question."* `[S12.5-L2-01]` measured that premise false — present mode suppressed two overlays
of about a dozen — D750 then overruled the suppression outright and said in as many words that
*"whether the feature wants a toggle of its own is open and is not decided here"*, leaving the
feature with **no global switch at all**. The maintainer has now answered it.

🚨 **It is an outer gate and not a write, which is the whole of the decision and the thing the test
exists to say.** A band has three gates on it now: `LayoutGrid::visible`, per grid, document state,
saved and round-tripped — D387's eye, the one the Layout grid card shows; `shown_visible`, the
frame's own; and this, workspace-wide and per session. The switch deliberately does **not** clear
`LayoutGrid::visible` across the document. That spelling would spend the per-grid state D387 built
the eye to keep, and would land in the undo history as an edit to the artwork — *"let me see it
without"* destroying what the eyes said. Turning the switch back on restores exactly what they said,
**because it never touched them**.

**The flip that matters is the second one, and it is the version somebody would plausibly have
written.** Deleting the `if !self.show_layout_grids { return; }` fails at *"the switch takes the
bands away"*, which is the predicted site and proves nothing much. Reimplementing the switch as a
write over `LayoutGrid::visible` leaves **every band assertion green** — the bands go, the bands come
back — and fails only at *"the switch left the document alone"*. So a test asserting only what
reaches the screen is green for the implementation this entry is about refusing.
`canvas::layout_grid_tests::the_workspace_switch_hides_every_band_and_spends_no_per_grid_state`
carries both, on a fixture of three grids with one eye deliberately off, so the restored state is
something there is a wrong answer about: a switch that wrote the document would come back with all
three on.

**Unbound, on D355's reasoning.** *Snap to baselines* has no chord because no app has that switch,
so there is no convention to match and none worth spending; the same holds here, and
`docs/shortcuts.md` has never reserved or declined one for a layout-grid toggle — grepped, not
assumed. `ViewSwitch::accel` now answers `None` for **two** variants where the sentence beside it
said one, and that sentence is corrected rather than dropped, because the count is what makes the
pair legible.

**Session state rather than a preference**, on §9.4's own rule: *"all of them are view state,
following `show_rulers`'s precedent rather than `canvas_background`'s (§15 D28), because none of them
has persisted geometric meaning."* The default is **on**, because a grid a designer went to the
trouble of adding to a frame is one they want to see — the switch is for taking it away for a moment,
not for turning the feature on.

⚠️ **The row's position is argued from adjacency, and the Illustrator attribution it was first
written on could not be corroborated.** The two grid rows sit together so that *"which grid did I
just hide"* is answered by reading one against the other — which is a sufficient argument and is
checkable against the menu. The brief's *"that is where Illustrator puts Show Column Guides relative
to Show Grid"* is not corroborated anywhere in `docs/`, and nothing available to this session could
confirm such a row exists in that application at all. It is therefore **dropped from the three
`input.rs` comments that rested on it** rather than left standing. This is D754's rule applied before
the premise had a chance to age: a true consequence resting on an unchecked premise is worse than a
plain error, because the reader who checks the premise discredits the consequence with it — and here
the consequence (adjacent rows, a second grid switch rather than a second meaning for `Grid`) is
right on grounds of its own.

⚠️ **Not in the canvas context menu — recorded here as an open question, and answered the same day
(D757).** `context-menus.md` §6.1 put four View rows there — *Show rulers*, *Show guides*, *Lock
guides*, *Show grid* — through `menu::view_rows`, and `menu::ViewState` had exactly four fields to
match, so `ViewState::get` answered `None` for `LayoutGrid` along with the seven switches that have
never been drawn in a menu. *Show grid* was therefore in both menus and *Show layout grid* in one,
which is the *"a rule stated in one place and broken in the two beside it"* shape. Adding it meant a
fifth `ViewState` field and a change to §6.1's table, which is a **spec** decision and was not this
change's to take — so it went to the maintainer, who answered *"keep it consistent"* within hours.
**Writing it down is what closed it**: an asymmetry recorded in §15 and in the spec table is one
somebody can settle in a sentence, where the same asymmetry left in the code is one nobody meets
until they open two menus in a row.

*(In no finding — the maintainer's decision, taken on D750's reopening. **D385 amended**: its struck
clause is closed rather than merely struck, and its reopened-question paragraph now names the answer.
**D750 amended** on the same point — its *"whether the feature wants a toggle of its own is open"* is
answered, and its *"there is now no global switch that takes a grid away at all"* is no longer true.
§5.3b's *"it has no global switch at all, and present mode is not one"* bullet and §9.4's View-menu
enumeration amended, the second in three places: the row list, the *"nine of the ten switches default
on"* count, and present mode's *"three of the other six View rows"*. `shortcuts.md` §6 gains the
**unbound row** its own rule asks for — *"this file holds the keymap bound, unbound and agreed … a
row saying 'none, on purpose' is what stops the next reader reaching for a free chord and calling it
parity"*, which had one such row and now has two — and `context-menus.md` §6.1 gains the ⚠️ naming
the fifth View row it does not carry. 🚨 **Four counts elsewhere were falsified by one variant and
are repaired**: §9.4's and D683's *"`[Self; 7]` and `[Self; 4]` over eleven variants"*, D37's
headline clause — which had already rotted once for exactly this reason and says so — and
`every_view_switch_is_on_exactly_one_menu`'s own doc, where the numbers are **deleted rather than
corrected**, the test being membership and not cardinality. ⚠️ **D683 predicted this variant** —
*"a twelfth variant compiles green … what nothing forces is that it appear on a menu"* — and its test
is why it could not land badly. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose layout-grid row is struck
already and which carries no row on a View switch.)*

**D754 — Five comments, a data file's header and §9.2 said `Phosphor.ttf` has *no* `post` table, and
every consequence they drew from it was right. *Measured and corrected 2026-09-10. Resolved.***

Measured by the session with a read-only script over the font's table directory: `post` **is** there
— 32 bytes at offset **488604**, version **`0x00030000`**. Version 3.0 is precisely the version that
stores no glyph *names*, so the claim was wrong about the file and right about everything it was used
for. Names cannot be read out of the font. `Phosphor.codepoints.txt` really did have to be recovered
from the font's own GSUB ligatures. A wrong codepoint really does lay out perfectly and render
nothing at all, and an atlas dump really is the only check on a new glyph. No production line
changed and nothing about the app moved; this is a record.

🚨 **A true consequence resting on a false premise is worse than a plain error, because checking it
is what breaks it.** A reader who doubts *"has no `post` table"* does the cheapest possible thing —
looks in the table directory — and finds the tag sitting there in 32 bytes. The natural conclusion
is that the paragraph is mistaken, and the paragraph goes on to say *dump the atlas before you trust
a codepoint*, which is the sentence that stands between them and an invisible button. **The premise
was falsifiable in one grep and the rule it carried was not**, so the check a careful reader runs is
the thing that discredits the advice.

⚠️ **This is not a comment that went stale, and the difference is where to look for the next one.**
Nothing changed underneath it: the font has not moved and the sentence was wrong the day it was
written. Staleness is found by reading prose against a tree that has changed; this shape is found
only by measuring a claim nobody thought needed measuring — and it survives *because* it is nearly
true. Seven copies and an unknown number of readings, not one of which had any reason to stop.

**The repair is to name the version rather than to deny the table**, and all seven say *version 3.0,
which carries no glyph names* now. That is stronger than the sentence it replaces in the one way
that counts: `0x00030000` is a fact the reader confirms in the same grep that would otherwise have
discredited the paragraph, so the check that used to end in doubt ends in agreement.

**The population, because a claim this cheap to copy is worth listing.** Four in `theme.rs` — the
*Adding an icon* note, `CIRCLE_HALF`'s, `icon::ALL`'s, and
`every_named_icon_has_a_glyph_behind_it`'s, which is where the atlas-dump rule lives — one in
`app.rs` beside `icon::SELECTION` in the view-switch row, the header of
`assets/fonts/Phosphor.codepoints.txt`, and `architecture.md` §9.2. ⚠️ **`icon::ALL`'s was found by
grepping the *claim* rather than by re-reading the list**, after the session's own account of the
repair had settled at five sites and been written into one of them as a **count** — *"four comments
and the codepoints file"*, which the sixth copy falsified the moment it was found. **A list of the
places you corrected is not a sweep**; the sweep is the phrase. The count is gone from that comment
rather than corrected, this entry holding the population instead, which is this project's standing
answer to a number in prose standing in for a check nobody built.

⚠️ **§9.2 was corrected one entry earlier, under D751**, whose own ⚠️ carries the same measurement in
a sentence because a painted dot rather than an icon-font glyph is what it argues for. That entry
records the *correction*; this one records the *claim*, its population and the number a reader can
check, and §9.2 cites both. Neither says more than the other about the font.

⚠️ **`CLAUDE.md` carries a different Phosphor claim — that the font has no `fvar` table — and it is
not in question here.** An earlier session measured it by grepping the binary, it is about variable
axes rather than about names, and nothing on this list touches it.

*(Measured and corrected 2026-09-10; **Resolved**. In no finding; record only, no production line
changed and no test written — the constants, the catalogue and the atlas-dump test are exactly as
they were. §9.2's Phosphor sentence already carried the correction under D751 and gains this entry's
number beside it. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row on the icon font or its
codepoint table.)*

**D753 — §5.6 said a handle dragged past its anchor flips the shape, and three kinds came through the
one resize path that threw the sign away. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-10.
Resolved.***

`[S13.1-L2-02]`. §5.6 states it unqualified — *"a handle dragged past the corner it is anchored to
**flips the shape**, and the flip *is* the sign of the scale factor"* — and every kind that goes
through `tools::resize_factors` obeys it, `scale_along` keeping the sign and `split_geometry_scale`
peeling it into `Orientation::mirror`. A `Rect`, a `Text` and an image-filled layer come through
`tools::resized_box` instead, whose extent closure takes `(at - held).abs()` and whose edge closure
reflects the box across the anchor: the box lands perfectly on the far side and **no sign survives to
become a mirror**. So a rect with one rounded corner carried that corner to the far side *unturned*,
where the same drag on a path put it against the held edge. The maintainer ruled that `Text` mirrors
as well, *"it keeps the action consistent"*, so there is no kind exempt.

**`resized_box` reports the crossing and `resize_to_handle` composes the reflection**, a third return
`(bool, bool)` rather than a transform built where the box is measured — that function knows nothing
about transforms and answers a question about a box.

🚨 **The crossing test is not `at < held`, and the obvious spelling is the one beside it answering a
different question.** `at < held` is the `edge` closure's — *which side of the anchor does the box lie
on* — and it coincides with *crossed* only for a handle on the high side. `Handle::Left` holds the
**right** edge, so an ordinary left drag already satisfies it. The predicate is a sign comparison:
the direction the box extends from its anchor is `span - 2 * held`, `held` being 0 or `span`, and a
crossing is the pointer's offset from the anchor having the opposite sign.

🚨 **Alt is the same rule and not an exemption, which was probed before the fix was written and is
the only reason it is not scoped to side handles.** With `symmetric` the anchor is the box's own
centre, and a `Path` dragged past that centre comes back `Mirror::X` exactly as one dragged past an
edge — so the same product answers both and there is one closure rather than two.

**The reflection is about the *new* box's own centre, composed on the right.** `resized_box` has
already placed the box beyond the anchor, so what is missing is only the content turning over inside
it, and a reflection about that box's centre maps the box onto itself. Reflecting about the *anchor*
would move the layer a second time; composing on the left would reflect the parent's axes and carry
it across the page. ⚠️ **The rail arm is excluded**: `geometry_moved_itself` marks
`GeometryPatch::TextPath`, where the type is placed by a curve rather than by a box, and a flip there
is D406's `on_path_flip` — a different question with its own control.

🚨 **The coverage result is the half worth carrying, and it runs both ways.** The change passed
**1,266** tests before a line of new test was written, because the existing flip test asserts where
the ink *lands* and the ink lands in the same place either way — measured to the unit, `Mirror::X`
against `Mirror::None` over an identical world box. Meanwhile the *wrong* predicate, `at < anchor`,
fails **six** tests, four of them older than this change (`an_ordinary_resize_flips_nothing`,
`resize_from_top_left_moves_the_origin_and_holds_the_far_corner`,
`dragging_an_auto_labels_left_edge_holds_its_right_edge`,
`dragging_the_top_of_a_trimmed_label_holds_the_bottom_the_handles_drew`,
`a_crop_drag_leaves_the_photograph_exactly_where_it_was`), because every one of those drives a
`TopLeft`, `Left` or `Top` handle where `at < anchor` is the *ordinary* drag. **The suite had real
teeth against the loud mistake and none at all against the quiet one**: a spurious flip is caught by
everything and a missing one by nothing. *Do not assert this on the ink's bounding box* —
`a_rect_flips_past_its_anchor_exactly_as_a_path_does` asserts `Mirror`, and
`a_drag_that_stops_short_of_the_anchor_flips_nothing` is its control, without which `crossed`
returning `true` unconditionally passes every row.

*(§5.6's flip bullet amended — it stated the rule unqualified and then explained it only through
`resize_factors`, which is the reading under which the second path was never wrong. §9.4's
`resized_box`/`resize_factors` divergence ⚠️ gains the second instance. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, which carries no row on the resize flip; the mirror bullet in *Later* is
`build::flip`'s rigid-body reading and a different verb. Closes `[S13.1-L2-02]`.)*

**D752 — The OpenType list drew every switch off over a selection whose runs disagreed, and toggling
one wrote the first run's whole list over all of them. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested
2026-09-10. Resolved.***

`[S6.2-L1-05]`, both halves, which D636 named and deliberately left.

🚨 **The section had the answer and spent it on the reset button.** `subject.mixed(Features)` is
called **zero** times across `features_section` and its rows, while `subject.ragged` is called
exactly once — one line above the readout, deciding whether a reset is lit. So the raggedness
question was asked within a screen of the control that needed it and the answer went somewhere else.

**The readout is the word "Mixed", which is D130's rule rather than an invention.** D130 is
*Resolved* and states it once: *"A control says **Mixed**. If it is too small to hold five letters it
says a dash, and there are exactly two"* — `ui::segment_mixed` and `ui::Swatch::Mixed`. A feature row
is the width of the card and the word is right-aligned to the margin the switch occupies, so five
letters fit with room over; a third dash would have been a departure from a live entry dressed as a
consistency repair. The maintainer ruled out the alternative independently: *"A three way switch
would be visually weird (thumb in the middle?) so I'll take the dim and tooltip approach."*
`ui::switch_row_mixed` is `switch_row`'s sibling over one `switch_row_inner` taking `on:
Option<bool>`, so the hover ground, the row height, the ink tiers and the right margin cannot come
apart between the definite row and the mixed one. **The row stays live** — dim is a readout and not a
disablement, clicking is how a mixed range is resolved, and the click turns the feature *on* because
a row that shows no position has to mean something predictable from the row alone. The tooltip says
which.

⚠️ **Per *tag*, not per attribute, and that is the whole readout.** `mixed(Features)` is true the
moment any one tag disagrees anywhere, so a readout built on it would mark all forty rows because one
of them differed. `TypeSubject::feature_mixed` compares one tag across the distinct lists
`CharSpans::values_in` hands back, reading an absent tag as `0` — exactly as the row draws it, a
missing tag meaning *whatever the font does by default*.

**The write is only the named tag**, which needed a per-run write core did not have.
`Spans::runs_of` is new: `values_in`'s answer without the deduplication and with the ranges kept, and
**`values_in` now calls it**, so the boundary rule has one implementation rather than a readout and a
write each walking the spans. `TextEdit::style_selection_per_run` takes a closure over each run's own
value; the OpenType merge stays in the panel, so the boundaries are core's and the merge is the
caller's. A bare caret does nothing there, deliberately — `style_selection`'s empty-range arm holds
the attribute as `pending`, and there is no *run* to compute from at a point.

🚨 **The flip is worse than predicted and it is the reason the loss is not recoverable.** Restoring
the flatten — `apply_char_attrs(subject, vec![CharAttr::Features(merge(&set))])` — fails at the
`tnum` assertion reading `left: [0]` where `[0, 0]` was expected: flattening does not merely set both
runs to the first one's list, it **collapses the two runs into one**, because identical neighbouring
spans have no boundary left to keep them apart. **What a mis-click destroyed was not a value but the
fact that the second word had ever been different**, and no undo-free edit puts that back.
⚠️ **The assertion order puts the loss first** — `tnum` surviving is what the user loses and `liga`
having changed is only the control that says the click did anything; a test asserting the second
alone passes against the flattening version.

*(D636's *"the OpenType half is deliberately left"* 🚨 is amended — both halves it named are answered.
§9.4's `switch_row` passage gains the mixed sibling, and its mixed-spelling ⚠️ is corrected: it read
*"this panel does not keep it"*, and the panel now keeps D130's rule in the OpenType list while its
numeric fields still do not — the dash population is unchanged and the size question D130 leaves open
is still unasked. §9.4's *"the write goes into the session's own spans"* bullet gains the per-run
door. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: its open Type-panel row is `[S6.1-L1-03]`'s zero-spacing
readout, which is a *structural-comparison* ruling this does not reach. Closes `[S6.2-L1-05]`.)*

**D751 — The library's failure message was bounded by the room beside the search field, so it faded
to nothing on the screen present mode exists for. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested
2026-09-10. Resolved.***

🚨 **`[S16.3-L1-03]`'s premise was already stale when it was ranked, and this is the ninth recorded
instance of that shape.** The finding says a failed save *"reports itself into a widget the library
never draws"*. **D426 had given the library a status line before the finding was written**; the
sentence was drawn. *A finding is a claim to check, including the half that reads as already
checked* — and here the wrong half is the premise rather than the verdict, because the verdict
survives for a reason the finding does not state.

**What was true is a width.** `status_label` took a `max_w`, and the library passed
`(bar width − SEARCH_W) / 2 − 48` — half the leftover room beside the search field, which is
**painted** across the centre of the bar rather than laid out in it, less the gear. That is a
function of the window: **382pt at the default 1200, 22pt at 500, and zero at 436**, with no
`with_min_inner_size` on the viewport, so all three are reachable by dragging an edge. The message
shrank to an ellipsis and then to nothing exactly where present mode says the user is working — a
laptop screen with the panels in the way.

**The maintainer chose an icon indicator with a tooltip**, and `app::status_dot` is a fixed box:
`ui.allocate_exact_size` rather than a `Label`, so the surface is the same width whatever the text
says, which is the property the old one lacked. `status_color` is lifted out of `status_label` so the
two screens differ in *surface* and cannot differ in what a failure looks like. The hit box is
`STATUS_DOT_HIT` (28, the header's control height) against ink of `STATUS_DOT_R` (4): a 4pt target is
a tooltip nobody discovers, and the whole point of the surface is that the sentence is one hover
away.

⚠️ **A painted circle rather than an icon-font glyph, and that is a measurement.** `Phosphor.ttf`'s
`post` table is version **3.0**, which carries no glyph names, so a codepoint cannot be checked
against the file by name; there is no warning or info picture among the 143 constants in
`theme::icon`; and a wrong codepoint lays out perfectly and renders nothing at all, which is the
failure mode §9.2 already records for the mask icons. Identifying a new glyph means dumping the atlas
and reading it by eye. A dot needs none of that and cannot come out blank. ⚠️ **§9.2 said the font has
**no** `post` table and that is corrected here**: the table is present — it is the *version* that
carries no names. Same practical consequence, and a reader checking the claim would have found the
tag and concluded the paragraph was wrong about everything.

🚨 **Three tests had to be re-aimed and D426's own is among them, because a tooltip's ink never
reaches `.shapes`.** They read the sentinel out of the frame's galleys, which is exactly what D426
built them to do and exactly what can never see this surface. The assertions **split**: the dot says
the screen is showing something and its colour says of which kind, `session.status().text` says what
the hover would read. ⚠️ **Asserting the text alone would be the original bug** — for two months this
file wrote 22 messages into a slot the library never drew and a test on `status().text` passed the
whole time. ⚠️ **And the colour pair matters more now than it did**: the sentence is gone from this
screen, so colour is the only thing left on it separating a failure from a report.

**Half (a) of the finding — should a failed save block the walk back — is answered no.**

*(§9.5's status-line ⚠️ amended: the two top bars no longer draw the same thing, and `max_w` is gone
with the caller that needed it. §9.2's Phosphor sentence corrected. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, which carries no row on the library's status surface. Closes `[S16.3-L1-03]`.)*

**D750 — Present mode is a chrome switch and not an overlay switch, so the guides and the layout
grids stay. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-10. Resolved.***

The maintainer's sentence is the ruling: *"Present Mode only hides the UI. The canvas works as
usual… Present Mode is for editing a large design and you want the chrome out of the way. Or for
editing in a small laptop screen."* So guides and layout grids stay on the canvas and the ruler bars
still go — the bars being window furniture at the edge of the frame rather than something you edit
with.

🚨 **Both sites argued the position that was overruled, and one of them was already false.**
`rulers::guides_on`'s doc read *"present mode promises to hide every piece of chrome at once, and a
guide is chrome by this module's own definition — it never enters the scene"*, and
`canvas::draw_layout_grids` opened `if self.present { return; }` under *"present mode … already hides
every other overlay. A second toggle of this feature's own would be a second answer to a question
that has one."* `[S12.5-L2-01]` measured present mode suppressing **two** overlays of about a dozen —
these two — while the frame name tags, the pixel grid, the size badge, the hover outline and the
handles all stayed. **Both quotations are kept at their sites rather than deleted**, because they are
what a later reader would otherwise reinstate the guards from.

⚠️ **"It never enters the scene" is a true sentence that answered the wrong question.** It
distinguishes chrome from *artwork*; the line present mode draws is between the app's chrome and the
**canvas**, and guides, layout grids, the selection box, the handles and the size badge are all on
the canvas side — things you edit *with* rather than parts of the app around them. `rulers_on` keeps
its `!self.present` for exactly that reason.

🚨 **D385 refused a per-frame *Show grid* toggle *because* of the false premise, so its argument is
gone and the question is reopened rather than answered.** D385's *"Two things deliberately not
built"* rests on *"present mode is the app's existing 'show me the artwork' switch and already
suppresses every overlay, so a second one would be a second answer to one question"*. There was then no
global switch that takes a grid away, which is a different starting point. **Whether the feature
wants a toggle of its own is open and is not decided here.**

⚠️ **It was decided five days later and the answer is yes** (D755): *View ▸ Show layout grid*, the
eighth row of the View menu, read by `draw_layout_grids` as an early `return`. So the two sentences
above are the state of the question on 2026-09-10 and not the state of the app — **there is a global
switch now**, and this entry's own suppression is still the thing that is gone: present mode does not
take the grids away, and the switch that does is one the user turned off.

🚨 **One ruling, two independent implementations — measured both ways.** Reinstating the grids'
`return` fails `canvas::layout_grid_tests` and leaves
`rulers::guide_grab_tests::present_mode_leaves_the_guides_on_screen_and_live` **green**; reinstating
`!self.present` in `guides_on` does the mirror. So a repair that "restores present mode" at one site
is half a repair with a full green board at the other, which is why each site is gated separately
rather than by one shared test. **The present-mode case in the grids' test is kept and *inverted*
rather than deleted** — the assertion that a grid still draws is what fails if somebody reinstates
the guard on the strength of the old comment.

⚠️ **`present`'s own field doc was wrong in a way the ruling makes worse and it is corrected**: it
claimed present mode *"overrides all six"* other View switches, where it reads three of them
(`rulers`, `layers`, `toolbar`) and never touched `Grid` or `GuideLock` at all — the pixel grid was
never suppressed, which `[S12.5-L2-01]` had said and nothing had carried back to the field. And
`show_guides`' doc still promised *"every reader goes through `guides_on`, which folds present mode
in the same way `rulers_on` does"*, which is now the opposite of the code.

*(§5.3b's layout-grid bullet and §9.4's `guides_on()` definition amended — the second stated
`show_guides && !present` as the predicate. §9.4's present-mode paragraph gains the ruling; its
enumeration was right all along and is worth reading as the *correct* list. **D385 amended**: the
premise is struck and the toggle question reopened, and its flip-check paragraph no longer describes
three suppressions in one test. Four `crates/` comments corrected —
`OndinApp::show_guides`, `OndinApp::present`, `rulers::draw_rulers_and_guides`' *"both halves now
hang off predicates that fold present mode in"*, and the two D541 docs
(`rulers::nudge_guides`, `inspector::remove_selected_guides`) that still name present mode as a way
to hide a guide. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose layout-grid row is struck already. Closes
the present-mode half of `[S12.5-L2-01]`.)*

**D749 — Pressing *sort* in the Trash set *Default page on open* to a value the Settings picker
refuses to offer. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-10. Resolved.***

`[S20.3-L1-02]`. `OndinApp::remember_dashboard` read the current `dash.nav`, `dash.sort` and
`dash.list_view` into the three `dashboard_*` preferences and saved — and its **only two callers**
were the view toggle and the sort cycle, each of which is about *one* of the three. So pressing
either wrote all three, and pressing sort while standing in the Trash set *Default page on open* to
**Trash**, the one value `library_settings`' picker refuses to offer, under a comment saying *"landing
there on launch would be a strange way to start"*.

**The maintainer ruled the three are settings and not sticky state**: *"Only settable on Settings,
not on navigation or any other action in the dashboard. The whole purpose is what to open when the
app loads, not to remember your last page visit."* The function is deleted, so
`apply_library_settings` is the only writer, and the header's controls change session state that
lasts until the app closes.

🚨 **Both readings were broken, which is why this was a defect rather than a naming quibble.** Read
as *sticky* state it was not sticky either: **no nav writer ever called it**, so the page was
remembered only if you also happened to touch the sort or the view on your way out. The two halves of
the finding close on one deletion.

⚠️ **`DashboardState`'s doc asserted the other half and is corrected.** It ended *"and the nav is
written back to preferences on exit"* — false in both clauses: `on_exit` writes none of the three
keys, and the writer that did exist ran from the sort and view controls rather than from any
navigation. The struct's three fields answer *what am I looking at now*; the three preferences answer
*what should be open when the app loads*, and the two are deliberately not the same state.

⚠️ **A *"Remember last"* option is the maintainer's own stated idea and is deliberately not built.**
It would be a **fourth preference** choosing between the two behaviours — not a fourth writer of
these three — which is the distinction that keeps the deletion from being re-argued as a regression.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §9.5's dashboard passage describes the three as defaults
chosen in Settings, which is what they now are and always should have been. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, which carries no row on dashboard preferences — and **the *"Remember last"* idea is not
one to add**, a decided non-goal belonging here rather than in the open-work file. Closes
`[S20.3-L1-02]`.)*

**D748 — The Group Colors reticle was a fourth selection door, and what it silently did was arm
`Delete` on a locked layer. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-10. Resolved.***

In no finding at all. D746 named this door in its own closing 🚨 and left it, on the ground that D71
had decided it with a reason; the maintainer has now extended the ruling to it and chosen the shape.

**D71's objection was right and its cure was not.** That entry decided *"**locked layers are
included** — they carry the colour, so the census counted them, and a button whose selection came out
smaller than the number printed beside it would be reporting one thing and doing another"*. The
objection holds; the conclusion does not, **because the button was reporting one thing and doing
another either way** — what it silently did was arm `Delete`. `group_color_scope` returns a selected
group or artboard's *children*, `delete_selection` reads no lock, so *select a frame → click a
swatch → Delete* destroyed a locked layer exactly as `Ctrl+A → Delete` did before D746.

**Filter the selection *and* make the message say so**, which is the maintainer's shape and answers
D71's objection without the selection: *"Selected 2 of 3 layers with this colour — 1 locked"*. The
census row's own count is left alone — it is `ColorUse::nodes`, the **layers carrying the colour**,
which is a fact about the document rather than a claim about what a click will select, and narrowing
it would answer *"where is this colour"* with a lie in the other direction. ⚠️ **It is not
`ColorUse::uses`**, and D71's *"do not tidy the label back onto `uses`"* is untouched: `uses` counts
paint slots and still orders the census, the two differing wherever a shape's fill and stroke share a
colour. ⚠️ **All-locked changes nothing at all** — no selection change, no
`entered_group` reset, just the message. Clearing the selection because the answer was empty would
spend a click on losing whatever the user had.

**`canvas_may_select` is renamed `may_select_in_bulk` in the same commit, because the rule is not
about the canvas.** What the four doors have in common is that the user described a *set* —
everything, everything under the band, everything using this colour — rather than pointing at a
layer. Clicking a row in the layers panel points at one, which is why that door reads no lock. **The
surface is not what separates them**: this fourth door is a panel. D746's name was true of its own
three doors and would have argued this one out of the rule.

🚨 **The flips split three ways and that is what says the rule has one statement.**
`may_select_in_bulk` returning `true` fails **six** tests across all four doors; dropping only the
`(n, l)` arm of the message match fails **one**, at the text assertion, with the selection already
correct. A test asserting only the selection would be green for the version this fix exists to avoid,
which is why the message is asserted separately rather than as a nicety.

*(**D71 amended** — its *"locked layers are included"* paragraph is false and its *"ask the
maintainer"* 🚨 is answered. **D746 amended**: it names `canvas_may_select` throughout, and its
fourth-door 🚨 left the question open. §9.2's Group Colors passage amended — the count and the
selection *can* now disagree, deliberately, and the message is what carries it. §9.4's locked-layer
paragraph takes the new name and the fourth door. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose last lock
row closed with D323.)*

**D747 — One `Tab` in the editor parks the keyboard on a chrome control that wears no ring, and the
next `Space` presses it. *Deferred by the maintainer 2026-09-10; the question is **open**. Record
only — no production line changed.***

`[S18.2-L1-01]`, a Medium, was put up as a standing ruling and the answer was to wait rather than to
choose: *"That's not an issue for now. I'll come back to it in the future after spending time with
it. Close it."* **A decision not to fix now is still a decision**, and `review/` is gitignored and
will be deleted when the round is retired — so without an entry here the measurement and the
question both go with it. That is the whole reason this exists; **nothing in it asks for work.**

**What was measured**, headless in debug, over three app controls in an ordinary `Ui` — no
`settings::card`, which is to say every panel in the app:

```text
frame 0  keys=-      focused=false  keymap_open=true   accent_rings=0  fired=[]
frame 1  keys=Tab    focused=true   keymap_open=false  accent_rings=0  fired=[]
frame 3  keys=Space  focused=true   keymap_open=false  accent_rings=0  fired=["field_button"]
frame 4  keys=Enter  focused=true   keymap_open=false  accent_rings=0  fired=["field_button"]
frame 6  (a press on empty ground clears it)
```

**Re-read against the tree rather than carried forward**, and every step of it is stated in the code
at `HEAD`. `ui::focus_ring` has exactly two production sites, its own definition and `settings::card`
— the same grep D621 leant on — so nothing outside a modal card paints one and `accent_rings=0` is
what the call graph says. `Sense::click()` is `CLICK | FOCUSABLE`, so `button_face`'s
`allocate_exact_size(box_size, Sense::click())` and both arms of `icon_button_padded` put every
`field_button`, `label_button` and tool-rail glyph in the tab order; `focus_ring`'s own ⚠️ says so
and D382 says so. `input::normal_mode`'s comment states the residue in as many words — *"`dispatch`
does nothing with this unless the node tool has a path, so outside point editing Tab reaches egui
untouched"* — and `took_tab` surrenders the focus only when `edited_path().is_some() ||
self.text.is_some()`, so with Select armed and no session nothing claims the key and nothing hands it
back. And the press is egui's, at the pinned `=0.35.0`: `context.rs` sets `FAKE_PRIMARY_CLICKED` when
`enabled && sense.senses_click() && memory.has_focus(id) && (key_pressed(Space) ||
key_pressed(Enter))`.

🚨 **`Space` and `Enter` fail differently, and the finding's *"`Enter` … does the same"* is the
looser half.** egui reads both with `key_pressed` rather than `consume_key`, so neither is eaten —
but `Enter` is `Action::Enter` and `Space` is not an `Action` at all. A focused widget makes
`egui_wants_keyboard_input()` true, `input::resolve` returns nothing, and the keymap is silent
(`input::tests::a_focused_widget_silences_the_keymap_and_tab_is_what_focuses_one` pins it), so
`Enter` is **hijacked**: the button fires and stepping into the selection does not. `Space` is read
straight off the input with `key_down` at all three canvas sites — `canvas_cursor`'s `armed`,
`normal_mode_input`'s `panning_armed` and `reshape_create` — behind no focus guard, so it
**collides**: the button fires *and* the pan arms, in the same frame, off one key. D293 already
decided the pointer version of this — an armed pan outranks every tool and a click while it is armed
is the same statement as the drag — and a keyboard-synthesized click goes nowhere near
`panning_armed`.

**What is unsettled is whether the chrome is meant to be keyboard-traversable at all**, and the two
fixes the finding offers imply opposite code. The smaller one widens `took_tab` to surrender after
any `Tab` the app did not claim, which makes every hand-rolled control unreachable from the keyboard.
The larger one calls `focus_ring` once per frame at the app level, which fixes the invisibility and
leaves `Space` doubling as pan and press. **Neither is implied by anything already decided.** D382
is the entry a reader will reach for and it does not answer this: its report was *"I think tab works
in modal forms. I just can't see where I'm tabbing at"*, its answer was to make the focus **visible**
rather than to take it away, and it enumerates **modals only** — its own ⚠️ notes that the panels'
controls are in the tab order *"whether or not anyone meant them to be"* without giving any of them a
ring. So the editor chrome is D382's un-enumerated remainder, which is why this is a gap rather than
a deviation.

⚠️ **The smaller fix is not the one-conjunct edit it looks like, which is worth knowing before
anyone reaches for it as the cheap option.** The surrender at the end of `<OndinApp as
eframe::App>::ui` is not scoped to the canvas — the only early return in that function is the
dashboard's — so a card reaches it too, and dropping the `edited_path() || text` term would take the
focus back inside a modal on the first `Tab`, which is the feature D382 built. *(Read off the call
graph rather than measured.)* Scoping it is the work, and D123's claw-back is the precedent for how
easily that is drawn too narrowly: `took_tab` is answered **before any of the frame's widgets run**,
because that is the only moment "our `Tab`" and "a rename field's `Tab`" can be told apart. The
