larger fix has its own load-bearing detail — `focus_ring` must be the **last** thing drawn in a body,
since it marks a widget already laid out, so "call it at the app level" means after every panel and
not merely once.

🚨 **A later reader must not take this entry as saying the chrome is not meant to take focus.** That
question has not been answered. What is recorded is the measurement, the mechanism and the shape of
the two answers — so that whoever comes back to it after spending time with the app is deciding
rather than rediscovering.

*Deferred by the maintainer and still open. Revisit with a ruling on whether keyboard traversal of
the editor chrome is a feature; the fix follows from the answer and not the other way round.*

*(Recorded 2026-09-10; no production line changed and no test was written. `[S18.2-L1-01]` is closed
in `review/` on the maintainer's decision with no commit against it. ⚠️ **The finding's site lines
have all rotted and its symbols have not** — `focus_ring` reads `ui.rs:2602` against 2782,
`button_face` 2750 against 2930, `icon_button_padded` 2453 against 2633, the three `Space` reads
`canvas.rs:1131/:1510/:3359` against 1161/1589/3551, `took_tab` `app.rs:1660` against 1892 — so read
by name. ⚠️ **The keyboard going quiet is D167's accepted trade and is deliberately not part of this**:
that trade weighs *failing to act* against corrupting the document, and it does not weigh a key that
**acts**. ⚠️ **The citation sits on `ui::focus_ring`'s own doc**, per D741's precedent, so this
record-only entry is one the closing census can find and the next reader of the function meets the
number where the decision would be made. **§9.5's focus-visible ⚠️ gains a clause naming the
remainder** — it was true and silent about it, which is the shape a reader mistakes for a ruling;
nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no row on keyboard traversal.)*

**D746 — A locked layer refused a click and refused a rubber band, and `Ctrl+A` took it anyway —
then `Delete` destroyed it, one undo step. *Decided by the maintainer; fixed and tested 2026-09-10.
Resolved.***

`[S16.2-L2-02]`. The maintainer's sentence is the whole ruling and it is wider than the finding:
*"A locked layer shouldn't be selected in any way except clicking on the layers panel. Not on the
canvas, select all or not."*

**Two doors read one list and applied two predicates.** `OndinApp::select_all` and
`canvas::apply_marquee` both take their candidates from `OndinApp::marquee_candidates`; the band
filtered what came back with `query::is_effectively_locked` — the filter D321 installed — and the
chord filtered nothing at all. So a locked rect refused the click (`query::hit_test`), refused the
band, and joined the selection on `Ctrl+A`. **The rule was never what disagreed, only its site**:
a predicate written at each door is a rule with one statement and several implementations, which is
D266's shape and the one this project keeps finding broken.

**The repair is at the selection door because there is no door behind it.** Every production reader
of the lock in `ondin-app` — `grep -n 'is_effectively_locked' crates/ondin-app/src` — refuses a
*gesture*, a *mode* or a *drop*, or dims the row that would open one: the anchors coming up on a
locked path (`canvas::edited_path`), image editing (`begin_image_edit` and the inspector chip that is
its door), a picture landing on a locked layer (`image_drop_target`), and `menu::LayerState`, which is
what dims the rows. **Not one of them is on a commit path.**
`delete_selection` builds a `DeleteNode` for each of `build::outermost(selection.ids())` and reads
the lock nowhere, and `nudge`, the restacks and the aligns are the same. So a door that hands a
locked id to `Selection::set` has already armed `Delete` — the refusal has to happen before the
selection exists, not in front of each verb.

**One statement, three doors.** ⚠️ **The function is `OndinApp::may_select_in_bulk` since D748 and is
named `canvas_may_select` throughout this entry**, which is left as written because the argument
below is about the three doors that existed; D748 adds a fourth that is a *panel*, and the rename
says the rule is about selecting a set the user **described** rather than about a surface. It is
`!ondin_core::is_effectively_locked(&self.session.doc, id)` and nothing else; `marquee_candidates`
`retain`s on it, so the shared list is filtered where it is *built* rather than by each caller
afterwards; and `select_all` passes whichever list it ends up with through the same predicate,
including the `root_artboards` fallback, which selects **frames** and so cannot reach the rule
through the candidate list at all. `apply_marquee`'s `selectable` keeps its visibility term and
loses its lock term as redundant, with D321's original sentence quoted at the site so the relocation
can be read rather than reconstructed. **Visibility is deliberately not in `canvas_may_select`** — a
hidden-but-unlocked layer is fully editable (`context-menus.md` §5.9), so the band's own flag test
stays the band's, and `Ctrl+A` still takes a hidden layer.

🚨 **The first cut leaked straight through the next door, and one assertion is what said so.**
Filtering inside `marquee_candidates` and then testing `is_empty()` on the *result* conflates two
different documents: frames with nothing in them, which is what the fallback exists for, and frames
whose contents are **all locked**, where the honest answer is to select nothing. With the filter in
and the emptiness test reading the filtered list, `Ctrl+A` selected the **frames** and `Delete` took
them with their locked children — the same layer lost by a different route, and
`ctrl_a_then_delete_leaves_a_locked_layer_where_it_was` was still red. `marquee_range` exists for
that one question and is deliberately `fn`-private: *which layers the gesture reaches*, as against
*which of them it may have*. **A repair at one door is where the next door starts.**

🚨 **`apply_marquee` had no test caller of any kind, so D321's guard was pinned by nothing.** Found
by flip-checking the relocation: with the lock filter off, **all 1,256 tests were green**. The
function is reached only from `finish_drag`'s `Drag::Marquee` arm and no test drives it;
`canvas::marquee_selectability_tests` is the first, and it asserts a locked layer and a hidden one
are refused for their two different reasons. Flipping `canvas_may_select` to `true` now fails
**three** tests across both doors and dropping `n.visible()` from `selectable` fails **one**, which
is the asymmetry saying the lock is one rule and the visibility term is not. ⚠️ **A relocation no
test disagrees with is a relocation nobody can check** — and this one had a live §15 entry behind it.

⚠️ **That falsifies a sentence in D709, which is amended rather than left standing.** It read
*"`marquee_candidates` had test callers only through the marquee's own suite, and that suite asserts
the **filtered** result"*. There is no marquee suite. The filtered result was asserted nowhere
either, so the entry that measured `Ctrl+A`'s coverage under-reported the hole beside it — the
narrower claim it could have made is that `marquee_candidates` had **no** test caller that was not
`select_all`'s. D709's third decision is reversed on its locked half and stands on its hidden one,
which is the standing offer in its own ⚠️ (*"if it is ever filtered, the third test is the place that
says so and the place to change"*) being taken.

**D321 is extended, not contradicted.** Its enumeration of the doors it guards does not include
`select_all`, and D746 adds that door and moves the predicate to the helper both doors read. The
rule D321 states — the marquee reads the lock *effectively*, through the ancestors, exactly as
`hit_test` does — is unchanged in every particular; a reader looking for it in `apply_marquee` now
finds a comment naming where it went.

**D71 and D323 are untouched, and the layers panel is why.** `layers::select_from_row` reaches
`Selection::toggle`, `set` and `set_one` directly, reads no lock and never calls
`marquee_candidates`, so clicking a locked row still selects it and the inspector's rules apply
unchanged — *"a locked layer can be selected and recoloured; what the lock stops is dragging it
about"* is as true as it was. **What D746 narrows is the canvas**, which is the half of the ruling
that names a surface. `canvas::edited_path`'s comment, the `Shift+D` selection-door test's, and
`arming_the_node_tool_finds_no_subject_on_a_locked_path`'s all already describe the panel as the
route by which a locked layer reaches the selection at all; each was *nearly* true when it was
written and is exactly true now.

🚨 **There is a fourth door, the ruling's literal words reach it, and it was not put to the
maintainer.** `inspector::select_by_color` — D71's reticle beside a Group Colors row — replaces the
selection with every layer using a colour and **includes locked ones on purpose**, because a button
whose selection came out smaller than the count printed beside it would be reporting one thing and
doing another. That is a panel, but it is not *the layers panel*, and it is not deliberate about the
layer the way clicking a row is: one click on a colour swatch can put a locked layer into the
selection, after which `Delete` takes it exactly as it did after `Ctrl+A`. **Left as it is here,
deliberately** — D71 decided it with a reason, and rewriting a decided entry on the strength of a
sentence about the canvas would be this file's own worst habit. *Ask the maintainer whether the
reticle counts as the layers panel for this ruling; if it does not, the fix is D71's argument that
has to move, not the filter.* ⚠️ **Asked and answered on 2026-09-10 — D748**, which is D71's argument
moving: the button was reporting one thing and doing another either way, so the selection is filtered
and the *message* carries the count. The predicate is one statement across **four** doors now and is
called `may_select_in_bulk`, the surface having turned out not to be what separates them.

⚠️ **D323's revisit condition had been met the whole time and nobody had noticed.** It closes with
*"Revisit if any path back into the selection stops being deliberate"*, on the premise that a locked
layer can only be reached by picking it — and `Ctrl+A` had never been a deliberate selection of any
particular layer. D323's rule survives, because it is about what a panel may do to a layer you
selected; what it was one step away from is now one step further.

*(§9.4's marquee and `Ctrl+A` paragraphs amended; D321, D709, D71 and D323 each gain a clause.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` — the lock's last open item there closed with D323 and its record
is a decided non-goal. One shipped comment corrected: `select_all_tests`' third test opened
*"**Locked and hidden layers are selected too**"*, which the same commit made false. Closes
`[S16.2-L2-02]`.)*

**D745 — vello drops a picture that will not fit its atlas and says nothing, so three ordinary
photographs on one page drew two. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the visibility half is not
fixed.***

`[S9.2-L1-01]`, an open **High**. vello keeps every picture a scene draws in **one 8192-pixel square
atlas**, and when the next one will not fit it sets that picture's position to `None` and carries on.
`vello_encoding-0.9.0/src/resolve.rs`'s own comment is the whole of the contract: *"If the atlas is
already maximum size, there's nothing we can do. Set the xy field to None so this image isn't
rendered and then carry on — other images might still fit."* **Not an error, not a `Result`, not a
log** — so the canvas cannot be told it has lost a picture and has to arrange in advance not to.

**Three ordinary 4500 × 3000 photographs are enough.** They need three shelves of 3000, the third has
nowhere to go, and the canvas drew **1 250 opaque pixels of 1 875** — an empty rectangle where the
third photograph is — while the layers row and the Fill swatch showed all three, because those read
the *store* and only the canvas reads the atlas. `ondin export --png` and `--svg` both wrote all three
correctly the whole time, which is the worst shape a defect of this kind can have: the drawing is
right everywhere except on the screen the user is working on. A single picture wider than 8192 — a
50-megapixel camera file, a stitched panorama — fails the same way and needs no second picture at
all.

**The maintainer's decision: full resolution until it stops fitting, then shrink.**
`ImageStore::prepare` computes one integer factor and `images::atlas_downscale` searches **upward
from 1**, so a page with two photographs on it is handed both at their own size exactly as before and
the third is what changes anything. The factor is taken from the store's own decoded population —
what the document's table carries — and **not from what a frame happens to draw**, which is the part
worth reading twice: a factor derived from visibility would change as the canvas is panned, so a
photograph would visibly resharpen when its neighbour scrolled off the edge. ⚠️ **It is recomputed
after the stale eviction**, so a photograph the document has stopped carrying does not go on shrinking
the ones it still does.

**One factor for all the pictures rather than one each.** Per-picture factors pack better, and they
make the page's photographs disagree with each other about sharpness — which reads as one of them
being wrong rather than as a budget — and make the answer depend on the order the pictures were
placed in. One number is also one cache key.

🚨 **The fit test is a *shelf* packing where vello uses a guillotine allocator (`guillotiere`), and
the direction of that difference is the licence to have written it at all.** Shelf packing is
strictly the worse of the two — it wastes the tail of every row — so **"the shelf fits" implies "the
guillotine fits"**, which is the one-way guarantee this needs. The converse does not hold, so
`fits_by_shelf` refuses some sets vello would have taken, and the cost of that is a photograph shrunk
when it need not have been. The alternative was depending on `guillotiere` directly and hoping our
copy matched vello's, which trades a conservative answer for a version-skew bug that draws nothing.
⚠️ **It reproduces every row of the finding's measured table** — 8192 fits and 8193 does not, two
photographs fit and three do not — and that is what says the model is the *right* model rather than a
plausible one. It is tallest-first, because in encounter order a short picture can open a shelf a
tall one then has to leave.

🚨 **The two backends now deliberately differ, and this is the first place they do.**
`color::Resolution { Source, Atlas }` is a parameter on `color::brush_to_backend`: the GPU painter
asks for `Atlas` (`ImageStore::atlas_pixels`) and the CPU painter for `Source` (`ImageStore::pixels`).
`color.rs`'s whole purpose is that the two cannot disagree — one conversion, one monotonic-stops
repair, one framing composition — so the exception is stated in the enum's own doc, in §6.2 and in
both painters. **A canvas that softens a photograph and an export that does not are both correct**,
and a reader who finds them different should reach for this rather than for a bug. The reason is not
symmetric and that is the point: the canvas has an atlas that is too small and the export has no
atlas at all.

⚠️ **The reduction is applied to whatever buffer `pixels` returns, not to the decode.** A picture
under a moving slider is already a preview (D186), so it is reduced once more — one step softer than
it needs to be, for the duration of a scrub, on a page that is over the atlas budget anyway. The
alternative is a second factor threaded through the derived cache to say how much of the budget each
buffer has already spent, which is a great deal of machinery for a case that resolves itself the
moment the slider stops. **Recorded as accepted rather than left to be discovered.**

⚠️ **The atlas cache is keyed on the *blob's* id, not the picture's**, and that is what makes it
correct for an adjusted picture as well as a bare one: the buffer handed back may be the decode, a
preview of it, or a derived copy carrying somebody's exposure slider, which are three different sets
of pixels under one `ImageId`. It is also the key **vello itself** uses for atlas residency
(`image_cache.rs`'s `self.map.entry(image.data.id())`), so a hit here and a hit there mean the same
thing. The factor is in the key too and `prepare` drops every entry not at the current one, so the
map holds one generation.

⚠️ **A residual, and it is the finding's deeper point rather than its headline.**
`MAX_ATLAS_DOWNSCALE` is 64; past it `atlas_downscale` gives up and the silent drop returns. At 64 a
4500-pixel photograph is 71 across, so reaching it takes thousands of pictures on one page — but the
gap it leaves is not about arithmetic. `ScenePainter::has_image` is answered by the **store**, which
knows nothing about the atlas, so **D179's grey-and-cross placeholder still cannot fire for an atlas
failure**. *The budget makes the loss not happen; it does not make it visible.* Closing that wants a
door from the backend back to the walk that does not exist today, and it is the reason this entry's
verdict names the half that is not fixed.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10 at `a5ea30f`; Keep. Closes `[S9.2-L1-01]`. **Tests**:
`images::tests::the_atlas_budget_agrees_with_what_the_device_measured`, which is the finding's own
table row for row and asserts factor **1** on the rows where the GPU and CPU columns agreed —
a model that shrank the two-photograph page would be *safe* and would break the maintainer's
decision; `whatever_factor_comes_back_makes_the_page_fit`, which is the property the function exists
for and is not the same claim as "the factor is bigger than one";
`a_short_picture_does_not_open_a_shelf_a_tall_one_has_to_leave`; and
`gpu_effects.rs::three_photographs_on_one_page_all_draw`, on-device and `#[ignore]`d, with **distinct
bytes per picture** because vello keys residency on the blob id and three copies of one photograph
would fit however this code behaved. 🚨 **Two flip results that are findings in their own right.**
First, **the obvious two-picture fixture for the tallest-first sort proves nothing**: a shelf's height
is the tallest thing on it, so with two pictures the order cannot matter — either they share a shelf
whose height is the max whichever went down first, or they are on two shelves and the total is the
sum — and the flip came back green. It takes **three**, two tall and one short, before the ordering
decides anything; both fixtures are kept, the two-picture one as the control that says the assertion
is about the ordering and not about shelf packing in general. Second, **flipping `atlas_downscale` to
return 1 fails on the *factor* assertion four lines before the pixels**, so it says nothing about the
drawing at all. The flip that reaches the picture is `atlas_pixels` returning `pixels` unchanged — the
budget still computed, the reduction not applied — and it comes back **`left: 1250, right: 1875`**,
the finding's own measurement to the pixel. **A test with a cheap assertion in front of an expensive
one is only as good as the flip that gets past it.** §5.5a gains the atlas-budget bullet, §6.2 the
one deliberate disagreement between the backends, and §6.3's *"the pixels come from
`ImageStore::pixels`"* sentence is corrected — it had become false for the GPU backend the moment
this landed; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose *Now · Images* list is closed but for linked
sources.)*

**D744 — Both backends bounded an effect layer's scratch buffer with a number neither of them can
build. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S11.2-L1-01]`, an open **High**. Both `push_effect_layer`s sized the buffer with
`.min(u16::MAX as f64)`, and that number bounds nothing either backend can build. On the GPU it is
**eight times** `max_texture_dimension_2d` — 8192 on this machine, which is also
`wgpu::Limits::default()`'s value and therefore what the app requests whatever the card could manage
— so a large layer made `fx_gpu` allocate scratch textures past the limit and **wgpu validation
aborted the process**, where the CPU backend and both exports drew the same document correctly. On
the CPU it is 127 pixels past `cpu::MAX_RASTER_SIDE` (65408), whose own doc says *"Not `u16::MAX`,
which is the one value the backend cannot take"* **twenty lines above the site that took it**.

**The maintainer's decision has two halves.** Too big is answered by **resampling, never by
truncating** — which is not a new mechanism but the one D395 already uses for a wide blur: `k` grows
until both sides fit, the layer is rasterized coarse and scaled back up on the way out. Truncating is
what the old `.min()` did, and it is wrong in a way that reads as a rendering bug rather than as a
bound, because **the silhouette a shadow is cast from is read out of this buffer** — a truncated one
cuts the shape off and casts a shadow from the stump. And **one fixed number rather than the
machine's own maximum**: D395's requirement is that the two backends choose the *same* buffer for one
drawing, and a device limit is a property of whoever opened the file, so a document would look
different on two machines with neither being wrong. `effects::MAX_EFFECT_BUFFER_SIDE = 8192` is the
floor rather than this card's ceiling, and it is also vello's `MAX_ATLAS_SIZE`, so one number bounds
both the effect scratch textures and the image atlas (D745).

**One function, because "identically" was the requirement and two hand-kept copies were how it was
being met.** `effects::effect_buffer(extent, k) -> ((u32, u32), f64)` is called by both
`push_effect_layer`s and returns the `k` that produced the size — dropping it and keeping
`buffer_downscale`'s would draw the artwork at one scale into a buffer at another, a picture subtly
the wrong size rather than an error. ⚠️ **This is the shape D601 and D615 have each already caught at
this very pair of sites**, which is worth saying plainly: two implementations of one rule, kept in
step by hand, at the seam whose whole design is that they cannot differ. `pack` gained a
`debug_assert!` that every size is inside the limit.

🚨 **The most valuable thing here is that the finding's own reproduction does not reproduce, and a
test written from it passes against the unfixed code.** The finding says *"a drop shadow at
`offset = 1000`, 8× zoom asks for an 8320-px buffer"*. Measured, it asks for exactly **8192** — the
viewport to the pixel. Two things bound the box first and both had to be measured rather than read:

- `effect::grow_to_escape` grows the target on each side by the escape from the **opposite** side (a
  shadow thrown right lets ink from off-screen *left* reach in) and then intersects with the layer's
  **own ink** — so a large offset grows nothing on the side it points at.
- `buffer_box_within` then bisects the escape down until the box's **area** fits the page's pixel
  count, so a big square layer is trimmed by area long before either side reaches 8192.

**What clears both is a wide, thin layer** — a 1600 × 12 banner, a rule, a divider — at 6×: measured
buffer **9672 × 144**, an area of 1.39 M against a 2.3 M budget, so nothing else trims it, and
`wgpu error: Validation Error` against the old cap. **That is an ordinary drawing, not a hostile
one.** ⚠️ *The reproduction a finding names is not the reproduction that reaches the code it names* —
a way for a row to be wrong that `review/index.md`'s list does not yet carry, and it is worth a line
there, because the failure mode is a green test that reads as a closed finding.

⚠️ **`pack`'s `min(limit)` is genuinely dead now, and the `debug_assert!` is what says so rather than
a fourth comment claiming it.** That function's doc has asserted the thing that needed checking three
times: D395 records the first, the *"a layer larger than that cannot exist"* claim the second, and
*"nothing depends on the false half"* the third — because `min(limit)` is unconditional and is
applied to the wrong value. It bounds where a layer is **placed** in the batch texture, while the
size handed downstream is `job.size`, untouched, so `Slice { size: job.size }` and the atlas
`ImageData` both described a texture larger than the chunk holding them. **The repair had to be where
the buffer is created**, not where it is packed.

`gpu_effects.rs::a_layer_needing_more_than_the_texture_limit_still_draws`, on-device and `#[ignore]`d,

struck already.)*

**D743 — The GPU's resample was the `k²`-per-thread spelling D403 says it was not writing, so the
pass that exists to bound a shadow's cost became the cost. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S10.2-L4-02]`, an open **High**. D403's own words are the finding: *"`coarsen` is dispatched over
the coarse grid, one thread per block, so the total work is one read per source pixel however large
`k` is — the full-size spelling reads `k²` texels per thread and is `k²` times the work, which is the
version that writes itself."* **That is true while `k ≤ min(w, h)` and nowhere past it.** Above the
buffer `effects::coarse_size` answers **1 × 1**, so a single thread iterates `k²` times over a buffer
holding `w·h` pixels and the pass *becomes* the very version the entry rejects. Nothing had to change
for that to happen — it is the same shader read at a dispatch size no test in the workspace reached,
the largest block factor anywhere being `k = 3`.

**Reachable at the two maxima the app itself sets**, which is what makes it a defect rather than a
degenerate curiosity: `inspector::MAX_BLUR` is 1 000 and `view::MAX_ZOOM` is 256. Measured on this
machine, a 4070 Ti, release, best of three, submit + `poll(Wait)` per frame, one drop shadow at
`k = 1 334` over `fx_gpu`'s 64×48 fixture: **116.3 ms before, 0.45 ms after — 258×**.
⚠️ **The control that isolates the mechanism is that the 116 does not move when the buffer does** —
the finding's own reading at the same `k` over a 200×220 layer is 126.8 ms, within 9% at fourteen
times the pixels. The cost is the **block's**, not the picture's, which makes it the one cost in this
pass that tracks nothing a user can see, and is why the test asserts a clock rather than a pixel.

**The repair is the finding's own second sketch and it changes no value.** `fx.wgsl`'s `coarsen` runs
its two loops from `base` to `hi = min(src_size, base + min(radius, src_size))` instead of running
the full `k × k` and skipping out-of-range taps with an `if`. It skips exactly the taps the `if`
skipped, so the picture is unmoved and **the divisor stays `k²`** — which is what the
transparent-off-edge rule requires and is the line a future editor "corrects" to the covered count,
drawing a bright rim down two sides of every resampled shadow. ⚠️ **`min(radius, src)` is taken
*before* the addition**, because `base + radius` on a block factor near `i32`'s ceiling wraps and the
clamped form cannot exceed twice the buffer; and the divisor is computed in `f32` because
`p.radius * p.radius` in `i32` wraps above 46 341. `MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK` (4096) keeps the host from
sending that today, and **a shader should not depend on its host's cap**.

**The CPU reference took the same bound, and not for symmetry.** `effects::coarsen` had the identical
`if … continue` shape and measures Θ(k) rather than Θ(k²), because the optimizer hoists the inner loop
away — the finding measured 41.6 ns per unit of `k`. So the reference was cheap for a reason the
implementation it stands for does not have, and **a reference whose cost model differs from the
implementation it is a reference *for* is worth less**: the shader has no optimizer and paid the whole
square. `saturating_mul` there rather than a plain multiply because `coarsen` is `pub` and takes `k`
as a parameter, where `shadow_layer`'s caller is capped at `MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK`.

🚨 **This falsifies a measurement in D454, and that entry is amended rather than left standing.** D454
bounds the same path from the other end and argues *"`coarsen` is Θ(k) regardless of the surface it
walks"*, with **≈180 s** at `u32::MAX` and a flip that printed **177.8 s**. Every one of those numbers
describes the loop replaced here: bounded by the source, `coarsen` costs `w·h` however large `k` is.
The two caps still earn their keep — `k as i32` above `i32::MAX` wraps **negative**, `coarsen` then
runs neither loop, and the GPU draws no shadow at all, which is the arm that is silent rather than
slow — but **the *cost* half of `MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK`'s argument is this entry's now**.
⚠️ **D454's first flip therefore wants re-running before it is quoted again.** It is recorded there
and here as a consequence of the loop bound, read off the code rather than measured a second time.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10 at `6a8b001`; Keep. Closes `[S10.2-L4-02]`. **Test**:
`ondin-render/tests/fx_gpu.rs`'s `a_deeply_resampled_shadow_costs_the_buffer_and_not_the_block`,
on-device and `#[ignore]`d, **written first and run red at 116.3 ms**. It asserts a **wall clock** —
under 50 ms, a hundred times the measured figure — because the property is a complexity and no pixel
expresses it; the bound is what fails, and the exact number is not portable and is not asserted.
⚠️ **Its fixture assertions are the anti-vacuity half**: `k` must equal 1 334 *and* exceed

path — which is what `a_resampled_drop_shadow_matches_the_reference` already covers, at `k = 3`, and
what this would quietly become. ⚠️ **This closes neither `[S10.1-L1-03]` nor `[S10.2-L1-03]`, which
D454 closed on 2026-09-07**, and the finding refuses the converse in as many words — *"a cap on `k`
… does **not** close this: at any cap above ~500 the frame is still over budget"* — so the two
repairs are independent and both are needed. §6.4's resample paragraph gains the precondition and its
`Θ(k)` sentence is corrected; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose two shadow-cost rows are D402's
and D403's and both are struck already.)*

**D742 — An inner shadow drew nothing at all on the shape it is most often put on, and the export
had the same bug by a third road. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S10.2-L1-01]`, an open **High** that had no entry here until now. An inner shadow on a shape whose
ink **is** its own bounding box — a rect, a frame, an image, a text node, which between them are most
of what is on a page — drew nothing whatever at offset `(0, 0)`, and a band one offset wide on one
side at the panel's own default. Measured through `VelloCpuRenderer::render_to_rgba` rather than read
off the code: `(255, 255, 255, 255)` at all four edges, pixel-identical to the same document with no
effect on it.

**Two edge rules in contradiction, one of them implicit.** `effects::shadow_layer` built the
silhouette **inverted** — `255 - v` — and then ran the passes over it. The offset lookup treats
outside the buffer as *"fully casting"* (255); `convolve`, `spread_alpha` and `coarsen` all treat
outside as *transparent* (0), which for an inverted silhouette means the opposite thing. On such a
shape the inverted silhouette is zero in **every pixel the buffer holds**, so the only thing that
ever rescued the picture was the lookup's branch — and at offset `(0, 0)` that branch never fires.
Both backends agreed, which is why `tests/fx_gpu.rs`'s byte comparison stayed green over two
implementations of the same wrong picture.

🚨 **§5.3a's `Insets::ZERO` for an inner shadow is correct and is *not* what was wrong**, and saying
so is half of this entry. `EffectKind::escape` answers where the effect's ink **lands**, and an inner
shadow lands nothing outside the shape however far its blur carries; the buffer being the ink box
follows from that and is by design. What the code did was read that answer as the answer to a second
question — where the primitives have to be **evaluated** — and for this one effect the two quantities
differ. Every other effect in the set hides the distinction, because for all of them they are equal.

**The repair is smaller than the finding's own sketch, and the argument for it is the load-bearing
part.** The sketch proposed threading an edge flag into `convolve`, `spread_alpha` and `coarsen` plus
their GPU twins. Instead the complement moved to the **tint**: the silhouette is the graphic's alpha
for both kinds of shadow, and `255 - v` happens once, at the end. No pass needs a flag, because every
pass between the two **commutes with the complement** — `blur(255 − v)` padded with 255 is exactly
`255 − blur(v)` padded with 0 for a normalized kernel, `coarsen` is a box average of the same shape
(partial blocks and the `k²` divisor included), the upsample is bilinear with weights summing to one,
and a dilation of the complement is the erosion of the original. ⚠️ **That is the sentence a future
editor breaks**, by inserting a pass between the silhouette and the tint that is neither linear nor a
max/min with a matching identity; the flag would then have to come back, and nothing would say so.
Sites: `effects::shadow_layer` (both halves), `fx.wgsl`'s `silhouette` and `tint`, and `fx_gpu::run`
moving the `inner` flag off `Pass::Silhouette`'s `Params` onto `Pass::Tint`'s.

⚠️ **A second defect fell out of it and is worth its own paragraph, because nothing pinned the
direction.** `spread_alpha`'s `grow` flag reads `(spread > 0) != inner` — grow the *shape's* alpha for
a drop shadow, erode it for an inner one — and it was being applied to an already-complemented buffer,
i.e. to the opposite operand, so a **positive spread on an inner shadow thinned it** instead of
thickening it. Complementing last puts the flag back on the value it was written for and the formula
is unchanged. `a_positive_spread_thickens_an_inner_shadow_inwards` is what says so now.

🚨 **The export is the third writer and had the same bug by a third road**, which is the shape §3's
one-model-three-writers rule exists to make findable. `ondin-export`'s `svg.rs` wrote the `<filter>`
region from `Resolved::ink_bounds`, and outside the filter region SVG defines every primitive's result
as transparent black — so a region equal to the layer's own ink left the
`feComponentTransfer tableValues="1 0"` that inverts the alpha **nothing outside the shape to invert
from**. `svg::inner_working_pad(effects)` returns `reach(blur) + |spread| + |offset|` maxed over the
visible inner shadows and `effect_region` adds it as uniform insets. Uniform and generous on purpose:
the exact answer is per-side and depends on the offset's direction the way `escape`'s does, and the
closing `feComposite operator="in"` confines the result, so extra region area cannot draw.

**This deviates from a rule the design states, and the rule is amended rather than the code excused.**
§7 said *"**The region is written explicitly**, `filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` from
`Resolved::ink_bounds` mapped into the wrapper's space"* and §5.9 said `ink_bounds` is *"what the SVG
writer's filter region is written from"*. Both are now false, and the general statement is the one
above: **a filter's working region and the layer's ink bounds are two quantities** — where the
primitives are evaluated against where the result lands. §5.3a and §6.4 carry the distinction so it is
stated once rather than inferred from the pad.

**Two independent implementations agreeing to the byte, and one sample that does not.** In a real
browser, on a hand-transcribed copy of the emitted filter chain differing only in the region
rectangle: region at the shape gives `(255, 255, 255, 255)` at every sample down from the edge,
region padded gives **165, 187, 207, 222, 234, 242, 248, 251, 253, 254** — and those ten bytes are
**identical** to what `ondin-render`'s `an_inner_shadow_on_a_rect_reaches_all_four_edges` reads off
our own renderer down the same edge, which is a stronger agreement than that test can ask for on its
own. 🚨 **The eleventh sample is the boundary row itself and it does not agree: 172 in the browser
against 140 here.** That is the shape's own antialiased edge under two rasterizers rather than
anything the filter does — the ten rows behind it are identical — so what this paragraph claims is
that *the falloff agrees*, not that *the picture is the same*.

⚠️ **The first version of that sentence said *"byte for byte"* over a run that started one pixel in,
and the sample it omitted is the only one that disagrees.** It is recorded rather than corrected away
because the shape recurs: **a comparison that begins where two implementations are known to agree is
not the comparison it reads as**, and the end it leaves out is exactly where somebody checking an
export against the canvas would look first. The corrected reading is on `svg::inner_working_pad`'s
doc and on the export test's, both of which name the disagreeing sample.

⚠️ **Be clear about what that check is not.** The browser measurement was on a **transcription** of
the emitted chain with the shape simplified to the degenerate case, not on an exported file; and on
the `every-kind.svg` golden — whose inner shadow sits on a **rounded** rect with a non-zero offset —
the padded and unpadded regions sample identically. That is part of why this survived: the shapes it
is visible on are the ones with no corners to spare, and the golden holds one of the others.

⚠️ **One flip-check result recorded as a method note, because it is this project's own trap in a new
spelling.** Flipping *only* `fx.wgsl`'s `silhouette` back to the inverted form is a **no-op**, and
green — `INNER` no longer reaches that pass, so the shader reads a flag nobody sets. The flip that
bites is the shipped spelling entire: the shader, plus `inner` back on the silhouette's `Params` and
off the tint's. **A one-line flip of a shader that no longer receives the flag it reads passes for the
wrong reason**, and it passes in exactly the way a correct flip fails to.

`an_inner_shadow_on_a_rect_reaches_all_four_edges` and
`a_positive_spread_thickens_an_inner_shadow_inwards`, `tests/gpu_effects.rs`'s

**D741 — `local_box` is asked fourteen times a frame, and the finding ranked itself on one call.
*Measured 2026-09-10; no production line changed. **The ruling is taken: §15 D778 declines the map**,
and `[S4.1-L4-08]` closes with it.***

`query::local_box` is uncached and walks the whole subtree on every ask. `[S4.1-L4-08]` ranked that
**Low** on the strength of a *single* call — 0.349 ms at 16,000 children — reasoning *"0.35 ms at
16,000 is a fraction of a 16 ms frame, so this is ranked Low deliberately."* Its own evidence
section had already said something else: *"roughly fourteen per-frame sites, several of which fire in
one frame for one selection."* **The evidence used the per-frame number and the ranking used the
per-call one.**

**The finding asked for the measurement in as many words**, which is why this is an entry rather
than a silent re-rank. Its confidence line reads *"**Medium on the per-frame total** — the call sites
were enumerated by grep, not driven through a headless frame, so 'several in one frame' is read
rather than counted. That is what would raise it."*

**Counted.** Through one real `eframe::App::ui` frame on an `OndinApp::headless`, with a 200-child
group selected: **2,814 calls for 201 nodes — exactly 14.00 top-level asks**, each of which re-walks
the whole subtree, and **0 with nothing selected**. The grep was exactly right, and all fourteen fire
in the same frame for one selection.

**Timed**, `--release`, 20 reps, fourteen walks per frame:

```text
children   per frame
 1,000      0.169 ms
 4,000      0.789 ms
16,000      5.400 ms
```

🚨 **5.4 ms is about a third of a 16 ms budget, and that is the entry.** Nothing downstream
re-derives a severity from the evidence it is filed with, so **a finding can hold the right
measurement in one section and rank itself on the wrong one in another** — and the wrong one was the
cheaper measurement, which is the direction to expect: a single call is what a grep and a bench
naturally produce, and the per-frame total needs a frame.

⚠️ **The finding's own "cheaper interim" is not available**, and it is worth recording so nobody
reaches for it. It suggests *"the cheaper interim is for the callers that ask several times in one
frame to ask once"*; the fourteen asks are **fourteen different functions across four files** —
`canvas.rs`, `rulers.rs`, `inspector.rs` and `picker.rs`. There is no single caller to hoist.

🚨 **That last sentence is false and §15 D764 is the hoist.** `selection_handles` asked
`preview_local_box` for its own box and then asked `preview_pivot`, which asks `preview_local_box`
again — so **eight of these fourteen were one function asking twice for one box**, four call sites
paying double, unconditionally. The interim was available, it needed no cache and no change to
`Resolved`, and it was worth 43% of the number above. ⚠️ **The arithmetic in the record had said so
the whole time**: `[S12.1-L4-03]` measured 0.6431 ms per selection-box build against
`[S4.1-L4-08]`'s 0.3490 ms per `local_box` call, a factor of **1.84**. *Two findings measured the
same work and neither divided* — and the count above, being a count of *asks* rather than of
distinct boxes, could not tell the difference either.

**Why the fix is left, and it is not timidity.** The named fix is **a new map on `Resolved`**, filled
by the same children-before-parents pass as `world_bounds`. ⚠️ **It cannot be derived from
`world_bounds`** — a world AABB is not a local box for anything rotated, which is the distinction
`local_box`'s doc opens with and the entire reason the function exists (§5.10). So it is a genuinely
new derived map: `update` has to keep it equal to `rebuild`, and the guard is one more assertion in
`ondin-core/tests/resolve.rs`'s `assert_resolved_matches_rebuild`. **That is a change to the
invariant-bearing cache**, and the number justifying it arrived at the end of a session.

⚠️ **Two claims in that paragraph were wrong and are corrected here (§15 D764).** It said *"a
**fourth** map"*, where `Resolved` holds **six** today — `world`, `world_bounds`, `ink_bounds`,
`inner_ink`, `text`, `boolean` — and D510 and `roadmap.md` independently call the rounded-outline
cache *"a **fifth** map"*, so the two documents read as describing one slot when they name two
different ones, both misnumbered. **The ordinal is deleted rather than corrected**, a count in prose
being a gate nobody built and the next map making any number here wrong again. And
`assert_resolved_matches_rebuild` does **not** compare *"field by field through the public API"*: it
compares **four of the six** — `world_transform`, `world_bounds`, `ink_bounds`, `text_layout` —
where `boolean` has only a fixed-fixture differential over four named nodes and **`inner_ink` is
compared by nothing anywhere in the workspace.** So a new map does not join a complete guard; it
joins a partial one, and the partiality is the thing to know before adding to it.

⚠️ **And the map would answer the resting frame only.** `session::preview_local_box` forwards to
`ondin_core::local_box` when no override is live and **re-walks the children itself** when one is —
so the frames of a live gesture, which are the frames where the handles are moving, keep paying the
walk unless the preview door gets the same treatment. *(Read out of the code rather than measured:
the count above was taken at rest.)*

⚠️ **Probe hygiene, since this entry is entirely a measurement.** `query.rs` was instrumented with a
thread-local counter and the instrumentation reverted with `Edit`; the throwaway `#[test]` in
`app.rs` was removed with `git checkout` **after** `git diff --stat` confirmed the probe was the only
uncommitted content in that file, at `+99/-0`. That check is the whole condition that makes the
destructive spelling safe. `git status` clean, workspace suite green.

*Fix with the map and the preview door together, or rule that a 16,000-node document is not
the case to spend a cache on — and if it is the second, the ranking still has to move, because the
number the finding was ranked on is not the number it costs.* ⚠️ **Six of the fourteen remain after
§15 D764**, which removed the other eight without touching either half of this; the preview door is
untouched and is still the half nothing measures.
🚨 **Ruled on 2026-09-15 and the second option is the one taken** (§15 **D778**): the map is not
built, on the six-ask arithmetic above and on the preview door — a cache bypassed exactly when a
gesture is live answers a frame nobody is dragging in. **The ranking moves with it**, as this
paragraph asks, and D778 carries the trigger that would re-open it.

*(Measured 2026-09-10 at `2e5243b`; no production line changed. **`[S4.1-L4-08]` stays open**, and
its Reachability line is now wrong rather than merely narrow. §5.10's `bounds`/`local_box` bullet
gains the per-frame figure. ⚠️ **The citation sits on `local_box`'s own doc**, deliberately, so the
next reader of the function meets the number before deciding it is cheap — which also means this is a
record-only entry the closing citation census **will** find, unlike D735, which changed no code and
so can never acquire one. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: it carries no row on per-frame query cost
at all — its `Per-edit cost` row is about `Document::apply` and `Resolved::update` per *edit* — and a
ruling with its options laid out is what this file is for.)*

**D778 — The derived-geometry map on `Resolved` is declined, and the frame it would answer is the one
nobody is looking at. *Ruling by the maintainer; recorded 2026-09-15; Resolved — D741's open ruling
and D510's open half are both closed, and the map is a decided non-goal.***

§15 **D741** leaves the choice in as many words — *"fix with the map and the preview door together,
or rule that a 16,000-node document is not the case to spend a cache on"* — and §15 **D510** leaves
a second, different map open for the rounded outline of a `Path`, which `roadmap.md` carries.
**Neither is built.** Two reasons, and the second is the one that decides it.

**The number the map was asked for on is stale, in the direction that matters.** D741 timed
*fourteen* per-frame asks; §15 **D764** then found that eight of them were `selection_handles`
asking `preview_local_box` for its own box and then asking `preview_pivot`, which walks for the same
box again — one repair, no cache, no change to `Resolved`. **Six asks remain**, so D741's 0.169 ms
per frame at 1,000 children is about **0.07 ms**, and its 5.400 ms at 16,000 is about **2.3 ms** —
at a selection size no document this project has drawn comes near.

🚨 **And the map answers the *resting* frame only, which D741 says about itself.**
`session::preview_local_box` forwards to `ondin_core::local_box` only while `overrides.is_empty()`;
with a gesture live it re-walks the children itself, in another crate. So every frame of a drag —
the frames where the handles are moving and a budget is the thing a hand can feel — keeps paying the
walk whatever `Resolved` holds. **A cache that is bypassed exactly when the work is being done is
not a smaller version of the fix; it is a different fix for a frame nobody has complained about.**

Against a saving under the noise stands a **seventh** derived map that `update` must keep equal to
`rebuild` for the life of every document. §5.9 holds six and says the count is load-bearing in
prose, and the guard a new map would join is partial rather than complete:
`assert_resolved_matches_rebuild` compares **four of the six** — `world_transform`, `world_bounds`,
`ink_bounds`, `text_layout` — while `boolean` has only a fixed-fixture differential and `inner_ink`
is compared by nothing anywhere in the workspace. **The cost of a map is not its fill pass; it is
the invariant somebody has to hold two implementations to.**

⚠️ **The trigger to revisit is recorded rather than left to taste, and it is deliberately not a
number of milliseconds.** Either a real document with **~10k nodes under one selection**, or **a way
to cache through the preview door**. A millisecond threshold is the wrong trigger here because the
only frame it can be measured on is the resting one, which is the frame the cache would answer and
the frame nobody is dragging in — so a threshold would be met by exactly the case that does not
matter.

*(Ruling by the maintainer; recorded 2026-09-15; no production line changed. **Closes
`[S4.1-L4-08]`, `[S12.1-L4-03]` and `[S4.2-L4-05]`.** ⚠️ **`[S12.1-L4-03]` survives the ruling in
both directions and D764 had already said so**: `selection_frame_extent` loops the selection while
`local_box` returns O(1) per leaf, so its `multi` row was never a beneficiary of this map and a
*yes* would have left it standing too. ⚠️ **`[S4.2-L4-05]` closes through D510 rather than through
D741** — it wants a scalar perimeter cached *beside* the rounded outline, and its own sketch says
*"otherwise leave it"*, so declining the outline map answers it without its ever being weighed.
⚠️ **`[S4.2-L4-04]` was not named in the ruling and nothing is left of it either**: D510 closed its
smaller half by measurement and this closes the map, so the finding has no residual — recorded as an
observation rather than as a closure somebody took, because the review's own ledger is where that is
counted and this entry is not it.
**The citation sits on `local_box`'s doc**, beside D741's, so a reader meeting the fourteen-asks
figure meets the ruling taken on it in the same paragraph. **D741 amended** — its verdict line read
*"Open — a ruling for the maintainer"* — and **D510 amended**, its larger half no longer *"still
open"*. §5.9's map-count bullet and §5.10's `bounds`/`local_box` bullet each gain the ruling.
🚨 **`roadmap.md`'s rounded-outline row is struck**, and it has to be: a declined map is a decided
non-goal and this file is what stops one being re-argued, so a row left standing would have re-opened
the question the next time somebody read that file for work.)*

**D740 — The guide's colour card and the canvas ground's were one card written twice, and the flip
that checked the merge did not bite at all. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the second of the
two reset guards is pinned by nothing, and the test says so.***

`[S14.1-L3-06]`. `guide_colour_row` and `canvas_ground_row` were **37 and 40 lines** running the same
five steps in the same order — `targeted` off the live picker's slot, `field_row_active`, a
`set_min_width`, 9pt spacing, a `swatch` that reports its click, then `paint_hex_field` on the root —
and their two call sites were another ~28 lines apiece of the same shape again: the row width, the
row, a 28×15 `ARROW_COUNTER_CLOCKWISE` under `FieldButton::enabled_if`, a two-armed hover, a re-test
of the same predicate, then `open_picker` on the anchor. `single_paint_row` and `colour_panel` are
the two halves now, the second taking a `ColourCard`.

🚨 **The reasoning had already come apart from one of the copies, and that is the finding's own
evidence.** `canvas_ground_row` carried the four-line explanation of why `set_min_width` is there —
*"The recessed ground shrink-wraps its contents… A paint row gets this for free from its
right-aligned opacity field; the canvas has no opacity, so it has to ask"* — while
`guide_colour_row` had the **identical line with no comment**, though the argument applies to it
verbatim. And the two reset hovers were the same `if` with the arms in **opposite order** —
`if any_override { "Reset…" } else { "Already…" }` against `if is_default { "Already…" } else
{ "Reset…" }`. **That is the fingerprint of a hand-re-derived copy rather than a shared helper**, and
it is what made the finding confident the two would drift. `ColourCard` is a struct rather than seven
parameters partly for exactly that: clippy asked, at **9 arguments against a limit of 7**, which is
the kind of signature the next person puts an `#[allow]` on rather than reads — and named fields make
the ordered pair unmistakable, `reset_hover` being `(live, dead)`, once.

🚨 **The flip did not bite at all, and finding out why was worth more than the merge.** Hard-coding
`FieldButton::enabled_if(false)` — the reset permanently dead in **both** cards — left all 1,254
tests green. ⚠️ **The finding had said no behavioural test was owed**, on the ground that *"the
assertion that should exist first is `[S14.1-L6-03]`'s, which would then cover both rows through one
helper"* — and **§15 D629 closed `[S14.1-L6-03]` with nine tests through `inspector_ui`'s dispatch,
not one of which reaches this leaf.** So the deferral had been honoured on paper and not in fact, and
nothing anywhere asserted that the button is live when there is something to put back, or that
clicking it puts it back. **A finding that defers its coverage to another finding is only as good as
what that one turned out to assert**, and nothing downstream compares the two.

🚨 **Writing the test then produced two predicted flips that both missed, and they are the entry.**

1. `enabled_if(false)` is green because **a disabled `field_button` still reports its click.**
   `ui::button_face` allocates `Sense::click()` whatever the state, and `FieldButton::Disabled`'s own
   doc has said so all along — *"Callers must still ignore the click; this only draws the state."*
   `enabled_if` decides how the button is **painted** and nothing else.
2. Dropping the `&& resettable` re-test after `.clicked()` is **also** green. With both guards gone
   the dead click really does commit, and what it commits is `SetCanvasBackground { DEFAULT }` over a
   ground that is already the default — **§15 D428's `Transaction::changes_nothing` absorbs it**, so
   the ground does not move and `undo_depth` does not either.

**So the assertions about the document pin neither guard**: the outcome they check is the one the
*wrong* version produces too. That is this project's own *"what would also pass this"* trap arriving
through a guard **three layers down** — not a weak assertion but a correct one standing in front of a
mechanism that makes the two versions indistinguishable. What pins `enabled_if` is the **glyph's
colour**, the one difference the two states leave in `.shapes` (`resting_ink(ui, false)` against
`text::MUTED`); the two hover strings cannot be asserted at all, because a tooltip's ink never
arrives.

⚠️ **Read the colour off `galley.job.sections[0].format.color` and not `override_text_color`**, which
measured `None` on **both** states: `Painter::text` bakes the colour into the `LayoutJob`'s section
format rather than overriding it at paint time. The override is for a galley laid out once and
re-coloured; this one is laid out per frame.

⚠️ **The `&& resettable` re-test is pinned by nothing and the test says so rather than papering over
it.** Pinning it would want a reset whose no-op is *not* absorbed, and neither caller offers one: the
guide card's reset builds one `SetGuideColor { color: None }` per **recoloured** guide, so over a set
with none it builds an empty transaction — the same no-op by another door. *Revisit if* a third
caller of `colour_panel` ever has a reset that moves something on a dead click; until then the guard
is belt-and-braces over `enabled_if` with D428 behind both, written where the next reader will be.

⚠️ **Two details both copies had and neither explained, kept and now stated once.** `reset` builds
its transaction rather than being handed one, so the two callers' very different answers — a
`SetGuideColor` per recoloured guide against one `SetCanvasBackground` — stay at the call sites where
they can be read against what the button says. And **`anchor` is taken before the card is drawn**: it
is where the picker opens, and it has to be the top of the card rather than wherever the cursor ended
up inside it.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep. Closes `[S14.1-L3-06]`. New test module
`inspector::colour_panel_tests`, which locates the reset **by its glyph** rather than by arithmetic,
so it does not have to know the row's widths and keeps working if the card is re-laid out — a
hard-coded click position is how this becomes a silently green test. §9.4's *"a control that does not
apply is shown and disabled"* passage gains the clause that the disabled state is paint only and the
call site owes the re-test, and the guide's Appearance passage gains the pointer at the shared card;
nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D739 — The stroke-position dropdown was fifty lines written twice, and the flip that checked the
merge found the *travelled* row uncovered. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S14.3-L3-07]`. `stroke_properties` and `mixed_stroke_properties` each hand-rolled the alignment
combo: the `free`/`combo_w` split, the `interact_size.y = 28.0` / `button_padding.y = 0.0` scope with
its two-paragraph explanation of why a `ComboBox` sizes its own height, the `ComboBox` with
`combo_chevron`, `width`, `height(140.0)` and `glyph_and_text`, the `if aligns { … } else { … }`
fork, the three `StrokeAlign` rows at `button_padding.y = 2.0`, and the *"Open shapes stroke
centred"* / *"Only closed shapes have an inside"* pair character for character. **Three things
differed**: the id salt, `selectable_label` plus a `picked` local against `selectable_value`, and the
*"Mixed"* label. `align_combo(ui, salt, aligns, combo_w, shown)` and `align_combo_width(ui)` now.

**`shown: Option<StrokeAlign>` is why the enum shape works.** `None` means the strokes in scope
disagree and the closed combo reads *Mixed*; *"nothing is lit while they disagree"* then falls out of
`shown == Some(a)` being false for every `a`, rather than wanting a second `mixed` flag beside a
value. **`Mixed` is deliberately not in the list** — it is a report and not a value, so offering it
would be offering a no-op, and the list is where the three real answers live.

⚠️ **`selectable_label(…).clicked()` replaces `selectable_value` on the single-stroke side and that
is not a behaviour change.** A `ComboBox`'s default `PopupCloseBehavior` is `CloseOnClick`, so both
spellings close the popup, and egui's own `ComboBox::show_index` is written as
`selectable_label(i == *selected, …).clicked()`. ⚠️ **Both read out of the dependency's source
rather than reasoned** — `egui-0.35.0/src/containers/combo_box.rs:337`
(`close_behavior.unwrap_or(PopupCloseBehavior::CloseOnClick)`) and `:294` — recorded with the line
numbers because the agent that wrote this entry had no shell and would otherwise have had to carry
the claim, and because this is a **dependency**'s behaviour, which no gate here pins and an upgrade
can change silently. What the merged function needs is the pick as a
**value**, which `selectable_value`'s in-place write cannot hand back across two callers that do
different things with it: `stroke_properties` folds it into the `Stroke` it returns,
`mixed_stroke_properties` fans it out through `edit_strokes_all`.

🚨 **The flip half-bit, and the half that did not is the finding.** Making `align_combo` return
`None` unconditionally turned **exactly one** test red —
`the_mixed_alignment_dropdown_lands_its_pick_on_every_stroke`. The **single-stroke** row, which is
what every drawing with one stroke on a layer uses and by far the more travelled of the two, had
**no assertion at all** that clicking a position writes it; the mixed row was covered because it is
the unusual case somebody thought to test. `the_per_stroke_alignment_dropdown_lands_its_pick` closes
that, and with it in place the same flip turns both red. **A flip that does not bite is a finding
about coverage**, and this one named the arm nobody would have picked to check.

⚠️ **The new test asserts the popup's three rows land at the same three `y`s the mixed test's do** —
**38.5, 66.5, 94.5 at x = 15**, measured on both — so the merge's claim is tested directly rather
than assumed. The coordinates are reused deliberately: both rows are one `horizontal` in a 320-wide
`screen_rect`, and if the two ever diverge again the test stops finding the popup and says so.

⚠️ **A trap that cost a debugging cycle, and it is written down at the test: egui hit-tests a press
against the rects the *previous* frame allocated.** A first frame carrying a press lands on nothing,
so without a warm-up frame the popup never opens and every frame draws the closed row — **which
reads exactly like a mis-aimed click**, and the reflex it invites is to move the coordinate.

⚠️ **The finding's cost argument had expired here too.** It leans on `[S14.3-L3-06]`'s stale `6.0`
sitting in *both* copies, where `CARD_COL_GAP` is 7 — **§15 D637 fixed both rows and pinned them with
a relation test**, every row of one unit ending on the same x, after the drift had been measured as
the stroke unit's properties row sitting two points right of every other control in the column. So
the drift the finding predicted had already happened, been paid off and been gated.
`align_combo_width` is what stops the **next** one having to be fixed twice.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep. Closes `[S14.3-L3-07]`. ⚠️ **`salt` is a parameter rather than a
`"stroke-align"` written inside**, because the difference is real: the per-stroke row salts by list
index, two strokes' dropdowns in one panel being two widgets that a shared id would open together,
and the mixed row has no index and takes a constant. ⚠️ **`aligns` is not cosmetic either** — with it
false the combo opens onto a sentence instead of a list, `geometry::stroke_align_applies` being the
predicate and `stroke_rule` asking it of the scope. §9.4's mixed-stroke paragraph gains a clause:
the position dropdown is one function for both rows, which is the second thing holding them in step
beside `paint_unit` placing both (§15 D196). Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D738 — Two paint walks that differed in one field access, and the flip the finding costed them by
had stopped being true. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the other two twin pairs the finding
names stay, deliberately.***

`[S14.4-L3-06]`. `inspector::shown_over_fills` and `shown_over_strokes` were **eleven lines each and
identical but for `paint().fills` against `paint().strokes`**: the same walk over `paint_targets`,
the same `display_node` read, the same fold. One `shown_over(list, of)` takes the list as an accessor
now, and the two wrappers are one line apiece.

**What was folded in the middle of them is the rule that decides whether a mixed row says *Mixed*.**
`spread.bare |= paints.is_empty()` — a paint target carrying no paint at all disagrees with
everything, so a bare layer beside a painted one cannot read as agreement — which is §9.4's *"any
disagreement, one unpainted layer among painted ones included"* and `build::paint_shown`'s *"there is
no third answer"*, asked of the previewed tree. It had two homes and has one.

🚨 **The finding's cost argument had expired, and it was nearly shipped as fact.** `[S14.4-L3-06]`
leans on `[S14.4-L6-05]`'s second flip — *"deleting the fill copy's `bare` line leaves the whole
workspace green"* — which was true at the review's SHA. **§15 D607 then gave both halves a test.**
Re-run here with the fold deleted outright, **three** tests go red:
`mixed_spread_tests::a_layer_with_no_paint_disagrees_with_the_one_that_has_some`,
`shipped_shared_readout_tests::a_layer_with_no_fill_disagrees_with_every_colour` and
`…::a_layer_with_no_stroke_has_not_got_the_others_width`. The comment written at the merge said the
workspace stayed green **until the flip was actually run**. So the justification is not *"the rule is
ungated"* — it is that those three tests are now about **one** line rather than about two that happen
to agree. **A fix sketch is a hypothesis about code the reviewer did not change, and about code
somebody else changed since**; D730 met the same thing from the other side, where the sketch's own
target had grown a branch that made it unavailable.

⚠️ **The finding names three twin pairs and only one had a shared body worth hoisting, which is a
decision rather than work left undone.** `strokes_shown`/`fills_shown` and
`strokes_in_scope`/`fills_in_scope` stay two named functions each, because **core does exactly the
same thing one level down**: `build::shared_fills` and `build::shared_strokes` are themselves two
named wrappers over one `build::paint_shown`, differing only in which list they hand it. A generic
here would take *two* closures at every call site — the accessor **and** which of those two core
functions to call — to replace two names that read, and it would break the one-for-one
correspondence with core that makes the app half easy to check against the model half. That
reasoning is written at `fills_in_scope`, **whose whole doc used to be *"`strokes_in_scope`'s
twin"*** — the tell the finding named, now carrying the argument for the twin instead of merely
announcing one.

⚠️ **The `shown_over_*` wrappers stay too, and not for symmetry.** `inspector_stroke` asks for
`align` and `width` through `shown_over_strokes` by name, two tests call each wrapper directly, and
their docs are where §15 D400's *"a frame keeps a real fill list now"* and D144's *"a frame's outline
strokes count"* arguments live — which are about **which list**, and a wrapper is exactly a name for
one list.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep. Closes `[S14.4-L3-06]`. **No new test**: the three D607 pinned
are the coverage, and what this changed is how many lines they are about — which is the merge's whole
claim and is why the flip was re-run rather than the finding's reading of it trusted. ⚠️
**`display_node`, not `doc.get`**, is the reason this family is not `build`'s at all: the app asks
core's question of the **previewed** tree so a value mid-drag reads as what is on screen, and D607
says that is a difference in the *tree* and was never meant to be a difference in the question.
§9.4's mixed-row paragraph gains a clause naming the one walk; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D737 — The Transform card's four-button row was two copies, and the rule that explains it sat
beside one of them. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S14.2-L3-08]`. `inspector_transform` and `inspector_multi_transform` each hand-rolled the
quarter-turn and mirror row. Stripped of comments the two copies were **44 lines and 36**, differing
in **four tooltip strings and one call** — `rotate_quarter(id, turn)` against
`rotate_selection_quarter(turn)`. The four-way split of the card's width, the button box, the glyph
order and the whole flip loop were identical token for token, so the row's layout arithmetic had to
be changed in two places to change it at all. `TurnScope` — `Node(NodeId)` or `Selection` — threads
the difference through as data, which is `PaintScope`'s shape and this module's own stated rule
arriving a second time: *"The Fill and Stroke panels are one implementation, not two."*

**The flip is one call on both sides, and that is what makes the second copy duplication rather than
a specialisation.** `build::flip` has always understood a selection — it mirrors the set about the
union's centreline, so the layers swap sides as one arrangement — so both copies wrote
`app.flip(axis)` and neither had anything of its own to say. The asymmetry with the quarter turns,
which go about **each layer's own** origin, is the model's rather than the panel's, and it is why
only the selection tooltips have a clause about it.

🚨 **A rule was moved as well as a row, and the rule is the same defect in prose.** The ten-line
argument for going through `rotate_node` rather than adding 90 to the rotation field above — wrong
for a **mirrored** layer, `Basis` reporting a reflection's angle in its own frame, so writing the sum
back turns it the other way; wrong for a **sheared** one, whose two axes are not square — sat at the
*single-layer* call site only, and the multi-selection card made the identical choice with nothing
saying why. It is on the shared function now. **D731 is this from the other end**: there, one
placement rule written twice with the reasoning on the copy that was *wrong*; here, one rule written
once, correctly, beside one of two implementations — and *a rule written next to one of its
implementations holds none of the others*.

⚠️ **The tooltips are a static pair chosen by scope rather than a base string plus a formatted
suffix.** That keeps the four strings byte-identical to the two copies it replaces and costs no
per-frame allocation on a row laid out every frame the card is open.

⚠️ **The module had already said this twice, about other rows.** `PaintScope` is the precedent the
repair follows, and `paint_unit`'s doc carries the same argument with a *report* behind it: *"One
function rather than two call sites because they have already drifted: the mixed-selection branch
once missed the tighter pitch and the properties row sat 3px lower on a mixed selection than on one
layer, which was reported."* The rule was stated, in this file, above the two copies.

**Two tests on the real function, which was not possible before.**
`ui::transform_row_tests::the_four_transform_buttons_split_the_card_evenly` asserts the same split
against a **replica** — it re-types the `(available_width − 3 × GAP) / 4` arithmetic beside four bare
`field_button_sized` calls — because while the row existed twice, neither copy was reachable from a
test. It stays as `ui.rs`'s statement about `field_button_sized`; the two new ones in
`inspector::quarters_row_tests` are the statement about the row.

🚨 **Both flips bit at the predicted site and both predicted *numbers* were wrong, which is worth
more than the sites being right.** `the_four_buttons_split_the_card_evenly_and_fill_it` was flipped
by changing the divisor from `4.0` to `3.0`, expecting the row to fall **short** of the card; it
reads `0.0..289.0 of 222`, sixty-seven points **over**, because a smaller divisor makes each button
*wider*. The assertion is an `abs()` and catches both — **an assertion written as "the row does not
reach the edge" would have been green for a row hanging a third of a card off the end.** The evenness
loop stayed green under that flip, which is the other half of the result: four equal buttons that
miss the edge are still four equal buttons, so that loop has no opinion about the split at all. Its
own teeth are against a different slip — three buttons at `bw` and the fourth at `quarter` — which is
exactly the shape a second copy drifts into.

⚠️ **`both_scopes_lay_the_row_out_identically` cannot fail while there is one implementation, and is
not a test of today's code.** The scope reaches nothing but the tooltip pair and the rotation call.
It is the test that goes red the moment somebody re-splits the row, which is the failure mode the
finding names and the one nothing else in this file would notice. Flip-checked by giving
`TurnScope::Node` its own `/ 5.0` split: red at `40.2 vs 50.2`, with the test above **green**,
because it only ever looks at one scope — which is the whole argument for the second test existing.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep. Closes `[S14.2-L3-08]`. §9.4's quarter-turn paragraph and the
multi-selection Transform passage each gain a clause saying the row is one function — **both of
them**, because leaving the pointer beside one copy of the description would be this entry's own
defect committed in the document. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: the *Later* row about a stored,
user-placed origin for a set cites `rotate_selection_quarter` as evidence that the app has answered
the *n*-layers question **deliberately**, which is untouched by where the button that calls it is
drawn.)*

**D736 — A flatten said the boolean was *empty* when it had been abandoned, and the two doors need
different mechanisms to say so. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the render walk's fail-open is
D282's decision and stays.***

`[S10.1-L2-06]`, narrowed. Both of `build::flatten`'s doors mapped `boolean::evaluate`'s `None` onto
`OpError::EmptyGeometry`, and that variant's own doc argues from **what the user can do next**: *"the
geometry was empty, which is a thing the user can fix by moving a shape rather than by selecting
differently."* **Moving a shape does not help an unwind.** The message was true about the outcome and
false about the cause, which is the only thing an error string has to be right about.
`OpError::BooleanAbandoned` is the second refusal — *"a boolean could not be computed, so there is
nothing to flatten"*.

⚠️ **§6.2's rule is the nearest thing to authority and this entry is reasoning by analogy, which it
says rather than implies.** *"A missing edit is recoverable and a lying one is not"* is stated about
**refusing** an edit — D481 and D714 apply it to a basis that cannot be represented, per node, so
that the member which cannot take the gesture is left where it was and the rest of the selection
still moves — and neither `architecture.md` nor §15 has ever extended it to *error text*.
`design-oracle` was explicit about that. The extension is sound and it is this entry's, not the
design's.

🚨 **The half of the finding that must not be fixed matters as much as the half that was.** As
written, `[S10.1-L2-06]` said the **render walk's** fail-open was the bug: `evaluate` answers `None`,
`scene::mask_geometry` reads that as *no clip*, and the masked layers draw unmasked. That is a live,
recorded decision, and D282 names this exact case in its own words — *"`None` means masks nothing,
never 'clip everything away': a hidden mask, an empty text node, an empty group and **a cancelled
boolean** all answer it"*, whose next sentence is that the other reading would make hiding a mask
look like deleting the artwork. Review pass S11.1 asked and got that back verbatim. **What survives
is the narrowed half — the failure is *unreported* at the doors that refuse an edit** — and that is
all this entry closes.

🚨 **The two doors need different mechanisms for the same distinction, which is why the finding's own
sketch (*"the four unbracketed sites do not each need a bracket"*, then "bracket the mask path")
would have been wrong at one of them.** `flatten_union` calls `evaluate` itself, so it reads
`boolean::failures` either side of the call: **the counter is the signal and never the `None`**,
which is that function's whole doc. `flatten_boolean` never calls `evaluate` at all — it reads
`Resolved::boolean_path`, filled on some earlier pass — so **this thread's counter has nothing to say
about it** and bracketing there would be the wrong question asked competently. It reads D298's
existing mark instead (`Resolved::boolean_failed`), which is already set for precisely this case, so
an abandoned boolean is refused with the right reason exactly when the layers row is already wearing
its warning colour.

🚨 **The builders are outside D298's bracket *by construction*, not by oversight, and that is the
entry's argument rather than a footnote.** D298 wires the counter into `commit_inner` — *"the one
door every edit goes through"* — reading it across `Resolved::update`, which is **resolution** and
happens after a transaction exists. A builder calls `evaluate` while *constructing* the transaction,
so a failure there refuses the edit before that bracket has anything to span. **That is why the
unbracketed call sites read as forgotten and are not**: they are on a different call path, and a
census of `evaluate`'s callers cannot see the difference.

⚠️ **The sites left are named rather than counted, and the count is exactly what has gone wrong here
before.** `scene::mask_geometry` and `scene::ghost_mask_geometry` are D282's fail-open, above, and
are deliberate. `renderer::reevaluate_booleans` stores an **empty `BezPath`** for a preview boolean
whose evaluation gave up, indistinguishable from one that came out empty — left because a preview has
no refusal to report and the commit behind it goes through `commit_inner`, so the durable answer
arrives at the release, from D298. ⚠️ **The brief for this entry said *"the other two"* and then
listed those three**; `boolean::poison_next`'s own doc has already refused to write this population
down, having carried *"four of the six"* and been one low within a release, and the sentence it
replaced it with is the one to copy: *"the shape of the caller set is the argument, and the number is
not."*

**Tests**, both in `crates/ondin-core/tests/build.rs`, both flip-checked.
`a_flatten_says_the_boolean_was_abandoned_rather_than_that_the_geometry_was_empty` is built from two
rects that genuinely **overlap** — the same fixture flattens to a 15000 union in the neighbouring
test — so nothing is empty and `EmptyGeometry` would be wrong on its own terms. ⚠️ **`poison_next(1)`
and not more**: `operand_path` on a plain rect goes through `local_path` and never reaches
`evaluate`, so the union is the *first* call and one token is exactly enough, where a fixture holding
a group or a nested boolean would spend it elsewhere and the test would go green for the wrong reason
— the hazard `poison_next`'s doc names.
`flattening_an_abandoned_boolean_says_so_rather_than_blaming_the_geometry` poisons before
`f.resolved()` and **not** before the flatten, because the failure has to happen while the *cache* is
being built, and it asserts the fixture is in the state it names — mark set **and** cache empty —
before the interesting assertion.

🚨 **The control in the first test is the load-bearing half.** Restoring either `ok_or(EmptyGeometry)`
fails at the predicted site and leaves the neighbouring flatten tests green; but a second flip on
`flatten_union` — returning `BooleanAbandoned` **unconditionally** — is caught *only* by the
un-poisoned control, which is why the control lives in the same test rather than being assumed. A
test that asserts which of two refusals fired is worth nothing without the case that must not fire.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep. Closes the narrowed `[S10.1-L2-06]`; **the fail-open half is
declined, not deferred** — D282 decides it and this entry is where a future reader finds that out
rather than re-opening it. §5.7's `OpError` listing gains the variant and §9.4's *Flatten* paragraph
now carries both refusals and which door tells them apart. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: the
Booleans section's one open item is `Intersect` losing half a thin result's area, which nothing here
touches, and its note that D298's machinery is unreachable for `Exclude` — a concatenation now, never
entering flo_curves — stays true of both new arms.)*

**D735 — Two invariants stated absolutely, each with its exception written down three thousand lines
away. *Recorded 2026-09-10; Keep — §4 invariants 2 and 4 amended, no code change.***

`[A1-L2-09]` and `[A1-L8-12]`, one entry for two findings, because it is the same failure twice:
**the code is right, the reasoning is written down, and the invariant's own prose denies it.**
Neither is a deviation to be fixed in code. Both are the record owing a clause — and the reader they
cost is the one who repairs the *code* to match the rule, which **D666** already showed is the
expensive direction: §9.4 stated `menu_place`'s order backwards, and correcting the function to agree
with the document would have introduced the bug.

**Invariant 2 and `Document::set_meta`.** The rule reads *"the only way to change a `Document` is
`Document::apply(Transaction)`. Node fields are private; no public `&mut` access."* `set_meta` is a
`pub fn(&mut self)` that replaces the `meta` block whole, outside `apply` and outside undo.

⚠️ **The reasoning exists and it is sound — it is simply nowhere near the rule.** §5.11a's meta-block
section has it in full: *"Not an `Operation`, so outside undo. A rename is a library action taken
from the dashboard, often while the document is not open; routing it through `apply` would put an
entry in the wrong document's history and make `Ctrl+Z` in the editor undo what the file browser
