did."* The same bullet adds that it reports no `DirtySet`, nothing about the drawing having changed.
**Invariant 2 stays true of what it is about** — no node, no edge, no geometry is reachable this way
— and the block is precisely the part of a `Document` that is *not* the drawing.

⚠️ **It has no §15 entry of its own and does not need one.** `grep set_meta docs/decisions.md`
answers nothing; the whole argument is in §5.11a, and what was missing is a pointer at it from the
invariant that reads as forbidding the call. Whether the carve-out also wants an entry of its own is
the maintainer's, and the finding says so.

🚨 **The count was wrong in both of the two places that gave one, and in opposite directions.** The
finding says *"roughly ten"*; the brief for this entry says **twenty-one**. Measured, it is **six**
production call sites — `library::store`'s `file_document`, `rename`, `move_to_project` and
`duplicate`, plus two in `panels::dashboard` (the import loop's fresh identity, and `follow_path`'s
patch when a document is renamed under an open editor) — with the remaining twenty inside
`#[cfg(test)]` modules and `ondin-core/tests/io.rs`. The command is
`grep -rn 'set_meta' crates/ --include=*.rs`, read against each file's `#[cfg(test)]` line, and it is
written here rather than a corrected number, because *a count in prose is a gate nobody built* (D720,
D726). **A grep that does not distinguish a test caller from a production one triples this figure**,
which is exactly how twenty-one was reached.

**Invariant 4 and the font set.** The rule reads *"`Resolved` … derived artifacts — never serialized,
always reconstructible."* Text layouts are shaped through the **thread-local** parley engine
`core::text` owns — §5.9 states it as a design property (*"No `FontContext` is threaded through:
`core::text` owns a thread-local parley engine"*) — and that engine holds whatever families the app
registered **on that thread**. `Engine::new` registers the two bundled Inter faces and nothing else.
So `Resolved::rebuild(&doc)` on a fresh thread shapes every text node against Inter and hands back
different bounds, **silently**: nothing errors, and every number downstream of a layout — the box, the
hit test, the cull, the export plan — is quietly wrong.

⚠️ **`Resolved::invalidate_text` is the same fact from the other side**, and `resolve.rs`'s own module
doc says so: *"Shaping depends on which fonts are registered with `crate::text`, so when the app
registers a newly downloaded or system-loaded family it must call `Resolved::invalidate_text`."* The
font set is an input to the derivation. The invariant's word for that is *reconstructible*, and it
names only the `Document`.

⚠️ **Latent, not live, and the reason to bother is what "latent" leaves out.** Nothing rebuilds
`Resolved` off the UI thread today: the five production `Resolved::rebuild` sites are in
`session.rs`, `canvas.rs` and `main.rs`'s export path, and `library/writer.rs` — the one background
thread this app has — is handed an owned `Document` and calls `io::save`, never `rebuild`. **But as
written §4 licenses a worker-thread rebuild**, and the symptom would be text bounds subtly wrong
rather than a failure, which is the class of bug this document exists to make un-writable.

**One lesson for both: an invariant stated absolutely, with its exception documented elsewhere, is an
invariant that reads as forbidding what the code does.** The exception then survives on the strength
of nobody having read the rule lately, and the first careful reader to hold both in view either
weakens the rule or breaks the code.

*(Prose only — no code change and no commit; nothing to gate. §4 invariants 2 and 4 amended, each
with a ⚠️ carrying the exception and a pointer at the section that argues it. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, which carries neither. Closes `[A1-L2-09]` and `[A1-L8-12]`.)*

**D788 — `ImageEntry`'s size is render-originated and accepted. *Recorded 2026-09-15; Keep — invariant
4 gains the clause, no code change.***

`[A1-L3-11]`. `ImageEntry::width` and `ImageEntry::height` are produced by `ondin-render`'s decoder,
written into the `Document` when a picture is placed, and serialized with it. That is **a derived
value cached in the model** — the pattern invariant 4 exists to prevent — and nothing anywhere
re-decodes to check them, so a hand-edited or truncated file carries whatever size it claims and
every box, hit test and layers row believes it.

**Two reasons it is right anyway, and the second is the one that settles it.** Entries are
content-hash-keyed and their bytes are immutable — a *Replace…* writes a whole new entry under a new
hash rather than mutating one — so the number cannot go stale in ordinary use. 🚨 **And for
`ImageSource::Linked` the bytes are not in the document at all**, so the stored size is the only
record of it there is. There is nothing to derive it from without the file, and **the entire reason a
link exists is that the file may be absent** — a document with a broken link still has to know how big
the picture was, or the layer's box collapses the first time the drive is unplugged. So this is the
point of a link rather than a shortcoming of one, and the caching is not an optimisation that could
be dropped.

⚠️ **This entry exists because a reviewer read it as a violation and nearly filed it as one.** The
fields are one grep from looking like an oversight and there was nothing to find:
`grep -n "ImageEntry" docs/decisions.md` answered six hits, **none** of them about the width/height
pair. **An accepted-by-necessity exception with no entry is indistinguishable from an oversight**,
and the reader it costs is the one who "fixes" it — which here means re-decoding on load, i.e. making
a linked picture's box depend on a file that may not be there.

*(Recorded 2026-09-15; no production line changed. **§4 invariant 4 gains a one-clause ⚠️ naming the
exception**, beside the font clause D735 gave it — because **D735**'s own lesson is that an exception
documented three thousand lines from the rule it excepts is an exception nobody reading the rule will
find, and the invariant is where a reader meets this field. ⚠️ **The citation sits on
`ImageEntry::width`'s doc and had to be planted by hand**: a record-only entry has nothing in
`crates/` to cite it, so it is invisible to the citation census until somebody writes one — D741's
fix for D735's shape, and it costs one comment. `ImageEntry::height`'s doc points at its twin rather
than repeating the argument. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, whose linking bullet is about *Relink*
and `is_linked`'s lost caller and says nothing about the stored size. Closes `[A1-L3-11]`.)*

**D734 — One dropdown, three refusals, and a tooltip that was false for two of them — beside a
control on the same row that named the reason exactly. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep —
`flatten_selection` deliberately left, below.***

`[S14.2-L3-06]`. `inspector::booleanable_selection` returned an `Option`, so the boolean dropdown
had one sentence for every way it could be dim: *"Boolean operations need two or more layers
selected"*. `build::boolean` refuses for **three** distinct reasons — fewer than two unique members
after `build::outermost`; a member that is `Artboard | Root | Text`; and members whose parents differ
— and **the sentence is false for two of them, over selections anybody can make**. A rect and a text
layer, two selected. Two rects in different groups, two selected. In each case two layers *are*
selected and the tooltip said otherwise.

It is `Result<Vec<NodeId>, &'static str>` now, the `Err` arm mapping `OpError::WrongKindForOp` to
*"Text and artboards cannot be boolean operands"* and `OpError::InvalidParent` to *"A boolean and its
operands have to be in the same group"*. Anything else keeps the count sentence, which is the least
wrong thing to say about a selection the panel should not have offered at all.

🚨 **The row contradicted itself, and that is the finding.** Over the *same* selection,
`inspector::mask_action` — one control to the right, in the same `ui.horizontal`, over the same
`selection.ids()` — named the real reason exactly. Its doc gives the rule this now follows: *"A
`Result` rather than an `Option` because every refusal here has a *different* thing to fix, and a
disabled control that cannot say which is the failure the identity row's tooltips exist to avoid."*
**A sentence that names this row and was honoured by one of its four controls.**

⚠️ **§15 D134 argues the same way and is the rule the row's dimming comes from**: *"a dimmed control
can say 'not for this selection' by itself but cannot say why, and the why is usually a real fact
about the model."* D134's own examples are per-node flags and a missing shared origin; a parent
mismatch and a wrong kind are the same kind of fact.

⚠️ **The `InvalidParent` sentence is `mask_action`'s with this row's own nouns.** *"A boolean and its
operands have to be in the same group"* against *"A mask and what it masks have to be in the same
group"* — the same fact about the same selection, said the same way. Two *unrelated* spellings of one
refusal on one row would be worse than the single wrong sentence this removes, which is the whole
reason the construction was copied rather than reinvented.

⚠️ **`apply_boolean` reports the refusal rather than returning silently.** The dropdown is dim
whenever this would fail, so anything that reaches the builder-side check got there by the
**keyboard**, and a chord that silently does nothing is the failure `flatten_selection`'s own doc
names two hundred lines up (*"the keyboard path would reach the builder with a lone rectangle and
report 'operation not valid for this node kind' — technically true, and no help at all"*).

**The test asserts the sentences, not `is_err()`**, which is the sibling test's own argument about
itself: a refusal test passes against exactly the version being replaced.
`every_boolean_refusal_says_which_thing_to_fix` drives the three `Err` arms over one fixture — a lone
shape, a shape and a text layer, and two shapes in different parents — and closes with an `is_ok()`
control, without which all three are satisfied by a function that refuses everything in nicer words.
**Flip**: both new arms collapsed back to the count sentence is red at the second assertion, printing
`left: Some("Boolean operations need two or more layers selected")` over a selection of two layers,
which is the defect verbatim.

⚠️ **`flatten_selection` still has the same shape and is left alone deliberately.** It asks
`selected_boolean().is_none() && booleanable_selection().is_err()` and says *"Select a boolean, or
two or more layers, to flatten"* — one sentence over the same three-way predicate — so it is now
**the only control on this row that cannot say why**. It is an `Act` on a menu row rather than a
tooltip, so the fix is not the same edit. *Fix by giving it the `Err` this function already computes.*

*(All six gates green. Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §9.4's identity-row passage states
D134's rule and the row's composition, not this tooltip's wording. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.
Closes `[S14.2-L3-06]`.)*

**D733 — A module doc named a mechanism the app never runs, and the arm it named is dead in
production. *Corrected 2026-09-10; Keep — the feature stays, the sentence goes.***

`[S6.2-L3-08]`. `panels::typography`'s module doc explained the bare-caret case of a *character*
write by saying it goes to `TextEdit::pending`, *"which holds the attribute for the next one
typed"*. **It does not, and cannot.**

`TextEdit::style_selection` is `pending`'s only door. It has exactly **one** production caller —
`apply_char_attrs`'s `subject.partial` arm — and `TypeSubject::read` sets `partial` **only** on
`Some((sel, _)) if !sel.is_empty()`. So the panel never calls `style_selection` with an empty range,
its `if range.is_empty()` arm is unreachable from the app, and a bare caret falls to the *"anything
else"* route instead, where it writes the node's **defaults** over the whole range. The rest of that
bullet — a caret being partial for a *paragraph* attribute and not for a character one — was true and
is unchanged; only the mechanism it credited was invented.

**The feature is real and stays.** §5.4's boundary-rule bullet designs it in as many words —
*"typing at the edge of a span inherits from the character to the left, unless the caret was
explicitly restyled while empty (`TextEdit::pending`)"*;
`styling_an_empty_caret_applies_to_the_next_thing_typed` and
`a_pending_style_does_not_survive_moving_the_caret` pin it in core, and it is
exactly what a caret-then-type gesture would need the day one is wired up. What cannot stay is prose
claiming it *is* wired up. **An unreachable arm is cheap; an unreachable arm the record calls live is
what sends a reader looking for a mechanism that is not there** — and the reader most likely to look
is the one implementing the gesture, who would find `pending` already populated by a path that never
runs and conclude the wiring existed.

A ⚠️ now sits on `style_selection` itself saying the same thing, so the next reader of *that* function
does not have to derive it from two files.

🚨 **No new test, and the reason is this entry's real content.** `bare_caret_readout_tests::shown_size`
— the fixture helper the readout tests share — already asserts *"the fixture: a bare caret is not
partial — that is the designed half"*, which is **exactly** the condition that makes `pending`
unreachable from the panel. So the behaviour was pinned the whole time and only the prose had
drifted. **A test can hold a fact firmly while a doc three thousand lines away denies it, and nothing
in this project compares them**: the doc gate resolves links, clippy reads code, the suite asserts
outcomes, and a sentence that is merely false passes all three.

⚠️ **The brief credited the design to §15 D217, and that is a wrong-but-resolving citation.** D217 is
the clipboard entry; it *depends* on `pending` (*"`insert` consumes `TextEdit::pending`, because a
pending style is waiting for the next thing typed, and a cut is not that"*) rather than deciding it.
The decision is §5.4's. Corrected in the shipped comment as well as here — the number resolves either
way, which is why nothing but a reader catches it.

*(Record correction only; no behaviour change, and all six gates green. Nothing amended in
`architecture.md` — §5.4's bullet was right all along, and is what the corrected comments now cite.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which carries no entry on either the bare caret or `pending`.
Closes `[S6.2-L3-08]`.)*

**D730 — A click through the picker's hex field that typed nothing quantised the colour and spent an
undo step. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — and the finding's fix sketch has aged out, below.***

`[S23.1-L1-05]`. `panels::picker::hex_row` committed on `lost_focus()` whatever `parse_hex` gave it
back, including its own unchanged text. `parse_hex` yields `u8`s and `Color::from_rgba8` re-expands
them, so **`0.5` came back `0.5019608`** on every channel, plus an undo step, for a click that typed
nothing. **Anything off the 8-bit lattice is affected, which is anything this picker's own HSV plane
produced** — so the control most likely to trip it is the one immediately above the field.

`inspector::paint_hex_field` has carried the guard since §15 **D517** and this
independently-written copy never got it. The comparison is on **bytes** rather than components, for
D517's reason: the floats really do differ, and what has to match is what the *field* can express.

**`PaintSlot::SelectionAll` is exempt**, the same exemption `paint_hex_field` makes and for §15
D540's reason — over a set that disagrees there is no one colour to compare against, `current` is the
stand-in brush, and comparing against it would refuse the edit whenever the stand-in happened to
match what was typed. Picking a disagreeing set to one colour is exactly the edit being asked for.

🚨 **The finding's fix sketch is no longer available, and the entry should say so.** It reads *"delete
`hex_row`'s field and call `paint_hex_field`"*. Since the review, `hex_row` has gained the
`SelectionAll` branch (D540) and — decisively — **it edits one stop of a gradient by `index`**
(`next[index].1 = rgb.with_alpha(a)`), which `paint_hex_field` has no concept of: that one reads
`paint::stops_of(brush)[0].1` and writes the first stop. They are not one control written twice any
more. **They are two controls that share a guard**, which is why the repair is the guard and not the
merge. *A fix sketch is a hypothesis about code the reviewer did not change, and this one aged out
between the review and the fix.*

🚨 **Three more landed in one batch the same day, and they expire in three *different* ways — which
is why this is a list rather than a rule.** D738's sketch cites a flip result (*"deleting the fill
copy's `bare` line leaves the whole workspace green"*) that a **later test invalidated**, D607 having
pinned both halves; re-run, the same mutation turns three tests red. D739's cites a **drift that was
since fixed and gated** — `[S14.3-L3-06]`'s stale `6.0` in both copies, closed by D637 and pinned by
a relation test. **D740's is the new one and the one worth expecting**: the finding *deferred its
coverage* — *"no behavioural test is owed; the assertion that should exist first is
`[S14.1-L6-03]`'s, which would then cover both rows through one helper"* — and D629 duly closed
`[S14.1-L6-03]` with nine tests through `inspector_ui`'s dispatch, **not one of which reaches that
leaf**. The deferral was honoured on paper and not in fact.

⚠️ **The third shape is the one nothing downstream can see.** A stale flip result is caught by
re-running the flip and a fixed drift by reading the site; but **a finding that defers its coverage
to another finding is only as good as what that one turned out to assert**, and the fix log records
that `[S14.1-L6-03]` was closed, not what its tests reach. **When a sketch says the coverage belongs
to another finding, read that finding's tests before believing the deferral** — the census, the fix
log and every gate agree the work was done.

🚨 **The test's first version was green and vacuous, and the way it failed is worth the space.** It
performed the gesture the finding describes, word for word — *"click once in the hex field, type
nothing, click away"* — and **the click away lands on the SV plane, which does not take focus**:
`picker.hex` was still `Some` three frames later, so `lost_focus()` never fired and the commit path
the test is about was never reached. The green run said nothing whatever about the fix. A probe
assertion on the field having lost focus is what caught it, is kept, and `Enter` is the door the test
uses now — `hex_row`'s own comment saying Enter triggers `lost_focus()`, so it is the same door.
**The gesture a finding describes is not always the gesture that reaches the code it names**, and a
click-away in a floating panel is exactly where the two come apart.

`a_bare_click_through_the_hex_field_writes_nothing` asserts the fixture is off the lattice before
anything else, then the colour unchanged and the undo depth unmoved, and closes with the typed
control — a guard that refused *everything* would pass the first three. **Flip**: `!mixed` inverted to
`mixed`, which applies the guard to the case it exempts and skips the case it is for, is red here at
`[0.5019608, …]` against `[0.5, …]` and leaves
`a_mixed_rows_hex_field_leaves_each_layer_its_own_opacity` **green** — the exemption being
unobservable from that test, which is what says the two are asking different questions.

*(All six gates green. Nothing amended in `architecture.md`. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`:
*Now · Inspector*'s hex-field row is about routing `paint_hex_field`'s write through
`app::edit_valve`, which this change does not do, and `hex_row` is a second control off that seam
rather than the one that row names. Closes `[S23.1-L1-05]`.)*

**D729 — The library's two floating menus were the same thirty-five lines twice, and the copy that
named the relationship copied it instead of sharing it. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — and
where the Escape did *not* go is the useful half.***

`[S20.2-L3-05]`. `panels::dashboard::project_filter_menu` and `panels::dashboard::file_menu_popup`
each hand-rolled a floating `Area`: the panel and its border, the rows at a fixed pitch, the hover
ground, the row hit test and the click-away test — identical down to the `+ 4.0` on the anchor and
the `+ 10.0` on the height. `project_filter_menu`'s own doc **named** the relationship, calling
itself *"the shape `file_menu_popup` already uses on this screen"*, and then copied it. One
`anchored_menu(ui, id, anchor, w, rows, paint) -> MenuOutcome` now, `MenuOutcome` carrying the row
clicked and whether the frame's click landed outside both the menu and its anchor.

**Only the shell is shared, and the closure is what says so.** `paint` is handed a `&Painter`, an
index and a rect, because what genuinely differs between the two is the row's *contents*: the filter
draws a colour dot and a tick, the ⋮ menu draws a label that turns red on *Delete*. Folding those
together would be the flag-and-branch function this panel already refuses elsewhere.

🚨 **Deliberately *not* where `[S20.2-L1-01]`'s Escape lives, and this is the entry's most useful
sentence.** The finding proposed extracting first, so that fix and `[S20.2-L1-02]`'s click-swallow
would both land in the shared helper. Both were closed before this extraction ever happened — §15
**D578** put the Escape in `dashboard_keys` behind `library_menu_open()`, and §15 **D558** put the
click-swallow behind the same predicate at the eight pointer-side doors that act. That is the better
place, and the reason generalises: **a keyboard rule that lives inside a *drawing* helper only runs
on the frames the menu is drawn**, where `library_menu_open()` is a question about state that can be
asked before anything is painted. **A shared implementation and a shared predicate are different
kinds of sharing, and this screen wanted both** — which is why doing the extraction first would have
produced a worse fix for the finding it was supposed to enable.

⚠️ **This was a prediction coming true one screen over rather than a violated invariant.**
`panels/mod.rs`'s popover paragraph states the rule — *"A hand-rolled copy is how the next popover
gets three of the six"* — about `ClickAway`'s six gating terms over the **inspector's** popovers.
These two menus implement no `ClickAway` at all; they hand-rolled a two-term dismissal of their own on
a different screen. So the rule is a good description of what went wrong here and **not** a count
these menus are an instance of, which matters because that same paragraph exists to say the count is
written *once, in that paragraph, and nowhere else*.

🚨 **A first version of the shipped comment got exactly that wrong and was corrected while this entry
was being written.** It quoted a *superseded* spelling — *"a fourth hand-rolled copy is how the next
one gets three of the exemptions"* — and called these menus *"the fifth and sixth copies"*, which
reintroduces into a second file the ordinal `panels/mod.rs` had removed from six. That paragraph
records the damage in as many words: the copy count was *"a fourth"* there and *"a fifth"* in
`inspector.rs`, and *"if a term is added, this is the sentence to change."* **A quotation is a copy,
so quoting a sentence that exists to be the only copy of a count is the failure it was written to
stop.** The comment cites the rule and names no ordinal now.

🚨 **No test drove either menu, so the whole 1,247-test suite was silent about this refactor.** *A
green suite is not evidence about code no test reaches, and an extraction is exactly the change that
looks safe because everything stays green.*
`both_library_menus_draw_their_rows_through_the_shared_shell` drives both callers and asserts row
**contents** rather than row count — a count passes against a shell that draws the right number of
empty rectangles, which is precisely what a mis-wired `paint` closure produces.

🚨 **Its first version was vacuous, and the flip is what said so.** `"All projects"` is the filter
**button's** own label and `"Kestrel"` is a **sidebar** row, so both strings are on screen with the
menu shut; `contains` found them and proved nothing. Under the flip — `paint` never called — the
file-menu assertions went red and the filter ones stayed green, which is the tell. The filter half is
asserted as a **difference** now: opening the menu paints each of those strings one *more* time than
the closed state does. **A string the closed state also paints is not evidence about the open one.**

⚠️ **`fn elide` narrowed from `&Ui` to `&Context`, and that did not force the other four call sites to
change.** `egui::Ui` is `Deref<Target = Context>`, so `elide(ui, …)` coerces silently — which is
worth one clause because it is the opposite of what a signature change is usually good for:
**reading `elide(ui, …)` is not evidence that a site was reviewed.** The narrowing bought the one
caller that has a `&Painter` and no `&Ui` to give.

Two smaller repairs went with it. `file_menu_popup`'s row height was a bare `28.0` written three
times where `FILTER_ROW_H` says the same number — the *width* difference between the two menus is a
decision (verbs against project names) and the height was not. And `let _ = label;`, a destructure
left over from a shape that function no longer has, is gone.

*(All six gates green. Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which describes neither menu's
construction; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S20.2-L3-05]`.)*

**D732 — Two crates with the dead-code lint switched off, and a claim whose own command could not
falsify it. *Fixed 2026-09-10; Keep — the platform arms nothing here compiles are an open class
rather than a fix.***

`[A8-L3-06]` and `[A8-L6-07]`, one entry for two findings, because they are the same failure twice:
**a check that was switched off or could not fail, and in both cases nothing in the repository could
see it.** One is a lint told not to fire; the other is a sentence offered with a command that can
only ever agree with it.

**The lint half.** `ondin-export/src/lib.rs` and `ondin-mcp/src/lib.rs` each carried a crate-root
`#![allow(dead_code)]`. That is stronger than the blind spot `CLAUDE.md` records under *Build /
test* — there a `pub` item in a library simply *cannot* be dead, because it is API; here every item
in the crate, **private ones included**, was forbidden to be reported. A private helper that lost its
last caller, and its now-false doc comment with it, would have sat in either crate with all six gates
green. Both are removed.

⚠️ **They were hiding nothing, and the measurement is the reason it was cheap.** Zero warnings each,
on clean rebuilds, under `check -p` (lib only), `clippy -p --all-targets`, `check --workspace
--all-targets` and `clippy --workspace --all-targets` — six spellings across the two crates. So the
cost was a disabled gate and the benefit was none. **The first run reported `Fresh` and was a cache
hit**; `rust-verify` distrusted it and re-ran after `cargo clean -p`, which is why the numbers are
quotable — *a lint that is not recompiled has not been re-run*, and a removed `allow` is exactly the
edit a fingerprint cache can decide is uninteresting.

**`ondin-export/tests/common/mod.rs` keeps its allow, and now says which kind it is.** A
`tests/common` module is compiled **once per integration test file** that declares it and each file
uses a different subset, so `fixture_with_stroke_align` is genuinely unused in `snapshot` and
genuinely used in `svg_roundtrip`; removing the line produces four warnings across two targets, every
one of them a false report. **That distinction is this half's practical content** — one of the three
attributes was load-bearing and two were not, and nothing in the tree distinguished them. The
surviving one carries the argument so the next reader does not have to re-measure it.

⚠️ **An inner attribute is invisible to the obvious census.** `grep '#\[allow('` cannot match
`#![allow(` — the `!` sits between the `#` and the `[` — so the *most far-reaching* kind of allow
there is was the kind nothing counted: `review/facts.md`'s census reported 38 outer attributes and
**zero** of the eight inner ones. Six inner attributes are left, five of them the rustdoc
`private_intra_doc_links` allow every crate root carries (D296) and one the `tests/common` one above.

🚨 **The cfg half is the same shape one step earlier, because there *is* a command and it is scoped
to its own answer.** `CLAUDE.md`'s release-gate paragraph asserted *"`debug_assertions` is still the
only cfg the app reads (`grep 'cfg(debug'` → `theme.rs` alone), so this is one gate rather than the
first of a class."* **The parenthesis is a self-confirming check**: that grep matches only cfgs whose
name *begins with* `debug`, so by construction it cannot report any other cfg and **can never
falsify the sentence it is offered as evidence for**. Both halves of the claim are false. Measured
with `grep -rhoE 'cfg\(([a-z_]+)' crates/ --include=*.rs | sort | uniq -c`: **302 `test`, 6
`windows`, 3 `panic`, 3 `not`, 3 `debug_assertions`, 2 `target_os`, 2 `all`, 1 `unix`.**

⚠️ **The narrow reading of the parenthesis has gone stale as well, which is worth one clause because
it shows what the command actually measures.** `grep 'cfg(debug' crates/` answers **two** files
today, `theme.rs` and `inspector.rs`, the second being a doc comment that names the attribute in
prose — the grep counts sentences as well as code. What remains true is the claim nobody was
disputing: `theme.rs` holds the only `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` this workspace *reads*.

⚠️ **So it is the first of a class, and the rest of the class has no gate at all.** Four functions in
`ondin-app` have an arm this machine never compiles, in either profile, under any of the six gates —
`canvas::os_cursor_desktop_px` and `library::clock::local_offset`, each with a `#[cfg(not(windows))]`
twin; `library::store::owner_may_write`, whose twin is `#[cfg(unix)]`; and
`panels::show_in_file_browser`, whose `cfg` is three-armed, so **two** of its arms are unbuilt. Five
arms, then, not four. A rename or a `rust-mechanic` sweep passes straight over every one of them.
🚨 **And two of the five are stubs while two carry real logic, which is the distinction to keep**:
`os_cursor_desktop_px`'s answers `None` and `local_offset`'s answers `0`, where the whole *reason*
`owner_may_write` is two functions is that `Permissions::set_readonly(false)` means mode `0o666` on
Unix and would make a briefly-writable file briefly **world**-writable — a correctness argument about
the one platform the arm is never built for. `show_in_file_browser`'s `open` and `xdg-open` arms are
the same. **Not fixable by adding a gate here**: it wants a cross-compile or a CI runner, and it is
recorded as an open class rather than as work.

⚠️ **Session 12 read that grep as *"true and answering the wrong question"*** — D597's closing
paragraph, written about egui defaulting `warn_on_id_clash` to `cfg!(debug_assertions)`. It was
neither: a command that cannot return a counter-example is not a true statement about our source,
because it could not have been an untrue one. D597's own point stands and is amended rather than
replaced — a dependency's use of the cfg is invisible to any census of ours — but the census was
also blind to four of our own cfgs, which is the half that made *"one gate rather than the first of a
class"* sound measured.

**The lesson to carry: when a claim comes with a command, read the command against the claim and not
only its output.** This is the same family as this round's *a count in a comment is a gate nobody
built* (D720, D726) with the failure one step earlier — there the number was a gate nobody wrote,
here the gate was written, run, quoted, and pointed at its own answer.

*(No production behaviour changes; both commits passed all six gates. D597's `grep 'cfg(debug'`
paragraph amended. Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which does not describe the gate list or the
crate roots' lint attributes; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. `CLAUDE.md`'s two copies of the claim
were corrected by the maintainer. Closes `[A8-L3-06]` and `[A8-L6-07]`.)*

**D731 — One placement rule written twice, and the copy that carried the reasoning was the copy that
was wrong. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — a third paste verb still disagrees, deliberately.***

`[S12.4-L3-09]`. `canvas::paste_text_as_layer` and `canvas::paste_svg` opened with the same fourteen
lines — the frame a paste is aimed at, the centre it lands on, and the parent transform that centre
has to be inverted through — **character for character**. They are one function now,
`canvas::paste_placement(&self, at) -> (Point, NodeId, Affine)`, sitting beside `paste_frame`.

**The cost the finding names is documentation rather than behaviour, and that is the interesting
half.** Both copies computed the same answer, so nothing was wrong on screen. What was wrong is that
`paste_text_as_layer` carried four paragraphs of reasoning about the rule and `paste_svg` carried
none — so **a reader tuning the rule at the documented copy would have left the other behind**, and
the two paste verbs would then land in different places for the same selection, which is a defect
neither function reads as having. This file already makes that argument against itself three times:
`pan_by_drag` is one function *"so the two cannot drift into panning at different speeds"*,
`preview_session` is *"one function rather than four copies of the same five lines"*, and
`restyle_session` is *"the one body behind the three entry points above, so 'who wins about the
spans' is a question asked in exactly one place."*

🚨 **And one of the four paragraphs was false, which is what this entry is really about.** It read
*"**A shape selected inside a frame takes the view's centre, not that frame's.** Deliberate and worth
one look on the machine"*, and it had been untrue since **D221** widened `paste_frame` to the
**enclosing** artboard — D221 says so in as many words (*"a shape selected inside a frame now pastes
into **that frame**, which D218 had recorded as a deliberate choice and was the wrong half of it"*),
and `paste_frame`'s own doc two hundred lines below said the same (*"the frame itself and anything
inside it both hand back the same answer"*). Measured before the correction was written: a shape
selected inside the fixture's frame hands back that frame's centre, `(200, 175)`, and that frame as
parent. **A false sentence that governed one call site was one lift away from governing two** —
*lifting a block carries its comments with it, which is the right instinct and is exactly how that
happens. A comment is not evidence, including one you are only moving.*

🚨 **The correction was applied to the new home and not to the old one, and for a commit the file
held both.** `paste_placement`'s doc carried the corrected rule with the false sentence quoted in
full, while `paste_text_as_layer` — two hundred lines above — went on *stating* it in the imperative.
A grep for the sentence answered three sites of which two were the correction, which is precisely
what makes the live one easy to read past. Fixed while this entry was being written: that doc now
points at `paste_placement` and quotes the old sentence rather than asserting it, and the
selection-versus-pointer reasoning it carried (Figma centres on the view unconditionally; the frame
is the tuning, D218) moved to `paste_placement`, where the rule is decided. **Moving a rule is not
the same edit as deleting the copy you moved it from**, and nothing in this project can see the
difference — the quotation and the claim are the same string.

⚠️ **The test exists only because of the lift, and it is D269's argument in miniature.** Both paste
verbs open with `crate::app::system_clipboard_text()`, so neither can be driven headlessly and
**neither has ever had a test**: the decision the two shared was locked behind a clipboard read. A
free `&self` decision function is testable, and
`canvas::paste_placement_tests::a_paste_takes_the_pointer_then_the_selected_frames_centre_then_the_view`
drives all four arms over one fixture — a pointer beating the selection, the frame itself, **a shape
inside it**, and nothing selected. The third is the arm the false paragraph denied, and it asserts
the frame's centre *and* the frame as the parent, since the sentence was wrong about both.

⚠️ **A third arm of `Ctrl+V` still disagrees and is left alone on purpose.** `app::paste_image`
places at `at.unwrap_or_else(|| self.viewport_centre())` with **no selected-frame arm at all**, and
its own doc states that as the behaviour — *"no point to place at, so … a new layer lands in the
middle of the view"* (§15 D224) — so an image pasted with a frame selected lands in the middle of the
view where text and SVG land in the frame. **Both halves are documented, so it is a disagreement
rather than drift**, and reconciling the three is a decision about what a chord paste means rather
than a lift. *Decide it or leave it; the change is one call either way.*

*(D218's closing note amended — it says the placement is read-verified because the verb cannot be
built headlessly, which is still true of the verb and no longer true of the rule. Nothing amended in
`architecture.md`: §9.4 states the placement only for `paste_at` and states it correctly, and
`roadmap.md`'s clipboard row already gives the true rule — *"the centre of the frame the selection is
in, else the middle of the view"* — so nothing was struck there either. Closes `[S12.4-L3-09]`.)*

**D728 — The sidebar counted the trash by scanning it, once per nav and once per frame. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the one invalidation door this entry left open was closed the same day, and
the hazard it is an instance of is not.***

`[S20.1-L3-07]`. `nav_count`'s `Nav::Trash` arm ran `store::trashed`, which is `scan::scan_dir` —
**one file open and one JSON prefix parse for every document in `.trash`** — and the sidebar paints
that count beside the heading on **every nav, every frame**, whether or not the trash is being looked
at. `visible_entries` scanned the same folder a *second* time in the same frame when it was. Two
hundred trashed documents was two hundred file opens a frame and four hundred on *Trash*, for a
number that changes only when the user acts. ⚠️ **And the opens are not the floor**: `scan::read_meta`
loops its read because a short one is routine *"on a hydrating cloud file"*, the base folder being
explicitly meant to be a directory a sync client is also writing into.

🚨 **The part worth recording is why it read as guarded: two module heads forbade exactly this, and
both named the wrong road.** `panels::dashboard`'s says *"a refresh reads every document's prefix…
Nothing in this file may call it from inside a layout loop"*, and `library::state`'s says *"a scan is
a real cost and must not be per-frame"* — both of `Library::refresh`, which nothing calls per frame.
This was the same hazard by a route neither sentence enumerates. **A rule that names one road is not
a rule about the destination**, which is D731's *one rule written twice* seen from the other end:
there, two copies of a rule and the reasoned one wrong; here, one copy, correct, and short of the
doors.

`Library::trashed: Vec<Entry>` holds the listing, `trashed()` reads it, and `refresh_trash()` is the
only thing that moves it. ⚠️ **The field is private where `entries` is `pub`, and that is the design
rather than an oversight**: a second way to get the answer is the wrong one to reach for, and one
reader plus one writer is what keeps the invalidation set *enumerable*. `refresh` calls
`refresh_trash`, so everything that already refreshed is covered without being touched.

🚨 **The invalidation point is the whole risk of caching this, and it is a standing hazard rather
than a solved problem.** `entries` has one producer, `scan::scan`. The trash is written by
`store::trash`, `store::purge_trash`, `relocate` and by a bare `fs::remove_file` — and **before this
cache existed none of them had to tell anybody**, which is the property being given up. Of the doors
as they stand, `trash_or_purge`'s trash arm, `delete_project`'s member sweep and `Act::Restore` all
call `refresh`; `relocate` is followed by `Library::open`; the two `purge_trash` calls —
`open_at_launch` and the library-settings *Save* — did not, and now call `refresh_trash`; and the
permanent delete is the door below, which did not either. **A writer added later has to know**, and
nothing will tell it — which is what the two greps now on `refresh_trash` are for.

🚨 **One door was missed and it was live for a day: permanent delete. *Fixed 2026-09-10.***
`trash_or_purge`'s first arm, taken when `dash.nav == Nav::Trash`, was `fs::remove_file` and then
`return` — no refresh of any kind — and both routes to it end there, the ⋮'s *Delete permanently* and
the *Delete* key through `delete_modal`. So a document deleted for good stayed in the Trash list
*and* in the sidebar's count until something unrelated refreshed. It calls
`self.library.refresh_trash()` now, **unconditionally rather than inside an `Ok` arm** — on a failure
the file is still there and re-reading the folder is still the right answer — and not a full
`refresh`, nothing outside `.trash` having moved. **The enumeration that missed it was of `store`'s
writers, and this is the one door that does not go through `store`**: a grep for `store::trash` /
`store::purge_trash` cannot see an `fs::remove_file` sitting in a panel.

🚨 **Before the cache that path was self-correcting and needed nothing, which is why it is the
hazard's first instance rather than a slip.** `visible_entries` rescanned `.trash` every frame, so
the row left the list the moment the file left the disk. **Caching a scan turns every writer that
never had to announce itself into one that must** — the door did not change, the contract around it
did — and the writers that never name `store` are the ones no enumeration of `store` can find.

⚠️ **`Library::refresh_trash`'s own doc has been corrected and now carries no count.** It read *"Two
of the five call sites already called `refresh` and three did not … a sixth writer added later has to
know"*, and **the sixth writer was already in the tree**, in a panel, on the day that sentence was
written: it read as a survey of a closed set at exactly the moment it was most wrong. Two greps stand
in the number's place, run from the repository root —

```text
grep -rn 'store::trash(\|store::purge_trash(' crates/ondin-app/src --include=*.rs
grep -rn 'remove_file\|fs::rename' crates/ondin-app/src --include=*.rs
```

— the first finding the doors that announce themselves and **the second the one that matters**,
because a writer that reaches `.trash` without naming `store` is precisely the writer this cache
cannot survive. *A count in prose is a gate nobody built* (D720, D726, D735), and this is the variant
where the count was not merely stale: it **was** the argument that the set was closed.

⚠️ **The launch ordering is load-bearing and carries a comment.** `Library::open` counts the trash
*before* `open_at_launch` sweeps it, so without the added `refresh_trash()` the sidebar's *Trash*
count is the pre-sweep one for the rest of the session — wrong from the first frame rather than
drifting later.

**Test** `the_trash_count_is_cached_rather_than_rescanned_every_frame`, asserted **by deleting
`.trash` behind the app's back**: a count that survives its own directory being removed was not read
from it, which is a direct test of *"this did not go to disk"* and needs no seam, where counting
`read_meta` calls would need one built and then maintained. ⚠️ **The third assertion is the one that
earns its place** — `refresh_trash` takes the count to zero — because without it this is a test for a
count that is merely *frozen*, and a cache nothing invalidates would pass the first two while being a
worse bug than the scan it replaced.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §9.5's `.trash` bullet is about the folder, the deletion stamp
and the retention window, and says nothing about how the count beside the heading is read. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md` — *"Filesystem is truth… no fact may live only in the cache"* stands, and a
held **scan**, re-read rather than patched, is inside it; with the permanent delete refreshing, every
door now re-reads truth rather than patching the listing. Closes `[S20.1-L3-07]`.)*

**D727 — Four creation builders no test had ever called, and the clamp two of them share is on the
door the tested one is not. *Tested 2026-09-10; Keep — this entry records coverage; no production
line moved.***

`[S13.2-L6-06]`. `create_ellipse`, `create_polygon`, `create_star` and `create_image_in_box` had
**zero** test callers workspace-wide, and every one of them is reached from one place — `canvas.rs`
committing a `Drag::Create` — so what was uncovered is the last step of four drawing gestures.

🚨 **The side-count clamps are the sharp half, because the identical bound is tested three times over
on the door beside them.** `tools::step_sides` is the **keyboard** door, `↑`/`↓` while the drag is
still in flight, and its doc says why the bound matters — *"`↓` held at three would wrap a `u32`
straight to four billion"*. `create_polygon` and `create_star` are the **commit** door, each clamping
to the same `geometry::MIN_SIDES..=MAX_SIDES`, and nothing asserted that the two agree: deleting
either `clamp` left the whole suite green.

⚠️ **The two doors fail differently, which is why one clamp cannot answer for the other.**
`step_sides` subtracts, so its lower end is where an overflow lives. A `u32` at the commit door
cannot go below zero, so what a bare `0` or `2` stores is a **count nothing honours**:
`geometry::star_path` clamps `n` again before it draws, so the canvas shows a triangle while the
model, the saved file and the inspector's *Sides* field all say `0`. **The clamp at this door defends
the document, not the drawing** — and a document that disagrees with its own picture round-trips that
disagreement.

🚨 **The shipped test comment gets that consequence wrong and it should be corrected.** It reads
*"what a bare `0` or `2` produces is a polygon with no area — `geometry` has no arm that draws one"*,
and `star_path`'s first line is `let n = n.clamp(MIN_SIDES, MAX_SIDES)`: the area is a triangle's.
The verdict the sentence supports is untouched — both doors need the clamp — and only the account of
the failure is false, which is the shape this round keeps producing. *Fix the sentence in
`the_creation_builders_clamp_their_side_count_at_both_ends`' doc.*

⚠️ **Nothing delivers an out-of-range count today, and the entry says so rather than implying a live
bug.** `Drag::Create` seeds `sides` from `POLYGON_DEFAULT_SIDES` or `STAR_DEFAULT_POINTS` and moves
it only through `step_sides`, so the commit door's clamp is defence against a *second* producer that
does not exist yet — which is exactly why deleting it costs nothing today and exactly why a future
editor would delete it. **Both builders are driven rather than one**, because the same constant
reaches them through two differently-named fields, `sides` and `points`, and a fix applied to one is
precisely the shape that misses the other. The same test pins the one path
`tools::STAR_DEFAULT_RATIO` has into a document — `create_star`'s `inner_ratio`, which nothing read
there.

🚨 **`create_image_in_box`'s contract is *negative*, and that is the general lesson.** Its doc's
headline is *"No fit, and no aspect lock. A drawn box is an instruction; second-guessing it is what
makes a tool feel like it is arguing"*: what it must **not** do is call `fitted_image_size`, which
its sibling `create_image` — the click door — does. **A negative contract needs a fixture in which
the positive one would visibly differ**, so the test draws a 400×200 image into a 50×300 box, the
wrong aspect *and* smaller than intrinsic, and asserts the fixture is a box the fit rule argues with
before asserting anything else.

⚠️ **The two image tests that look as though they cover this do not, and the flip is what says so
rather than an assertion.** Inserting `fitted_image_size` into `create_image_in_box` is red here at
`50×25` against `50×300`, and **`a_placed_image_shrinks_to_fit_and_is_never_scaled_up` and
`a_placed_image_is_centred_on_the_click` both stayed green** — both drive the **click** path, so the
one distinction between the two placement gestures was asserted nowhere. *A flip that leaves a
neighbouring test green is a measurement of where that test's coverage stops*, and it is why this
could not be folded into either of them.

⚠️ **`create_ellipse` is the fourth and the plainest, recorded because of what its name collides
with**: `create_shape_box_is_order_independent` reads like the ellipse builder's test and calls the
private `local_box` directly, never reaching a builder at all. What was unasserted is that the
builder passes that box through to an `Ellipse`, so `an_ellipse_is_made_at_the_box_it_was_dragged`
gives the corners the other way round — `local_box`'s own property arriving at a builder for the
first time.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §5.5a's *"A click fits, a drag draws"* and §9.4's copy of it
both state the distinction correctly, and have since before the builders existed — the design was
right and the tests were silent. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S13.2-L6-06]`.)*

**D726 — §8.4's tool list had a second copy in a crate nobody opens for three milestones, and nothing
compared them. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — and coupling a crate to this document is a shape
with a boundary, stated below.***

`[S22-L3-06]`. `ondin-mcp/src/tools.rs` was fourteen lines of module doc and **no code**, and the doc
held §8.4's twenty-eight tool names a second time. Identical name for name and phase for phase on the
day the finding was written — checked, not assumed — so nothing was wrong yet. **What was wrong is
that nothing could ever say so**, and the window in which the two can drift is the *whole* of the time
nobody is reading this file: `roadmap.md` files M6 under *Later · Post-v1*, and §15 D4 defers
`serve`/`mcp-proxy` until the editor is feature-complete. The copy that is **not** the design would
therefore sit unread across every milestone in which a tool list is most likely to change, and would
read as the design to anyone who opened the crate.

⚠️ **`cargo doc` reads this crate and could not help.** A prose list of tool names contains no
`[link]`, so the one gate that reads doc comments had nothing to resolve — which is worth stating
because the usual excuses do not apply here: `ondin-mcp` is a lib crate with a `deny`, not a
`#[cfg(test)]` module (D319), not a `tests/` target and not a `build.rs` (D622). **The list had to
stop being prose before anything could check it.** This is the round's *a count in a comment is a
gate nobody built* with a list in place of the count, and the repair has the same shape: not a
corrected copy, but the copy made comparable.

`PHASE_1: [&str; 8]` and `PHASE_2: [&str; 20]` are constants, and a `#[cfg(test)]` module
`include_str!`s `docs/architecture.md` and diffs both phases **in order**. Ordered rather than
set-compared on purpose: §8.4 gives Phase 1 in the order it wants shipped, and a set comparison would
call a reordered list identical and lose exactly what the phases carry. Names are parsed from §8.4's
backticks with any signature dropped at the `(`, because the document writes `get_document() ->
Snapshot` and `group(ids)` where the crate writes bare names — a comparison demanding the same
*spelling* would fail on a difference that is not one.

⚠️ **`include_str!` rather than a runtime read, and that is the half that makes it a gate.** It
registers the dependency, so editing §8.4 rebuilds and re-runs the test; a `fs::read` would depend on
the working directory and would leave a stale binary passing. Verified green under both
`cargo test -p ondin-mcp` and `cargo test --workspace`, which is not a formality in this workspace —
§15 D600 is where a test came out green under `-p` and red under `--workspace`, the two spellings
resolving features differently and so not compiling the same dependency graph.

🚨 **A gate whose subject is prose has two failure modes and only one of them is interesting.**
Renaming an entry is red at the comparison, which is the case it was written for. Rewording the
*heading* the parser looks for is red at `listed`'s own panic — **loudly, rather than by returning an
empty list that compares equal to an empty list**, which is this project's vacuity trap in its purest
form: the gate would go quiet at the exact moment the document it watches was edited. The parse
panics and the parsed list is asserted non-empty before it is compared, and both were flip-checked.
*A gate that reads a prose document must fail loudly when the prose moves, or it stops being a gate
at the moment it is needed.*

⚠️ **The load-bearing detail for a future editor of §8.4 is that the two phase paragraphs are now
parsed.** Their opening sentences are the parser's anchors, each paragraph ends at the first blank
line — which is what keeps the *Selection* and *Notes* paragraphs, both of which contain backticked
names, out of the answer — and every backticked token inside them is read as a tool name. Reflowing
either paragraph, or moving a name into it as an aside, breaks the build rather than the record.
§8.4 says so in place now.

🚨 **This is the first thing in the workspace that couples a crate's source to `docs/architecture.md`,
and the maintainer asked whether the shape should be repeated. The answer is yes, narrowly, and the
boundary is what makes it safe.** The technique is not new — `app::only_the_layers_panel_commits_without_the_committer`
(§15 D679) `include_str!`s seven panel sources and greps them, and `theme.rs` reads its own file — so
what is new is only the *subject*. Repeat it where all three hold: the document states an **exhaustive
list or an enumerated set** rather than an argument; the code holds a copy of that same set; and the
document's spelling of it is stable enough to parse without the parser becoming the thing that breaks.
**Do not repeat it for prose that carries a reason**, which is most of this document — a test that
diffed a paragraph of argument would be red on every honest edit, and the second time that happens
somebody deletes the test rather than reads it. The tell for a candidate is a list somebody would
otherwise be tempted to write down twice.

*(§8.4 gains the note that its two phase paragraphs are parsed and by what. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`: the *Later · Post-v1* MCP row is about M6 being deferred, which this does not touch,
and it already describes `ondin-mcp` as *"a stub: message shapes and the tool list, no handlers, no
socket"* — still true. Closes `[S22-L3-06]`.)*

**D725 — The Transform card's numbers changed shape when a second layer was selected, and its corner
radius reported one the document does not hold. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S14.2-L3-07]`. §9.4 states the rule once — *"Every scrubbable field therefore pins its own:
`ui::number(n)` as a `custom_formatter` where trailing zeros should be trimmed"* (§15 D66) — and the
multi-selection card pinned a formatter without pinning **that** one. `inspector::multi_number` handed
`custom_formatter` a raw `format!("{v:.2}")`, which does not trim, so every number on the card gained
two trailing zeros the moment a second layer was selected: `20` beside a single-layer field still
reading `20` became `20.00`. `spacing_row` carried the same raw `{v:.2}`.

🚨 **And `inspector_multi_appearance`'s corner radius printed at *zero* decimals** where its
single-layer twin prints two, so a shared **4.5 read `4`** and 5.5 read `6` — the panel reporting a
radius the document does not hold, which is a different and worse failure from a cosmetic one. **Half
integers are what the control beside it produces**: `Scrub::whole(0.5)` steps by half units, and
photographic scaling carries corner radii, so 5 becomes 4.5 at 90%. All three now call
`crate::ui::number(2)`.

⚠️ **The card claims this parity in its own comment**, three hundred lines above the formatter that
broke it: *"the single-layer panel's arithmetic, to the pixel — walking from one layer to two shifted
the numbers sideways, which is what makes a panel feel cheap."* That comment was written about the
**widths**, and the widths were fixed. *A parity claim scoped to one axis reads as a claim about the
control.*

⚠️ **Bounded to the readout, which is what separates this from `[S14.2-L1-02]`.** A `custom_formatter`
cannot commit anything; what stops leaving the multi radius field by click, Enter or Tab from writing
is `edit_valve`'s engagement latch (§15 D316, D519), and `a_bare_click_through_a_mixed_corner_radius_field_writes_nothing`
is what pins it. ⚠️ **`interacting` is not that guard and it is easy to read as one** — it answers
`dragged() || drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()` and so is **true** on the frame the field
is tabbed away from; its own comment says it decides whether to *build* a transaction and that
*"nothing downstream of it commits on its answer — the valves ask their own latch"*. The brief for
this entry had the two the wrong way round.

**Test**: `inspector::a_number_reads_the_same_with_one_layer_selected_and_with_two`, asserting on the
**galleys of both cards over one document** rather than on the formatters — a test of `ui::number`
would pass while the card called something else, which is exactly what had happened. The fixture is
asserted to hold 4.5 before anything is painted. **Flips**, run separately, one per assertion:
restoring the radius's `{v:.0}` gives `… "APPEARANCE", "100%", "4", …`, and restoring
`multi_number`'s `{v:.2}` gives `… "0.00", "X", "0.00", "Y", "100.00", "W", …` with the radius still
reading `4.5` beside it. Neither flip touches the other's assertion, which is why they are two.

⚠️ **The multi opacity field's `{v:.0}%` is left alone deliberately** and is not a fourth instance:
its single-layer twins spell the same thing as `.suffix("%").max_decimals(0)`, so the two agree, and a
percentage is the one quantity on these cards that is meant to read whole.

*(§9.4's D66 paragraph amended to say that the rule is the single-layer field's *spelling* and not
merely "a formatter". Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S14.2-L3-07]`.)*

**D724 — A tool switch cleared five pieces of gesture state by name and not the drag. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-10; Keep — `cancel_gesture` deliberately not reused, and the reason is the argument.***

`[S12.4-L1-07]`. `OndinApp::choose_tool` cleared the text session, the pen, `pen_bias`, `points` and
`pending_images` — each by name, each with a sentence saying why — and never touched `self.drag`. So
pressing any tool key, or a rail button, mid-crop-drag left a live `Drag::CropResize` **and last
frame's crop preview installed**, while `edited_image()` went `None` and brought the layer's selection
box and handles back: a crop preview of a layer no longer in crop mode, under transform chrome
answering a gesture that is not the one in hand. Measured headless — `drag live = true, gesture
preview = true` after `choose_tool(Select)`. §9.4 names picking another tool as one of the three ways
out of image editing (§15 D268, D270), and it was the one that did not finish the gesture.

⚠️ **`Escape` was already clean by ordering rather than by design.** Its ladder reaches
`cancel_gesture` before its `choose_tool(Tool::Select)` rung, and that gate is `self.drag.is_none()`
— kind-agnostic, so it caught this without knowing about crops. **Every other route to a tool change
skipped it**, which is why the finding rated Low: the one door anybody would test was the one door
that worked.

Three lines at the top of `choose_tool`: `self.drag = Drag::None`, `self.alt_clone = None`,
`self.session.clear_gesture_preview()`.

- **`clear_gesture_preview`, not `clear_preview`** (§15 D109). The two share one override set and
  only one of them belongs to the drag; `[A1-L2-04]` is that mistake made once already, and a live
  text session's uncommitted content is what the wrong one takes.
- **`alt_clone`, because the release will not clear it.** `finish_drag` drops it on its no-pointer arm
  and at the end of the `Drag::Move` arm — with `self.drag` already `Drag::None` and a pointer
  position in hand the match falls through `Drag::None => {}` and neither runs, so a stale copy stays
  armed. *"What the next Alt-drag would silently insert"*, in `cancel_gesture`'s own words.

🚨 **Not routed through `cancel_gesture`, though the finding's sketch prefers it, and the reason is
worth the paragraph.** That function takes a `&egui::Context` `choose_tool` has not got across
**seventeen** call sites, and its gate answers for inspector field scrubs, a Settings nudge, an export
quality scrub and a guide-position drag — states a tool switch cannot be in the middle of, the
keyboard belonging to the field. What the two share is the **list**, not the funnel; these three lines
are the part of that list a canvas drag owns. `[A2-L7-02]` is the architectural cause and is not
closed by this: with 101 fields and one privacy scope, *"is a gesture in flight?"* is a hand-written
list at every site that needs one, and this entry adds a fourth such list rather than removing one.

**Test**: `canvas::tool_switch_drops_the_drag_tests::changing_tool_mid_drag_drops_the_drag_and_its_preview`.
⚠️ **The `Drag::CropResize` is built by hand rather than driven**, deliberately: what `choose_tool`
owes is an answer to *any* live `Drag`, and driving the crop mechanics — handle hit-testing, the fill
index, the limit rect — would make the test fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the tool
switch. The fixture is asserted live before the switch, or the two assertions after it pass for the
wrong reason. Flip-checked; **all 1,242 app tests pass**, which is the real check here, seventeen call
sites having gained a clear.

⚠️ **`Escape` is the control this entry claims and it is *not* asserted anywhere** — the test's own doc
said *"asserting it here"* and was corrected in the same pass. The ordering claim above is read out of
the ladder rather than pinned, and the ladder is free to be reordered without anything going red.
*Fix by adding the Escape arm to that module if the ladder is ever touched.*

*(§9.4's *"arming a tool whose verb is create clears the selection"* paragraph gains the drag. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S12.4-L1-07]`.)*

**D723 — Three copies of one `DragValue` chrome strip, and one of them overrode a default with the
default. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S18.1-L3-06]`. `ui::value_field_f64`, `ui::badge_field` and `ui::bare_drag_value` each held a
verbatim eight-line sequence stripping a `DragValue`'s own grounds and borders, and each held its own
paragraph restating the same two egui facts. New `ui::strip_drag_value_chrome` is the one block, and
the two facts are stated once:

- **A `DragValue` has two faces and both ground themselves.** The resting face is a `Button`, filling
  from `bg_fill`/`weak_bg_fill` and outlining from `bg_stroke` across all four widget states; the
  keyboard-editing face is a `TextEdit`, filling from `extreme_bg_color` and, once focused, outlining
  itself in `selection.stroke`. A caller that has drawn its own field, pill or row wants none of them.
- 🚨 **The width goes and the colour stays, and that distinction is a reported bug.**
  `selection.stroke` has two jobs in egui: it is that focus outline, *and* it is the colour selected
  glyphs are repainted in — `text_selection::visuals::paint_text_selection` writes it straight into
  the galley's vertices. `Stroke::NONE` is transparent, so zeroing the whole thing turned **every
  selected digit invisible** and left an opaque selection block with nothing legible in it. A
  zero-*width* stroke is skipped by the tessellator, so the outline goes either way; keeping the
  colour is what keeps the text.

🚨 **The "parser precedence divergence" the finding names is the signature and not two decisions.**
`value_field_f64` and `badge_field` build the `DragValue` themselves, so they can set a parser the
caller's `build` closure is free to replace; `bare_drag_value` is handed a **finished** one and has
nowhere earlier to put it. **The rule is the same in all three — the parser is a default a caller may
replace** — and only in the third is the rule unofferable. Both docs stated it as though each were the
only copy, one calling it a feature of that helper and the other a limitation of this one, which is
how one rule came to look like two contracts. *Three copies of a paragraph are three chances to
describe the same thing differently, and the differences read as decisions.*

⚠️ **`badge_field`'s `.update_while_editing(true)` is removed.** Measured against the vendored source
— `egui-0.35.0/src/widgets/drag_value.rs:81` has `update_while_editing: true` in the default
constructor — so it did nothing, and it sat **after** `build`, so it would silently have overridden a
caller asking for `false` the day one wanted to. The other two helpers leave the default alone. *An
override that is a no-op is the worst kind: nothing tests it and nothing announces it.* ⚠️ **The
behaviour it names is load-bearing elsewhere and comes from the default, not from any call site**:
`inspector::escaping_the_field_abandons_the_edit`'s doc turns on each keystroke having already been
written through the `&mut` before `Escape` arrives, and it credited that to *"`ui::value_field` builds
every field with `update_while_editing(true)`"* — which `value_field_f64` has never done. Corrected
there; the conclusion, that `edit_valve`'s `Escape` guard is load-bearing and looks redundant (§15
D315, D316), is unchanged.

⚠️ **`ui::selected_digits_are_never_painted_transparent` covers all three helpers now.** `badge_field`
was the third and had never been in that table — which is that test's own doc argument (*"the bug was
fixed in `value_field` and left live in `bare_drag_value` … a test that covered only the reported one
would have let that stand"*) happening a second time, to the test written to stop it happening. The
per-helper arm is kept even though the three now share one function: what it pins is that each helper
is still **wired** to the rule, and the cheapest way to break that is for one of them to stop calling
it. **Flip**: `Stroke::NONE` in the extracted helper is red.

*(§9.4's numeric-field family gains a paragraph naming the helper and what it deliberately does not
strip. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S18.1-L3-06]`.)*

**D722 — A disabled cell was a keyboard tab stop that could not be activated, on the argument that it
might carry a tooltip nothing can hang. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S18.2-L3-04]`. `ui::segmented_enabled` registered **every** cell with `Sense::click()`, disabled
ones included, and the only reason its comment gave was *"so the cell can carry a tooltip explaining
why it is unavailable"*. **No caller can carry that tooltip**: the function returns `Option<usize>`,
the per-cell `Response` is a local that never escapes, and `paint` is handed a `&Painter` rather than
a response. There is one production caller with disabled cells (`picker::picker_body`), it hangs
none, and `ui::segmented` passes `|_| true` so it has no disabled cells at all. *An affordance the
signature cannot deliver is not a reason; it is a plan nobody wrote down as one.*

🚨 **What the registration bought instead is a tab stop that swallows Return and Space and offers
neither the click nor the explanation.** `Sense::click()` is `CLICK | FOCUSABLE` — which
`ui::focus_ring`'s own ⚠️ states from the other side, *"every hand-rolled control in this app is
already focusable … whether or not anyone meant it to be"*, and which §9.4 records again at §15 D290
for the value field's strip and unit. **The same egui fact, read for the third time, and the first two
readings were both about not creating a stop by accident.**

A disabled cell now senses `Sense::hover()`, which **is** `Sense::empty()` (§15 D688): the rect stays
claimed, so the cell still reports hover for the ground and for any future tooltip, and it takes
neither focus nor click. ⚠️ **Still registered rather than not sensed at all**, because dropping the
`interact` would take the hover the ground is drawn from with it. If the tooltip is ever wanted, the
change is to hand `paint` the response — **widening the signature is the honest way to offer it, and
a sense nobody can read is not.**

⚠️ **The bargain the doc describes is otherwise unchanged and is cited elsewhere correctly.** §9.4
records it at §15 D134 — a slot that cannot hold a gradient keeps its tabs rather than losing them —
and the inspector's layout-grid row cites *"`ui::segmented_enabled`'s bargain"* for its dimmed margin
and gutter fields, quoting only the visible-but-unavailable half. That half was true and stays true;
it is the tooltip clause that was never cashed.

**Test**: `ui::segmented_disabled_tests`, counting **tab stops** rather than naming cell 1 — naming it
would mean copying `segmented_enabled`'s id formula into the test, and an assertion that copies a
formula goes vacuously green the day the formula changes. ⚠️ **Flip-checked twice, and the *control*
is the one that earned its place**: restoring `Sense::click()` for both cells is red at the second
assertion, 3 against 2; dropping to `Sense::hover()` for **both** — the over-broad reading of the fix
— is red at the *first*, 0 against 3, the whole control becoming unreachable from the keyboard.
Without that fixture line the second flip is green, which is the finding this pair actually makes: the
assertion that says what must **stay** reachable is the one a plausible wrong fix trips.

*(§9.4's `segmented_enabled` passage gains the sense. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes
`[S18.2-L3-04]`.)*

**D721 — A group separator was one *device* pixel where every other hairline in the chrome is one
*point*. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — the alternative is named, and overruling it is one
constant.***

`[S18.1-L3-04]`. `ui::menu_sep` painted `1.0 / ppp` **points** — exactly one device pixel — where its
own doc says *"**1pt** of `text_a(20)`"* and, two paragraphs down, *"the rule stays 1pt and only the
air moved"*, where `ui::MENU_SEP_H` allocates `1.0 + SEP_AIR * 2.0`, and where §9.4 carried the same
pair of sentences. Measured out of `FullOutput::shapes`: **1.0 pt at ppp 1.0, 0.667 at 1.5, 0.5 at
2.0.** The doc was true at 100% and at no other scale.

🚨 **The cost is a comparison inside one card.** `ui::MENU_BORDER` is a 1-*point* stroke around the
very frame the separator sits inside, five points away — and so are `ui::field_frame`'s,
`ui::button_face`'s, `ui::SEGMENT_BORDER` and `inspector::popup_rule`, which is this same separator
one menu over. All five verified as `1.0` rather than taken from the finding. **At 200% a group rule
was half the weight of its own card's border; at 300%, a third.**

⚠️ **It was the only *chrome* hairline denominated in device pixels, and the qualifier is
load-bearing.** `grid::draw_pixel_grid`'s line is `1.0 / ppp` on purpose — one device pixel *is* its
subject, and §9.4 says so — and `picker`'s two `1.0 / ppp` are **insets**, not weights. A future sweep
unifying widths must not take any of the three.

⚠️ **The snapping was never the defect and is kept.** The doc argues for it — *"a 1pt rule landing on
a half pixel is the one width where the rounding shows as a colour change rather than a position
change"* — and it is the only technique in that file crisp at every scale. What was wrong is the
**width**. The rule is now `round(ppp).max(1.0)` device pixels: a *nominal* point, snapped, which is
what the doc's two sentences mean together. ⚠️ **That arithmetic is not new here** —
`layers::snap_across` computes the drop line's width as `(width * ppp).round().max(1.0) / ppp`, which
is this expression with the nominal passed in — so the separator is joining a form the app already
had rather than inventing one.

🚨 **At ppp 1.5 that is 1.333pt rather than 1.0, and the finding's own suggested assertion — *"equals
`MENU_BORDER` at ppp ∈ {1, 1.5, 2}"* — would fail on it. This is a choice and not the finding's.**
Painting exactly 1.0pt there covers 1.5 device rows: half a row of partial coverage, which is
precisely the smear the paragraph above exists to avoid. **A third of a point heavy and crisp beats
exact and smeared**, and it errs toward the rule being *seen*, which is the whole reason a separator
is here rather than more air. *The alternative is a bare `1.0`, one constant and one paragraph, and it
is the maintainer's to take if the extra weight at 150% ever reads wrong on screen.*

⚠️ **`MENU_SEP_H` does not move and must not.** `menu::height` sums it *before* the menu is on screen,
because `ui::menu_place` flips and clamps against a size it does not yet have, and
`a_menus_computed_height_is_the_height_it_paints` is the other half of that guarantee. The rule
growing from 0.5pt to 1.333pt at ppp 1.5 stays well inside the 7pt already allocated, and
`the_rule_still_fits_the_height_the_menu_reserved_for_it` is the assertion that says so rather than
leaving it to be noticed. That test still passes unchanged.

**Tests**: two, in `ui::hairline_weight_tests`. ⚠️ **Flip-checked in both directions and each bites a
different assertion**, which is what says the three assertions ask three questions: restoring
`1.0 / ppp` fails the *nominal-point* one (0.667pt = 1 device pixel where a nominal point snaps to 2),
and painting a bare `1.0` fails the *whole-device-pixels* one at `1.4999996`. The middle assertion —
at least one device pixel — bit under neither and is kept anyway, being the one that would catch a
future weight derived from a smaller nominal.

*(§9.4's `menu_sep` passage amended: it asserted 1pt and then recorded the code as one device pixel
with the disagreement parked. `roadmap.md`'s *"Two chrome hairlines"* entry is **edited down rather
than struck** — the `rulers::snap_across_axis` **base** half is untouched and still open, and it now
moves the pixel grid as well as the guides (§15 D484). Closes `[S18.1-L3-04]`.)*

**D720 — Turning web fonts off did not reach the fetch that was already out. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-10; Keep — the queued warm is the standing residual.***

`[S21-L5-06]`. §15 D330's promise is *"off means no request leaves the machine"*, and §5.4a states it
as a switch with two doors to close. There is a third, and it is the one nothing could see from
either door: `fonts::spawn_catalog`'s thread captured a `Receiver`, an `Agent`, a path and a
`Context`, and nothing cancellable. A user who turned the switch off while that thread was inside
`fetch_catalog` still had **two** calls go to `api.fontsource.org` — the list endpoint and the
variable-axes endpoint — still had `catalog.json` written to their disk, and still had the entries
merged into `self.catalog`, all of it after they had said no.

`FontService::catalog_live: Arc<AtomicBool>` is the cancel, passed into `spawn_catalog` and read
twice: immediately before `fetch_catalog`, and **again before `write_catalog`**. The disk copy above
those checks is sent either way, because reading a file this app already wrote is not a request
leaving the machine.

**The second check is the half that matters.** `fetch_catalog` blocks, so the whole window this
closes is the one where the user turns the switch off *while it is out*; a version that asked only
on the way in would close the window nobody is in. Coming back to write `catalog.json` and merge the
entries after a cancel is the request having left the machine **and left something behind**.

🚨 **One flag per spawn rather than one on the service, and the first version of this fix got it
wrong in the direction that looks obviously right.** `self.catalog_live.store(on, …)` is one line
and reads as the whole of it — and it writes `true` back into the flag the *cancelled* thread is
still holding. A thread blocked inside `fetch_catalog` across an off-then-on then returns, reads
`true`, and writes the response the user cancelled: the fix reintroducing the race its own doc
comment described. Each thread instead holds a flag that only ever goes `false`. `set_web_fonts`
cancels on the off path; on the on path it either allocates a **fresh** flag with the thread it
spawns, or — when the catalog is still in memory, which is the common case — spawns nothing and
leaves the old flag cancelled where it is.

**What caught it was the assertion that holds the old handle after the service's field has
legitimately moved on.** The first two assertions were green against the broken version. *A guard
that is correct in the direction you were thinking about is not a guard*, and the direction nobody
thinks about here is the second click.

⚠️ **It does not interrupt a `ureq` call in flight, and nothing in this crate can.** What it
guarantees is that the *result* is dropped rather than written or merged, and that the second of the
two calls is never made. One already-open socket is the residual, bounded by one request, and that
is stated at the field rather than left to be discovered.

🚨 **A false comment corrected, and it is this round's *count in prose* shape.** `prefetch_popular`'s
doc said the queued warm was *"**the one hole** in D330's 'off means no request leaves the machine'"*.
It was not: the catalog thread was a second, and the more visible one — it talks to
`api.fontsource.org` rather than to the CDN, and it **writes to the user's disk**. Closing it makes
the old sentence true again *by arithmetic*, which is exactly how it would go wrong the next time
somebody adds a caller, so it is written as a **rule** instead: the hole is *requests already queued
or already in flight when the switch is turned off*, the queued warm is the only one left, and
anything new that reaches the network must either be startable only while the switch is on or hold a
cancel flag the way `spawn_catalog` does. `grep -n 'agent' crates/ondin-app/src/fonts/mod.rs` is the
enumeration, in place of a number. **D330's *"two doors"* paragraph and D352's *"one hole"* paragraph
both carried the same claim and both are amended.**

⚠️ **The queued warm stays open on purpose.** `set_web_fonts` does not drain the queue, so up to
fifty prefetch jobs can still go out after the switch is off; the fix wants `queue` to grow a drain
operation nothing else needs, which is a change to the queue's interface for one caller. Bounded and
brief, and now the only one.

**Test**: `fonts::turning_web_fonts_off_cancels_a_catalog_fetch_that_is_already_out`.
⚠️ **The finding rated this *"hard to write honestly without a network seam"* and proposed saying so
rather than asserting — and the cancel flag *is* the seam.** What the test asserts is the thing
`spawn_catalog` actually reads, not that a socket was or was not opened, which nothing here can see.
No thread is started anywhere in it: `FontService::inert` starts none, and `set_web_fonts(true, …)`
spawns only when the catalog is empty, which the fixture's is not. **Flip**, run: `if !on { … }` back
to `store(on, …)` is red at the third assertion and green at the other two, which is what says this
test is not a restatement of the switch test above it.
