*(§5.4a's switch bullet gains the third door and its prefetch bullet's hole is restated as a rule.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: the queued warm is a named residual inside this entry rather than
an open item, and a decided residual with its fix written down is a §15 clause. Closes
`[S21-L5-06]`.)*

**D719 — An unedited *Edit project* card rewrote `projects.json` and rescanned the whole library.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — folding both project cards onto `settings::modal_footer` is the
remaining half.***

`[S20.3-L3-06]`. `panels::dashboard::EditProject::of` seeds the card from the project as it stands,
so opening *Edit project* and clicking **Save changes** — or pressing Enter, which is gated on the
same predicate the button was — reached `OndinApp::save_project` with every field equal to what was
already stored. It ran anyway: `save_projects()` rewrote `projects.json`, `reload_projects()` re-read
it, and `refresh()` **rescanned the whole library**, a price `refresh`'s own comment accepts on the
assumption that something moved.

⚠️ **The failure is the message, not the wasted work.** If that write fails, the user is told *"Could
not write projects.json"* about a change they did not make — and `may_write_projects` cannot prevent
it, having passed a moment earlier, so a sync client holding the file for a second is enough.

🚨 **That alarm reaches the user *because* `[S20.1-L1-01]` was fixed, which is the opposite of the way
the finding frames it.** That finding is the one about the library screen writing 22 status messages
and painting none of them; §15 D426 gave the screen a status line of its own. So the channel is not
invisible any more, and a spurious *"Could not write projects.json"* now lands where it would once
have been swallowed. **A citation to a *fixed* finding still resolves, and it reads as though the old
state held** — which is the same trap `[S16.3-L2-06]` set in session 18, met here in a premise rather
than in a fix sketch.

`EditProject::differs_from` is the guard, written directly under `of` as its mirror so the two stay
one: every field `of` copies as *content* is compared, `id` being identity and `name_focused` a caret
latch. ⚠️ **`name` is compared trimmed, because that is what gets written** — `save_project` stores
`ep.name.trim()`, so a name gaining a trailing space is not an edit, and comparing untrimmed would
relight the button for a keystroke that changes nothing on disk.

**Two askers, one statement.** `save_project` refuses the write however the card was dismissed, which
is `set_archived`'s `if p.archived == archived { return; }` asked of the whole card rather than of one
field; and the footer dims *Save changes* on the same predicate, so the refusal is drawn as well as
performed. The button is not the thing under test: Enter reaches the write through a different door,
and a card that opened before another window changed the project would be dirty at draw time and
clean by the time it committed.

🚨 **A false doc claim corrected in the same pass, and it is G20's shape.** `library_settings_modal`'s
doc says the two cards *"are now the same card: … same footer with the commit lit only when the draft
differs from what is saved"* (§15 D368). *"The two"* is Settings and Settings —
`new_project_modal` and `edit_project_modal` each hand-roll their footer rather than calling
`settings::modal_footer`, so *"same footer"* has never been true of them. **The same control written
three times is how the rule that matters came to be in only one of them.** The two now agree about
the *rule* and still not about the footer. *Fix by folding both project cards onto `modal_footer`*: a
layout change rather than a behavioural one, and unfixed.

**Test**: `panels::dashboard::a_card_with_nothing_edited_neither_writes_nor_rescans`, with
**`projects.json`'s mtime as the witness**, which is what the finding asked for — the record is
identical either way, so an assertion on the projects list is green through the bug. The stamp is set
a minute back rather than read and compared, because whole-second mtimes make *"was this rewritten in
the same second"* a coin toss; that is `recovery`'s intermittent-red lesson borrowed. Both ends are
asserted together, since a `save_project` that refused *everything* would pass the first half alone.
⚠️ **The fixture assertion caught a wrong premise**: `seed` pushes into memory and writes nothing, so
the test has to `save_projects()` once before there is a file to watch at all. **Flip**, run:
disabling the `differs_from` guard in `save_project` is red at the first mtime assertion.

*(§9.5's *Edit project* paragraph gains the rule. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: the shared-footer
remainder is a decided route with a named fix and belongs here, where an item in that file would be a
second copy of it. Closes `[S20.3-L3-06]`.)*

**D718 — A rule stated in the imperative, with no test caller, beside the same shape with five.
*Tested 2026-09-10; Keep — this entry records the rule, it does not change it.***

`[S6.3-L6-05]`. No production change. `panels::typography::step_length` moves a `Length` by one press
of `Alt+←`/`→` or `Alt+↑`/`↓`, and its doc states a rule outright: *"A chord must not silently convert
the value: a tracking of `2%` nudged up stays a percentage, and one of `0.4px` stays absolute.
Converting would make the same key mean different things depending on a unit chip the user set
deliberately, and would strand the value the next time the font size changed."* It had **zero** test
callers workspace-wide.

🚨 **The finding predicted the flip would come back green and it did.** Rewriting the `Em` arm as
`Length::Px(v + d * em)` — precisely the silent conversion the doc forbids, and the slip a careless
edit makes — left the whole workspace at exit 0. One `Alt+→` on a `2%` tracking would have stored
`0.01px` and flipped the field's unit chip under the user's hand, with every gate green.

⚠️ **The contrast is the finding rather than a decoration.**
`next_line_height` is free, pure, `Copy` in and `Copy` out — the shape §15 D269 says to lift a
decision into, precisely so a test can reach it — and it has five callers in the test directly above
this one. Two functions of the same shape on the same type, one covered five times over and one not
at all. *Being the ideal test subject is not the same as being tested*, and the two sitting side by
side is what makes that legible rather than arguable.

**Test**: `panels::typography::a_chord_steps_a_length_without_changing_its_unit` — the doc's own two
examples, a step down across zero where a sign slip would show, leading's constants through the same
function, and a step of zero as the identity. The step **sizes** are asserted with the unit because
they are the other half of the same promise: `TRACKING_STEP_PX` is a tenth of `TRACKING_STEP_EM`'s
magnitude on purpose, px tracking being a fine adjustment where em tracking is a coarse one, so a
test that checked only the *unit* would pass against arms that had swapped their step constants.
**Flip**, run: the finding's own mutation is red at the first assertion, `Px(0.03)` against
`Em(0.03)`.

⚠️ **The finding names two more items with no test caller and only one of them still has none.**
`optional_length_field` has none, and that is left open. **`Bounds` does** — 
`both_ends_of_every_length_field_bound_the_same_quantity` drives `Bounds::TRACKING`,
`Bounds::SIGNED_TRACKING` and `Bounds::px` at three font sizes, and its own doc states its scope,
including that it does *not* reach `optional_length_field`, `length_field` or
`type_line_height_field`, each of which calls `px_range_for` inline. **A finding's list of uncovered
items is a claim about the day it was written**, and this one had been half-closed by a §15 D546-era
test before it was ranked.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §5.4's `Length` rules are about the model and the unit chip,
and the chord's unit discipline is a panel rule that lives on the function. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`. Closes `[S6.3-L6-05]`.)*

**D717 — Five lines of a function's doc filed under a string constant, and the stolen sentence was an
instruction. *Corrected 2026-09-10; Keep.***

`[S23.1-L3-06]`. In `panels::picker`, the five lines describing `picker_window` were stacked at the
**bottom** of `WINDOW_NAME`'s own doc comment with no blank `///` between the two. So a `&str`
constant claimed to be *"the picker's window, minus its position and its contents"* and to be
*"shared with the test below"*; `WINDOW_NAME`'s real summary line — the one rustdoc uses — was buried
mid-paragraph; and `picker_window` documented itself nowhere. ⚠️ **`pub(super) fn layer_id` sits
between the two and kept its own doc**, which is what makes the boundary hard to see on a read: the
file looks like three well-documented items and is two.

🚨 **What it cost is that the stolen sentence is an *instruction*.** *"A test that rebuilt it would
keep passing after someone removed the line it exists to defend"* tells a maintainer not to inline
`picker_window` into `the_picker_opens_where_it_was_spawned_on_the_very_first_frame` — the very
edit somebody reaching for tidiness would make — and it was filed under a string constant, where that
person would never meet it. **A stolen doc comment is not merely misfiled: it is invisible to the
person changing the thing it describes** — `CLAUDE.md`'s *Editing files* list records the instance
that proved it, where a paragraph filed under the wrong name was still asserting a claim a fix had
falsified an hour earlier.

⚠️ **Both detectors were blind and would be again.** The merged run is far under the length ranking's
floor, so that sweep cannot reach it; and the neighbour grep asks *"did the item below lose its
comment"*, which `layer_id` — the item immediately below — had not. This is the same shape as the
duplication cases: nothing lost anything, so the check that looks for a victim answers no.

⚠️ **No ordinal is written into the repair.** The finding's title gives one, and that is the review's
count on the day it was written, where `CLAUDE.md`'s *Editing files* list is the running tally. **A
position in a tally is a count in prose**, so the corrected doc points at that list — and at the two
checks that find these — rather than restating a number that goes stale the next time one is found.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which does not describe this file's internals; nothing struck
from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S23.1-L3-06]`.)*

**D716 — Two "I do not know" sentinels that read as "delete it". *Fixed and tested 2026-09-10;
Keep.***

`[S1.2-L1-06]`. `library::recovery::pending` had two I/O sentinels, both written the unsafe way
round, and on the other side of the branch both of them guard is the **permanent deletion of the
user's only unsaved copy**. `app::open_at_launch` runs this over the whole of `.recovery/`, which
means immediately after a crash, at the one moment the folder's contents matter most.

- `modified_secs` ended `.unwrap_or(0)`. Zero is not a neutral value here, it is *the beginning of
  time*: an unreadable or pre-epoch stamp became `written = 0`, `entry.modified > written` held
  trivially, and the branch `remove_file`d the snapshot. **A sentinel meaning "unknown" read as
  "older than everything."** It returns `Option<u64>` now, so `None` settles nothing in either
  direction and the byte comparison decides.
- `identical` was `read(&entry.path).ok() == read(&path).ok()`. Two `None`s compare **equal**, so one
  lock catching both files in a single antivirus or sync sweep read as *byte-identical* and deleted
  the snapshot. It requires `(Ok, Ok)` now.

🚨 **The two branches sat eight lines apart disagreeing about what an unreadable file means.** Five
lines below them, `scan::read_meta(&path)` answering `None` for the identical reason `continue`s and
deletes **nothing**. The comment on the byte test called the two-`None` case *"the right answer by
luck and by intent: neither file can be read, so there is nothing to offer either way"* — which is
true only if deleting is not part of the answer, and it was. **One function, one kind of failure,
two opposite conclusions, neither of them wrong on its own terms.**

**`Pending::written` is an `Option<u64>` and the recovery card drops its time clause rather than
inventing one.** The *"has changes from {} that were never saved"* label loses *"from N hours ago"*
and keeps every word the user acts on. The two available fudges are both lies they would act on: `0`
reads as *"56 years ago"* and `now` reads as *"just now"* about a file that may be a week old. That
is an omission and not a copy decision — the label is the only user-visible half of this entry, and
it is recorded here so the next reader knows the missing clause is deliberate.

**Test**: `recovery::a_snapshot_with_an_unreadable_stamp_is_offered_rather_than_deleted`, stamping
the snapshot to `UNIX_EPOCH − 1s` — `duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)` is `Err` for it, which is the same
door an unreadable `modified()` comes through and the one of the two that can be arranged portably.
⚠️ **The fixture edits the document's `meta.name` after filing so the two files differ**, and that is
load-bearing: written the obvious way, with the snapshot a copy of what was filed, it is deleted for
the **right** reason and stays green straight through the bug. It asserts the two files differ before
asking `pending` anything. **Flip**, run: restoring `unwrap_or(0)` is red at *"an undatable snapshot
must not be deleted — this is the user's only copy of work that never reached the file"*, which is
the loss stated before the report.

⚠️ **The `identical` half is closed by construction and is not staged**, and saying so plainly is
better than implying coverage: it needs two simultaneous read failures on two named files, which no
portable fixture arranges. The control for it is the existing byte-equality assertion in
`a_snapshot_older_than_its_document_is_dropped_rather_than_offered`, which says the comparison still
drops a snapshot the document really does contain.

*(§9.5's crash-recovery paragraph gains the rule that neither sentinel may decide to delete. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S1.2-L1-06]`.)*

**D715 — Every refusal out of `atomic::write` named neither the file nor the step. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-10; Keep — and the finding's headline had already been closed by §15 D548.***

`[S1.2-L1-08]`. An `io::Error` carries a *kind* and a sentence and **no path**. `atomic::write` has
four failure points and returned all four bare, so `OndinApp::save_file`'s
`format!("Save failed: {e}")` reached the status line as *"Save failed: Access is denied. (os error
5)"* — naming neither the file nor which step was refused, on a message whose whole job is to be
acted on. `atomic::at` wraps each with the step and the path and keeps `kind()`.

🚨 **The finding's headline is closed and by another entry, and that is recorded here rather than
quietly dropped.** `[S1.2-L1-08]` is about a stale `.writing` that another process holds open making
`File::create` fail *forever*. **§15 D548 removed that mechanism**: `temp_for` appends
`<pid>-<counter>`, so the name a write is about to create has never existed, and
`two_writes_of_one_path_get_different_temp_files` pins it. The finding was taken at a SHA before D548
and its measurement was correct then.

🚨 **What survives is wider than the finding's own fix sketch, and that is the lesson worth carrying
past this entry.** The sketch asks for the **temp** path in the message. The step reachable today is
the **rename** — refused by a destination something else holds open, which is a sync client or an
indexer on the user's own `.ondin` rather than on a leftover — and the path worth printing there is
the *destination*, the file the user has heard of. Flip-checked: removing the rename's `map_err` and
leaving the three temp-file steps wrapped is red at the same assertion. **So the sketch, followed
literally, would have left the one case a user actually reaches as unattributable as it was.** *A fix
sketch written against the mechanism that was reachable when it was written is not a sketch of the
fix once another entry has closed that mechanism.*

⚠️ **`Error::new` keeps `kind()` and drops `raw_os_error()`.** Nothing in `crates/` reads either off
a save — checked rather than assumed: `raw_os_error` appears nowhere, and the only `ErrorKind`
matches in the workspace are `NotFound` on *reads* in `prefs::load_from`, `library::cache` and
`library::project::read`, plus `Interrupted` in `scan`. The kind is preserved because it is the half
a caller would plausibly classify on, and the raw code is already inside the message text the OS
wrote.

**The verbs are the four steps rather than the four function names** — a user reads *"could not
replace"*, not *"rename failed"* — and `flush` is `sync_all`, which is the durability barrier rather
than a buffer flush and is the word that means anything outside that module.

**Test**: `atomic::a_refused_write_names_the_file_it_could_not_write`, staged with a read-only
destination, which is the same portable lock `a_failed_write_leaves_the_old_file_intact` uses.
**Asserted on the substring and on the kind rather than on the whole sentence**, because the OS's
text differs by platform and locale and pinning it would make this a test of Windows' phrasing.

*(§9.5's atomic-write paragraph gains the message rule. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes
`[S1.2-L1-08]`, whose headline D548 had already closed.)*

**D714 — `Basis::of` was total, lossy, and had no way to say which of the two it was being. *Fixed
and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — and two doors onto the same loss are still open.***

`[S13.1-L1-07]`. `build::Basis::of` splits a transform's basis into the orientation a node may store
and the scale its geometry takes (§5.6). `Orientation::to_affine` is `R · skewX · mirror`, whose
determinant is always ±1, so `orientation · diag(sx, sy)` can produce a second column of **zero** and
nothing else once `sy` is zero. A **rank-1** basis has a second column that is emphatically not zero
— `[1, 2, 2, 4]`'s is `(2, 4)` — so **no return value of `of` could have been exact for one, and the
function had no way to say so.** It returned something plausible and the caller believed it:
`tools::rotate_node` on that transform wrote `R(63.43°)` with `csy = 0`, `tools::scale_geometry`
turned that zero into `(40 · 0).max(1.0)`, and a 40×40 rect came out **1 unit tall at 63°**, from one
turn.

🚨 **It is representability, not float error, and that is exactly why the non-finite family never saw
it.** Every number in that sequence is finite. `build::affine_is_finite` is happy, `OpError::NonFinite`
is happy, `Document::apply` stores it, the file saves and reopens, and all six gates are green — the
loss is a shape, not a `NaN`. D421's guards answer *"will `serde_json` write this"*; this answers
*"can the pair I am about to return be multiplied back into the matrix I was given"*, and nothing in
the tree had ever asked it.

`Basis::exact(transform) -> Option<Self>` is the half that can refuse, sitting beside `of` in
`build.rs`. `tools::split_geometry_scale` answers `Option<(Affine, f64, f64)>` now and routes through
it, and all six of its call sites refuse **per node** — `return Transaction(…)` where the caller is a
single-node verb, `continue` where it is a loop over a selection.

**The second degenerate arm is the one a reader misses**, and it is why `exact` refuses on both of
`of`'s rather than only on the rank-1 case. `Affine::scale(1e-13)` is invertible in principle and
falls under `of`'s `DEGENERATE` floor of `1e-12`, so `of` reports `sx = 0` with an *identity*
orientation — a real scale read back as no scale at all. Under `Scaling::Photographic` that makes
`s = sqrt(0 · sy) = 0` and zeroes every stroke width in the node.

⚠️ **The threshold is deliberately not restated at the guard.** `exact` reads `basis.scale.x` and
`basis.scale.y` — the very numbers `of`'s two degenerate arms tested — instead of recomputing `sx`
and `sy` beside them, so the guard cannot drift away from the arms it guards. That is this round's
*one rule, more than one implementation* shape refused in advance rather than filed later. A
non-finite input makes both comparisons false through `NaN` anyway, and `affine_is_finite` is spelled
regardless, because relying on that is a subtlety rather than an argument.

**Refusing per node is §15 D481's answer one function up, and the two now live side by side.**
`tools::scaled_about` catches a basis whose product overflows to `inf`; this catches one that is
entirely finite and cannot be represented as `orientation × scale`. §6.2's rule is the argument for
the shape in both: a missing edit is recoverable and a lying one is not, so the member that cannot
take the gesture is left exactly where it was and the rest of the selection still moves. The two test
modules are siblings — `tools::overflow_tests` and `tools::unrepresentable_basis_tests` — for that
reason, and a reader who finds one should read the other.

🚨 **Three sentences claiming exactness for every matrix were corrected, and the third is the finding
in miniature.** `split_geometry_scale`'s doc said *"exact for every matrix"*. The core test
`a_basis_splits_into_a_storable_orientation_and_a_scale` opened *"The split is exact for every
matrix"* and drove only invertible cases, so nothing under that heading could ever have disagreed
with it. And two tests above it in the same file,
`a_collapsed_basis_decomposes_to_numbers_not_nan` says outright that *"exactness is not on offer here
— a matrix that has lost a dimension cannot be rebuilt from anything"* **and drives
`Affine::new([1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 0.0, 0.0])`, a rank-1 basis.** The contradiction sat forty lines
apart in one file, both halves green, for as long as both tests existed. **A file that states a rule
and its own counter-example is not a file anything will flag** — the two tests are about different
questions, so neither is wrong, and only reading them together says the caller had no way to tell
which regime it was in.

🚨 **The design did *not* have the narrow wording, which is the correction to the framing this fix
was written under.** §5.7a does say *"every invertible 2×2 factors uniquely"* — and then throws the
word away in the next clause: *"four degrees of freedom for a four-coefficient matrix, so it is exact
for any matrix whatsoever, not just the ones a well-behaved editor produces."* §5.6's group-resize
bullet had the same generalisation with no qualifier at all (*"exact for any matrix whatever"*). So
this was not the code dropping a word the design still held; **the design stated the correct premise
and drew the wrong conclusion from it in the following sentence, and the code was faithful to the
conclusion.** Both passages are amended, and the arithmetic — a four-coefficient matrix has four
degrees of freedom only when it has four *independent* ones — is now written where the wrong
inference was made, because that inference is the thing a future editor would make again.

🚨 **`Basis::of` deliberately keeps its lossy arms, and two callers that should not have them are
left open.** `of` is total on purpose: the inspector's angle and scale readouts want a *number* for a
collapsed node — 0° rather than a blank — and `Orientation::of` and `shared_angle` are pure reporting.
But `inspector::multi_angle_tx` and the **skew** half of `inspector::inspector_transform` do not
report: they rebuild a whole transform as `orientation · diag(scale.x, scale.y)` from a lossy split
and commit it through `place_at` → `build::place_at_world`, which never touches
`split_geometry_scale` and so never meets this guard. On a rank-1 node the rebuilt second column is
zero where the stored one is `(2, 4)`, and `multi_angle_tx` is reachable **without an edit at all** —
its own comment records that a field losing focus arrives as a nudge of zero, and a nudge of zero on
such a node still produces a transform that differs from the stored one and is therefore pushed. The
rotation half of the single-layer panel is safe by a different mechanism and not by luck:
`turned_about` *composes* onto `Affine::new(world)` rather than rebuilding from the split (§15 D206),
which is exact under any basis. ⚠️ **The comment on the unguarded rebuild is a fourth copy of the
false sentence** — *"the residual `Basis::of` reports is multiplied back on — which is what makes the
round trip exact for any matrix at all"* — sitting on the one path that is not guarded, which is the
worst place for it to be. *Fix: route both through `Basis::exact` and decide what a refused skew or
multi-angle edit shows.* It is left open because the answer is a **UI** question this entry has no
standing to settle — a field that silently declines to write is not obviously better than one that is
dimmed or absent, and the single-node verbs `split_geometry_scale` guards had no such field to
answer for.

**Test**: `build::an_unrepresentable_basis_is_refused_rather_than_approximated` in
`ondin-core/tests/build.rs` for the predicate — rank-1, the `1e-13` arm, a `NaN`, and a control loop
re-driving the exactness test's own cases so this is not a guard that simply refuses everything — and
`tools::unrepresentable_basis_tests::a_rank_one_member_is_left_alone_rather_than_collapsed` for the
behaviour. **The fixture is asserted singular first**, because a merely unusual transform splits fine
and the gesture *should* rewrite it.

⚠️ **Flipped twice, separately, and the reason is worth carrying past this entry.** Putting
`Basis::of` back inside `split_geometry_scale` fails on the **first** assertion, with the defect in
the message — `SetGeometry { geometry: Size(89.44W × 1.0H) }` — and **aborts there**, so the
`continue` arm at `resize_selection` is never reached by it. A second flip restoring the old splitter
at that one call site is what fails on *"the rank-1 member is untouched"*. 🚨 **Where a test asserts
two consumers of one function, flipping the function proves only the first**; the second consumer
needs a flip at its own call site, and the obvious single flip reads as though it had covered both.
⚠️ `skew_to_handle` was the first choice for that second consumer and is the wrong one — it returns
early when `side_shear` answers `None`, so the assertion would have been green either way.

*(§5.6's group-resize bullet and §5.7a's RQ paragraph are amended — both stated exactness for *any*
matrix, and §5.7a's is the sentence the code was faithful to. §9.4's `scaled_about` paragraph gains
the sibling refusal. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: neither the exactness claim nor the split's
refusal is open work there, and the two `Basis::of` rewrite sites above belong here rather than
there, because a decided open route with a named fix is a §15 clause and an item in that file would
be a second copy of it. Closes `[S13.1-L1-07]`.)*

**D713 — A safety argument that enumerated its producers, in a field that had gained a second one.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-10; Keep — and the loader's half was ruled on at D762, against
normalising.***

`[S23.2-L1-02]`. `panels::paint`'s four gradient-geometry accessors speak the shape's space and the
brush's geometry may not, so a reader maps forward through `GradientBrush::transform` and a writer
maps back through its inverse (§15 D412, §9.2). The constant that carries that rule,
`_GRADIENT_GEOMETRY_IS_IN_SHAPE_SPACE`, closed with: *"The inverse is safe because `svg_in` only
stores a transform whose smaller singular value exceeds `1e-9` (`Paint::squashed_radial`), so the
determinant is bounded away from zero."* **That is true of `svg_in` and false of the field.**

The field has a second producer. `GradientBrush::transform` is `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if
= "is_identity")]`, nothing in `io` validates it, and so any six numbers in a `.ondin` become the
transform. A **singular** matrix is *finite*, so `build::brush_is_finite` — which asks
`affine_is_finite(g.transform)` — accepts it at the op boundary and stores it. `Affine::inverse`
divides by the determinant, so `with_linear_angle` and `with_radial_centre` then wrote `NaN` into
every endpoint; measured, both returned `[(NaN, NaN), (NaN, NaN)]`. `serde_json` writes `NaN` as
`null`, and the next load answers *"invalid type: null, expected f64"*. **One bare click in the
picker's `CX` field turns a document that opened a moment ago into one that never opens again** —
invariant 8's terminal failure arriving through a door invariant 8's own predicate holds open.

`build::affine_is_invertible(t)` is `affine_is_finite(t) && affine_is_finite(t.inverse())`, and both
writers ask it and return the brush untouched when the answer is no. A gradient whose space has
collapsed to a line has no centre and no angle to address, so doing nothing is the honest answer, and
`Transaction::changes_nothing` (§15 D428) keeps it off the undo stack.

**Threshold-free, and that is the choice rather than an accident of spelling.** This tree already
carries four different guards asking "is this affine safe to invert" and no two are alike:
`determinant().abs() > 1e-12` and `determinant() == 0.0 || !finite` in `svg_in`,
`determinant().abs() < f64::EPSILON` and `!det.is_finite() || det == 0.0` in the SVG writer. Every
one of them is an argument about an epsilon nobody can defend, and a fifth would have been a fifth
number to defend. The question the *caller* has is *"will the inverse be representable"*, so that is
the question the predicate asks — no constant to tune, right by construction rather than by choosing
a number small enough. ⚠️ **The four is a measurement and not a gate**; the site says to re-run
`grep -rn 'determinant' crates/ --include=*.rs` rather than to trust it, most of whose hits are prose
or an area measure.

⚠️ **All four call `affine_is_invertible` since 2026-09-15** (§15 D762), so this paragraph is history
rather than a description of the tree. Two corrections came with them. ***"No two are alike"*
overstates by one**: `svg_in`'s transform fold and the SVG writer's `sweep_radius` are the same test
with the operands reversed, in two crates — which is worse than four different opinions, being one
opinion nobody knew was shared. And **the `f64::EPSILON` guard was not an indefensible epsilon, it
was a category error**: ≈2.22e-16 is a *relative* quantity, the gap between 1.0 and the next double,
where a determinant is in *squared world units*, so it stopped guarding at large coordinates
altogether. *A number chosen because it is spelled like a small number.*

🚨 **And this entry's own revisit trigger had already fired on the day it was written, which is the
sharpest thing on it.** *"Revisit when a second reader wants an inverse"* — `svg::sweep_radius` is a
**third** inverting reader of `GradientBrush::transform`, it predates this entry, and **it is one of
the four guards counted two paragraphs up**. So the count that was offered as the reason to wait
contained the condition for not waiting. **An enumeration made to argue a deferral is worth reading
against the deferral's own trigger**, and nothing here could have caught it: every number resolves,
every guard is real, and the two facts are four paragraphs apart in one entry.

🚨 **The general lesson is about the *scope* of a safety argument and not about gradients.** The
sentence was correct on the day it was written and named the producer it had checked. What made it
dangerous is that it reads as a property of the **field**, so the next person to add a producer had
no reason to look at it and nothing anywhere would have told them. **An argument that enumerates its
producers is false the day a second one appears, and no gate, test or census in this project can
see it happen.** The corrected comment keeps the old sentence quoted in full, because the shape is
worth more than the correction.

⚠️ **The loader still accepts a singular gradient brush transform, deliberately, and that half is
open.** Normalising it to the identity on load would be the durable answer — it is what `svg_in`'s
`transform=` fold does for a singular `transform=` attribute — but it **silently rewrites the content
of the user's file**, which is a different kind of decision from refusing an edit and belongs to the
maintainer rather than to a fix. So `affine_is_invertible` is documented as *the guard a reader asks
before inverting, not a rule about what may be stored*, and every other reader of that field is
unguarded. *Revisit when a second reader wants an inverse* — at two, the choice is between spreading
the guard and normalising once at the door.

⚠️ **Ruled 2026-09-15 and the answer is to spread the guard** (§15 D762). The ruling also corrects
the weighing above, which understates its own case: this paragraph worries about *"silently
rewriting the content of the user's file"*, and a singular brush transform paints a **degenerate**
gradient where the identity paints the ramp across the whole shape — so normalising does not quietly
substitute one invisible thing for another, it makes an **invisible paint visible**, in artwork
nobody authored. The *"draws nothing either way"* argument borrowed from `svg_in`'s `transform=` fold
is about a matrix applied to *geometry* and does not transfer to a stored brush transform.

⚠️ **`svg_in`'s own precedent citation was looser than it read, and is corrected here.** The
`transform=` fold justified dropping a singular matrix by saying *"the identity is the same answer
`image.rs` already gives for a singular brush transform
(`degenerate_inputs_resolve_to_the_identity_framing`)"*. That test is about `ImageFit`/`Framing` — an
image brush's framing affine, which is **computed** from a frame and a source size and never stored —
so it is a precedent for *deriving* the identity rather than for normalising a stored field, and
`GradientBrush::transform` is precisely the stored field with no normalisation anywhere. Both halves
resolve and the conclusion survives; the argument for it did not. **A reference that resolves is not
a reference that agrees**, which is the third time this round that shape has been filed.

**Test**: `panels::paint::tests::a_singular_gradient_transform_is_refused_rather_than_inverted`,
driving `Affine::new([1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 4.0, 0.0, 0.0])` through both writers. **The loss is asserted
before the mechanism** — what it checks is that the geometry stays representable, not which guard
refused it — and **the fixture is pinned singular first**, because a transform that is merely unusual
is invertible and both writers are right to use it, so without that assertion the test passes against
a fixture that never reaches the bug.

*(§9.2's `paint.rs` paragraph gains the guard and invariant 8's derived-value clause gains this as
its second instance beside §15 D495's — a validated operand is still not a usable *derived* value,
and an inverse is the second way to manufacture one from numbers that all passed. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`, which carries no entry on gradient-transform validity in either direction; the loader's
open half is recorded above rather than there, because a maintainer's ruling with the options laid
out is what §15 is for. Closes `[S23.2-L1-02]`.)*

**D712 — The library's search chord answered to Alt and to Shift. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep.***

`[S20.1-L1-06]`. `dashboard::search_field`'s gate was `i.modifiers.command` alone, so
`Ctrl+Shift+K`, `Ctrl+Alt+K`, `Ctrl+Shift+P` and `Ctrl+Alt+P` each opened the library search — four
spellings `shortcuts.md` §8's dashboard row does not list, on the one chord site on this screen that
carried no exclusion. It is `command && !alt && !shift` now, which is how the screen's other
context-reading site has always spelled it.

🚨 **The reason not to was already written in the same file, and in the same `impl`.**
`dashboard_keys`' own chord gate carries it: *"Spelled the way `input::normal_mode` spells it —
`Ctrl` without Alt and without Shift — so `Ctrl+Alt+N` and `Ctrl+Shift+D` stay unbound here exactly
as they are there, rather than becoming second doors this screen invented."* **`search_field` was the
second door that comment forbids.** That is this round's recurring Low shape — *a rule stated in one
place and broken in the one beside it* — at the shortest range it has been found at, and the range is
the finding rather than a detail of it: the two gates are about 2,300 lines apart inside one `impl
OndinApp`, and **proximity is not what makes a rule hold.** A rule holds where it is *called*, and
this one was prose.

🚨 **D710 is the identical rule and could not have closed this.** That entry put `!m.shift` on eight
arms of `input::normal_mode` earlier in this same session, and none of it reaches this screen:
`input::resolve` is not called at all while the library is up — `OndinApp::ui` calls `dashboard_ui`
and **returns** before it (§9.5) — so the editor's keymap and its modifier discipline are simply not
running. **A keymap rule stated for one screen holds nothing on the other**, and this file is where
that has to be said twice on purpose. The two entries are one rule at two doors, and a reader of
either should be sent to the other; both sites say so.

⚠️ **`Ctrl+Shift+K` is bound in the editor** — *Place image* (`shortcuts.md` §8, `architecture.md`
§5.5a) — and the two screens cannot collide, for the same reason D710 could not close this. So
nothing here was a collision: what was wrong is that **one chord meant two things and only one of
them was written down**, which is the quieter half of the same defect and the half no test anywhere
would have caught.

**Test**: `panels::dashboard::tests::the_search_chord_does_not_answer_to_alt_or_shift`. **The two
bare chords are asserted first, and that ordering is what gives the rest teeth** — a "fix" that
simply deleted the chord passes every negative assertion under it, which is D542's control
assertion in the same module doing the same job. **Flip**, restoring `i.modifiers.command` alone:
red at the first `Ctrl+Shift+K` assertion, `Some("")` against `None`.

⚠️ **D542 shared the *modal* list between these two readers and not the modifier discipline, and its
entry gains a clause saying so.** `library_keys_are_free` was built to be *"what makes a ninth modal
join both readers or neither"*, and it did exactly that — it is a question about **what is on
screen**, and `search_field` calls it. The other half of `dashboard_keys`' gate is a question about
**what is held down**, and that half stayed at one site, so the two readers of one context went on
disagreeing about which spellings of one chord answer. **A predicate that closes one asymmetry
between two callers is evidence about that asymmetry and about no other.**

⚠️ **The discipline is still spelled at each site rather than named once, and that is left
deliberately.** The two callers want different answers — `dashboard_keys` reads plain keys past
`modifiers.is_none()` *and* chords above it, `search_field` reads only a chord — so a shared
predicate would have to be parameterised, and a two-caller predicate with an argument is not
obviously better than two lines that say the same thing. *Fix with a shared predicate if a third
context-reading site ever appears on this screen*: two hand-kept copies is the state D542 found the
modal list in, and the third copy is where it stopped being affordable.

⚠️ **D383 was checked and wants nothing.** Its `cmd_only && !m.shift` enumeration is about the
**editor's** `Ctrl+N` and `Ctrl+W` arms, and its dashboard half describes `modifiers.is_none()` and
the chord arm read above it — both of which were already right, this being the site D383 never
touched.

*(`shortcuts.md` §8's `Ctrl+K`/`Ctrl+P` row states the modifier discipline now, and the *Deliberately
unbound* section's `Ctrl+Shift` bullet gains the second screen. **The four spellings are deliberately
not listed there**: the rule already covers them, and a per-spelling list is the *count in prose
standing in for a gate nobody built* that this round keeps filing against itself. §9.5's
`library_keys_are_free` paragraph gains the discipline, which is the passage D710's closing note —
*"`architecture.md` … does not carry the keymap's modifier discipline"* — was right about for the
editor and would have been wrong about here. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`; the keymap's open work
is the palette and the cheatsheet, and neither is this. Closes `[S20.1-L1-06]`.)*

**D711 — An unknown family fell back to Inter's *face* and not to its *axes*. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`[S5.1-L1-06]`. `text.rs`'s module doc promises *"Unknown families fall back to Inter"*, and the
**face** did: `push_style` names `default_family` as the second entry of every run's family list, so
parley resolves the bundled Inter for a family the machine does not have. The **axes** did not.
`shape` gathered axis metadata for the families the runs *name*, so `axes_for` answered `&[]` for a
family fontique cannot find, `axis_settings` found no `OPSZ` in an empty list, no `opsz` variation
was pushed, and the face shaped at its axis default of 14 instead of the clamped 32 the same text
gets when the family is spelled `"Inter"`.

**Measured in release**, `"Hamburgefonstiv"` at 96pt: `"Inter"` gives run coords `[16384, 0]` and a
last-glyph x of **670.500**; `"NoSuchFamilyAnywhere"` gives coords `[]` and **726.609**, **8.4%
wider**, both shaped in the same bundled face. And it snaps to the narrower one the moment that
family becomes real — a font install, a web-font download landing — which is a silent reflow of a
document nobody edited, in a session where the user was told the font was absent (§5.4a's warning,
§15 D227) and not that the metrics differed from the ones on screen.

🚨 **It is the exact symptom `axis_settings`' own doc names as its reason to exist** — *"leaving it
at the axis default is what makes a 96pt heading look like blown-up body text"* — implemented for the
requested family and not for the fallback the module doc says every unknown family gets. **A rule
stated in one place and not applied on the path beside it**, which is this round's recurring Low
shape. The fix gathers `default_family` into the axis table alongside every family the runs name, and
`axes_for` answers the fallback's list for a family that is not there.

🚨 **The care is one predicate, and it is the thing a later reader will simplify.** `known` is
`engine.font_cx.collection.family_id(f).is_some()` and **not** `!axes.is_empty()`.
`family_axes_locked` answers an empty list for both of two different states — a family fontique
cannot find, and one it can find whose default face declares no axes at all — and only the first may
inherit. A bool on emptiness would push Inter's `opsz` at a **static** face the user really asked
for, which is asking for a variation that font does not carry. ⚠️ **`known` asks whether the family
is *listed*, not whether its face can be read**: `family_axes_locked` also returns an empty list when
the family resolves and its default face cannot be loaded or parsed, and that path is `known` and so
does not inherit — i.e. it reproduces this defect. Registered faces are memory blobs, so it is not
reachable today; it is where to look if it ever is.

**Test**: `text::tests::an_unknown_family_measures_the_same_as_the_fallback_it_is_shaped_in`, and
three of its choices are as much the record as the assertion. **96pt on purpose** — the defect is
optical sizing, so at body size the clamped value is near the axis default, both spellings measure
almost the same, and a 20pt fixture passes whichever way the code goes. **The width is compared
against `"Inter"`** rather than against a literal, because a number here is a measurement of the
bundled face's version and the claim is that the two spellings *agree*. **Flip**, restoring
`axes_for`'s `.unwrap_or(&[])`: fails at **780.5625 against 719.625**, 8.5% wider — *debug* numbers
against the finding's release 726.609/670.500. The absolute widths differ between profiles and the
**ratio** does not, which is the second argument for comparing the two spellings; the first assertion
is the fixture control and stays green under the flip, so the test is about the fallback rather than
about shaping at all.

🚨 **D571 says *"Inter ships no `opsz`"*, and this entry's measurement is what settles that it is
false.** The bundled `Inter-Variable.ttf` ships `opsz` and `wght` — `text::family_axes`' own doc says
so in the same file, *"bundled Inter's two faces carry the same `opsz`/`wght`"* — and the argument
needs no font table read: if Inter had no `opsz`, `axis_settings` would synthesize nothing
for **either** spelling, the two would already have measured alike, and there would have been no
defect to fix. D571's parenthetical is corrected. *Fix — the same false sentence is in two comments
in `text.rs`*, on `a_stored_opsz_reaches_the_shaper_raw_and_an_absent_one_tracks_the_size`'s doc and
in `optical_size_auto_reaches_the_shaper`'s body. **Both tests are right either way** — handing the
axis in by hand is what makes its three ends explicit, and the plumbing test drives `WGHT` — so what
is wrong is only the reason given, which is the kind of sentence a reader trusts precisely because
nothing gates it.

*(§5.4's *"which face is asked differs by question"* paragraph gains the shaper as a third question,
and §5.4a's fallback bullet gains the metrics half: neither document had said anything about the
fallback's **axes**, and no §15 entry claimed or implied that the two spellings agree — checked
before this entry restated it. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`; the one open font item there is the
snapshot-versus-panel *warning* split, which is a different question and stays. Closes
`[S5.1-L1-06]`.)*

**D710 — `Ctrl+Shift+…` was a silent second spelling of eight `Ctrl` chords. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`input::normal_mode` has stated this rule three times and never generalised it. `Save`'s comment is
the clearest of the three: *"Dropping it would make the freed chord a second spelling of Save —
silently, and only for the user who still has the old habit in their fingers. A chord that does
nothing is the honest state for one whose action was removed."* Fifteen arms carry `!m.shift`.
**Eight carried `cmd_only` alone** — `Open`, `SelectAll`, `Duplicate`, the `Y` half of `Redo`,
`ZoomOut`, `ZoomReset`, `ZoomFit`, and `ZoomSelection`'s `cmd_only` half — so each of those verbs had
a second, undocumented spelling on a chord `shortcuts.md` binds to nothing. All eight are guarded now,
and `ctrl_shift_is_not_a_second_spelling_of_ctrl` asserts both directions for each key: that `Ctrl+…`
still answers, which is the fixture check without which the other assertion is about nothing, and that
`Ctrl+Shift+…` answers nothing at all.

**`Ctrl+Shift+D` is the one that was doing harm.** It duplicated the selection and spent an undo
step, and §11 binds `Shift+D` to *reverse subpath direction* one modifier away — which is precisely
the hand-slips-onto-a-neighbour hazard §8's `Ctrl+Shift+E` row is guarded against **by name**, plain
`Ctrl+E` being *Flatten*.

**This is D207's Shift, and the two fail differently.** D207 ends *"the harm from a missing `!alt` is
not visible until a second chord claims the spelling"* — true of Alt, where the collision has to be
built before it can bite, and where D545 found eight `Ctrl+Alt` bracket spellings restacking the
selection for chords nothing binds. A missing `!m.shift` is live from the moment a hand is still
resting on Shift, which is the ordinary state between two chords in the same block.

🚨 **The finding names twelve doors and four of them must stay open, and checking those was worth
more than closing the other eight.** Each was tried, and each failed something:

- **`Ctrl+Shift+=`** is the *primary* spelling of `Ctrl++`. On a US layout `+` is `Shift+=` and egui
  reports the **logical** key, so `Key::Plus` is unreachable without Shift. `shortcuts.md` §3 says so
  in the row itself — *"both spellings already accepted"* — and §0's L1 worked example is this same
  mechanism for `Shift+1` → `!`. A blanket `!m.shift` here removes zoom-in outright for anyone who
  types the chord the way it is written. The guard went on the **unshifted** spelling only: `Equals`
  needs no Shift and must not accept one, `Plus` cannot be produced without.
- **`Event::Copy` / `Event::Cut` under Shift** are pinned by
  `shift_makes_the_paste_event_a_paste_in_place`, which states the reason: copy and cut are *not*
  given a Shift reading, because `Ctrl+Shift+C` is the **text session's** centre-align — and this is
  `normal_mode`, where that chord does not exist. Guarding here frees no unspent combination; it
  makes `Ctrl+Shift+C` fail to copy outside a text session, for a collision that is not in this
  function. Tried; the test failed at `Copy under Shift: []`.
- **`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+V`** is pinned by `a_property_paste_is_not_also_a_paste_in_place`, whose subject
  sentence is *"Alt beats Shift on a paste, so a hand still resting on Shift cannot turn a property
  paste into a paste-in-place."* The guard makes that chord do **nothing**, which is the
  hand-still-on-Shift case the rule exists for. Tried; the test failed at `left: []`.
- **`Ctrl+Shift+Z`** stays Redo — the documented alternate spelling (§11) — so only the `Y` half of
  that arm took the guard.

⚠️ **`design-oracle` was asked before any of this was written, and is the reason three of the four
were caught before they shipped**: it quoted §3 and §10 against the finding. 🚨 **A finding measured
twelve behaviours correctly and was wrong about what four of them mean.** That is a different failure
from the wrong *fix sketches* this round keeps turning up, and a quieter one: every observation in it
was true, and the whole error is in what a true observation was taken to imply. Each of the four
sites now carries the test that would have failed and the line it failed with, so the next reader
sweeping `Ctrl` chords for consistency finds the answer rather than the finding.

*(`shortcuts.md`'s **Deliberately unbound** section states the rule once now, with the eight
combinations and the four exceptions; nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which does not carry the
keymap's modifier discipline. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S17-L1-05]`.)*

**D709 — `Ctrl+A` decided three things and no test reached any of them. *Tested 2026-09-09; Keep —
this entry records the rule, it does not rule on it.***

`OndinApp::select_all` is four lines and every one of them is a decision. It takes its candidates
from `marquee_candidates` — the direct children of every root frame, plus the root's own children
that are not frames. It falls back to `root_artboards()` when that set comes back empty. And by not
filtering the list at all, it selects a locked or hidden layer like any other. ⚠️ **The lock half of
that last sentence was reversed on 2026-09-10 by D746**, on the maintainer's ruling that the canvas
selects a locked layer by no gesture at all; the hidden half stands. What is below is the state this
entry recorded, and it is left standing because the reversal is what it invited.

**The finding's measurement is the whole argument.** Adding `visible && !is_effectively_locked` to
the candidate set — a change to what the chord answers for *any* document holding a locked or hidden
layer — left **969 tests green**. `marquee_candidates` had test callers only through `select_all`
itself; the list it hands back was asserted nowhere, and the fallback arm had no test caller anywhere
in the tree. **Any implementation of `Ctrl+A` passed** — which is this project's own question about a
green suite, *what would also pass this*, answered in the worst possible way.

🚨 **The sentence above said something else until D746 and it was false in the direction that
under-reports the hole.** It read *"`marquee_candidates` had test callers only through the marquee's
own suite, and that suite asserts the **filtered** result, because `canvas::apply_marquee` does its
filtering after the call rather than inside it"*. **There is no marquee suite.** `apply_marquee` is
reached only from `finish_drag`'s `Drag::Marquee` arm and had **no test caller of any kind** —
measured on 2026-09-10 by flipping its lock filter off, which left all 1,256 tests green. So the
filtered result was asserted nowhere either, and this entry credited coverage to the one door it was
not measuring. *A claim about what a neighbouring test asserts is worth checking against the test.*

`app::select_all_tests` is three tests, one per decision: the candidate set (the contents of frames
plus the loose non-artboard layers, and **not** the frames themselves), the empty-set fallback (a
document of empty frames selects the frames), and locked and hidden layers being **included**. The
same flip now breaks exactly one test.

⚠️ **This is not an endorsement of either answer on the lock.** `Ctrl+A` taking a locked layer is
arguable — the marquee does not, and someone could reasonably want them to agree — and if it is ever
filtered, the third test is the place that says so and the place to change. What the test stops is
the rule moving **silently**, which is what it had been free to do. 🚨 **That offer was taken a day
later**: D746 carries the maintainer's ruling, the third test is
`ctrl_a_skips_locked_layers_and_still_takes_hidden_ones` now, and a fourth was added for the loss the
ruling was taken over — `Ctrl+A` then `Delete` destroying a locked layer. **The mechanism is what
made the offer worth writing**: a decision recorded as a test is a decision somebody can reverse in
one place, and this one was reversed by editing the assertion the entry pointed at.

🚨 **The asymmetry with the marquee is what a reader will trip over, and until today it was written
down on one side only.** §9.4 read *"a rubber band and a click agree about the lock"* (§15 D321) —
true of those two doors; `Ctrl+A` was a **third** door that agreed with neither, taking the same
candidate set through no filter at all. Nothing in `architecture.md` said so, and
nothing said the fallback existed. Both are in §9.4's marquee paragraph now, beside the rule they are
the exception to. ⚠️ The *other* half of `select_all`'s comment — *"layers, whatever is selected —
guides included"* — was already there, in §9.4's guide paragraph and in almost the same words, so the
design and the code agreed about that one all along.

⚠️ **A predicted failure site was wrong, and it is the third time this session.** Dropping the
`!matches!(… Artboard …)` filter from `marquee_candidates` was predicted to fail the `!contains`
assertion written for exactly that case; it fails the **set equality** first
(`left: [5a11:2, 5a11:3, …]`) and the negative assertion never runs. So that assertion has teeth only
against a version that admits the frames **without** otherwise changing the set — which this mutation
is not. It is kept, with its narrower job written on it rather than trimmed as redundant, and the
correction is the part worth carrying: *write the predicted site down, run it, and correct the prose
to what actually happened.*

*(§9.4's marquee paragraph amended; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S16.2-L6-07]`.)*

**D708 — A doc comment that was true of its function and false of the program. *Corrected
2026-09-09; Keep the cache — the sentence was the defect.***

`library::cover::Covers::clear`'s doc said the disk cover cache *"is not cleared: it is keyed by
document id, so it stays correct across a move and is exactly what makes the new folder's covers
appear immediately if they have been seen before."* Every clause of that is true of `clear`, which
empties the in-memory texture map and touches no file.

**It is false of the program.** `Covers::sweep(live)` runs on the same transition — the next
`go_to_dashboard`, from `app.rs` — and its keep set is built from the **current** library alone, over
one shared directory (`dirs::cache_dir()/ondin/covers`) that nothing in the path and nothing in
`cover::key` namespaces per library. So switching from library A to B and entering the dashboard
deletes every one of A's cached covers, and switching back re-renders all of them at one document per
pass. **The claim was correct about its own three lines and wrong about what happens**, which is the
worst shape a doc comment has, because there is no version of reading the function that catches it.

🚨 **It was written in two places and both said it** — `clear`'s doc and the comment on
`apply_library_settings`' `self.covers.clear()`. Corrected in both, with the whole account and the
options on `clear` and a pointer from the other, so there is one statement of it rather than two that
can drift apart.

⚠️ **The cost is bounded and the sentence was not.** Covers are deliberately disposable (§15 D366)
and `Covers::get` renders lazily against an 8 ms per-pass budget with a one-render progress
guarantee, so what the user sees is a grid filling in over a few passes rather than a wrong picture.
That is why this is a corrected sentence and not a rewritten cache: the promise was worth more than
the behaviour, and withdrawing it costs nothing anybody can see.

**Two ways to make the old claim true, neither taken.** Namespace the cache directory by a hash of
the library root — which would also stop two libraries holding the same synced document from sharing
an entry, a second and independent reason to want it. Or sweep on an **age** bound rather than on
membership, so a cover no current document claims survives a switch and a genuinely dead one still
goes. Both change eviction semantics and the first changes the cache layout, so both are decisions
rather than repairs. *Revisit if a user is ever expected to keep two libraries and move between them
often*; today the base folder is changed rarely and by hand.

🚨 **Neither the sweep's scope nor the promise was recorded anywhere.** Checked rather than assumed:
`architecture.md` mentioned covers only as a thing that lives in the cache directory, and this file
had no entry naming `Covers` or `sweep` at all. So a doc comment on a three-line function was the
project's only statement of a rule that decides the fate of every cached cover in the library — and a
claim about the *program* written on a *unit* is invisible to anyone changing either one.

*(§9.5's `dirs::cache_dir()` bullet amended; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes
`[S1.3-L8-07]`.)*

**D707 — Two vestigial signatures, and one of them made a real distinction look like an oversight.
*Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — no behaviour changed.***

`panels::dashboard::dashboard_header` took `_act: &mut Option<Act>` and never read it. `Act` is that
file's deferral discipline, and its own doc says why: *"Deferred rather than done in place, because
every one of these mutates the entry list the layout is iterating."* So a header handed `act` reads
as a function that may emit one, and the next reader has to walk all 124 lines of it to find that the
two things it **does** commit — `dash.deleting_project` and `dash.edit_project`, both of them
assignments that open a card — bypass the mechanism **correctly**, because a card mutates no list.
**The parameter made a real distinction look like an oversight**, which is the expensive kind of
noise: it does not mislead about behaviour, it misleads about whether anybody thought about it.

`search_panel` took `&self` and its body reads only `ui.ctx()`, `anchor`, `height` and `body`.

⚠️ **Neither is visible to any gate.** The `_` prefix silences `unused_variables` by design — that is
what it is for — and `clippy::unused_self` is `pedantic`, which this project does not run as a gate.

⚠️ **`search_panel` stays in the `impl` as an associated function** rather than being lifted to module
scope. Both call sites already spell it `Self::search_panel`, so moving the body would be churn with
the same outcome.

🚨 **The comment written for that choice credited it to §15 D269, and D269 is a different and stronger
argument.** Corrected here and at the site. D269 is about a `&mut self` method's **call site** being
unobservable — *"no test in this crate can say where a `&mut self` method is called from"* — after a
`draw_crop_box` call had sat for months in a place it could never run from; its remedy is lifting the
**decision** into a free function so the arithmetic can be pinned even though the placement cannot.
The *reachability* half was answered separately by D303's `OndinApp::headless`, whose entry says in as
many words that a headless app *"makes the method callable without making the call site observable"*.
`search_panel` decides nothing and has been reachable since D303, so dropping the receiver is the
smaller thing: a signature that stops claiming to read state it does not read. **A citation that
resolves is not a citation that agrees** — both numbers exist, both entries are live, and nothing in
this project can see the difference.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which describes neither signature; nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`. Closes `[S20.1-L3-08]`.)*

**D706 — `atomic::write` cleaned up after the rename and after nothing else. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

🚨 **The finding's headline was closed before it was ranked, and that is where this entry has to
start.** `[S1.2-L2-07]` says a failed `pin_version` leaves a **permanent** `.writing` orphan, on the
argument that this caller's target is a fresh name that will never be written again, so the
self-clearing the old scheme relied on can never happen for it. That was true of D378's *derived*
temp name and has been false since §15 D548, which made temps unique
(`<target>.<pid>-<counter>.writing`) and put a swept, age-gated directory pass where the
self-clearing had been. **This is the sixth finding this round found to have been answered by an
entry written before it was ranked**, and the second this session.

**What survived is smaller and real.** The cleanup lived in the `rename` error arm alone, so a
failure at `File::create`, `write_all` or `sync_all` returned through `?` and left the temp behind —
**and disk-full, which is the reason the cleanup comment gives for existing, surfaces at
`write_all`**, the one of the four arms that had none. The whole write is a closure now and a single
`if result.is_err()` covers all four.

🚨 **It is a gap in D548's own argument, which is why reading the superseding entry was worth the
minute.** D548 bounds `sweep_once` to once per directory per process and defends the bound with
*"debris left by a **dead** process was there before this one started, so the first write into a
directory is the only moment that can find any that matters."* That is true of debris the process
**inherits** and false of debris it **creates after its own sweep has run** — which is exactly what a
failed write leaves. It is bounded rather than permanent, since a later launch sweeps it once
`STALE_TEMP` has passed and nothing accumulates without limit; but an hour is a long time to keep a
temp file for a failure that happened in this process, and the honest place to clean up a write's own
failure is the write. **D548's bullet is amended** to say what its bound does not cover.

⚠️ **The three early arms are covered by construction and exercised by no test, and that is said at
the site rather than papered over.** A read-only *destination* is the only failure this module can
stage portably — it is what `a_failed_write_leaves_the_old_file_intact` uses — and `File::create`,
`write_all` and `sync_all` want a full disk or a revoked ACL. Writable-with-difficulty rather than
written, which is a queue and not a fact.

**Flip:** disabling the cleanup fails that test's temp-file assertion **and that line alone** — the
content and `is_err` assertions above it stay green, which is what says the temp-file question is
asked there and nowhere else. Predicted correctly.

*(§9.5's atomic-write paragraph is widened from the refused rename to all four steps, and §15 D548's
`sweep_once` bullet amended. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S1.2-L2-07]`.)*

**D705 — A ratio test took one sample, and a scheduler stall failed it. *Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep —
test-only, no behaviour changed.***

No finding. `ondin-export/tests/svg.rs · collecting_defs_does_not_grow_with_the_square_of_their_count`
is §15 D593's regression test: it exports a 1,500-def document and a 6,000-def one and asserts the
ratio is under 6.0, an absolute bound being a measurement of the machine rather than of the code. It
took a **single** wall-clock sample per size, and went red at **7.04×** during a full
`cargo test --workspace`, then passed 3/3 in isolation and clean on two later full runs.

**Nothing was wrong with the code.** Cargo runs the crates' test binaries in parallel, the absolute
times here are ~0.009 s and ~0.066 s, and one scheduler stall inside a nine-millisecond window moves
the **ratio** far more than it moves either measurement — the small sample is the denominator, so a
stall there is the cheapest possible way to counterfeit a quadratic regression. Best of three per
size now.

**The minimum is the right statistic and the mean is not.** Contention can only ever make a sample
*slower*, so the fastest of a few is the closest estimate of the work's own cost, where an average
carries whatever else the machine was doing.

🚨 **It is not a widened threshold, and widening is the repair to refuse.** Moving the bound towards
the 8.3× the broken version measures gives up precisely the discrimination this test exists for, and
raising it far enough to absorb a 7.04× stall would leave it unable to tell a stall from the square
coming back.

**Re-measured on both sides rather than assumed**: 3.97× with the `HashSet` and **8.12×** with the
linear scan restored — 0.0082 s / 0.0327 s against 0.0117 s / 0.0949 s — so 6.0 keeps 51% headroom
above the fixed version and 26% below the broken one. That is the thing a sampling change has to be
checked against: it must buy stability without costing separation, and only measuring both sides says
whether it did.

⚠️ **It does not make the test immune, and pretending otherwise is how a flake comes back as a
mystery.** Three stalls in a row still fail it. The failure message prints both times, so the next
reader can tell a stall (both inflated, ratio near 4) from the square coming back (the large one
alone inflated).

⚠️ **Found by `rust-verify` while running the gates**, which is worth a clause: it is the second time
this session a subagent turned up something no finding names.

*(D593's measurement paragraph gains a pointer here. Nothing amended in `architecture.md` — §7 and
§11 record D593's fix rather than its sampling; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D704 — The Language combo showed a raw BCP-47 tag when closed and a friendly name when open.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`panels::typography::language_section`. `LANGUAGES` is a `(tag, name)` table whose doc states its job
— *"Languages worth offering by name"* — and the open list used the name while the closed control
used `current`, the stored locale, verbatim. So picking *German* from a list that says "German" left
a field reading `de`, and *Chinese (Simplified)* left `zh-Hans`. **One control disagreeing with itself
between its two states**, with the mapping that resolves the disagreement sitting in the same file and
already used by the other half of the same widget.

It was also the one control in that file showing the user a raw wire value: the two combos beside it,
`enum_combo` and `feature_choice_row`, both resolve their closed text through the same table their
list uses — `enum_combo` calls one `label: fn(T) -> &'static str` from both places, and
`feature_choice_row` reads `feature_value_label` closed against `feature_values` open.

🚨 **`feature_values`' own doc states the rule this control was breaking, three thousand lines up the
same file**: *"The list and the closed dropdown are two readings of the same mapping."* It says so
while explaining a different hazard — where the `+ 1` between a label's index and its value lives —
so the sentence is a premise there and was never a claim anyone checked the third combo against.
**A rule stated in one place and broken in the one beside it**, which is this session's recurring
shape and is why the fix is worth more than the three strings it changes.

🚨 **An unlisted tag falls back to itself and not to *None*, and that is the assertion with teeth.** A
document can carry a locale this table does not offer — an imported `xml:lang`, or a file written
against a longer list — and that is a real setting the panel must not describe as absent. **Run:** the
obvious `find(…).map(…).unwrap_or("None")` passes the `None` case and the German case and reports a
real setting as absent; it fails on exactly that third assertion, which is why the third assertion is
there.

`the_language_field_reads_its_name_rather_than_its_tag` drives `language_section` headlessly and reads
the painted galleys. **Flip:** restoring `current` verbatim fails the second assertion — the field
reads `de` where "German" is wanted — and leaves the first and third green, `None` and an unlisted tag
being the two inputs the old spelling happened to get right. Predicted correctly.

⚠️ **The test lives in `type_popup_readout_tests`, which is D691's `features_reveal_count_tests`
renamed and widened.** The two controls share a fixture rather than a subject — both need a headless
app holding one text node — and duplicating thirty lines of it to keep two module names apart is the
shape this codebase keeps filing against itself. ⚠️ **The rename is drift in this file and was caught
rather than left**: D691's body and index row both named the old module, and a module name written in
prose is gated by nothing. Both are corrected.

*(§9.4's Character-tab paragraph gains the rule; §15 D691's test citation corrected in its body and

**D702 — "SVG needs core only" was false in three places, and the sentence is the cost rather than
the code. *Corrected 2026-09-09; Keep the code — **the move was ruled on and declined**, §15 D783.***

`crates/ondin-export/Cargo.toml`'s head comment and `architecture.md` §3's inline comment on the
dependency graph both said it. `ondin-export/src/svg.rs` calls `ondin_render::effects` three times:
`filter_matrix` once from the `<filter>` emitter, and `any_ink` twice — once to decide whether a node
earns a filter at all, once to decide whether its id has a def to point at.

**The code is right, and that is worth saying first.** §6.4 exists because there must be one
implementation of the effect arithmetic; a writer computing its own colour matrix would be a third
implementation of a thing the two backends are held byte-identical on, which is the opposite and
worse mistake.

**The sentence is what costs.** It is the one a reader cites to budget an SVG-only path — a `--svg`
build, a wasm target, an MCP `export_svg` handler — for `ondin-core` alone, and gets `ondin-render`,
`vello`, `vello_cpu` and `wgpu` instead. A dependency-graph comment is read for that question and for
nothing else.

⚠️ **The other repair was costed here and is declined** (§15 **D783**, 2026-09-15). Both helpers are
pure functions of `&Filters` and `&[Effect]` over `ondin_core::effect` types — no `Surface`, no
device, no texture — so moving them into `ondin-core` is two functions and their call sites, and that
would make the *original* sentence true rather than soften it. **The softened sentence stands
instead**, on §6.4's ground below: the move splits the specification the shaders are written against,
and a literal dependency comment is not worth that.

⚠️ **Count the sites rather than carrying the number, and the brief that produced this entry is why.**
It said *"about fifteen call sites, twelve of them inside `ondin-render`"*;
`grep -rnE '\b(any_ink|filter_matrix) *\(' crates/` reads **14** on 2026-09-09 — eleven inside
`ondin-render` (two in `scene.rs`, two in `fx_gpu.rs`, one in `effects::run` and six in that module's
own `#[cfg(test)]` block) and three in `svg.rs`. Nothing turns on the difference and that is the
point: a cost written as a number goes stale on the next call site, where the command does not. This
is session 17's recurring shape — *a count in prose standing in for a gate nobody built* — met on an
estimate rather than on a claim.

🚨 **§3 would permit it and §6.4 is the passage that would have to give.** §3's rule is an allow/deny
list of *external* crates, and neither helper needs one — the types are core's already — so nothing in
the dependency rules stands in the way. What does is §6.4's reason for `effects.rs` living where it
lives: *"these functions are the specification, the CPU backend is the reference, and the GPU shaders
are written against it"*, with `fx.wgsl` carrying one entry point per step of `effects::run` and
packing `filter_matrix`'s twenty coefficients five to a row. Moving two of those functions splits the
specification, leaving a shader's colour-matrix order in a crate that has no backend and is cited
across two crate boundaries. **That is the trade, and it is a §6.4 question as much as a §3 one** —
which is why it is a decision rather than a tidy-up and is left to the maintainer.

🚨 **This entry and D703 are cited from a `Cargo.toml` and the citation census cannot see either.**
The prescribed command is `grep -rhoE 'D[0-9]{1,3}\b' crates/ --include=*.rs`, and a manifest carries
neither the extension nor, in D703's case, the directory. D703 has the note.

*(§3's dependency-graph comment amended, and `ondin-export/Cargo.toml`'s head comment corrected in the

**D783 — `any_ink` and `filter_matrix` stay in `ondin-render`: the dependency comment is corrected
rather than made true. *Ruling by the maintainer; recorded 2026-09-15; Resolved — D702's open half
is closed, and the move is a decided non-goal.***

§15 **D702** leaves one repair open and costed: moving `effects::any_ink` and
`effects::filter_matrix` into `ondin-core` would make `ondin-export`'s original head comment —
*"SVG needs core only"* — **true**, rather than softening it to say what the crate actually needs.
**The move is not made.**

**§3 would permit it, so the dependency rules are not what stands in the way.** Its rule is an
allow/deny list of *external* crates, and neither helper needs one: both are pure functions of
`&Filters` and `&[Effect]` over `ondin_core::effect` types, with no `Surface`, no device and no
texture anywhere in them. A reader who weighs this against §3 alone will conclude it is a tidy-up.

🚨 **§6.4 is what gives, and it is the passage the move would have to break.** `effects.rs` lives in
`ondin-render` because *"these functions are the specification, the CPU backend is the reference,
and the GPU shaders are written against it"* — `fx.wgsl` carries one entry point per step of
`effects::run`, in the same order, and packs `filter_matrix`'s twenty coefficients five to a row.
Moving two of them **splits the specification**: a shader's colour-matrix order would live in a
crate that has no backend and cannot compile one, cited across two crate boundaries, with nothing
at either end saying the two halves are one document. **Buying a literal dependency comment with a
split specification is the wrong trade**, and the comment is the cheaper thing to fix — which D702
already did.

⚠️ **So the softened sentence stands, and stands as the honest one.** *"SVG needs core plus
`ondin_render::effects` for the filter maths"* is what a reader budgeting an SVG-only path — a
`--svg` build, a wasm target, an MCP `export_svg` handler — actually needs to know, because that
path really does pull `ondin-render`, and a comment that reads true while the graph reads otherwise
is worse than one that admits the edge. **Correcting a comment costs nothing; a reader acting on a
wrong one costs a re-plan.**

*(Ruling by the maintainer; recorded 2026-09-15; no production line changed. **D702 amended**, its

**D786 — The headless half of `tools/` moves to core before the first MCP handler, and the trigger is
written down. *Deferred with a trigger; recorded 2026-09-15; Fix when the trigger fires —
`[A2-L7-01]` stays open, and this is not a decline.***

`[A2-L7-01]`. The production halves of `crates/ondin-app/src/tools/mod.rs` and
`crates/ondin-app/src/preview.rs` are **headless geometry sitting in a crate nothing can link
against**. Neither file's `use` list names egui, winit or wgpu — `tools/mod.rs` imports
`crate::preview::{…}` and `ondin_core::{…}` and nothing else — and every egui mention in either is
inside a doc comment. `resize_box_to`, `rotate_node`, `pen_outline`, `pen_anchors`, `insert_point`,
`align_points`, `distribute_points` and `space_points` are not *"turning a drag rectangle into a
node"*, which is what that module's own head says stays there.

**The reason it matters is that the wall is absolute rather than a matter of taste.** `ondin-app`
declares only `[[bin]] name = "ondin"` and has no `src/lib.rs`, so nothing outside that binary can
link any of it at all, and §3's graph puts `ondin-mcp` **below** `ondin-app`, so the edge cannot be
added without inverting the graph. An MCP handler for `set_geometry`, `resize` or `rotate` therefore
has two choices: duplicate the arithmetic, or move it. `build::align` and `build::distribute` are
already the node-level twins of two of these functions, in the other crate, which is what the right
answer looks like.

🚨 **Deferred rather than declined, because the cost is asymmetric in time.** Done before the first
MCP handler exists, this is a compiler-enumerated sweep — `rust-mechanic`'s shape, every call site
named by the build. Done after, the duplicate is already written, and two implementations of the same
arithmetic have to be reconciled by somebody who has to work out which of them is right: §15 **D2**'s
shape, and `[A1-L7-07]`'s.

⚠️ **The trigger is the first MCP tool handler — not a date, and not M6 in general.** §15 **D4**
defers `serve` and `mcp-proxy` to M6, so the window this can be done in is long and there is no
urgency to invent; what closes it is somebody needing `set_geometry` from outside this binary. **What
moves** is everything taking only `Document` / `Resolved` / kurbo types. **What stays** is the gesture
state — `Drag`, `PenState`, `TextSession`, `CaretBlink` — which is app-shaped by definition and is the
half `tools/mod.rs`'s head already describes correctly.

*(Deferred with a trigger; recorded 2026-09-15; no production line changed — the citation sits on
`tools/mod.rs`'s module head, directly under the rule it is not keeping, so the next person to read
that head meets the deferral rather than the promise. ⚠️ **The finding's figures are a year old and
were re-measured rather than copied forward**: the production halves are lines **1–4,114** and
**1–1,337** today — first `#[cfg(test)]` at 4115 and 1338 — **5,451** lines between them, against the
`1–3,609` / `1–1,244` and *"~4.8k"* the finding recorded. And not every line of a production half is
headless geometry: `CaretBlink` is in `preview.rs`'s and stays. **§4 invariant 10 gains the clause**,
because a reader budgeting an MCP handler reads the invariant that promises a thin adapter and not
this file. `roadmap.md`'s post-v1 **MCP and headless (M6)** row gains the trigger; **nothing is
struck there**, since a deferred move is open work and not a landed one.)*

**D701 — `card_modal` respelled `color::DIVIDER`'s value instead of naming it. *Fixed 2026-09-09;
Keep — no behaviour changed, and none could.***

`settings::card_modal` stroked the card with `theme::color::text_a(23)`.
`grep -rn "text_a(23)" crates/ondin-app/src` returns exactly two lines: the constant's own
