definition, `pub const DIVIDER: Color32 = text_a(23)`, and this. So the hairline round **every modal
card in the app** was the one hairline in the workspace that would not follow a retune of the
constant named for it — while `theme.rs`'s module doc ends *"change a token here and the whole chrome
follows"*. It would not have: retuning `DIVIDER` moves the panel dividers, egui's
`noninteractive.bg_stroke` and the window stroke, and would have left the modal cards behind at the
old weight.

⚠️ **The two fold to the same `Color32`, so nothing on screen disagreed and no gate could ever have
said so.** That is the whole reason it is worth fixing while it is still harmless: a respelt token
costs nothing until the day somebody changes the token, and on that day the divergence arrives
already shipped, in a control nobody was editing, with every gate green. One keystroke away, and
invisible when it lands.

**There is no test and there should not be.** The constant *is* the assertion. A test comparing
`DIVIDER` against `text_a(23)` would pin the very value the token exists to let somebody change, and
a test comparing the card's stroke against `DIVIDER` passes equally against the literal, both sides
of the comparison folding to the same number. What catches the next instance is the grep in this
entry, run over `theme::color`'s definitions.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which names no colour token; nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`. Closes `[S18.3-L3-05]`.)*

**D700 — A base folder naming an existing file was adopted and persisted. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`panels::dashboard::apply_library_settings` ended its base-folder branch with
`let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(&new_root);` — **after** the migration had run and **after**
`prefs.base_folder` had been assigned — and discarded the result. So a path that names an existing
*file* rather than a directory became the library root, and the three ways to get one are all
ordinary: a mis-copied path, a `.lnk`, a cloud client's placeholder.

Measured: the root became the file, `may_write` went false, `root_unavailable` true, `entries` 0,
the preference was **persisted** so the state survived a relaunch, and the card said nothing at all.
With *Move my existing files there* on, `relocate` ran against a destination that cannot be a
directory.

The call moves to the **top** of the branch and its failure *is* the refusal: nothing moves, nothing
is written, and the card says so. ⚠️ **Before the migration and not merely before the assignment**,
which is the half that matters — the old order had the copy loop pointed at a non-directory before
anything checked whether one could exist there.

⚠️ **Only the base folder is refused; the card's other settings still apply.** A refusal spelled as
an early `return` would discard the autosave interval because a path was mistyped, which is a second
surprise and a worse one, since nothing on screen would connect the two. The test asserts it.

⚠️ **The sentence is asserted on the *screen*, not on `session.status().text`** — §15 D605's rule,
learnt on this very panel, where a test named for something the user is told asserted a field whose
only production reader sits below the dashboard's own `return`.
`a_base_folder_that_names_a_file_is_refused_and_not_persisted` is D693's import test's neighbour and
reads the painted galleys.

**Flip:** restore the `let _ = create_dir_all(…)` at the foot of the block and it fails the first
assertion — the root becomes the file — and then the second, the preference having been persisted.

🚨 **§9.5 already stated the rule this restores**, in the paragraph about `root_unavailable`:
*"Settings creates the folder it is pointed at rather than opening a library that refuses the write
that would have made it."* True of the call and false of what was done with its answer — the
code-wrong, design-right shape D694 records five entries below. The passage is not softened; it
gains the ordering and the refusal.

*(§9.5's `root_unavailable` paragraph amended; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes
`[S20.3-L1-05]`.)*

**D699 — A `dead_code` receipt that outlived its condition by a fortnight, and what it was hiding.
*Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — no behaviour changed.***

`main.rs` carried `#[allow(dead_code)] mod library` under a comment reading *"unwired on purpose …
delete this attribute the moment the first real caller lands — leaving it is how an abandoned module
comes to look finished"*. The dashboard that calls the module landed on 2026-08-26 (§15 D362–D366)
and `panels/dashboard.rs` is 4,600-odd lines. The instruction was right, it named its own expiry, and
it went unfollowed — so a blanket `allow` sat over every item in a module that is now thoroughly
wired.

Removing it surfaces **exactly one** thing, under both `cargo check -p ondin-app` and
`--all-targets`: `library::store::versions`, whose six call sites are every one of them inside a
`#[cfg(test)]` module. The app **pins** versions — `pin_version`, reached from `save_file` — and has
no path that ever **lists** them.

🚨 **`#[cfg(test)]` was tried first and the doc gate refused it, which is the entry's real content.**
`pin_version`'s doc is on a *production* item and carries `` [`versions`] ``, and that link is
load-bearing rather than decorative: it is the argument for D378's read-then-atomic-write, namely
that a half-copied pin is *listed as a version*, offered for restore, and fails when taken. `cargo
doc` builds without the `test` cfg, so under `#[cfg(test)]` the item is simply absent from the crate
rustdoc reads and the gate exits **101**. **That is D319's mechanism from a third direction** — not a
link nothing checks, and not a target the gate cannot see, but a production doc that cannot name a
test-only item at all.

🚨 **So the attribute is `#[allow(dead_code)]` on the function, and the distinction from D672 is the
load-bearing part.** D672's lesson is that an allow-listed item is still a live *root*, so an allow
can shield a whole graph hanging off it — and it was found on a `pub const ALL` listing 143 icon
constants, where the shield is the list. That needs the item to **name** other dead things.
`versions` names only `VERSIONS_DIR` and `DOCUMENT_EXT`, both of which `pin_version` uses too, so it
shields nothing but itself. **Verified rather than argued**: with the narrow attribute in place, a
throwaway `fn` added to `store.rs` is reported by the **plain** build, which is the gate that catches
the next dead thing in `library`. A reader who has only D672 in front of them will reach for
`cfg(test)` and break the doc gate; a reader who has only this one will put an allow on a catalogue
and shield everything under it. **The two entries are a pair and neither is the general rule.**

⚠️ **Whether `versions` should exist is deliberately not decided here.** Dead code, or the back half
of a version-history screen nobody has built — §9.5 describes the directory and no document
describes a way to browse it. Marking it decides neither; it makes the choice visible instead of
shielded. *Delete the attribute the moment a real caller lands*, which is the instruction the
blanket receipt gave and the one this entry is about somebody not having followed.

*(§9.5's `.versions` bullet gains the fact that nothing reads the directory; nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`. Closes `[S16.5-L3-04]`.)*

**D698 — `OndinApp::update` names a method the app does not have, and D330 argued from its
signature. *Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — prose only.***

`impl eframe::App for OndinApp` has exactly two methods, `on_exit` and **`ui`**;
`grep -rn "fn update" crates/ondin-app/src/` returns only `canvas::update_drag` and
`rulers::update_guide_drag`. eframe's *conventional* method is named `update` and takes an
`eframe::Frame`, so the wrong name reads as obviously right to anyone who knows the framework and
has not checked this impl. Every occurrence is plain backticks in prose, which is D319's hole:
`rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links` never looks at a name written that way, so the drift is the
cheapest kind to introduce and the only kind no gate reads.

🚨 **The cost was not tidiness.** D330 excused an untested decision on the ground that the guard
*"is in `OndinApp::update`, which takes an `eframe::Frame` and is not reachable from a test even with
`OndinApp::headless`"*. `fn ui` takes `&mut egui::Ui` **plus** `&mut eframe::Frame`, is reachable by
`eframe::Frame::_new_kittest()` plus `ctx.run_ui`, and was already being driven by a test at the
time. **An excuse argued from a signature that is not the signature** — and the thing it excused was
a keyboard guard that turned out to be missing on two of three modals.

⚠️ **D464 caught that half on 2026-09-07 and its correction is complete**, checked rather than
assumed: D330's paragraph now names `<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui`, says it is reachable, says how,
and names the crash-recovery card its original sentence had left out. D464 also fixed four code
comments in the same commit. What was left is the *name* everywhere else, which is what this entry
closes; the whole account now sits on `<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui`'s own doc, where the next
person to write the wrong name will be standing.

⚠️ **The finding's ten-site census was stale and was re-derived** with
`grep -rn "OndinApp::update" docs/`. Four sites in `crates/`, `context-menus.md` §0's right-click
paragraph, `shortcuts.md` §2's repaint note and §10's `took_tab` note, and two prose uses in this
file — D123's focus-return sentence and D173's `Tab`-in-a-session one. 🚨 **Six occurrences in this
file are corrections that quote the dead name on purpose in order to say it is wrong**: D464's index
row and body, and D330's amended paragraph. Those survive verbatim, and a sweep that treats the name
as a rename target destroys the record of the mistake. `architecture.md` never used it — §9.4 has
said `<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui` all along, which is why nothing there is amended.

*(`context-menus.md`, `shortcuts.md` and two passages here corrected; nothing amended in
`architecture.md`; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S17-L3-07]`.)*

**D697 — Two more doc-comment thefts, and in each the thief is a rung of the ladder the stolen
paragraph describes. *Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — prose only.***

In `app.rs`, `escape`'s twenty-line rationale for the Escape ladder — the order of specificity, why
an in-flight pen path is committed rather than discarded, why falling back to Select is what makes
the key safe to lean on — sat on `cancel_gesture`, a merged run of 33 lines. And `enter_action`'s
*"a toggle, where Escape is a ladder"* argument sat on `enter_container`, 22 lines. **Both victims
had no doc at all.**

🚨 **They read as preambles rather than as mistakes, and that is not luck.** `cancel_gesture` *is*
one rung of the ladder `escape` walks, and `enter_container` *is* what `enter_action` calls — so a
stolen paragraph about a ladder is at its most plausible sitting on a rung of it. The reader who
would catch a misfiled comment by noticing it describes something else entirely gets no such signal
here.

Split back apart. All four items now open with a line that describes the item beneath them.

⚠️ **Neither detector in `CLAUDE.md` reaches these.** Both runs sit far under the length ranking's
52-line floor, so the outlier sweep cannot see them; and the neighbour grep asks *"did the item below
lose its comment"*, which answers yes only if somebody runs it on these two functions, which nobody
had. **The check that catches both in one read is the first-line test** — does the run's opening
sentence name the item under it? *"Leaving a tool or pressing Escape abandons whatever is half-done"*
does not describe *"abandon whatever gesture is in flight"*, and *"Enter: step into the selection, or
step back out"* describes a key binding sitting on a function that has no idea a key exists.

⚠️ **The running count of this class lives in `CLAUDE.md` and deliberately not here**, so there is
one tally and not two. A number written into a code comment is a gate nobody built, and this one was
wrong when it was shipped.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, whose §9.4 states the Escape ladder's order and was right
about it; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S16.2-L3-05]`.)*

**D696 — The zero-travel `finish_drag` census, and behaviourally there was nothing to fix. *Tested
2026-09-09; Keep — test-only.***

`[S12.1-L1-05]`, `[S13.1-L1-08]` and `[S12.5-L1-04]` each tabulated an arm of `finish_drag` buying an
undo step for a gesture that ended where it began, and each proposed a per-arm epsilon — and each
*also* said, in its own fix sketch, that the guard really belonged one level up as
`Transaction::changes_nothing(&doc)` beside `commit_inner`'s empty test. **That is exactly where D428
put it, for its own reasons, two sessions before these three were ranked.** The arms still push their
unconditional `SetGeometry`/`SetTransform`; the transaction is absorbed at the commit.

What did not exist is the table all three asked for: *"one over every arm `finish_drag` commits from,
so a sixth arm added later cannot join the list silently."* `session.rs`'s
`an_edit_that_writes_back_what_is_already_there_is_not_an_undo_step` pins the absorber against a
hand-built transaction, which is a claim about `commit_inner` and not about the gestures.

🚨 **Running it corrected `[S12.1-L1-05]`.** That finding names **Rotate** as unguarded and tabulates
it at `undo_depth 0 -> 1`. With D428's guard switched off the collected offenders are
`["Resize", "LineEnd", "RailOffset"]` — Rotate is not among them, because `tools::rotate_node` ends
with `if transform.as_coeffs() != node.transform().as_coeffs()` and emits no operation for a zero
turn. **So only three of the six committing arms reach D428 at all**, and each of the other three is
stopped by a different mechanism before it gets there:

- **`Move`** has its own epsilon in the arm, `raw.hypot() > 1e-4`.
- **`Skew`** is caught by `commit_inner`'s *emptiness* test rather than by D428, because
  `tools::side_shear` answers `None` for a zero drag and `skew_tx` therefore returns an empty
  transaction. A `side_shear` returning an identity shear instead would move it onto the other
  mechanism with no other change.
- **`Rotate`** is guarded at its *producer*, above.
- **`Resize`, `LineEnd` and `RailOffset`** push unconditionally and reach D428 alone.

⚠️ **What Rotate did at the SHA the finding was taken at is not claimed here.** What is measured is
today. The finding's *verdict* — the guard belongs one level up — stood and was acted on; its census
of which arms needed it was one row over, and nothing anywhere would have said so.

**Four routes to one outcome is the reason the test asserts the outcome rather than the route.** Two
of the three that are not D428 are accidents of a producer's internals, and neither is written down
anywhere as a contract, so
a test naming `changes_nothing` would pin the wrong thing for half the table.
`canvas::zero_travel_release_tests::no_committing_drag_arm_spends_an_undo_step_on_a_zero_travel_release`
drives all six at the seam the user presses.

⚠️ **It *collects* the offending arms and asserts the list is empty rather than asserting per row.**
A per-row `assert_eq!` aborts at Resize and never reaches the Rotate question — which is precisely
how the finding's census survived being read three times.

🚨 **This is D428's own closing warning coming true, and it is worth reading beside that entry.**
D428 records the price of closing at one seam: *"a guard placed at a choke point closes doors nobody
enumerates, so the doors it closed are not recorded anywhere and the next reader cannot tell a
covered door from an uncovered one … the only repair is a test at the door that names the entry."*
Three findings' worth sat open across three sessions with fix sketches pointing straight at the guard
that had already answered them. This is that repair, for six doors at once.

*(§9.3's zero-travel bullets gain the three mechanisms and the census; nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`. Closes `[S12.1-L1-05]`, `[S13.1-L1-08]` and `[S12.5-L1-04]`.)*

**D695 — The pivot snap radius was multiplied by the node's own scale, under a comment saying that
could not happen. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`canvas::pivot_at` compares in the node's **local** space, so the screen-pixel threshold
`PIVOT_SNAP_PX` (6) has to be converted before it can be used there — and it was divided by the
camera zoom alone, under a sentence reading, verbatim, *"and by nothing else — the node's own basis
is a rotation, which preserves distance"*.

🚨 **That sentence is false in this app, and it is the load-bearing part of the defect**, because it
is the reason the second divisor was left out rather than forgotten. A group carries scale; skew is a
shipped canvas gesture (§15 D324, D326); and `[S13.1-L2-04]` records `tools::rotate_node` storing
`scale = (1.4547, 0.6875)` on an ordinary turn, so even the one transform the comment names as safe
is not. Measured: a corner held the marker out to **24.25** screen units on a rect inside a 4× group
against **6.25** at scale 1 — exactly 4×, with the scale-1 row as the control. On a small layer
inside a heavily scaled group most of the box sits inside one of the nine radii, which leaves
nowhere to put the pivot at all.

**Two tolerances now, one per axis, from the world basis's column norms.** `|column 0|` is how long
one local unit along local x is in world space and `|column 1|` the same for y — which is exactly the
conversion this comparison needs, because the loop below already asks each axis its own question.

🚨 **The per-axis half is D694's lesson arriving from somewhere else entirely, and the two entries
are a pair.** The
tempting repair is a single scalar taken from the basis's geometric mean, and it was run: under
`scale(4, 1)` it **passes** the uniform test and **fails** the non-uniform one, because 2.5 local
units is inside a mean-derived tolerance of 3 and outside x's true 1.5. So the mean is wrong here for
the same reason §5.6 says it must not decide a guide: **the same quantity chosen for the same
plausible reason, in two files that share no code** — `tools::scale_scalars` and `canvas::pivot_at` —
and found in one session by two unrelated findings. A reader of either entry should find the other.

`canvas::pivot_snap_scale_tests::a_scaled_basis_does_not_widen_the_pivot_snap` and
`…::a_non_uniform_basis_gives_each_axis_its_own_snap_radius`. ⚠️ **The first assertion of each is a
control**: it says the snap still fires at all, which is what catches a repair that divides by the
basis *twice* — the obvious over-correction, and one a test asserting only "it no longer snaps too
far" would pass.

**Flip:** the scale-blind `PIVOT_SNAP_PX / zoom` fails both tests. The message on the `assert_ne!` is
`left: 0.0, right: 0.0`, which is what an `assert_ne!` prints when the two sides agree, and reads at
a glance like a test asserting nothing — it is worth knowing that is the expected shape of this
particular red.

*(§9.4's pivot-marker paragraph gains the conversion and keeps its *"within 6 screen px"*, which was
the rule all along; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S12.5-L3-05]`.)*

**D694 — A frame's guides were gated on the geometric mean, which §5.6 names as the one quantity that
must not decide them. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`tools::scale_scalars` opened with `let Some(s) = scaling.scalar(csx, csy) else { return; };` and
called `scaled_guides` from **inside** that guard — the one item in the function that does not use
`s` at all. `Scaling::scalar` answers `None` for **two unrelated reasons**: a Geometry drag, which is
a resize and must leave a guide alone; and a Photographic one whose `sqrt(|csx·csy|)` is within
`SCALE_NOOP` (1e-9) of 1, which is a scale and must not. One guard, two questions, and only one of
them was the guard's own.

So a photographic `(2.0, 0.5)` — mean exactly 1 — scaled a 400 × 200 frame to 800 × 100 and left its
centre guide at 200: a quarter of the way across instead of halfway, with no undo step of its own to
notice and nothing on screen saying the guide had stopped meaning what it was placed to mean.

🚨 **This is code-wrong and design-right, and the design was right in as many words.** §5.6 has said
since the feature landed that a guide scales by the **axis** factor *"because the geometric mean
would drift a guide off the feature it was placed against under any non-uniform scale"* — and the
gate in front of the call **was** the mean. The rule was not softened to match: the fix is the code,
and §5.6 gains one sentence saying the `Scaling` fork is what gates the call, because the fork is the
line the bug was on. **A reader repairing the design to match the code here would have written the
defect into the invariant.**

The call is hoisted above the guard and asks `scaling == Scaling::Photographic` directly. Everything
below the early return genuinely does not move at mean 1 — a stroke width, a dash pattern, a corner
radius, a font size, all of which are multiplied by `s` — so the early return is right for all of it
and was wrong for exactly this one member of the list.

⚠️ **The coverage fact is the half worth carrying.** `the_scale_tool_multiplies_a_frames_guides_and_a_resize_does_not`
predates this and names the feature, and it drives only `(2.0, 1.0)` — mean 1.414, the case that
works — so it **stayed green under the flip**. A test can name the feature, pin the fork it is about,
and cover only the arm that was never broken; that is the shape `CLAUDE.md` records as *"a flip that
does not bite is a finding about which paths the tests actually take"*, arriving from the other end.
`tools::…::a_photographic_scale_with_a_mean_of_one_still_moves_the_guides` is the case that was
missing.

**Flip:** put the call back behind the guard and it fails with `left: 200.0, right: 400.0`.
Predicted correctly. The Geometry half is unchanged and is still asserted by the older test's first
arm, which is what keeps the fix from having widened the verb.

🚨 **Read D695 beside this.** The same session found the geometric mean deciding something it must
not decide a second time, in `canvas::pivot_at`, reached by a different finding through code that
shares nothing with `tools::scale_scalars` — and there the single scalar was not a gate but the
tolerance itself, so the repair had to be *two* numbers rather than a hoisted call. **The mean is the
plausible wrong answer whenever two axis factors have to become one**, and this pair is the evidence
that it is a habit rather than a slip.

*(§5.6's guide bullet gains the gate; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S13.1-L2-06]`.)*

**D693 — An import never said what it skipped as already present, and the one arm that could mention
it *asserted* the reason. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`panels::dashboard::import_counting` dropped an already-in-the-library file with a bare `continue`
and returned `(ok, failed)`. Nothing downstream was ever told the skip had happened — so the only
place in `import_summary` that could mention it was the `(0, 0)` arm, and that arm did not *report*
the reason, it **asserted** it: *"Nothing to import — those files are already in the library"*, a
sentence inferred from two zeroes.

**Two harms, both measured.** Importing three documents of which two were already under the base
folder said *"Imported 1 file(s)"* and nothing whatever about the other two — the user's two
documents simply did not appear and no sentence accounted for them. And a drop of forty pictures and
no documents is *also* `(0, 0)`, so that same arm claimed forty files were already in the library
when not one of them was.

🚨 **This is the defect D373 records having fixed, surviving in the arm beside the one it fixed.**
That entry's own comment in this module reads *"a drop of one document and forty pictures reported
the document and said nothing whatever about the forty — a silent partial failure of exactly the kind
this project does not leave lying around"*, and the second skip category went on doing it. **A rule
stated in one place and broken in the two beside it** is the recurring shape of this review's Low
tail, and here the two places are forty lines apart in one file.

🚨 **D373 is a `Keep` entry that claimed the opposite, and it is amended.** Its body and its §15.0
index row both said `import_paths` *"already announces its own outcome — the count, the failures and
the already-in-the-library skip"*. That was true only of a drop where nothing else happened; the
clause is now true rather than aspirational, and both copies of the signature it names have been
corrected.

`import_counting` returns `(ok, failed, already)`, `import_summary` takes a fourth parameter with a
clause of its own — ` — {n} file(s) already in the library` — appended to **every** arm as `skipped`
already was, and the `(0, 0)` arm states only what it knows.

**A user-visible string change in a status toast, and it is taken deliberately rather than fallen
into.** The argument is D373's own and does not need restating so much as extending: a partial
refusal that says nothing is indistinguishable from files that never arrived, and that is as true of
*"these were already here"* as it is of *"these were not documents"*.

`an_import_of_files_already_in_the_library_says_so` drives `import_counting` itself rather than the
formatter, so it pins the count arriving rather than the sentence. **Flip:** restore the bare
`continue` and it fails with `left: (1, 0, 0), right: (1, 0, 2)`. Predicted correctly.

⚠️ **The existing `an_import_says_what_it_took_and_what_it_left` is what made this look covered.** It
is formatter-only — four `(ok, failed)` arms against a free function needing no app, library or
filesystem — and it grew from five assertions to seven, because its **third** had asserted the old
`(0, 0)` sentence as correct. *A test that pins a sentence pins whatever the sentence claims*,
including the half nobody told it.

*(§9.5's library-drop paragraph carries `import_summary`'s signature and is corrected to four;
nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S20.2-L1-06]`.)*

**D692 — A stop opacity above 1 put 500 into a `0..=100` field, and two sites had to clamp.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

**The importer.** `svg_in::stop_of` read `stop-opacity` and did not clamp it — where `resolve` clamps
`fill-opacity` and `stroke-opacity`, and the `offset` **two lines below in the same function** clamps
too. So `stop-opacity="5"` survived the import, survived the save and survived the load. The
asymmetry was two lines apart and was not a decision: `Color::multiply_alpha` is
`add_alpha(opaque, alpha * rhs)` and does no range work of its own.

**The reader.** `panels::paint::alpha_of` returned the raw maximum stop alpha, and it is the producer
for the inspector's opacity field, for the picker's, **and** for `with_alpha`'s `peak`. A
`range(0.0..=100.0)` control handed 500 shows 100, and egui's `clamp_existing_to_range` then makes one
bare click write `with_alpha(brush, 1.0)` — which divides every stop by the peak. With a raw peak of
5.0 that rescaled the whole ramp: a second stop at 25% came back at **5%**, a visible change to the
picture from a click that typed nothing.

⚠️ **Clamping `alpha_of` repairs the rewrite as well as the readout, and the finding did not name
this.** With a clamped peak of 1.0 the out-of-range stop is brought back to 1.0 and every other stop
keeps the alpha it had — so the same bare click that used to destroy the ramp now normalises the one
component that was wrong and touches nothing else. *Fixing the producer fixed the consumer*, which is
the argument for the clamp being here rather than at the field.

🚨 **Both paragraphs above are history now, and the accidental repair is what was lost** (§15 **D767**).
A gradient's opacity is a **field** on `GradientBrush`, `with_alpha` writes it, and `alpha_of` returns
it — so there is no `peak`, nothing divides the ramp, and an out-of-range *stop* cannot reach the
opacity control **by any route**. The first harm is unreachable rather than mitigated and the second
is gone with the division. But the normalisation above was a *side effect* of dividing by the peak,
not a designed behaviour, and it went with it: **a hand-written `stop-opacity="5"` now stays 5.0 in
the document.** `brush_is_finite` accepts it — it checks finiteness, not range — and the raster clamps
it, so nothing the user sees changed. ⚠️ **That is a stop-validation gap and it always was**: this
entry's own *"a document already carrying such a stop keeps it"* describes exactly that state, and
the opacity field was never the right place to close it. *Recorded, not fixed.* Both tests were
rewritten rather than deleted, `a_stop_alpha_above_one_no_longer_reaches_the_opacity_field` and
`a_negative_stop_alpha_cannot_move_the_opacity_field`, on the ground that a test deleting itself here
would leave nothing saying a rogue stop cannot move the control.

🚨 **One step of the finding's mechanism is wrong and is corrected here.** `[S23.2-L1-03]` says
`stop-opacity="-1"` gives `alpha_of == -1.0`. It cannot: the fold is seeded at `0.0` and
`f32::max(0.0, -1.0)` is `0.0`, so a negative peak was already floored before this entry's clamp
existed. What *is* true is that the stored component is `-1.0` — measured from the `min`-only flip's
failure output, not reasoned — and the consequence the finding names is unchanged. **The verdict
stood and one step of its argument did not**, which is why `a_negative_stop_alpha_reads_as_zero_and_not_as_itself`
asserts the floor: the claim that was checked is the one worth pinning.

⚠️ **Flips, both run.** Dropping `alpha_of`'s clamp fails with `left: 5.0, right: 1.0`. Writing the
importer's clamp as `.min(1.0)` — the plausible wrong version, and the one somebody reaching for "cap
it at 1" writes — fails the low assertion with `left: -1.0, right: 0.0`, which is what says the
importer's clamp is two-sided for a reason.

**Nothing in either document stated a `0..=1` rule for a stop's alpha, and that was checked rather
than taken from the finding.** §5.7's *"opacity out of range"* validation is `Node::opacity`, a
different field on a different type; invariant 8 weighs a gradient stop's colour, but for
**finiteness**, which 5.0 passes without comment. So the range question had no home, which is exactly
why two sites could disagree about it in silence. Invariant 8 now names this as the fourth instance
of its own *"a finiteness guard answers what `serde_json` will write, not what the arithmetic
downstream can survive"* shape, and says why the answer here is a clamp at the two doors rather than
a refusal at the operation: a stop alpha out of range is a *file* being out of spec, and the model
has always chosen to read such a file rather than refuse it.

*(§5.5a's gradient-stop paragraph gains the sibling rule beside its own "nothing clamps on load";
invariant 8's instance paragraph amended. §7 is not amended — it describes what the reader maps, not
what it normalises. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S23.2-L1-03]`.)*

**D691 — The *Show all features* offer counted past the search box. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep.***

`panels::typography::features_section` computed `hidden` as
`ordered.iter().filter(|(t, l)| !shown(t, l)).count()` **before the search field is drawn** — so it
applied the curation filter and not the needle, while the row loop twenty lines below applies both.
Two filters decide what the list contains and the count knew about one of them, because at the point
it was taken the other did not exist yet.

With a needle typed, the collapsed reveal offered *"Show all features (43 more)"* and the click added
nothing at all: every one of the 43 was withheld by the curation **and** excluded by the needle, so
expanding the list changed no row on screen.

🚨 **`features_reveal`'s own doc states the rule that was broken**, and reasons about exactly one way
the offer can be unreal. It says the collapsed offer *"is only real if something is actually
hidden"*, and the mechanism it holds is the withheld feature the document has an opinion about —
touching one writes it into the set and moves it out of the count. This is a **second** door onto the
same *"control that cannot change anything"* state, reached past the paragraph that owns the
question. *A guard written against one route is a guard against one route*, however completely it
argues its case.

The fix is a `matches` closure written once and asked by both the row loop and the count, with the
count moved down to sit beside the loop it has to agree with. **The two filters are now one
expression each and neither can be applied by half the code.**

🚨 **The fixture correction is worth more than the fix.** The first probe built its 43 withheld
features as `cv01`..`cv43`. `feature_label` routes a character variant through `font_defined`, which
sets `offered = true` — so the face had **nothing** withheld, `features_reveal(false, 0)` is `None`,
and the probe read *exactly like the fix working*. It was the control assertion that caught it. The
withheld shape is a **private four-letter tag** (`Zk01`..`Zk43`), which
`a_mechanic_is_withheld_a_stylistic_set_is_named_and_a_private_tag_is_neither` already pins. That is
`CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity — *"its fixture never reached the state"* — met again, and the habit that
caught it is the one that paragraph asks for: assert the fixture is in the state you think before the
interesting assertion.

`type_popup_readout_tests::a_needle_that_hides_every_withheld_feature_hides_the_offer` and
`::a_needle_that_matches_withheld_features_offers_exactly_those` are the pair, one for each direction
the count can be wrong. **Flip:** count over `!shown` alone and both fail with
`Some("Show all features (43 more)")`. ⚠️ **The module was `features_reveal_count_tests` when this
entry was written and was renamed and widened by §15 D704 the same day**, the Language combo needing
the same fixture; this citation and the index row above were corrected then, and a module name in
prose is gated by nothing.

*(§9.4's OpenType-list paragraph gains what the offer counts; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.
Closes `[S6.3-L1-07]`.)*

**D690 — The rail of the text node being edited was drawn twice. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep.***

`canvas::draw_text_rails` iterated `selection.ids().chain(live)`, `live` being the live
`TextSession`'s id, with no dedup — under a comment describing that node as *"normally in the
selection and need not be, since a session survives things that change it"*. **"Normally" is in fact
"always, at the moment it opens"**: `begin_edit_text` calls `Selection::set_one(id)` immediately
before installing the session, so the two halves of the chain do not merely *overlap* in the common
case, they agree on it.

Two coats of `SELECT_DIM` (alpha `0x8c`, 55%) composite to 1 − 0.451² ≈ 79.7%. So the one rail the
user was actually working on was the one drawn at a weight no other rail on screen had — which reads
as the app emphasising the right thing and is a compositing artefact.

The repair is `live.filter(|id| !selection.contains(*id))`. **An `Option` filter rather than a dedup
set**, because a chain that can carry exactly one extra id needs no set, and a set here would be
answering a question this iteration cannot ask.

🚨 **The inconsistency this exposed is deliberately left standing.** `draw_text_line_boxes` and
`draw_text_baselines`, the two siblings called from the same `chrome` block of `draw_canvas`, iterate
`selection.ids()` **alone** — so they never doubled, and so a session that has left the selection
loses its line box and its baselines while keeping its rail. That is the other half of the same
asymmetry and it is a different question: *whether the three overlays should follow the session or
the selection*. Nothing here changes which of them tracks what, and this entry is not the place to
decide it — the fix removes a compositing defect and does not widen or narrow what any of the three
draws.

`canvas::rail_drag_tests::the_edited_nodes_rail_is_drawn_once` counts the `Shape::Path`s the overlay
puts on the painter. ⚠️ **The first assertion is a control and it is load-bearing**: without it a
green second assertion is equally consistent with the overlay having stopped drawing anything at all.
**Flips, both run** — dropping the filter fails the second assertion with `left: 2, right: 1`, and
filtering the *selection* half instead, which is the plausible wrong version, fails the **first**
with `left: 0, right: 1`. That is why the control is asserted before the subject.

⚠️ **D408 introduced this rail and was read against the change.** Its statement is *"the rail is
drawn while a railed node is selected or being edited"*, which is a union and is still exactly true;
nothing in it asserts how many times. §5.4 carries the same sentence and gains the word *once*, since
that is the passage a future editor restating the union would reach for.

*(§5.4's rail-chrome sentence amended; D408 read and unchanged; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.
Closes `[S12.4-L1-08]`.)*

**D689 — The zoom range had two statements and only one of them was enforced. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`view::MIN_ZOOM` (0.02) and `MAX_ZOOM` (256.0) were **private**, so `Camera::zoom_by` was the only
site that could read them — and `Camera::zoom` is a `pub` field, so `zoom_by` was never the only
*writer*. `OndinApp::zoom_to`, which is *Fit to page* and *Fit selection* (`Action::ZoomFit`,
`Action::ZoomSelection`), wrote `zoom.clamp(0.02, 256.0)`: the same two numbers as bare literals,
**because there was nothing to name**.

So changing a bound moved every wheel, chord and menu zoom and left both fits on the old one, with
every gate green — a rule with one statement in the code and two in the tree, which is the recurring
shape of this review's Low tail.

Both consts are `pub(crate)` now, `Camera::set_zoom(zoom)` clamps, `zoom_by` goes through it and
`zoom_to` calls it.

⚠️ **`set_zoom` does not close the `pub` field, and it is not meant to.** A caller can still assign
`zoom` directly and `Action::ZoomReset` deliberately does, writing `1.0` — a known-good constant that
needs no clamp and would read worse behind one. What the function is, is a **named place to put a
computed zoom**, so the rule has a single implementation rather than one per caller. The invariant is
still *"every writer that is not setting a known-good constant goes through here"* and is still
upheld by reading, not by the type system. **The door is not shut; it has a sign on it.**

**The writer census was measured, not assumed**: `grep -rn "camera.zoom =" crates/`, each hit read
against its enclosing module. Production writers are exactly two, `ZoomReset` and `zoom_to`; the
other three are inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules in `grid.rs` and `canvas.rs`.

`app::zoom_range_tests::a_fit_cannot_leave_the_camera_outside_the_zoom_range` asserts **by the
constants** rather than by `256.0`, which is what makes it a test of the rule instead of a second
copy of the literal. ⚠️ **The flip is two steps and both were run**, which is the part worth keeping:
`MAX_ZOOM = 100.0` **alone leaves it green**, because the fit now follows the constant — and only
that *plus* the literal restored at the call site fails, `left: 256.0, right: 100.0`. A one-step flip
here would have read as a vacuous test when it was in fact the fix working.

🚨 **A third statement of the number survives and `pub(crate)` cannot reach it.** D402 closes on
*"the app's own `MAX_ZOOM` is 256"*, and D403's cost table gives its top row as 256× with `MAX_ZOOM`
named beside it — both about GPU work that lives in `ondin-render`, whose instrument is
`tests/zoom_sweep.rs`. **`ondin-app` declares only `[[bin]] name = "ondin"` and has no lib target**,
so nothing in `ondin-render` can name this constant at any visibility. Those two entries are readers
of the *number*, in prose, and they were read and left alone: writing *"the constant is nameable
now"* into either would be false, and a resolving citation that is wrong is invisible to every check
in this project. **The zoom bound crossing a crate boundary as a bare 256 is a real third statement
that this fix does not close**, and it is recorded here rather than claimed away.

*(`architecture.md` states the zoom range nowhere — checked — so nothing there is amended; D402 and
D403 read and unchanged; nothing struck from `roadmap.md`. Closes `[S16.5-L3-06]`.)*

**D688 — `Sense::hover()` *is* `Sense::empty()`, and the one value carried two opposite explanations.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — no behaviour changed.***

egui 0.35 defines `const HOVER = 0` and `pub fn hover() -> Self { Self::empty() }`. One value, two
spellings — and this app used both, with prose in front of each explaining it as the opposite of the
other.

`ui::menu_row` passed `Sense::hover()` for a **dimmed** row and explained it as *"it must still win
the hit test so the tooltip explaining why has somewhere to hang"*. `badge_field`, `grip` and
`value_field_f64` passed `Sense::empty()` for a rect that must **not** sense, all three citing
`icon_button_padded` as the rule — while `icon_button_padded` itself spelled that same job `hover()`.
So the two halves of the file disagreed about what a zero sense means, and neither could be wrong in
a way the compiler would notice, because they are the same constant.

🚨 **The dimmed row's sentence is false, and the row works anyway, which is exactly how it survived.**
A zero-sense widget does not win the hit test: egui's `hit_test_on_close` filters candidates on
`senses_click()` / `senses_drag()`, so such a widget never enters `hits.click` or `hits.drag` at all.
What the tooltip rests on is `interaction.rs`'s `is_on_top_of_the_interactive_widget`, which grants
hover to a non-interactive widget while it sits **above** the top interactive widget under the
pointer. **A claimant works by being last, not by being interactive.**

⚠️ **That is a *conditional* guarantee, and its condition is the arrangement three functions in
`ui.rs` deliberately construct.** `badge_field` allocates a silent rect under two live claimants;
`icon_button_padded` allocates the painted box without a sense and reads the press off a larger
rect; `value_field_f64` and `grip` do the same for the same reason. `inspector::menu_action` breaks
the condition on purpose from the other end, putting a second claimant over a disabled scope. In a
menu `Area` with nothing interactive beneath it, `menu_row` is simply the lucky end of one rule —
and the comment that read as stating the rule was stating a different one.

One spelling now, `Sense::empty()`, across the nine files that use it; `Sense::hover()` survives only
inside the three corrected paragraphs, quoting itself. **No behaviour changed and none could**, the
two being the same value, which is what makes this a documentation defect with a mechanical
consequence rather than a bug.

🚨 **One of the three corrections was itself wrong on the first pass, and that is worth the entry
recording.** `inspector::menu_action`'s doc was rewritten to say its claimant senses **clicks**. It
senses nothing and is hovered anyway, for the on-top reason — which that function's own test
asserts. It was caught by reading the test, not by the compiler. **A correction to a false sentence
can be a second false sentence**, and nothing gates either one: the code compiles, the links resolve
and the tests pass under both readings.

`ui::zero_sense_hover_tests::a_row_that_senses_nothing_is_hovered_only_while_it_is_on_top` pins the
half nothing pinned. `menu_action`'s existing
`a_dimmed_control_can_be_hovered_only_through_a_claimant_of_its_own` already covers the **positive**
half — a zero-sense claimant allocated after a disabled scope does see the pointer. The new one
covers the **negative** half, which is the half the false sentence denied: register something
interactive over the same rect *afterwards* and the zero-sense row stops being hovered. Two passes
are pumped, interaction state being last frame's, and the uncovered case is the control — without it
the test could pass over a row that is never hovered at all.

**Flip:** drop the `ui.interact(rect, …, Sense::click())` line and the second assertion fails, the
row hovered again because nothing is above it. Predicted correctly.

*(§9.2's dimmed-control paragraph and §9.4's image-editing card paragraph each name the old spelling
and are amended to the surviving one; the rule they state — `on_disabled_hover_text` where there is a
`Response` to hang it on, an explicit claimant where there is not — is unchanged, and is D182's and
D234's. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D687 — A point box's side handles snapped an axis they cannot move, and two doc comments in one
file disagreed about whether they existed. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`canvas::snapped_point_box` passed `(true, true)` to `snap::snap_point` under *"Both axes, because a
corner travels along both — the point box **has no side handles** (`draw_point_box` has why)"*.
`draw_point_box`, the function that sentence cites for its authority, says *"**Four corner squares
and four invisible side bands**, as a layer's box has"* — and `node_grab` arms `Handle::EDGES` beside
`Handle::CORNERS`, under its own comment about a report that only the diagonals resized. **Two doc
comments in one file contradicting each other, with the code on the wrong side of the argument.**

🚨 **The geometry was safe and the mark was not, which is why nobody had reported it as a wrong
shape.** `tools::resize_factors` returns `1.0` for the axis a side handle does not drive, so nothing
moved that should not have. What was wrong is that `snap_point` handed back a `snap::Guide` for the
axis the drag cannot move, and the `Drag::PointBox` arm of the snap-mark pass **painted** it — a pink
line taking credit for a match the gesture did not make. `snap_point`'s own doc states the rule the
call was breaking: *"Snapping an axis the handle cannot move would move the anchored edge."*

Fixed by passing the handle down and asking `Self::resize_axes`, which is exactly what
`snapped_resize` already asks — so the answer is the handle's box-local outward direction mapped
through the node's world transform, and a rotated node's side really does claim both axes when it
travels along both. **One statement of the rule for both boxes**, rather than a constant beside one
of them.

⚠️ **Two fixture lessons, both learnt by probing rather than by reading, and both worth the next
person's time.** The first version of the test built its snap targets out of two **ruler guides** and
every case came back empty: `snap_point` deliberately emits no `Guide` mark for a ruler guide —
*"it is already a drawn line"* — so the mark this test is about exists only for a **node** target. And
a headless app's canvas is one pixel square, so `snap::targets`' view test rejects everything unless
`canvas_px` and the camera centre are set; without them nothing is a candidate at all and every
assertion is about an empty vector.

`canvas::point_box_snap_tests::a_side_handle_snaps_one_axis_and_a_corner_snaps_both` asserts a
`Right` handle returns the vertical guide only, a `Bottom` handle the horizontal only, and — the
control — that `BottomRight` still returns two. ⚠️ **The control is what says why the old sentence
read as true**: the unconditional answer was right for four of the eight handles, and those four are
the ones anybody demonstrates the feature with.

**Flip:** put `(true, true)` back and the `Right` case fails with two guides where one was expected.
Predicted correctly.

*(§9.4's resize paragraph gains the axis rule beside `snapped_resize`'s exclusion of the whole
selection — the two are the same function's two obligations and only one of them was written down.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D686 — `convert` was the one image-unsafe helper in a module that had decided the rule twice.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

Three helpers in `panels::paint` can be handed a `Brush::Image`, and the module states what that must
mean in two of them. `with_stops` refuses outright, its comment recording the bug that earned the
rule — *"one nudge of an image row's opacity scrubber replaced the photograph with a grey
rectangle"*. `default_brush`'s `Image` arm carries a `debug_assert!(false, …)` so a test finds it
first. **`convert` had neither.** Asked for any kind but `Image` it called `stops_of`, which hands
back a placeholder grey *by design, for the swatch to draw*, fanned it into a two-stop fade and
returned a grey gradient. The photograph is gone.

⚠️ **There is no failing input today, and the guard is the point rather than the objection to it.**
The only caller is `picker::picker_body`, protected twice over: `PaintKind::Image` is deliberately
absent from `PaintKind::ALL`, so the tab strip cannot ask for it, and that function returns early for
an image brush before it draws anything. What this cost is **altitude**. The identical bug shipped
once already through `with_stops` and was fixed *in this module*, on the stated ground that the rule
belongs where the brush is; the third helper's protection lived in `picker.rs`. A second caller — the
Group Colors row, a *Convert to gradient* menu item, an MCP verb — would inherit none of it, and
nothing in this file would have said so.

The guard is `matches!(brush, Brush::Image(_))` beside the existing early return, which had covered
only the case where the *target* kind was already `Image` — the one target the tab strip cannot ask
for. The arm that matters is every other one.

⚠️ **The flip was predicted wrongly twice over, and the correction is the plainer symptom.** The
prediction named `PaintKind::Linear` and a grey **gradient**, on the strength of the finding's own
headline. Removing the guard fails first on **`Solid`**, with `Solid(0.851, 0.851, 0.851, 1.0)` — the
placeholder grey — because `default_brush`'s `Solid` arm returns the first stop rather than building
anything, so the picture comes back as a flat grey swatch. The loop starts there. **A test that
sweeps a set catches the defect at the first member, not at the memorable one.**

`panels::paint::tests::an_images_opacity_dims_it_rather_than_replacing_it_with_grey` gains the third
door: it already drove the sampler-alpha path and the `with_stops` refusal, and now asserts
`convert(&image, kind, …) == image` for all three of `Solid`, `Linear` and `Radial`. One test for
three helpers is right here, because the three are one rule — *a picture is not a colour* — and
splitting them would let the next one be added without a case.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`. §9.4 already states the model half — `PaintKind::Image` is
*"deliberately absent from `PaintKind::ALL`"*, and the other three convert to one another *"where an
image does not"* — which is the rule this fix makes the code keep. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D685 — `stack_escape`'s square overflowed and the ink box came back unchanged. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

**The sibling D676 recorded and deliberately did not fix**, closed the same day that entry was
written. No finding named it: `arch-scribe` found it sweeping for D676's shape, and it was measured
red before anything was repaired.

Stage 1 of `effect::stack_escape` composed the visible layer blurs by summing
`deviation(radius).powi(2)` and rooting the sum once. `BLUR_DEVIATION` is 0.5, so a radius past
about `2.7e154` is finite — and therefore accepted by `build::effect_is_finite` at both its doors,
`SetEffects` and `op_insert_subtree`'s field loop — while its **square** is not. The sum came back
infinite, `stage1` with it, and `effect::escaped` was handed `Insets::uniform(inf)`.

**Which is D641's swallow, reached from a direction D641's own repair cannot see.** `escaped` splits
the insets back into an offset and a radius, so `x1 - x0` is `inf − inf` — `NaN` — and `f64::min`
answers the operand that is *not* `NaN`, so every edge contributes zero and **the box comes back
unchanged**. D641 puts the guard at the operation because the value it weighs is authored; here the
authored value is finite and the infinity is *derived*, so there is nothing at the operation to
refuse.

🚨 **This is the dangerous one of the pair, and the entry exists to say which way each fails.**
D676's overflow answered an **infinite** box: every cull passes, every raster is enormous, the
export plan asks for a picture nobody can allocate — loud, and impossible to ship without noticing.
This one answers the **original** box, so a layer whose blur reaches across the page reports the
extent of a bare rectangle, and `scene::paint_node` culls artwork that is on screen. §5.9's rule is
that **too small is the one error these bounds may not make**, and `resolve::mask_extent`'s doc
spends a paragraph on it.

**Three parts, and they are a fix, a floor and a store rather than one rule written three times.**

1. **The fold.** `f64::hypot` is the overflow-safe spelling of a *pair* and D676 could use it; a sum
   over a list cannot. The safe spelling for a fold is the classical one — divide through by the
   largest deviation, sum squares that are all `≤ 1`, multiply back — which is exact for every input
   the old form got right and finite for the ones it did not.
2. **The floor in `escaped`.** An escape whose four insets are not all finite now answers the
   **unbounded rect** rather than being decomposed into `NaN`. That is a change of failure and not a
   change of answer: an escape nobody can measure covers everything, and the one thing it must not
   read as is covering nothing.
3. **The store.** `.and_then(geometry::measurable)` on the ink written by `recompute_bounds` **and**
   by `resolve_subtree`, so the unbounded rect becomes the absence D495 chose over an infinite box —
   *"an infinite box unions all the way up"*. Both passes, because `update` and `rebuild` are
   asserted equal by a randomized differential test and a guard on one of them is a divergence.

🚨 **Running one flip was misleading, and the pair is the argument for both repairs.** Restoring
`deviation(radius).powi(2)` on its own fails at `expect("the node has ink")` — the floor catches the
infinite escape, `measurable` drops the box, and the node simply has no ink, which reads like a
different bug. Removing the floor **as well** is what reproduces the original defect, and it prints
it exactly: *"the blur reported reaching nowhere: ink `0,0 .. 100,100` against box
`0,0 .. 100,100`"*. Only running both says which of the two is the fix and which is the floor.

`resolve::measurable_bounds_tests::a_blur_whose_square_overflows_still_reports_the_ink_it_covers`
asserts the ink is wider than the box on both sides and that both edges are numbers, at a radius of
`4e154` — the last decade before the old spelling overflowed. Its control is an `f64::MAX` radius,
where the escape genuinely does overflow: the node then has **no** measurable ink, rather than the
box it started from. That control is what separates *the arithmetic was wrong* from *this input has
no answer*.

*(§5.9's *"`ink_bounds` needs no guard of its own and the reason is arithmetic"* is amended — true
of D676's door, and false of this one, since both ink stores are guarded now. §5.9's D676 paragraph
carried a `*Fix.*` for this sibling and it is struck. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D684 — An empty badge label overflowed one statement before its own guard. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`cursor::digits` lifts a short string's coverage out of the font atlas and folds a bounding box out
of the glyphs it placed, seeded `(i32::MAX, i32::MAX, i32::MIN, i32::MIN)`. Place none — an empty
label, or one whose every glyph is missing — and those seeds come straight back out, so `hi_x - lo_x`
is `i32::MIN - i32::MAX`.

**That is not a small wrong number, it is an overflow.** A debug build panics with *"attempt to
subtract with overflow"*; a release build wraps to `1` and carries on to allocate a one-byte buffer
and index it with glyph offsets. And the guard written for exactly this state — `if w <= 0 || h <= 0`
— sat one statement *past* it, so it could only ever have caught a box that was measured and came out
empty, never a box that was never measured at all. `rasterize`, the sibling that lifts a single
glyph the same way, has always tested before it subtracts.

The emptiness test is above the fold now.

⚠️ **Not reachable from the app today, and the arithmetic is why it is written down anyway.** The
only labels that reach here are `Remaining::label`'s `"1"`–`"99"` and `"99+"`, Inter carries every
one of those characters, and `theme::install` has run before any cursor is built. What is one line
from being right is the guard the whole `Option` chain above it is written to receive: `badge(…)?`
in `loaded_crosshair` says in its own punctuation that a label with nothing to draw is an answer this
function is allowed to give.

`cursor::tests::a_badge_with_nothing_to_draw_refuses_rather_than_overflowing` asks for `""` and
expects `None`, with `"99+"` as the control so the guard has not eaten the ordinary case.
⚠️ **The empty string is the honest input rather than a contrivance**: it is the one label whose
glyph list is empty for a reason nothing about font loading can change, where a missing-glyph label
would need a font this repository does not have. What the test is about is the guard's *position*,
and both inputs reach it the same way.

**Flip:** move `if placed.is_empty()` back below the `let (w, h) = …` and the test fails by
**panicking** rather than by an assertion — which is the finding, and is the reason the test's own
doc says so. Predicted correctly.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, whose §5.5a bullet specifies what the loaded cursor's badge
*says* (§15 D236, D9) and never how its digits are rasterized. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D683 — Nothing asserted that the View and Snap menus between them cover `ViewSwitch`. *Tested
2026-09-09; Keep — test-only.***

`ViewSwitch::VIEW_MENU` and `SNAP_MENU` were `[Self; 7]` and `[Self; 4]`, written out by hand over an
enum with **eleven** variants, and 7 + 4 = 11 was a coincidence nothing checked. A twelfth variant
compiles green: `label` and `accel` force a string for it — they are exhaustive since D675 —
`set_view_switch` and `view_switch` force a field, and `input::resolve` can give it a chord. What
nothing forces is that it appear on a menu, so it would be a switch with a keyboard binding and no
row, silently.

⚠️ **The twelfth variant arrived on 2026-09-15 and this entry is why it could not land badly**
(D755): `ViewSwitch::LayoutGrid` is on `VIEW_MENU`, which is `[Self; 8]` now, and the test is what
would have said so had it not been. **The three numbers above are as-of-D683 and are left in the past
tense**, since rewriting them to today's would make the account of the defect wrong — and they are
struck out of the test's own comment rather than corrected there, because this assertion is
**membership and not cardinality** and a count beside it is a gate nobody built.

**That is the exact failure the type was introduced to prevent**, and `Action::ToggleView`'s own doc
says so: *"the same set the View and Snap menus show, so a row and its chord cannot come to mean
different things."* D675 had just finished removing two wildcards that made the same absence look
like an answer; this is the third place the coupling was asserted by nobody.

🚨 **Membership, not cardinality, and the difference is the whole test.**
`assert_eq!(VIEW.len() + SNAP.len(), ALL.len())` is what anyone writes first and it is
`[S6.3-L6-04]`'s trap in miniature: it passes for two arrays that both hold `Grid` and neither holds
`Present`. `menu::view_switch_registry_tests::every_view_switch_is_on_exactly_one_menu` asks each
switch how many of the two menus it is on and demands **one** — which catches an omission and a
duplication with one assertion, and names the offender by its own label rather than by an index.

`ViewSwitch::ALL` is what makes it askable, and it landed under D675; this entry is the membership
half only.

**Flip:** drop `Present` from `VIEW_MENU`, making it `[Self; 6]` — the plausible slip, present mode
not being a peer of the others — and the test fails naming *"Present mode"* with `0` menus. Site
predicted correctly.

*(§9.4's registry paragraph gains the check. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D682 — Four cursor hotspots nothing read, and two of them carried a *reason*. *Fixed 2026-09-09;
Keep — no behaviour changed.***

`Cursors::image` routes `Crosshair`, `Rotate`, `Loaded` and `TextOnPath` to functions that draw them
outright and pass their own `Hotspot`, so the only caller of `Bitmap::hotspot()` was the
`other => rasterize(…)` arm — and `other` is exactly the five variants that have a Phosphor glyph.
Four of the nine variants' answers were therefore dead, and the two lists had to be kept in step by
somebody remembering that they were two lists.

**The two halves failed differently, and the worse half is the one that looks better.** `Loaded` and
`TextOnPath` said *"Read by nothing"* in their own arms, which is honest and is D236's own note
arriving twice more. `Crosshair` and `Rotate` instead carried an **argument** for a value nothing
read — *"a crosshair points at its own centre, which is why it has a gap there"* — so somebody moving
the crosshair's aiming point would edit that line, run the app, see no change, and have to go and
find `Cross::aim`. A dead value that says it is dead costs a reader nothing; a dead value with a
rationale on it costs them the afternoon.

⚠️ **D236 is the precedent and it is the argument for merging rather than annotating.** That entry
closes with *"`Bitmap::hotspot`'s `Loaded` arm is read by nothing and says so — the real hotspot
comes from `loaded_crosshair`, not from there"*, which was written for this exact shape on one arm.
The shape came back on two more, which is what says the annotation does not hold: a note is a claim
about today's routing, and the routing is what grew.

So `glyph()` and `hotspot()` are one function,
`glyph_and_hotspot(self) -> Option<(&'static str, Hotspot)>`. A variant with no glyph now has
nowhere to put a hotspot, the four drawn cursors take the single `None` arm together, and the
routing in `image` is the only place that decides which of the two lists a variant is on. D236's
closing note is amended, the arm it names no longer existing.

**No new test, and both existing ones were read against the claim rather than assumed.**
`cursor::tests::the_badge_does_not_move_the_aiming_point` asserts the loaded cursor's hotspot
*equals* the plain crosshair's over 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0/3.0 and six counts, and that the aiming point is
still transparent in each; `the_crosshair_can_be_seen_through_at_its_aiming_point` asserts the alpha
at the hotspot is `0`. Between them the outcome the deleted arms could have changed is already
pinned, which is why this is a shape change with no assertion behind it.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`. It specifies what each cursor *says* — §9.4's discard bin and
Scale glyph, §5.5a's loaded count badge — and never how a hotspot reaches one. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D681 — Recovering strands the snapshot it replaced, and the one-line fix made the reachable case
worse. *Resolved 2026-09-15 by the maintainer's ruling — see D768. The leak is gone and the guards
are why.***

🚨 **The ruling is D768 and it is the shape this entry asked for**, not the one line: `open_path`'s
save-then-`confirm_discard` pair is lifted into `OndinApp::may_replace_current_document` and asked by
both doors, and `drop_recovery` sits behind it. **The rest of this entry is the argument that got
there and is kept in the past tense** — in particular the reason the one-line repair was reverted,
which is the thing a future reader is most likely to undo.

`OndinApp::recover` reads the pending snapshot, adopts it into the session, and then sets
`recovery.key` to that snapshot's key. What it never does is drop the key it is **overwriting**. So
the outgoing session's own snapshot is left in `.recovery/` with nothing naming it: it is offered at
every future launch, and *Later* only pops it for that launch, so the prompt returns for ever.

**The rule is already written down and already applied at the sibling door.** `open_path` calls
`drop_recovery` immediately before `adopt_document`, under a ⚠️ comment that states this failure
verbatim — *"Past this line the app is holding a different document and has no way to name the old
one's snapshot, so the file would sit in `.recovery/` until the next launch asked about it."*
`recover` does the adopt and never calls it at all.

🚨 **That line was written, tested, and then reverted, and it is the most useful sentence in this
entry.** The fix passed, the flip bit where it was predicted to, and on the only route anybody can
actually reach it **deletes the last copy of the user's work**. Leaking a snapshot offers it again;
dropping it takes it away. So the repair that closes the finding as written is strictly worse than
the defect, and this is a decision rather than an unattended fix.

**Two facts make it so, and the first is that the finding's own route is closed.** Its argument is
that the recovery card does not own the keyboard (`[S16.1-L2-01]`), so the document underneath can be
edited while the card is up, marking the session dirty and making `recovery_tick` mint a second key.
**D464 fixed that on 2026-09-07**: `eframe::App::ui`'s guard chain names `recovery.pending` beside
`settings` and `confirming_close`, so the keyboard cannot reach the document behind the card.
⚠️ **A citation that resolves to a *fixed* finding is worse than one that dangles**, because the
reader checks the number, finds an entry, and stops.

🚨 **The sentence that stood here — *"the card blocks the pointer, so nothing behind it can be edited
and no second key can be minted that way"* — was false for eight days, and it was false about the
very route this entry exists to weigh** (§15 D759). The backdrop blocks a **click**; it does not
block a **drop**, because `raw.dropped_files` is filled from winit before any widget runs. So a
picture dragged onto the window while the recovery card was up committed ops to the document behind
it, marked the session dirty, and minted the second snapshot key this paragraph said could not be
minted. D759 guards it and the claim is true now — **but the reason to keep the old wording quoted is
that it was written the day the keyboard hole closed and generalised from the keyboard to "the
pointer" without anybody asking the pointer.**

**The second is that the live route needs no keyboard at all — it is the queue.**
`recovery::pending` is a queue, and `recovery_modal` prints *"N more after this one"* when it holds
more than one, so a launch that finds two snapshots lets *Recover* be pressed twice. The second press
is the one that finds `recovery.key` already set — naming the snapshot the user recovered **one press
ago** and has not saved. On that route `drop_recovery` deletes exactly that.

*Fixed with `open_path`'s whole shape — save if it can, then `confirm_discard` — and not with the one
line*, which is what this entry asked for and what **D768** did. Neither guard was here, and adding
them changes what a button does, which was the maintainer's call rather than a fix phase's. Until it
was made the leak was the safer of the two states and the comment at the site said so.

**The test was kept and inverted, which is unusual enough to say out loud.**
`app::recover_snapshot_tests::recovering_leaks_the_outgoing_snapshot_until_someone_rules_on_the_guards`
wrote two snapshots into a scratch root, set `recovery.key` to the first by hand — so it depended on
neither route above — recovered the second, and asserted the first was **still there**. Its failure
message was the ruling: *"a `drop_recovery` has been added to `recover` without `open_path`'s
save-then-confirm guards."* ⚠️ **A test that pins an unfixed state is a tripwire and not an assertion
of correctness**: if it goes red, the question the entry is waiting on has been answered by accident.
It went red on purpose and is
`recovering_drops_the_outgoing_snapshot_now_that_the_guards_are_there` now, with
`a_second_recover_asks_before_it_spends_the_first` beside it for the queue route it cannot see.

*(D377's drop-site enumeration was left at **four** — `open_path`, `go_to_dashboard` and
`close_confirmation`'s two arms — and *"Discard is the only thing that deletes"* stood, both of them
having been amended to five for the half-day the reverted fix was in the tree. **Both are at five
now, by D768, and this time the code is at `HEAD`.** §9.5's copy of that list moved with them.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D680 — A locked paste counted nothing. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`app::paste_guides` built its ops, committed them, called `select_pasted_guides`, and then read the
count it reports off `self.session.selection.guides().len()`. `select_pasted_guides` opens
`if self.lock_guides { return; }`.

**That early return is the correct rule, which is what makes this worth an entry.** Locked means
unselectable — `guide_at` refuses a locked guide — so selecting a fresh copy would produce a guide
that is *selected and unpickable*, the state the ruler drag's release is careful not to create and
that `architecture.md` §9.4 already writes out. The rule is right and it is exactly what stranded the
count: with *Lock guides* on, a paste that added three guides and committed reported **"Pasted 0
guide(s)"** — or, if some unrelated guide happened to be selected, that guide's count. The orphan arm
contradicted itself inside one sentence: *"Pasted 0 guide(s) — 2 whose frame is gone are now on the
canvas"*.

**The twin had it right all along.** `duplicate_guides` takes `ops.len()` before it commits. The two
share `pasted_guide` — the placement rule — and nothing else, so they are two doors onto one feature
that disagreed about how to count what they had placed. It is `ids.len()` here now, taken from the
ids the paste minted.

⚠️ **The unlocked case is why it survived to be found by review.** With guides unlocked the selection
*is* the paste, so the wrong expression returns the right number, and every ordinary use of the
feature — which is every use with the default preference — looks perfectly correct.

`app::guide_copy_tests::a_paste_counts_the_guides_it_made_even_when_they_cannot_be_selected` runs
both, `for locked in [true, false]`, and asserts the status line and that the guides really did reach
the document. The unlocked half is the control: without it the test is about a message rather than
about a count. **Flip:** put `self.session.selection.guides().len()` back and the locked case fails
with *"Pasted 0 guide(s)"*. Predicted correctly.

*(§9.4's guide-clipboard paragraph gains the rule, two sentences from the lock it already states.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D679 — A fourth panel committed for itself, and D128's enforcement sentence was false rather than
incomplete. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`OndinApp::commit_edit`'s doc calls routing through it *"the whole guard against the chrome hide
becoming a roll-call"*, and D128 states the enforcement as a grep: *"the only `session.commit` left
under `panels/` is in `layers.rs`"*. `inspector::remove_selected_guides` — the guide card's Trash
button — committed through `session.commit` directly, and had since it was written.

**The distinction is that the sentence was false, not merely out of date.** The exceptions
`commit_edit`'s doc already names are exceptions *from* the rule and say so — `commit_chrome_edit`
for box trim, the layers panel, and the identity row's *Group* and *Ungroup* buttons (D562), which
reach `session.commit` through an `OndinApp` method declared in `app.rs`, so D128's grep passes over
them honestly and the doc says as much. This one was under
`panels/`, spelled `self.session.commit`, and named nowhere: not in that function's list, not in
`architecture.md` §9.4's chrome-hide paragraph, and not in D128.

Routed through `commit_edit`. **Behaviourally identical**, because `RemoveGuide` is one of the eleven
operations `op::changes_ink` answers `false` for, so the hide was never armed either way. What it
cost to leave is that this function is what the next guide control gets copied from, and the next one
may not be an op the predicate excuses.

**The grep nobody was running is a test now.**
`app::tests::only_the_layers_panel_commits_without_the_committer` reads the seven sources under
`panels/` through `include_str!` and asserts the committing set is exactly `["layers.rs"]`.
⚠️ **`self.session.` rather than `.session.` is the discriminator, and it is not cosmetic**: every
test in those files commits through a *named* app (`app.session.commit`), so the receiver is what
tells production code from a fixture. A predicate matching both reports six files and gets abandoned
as noise.

⚠️ **The control on the array is a `read_dir`, and the obvious one was a tautology.**
`assert_eq!(panels.len(), 7)` was written first and cannot fail: a hand-written array of seven has
seven entries whatever the directory holds, so an eighth panel would join the tree unscanned with
this test still green. `include_str!` resolves at compile time and takes no glob, so the array cannot
be generated — what *can* be checked is that it matches `src/panels` read at run time, minus
`mod.rs`, which is the module declaration rather than a panel.

🚨 **The method note is the half worth carrying past this entry: a census like this has to be run per
file, and a truncating sweep is how the finding's own subject was missed.** `inspector.rs` is the
largest file in the tree — over twenty-three thousand lines — and holds **37** `#[cfg(test)]`
attributes at column 0 and **36** top-level test modules, with production code running between them
to within a hundred lines of the end. The *first* of those attributes
is a one-line `const` at line 876 with production code continuing straight underneath, so a sweep
that treats the first `#[cfg(test)]` as the end of the file loses better than twenty-two thousand
lines — which is how a review pass whose whole subject was this convention certified a file that
broke it.

🚨 **And that mechanism does not explain this finding, which is the correction worth more than the
note.** The comment shipped with the fix called line 876 the first `#[cfg(test)]` **module** and put
the module count at *"nine"*; the first top-level module is at **11,683** and there are **36** of
them, and `remove_selected_guides` sits at ~10,012 — *before* it. So a module-aware sweep would have
found this outright, and only the **attribute** reading loses it. That is what the sweep actually
run did. Corrected in the tree, with the distinction stated rather than the wording patched, and the
test sidesteps the whole question by discriminating on the **receiver** instead of trying to know
where test code begins. *The repair for a count in prose is the command, not a better number.*

*(D128 is amended — a *Resolved* entry whose own claim had stopped being true. **§9.4**'s chrome-hide
paragraph gains the test and the two exceptions it cannot see; the rule is stated there rather than in
§9.3, whose valve it cross-references. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D678 — The save pill could never say "1h". *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`app::save_label`'s four bands each round half-up: `(secs + unit/2) / unit`. A band therefore prints
`1` as its **first** value only while its opening lies in `[unit/2, 3·unit/2)`. The hours band opened
at **5400**, which is `3 × 3600 / 2` exactly — one second outside — so the smallest value it could
produce was `2`.

**So *"Saved · 1h ago"* was unreachable for every input in the function's domain.** An hour-old save
read *"Saved · 60m ago"*, the minutes band ran on to *"90m ago"*, and the pill then jumped straight
to `2h`.

⚠️ **The days band was already right, and it is what makes 2700 a rule rather than a taste.** It
opens at 79200 — 22 h — which is inside `[43200, 129600)`, so its first value is `1d`. The property
the ladder already kept everywhere else is *a band's first value is 1*, and the hours band was the
one place it had been broken.

🚨 **Two plausible restatements of that property are wrong, and both would move a boundary that is
correct.** It is **not** "three quarters of the unit": that is what 45 s and 45 min look like, and
22 h is not it, `0.75 × 24 h` being 18 h. And it is **not** "the earliest second at which the band
could say 1": for days that is 43200, i.e. 12 h. ⚠️ **The comment shipped with the fix and the test's
own doc both used the second wording** — *"22 h … is where half-up first gives one day"* — and both
put the cost at *"`45m`…`59m` now read `1h`"* where the readings actually replaced are **45m through
90m**, the old minutes band having run to 5399. **Both are corrected in the tree**, each carrying a
sentence saying what it used to claim, because the wrong wording is the one anybody re-derives.
🚨 **Neither error was in the code and the code was right the whole time**, which is the thing to
carry: a boundary can be correct and its *justification* wrong, and nothing here reads a
justification — `cargo doc` resolves links, clippy reads code, and this test asserts eight strings.

The cost is worth stating plainly all the same: `45m` through `90m` now read `1h`, which is the same
trade `just now` → `1m` makes at 45 seconds, and the pill is a relative time rather than a clock.

`app::tests::every_band_of_the_save_pill_can_say_one_of_its_unit` is eight rows across all four
bands. ⚠️ **The `1d` row is not filler**: it is the band that was already right, and asserting it is
what stops a later tidy moving all three boundaries onto one wrong rule.

**Flip:** put the hours band back to `45..=5399` / `5400..` and it fails at the **2700** row — *"the
hours band opens where it can say 1: left `"Saved · 45m ago"`, right `"Saved · 1h ago"`"*.
⚠️ **Predicted wrongly**: the prediction named the `3600` row, on the strength of *"60m ago"* being
the symptom anybody would report. The row that bites is the band's **edge**, which is the general
shape — a boundary defect is caught at the boundary, and the memorable middle of the band is caught
second.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`. §9.5 specifies the pill's amber dot and its *Saving…* label
(§15 D393) and has never specified the *ago* ladder, which is a wording rule the code owns; the entry
above is where it is written down. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D677 — A picture too big to draw is not a picture that could not be read. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`ondin_render::images::DecodeError` had **no reader anywhere in the workspace**. `ImageStore::failure`
and the whole three-way distinction — `Corrupt`, `TooLarge`, `TooMuchPixelData` — were consumed
nowhere outside `images.rs`'s own tests, and both callers of `insert` discarded the error with
`.ok()?`. `dead_code` never fires on a `pub` item in a library crate, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s recorded
blind spot; it was swept for `ondin-core` at Pass 0 §11 and never for `ondin-render`.

So a **70000 × 100 panorama** — 34 KB of PNG that `image` decodes without complaint, refused because
`vello_cpu` builds its `Pixmap` from `u16` dimensions — came back as **"Could not read"**. The file
reads perfectly well; what it cannot do is be drawn. `DecodeError`'s own doc states the intent nobody
