took up: *"Why an image could not be decoded, for the caller that wants to say so."*

🚨 **The standard was already written eleven lines above the message.** `place_image_action`'s SVG arm
says it in as many words — *"'could not read' would be a lie about a file that reads perfectly well
and is simply not an image"* — which is the whole reason the drop path sniffs the bytes at all.
`TooLarge` is the third member of that set and was the one nobody counted separately, so the app was
careful about one lie and casual about the other.

`app::ImageRefusal` is the type: `NotAnImage` for *this is not a picture*, `Decode(DecodeError)` for
*it is a picture and Ondin will not draw it*, with `DecodeError`'s three variants saying which reason.
`load_image_bytes` and `load_image_file` return a `Result` of it. Three sites that tell the user
something now say which of the two went wrong — the drop, the file picker and *Replace…* — and the
fourth deliberately says nothing: `paste_image` decodes the app's **own** freshly encoded PNG, so a
refusal there is a bug rather than something to explain.

**The message carries both numbers and the limit**, not a category. *"panorama.png is 70000 × 100;
the largest Ondin can draw is 65535 on a side"* tells somebody what to change and by how much, where
*"too large"* sends them back to a file to guess. `TooMuchPixelData` gets a sentence of its own, in
`human_bytes`, because it is a different bound with a different remedy — which is exactly why
`DecodeError` keeps the two apart, and why flattening them here would have thrown away the reason the
enum has three variants.

⚠️ **The negative assertion is the finding.** The old sentence is *false*, not merely unhelpful, so
`app::svg_sniff_tests::a_picture_too_big_to_draw_says_so_rather_than_could_not_read` asserts the
message does **not** contain *"Could not read"* as well as that it contains 70000, 100 and 65535 — a
test that only checked for the new numbers would pass a message that said both. The control is twenty
bytes of prose, which still gets the plain sentence, so the change is about telling two failures apart
rather than about replacing one message with another. **Flip:** put `.ok().ok_or(ImageRefusal::NotAnImage)`
back on `load_image_bytes`' `insert` and the first assertion fails, `NotAnImage` against
`Decode(TooLarge { .. })`. Predicted correctly.

**Behaviour change worth recording**: a multi-file failure is joined with `"; "`, one sentence per
file, where it used to be one *"Could not read: a, b, c"*. That is the point rather than a side
effect — two files can now fail for two different reasons in one drop, and a single list of names
could only ever have said one thing about both.

⚠️ **`ImageStore::failure` still has no production reader.** This fix takes the error off `insert`,
which is where the caller already was; the store's *remembered* failure — the thing that stops a
corrupt entry being re-decoded every frame — is read by nothing outside its own tests. The
`pub`-in-a-library trap is narrowed here and not closed, and the same sweep is owed for the rest of
`ondin-render`.

🚨 **A defect this change shipped, found while checking it.** The new test was inserted into
`app::svg_sniff_tests` by anchoring an `Edit` on D671's
`#[test] fn the_drop_door_and_the_paste_door_agree_about_a_file` — **the item line** — so it landed
between that test and its own doc comment. D671's eighteen-line paragraph, ending *"Flip: put back the
old body … Predicted correctly"*, now sits on **this** test, and `the_drop_door_and_the_paste_door_agree_about_a_file`
has no doc at all. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s nineteenth instance and the plainest spelling of it: the
merged run is 38 lines against a length ranking whose floor is 52, so that detector cannot reach it,
and every gate is green. The neighbour grep *would* have caught it — the item below did lose its
comment — and it was not run on this insertion. ~~*Fix by splitting the run and putting D671's half back
on its own test.*~~ ⚠️ ~~The module's name is now wrong as well: `svg_sniff_tests` holds an
image-refusal test.~~ **Both done 2026-09-09.** The eighteen lines are back on
`the_drop_door_and_the_paste_door_agree_about_a_file`, with a ⚠️ note on them recording that they
spent one commit on the test below and that the anchor chosen was the `fn` line — *the unique string,
and the wrong one*, which is the tension `CLAUDE.md` names: the uniqueness of an anchor and its
correctness pull in opposite directions, and the unique one is always the item line. `svg_sniff_tests`
has a module doc naming both halves, so the name is documented rather than renamed — the two findings
are the same sentence from two sides, *"could not read"* about a file that reads perfectly well.

*(§5.5a's image bullets gain the refusal rule — that a refusal names which of the two things went
wrong, and that the numbers are in the message. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D676 — A blur's escape squared its way to an infinite ink box. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep.***

No finding named this. It came out of `arch-scribe` reading D667's brief against `effect::escaped`,
and D667's own body carries the arithmetic **read rather than run**; this is that reading confirmed
red and repaired.

`escaped` maps the escape radius as an **ellipse** rather than as a box — the right answer, and D641's
paragraph above it explains why: a blur's reach is a disc, so what maps is an ellipse and its extent
is the row's euclidean norm, which comes back to exactly `r` under any rotation. It was spelled
`((a * rad.x).powi(2) + (c * rad.y).powi(2)).sqrt()`, and **the square is where it breaks**: `x²`
overflows at about `1.3e154`, where the product `x` itself stays finite all the way to `1.8e308`.

**So every input is legal and every guard passes.** `build::effect_is_finite` takes the radius (§15
D641), `build::affine_is_finite` takes a `scale(1e155)` — every coefficient finite, which is all it
asks — and `geometry::measurable` takes the resulting world box at `1e157`, ordered and finite. Then
`h` comes back infinite, `(t.x − h.x).min(0.0)` is `−inf`, and the ink box is
`(−inf, −inf, inf, inf)` under a world box that passed.

**That box is not `world_bounds`**, which is why §15 D495 and D667 never look at it. It is what
`scene::paint_node` culls whole subtrees on, what `ondin_export::plan::raster_size` sizes a raster
from, and what the SVG writer measures for `filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` (§5.3a, §7).

**The repair is `f64::hypot`, and it is deliberately not a guard.** There was nothing wrong with the
*answer*, only with the route to it — `hypot` is the same value computed without an intermediate that
can overflow — so the box stays finite and stays right, and no input has to be refused. ⚠️ **This is
not D641's shape and the difference is worth stating**, because the two sit three lines apart in the
same function. D641 is about an escape that is *itself* non-finite, which `escaped` has nowhere to put:
its signature returns a `Rect`, an infinite box is the failure D495 removed, and so the check belongs
at the operation. Here the escape is finite, the world transform is legal, and there is no operation
to guard — the defect is arithmetic and the fix is arithmetic.

`resolve::measurable_bounds_tests::a_blur_under_a_huge_scale_keeps_the_documents_ink_finite` asserts
the node's ink is finite on all four edges and that the root inherits exactly it, then runs the same
blur at scale 1 as a control, asserting the ink is the box grown by `stack_escape` on **both** sides.
That control is what says the change is about overflow rather than about the arithmetic: a clamp would
have passed the first assertion and failed the second. **Flip:** put back the `powi(2)` spelling and
the first assertion fails with an infinite box while the control stays green. Predicted correctly.

🚨 **The sweep for the same shape found one sibling, and it is recorded rather than fixed.**
`effect::stack_escape` composes stage 1 in deviations — `sigma2` is a **sum of `deviation(radius).powi(2)`**
over the visible layer blurs, rooted once — which is the same overflow with a list instead of a pair.
A radius past roughly `1.3e154 / BLUR_DEVIATION` is finite, so `build::effect_is_finite` accepts it at
both its doors, and `sigma2` comes back infinite; `stage1` is then infinite, and `escaped` is handed
`Insets::uniform(inf)` — which is **D641's `inf − inf = NaN` swallow**, returning the box *unchanged*.
So the symptom is D641's exactly, an unbounded blur reporting that it reaches nowhere, reintroduced by
a **derived** infinity rather than an authored one. D641's repair cannot see it, because the field it
weighs is finite; `hypot` cannot help either, the operands being a fold rather than a pair. ~~*Fix
separately — the answer is a bound on the radius at the operation, or a fold that cannot overflow, and
which of the two it should be is a decision rather than a spelling.*~~ **Fixed the same day: it is
the fold, and it needed a floor and a store beside it — D685.** ⚠️ **And the sibling fails in the
*opposite* direction to this entry**, which is the reason it deserved its own: an infinite box is
loud, and a box that has silently not grown makes the cull drop artwork that is on screen.

⚠️ **Two other `(x² + y²)` sites were read and cleared**, so the sweep is a result rather than a
sample. `geometry::distance_point_segment` takes `ab.hypot2()` and divides by it, so an overflow makes
`t` zero and degrades a hit test to "distance to the segment's start" — a wrong `bool`, not a box that
escapes. `svg_in::squashed_radial` squares four affine coefficients to compare singular values; an
overflow gives `lo = NaN` and the predicate answers `false`, which is the conservative side of a
heuristic. Neither produces a bound anything caches.

*(§5.9's *"`ink_bounds` is not yet guarded this way and is a known gap"* is struck and replaced with
what closed it; §5.9's D641 paragraph gains the derived-infinity sibling — ⚠️ **this line said
§5.3a and was wrong**, the D641 paragraph being in §5.9's `ink_bounds` bullet, which is the
resolves-but-does-not-agree shape D672 records for the third consecutive session. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D675 — `ViewState` answered for seven switches with the grid's, and `spec` gave them its chord.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`menu::ViewState` is a four-field struct read once by the caller so that building a menu takes no
borrow of anything. Its `get` closed on `_ => self.grid`. `input::ViewSwitch` has **eleven** variants,
so there was no value that wildcard *could* return for `Layers`, `Toolbar`, `Present` or the four
`Snap` switches — and it returned one anyway, which is the whole defect: **the absence was made to
look like an answer.** `Item::spec`'s accelerator arm closed the same way, on `_ => "Ctrl+'"`, so
those same seven would have rendered wearing the grid's chord, four of them switches with chords of
their own.

⚠️ **The finding counts `ViewSwitch` at seven variants and it is eleven.** That is the same defect one
level up — a number in prose standing in for a gate — and it is the argument for the repair being an
exhaustive `match` rather than a corrected count. Both matches are one now, and a twelfth variant is a
compile error at each.

**Not reachable today, and that is why it is a trap rather than a bug.** `view_rows` and `guide_menu`
between them build rows for the four the struct holds, and `Item::ALL` lists only those. The day it
becomes reachable is written down: `context-menus.md` §6.1 keeps *Show layers*, *Show toolbar* and
*Present mode* out of the canvas menu deliberately, so a row shipped with the grid's tick and the
grid's chord the moment that is reversed, and nothing anywhere would have said a word. The file is
otherwise built on the opposite habit and says so — `LayerState::text_sizing` is an `Option` *"so the
one state that has no answer cannot be spelled"*.

`get` returns `Option<bool>`, and `Row::checked` takes `impl Into<Option<bool>>` so a caller with no
answer can say so; `checked` was `Some(on)` unconditionally, which is precisely why `ViewState::get`
had to invent a `bool`. Of `Row::checked`'s **nine** call sites, six pass a plain `bool` and read
unchanged, and the three that ask `ViewState::get` pass its `Option` straight through — a `None`
leaves the row with no tick rather than with a borrowed one.

`ViewSwitch::accel()` is new, beside `label()`, for the reason `label` gives: the enum was bought so a
switch's text lives in one place, and its chord is the same kind of fact. It is exhaustive, and `None`
for `SnapBaselines`, which has no chord — deliberately, no app having this switch, so there is no
convention to match and no chord worth spending. ⚠️ **Nothing makes `accel` and `input::resolve`
agree.** These are the menu's *spellings* and `resolve` holds the bindings; the strings here were read
off the chords `resolve` tests for, by hand. `shortcuts.md` is the document that fixes how a chord is
written and is what a reader should check both against — but no gate compares any of the three, and
the test below deliberately does not pretend to, asserting distinctness rather than correctness.

The glyph arm is spelled out too, and it is the one place the answer is honestly unknown: none of
those seven rows has ever been drawn, so `SLIDERS_HORIZONTAL` is a **placeholder** rather than a pick
— *"what a switch looks like when nobody has chosen yet"* — and spelling it out means the compiler
puts the author on that line the day one lands, which is where `context-menus.md` §8 wants the verb's
glyph named.

`ViewSwitch::ALL` is new and `#[cfg(test)]` — the same admission `Item::ALL`'s doc makes and the shape
D672 had to reach for in `theme::icon`, an `#[allow]` on a list like this keeping every item it names
alive. It is hand-written, so it cannot police the enum on its own; what makes it answerable is that
`label` and `accel` are exhaustive `match`es three lines above it. Two tests in
`menu::view_switch_registry_tests`: every switch takes its chord from the switch and no two chords
collide, with a chordless one staying expressible; and `ViewState` answers for its four and for
nothing else.

⚠️ **The accel flip's site was predicted correctly and its *assertion* was not.** Putting the wildcard
back fails the registry-asks-the-switch check rather than the distinctness scan below it, because that
check runs first and is strictly stronger. The scan is not redundant for that — it is what would catch
a *wrong* chord written into `accel` itself, which is the half the first assertion cannot see.

*(§9.4's context-menu registry paragraph amended — that a `Spec` field a target cannot answer is an
absence rather than a default. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D674 — One definition of "container" behind the collapse-all button. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep.***

`layers::tree_is_all_collapsed` re-ran `subtree_nodes` over the root and re-inlined
`tree_containers`' two-clause filter — *not the root, and has children* — with
`&& !self.collapsed.contains(&id)` bolted on the end. So the button's **glyph** and the button's
**action**, `toggle_collapse_all`'s `anything_open`, reached *"what counts as a container"* by two
independent walks. Widen or narrow one and the arrow points one way while the press does the other,
with nothing in between to disagree.

🚨 **The coupling was stated in the design and enforced by nothing.** §9.4 names the two functions in
one breath as the argument for the control existing at all: *"a control that looks and does the other
thing costs one button instead of two (`tree_is_all_collapsed` / `toggle_collapse_all`)"*. A control
whose whole justification is that it reads the room had two readings of the room.

It is `self.tree_containers().iter().all(|id| self.collapsed.contains(id))` now — the exact negation
of `anything_open`, which is what makes the pair one sentence rather than two that happen to agree.
`tree_containers` already had a third reader in `collapse_all`, the answer to
`Prefs::collapse_groups_on_open`, so the shared definition was there and this was the one caller not
using it. It also drops a second full `subtree_nodes` walk **per frame**: the glyph is read on every
frame the panel draws, where the toggle's walk is per click.

`layers::collapse_all_tests::the_glyph_and_the_press_read_one_definition_of_container` drives the
button rather than comparing the two predicates — press it until it stops changing anything, and
assert the glyph says the opposite each time — which is the assertion that survives a future third
reader. The fixture holds an Artboard, a Boolean and a **childless** `Group`, and the childless one is
its point: it is a container by the tree's eye and by neither predicate, so a "fix" that folded it
would be caught here and nowhere else.

**Flip:** put back the inlined walk with the `id != root` clause dropped — the plausible slip, since
the root is not a row — and the second assertion fails, the glyph reading *"not all folded"* on a tree
the press has just folded, because the root is a container nothing can collapse. Site predicted
correctly.

*(§9.4's collapse-all paragraph amended — one definition, and which function owns it. Nothing struck
from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D673 — `SLIDER_H`'s doc called the knob the tallest thing in the row. *Doc fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep — the drawing was right and the record was not.***

`ui::SLIDER_H` is `pub` and is the number every caller reserves. Its doc read *"the knob's diameter,
which is the tallest thing in it"*. The tallest thing in it is the knob's **shadow** — a `half`-radius
disc drawn at `rect.center().y + 1.0`, which is the design's `box-shadow: 0 1px 3px` — so `slider`
paints `SLIDER_H + 1` of ink into the `SLIDER_H` it allocates. Measured at ppp 1.0 over a 120pt
slider: row `120 × 11`, ink `120 × 12`, bottom overflow exactly 1.0.

**The bleed is kept.** A shadow outside the box is what a shadow is, and it lands in the caller's row
gap; the one production caller, `typography::axis_slider`, has the room. What could not stand was a
`pub` constant telling its callers it bounded the drawing, because that is the sentence somebody packs
a row against.

⚠️ **A corrected sentence would rot the same way, so the number is a test now.**
`ui::slider_ink_tests::a_sliders_shadow_leaves_the_row_by_exactly_one_point` unions the frame's shapes
and measures the overflow. It also asserts the other three sides are **tight**, and that is the
load-bearing half: a test bounding only the bottom would pass for a knob that had grown in every
direction, which is the change somebody adjusting a radius would actually make. Two flips, both
predicted correctly and failing in opposite directions — the offset at `+2.0` fails with 2 against 1,
and at `0.0` it fails the other way, which is what stops this being a one-directional bound.

🚨 **The app's other slider answers the same question the other way, and that is recorded rather than
fixed.** `panels::picker::slider_track` allocates its own `SLIDER_H + 6.0`, under the doc *"A 9px
slider track with room for its knob to overhang"*, because its knob is radius 6.5 on a 9pt rail. Two
hand-rolled sliders, two answers about whether a row owes its knob any room — and `picker` carries a
**second `SLIDER_H`, of a different value**, in a module that also imports `ui::`. They are never
mixed today and nothing says they may not be.

🚨 **Ruled by §15 D766, and the answer is that the two bound *different axes* — so the question had
no side to take.** Measured: `picker`'s bounds its knob **vertically**, which is what the `+ 6.0`
buys (7.0 of reach against a 7.5 half-row), and lets it hang **7pt off each horizontal end,
unclamped**; `ui::slider` bleeds 1pt below and **clamps travel** so its knob cannot leave the rail.
⚠️ **The sentence above — *"its knob is given room where `ui::slider`'s overhangs"* — is therefore
true of one axis and silent about the one where the answers are reversed**, and is corrected here
rather than left standing. ⚠️ **And the two constants were never one quantity**: `picker`'s is the
**rail's** thickness and is `TRACK_H` now, where `ui::SLIDER_H` is the **knob diameter** with
`SLIDER_RAIL_H` under it — so unifying the values would have thickened the picker's gradient strips
and left its knob exactly where it was.

⚠️ **Nothing in the record settles it, which was checked rather than assumed.** §9.4's `ui::slider`
paragraph specifies the 3pt rail, the 11pt knob, the two accent tiers and *"a soft shadow under it"*,
and says nothing about what the allocated row bounds; `design/handoff-type-popups.md` asks for a
slider per axis row and gives no geometry at all. *A ruling for the maintainer: either a row bounds
its control's ink or it does not, and the two sliders should then agree.* 🚨 **Answered by D766, and
not as posed** — see above. ⚠️ **This entry cited that paragraph as *"§9.2's"* three times and the
paragraph is in **§9.4***; §9.2 is *Layout*. Corrected throughout, per D766: a section reference that
names the wrong neighbourhood reads as having read it.

*(§9.4's `ui::slider` paragraph amended — what `SLIDER_H` measures, and that the shadow leaves it.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D672 — A working `dead_code` for `theme`'s two catalogue modules. *Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — no
behaviour changed.***

`pub mod color` carried `#[allow(dead_code)] // full ramp kept as a palette for later phases`, and
`pub mod icon` one reading *"full icon catalog kept for later phases"*. Both read as policy. Neither
was: they were blanket shields over catalogues nobody could measure, which is the state
`CLAUDE.md`'s *"a clean clippy run does not mean there is no dead code"* paragraph is about, arrived at
from the other end — not a lint that cannot see, but a lint switched off across a module.

**The colour allow is gone outright.** Measured with the attribute removed, `cargo check -p ondin-app`
reports **zero** warnings there: every constant in the module and both `const fn`s have a production
reader outside the file. The receipt described a state that no longer exists, and had been describing
it for long enough that nobody would have known.

⚠️ **The count that stood in this paragraph and in the shipped comment is gone rather than
corrected, and that is the decision to keep.** The comment read *"all 34"* and this entry read *"all
forty"*, which is `mod color`'s **35** `Color32` constants plus the five in the sibling `mod text`
that the `allow` was never on — a number taken over the wrong population, which is the shape session
14 recorded for `settings::card`. Neither figure was checkable by anything: **a count in prose is a
gate nobody built**, and the gate here is the two words above it, so the comment now says *"every
constant"* and names the command. The rule generalises past this module — where the claim is *"the
lint is live"*, print the lint's own answer rather than a tally of what it was asked about.

`icon`'s was switched off across **143** constants to silence **four**. Each of the four carries its
own allow now, with the reason it is kept, so the module has a working `dead_code` for the first time
and the *next* icon to lose its last call site is a warning rather than a silence.

🚨 **The finding's own fix sketch is wrong, and this is the entry's most useful sentence.**
`[S18.3-L3-04]` says to put the allow on `icon::ALL` — the catalogue list — alone. That **restores the
blanket shield**, because an allow-listed item is still a live *root*, and `ALL` names every one of
the 143 constants. Measured both ways: with `#[allow]` on `ALL`, zero dead constants are reported;
with it removed, the leaves with no other reader appear. `ALL` is `#[cfg(test)]` instead, which is
also what makes its own doc's *"read only from tests"* true rather than aspirational.

⚠️ **Under `--all-targets` it is live again and shields everything.** That is §15 D302's shape from
the other side: D302 is a gate that never sees the tests, and this is a gate that stops seeing the
*code* the moment the tests are compiled in. **The gate that catches the next dead icon is the plain
build** — `cargo check`/`cargo build`, and `check --release -p ondin-app` is the one on the standard
list — and the test build cannot be it. Worth knowing before somebody normalises the two commands.

🚨 **That paragraph is wrong, measured while removing one of these allows on 2026-09-15** (§15 D761).
Taking the attribute off a constant with no reader warns under **both** spellings —
`cargo check -p ondin-app` and `cargo check -p ondin-app --all-targets`. `icon::ALL` being
`#[cfg(test)]` shields the *test* target, and the **bin** target is compiled without that cfg either
way, so the bin's own analysis still reports the dead constant and `--all-targets` builds the bin
too. **The gate is better than this entry claims, in both spellings** — and the claim is exactly the
sort a reader trims a command on, which is why it is corrected here rather than quietly dropped.

**The four constants stay, and that is a `design-oracle` result rather than caution.** `CARET_UP` is
the unused third of a trio whose other two every disclosure draws; `ARROWS_HORIZONTAL` is the unused
half of a symmetry, letter spacing having taken `TEXT_AA` on its own argument. The interesting pair is
`ARROW_LINE_UP`/`ARROW_LINE_DOWN`, the *all the way* halves of the z-order family, and **the app draws
neither**: `menu.rs`'s four *Restack* rows give `Forward` and `Backward` the plain arrows and hand
**both** `Front` and `Back` `icon::STACK`, so *Bring to front* and *Send to back* wear one picture as
the first and last rows of one four-row group. Asked directly, `context-menus.md` §4's *Order* table
lists those four rows with their chords and **no icons**, and neither `architecture.md`, `shortcuts.md`
nor §15 assigns a glyph to any of them. Meanwhile `theme.rs`'s own comment groups the four arrows as
*"Z-order: one step vs all the way"*, which reads as these having been meant for those rows, while
`STACK`'s doc endorses what ships. **Two code comments disagree, no document settles it, and deleting
the pair would take a side** — a ruling for the maintainer, not a bug.

🚨 ***"No document settles it"* is wrong and is corrected here** (§15 D761). `design/Editor.dc.html`
assigns `ph-stack` to *Bring to front* and `ph-stack-simple` to *Send to back*, and
`context-menus.md` §8 makes that export **normative for what a row looks like**. The census that
produced the sentence asked `context-menus.md`'s tables, `architecture.md`, `shortcuts.md` and this
file, and the design export is a document none of those four is. ⚠️ **What it would have changed is
nothing about the conclusion and everything about the shape of it**: the export's own answer spends
`ph-stack-simple` on *Flatten* as well, so following it moves the duplication rather than removing
it, and the ruling would still have gone the other way — but as a **recorded deviation** from §8
rather than as a free choice, which is what D761 files it as. *A document you did not think to ask is
not a document that does not exist.*

⚠️ **Ruled 2026-09-15 and the pair is live**: `ARROW_LINE_UP` / `ARROW_UP` / `ARROW_DOWN` /
`ARROW_LINE_DOWN` across the four Order rows, both stale allows removed, `STACK` drawn by nothing and
keeping one allow with its reason. §15 D761 has the argument.

🚨 **Two false citations corrected in code, and one of them was in this file.** The first: `EXPORT`'s
doc glossed `ARROW_LINE_DOWN` as *"Send to back"* while arguing about tray shapes, and **D225 carries
the identical parenthetical**, which is amended above. It is not the *Send to back* glyph — `STACK` is
— and `ARROW_LINE_DOWN` is drawn nowhere at all; the *shape* argument the parenthetical sits inside is
unaffected, which is why both are corrected rather than removed. The cost of leaving it is concrete:
the next person choosing a glyph near this family reads that sentence, reaches for the constant, and
ships a second picture for a row that already has one.

The second is sharper. `FOLDER_SIMPLE`'s doc read *"Two rows in one card wearing one glyph is what
`context-menus.md` §8 is about"*. §8's own words are *"name them in the registry rather than at the
call site, **so the same verb cannot be two pictures in two menus**"* — one verb, one glyph, across the
app. That is the **converse**. The one-glyph-two-verbs direction is named only in §15 **D225**, and
named there as *"§8's glyph rule failing in the direction nobody checks for"*. Both readings condemn
the wrong glyph in that slot, so the conclusion survived; only one of them is §8's.

⚠️ **That is the third consecutive session with a citation that resolves and points at the adjacent
claim** — session 16's `§15 D54` for a quotation that is D127's, session 17's *"§5.3a's question"* for
a decision §6.4 makes, and this. **A reference that resolves is not a reference that agrees**, and
nothing in this project can see the difference: the doc gate reads links, the census reads numbers,
and only somebody reading the cited text reads the cited text.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which describes the icon font and the atlas-dump technique and
never the catalogue's `allow`. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D671 — Two implementations of *"is this SVG"*, and the one on the drop path refused the commonest
file there is. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`app::looks_like_svg` sniffs a dropped file's leading bytes so vector art can be **refused rather
than rasterized** (§5.5a); `svg_in::looks_like_svg` is the gate the paste path asks of a clipboard
string. They were two implementations of one question and they disagreed. Measured over five byte
runs, the doctype-first case came back `app = false`, `core = true` — so a file opening `<!DOCTYPE
svg PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN" …>`, which is the shape most SVG written before about 2015 has,
was **"Could not read: logo.svg"** when dropped on the canvas and imported as layers when the same
bytes were pasted.

**That is precisely the lie the arm above the call site exists to avoid**, and it says so in its own
words: *"'could not read' would be a lie about a file that reads perfectly well and is simply not an
image."* The whole point of sniffing the bytes rather than the name is to report the right thing;
half of the report was wrong about the ordinary case.

`app::looks_like_svg` is now the **byte-to-`str` adapter and nothing else**. What stays on this side
is what is genuinely about bytes: the 512-byte cap, and `String::from_utf8_lossy` rather than a
`from_utf8` that gives up, because the cap can split a multi-byte character and did. A root element
past 512 bytes of prolog and comments still reads as not-SVG, which is the pre-existing behaviour and
is well beyond anything a generator writes.

**The second half is a separate defect, in core, and it is a sentence rather than a branch.**
`looks_like_svg`'s comment read *"A leading `<?xml …?>` or a comment is ordinary; skip to the first
element"* above code that skipped a prolog and **no comment at all**. The half it was false about is
exactly what Illustrator writes — a `<!-- Generator: Adobe Illustrator … -->` line between the
declaration and the doctype. The skipping is implemented now, as a loop in a new private
`before_root`, because a generator comment followed by a licence comment is an ordinary way for a
file to open. **The sentence is true rather than corrected**, which is the better of the two repairs
available: a comment before the root really is ordinary and `import`'s parser has never minded one.

🚨 **A byte-order mark is still refused, and this is an *open* question rather than a settled one.**
It is not the same question the doctype was: a BOM reaches `roxmltree` as well, so admitting one here
would trade a wrong refusal for an error message from the parser. That wants driving rather than
reasoning and is left where the finding put it. *Revisit with a real BOM-prefixed file in hand.*

**Three flips, all predicted correctly.** Deleting the `while let Some(rest) = head.strip_prefix("<!--")`
loop fails on the plain generator comment; answering `rest` rather than `""` for a comment with no
`-->` fails on the fourth row; and putting back the app's old body — `text.starts_with("<svg") ||
(text.starts_with("<?xml") && text.contains("<svg"))` over a `str::from_utf8` that gives up — fails
the doctype assertion on the drop side.

⚠️ **One test row had to be rewritten to make the second of those bite at all.** It read *"`<!-- never
closed, and then <svg/>`"*, which is refused whichever way the unterminated-comment arm answers,
because the text after `<!--` is a **space** and nothing there starts with `<svg`. The case the arm
is actually for is a comment whose contents *open* with the element — `"<!--<svg/> and never
closed"` — and the difference is one character. `CLAUDE.md`'s *"what would also pass this"* in
miniature.

⚠️ **Asserting that the two doors agree would be worthless now**, the app's function being three
lines over core's, so `app::svg_sniff_tests` asserts the **answers** instead, and its last two rows
are the two things that are still this side's own: the cap, and a multi-byte character cut in half by
it.

⚠️ **Not re-raised, and it is the maintainer's call.** `app.rs`'s user-facing string *"SVG is vector
art, not an image — dropping one will create layers once the parser is built"* is stale: the parser
exists and pasting works. The finding hands that to A7 and changing user-facing copy is not this
entry's to make — but note the direction, because it is the improvement the finding asked for:
widening the sniffer means **more** files now reach that message rather than "Could not read".

*(§5.5a's SVG-refusal bullet amended — one predicate, and where the parser's branch went. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D670 — The export CLI accepted two things its own comment says it refuses. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`main::parse_export`'s `-o` arm took `args.get(i)` unconditionally. So `ondin export doc.ondin -o
--png` set the output *to* `--png`, and — this is the half that matters — the token then never
reached the top of the loop, so the `other if other.starts_with('-')` arm could not object, the
format fell to the SVG default, and the command wrote **SVG bytes into a file literally named
`--png`** and printed `wrote --png`. **The lost format flag is the interesting failure, not the silly
filename.**

The positional arm overwrote rather than refusing, so `ondin export a.ondin b.ondin --png` rendered
`b.ondin` and never mentioned `a.ondin`. A build step whose glob matched twice exports the wrong
document into the right name and has no way to notice.

**Both are refused now, in the parser's own words**: *"Refused rather than ignored, which is this
parser's rule everywhere else … a build script that believes it asked for 2× and got 1× has no way to
notice."* The `-o` refusal is the same one the three size flags already make with their `ok_or_else`,
one argument earlier — this arm was simply the one that did not. The second-document message names
**both** files, because the interesting half is which two.

⚠️ **Scope, checked against the design before writing.** §7 states the refusal rule and scopes it to
the size flags and `--all`, and it records that `--png --svg` **takes the last one** on purpose —
*"two formats have an obvious ordering and two sizes do not"*. That case is not a finding and must
not be changed. A second positional file was addressed in neither document, which is a gap rather
than a deviation; §7 now says what it does.

Two flips, both predicted correctly, added to `export_rejects_missing_input_and_bad_flags` — put back
the unconditional `args.get(i)` and the first fails; put back `other => file = Some(…)` without the
`file.is_some()` guard and the second fails. A third assertion says the order does not matter: the
second name is refused wherever it sits among the flags.

🚨 **A defect this change shipped, found while checking it.** The comment on the second-document arm
went into `main.rs` **twice, byte-identical** — six lines, repeated immediately. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s
eleventh and twelfth instances again, the *duplication* rather than the theft, and it arrived by the
same door both of those did: **a hand revert that re-added the block rather than restoring it**, so
the copy that had survived and the copy that came back sat one under the other. Neither detector on
that list can see one — the length ranking never reaches a doubled six-line run, and the neighbour
grep asks *"did the item below lose its comment"*, which here answers no — and a duplicated comment is
valid Rust describing the right item, so there is nothing for a gate to object to either. ⚠️
**Resolved the same day**: one copy deleted, and a scan for repeated long comment lines across all
eleven files this session touched found no others. *Resolved.*

*(§7's CLI bullet amended — what a second positional does, and that `-o` refuses a flag. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D669 — `expr`'s descent had no depth bound, and a stack overflow is not a panic. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`expr::eval`/`eval_in` is the `custom_parser` on **every numeric field in the app** (§9), and its
descent recursed once per `(` and once per leading `-` with nothing counting. A pasted run of
punctuation was therefore a paste that killed the process.

🚨 **The consequence is this round's *work that is never written at all* class, and it is the reason
this is a Critical-shaped bug in a calculator.** `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` (`0xc00000fd`) is not a
panic: nothing unwinds, so neither `OndinApp::on_exit`'s `disk_settle` nor `library::writer::Writer`'s
`Drop` runs, and **the unsaved document and the crash snapshot go with the process**. The recovery
machinery §15 D377 and D392 exist for is precisely what this failure mode skips.

The finding measured ~500 bytes of stack per bracket in a debug build, which puts the 8 MiB main
thread between 8,000 and 20,000 characters and a 1 MiB thread at 2,000.

**The fix is a `depth: u32` on `Parser` and `const MAX_DEPTH: u32 = 64`, counted in `unary` — the one
rule on both recursion cycles.** A bracket recurses `atom` → `expr` → `term` → `unary` → `atom`; a
leading sign recurses `unary` → `unary`; `unary` sits on each, so counting there rather than at the
two call sites means a rule added later that recurses through the grammar at all is bounded without
anyone remembering to bound it. The old body is `unary_nested`.

⚠️ **64 is chosen against what a *field* can hold, not against the measured stack figure**, and that
is deliberate: setting it near the measured limit would leave the failure reachable on a thread with
a smaller stack, and this parser is reached from every field in the app. Nothing anybody types into
one nests past a handful. `None` is what a field already does with an expression it cannot read —
leave the value alone — so the guard needs no new failure path.

🚨 **The test could not have been written before the fix, which is unusual enough to record.** The
case *aborted the test binary* rather than failing it — no assertion, no name, nothing in the output
saying which test died — so there is no "run it red first" here and **the flip is the whole of the
evidence**. Flip confirmed: `MAX_DEPTH = 100_000` and `cargo test -p ondin-app expr` exits
`0xc00000fd` with no test result at all. Worth doing once rather than trusting the comment, because a
test that merely returns `None` looks identical whether the guard is doing anything or not.

⚠️ **Second flip, and a site correction worth carrying.** Deleting `self.depth -= 1;` fails on the
**flat** thousand-term sum, not on the sixty-nested expression — 60 still fits under 64 without the
decrement. *Depth is a property of an expression's shape, not of its length*, which is both why that
assertion is the one with teeth and why the bound costs nothing anybody was ever going to type.

*(§9's `expr::eval` paragraph gains the bound and its reason. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D668 — Six `matches!` predicates decide behaviour from `NodeKind`, and every one of them answers
`false` for a variant nobody added. *Tested 2026-09-09; Keep — test-only apart from two pure
extractions.***

`NodeKind` has eleven variants, they carry payloads, and it is the one kind-like enum in `node.rs`
with no `ALL` — `MaskMode`, `BoolOp`, `DashStyle` and `Side` all have one. So a twelfth variant is
**not** a compile error at a `matches!` arm nobody wrote: the predicate simply answers `false`, all
six gates stay green, and the symptom arrives later and somewhere else.

**The codebase has paid for this twice, and both notes are still at the site.**
`resolve::is_indexed`'s says the kind was *"left out at first, and the symptom was a boolean that
could be selected from the layers tree and not from the canvas"*; `NodeKind::takes_paint`'s says
*"the transaction came back `WrongKindForOp`"*. Neither is the sort of failure a reader traces back
to a missing `|` in another module.

The fixture is `#[cfg(test)] pub(crate) mod node::kind_fixture`, three items: `tag`, an exhaustive
`match` with **no wildcard**, so a twelfth variant breaks the compile there — which is where the
instruction to add a sample lives, at the point the error lands rather than in a doc nobody is
reading at the time; `all`, one sample per variant with the smallest legal payloads, since no
predicate in the matrix reads one; and `split`, which returns a predicate's membership as the
accepted **and rejected** name lists.

🚨 **The rejected list is the whole mechanism.** Asserting only the accepted set converts nothing: a
twelfth variant answers `false`, the accepted set is unchanged, the test stays green — which is the
failure being guarded against, reproduced inside its own guard. Spelling both means the new name has
to land in one list or the other, and either way an assertion goes red naming the predicate it
belongs to.

Two pure extractions, **behaviour unchanged**: `resolve::is_indexed` becomes `pub(crate)`, and
`group_chain`'s inline `matches!` becomes `query::steps_into`. The second is the point of the pair —
an expression buried in a `while` loop was the one of the six no test could name, and a predicate a
test cannot reach is a predicate outside every guard anybody writes for the class.

**`is_indexed` and `takes_paint` have identical membership today**, spelled twice in two modules for
two unrelated reasons, and `takes_paint`'s own doc predicts they will drift. One test rather than six
is what puts them side by side, so a change made to one that was meant for both shows up in the diff.

**Three flips, all predicted correctly.** Deleting `NodeKind::Boolean { .. }` from `is_indexed` fails
on the `is_indexed` pair — the regression that comment records, now a red test rather than a canvas
nobody can click. Deleting `Artboard` from `stroke_sides_apply` fails there and nowhere else. ⚠️ **The
third is a flip of the *expectation* rather than of the code, because the case cannot be reached from
the code at all**: simulating a twelfth variant means adding one. So the shape was reproduced instead
— `Root` is rejected by all six predicates, i.e. it is exactly what a new variant looks like here, and
removing `"Root"` from `clips_children`'s rejected list fails with the actual list naming it and the
expected one not.

⚠️ **A residual gap, recorded rather than glossed: nothing checks that `all()` is complete.** A
variant added to `tag`'s match and forgotten in `all()` leaves eleven samples for twelve variants and
no gate in the crate disagrees. The compile error in `tag` is the only thing that ever says so, which
is why the instruction is written there and why `the_fixture_holds_each_kind_once` says in its own
doc that it cannot check this. **Do not "simplify" `tag` with a wildcard arm** — the arm that does
not exist is the entire guard.

*(§5.3's `takes_paint` bullet amended — the enforcement is a matrix now rather than a copied list.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D667 — A failed boolean's placeholder was the last unguarded route into `world_bounds`, and the
R-tree turns a bad box into the whole plane. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

§15 D495 added `geometry::measurable` — a rect that is **ordered** *and* **finite**, either test alone
letting half the bad boxes through — and routed `world_bounds_of_parts` and `world_bounds_of_path`
through it. That left exactly one arm of `Resolved::recompute_bounds` reaching
`geometry::transform_rect` raw: the placeholder box a boolean that gave up still draws (§15 D298),
`query::boolean_placeholder(doc, self, id).map(|b| geometry::transform_rect(world, b))`.

**And it is reachable from an ordinary document, because the guard on the operands cannot see it.**
`query::local_box` composes child transforms itself, so a `scale(1e308)` on an operand — every
coefficient finite, which is what `op_create`'s and `op_set_transform`'s `build::affine_is_finite`
ask — gives an ordered *infinite* local box. Measured: the boolean stored `Rect { x0: 0.0, y0: 0.0,
x1: inf, y1: inf }`, and its container unioned it, so **one leaf takes its ancestors' extent up to
the root** — which `plan::raster_size` reads (§15 D334 names that consumer). This is invariant 8's own
*"a validated operand does not make a usable **derived** value"* paragraph happening again, at the one
site D495 did not reach.

The fix is `.and_then(geometry::measurable)` on the placeholder arm, and `build_index`'s `.map(…)`
becoming `.filter_map(|(id, r)| geometry::measurable(*r).map(|r| entry(*id, r)))`.

🚨 **Two statements of one rule, on purpose, and it is a deliberate exception to this project's usual
"one rule, one statement".** The writer guards what it *stores*; the index guards what it *accepts*,
however the map came to hold it. The argument for the second is not symmetry: `world_bounds` is
derived from geometry as well as from transforms, the doors onto a non-finite one are not enumerable,
and the door that was open when this was written was three call frames away in `query::local_box`.
Where a rule has one statement and several implementations this project calls it a defect; here the
rule has one statement per *boundary*, and the boundaries are the writer and the container.

The index guard earns its place on its own measurement. `rstar`'s `AABB::from_corners` takes its
corners **component-wise**, so an *inverted* rect — which is what `transform_rect` answers for a
`NaN` transform, `f64::min` returning the operand that is not `NaN` and leaving both seeds where they
started — normalises to the **maximal** box, and the node becomes a candidate for every spatial query
for the life of the session. The finding measured `nodes_in_view` over a 100×100 view at −5000,−5000
containing nothing at all: it returned exactly the broken node and correctly excluded the artboard
beside it.

`resolve::measurable_bounds_tests` is the new inline module, two tests, both flip-checked. The second
writes `res.failed` and `res.boolean` **by hand**, on the argument that a boolean enters `failed` only
when `boolean::failures()` moves — i.e. when flo_curves unwinds — and that S4.1's pass report records
nothing having forced that since flo_curves 0.8.1.

🚨 **That argument is wrong, and the reason is one function away.** §15 D239 built
`boolean::poison_next` for exactly this problem when the real fixture stopped existing, and the
poison is read in **`guarded`**, which is deliberately the one guard *both* entry points share —
`evaluate` and `evaluate_node` alike, D239's own doc saying so in as many words so that a boolean
cannot be recoverable from one door and fatal from the other. `Resolved::reevaluate_boolean` brackets
`evaluate_node` with `failures()` and inserts into `failed` when the count moves, so
`poison_next(1)` before a `rebuild` over a document holding one boolean reaches this arm through the
front door, with `scale(1e308)` on an operand supplying the infinite box independently. **The test was
sound and its stated reason was not**, which is the shape `CLAUDE.md` records as a verdict outliving
its argument. ⚠️ **Resolved the same day, and the repair is the first of the two that were on offer.**
The fixture poisons one `guarded` call and asserts `res.boolean_failed(boolean)` **before** it looks at
the bounds, so a poison landing on some other `guarded` call fails loudly instead of leaving the test
about nothing — which is exactly what the hand-written `res.failed` could not do, a hand-written state
being true whether or not the code put it there. *Resolved.*

⚠️ **The first test's flip was predicted at the right site and the wrong *count*** — it said two
candidates would come back and it is one, because the good sibling's own box is nowhere near that
view either. That is the control doing its job in the direction nobody plans for: it is not there to
be found, it is there to prove `build_index` is not simply returning an empty tree.

🚨 **`ink_bounds` is the same shape and is *not* closed here — read this before assuming the class is
done.** The audit behind this entry covered `resolve_subtree` (no `Boolean` arm; booleans go through
`update`), the `Group | Root` union arms (children are already measurable) and `clipped_to`, and
stopped at the ink half. `recompute_bounds` ends `ink.map(|b| effect::escaped(b,
effect::stack_escape(node.effects()), world))` and stores the result **with no `measurable` in front
of it**. `effect::escaped` maps the radius as an ellipse, `((a * rad.x).powi(2) + (c * rad.y).powi(2)).sqrt()`
— and the *square* overflows at about `1.3e154`, where the product itself would stay finite to
`1.8e308`. So a finite escape, a measurable box and a `scale(1e155)` that `affine_is_finite` accepts
give `h = inf`, `(t.x − h.x).min(0.0) = −inf`, and an ink box of `(−inf, −inf, inf, inf)` under a
world box that passed. `ink_bounds` is not in the R-tree, which is why this is not the same bug — but
`plan::raster_size` reads it too, and so does `scene::paint_node`'s cull. **Read rather than run**:
the arithmetic is from the source, not from a measurement. ⚠️ **Measured and fixed the same day —
§15 D676**, which confirmed every step of the reading and replaced the square with `f64::hypot`. Read
that entry rather than this paragraph for what happened, and in particular for the sibling it turned
up in `effect::stack_escape` that is **not** fixed. *Resolved at D676.*

*(§5.9's `measurable` bullet amended — the placeholder arm, the index guard, and why there are two.
Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D666 — `menu_place` clamps last, and its doc said the opposite twice — as did §9.4. *Doc fixed and
tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the code was right and the record was not.***

`ui::menu_place` flips a menu away from the edge it would hang off, rounds the result to the device
pixel grid, and then clamps it into `content_rect()`. Its own doc comment said *"Flip first, then
**clamp, then round**; and the order is the whole of the function"* — and two sentences later
*"**Rounding comes last** because rounding a clamped value can push it back out by a fraction of a
point"*, which offers, as the reason for rounding last, the argument **against** rounding last. The
code has always been `snap(pos).clamp(…)`.

**The code is right, which is why this is a doc fix.** Half a pixel past the right edge is a menu
with its last column cut; half a pixel off the pixel grid is a hairline that looks soft. Staying on
screen is the thing this function exists for and crispness is the thing it does on the way, so the
clamp has to have the last word.

🚨 **The review named the code comment, and the same sentence is in `architecture.md` §9.4 — same
wrong order, same argument underneath it.** That is the half that matters: it is the design document,
so a reader correcting the code *to* the design would have introduced the bug this entry is about.
Amended. ⚠️ `docs/context-menus.md` §8 is cited by `menu_place`'s own doc and was checked in the same
pass: its *Edge flipping* bullet says a menu near an edge must flip and one taller than the viewport
must clamp, and says nothing about rounding at all. Nothing to fix there.

`ui::context_menu_chrome_tests::a_menu_is_clamped_after_it_is_rounded_and_not_before` is the new
test, and **its fixture is the one input where the two orders differ.** It takes three things at
once: a fractional `pixels_per_point`, a right limit that rounds *outward* at that scale, and an `at`
far enough right that the clamp still bites after the flip. At ppp 1.5 the limit is `1400 − 137 =
1263`, and `1263 × 1.5 = 1894.5` rounds *up* to 1895, i.e. `1263.333` — a third of a point past the
edge. Every ordinary placement gives the same answer under both orders, which is why this went
unnoticed for as long as it did and why the assertion is an exact `f32` comparison.

⚠️ **`at` is outside the viewport, and it has to be.** Flipping subtracts the same `size.x` the limit
does, so an `at` that is on screen always lands on screen and the clamp never gets a turn. A pointer
position carried over from before a viewport resize is exactly the case this function exists to
survive.

⚠️ **The first draft never reached the state it named.** It called `menu_place` outside a frame, where
`content_rect()` is egui's 10,000pt fallback — 6666.7 points at this scale — which clamps nothing, and
it got `1450` back untouched. It runs inside `ctx.run_ui` now. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity
shape, *the fixture never reached the state*, caught by an assertion failing rather than passing,
which is the lucky direction.

⚠️ **Flip run, predicted site right**: the two operations swapped to `snap(pos.clamp(…))` fails the
clamped assertion against `1263.0`, and the crisp case below it stays green — which is why both are
there. ⚠️ **The failing value written into the shipped comment is `1263.3333` and the run reported
`1263.3334`.** The nearest `f32` to `1895 / 1.5` is `1263.333374…`, so `1263.3334` is what Rust
prints and the comment is the one to correct. *Fix the figure.*

*(§9.4's placement paragraph amended — the order and the reason under it. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D665 — Two comments in `ui.rs` asserted facts about the code, and both facts were false. *Fixed
2026-09-09; Keep — comment-only, no behaviour changed.***

One entry for the pair, because they are one shape: **a doc comment standing in for a gate that
cannot exist.**

*First.* `ui::combo_chevron`'s doc says why every new `ComboBox` owes the `.icon(ui::combo_chevron)`
call — `Style` has no field for a combo's icon, so it cannot be made a theme default — and it closed
*"a dropdown that forgets it silently draws egui's white triangle next to **seven** that do not"*,
one sentence above *"`combo_chevron_tests` pins the pair; it cannot pin the call site that does not
exist yet"*. **So the count was the coverage claim**, and it was seventeen when the review counted
it: stale by a factor of two and a half, in the one sentence standing in for the gate the sentence
itself says cannot exist. `[A8-L6-04]`'s class, one level down — a rule whose only enforcement is a
figure in a comment.

**The figure is gone rather than corrected**, because it rots on exactly the day somebody adds a
dropdown, which is the day it is being read. The doc carries the two greps instead, and one dated
result to compare against. Measured over `crates/ondin-app/src` at the close of this session:
**23 `ComboBox::from_id_salt` constructions, 17 `.icon(ui::combo_chevron)` calls, and four
constructions with no chevron anywhere near them** — `inspector.rs`'s two, `typography.rs`'s and
`ui.rs`'s, all four `"probe"` combos inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules where egui's own triangle is
irrelevant. **The rule holds at every production dropdown**, and the positive result is written down
so that the next reader compares rather than re-derives.

🚨 **Three corrections to that measurement, and the first is a trap the recipe made for itself.** The
doc comment now contains the two greps, so it matches them: run today they return **24** and **18**,
one of each hit being the recipe's own line, and the real counts are 23 and 17. A reader re-running
the check will get two numbers that disagree with the two beside them and conclude the tree has
drifted. ⚠️ **`ui.rs:7982` is `ui.rs:8117`** — the four line numbers were taken before this session's
own additions to `ui.rs` moved them down 135 lines, and the other three still resolve, which is the
usual shape of a stale line number: mostly right. ⚠️ **And `23 − 4 = 19` against 17 chevron calls is
closed rather than left hanging.** The two unaccounted constructions are `combo_chevron_tests`' own,
which call `.icon(combo_chevron)` **unqualified**, being in the module that owns the function. That
is session 14's `settings::card` shape again — *a grep qualified with the module path undercounts by
exactly the module that owns the function, which is the likeliest interesting caller* — and
`17 + 2 + 4 = 23` accounts for every construction in the crate.

*Second.* `ui::paint_switch`'s doc explains why there is no standalone `switch` widget yet, and closed
*"adding it now would be a builder with no callers, **which in a library crate `dead_code` never
notices**"*. `ondin-app` is not a library crate: `Cargo.toml` declares only `[[bin]] name = "ondin"`,
there is no `src/lib.rs`, and `main.rs`'s `mod ui;` carries no `#[allow(dead_code)]` — the crate has
exactly **one** module that opts out, `mod library;`, which is the control saying the lint is live
everywhere else. So an uncalled `pub fn switch` would surface on the plain
`cargo check --release -p ondin-app` gate.

**The decision is unchanged; its stated reason was void in the file it was written in**, which is
worse than no reason at all, because it told the next reader that this module can hide an uncalled
`pub` builder. The true version of the rule is `CLAUDE.md`'s and it is about **`ondin-core`**, where a
`pub` item is the crate's API and `dead_code` never fires on one — plus the half that is not about
`pub` at all: a derived `PartialEq` hides an unread **field** anywhere in the workspace, this crate
included.

*(§9.2's chevron paragraph gains the check and its result. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D664 — `TextStyle::scaled`, and the app's byte-identical twin of it deleted. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

Core owned the photographic-scale rule for the **span** scope — `CharAttr::scaled_by` encodes all six
decisions, `Size` clamped to `MIN_FONT_SIZE..=MAX_FONT_SIZE`, the four lengths through
`Length::scaled`, both decorations through `scale_decoration` — and it published
`ParagraphStyle::scaled` for the **paragraph** scope and **nothing for the node scope**. So
`ondin-app::tools::scaled_text_scopes` re-stated every one of those six in a `TextStyle` literal,
above a **byte-identical private twin** of `typography::scale_decoration`, with
`ParagraphStyle::scaled` called one line below the copy. The two agreed; nothing made them agree
tomorrow, and the asymmetry was the tell.

`TextStyle::scaled` is added to core; the literal and the twin are deleted from the app, which now
calls all three.

🚨 **Written as a field literal and *not* as a loop through `TextStyle::set`, which is the obvious
spelling and would have been a live behaviour change.** `set` canonicalizes, and `Spans::scaled` does
not — it maps `scaled_by` over the span attributes and hands the results to `from_parts` raw. A
canonicalized default compared against an un-canonicalized span is a different comparison from the one
`Spans::normalize` makes, so a span that equalled the default before the scale could stop equalling it
after and be **stored** where it used to vanish. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s *"narrowing a predicate turns
every omission in the narrower one into a live bug"* from a new direction: here it is a **widening** of
canonicalization, and it would have changed *which spans exist* rather than what any of them says.

⚠️ **The gap is narrower than that paragraph reads, and it is still real — which is worth stating
because the narrow version is the one a future editor will check.** `Length::scaled` already
canonicalizes its `Px` arm, so the two spellings agree on every `Px` length by construction. What a
`set` loop would have *added* is `Length::canonical` on the `Em` arm, `canonical_decoration`'s zero
floor and colour rounding on the two decorations, and — asked over `CharAttrKind::ALL` — the variation
sort, the feature dedup and the locale filter on fields a scale does not touch at all. **What makes
that reachable rather than theoretical is §5.4's own record** (§15 D443): the scope *defaults* are
still not canonicalized on load, `TextStyle` being a plain `#[derive(Deserialize)]` that serde builds
field by field, so a style off disk can be non-canonical — and a `set` loop would have quietly
canonicalized it in the middle of a scale gesture while the spans beside it stayed raw.

What keeps the node rule and the span rule in step is therefore a test rather than the type system:
`typography::tests::a_scaled_style_agrees_with_the_span_rule_attribute_by_attribute`, asked over
`CharAttrKind::ALL` so that a sixteenth attribute is covered the day it exists rather than the day
somebody remembers this test. It is also why `scale_decoration` is *called* from both sides rather
than copied into either.

⚠️ **The fixture has to be non-default in every scalable field, or the test is about nothing**:
`TextStyle::default`'s lengths are all zero and `0 × 1.75 == 0`, so a `scaled` that returned
`self.clone()` would pass over the defaults. The `assert_ne!` is what says the fixture moved.
⚠️ **Flip run, predicted site right**: leaving `baseline_shift` unscaled — the plausible slip, since it
is the one field of the six whose name does not say "length" — fails at `BaselineShift(Px(-3.0))`
against `Px(-5.25)`, naming the attribute in the message, which is the whole reason the loop asserts
per kind instead of comparing two structs.

🚨 **This is also the entry that was written twice, and it is the strongest evidence this project has
for why the D-number block is reserved up front.** D663 was placed by hand into `io/schema.rs` and
`tests/io.rs` for `[S1.1-L1-06]`, and then, an hour later, into `typography.rs` and `tools/mod.rs`
for this finding; `22ecd28` renumbered the second. **Nothing could have caught it.** Both numbers
resolved to entries that did not exist yet, so the doc gate, clippy and the citation census were all
blind — only a grep of the reserved range would have said so. The habit held perfectly for D647–D662,
taken as one block from §15.0's last index line before a line of documentation was written, and it
broke the moment numbering went ad hoc *between* batches. **That is a fact about the habit rather than
about anybody**, and it is the mirror of the paragraph `CLAUDE.md` has carried since D400: the
reservation is the thing that works, and the census is only what checks it.

*(§5.4's `Length::scaled` sentence amended to name the three published rules. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D663 — An inert `clip` reached the file and the loader threw it away, so a document's bytes moved on
its first open-and-save. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — fixed at the writer, and the loader's
normalization stays.***

Two halves that are each right and were wrong together. `Document::op_set_clip` deliberately accepts
`clip: true` on a kind with no frame to clip to — §15 **D282**, *"an inert `clip` is a switch nothing
reads"*, where `SetMask` refuses the same node outright — and `io::schema::into_document` zeroes the
flag on the way in (`dto.clip && dto.kind.clips_children()`). So the writer wrote a flag the reader
discarded: `load(save(d)) != d`, and `save(load(save(d))) != save(d)` for **every** group carrying it,
with no edit made and nothing on screen to say so. §5.11 documents the loader's end and D282
documents the operation's, and **neither says that the model therefore holds a state the format
discards**; each is a true statement about its own half.

⚠️ **The re-save is one byte *longer*, not shorter.** `clip` carries a named serde default
(`clips_by_default`) and no `skip_serializing_if`, so the key is always present: the first save writes
`"clip":true` and the second `"clip":false`. Both the shipped comment in `io/schema.rs` and the test's
own doc say *shorter*, which is the one thing about the loss neither of them has right. *Fix the
direction in both.*

**Fixed at the writer**, `clip: n.clip() && n.kind().clips_children()` in
`DocumentDto::from_document` — the projection saying what the format's `clip` actually means, which is
*"clips its children"*. The loader's normalization **stays**: that one is the guard against a
hand-edited or foreign file, and is what `a_mask_on_a_frame_does_not_survive_being_loaded` pins for the
sibling flag. The model is untouched, so D282's property — drag a shape through a frame and back and it
keeps its setting — is untouched, and the test asserts that first.

🚨 **The finding's third fix option would have been a live bug, and it is the one that reads as
cheapest**: *"the loader stops normalizing and the readers keep asking the kind — which they already
do"*. **They do not.** `render/scene.rs`'s and `canvas.rs`'s `bounds_cover_subtree` are
`node.children().is_empty() || node.clip() || matches!(kind, Group | Root | Boolean)`, with the `clip`
term **not** kind-gated, so a group arriving with the flag live would have had its whole subtree culled
against its own bounds. `menu.rs`'s `clips: node.clip()` and the SVG writer's `split_clip` are the same
shape; the only kind-gated readers are the two `Artboard` `match` arms, in `scene.rs` and `svg.rs`, and
those gate by the arm rather than by the predicate. **Two of the three options were safe and the one
that reads as free was not.**

🚨 **And the sentence that would have argued that option back in is `NodeKind::clips_children`'s own
doc comment**, which says *"three places ask — the scene walk, the SVG writer, and the loader"*. Two of
those three do not ask it at all. The three real callers in `crates/` are `op_create`'s creation
default (`clip: kind.clips_children()`), this projection, and the loader. §5.3 carried the same claim
and is amended with it. **A predicate's doc naming readers that read something else is invisible to
every gate here**, and it is the second time in two sessions that the sentence a fix had to disprove
was sitting on the function itself.

`crates/ondin-core/tests/io.rs · an_inert_clip_flag_never_reaches_the_file`. ⚠️ **Two things it had to
learn.** The *artboard* clips legitimately and by default, so `"clip": true` is a substring of every
file this fixture produces and a grep for it asserts nothing — the group's own record has to be read
out of the parsed JSON by id. And the byte comparison is an `assert!` rather than an `assert_eq!` on
two buffers, because the first run printed 53 KB of decimal that nobody reads.

⚠️ **Flip run, and the predicted site was wrong in the useful direction**: with the writer's guard
removed the test fails one assertion *earlier* than predicted — on the group's own `clip` record,
`Bool(true)` against `Bool(false)`, rather than on the byte-stability one. That is the better site and
is why the record assertion was added at all: it names the flag rather than the file.

*(§5.3's `clip` bullet and §5.11's `clip` sentence amended. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D662 — `from_wire` reads untrusted bytes and nothing asserted a byte of what it accepts. *Tested
2026-09-09; Keep — pinned rather than tightened, and the tightening is an open ruling.***

`crates/ondin-core/src/id.rs` had two tests: `mint` and the `Debug` format. Neither touches the
parser. `NodeId::from_wire` sits behind `io/schema.rs`'s `parse_id` and therefore behind **every node
id, every `parent`, every entry of every `children` list** and — through `GuideId::from_wire`, which
shares this function — every guide id in every file the app opens. It is the one function in that
file that reads bytes nobody in this process wrote, and `tests/io.rs` exercised it only through
well-formed saves of its own making.

`from_wire_accepts_the_canonical_form_and_six_aliases_of_it` tables what parses and what does not, in
both directions, plus the round trip.

**Pinned, not tightened, and that is the decision this entry records.** Five of the accepted
spellings are strings `NodeId::to_wire` can never produce — a leading `+` on either half, uppercase
hex, leading zeroes on either half — and a sixth, `"0:0"`, names an id the minter guarantees is never
minted, `IdSource::new` starting `seq` at 1. **None of them is a defect.** Every alias parses to the
*same* `NodeId` as its canonical form, so `into_document`'s duplicate check still catches a file that
spells one node two ways, and a cross-reference written non-canonically still resolves to the node it
names. `"1a2b:"` and `":42"` are already refused, which is the control saying the parser is not
simply permissive: an empty half fails `from_str_radix`/`parse` rather than defaulting to zero.

🚨 **Whether the aliases should be *rejected* is a ruling and is left open for the maintainer.** The
case for it is §5.2's own words — the serialized form is *"compact and diff-readable"* — and a diff
is only readable if one id has one spelling. The cost is that it narrows what `io::load` accepts,
which is a **compatibility** decision rather than a repair: a file written by a tool that pads its
hex would stop opening. The test is written so that tightening it is a *visible* edit — move a row
from `accepted` to the rejected list and the intent is on the diff — which is the most this entry can
do without taking the decision.

🚨 **Two counts in the comment this change shipped are one over, and the test's own name is one of
them.** The `accepted` table holds eight rows: the canonical form, **five** aliases of it, `"0:0"`,
and `"ffffffffffffffff:1"` — which `to_wire` *can* produce, being the `u64::MAX` actor, and which is
a boundary case rather than an alias at all. So *"six of the accepted spellings are strings
`NodeId::to_wire` can never produce"* is five, and `…_and_six_aliases_of_it` is five. ⚠️ **And the
quotation in the same paragraph is credited to the wrong place**: it attributes *"compact and
diff-friendly"* to §5.2, which says *"compact and diff-**readable**"*; *"diff-friendly"* is
`NodeId::to_wire`'s own doc comment, one screen above. That is session 14's `Prefs::ephemeral` shape
again — a real sentence quoted against the wrong owner — and no gate reads either. *Fix the name, the
count and the attribution.*

**The second test is `skip_to_only_ever_moves_the_counter_forward`.** Invariant 3's whole mechanism is
one `max`: a deleted node's id must never be re-minted, and `document::reserve_existing_ids` calls
`skip_to` with `seq + 1` for every id in a loaded file. A file holding a *high* id must push the
counter past it, and a file holding a *low* one must not pull it back — which is the half a plain
assignment would break and the half nothing asserted. ⚠️ **Flip run, predicted site right**:
`self.next_seq = seq` fails at *"a lower seq must not pull the counter back"*, 2 against 3, and the
other three assertions stay green under it, which is why the backwards case has to be there at all.

⚠️ **Unnumbered, and recorded here for want of a better home.** The same session converted nine
`[`link`]`s it had written into prose no gate reads — two inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `id.rs`
and seven in `crates/*/tests/` files — to plain backticks per §15 D319 and D622, taking the `tests/`
population back to **23 files and 18 links**, measured.

*(§5.2 gains a sentence on what the parser accepts and on the open ruling. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D661 — `can_frame`'s contract with `frame` was stated in a sentence and checked by nothing. *Tested
2026-09-09; Keep — test-only, no production code changed.***

`build::can_frame` had **zero test callers workspace-wide**. Its doc states its contract in one
sentence — *"the builder's own question, so a row cannot offer what the verb would refuse"* — and
nothing checked it. **One** test in `menu.rs` sets `cx.can_frame` by hand as a literal `bool` —
`frame_selection_is_offered_where_group_is_and_on_the_frames_group_refuses` — and the menu fixture
hands every other test a hard-coded `can_frame: true`. Which proves the row reacts to the flag and
says nothing whatever about whether the flag is right; the path from a real document to a dimmed
*Frame selection* row was never exercised. ⚠️ **The shipped comment says *"`menu.rs`'s two tests"***;
there is one that sets it and a fixture default behind the rest. *Fix the comment.*

`crates/ondin-core/tests/build.rs · can_frame_answers_what_frame_would_do` runs six selections —
nothing selected, the root, two different parents, a selection inside a group, an ordinary pair, and
a frame among the members — asserting `can_frame == frame(…).is_ok()` on each.

**The one deliberate disagreement is asserted separately**, not folded into the equality. An empty
group has no measurable extent: `can_frame` answers `true`, because it does not measure and its doc
says so on purpose — *"that needs a `Resolved` and it is not a thing a user can act on"* — and `frame`
answers `Err(MalformedSubtree)`. A test demanding plain equality would report the **documented** case
as the bug, and the point of asserting it as the contract is that the exception cannot later be
"fixed" into a divergence.

🚨 **The flip the review proposed does not bite, and that is a finding about the code rather than a
failed experiment.** Deleting `can_frame`'s `matches!(node.kind(), NodeKind::Root)` arm leaves every
row green. The reason is the guard two lines below it: **`Root` is the only node in a `Document` with
no parent.** `Document::new` is the one place a node is given `parent: None`; `op_create` writes
`Some(parent)`, `op_insert_subtree` overwrites the subtree root's with `Some(parent)` after the
structural checks, and `Reparent` writes one too. So `let Some(p) = node.parent() else { return
false }` already refuses the root and the kind test is **expressive rather than load-bearing**. It is
kept for exactly that reason — a reader asking *"can you frame the root?"* should find the answer at
the function and not have to infer it from a field — with a comment saying nothing would notice if it
went.

⚠️ **The literal `parent: None` occurs at two sites in `crates/` and only one of them is in a
document**: `document.rs`'s constructor, and a `#[cfg(test)]` fixture in `geometry.rs` that builds a
bare `Node` never inserted anywhere. So the claim holds, and it is not a one-grep claim.

⚠️ **A flip that does bite**, for the row that has no other guard behind it: neutering the
shared-parent comparison fails on *two different parents*, `true` against `false`. ⚠️ **And spelling
that same flip `if false && …` fails the *wrong* row** — the short-circuit skips `get_or_insert`, so
`parent` stays `None` and every case comes back `false`. A mutation with a different meaning and the
same one-line description, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s own warning about naming the mutation precisely,
arriving in miniature.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which states the frame verb's rules and has never mentioned
`can_frame` as a separate predicate. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D660 — The SVG reader collapsed Unicode's twenty-three whitespace characters where XML has four.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep.***

`svg_in::push_collapsed` asked `c.is_whitespace()` — Unicode's `White_Space` property — while its own
doc comment said *"XML whitespace collapsing, which is what `xml:space="default"` means"*. XML's `S`
production is `#x20 | #x9 | #xD | #xA`, and CSS's `white-space: normal` collapses the same four. So
the predicate was wider than both specifications **and** than the sentence directly above it.

Measured on import, reading the content off the transaction:

| `<text>` content | imported as |
| --- | --- |
| `10\u{00a0}km` (no-break space) | `"10 km"` — breakable |
| `1\u{2007}5` (figure space) | `"1 5"` — a different width |
| `1\u{202f}2` (narrow no-break space) | `"1 2"` |
| `\u{3000}a` (leading ideographic space) | `"a"` — gone entirely |

Four of the twenty-three are exactly the characters an author reaches for *because* they are not
ordinary spaces, so collapsing them threw away the reason they were typed: a pasted price,
measurement or date the source file deliberately kept unbreakable came back breakable, and nothing
was reported. ⚠️ **`\u{feff}` was always preserved** — it carries no `White_Space` property — which is
the control saying the rule really was `char::is_whitespace` rather than something narrower that
happened to include these four.

`const XML_SPACE: [char; 4]` now, used by `push_collapsed` **and** by `text_node`'s two trims.

⚠️ **The trims are the second half, and the ideographic-space row is the one that needs them.** A
`str::trim` on the wider set removed a leading `\u{3000}` **outright** rather than collapsing it to a
space, which is why that row lost a character where the other three merely lost a distinction.

⚠️ **`lead` is why the two must not drift.** It re-bases every span's byte range onto the trimmed
string (§15 D396), so a front trim that removes characters `push_collapsed` would have kept moves
every run in the node. D396's argument that the front trim is structurally zero — `push_collapsed`
refuses to emit a leading separator — still holds under the narrower set, because narrowing only ever
removes reasons to trim.

`a_no_break_space_is_not_collapsed_into_an_ordinary_one` covers four separators and two controls, the
second control being the ordinary newline-and-indent case, which still has to collapse or the fix
would simply be *"stop collapsing"*.

⚠️ **Two flips, failing different assertions, which is what says the fix is two lines rather than
one**: restoring `is_whitespace` fails the NBSP row, and restoring the wide trims leaves that green
and fails the ideographic one.

*(§7's SVG-reader text bullets gain the rule — neither document had ever stated what the reader does
with whitespace. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D659 — `absorb` treats thirteen operations as a no-op, not the eleven §5.3b and §5.7 enumerated.
*Fixed 2026-09-09; Keep — the code was right and the record was not.***

`op::changes_ink` answers `false` for **eleven** chrome-and-bookkeeping operations, pinned by
`op::changes_ink_tests::only_the_chrome_operations_change_no_ink`, which asserts its own length —
**not `op::tests::`**, which is what the brief and the new test's own doc comment both say; `op.rs`
has no `mod tests` at all. *Fix the comment.*
`RenderOverrides::absorb` holds those same eleven in one arm **and a second no-op arm further down the
same `match`**, behind a comment of its own: `AddImage | RemoveImage`. Thirteen. ⚠️ **The brief's
*"nineteen lines below it, behind a sixteen-line comment"* is wrong in both states of the file and the
shipped test comment repeats it** — before this fix the arm sat **fourteen** lines below, behind a
**thirteen**-line comment; after it, twenty-eight lines below behind a twenty-seven-line one, the
growth being this entry's own note. *Fix the comment*, or better, drop the numbers: a distance in
lines is the one measurement that a comment inserted between the two sites invalidates.

Two passages said otherwise, and both closed off the possibility of noticing:

- **§5.3b**'s layout-grid bullet: *"Those two lists are the same eleven operations and the test that
  pins them now asserts its own length."*
