- **§5.7**'s `changes_ink` bullet: *"which is **the same eleven `RenderOverrides::absorb` treats as a
  no-op** (§6.2), deliberately … if the two lists ever disagree, one of them is wrong."*

**The correct statement is a subset.** `changes_ink`'s eleven are all no-ops in `absorb`; the two
extras are the image operations, and they are there for the reason the arm's own comment gives —
*"it is here because `RenderOverrides` has no image table to patch"* — rather than because they are
invisible. An image op changes what is drawn, so the honest reading of that arm is *"cannot preview
this"*, not *"nothing to preview"*.

**Why this is worth more than a corrected sentence.** `EditorSession::has_gesture_preview` is
`!self.overrides.is_empty() && …`, so *every* transaction `absorb` no-ops is invisible to
`cancel_gesture`'s gate. Anyone repairing `[A1-L2-02]` from the design's list repairs the wrong list:
that repair list has to be derived from `absorb`, and this entry is where the next reader is told so.

🚨 **`[A7-L8-04]` certified the opposite as a verified fact** — *"the corresponding no-op arm … holds
the same eleven, **so the two lists do agree**"* — and on that basis certified §5.3b's sentence as
correct. The hand-count stopped at the first no-op arm. That is `[A6-L8-02]`'s shape: a check's own
baseline carrying the thing it checks for. It has no §15 entry of its own, so **D336 is amended
instead**, being the entry a reader arrives at and the one that carried the claim in the record:
*"`absorb`'s no-op arm holds the same eleven. The two lists have never disagreed. Only the sentences
about them have."* Wrong about the arm, and wrong in its last sentence about what kind of drift this
was. D336 is about a **count** going stale in five copies; this is a **relationship** stated wrongly
in every copy at once, which no recount could have found.

⚠️ **The brief that produced this entry had both section numbers and the count wrong, in the
direction that makes the finding look smaller.** The *"same eleven … asserts its own length"*
sentence is §5.3b's, not §5.7's; the *"Exactly eleven answer `false`"* bullet is §5.7's, not §6.3's;
and neither still read *ten* — D336's third round of copy-drift was cleared on 2026-09-07 and both
prose copies say eleven. **There was no sixth copy of the count to fix. The count was never the
problem.**

Code side: a comment on the image arm carrying the argument, and
`ondin-render/tests/overrides.rs · every_no_op_of_absorb_is_a_no_op_and_two_of_them_still_change_ink`
— thirteen operations absorbed to an empty preview, eleven of them `!changes_ink` and two of them
`changes_ink` — asserting its own list lengths, as `op.rs`'s test does, so the counts in the comment
above it are checkable.

⚠️ **What it cannot do is prove there is no fourteenth.** That needs a value of every `Operation`
variant, which is `op.rs`'s fixture's job; this is a **sibling** of that test rather than a
replacement. What it does catch is the two lists drifting apart again, which is how they got here.

*(§5.3b, §5.7 and §6.2 amended. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D658 — The goldens' fixture reached neither `effects` nor `pivot`, and `EffectKind` had no
tripwire. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — test-only, no production code changed.***

`goldens.rs`'s header says a golden *"notices … the field that quietly left the snapshot schema"*.
Measured against `tests/goldens/every-kind.json`, the `effects` field and the whole of
`EffectSummary` — `blur`, `spread`, `brightness`, `contrast`, `saturation`, `hue` — appeared in
**none** of its keys, and neither did `pivot`. Both are `skip_serializing_if`-elided, so that was
correct *output* for a fixture carrying neither, which means **deleting `NodeSnapshot::effects`
entirely would have left both goldens byte-identical.** The stated purpose named a case the file
could not answer.

`EffectKind` is covered elsewhere — `snapshot.rs`, `svg.rs`'s shadow and filter tests,
`svg_roundtrip.rs` — so nothing was uncovered outright. What was missing is the **change-detector**,
which is a different thing and is what a golden is for.

`golden_document` gains all four effect kinds on the rect and a `Normalized(0.25, 0.75)` pivot on the
ellipse, plus `EVERY_EFFECT` and an exhaustive `effect_name` beside the existing `EVERY_KIND`/
`kind_name` pair — so a fifth `EffectKind` breaks the file's compile the way a twelfth `NodeKind`
does, and `the_fixture_holds_one_node_of_every_effect_kind` is what then forces the *fixture* to grow
it. Written out twice rather than shared, the two enums having nothing in common but the hazard.

**The regeneration diff was read, and this entry records the reading**, which is that file's own rule:
*"a regenerated golden that nobody read is worse than no golden at all, because it converts a question
into a record."* SVG: one `<filter id="fx-601d_3">` in `<defs>` and a `<g filter=…>` around the rect,
28 lines. Every number checks out by hand — `stdDeviation` is half the typed blur at all three of
6/4/2, `spread: 1` is `feMorphology dilate radius="1"`, the offsets are verbatim, `flood-opacity` is
`90/255 = 0.3529` and `120/255 = 0.4706`, and the colour matrix's `0.05` column is contrast 0.9's
intercept `(1 − 0.9)/2`. JSON: the four effect objects and `"pivot": [17.5, 33.75]` on the ellipse,
which is `70 × 0.25` and `45 × 0.75` against its 70 × 45 box — the **derivation** rather than the
stored fraction, which is the whole reason a `Normalized` pivot is the one worth putting here (D651).

⚠️ **The pivot produced no SVG change at all, and that is correct.** `Operation::SetPivot`'s own doc
says the render boundary, `Resolved`, hit-testing and the SVG writer never see it. A diff on the SVG
side would have been the finding.

🚨 **The effect order was filed as an open question of §5.3a's and it is a settled one.** The filter
emits the blur and the colour matrix **first** and casts both shadows off the result — `fxa0` derives
from `fx3` — with the stack written `[DropShadow, InnerShadow, LayerBlur, Filters]`, and that is not
the list order leaking through. §6.4 states it as a decision: *"`run` is two stages, not one fold, and
the SVG writer is arranged the same way for the same reason … every shadow is then cast from that
result"*, with the one-fold spelling rejected because an inner shadow following a drop shadow would
take its silhouette from the layer **plus the shadow**. §5.3a's `stack_escape` bullet computes the
escape per stage on exactly that basis (§15 D473), and §7 says the graph *"is built in the same two
stages the CPU pass uses and for the same reason"*. So the emitted order **implements** the design
rather than raising a question about it, and a reordering here would be a change to `stack_escape`
too. *Fix the comment*, which cites §5.3a for a question §5.3a and §6.4 answer.

⚠️ **Still not covered: `<mask>`**, which both goldens lack along with `<radialGradient>`, `<image>`,
`<textPath>` and `<use>` on the SVG side. One masked node would close most of that on both sides at
once; it is left deliberately, because a mask restructures the markup around the run it covers and
that diff wants reading on its own. A standing gap rather than an oversight.

⚠️ **D651 is amended by this change** — it says `golden_document` sets no pivot on any of its nodes,
which was true when it was written an hour earlier and is not now.

*(§11's golden-blind-spot paragraph gains the field case and the standing `<mask>` gap. Nothing struck
from `roadmap.md`, whose golden item is the parked PNG third and is untouched by this.)*

**D657 — The export background chip was blank of the truth over a multi-selection. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep.***

`panels/export.rs`'s `background_swatch` resolved the chip from `export_subjects().first()`. Two
rects in two frames — one white, one black, **both set to *Frame's own*** — painted **white** and
exported one of each, with the tooltip beside them reading *"the nearest frame's background"*,
singular. Nothing on screen said the answer was per-layer.

🚨 **The panel states this rule twice in the same file and broke it one control away.**
`export_size_label`, one function up: *"Blank over a multi-selection rather than a guess. `Width(512)`
is a different multiplier on every differently-shaped layer, so one number for thirty icons would be
true of at most one of them — and the row that carries it is the same row for all thirty."* And
`inspector_export`'s own body, deriving the value: *"One subject's box sizes every row; over a
multi-selection there is no single answer, so the size cell says so rather than picking a member's
arbitrarily."* The chip is the same sentence about a colour.

The `sizing: Option<NodeId>` that already carried *"there is exactly one subject"* down `export_row`
is threaded through `export_settings_popup` into `background_swatch`.

⚠️ **Only `Frame` varies per layer, so the fix is a `match` and not a gate on `sizing`.**
`plan::background_color` reads the node in that one arm and nowhere else: `Solid` and `Transparent`
are properties of the **spec**, and are exactly as true of thirty layers as of one. Muting them would
be a second wrong answer in the other direction — a chip saying nothing about a setting that does
have a colour. The tooltip gains a plural arm for the `Frame`/no-subject case, because a chip that
goes muted under a sentence still promising *"the nearest frame's"* reads as the setting having
failed rather than as the panel declining to guess.

`a_frame_background_chip_says_nothing_over_a_multi_selection` asserts the fixture first — the two
subjects really do resolve to different colours, so "one member's answer" is a wrong answer for the
other — then the multi-selection case, then the `Solid` case.

⚠️ **Two flips, and they fail different assertions, which is why both cases are asserted.** Deleting
the `(Frame, None) => None` arm fails the multi-selection one, `Color32::WHITE` against
`theme::text::DIM`. Gating the whole resolution on `sizing` — `sizing.and_then(…)`, the obvious
one-line spelling of "be honest over a multi-selection" — leaves that green and fails the `Solid` one,
the muted ink against white. **Either flip alone would bless one of the two wrong answers.**

*(§9.4's Export-panel passage gains the rule beside the size line's. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D656 — A planned path is a folder and a name, and the export panel's two destination arms
disagreed about both halves. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the File arm gains the folder
arm's one line, and the dialog gains a split.***

Two halves of one asymmetry, in `panels/export.rs`.

**`write_export`'s `Destination::File` and `Destination::Folder` arms differed by exactly one
`create_dir_all` and nothing else.** With *Slashes in names make folders* on, a layer called
`icons/close` plans `icons/close.png` — the `/` is the feature, not an accident of the name — so
that layer exported fine as one of several, where the folder arm creates the directory, and failed
with *"the system cannot find the path specified"* on its own. **Whether an export worked depended
on how many other layers happened to be selected**, which is not a rule anybody could have guessed
from either arm.

The File arm has the same line now. Every path it is given has just come out of a save dialog, so
normally the parent exists and the call is a no-op; it is not free of doubt, because the dialog was
handed a name that may itself carry a folder — which is the other half.

**`run_export`'s `SaveFile` arm called `set_file_name(files[0].path.clone())`**, handing a relative
*path* to an API that wants a name. `save_dialog_target(start, planned) -> (PathBuf, String)` splits
it: the folder half goes to `set_directory`, the name half to `set_file_name`. Lifted out of
`run_export` for §15 D269's reason — that function opens a modal, so the arithmetic is the only part
of it a test can reach.

⚠️ **The joined directory is used only when it already exists**, and that is what keeps the function
deterministic. Platform dialogs differ on a `set_directory` that does not resolve — some fall back to
the last-used folder, some to the home directory — and the export's own remembered folder is a better
start than whichever of those the machine picks. Nothing is lost by starting one level up, because
the folder is created on the write side regardless.

**What is not claimed**: what the Windows common dialog makes of `icons/close.png` in
`SetFileName`. That cannot be driven from a test and is asserted nowhere. The **asymmetry** is the
finding, and it holds however the dialog behaves.

`a_planned_path_reaches_the_save_dialog_as_a_folder_and_a_name`, three cases: a bare name, a folder
that exists, and a folder that does not — the last being the ordinary first run, where the name is
still split off and only the directory falls back.

⚠️ **Flip run, and the predicted site was wrong.** `(start, planned.to_string())` — the old
behaviour — was expected to fail on the name. It fails on the **existing-subfolder** assertion, both
halves of it at once, and the bare-name case above it is **green under the old behaviour**. Which is
exactly why the bug survived: the only planned paths anybody tries by hand have no `/` in them.

*(§7's app-door sentence gains the split. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D655 — The pad test asserted one of the two orientations a pad can have. *Tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — test-only, no production code changed.***

`crates/ondin-export/tests/raster_opts.rs`'s `a_pad_squares_the_result_and_takes_the_background`
runs against `png::padded_square`, and its fixture is 100 × 50. So `side == r.width`, `dx` is **0 in
every run**, and the three samples are one column at three rows: they pin `dy` and say nothing
whatever about `dx`. Replacing `let dx = ((side - r.width) / 2) as usize` with `let dx = 0` left the
test green, and `trim_runs_before_pad` with it, since that one asserts only the size.

**The consequence is the property the function's own doc claims.** A *tall* subject padded that way
is left-aligned rather than centred, and `padded_square` opens *"Centred, and biased to the left/top
on an odd remainder … an icon set padded this way is consistent with itself, which is the point"*.
An icon set of mixed orientations would have come out with its portrait members flush left, which is
the one thing the option exists to prevent.

`CLAUDE.md`'s first vacuity shape — *it asserted one of two boundaries* — with the boundaries here
being the two **orientations** rather than two ends of a range. A 50 × 100 case is added through
`SetGeometry` on the same rect, asserting the padding on both sides and the artwork between them.

⚠️ **Flip run, predicted site right**: `dx = 0`, red at the tall case's *"padding to the left"*,
which is the first sample the mutation moves ink into. The eight other tests in the file stay green.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`, which states the pad's effect on a file's size and not its
alignment. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D654 — The export row's spacing test asserts an accurate replica of the row, which is why it
cannot see the row. *Tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the replica stays and a real test sits beside it.***

`an_export_row_and_its_size_line_sit_where_they_are_told` never calls `export_row`. It builds its own
two-unit column out of `ui.scope`, `ui.horizontal` and `ui.allocate_space` and measures **that**, so
what it proves is that egui behaves the way the recipe expects. It cannot see whether `export_row`
follows the recipe. Measured: swapping the two arms of `export_row`'s trailing `match lined` — which
undoes exactly the correction `ROW_UNIT_GAP`'s own doc records — leaves it green, and so does
deleting the `if !last` block outright.

That is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape, *its fixture never reached the state it names*, with a
twist worth knowing: **the fixture reaches an accurate copy of the state**, which is what makes it
read as covered rather than as obviously beside the point.

**The replica is kept.** It is the thing that caught `interact_size.y`'s 24pt minimum — 13pt of ink
painting in a 24pt slot and adding five points to the gap at each end while both constants stayed
correct in the source — and that is a fact about egui rather than about this function, so it is worth
pinning where somebody will read it.

🚨 **Its doc names two numbers and both have since moved.** *"An 8 painted as 13 and an 18 as 23.
Nothing about that is visible in `ROW_LINE_GAP = 8.0`"* was true when it was written; the constant
is **3** today and `ROW_UNIT_GAP` is **6**, both having come down on the machine (their own docs
carry the 8 → 5 → 3 and 18 → 15 → 6 ladders). The mechanism is right and the arithmetic is a museum
piece, which is why nothing objected: the test uses the constants symbolically and passes either
way, and no gate reads a sentence. *Fix the comment* — state the mechanism without the two figures,
the way `export_row`'s own comment beside the `allocate_space` already does.

⚠️ **The finding's own cheap fix does not work, and this entry says so rather than leaving the next
reader to try it.** It proposed adding the un-captioned case *to the replica*, *"with the same
teeth"*. It has none: the replica's arithmetic **is** the test's, so an assertion over it is an
assertion about the fixture. The only thing that can see `export_row`'s allocation is `export_row`.

`export_rows_trailing_gap_is_the_one_the_unit_asks_for` drives the real function from
`OndinApp::headless` (§15 D303), **one row per frame** — two in one frame clash ids — and measures
the gap as a **difference**: the same row laid out with `last` false minus the same row with `last`
true is exactly the block under test, so the row's own height, the theme's minimums and the size line
all cancel. Captioned is `ROW_UNIT_GAP`, 6; un-captioned is `ROW_UNIT_GAP + ROW_LINE_GAP`, 9. The
fixture asserts it is in both states it names, through `export_size_label`.

⚠️ **Flip run, and the predicted site was wrong.** The mutation is the finding's own — `match
lined`'s two arms swapped — and it was expected to bite on the *un-captioned* assertion, that being
the arm the replica never builds. It bites on the **captioned** one, at 9 against 6, simply because a
swap breaks both and that assertion is written first. The un-captioned assertion is what makes the
flip unrecoverable rather than what catches it. Run in the same command, the replica stays green,
which is the finding in one line.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md`: §9.4 already states the 6-and-3 rule and the no-caption case,
and this changes only what checks them. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D653 — `at_rest` is a conjunction of five terms and its test built four. *Tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — test-only, no production code changed.***

`panels/export.rs`'s `settings_button_state` decides whether a collapsed export row admits it is
holding a setting. `at_rest` is `prefix.is_empty() && suffix.is_empty() && background ==
ExportBackground::Transparent && !trim && !pad_square`, and `a_closed_row_still_declares_a_setting`
built the first four and never `pad_square`. Deleting `&& !spec.pad_square` therefore left **every**
assertion in it green — and a row with *Pad to a square* on, collapsed, was indistinguishable from a
row at rest, which is precisely the state §15 **D72**'s third button state exists to prevent. Three
lines added; flip run, predicted site right, `Off` against `Set`.

🚨 **`pad_button_state` beside it is tested by nothing at all**, and that is a standing gap this
entry names rather than closes. It is one line today — `ui::FieldButton::on_if(spec.pad_square)` —
so there is little to get wrong; what makes it worth writing down is that `trim_button_state`,
directly above it, has a test *because* it grew a third state, and the two read as a pair on the
screen. *Fix if padding ever gains an unavailable case*, which is the shape trim already has.

*(Nothing amended in `architecture.md` — §9.4 describes the popover's five labelled sections and the
settings button without enumerating the terms. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D652 — `de_collide` promised something no function in `ondin-export` can deliver, and the CLI is
the other door that owes a count. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the doc half is a scoping,
the behaviour half is D636's rule at D636's other door.***

**The doc half.** `crates/ondin-export/src/plan.rs`'s `de_collide` opened *"Nothing is silently
overwritten"*. That absolute is false and this function cannot make it true: `taken` is a local
`Vec<String>` created in `plan()` and dropped with it, and nothing in the crate reads the filesystem
— which is a property `architecture.md` §7 states as a *virtue* two sentences earlier (*"Nothing here
touches the filesystem — the app and the CLI own that, which is what keeps the crate testable without
one"*). What the function actually guarantees is that **no two files in one plan share a name**, and
that is what it says now.

🚨 **The behaviour half reversed this entry's first reading, and that is the part most worth
recording.** It was drafted declining the obvious repair — a `(n replaced)` count — on the ground
that counting does not separate the cases, a re-run of an export legitimately replacing everything it
wrote last time. **That argument contradicts a live entry.** §15 **D636** had already shipped exactly
that count for the export panel's folder arm, and its ruling is that **the disclosure belongs to the
door**: a *File* or an *Archive* was named in a save dialog a moment earlier and the OS has already
warned, so a door that writes with **no dialog at all** owes the user a count instead. D636 names the
File and Archive arms as the deliberate exclusions and never mentions the CLI, and nothing else in
§15 or in `architecture.md` argues against extending it.

**The CLI is the other no-dialog door, and it is the worse of the two.** It is a separately
implemented walk (§15 D626), and `main.rs`'s `run_export_all` falls back to **the folder holding the
`.ondin`** when `-o` is absent — which, for a document in the library, is a project folder the user
keeps other things in. So `ondin export brand.ondin --all` on a document with a layer named `logo`
replaced a hand-authored `logo.svg` beside it and printed `wrote 1 file`. It prints `wrote 1 file (1
replaced)` now.

**Two free functions were lifted out of `run_export_all` so any of this is assertable at all** — §15
D269's shape, the run's only report of the number being a `println!` a test cannot read.
`write_planned(&[(PathBuf, Vec<u8>)]) -> Result<usize, String>` asks `path.exists()` **before** the
write, which is the whole of it: afterwards every one of those paths exists and the count would come
back as the file count. `export_all_report(written, replaced, skipped, dir) -> String` is the
sentence.

⚠️ **The message's order is this door's and not the panel's.** D636 put the count first and the path
last because `app::status_label` draws it with `.truncate()`, so what falls off the end is what the
reader can most afford to lose. A terminal line is not truncated, so the folder stays where a reader
of `wrote N files to …` looks for it and the two parenthetical counts follow it. What the two doors
share is *which* counts are owed, not where they sit.

⚠️ **The second `write_planned` in the test is the half that says what the number means.** A re-run of
the same export legitimately replaces everything it wrote last time, so it returns 2 — and that is
the ordinary reading rather than an alarm. The count is a fact about the folder, not an accusation,
and asserting only the first run would leave that unstated.

⚠️ **Flip run, predicted site right.** Deleting the `if path.exists()` branch fails the first
`write_planned` assertion at 0 against 1 and leaves the three report-spelling assertions green: those
are about the sentence, and only this one is about the counting.
`main.rs · export_all_says_how_many_files_it_replaced`.

*(§7's plan paragraph is rescoped, its no-dialog sentence now names both doors, and the CLI bullet
gains the `-o`-less default directory — which neither document had ever stated, and which is the
reason `--all` is the door that most needs the count. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D651 — `pivot` was the one field of the MCP snapshot surface with no test and no golden. *Tested
2026-09-09; Keep — test-only, no production code changed.***

`crates/ondin-export/src/snapshot.rs`'s `NodeSnapshot::pivot` had **no reader outside its own module
anywhere in the workspace** — `ondin-mcp` does not mention the word — and `goldens::golden_document`
set no pivot on any of its nodes, so `json_snapshot_matches_its_golden` compared a file the field
never appeared in. (**It does now**, an hour later: §15 D658 gave the fixture a `Normalized` pivot on
its ellipse for that reason and the golden was regenerated.) Every other schema addition since
version 4 has both halves covered:
`PaintSummary::Image`'s id, framing mode and alpha, then `adjust`, then `effects`.

**It is also the only field in `node_snapshot` that derives rather than projects.** The others read
the node and hand the answer on. This one measures `ondin_core::local_box` and resolves the model's
fraction-or-point enum against that box through `geometry::pivot_point`, which is exactly what the
field's own doc promises — *"reported as the resolved point rather than as the model's
fraction-or-point enum"*. So the two `Pivot` variants have to be asserted **separately**: a `Local`
point passes through untouched and a `Normalized` fraction does not, and only the second one can be
wrong.

`tests/snapshot.rs · a_pivot_is_reported_as_a_point_and_only_when_it_has_been_moved` takes four
readings on the suite's own fixture. An untouched rect carries `None`, and the JSON has **no `pivot`
key at all** rather than a null — `skip_serializing_if` is what keeps every document in the world
from carrying it. `Normalized(1, 1)` on the fixture's 80 × 40 rect is `[80, 40]`, its bottom-right.
`Local(7, 9)` is `[7, 9]`.

⚠️ **The fourth reading pins a rough edge, and it is recorded rather than endorsed.** `local_box` is
`None` for a node it cannot measure — an empty `Group` falls through to a union of no children — and
the writer's `unwrap_or_default()` makes that `Rect::ZERO`, so a *fractional* pivot on an empty group
resolves against a zero box and reports `[0, 0]` whatever the fraction says. It is here because it is
the one input that makes the derivation observable at all, not because anybody can reach it: nothing
in the UI sets a pivot on an empty group.

⚠️ **Two flips, and the predicted site was right both times** — the `Normalized` assertion.
`pivot: node.pivot().map(|_| [0.0, 0.0])` fails there at `[0, 0]` against `[80, 40]` and leaves the
*absent* assertion green, which is why that one is asserted at all. Replacing `geometry::pivot_point`'s
`Normalized` arm with `local.center()` — the plausible wrong version, since `None` already means the
centre — fails the same assertion at `[40, 20]` and leaves `Local` green.

**The neighbouring worry was checked and cleared**: `pivot`'s absence from `SNAPSHOT_VERSION`'s bump
list is correct, and §7 already says why — the field is additive and write-only, so a reader on
version 8 loses nothing by not knowing about it. The version stays at 9.

🚨 **The count in the comment this change shipped is wrong, one entry after D650 recorded the same
shape.** The test's doc says `golden_document` sets no pivot on *"any of its eleven nodes"*; the
fixture issues **thirteen** `CreateNode`s and the golden JSON holds **fourteen** node snapshots, the
document root included. *Fix the comment* — the argument does not depend on the figure, which is why
nothing caught it.

*(§7's `NodeSnapshot::pivot` sentence gains the derivation and its empty-container edge. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md`, whose open MCP-snapshot items are about run colour, list markers and the
paragraph scope, none of which this touches.)*

**D650 — One test in the round-trip suite was not a binding, and the writer's own `<clipPath>`
spelling was what it was standing in for. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the suite gained a
binding and its header gained the rule that says what a binding is.***

`crates/ondin-export/tests/svg_roundtrip.rs` opens by calling itself *"the only thing that binds"*
`ondin_export::svg` to `ondin_core::svg_in`, which is the whole risk of the writer and the reader
living in different crates. It held fifteen tests, and fourteen of them earned that by calling
`svg_of` and feeding the result to `reimport`. `an_imported_clip_path_is_empty_outside_the_clip`
takes **hand-authored** markup and never touches the writer.

It is honest as what it is — a *renderer* test, and its own doc says so: *"this is the layer where
'there is a mask node in the tree' becomes 'the ink stops'"*. What it is not is coverage of the
writer, and it was being read as this suite's clip coverage because its name reads like it. **Both
sides of a hand-written fixture agree about what SVG looks like**, so the only thing that can
disagree with you is the writer's own output.

**Which left the one spelling that most needed binding unlooked-at**: the writer puts the artboard
clip **at top level**, before `<defs>`, rather than inside it. That is legal and it is unusual, and a
reader is written against `<defs>` — so it is exactly the shape a round-trip suite exists for.

The module doc now says so and generalises past clips: *a test in this file that does not call
`svg_of` is not one of the things that binds*, however much its name reads like it.
`the_writers_own_clip_spelling_round_trips` is the binding it was standing in for — a 100 × 100
artboard holding one rect, exported through `svg_of`, asserted first to be in the state the test
names (the `<clipPath>` is emitted before `<defs>`, and the frame's `<g>` references it), then
re-imported with **both** report lists empty, then with the clip back as exactly one mask node,
which is how this model spells a clip.

⚠️ **The predicted failing site was wrong, and that is the useful half.** The flip is on the
*reader*: `Gradients::collect`'s `if name == "clipPath" || name == "mask"` narrowed to `mask` alone,
so the writer's markup is byte-identical and only the reading of it changes. The prediction was that
the report lists would stay empty and the **mask** assertion would carry it. Both fail, and the
reports one goes first, at `skipped: ["clip-path"]` — an unresolvable `url(#…)` is reported by the
**attribute** name rather than by the element's, which is a spelling neither the finding nor the
test's author had in mind. Relaxing that assertion and re-running shows the mask one failing behind
it at 0 against 1, so both have teeth and the order is reports-then-structure.

**The finding's other half was closed by another finding's fix**, which is worth naming rather than
leaving as a silent gap in the ledger. That half was the writer's top-level `<clipPath>` being
reported **skipped** — a false positive on the one list that tells a user what a paste lost — and it
went with `[A5-L6-01]`, whose repair put `clipPath` and `mask` on `svg_in`'s
definitions-wherever-they-sit list (§15 D477) and is asserted in
`an_image_fill_is_reported_lost_rather_than_silently_blackened`. What had no assertion anywhere was
the other half: that the clip is actually read back **as a clip**.

🚨 **The count in the comments this change shipped is wrong, and it is the same shape it is a finding
about.** The module doc and the test's own doc both say *"twelve of its thirteen tests"*; the file
held **fifteen** before this one, of which **fourteen** called `svg_of`, and holds sixteen now. *Fix
the two comments* — and note that the argument does not depend on the figure, which is why nothing
caught it.

*(§7's model-completeness paragraph gains the rule: the gate is only as wide as the tests that call
the writer. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` — the *Now · SVG import* section's ⚠️ *"a suite only
binds what it covers"* is a note on landed work rather than an open item, and this is its second
instance.)*

**D649 — The sort owns document order in `exportable_layers`, and a `.rev()` three lines above it
claimed the walk did. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the redundant call was never the
damage.***

`panels/export.rs`'s `exportable_layers` pushed each parent's children reversed onto its stack,
under: *"Reversed, so the traversal comes out in document order rather than with each parent's
children back to front — which nothing downstream would notice today and everything would inherit
tomorrow."*

**Both halves were false.** The next statement is `ondin_core::build::all_in_document_order`, whose
first line collects its input into an `FxHashSet` and which then re-walks the document from the root
— so the order the stack produced is **discarded**, not merely unnoticed. And nothing inherits it
tomorrow, because the sort is unconditional: there is no path out of this function that does not go
through it. `document_exports_anything`, immediately above, writes the same walk with no `.rev()`
and needs no explanation for it.

**The damage was never the redundant call.** It is that a comment states a rule — *a `.rev()` on a
`children()` extend is what makes a stack walk come out in document order* — three lines from a
place where the rule is inert, so a reader takes the pattern somewhere no sort follows, where it is
load-bearing and where getting it wrong is silent. Both the `.rev()` and the comment are gone and
the replacement says what actually orders the output.

`export_all_scope_tests::export_all_collects_siblings_in_document_order`, **three siblings and not a
nested pair**: `a_nested_layers_export_settings_are_not_dropped_by_export_all` already asserts a
parent and its child come out outermost-first, and that pair is in the same order whichever way
children are pushed — so it could not have seen this at all. Three siblings is the smallest fixture
where the two orders differ.

⚠️ **Flip run, and the first flip deliberately does not bite.** Putting the `.rev()` back leaves the
new test green, which *is* the claim: the walk's order is unobservable. What bites is returning `out`
from `exportable_layers` instead of the sort — `[c, b, a]` against `[a, b, c]`, on the one assertion
— and that is what says the sort is load-bearing rather than decorative, which is what the removed
comment should have said in the first place.

*(§7's *Export all* passage gains the clause. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`, which holds no open
item about export ordering.)*

**D648 — A hidden alpha mask erased the whole drawing on export, and the dead arm that was meant to
say otherwise. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — D566's `visible()` guard, in the writer this
time.***

`[S8.1-L3-07]` is the small half and it is a *shape* finding. `svg::emit_node`'s mask loop matched
`doc.get(*child).map(|n| n.mask_mode())`, which gives a three-armed match with a dead `None`.
`Node::mask_mode` returns a `MaskMode` and never an `Option` of one — the `Option` came from the
lookup, and the `is_some_and(|n| n.mask())` guard two lines above had already made it. The dead arm
carried the hidden-mask sentence, *"`None` — a hidden mask, an empty one — masks nothing, so the run
simply carries on unwrapped"*, which is true of [`Resolved::mask_path`] and not of that lookup.
`scene.rs`'s equivalent walk has two arms; this had three, and the extra one was where a reader
tracing *"what happens to a hidden mask"* was sent.

🚨 **Reading it against the code in order to write that down is what found the live defect, and the
finding did not name it.** The `Alpha` arm had **no visibility guard at all**. It opened a `<mask>`
and filled it by calling `emit_node` on the mask child — and `emit_node` returns early for an
invisible node. So a hidden alpha mask produced an **empty** `<mask>` wrapping the run: the file
opened and showed a blank page.

**That is the one reading D282 forbids**, quoted: *"`None` means *masks nothing*, never 'clip
everything away': a hidden mask, an empty text node, an empty group and a cancelled boolean all
answer it"*, whose next sentence is *"The other reading would make hiding a mask look like deleting
the artwork"* — which is exactly what the export did. The `Shape` arm honoured the rule, and **only
by accident of routing**: it goes through `mask_path`, whose first act after the lookup is a
visibility test. Nothing in this writer had ever asked the question on purpose.

🚨 **This is D566's defect in a second walk, one day after the canvas was repaired.** That entry
found the same asymmetry in `scene::paint_node` — `mask_geometry` asks visibility, the arm storing
`RunKind::Alpha(child)` did not — and fixed it with one named expression asked by both arms,
`scene::visible(ov, node, id)`, on the argument that *"the same line written twice in two arms is how
the two came to disagree in the first place"*. It repaired `scene.rs` and `paint_ghost` and left this
writer alone. **So the same document drew one picture on the canvas and exported another**, and the
entry that fixed half of it is the entry that explains why the other half was there.

The arm is now `MaskMode::Alpha if child_node.visible()` with a fall-through `MaskMode::Alpha => {}`,
and the loop binds the node once — `if let Some(child_node) = doc.get(*child) && child_node.mask()` —
so the match has the two arms the rule has and the third cannot come back. ⚠️ **The `None` sentence
moved rather than being deleted**: it sits on the `Shape` arm's `if let Some(path) =
res.mask_path(…)`, which is the line where it is true.

`tests/svg.rs · a_hidden_mask_leaves_the_run_unwrapped_in_both_modes` is a table over both modes and
asserts three things in order: the fixture — a *visible* mask of that mode really does wrap the
siblings above it — then the loss, that hidden there is no `<g mask=` and no `<g clip-path=` wrapper,
then the strong one, that the file with the mask hidden is **byte-identical** to the same document
with the mask flag simply off. *A hidden mask is not a weaker mask; it is not a mask.*

⚠️ **Flip run**, the `if child_node.visible()` guard removed: red at the wrapper assertion on
`Alpha`, with the identity assertion behind it, and **`Shape` stays green under the same flip**,
because its arm never reads the flag directly. That asymmetry is what the finding is about and it is
why the test is a table over both modes rather than one case.

*(§7's mask paragraph gains the rule for the `Alpha` arm. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`: masks
closed there on 2026-08-21 with *"Nothing is left"*, and a writer that disagrees with the canvas is a
defect rather than an open item.)*

**D647 — A sweep gradient's exported radius was a literal `50`. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep —
it comes off the shape now, measured to the far corner.***

SVG 1.1 has no sweep gradient, so `svg::gradient_def` approximates one as a `<radialGradient>` rather
than dropping the paint. The other two arms take their geometry from the gradient — `Linear` writes
its endpoints, `Radial` its `end_radius` — and this one had nowhere to take it from, a sweep's
payload being a centre and two angles and no radius at all. So a number was invented, and written
verbatim whatever the shape.

**It is the one number in this writer that does not survive a change of scale.** On a 1 000 × 600
rect the export is a 50-unit blob at the centre with the last stop flooding everything else; on a
10-unit shape it overflows the other way. The document is right, the canvas is right, and the file a
browser opens is not.

🚨 **Half the frame's diagonal is the obvious answer and it is wrong**, and the finding's own fix
sketch proposed it with the parenthetical that makes it look right — *"half the diagonal of the
frame, which covers the whole shape from any centre"*. It covers the shape only from the frame's
**own** centre. A sweep centred on a corner — which is exactly where a sweep is most often put —
needs the whole diagonal, and anywhere in between needs something else again. So `sweep_radius`
measures the distance to all four corners and keeps the largest, which is exact from any centre and
costs three more subtractions.

⚠️ **And the measurement is in the gradient's own space, not the node's.** `cx`/`cy`/`r` are read
*before* `gradientTransform`, and this arm writes `p.center` raw exactly as the radial arm writes
`end_center` — so the box has to be pulled back through `brush.transform.inverse()` first, or a
squashed gradient gets a radius measured in the wrong units. [`None`] for a singular or non-finite
transform, where there is no pull-back to make; the caller's `unwrap_or(50.0)` keeps the old literal
there, and where it had no box to give at all, a node with no outline painting nothing and the number
being unobservable.

**Only the sweep arm asks for a frame, and the gate is on the kind rather than on the caller.**
Finding one costs an outline walk — `paint_frame` is `outline` plus a bounding box for everything but
an artboard and a text layout — so `collect_defs` asks for it under
`matches!(g.gradient.kind, GradientKind::Sweep(_)).then(…).flatten()` rather than handing every
gradient in the document a box two of the three kinds will not read.

`tests/svg.rs · a_sweep_gradients_radius_is_the_shapes_and_is_measured_from_its_centre`, one
1 000 × 600 rect and two centres: at `(500, 300)`, the box's own middle, the answer is half the
diagonal, **583.1**; at `(0, 0)`, a corner, it is the whole diagonal, **1166.2**.

⚠️ **Flip run, both measured, and only the second assertion has teeth against the plausible wrong
version.** Restoring the `r="50"` literal fails *both*, at 50 — so the first assertion is worth
having against the old behaviour and against nothing else. Replacing the corner walk with half the
transformed frame's diagonal leaves the centred case green at 583.1 and fails the corner one at 583.1
against 1166.2, which is the flip that matters and is the reason the test carries two centres rather
than one.

⚠️ **Reachability is thin and is stated rather than assumed.** `panels/paint.rs` carries *"Sweep is
not offered by the UI; nothing constructs one"*, and `svg_in` has no arm that builds one either — so
the input is a `.ondin` holding a sweep that `serde` deserializes, which is the hand-edited or
foreign file D643's overlap arm is reachable through and the same door D455's descending ramp comes
in by. Low for that reason, and recorded because the two arms beside it had made the rule obvious and
this one had been exempt from it since the day it was written.

*(§7's gradient sentence gains the sweep arm. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D646 — The colour census's layer list was in pick order, not document order. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep — the ordering is fixed at the walk, and the walk is on more per-frame paths than
the census.***

Three places state the rule. `architecture.md`: *"`ColorUse` carries **both** numbers a caller can
want: `uses` counts paint slots and `nodes` the distinct layers, **in document order**."*
`ColorUse::nodes`' own doc repeats it. So does `build::census`'s dedupe comment — *"`subtree_nodes`
is pre-order, so checking the tail is enough to keep this list distinct and in document order."*

**The pre-order claim is true within one root, and none of the three says so.** `subtree_nodes`
seeded its stack from `outermost`, whose own doc is explicit that it returns *"in input order"*.
Measured, three red rects `a`, `b`, `c` created in that order under one artboard:

| scope passed | `colors_in(&doc, scope)[0].nodes` |
| --- | --- |
| `&[artboard]` | `[a, b, c]` |
| `&[c, a, b]` | `[c, a, b]` |

**The second is the shape the panel actually passes.** `inspector::group_color_scope` returns
`node.children()` only when the selection is a *single* container, and `selection.ids().to_vec()` for
every multi-selection — pick order, since `Selection::ids` pushes as you shift-click. The row's
reticle hands `ColorUse::nodes` straight to `select_by_color`, which is a `selection.set(ids)`, so
shift-clicking two red shapes front-to-back and pressing *Select 2 layers with this colour*
re-selected them front-to-back.

**Fixed at the source rather than at the census.** `subtree_nodes` orders its roots through
`all_in_document_order` before the walk, **and only when there is more than one root**, because that
is the only case it can matter and `all_in_document_order` is a walk of the whole document.
`all_in_document_order` rather than `in_document_order` because the latter re-runs `outermost`'s
filter, which this function has already applied. ⚠️ **`subtree_nodes`' own doc claimed document order
too** and is amended; the claim was never qualified to "within a root".

**Two consumers beyond the one the finding names.** `gradients_in` is the same walk, so its rows had
the identical defect — and with them `GradientUse::at`, the *"first place the census found it"* that
`PaintSlot::GroupGradient` is keyed by, which means the picker slot's identity for one gradient in
one document depended on the order the layers were clicked in. `recolor`, `repaint`, `guides_of` and
`set_corner_radius_all` walk it too, so their operation lists were pick-ordered as well; those are
independent per-node operations, so what changed there is the shape of the transaction and not its
result, and it is recorded here so nobody reads the fix as narrower than it is.

🚨 **The cost is right about the census and short about the frame.** `census` calls `subtree_nodes`
once, in its own `for` header, so `colors_in` and `gradients_in` are one extra full-document walk
each per frame the Group Colors panel draws. But `inspector_multi_appearance` calls
`shared_radius_shown` **and** `any_rect_in` on `selection.ids()` on every frame it draws, and both go
through the same walk — so a multi-selection with both panels up pays **four**, not two. Root-only
callers pay nothing, which is what the length test is for. ⚠️ **And the enumeration of them in the
new code comment is short by two**: `layers::tree_containers` and `layers::tree_is_all_collapsed` are
root-only as well as the three it names (the layers panel's order index, the frame index,
`resolve`'s boolean sweep). *Fix the comment* — a scoped list reading as exhaustive, which is the
shape `settings::card`'s modal count had.

`tests/bulk.rs · the_censuss_layers_come_back_in_document_order` gains a second assertion passing the
scope back-to-front. 🚨 **The test written for the rule passed a single root**, which is the one case
where the claim holds for free — and it painted out of order and called *that* the discriminating
half, when paint order was never what could break it: the walk visits nodes and asks each one what it
carries, so the paint sequence is not consulted at any point. Flip run, the root ordering removed:
red at the **second** assertion with `[c, a, b]`, first assertion green, which is exactly the gap
this test had.

*(§5.7a's `subtree_nodes` paragraph gains the root ordering, and §9.4's gradient-row sentence says
its key is now stable against the order the scope was passed in. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` —
it holds no open item about the census or its ordering.)*

**D645 — `ZMove::Backward` was only ever tested where its direction is invisible. *Tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — test-only, and one of the three assertions came out of a flip that did not bite.***

`build::restacked`'s `Backward` arm is `for i in 1..out.len() { if sel.contains(&out[i]) &&
!sel.contains(&out[i - 1]) { out.swap(i, i - 1) } }`. Reversing that loop to `(1..out.len()).rev()`
makes a swapped member match again on the next iteration and walk all the way to index 0 — *Send
backward* becomes *Send to back*.

**`ZMove::Backward` reached `z_order` at exactly two sites in the whole tree, both in
`tests/build.rs`**: one with a single member at index **1**, and one with a single member at index
**0** asserting an empty transaction. From index 1 the two spellings agree, and from index 0 the loop
is never entered, so both stayed green under the reversal. Its mirror `Forward` **is** covered, which
is what makes the pair asymmetric and is worth saying rather than leaving as a symmetry argument:
**the spelling that carries a comment is the one that was checked.**

Three assertions:

- The index-2 case in `z_order_one_step_swaps_with_the_nearest_unselected_neighbour`. Flip run:
  reversing the `Backward` loop is red here with `[c, a, b]` — the member walked to the front.
- `z_order_moves_each_run_of_a_split_selection_on_its_own` — `{a, c}` in `[a, b, c, d]` under
  `Forward`, expecting `[b, a, d, c]`, which is the non-contiguous shape
  `z_order_preserves_relative_order_within_the_selection` misses by covering only an adjacent pair.
  🚨 **Two flips bite nothing here and that is written into the test's own doc.** Dropping `Forward`'s
  `.rev()` was predicted to fail it with `[b, d, a, c]` and does not: neither selected member is ever
  adjacent to the other in the direction of travel, so both the loop order and the neighbour clause
  are unobservable and every spelling gives `[b, a, d, c]`. **The test covers the shape the finding
  named and pins no mutation of its own**, and saying so is worth more than the assertion.
- 🚨 **The one that came out of a flip that did *not* bite**, and the reason this entry is more than a
  coverage note. Dropping the `!sel.contains(&out[i + 1])` clause from the `Forward` arm left **all
  six** `z_order` tests green, including the two written above. Because the loop runs `.rev()`, by the
  time index `i` is reached a selected `i + 1` has already moved up, so the neighbour under test is
  unselected either way — the clause is redundant everywhere except at the **top of the stack**, where
  there is nothing above to move into: without it, `[a, b]` with `{a, b}` selected swaps them anyway,
  reversing the selection's internal order *and* spending an undo step doing it. That assertion is
  now the last line of `z_order_at_the_end_of_the_stack_is_not_an_edit`, and it is red under the
  clause-dropping flip.

🚨 **`restacked`'s own comment was the only record of the rule.** `design-oracle` reports that
neither `architecture.md` nor §15 states which neighbour a one-step move trades with, or whether a
run of adjacent members moves as a unit — and that comment was checked on one of two arms. §9.2's
arrangement paragraph says it now, so the next reader who "simplifies" either loop has something to
fail against as well as a comment to read.

*(No production code changed. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`.)*

**D644 — SVG import installed layer names both rename fields refuse. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — one home and two copies, and the entry says so rather than claiming a unification.***

`svg_in::element_name` took `data-name`, else `id`, and passed it through `map(str::to_string)`
verbatim. Measured end to end through `svg_in::import` → `Document::apply`: `<rect id="">` gave a
layers row with **no label at all**, `id="   "` a row labelled with three spaces, and a `data-name`
carrying a newline a name with a line break in a panel that lays out one line.

**Every other door into a name refuses exactly this.** `layers::layer_rename_field` does
`let name = buf.trim().to_string(); if !cancelled && !name.is_empty() && …`, which is D54's *"a name
typed empty is discarded too"*. The inspector's name field does the same, with the argument written
beside it: *"selecting all and pressing Delete here left a row with no label at all, where doing the
same thing in the tree two panels away did nothing. Two surfaces for one edit have to agree on what a
name is."* Import was a **third** surface agreeing with neither.

The cost is more than cosmetic and `naming.rs`'s own module doc names it: `snapshot.rs` emits
`node.name()` into the AI-handoff projection and Command Mode (§13) addresses layers by name as a
fallback. **A blank name makes that fallback unusable for the node, where a duplicate merely makes it
ambiguous** — which is the difference between this and D127's non-goal.

`naming::usable(raw) -> Option<String>` is the predicate, and `element_name` ends
`.and_then(crate::naming::usable)`. Three things about it are load-bearing:

- **`None` rather than a repaired string**, which is the whole point at the import site:
  `op_create` turns `None` into a generated name, exactly what an element carrying no `id` already
  gets, so an unusable name falls through to the answer the document already has for "unnamed".
- **Every interior whitespace character becomes one ordinary space** — a no-op for a space itself,
  and what turns `"a\nb"` into `"a b"`. An SVG `id` cannot contain whitespace at all (XML forbids it
  in a `Name`), so this only ever fires on `data-name` or on a file no validator would pass.
- **Runs are not collapsed.** `"Hello   World"` keeps its three spaces: somebody typed that, and
  squeezing it would be inventing an intent the way `naming::numbered` declines to read `"Layer 007"`
  as a number.

⚠️ **This is not a uniqueness rule and must not become one.** D127's recorded non-goal is that
uniqueness never becomes load-bearing; this is about whether a name is *displayable*, which is the
question the two fields already answered.

🚨 **Which of them answered it is worth getting right, because the change shipped a citation that is
wrong and resolves.** The paragraph quoted above is `inspector.rs`'s own comment and it cites **D127**,
not D54; D54 is the layers panel's entry and says only that an empty rename is discarded.
`naming::usable`'s doc credits the quotation to D54. Both numbers resolve, so no gate and no census
can see it — *fix the doc comment.*

🚨 **The rule now has one home and two copies, and this entry deliberately does not claim a
unification.** Both rename fields still hand-roll `trim`/`is_empty`, and `naming` is a `pub mod`, so
`ondin_core::naming::usable` is reachable from `ondin-app` and nothing mechanical stops them routing
through it. ⚠️ **They are also three surfaces with three rules again in the small**: the *refusal*
agrees everywhere, the whitespace normalisation is import's alone, so a name carrying a tab would
survive a rename field and not a round trip through SVG. *Fix by routing both fields through
`naming::usable`, or record here why a typed name should keep whitespace an imported one may not.*

🚨 **Nothing in `architecture.md` or §15 had ever stated that a layer name may not be empty.** D54
states it as one field's behaviour, not as a rule about names; §5.7b, which holds the naming rules,
said only that *"everything else that writes a name is the user typing one"* — which import is not.
This entry and the §5.7b bullet are the first record.

`naming::tests::a_name_is_usable_when_something_is_left_after_trimming` is table-driven, and **the
last two rows are what keep this from becoming a cleaner-upper**: a run of interior spaces survives,
and so does a name that is nothing but punctuation. The question is *"is there anything to show"*,
never *"is this a good name"*, and the second is not one core is entitled to ask.
`svg_in::tests::an_unusable_id_falls_through_to_the_generated_name` drives the whole path, and its
**fourth rect is an ordinary `id="Roof"`** — the assertion that says this is a filter rather than a
rename, without which an `element_name` returning `None` unconditionally passes everything above it.
Flip run: `.map(str::to_string)` restored, red on the first rect.

*(§5.7b gains the rule and the third door. §7's `data-name` paragraph gains its one exception: the
writer still round-trips a name byte for byte, and the **reader** no longer does for a name holding
whitespace other than a space. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` — the *SVG import* section's open
list holds nothing about names.)*

**D643 — `normalize`'s overlap arm depended on the file's array order, and ate bytes outside the
overlap. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — overlaps are resolved by painting, and this entry is
the first record of what the rule is.***

`typography::Spans::normalize` merged two overlapping spans of one kind through a three-way `Join`,
under this comment: *"equal values join, unequal ones let the **later** span keep the shared bytes
(it is the one a caller set most recently)."* **Both halves of that sentence were false.** The list
has just been sorted by `(kind, start)`, so *"later"* meant "starts further right", which has nothing
to do with recency; and for two spans sharing a start `sort_by_key` is **stable**, so the winner was
decided by the order the file's array happened to be in.

Measured, stock `TextStyle`, weight 400:

| file order | result | bytes 5..10 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[{0..10, W700}, {0..5, W300}]` | `[{0..5, W300}]` | lost their 700 to the node default |
| `[{0..5, W300}, {0..10, W700}]` | `[{0..10, W700}]` | the 300 is gone entirely |

**Two documents from one set**, which is the headline. The second loss is the `Join::Truncate` arm's
own: it set `prev.end = span.start` and then popped `prev` when that emptied it, discarding `prev`'s
**whole** range including the part beyond `span.end` — bytes nothing overlapped. ⚠️ **The straddling
control behaved exactly as documented** (`[{0..6, W700}, {4..10, W300}]` → `[{0..4, W700}, {4..10,
W300}]`), and that is what localised the defect to **containment** rather than to overlap in general.

**Painting, not truncating.** Spans of one kind are laid down in sorted order and each byte takes the
value of the last one covering it; a span painted over keeps whatever lies outside the shared bytes,
on **both** sides. The runs a new span paints over are always a suffix of what is already laid down,
so the whole repair is one head, one tail, and everything between them gone.

⚠️ **`std::cmp::Reverse(end)` joins the sort key and is load-bearing.** With equal starts the widest
is laid down first and the narrower paints over it — which is what makes the answer
order-independent, and it is the *only* reason two spans sharing a start have a defined winner at
all. The equal-value merge is a pass of its own now rather than an arm of the loop, because painting
can split a run around one of equal value and produce a pair the loop has already walked past.

Two things that are the reasons this is safe, and both would be the first casualties of a
"simplification":

- **The `(kind, start)` save order is unaffected** (§5.11, invariant 9). After `normalize` runs, one
  kind's spans do not overlap, so no two share a start and the third key never breaks a tie in the
  output. The third key changes which *input* survives, not how the survivors are written.
- **Two spans with an *identical* range and different values are still decided by array order**,
  because nothing here compares values. That case has no defensible answer and is not one this crate
  can produce, so it is recorded rather than guarded.

🚨 **Nothing had ruled on this before.** §5.4 states only the postcondition — *"no two spans of one
kind overlapping"* — and no §15 entry and no other architecture passage says what a file's
overlapping same-kind spans should *become*. So the misleading comment was the whole of the record,
and it was wrong in both of its clauses. This entry is the rule now.

**Reachability is IO only, and that is the honest bound.** `Spans::set` splits the old span around
the new range and cannot produce a containment; `edited`'s two maps are monotonic; and `clamped`,
`restated` and `scaled` preserve ranges. So the producer is a hand-edited or foreign-written file —
which `io/schema.rs` explicitly chooses to **normalize rather than reject**, on the stated grounds
that clamping *"loses nothing a designer would notice"*. Here it lost styling, and which styling
depended on array order.

`typography::tests::an_overlap_resolves_the_same_way_whichever_order_the_file_lists_it_in`, built
with `from_parts` rather than `set` **on purpose** — a test driven through `set` cannot reach the
state and would be green against the old code. Two flips run, and **each bites at exactly one
assertion with the other green**, which is what says the tie-break and the split are two halves of
the fix rather than one written twice: the sort key without `Reverse(end)` is red on
order-independence and green on the tail; the tail dropped from the split is **green** on
order-independence — both orders agree on the wrong answer — and red on the tail. The straddling
control survives both.

*(§5.4's span bullet gains the resolution rule, which it stated only as a postcondition. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md` — its one open `Spans::normalize` item is `[S6.1-L1-03]`'s *Mixed* readout,
a structural-comparison ruling this change does not touch.)*

**D642 — A duplicate id was first-wins in one of three maps. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the
rule was written three lines from one of its three implementations and held none of the other two.***

`svg_in`'s `Gradients::collect` builds three maps from one pass over the document. `ids` was written
with `ids.entry(id).or_insert(el)` under a comment stating the rule verbatim:

> **First wins**, which is what a browser does with a duplicate id and is the only answer that does
> not depend on document order twice.

`clips` and `by_id` were plain `insert`s, i.e. **last**-wins. So one document had two answers for
`#g`: `Gradients::element`, `Gradients::filter` and `gradient_chain`'s `href` walk took the first,
while `Gradients::get` — the fill and stroke path, and by far the common one — and `Gradients::clip`
took the last.

Measured against Chrome, serving the same file as `image/svg+xml`: two `<linearGradient id="g">`,
red then blue, on one rect. Chrome paints **red**; Ondin painted **blue**.

The fix is `by_id.entry(id).or_insert(…)` and `clips.entry(id).or_insert(el)`.

🚨 **The obvious enumeration of who took which is wrong, and it is wrong in this change's own
comments.** `Gradients::clip` reads `clips`, which was last-wins until this fix — so it belongs
beside `Gradients::get` and *not* among the first-takers, where both the comment at `by_id`'s
insertion and the gradient test's doc put it. The `ids` readers are three: `Gradients::element`,
whose only caller is the `<use href>` resolver; `Gradients::filter`, which looks a `filter="url(#…)"`
up off the same map and therefore was **never** affected by this defect; and `gradient_chain`'s
`href` walk. *Fix the two comments.*

⚠️ **`clips` holds `<mask>` as well as `<clipPath>`** — the arm is `if name == "clipPath" || name ==
"mask"` — so the same defect covered a duplicate `<mask id>`, which the finding's name does not say.

⚠️ **The gradient test's `href` half is the assertion that says the maps *disagreed*, not merely that
the fill changed.** `#h` inherits its stops from `#g` through `gradient_chain`, which reads `ids`, so
under the old code the two rects came back `["blue", "red"]` — one document, two answers. Asserting
the fill alone would have passed against a fix that flipped `ids` to **last**-wins instead, which is
the opposite repair and equally consistent with the symptom. Both rects are read before either is
asserted for the same reason: a failure message naming only rect 0 hides the pair.
`a_duplicate_gradient_id_resolves_to_the_first_definition` and
`a_duplicate_clip_path_id_resolves_to_the_first_definition`, both flips run.

Severity is Low because a duplicate id is invalid SVG and no file in the tree has one. It is recorded
because of the shape rather than the blast radius: **a rule stated next to one of its three
implementations is not a rule the other two are held to by anything**, and nothing in this project
can see the disagreement — the two maps are built eight lines apart, both compile, and every test was
green.

*(§7's SVG reader paragraphs gain the id rule, which no passage stated. Nothing struck from
`roadmap.md`.)*

**D641 — An infinite escape became *no* escape, and the fix is one level out. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-09; Keep — invariant 8's third family, and the check belongs at the operation because the
derived function has nowhere to put an absence.***

`effect::escaped(bounds, escape, world)` grows a world box by a local escape. It splits the insets
back into an offset and a radius — `off = (x1 − x0) * 0.5`, `rad = (x0 + x1) * 0.5` — so with
`x0 = x1 = inf` the offset is `inf − inf`, which is `NaN`. The final `(t.x − h.x).min(0.0)` is then
`NaN.min(0.0)`, and `f64::min` resolves that to the **non-`NaN`** operand, i.e. `0.0`. Every edge
takes the same path, so the whole escape is discarded and the function returns `bounds` **unchanged**.
The early `if escape == Insets::ZERO` return does not fire and there was no other guard.

A layer carrying `EffectKind::LayerBlur { radius: f64::INFINITY }` therefore reported an `ink_bounds`
identical to its geometry, and the viewport cull, the export plan and both backends' buffer boxes all
believed an unbounded blur reached nowhere. Not a refusal and not a `NaN` box: the bare geometry, out
of a function whose whole job is to grow it.

⚠️ **The contrast is worth the entry on its own.** `reach(f64::NAN)` is `0.0` by the same
`max`-against-zero convention, so a `NaN` radius was always a benign no-op while an infinite one was
a bounds *lie* — two non-finite inputs, two silent answers, from one idiom. This is `[S4.2-L1-06]`'s
mechanism (D640) with the sign reversed: there `f64::min` made a `NaN` the **largest** trim, here it
makes an infinity the **smallest** escape.

🚨 **The finding's own fix sketch is wrong, and the thing that makes it look right is its citation.**
It asks for *"the conservative one (an infinite box)"* and cites §5.9 for it. An infinite box is
precisely the failure **D495** removed: it unions all the way up, so `world_bounds(root)` stays
infinite for the life of the session, with `plan::raster_size` and `plan::raster_opts` reading it
(D334). ⚠️ **§5.9 holds two rules and the sketch read one.** *"Too small is the one error these bounds
may not make"* is about how a bound may err **among numbers**, and it is the sentence a reader lands
on. D495's *"a bounds function's `None` means no measurable extent, not only no geometry"* is what
§5.9 says about a bound that is **not** a number, `geometry::measurable` requiring the rect be
ordered *and finite*. The sketch applies the first rule to a case governed by the second.

So the fix is neither an infinite box nor a sentinel. `escaped`'s signature has no room for absence —
several of its callers have a `Rect` to return and nowhere to put one, which is `transform_rect`'s
position exactly — and **the check belongs at the operation**, which is where invariant 8 puts it
anyway. `build::effect_is_finite` is the predicate, beside `brush_is_finite` and
`image_ref_is_finite`: it weighs a shadow's offset, blur, spread **and colour**, a layer blur's
radius, and the four filter factors. ⚠️ **The colour arm is the one a check written by reading the
word "distance" leaves out**, and it is `brush_is_finite`'s argument again — the question is what
`serde_json` will refuse to write, not what looks like a coordinate.

Two doors take it: `op_set_effects`, and `op_insert_subtree`'s per-node field loop. `escaped`'s doc
now records the swallow and why the repair is upstream, and `OpError::NonFinite`'s doc names effects.

⚠️ **The preview path does not come through an operation, and what bounds it is the panel's ranges.**
A blur being scrubbed reaches the renderer through `RenderOverrides` before anything is committed, so
the operation guard is not what covers it. `inspector.rs`'s `MAX_BLUR` (1000) is **half** of the
answer and not the whole one: `stack_escape` reads a shadow's offset and spread as well as its blur,
and those three fields are ranged at `±MAX_OFFSET` (10,000), while `Filters` escape nothing at all —
so it is two constants on five fields rather than one on two. `svg_in::deviation_of` filters
`is_finite` on the import side. **Three bounds, none of them `escaped`**, which is worth knowing
before somebody removes one of them as redundant.

⚠️ **This *is* invariant 8 gaining a family**, unlike D639 the same day: a blur radius is not a
coordinate, so the rule genuinely did not name it, and effects join coordinates (D421) and paint
(D451, D452) as the third. 🚨 **And it is the only one of the three whose value does damage before the
file is ever saved.** The other two end at `serde_json` writing `null` and `load` refusing it; this
one corrupts a cached bound in a running session as well.

Tests: four `SetEffects` arms in `tests/io.rs ·
no_operation_may_write_a_number_that_is_not_finite` — blur radius, shadow offset, shadow **colour**
and filter factor — and `document::tests::insert_subtree_refuses_a_non_finite_effect`, which lives
in-crate for D639's reason: every field of `Node` is `pub(crate)`, so a test outside the crate can
only obtain a `Vec<Node>` from `capture_subtree`. **Both flips run, and each is red at its own door
with the other green**, which is what says `op_set_effects`' guard does not cover `InsertSubtree`.

*(§2's invariant 8 gains the effects family and §5.9's `ink_bounds` bullet gains the swallow. Nothing
struck from `roadmap.md` — its effects entries are the parked *Background blur* non-goal and
`[S4.2-L4-04]`'s open performance half, neither touched by this.)*

**D640 — A `NaN` corner radius was the *largest* radius, not none. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — the pair of guards is the finding, and neither half alone produced the reported symptom.***

`geometry::round_corners`' fast path was `radii.iter().all(|r| *r <= 0.0)` and `round_run`'s
per-corner guard was `if radius <= 0.0 { continue }`. Every comparison against `NaN` is false, so
both let it through — and what it reached is `fillet`'s
`let t = (radius / (theta * 0.5).tan()).min(la * 0.5).min(lb * 0.5)`, where `f64::min` returns the
**non-`NaN`** operand. So the trim came back as the largest one the clamp allows. A 100 × 100 square
carrying a `NaN` radius drew, exported and hit-tested as its **inscribed circle** — measured area
7856 against 10000, byte-identical to what an infinite radius gives. Not a refusal and not a `NaN`
path: the maximum fillet, out of a guard that reads as excluding it.

`!radii.iter().any(|r| *r > 0.0)` for the fast path and `radius.is_nan() || radius <= 0.0` per
corner. ⚠️ **The second is spelled with `is_nan()` rather than as `!(radius > 0.0)`** — the same
predicate — because `clippy::neg_cmp_op_on_partial_ord` objects to the negated form, for precisely
the reason this bug happened: a negated comparison hides the incomparable case, and hiding it is
what the old guard did.

⚠️ **`inf` is deliberately unchanged and the test asserts it still rounds.** It is a magnitude, and
*"each radius is clamped to half of each adjoining segment"* is this function's documented answer to
a radius that is too big — the same answer 500 gets. Without that assertion the fix reads as "reject
anything not finite" and the next reader tightens the guard onto a case the function has always
answered on purpose. That the two used to be byte-identical is also what identified `f64::min` as
the mechanism in the first place, rather than a `NaN` propagating through the arithmetic.

🚨 **Three flips run, and the pair is the finding.**

- **Fast path alone reverted** to `all(|r| *r <= 0.0)`: red at the first assertion, and the left side
  is **the square**, not a circle — the per-corner guard catches every `NaN` on the way through, and
  all the walk changes is that the closing edge arrives as an explicit `LineTo`. So that assertion
  pins *which route* `[NaN; 4]` takes, which is stronger than "was not rounded" and is deliberate.
- **Per-corner guard alone reverted**: the first assertion stays **green**, because the fast path
  answers `[NaN; 4]` before the walk ever runs, and it is red at the mixed case with `(0,0)` filleted
  50 units, i.e. the maximum.
- **Both reverted**: four `CurveTo`s and no straight edge left, which is `[S4.2-L1-06]`'s measured
  inscribed circle reproduced exactly.

⚠️ **So a fix at either site alone would have closed the reported symptom and left the other guard
reading as doing the opposite of what it does.** That is why both are here and why
`a_nan_radius_is_no_radius_where_an_infinite_one_is_the_largest` carries a mixed list — one live 20
beside the `NaN` — at all: `[NaN, 0, 0, 0]` would not do, no element of it being `> 0`, so it takes
the early return and never reaches `round_run`. The test sits beside
`an_over_large_radius_clamps_instead_of_inverting` because that test asserts the very answer this bug
produced.

⚠️ **Nothing reaches this today, and the entry says so rather than claiming a closed hole.**
`NodeKind::geometry_is_finite` weighs a `Rect`'s four radii and a `Path`'s whole list,
`GeometryPatch::is_finite` weighs `CornerRadius`, `CornerRadii` and `Path`, and `serde_json` cannot
carry a non-finite number into the loader at all (§15 D421) — so the review's own reachability note,
*"only through G1's open doors"*, names doors `[S2.1-L2-01]` has since shut. What is repaired is the
function's **own** contract: `round_corners` is `pub` in `ondin-core` and its two guards were the
statement of what a radius means to it.

🚨 **The two spellings had already drifted apart in the tree, and the disagreement was visible from
the menu.** `build::can_outline` answers a `Path` with `corner_radii.iter().any(|r| *r > 0.0)` — the
predicate this change gives `round_corners` — so on a `NaN` list the menu row was dimmed for having
nothing to bake while the canvas drew the inscribed circle. Both now ask the same question. ⚠️ **The
comment beside `can_outline`'s line still explains itself as *"`round_corners` returns the path
untouched when every radius is `<= 0`"***, which is the sentence this entry disproves; it is the
thing a later editor would "simplify" the guard back to. *Fix the comment.*

*(§9.4's *Outline shape* paragraph amended, where the same `<= 0` phrasing was the documented
justification for `can_outline`'s predicate. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` — its one rounded-path
bullet is `[S4.2-L4-04]`'s open performance half and is untouched by this.)*

**D639 — A non-finite pivot saved as `null` and killed the file. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09;
Keep — the pivot was inside invariant 8's rule and outside its code.***

`Document::op_set_pivot` validated nothing. `apply(SetPivot { pivot:
Some(Pivot::Normalized(Vec2::new(f64::NAN, 0.0))) })` returned `Ok`, `io::save` succeeded —
`serde_json` writes a non-finite `f64` as `null` — and `io::load` then failed with *"invalid type:
null, expected f64"*. That is `[A1-L2-01]`'s terminal shape reached through a field nobody had
counted: a document that saves cleanly, saves again through autosave and the crash snapshot, and
never opens again.

⚠️ **The arithmetic downstream was already safe and that was never the question.**
`geometry::pivot_for` falls back below `MIN_EXTENT` and `canvas::origin_pivot` has its own
`ORIGIN_MIN_EXTENT` floor, so nothing here divides by a zero extent — which is what a reader
checking this field would find and stop at. What neither guards is a coordinate that was **never
finite**, and there are two ways one arrives: `canvas::pivot_at` inverts the node's world transform
to place the marker, and a singular transform's inverse is `NaN` in every coefficient; and any
hand-authored or MCP write hands the value straight over.

`Pivot::is_finite` is the predicate and it lives **on the enum rather than at the call site**,
because the two variants hold different types — `Normalized` a `Vec2`, `Local` a `Point` — so a
guard written against one compiles happily while missing the other. Two doors ask it: `op_set_pivot`,
and `op_insert_subtree`'s per-node field loop, which was already asking `kind.geometry_is_finite()`
and `affine_is_finite(transform)` and not the third coordinate a node carries.

⚠️ **No external route reaches the `InsertSubtree` guard, and this entry says so rather than claiming
a closed hole.** Every field of `Node` is `pub(crate)`, so outside the crate a `Vec<Node>` can only
come from `capture_subtree` — from a document the operation guards have already vetted. It is kept
for the same reason and in the same register as `io::MAX_TREE_DEPTH`'s doc, *the traffic the model
cannot vouch for*, and that is why its test lives in `document.rs`'s own `mod tests`
(`insert_subtree_refuses_a_non_finite_pivot`) rather than in `tests/io.rs` beside the operations a
caller outside the crate can actually reach.

⚠️ **This is not invariant 8 gaining a family.** A pivot *is* a coordinate — the rule has said
geometry, transform and guide position since it was written, and the enforcement test's own name has
said **number** since D451 renamed it from `…_a_coordinate_…`. So the rule covered this from the
first day and only the code did not, which is the opposite direction from D451's paint and is the
harder one to see: the value looks exactly like the values already guarded.
🚨 **Which makes `no_operation_may_write_a_number_that_is_not_finite`'s *"at every door that writes
one"* false twice over** — once for a family outside the rule and once for a value inside it. That
sentence is prose in a `#[cfg(test)]` module, so no gate in this project has ever read it (§15 D319).

Two `SetPivot` arms in that test, one per variant, plus the in-crate insert one.
`OpError::NonFinite`'s doc names the pivot now. **Three flips run, and the sharpest is not the
obvious one**: blinding the clause in `op_insert_subtree`'s loop fails at the predicted site, and
blinding only `Pivot::is_finite`'s `Local` arm — the predicate somebody writes who reads the enum as
one shape — leaves the `Normalized` assertion **green** and fails at *"Local((inf, 0.0)) was
inserted"*. That is what says the second half of the predicate is carrying its own weight rather
than restating the first.

*(§2's invariant 8 gains the pivot in its enumeration and a paragraph; §5.3's pivot bullet names the
two doors. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md` — it was carrying no item for this.)*

**D638 — The schema-version guard ran on a truncated `u32`. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Keep — the
error type's payload being narrower than the input is what made the cast look free.***

`io::migrate` read `schema_version` off the parsed JSON as a `u64` and cast it `as u32` *before* both
comparisons, so `version > CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` did not mean what it read as. Measured on an
otherwise-valid save, three headers:

- **`8589934592`** (2³³) — its low 32 bits are zero, so it truncated to **0**, passed the guard, was
  migrated through the whole v0→v4 chain and **opened**, reported as v4. A file claiming a version
  from the future was read as the oldest one this loader knows.
- **`4294967300`** (2³²+4) — truncated to 4, which *is* `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION`, so `migrate`
  returned early and the failure arrived from the DTO instead, as a serde error about a `u32`. An
  answer to the wrong question.
- **`u64::MAX`** — refused as *"unsupported schema version: 4294967295"*, a version the file does not
  claim.

The fix is to compare in the header's own denomination and never narrow: both comparisons are against
`u64::from(CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION)`, and the `match` runs on the same value the guard read rather
than on a second copy that could disagree with it. Below `CURRENT` the value provably fits, so
nothing downstream changes.

🚨 **`IoError::UnsupportedVersion` carries a `u64` where it carried a `u32`, and that is the
load-bearing half of the change.** While the variant was narrow, casting at the read was free
everywhere — which is how the guard came to be written on a number nobody had checked. With the
