*(§9.4's wrap paragraph now names `wrap_gate_tests`, and D624's closing *"`architecture.md` is

**D623 — `node_grab` walked every segment of the path to answer "what is the pointer over".
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — a control-hull reject, and a second rebuild taken out of
`point_box`.***

`canvas::node_grab`'s tail allocates a whole `BezPath` through `tools::pen_path`, hands it to
`geometry::nearest_segment`, which walks **every segment of it**, and then throws both away. It does
that on every call, and the calls are per frame: `draw_points` makes one on every hover frame while
the Node tool is armed, `select_cursor`'s `Drag::None` arm makes a second whenever a point box
exists, and `menu::on_segment` reaches it through `segment_at` while a context menu is open.
Measured in release on one open path with the pointer *off* the ink — so every filter above the walk
runs to the end and refuses — **0.020 ms at 512 anchors, 0.177 at 2048 and 0.868 at 8192**: 1.74 ms
a frame for answering *"what is the pointer over"*, before anything is drawn, on a path size an
imported SVG map or a flattened boolean reaches without trying. `[S12.3-L4-05]`.

**The fix is a reject and it is exactly lossless, which is what makes it a fix rather than a
threshold.** A cubic lies inside the hull of its own control points, so the box over every anchor
and every handle *contains* the ink. Taking that box, inflating it by `slop` and answering `None`
when the pointer falls outside cannot change an answer: anything the walk would have found is on the
ink, and therefore inside the box. It costs one pass over the anchors with no allocation, and it
fires for the whole canvas outside the path's own bounds — which is where a pointer usually is, and
is exactly the case the measurement above is of.

⚠️ **The cache the finding also sketched is deliberately not built, and the reason generalises.**
The subpaths here are **preview**-aware, and a preview changes within a frame without moving
`EditorSession::revision` — so keying a memo on the revision, which is what **D616** does correctly
for the artboards, would reintroduce the committed/preview split that `edited_subpaths` and
`preview_subpaths` exist to keep apart. That is a correctness bug bought with a cost saving. **The
same key is right for one of these two and wrong for the other, and the difference is whether the
thing being memoized is committed.**

**A second cost, in `point_box`, and for the commonest state it was the larger one.** It called
`preview_subpaths` — a full `pen_anchors` rebuild over the node — and *then* asked `points_box`,
which refuses fewer than two points. So every hover frame with nothing selected paid for a complete
second rebuild whose answer was always `None`. The refusal is `points_box`'s own rule and is
restated one allocation earlier rather than moved, since *"below two anchors there is no extent to
scale about"* belongs where the box is built. At 4096 anchors over twenty calls the two changes
together take `node_grab` from **40.5 ms to 2.5**.

🚨 **The test counts rather than times, and the clock is what said so.** The first draft asserted a
5× timing ratio. It passes in **release** — the profile the finding measured in, where the segment
walk dominates — and **fails in debug** at 21.9 ms against 35.7, a ratio of 1.6, because in debug
`edited_subpaths` dominates instead and runs *before* the reject either way. ⚠️ **So the finding's
own attribution — *"`edited_subpaths` is only 5 % of the cost at 8192"* — is a release fact, and it
inverts under the profile `cargo test` runs in.** A wall-clock bound is therefore either too tight
for the suite or too loose to mean anything, and the claim was never about time: it is *"the pointer
is nowhere near the path, so do not walk it"*, which is **countable**. `OndinApp::segment_walks` is
that count, D616's shape at a second site. **This is `[A8-L3-02]`'s lesson arriving from a third
direction — ask which spelling, or which profile, a measurement was taken under.**

⚠️ **And the fixture's first draft never reached the code under test.** Anchors one unit apart put
every point on the ink inside `slop` of an *anchor*, so `node_grab` returned `Anchor` before the
segment walk it is about. Spaced at 100 now, with the trap written into the test — this project's
*"its fixture never reached the state"* vacuity shape, caught by an assertion rather than by
reading. `canvas::a_pointer_away_from_a_path_does_not_walk_it` asserts the two correctness cases
first, on the ink and one unit off it inside the slop, and only then the count; the flip that
deletes the reject leaves both correctness assertions green and fails the count at **1 against 0**,
which is the whole claim.

Neither document changed. §9.4's `node_grab` paragraph is about which handles the tool offers, and
nothing in the design says anything about what the query costs.

**D622 — D319 is corrected in three places: its counts, a third blind target, and a paragraph
that argued a working gate away. *Recorded and corrected 2026-09-09; Fix for the record, Keep for
the gate.***

D319 is a live *Keep* entry — the one this project points at when somebody asks what checks the
comments — and three separate things in it were wrong. It is amended in place rather than superseded,
because the entry's core claim is still true and still the reason the hole exists.

**(a) Every count in it was stale, and the same figure had seven copies.** *"The eighteen files under
`crates/…/tests/`"* is **23**, and *"nine intra-doc links live there today"* is **18**. The other six
copies were `CLAUDE.md` (three), `.claude/skills/codebase-review/SKILL.md` (two) and
`.claude/agents/rust-verify.md` (one), the last three of which said **21** — so one number was stale
in seven places at **two different values**.

⚠️ **It did not rot by neglect, and that is the part worth carrying.** `git log --diff-filter=A` puts
21 of these files in the tree on 2026-08-28, the day the figure was last re-run; the two added since
are `svg_roundtrip.rs` and `zoom_sweep.rs`. **A commit that lands a test suite has no reason to think
about a count in a §15 entry**, so the number rots on exactly the days somebody is doing the right
thing. The copies outside D319 therefore carry **no number at all** now and say to count during the
sweep — the only version of this claim that cannot go stale, and the same answer `rust-verify.md`
had already reached on its own.

**(b) `build.rs` is a third target the doc gate never reads, and nothing had written it down.**
`crates/ondin-app/build.rs` carries 22 lines of `//!` prose. Measured: `//!` plus a link to a
nonexistent item, left in that file, passes `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`
at **exit 0** — while `cargo fmt --all --check` prints a diff for the same probe and clippy warns
under both spellings. **Of the six gates, the doc gate alone is blind to it.** Links have lived
there: D409's paragraph records two now-deleted `pub fn`s in that file carrying D405 citations in
their doc comments. D319 named two mechanisms and there are three.

⚠️ **And D319's crate-root claim has a sharper form than it states.** It says the only crate-level
attribute *"in any of the eighteen"* is `#![allow(dead_code)]` in `tests/common/mod.rs`. That file is
**not a crate root** — it is reached through `mod common;` — so the set of test crate roots carries
no crate-level attribute at all, which is a stronger statement of the same fact.

**(c) 🚨 The paragraph deciding `--document-private-items` off the gate command is false, and it was
never measured.** Verbatim: *"a broken link is reported whatever the item's visibility, which is the
only thing this gate is for, so the flag would change what gets rendered and nothing about what gets
caught."* **rustdoc does not read what it does not document.** A deliberately broken link on
`svg_in::Builder::pick_family` — a private method — leaves the bare gate at **exit 0**, and the flag
catches it. The flag was consequently absent for the nine days between D319 (2026-08-23) and
2026-09-01, over a body of code that is almost entirely private; the day it was added it surfaced
**three** broken links plus **eight** naming a struct with no `impl` block at all.

🚨 **That is the worst shape a record can take, and it is worse than an ordinary stale sentence: a
live *Keep* entry telling the next reader to remove a working gate.** Every other hole on this list
is a gate that does not cover what it claims. This one is a gate that *existed*, was argued away in
§15 from what a gate is "for" rather than from a measurement, and had to be re-discovered by probe.
**When the record says a check is unnecessary, check** — which is the mirror of D445's *"when the
record says a check is impossible, check"*, and the two now bracket D319 from both sides.

⚠️ **The session writing this entry added the nineteenth `tests/` link while counting them** —
`[`svg::name_attr`]`, written into `svg_roundtrip.rs` by D611 an hour earlier, straight into the
population under audit. Converted to plain backticks per D319's own convention, which is what took
the number back to 18. **The habit that grows this population is the habit of writing good prose**,
which is why the convention rather than a gate is the answer.

*(Closes `[A8-L6-01]` and `[A8-L6-05]`. No `Fix` is claimed for the gate itself: `--tests` still does
not exist, `build.rs` has no flag either, and the test crate roots still carry no `deny` — what is
fixed is the record that described all three wrongly. `SKILL.md` and `rust-verify.md` amended;
`CLAUDE.md` is the delegating session's own job and carries the counts at the close of each session)*

**D621 — The one card in the app outside the modal vocabulary was the one that throws work away.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — through `settings::card`, with *Discard* on `Danger`.***

`OndinApp::close_confirmation` was built with `egui::Modal::new` and three bare `ui.button`s. Every
other modal in the app is drawn on `settings::card`; this was the one that was not, and it is the
one that decides whether a document's unsaved work is kept or thrown away. `[S18.1-L3-02]`.

**Three things it was missing, in order of what each cost.** The **focus ring** first:
`ui::focus_ring`'s own doc says *"call it once at the end of a modal's body; `settings::card` does
that for every card in the app so a new one cannot forget"*, and `grep` returns exactly **two**
production sites for that function — its definition and `settings::card`. So the sentence was false
of this card, which painted no ring **at any point in the tab order**: a keyboard user tabbing
between the three buttons had nothing on screen saying which one `Enter` would press, which is
precisely the gap **D382** put the ring into the modals to close. Then **`FieldButton::Danger` on
*Discard***, whose own doc is about this exact shape — *"a confirm that read as an ordinary
`FieldButton::Off` button beside Cancel — two grey buttons, one of which removes a project that has
no trash to come back from"* — and here the two grey buttons were *Discard* and *Cancel*, where what
the first discards is the document on screen. And last the card's **frame and backdrop**:
`color::CARD`, the `text_a(23)` hairline, the 10pt radius, the 24/60 shadow, and
`from_black_alpha(128)` against egui's default 100, whose own doc argues that at 100 *"a light
document still read as the thing in focus"*.

It routes through `settings::card` and `settings::modal_title` now, with *Save and close* on
`FieldButton::On`, *Discard* on `Danger` and *Cancel* on `Off`, in a right-to-left footer like every
other card's. ⚠️ **`modal_title`'s ✕ maps to *Cancel*, not to a fourth answer** — the same reading
`should_close` already gives `Escape` and the backdrop, for **D377**'s reason: a reflex gesture must
not land in the arm that throws work away.

🚨 **Three measuring findings came out of writing the tests, and the third is the one that matters
most for the record.**

1. **`FullOutput::shapes` is not flat.** `CLAUDE.md` records it as already *layer*-flattened, which
   is true and is not the whole story: an individual entry can be a **`Shape::Vec`** holding more
   shapes, and that is exactly what an `egui::Frame` paints its background and its shadow as. A
   first draft scanned the top level, found the three buttons and not the card they sit on, and read
   as a missing frame. The helper walks `Shape::Vec` recursively.
2. **The `Area` fade again.** Read two frames in, the ring came back at `#29_34_51_5F` — the accent
   at 0.37 — which matches no constant in the theme. The helper puts the events in on the first
   frame and reads off the last of thirty; `focus_ring`'s own visibility latch survives the idle
   frames, so the key is still spent.
3. **The obvious assertion had no teeth, and only the flip said so.** *"The ground is `color::CARD`"*
   is satisfied by the version that shipped, because `theme::install` puts that colour into egui's
   own window fill — so the bare `egui::Modal` painted `#252526` too. What actually discriminates is
   the **backdrop weight** and the card's **hairline on a 10pt corner**, which egui's default frame
   does not draw at all. The flip fails at the backdrop with `#00_00_00_64`, alpha 100.

⚠️ **Not a duplicate of `[S16.3-L1-01]`**, which is this same modal's missing `CancelClose` on a
second ✕ click. That one is about the close path and this one is about the chrome; fixing either
leaves the other standing.

⚠️ **One count in the brief and in the shipped test-module comment is one low, and the document was
already right.** Both say *"seven modals go through `settings::card`; this was the eighth"*. It is
**eight** and this is the **ninth**: the editor's own Settings card calls `card` unqualified from
inside `settings.rs`, so a grep for `settings::card(` misses it. §9.5's *"eight modals stand on it"*
was correct before this change and reads **nine** now, and §9.5's paragraph recording the *Unsaved
changes* card as the ninth modal and the one **not** on the shared card is amended, since D525's
history is still worth keeping and its conclusion is no longer the current state.

**D620 — A library migration counted what it could not move and never said what it was.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `failed` names the source paths, and the failure arm gets its
first test.***

`library::relocate::Moved::failed` was a `usize`, incremented from **twelve** sites: a document, a
version file, a trashed document, a crash snapshot, a directory that could not be created, a
`projects.json` that would not parse. What the user saw was *"Moved 37 file(s); 23 could not be
moved"* — no names, no paths, and no way to tell a document from a sidecar. `[S1.3-L6-06]`.

⚠️ **A migration is not re-runnable in place, which is what turns a bad status line into lost work.**
`panels::dashboard::apply_library_settings` re-points the app at the new root **outside** the
`if d.migrate` block, so it does so whether the migration succeeded, partly succeeded or did
nothing. There is no retry and no rollback. The only recovery is to go and find the files by hand —
which is impossible without knowing which they are.

**Source paths and not destinations, deliberately.** A failure means the file is still where it was,
and `move_file` is copy-then-delete with the **delete last**, so the source is the thing that exists
to be gone and looked at. There is one spelling, `Moved::fail(&Path)`, so no site can record a
failure without naming one — which a bare `failed += 1` allowed at all twelve. `summary()` names the
**first**: a status line cannot hold twenty-three paths, but one name says which folder to go and
look in, and whether what was left behind is a document or a sidecar.

🚨 **The compiler found every reader and there were four, all of them in tests.** No production code
read the count at all — `apply_library_settings` uses `destination_of` and `summary()` and nothing
else — which is its own small statement about what the number was worth. Two of the four are
*strengthened* rather than adapted: `an_unanswered_crash_snapshot_moves_with_the_library` and
`an_unreadable_destination_project_list_is_left_alone` assert the **path** now and not the count,
because `failed == 1` is satisfied by a migration that strands the *wrong* file, and that is the
whole complaint.

**And the test that did not exist.** All seven tests in the module were happy paths; `failed` was
asserted non-zero in exactly one, and that path never calls `move_file`. So `Moved::summary`'s
failure arm had no test caller either — **deleting it and returning `"Moved {d} file(s)"`
unconditionally left the module green**, which means the app could report a partial migration as a
complete one and nothing anywhere noticed.
`a_document_that_cannot_be_moved_is_named_and_left_where_it_was` **arranges** the failure rather
than mocking it: a *file* is put where the project's *folder* has to go, so `create_dir_all` fails
for exactly one document and the rest of the migration runs normally. That is a real arm of
`relocate` and it is deterministic on every platform, which a permission-denied directory or a
held-open handle is not. ⚠️ **The second document is the control**, and it is not decoration: a
version that gave up on the whole migration at the first failure would satisfy every assertion about
the failed one.

⚠️ **Both flips bite at their predicted sites, and one message corrects the write-up.** Deleting
`summary`'s failure arm — the review's own flip, the one that left this module green — reports
**`"Moved 1 file(s) and 1 project(s)"`**, not the `"Moved 1 file(s)"` that was predicted: the arm
being flipped is not the only one composing the sentence. It also bites
`a_snapshot_that_would_collide_is_left_behind_and_reported`, the other test that reads the summary.
Replacing `moved.fail(&entry.path)` at that site with a fail on `dir` keeps the count at one and
fails the **name**, which is precisely the difference between this test and the `usize` it replaced.

**What is left is named in the code and is the maintainer's**: the full list belongs in the *Library
settings* modal, and so do rollback and a *re-run the migration* button. The module's own defence —
*"a migration run twice leaves duplicates rather than being idempotent, which is the right way
round"* — is an argument for a retry the UI does not offer, and the retry that exists today is a
three-step dance back through Settings whose middle step looks like the operation that lost the
files. That is a `roadmap.md` bullet under *Now · Files, library and storage* rather than a verdict
here. ⚠️ **Two of those three were built on 2026-09-19 and this hand-off now names one thing** — the
list and the retry are D810's; **rollback alone is still the maintainer's**, and it is a decision
rather than work.

§9.5 amended, where the migration paragraph described the map the session is re-pointed through and
said nothing about what happens to a file that does not go.

**D810 — A partly-failed migration had no way back and no list. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Keep —
two of the three asks, and the third is still a decision.***

D620 gave `Moved::failed` the names of everything that stayed behind and put the **first** of them in
the status line, then handed the rest to the maintainer as three separable asks: the full list in the
*Library settings* modal, a *re-run the migration* button, and rollback. **The first two are built.
Rollback is not and stays open**, because `relocate` deliberately overwrites nothing, so "undo" means
deciding what to do with everything that *did* arrive — which is a decision rather than a fix, and is
what is left in `roadmap.md`.

`OndinApp::stranded: Option<panels::dashboard::Stranded>` holds `{ from, to, failed }` after a migration
that left anything behind, and is assigned in **both** directions so that a clean run *clears* a
previous one's report and the modal cannot go on offering to retry a move that has already finished.
**Session state and not a preference**: the files are the record, and a stranded list in `prefs.json`
would be a second copy of a fact the filesystem holds. It is deliberately not a `Moved` — that type is
the whole of what a migration did, including the path map a caller re-points an open document through,
and what has to survive the operation is the part nobody can reconstruct afterwards.

The modal draws it under the migrate switch: a warning line with the count, the old folder's path, up
to `STRANDED_ROWS` = **6** filenames, an *"…and N more"*, and a *Try again* button. It sits below the
switch rather than beside it because the switch is a question about the *next* move and this is the
report on the last one. ⚠️ **Six is a bound on the modal's height and not a judgement about how many
names are useful.** That card has no scroll area and a partly-failed migration can strand every document
in the library, so an uncapped list takes *Save changes* off the bottom of the window. The folder above
is what the user opens; the names are what to look for in it.

`OndinApp::retry_migration` re-runs `relocate(from, to)`. **It is not idempotent and does not need to
be**: a successful move deletes its source, so the second walk meets only what was left behind, and what
fails again fails for the same reason — a name already taken at the destination is `Collision::Stranded`'s
case and stays stranded however many times it is asked. This is the run the module's own defence already
assumed was reachable — *"a migration run twice leaves duplicates rather than being idempotent, which is
the right way round"* — where until now the only route was a three-step dance back through Settings
**whose middle step looks exactly like the operation that lost the files**.

The re-point loop that was inline in `apply_library_settings` is `OndinApp::follow_moved_documents` now,
because a retry is a second migration and owes everything the first one did; D430's whole argument — the
forked open document, the map rather than a prefix swap, `prefs.last_document` — moved onto the function
with it. ⚠️ **The retry is answered *after* the Save/Cancel match**, so it cannot race a base-folder
change: both touch the library and `apply_library_settings` is the one that may **re-point** it, so
running the retry first would move files into a root the next line is about to change. Cancel takes the
draft away and leaves the report standing, which is right — the files are still stranded whatever the
user did with the card.

**Test `panels::dashboard::tests::a_partly_failed_migration_is_listed_and_can_be_run_again`**, driving
the real modal and reading the list out of `galleys`. Asserting it on a `String` instead would be D426's
own bug: 22 status messages went into a slot nothing drew for two months while every test that read the
slot passed. 🚨 **Two flips, and the second is the finding.** Dropping the `stranded` assignment fails at
the report, predicted. **Dropping `retry_migration`'s `library.refresh()` left every assertion green on
the first reading** — the retry's effect on the dashboard *behind* the modal was untested — which is what
the `library.entries` assertion was added for. *A flip that does not bite is where the coverage gap is,
not a failed experiment.*

§9.5's *"there is no retry and no rollback to offer instead"* sentence is amended.

🚨 **Rollback was refused the same day (D814), so this entry's *"stays open"* is discharged** and the
three asks are closed as two built and one decided.

**D814 — A library migration has no rollback, by decision, and the retry is the recovery. *Ruled by
the maintainer 2026-09-19; Resolved — a decided non-goal, and no production line changed.***

D620 handed over three asks and D810 built two. The third is refused, and the reason is that it is
not the operation it sounds like.

**`relocate` deliberately overwrites nothing, so "undo" is not the reverse of a known operation.** It
is a fresh decision about everything that *did* arrive — a document already sitting at the
destination, a `.versions` tree merged into another library's, and worst of all a `.trash` file
renamed on the way in by `Collision::Rename`, which no longer carries the name it left under and is
therefore indistinguishable from a document that was always there. A rollback would have to guess,
per file, and a wrong guess deletes work.

⚠️ **And a reverse migration can itself partly fail**, which leaves a second and worse partial state
with nothing to offer after it. The thing being asked for is a recovery, and a recovery that can
strand files is not one.

**What the ask was really about is reachable now.** The retry moves in the **migration's own
direction** over whatever is still in the old folder, and D810 made it a button on the card that
reports the failure — where until then the only route was a three-step dance back through Settings
whose middle step looks exactly like the operation that lost the files. ⚠️ **Do not read the retry
as half a rollback**: nothing in the app moves anything back, and that sentence is kept on
`relocate`'s module head rather than only here.

**Record-only, so the citation is planted by hand** on `library::relocate`'s module head, beside the
*"a migration run twice leaves duplicates rather than being idempotent, which is the right way
round"* note — which is this same argument seen from the forward direction, and the place a reader
meets the question.

---

**D619 — *Recent searches* is a persisted, disk-writing feature with no assertions at all.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — with one side effect recorded rather than fixed.***

`grep -rn "recent_searches\|remember_search" crates/` returned six hits and **none of them was in a
test**. All four of `remember_search`'s decisions live in five lines: the refusal of a blank query,
the `retain` that dedupes and promotes to the front, the `truncate(SEARCH_RECENTS)` that caps the
list at five, and `self.library.local.save()`, which puts the list on disk. Delete the `retain` and
the list fills with repeats of one word; change the cap to fifty and nothing goes red.
`[S20.1-L6-05]`.

⚠️ **It was *executed* and unasserted, which is the distinction that makes a gap like this invisible
to a coverage number.** The search-arrows test drives `remember_search` through the `nav_to` arm and
looks at none of what it did. `[A5-L6-02]` draws the same line for `grid.rs`, and the pair is worth
holding together: *reached* and *checked* are different properties, and only one of them is
countable.

**And the display half had never been laid out at all.** `recents` is non-empty only when the needle
is empty, and the one test that opens the search with an empty query has an empty list — so
`search_results` returned before drawing a row. `a_remembered_search_is_deduped_promoted_capped_and_shown`
asserts all four decisions, the persistence, and the rows on screen; the rows are the first time that
branch has been drawn.

🚨 **A side effect worth a decision of its own, recorded rather than fixed: the test suite writes to
the user's real cache directory.** `LocalIndex::save` goes to `dirs::cache_dir()/ondin/library.json`
with no injection point, and `Library::open` *loads* from there — so the `app()` fixture, which
redirects the base folder, cannot redirect this. **The first run of this test found its fixture
already populated from a previous run**, which is that side effect surfacing rather than a fixture
mistake. The test clears the list and says why, and asserts persistence through `save_to`/`load_from`
against a temp path instead. ⚠️ **The `load_from`/`save_to` pair D370 built is the right answer and
nothing routes the app through it**: `remember_search` calls the global `save`, so running the suite
edits the person's own *Recent searches*. **This wants an injection point and is left for the
maintainer** — it is real work rather than a ruling, so it is a bullet under `roadmap.md`'s *Now ·
Files, library and storage* and not a verdict here.

⚠️ **All four flips bite, and two land earlier than predicted.** Dropping the `retain` fails the
promote assertion — the predicted site — with `["alpha", "gamma", "beta", "alpha"]`; `truncate(50)`
fails the cap with a sixth entry still on the end, predicted; dropping the empty-query guard fails
the blank assertion, predicted; and `insert(0, ..)` → `push` was predicted to fail the promote
assertion and fails **"newest first"** two assertions earlier, with the list simply reversed. **An
order flip bites at the first assertion that reads an order, which is rarely the one the claim is
filed under** — worth expecting, because the prediction reads the *claim* and the test reads the
list.

§9.5 amended, where the paragraph on `load_from`/`save_to` implied that pair was the whole mitigation.
⚠️ **The hand-off above was answered on 2026-09-19 and this paragraph is the one it corrects** — see
D807, which is the injection point, and note that it is none of the four shapes this entry and
`roadmap.md` between them proposed.

**D807 — The per-machine index had no injection point, so the suite edited the developer's own
*Recent searches*. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Keep — a `cfg!`, because there is no constructor here
that can be trusted to set a flag.***

D619 recorded this as a side effect rather than fixing it and left the *where* to the maintainer.
**It was established rather than reasoned.** `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\library.json` on the maintainer's
machine held `recent_searches: ["alp", "d", "alpha", "gamma", "beta"]` — the fixture strings of
`panels::dashboard`'s `a_remembered_search_is_deduped_promoted_capped_and_shown`, and nothing else —
with an mtime from a suite run earlier the same day. The `app()` fixture redirects the **base folder**,
which is a different knob, so anything driving an `OndinApp` reached the real file.

`library::cache::index_is_reachable()` answers `!cfg!(test)`; `LocalIndex::load` returns
`Self::default()` and `LocalIndex::save` returns, each on its **first line**, when it is false.
`load_from`/`save_to` are untouched and stay past the guard.

🚨 **`roadmap.md` named four possible answers and none of them was taken, which is the half worth
recording.** It called `prefs::Prefs::ephemeral` — a `#[serde(skip)]` flag `OndinApp::headless` sets and
`Prefs::save` reads before anything touches the filesystem — *"the cheapest of the four"*. It does not
work here, and the reason is `library::state::Library::open`: `Prefs` is built **once**, by the one
constructor that knows a test's app is different, whereas the index is rebuilt by `Library::open`, which
tests call **directly, after building the app** — `app.library = Library::open(root)` at two sites, in
`app.rs` and in `panels/dashboard.rs` — so a field the constructor set would be silently discarded by
the very fixture that needs it. A process-wide flag stored by `headless` (D798's `CLIPBOARD_OFF`
spelling) fails one step further out: every `Library::open` in `library::state`'s own tests would go on
reading the machine's file until some *other* test in the binary happened to build an app first.
**A `cfg!` has no door to forget.**

🚨 **Why a profile-dependent guard is allowed here and was refused for the other two resources in the
class.** `load` and `save` hold no behaviour beyond resolving `path()` — the three-way read, the
`unreadable` write latch and the round trip are all in `load_from`/`save_to`, which take a path and are
asserted. That is not true of `Prefs`, whose latch test drives `save_to`, and it is emphatically not
true of the clipboard: `clipboard_gate_tests` has to open a **real** `arboard` handle to prove D796's
lock holds under eight threads, which is exactly why D798's refusal sits in the four callers and not
inside `with_clipboard`. *The question to ask of a `cfg!` is what it costs in coverage, and here the
answer is nothing.*

**Test `library::cache::tests::the_machines_own_index_is_unreachable_from_a_test`**, which asserts the
guard **and then** the one consequence observable without writing — `a_headless_app_cannot_reach_the_clipboard`'s
order, and it matters for the same reason. Flip-checked by deleting the `if !index_is_reachable()` from
`load`: red on the second assertion with `["alp", "d", "alpha", "gamma", "beta"]` against `[]`, which is
the reported symptom itself rather than a stand-in for it. ⚠️ **The `save` half cannot be caught by any
test** — the only thing that would observe it is a write nobody may perform — so deleting *that* guard
leaves the test green by construction, and that half rests on the first assertion and on the `cfg!`.
⚠️ **The second assertion can false-*pass* and never false-fail**: on a fresh runner with no file an
unguarded `load` answers `Default` too, which is the other reason the flag is asserted directly.

Two test sites had their reasoning corrected rather than their behaviour.
`a_remembered_search_is_deduped_promoted_capped_and_shown` **asserts** the empty list where it used to
clear it, and `a_missing_library_folder_says_so_instead_of_reading_as_empty` dropped its
`LocalIndex::default()` overwrite; its `mark_opened` is still the fixture. *An assertion is what a
cleared list should always have been — clearing it says the suite expects contamination and works
around it.*

§9.5's *"an injection point for the local index is open work"* paragraph is amended, and the bullet is
struck from `roadmap.md` with the clause in that section's table row.

**D618 — Two of the library's destructive modals, on screen for the first time.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — the sentence and the switch, asserted where the eye reads them.***

`dash.deleting` and `dash.deleting_project` are **never assigned in any test module in the
workspace**, while `dash.new_project`, `dash.edit_project` and `library_settings` all are. So the two
cards that *destroy* something were the ones no test had ever drawn. The review ran five simultaneous
flips of five documented decisions with the whole `ondin-app` suite green — 977 passed — and this
entry closes the two that matter most. `[S20.3-L6-04]`.

**The first is the one worth writing down first.** `delete_modal`'s `let purge = self.dash.nav ==
Nav::Trash` flipped to `!=` makes **every *Delete file* card in the library read "is deleted for
good. This cannot be undone", and every card in the Trash read "moves to Trash"** — which is exactly
the sentence that function's own ⚠️ calls *"the worst sentence on the screen"*. The test asserts
**both navs**, because one of the two is satisfied by a build that shows that sentence everywhere,
and it asserts the **title with the body**, because a card that contradicts itself is the same
failure by a different door. ⚠️ **`nav` is set directly rather than reached by clicking**: the route
in is `dashboard_keys`' Delete, which is `[S20.3-L1-02]`'s territory and still an open ruling. What
this pins is the *card*, which is where the sentence lives and where the flip was.

**The second is `delete_project_modal`'s switch, which reads the inverse of the field it writes**
(`!dp.keep_files`) — and the flip draws it *off* when it will delete and *on* when it will not, on
**the one destructive card in the app with no trash behind it**. Asserted through
`ui::switch_row_ink`, the label's colour, because that is what the eye reads the state off and the
field was never in doubt. ⚠️ The count in the label is asserted too: `if count > 0` means a fixture
with no documents draws no row at all, and a test of a row that is not there asserts nothing.

🚨 **`CLAUDE.md`'s `Area`-fade trap, hit and recorded.** A modal is an `Area` and an `Area` fades in,
so every colour it paints is gamma-multiplied by how far through the fade the pass is: read at four
passes the label came back `#7C7C7D88` against a `MUTED` of `#909092 9E`, a uniform 0.86 of it. The
`galleys` helper can afford four passes because a **string** does not fade; a **colour** has to be
read after the animation settles, and this one reads at thirty. The flip's own values —
`#CCCCD0E0` against `#909092 9E` — differ in alpha as well as in RGB, which is what says the fade had
settled and that the alpha is part of the theme's two inks rather than an artefact of the pass count.

Both flips bite at their predicted sites. Neither document changed: §9.5 specifies the library screen
and its dialogs, and both cards are already described there exactly as they behave.

**D617 — Three `tools` verbs that nothing called.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `side_shear`'s four arms, `rotate_points`, `space_points`.***

**Two findings under one entry**, `[S13.1-L6-05]` and `[S13.2-L6-05]`, both **G9**, because they are
the same gap in one module and were closed in one pass.

**Half of `side_shear` was executed by nothing.** The four skew call sites in the whole workspace pass
`Handle::Top` three times and `Handle::Right` once, and **all four pass `snap_to_steps: false`** — so
`Handle::Bottom`'s span sign, `Handle::Left`'s held edge, `SKEW_SNAP` and `MAX_SKEW` had no caller
anywhere. **D322 exists because this function got its *origin* wrong**, and it pinned `Handle::Top`
alone. The review ran two flips, both green across the whole workspace: `Bottom`'s span sign reversed
together with `Left`'s held edge moved to `min_x()` — a bottom drag then leans backwards and a left
drag slides the layer sideways instead of leaning about the far side — and the entire snap-and-clamp
body of `lean` replaced by a bare `(offset / span).atan()`. ⚠️ A third flip was run as a **control**
and did bite (neutering `paired_size` failed four tests), so the suite is not blind everywhere in
that file — only here, in the function with the most arms.

**Three tests in a new `side_shear_tests` module, and the four arms are asserted as the bargain the
doc promises rather than as numbers**: the side facing the grabbed one does not move, and the grabbed
one moves by the drag. That is one sentence for all four arms and it is what a sign error breaks.
⚠️ **The probe points are corners of the held side, not its midpoint.** A midpoint is fixed under a
shear about that side for a trivial reason — it lies on the axis — so it would stay put under a shear
about the box's *centre* too. ⚠️ **Every case presses at the middle of its own side**, because D322
measures the offset from the press and pressing anywhere else is a legitimately different answer.

**The snap test needs its third case, and that is what makes the ordering assertable at all.** A drag
far past the clamp snaps to 90°, which *is* a step, and is then pulled in to `MAX_SKEW`; snapping
after the clamp would round 89° back up to 90° and leave the degenerate matrix the clamp exists to
avoid. Its first case is the anti-vacuity control, asserting the fixture's own raw angle is 18.43° so
that "snapped to 15" means something moved rather than 15 arriving by coincidence.

🚨 **The lean is signed and the sign is asserted rather than taken away with an `abs()`.**
`Handle::Top`'s span is `min_y − max_y`, so a rightward drag on the top edge is a *negative* `skew_x`;
asserting the magnitude alone would pass for the arm that leans the wrong way, which is one of the two
the review's green flip produced.

⚠️ **The interesting flip result is a wrong *correction* rather than a wrong prediction.** `Bottom`'s
reversed span was first predicted to fail the grabbed-side assertion; the write-up then "corrected"
that to the held-side one, on the reasoning that a reversed span leans the box the other way about the
same edge. **The original prediction was right.** The held edge is pinned by the `Vec2` beside the
span and is untouched by its sign — what a reversed span changes is the direction the grabbed side
travels. Only running it said so, and a correction written over a prediction is exactly the sentence
nobody re-checks.

**`rotate_points` and `space_points` each have one production call site and had zero test callers.**
Neither name appears in any `#[cfg(test)]` module or in any file under `crates/*/tests/`;
`rotate_about_pivot_moves_points_correctly` is *named* for the first and exercises
`turn_about`/`rotate_selection` instead. Their neighbours `align_points` and `distribute_points` do
have a test, which is the contrast that makes this a gap rather than a policy, and both of the
review's flips were green across 972 tests. ⚠️ **D243's verdict line reads *"Built and tested"*, which
was drift** — the point arm of that entry had no test at all — and this entry is where it is
corrected. D123's half is the weaker case and worth distinguishing: it *states* `rotate_points`'
handle rule as a fact about the code, and the statement was true and merely unasserted. **A true
sentence nothing checks and a verdict claiming a test that does not exist are two different
failures**, and only the second is a lie.

`rotate_points` carries each handle through the transform **via the control point it describes**,
which is D123's rule, *"so a zero-length handle stays at zero rather than at a rounding error"* —
hence a corner anchor with no handles in the fixture, a case no assertion on the *anchor* can see.
`space_points` holds **the first point on the axis**, and its selection is passed deliberately
scrambled, because `points_along` sorts and the guarantee is about the axis rather than about the
order the user clicked in.

⚠️ **Two recorded values were wrong and the runs corrected them.** The expected handle after a quarter
turn: `Affine::rotate(FRAC_PI_2)` sends `+x` to `+y`, so `leaving()` is `(10, 25)` and not the
`(5, 20)` first written, which is where a −90° turn would put it. And the reversed-order flip gives
**`[50, 45, 40, 90]`**, not the finding's predicted `[30, 35, 40]`: the gap still accumulates
*forwards* from `start`, so reversing the order moves the whole run to the far side of the anchor it
held. **A flip's failing value is worth reading even when its site was predicted correctly.**

`architecture.md` did not change: §5.6 describes the skew gesture exactly as it behaves and §9.4
describes the point arrangements, and nothing in either was falsified — what was missing was the
coverage, not the rule. **D243's paragraph on the point arrangements gained the correction**, since
that is the entry whose verdict was the untrue one.

**D616 — The artboard index is memoized on the document revision.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `FrameIndex`, keyed on `EditorSession::revision`.***

`OndinApp::artboards` was a full-document walk — `subtree_nodes` over the whole tree, building a
`Vec<NodeId>` of *every* node — to answer a question about four of them. And it was asked per node,
per call: `canvas::move_destination` → `frame_covering` → `artboards`, with `leaving_their_frames`
running once a frame, `draw_frame_drop_outline` running `move_destination` over the same roots again
on the same frame, and an Alt-drag's `clone_tx` a third pass. Measured in release at 16,000 nodes over
200 iterations: `artboards()` alone **0.157 ms**, `move_destination` at one layer **0.155**,
`leaving_their_frames` **0.156** at one root and **3.037** at twenty. So a twenty-layer move was
**6.07 ms a frame** and **9.11 with Alt**, against a 16.7 ms budget, before anything is drawn.
`[S12.2-L4-04]`.

⚠️ **The one-root figure against the bare call is what says the whole cost is the walk**, and it is
the half that decides who feels it: this scales with the **document**, not with the artboard count. A
drawing with four frames and sixteen thousand nodes pays exactly as much as one with forty, so the
worst case is not a document anybody would call complicated in the frames.

**`FrameIndex` on `OndinApp` behind a `RefCell`**, holding the artboard list, their world boxes and a
walk counter, filled by `with_frames`. **A closure rather than a returned `Ref`**, so no caller can
hold the borrow across something that might want the memo again — which is what a `RefCell` panic is
made of, and is exactly what a nested `frame_covering` inside an `artboards()` loop would do.
`artboards()` becomes a memo read and a four-element clone; `frame_covering` reads the `(id, Rect)`
pairs directly rather than re-deriving a box per frame.

🚨 **Keyed on `EditorSession::revision`, which is an existing invalidation rule rather than a new
one.** That counter is bumped in exactly two places — `commit_inner`, which undo and redo also go
through, and `adopt_document` — and those are precisely the events that can add, remove or move an
artboard. Nothing else assigns it. **The rule this leaves is the one to keep**: anything that can
change the artboard set has to reach it through a commit, and a future path that edits `session.doc`
outside one would leave this memo stale with nothing to say so. ⚠️ **A gesture in flight does not bump
it and must not**: these are the **committed** world bounds, which is what `frame_covering` read
before this change and what the drop rule is defined against — a memo that tracked a drag would change
the feature rather than its cost.

`canvas::a_move_drag_walks_the_document_once_however_many_layers_are_selected`. **A counter and not a
clock**, which is the finding's own suggestion and the more durable of the two — a wall-clock ratio
says the same thing and still passes on a fast machine with the memo defeated. ⚠️ **`frame_walks` is
`#[cfg(test)]` on the *accessor* and not on the counter**, so the production build and the tested
build do not differ in the one place this could go wrong; the increment is one add on the cold path.
An ungated accessor is reported dead on the `bin` target by `clippy --all-targets`, which is **D302**'s
gate working correctly rather than an obstacle.

⚠️ **Both flips bite at their predicted sites, and the written prediction still had the numbers
wrong.** Always-walking gives **20 against 0** — one walk per selected root, the finding's *"40
times"* at this fixture's own size — and a memo keyed on something that never moves leaves that
assertion green and fails the **second** at **0 against 1**. The write-up said "21 against 1" and "1
against 2" beforehand: both assertions are on a *delta* from `before`, not on the absolute counter,
and the prediction quietly read them as absolute. **The second assertion is not a formality — it is
the whole invalidation rule, asserted.**

§9.4 amended.

**D615 — A shadow's spread is bounded by the buffer it runs in.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `effects::spread_steps`, one helper both backends count to.***

`n`, the box dilation's half-width, is in **device pixels**: `effects::shadow_layer` passes
`sh.spread × scale`, so the authored number is multiplied by the zoom. The only bound anywhere was
`panels::inspector::MAX_OFFSET = 10_000`, whose own doc calls it *"the reach of an offset or a
spread, in both directions"* — and which the panel applies to the **Offset** fields as well. **An
offset costs nothing**: it is a shifted texture read, O(1) per pixel. A spread is Θ(n) per pixel.
Two fields sharing one range is exactly the **G10** shape — *the cap measures how far the shadow
goes, and what grows is how many samples each pixel takes*. Measured in release on a real adapter,
one shadow with `blur: 0`: **23.8 ms** at `spread: 200` and zoom 256, **117.1 ms** at 1 000,
**277.9 ms** at 10 000 and zoom 64, and **1 092.7 ms** at 10 000 and zoom 256 — one shadow, one
frame. `[S10.2-L4-04]`.

⚠️ **D403 does not cover this and could not.** That entry bounds the *blur*, and it does so by
resampling: past twice the budget the silhouette is coarsened into blocks and blurred on the coarse
grid. `spread_alpha` runs at **full resolution and before** `blur_coarse` ever sees the surface, so
the one term the design had bounded was the one beside the term that went on growing with the zoom
untouched.

**The cap is exactly lossless, which is what makes it a fix rather than a clamp.** Both loops read
outside the buffer as **empty** — `effects::spread_alpha`'s `t < 0 || t >= inner_len` arm and
`fx.wgsl`'s `inside()` test — so once the window covers the whole line the answer stops moving: a
dilation takes the line's maximum and can find nothing further, and an erosion has already met a
zero. At `n ≥ extent − 1` that is true of every pixel on the axis. So no picture changes, including
the ones that render today; only work that could not have changed one is stopped. **`extent − 1` and
not `extent`** is the boundary, because the window is `[i − n, i + n]`.

**One helper, both backends**, and `fx_gpu::run` calls it rather than spelling the arithmetic a
second time. That is the mistake §15 D601 records at this very pair of sites: both backends computed
the radius from `scale.0.max(scale.1)`, both were wrong in the same way, and every fixture in
`tests/fx_gpu.rs` is at `SCALE = (1.0, 1.0)`, so the CPU/GPU comparison harness agreed with itself
and stayed green. A cap the two could disagree about would be the same defect with a new value in
it.

Two tests. `a_spread_wider_than_the_buffer_is_capped_without_changing_the_picture` asserts the
picture is byte-identical at spread 200 and 200 000 on a 120-wide buffer **and** that the work stops
— the second is needed, or the first is satisfied by a build that does nothing at all. The timing
bound is a deliberately loose 20× ratio, because a wall clock in a test suite is a flake waiting to
happen and what is being pinned is Θ(n) against Θ(1). ⚠️ **Flip-check, run**: `spread_steps`
returning `v.abs().round() as i32` uncapped fails at **12.3 ms against 9.24 s**, a ratio of about
754, so the 20× bound has nearly two orders of magnitude of margin and nothing here is close to a
clock. **The flip leaves the picture assertion green**, which is the whole claim.
`a_spreads_reach_is_capped_at_the_axis_it_runs_along` pins the arithmetic at the boundary — under,
at, over — per axis, for a negative radius, and for a zero-width buffer.

🚨 **What this does not do, and the record should not read as if it did.** The cost is still
Θ(w·h·n) for `n` up to the buffer's own size — the finding's **1 026.9 ms at 960×540, n = 500** on
the CPU export and cover path. Bounding *that* means running the dilation on `shadow_downscale`'s
coarse grid the way `blur_coarse` does, which is a real approximation rather than a lossless cap,
guarded by `fx_gpu::a_resampled_shadow_with_a_spread_matches_the_reference`, and **a separate
decision left open**. This removes the *unboundedness*; the remaining growth is bounded by the
viewport. ⚠️ **The finding also asks that the panel's *Spread* field stop borrowing the offset's
range, and that is not done** — it is a UI nicety now rather than a correctness bound, since the
renderer no longer cares what number reaches it.

§6.4 amended.

**D614 — A union is folded as a balanced tree.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `Subtract` keeps the left fold, the other two do not.***

A group used as a shape mask unions all of its members, and there is no cache anywhere on that
path: `scene::mask_geometry` runs it on the scene walk, once per repaint, and `resolve::mask_path`
runs it from `query.rs`, once per pointer move. `boolean::fold_operands` folded **left**, so step
*i* handed flo_curves an accumulator of *i* subpaths and the total was Θ(N²) — worse in practice,
`path_add` being superlinear itself. Measured in release on N disjoint 20×20 rects, which is a group
of icons and is both the common case and the expensive one: **0.56 ms at 16, 1.39 at 32, 5.94 at 64,
26.7 at 128, 103 at 256, 471 at 512.** At 128 a single mask costs more than a whole 16.7 ms frame.
`[S10.1-L4-04]`.

⚠️ **§15 D239's cost table measured the wrong shape for this, and said so honestly at the time.** It
timed `evaluate` on an overlapping **ring**, whose union collapses to a handful of subpaths however
many operands went in — which is why *"under 4 ms at sixty-four overlapping operands"* was true and
was not the case that grows. The disjoint set is the one where the accumulator's subpath count is
the operand count.

Merging adjacent pairs, then pairs of pairs, makes it log N levels of N subpaths each. **After: 0.13
ms at 16, 2.1 at 128, 6.4 at 256, 20.3 at 512** — 24× at the top, and the curve is N log N rather
than ≈N².

**Union and intersection are associative and `Subtract` is not**, which is the whole of the arm that
did not change. `a − b − c − d` is `((a−b)−c)−d`; a tree computes `(a−b)−(c−d)`, and everything `d`
takes out of `c` comes back. So `fold_operands` keeps the left fold for `Subtract` and reassociates
only the other two. ⚠️ **This is associativity and not the commutativity §9.4 already states** — the
two are different properties and only one of them licenses a tree. The intersection's early exit is
preserved per level (empty anywhere is empty overall), and at odd counts the leftover rides up a
level untouched, which is what keeps the tree balanced.

Two tests. `a_union_folded_as_a_tree_is_the_shape_the_left_fold_gives` computes the left fold by
hand and compares it against `evaluate`, **because reassociating is a pure optimisation and no
assertion about the shape can bite the change** — any correct fold passes. What it pins is the
*premise*: that `combine` is associative here to within `ACCURACY`. ⚠️ The delta is exactly `0.0` at
every count tried, 16 through 512, which is stronger than the tolerance asserted and is deliberately
not what is asserted — two bracketings of a floating-point boolean are entitled to differ, and a
test demanding they never do would be pinning luck.
`a_subtraction_is_still_bracketed_from_the_left` guards the arm that was *not* changed. ⚠️ **It
needs four operands**: with three, the tree pairs the first two and carries the third up untouched,
so it computes exactly the left fold and stays green under the flip. Flip-check, run: deleting the
`Subtract` arm fails there at **1000 against 800** — the predicted site, and the predicted gap of
200, at numbers 600 lower than the write-up said, the arithmetic having been done before it was run.

🚨 **The measurement contradicted the finding's own fix sketch, and the finding says its attribution
was reasoned rather than measured.** That sketch proposed hoisting `Shape::area` out of `from_flo`'s
O(subpaths²) nesting loop. Timed apart at N = 256 the fold is **96.2 ms** and `from_flo` **2.8 ms**,
so that fix removes 3% of a 103 ms cost. **The finding's second recommendation — a cache slot in
`Resolved` beside `boolean` — is not built and is not needed for this**: what is left is N log N,
and the invalidation rule a cache would have added is a cost that stays unspent.

§9.4's Booleans subsection amended, where the cost was recorded as settled.

**D613 — The corruption mark is drawn, and it is made to mean something.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — one `Mark`, two sources, and `Cover::Failed` split in two.***

`library::scan::Entry::unread` was computed on every scan and had **no reader outside `library/`** —
`panels/dashboard.rs`, 7,600 lines and the only consumer of `Entry`, did not contain the string
once. So a `.ondin` this build cannot parse got a card carrying a de-slugged filename, a created
date, a hover menu and *Open*, identical in every pixel to a healthy document, and the only feedback
the user ever got was the status line saying *"Load error: …"* after they had clicked it. `Entry`
derives `PartialEq`, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s measured mechanism for `dead_code` staying silent on a
written-never-read field — and `scan.rs` had a test asserting the field, so the suite read as
covering a feature that did not exist. `[S1.3-L3-05]`.

**Half one, the drawing.** `conflict_chip`/`conflict_chip_size` become `mark_chip`/`mark_chip_size`
over a new `Mark { Unreadable, Conflict }`, so the broken file gets the treatment the conflict copy
already had, at both call sites — the card's bottom-left corner and the list row's name column,
which takes the chip's width out before eliding. **Red rather than amber, and the colour argument is
this entry's**: `theme::color::WARN`'s own words are *"the usual cause is a file that moved, which is
a thing to fix rather than a mistake in the document"*, which is true of a conflict copy and not of
a document that will not open. The objection that kept red away from the conflict mark — *"red would
read as `this click removes it`, which is what the ⋮'s Delete means two inches away"* — **does not
apply here, because the thing it warns about is exactly the click.** ⚠️ `mark_chip_size` measures
per mark: `UNREADABLE` is four characters longer than `CONFLICT`, and the list view takes that width
out of the *Name* column before eliding, so one size shared between the two is the fixed guess the
function exists not to be. **One mark, most severe first**, rather than two chips: a conflict copy
of a broken document is both, they would share one corner, and *this will not open* is what has to
be acted on first, because until it is fixed there is no choosing between two copies.

🚨 **Half two, making the flag honest — and the finding's account of the gap does not survive
reading `read_meta`, while the real gap is worse.** The finding names a document *truncated* past
its 4 KB `meta` block. That is not the hole: a truncation makes `probe::scan_value` fail on the
`root` key, which is `MetaProbe::Inconclusive`, and **that arm already reads the whole file and runs
`io::load`** — it is the arm D485 pinned. What is *not* caught is a document whose JSON is
well-formed and which `io::load` nonetheless refuses: the probe walks to `root`, answers `Found`,
and nothing ever parses it. **A file written by a newer build is exactly that** — one number
changed, structurally perfect, refused by `migrate`'s `version > CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` guard — and a synced
library is precisely where one turns up.

The answer was already being computed and thrown away. `cover::rasterize` runs `io::load` over the
whole file to draw a thumbnail, and `Cover::Failed` conflated *will not load* with *empty document*;
it splits into `Cover::Unreadable` / `Cover::Blank` behind a private `NoCover`, and
`Covers::unreadable(entry)` is a map lookup on the key `get` already built, with no parsing of its
own — everything that reads it is drawing. `mark_of` asks `entry.unread || covers.unreadable(entry)`
and **neither alone is sufficient**: the flag carries the early passes, because the cover cache is
lazy — and per-pass budgeted until **D820** moved the render onto a thread — so a document whose
cover has not come back yet answers `false`. `get` requests a repaint, so late arrives.

Two tests, and neither is the other.
`cover::a_document_the_loader_refuses_is_unreadable_where_an_empty_one_is_merely_blank` asserts the
*fact*, on a **version bump** rather than a cut, since a cut is the case that was already caught;
`dashboard::a_document_this_build_cannot_open_wears_the_mark_and_a_healthy_one_does_not` asserts the
*drawing*, in both views, with a healthy document in the same library as the control and two passes
pumped for the cover cache's laziness. 🚨 **Those two passes became a *race* on 2026-09-19 and this
test flaked 2 runs in 20** — with the render on a thread, "the next pass" stopped being a fact — so
it calls `Covers::settle` before asserting now; **D820** has the mechanism and why six clean runs
were not evidence. `an_empty_document_has_no_cover` was strengthened from
`is_none()` to `Some(NoCover::Blank)` — **it could not have told the two failures apart**, which is
exactly why an empty document used to get the same answer as a corrupt one. All flips run and bite
at their predicted sites; dropping `covers.unreadable` from `mark_of` fails at 0 marks against 1,
which is the half the scan flag cannot see.

⚠️ **Left undone deliberately**: the finding also asks for a disabled or warning-styled *Open* row.
That is a behaviour decision rather than a drawing one, the mark plus the existing status line
already say it, and refusing to open a file the user may want to inspect or repair is not obviously
right. **The maintainer's call**, and it was taken on 2026-09-19 — **neither**, D818.

**D818 — An `UNREADABLE` card keeps its *Open*, and the reason is which file actually arrives.
*Ruled by the maintainer 2026-09-19; Resolved — a decided non-goal, and no production line
changed.***

D613 built the mark and closed by handing this over: whether *Open* should be **disabled** or
**warning-styled** on such a card. The answer is neither, on two grounds.

**The mark and the status line already say the file will not load**, so a refusal at the click is a
third statement of one fact — and the one statement that also takes something away. D613's own
colour argument is the same shape from the other end: red was chosen there *because* the thing being
warned about is the click, which only works if the click remains the user's to make.

🚨 **And the case that actually reaches a synced library is a document written by a *newer build*** —
D613 established that as the gap the scan flag could not see: one number changed, structurally
perfect, refused by `migrate`'s version guard. Such a file is not corrupt; it is **ahead of this
build**. Refusing to open a document the user may want to inspect, or may be about to update the app
for, is the wrong way round. The mark warns, and the click stays theirs.

**Record-only, so the citation is planted by hand** on `panels::dashboard::Mark::Unreadable` — the
variant a reader meets the question at, and the one place the decision would otherwise be invisible
to the census. *Nothing in the code changed, which is the whole of the ruling.*

§9.5 amended; `roadmap.md`'s *"`scan::Entry::unread` has no production consumer"* entry is struck,
its two answers having been "a mark on the card" and "remove the field" and the first one having
landed.

**D612 — "No clip" is the render target's own box, not ±1e7 in the node's local units.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — one lifted `layer_shape`, both GPU sites through it.***

vello needs a shape for every layer, so `GpuScenePainter::push_layer` substituted
`Rect::new(-1e7, -1e7, 1e7, 1e7)` when `clip` was `None` — and drew it under `self.base * transform`,
i.e. **±1e7 in that node's own local space**. Any ancestor scale below 1 shrank it in world terms:
at `Affine::scale(0.001)` an "unbounded" layer covered ±1e4 world units and cut away everything past
it. Measured in release — a group at `scale(0.001)` with `opacity: 0.5` holding one 100×100-unit
rect at world (20000, 100), viewport over world (19000, 0)–(21000, 2000) at 400×400 — **CPU 400
green pixels, GPU 0**. The layer was in the export and absent from the canvas. `[S11.2-L1-04]`.

**Invariant 11 broken *below* the shared walk, which is why nothing caught it.**
`CpuPainter::push_layer` passes `clip` straight through, so `None` reaches `vello_cpu` as no clip at
all; this backend substituted, and a substitute is a decision the document→scene walk never sees.
`gpu.rs`'s own module header — *"the CPU pixel tests validate that logic"* — is true of the walk and
cannot be true of this.

⚠️ **And the two GPU sites did not agree with each other.** `push_mask_layer` used the same ±1e7
under `self.base` alone — ±1e7 in **world** units, a different and much wider bound — so "unbounded"
meant two things one function apart, and only one of them was wrong in the direction that loses ink.

**The answer is the target's own pixel box under the identity.** A lifted free function
`gpu::layer_shape(limit, base, transform, clip) -> (Affine, Cow<BezPath>)`: with a clip,
`(base * transform, borrowed)`; without, `(Affine::IDENTITY, limit inflated by one pixel)`. The
target's pixel box is what "no clip" *means* for a render target, it is the one shape no transform
can shrink, and `limit` already follows the stack, so a nested effect buffer gets its own. The
inflation keeps the clip's antialiased edge off the target's outermost row. Both GPU sites go
through it.

⚠️ **Not `(base * transform).inverse() * limit`**, which the finding sketched first: a degenerate
`transform` — a zero scale, which this document model permits — makes that inversion non-finite, and
a non-finite clip path is **G1**'s shape. The identity has no inverse to take.

`gpu::tests::an_unclipped_layer_covers_the_target_under_any_transform`. **Asserted on the decision
rather than on pixels, and that is the point**: the divergence lives below the shared walk where the
CPU pixel tests cannot reach it, and `tests/gpu_effects.rs`'s comparison harness needs a device this
machine does not have. §15 D269's move applied here — the choice is lifted out of `push_layer` so a
test can ask it directly, and what it asks is the invariant itself, that the substitute does not
depend on the node's transform. The scales are the ones that break it rather than a sample: `0.001`
is the measured failure, `1000.0` the mirror, `0.0` the degenerate case the *other* candidate fix
dies on. A real clip is the control, or the fix would be "stop clipping", which is a different bug.

⚠️ **Flip-check, run**: restoring `(base * transform, ±1e7)` fails at the `0.001` case — the
predicted site — and the message is starker than the written prediction. The substitute lands at
`x0: -23000 … x1: -15000`, so it does not fall short of the 800-wide target, it **misses it
entirely**. The prediction said "a device-space width of 20000", which was arithmetic done in the
head that dropped `base`'s translation term; `base` translates as well as scales, and that is
exactly the term a reasoned prediction loses.

§4 invariant 11 and §6.2 amended.

**D611 — A layer's name reaches the SVG file, and comes back.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `data-name`, written at three sites and read at six.***

`ondin_export::svg` never called `Node::name()`. No artwork element carried an `id`, or anything else
derived from one; the only ids in the file are the `grad-`, `img-`, `clip-`, `mask-` and `fx-` ones the
writer synthesises from `NodeId::to_wire` for defs. Meanwhile `svg_in` reads an element's `id` **as**
the layer's name, at six sites. So the pair was asymmetric in the one direction that loses data: a
document with named layers exported and re-imported came back with **every layer unnamed**, and nothing
said so — `svg_roundtrip.rs`, which its own module doc calls *"the only thing that binds"* the two,
asserts geometry, paint and structure and never a name. `[S8.1-L6-04]`.

**Not a recorded non-goal, which is why this is a defect rather than a trade.** §7 discusses ids for
defs only, §5.7b governs name *generation* inside the document, and there was no §15 entry and no
roadmap line. `naming.rs` exists to produce those names and the `.ondin` format keeps them; handing
another tool a structure with no labels on it is most of what "editable elsewhere" means.

**The decision is the attribute, and it is `data-name` rather than `id`.** An `id` must be an XML
`Name` and unique in the document. `"Rectangle 1"` — which is exactly what `naming::created_name`
produces — is neither, so writing names as ids means sanitising and uniquifying them: ordinary names
mangled on the way out and read back mangled, and §5.7b's *"uniqueness is never load-bearing"* turned
into a promise this writer would have to keep. Worse, it puts free user text into the same namespace as
the synthesised ids above — a layer someone happens to name `clip-601d_2` would shadow a real
`<clipPath>` and silently redirect its own frame's `url(#…)`. `data-*` is valid markup every viewer
ignores, it is what Figma writes for exactly this, and it round-trips the name **byte for byte**.

**The reader prefers `data-name` and still falls back to `id`, and the fallback is not a compatibility
shim.** `id` is where Illustrator and Inkscape put a layer's identity; reading it was right before this
and is still right. What changed is only which one wins when a file carries both, and a file this writer
produced always will.

`svg::name_attr(node)` is empty for an unnamed node — the discipline every other attribute here keeps —
and is called at the three places this writer opens a node's *own* element: the leaf `t` in
`emit_shape`, the container `<g>` in `emit_node`, and `emit_stacked`'s `<g>`, whose children are that
node's own paints and must therefore not carry it. ⚠️ **In the split-clip case it goes on the *outer*
group**: the inner one exists only to hold the clip apart from the transform, and a reader taking the
name off it would report a container the document does not have. On the reading side
`svg_in::element_name(el)` is one function replacing six copies of
`el.attribute("id").map(str::to_string)` — a copy that forgot the new attribute would silently be the
old behaviour in exactly one element kind, and nothing downstream could tell.

`svg_roundtrip::a_layers_name_survives_the_round_trip`. Four names chosen for what they do to markup: a
group and a leaf, because those are two different writers; a name with a **space**, which is not a valid
XML `Name`; and one holding `&`, `<` and a quote, which is the escaping and the only case that can make
the file unparseable. The two-fill rect is what reaches `emit_stacked`'s arm.

🚨 **The first flip did not bite, and that is a finding about the test rather than about the code.**
`name_attr` writing ` id="…"` instead of ` data-name="…"` — the other candidate fix, and the one the
review sketched first — **round-trips all three names perfectly**, because `roxmltree` hands back an
attribute value verbatim and never asks whether an `id` is a valid `Name`. The round trip cannot tell
the two spellings apart, so a test that only round-tripped would have blessed the wrong answer. A second
assertion says every `id` the writer emits is an XML `Name`, and *that* one bites the flip, at the group
with `id="Outer group"`. **The written-up flip and its predicted site were both wrong before it was
run.**

**The golden moved and was read**, per `goldens.rs`'s own instruction: `every-kind.svg`, 2733 → 2954
bytes, thirty lines unchanged, exactly one `data-name` added per artwork element and none on the
artboard's own background `<rect>`, which is a fill rather than a node.

⚠️ **Three assertions in `ondin-export/tests/svg.rs` had to change and the change is not cosmetic.**
`a_frames_border_is_written_outside_the_group_that_clips_it`,
`a_frame_without_a_border_is_still_one_group` and `unequal_corners_are_exported_as_a_path_not_a_rounded_rect`
matched exact strings that assumed `transform` was the element's **first** attribute. Their claims were
never about attribute order — they are about which element carries the transform and whether it also
carries the clip — and they are spelled that way now. A test that pins the order of attributes it does
not care about is a test that breaks on the next one added.

§5.7b and §7 amended.

**D610 — Room for a truncation ellipsis is made by moving the line, not by moving the ellipsis.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — the last line shifts left by the overlap.***

`text::ellipsis_run` placed itself at `x.min(w - advance)`, where `x` is the last visible line's right
edge. Under `TextAlign::Center` and `TextAlign::End` that edge reaches the box edge **by
construction**, so the `min` always bit and pushed the `…` back over the last characters by its own
advance. Measured in release on one 10pt node, `AutoHeight(120.0)`, `max_lines = 1`: body glyphs at or
past the ellipsis origin were **0** for `Start`, **1** for `Center`, **2** for `End` — ellipsis origin
110.1 / 111.4 / 111.4 against body last-glyph origins 107.3 / 113.7 / 120.0. `[S5.2-L1-01]`.

**The clamp's own comment stated its aim and the aim was the wrong quantity.** *"Past the wrap width it
would be the one glyph hanging out of a node that was truncated precisely to fit"* is a claim about the
**box**; what fails is the relationship to the **ink**. T2's *a bound that bounds the wrong quantity*,
from the drawing side.

`extract` now records where the last line's ink starts in `runs` and in `decorations` and how far left
it reaches, then shifts that whole line left by the overlap `(x + advance - w)`, clamped so it never
crosses the line's own left edge — a box narrower than the ellipsis would otherwise drag the ink out of
the node entirely, and one glyph clipped at the right is the better failure. `ellipsis_run` no longer
takes the wrap width and no longer decides where it goes; it is handed `at`. A new
`const ELLIPSIS: &str = "…"` is shared between them, because `extract` asks `marker_advance` how much
room to make and `ellipsis_run` shapes what goes in it: **two spellings of one glyph is a gap that opens
silently.**

**Shifting rather than dropping trailing clusters**, which was the finding's own preferred sketch and is
CSS's actual rule. Two reasons. It changes **no visible string**, so no document already using
`BlockStyle::overflow == Ellipsis` loses a character. And it is a uniform translation, which is the only
thing that is right for a **bidi** line, where "the trailing clusters" are at the *left* and a naive
`x >= limit` drop would eat the beginning of the text — `TextDirection::Rtl` is a supported value here.
It is also what a browser does with `text-align: right; text-overflow: ellipsis`: the ellipsis lands
where the line used to end and the text is pushed off the edge it was flush against.

⚠️ **Two things are still open rather than fixed, and both are said in the code.** The ellipsis is placed
at the line's *right* edge for every direction, and an RTL line's logical end is at its **left** — a
second defect at the same call site, pre-existing, and `parley_alignment` is where the direction is
known. And the decoration bands' `gaps` need no shifting **only because this sits above `skip_ink`**,
which has not populated them yet; move the block below it and the gaps are stale by exactly the shift.

`text::tests::an_ellipsis_never_sits_over_the_text_it_ends`, all three alignments in one loop with
`Start` as the passing control — its line ends short of the box, so nothing moves, which is what stops
the test reading as "ellipses are fine now". Two assertions: no body glyph at or past the ellipsis
origin, **and** the ellipsis ends inside the box. The second is what stops the fix being "let it hang",
since dropping the clamp entirely also passes the overlap test. **Both flips run and bite**: the old
clamp fails at `Center` with *"1 of the line's glyphs are at or past the ellipsis at 111.357"*, matching
the finding's measurement; no clamp at all fails the box assertion at `Center`, the ellipsis ending at
125.1 against a 120 box. ⚠️ **The predicted failing site was `End`**, on the reasoning that it overlaps
by the most — the loop reaches `Center` first and both are wrong by the same rule, so the fixture order
decided it and not the size of the defect.

⚠️ **The region had no assertion about placement in either direction before this.** The review replaced
the whole clamp with `let at = x;` and the entire workspace stayed green:
`ellipsis_adds_a_glyph_where_clip_does_not` counts glyphs and reads no position,
`an_ellipsis_is_set_in_the_type_it_follows` reads the size. Both of this finding's siblings are closed —
**D490**, the ellipsis taking its type from text that is not on screen, and **D506**, the export walk
emitting no ellipsis at all — and this was the last part of the region still wrong.

§5.4 amended, where the clamp was described as deliberate-for-now; `roadmap.md`'s entry is struck.

**D609 — An inspector field engaged over a live text session composes with it instead of replacing it.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — two previews, spelled as two fields.***

`EditorSession::set_preview` built `RenderOverrides` from the field's transaction alone and set
`preview_holds_session = false`. A live text session's preview is installed by `set_session_preview`,
which is the same call plus that flag. One override set, one flag, and whichever call came last owned
both. So clicking the Transform card's **X** during a live text session took the typed text off the
canvas — from the probe: double-click a text layer, type ` world!!`, click **X** without ending the
session, and the typed text vanishes while the committed text comes back. **And it did not come back**,
because `OndinApp::preview_session` is event-driven — a keystroke, a cut, a paste, four restyles — never
per frame, and the valve's release path cleared rather than restored. `[S16.4-L1-03]`.

⚠️ **Worse than a drawing bug, because the panels read the same overrides.** `display_node` is what every
panel reports through, so for as long as the text was off the canvas the typography panel was describing
the **committed** string: two readings of one edit, from two sources, which is the exact phrasing D109's
original report used.

**This is D109 arriving a third time, at the one site its two fixes did not reach.**
`clear_gesture_preview`'s doc records both, and both are on the **clear** side — the commit's and the
cancel's. Nothing had ever been done on the **set** side, and what kept it hidden is that the bug needs a
*gesture over a session*, which only an inspector control can produce.

`preview_holds_session: bool` is now `session_preview: Option<Transaction>` beside a separate
`preview_holds_gesture: bool`. `set_preview` composes: the session's operations first, then the field's,
because `RenderOverrides::absorb` is last-one-wins per field — so a field editing the session's own node
wins the transform and leaves the text alone, which is the case the finding was measured on. `Some` is
also the answer to "does a session hold this preview", which is what the flag it replaces meant; two
spellings of one fact is how they come to disagree.

**`clear_gesture_preview` stopped being "leave it where it is" and became "put it back", and that half is
not optional.** Once the override set holds both, doing nothing leaves the released field's patch standing
for the rest of the session. It rebuilds from `session_preview` alone — **without** the already-shaped
layout `set_session_preview` is normally handed, which is correct and merely slower (**D592**) and is paid
once per gesture rather than once per keystroke. `clear_preview`, the "drop everything" spelling
`finish_text_edit`, `adopt_document`, `fonts_changed` and the end of a canvas drag use, drops
`session_preview` too.

🚨 **`has_gesture_preview` reads `preview_holds_gesture` and not `!preview_holds_session`, and this is the
half worth stating.** A scrub engaged over a live session is *both* things at once, and the old spelling
answered `false` for it — so a right-click cancelling that scrub fell through to `ctx.dragged_id()`, the
blinking witness `cancel_gesture`'s own comment says must never stand alone (**D168**, **D588**). One
`bool` could not tell "a session with a scrub over it" from "a session alone"; **all four combinations are
reachable**, which is why the repair is two fields and not a third value on one.

**Spelled once, at `set_preview`, rather than guarded at the caller** — which is what D109 itself asks for,
*"add no third spelling"*. A canvas gesture cannot reach it during a live session, `Mode::TextInsert`
owning the pointer, so the callers that can compose are the inspector's: `edit_valve`, `multi_valve`,
`char_valve`, and the press-only `preview_slot`.

`canvas::headless_app_tests::a_valved_edit_engaged_over_a_live_text_session_previews_over_it_not_instead_of_it`.
**Three flips run, all bite**: un-composing `set_preview` fails the first assertion at
`left: Some(1.0)  right: Some(0.5)` — the predicted site, for once; making `clear_gesture_preview` a no-op
over a session fails the third at `left: Some(120.0)  right: Some(0.0)`; and restoring the old
`has_gesture_preview` spelling fails the gesture-witness assertion. ⚠️ **The third assertion's first draft
was wrong and the run said so**: the field was released on the *committing* arm, where a
`preview_local_transform` of 120 is the **document** rather than a leftover override, so it would have read
