green for a preview that never went away. `Escape` is the arm that discriminates, and the test says so.

*Also amended:* `EditorSession::fonts_changed`'s doc said *"rebuilding the overrides would need the pending
transaction, which the session does not keep"*, which is half-false now — it keeps a session's, so the
clear there is a deliberate choice rather than a forced one. `panels/typography.rs`'s comment naming
`preview_holds_session` names `session_preview`. §9.3 and §9.4 amended.

**D608 — The static-family arm's decisions are lifted where a test can reach them.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `ordered_cuts`, and two tests that need no font at all.***

`text::family_variants` builds the variant dropdown's list from two sources — a variable family's
`fvar` named instances, a static one's faces — and returns early whenever the first is non-empty. The
other arm is the one serving nearly every **static** system font: Arial, Georgia, Helvetica, most of
what a Windows or macOS font folder holds. It **had zero test callers anywhere in the workspace**, and
so did `face_name`, whose only caller it is. `[S5.1-L6-05]`, group **G9**.

**Nothing in the tree can reach it, and that is a fact about the fixtures rather than about the
code.** `Engine::new` builds its fontique collection with `system_fonts: false`, deliberately and with
the reason on it, so the only faces core ever holds are the ones something registers — and both
bundled files, `Inter-Variable.ttf` and `Inter-Italic-Variable.ttf`, are variable. So
`inters_variant_list_offers_both_slopes`, the one test `family_variants` had, exercises the
named-instance arm and only it; and the workspace's one other test that registers a face with core is
`#[ignore]`d, needs the network, and downloads Roboto, which its own assertion pins as variable
(*"Roboto is variable on wght+wdth"*). Both doors into the static arm are production doors:
`FontService` registers system faces and downloaded ones, and §5.4a's *"a family whose file the decoder
cannot read falls back to the static cuts automatically"* lands there too.

Three decisions with no teeth, then. `out.sort_by_key(|v| (v.italic, v.weight))` — uprights before
italics, ascending weight within each, which is the order the dropdown draws. `out.dedup_by(…)` — a
family registering the same cut twice must not offer it twice. And `face_name`'s nine weight buckets
with their `("Regular", true) => "Italic"` exception, a wrong answer in which is a wrong *word* under
the user's pointer rather than a gap.

**The fix is D269's move rather than a fixture.** The finding's own sketch was to strip the `fvar`
table from the bundled Inter at test time, or to add a static OFL face to `assets/`; both buy the
whole arm and both cost an asset or a build step. `ordered_cuts` — a free
`fn(&mut Vec<FontVariant>)` lifted out of the `ENGINE.with` closure — buys the two decisions for
nothing, and `face_name` was already free and is now called directly. **No font fixture, no new
asset.**

⚠️ **What that does not buy is stated on `ordered_cuts` rather than glossed**: the parley query above
it — `collection.family_id`, `collection.family(id)`, and the `f.weight()` / `f.style()` reads that
build the list — still has no caller but production, and reaching it needs a registered static face
the tree has not got. **The decisions are tested; the plumbing is on trust.** Asserting a decision
that was previously unreachable is worth more than leaving the whole arm dark, and saying the *arm*
is covered would be the thing this finding is about. ⚠️ **The repository does hold one static face and
it is not the answer**: `ondin-app`'s `Phosphor.ttf` has no `fvar`, but it is an icon font installed
into *egui*, in the wrong crate for a core test, and a single-face family exercises neither the sort
nor the dedup — it would reach the query and nothing else.

`face_name_names_every_weight_bucket_at_its_own_boundary` samples `1/149`, `150/249`, `250/349` and so
on to `850/1000` — **the ends of every bucket, never the middles**, because a range is only ever wrong
at its ends and a test walking `100, 200, 300…` passes against an off-by-one in the table. The
`("Regular", true)` case is asserted beside `Bold Italic` and `Extra Light Italic`, being the one
entry that is not the pattern and the one a rewrite would flatten.

🚨 **The first fixture for the sort could not see the sort, and the flip is what said so.** With only
a 400-upright and a 700 in either slope, `(italic, weight)` and `(weight, italic)` order the same
list, so reversing the tuple left the test **green** — a fixture that could not tell the shipped rule
from the wrong one. A **light italic** is what makes the two keys disagree: it must sort *before* an
upright on weight and *after* it on slope. With one in the fixture both flips bite at the single order
assertion — the reversed tuple gives `[(400, false), (400, true), (700, false)]`, the italic
interleaved between the two uprights, and the `dedup_by` disabled gives
`[(400, false), (700, false), (700, false), (400, true)]`, the doubled cut offered twice. That
sentence is in the fixture's own comment, where the next person to shorten the vector will read it.

Neither document changed: nothing in architecture states the variant list's order, and §5.4's rule on
which face each question asks — the list from every face, the axes and features from the default one —
is **D149**'s and is still exact.

**D607 — One agreement rule, and the readouts that ship get tests.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — two constants in core, one deletion, and four tests on the
copies the panel calls.***

A production call-site census over all of `crates/`, which is what `[S3.2-L6-03]` is about:

| function | production callers | test callers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build::shared_over_fills` | 0 | 5, in `tests/bulk.rs` |
| `build::shared_over_strokes` | 0 | 2 |
| `build::shared_corner_radius` | 0 | 3 |
| `build::shared_opacity` | **0** | **0** |

What ships is `inspector::shown_over_fills`, `shown_over_strokes`, `shared_opacity_shown` and
`shared_radius_shown`, and **none of those four had a test caller either**. So the tested copy was
not the shipped copy, in both directions at once.

🚨 **Two of the four twins asked a different question, which is what turns a duplication into a
defect.** Core compared a radius and an opacity with `==`; the panel used `< 1e-9` and `< 1e-6`. So
`bulk.rs`'s `corner_radius_is_shared_only_when_every_rect_agrees_evenly` pinned a rule **no user
could reach**, and the rule that actually decides whether the field says *Mixed* was asserted
nowhere at all.

The tolerances are `build::OPACITY_AGREEMENT` and `build::RADIUS_AGREEMENT` now, in core beside the
argument for each: opacity is the coarser because the field formats as `{v:.0}%`, so anything this
side of a part in a million is the same number on screen and reporting *Mixed* for it would be the
readout disagreeing with itself; a radius is tighter because it is a length in document units rather
than a normalized fraction, and a billionth of a unit is below what any drag or parser can author.
**Core's copy was brought onto the shipped rule and not the other way round.**
`build::shared_opacity` is **deleted** rather than left standing as a second answer, and the `lib.rs`
re-export goes with it.

⚠️ **The twins cannot be collapsed into core's and are not meant to be.** They read `display_node`,
which is the rule §9.4 states: the app asks `build`'s question of the *previewed* tree, so a scrub
reads back its own drag rather than the last commit. **That is a difference in the tree, and it was
never meant to be a difference in the question.** A future reader tempted to delete one side of the
pair should delete the *core* side, as this entry did for opacity, and only where the panel is the
sole caller.

`inspector::shipped_shared_readout_tests` has four, each with its own control:

- two radii a billionth apart are one radius; two a thousandth apart are *Mixed*;
- the same for opacity at its own coarser tolerance;
- a layer with **no fill at all** disagrees with every colour — `Spread::bare`, the rule
  `shared_over_fills`' doc argues for at length and which no test had ever asked of the shipped copy;
- the stroke twin of that rule, where the sentence it was written for is easiest to see.

Flips, all run. `RADIUS_AGREEMENT` at `0.0` — the exact `==` core carried until this entry — fails
the first radius assertion, `None` against `Some(6.0)`; raised to `1e-2` it fails the **control**
instead, which is the pair that says the tolerance is bounded on both sides. The same both ways for
opacity. ⚠️ **Deleting `spread.bare |= fills.is_empty()` fails the third fill assertion while the
first two stay green**, which is why the bare case is asserted separately rather than trusted to
fall out of the agreement walk.

⚠️ **A deletion leaves names behind in prose, and two survived this one.** §13's `vm.md` summary said
a property read across a disagreeing selection *"reuses core's existing `PaintShown::Mixed` /
`shared_opacity` answer"*; it names `shared_corner_radius` now. **`vm.md` itself still names
`shared_opacity` twice** (its property table and its multi-select semantics) and is left alone — it
describes a language nothing has built, and it is not one of the three documents this file is
maintained beside. *Fix with* the same substitution when that file is next opened.

**D606 — The ⋮ file menu's four rules, driven through the painted rows.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `menu_row_centre`, and two tests that click the menu.***

`file_menu_popup` had **zero test callers**, and the string `file_menu_popup` did not occur once in
`dashboard.rs`'s 2,300-line test module — this of a pair whose doc, the one on `file_menu_button`,
calls it *"the one place every per-document action lives"*.
Three simultaneous flips left **975/975 green**. The worst is `Act::Trash(path) if !trashed`
inverted to `if trashed`: *Delete* outside the trash then falls through to
`other => *act = Some(other)` and `trash_or_purge` trashes the document **with no confirmation card
at all** — a destructive verb losing its only guard, silently, `[S20.2-L6-04]`.

⚠️ **The suite reached this file the whole time and simply never entered the function.** The
finding's control — `can_open` reduced to `true` — failed
`nothing_opens_a_document_out_of_the_trash` at the assertion that test's own doc predicts. The
harness had teeth; the door was the gap, which is the distinction worth carrying out of G19.

The door turns out to be drivable in six lines on helpers that were already in the module:
`menu_row_centre` finds the row's painted label through `galleys` and `click_at` takes its centre.
It matches **exactly** rather than by `contains`, because *Delete* and *Delete permanently* are rows
of two different menus and one is a prefix of the other. Four rules are asserted now: *Delete*
raises the confirmation card **and** nothing is trashed on the way — two assertions, because a
version that did both would pass the first alone; the *Star*/*Unstar* label follows `is_starred`;
*Move to project* opens the sheet rather than becoming an act; and a trashed document gets two rows,
neither of them *Open*.

🚨 **The first draft could not see one of the three flips, and the flip is what said so.** Deleting
the `("Open", …)` row from the non-trash arm left both new tests **green** — *"the trash menu must
not offer Open"* is satisfied for free by a build that offers it nowhere. **An absence is only
evidence beside the presence it is an absence of.** The ordinary menu's rows are asserted present
first now, and that block is the whole reason the eight absences below it mean anything. It
generalises past this test: every one of this project's *"X is not offered here"* assertions wants
the same companion.

⚠️ **Both predicted flip sites were wrong.** The *Open* flip fails at the new control rather than at
the trash list. Inverting `if starred` fails at the `menu_row_centre("Star")` **lookup** — an
unstarred document paints *Unstar*, so the row the test reaches for is not on screen and it dies at
the fixture step, twenty lines above the *Unstar* assertion it was predicted to fail. The panic
prints the whole frame's text, which is what makes that read as a finding rather than as a helper
falling over.

**D605 — The library's import sentence is asserted on the screen, not on the field.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — the assertion moved onto `galleys`.***

G19's shape: a test named after a rule, green while the rule was false.
`a_dropped_document_is_imported_and_a_dropped_image_is_not` asserted `app.session.status().text` —
a `String` whose only production reader is the editor's top bar, which sits **below**
`OndinApp::ui`'s `View::Dashboard` return (**D426**). So the test was named for a sentence the user
is told and asserted a value nobody could see. **No flip demonstrated that at the time, because the
plausible wrong version was what shipped**: the message really was being written, into a slot with
no reader on that screen.

`[S20.1-L6-04]` named two sites. The other,
`a_missing_library_folder_says_so_instead_of_reading_as_empty`, was converted when `[S20.1-L1-01]`
was closed — there being a status line on that screen to assert on only since **D426** — so this is
the second and last. The mixed-drop assertion reads
`galleys(&mut app, &ctx)` now and looks for *"Imported 1"* and *"1 other file(s)"* in one painted
run.

Flip-check, run now that there is something to flip: deleting the `status_label` call from the
dashboard's top bar fails it, and the failure prints the whole frame's text — thirty-odd runs of
chrome with no sentence among them. ⚠️ **The field assertion it replaces stays green under that
flip.** That is the finding in one line, and it is the only demonstration available: nothing about
the field is wrong, and everything about asserting on it is.

⚠️ **One field assertion survives in the same test** — the single-image refusal,
`status().text.contains(".ondin")`, a few lines above — and it is the same class for the same
reason. It is narrow and it is real. *Fix with* the same `galleys` read, which is four lines.

**D604 — A railed resize solves against the type the transaction will leave, not the type it found.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `kind_to_solve_against`, at both rail doors.***

`railed_resize` converges the rail's scale against `railed_box`, which lays the text out — the real
box, through the same layout the canvas draws, because on a rail the type keeps its size and
re-flows and every cheaper model of that box is wrong. `scale_scalars` then writes `font_size * s`.
So the solve converged on `layout(new rail, old font)` while the document ended up with
`layout(new rail, new font)` — **the second argument, and only the second argument**.

Measured before the fix, both tools, the same `BottomRight` drag on the same fixture:

```text
Select : asked 317.173 x 61.494 at (-6.708, -20.773)
         got   318.427 x 58.324 at (-6.708, -20.773)   <-- anchor exact
Scale  : asked 317.173 x 61.494 at (-6.708, -20.773)
         got   330.690 x 77.524 at (-16.289, -35.773)  <-- anchor moved (9.58, 15.00)
         font 16.00 -> 32.00
```

⚠️ **The Select run is the control and it is what localises the fault.** The solve lands the anchor
to the bit whenever nothing else touches the type, so this was never `railed_resize` being
imprecise — it was the **composition of two correct steps in the wrong order**, which is the kind of
defect that survives a suite testing each step. `railed_resize`'s own doc names the symptom as the
thing that *"could not stand"*: *"a corner drag is a promise about the **opposite** corner, and a
layer that slides out from under the pointer reads as a broken gesture"*. `[S13.2-L1-03]`.

`scaled_text_scopes` is split out of `scale_scalars` — the four text scopes as a photographic scale
of `s` leaves them — and `kind_to_solve_against` sits above it, answering *which kind should this
solve measure against*. Both rail arms are rewired, `resize_to_handle`'s and `scale_geometry`'s.
⚠️ **Only the kind the solve *measures* moves**: `drawn` stays the **unscaled** box, being where the
node is now, and `want` is the target derived from it. A reader who moved `drawn` too would be
scaling the box twice.

⚠️ **`kind_to_solve_against` clones the kind and mutates the four text scopes rather than rebuilding
it field by field, deliberately.** `NodeKind::Text` has eight fields and gained two of them —
`on_path_flip` and `on_path_offset` — since the code around it was written, so a ninth travels
through here on its own instead of being an omission the next person silently copies past. That is
the line to leave alone.

⚠️ **`Scaling::Photographic` and `on_path` had never met in any test.** Grepped at the time: nine
`Photographic` sites, none railed; three rail sites, none photographic. The two features are three
years of gestures apart and the suite had no fixture holding both — which is the general shape of
this finding rather than an aside, since the defect is in the composition and nothing composed them.

`tools::tests::the_scale_tool_on_a_rail_holds_the_corner_the_select_tool_holds`, with the anchor
asserted tightly and the extent loosely: a ribbon's box is affine rather than linear in the scale,
so the far corner is a target where the near one is a promise. Flip, run: `kind_to_solve_against`
returning `None` unconditionally — the solve back on the unscaled kind — fails at the **anchor**
assertion, `x0: -16.2887…, y0: -35.7732…` against `-6.7082…, -20.7734…`. **That is the finding's
`(9.58, 15.00)` to the decimal, three sessions after it was measured**, which is worth more than the
assertion passing: the fixture reproduces the report.

**D789 — A railed resize holds the corner the gesture held, not the box's origin. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-15; Resolved — `railed_resize` takes the `Handle`.***

Reported from use and in no review finding: *"I held the bottom-left corner handle and the box
started shifting to the right."* Text on a sharp-cornered rectangle rail, dragged smaller.

`tools::railed_resize` ended with `Affine::translate(want.origin() - got.origin()) * out`, which pins
the box's **top-left**, under a comment reading *"the anchor, exactly: whatever the extent came out
as, the corner the gesture held is where it said it would be."* **That sentence is true of one
handle.** `Handle::BottomRight` holds the top-left, so for it the origin *is* the anchor; the other
three hold a corner the origin is not. Pinning the origin fixes `x0`, and `x1 = x0 + got.width()`
then carries the solve's **extent residual** — which this function leaves on purpose and says so two
paragraphs above the line: *"The placement comes out exact and the extent comes out close … the
anchor is a promise and the far corner is a target."* **The promise was being kept about the wrong
corner.**

Measured on the reporter's own document — 24pt Inter on a 341 × 172 rectangle rail, cap-to-baseline
trim — dragging `BottomLeft`, whose held corner is the top-right:

```text
shrink   got width   held-corner drift
  55%      207.29         +0.41
  25%       96.65         +2.61
  10%       47.99        +10.37
```

At 10% the wanted width was 37.61 and the residual +10.38 against a drift of +10.37 — **the same
number**. ⚠️ **`y0`, the coordinate the origin genuinely does pin, held at +0.00 throughout**, which
is the control that makes this the diagnosis rather than a plausible story: the axis the old line was
right about did not move.

The fix is the handle. `railed_resize` takes it and anchors through `Handle::anchored`, which already
answers the question — *"the local coordinate this handle holds still on each axis, or `None` for an
axis it does not touch"* — and which §5.6 already cites for the *other* thing a handle decides about
a text box, whether the drag authors the height. ⚠️ **It is asked of *both* boxes, and that is the
whole of the fix**: the held edge is `origin + width` on one side and `origin + 0` on the other, so
`want`'s offset and `got`'s differ by exactly the residual being corrected for. **Asking it once and
reusing the answer looks like the same thing and reintroduces the bug in a subtler spelling.**

🚨 **Why it went unseen is the part worth carrying, and it is not subtlety.** Every resize test in
`tools/mod.rs` drags `Handle::BottomRight` (38 sites) or `Handle::TopLeft` (11); **`BottomLeft` and
`TopRight` appeared zero times.** And the drift exists only on a **railed** node, because only that
path solves and therefore only that path leaves a residual — ordinary geometry resize is exact. So
the single railed test, `dragging_railed_text_scales_its_rail`, drags the one handle where the origin
*is* the anchor, and could not have shown this however carefully it was read. **A rule with one
implementation, one test, and that test on the arm where the rule holds.**

`tools::tests::every_handle_holds_its_own_corner_on_a_rail` runs all four corners.
⚠️ **It shrinks to 0.25× deliberately**: the residual scales with the distance from 1, so a 2× *grow*
— which is what the existing test does — hides what a shrink shows.
⚠️ **Flipped by restoring `want.origin() - got.origin()`, only `BottomLeft` fails**, at 2.844 units,
and `dragging_railed_text_scales_its_rail` stays green — which is the whole argument for a second
test rather than an assertion added to that one. `TopRight` and `TopLeft` pass under the flip on this
fixture, its gentle-S rail leaving their residual under the tolerance. **One handle out of four is
enough**, and the test's own doc says which one, because a test that fired only when every arm was
wrong would have been green for this bug.

⚠️ **`scale_geometry`'s call site passes `Handle::BottomRight` and the reason is written beside it**:
there is no handle at that door, and `want` is `drawn` scaled about `drawn.origin()`, which is
exactly the corner `BottomRight` holds. Naming it says what that site wants rather than borrowing a
default, and behaviour there is unchanged.

🚨 **This function has now broken the same promise twice, for two unrelated reasons, and both times
the covering test was on the handle that could not see it.** **D604** above fixed the Scale tool
sliding a rail's held corner by 9.58 × 15.00 units, by solving against the type the transaction would
*leave*; the test it added drags `BottomRight` too, and quotes the same *"a corner drag is a promise
about the **opposite** corner"* sentence this entry does. **Two causes, one symptom, one blind spot**
— so the thing to distrust here is the handle coverage rather than the arithmetic, and a third defect
at this anchor should be looked for at `TopRight` and `BottomLeft` first.

**D790 — A pronoun rebound when a passage grew above it, and §5.6 credited `railed_resize` with a
rule it has no line of. *Record fixed 2026-09-15; Resolved — the subject is named.***

§5.6's text-resize bullet ended: *"… and share `tools::railed_resize`. That function scales each axis
exactly when the *user* authors it: `Auto` has nothing at all, `AutoHeight` has only its wrap width,
`Fixed` has both."* That rule is `tools::scaled_text_sizing`'s, stated almost verbatim in its own
doc. **`railed_resize` contains no `TextSizing` of any kind** — it solves a rail scale factor against
`railed_box` with two correction passes and translates by `Handle::anchored`, which is all it does.

🚨 **And the sentence contradicted the paragraph immediately above it.** That paragraph is **D472**'s,
and its whole finding is that on a rail `TextSizing` is *inert* — the rail's length is the measure, so
for `Auto` `scaled_text_sizing` answers `None` and there was nothing left to write. So the design
document spent eight days crediting the rail function with the one rule the rail path does not have,
three lines under its own statement that the rail path does not have it.

**Nothing was written wrongly. The sentence was correct when it was written and no edit has touched
it since.** Before `700b51b` the passage read *"… hands text to `tools::scaled_text_sizing` ahead of
the generic path and returns. **That function** scales each axis exactly when …"*, and the pronoun
pointed at the function named eleven words earlier. `700b51b` — D472's documentation — inserted the
railed ⚠️ **between** the antecedent and the pronoun, and its own last clause ends on
`tools::railed_resize`. The diff changes not one character of the sentence it broke.

🚨 **This is `CLAUDE.md`'s *anchor above, never below* rule with its sign reversed, and the reversal
is the thing to carry.** That rule exists because a doc comment **precedes** its item, so an insertion
placed below one steals it. Prose binds the other way round: an antecedent **precedes** its pronoun,
so an insertion placed *above* — the safe direction, the one the rule tells you to take — is exactly
what orphans a reference below it. **The same edit, the opposite half harmed.** A reader who has
internalised the code rule has internalised the wrong reflex for the document, and the document is
where this project keeps the rules the code is checked against.

⚠️ **The two defects have now happened in the same pair of functions, in the two different media.**
`railed_box`, inserted above `railed_resize`, took its 26-line doc — the code half, recorded in a ⚠️
still sitting on that doc. This is the prose half, at the passage describing the same neighbourhood.
Insertion is the hazard; which end of the insertion gets hurt is decided by which way the medium
binds.

🚨 **A pronoun is a citation with no name in it, and that is why nothing here could have caught this.**
`cargo doc` resolves `[link]`s and exits 101 on one that dangles. The citation census resolves
`D<n>` and says which numbers are owed. A `§` reference at least names a neighbourhood a reader can
open and disagree with. **Nothing anywhere resolves *"That function"*** — not a gate, not a census,
not the length ranking, not the neighbour grep — and the failure is silent in both directions: the
sentence stays grammatical, and the reader who checks it lands on a real function and reads a real
rule that belongs to something else. **Name the subject in any sentence a later insertion could come
between.** A repeated noun is four words and cannot rebind.

⚠️ **The sweep was the phrase, not a list of places.** `grep -rn "scales each axis\|axis is scaled
exactly"` and a grep for the `AutoHeight` clause over `docs/`, `crates/` and the root markdown return
exactly two live sites — this passage and `scaled_text_sizing`'s own doc — plus the generated copies
under `target/doc`. No other statement of the rule exists and no other site misattributes it, which
is session 23's lesson applied before rather than after.

*(Record fixed 2026-09-15; Resolved. **No production line changed and nothing in the code was
wrong** — the code has always been what §5.6 was describing incorrectly. §5.6's bullet now opens the
sentence **"Off a rail, `tools::scaled_text_sizing` …"**, naming the function instead of pointing at
it, gains "on either arm" on the sentence about the layer still travelling with the box, and carries
a ⚠️ stating the misattribution and the pronoun rule. ⚠️ **"On either arm" was checked rather than
assumed**: in `scale_geometry` the railed arm returns after pushing its `TextPath` patch and the
generic text arm returns after `scaled_text_sizing`, and **neither pushes a transform** — that half
is the caller's at both doors, so the layer travels either way. ⚠️ **The bullet's later sentences —
`resizable_size` reporting `Size::ZERO`, the `max(1.0)` floor, the `Fixed(1×1)` collapse — are about
the *generic* path and resume after the ⚠️ by naming it**, which is the same repair as the headline
one: "the generic path" is a noun and survives whatever is inserted above it. The citation sits on
`scaled_text_sizing`'s doc, where a reader meets the question of who owns this rule — a record-only
entry acquires no `crates/` citation on its own and is invisible to the closing census until somebody
plants one by hand, which is **D741**'s fix for **D735**'s shape. Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`,
which carries no row on text resize or on the design document's prose)*

**D603 — A unit chosen at amount zero survives the file, and the finding's headline no longer
reproduces. *Tested 2026-09-09; Keep, with a ruling — the guard, and the readout left to the
maintainer.***

`[S6.2-L1-03]`: a text layer at the stock `Px(0.0)` letter spacing, one click on the `%` chip — an
ordinary first move for a designer who works in percent and sets the unit before the number.
Measured then: `Px(0.0) → Em(0.0)`, `undo_depth 0 → 1`, and `io::save` → `io::load` gave back
**`Px(0.0)`**. The click cost an undo step, changed no ink, and was silently discarded by the next
round trip.

🚨 **The save/load half no longer reproduces, and this session's contribution is the guard rather
than a fix.** **D537**'s repair — the core half of `[S6.1-L1-03]` — moved all seven optional lengths
from `skip_serializing_if = "Length::is_zero"`, which elides `Em(0.0)` and `Px(0.0)` alike, to
`Length::is_default_zero`, which elides only the `Px(0.0)` an absent key reads back as. **Nothing
asserted that end to end.** D537's own test serializes two of the seven *structs* and reads the JSON
text, which says the key was written and says nothing about what `io::load` hands back through a
whole document.

`ondin-core/tests/io.rs · a_unit_chosen_at_zero_is_not_thrown_away_by_the_next_save` covers all seven
together — `letter_spacing`, `word_spacing` and `baseline_shift` on `TextStyle`, `spacing`, `indent`,
`indent_start` and `indent_end` on `ParagraphStyle` — **because they were changed together and would
regress together**, one predicate named seven times. It carries a fixture assertion,
`assert_ne!(Em(0.0), Px(0.0))`, so the seven assertions below it are about a value that is genuinely
distinct rather than about two spellings of the same one. Flip, run: `letter_spacing` back to
`Length::is_zero` fails at that field, `Px(0.0)` against `Em(0.0)` — the key simply absent from the
file and `#[serde(default)]` supplying the `Px` zero.

⚠️ **What is left of the finding is a ruling, not work.** Over a *selection* the same click writes a
`LetterSpacing(Em(0.0))` span, which `Spans::normalize` will not elide against a `Px(0.0)` default —
`Length` derives structural `PartialEq` — so `shared_in` over the whole node answers `None` and the
panel reads **Mixed** for text whose letter spacing is zero everywhere. Whether `Em(0)` and `Px(0)`
should be *one* value is a design question with two defensible answers — the unit is deliberate state
the user set, and the two are the same ink — and the two halves pull opposite ways, since preserving
the unit **requires** keeping the span. **That ruling has been taken — see D799**, which puts the
comparison at the reader on the resolved value and stops at zero. Until then it sat on
`roadmap.md`'s *Now · Text* where D537 filed it; the bullet is struck.

**D799 — A letter spacing of zero everywhere no longer reads *Mixed*, and the comparison is at the
reader on the resolved value. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — `[S6.1-L1-03]`'s open half,
and `[S6.2-L1-03]` with it.***

**The maintainer's ruling**, and `Length::is_default_zero`'s doc **predicted it verbatim** — *"The
readout is a comparison on the resolved value and belongs at the reader; it is left open rather than
guessed at."* That last clause is spent; the sentence now says where the comparison landed. *A
prediction left in a doc comment is a cheap thing to write and an expensive thing to leave standing
once it comes true.*

**Where it landed**: `TypeSubject::shared` and `TypeSubject::para_shared` in `panels/typography.rs`,
each falling through to a new free helper `agreed_zero` when `Spans::shared_in` answers `None`.
**`Spans::normalize` and `shared_in` are untouched, and must be** — they compare structurally because
**D537** keeps `Em(0.0)` distinct from `Px(0.0)` precisely so that a user's choice of unit survives
at amount zero, and making the model compare them equal would fix the readout by throwing away the
thing D537's predicate exists to keep. The two halves pull opposite ways, which is why the answer is
at the reader and not in the model.

It covers **seven lengths, which is all of D537's**: letter spacing, word spacing and baseline shift
in the character scope, through the one shared field `length_char_field`; spacing, indent,
indent-start and indent-end in the paragraph scope.

🚨 **It stops at zero, and that is a decision inside the ruling rather than a partial
implementation.** The general resolved comparison — two lengths that resolve alike *at the current
font size* — was considered and refused: `Em(0.02)` and `Px(0.32)` are the same ink at 16pt and
different ink at 24, so a field would flip between a number and a dash as the user resized the text,
and the unit chip would have to name one of two units the document genuinely holds. **Zero is the
only amount at which the unit carries no information about the ink**, which is exactly why it was the
only amount that read wrong. **Widening this is a further decision and should be recorded as one, not
arrive as an oversight.**

⚠️ **`agreed_zero` hands back the *first* value, not the default**, because the unit chip reads its
suffix off whatever comes back: returning `Px(0.0)` for a document the user had set to `%` would flip
the chip under them, which is D537's own symptom arriving by a new road.

**Two tests, and three flips run between them.**

`a_zero_letter_spacing_in_two_units_is_not_mixed` opens on a fixture guard, `assert_ne!(Em(0.0),
Px(0.0))` — if `set` ever canonicalized on the way in, the spans would agree structurally, `shared_in`
would answer on its own, and every assertion below would pass **without `agreed_zero` existing**.
Flip 1, deleting the `or_else` arm: red on the `mixed` assertion, the predicted site. Flip 2,
returning a different one of the agreeing values (`.last()` for `.next()`): the `mixed` assertion
stays **green** and the second fails at `Px(0.0)` against `Em(0.0)`. **A test that only asked "is it
mixed" would have shipped D537's symptom by a new road**, which is why there are two assertions.

`two_different_letter_spacings_still_read_mixed` is the control. 🚨 **Flip 3 — dropping
`agreed_zero`'s `is_zero` test so that any two lengths count as agreed — proved the predicted site
wrong.** It is red on the *first* assertion, two non-zero amounts, and never reaches the second. The
prediction assumed a zero beside a number is the harder case for an over-broad predicate; it is not,
because such a predicate stops looking at amounts at all and fails on the first pair it meets. Both
assertions are kept: the first is what this flip catches, and the second is what would survive a
predicate checking *one* side for zero rather than all of them.

*(§5's D537 bullet gains the reader half — the passage that says the unit is *"unobservable in the
drawing and still observable in the panel"* is where a reader meets the question of what the panel
then does with it. `Length::is_default_zero`'s doc is amended in `crates/`, its open clause replaced
by a pointer. The *Now · Text* bullet and the `[S6.2-L1-03]` ⚠️ under it are **struck from
`roadmap.md`**, one decision having been holding the last of two findings.)*

**D602 — The hover and key rings cull to the viewport and skip what is switched off.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `outline_view`, and two rejects at the top of the recursion.***

`canvas::stroke_outlines` recursed into every child of a container with **no bounds test and no
visibility test at any level**, and read the committed `doc.get(id)` rather than `display_node`.
`hover_target` resolves a plain hover to the outermost group, so what that costs is the **resting
frame of an ordinary document** rather than a stress case: put the pointer on a group and every leaf
in it is resolved, built into a path, transformed and flattened, whether it is on screen or drawn at
all — up to twice a frame, from `draw_hover_outline` and from `draw_key_outline`, both gated only on
`hover_chrome_live`.

`[S12.4-L4-05]` is the cost, measured in release over 20 iterations with the cost isolated against a
bare `run_ui` at 0.0047 ms/f:

| leaves | hovered | the same group 1e6 units off screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.0398 ms/f | 0.0016 |
| 1000 | 1.4809 | 1.4763 |
| 16000 | **26.3337** | **25.9181** |

Linear in leaf count and **flat against the viewport**. The off-screen column is the control and it
is the half that says the cull was *absent* rather than coarse — a 26 ms frame for chrome that is
not on screen.

`[S12.4-L1-06]` is the other filter, and it is a wrong picture rather than a slow one: a group of two
100×100 rects with the second at `x=300` and `SetVisible { visible: false }` painted **2** path
shapes with a screen bbox of `[0,0]–[400,100]`, where the renderer draws only the first. Two
functions along in the same file, `shown_visible` gates the frame name tag and the layout grids for
exactly this reason — *"chrome hanging off a box nobody can see is chrome over nothing"*. Read
through `display_node`, so a layers-panel eye **preview** counts too, which the committed document
the walk reads does not see.

`stroke_outlines` takes a `view: KRect` now, from the new `outline_view`: the camera viewport
inflated by the ring's **own** stroke width. Padding by the whole width rather than half is
deliberate slack — a 3px ring is centred on the outline, so a node whose box ends at the edge of the
view still paints inside it, and the cost of over-drawing one node is a path build where the cost of
under-drawing it is a missing mark.

⚠️ **`bounds_cover_subtree` is `scene.rs`'s own predicate, copied rather than approximated**, and it
is the load-bearing detail. A group's bounds are the union of its children and a *clipping* frame's
are the limit of what its children may paint, so either may be rejected whole; **a frame with
clipping off is neither**, and its contents are free to sit outside it. Culling on such a frame's own
box would lose the ring on a child that is perfectly visible, which is the failure a reader
"simplifying" this to a plain bounds test would introduce.

⚠️ **The visibility reject covers the entry node and everything below it, and not the chain above
it** — the recursion returns before descending, so a hidden group takes its whole subtree with it,
but an entry `id` under a hidden *ancestor* is the caller's business. The two hover doors resolve
through `pick_leaf`, which already respects visibility; `draw_key_outline` names a node directly, so
it asks `shown_visible` first.

⚠️ **That enumeration is one door short and the function's own comment repeats the shortfall.**
`draw_drop_indicator` is a fourth call site, and it names a node directly too — `image_drop_target`
answers from the **selection**, checking the lock and the pointer's containment and nothing about
visibility. So a selected picture inside a hidden group, with a file dragged over it, is rung on
artwork nobody can see. It is narrow and it is real. *Fix with* the same `shown_visible` call
`draw_key_outline` takes, and note that the *operation* behind it has the larger version of the same
question — a drop replacing a picture that is not drawn — which is a decision rather than a slip and
is not this entry's to take.

`canvas::outline_reject_tests` has both halves: `a_group_off_screen_is_not_traced_and_one_on_screen_still_is`
(3 marks on screen, **0** off, the on-screen row being what stops the cull being satisfied by drawing
nothing at all) and `a_hidden_child_is_not_traced` (1 mark, plus a hidden group being no ring at
all). Both flips were run and both bit at the predicted assertion, 3 against 0 and 2 against 1.
⚠️ **A third flip did *not* bite and is written into the test**: with the reject present and the
padding dropped from `outline_view`, both rows stay green, because neither fixture has a node whose
box **ends** at the edge of the view. Nothing here is evidence for the padding.

⚠️ **No "after" timing is quoted anywhere, deliberately.** The reject sits above `local_path`,
`apply_affine` and `flatten_to_screen`, so a shape count of **zero** says none of that work runs —
which a millisecond figure on one machine would only suggest.

**D601 — A shadow's spread takes one radius per axis, as the blur beside it already did.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `spread_alpha` takes a pair, and each separable pass takes its
own half-width.***

`effects::shadow_layer` passed `sh.spread * scale.0.max(scale.1)` — one number — while `device_sigma`
directly next door takes **two** deviations on purpose, its own doc saying why: *"a non-uniform scale
blurs unevenly … Passing one averaged sigma … makes a blur on a skewed layer round rather than
lean"*. `push_effect_layer` computes `scale` as the two **column norms** of the composed device
transform, deliberately and with a comment saying so, and a skew is a shipped gesture
(`tools::side_shear`). So the pair was in hand at the call site and one of the two consumers threw it
away.

`[S10.2-L1-05]`'s own measurement, through `effects::run` on a 40×40 opaque square with
`DropShadow { blur: 0, spread: 10, offset: 0 }` — **the finding's numbers rather than this session's**,
which are the test's below:

| `scale` | drawn right | drawn down | correct |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1, 1) | 10 px | 10 px | 10 / 10 |
| (4, 1) | **40 px** | **40 px** | 40 / **10** |
| (1, 4) | **40 px** | **40 px** | **10** / 40 |

The factor is the ratio of the column norms, so it is unbounded rather than a rounding.

⚠️ **And the excess was outside the bounds the model had allocated for it**, which is what turns a
too-thick shadow into a visibly ruled one. `effect::escape` adds the spread in *document* units per
side; `escaped` maps that radius through the linear part of the world transform as an **ellipse**, so
the box says `spread × scale` per axis and answered 40/10 for the middle row — correct, and
disagreeing with the ink. `grow_to_escape` then ends `device_ink.intersect(grown)`, so the surplus 30
device pixels on the short axis were cut off with a straight edge. §5.9's *"too small is the one
error these bounds may not make"* was kept by the bounds and broken by the drawing.

`spread_alpha` takes `r: (f64, f64)` now, and the separable two-pass loop already had the structure
for it — each pass reads one axis, so the change is which number each pass takes. A pass whose radius
rounds to zero is skipped outright, zero being the identity for both a dilation and an erosion. The
sign comes from `r.0 + r.1` rather than from either half, **so an axis scaled to zero cannot take the
sign with it**: that is the line a later reader would simplify to `r.0 > 0.0` and thereby turn an
inner shadow inside out on a flattened layer. `fx_gpu::run` makes the same split per `Pass::Spread`
dispatch, from the same reasoning.

🚨 **Both backends did it identically, which is why the GPU suite could not see it.** `tests/fx_gpu.rs`
compares the two implementations against each other and every fixture in it is at
`SCALE = (1.0, 1.0)` — the one scale at which the wrong answer and the right one coincide. A
differential test agrees about a shared mistake, and a fixture set with no non-uniform scale in it
cannot ask the question this entry is about.

`effects::tests::a_spread_follows_the_scale_on_each_axis_the_way_the_blur_does`. Flip, one radius on
both passes again: it fails at the `(4, 1)` row, `left: (40, 40)` against `right: (40, 10)` — the
*across* number is right in both versions and the *down* number is the whole of the loss. ⚠️ **The
`(1, 1)` row is green under the flip and is the first row**, which is exactly the shape of test that
shipped this: a uniform-scale case, passing, at the top of the file.

**D600 — The four image formats v1 accepts are decided in code, because a feature list cannot decide
them. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `signature_is_accepted`, on magic bytes.***

`Cargo.toml`'s `[workspace.dependencies]` asks `image` for exactly `png,jpeg,webp,gif` with
`default-features = false`, and its comment said the list was *"named here so adding a fifth is a
decision"*. **That was false, and it was the kind of false that reads as a guarantee.** Cargo unifies
features across the dependency graph, and `arboard` — which this workspace declares for the image
paste (**D183**) — asks the same `image` build for `bmp` under `cfg(windows)` and `tiff` under
`cfg(target_os = "macos")`. Measured: `cargo tree --workspace` reports `bmp,gif,jpeg,png,webp` here,
`cargo tree -p ondin-render` the declared four. TIFF is the exact format `ondin_core::ImageFormat`'s
own doc names as excluded on purpose (§5.5a, **D191**), and it is compiled on macOS.

`images::decode` calls `image::load_from_memory` first — which sniffs with whatever is compiled — and
only falls back to `load_from_memory_with_format(bytes, hinted)`. So BMP bytes labelled `image/png`
**drew the picture on Windows and the missing-image placeholder on Linux**: one document, two
platforms, no report on either.

**Both doors are real.** `app::image_format_of` sniffs first and, for anything the sniff recognises
and v1 does not accept, falls through to the **file extension** — so a BMP named `.png` arrives at
`decode` hinted as a PNG. `svg_in::data_uri` maps the declared MIME type straight through with no
sniff at all, which is untrusted input from a foreign file. `[S22-L2-02]`.

The guard is `signature_is_accepted`, on `image::guess_format` — magic bytes, and **not** gated on
the compiled decoders, which is what makes it answer the same thing on every platform. Only a
*recognised* format outside the four is refused; bytes `image` cannot place at all are still handed
to the hinted decoder exactly as before, so nothing that decodes today stops decoding. The manifest
comment now says what it can say: the list bounds what we *ask for*, not what is compiled, and the
decision lives in the function.

🚨 **The guard is a named function rather than two lines inside `decode`, and that is a finding
rather than a preference.** The end-to-end test — BMP bytes in, `Err(Corrupt)` out — **cannot
discriminate under `cargo test -p ondin-render`**, because that spelling compiles no BMP decoder and
the bytes are refused with or without the guard. Widening the four to admit `Bmp` is **green under
`-p` and red under `--workspace`**, `left: Ok((1, 1))` against `right: Err(Corrupt)`. That is
`[A8-L3-02]`'s **hole 4** — `--workspace` and `-p` compiling different code — deciding *whether a
test can fail*, where every previous instance of it has been about what a lint reports or what a
`size_of` measures. A predicate on magic bytes has no such dependency, so a test on it is worth the
same under either spelling; **the split is what makes the assertion portable.**

`images::tests` has both: `a_format_outside_the_four_is_refused_whatever_the_platform_compiled`,
whose hand-written 1×1 24-bit BMP fixture is asserted to *be* a BMP before anything else — or the
refusal below it is only the news that some bytes failed to decode — and the control
`a_png_is_still_a_png`, which is what says `guess_format`, now consulted on every decode, does not
refuse the four it is there to admit.

**D599 — The feature registry is asserted as a set, and the failure message is the difference.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — a sorted `EXPECTED` and a set difference.***

`panels::typography::REGISTRY` is 124 individually registered OpenType 1.9.1 tags, and it is not a
lookup table that can be incomplete: `feature_label` reports a tag that misses the table as the
font's own **private** tag, hidden behind *Show all features* and carrying the raw four letters where
a name and a description belong. `REGISTRY`'s own doc says so — *"a tag **missing** from this table
is reported to the user as private, so an omission is a wrong answer rather than a gap"*.

The test asserted the table's **cardinality**: `REGISTRY.len() == 124`, a dedup, four-byte ASCII
tags, non-empty names, `offered == !what.is_empty()`, and no `ssXX`/`cvXX`. **Every one of those is
preserved by a same-length substitution**, which in a table of 124 four-letter literals is the
likeliest edit there is. Measured: `("qwid", …)` retyped as `("qwix", …)` left `cargo test -p
ondin-app` at **970 passed / 0 failed**. The control — `kern` retyped as `kzrn` — did go red, but
only in a neighbouring test whose `["tnum", "liga", "kern", "smcp"]` loop names **four** of the 124
by hand. So the machinery worked and the coverage was four. `[S6.3-L6-04]`.

A sorted `const EXPECTED: [&str; 124]` closes it, asserted as a set difference. The length and dedup
assertions are kept — they are what says the list is not being satisfied by a duplicate — but they
are no longer the only thing holding the data. `EXPECTED` is deliberately **not** in `REGISTRY`'s own
order: the table is grouped by what the features *do*, which is the right order to read it in and the
wrong one to diff it in.

⚠️ **The message is the second draft and the first one is the lesson.** `assert_eq!(tags, EXPECTED)`
is the same assertion and it printed both 124-element lists — 248 strings, with the one that moved
buried in them. The difference prints `gone: ["qwid"], arrived: ["qwix"]`, and the flip was re-run
against that message rather than reasoned about. **A set assertion needs the set difference in its
message, or it reports the haystack.**

This is `[A8-L6-04]`'s mechanism — *the test asserts a count* — at its second site, `theme.rs`'s icon
catalogue being the first. Worth reading the two together: a count is the assertion somebody writes
when the data is long, and length is exactly the property an edit to long data preserves.

**D598 — The span order is a written-out list now, and D154's reason was a proxy.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-09; Fix — `CharAttrKind::ALL`, `ParaAttrKind::ALL`, and a fixture that
exercises the key it is named for.***

The declaration order of `CharAttrKind` *is* the `(attribute, start)` sort every saved document's
span list is written in: `Spans::normalize` ends `sort_by_key(|s| (s.attr.attr_kind(), s.start))`,
which is §5.11's invariant 9 and the reason two saves of an untouched document are byte-identical.
**D154** knew that and named a test as the enforcement of it —
`colour_sorts_after_every_other_attribute`, which compared `CharAttrKind::Color > kind` against a
hand-written list of the other fourteen.

**Every one of those fourteen comparisons survives any permutation of the fourteen.** Measured before
the fix: `CharAttrKind::Family` and `CharAttrKind::Size` exchanged, one line and nothing else, left
the whole workspace green — **1,479 tests**, the `every-kind.json` golden included. `[S6.1-L6-02]` is
a verdict whose reason names a code fact, where the code fact was not one.

🚨 **And D154's reason is wrong in the direction that matters, which is worth correcting rather than
quietly restating.** D154 says `Color` is appended because "inserted anywhere else it reorders the
spans of every document already on disk". A kind that *arrives* reorders nothing: the fourteen
already there keep their relative order whatever index a newcomer takes, and a document that does not
use the newcomer sorts and serializes byte-for-byte as before.

⚠️ **Two facts carry that and the entry originally stated only one.** `CharAttr` is serialized by
serde in its externally-tagged default form, keyed by variant **name** rather than by position — and
`CharAttrKind` itself **never reaches disk at all**: it derives `PartialOrd, Ord` and no serde trait,
so the declaration order feeds `normalize`'s sort key and nothing else. The first is necessary; the
second is what makes it sufficient, because an index that shifts has no representation anywhere to
change. `arch-scribe` supplied the second reading against the code.

What churns is a kind that **moves** — and then only in the documents holding spans of **both** of
the kinds it moved past, which is what the new test's own failure message says
(*"every document on disk holding both re-sorts on its next save"*). Appending remains the rule,
because it is the one edit that *cannot* move an existing
variant — but it is the proxy, and the rule underneath it is **an existing variant never moves**. The
`CharAttrKind::Color` doc had repeated D154's wording and states the real rule now.

`CharAttrKind::ALL` (15) and `ParaAttrKind::ALL` (7) are `pub const` literals in declaration order,
and `char_attribute_kinds_keep_the_order_a_saved_file_is_written_in` asserts the list is strictly
ascending, naming both kinds and the index when it is not. The character test also keeps `ALL.last()
== Color`, which is D154's own rule restated for the reader who arrives from that entry; only the
ascending assertion is load-bearing. The paragraph twin covers `ParaAttrKind`, **which had no guard
of any kind** — not even the fourteen comparisons — so a swap there was invisible from the start.

⚠️ **Completeness is deliberately not compiler-checked, and that is the right answer rather than a
hole.** A sixteenth variant left out of `ALL` makes no test red — and it moves none of the fifteen,
so no document on disk changes and there is nothing to catch. The list exists for the edit that
*does* churn every file, and for that it is exact.

⚠️ **The test named for the sort key never exercised the key.**
`spans_sort_by_attribute_then_start_for_byte_stable_saves` used `Size 0..2` and `Weight 4..8`, whose
**starts** already order them the way the kind does. Measured before the rebuild: deleting the
attribute from the key outright — `sort_by_key(|s| (s.start, s.start))` — left it **green**, and the
only casualty anywhere in the workspace was `a_paragraph_span_list_round_trips_through_json`, one
failure out of 1,479 in a test that is not about the sort at all. Both spans start at 0 now and the
resulting kind order is asserted explicitly, so that same flip fails **twice**, and once at the test
named for the thing it broke. The old `a == b` is kept beside it: it says the *insertion* order does
not survive, which is the property a byte-stable save actually needs.

⚠️ **A permutation is only visible to a test that holds both of the kinds it permutes**, and that is
the argument for asserting the list rather than sampling it. The `Family`/`Size` swap fails the new
order test **and nothing else** — including the rebuilt byte-stability test, whose two spans are
`Size` and `Weight`, a pair that exchange does not reorder. The first draft of that test's own doc
predicted it would fall there too, and was corrected against the run.

**D597 — A test whose subject exists only in a debug build, and a release suite nobody runs.
*Fixed 2026-09-08; Fix — the option is set rather than read. Both instances closed and the open
ruling answered at D771, 2026-09-15.***

**This is not a review finding.** `cargo test --workspace --release` was run while waiting for
something else, which is a command no gate in this project issues, and it came back **red** —
on `ui::scrub_tests::a_row_of_value_fields_has_no_id_clash`, and on that test's own fixture check:
*"the clash warning is off, so this test cannot fail"*.

The assertion was right, and it is the thing that makes the test mean anything: the test looks for
egui's id-clash overlay in `.shapes` and demands there is none, so the warning has to be **on** or an
absence proves nothing. What it read was the *ambient* value. egui defaults
`Options::warn_on_id_clash` to `cfg!(debug_assertions)` (`egui-0.36.1/src/memory/mod.rs`) and
`Context::check_for_id_clash` returns before painting anything when it is false — so in a release
build no overlay is ever drawn, and a test that hunts for one is asserting nothing at all. Reading
the default therefore made the test say one thing in debug and fail outright in release.

The fix is one line, `ctx.options_mut(|o| o.warn_on_id_clash = true);` ahead of the assertion, so the
test means the same in both profiles. **The assertion is kept rather than deleted**: it now checks
the value that was just set rather than a default, which is still what stands between this test and
vacuity if `theme::install` ever grows a line that turns the option off — it already quiets the
noisier sibling `warn_if_rect_changes_id` (**D65**) and deliberately leaves this one alone.

⚠️ **This is a gate observation and not a product defect.** Nothing a user can do was broken and the
release binary is unaffected. What was broken is a claim about coverage.

🚨 **No gate in this workspace runs the tests in release.** The six are `cargo build`, `cargo test`,
`cargo clippy --all-targets`, `cargo fmt`, `cargo doc --document-private-items` and
`cargo check --release` — and the last of those *compiles* without `debug_assertions` and does not
run a single test. So a test whose subject exists only in debug is invisible to the whole set, in
both directions: **red in release with nobody looking**, which is this one, or **green in release
while asserting nothing**, which is the worse half. **D161** is the same cfg seen from the other
side — a line behind egui's own `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` broke the release *build* with the other
four gates green, and is the reason `check --release` exists at all. That gate catches a line that
fails to compile. It cannot catch a test whose *meaning* changes.

⚠️ **And the worse half is not hypothetical — there is a live instance, found writing this entry.**
`app::library_wiring_tests::the_dashboard_draws_without_egui_complaining` runs the dashboard through
ten passes (five `Nav`s × grid and list) and asserts that egui painted no red-stroked `Shape::Rect`,
which is half of what a clash draws. It never sets the option. In release `check_for_id_clash`
returns early, the count is zero by construction, and the test passes while checking nothing — over
the one screen whose rows are hand-built and whose ids come from paths and indices, which is exactly
the bug class it was written for. Its own doc records a flip that draws **4** warning rectangles;
that flip can only ever have been run in debug. ⚠️ **Closed 2026-09-15** — it carries the same one
line after `theme::install`, with the assertion beside it (D771).

⚠️ **The third reader of an egui debug overlay is legitimately debug-only, and must not be "fixed"
the same way.** `panels::inspector::carry_tests::shrinking_a_paint_list_paints_no_warning_outline`
guards that `theme::install` keeps `warn_if_rect_changes_id` off (**D65**), and that flag lives on
`Style::debug` — which egui puts behind `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]`, the whole `DebugOptions` type
being absent from a release build. There is no option to set there and nothing for the test to be
about, because the overlay it guards against cannot be painted in the profile in question. Leave it,
and read this paragraph before generalising the one above.

**Whether `cargo test --workspace --release` joins the gates was left open for the maintainer, and
was answered at D771: a *session-close step*, not a gate.** It catches exactly this class. The
release suite is green today — 31 targets, the same as the debug run — and **nothing keeps it that
way**, because a written step is a habit rather than a gate.

🚨 **The cost figure that stood here was false, and it is the thing the ruling turned on.** This
paragraph read *"it roughly doubles the test time"*, and the index row and `CLAUDE.md` carried the
same phrase — three copies of a number nobody had measured. **Measured 2026-09-15, warm: the release
*run* is 6 s against the debug run's 20 s**, three times *faster*, `[profile.dev.package.ondin-render]
opt-level = 3` already optimising the hot crate in debug. **The cost is the build, not the run** — 26 s
of warm fingerprinting, 96 s cold, and 2.4 GB of a second profile's artifacts. It landed near the right
total for entirely the wrong reason, and the reason is what decides the question: what a maintainer
feels is the **marginal release recompile** after each edit, which *"doubles the test time"* does not
describe. See D771 for the full measurement and for why `-p ondin-app --release` was rejected despite
costing 1 s.

⚠️ **One distinction the record did not draw, and it is why this was easy to miss.**
`grep 'cfg(debug' crates/` still answers `theme.rs` alone, so *our* code reads the profile in exactly
one place, and that grep has been carried as though it bounded the problem. It does not: this
finding is about a **dependency's** use of the cfg, an egui default that changes the meaning of code
which never mentions `debug_assertions` at all. A census of our own `cfg(debug_assertions)` says
nothing about what the profile changes underneath us.

🚨 **That paragraph is half the correction and it credits the grep with more than it can do** (D732).
`grep 'cfg(debug'` matches only cfgs whose name **begins with** `debug`, so it cannot report a
`cfg(windows)`, a `cfg(unix)` or a `cfg(target_os = …)` — it **cannot return a counter-example to the
claim it is quoted as evidence for**, which was that `debug_assertions` is the only cfg the app
reads. `ondin-app` reads `windows`, `unix` and `target_os` as well, and `ondin-core` reads `panic`
(D445). So the sentence above is right that our census says nothing about a dependency's use of the
profile, and it is *also* true that the census was never a census: **the only thing that command
establishes is where the string `cfg(debug` appears**, which today is two files, one of them a doc
comment. `theme.rs` is still the only place we *read* the profile.

**D596 — The derived-buffer budget is enforced where a buffer is inserted, not only from `prepare`.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — `trim_derived`, called from `pixels` too, and a candidate list
that will take a live buffer.***

`[S9.2-L4-03]`. `ADJUSTED_BYTES` (256 MB) was checked in exactly one place, `evict_derived`, whose
only caller is the last line of `prepare`. **Every non-interactive caller runs `prepare` once, before
the first read**: `png::png` and `png::raster_of` both open with
`let mut images = ImageStore::new(); images.prepare(doc);` and then hand the store to the renderer,
which asks `pixels` once per distinct fill for the whole render. Nothing calls `prepare` again, so
`derived` only grew and the cap was never consulted on the export or library-cover paths.

**Measured in release on one 4000×3000 picture, driven in the export's own order** — one `prepare`,
then `pixels` per fill:

```text
distinct adjustments | derived_len | held
                   4 |           4 |  192 MB
                   8 |           8 |  384 MB   (budget 256 MB)
the canvas shape     |           5 |  240 MB   (six further `prepare`s)
```

The last row is the control: where `prepare` keeps running the two eviction rules do their work and
the store sits under the cap. The other two are unbounded above — one buffer per distinct
`(ImageId, AdjustKey)` the walk visits, each read exactly once and never again.

🚨 **Two defects, and either alone leaves it unbounded.** Moving the check into `pixels` is not
enough, because the old budget loop filtered its candidates to `!live(d.asked)`, and
`live(asked) = asked + SETTLED_FRAMES >= clock`: a single `prepare` sets `clock` to 1, every entry a
one-shot walk creates is asked at 1, and `live(1)` is true of all of them for the whole render — so
the loop had nothing it was willing to evict. **A cap that cannot evict anything is not a cap.** The
retain above it compounds the same thing from the other side: its `d.full || live(d.asked)` term
keeps every entry a non-interactive store creates, since `full` is `to_source == Affine::IDENTITY`
and the `previews` arm is `false` there.

The fix is the free function `trim_derived(cache, budget, clock, keep)`, called from `evict_derived`
and from the end of `pixels`. It sorts candidates by `(is_live, asked)` — `false < true`, so **stale
before live, and within each the least recently asked first** — and will take a live buffer as a last
resort. **`keep` is the entry the caller has just built and is about to return, and is never a
candidate**, or `pixels` could hand back a buffer it had already dropped.

⚠️ **Preferring stale is `evict_derived`'s own rule and §15 D160's reason** — a buffer the walk is
about to ask for again costs a recomputation to evict, which is the thrash `PREVIEW_FLOOR` exists to
prevent in the font cache. What changed is only what happens when there is **no** stale candidate:
previously nothing, now the oldest. **The floor D160 reaches for is deliberately not copied**, and
that is the load-bearing half: a floor here would reinstate this defect exactly, since on a one-shot
walk every entry is live and any refusal to evict one is a refusal to evict at all. The trade is
therefore real and is stated rather than hidden — where the working set genuinely exceeds 256 MB the
store now recomputes instead of growing, which is the thrash D160 refuses in the picker, accepted
here because the alternative is no bound. `ADJUSTED_BYTES`' own doc claims to be *"a working-set
bound rather than a waste bound"*, unlike `DECODED_BYTES`, and that claim is what measurement
contradicted on this path. *Revisit if* a canvas is ever measured over the budget.

`set_derived_budget` is `#[cfg(test)]` and deliberately **not** the public twin `with_budget` is:
nothing in the app has any business choosing this number, `ADJUSTED_BYTES` being the one answer and
its doc the place the argument for it lives.

Two tests, both in `images::tests::adjust_tests`.
`an_export_shaped_run_does_not_exceed_the_derived_budget` reads six distinct adjustments once each
with the clock standing still, against a budget of three buffers, and asserts `derived_len() == 3`;
its **fixture assertion comes first**, because if a single buffer already exceeded the budget
`derived_len` would sit at 1 for reasons that have nothing to do with eviction.
`a_stale_derived_buffer_goes_before_a_live_one` ages two entries past `SETTLED_FRAMES` with three
`prepare`s, leaves a third live, and inserts a fourth over budget. **Both flips run separately and both fail at 6 against 3**: (1) `trim_derived`'s
call removed from `pixels`; (2) the call kept and the candidate list filtered back to
`!live(d.asked)`. ⚠️ Flip (2) leaves the second test **green** and flip (1) takes it down at 4
against 3, which is the pair that says the *time* of the check and the *predicate* are two
independent defects rather than one described twice.

⚠️ **The second test does not pin the preference it is named for, and that was found writing this
entry rather than by any gate.** `derived_len` is the only thing it can observe, and `trim_derived`
runs on every insertion — so the count comes back to the budget's three whichever buffer was
dropped, including under a *reversed* order, where asking for the live value again simply rebuilds it
and evicts another. What it really pins is that the budget holds when the candidates are of mixed
age. *Fix with* a `#[cfg(test)]` predicate that answers whether a key is held **without building
it**, which is the one observation the store does not currently offer; then assert which buffer
survived.

⚠️ **A second and larger idea was declined for now rather than missed.** A non-interactive store need
not cache derived buffers at all — the walk reads each `(id, adjust)` exactly once, so the
`previews == false` arm could answer without inserting and hold one buffer instead of N. That is a
behaviour change with its own trade, a second fill sharing one `(id, adjust)` paying the adjustment
pass twice, and `png.rs`'s own doc already flags the store-per-export shape as *"right for a one-shot
export and wrong for anything else"*. **Worth revisiting if export memory is measured again.**
`[S9.2-L5-02]` is a different budget (`DECODED_BYTES`) and is not this. §5.5a amended, and D186's
sentence with it.

**D595 — One picture on many shapes is written once. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — a shared
`<image>` in `<defs>` and a `<use>` inside each pattern.***

`[S9.1-L4-03]`, Medium. Every def was keyed per node **per slot** — `image_id(id, slot)`, and
`Defs::add` dedupes on that string — so **nothing was keyed on the picture**. Two shapes showing one
photograph were two defs, each carrying a full base64 copy of it.

**Measured in release, one embedded 200 KB image shared by N rectangles:**

```text
shapes | document | exported SVG
     1 |  0.27 MB |  0.27 MB   (1.0x)
     2 |  0.27    |  0.53      (2.0x)
    10 |  0.28    |  2.67      (9.6x)
    30 |  0.30    |  8.01     (26.6x)
```

**The document column is the control and it is flat**, because `ImageId` is a content hash and the
table holds the blob once. The export threw that away exactly. A moodboard, a photo grid and a
repeated logo are ordinary documents, and *Export SVG* is not an exotic path. The cost is not only
what lands in the file: `ImageEntry::href` returns a fresh `String` of 4/3 × the blob per call and
`escape_xml` copies it again, so the transient cost per shape was about 2.7× the blob on top of the
~1.33× that was written.

**One `<image id="pix-<hash>">` per distinct `ImageId` goes in `<defs>`, and each `<pattern>` holds a
`<use href="#pix-…">`.** ⚠️ **The per-node `<pattern>` is not the duplication and stays**: its
`patternTransform` carries that node's own `ImageRef::framing`, which genuinely differs per node, and
a fix that hoisted the pattern too would look right in bytes and lose every framing. This extends
**D185** rather than revising it — an image is still a paint server reached through the `Defs`
machinery, and `write_element` still learns nothing.

Three details are load-bearing. **The `opacity` and the `filter` moved onto the `<use>`**, which is
where they have to be now: both are the *node's* — the sampler's alpha and that node's adjustment
`<filter>` — and the `<image>` is shared by every node showing the picture. **No `width`/`height` on
the `<use>`**, deliberately: those apply only when the reference is to an `<svg>` or a `<symbol>`, so
writing them here would be inert and would read as though they were doing something, and the
`<image>` already carries the tile's intrinsic pixel box. And **`payload_id` sanitises the hash to
ASCII alphanumerics**, because an `ImageId`'s spelling is not this file's to assume; an id that is
not an XML name produces a document no reader can resolve, and the failure mode is a picture that
silently does not draw.

🚨 **Verified against a real browser, because nothing in this workspace renders SVG.** The round-trip
suite cannot see this — `svg_in` has no `<pattern>` handling at all (`[A5-L6-01]`) — and the §11
golden holds one node of every kind and **no image**, so *no gate in the workspace looks at image
markup*. A three-rect document sharing one 4×4 PNG was exported, a copy of it rewritten by hand into
the old inline form, both served over HTTP, drawn into canvases and differenced: **10,800 opaque
pixels (3 × 60 × 60), 0 channels differing, worst delta 0.** That is the technique `CLAUDE.md`
records for checking an *import*, used here on the writer, and it is what says `<use>` of an
`<image>` in `<defs>` is not merely valid but identical.

`ondin-export/tests/svg.rs · one_picture_on_many_shapes_is_written_once`: ten `<pattern>`s, one
`data:`, ten `<use>`s, and the byte ratio under 1.5×. ⚠️ **The pattern count is asserted on purpose**
— a byte-ratio assertion alone is passed by the hoist that loses the framings. Flip, the `<use>` put
back to an inline `<image href="data:…">`: fails on *"the payload is written once"* at **11 against
1**, eleven rather than ten because the hoisted def is still emitted under that flip, which is the
honest picture of a half-applied fix. §7 and §11 amended.

**D594 — The incremental update stops re-walking to the root. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`collect_subtree` records depth on the way down, and the sort caches its key.***

`[S4.1-L4-03]`, Medium. `Resolved::update` sorted its affected set by `depth` with `sort_by_key`,
which the standard library documents as calling the key function on **every comparison** — and
`depth` walks the parent chain to the root. `ordered` was collected from an `FxHashSet` — it is that
hash container's keys still — so it arrives scrambled and Rust's adaptive sort gets no help from a
nearly-ordered input either. So the one line that puts parents before children was Θ(n log n) walks
of O(d) each, per commit.

**Measured in release with the node count held near constant and the depth varied**, `update` against
the full `rebuild` it exists to avoid:

```text
depth x per-level   nodes | update | rebuild | this line
  200 x   1           402 |  5.819 |  0.122  | 5.431  (93% of update)
   20 x  10           222 |  0.357 |  0.075  | 0.357  (100%)
    4 x  50           206 |  0.098 |  0.066  | 0.045  (46%)
    1 x 200           203 |  0.063 |  0.060  | 0.010  (16%)     (ms)
```

At depth 20 — ordinary for imported SVG — **the incremental path was 4.8× the full reconstruction**,
and at depth 200, 47×. `rebuild` needs no sort at all, `resolve_subtree` being a recursion that puts
parents before children structurally, so it wins outright the moment depth costs anything. The bill
is per commit: every arrow-key nudge at a held ~30/s, every undo, every redo, every released scrub.

🚨 **`sort_by_cached_key` is the obvious one-word fix and it is not enough.** Three versions on a
200-deep chain in debug, three runs each, as a ratio against `rebuild`:

```text
sort_by_key over a depth walk          42.9x   <- the finding
sort_by_cached_key over a depth walk    3.2x   <- one word, and still 3x
depth recorded on the way down          1.2x   <- this
```

**The middle row is the one worth carrying.** It takes 93% of the cost out and still leaves the
incremental path three times the price of the thing it exists to avoid, because the walk still runs
once per node — and a fix accepted on *"much faster than before"* would have stopped there. So
`collect_subtree` records each node's depth as it descends, a child's being its parent's plus one and
therefore free; `affected` is an `FxHashMap<NodeId, usize>` rather than a set; and the sort is
`sort_by_cached_key` over a lookup.

⚠️ **The review's own attribution had to be corrected before any of this was believed.** Its first
replica of the line read *10% of `update`*, which would have sent the finding to Rejected. It was
wrong because it sorted ids in **creation** order, which is already sorted by depth, so the adaptive
sort called the key O(n) times instead of O(n log n). Scrambling the replica's input — which is what
`affected.iter()` does for real — moved the same line from 10% to 93%. **A replica that matches the
code's shape but not its input distribution measures a different function**, and nothing about the
replica looked wrong.

⚠️ **This composes with §15 D590 and neither makes the other cheaper.** D590 changed what
`op_set_transform` puts in the dirty set and narrowed the *text* pass to it; the sort still runs over
the **expanded** set, because a descendant's world transform really does depend on a dirty ancestor.
The two are the same function's two independent costs.

`ondin-core/tests/resolve.rs · an_incremental_update_is_not_slower_than_the_rebuild_it_replaces`
asserts the **ratio against `rebuild`** — the property the incremental path exists to have, rather
than a duration, which would be a measurement of this machine — and asserts that the two passes still
agree about the world transform, so it is not a test about speed alone. ⚠️ **The fixture is deep and
narrow on purpose.** Depth is the quantity that made this superlinear, and `[A4-MAP]`'s cost model
has **no depth axis** — it denominates this path in node count, and 402 nodes at depth 200 cost more
here than 4,000 flat ones, so a wide fixture measures nothing. That is G10's shape applied to a cost
model rather than to a cap. Flip, back to `sort_by_key` over a `depth` walk: fails at 42.9×, naming
both timings. §5.9 amended.

**D593 — Collecting SVG defs is linear in their count. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — a
`HashSet` beside the insertion-ordered `Vec`.***

`[A4-L4-02]`, Medium. `Defs` stored `entries: Vec<(String, String)>` and deduped by scanning it —
`add` with `self.entries.iter().any(|(k, _)| *k == id)`, and `has` the same — while `collect_defs`
calls `add` once per gradient fill, per gradient stroke, per image (three ids: `image_id`,
`image_clip_id`, `adjust_id`), per effect stack and per text rail. So D defs cost **Θ(D²)** string
comparisons, over ids of the form `grad-{node}-{slot}` that share a long common prefix and therefore
run past it before differing. `has` is asked **per image paint during emission**, adding an
O(nodes × D) term of its own on top.

**Measured with the node count held fixed at 16,000**, so the tree walk, the transforms and the
string building are constant across the row and only the def count moves:

```text
  defs | export
 1,000 |  21.34 ms
 2,000 |  23.52
 4,000 |  32.51
 8,000 |  63.42
16,000 | 166.89
```

The excess over the D=1,000 row multiplies by **≈3.4 per doubling** — a pure square would be 4.0, and
the shortfall is the linear byte-growth term riding along — and at D=16,000 the quadratic term is
about **87% of export time**. **The emitted bytes grow exactly linearly over the same row**, 169 KB
to 5.49 MB for ×32 nodes, which is what says the time is not the extra markup. 16,000 gradient fills
is ordinary for a detailed vector illustration, and `svg_in` accepts arbitrary files up to a
`nodes_limit` of 500,000.

The fix is a `std::collections::HashSet<String>` beside the `Vec`. ⚠️ **The `Vec` stays and its doc
now says why**: `emit` depends on insertion order, and a `<defs>` block that reshuffled between two
exports of one document would break invariant 9's byte-stability and every golden in §11.
**`std::collections::HashSet` rather than `FxHashSet`**: this crate does not depend on `rustc_hash`,
§3's dependency rules are not worth spending on a hash function here, and the win being asked for is
O(D) against O(D²) rather than a constant factor.

⚠️ **The output is byte-identical, which is why the §11 goldens could not see this and are not its
regression test.** `ondin-export/tests/svg.rs ·
collecting_defs_does_not_grow_with_the_square_of_their_count` asserts a **ratio** rather than a
threshold: this project measures a 40× spread between debug and release on the same work
(`fonts::preview::FRAME_BUDGET`'s own note), so an absolute bound would be a measurement of the
machine. A 4× document costs **4.06×** with the set and **8.3×** with
the scan, three runs each, stable to two decimal places; the bound is 6.0, and the fixture assertion
that both documents really carry one def per rect comes first, since a build that emitted nothing
would have the flattest curve of all. ⚠️ **The sizes 1,500 and 6,000 are chosen for separation, not
for speed** — at 1,000/4,000 the two versions measure 4.1× and 7.0×, which leaves the bound very
little room on either side, and the extra fixture-building is what buys the margin. §7 and §11
amended.

⚠️ **Those figures are single-sample and the test no longer takes single samples** (§15 D705). One
wall-clock reading per size failed at 7.04× under a full `cargo test --workspace` a day later, on a
scheduler stall inside a nine-millisecond window; it is best of three per size now, re-measured on
both sides at **3.97×** and **8.12×**. The bound is still 6.0 and the discrimination is what D705
refused to trade away.

**D592 — A keystroke shapes the edited node once. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`from_transaction_shaped`, and the session hands over the layout it already has.***
