`[A4-L4-01]`, Medium. `RenderOverrides::set_kind` carries a *"re-shape only when the text actually
changed"* guard — it compares the edited kind against `doc.get(id)` and reuses `res.text_layout(id)`
where they are equal — and **it cannot fire for a live text session**. `doc.get(id)` is the last
*commit*, and a session commits exactly once, at `finish_text_edit` (§9.3). So the two kinds are
unequal for the whole session by construction, every keystroke took the `shaped(&kind)` arm, and
parley ran over the whole node a **second** time on top of the `TextEdit::reshape` the keystroke had
just paid for.

**Measured in release, one node, mean of 20 inserts**: at 4,000 characters 1.171 ms in
`TextEdit::insert` and 1.325 ms again in `from_transaction`; at 16,000, 4.755 and 5.435; at 64,000,
18.999 and 21.753. `from_transaction ≈ insert + extract` at every size, which is what *attributes*
the second shape rather than assuming it — the preview's cost tracks a shape plus an extract, not an
extract alone.

**The fix hands the answer over rather than deriving it twice.**
`RenderOverrides::from_transaction_shaped` takes `Option<(NodeId, TextLayout)>`;
`canvas::preview_session` passes `s.editor.text_layout()`, which is `extract(&self.shaped,
self.parts())` — the half of the work the session has already done, 0.63 ms at 16k;
`EditorSession::set_session_preview` carries it through. `from_transaction` is **unchanged** and is
still what every gesture preview in the app goes through, which is what keeps the other eleven
`absorb` arms reading the way they did. The second test is that control.

🚨 **`prepared_text` is a construction argument wearing a private field, and that is deliberate.**
`set_kind` is reached from eleven arms of `absorb` through `patch_text`, so threading a parameter to
say something about *one* node would put the same `None` at ten call sites. It is set before the
absorb loop, read by `set_kind`, and cleared before the value is returned, so no `RenderOverrides` a
caller can observe ever holds one. ⚠️ **The risk is what a session's preview now *carries*, which is
§15 D109's and `[A1-L2-04]`'s path**: a layout that disagreed with the kind beside it would have the
canvas drawing one thing while every measurement read another. That is why the argument is a whole
`TextLayout` keyed to a `NodeId` rather than a flag — a caller cannot pass it by accident, and the
session's `text_layout()` is derived from the same `parts()` its `SetText` is built from.
⚠️ **And §6's *"preview and result cannot describe different edits"* rests on that**, because the
differential suite in `ondin-render/tests/overrides.rs` builds every one of its scenes through
`from_transaction` — twenty-odd call sites, all `None`. The prepared-layout door is covered by the
two app-side tests and by the shape of the argument, and by nothing that renders both ways. §6's
point 1 says so now.

`canvas::session_preview_shape_tests`, two, counted through `ondin_core::text::shapes()` rather than
timed, since a duration is a measurement of this machine and a count is a measurement of the
program. ⚠️ **The fixture asserts the editor's own count is 1 first** — with no live session, or a
caret that never landed, the preview assertion below would read `0` for the wrong reason — and the
preview is asserted to *exist* afterwards, because "shaped nothing" is also what a
`from_transaction` that bailed out reports. Flip, `preview_session` passing `None`: fails on *"the
preview re-shaped what the editor had just shaped"* at 1 against 0. §9.3 and §6 amended.

**D591 — A preview face does not re-shape a document that never names its family. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — `FontPoll::registered` and `FontPoll::touches`.***

`[A4-L4-04]`, Medium. §5.4a has said the right thing all along — *"treat font arrival as dirtying all
Text nodes **using that family**"* — and the app read it as far as the comma. `FontService::poll` set
`fonts_registered` on any successful registration, with no notion of who had asked for the face, and
`OndinApp::ui` turned that into `EditorSession::fonts_changed` → `Resolved::invalidate_text` over the
whole document.

**The picker is what makes that expensive.** It fetches preview faces for as long as it is scrolled —
the `preview` lane, backlog 48 — so scrolling the family list re-shaped every text node in the
document on every frame one of them landed: ~23 ms on a twenty-block document, in exactly the
interaction that has to stay smooth, and the reason that row list was virtualized in the first place.

**Half of the distinction already existed** (§5.4a, §15 **D352**): a longer family *list* is a
repaint and not a re-shape, because the catalog landing changes what the picker offers and nothing
about how a node shapes. Font *data* is the other half, and the same argument goes one step further
down — data for a family nothing in the document names cannot change a glyph of it either.

`FontPoll::registered` is a `Vec<String>` of lowercased family names and
`FontPoll::touches(&HashSet<String>)` asks the question; `OndinApp::document_families()` is one walk
for two callers, the gate and `ensure_document_fonts`. **`FontPoll` is no longer `Copy`**, which is
the price of carrying names. ⚠️ **`previews.retry_misses` is deliberately *not* narrowed**: a picker
miss is a family whose preview strip could not be drawn, and an arriving preview face is precisely
what it was waiting for, whether or not the document has ever heard of it. ⚠️ **`ensure_document_fonts`
is now handed lowercased names**, which was checked rather than assumed: `FontService::keys` is
already the lowercased family list, `faces_of` resolves through it and core's `is_family_available`
does the same, so case is not part of a family's identity anywhere on this path. Keeping two forms
would let the gate and the loader disagree about one family, which is this finding's own failure
shape.

🚨 **Two things this does not do, and the second was a hole rather than a boundary.** The *gate* is
narrowed and `Resolved::invalidate_text` is not: once an arriving family is one the document names,
every text node in it re-shapes, including the ones set in something else. That is the coarser half
of §5.4a's sentence and it costs one walk of a document that had work to do anyway. ⚠️ **And
`document_families` read `TextStyle::font_family` alone, so a family applied to a *selection* was not
in the set** — `panels::typography::type_family_row` writes `CharAttr::Family` into the spans
whenever the range is partial, and calls `ensure_loaded` for it, so the bytes really did arrive a
frame or two later and the narrowed gate then declined to invalidate. That run kept drawing in the
fallback face until something else touched the node, and the coarse gate had covered it by accident,
so the narrowing is what made it reachable at all.

**Amended 2026-09-08, in `428d834`.** `document_families` unions the node's default
`TextStyle::font_family` with every `CharAttr::Family` in its character spans, which closes
`ensure_document_fonts`' identical gap on the *loading* side in the same walk — the one place, as the
instruction here predicted. `a_family_applied_to_a_selection_is_one_the_document_names` pins it.
⚠️ **Its fixture asserts the node's own default is still `Inter`**, or the span would be the only
family in the walk and the test would pass against a version that had started reading spans
*instead of* defaults, which is the same bug with the operands swapped. Flip, the `spans.as_slice()`
loop removed: fails on *"a family applied to a selection is not in the set"*.

`app::font_arrival_tests`, three. The predicate test asserts the `Roboto` case, the `Inter` case —
which **must** still invalidate, since a fix that simply stopped invalidating would leave such a
document in the fallback for the rest of the session with nothing to say so — and `INTER`, because a
fix where only one end lowercased would be invisible until somebody typed a family name in the wrong
case. The selection test above is the second. The third measures the cost of the branch through
`text::shapes`, passes in both builds, and says so: it is the price of the thing the fix stops doing
rather than a flip-check of the fix.
⚠️ **The `poll` end cannot be driven headlessly** — `register_fonts` is what decides whether a face
counts, and only Inter is bundled — so the module says which half is asserted and which is read.
§5.4a and §5.9 amended.

**D590 — A translate does not re-shape the text it moves. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — the
text pass runs over the dirty set, and the op stops expanding it.***

`[A4-L4-03]`, Medium. `Resolved::update` expands the dirty set to whole subtrees — correctly, since a
descendant's *world transform* depends on a dirty ancestor — and then ran `reshape_text` over the
expansion. **A text layout depends on nothing outside its own node**: `text::layout` reads
`TextRef::of(node.kind())` and nothing else, so content, style, both span lists, sizing and the rail
are all the node's own. A node whose layout needs redoing is a node whose own kind changed, and the
`op_*` handlers dirty exactly those — `op_insert_subtree` and `op_delete_node` enumerating every node
they touch rather than only a subtree root, which is what makes this safe for the two structural
doors.

What it cost: select a group of twenty 4,000-character blocks and hold an arrow key. Every nudge
commits, the whole subtree lands in `affected`, and all twenty were re-shaped for a **translate** —
about 23 ms per keypress at a measured 1.17 ms per 4k-character shape, against a Windows key repeat
of ~30/s. The same on opacity, visibility, paint, lock and reorder, and on every undo and redo of
one. Not one glyph can move in any of them.

🚨 **Two halves, and either alone changes nothing — which is this entry's own correction to the
finding.** It said *"`DirtySet` itself is minimal (the `op_*` handlers insert only what they
touched)"*, and `op_set_transform` was running `for d in self.subtree_ids(id) { dirty.0.insert(d); }`
— performing by hand the same expansion `update`'s `collect_subtree` performs. So narrowing the text
pass moved no count at all until the op stopped duplicating it. The op dirties the node it changed
now; `Resolved::update` is `DirtySet`'s only consumer, which was checked before the narrowing.
**The review's fix sketch was the equality guard `set_kind` has** (§15 D592, next door) and the
answer is cheaper than that: the pass has no comparison in it at all, because the set it runs over is
already the set of nodes whose kind was written.

⚠️ **Four ops are not narrowed and still pay it.** `op_set_clip`, `op_set_mask`, `op_set_mask_mode`
and `op_set_geometry` each insert their whole subtree, and each for a real reason — a clip released
or a mask mode switched changes how everything under it is *drawn*, and a resized frame changes what
its children are clipped to — but the text pass cannot tell any of those reasons from a kind change,
so toggling *Clip content* on a frame holding twenty text blocks re-shapes all twenty exactly as the
nudge used to. **Revisit if a compositing toggle or a frame resize turns up in a measurement**:
the shape of the answer is a dirty set that says *why* a node is dirty, which is a much larger change
than this one and not worth making for a gesture nobody holds down.

⚠️ **Nothing that existed could see any of this.** `update`'s correctness is owned by a randomized
differential against `rebuild`, and the layouts produced are identical either way, so that test is
green under the bug and under the fix. `ondin_core::text::shapes()` is the observable that separates
them: a thread-local monotonic counter, `boolean::failures`' shape and its two arguments — a *count*
so brackets nest without treading on each other, thread-local because parley's engine is, so the
preview path and the edit path cannot report each other's work. 🚨 **It is counted in `shape` and not
in `layout`**, which was found the hard way while writing D592's test: `TextEdit::reshape` shapes
without going through `layout` at all, so a counter on `layout` reports **0** for a keystroke.

`ondin-core/tests/resolve.rs · a_translate_on_a_group_does_not_reshape_the_text_inside_it`, with the
initial `rebuild`'s count as the fixture assertion, a `SetText` as the control, and the descendant's
world transform asserted to have moved — a descendant that stopped following its parent is the way
this fix goes wrong. Both flips are run separately and each fails at **3 against 0**. The randomized
differential passes with the fix in, which is the only thing that can say the narrowed set is still
enough. §5.7 and §5.9 amended.

**D589 — A bare caret's character fields describe the run typing will join. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — `TypeSubject::resolve_at`, on the readout only.***

`[S6.2-L1-06]`, Medium. `TypeSubject::read` falls back to `0..len` for a caret with no selection.
That is right, and it is what §9.4 and §15 **D164** settle about the *write*: a bare-caret character
write sets the node's default and drops that attribute's overrides, because *"make it all 24pt"*
leaving a 16pt run behind is the worse answer. `shown` then resolved the attribute at `range.start`
— i.e. **byte 0**, whatever the caret was doing — and `mixed` is `self.partial && …`, which is
structurally `false` over a whole-node range, so nothing on the row said the number was a guess.

Measured on `"hello world"` with `Size(40)` over the first five bytes and a node default of 16: with
the caret at the end, the Size field read **40** and the next keystroke came out at **16**. The field
named a size the very next character contradicted, and a scrub started from it would have flattened
the whole node to 40 — which nobody asked for and which the panel gave no way to see coming.

**The resolve point is a field of its own now.** `TypeSubject::resolve_at: Option<usize>` is
`range.start` for a selection, and for a bare caret it is the byte to the caret's **left**, because
that is what an insertion inherits: `Spans::edited`'s `map_end` sends a span whose `end == at` to
`at + inserted`, and its `map_start` sends one whose `start == at` to `at + inserted` as well, so
typing joins the run that *ends* at the caret and never the one that begins there. `None` at byte 0,
where there is no run to the left and an insertion takes the node's defaults — read as
`self.style.get(kind)`. **`None` is a real answer rather than a missing one**, and byte 0 is the one
caret where "the value at the caret" and "the value typing inherits" disagree in the other
direction: byte 0 carries the 40pt span, and an insertion there does not join it.

⚠️ **The write is untouched and must be.** This is the readout, and `design-oracle` reports that
neither document had a passage on it — §9.4 rules on where a character write *goes* and said nothing
about what a field shows while the caret is bare. §9.4 carries the rule now.

`panels::typography::bare_caret_readout_tests`, two: the three carets the resolve point has — inside
the run, at the boundary and past it — plus byte 0, and a control that a selection still resolves at
its own start and an unedited node still reads byte 0. ⚠️ **The fixture asserts `!subject.partial` at
each caret**, because a caret that had somehow become partial would be answering a different question
and every number under it would be right for the wrong reason; the control's own fixture assertion is
the opposite, that its selection *is* ragged and can still say *mixed*. Flip, `resolve_at` put back
to `Some(self.range.start)` throughout: fails on the first assertion at 40 against 16, which is the
finding's own measurement.

**D588 — A paint-row reorder is a gesture `cancel_gesture` can find. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08;
Fix — one non-blinking term in the gate.***

`[S14.3-L1-02]`, Medium. There are two hand-written lists in that function — the gate that decides
whether anything is in flight, and the clearing below it — and they were out of step by one. The
clear had `paint_drag` all along, under a comment saying it is *"the fourth, for the same reason"* as
the layers-tree row drag; the gate never mentioned it, so the whole body was unreachable whenever a
paint reorder was the only gesture in flight.

🚨 **The one term that ever answered for it was `ctx.dragged_id()`, which is the blinking one this
function's own comment warns about.** egui clears `dragged` on the release of *any* button and
`cancel_gesture` runs on `button_pressed(Secondary)`, so a right-click whose press and release fall
in one rendered frame reads a snapshot that has already been cleared — at 60 fps, any click under
~16 ms, which is why the *slow* right-click worked and made this look like no bug at all. ⚠️ **And it
does not recover**: egui will not re-arm the drag while the primary stays down, so a second and
slower right-click failed too and one fast click made the reorder uncancellable for the rest of the
gesture. Measured: the release committed `[4.0, 9.0] → [9.0, 4.0]` with `undo_depth +1`, after two
cancels that were supposed to have abandoned it.

The fix is `|| self.paint_drag.is_some()` — a term of exactly the kind the comment asks for, and
absent whenever nothing is in flight, so the gate stays the strict no-op that leaves
right-click-to-remove-a-gradient-stop alone.
`app::paint_drag_cancel_tests::a_right_click_cancels_a_paint_row_reorder`, with an idle app as the
control so the flip cannot be read as the gate having been opened to everything. ⚠️ **The fixture
asserts `ctx.dragged_id()` is `None` first**: that is the state a one-frame right-click leaves
behind and the only one in which the gate's other terms have anything to say, so a test that did not
pin it would be measuring the pre-blink case — which worked before the fix and is not what the
finding is about. §9.4's list of hand-written clear lists is amended: this is the fourth omission of
that class and the first in a *gate* rather than in a clear.

**D785 — In-flight gesture state gets one owner, and the gate stops being a list. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-15; Fix — the narrow half of `[A2-L7-02]`, which stays open for the wide one.***

`[A2-L7-02]` is a Debt finding about `OndinApp` — 101 fields, 681 methods across twelve files, one
privacy scope — and **its own fix sketch names this move as the cheap one**: *"not a rewrite. The
cheap, targeted move that answers the named failure is to give in-flight gesture state one owner."*
That is what landed. **The wide half did not**, and this entry says so rather than leaving it to be
inferred: per-panel state structs, the field count and the single privacy scope are all untouched and
none of them is proposed here.

🚨 **The named failure is a `||` chain that went stale twice, and both times silently.**
`cancel_gesture`'s gate was hand-written over nine fields scattered through the 101. `[A1-L2-02]`
found it **two short** — `export_quality_scrub` and `guide_position_drag` — so a right-click to
cancel a scrub on the export-quality field or on the inspector's guide-position field **did nothing
at all, and the value committed on release**. Neither shows through `has_gesture_preview`, and for two
different reasons: `SetExports` never reaches `set_preview`, and `SetGuidePosition` is absorbed as a
no-op, so `overrides` stays empty and there was no second signal to fall back on. `paint_drag` had
been a third, §15 **D588**, covered only by the blinking `ctx.dragged_id()` term. **Three of that
chain's clauses had been added one at a time**, each after a field appeared elsewhere and nothing told
the gate — and the comment on one of them said as much: *"which is the shape of bug this whole list is
made of"*.

`app::InFlight` holds the **seven** values a gesture carries: `session_scrub`, `settings_scrub`,
`paint_drag`, `export_quality_scrub`, `grid_scrub`, `grid_paint`, `guide_position_drag`. **The whole
of the fix is `InFlight::any`**, which is `*self != Self::default()` — a `PartialEq` against
`Default`, and therefore **exhaustive by construction**. An eighth value a gesture holds is covered on
the day it is added to the struct, with nothing anywhere to remember. *That property, and not the
tidiness, is the reason it was worth moving fields out of `OndinApp` at all* — a `fn any(&self)` that
`or`ed seven names would be the same list in a better postcode.

⚠️ **`drag` and `layer_drag` stay on `OndinApp`, and the boundary is "a value a gesture is holding"
rather than "a gesture".** Three reasons, and they compose: `cancel_gesture` **acts** on those two —
it writes `Drag::None` and drops the dragged row — where everything in `InFlight` is read back by its
*own owner* on the `gesture_cancelled` flag; neither has ever been the one forgotten, being the two
fields any reader of a gesture bug looks at first; and `grep -rn 'self\.drag' crates/ondin-app/src`
reads **101**, so folding them in is about 150 renames buying nothing. A type whose membership rule is
*"everything that sounds like a gesture"* would have had to take them and would have been a worse
type for it.

⚠️ **Clearing is deliberately not in the type, and a later editor will want to put it there.** The
seven fields are **not** all dropped by the cancel: `grid_scrub` and `grid_paint` are, because their
in-flight value is on the canvas and nothing else will drop it, and the rest are read back through
`gesture_cancelled` — which is how a field that has to **restore** something gets the chance to.
`session_scrub` is the clearest case: it is the only record of what the typographic spans were, and a
cancel that had already zeroed it would have nothing to wind back. **A blanket
`*self = Self::default()` inside `InFlight` would read as the obvious completion of this change and
would take that away**, silently, in the direction nothing on screen shows.

*(Fixed and tested 2026-09-15; `[A2-L7-02]` **stays open** for the structural half. `panels::paint`'s
`PaintDrag` and `Slots` gain `PartialEq` so `any` can compare the whole struct; nothing compares two
*live* ones, and `Slots` is last frame's layout in `f32`, so equality on it is a question about pixels
rather than about the drag. **Two tests** in `app::in_flight_tests`, written as seven separate
`InFlight::default()`s rather than cumulatively, since setting them one on top of another leaves every
assertion after the first green for the first field's sake. 🚨 **Flipped with the exact shape that
caused the bug** — `any` rewritten as an `||` chain over six of the seven, omitting
`export_quality_scrub` — and it fails **both** the new predicate test *and* the pre-existing
behavioural `canvas::headless_app_tests::cancelling_needs_a_witness_and_our_two_do_not_blink`, which
drives the real `cancel_gesture`. **Two independent detectors for one defect, saying different
things**: one that the predicate is short, one that a user's right-click does nothing. ⚠️ **The new
test's own list of seven is itself hand-written and would go stale exactly as the chain did**, and its
doc says so — the difference is *where the staleness lands*. A chain that forgets a field is a cancel
that silently does nothing; a test that forgets one checks six of seven while the production answer
stays right by construction. §9.4's three-hand-written-lists paragraph is amended — the gate is no
longer one of them and the **clear** still is — as is its sentence naming `[A2-L7-02]`'s cost at every
site that needs the list. §5.3b, §9.3 and §9.4 each spelled one of these fields `OndinApp::<field>`
and now spell it `InFlight::<field>`. ⚠️ **Six older entries in this file still spell them that way and
are deliberately left** — D168, D274, D330, D387 and D535 among them — because each is a dated record
of what was decided and where the value lived, and rewriting a path inside one edits the evidence.
`grep -rn 'OndinApp::session_scrub\|OndinApp::grid_scrub\|OndinApp::settings_scrub\|OndinApp::guide_position_drag' docs/`
is the population, and **this entry is what they now resolve to.** Nothing struck from `roadmap.md`,
which carries no row on the gate.)*

**D587 — The I-beam is measured from the figure's middle, like the arc. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — one centre for both marks, and the test loops the scales.***

`[S17-L1-04]`, Medium. `cursor::text_on_path` builds its arc from `ccx = f64::from(w) / 2.0`, a
**length**, and built the I-beam's stem and serif from `cx = w / 2`, an **index**. The buffer's
mirror is `x ↔ w − 1 − x`, whose fixed point is `(w − 1) / 2`, so `cx` is that axis only when `w` is
odd — and `w = half_w * 2 + thick`, so only when `thick` is odd. `pt(v) = ((v * scale).round() as
i32).max(1)` makes `pt(1.0)` **even** at exactly 1.5×, 1.75×, 2.0× and 2.5×, the first three of
which are the display scales this project's own notes call the Windows norms. Measured over the
mirror: 0 lopsided texels at 1.0× and 1.25×, **16 at 1.5×, 16 at 1.75×, 22 at 2.0×**, and 0 at 2.5×
and 3.0× — 2.5× coming out clean only because `half_w`'s own parity shifts the axis back, which is
what makes it a control rather than a case.

**This is the function's own ⚠️ happening a second time.** That comment records the half-texel
between a length and an index being found and fixed **for the arc** — *"sampling texel middles
against a circle centred on an index put the arc's right end a whole row below its left, on a figure
that is symmetric by construction"* — and the beam was left on the index it had. So the two marks
were centred half a texel apart, and the serif, spanning `cx − serif ..= cx + serif`, was one column
right-heavy. Both marks test `(x + 0.5 − ccx).abs()` now. The cost is one extra serif column on an
even-width buffer, which is what symmetry means there: an even figure has no centre column, so a
symmetric serif has to be even too.

⚠️ **The test named for the symmetry ran at one scale.** It called `text_on_path(1.0)` and nothing
else — the one scale where `pt(1.0)` is odd and the parity happens to be right — while the two badge
tests four hundred lines up in the same module both loop `SCALES`. The habit and the constant were
already in the file; the test that most needed them was the one not using them. It loops **seven**
scales now: `SCALES`' five, plus 1.75 and 2.5 added at the call rather than to the constant, so the
badge tests keep the coverage they were written against. Flip, the beam built from `cx` again: fails
at *"at 1.5x, row 0 is lopsided at column 5"*, which is the site the finding predicted.

Neither document changed. `architecture.md` rules on which cursors are drawn and why (§9.2, §15 D9)
and nowhere on how one is centred; the *"sizes are in points and scaled"* rule lives in `cursor.rs`'s
own doc comments, and the parity note belongs beside it rather than in §9.2, because it is a fact
about `pt`'s rounding and not about the design.

**D586 — A preview strip too big for the backend is refused, and `MAX_RASTER_SIDE` moves to the crate
that owns the limit. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — two guards, and one number in one place.***

`[S21-L1-05]`, Low. Two guards, both needed, at the two ends of one call.

**The strip had a bound on one axis.** `fonts::preview::rasterize` capped the width at `MAX_STRIP_PT`
— a long family name is clipped by the row, because the useful part of a name is its beginning — and
left the **height** unbounded, on the reasonable-looking ground that a line of type at 15 pt is about
18 pt tall. The hazard is a font declaring a small `unitsPerEm` against maximal `ascender` and
`descender`: the spec allows `unitsPerEm` down to 16 and both metrics are `i16`, so a line-box ratio
of ~2,048 is representable, and 15 pt × 2,048 × ppp 2 is about 61,000 px. Inter measures 18.15 pt at
15 pt, a ratio of 1.21, so nothing in the tree comes near it.

🚨 **`ondin_render::rasterize_glyph_run` then cast both dimensions to `u16`, which is a silent wrap
and not a clamp.** Measured by the review: `rasterize_glyph_run(w=8, h=70000)` returns 142,848 bytes
— `70000 as u16` is 4464 — where the caller pairs that buffer with the untruncated numbers and
`ColorImage` wants 2,240,000, so epaint asserts. **On the UI thread, from one picker row, out of a
font's own metrics.** And the wrap is not the only cost: well below it the same arithmetic is a 128 MB
allocation for a row in a scrolling list, which `paint`'s own budget cannot catch — the progress
guarantee rasterizes the first strip of a frame *before* it looks at `FRAME_BUDGET`, deliberately, or
a machine slow enough to spend the whole budget on one strip would leave every row in the fallback
font for ever.

**The height is refused rather than clipped, and that asymmetry is the decision.** `MAX_STRIP_H_PT`
is `PREVIEW_PT * 6.0`, five times the widest real ratio, and a family whose line box exceeds it draws
its name in the UI font — the fallback `paint` already has for three other reasons. A strip is one
line: clipping the height the way the width is clipped would draw a *sliced* name, where a clipped
width is merely a shorter one. The size decision is lifted into `fn strip_px(width, height, ppp) ->
Option<(u32, u32)>` for D269's reason — no font in the tree has such metrics, so with the guard inline
the only test that could reach it would have to build an sfnt by hand.

**And the backend refuses too**, `rasterize_glyph_run` answering `Option<Vec<u8>>`. The two are not
one guard written twice: the caller's keeps a merely *large* strip from being an allocation nobody
asked for, and the backend's is the one that cannot be got round by a second caller.

🚨 **The bound is not `u16::MAX`, and the control is what said so.** Written first with
`u16::try_from`, the test's control at `65535 × 1` panicked inside `vello_common-0.2.0`'s
`util.rs:174` on an `Option::unwrap` — which is **D434**'s finding arriving at the second site
`[S21-L1-05]` had predicted (*"the same `as u16` mechanism as `[S8.2-L1-01]`, at a second site; a fix
for one should sweep for the other"*). So `MAX_RASTER_SIDE = 511 * 128` **moved** from
`ondin-export/src/png.rs` to `ondin-render/src/cpu.rs`, is re-exported from `ondin_render`, and
`png::MAX_RASTER_SIDE` is an alias keeping its own doc. The limit is the CPU backend's and this is the
crate that owns it; the alternative — the argument for the number living in `ondin-export` while
`ondin-render` made the same mistake one crate away — is how the two came to disagree in the first
place. **One number, one argument for it, two callers.**

⚠️ **D434's warning that neither vello constant is public still stands**, so an upgrade can silently
invalidate it and no gate here would notice. What stands in for one is a test that *renders at the
cap*, and there are two of them now rather than one: `ondin-export`'s
`a_raster_at_the_cap_renders_on_either_axis` and
`cpu::preview_tests::a_strip_too_big_for_the_backend_is_refused_rather_than_truncated`. The second
one's control renders `MAX_RASTER_SIDE × 1` and then checks the buffer against `w × h × 4`, because
*"returns `None` for a big number"* is satisfied by a function that returns `None` for everything, and
because the bound is **inclusive** — an off-by-one there would be `[S8.2-L1-01]` again. Flip,
`u16::try_from` put back to `as u16`: fails on *"a size past the backend's u16 must be refused"*,
having answered with a 142,848-byte buffer for a 70,000-pixel request.

`fonts::preview::tests::an_extreme_line_box_is_declined_and_a_long_name_is_only_clipped` is the other
half, and it is the one that says the two axes are guarded differently on purpose rather than by
accident. §7 and §9.4 amended; §6.3's note that `rasterize_glyph_run` keeps the detected SIMD level
now also says it can decline.

**D585 — A fetch failure is not a decoder verdict. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — `FaceFailure`,
and the downgrade on `Decode` only.***

`[S21-L1-04]`, Low. §5.4a's rule is about the **decoder**: *"a family whose file the decoder cannot
read falls back to the static cuts automatically"*, and `FaceSpec::variable`'s own doc says the same —
*"the one failure the service reacts to: if the variable file cannot be decoded, the static cuts are
tried."* `FontMsg::Failed` carried `family`, `key` and `variable` and **no reason**, and `poll`'s
`variable` arm wrote `entry.cut = None` unconditionally. So the rule was being applied to the network.

One 503 on `roboto:vf@latest/…woff2` made Roboto a **static** family for the rest of the session:
`text::family_axes("Roboto")` empty, so no `wght` or `wdth` rows in the Font tab; the static cuts in
place of the nine named instances; six files fetched where one would have done. ⚠️ **The downgrade is
unrecoverable in memory** — `entry.cut`'s only other writer is `fetch_catalog`, gated on
`CATALOG_MAX_AGE` and running at most twice a session — **and the disk catalog is untouched**, so a
restart fixed it and nothing anywhere said so. A transient failure had a permanent consequence that
looked like a fact about the typeface.

A private `enum FaceFailure { Fetch, Decode }`, and `load_face` returns `Result<Vec<u8>,
FaceFailure>`. `Fetch` says nothing about the face and must not be treated as a verdict on it, so the
family keeps its `cut` and the `ensure` beside the arm asks for the variable file again — which is
what reopening the picker ought to do.

⚠️ **A caught unwind counts as `Decode`, not `Fetch`.** `load_one_face`'s `catch_unwind` is D450's
guard, and by the time a decoder can panic the bytes are in hand — so calling an unwind a transport
failure would take the fallback away from the exact case the guard was written for, a woff2 this build
cannot read. The `FaceSource::File` arm distinguishes on the same principle rather than defaulting: a
read error is `Fetch`, because nothing has looked at a face, and a file that opens and is not sfnt is
`Decode`, which is the verdict the web arm reaches through `sfnt_from`.

`fonts::tests::a_variable_file_that_failed_to_download_is_still_a_variable_family`, with the `Decode`
case as an **in-test control**. That control is the point of the test rather than decoration:
asserting only the `Fetch` half is satisfied by a build that never downgrades at all, and a family
whose variable file genuinely cannot be read would then never fall back and simply not draw — the
worse of the two bugs. Flip, the `reason == FaceFailure::Decode` term removed: fails on *"a download
failure took the family's variable file away"*, `None` against `Some("standard")`, with the `Decode`
half still green.

§5.4a is amended rather than added to. The sentence was already right, and what it needed was for the
word *decoder* to be load-bearing where the code had read it as *"could not be had"*.

**D584 — A text session's base moves with the document. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`restyle_session` re-bases `original` onto the document.***

`[S19.2-L2-02]`, Medium. `TextSession::original` is *"content and both span lists as the document last
held them, so a session that changed nothing can be closed without creating an undo step"*. It was a
snapshot taken once at `begin_edit_text` and never touched again.

**Every one of the three helpers that re-open the editor exists because something outside the session
has just written to the very node it is editing** — `text_session_restyled`,
`text_session_restyled_after` and `restyle_session_with`, all through `restyle_session` — and every
one of them re-based the **editor** while none re-based `original`. So from the first such commit
onwards, `changed()` was comparing a re-based editor against a pre-session document and could only
answer yes. Measured: open a text node, type nothing, apply one character attribute from the Type
panel, press Escape — a *"Text updated"* toast for an edit that updated nothing, against §9.3's *"one
editing session is one undo step"*.

⚠️ **The document's content, and not the editor's, which is the whole care needed here.** A live
session is a commit *ahead* of the document — `text_session_restyled_after`'s own doc says so, which
is why it exists separately — so re-basing onto the editor makes `changed()` answer **no** for text
that has been typed and never committed, and Escape throws it away. That flip is run, and it is the
second test. Re-basing onto the document leaves the typed difference exactly where it is, which is
what makes this a *narrowing* of `changed()` rather than a change of its meaning.

⚠️ **The undo-step half of the finding was already unreachable, and the entry has to say so or the
finding's own measurement misleads the next reader.** It recorded `undo_depth 1 → 2 → 3`, with the
third step a `SetText` byte-identical to the panel's — and that half has been dead since **D428**,
whose `changes_nothing` guard refuses exactly this transaction at `commit_inner`. **What D428 cannot
refuse is the toast**: `finish_text_edit` calls `info("Text updated")` after `commit` returns, and an
absorbed commit returns `Ok`. So the visible remainder is a status line claiming an edit that did not
happen, and the depth assertion in the test is a **control** — it is there to say D428's guard is
still holding, not to say the fix worked.

Door (b) of the finding — an Undo taken under a live session being overwritten when the session
closes — is **not** closed here, and did not need to be: `[S16.4-L1-02]` had already closed it at its
own door by gating the top bar's Undo, Redo, Save and Open in `Mode::TextInsert`.

`canvas::session_rebase_tests`, two: the symptom, and the flip that pins which side `original` is
re-based onto. §9.3 amended — it stated the one-undo-step-per-session rule and said nothing about what
happens when something outside a session commits to the node, which is the state the rule was being
broken in.

**D583 — `rewrite_path`'s no-op guard compares canonical forms. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
both sides through `pen_anchors`, for the comparison only.***

`[S14.1-L1-02]`, Medium. `pen_path(&pen_anchors(&p, &[]))` is **not** `p` for the ordinary SVG
spelling of a closed shape, and that is the whole finding. `pen_outline` draws the closing segment
*and* emits `ClosePath`, so `MoveTo(0,0) LineTo(80,0) LineTo(80,60) ClosePath` — byte for byte what
`svg_in::node_ignoring` builds for a `<polygon>`, and what `BezPath::from_svg` gives for any `d`
ending in `Z` — comes back with an extra `LineTo(0,0)`.

`rewrite_path`'s no-op guard compared the stored path against the rewritten one **raw**. So a bare
*click* into the Appearance card's corner-radius field committed a `SetGeometry`, and the saved
outline grew a segment the user never drew. `pen_radii`'s trailing-zero trim is the same miss on the
other half of the comparison: a stored `[0, 0, 0]` is never `[]`.

**Comparing forward rather than normalising the model**, which is the other half of the choice D117
left open. Both sides go through `pen_anchors` → `pen_path`/`pen_radii` **for the comparison only**;
nothing about what is stored changes, so this is not a load-time normalisation and therefore not
invariant 9's migration. Nothing is lost by it either — the two forms differ only in a segment of zero
length and in radii that are already zero, so a `true` here is never a dropped edit, and a quad
canonicalises to the cubic with the same curve, which means a bare click on an imported quad stops
rewriting it as well.

⚠️ **`pen_path`'s own doc was wrong and is corrected.** It claimed the round trip was the identity *up
to* a quad elevated to a cubic and a closing duplicate folded away — two ways it moves, both of which
*remove* something. The third way **adds**: a closed subpath whose last point is not the first comes
back with the closing `LineTo` written out. That is the ordinary SVG spelling, so it is the common
case rather than a corner one, and being the one that adds is why it was the one nobody noticed.

**This amends D117 and D118.** D117 closed the *read* side — *"a `ClosePath` whose last point is
already the first folds"* — and left the write side emitting the segment, which is correct for
`pen_outline` and is what makes the round trip asymmetric; D117's other claim, that `rewrite_path` can
recognise a gesture that changed nothing by comparing the finished path against the stored one, was
then true only of paths already in `pen_path`'s output shape. D118's *"a click on a point was leaving
an empty undo step"* rests on that same comparison and inherited the same limit.

`tools::rewrite_no_op_tests`, three, with a fixture assertion that the round trip really does move —
without it the tests are about a path the guard never had trouble with — and a control that a real
radius edit still commits. Flip against the old raw comparison: both no-op tests fail, carrying the
extra `LineTo((0.0, 0.0))` in the message. §9.4's pen passage amended, which had enumerated two of the
three movements as though they were all of them.

**D582 — Releasing the primary over the layers tree landed nothing at all, for a day. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-08; Fix — admit the release frame and clear the stranded drag.***

A regression against **D471**, introduced by it on 2026-09-07 (`3e9b3ee`) and found while fixing
`[S15.1-L1-04]` next door. Not a review finding: nothing in the review saw it, and nothing in the
suite could.

D471 gave `drop_hint` a bare `return` on `!ui.input(|i| i.pointer.primary_down())`, so that a drag
stranded by the panel's own view-switch chord could neither paint nor land. But `layers_tree` clears
`LayerDrag::target` at the top of **every** frame and `drop_hint` is the only thing that re-derives
it — and egui clears `pointer.down[Primary]` on the frame it *processes* the release
(`egui-0.36.1/src/input_state/mod.rs:1203`).

🚨 **So the one frame that ends a drag was the one frame that could not resolve one.** From
2026-09-07, releasing the primary over the layers tree landed nothing: `finish_layer_drag` took the
drag, found `target: None` two lines in, and returned, silently. Measured both ways — with the
`return` in place a press-move-release over the tree leaves `undo_depth` at 0 and the root's child
list byte-identical; with the guard disabled the same events give status *"Reordered"* and the move.
The panel's whole point, dead, with every gate green.

The guard now reads both edges and **clears** rather than ignores:

```rust
let (down, released) = ui.input(|i| (i.pointer.primary_down(), i.pointer.primary_released()));
if !down && !released {
    self.layer_drag = None;
    return;
}
```

**Clearing is strictly stronger than D471's ignoring**, which is why admitting the release frame costs
nothing. A stranded drag meets an ordinary frame — no button down and no release — before any later
click can reach it, and dies there; D471 had to refuse the release frame *precisely because* it left
the drag live and merely unpainted. The class D471 closed stays closed, and the recovery on the
present-mode route is still here rather than at the view switch.

`drag_start_sync_tests::releasing_the_primary_over_the_tree_lands_the_drop` is new, and **nothing in
the suite drove a press, a move and a release end to end** — which is the entire hole.
`[S15.1-L1-04]`'s own probe used a *middle*-button release, which leaves the primary down, so
`drop_hint` runs and the target is there; the eight `drop_indent_tests` set `layer_drag` by hand and
never release at all. So a day-old regression in the panel's central gesture survived a review finding
written against the very function. Its fixture assertion is that the drag is in flight *with a target*
before the release, or a build that never resolves one passes. Flip, `!down && !released` narrowed
back to `!down`: fails here at `undo_depth 0`, and takes
`a_middle_button_release_does_not_land_a_layer_drag`'s control with it, which is that control doing
its job. `a_drag_with_no_button_behind_it_paints_nothing` stays green under **both** flips — it never
releases anything — and its doc now says so, because a green run there says nothing at all about this.

🚨 **The lesson is about frames and it generalises.** A guard written for one frame's question can be
wrong about *which frame* it runs on, and nothing in this workspace reads frame ordering: the code
compiles, the tests pass, the doc links resolve, and the behaviour is gone. D471's own test passes
either way. **The tell is a predicate over `pointer` state read in a function whose caller resets what
it writes each frame** — ask what that predicate says on the release frame specifically, because that
is the frame the feature exists for. D471 amended; §9.2 amended.

**D581 — All three selection doors in the row walk tell the panel, and the drag ends on the primary
button. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — two lines, in `layers.rs`.***

`[S15.1-L1-02]` and the button half of `[S15.1-L1-04]`, both Medium. Two one-line fixes in one file,
kept in one entry because they are the same shape: a rule the neighbouring code already followed and
one door that did not.

**The third selection door.** `layers_row` changes the selection from inside the walk at three
places — the click arm, the right-click arm, and the `resp.drag_started()` arm's `else` branch, which
`set_one`s a row that was not already selected so the drag carries something. The first two closed
with `self.layers_synced_selection = self.session.selection.ids().to_vec();` under a comment saying
exactly why — *"the panel already knows about the selection it just made, so `sync_tree_to_selection`
must not treat it as news and scroll the row the user is pointing at out from under them"* — and the
drag arm did not.

So `sync_tree_to_selection`, at the top of the next `layers_tree`, read the picked-up row as news, set
`scroll_layers_to_selection`, and `layers_row` consumed it in the same frame with
`ui.scroll_to_rect(rect, Some(Align::Center))`. That is gated on
`!ui.clip_rect().contains_rect(rect)`, which is why it is invisible in the middle of a list and bites
where it hurts most: **picking up a row that is only *partly* in the viewport scrolls the whole tree,
and every drop boundary in it, out from under a held pointer.** The finding measured 20.7 pt for the
drag against 0.0 for a click ending in the identical selection.

**The release check.** `layers_tree` ended a row drag on `ui.input(|i| i.pointer.any_released())` —
the workspace's only `any_released()`, against three `primary_released()` in `canvas.rs`. Clicking the
scroll wheel part-way through a row drag therefore landed the drop wherever the pointer happened to
be, and left the still-held primary controlling nothing. The **secondary** button was already answered
one layer up, `app::update` running `cancel_gesture` before the panels and that clearing `layer_drag`
by name, so the **middle** button was the one door with no answer at either end.

`layers::drag_start_sync_tests`, with the click as an in-fixture control. ⚠️ **The fixture assertion
is what stops the scroll test being vacuous**: a row wholly inside the viewport is never recentred at
all, so a fixture whose rows all fit passes with the fix removed, and the row is asserted to straddle
the clip edge before anything is claimed. Flip, the new `layers_synced_selection` line removed: fails
at `3.6296296` on the **fourth** offset, with the click control still at `0.0`. ⚠️ **That is not the
finding's 20.7, and the difference is the assertion's whole shape** — `scroll_to_rect` is animated, so
the offset arrives over several frames, and what is asserted is *zero on every frame* rather than a
magnitude. `lit_rows`, the helper that measures the row boxes, has to put `layers_synced_selection`
back after it selects, or the very bookkeeping under test starts the real run in the wrong state.

§9.2 amended: it described `target` being cleared every frame and the drop hint's button test, and
said nothing about which button ends the drag or about the panel telling itself what it just selected.

**D580 — One retarget for both picker doors. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — `retarget_after`,
called from the click door as well as the drag door.***

`[S14.5-L1-03]`, Medium. `valve_slot` called **both** `retarget_group_color` and
`retarget_mixed_paint`; `write_slot` called only the second. So a **click** on the hue strip, or a
preset, over a Group Colors row recoloured the fills and left `PaintSlot::GroupColor` naming a colour
the document no longer held — `slot_brush` → `group_color_shown` found nothing, and `picker_ui`'s
`let Some(brush) = … else { self.picker = None; return; }` shut the picker on the next frame.
**Dragging on the same strip worked**, because `picker::pointer_slot` routes a click to `write_slot`
and a drag to `valve_slot`: one control, two verbs, and the machinery on one of them. Measured with
the mixed row as the control in the same probe — `GroupColor([30,120,200,255])` unmoved after the
write and `slot_brush` not resolving, against `SelectionAll(Fill)` moving to `Selection(Fill, 0)` and
resolving — and the fills read back `[0.863, 0.157, 0.157, 1.0]`, so the key genuinely named a colour
nothing in the document had.

⚠️ **The click is not the rare door.** `write_slot` is reached from `pointer_slot`'s every ordinary
press, from the picker's kind tabs, from four places in the stop bar and from the hex field; the drag
door is the one that needs a control travelled across.

**Both retargets are one helper now** — `retarget_after(slot, &brush)` — called from both verbs, so
the two doors cannot carry different answers. `write_slot` clones its brush to call it, because
`slot_transaction` consumes one and the retarget has to read the other *after* the commit: a
`GroupColor` row is renamed by the colour that landed. `valve_slot`'s `committing` guard stays where
it is and deliberately does **not** move into the helper — a preview frame must not retarget, since
the row it would move to does not exist yet.

**The two cases are the same shape from opposite directions**, which is worth stating because the
record has them as separate stories: a `GroupColor` key **is** the colour, so changing the colour
renames the row; a `SelectionAll` slot is a stand-in for *disagreement*, so an edit that makes the
targets agree deletes it. Either way the picker is left pointing at a row that is no longer on screen.
Both doc comments already knew it — `retarget_mixed_paint`'s calls its own failure *"the failure
`retarget_group_color` exists to prevent, arrived at by another road"* — and both were true. Only one
of the pair was called from both doors.

**Nothing ruled on the asymmetry, and read against the code it was not immaterial.** §9.4 says of the
mixed row that *"`write_slot` **and** `valve_slot` call `retarget_mixed_paint`"* and, two panels
later, of Group Colors that *"`valve_slot` retargets the row and the picker onto the colour it
became"*; **D53** carries the same sentence. One slot naming both verbs and the other naming one reads
as a detail until you know the two verbs are the click door and the drag door. §9.4's Group Colors
passage was **false by omission** and is amended; D53's sentence is amended to point here.

`inspector::frame_fill_tests::a_click_over_a_group_colors_row_takes_the_picker_with_it`. Two
assertions, and the second is the one the user sees: the slot having moved is the mechanism,
`slot_brush` resolving is the picker *staying open*, and a retarget onto the wrong key passes the
first and fails the second. Flip, `retarget_after`'s `GroupColor` arm removed: fails on *"the slot
follows the colour it became"*, the key coming back as the old red `[235, 110, 90, 255]` against
`[60, 120, 220, 255]`. ⚠️ **There is no `SelectionAll` control here and the test says so** — the two
arms need different documents, and a fixture that reached neither would fail the `slot_brush`
assertion for the wrong reason. Its control is the fixture assertion *above* the write, that the Group
Colors row was on screen before it, which is what makes *"it resolves afterwards"* a statement about
the retarget rather than about a row that never existed. ⚠️ **Neither half of the pair was pinned by
anything until this test**: `[S14.5-L6-05]` had already flip-checked that deleting `write_slot`'s
*surviving* `retarget_mixed_paint` call left 973 of 973 tests green.

**D579 — Every tool clears `autopan_total` at both ends of a drag. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08;
Fix — one reset above the tool routing, on both edges.***

`[S19.2-L2-03]`, Medium. `autopan_total` is what `cancel_gesture` subtracts, and §9.4 defines it as
**this drag's** scrolling: *"a running total rather than a camera snapshot, so a zoom or a wheel-pan
made during the drag is left alone."* It had exactly two resets, and **neither was on the path of a
node, pen or image-edit gesture.** `normal_mode_input` returns at its `pen_input`, `node_input` and
`image_edit_input` arms *before* the `drag_started()` block the press-side reset lived in; and
`finish_drag`, whose head carries the release-side one, has **one production caller**, inside the same
function and below those same returns. `node_input` ends each of its drags with
`self.drag = Drag::None; self.session.commit(tx);` and never calls it. All five of its drag kinds —
`Handle`, `Points`, `PointBox`, `PointRotate`, `Segment` — answer `true` from `Drag::autopans`, so all
five accumulate.

🚨 **The release half is the one that costs a picture, and a press-side fix does not touch it.**
Measured: drag anchors into the right edge under the node tool until the view auto-scrolls, then let
go — a *completed* gesture, which correctly keeps the view where it scrolled to. Then scrub any
inspector field and right-click to cancel. **The view jumps back 42.231 units** it scrolled for a drag
that landed. Nothing presses on the canvas between the two, so no press-side reset can reach it; and a
second node drag adds to the leftover, so cancelling *that* one puts the view further back than the
gesture found it — the opposite of what cancel promises. The finding's table is five tools in one run:
`Select` and `Rect` at `(0,0)`, `Node`, `Pen` and `ImageEdit` at `(300,0)`.

One `if resp.drag_started() || resp.drag_stopped()` at the **head** of `normal_mode_input`, above the
tool routing, because above the routing is the only place every tool is still on the path.
`finish_drag`'s own reset **stays**: it is idempotent, and it is the sentence that says *why* — *"a
completed gesture keeps the view where it scrolled to — the layer is there now. Only a cancel unwinds
it."*

⚠️ **The ordering against the cancel was checked rather than assumed, and the load-bearing half is not
the one the code comment leads with.** A right-click's `cancel_gesture` runs from `OndinApp::ui`
*before* any panel is drawn, so the total is spent before this line can zero it — and it sets
`gesture_cancelled`, on which `normal_mode_input` bails four lines *above* the new reset, so on a
cancel frame the reset does not run at all. The comment's other clause, that a secondary press does
not stop a primary drag, is true of a *press* and not of a fast *click*: `typography::cancel_gate`
pins egui clearing `dragged` on the release of **any** button, and `drag_stopped` is derived from
`dragged` changing, so a right-click whose press and release land in one frame does make
`drag_stopped()` true. *Do not reorder `cancel_gesture` after the panels on the strength of that
clause* — it is the ordering that makes the case safe, not the claim.

`canvas::autopan_ownership_tests::every_tool_clears_the_autopan_total_at_both_ends_of_a_drag`, the
finding's table with both edges asserted per tool. `Select` and `Rect` are the controls in the same
run: they always cleared, being the two families that reach the old site. **Two flips, each biting its
own half.** The reset put back inside the `drag_started()` block below the routing fails on *"Node
clears on the press"* at `(300.0, 0.0)`, the finding's own number, with both controls green; dropping
only the `|| resp.drag_stopped()` fails on *"Node clears on the release"*, also at `(300.0, 0.0)` and
again with both controls green, because `Select` and `Rect` reach `finish_drag` and the other three do
not. ⚠️ **The first flip was predicted at the release assertion and bit at the press one** — the loop
asserts the press first and the tools run in order, so the first thing to go wrong is not the thing
the finding is about, and only the second flip separates them.
`headless_app_tests::app_with_two_rects` became `pub(super)` to be shared rather than copied: two
fixtures both claiming to be *the* two-rect app is how the assertions in one module quietly stop being
about the same document as those in the other.

**Neither document ruled on which gestures reset the accumulator**, read by hand rather than asked of
`design-oracle`. §9.4's passage says the total accumulates and that a cancel subtracts it and stops
there, and no §15 entry mentions the reset at all — the nearest is **D535**'s enumeration of what
`cancel_gesture` clears, which names `autopan_total` as a thing *spent* rather than a thing reset. A
gap, not a decision. §9.4 amended to say the total is cleared at both ends of one drag and where.

**D578 — The filter dropdown owns the keyboard while it is up. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`library_menu_open()` reused rather than a term added.***

`[S20.2-L1-01]`, Medium. The library's *All projects ⌄* dropdown owned no keyboard at all.
`dashboard_keys` returns early on ten things — the recovery card, the two confirmations, the *Move to
project* sheet, *New project*, *Edit project*, the library's Settings card, the rename field, the
search overlay and `egui_wants_keyboard_input` — and handles `Escape` for an eleventh, `dash.menu_for`.
**`dash.filter_open` was in neither list**, and `project_filter_menu` reads no key of its own: its only
exit was the pointer. Measured with the ⋮ menu as the passing control in the same probe, so the
difference is between the two and not between two runs — with the dropdown open, `Escape` **left it
open and cleared the card cursor behind it instead**, `Delete` opened the *Delete file* confirmation
**underneath** it, and an arrow stepped the cursor behind it.

**Two twins, one of them given a keyboard.** `project_filter_menu`'s own doc says it *is* the ⋮'s
shape — *"the shape `OndinApp::file_menu_popup` already uses on this screen"* — and `dashboard_keys`'
doc is written against exactly this case: *"Every guard is something that owns the keyboard while it
is up."* So this is not a rule that was traded away; it is a rule with one member of an enumeration
missing.

**The fix reuses `library_menu_open()` rather than adding a term**, which is the predicate D558's
eight pointer-side doors already ask — so the keyboard side cannot fall out of step with them, which
is the whole reason that predicate exists. D558's enumeration is **cross-referenced rather than
amended**: it is a list of *pointer* doors and is still true as written, with the keyboard now a
ninth caller of the same question. The `Escape` arm clears both `menu_for` and `filter_open`, so one
key shuts whichever is up.

🚨 **`library_menu_open`'s own doc still describes this as open, and it is the doc on the function the
fix calls.** Two paragraphs of it were written when the gap was live: *"The **filter dropdown** is the
one that reads nothing, and it is in no guard at all — not `library_keys_are_free`, not that early
return. So with it open the arrows, `Enter`, `Delete`, `F2` and `Ctrl+D` all still act on the grid
behind it … **That, alone, is the open finding**"*, and above it *"A pointer question"*, which is now
half of what the predicate is. Every gate is green on both, because a doc comment describing the
opposite of what the code does compiles perfectly. **This is the worst placement such a claim can
have** — the next reader of the guard reads the sentence saying the guard does not exist. ✅ **Fixed
the same day**, the enumeration of eight doors under it kept intact, and the repaired paragraph
records why the shape is likely: *a comment that describes a bug is the one most likely to survive its
fix, because the fix's author reads it as the statement of the problem rather than as a claim about
the code.* `dashboard_keys`' own *"the ⋮ menu is the one that does not merely block"* went with it —
it names both floating menus now — and the flip note three paragraphs down, which had been written
into the **next** test's doc comment (the `Ctrl+K` one, D542's), was moved back onto the test it is
about. ⚠️ **That last one is not a doc-comment theft and neither detector in `CLAUDE.md` can see it**:
both functions kept their own comments, and a flip note filed under the wrong name is simply
invisible to the person changing the thing it is about.

`design-oracle` had reported the area clean under G15 and the enumerations are why: `shortcuts.md`
§8a lists the guards verbatim and D374 repeats the list near-verbatim, **neither naming the filter
dropdown**, and **D369**, the entry that built the control, says nothing about keyboard ownership at
all. A gap, not a decision — and this also closes what the last three fix sessions have been carrying
as *"the fifth class of floating thing"*.

Three rows added to `dashboard::tests::the_keyboard_moves_the_selection_opens_it_and_asks_before_deleting`.
⚠️ **Two test traps, both found by an assertion failing rather than by reading.** `filter_open` cannot
be raised by clicking the control in a fixture with no projects — `project_filter` returns early and
*clears* it — and it does not survive a frame either, because `press` runs a whole `dashboard_ui`
whose header runs *after* `dashboard_keys` and clears the flag on the way past. So the flag is set
directly and **before every press**: one assignment covers exactly one press, and a version making
three presses on one assignment measured the guard once and nothing twice. Flip — the guard put back
to `menu_for.is_some()` — fails on the **first** of the three rows, the arrow one, Beta against
Alpha. ⚠️ **Predicted at the `Escape` assertion**, which is the one the finding's title is about;
the guard is one predicate for all three, so there is one flip site under three assertions and a
fourth row would not be independently covered either. §9.5, `shortcuts.md` §8a and D374 amended —
each of the three carried the *"the ⋮ menu is the one that does not merely block"* sentence, written
of the ⋮ alone.

**D577 — `rotate_node` splits, like every other transform-writing gesture. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — `split_geometry_scale` before the write, with `skew_to_handle`'s `SCALE_NOOP`
gate.***

`[S13.1-L2-04]`, Medium. `rotate_node` wrote `parent_world⁻¹ · turn_about(pivot, angle) · old_world`
straight into `SetTransform`. `P⁻¹ · R · P` is a rotation only when `P` is conformal; a **skewed**
parent makes it a general unimodular matrix, so the child stored a scale. Every *other*
transform-writing gesture in the file splits first — `resize_geometry`, `resize_selection`,
`scale_subtree`, `skew_to_handle`, `skew_selection` — and `resize_to_handle` writes a pure translation
onto the existing basis. This was the one that did not, and its own doc stated the formula and said
nothing about the split.

§5.6 is the rule it broke, verbatim: *"`transform` carries translation, rotation, skew and flip. **It
does not carry scale in normal editing.** Scale is the one factor kept out, and for a reason the
others do not share: a layer's size must be one number in one place (its geometry)."* `design-oracle`
reports **no §15 entry** covering `rotate_node` not splitting — D50 endorses the compose-and-project
mechanism and D52 scopes the split to *resize*, and §5.6's note that a **world** basis may carry
residual scale is a different claim about a different matrix.

🚨 **Nothing rendered wrong, which is why this survived — and the *next* gesture is where it is
paid.** The split reproduces the world placement exactly, so the pixels were right; what was wrong was
that the node's stored `size` went on reading `100 × 100` while it drew 223 units wide. Then a 0.006°
lean — `skew_to_handle`, a pointer moved one hundredth of a unit — ran the accumulated basis through
`split_geometry_scale` and moved the stored size to `145.47 × 68.74`. **The W/H fields jump 45% on a
gesture that asked for a hundredth of a degree**, and `resize_box_to` — *"make it 200 wide"* — has
quietly changed meaning. **A transform carrying scale is not a wrong picture, it is a wrong *number*,
and the number surfaces later and somewhere else**, which is the whole argument for §5.6 and is the
reason a rendering test could never have found this.

The `SCALE_NOOP` gate is `skew_to_handle`'s and is here for its reason: the factors come out of a
square root, so an ordinary rotation lands a few ulps off 1 and a tighter test would put a phantom
resize in the undo stack beside every turn.

`tools::tests::a_rotation_under_a_skewed_parent_leaves_the_scale_in_the_geometry`, with an unskewed row
as the control — without it a `split_geometry_scale` that always answered `(1, 1)` would pass, and so
would a build where `rotate_node` had stopped rotating. ⚠️ **The world-placement assertion is a control
and had to be written twice.** Comparing local point `(100, 0)` before and after fails by **61 units**
with the fix working perfectly, because the split moves scale into the geometry and the same local
coordinate then names a different place; it reads through the node's own `size` instead. **The corner
is what has to stay put — its local coordinate is not.** Flip, the split removed: fails on *"a rotation
under a skewed parent stores no scale"* at `(0.6197, 1.6138)` with both world-placement controls green
in the same run, which is the finding's shape exactly. ⚠️ **Not the finding's `(1.4547, 0.6875)`** —
the test leans by a unit shear and turns 30° about the rect's own centre where the finding turned about
the group's, so the residual is a different pair. Same fact; **neither number is a constant to check
against.**

⚠️ **The blast radius is wider than the function**: `rotate_node` is also `rotate_selection`'s
per-member step and the inspector's quarter-turn, so the split changes what those transactions contain
— a rotation may now carry geometry ops beside the transform. All 1099 `ondin-app` tests stay green.
No design section needed changing: §5.6 already said this and the code now obeys it.

**D576 — One drag-to-edge autoscroller, not two. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — the second one
deleted.***

`[S15.1-L1-01]`, Medium. The layers tree had **two** drag-to-edge autoscrollers, both reached every
frame a drag was live and on the identical y range. `app::layers_panel` runs its band
(`ui::edge_scroll_speed`, `LAYER_SCROLL_BAND`, `LAYER_SCROLL_MAX`, `* dt`, `ScrollAnimation::none()`)
immediately before calling `layers_tree`, inside the same `ScrollArea`; `layers_tree`'s second
statement called `autoscroll_while_dragging`, whose own 28pt/9pt linear ramp used plain
`scroll_with_delta`. Both read `ui.clip_rect()` and the tree's only margin is horizontal, so the two
bands sat on the same pixels.

`egui::Ui::scroll_with_delta_animation` **accumulates** (`state.scroll_delta.0 += delta`), so they
added, and three separate consequences were measured. **16.0 pt/frame, 960 pt/s at 60 Hz**, against
`LAYER_SCROLL_MAX`'s own doc — *"420 … points per second. Slower than the canvas: the target is one
20px row, not a region, so the last stretch has to be steerable rather than quick."* **1500 pt/s at
120 Hz**, because only one of the two was `dt`-scaled, which is the thing `* dt` exists to prevent.
And **the creep was gone**: the linear term is 4.8× the quadratic one 14pt into the band, against
`ui::edge_scroll_speed`'s stated design that *"`t²` keeps a creep available for most of the band"*.

⚠️ **The animation is last-write-wins, so the deleted one silently undid the other's decision.**
`layers_panel` passes `ScrollAnimation::none()` under a comment saying *"egui's default easing would
keep gliding after the hand stopped and overshoot the row being aimed at"*; the later plain
`scroll_with_delta` is the style default (`points_per_second: 1000.0`, `duration: 0.1..=0.3`), and
nothing in `crates/` sets `scroll_animation`. **The glide that comment says was removed was reinstated
one call later, every frame** — which is the cost of a second implementation that no gate can see, and
is worth more than the speed: a fix to the first one would have been a fix to the loser of a race.

**Both doc comments claimed to be the only implementation.** The deleted one said *"without this the
panel can only be reordered within one screenful"*, which was true — of the other. The record
describes one mechanism and it is `layers_panel`'s: §9.4 and D278's discussion say *"the layers tree's
drag-to-edge scroll while a row is dragged (§9.4, `ui::edge_scroll_speed`, the same curve as
`canvas::autopan`) lives *inside* that scroll area and is untouched"*. `autoscroll_while_dragging`
appears in no §15 entry and in neither document, so deleting it is the code catching up rather than a
choice between two designs; **D278 is cited from the deletion comment**, an old number reaching code
for the first time.

`layers::autoscroll_ownership_tests::the_tree_does_not_scroll_itself_when_a_drag_reaches_its_edge`,
which asserts the deletion as behaviour: the pointer past the far end of the band, eight frames, and
the offset must not move. ⚠️ **A flip that did not bite, and the reason is a fixture that could not
reach the state.** The first version parked the pointer above the **top** edge, where the autoscroller
scrolls content *down* to reveal what is above — and a `ScrollArea` at offset 0 has nothing above, so
egui clamps the delta to nothing. The flip stayed green with the deleted function fully restored and
running. Confirmed by probe rather than reasoned: the pointer was seen at `(150, -4)` against a clip
rect of `[0,0]-[300,120]` and the step computed to its full 9pt; the offset simply could not move.
Moved to the **bottom** edge, the flip fails on *"the tree scrolls itself on pass 1"* at `0.6666667`.
⚠️ **The offset lags by one frame** — `scroll_with_delta_animation` writes a delta the area consumes
on its next pass — so a single-frame test is green under the bug, and the failure is on pass 1 rather
than pass 0. A fixture assertion that 40 rows overflow a 120pt viewport is what stops the whole test
being vacuous. §9.4 amended.

**D575 — A nested `<tspan>` is a run like any other, at whatever depth. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08;
Fix — one piece per text node, not one per element.***

`[S7.1-L1-04]`, Medium. `fn text` walked `body.children()` and read exactly one level, so
`<text fill="black">a<tspan><tspan fill="#ff0000" font-size="40" font-weight="700">b</tspan></tspan></text>`
imported with **`spans: Spans([])`** — no colour, no size, no weight — where the identical markup one
level flatter gives three spans. `skipped` and `approximated` were both **empty**. ⚠️ **The text
arrived**, because the collection underneath was already `descendants()`, and that is precisely what
made the loss silent: the content was right and only the styling was gone, so nothing looked broken. A
nested *positioned* tspan was worse — one node where SVG places two.

**The module's own contract is what this restores.** `fn text`'s doc says *"Nothing on a `<tspan>` is
lost silently any more, which was this module's one breach of its own contract"* and D398 closed *"the
importer's last silent loss"*; neither carves out nesting, and a depth-one reader is exactly the
*"field read into `Style` and compared nowhere below"* shape that D398's own warning names.

**The shape is one piece per *text node*, not one per element**, and that is the load-bearing choice:
`TextPiece::Run` carries the innermost element its characters came from plus that element's fully
resolved `Style`, so `<tspan>x<tspan>y</tspan>z</tspan>` is three pieces and `z` correctly reads the
**outer** tspan's style. A per-element walk cannot express that at all — it would give `z` the inner
style or lose it — and no amount of recursion fixes it, which is why the interleaved case is asserted
rather than left to the reader. A `Break` is emitted *before* the pieces inside it, so a positioned
tspan starts its node and then contributes its own text to it. The old `if positioned { continue; }`
generalises to `if child == run_el { continue; }`, which covers three cases at once: the `<text>`'s
own leading text, a positioned tspan's own text — it *became* the run — and any tspan nested inside
the one that became it.

`svg_in::tests::a_nested_tspan_carries_its_style_like_a_flat_one`, with the flat spelling asserted in
the same run as the control, and `text_after_a_nested_tspan_reads_the_outer_ones_style`. ⚠️ **The
first attempt at the flip was faithful in colour and wrong in mechanism**: dropping the recursion *and*
using `children()` instead of `descendants()` loses the nested text as well, so it failed on a fixture
assertion three lines above the interesting one, at `"a"` against `"ab"` — proving that a reader which
drops nested text is broken, which nobody doubted. Rewritten as the code that actually shipped —
per-element, `descendants()` kept — it fails on *"a nested tspan carries its own style"* with
`Spans([])` against the flat spelling's three spans, **the finding's own measurement reproduced by the
flip**. ⚠️ **And a prediction was wrong.** The second test's flip was expected to bite at *"the tail
reads the outer tspan's size"* and bites at the **control** instead, `y` reading 12 where it should
read 40, because under a per-element flatten all three characters carry the outer style and the tail
assertion is green. So that assertion is **not** falsified by that flip; it pins the ordering a
per-text-node walk gives and nothing simpler produces a wrong answer for it. Left standing, recorded
so nobody reads it as the one with teeth. §7 amended.

**D574 — The click-away test asks the local box, like the I-beam. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
one expression, called rather than paraphrased.***

`[S12.4-L1-04]`, Medium. `text_mode_input` decided *"is this click inside the node"* from
`preview_world_bounds` — the **upright** world AABB — where the I-beam asks
`preview_local_box(id).contains(text_local(id, world))`, the node's own rectangle. For any rotation
that is not a multiple of 90° the first strictly contains the second, so in the corners between them
the pointer had already stopped being an I-beam and the click nevertheless kept the session open and
moved the caret. **The gesture that means *"I am done"* silently became *"put the caret at the
start"*.**

Measured on a 45° `"Hello world"` node over a 120×120 grid of screen points spanning its world AABB:
**1885 of 14400 disagree**, every one of them the same way round — the click said *inside* where the
cursor said *outside*, never the reverse. Upright, 0 of 14400, which is why nothing had ever seen it.

**D155 answered this question once and only for the cursor**, and gave the rotation as its reason: *"A
live session now owns the cursor over its own layer whatever tool opened it (`over_edited_text`,
against the node's *local* box so a rotated layer answers about its own rectangle)."* The
finish-or-not half was never moved with it, and `over_edited_text`'s own doc had gone on asserting
that the two *cannot* differ — the caret placement using the same mapping, so the cursor and what a
press would do could not disagree. **A doc comment claiming two things agree is worth exactly as much
as the number of expressions computing them**, and there were two. There is one now: the call site
calls `over_edited_text` rather than paraphrasing it. `design-oracle` found nothing in either document
stating which box a click-away should use, so **the two halves of one question were answered
deliberately once and by default once** — which is the whole shape of the finding, and the reason it
is a gap rather than a disagreement.

⚠️ **It narrows where a click ends the session, and the finding asked for the maintainer's eye once on
that account**: the corners between the two boxes now finish the edit where they used to move the
caret. **The narrowing is D155's rule reaching its other half rather than a new decision** — nothing
about which box is right is being settled here, only that both halves ask the same one.

`canvas::rotated_click_away_tests`, two tests.
`the_world_box_and_the_local_box_disagree_only_when_the_node_is_rotated` sweeps the grid and asserts
the **shape** of the result rather than the count — many under rotation, none upright, every
disagreement the same way round — because the number depends on the grid and on the shaped width,
where the shape does not; the upright row is the control that stops it passing against a predicate
which has stopped answering `true` anywhere.
`a_click_between_the_two_boxes_ends_the_session` drives a real pointer through `canvas_ui`, with a
click in the middle of the letters as the control, and its flip — the call site put back to
`preview_world_bounds(id).is_some_and(|b| b.contains(world))` — fails on *"a click outside the letters
ends the session"*, predicted correctly for once because there is only one assertion it can bite.

⚠️ **Two test-writing traps, both found the hard way and both recorded on the test.** The screen rect
`canvas_ui` allocates is **not** the one a test passes in `RawInput` — it comes off
`ui.available_size()` — so a point computed against the wrong rect lands outside the response and **no
click is delivered at all**, which reads exactly like the fix not working and which the control cannot
distinguish from it. And the camera has to be moved onto the fixture or the same thing happens. There
is now a fixture assertion that the point is on the canvas, which is what turns both into a failure
that names itself. `architecture.md` ruled on none of this and needed no change.

**D573 — A `<text>`'s chrome reaches every run it splits into. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — an
`over` element on `chrome`, composed rather than substituted.***

`[S7.1-L1-05]`, Medium. A positioned `<tspan>` becomes a node of its own — the rule
`a_positioned_tspan_starts_a_new_layer_and_a_bare_one_does_not` pins — and `chrome` was handed that
`<tspan>`, which carries none of `opacity`, `display`/`visibility` or `filter`. Measured:
`<text x=0 y=20 opacity="0.3" display="none">A<tspan x=0 y=60>B</tspan></text>` imports as two nodes,
the first with `SetOpacity 0.3` and `SetVisible false`, the second with **neither**, and `skipped`
empty. A diagram pasted from a file that hides a layer therefore arrived with half of that layer on
screen and nothing said why — a silent loss, which is the one thing `Import::skipped` exists to
prevent.

**This is the treatment the run's own *transform* already had**, arrived at separately and for the
same reason: `text_node` takes an `outer` transform rather than reading one off the element, on the
stated grounds that a `<tspan>` cannot carry one. The three chrome properties were never moved with
it. `chrome` takes an `over: Option<Node>` now, `text_node` passes the `<text>`, and the other three
call sites pass `None`.

⚠️ **It composes, it does not replace, and that is the difference between this fix and the obvious
one.** `opacity` on a `<tspan>` is legal and multiplies with its parent's, exactly as SVG nests it for
groups, so the test asserts `0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15`; a fix spelled *"read the `<text>` instead"* passes the
visibility half and silently drops every per-run fade. `display` and `visibility` are the degenerate
case of the same composition — either one hides. **`filter` is the one property that does not
compose**, two filters being a graph where the model holds one effect stack per node, so the run's own
wins if it states one and the `<text>`'s is used otherwise; a `<tspan filter=…>` is legal and rare
