where a `<text filter=…>` is ordinary, and before this it reached the first run only. `over` is
ignored when it is the same element as `el`, which is what keeps the first run's opacity from being
squared — asserted, not assumed.

`svg_in::tests::a_texts_own_chrome_reaches_every_run_it_splits_into`. Flips: `Some(text_el)` put back
to `None` gives `Some(1.0)` against `Some(0.3)`, and the product replaced by "outer wins" gives `0.3`
against `0.15`. ⚠️ **The first was predicted at the *visibility* assertion and bit at the opacity
one** — the two are one `if` apart in `chrome` and opacity is simply written first — which is the
fourth wrong flip-site prediction of the session.

**Neither document ruled on this and one of them now carries a pointer.** `architecture.md` said
nothing about how a `<text>`'s properties reach its runs; D394's second amendment does, and it is the
sentence to read against this one — *"a positioned `<tspan>` is the source of its own run's font, id
and opacity"*, written directly beside the observation that the `<text>`'s transform has to be passed
in. It is still true of the `<tspan>`'s own opacity and it was never the whole rule, the outer
element's multiplying into it; that amendment now says so. §7 amended.

**D572 — A zero `stdDeviation` and a `currentColor` flood are readable. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08;
Fix — `>= 0.0`, `current` threaded to `flood_color`, and a refusal that reads values instead of
presence.***

`[S7.2-L1-04]`, Medium. `deviation_of` answered `None` for anything but `dev > 0.0`, and all three of
its callers propagate that with `?` — so under D411's all-or-nothing-per-`<filter>` rule a stated zero
took the **whole filter** down. Measured before:
`<feDropShadow dx="1" dy="1" stdDeviation="0"/>` → 0 effects, `skipped: ["filter"]`. A hard-edged
offset shadow is an ordinary design idiom and `effect::Shadow` holds it exactly, `blur: 0.0`. The
`is_finite()` half of that guard was doing the junk-file job it was written for; `> 0.0` was a second,
stricter claim nothing had ever argued for. It is `>= 0.0` now, and **negative stays a refusal**,
which is what SVG says: a negative deviation is an error where a zero explicitly *disables* the
primitive.

**A lone `<feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="0"/>` now contributes no effect and no skip**, joining the
bare `<feOffset/>` on D411's list of identity primitives. That row is a *reporting* fix rather than a
rendering one — the spec's zero disables the primitive, so Ondin already drew the right picture and
merely claimed a filter had been dropped — and the assertion to watch is `skipped.is_empty()` rather
than the effect count, which does not move.

`flood-color="currentColor"` refused the whole filter for a different reason: `parse_paint_color` does
not know the keyword, because it is a **reference** and not a colour, so the `?` in `flood_color` took
the shadow and every primitive beside it. It resolves against the **referencing** element's `color`
now, which is what SVG says and is the same value `parse_paint` has always used for a `fill`; a
`<filter>` lives in `<defs>` and inherits nothing, so `current` had to be threaded from `chrome` down
through `effects_of` and `shadow_chain` rather than read where it is used.

🚨 **The half of this entry worth carrying: widening a reader opened a hole in a guard that read
*presence* rather than *effect*.** `shadow_chain` refuses a silhouette *"neither moved nor
softened"* — the model has no row for a shape restated in another colour — and that guard was
`!seen_offset && !seen_blur`. It was sound only because a zero `stdDeviation` refused the whole filter
one function away. With the zero legal, `feOffset dx="0" dy="0"` followed by
`feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="0"` is a chain with two primitives, both flags set and no effect at all:
a solid slab imported exactly on top of the artwork, which nothing downstream would object to, because
it is a perfectly valid shadow that happens to be invisible and un-findable. The guard is
`offset == Vec2::ZERO && blur == 0.0` now — the old condition wherever it was right and stricter only
where it was wrong, a missing primitive still landing there through the zero it was initialised to.
**`spread` is deliberately not in the test**, which keeps the rule exactly what it was: a chain whose
only content is an `feMorphology` was refused before and is refused now, and whether a spread-only halo
should import is a separate question nobody has measured and not one to answer inside a bug fix.

⚠️ **A flip that did not bite is what found that hole.** The first attempt kept the presence test and
split the blur flag into `read_blur`/`seen_blur`; all 79 `svg_in` tests stayed green **and so did the
new fixture**, because `feOffset` sets `seen_offset` whether or not it moves anything. The hole was one
primitive wider than the change that opened it, and only writing the fixture said so. ⚠️ **And two
flip-site predictions went wrong the same way**: both were aimed at the *loss* assertion — `fx.len()`,
the blur value — and both bit on the `skipped` assertion in front of it. **A refused filter reports
itself before it fails to be a shadow**, which is this file's own *put the loss before the mechanism*
advice arriving by luck rather than by design.

Three tests: `a_zero_deviation_is_a_hard_edge_rather_than_an_unreadable_filter`, four inputs with two
controls and the negative row; `a_chain_that_neither_moves_nor_softens_is_still_refused`, with two
controls, because a reader that had stopped reading chains at all would pass the refusal; and
`a_current_color_flood_resolves_against_the_referencing_elements_color`, which asserts the **colour**
and not merely the arrival — a fix resolving `currentColor` to black would pass *"a shadow arrives"*
and be wrong on every file that uses the keyword for the reason anyone uses it. **D411 is
cross-referenced rather than amended**: its enumeration of what `effects_of` reads is still true as
written, and the zero-deviation blur simply joins the identity case it already names. §7 amended.

**D571 — One `opsz` rule, on the function that runs it. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — the copy
nothing called is deleted and its coverage moved.***

`[S6.1-L3-04]`, Medium. `TextStyle::optical_size` had **zero production callers** — the only caller in
the workspace was its own test — while the value that actually reaches the shaper is computed by
`text::axis_settings`. So the tested copy was not the one that ran, and `dead_code` cannot say so: a
`pub` item in a library crate is API whatever calls it. **The two disagreed about exactly one case and
neither of them was driven on it**: `optical_size` **clamped** a stored coordinate to the axis range
where `axis_settings` passes it through raw.

**Settled in favour of pass-through**, on three grounds in order of weight. The panel already refuses
to *rewrite* a stored out-of-range value (§15 D425, `clamp_existing_to_range(false)`), so clamping here
would make the readout and the file disagree with the ink for no gain. The shaper clamps it anyway, so
nothing renders differently. And clamping `opsz` while passing `wght`, `wdth` and every other axis
through would be the same divergence in miniature, one function along. **The synthesized value is the
exception and is still clamped**, because it is not a coordinate anybody stored — it is the font size,
which has nothing to do with this axis's range and is routinely outside it.

**The old test's three value assertions were the only coverage the Manual arm had anywhere**, so they
are *moved* rather than deleted — onto
`text::tests::a_stored_opsz_reaches_the_shaper_raw_and_an_absent_one_tracks_the_size`, with the axis
handed in by hand, which is what makes the three ends of the range explicit and the Manual arm
assertable at all. ⚠️ **The reason first given for handing it in was *"Inter ships no `opsz`"*, and
that is false** (§15 D711, 2026-09-09): the bundled `Inter-Variable.ttf` ships `opsz` and `wght`, and
`text::family_axes`' own doc says so — *"bundled Inter's two faces carry the same `opsz`/`wght`"*.
The argument needs no font table read, because D711's defect could not have existed otherwise: it is
precisely the `opsz` this family *does* have being synthesized for one spelling of it and not the
other. Nothing about the fix or the test changes — the axis is still handed in by hand, and
`optical_size_auto_reaches_the_shaper` still drives `WGHT` — but the claim was carried into two
comments in `text.rs` and is wrong in both. `typography::tests::optical_size_is_auto_until_a_coordinate_is_typed` keeps the *predicate*
half and now says where the value half went. Flip: `axis.clamp(style.font_size)` replaced by
`style.font_size` gives `96` against `32`. ⚠️ **Predicted at the *Manual* assertion and wrong** — the
two arms read different inputs and only Auto touches the clamp.

Two smaller items went in the same sweep. `Length::with_amount` had zero mentions workspace-wide
including its own definition, and is deleted. `Spans::values_in`'s doc opened *"What the panel's
**mixed** state is computed from"* and named a caller it does not have: the panel asks `shared_in`, and
`shared_in` is `values_in`'s only caller anywhere. Harmless as prose and not as a lead — it is the
sentence that stops a reader looking for the mixed rule one function short of where the collapse to
`Option` actually happens.

**No design section needed changing.** Neither document rules on which function owns the `opsz` rule —
§9.4 names the Optical size row and its Auto/Manual mode and nothing under them — so the rule's home is
stated where it runs, in `axis_settings`' own doc, and this entry is the record that there was ever a
second copy.

**D570 — Leaving *Font* on a decoration thickness seeds what the face was drawing. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — `TextLayout::decoration_sizes`, threaded to the chip.***

`[S6.3-L1-01]`, Medium. `optional_length_field`'s unit chip cycles `auto → px → % → auto`, and its
`None` arm seeded `Px(0.0)` on the stated argument that *"the font's own value is not knowable here,
and a made-up number would move the ink"*. The premise was true when it was written and is no longer;
**the conclusion never followed from it either, because zero moves the ink further than any guess
could — it removes it.** `render::scene::decoration_path` and `core::text::crossings` each open by
refusing a band of zero height, so one click on the *Font* chip — the click that means *"show me this
in px"* — erased the underline, leaving `0.00 px` on screen and no number to guess back.

`next_line_height` had solved exactly this two fields away (§15 D162) and this field did not know.
**What was missing was the metric.** `TextLayout::line_height` had no decoration counterpart, and
`DecorationInk::band` cannot answer for one, because a band's height is what the *style* resolved to —
and on the node this is about, that is already the zero. `TextLayout::decoration_sizes` is
`(underline, strikethrough)` taken from the **first run**'s `run.metrics()`, pre-clamp and
pre-override, captured in `extract` in the walk that is already there rather than beside the
`decoration_ink` calls, which only run for a decoration that exists. The panel carries it on
`TypeSubject`, `optional_length_field` takes a `resolved: Option<f64>`, and `next_optional_length` is
factored out beside `next_line_height` for that function's reason: it is the decision, and the field
around it needs a `Ui`. Measured — Inter at 20pt reports `(1.3671875, 1.3671875)`, doubling at 40pt;
an empty node reports `None`; a face reporting zero is filtered back onto the old fallback rather than
allowed to pretend. ⚠️ **The two numbers are equal for Inter**, so no test claims they differ: they are
two fields because `run.metrics()` reports two, not because a measurement here separated them.

⚠️ **The *offset* field still passes `None` and still seeds zero, deliberately.** The face's own offset
is on the same metrics, but the panel's offset is positive-*up* against parley's convention (§15 D151),
and getting that sign wrong silently moves every underline in the document. Seeding zero on an offset
puts the band on the baseline, which is visible and recoverable; seeding zero on a thickness is not.
Asserted, so a later reader does not "finish the job" on a sign nobody has checked.

⚠️ **The two cycles differ, and a fix transplanted from the twin gets the unit wrong.** These fields run
`auto → px → %` where line height runs `auto → % → px`, so the arm that reads `None` here produces a
`Px` and the equivalent there produces an `Em` — and at 20pt `Em(1.37)` is a 27px underline with the
right number in it and nothing to say so. The panel test pins the unit for that reason.

`typography::tests::leaving_the_font_seeds_the_thickness_the_face_was_drawing` is the panel half;
`text::tests::a_shaped_node_reports_the_faces_own_decoration_thicknesses` and
`the_seeded_thickness_draws_a_band_where_zero_draws_none` are the core's, the second being what makes
this a *fix* rather than a different arbitrary number. Flips: the seed forced back to zero gives
`Some(Px(0.0))` against `Some(Px(1.3671875))`, and `decoration_sizes` never set in `extract` fails the
core test's `expect`. **Neither document ruled on this**: D151 covers the decoration sign convention
only, and D162's Auto-seeding rule is stated for line height and nothing else. §9.4 amended.

**D569 — The variable-axis number field is valved, and the valve keeps `clear_at_default`. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-08; Fix — `axis_valve` for the field too, with the flag threaded through it.***

`[S6.2-L1-04]`, Medium. `axis_field` discarded the `egui::Response` `value_field` hands back, so there
was nothing for a valve to key on, and wrote through `write_axis` → `apply_char_attrs`, the **click**
path. Measured: five frames of a prefix-strip drag gave `undo_depth 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5`, five
committed values the user never stopped on. That is §9.3's *"one gesture = one transaction = one undo
step"*, and it is §15 D108's bug still live on the one control the paragraph fields' fix never reached
— while `axis_slider`, two functions below in the same file, was already valved and carried a comment
saying why. ⚠️ **`write_axis`'s own `if value == current` guard could never have absorbed it**, which is
why nothing here looked wrong: `apply_char_attrs` sets no preview, so `current` is the last committed
value on every frame of the drag and the two are unequal every time.

The response is kept and routed through `axis_valve`. **The reset slot returns early on the immediate
`write_axis`**, the same fork `decoration_write` and `paragraph_length` already make: a click has no
drag for a falling edge to wait on, and a valve handed one would hold the edit until some later frame
the field happened to be engaged on.

**The second half is a real second change rather than plumbing.** `axis_valve` pushed a coordinate
**unconditionally**, so moving the field onto it would have started storing `wght=400` where the field
had always dropped it — silently, in the save format. `clear_at_default` is threaded into the valve and
passed from both callers: `true` from `axis_row`, where the reset slot lives, so that *"back to the
font's own value"* means **no coordinate** whichever of the two controls arrives at it; `false` from
`opsz_row`, where an absent coordinate is the **Auto** state and dropping one would silently change the
mode. ⚠️ **It also makes the two controls agree**, which is worth stating as a defect of its own:
before, sliding exactly onto the default stored a coordinate and typing the same number dropped it, so
the same axis at the same value saved two different files depending on which control set it.

⚠️ **This threaded the flag through the valve and left the *rule* written out twice** — the same eight
lines in `write_axis` and in `axis_valve` — of which only the valve's copy was ever reached by a test,
which is what D624 then warned readers about and D804 repaired: both arms call one free
`axis_coords_after` now, and the rule is pinned rather than the caller.

`panels::typography::axis_valve_tests` drives the field through real pointer and key events, undo depth
being a witness no single call can give. Three flips, each biting its own assertion and leaving the
other two green. The valve reverted to the immediate write: `undo_depth` **4** against 1.
`clear_at_default` removed from `axis_valve`: `Some(400.0)` against `None`, with the 500 control
staying green — ⚠️ **and since D804 that mutation has to be named by the argument and not by the
line**, `false` passed from `axis_valve` rather than a guard deleted in place, D803's lesson on a
second file. The reset arm's `return` removed: **green** — a finding rather than a failure, because
the frame a reset lands on is not an engaged one, so `char_valve`'s falling edge never fires and the
immediate write is the only one either way; the `return` is insurance against a reset clicked *during*
a scrub, which is reachable and which the test does not stage. ⚠️ **A measuring note, the same one D565
paid for**: `egui::Memory::request_focus` called before a frame leaves `gained_focus()` false, so the
typing test drives the field by real click, type and click-away rather than by requesting focus.
**Neither document ruled on this control.** §9.3 amended, where the standing claim that *"every
character-attribute field routes through `char_valve`"* was false for this one until now.

**D568 — Undo drops the point set and any live pen run. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — one
`document_rewound` on the app, because neither field lives on the session.***

`[S19.2-L1-01]`, Medium. `PointSet` holds `PointRef`s, which are `(subpath, anchor)` **indices**, and
`PointSet::retain_valid`'s own doc states the rule every structural edit in the node tool obeys —
*"deleting an anchor renumbers every anchor after it in that subpath, so a set kept across the edit
would silently point at the wrong points, near-miss selections being the kind of bug that only shows up
three edits later"*. `canvas::delete_points`, `remove_segments`, `insert_point`, `join_points` and
`end_pen_gesture` each clear or re-set it. **Undo and redo were the two doors with nothing.** Measured:
delete the middle anchor of a three-anchor path, click the last anchor, `Ctrl+Z` — the selection
survives the rewind and now names a *different* anchor, `(100,0)` where the user clicked `(100,100)`,
so one arrow tap moves the point nobody picked and the inspector's X/Y, `draw_points`' markers, align
and every drag read it, all of them going through `subject_points`.

⚠️ **`retain_valid` is the wrong guard here, and truncating would have hidden the bug rather than
closed it.** The failing case leaves every index in range, so a re-validation is a no-op; the test says
so directly, running `retain_valid(&[3])` against the restored path and showing that `(0, 1)` survives
it. **A test written against the index set would therefore have been green under the bug and green
under a fix that does not work**, which is why both assertions are on a *position* —
`selected_point_positions` — rather than on `points.on(id)`.

**`EditorSession` structurally could not have fixed this**: `points` and `pen` live on `OndinApp` and
not on the session, so `session.undo()` returns a `bool` now — *did the document move* — and the app
owns the clearing. ⚠️ **The `bool` is about the document and not about the keystroke**: `Ctrl+Z` at the
bottom of the stack must not deselect anything, and a second test pins that. `Selection` is the half
that does live on the session and needs none of this, being a set of `NodeId`s where `retain_existing`
is a truncation and a survivor still means the same layer.

**`PenState` is the second half and is worse than a stale reference.** `PenEdit::subpaths` is a
**snapshot** of every subpath the node had at the resume and `finish_pen` writes the whole list back
through `rewrite_path`, so a pen run spanning an undo *resurrects* the geometry the undo removed. It is
dropped for the argument `end_pen_gesture` already gives for the identical case, and the assertion is
that the pen is *gone* — a live `PenState` after a rewind is the bug whatever the next click does with
it.

Three flips, each biting its own assertion and leaving the other two green: `points.clear()` removed →
`[(100.0, 0.0)]` against `[]`, the predicted site for once, and only because the assertion is on the
position; `self.pen = None` removed → the pen assertion; the `if` made unconditional → the
bottom-of-stack test at `[]` against `[(100.0, 100.0)]`. `app::undo_rewind_tests`, three cases. **No
entry covered this.** The truncation rule is **D118**'s — *"`retain_valid` is a truncation, not a
remap … an index surviving an edit and pointing at a different anchor is the silent failure"* — and it
is stated there about edits inside the node tool, with D125's insert and the join's splice restating it
for their own gestures; **D114 is the per-anchor-identity argument D118 cites and does not mention
`PointSet` at all**, which is worth saying because the brief for this entry credited it with the rule.
Nothing anywhere ruled on what Undo does to a `PointSet`. §9.4 amended.

**D567 — A ghost's effect buffer is measured the way the committed one is. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — `ghost_ink`, which is `effect_bounds`' three arms for a node `Resolved` has never
seen.***

`[S11.1-L1-04]`, Medium. `paint_ghost`'s `ghost_effects` binding read
`geometry::local_path(&ghost.kind)?.bounding_box()`, and that is wrong in **two** ways at once —
neither of which the binding's own doc described, which is why it survived a paragraph of reasoning
sitting directly above it.

**The `?` was the first.** `local_path` answers `None` for `Root | Group | Text | Boolean`; the arm
is explicit and it is `None` on purpose, because those kinds have an outline that this argument
cannot build. So the whole computation was swallowed and a ghost of any of them pushed **no effect
layer at all**. Alt-dragging a copy of a shadowed *group* previewed flat for the entire drag and
gained its shadow at the instant of release — which is verbatim the twitch the binding's own comment
says it exists to prevent, and it was true of the commonest thing anyone Alt-drags. Measured against
`RenderOverrides::from_transaction` of the `InsertSubtree` the drag commits: 1 effect layer in the
previewed stream against 2 in the committed one.

**The outline's box is not the ink's box, and that is the second.**
`ondin_core::geometry::world_bounds_of_parts` is the function `Resolved` measures a leaf with —
**including the stroke expansion** — and `effect_bounds`' own comment says so in as many words, so
the committed path had it and the preview did not. A 40pt-stroked shadowed rect's ghost box came out
`(-12,-4)–(112,120)` against the committed `(-32,-24)–(132,140)`: 20 units short on every side,
exactly half the stroke, so the preview's shadow was cropped and snapped out at release.

`ghost_ink` gives the ghost `effect_bounds`' three arms, and each is there for its own reason. A
**container** has no outline of its own, so its box is its children's, each grown by that child's
own stack — the arm the old code had no equivalent of at all, and the expensive one, since
`res.inner_ink` is a cache lookup where this is a walk. It is affordable because a ghost forest is
what one gesture is dragging rather than the document. A **boolean**'s box is `GhostNode::path`, the
evaluated outline the ghost already carries, which is the ghost's share of what `Resolved` keeps for
a committed one — `world_bounds_of_parts` declines a boolean for the same reason `geometry::local_path`
does. Everything else goes through `world_bounds_of_parts`. The result is then grown by
`effect::escaped` and mapped back to local **exactly as `effect_bounds` does**, which is the point of
writing it as three arms rather than as one clever expression: the two halves of invariant 5 have to
land on the same number, and the cheapest way to be sure is for them to be the same arithmetic.
Hidden and masking children contribute nothing, which is the filter `ghost_mask_geometry` already
applies — a mask is not artwork, so a buffer sized to include one is sized for ink that is never laid
down.

The invariant is §4 invariant 5's corollary — the preview is what the commit produces — and the
existing harness is `overrides::assert_preview_matches_commit`, which compares the whole draw-call
stream rather than a count. `a_ghost_of_a_shadowed_group_previews_with_its_shadow` asserts the
committed effect-layer count **first**, so *"the ghost pushed one"* reads as a defect rather than as a
document that only has one shadow in it; `a_ghost_of_a_shadowed_stroked_shape_reserves_the_strokes_reach`
is the second half. **The two are flip-checked separately and each is green under the other's flip**:
making the container arm answer `None` is red on the first only, and putting the outline's box back
in the leaf arm is red on the second only, at `[-22,-14,122,80]` against `[-42,-34,142,100]` — 20
units all round. ⚠️ **The stroked case is the half a layer count cannot see**, one effect layer either
way, which is why this needed the stream comparison and why a test written to the first symptom would
have covered half the entry.

🚨 **The boolean arm's unwind stops being defensive and becomes live, and two places still say
otherwise.** `paint_ghost`'s `Boolean` early return pops the effect layer, and its comment justifies
writing the pop at all by saying it *"is saved today only by `geometry::local_path` answering `None`
for `Boolean`, so `ghost_effects` is always `None` here"* — a fact about a function two modules away,
recorded precisely so that *"the day a ghost boolean gets a path this does not become the same bug in
the preview"*. This entry is that day: `ghost_ink` answers a boolean ghost from its own `path`, so the
layer can now be pushed and the pop is the thing keeping D436's bug out of the preview. The code is
right and was right in advance, which is the reason for writing an unwind rather than arguing it away.
The prose is not: the comment in `scene.rs` still claims it cannot fire, and §6.2 carried the same
sentence. *§6.2 corrected 2026-09-08; fix the code comment*, and say there that the pop is
load-bearing rather than a precaution.

§6.2 amended in two places — the ghost's effect box, which said *"measured from the ghost's outline"*
and now names `ghost_ink`, and the `Boolean` unwind's stale reason.

**D566 — A hidden alpha mask masks nothing, which is what D282 already said. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — one named `visible`, asked by both arms.***

`[S11.1-L1-03]`, High. The `Shape` arm of `paint_node`'s mask branch routes through `mask_geometry`,
whose **first act** is a visibility test; the `Alpha` arm consulted no visibility at all and stored
`RunKind::Alpha(child)` unconditionally. `end_run` then pushes a `DestIn` layer and draws a node that
returns immediately for being invisible — and **an empty `DestIn` layer multiplies the run's alpha by
zero**. So switching a mask off did the one thing a mask is never allowed to do: it erased everything
the mask covered instead of revealing it. Measured in release on a 100×100 white mask over a 200×200
red rect, counting non-transparent pixels of a 220×220 render — `Shape` visible 10,000, hidden
**40,000**; `Alpha` visible 10,000, hidden **0**.

**And the rest of the app disagreed with the render, which is what settles this against the
counter-quote below.** With the alpha mask hidden and nothing drawn at all, `ondin_core::query::hit_test`
still returned the content node and `res.world_bounds(group)` was still the hidden mask's own box. One
document behaving three inconsistent ways at once is not a rendering mode being honest; it is one of
the three being wrong, and the other two agree with D282.

**The invariant is D282, quoted:** *"`None` means *masks nothing*, never 'clip everything away': a
**hidden mask**, an empty text node, an empty group and a cancelled boolean all answer it"*. A hidden
mask is the **first item on that list** and only the shape arm honoured it, through a line in a
function the alpha arm does not call.

⚠️ **State the counter-quote, so the next reader does not have to go and find it.** D282 also says
*"an alpha mask with **no ink** legitimately erases the run — that is the mode being honest, not a
case to guard"*, and read alone that sentence sanctions exactly the behaviour this entry removes. It
does not: it is about **content**, and the sentence above it is about the eye icon. A mask the user
has switched off has not been asked to erase anything. D282 covers both cases and this entry says so
rather than carving out an exception to it.

The fix is one named expression — `scene::visible(ov, node, id)`, the override-aware read
`mask_geometry` opened with — asked by both arms, **because the same line written twice in two arms
is how the two came to disagree in the first place**. In `paint_ghost` the `alpha_ghost` binding has
to stay `None` as well, or `end_run` pushes the `DestIn` layer the arm has just declined;
`ghost_mask_geometry` already refuses a hidden ghost on the `Shape` side, so without that half a
preview and its commit would part company exactly where `assert_preview_matches_commit` looks.

`ondin-render/tests/render.rs · a_hidden_mask_reveals_the_run_above_it_in_both_modes` asserts on the
**walk** rather than on pixels: `mask_layers` counts the `DestIn` composite itself, so a hidden alpha
mask that pushes no mask layer is the mechanism rather than a consequence of it. The visible row is
the control — without it, "0 mask layers" is equally consistent with a walk that stopped compositing
altogether.

⚠️ **Flip-checked, and it bit somewhere other than predicted.** Dropping the `visible(…)` term was
expected to fail on the fill count; it fails on `mask_layers`, `(1, 1, 0)` against `(1, 0, 0)`. The
fill count is **1 either way** — the hidden mask paints nothing whether or not a composite is opened
for it, and the empty layer multiplies the alpha away *after* the run has been drawn. So the pixels
vanish while the walk still records one fill, and `mask_layers` is the only assertion here with
teeth: **a test written from the reported symptom — "nothing is on screen" — would have counted fills
and gone green.**

§6.2 amended: the asymmetry it records is about ink and not about the eye icon, and it now says which.

**D565 — The custom dash-list field writes only what the user typed. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08;
Fix — the `lost_focus` arm compares the text, not the parsed list.***

`[S14.3-L1-04]`, Low. On `lost_focus` `inspector::dash_list_field` handed back
`Some(Stroke { dashes, .. })` for **any** parseable text — including the text it had printed itself a
moment earlier — with no comparison of any kind.

⚠️ **Half of the reported failure was already closed before it was read, and this entry says so
rather than taking credit for it.** The finding measured a bare click in and out as `undo_depth +1`
on a single layer and `+0` over a selection, and attributed the asymmetry to `write_strokes`'
`PaintScope::Node` arm having no equality test where `ondin_core::set_strokes_all` has one.
`Transaction::changes_nothing` (**D428**) absorbs an identical `SetStrokes` at `session::commit_inner`,
and `write_strokes` commits through `commit_edit` → `session::commit`, so both arms are covered and
that half of the finding is gone.

**What D428 cannot absorb is a write that genuinely changes the document, and the round trip is
lossy.** `inspector::dash_list_text` prints a number whose fractional part is within `1e-9` of zero
as `d.round()` — deliberately, because a pattern is typed as whole numbers far more often than not
and `5.0, 10.0` reads as something the field did to it. So a `stroke-dasharray` imported from SVG as
`5.0000000001` was silently rewritten to `5` by opening the dash popover and closing it again.
Comparing the **parsed lists** cannot catch that: they genuinely differ, which is the point.

The arm compares the *text* against `dash_list_text(&s.dashes)`, which asks the only question that
means anything here — *is what is in the box what this value looks like* — and answers no-op for the
bare click while leaving every real edit through. A retyping that differs only in spacing still
writes, and D428 absorbs it at the commit, which is the right division: the field decides whether the
user said anything and the transaction layer decides whether it changed anything.

This is `[S14.1-L1-02]`'s shape — `tools::rewrite_path` comparing a round-tripped path against a
stored one with no canonical-form rule — **met from the other side**: there the comparison existed and
had no canonical form, here there was no comparison at all. Worth carrying together, because the fix
in each direction is the same question asked once.

`panels::inspector::dash_list_field_tests::opening_the_dash_list_and_closing_it_does_not_round_the_numbers`
asserts the fixture really is in the lossy state first — that `dash_list_text` prints `5, 10` and that
parsing it back does *not* give `[5.0000000001, 10]` — without which a `dash_list_text` that started
printing full precision would make the test pass while asserting nothing. Flip-checked by dropping the
`text != dash_list_text(&s.dashes)` term: red at the first assertion, handing back `[5, 10]`, the
reported symptom. `a_dash_list_the_user_retypes_still_reaches_the_stroke` is the control that says the
field has not gone inert.

⚠️ **A measuring note worth keeping.** `egui::Memory::request_focus` called *before* a frame leaves
`Response::gained_focus` **false** — egui asks whether the id was focused last frame, and the request
has already made it so by the time the frame starts — so driving the field's *entry* takes real
pointer events. The test stages `stroke_dash_text` to exactly what `gained_focus` would have put
there, asserts that equivalence in the fixture, and drives only the `lost_focus` arm, which is the
arm the entry is about.

§9.4 amended, and D428 with it.

**D564 — The gradient chip clamps its stops the way the canvas clamps them. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — D455's rule, spelled once, at the fourth door.***

`[S18.2-L1-03]`, Low. `ui::paint_ramp`'s doc stated *"offset 0..1, **sorted**"* as a precondition, and
the body neither sorted, clamped nor asserted — while **nothing on the read path established it**.
`panels::paint::with_stops` sorts on the *write* path, so a gradient the user has touched is fine;
`panels::paint::stops_of` hands an imported list over verbatim. Measured through `ctx.run_ui`, reading
the mesh's column vertices back out: the control `[(0.0, blue), (1.0, red)]` builds columns at x
`[0, 0, 100, 100]` with colours `[blue, blue, red, red]`, and `[(1.0, red), (0.0, blue)]` — which is
what a `<linearGradient>` with descending offsets imports as — built `[0, **100**, **0**, 100]`. Two
of the four triangles wound backwards, and the chip painted the ramp mirrored.

🚨 **This is D455's fourth door and it was missed.** D455 put `make_stops_monotonic` on the importer,
the renderer and the SVG writer, and picked SVG's rule — *"each gradient offset is required to be
equal to or greater than the previous"* — over a **sort**, on the argument that a file is to be read
rather than guessed at. The chip is the fourth reader: `inspector::paint_row`'s swatch and
`typography`'s, both through `ui::Swatch::Ramp`, plus `picker::preview_chip` and `picker::stop_bar`,
all funnel through `paint_ramp`. So **one document was drawn two ways in one frame** — the swatch
mirrored, the artwork beside it clamped — and the swatch is the control the user checks the artwork
against. It is exactly the shape of the note D455 already left standing in `ondin-export/src/svg.rs`,
*"the third door of §15 D455, and the one that was missed"*, which is now a family of two.

Rather than spell the running maximum a second time — which would have been **G8**'s own shape inside
the entry that is *about* a rule living in four places — `make_stops_monotonic`'s step is named
`ondin_core::image::monotonic_offset(&mut hi, offset)` and both callers go through it, so the two
cannot drift. `paint_ramp`'s doc no longer states a precondition nothing establishes.

`ui::ramp_tests::a_descending_ramp_is_clamped_the_way_the_canvas_clamps_it`. ⚠️ **The assertion is
that the columns are non-decreasing, not that the left edge is red.** The second is true and is a
consequence of *this* input; the first is the property — a mesh whose columns walk backwards is a
folded ramp whatever colours it happens to carry, and a three-stop fixture would satisfy a left-edge
assertion while still folding in the middle. The ascending row is the control, and it is also what
stops a "fix" that sorted: a sort and a clamp give different pictures (D455's own argument) and the
ascending row is unchanged under either, so it is the descending row that has to say which rule was
applied. Flip-checked by dropping the `monotonic_offset` call — red at the non-decreasing assertion,
reading `0` after `100`.

⚠️ **And it settles the one thing the finding could not.** The finding filed itself as *"the function
violating its own stated contract"*, because the **canvas** half was never measured. It is measured:
`ondin-export/tests/png.rs · a_gradient_with_descending_stops_draws_the_ramp_svg_says_it_means`
renders the clamped reading through `VelloCpuRenderer`. So this was a genuine chip/canvas
**divergence** rather than a contract violation — which is worth more, because a contract nobody
depends on can be deleted and a divergence cannot.

§5.5a amended: its *"asked at three doors, and no one of them covers another"* now names four, and
says why the chip is a door rather than a consumer of one.

**D563 — A boolean's hover outline is its own silhouette, and `Resolved::local_path` finally has the
caller §9.4 always claimed it had. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — the wrapper, and a `Boolean`
arm under it.***

`[S12.4-L2-02]`, Medium. `canvas::stroke_outlines` asked the bare `ondin_core::geometry::local_path`,
which returns `None` for a `Boolean` **on purpose** — a boolean's outline is no more a function of
its kind than a text layout is, and §9.4 says so — and the `match` under it had arms for `Text` and
`Artboard` and none for `Boolean`. So a boolean fell into the container arm, the one written for a
`Group`, and its hover and key-layer ring was drawn as **every operand's full outline**: an
`Intersect` of two 100 × 100 rects offset by 50 traced `(0,0)–(150,100)` where the artwork is
`(50,0)–(100,100)`. Three times too wide, two shapes painted instead of one, edges that are nowhere
on the drawing — and reached by the ordinary hover, since `pick_preview` with no modifier hands
`hover_target` the outermost container. `draw_key_outline` had it through the same function.

This is **D93**'s generalisation — *"any new `is_…(kind)` reading `local_path` owes a `Boolean` arm"*
— reaching `ondin-app` for the first time; D93's own three sites are in `ondin-core` and
`ondin-export`. It is also the third member of the review's *"`Boolean` falls through a kind list"*
family, after the scene walk's subtree cull (**D536**) and `group_chain`'s untested boolean arm
(**D503**), which is `CLAUDE.md`'s named `matches!(kind` sweep hazard one crate over from where it
was last swept.

**Two parts, and they are not redundant.** `stroke_outlines` calls
`self.session.resolved.local_path(&self.session.doc, id)`, which is the wrapper §9.4 mandates, with
`Artboard` keeping its early-out for D144's reason — a frame's outline and its selection quad are the
same rectangle, so routing it through `local_path` would be a second drawing of one mark. And
`NodeKind::Boolean` joins the `Text | Artboard` arm, so a boolean with **no** derived outline —
legitimately empty, or abandoned (**D239**) — is traced by its box rather than falling to the
container arm. There is still something under the pointer, and the box is what the selection outline
draws for it anyway, so the two marks agree.

⚠️ **The two halves were flip-checked separately and the second flip did not bite on the first test,
which is what turned the fixture into an L.** With `Resolved::local_path` in front of it the `match`
arm never runs for a boolean that *has* a silhouette; and the finding's own `Intersect`-of-two-rects
result is a **rectangle**, so the `match` arm alone — which traces the selection *quad* — passes a
box-and-count assertion with the real fix reverted. `canvas::boolean_outline_tests::a_booleans_outline_is_its_own_silhouette_and_not_its_operands`
therefore uses a `Subtract` L and asserts three things, each load-bearing for a different half: the
box catches the operand outlines, which reach `(0,0)–(150,150)`; the **shape count** catches a fix
that drew the right outline and left the operands under it, which the box cannot see because the
union of a shape and something it contains is the same box; and the **bend at `(50,50)`** — strictly
inside its own bounding box, where a quad has no point — catches the `match` arm doing the work
alone. A plain rect operand is the control that says the probe can report agreement.
`a_boolean_with_no_result_is_traced_by_its_box_and_not_by_its_operands` is the second half, on two
disjoint rects intersected.

⚠️ **A deliberate limit, recorded rather than closed.** The geometry is **committed** and the
transform is **previewed** — `node` comes from `session.doc` and not from `display_node`, which is
what this function already did — so a boolean whose operand is mid-drag traces its last committed
silhouette under a live transform. *Revisit if that reads wrong on screen*;
`session::preview_local_box` shows the shape it would take.

§9.4 amended. Its *"`Resolved::local_path` is the canvas's"* was false as written for as long as it
stood: the wrapper's only caller was `Resolved::mask_path`, and no gate could have said so — it is a
`pub` item in `ondin-core`, where `dead_code` never fires however many callers an item has lost. It
has two now.

**D562 — The inspector's Group and Ungroup buttons call the verb instead of re-implementing it.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — two functions deleted, two call sites rerouted.***

`[S14.5-L1-04]`, Medium, group **G8**. `ungroup_selected_from_panel` was a six-line second
implementation of `OndinApp::ungroup_selection`, and the two had diverged in the **aftermath**, which
no gate looks at. Measured down both doors on one fixture — a group holding one rect — the keyboard
door left the freed layer selected and said *"Ungrouped"*; the panel's left the selection **empty**,
dropping the user into the empty-canvas card, said nothing at all, and discarded `build::ungroup`'s
`Err`, so a refusal was silent. It also committed inside a loop, which is the per-container undo step
**D521** took out of `ungroup_selection`: two containers dissolved from the panel needed two
`Ctrl+Z`, and a refusal on the second left the first already gone under a status line that never
appeared.

`group_selected_from_panel` was the same shape with a smaller divergence — only the committer — and
is deleted too, on the argument that a pair differing only in the committer is a pair the day before
it matters. **G8's rule held**: the `app.rs` copy is the one with a test caller, so it is the one
that survives.

🚨 **The committer the group copy used was `commit_edit`, and dropping it is a real change rather
than a tidy.** `commit_edit` arms the selection-chrome hide (**D128**) and `session.commit` does not,
so the identity row's two buttons now behave exactly as `Ctrl+G` and `Ctrl+Shift+G` always have —
which is this entry's whole point — at the cost of putting two inspector controls outside the rule
that *"every inspector control commits through `OndinApp::commit_edit` or `edit_valve`"*. ⚠️ **And
that rule's own enforcement cannot see them.** D128 states it as *"the only `session.commit` left
under `panels/` is in `layers.rs`"*, which is a grep over one directory, and these two reach
`session.commit` through an `OndinApp` method instead — so the rule reads as unbroken and is not.
**Settled the same day: the third exception is *named*, and `session.commit` is the right committer
for it.** Grouping does not change one pixel of the artwork, so there is nothing to get the selection
box out of the way *for*, and the old panel copy's `commit_edit` was the wrong half rather than the
half worth keeping. `commit_edit`'s own doc now enumerates three, says why the predicate cannot be
left to decide it — `Transaction::changes_ink` answers `true` all the same, classifying `CreateNode`
and `Reparent` by op rather than by outcome, which is right for its own purpose — and records that
D128's grep still passes and therefore cannot see this. *Keep.*

`app::ungroup_tests::ungrouping_selects_the_freed_layer_and_says_so` asserts the aftermath the panel
copy got wrong, on the finding's own single-container fixture — where "the selection is empty
afterwards" reads as an ordinary deselect rather than as a bug — with the fixture's own state
asserted first. The flip is the status line: dropping `session.info("Ungrouped")` is red at the last
assertion and green at every other one, which is the panel copy's exact signature. There is
deliberately **no** test of the button itself; the click site is one line inside `inspector_ui`'s
identity row, and what replaces a test is that there is nothing left to disagree.

⚠️ **Two stale names came out of the deletion and neither was a `[link]`.** `inspector::group_actions`'
doc named `ungroup_selected_from_panel` in plain backticks — D319's convention, correctly applied, and
therefore a name `cargo doc` has nothing to resolve — and §9.4 named it in prose, where no gate looks
at all. Both were found by grepping the deleted name, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s other half of the
deletion rule and the only thing that finds either.

§9.4 amended in two places — the committer rule and the identity row's own paragraph.

**D561 — Entering the crop on a `Fit` picture moves it, and cover is the closest rectangle a crop can
name. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Keep the code, fix the record.***

`[S12.3-L1-03]`, Low. `canvas::crop_and_limit` seeds every non-`Crop` fill from
`ImageRef::cover_crop`, and its doc promised *"A picture that has never been cropped starts where the
eye already is"*. For `Fill` that is exact and there is a test that says so —
`entering_crop_at_its_cover_rectangle_draws_exactly_what_fill_drew`, which compares the two
`framing`s corner by corner. For `Fit` it is false: a 400 × 300 picture letterboxed in a 100 × 100 frame at `(0,12.5)–(100,87.5)` becomes
`(-16.67,0)–(116.67,100)` on the first previewed frame — 33% larger, and 33 units of width outside
the frame, from a mode whose entire job is not to change the picture.

🚨 **The finding's preferred fix is impossible, and working that out is the result.** A `Crop`
framing maps its rectangle onto the **whole** frame, so reproducing a letterbox needs a crop
rectangle *larger than the source* — and `ondin_core::crop_clamped` shrinks any such rectangle back
about its own centre, uniformly, before it can be stored. There is no representable seed that leaves
a `Fit` picture where it was, which makes this a limit of the model rather than a defect in the seed.

What replaces the promise is a stronger statement, now asserted: **`crop_clamped` of the exact `Fit`
rectangle *is* `cover_crop`**, to the last bit, at every one of the eight orientations. So cover is
not a convenient seed but the closest one that exists, and that is a better thing to be able to say
than the guarantee it replaces.

The exact rectangle is read off `ImageRef::picture_box` — where the whole picture actually lands,
normalised the way a crop is — rather than re-derived from aspect ratios, which would be this file's
own arithmetic checked against itself. ⚠️ **The `Fill` row is the control that makes the derivation
credible**: there the exact rectangle needs no clamping at all and equals `cover_crop` on its own, so
the equality below cannot be an artefact of clamping everything onto one rectangle.

⚠️ **Flip-checked, and it bit at the control rather than where it was aimed.** `cover_crop`'s `.max`
turned into `.min` — cover made contain, which is the implementation somebody would actually have
written — fails the *Fill* row first, at `(-0.5,0)–(1.5,1)` against an exact `(0,0.25)–(1,0.75)`, so
the clamped assertion never runs. The control is not decoration here; it is the assertion with the
teeth. `ondin_core::image::tests::a_fit_pictures_exact_crop_leaves_the_source_and_clamps_to_the_cover_one`.

`crop_and_limit`'s doc now says a `Fit` picture moves and why the model cannot honour the old
promise. **Both documents were silent on the non-`Crop` seed** — D268 sanctions only the mode being
*forced*, which is a different question — and §5.5a carried the general claim that picking the mode
changes nothing on screen. §5.5a amended.

**D560 — An endpoint that already carries a handle gets no second one either. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-08; Fix — the endpoint question asked before the mirror, not after.***

`[S13.2-L2-04]`, Medium. `tools::smoothed_handles`' *already shaped* early return — mirror the handle
that was aimed on purpose, keeping the longer one — ran **before** the function worked out whether
the anchor is an endpoint. So the two arms at the bottom that deliberately answer `Vec2::ZERO` on the
missing side were unreachable for any anchor that already carried a handle. *Convert to smooth* on
the first anchor of an open path beginning `M 0 0 C …` gave it a `back` pointing off the end of the
path: `out (10,0) back (-10,-0) is_smooth true`, against the control — an endpoint with no handle,
which takes the derive-from-neighbours arm — at `out (10,0) back (0,0) is_smooth false`.

**Two consequences worth recording.** The phantom handle is **drawn and grabbable**:
`canvas::node_grab` builds a candidate for each of `Side::BOTH` and filters on the handle being long
enough to draw (`HANDLE_DRAWN`) and on distance, and the overlay draws them under the same test —
neither asks whether the segment exists, and a handle 10 units long clears the threshold. And because
`is_smooth()` then answered `true`, the next drag on the **real** handle took the mirror arm instead
of the break arm, so pulling the visible handle swung the invisible one.

This is **D250** verbatim, and the function's own doc already stated the rule it broke: *"An endpoint
of an open subpath gets one handle, not two. It has one segment, so a mirrored handle would point at
nothing and still be draggable — a control over a curve that does not exist."* `prev` and `next` are
computed first now and the shaped branch masks the side that does not exist.

⚠️ **One deliberate non-change.** A **lone** anchor — no neighbour on either side — keeps the
mirrored pair rather than being zeroed. D250's argument would zero both handles, since it has no
segment on either side; but `making_a_point_smooth_mirrors_a_handle_or_derives_one_from_the_neighbours`
asserts the mirror on exactly that fixture, and the derive arms answer `None` for a lone *corner*
rather than inventing a direction. The standing rule is *no invention where there is shaping to
read*, and this entry does not reopen it.

The test is the one whose **name described a case it had never constructed**: every fixture in
`an_open_subpaths_endpoint_smooths_on_the_side_it_has` was a `PenAnchor::corner`, so the *"side it
has"* clause was answered entirely by the arm the rule was never broken in. A shaped **first** anchor
and a shaped **last** one are added, built twice rather than looped, because the two one-sided cases
are separate lines in the shaped branch and each bites only at its own end — flip-checked separately
per end.

No design section needed changing: §9.4 states the rule by citing D250, and the code now obeys it.

**D559 — Alt+Shift on a *side* handle centres the axis the ratio lock drove, in both copies of the
anchor rules. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix — one guard, moved ahead of the anchor question.***

`[S13.1-L2-01]`, Medium, group **G8**. `tools::resize_factors`' `pin` closure chose each axis's
anchor from whether the **handle owns** the axis — `hold: Option<f64>` — and so pinned `box_.min` on
an axis the handle leaves alone. Eleven lines above it, the `keep_ratio` block has already given that
axis a factor taken from the other one, so it is no longer the identity the `None` arm assumes: under
Alt **and** Shift on a *side* handle it was scaled about the box's top or left edge while the dragged
axis was scaled about the centre.

Measured on a 100 × 50 subject at the origin, right side handle dragged to x = 80, driven through
`tools::resize_layer`: a `Rect`, which goes through `resized_box`, lands at `(20,10)–(80,40)`; a
`Path` of the same rectangle, which goes through `resize_factors` → `resize_geometry`, landed at
`(20,0)–(80,30)` — **ten units up, from the same modifiers and the same pointer**.

`pin` answers `mid` on both axes whenever `symmetric` now, which is exactly what `resized_box`'s
`edge` closure does: it returns `mid - extent / 2.0` **before** it looks at `hold`, and its own
comment already spelled the reason out — centring an untouched axis is a no-op in the ordinary case,
its factor being 1, and *not* a no-op once `keep_ratio` has driven it. So this is **G8**: one
decision implemented twice, and the copies disagreed. `resize_factors`' own doc says it exists so
that *"a second copy of the anchor rules is a second place for Alt to stop meaning what it means"*,
which is the failure, described in advance, by the function it happened to.

`tools::tests::alt_and_shift_on_a_side_handle_centre_the_followed_axis_for_a_path_too` drives the
whole verb rather than the helper — a `Path` through `resize_layer`, with the fixture's own box
asserted first so a changed fixture reports as a fixture — and takes its expected numbers from
`alt_and_shift_resize_proportionally_about_the_centre`, which covers only `resized_box`. ⚠️
**Flip-checked, and the interesting half is the *y* pair**: reverting `pin`'s guard to
`Some(_) if symmetric` leaves the width assertion green and fails at `0`/`30` against `10`/`40`,
which is `CLAUDE.md`'s predicted-failure-site note again — the box is not what this test is about.

§9.4 amended.

**D558 — A click that dismisses a library menu is spent doing so. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
gated at every door that acts, off a flag latched at the top of the frame.***

`[S20.2-L1-02]`, Medium. This is `context-menus.md` §0's left-click clause, which `canvas_ui` quotes
and obeys: *"A click that dismisses a menu is spent doing so: it must not also select what it landed
on. The menu was aimed at something, and a click to get rid of it that retargets the selection turns
dismissal into an edit."* The dashboard obeyed it at neither of its two floating menus. Both
dismissals are the same six lines — `input(|i| i.pointer.any_click())` and two `contains` tests —
and **neither consumes the click**; the cards sense clicks and the menus are `egui::Area`s covering
only their own rects, so the click reached the card and `pick_or_open` turned it into `Act::Open`.
Open the ⋮ on *Alpha*, decide against it, click *Bravo* to get rid of the menu: the menu closed
**and Bravo opened** — the library gone and the editor up on a document the user only clicked to
dismiss a popup. ⚠️ **On the canvas the cost is a retargeted selection; here it is a whole
navigation**, which is the same rule with a larger consequence. There was no pointer gesture that
dismissed either menu without acting, short of a click on empty body space or on the ⋮ itself.

Gated at the acts rather than at the two dismissals, which is `canvas_ui`'s shape: a dismissal
cannot consume a click the card has already turned into an `Act::Open`, so gating the act is the only
order that works.

🚨 **And the interesting half is that the obvious one-line fix is wrong, and its own test caught
it.** The first version read `self.library_menu_open()` live at `pick_or_open`. `file_menu_button`
draws the popup — *and runs its dismissal* — from inside the card that owns it, so a menu anchored on
*Alpha* is already closed by the time *Bravo*'s card is drawn: **the live flag answers "no menu" for
every card after the anchor**, and the fix therefore worked or did not depending on sort order.
`DashboardState::menu_was_up` is latched at the top of `dashboard_ui` before anything is drawn, which
is the only point in the frame where *"was a menu on screen when this click arrived"* still has the
right answer. Both spellings are flip-checked and both fail at the same assertion, which is what
makes the distinction worth recording rather than looking like fussiness. ⚠️ **And the dropdown is
the worse case rather than a second copy of the same one**: `project_filter` runs in the top bar,
*before* any card is drawn, so the live flag would have been `false` for **every** card on the
screen and not merely for the ones sorting after an anchor — which is why that row of the test earns
its place.

⚠️ **The gate belongs at every door that acts, and the first version put it on one.** `pick_or_open`
is the file card and the file row; a dismissing click on a sidebar nav row still navigated
(`project_row` → `Nav::Project`), and one on the dashed *New file* card still fired `Act::NewFile`
and **created a document** — worse than opening one, and the door nobody thinks of because it is the
only one on this screen that is not a navigation. Closed the same day with the same flag at each:
`nav_row` ends `resp.clicked() && !self.dash.menu_was_up`, which covers *All files*, *Recent*,
*Starred*, *Trash* and *New project* as well as the project rows, and `project_row` gates **both** of
its hits — the `undo.clicked()` early return for *Unarchive* as well as the `resp.clicked()` →
`Select`. The *Unarchive* button shares the row's rect, so a dismissing click can land on either,
and *"the click did something I did not ask for"* is the same complaint whichever of the two it was.

The two new gates the test reaches were flipped and both bite: the `new_file_card` gate removed fails
at **4** documents against 3, and `project_row`'s at `Project("p-1")` against `All`, with the two
controls — a sidebar row and the *New file* card with nothing floating — staying green. ⚠️ **Two
fixture traps had to be got round to write those rows, and both are facts about the screen rather
than about the test.** `file_menu_popup` is drawn from inside its **own** card, so a ⋮ menu anchored
on a document the current nav does not show is never drawn and therefore **never dismissed** —
`menu_for` simply stays `Some`. And the filter dropdown is no substitute on a project nav,
`filter_applies()` being false there and `project_filter` clearing `filter_open` on its way out,
which is the trap the dropdown row needed a project to escape. The fixture that works is a document
filed *in* the project whose grid is on screen.

🚨 **And two doors are still ungated after the second pass, one of them the same create-a-document
case.** `dashboard_sidebar`'s accent *New file* button — the first thing in the sidebar, the only
accent button on the screen — is a hand-rolled `allocate_exact_size` whose `if resp.clicked()`
fires `Act::NewFile` with no flag anywhere near it; it is not a `nav_row`, which is why gating that
function did not reach it. And `project_cards` → `project_card` on *Recent* returns a bare
`resp.clicked()` that sets `Nav::Project`, which is the sidebar row's failure on a card. So the
count is **five gated call sites and seven doors**, and the two that are left were found by reading
every `.clicked()` in the module against the gate rather than by reading the fix. *Fix, with the
same flag at both* — and the rule for the next reader is the one this entry has now demonstrated
twice: **enumerate the acts, not the functions the finding named.**

⚠️ **`nav_row` and the *Unarchive* return are gated and unasserted.** The test's sidebar row is a
`project_row` and its `Select` hit, so what is pinned is that door and the card; the other two carry
the same one-line predicate and nothing would fail if one of them lost it. *Revisit if either grows
a condition of its own* — seven hand-written copies of one predicate is what §9.3's rule costs on
this screen, the same shape as the two hand-maintained modal lists §9.5 records, and nothing makes a
new door join.

⚠️ **`library_menu_open` is deliberately not folded into `library_keys_are_free`** (D542). That
predicate is about the *keyboard*, and this is a pointer question; the two menus do not even have the
same keyboard story, which is why one predicate could not serve both. 🚨 **The fix's own doc comment
says *"they read no key at all"* and that is false for the ⋮ popup**: `dashboard_keys` returns early
while `menu_for` is set and answers `Escape` on the way, which D374 built and
`the_library_answers_its_own_keys` asserts, and §9.5 states in as many words. The **filter
dropdown** is the one that reads nothing — it is in neither list, so the arrows, `Enter`, `Delete`,
`F2` and `Ctrl+D` all still act on the grid behind it and `Escape` clears the keyboard cursor
instead of closing it. *Comment corrected 2026-09-08*: it now names `dashboard_keys`' early return
and its `Escape`, and records the dropdown as the one in no guard at all. That dropdown alone is the
open finding, and it is `roadmap.md`'s *Escape* question rather than anything R4 decides — narrower
than session 7's *"fifth class of floating thing"* was stated.

`panels::dashboard::tests::a_click_that_dismisses_a_library_menu_does_not_also_open_a_document`
drives both menus and three of the five gated call sites through real frames, with press and release
in **separate** frames because egui reports `clicked()` on the release against last frame's rect. The control — the same click with
nothing floating, which must still open the document — is asserted **first**, so a fix that simply
stopped cards opening reports as a broken fixture rather than as a pass; and the menu still having
closed is asserted too, since a gate that swallowed the click *and* left the popup up would be a
menu with no pointer route out of it at all. ⚠️ **A fixture note worth carrying, because it cost a
wrong diagnosis**: `project_filter` returns early where `filter_applies()` is false and **clears
`filter_open` on the way out** (*"closed as well as hidden, or the dropdown survives a nav
change"*), so on a library with no projects the flag was gone by the end of the first layout frame
and the dropdown row measured a click with nothing floating — it read as the fix failing when the
fixture had never reached the state. The test now asserts the flag survives the layout frame before
clicking, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape caught by its own precondition.

§9.5 amended, and `context-menus.md` §0 and its §9.6 ledger with it — the rule now has a **third**
enforcement site, the canvas's mode input and the layers row's click being the other two.

**D557 — An archived project is not a destination. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`Projects::destination`, read by all three doors.***

`[S20.3-L1-03]`, Medium. Stand on a project's grid, open *Edit project*, turn *Archive project* on
and Save. The grid stays on screen with the dashed *New file in {project}* card still on it; click it
and a brand-new document is filed straight into the archived project. Open the ⋮ on that document,
choose *Move to project*, and the sheet offers **nothing** — because the project it is in is
archived. `dashboard::move_modal`'s own ⚠️ states the rule the card had just broken: *"a document
cannot be filed into an archived project without unarchiving it first."*

⚠️ **`Projects::get` resolving an archived project is correct and is not the bug.** Its neighbour
`active()` carries the distinction in as many words — *"a list is a set of things to choose between,
and a lookup is 'what is this id' — a document filed in an archived project must still resolve to its
name and its colour, or archiving would silently unfile every file in it"* — and both halves of that
are right. **A destination is a third question**, and it had no name, so `get` was answering it at
what the finding took to be two call sites and turned out to be three.
`Projects::destination(id)` is `get(id).filter(|p| !p.archived)`.

**`move_modal`'s exception does not apply, and that is the difference between the two lists.** It
keeps the archived project a document is *already* in, so the sheet can show where it is; there is no
"already" for a document that does not exist yet.

Two of the three doors take it and **they have to answer alike**: `dashboard::new_file_into` decides
whether the card is drawn and what it promises, `OndinApp::nav_project` decides where `Act::NewFile`
files. A
fix to one alone is either a card promising a project the act will not use, or an act filing
somewhere no card offered — and `Ctrl+N` reaches the second without going near the first. With the
nav on an archived project both now answer *no project*, i.e. unfiled, which is the honest answer and
the same as `Ctrl+N` on *All files*.

⚠️ **The finding named two doors and there were three.** `dashboard::import_counting` resolves
`Nav::Project(id)` the same way — *"into the project being viewed, which is the answer the design's
Target project field asks for and the one the user has already given by being where they are"* (D365)
— so an import taken while standing on an archived project's grid filed every copied document into
it, which is `move_modal`'s refused destination reached in bulk. And that nav is ordinary rather
than a corner: an archived project's row is selectable from the sidebar's own *Archived projects*
group, so *"the project being viewed"* can legitimately be an archived one. Fixed the same day, one
line at `import_counting`, reading `destination` like the other two; the honest answer there is
unfiled as well. *Which is the shape to expect of a finding that counts call sites* — the two it
named were the pair that had to agree with each other, and the third was the one nobody was
comparing anything to.

⚠️ **The third door is fixed and unasserted, and it is writable rather than unreachable.**
`import_counting` takes a `&[PathBuf]` and copies real files, so a test wants a temp source
directory and nothing else; the entry's own instruction was *"it wants the same test"* and only the
one line was taken. Nothing pins it, and the test's doc still treats the two wrappers it drives as
the whole population — which is exactly the reading that let the third door hide the first time.
*Fix with a third row on `an_archived_project_is_not_a_destination_for_a_new_document`* — the same
nav, one file imported, the copy's `meta.project` asserted `None`.

`app::library_wiring_tests::an_archived_project_is_not_a_destination_for_a_new_document` asserts both
halves, with an active-project control first, and asserts the **unfiled** answer rather than merely
the absence of the archived one — *no project* being the honest destination and what distinguishes
the fix from one that refuses to create anything. Flip: `destination` reverted to `get`, which fails
on the card assertion with `Some("Kestrel")`, the promise drawn over the archived grid. ⚠️ **The
second assertion is deliberately not separately flip-checked**: both functions are one-line wrappers
over the same call, so no version of the code answers one and not the other. What the pair is for is
the *opposite* risk — a future fix applied to one wrapper and not the other, which is how the two
came to disagree in the first place.

§9.5 amended.

**D556 — A project whose files could not all be moved is kept. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
the `retain` and the nav reset both gated on `failed == 0`.***

`[S20.2-L1-03]`, Medium. 🚨 **`delete_project`'s own ⚠️ doc argued for the file-first ordering on the
grounds that *"a failure leaves the project standing with some of its files already moved, which is a
state the user can see and repeat"* — and the `retain` under it ran unconditionally, so the ordering
was doing nothing.** A run that failed halfway removed the project row anyway, producing exactly the
state the ordering was chosen to avoid, and producing it *silently*, because the `failed` counter's
only consumer is a status line.

Measured end to end with `.trash` present as a **file**, so `store::trash`'s `create_dir_all`
refuses: the row was gone, both members were still on disk with `meta.project = Some("p-1")`, and
`Library::project_of` answered `None` — so the user watched a project and its files disappear and the
documents were still in the library, listed under *All files*, wearing a project id nothing lists.

Fixed by gating the `retain` on `failed == 0`. **The nav reset is gated too**, and that half is worth
its own sentence: a reset to *All files* on the failure path takes the user off the one heading that
now holds the files they have to deal with, which is the screen where the retry is a click away.
`save_projects` is still called either way — on the success path it is the removal being written, and
on the failure path a no-op write that still reports a `projects.json` that cannot be written, which
is worth knowing before the retry. The status line now ends *"the project has been kept"*.

`app::library_wiring_tests::a_project_whose_files_could_not_move_is_kept` stages the failure rather
than injecting it, which needs no seam, and keeps the same delete with a writable trash as its
control — without which a version that never deleted anything would pass every assertion above it.
Flip: the guard removed. It fails on the row assertion and the *files* assertion stays green —
measured, not assumed — which is the whole shape of the bug: **nothing was lost, and the record of
where it belonged was.**

§9.5 amended.

**D555 — The rulers are latched for the life of a guide drag. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-08; Fix —
`GuideDrag::rulers_shown`, read by both terms that folded `rulers_on()`.***

`[S19.1-L1-02]`, Medium. `rulers::update_guide_drag`'s `over_own_ruler` was `self.rulers_on() &&
ruler_at(rect, p) == Some(axis)`, and `rulers_on` is `show_rulers && !present`. **Both halves are
live chords** — `input.rs` binds `Shift+R` to `ViewSwitch::Rulers` and `Ctrl+\` to
`ViewSwitch::Present` — and `OndinApp` dispatches the resolved action with **no drag guard**, though
the shape exists elsewhere in that file (`Action::Nudge(_) if matches!(self.drag, Drag::Create {
.. })`). That term is the **only** thing feeding `GuideDrag::discarding`.

So pressing either chord with the button still down turned the guide **cancel** gesture into a guide
**create** gesture. Drag a horizontal guide out of the top ruler, press `Ctrl+\`, drag back to where
the bar was and release — the gesture this module documents as *"the gesture that made it, run
backwards"* — and it committed a guide at whatever coordinate the vanished bar sat over, selected it
and dirtied the document, while the remaining frames of the drag drew **0 shapes** and the cursor
still promised a live guide drag. `ruler_cursor` drops the bin bitmap and `draw_guide_faded`'s
discard fade is never asked for, so nothing on screen said the release would do something different
from what it had a frame ago. **Reverse direction, same term**: turning the rulers *on* mid-drag made
`over_own_ruler` true, so a guide dragged to the top of the canvas became discarding without moving.

⚠️ **The function's own comment was written against precisely this hazard and named the wrong
input** — *"a mismatch here would have the press and the frames after it disagreeing about where the
bars are"* — where the mismatch it guarded against was between two *functions*, and a toggle mid-drag
produces the same disagreement between two *frames*.

The fix is `GuideDrag::rulers_shown`, latched at `begin_guide_drag` **for the same reason
`left_ruler` already was**: that field's comment says *"one rule, evaluated the same way at the press
and on every frame after it"*, and this is that rule's other half — `left_ruler` latches the
pointer's position against the bars, `rulers_shown` latches the bars' existence. The alternative,
refusing the two `ViewSwitch` actions while a `Drag::Guide` is live, was **not** taken: it makes a
view toggle silently fail, where this makes a gesture behave.

🚨 **The first version of this fix latched one of the two terms, and the shape of the miss is the
lesson.** It covered the term that decides the **commit** — `discarding`, off `over_own_ruler` — and
left the term that decides the **announcement** reading a method that folds the same two chords:
`off_rulers` was `self.ruler_at(p, rect).is_none()`, and `ruler_at` is `rulers_on().then(…)`. So
taking the bars away mid-drag answered *"the pointer is off both rulers"* on the frame they
vanished, latching `left_ruler` without the pointer ever having left one, and `announces_discard()`
then drew the fade and the bin cursor over a *new* guide that does not exist yet — the exact state
D140 added `left_ruler` to prevent, reached by the other door. Nothing committed differently; the
gesture merely lied about what it would do. **One field, two consumers, and only one of them was
latched** — which is worth carrying because the field's *own* comment says the rule is *"evaluated
the same way at the press and on every frame after it"*, and a reader auditing the fix against that
sentence has to enumerate the consumers rather than the fix.

Closed the same day: `off_rulers` is now `!d.rulers_shown || ruler_at(rect, p).is_none()` — the free
function against the latched flag rather than the method that folds the live one. **With the latch
this is a pure geometry test against the layout the press saw**, which is what the paragraph above
was already asking for: the bars' *region* does not move, so *"is the pointer off the bar"* stops
depending on whether the bar is currently painted. Rulers off at the press makes it unconditionally
true, which is right — the pointer is off bars that are not there — and it is how `begin_guide_drag`
seeds `left_ruler` in the first place. The repair's own comment cites **D140** by name, that being
the entry which added `left_ruler` precisely so a new guide could not announce a discard before it
had been off the bars once: the promise this half had broken, and the only way to say what was being
restored rather than merely changed.

`rulers::guide_grab_tests::toggling_the_rulers_mid_drag_does_not_change_what_the_release_means`
drives the finding's own gesture — a **new** guide pulled out of the bar, where cancelling must
create nothing at all — for both chords, plus the reverse direction with an existing guide, plus two
controls, plus a fourth row for the announcement: a new guide pressed on the bar, `present` set
**with the pointer not moving**, and `announces_discard()` asserted false before and after. The
pointer standing still is the whole point of that row — it is what makes the bars' existence the
only thing that changed. ⚠️ **The undo assertion only means something on the new-guide path**, which
the first draft got wrong: an existing guide dropped on the bar is a legitimate delete and *does* spend a step, so a
test asserting `undo_depth` unchanged there fails for the right reason. ⚠️ **The leading control
asserts `announces_discard()`** and not merely an empty guide list, because *"no guide, no undo
step"* is satisfied by a version that never creates guides at all.

Flips: the latch reverted. It fails at the present-mode row, and — measured by skipping that row and
re-running — **also at the reverse-direction row**, so both directions of the conjunction bite; both
controls stay green. The announcement row has a flip of its own: `off_rulers` put back to
`self.ruler_at(p, rect).is_none()` fails it with *"a guide still sitting where it was pressed has not
been 'off both rulers' just because the rulers were switched off underneath it"*.

⚠️ **The `dead_code` observation recorded against the first flip is no longer reproducible, and why
is the useful half.** Reverting the commit term alone left the field unread and the lint said so,
which was a free confirmation that there was no second copy of this rule anywhere. There is a second
*reader* now — the two terms of this one function — so neither flip can raise it, and the
confirmation is gone with the one-site claim it rested on. (It fired at all only because `GuideDrag`
does not derive `PartialEq`, `CLAUDE.md`'s measured mechanism for a field nothing reads staying
invisible to every gate.) *The test's doc still says the field is read at exactly one site;* **fix
the comment** — and notice that the sentence which made the fix look complete is the same one that
made the second reader easy to miss.

§9.4 amended.

**D554 — `frame_label_at` takes the last match, like every other reader of `artboards()`. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-08; Fix — one `.rev()`.***

`[S12.5-L1-02]`, Medium. `OndinApp::artboards` is depth-first in child order — paint order — and its
own comment states the contract its readers are built on: *"everything that reads this list relies on
that: 'the topmost frame containing the point' and 'the frame that owns these bounds' both take the
**last** match, and the last match of two nested frames is the inner one, which is the one the
pointer is really in."* `canvas::frame_label_at` took the **first**.

⚠️ **Which made the word on screen and the frame a click picks two different frames.** A page frame
with a full-bleed header flush in its top-left corner — the commonest nesting there is — puts the two
name tags on exactly the same pixels, every tag being placed 5px in from its own frame's left edge
(`frame_label`). `draw_frame_labels` paints in `artboards()` order, so it paints `Page` and then
`Header` and *Header* is the only word legible there; the click selected `Page`. `hover_target`
resolves through the same function, so the outer frame lit up first and the outline lied about it
before the click took it. It fires for **siblings** as well: two frames in a row at one `y` with a
long name on the left put its tag over its neighbour's.

⚠️ **The count in the fix's own doc comment was one short, and it was worth correcting rather than
repeating**: `artboards()` has **six** readers, not five. Four honour the rule — `target_artboard`
and `rulers::frame_at_world` spell `.rev().find`, `frame_covering` keeps the last qualifying match by
overwriting `chosen` as it walks, and `draw_frame_labels` paints in order so the last one wins the
pixel — the fifth is `draw_layout_grids`, which reads the list and is indifferent to its order
because every frame draws its own tracks, and the sixth was this one. *Comment corrected 2026-09-08*,
and it names the sixth and says why it is not a bug: an indifferent reader is still a member of the
population the sentence enumerates, which is the whole reason to state a count at all.

`canvas::frame_menu_door_tests::the_name_tag_you_can_read_is_the_one_a_click_picks` asserts **both halves
in one test**, which is the finding's own instruction: *"the word on screen"* is not a property of
`frame_label_at` — it is `draw_frame_labels`' paint order — so a test asserting only the pick would
go green if a later change fixed the disagreement by flipping the *paint* order instead, which is the
same bug with the frames swapped. It reads the last `Shape::Text` at the shared position out of
`FullOutput::shapes`, and asserts the fixture's overlap and `artboards()`' own order first, so a
fixture that stopped being ambiguous reports as a fixture.
