a batch passes a document advanced by the placements already built. `None` reads the live document,
which is every single-picture caller, the Image tool's per-click placement included: that one
correctly wants one transaction each, because each click is its own gesture.

**The *placement* is read from the live document either way, and deliberately.** Which artboard is
under `world`, and the frame the picture is fitted into, come from `draw_target` — a picture is not a
container, so nothing a batch creates can change the answer, and `draw_target` needs the camera as
well as the tree. `drop_images_at` concatenates and commits once, and selects **every** picture the
drop made rather than the last, which is also what gives the user something to press Delete on.

Tests in `ondin-app/src/app.rs · mod image_drop_tests`:
`one_drop_of_three_files_is_one_undo_step`,
`a_batch_numbers_its_layers_against_the_siblings_it_is_adding` and
`one_blob_dropped_twice_is_embedded_once`.

⚠️ **Both predicted failure sites for the advancing document were wrong, and the second is the
sharper finding.** Committing per file is red at the count, 3 for 1, with *"three layers landed"*
green above it — that one as predicted. Building every placement against the untouched document
(`image_tx(None, …)` in the loop) is red at the **names**, all three coming back `"Image 1"`, with
the layer count green: three layers still land, they are just indistinguishable. The same flip in the
dedupe test is red at the **layer count**, 1 for 2, and not at the image count where it was predicted
— both placements embed the blob, the second transaction is then refused when it is applied to the
advancing document, and the layer never lands at all. **A duplicated write does not merely duplicate:
here it loses the picture.** That is why the layer count is asserted before the image count in
`one_blob_dropped_twice_is_embedded_once`.

§5.8, §9.3 and §9.4 amended.

**D521 — One `Ctrl+Shift+G` was one undo step per container. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the
accumulation moved into a builder, the run mechanism being unavailable to a structural command.***

`[S16.2-L2-03]`, Medium. `app::ungroup_selection` was a `for group in groups` loop with
`self.session.commit(tx)` **inside it** — the only per-subject commit loop in the file. Measured: an
ungroup of two groups gave `undo_delta=2, groups_left=0`, and one `Ctrl+Z` brought **one** group back
and left the other dissolved. Every sibling verb in the same `impl` builds one transaction and
commits once, and `delete_selection` says why in as many words: it folds a frame's guides into the
same `Vec<Operation>` so *"one Ctrl+Z brings back both"*. `toggle_hidden`, `toggle_locked`,
`paste_guides`, `duplicate_guides`, `insert_all` and `paste_properties` all do the same.

⚠️ **`commit_run` cannot fix this, and the review measured that before the fix was written.**
`history::commit_into_run` refuses to merge unless `shape(&tx)` is `Some`, and `shape` requires
`op.overwrites()` on **every** operation — which is `None` for the structural ops an ungroup is made
of, `Reparent` and `DeleteNode`. So **the run mechanism is structurally unavailable to every
structural command in the app**, and that is the general fact worth taking off this entry rather than
the ungroup itself: it is why D522 needed the same treatment for `CreateNode`, and it means *"use
`commit_run`"* is never the answer for a verb that changes the **shape** of the tree. The folding has
to happen before the commit, which is to say in a builder.

`build::ungroup_all(doc, ids)` is that builder, beside `build::group`. ⚠️ **It simulates rather than
concatenating, and that is the whole of its design.** `ungroup` reads the container's own position
among its parent's children, so the second container's index is measured against a child list the
first one's ops have already spliced — and a container nested *inside* an earlier one has a different
parent and a different local transform by the time its turn comes. A whole `Document` is cloned and
advanced as each container's transaction is built. That is heavier than `layers::plan_layer_move`'s
map of child lists, deliberately: an ungroup rewrites transforms as well as parentage, so a map of
child lists does not carry enough to build the next transaction against. The clone is skipped for the
one-container case, which is every ungroup but a multi-selection.

⚠️ **The wrong answer a concatenation gives is not the interleave anyone predicts, and it is invisible
to the obvious assertion.** Flipped by concatenating against the original document: red at the first
`children_of` with `[behind, a, c, d, b]` — the second group's children land at stale indices
*inside* the run the first has already spliced, and `b` is pushed off the end — while **every
world-position assertion stays green**, because the wrong indices still name the right parent. *A
test asserting positions alone would have passed.*

⚠️ **The half-applied *failure* the finding also names turned out to be unreachable from this verb,
and that is stated rather than claimed as fixed.** `ungroup_selection` filters the selection to live
`Group`/`Boolean` nodes, which rules out every error `build::ungroup` can return: `WrongKindForOp`
and `NoSuchNode` are filtered out, and `CannotModifyRoot` cannot arrive because the root is not a
`Group` and so never survives the filter either. Measured while trying to write the test — a first
attempt selected the root, watched the filter drop it, and saw the *good* group ungrouped normally.
So *"a command that half-applies and then says it failed"* was a latent hazard in the loop rather
than a reachable one. The guarantee now lives where it can be stated at all, in the builder, and
`one_bad_container_builds_no_ops_at_all` is what states it.

Tests. `ondin-core/tests/build.rs`:
`two_containers_ungroup_in_one_transaction_without_interleaving`, run over both orderings of the two
containers, and `one_bad_container_builds_no_ops_at_all`, which is the only assertion the skip-the-
failure flip can reach. `ondin-app/src/app.rs · mod ungroup_tests`:
`one_ungroup_of_two_groups_is_one_undo_step`, whose flip — the commit back inside a per-container
loop — is red at the **count**, 2 for 1, so the count is the load-bearing assertion and the `Ctrl+Z`
round trip below it corroborates rather than proves.

§5.7a, §5.8, §9.3 and §9.4 amended.

**D520 — The box fields skipped a no-op write only in the arm beside them. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the guard `multi_angle_tx` already had, in the other four arms.***

`[S14.2-L1-02]`, Medium. `inspector::multi_transform_tx`'s X, Y, W and H arms call
`build::move_by_world` and `tools::resize_selection`, which emit one op per member
**unconditionally**. So a nudge of zero — a field losing focus without having been edited — built a
transaction of N writes that each set a layer to the transform or the size it already had. The
finding measured `undo_depth 0 → 2` for a click through X and then Y, `is_dirty` false → true, and an
autosave and a crash-snapshot write for a click that changed nothing. Forty no-op writes on a
twenty-layer selection.

**The guard existed one arm away and said what it was for.** `multi_angle_tx`'s per-op `unchanged`
filter carries the comment *"Skip the layers this leaves alone. A field losing focus without having
been edited arrives here as a nudge of zero…"* — this failure named exactly, in a sibling arm of the
same function, and the angles have been skipping it since they were written. X and Y return an empty
`Transaction` when the delta is zero; W and H when `size == now`, asked **after**
`tools::paired_size` has had its say, because a locked pair can turn a zero on one axis into a real
change on the other, and a comparison taken before the lock would let that through as a no-op or
refuse a real edit as one.

⚠️ **This amends D53, which is a live *Intentional* entry, and the sentence it amends is false
rather than merely stale.** That entry states *"Every bulk builder skips no-op writes"* and *"the six
multi Transform fields skip building their transaction at all unless the control is mid-edit"*. Both
halves failed on the one frame that matters: `inspector::interacting` is `dragged() ||
drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()`, so the field **did** build on the defocus frame, and
two of the four box builders did not skip the write. D53's *reasoning* — why `multi_valve` exists
separately, and the drag total it is there to clear — is untouched and stands.

⚠️ **D428's `changes_nothing` at `commit_inner` is downstream of this and does not make it
redundant.** A transaction whose every operation writes back the value already there is dropped
before it reaches the history, so over a top-level selection the *symptom* the finding measured is
now caught twice. Two things are still this guard's own. The transaction is never **built**, which is
where the cost is: a W or H edit runs `resize_selection`, and that recurses into the geometry of
every descendant, six fields being laid out every frame. And D428's comparison is exact —
`Operation::SetTransform`'s arm is `n.transform() == *transform` — while `build::local_for_world`
returns `parent_world.inverse() * world`, so a move of nothing under a non-identity ancestor is not
guaranteed to come back bit-identical, and a coefficient off in its last place is a write
`changes_nothing` correctly calls a change. *Do not remove either guard on the strength of the
other.*

Test `inspector::multi_valve_tests::a_zero_nudge_builds_no_transaction_at_all` walks all six fields
with `MultiEdit::Nudge(0.0)` and asserts each builds nothing, with a real move as the control.
**Flipped by removing the `size == now` guard alone: red at W, building 2 ops for a nudge of nothing,
with X and Y already past.** H is never reached — the loop stops at the first field that fails — so
the flip says the W/H arm is guarded and says nothing about H's own path; they share the one guard,
which is why that is enough.

⚠️ **`a_bare_click_through_a_multi_field_commits_nothing` pins nothing at all on this fixture, which
is measured rather than suspected.** Three flips were run: removing D519's engagement latch, removing
this guard, and — the one that settles it — removing **both at once**. All three are green. The
reason is a third door neither the finding nor the session that wrote the test knew about: D428's
`changes_nothing` at `commit_inner`, which over this fixture — two rects on the root, identity parent
— finds the zero-nudge ops bit-identical and refuses the commit before the history sees it. So that
test is a *symptom* guard over three independent doors, useful the day one of them is changed and
evidence about none of them. The mechanisms are pinned elsewhere:
`a_zero_nudge_builds_no_transaction_at_all` for this guard,
`typing_a_multi_width_leaves_exactly_one_step_in_the_history` for the latch. **A green run there must
not be read as evidence that either is present**, and the test's own doc comment now says so at
length.

⚠️ **The finding's measured `undo_depth 0 → 2` is not reproducible today and was not when this fix
was written**: it was taken at the review's own SHA, which predates D428, so the symptom had been
closed from underneath months earlier by a change made for a different reason. **That is the shape
worth carrying off this entry.** A later fix can make an *earlier* finding's symptom unreachable, and
a test written to the finding's own measurement is then vacuous the day it is written, with every
gate green — this is `CLAUDE.md`'s "what would also pass this" with the answer being *the code as it
already stood*. The tell is a flip that does not bite. The move that finds it is the **double** flip
— every suppressor removed at once rather than one at a time — and it only happened here because a
documentation pass asked for it, which is `arch-scribe` finding what no gate can, again. *Whenever a
fix closes a finding older than the last release of work, flip the guard the finding named before
believing the test that guards it.*

§9.4 amended, and D53 with it.

**D519 — A typed number on the multi-selection Transform card was five undo steps. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the shared valve's engagement latch, in the second valve it never reached.***

`[S14.2-L1-01]`, Medium. `inspector::multi_valve` committed on `resp.drag_stopped() ||
resp.lost_focus() || resp.changed()` — **the exact expression §15 D316 removed from
`OndinApp::edit_valve`**, whose doc quotes it and says why: a `DragValue` being typed into reports
`changed()` on every keystroke and `lost_focus()` on **two consecutive frames**. D316 reached the
shared valve and never reached this second, hand-rolled one.

**Measured headless.** Select two layers, click into the Transform card's W field, type `500`, click
away: **five** entries in the history — one per keystroke, then the finishing frame, then the
settling frame — which is five autosaves, five crash-snapshot writes and five presses of `Ctrl+Z` to
undo one number. The single-layer card gives one. Pointer-only; no key but the digits.

**The fix is not a second mechanism.** `multi_valve` carries the same latch `edit_valve` does —
`engaged = resp.dragged() || resp.has_focus()`, stored under `resp.id.with("multi-valve-engaged")` in
`Context::data`, **read before the `gesture_cancelled` bail**, which is D317's ordering — commits on
the falling edge, and refuses on `key_pressed(Escape)`, which is D315's rule reaching this valve for
the first time. The one thing this valve exists for is kept: D53's drag total `multi_transform_drag`
must outlive the frames of a drag and must not outlive the drag itself, so it is cleared on the
committing frame. The clear is `clear_gesture_preview` and not `clear_preview`, which is D109's one
spelling — on the new `Escape` path nothing commits, so this is the only clear, and the broad one
would take a live text session's uncommitted content off the canvas with it.

⚠️ **The falling edge of engagement arrives one frame before the number does, and that is the subtle
half.** Measured frame by frame: the three keystroke frames report `changed()` with the field focused
and the value written back each time; the click away reports `lost_focus()` **with the value still at
the old one**; and egui writes the parsed edit string back on the *next* frame, when the field is
already disengaged. A valve that built its transaction from the committing frame alone would commit
`Nudge(0)` and throw the typed number away — which is exactly what the first attempt at this fix did.
So `multi_number` **remembers** the typed value, keyed on the widget's own id
(`resp.id.with("multi-typed")`, an `Option<f64>`), and the valve spends it on the way out — both ways
out, so an abandoned edit leaves no number behind for the next engagement to re-apply. *That memory
is the load-bearing line, and not the predicate in front of it*: a flip that swaps `step != 0.0` back
to `resp.changed()` leaves all five tests green, and a flip that drops the `pending` arm is red.

`multi_number` now returns its `egui::Response`, as `scale_row` does and for the same reason: the
widget's rect is not predictable from outside, so a test has to draw the field once to find where it
is. Nothing in production reads the value. **That is what unblocked the finding** — session 6 wrote
this fix, could not make a test reach the widget (a guessed coordinate produced a multi card
reporting `0` undo steps, a passing assertion about a click that missed), and backed the whole thing
out.

Five tests in `inspector::multi_valve_tests`, driving real pointer and key events over a two-rect
fixture whose union is 100×60: `typing_a_multi_width_leaves_exactly_one_step_in_the_history`,
`escape_abandons_a_typed_multi_edit`, `a_bare_click_through_a_multi_field_commits_nothing`,
`a_zero_nudge_builds_no_transaction_at_all` and
`a_scrubbed_multi_width_is_one_step_and_leaves_no_total_behind`. ⚠️ **One of the five pins nothing,
and D520 has the measurement**: `a_bare_click_through_a_multi_field_commits_nothing` stays green with
this latch and D520's guard **both** removed, because D428's `changes_nothing` refuses the commit
underneath them. It is a symptom guard, and the latch is pinned by
`typing_a_multi_width_leaves_exactly_one_step_in_the_history` alone. ⚠️ **This is the first coverage
the card's typed path has ever had.** `[S14.2-L6-04]` counted three test callers, every one of them
`MultiField::W` or `H` with `MultiEdit::Absolute` and none of them through a valve; that finding is
**not** closed, because the angle half — `multi_angle_tx`, `shared_angle` and the `MAX_SKEW` clamp —
is still reached by nothing. `roadmap.md` carries it.

**Five flips were run and three of the predictions were wrong**, which is worth the space:

1. Restoring the old commit condition is red at `undo_depth` reading **3** — but at the assertion in
   the *middle* of the test rather than at the count at the end, because the keystrokes are in the
   history before the click away happens.
2. Dropping the remembered typed value is red at the **count**, 0 against 1 — not at the width, where
   it was predicted: with D520's guard in place the abandoned edit builds an *empty* transaction, so
   the commit is a no-op rather than a wrong write.
3. Swapping the `typed` predicate back to `resp.changed()` does not bite at all.
4. Dropping the `Escape` refusal is red at the width (500 for 100) and **green at the count**,
   because abandoning and committing both spend the engagement exactly once.
5. Moving `multi_transform_drag = None` out of the committing branch is red at the last assertion of
   the scrub test and nowhere else in 1,036 tests.

§9.3 and §9.4 amended, and D53 with them.

**D518 — A text layer emptied in an earlier session is not deleted by opening it. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — freshness carried on the session rather than inferred from `original`.***

`[S12.4-L2-03]`, Medium. `canvas::finish_text_edit` guarded the empty-close delete with
`session.editor.content().is_empty() && session.original.0.is_empty()`.

§9.3 scopes that delete to a **fresh** node — *"undo after typing restores the pre-session content (**a
fresh node left empty is removed instead**), matching Figma's one-undo-step-per-editing-session
model."* An empty `original` is true of a freshly created node and **equally true of any pre-existing
node that is already empty**. Nothing distinguished the two.

**Measured headless, driving the app's own verbs.** Session 1 — open, select all, backspace, close —
leaves the node present with content `Some("")` and one undo step, which is correct: a layer the user
cleared on purpose is still a layer. Session 2 — open, close, **nothing typed** — removed it, taking
the undo depth from 1 to 2. The control, a node still holding content through the same open and close,
survives.

⚠️ **The empty state is reachable and it persists**, which is what makes this more than a curiosity.
`SetText { content: "" }` is accepted — `Document::op_set_text` has no emptiness check, only a span
clamp — and session 1 above is the ordinary route to it: select all, backspace, Escape.

⚠️ **SVG import does *not* produce one, though two code comments here say it does.** `svg_in`'s only
`NodeKind::Text` construction sits behind `let content = content.trim(); if content.is_empty() { return
None; }`, so an empty `<text>` mints no node at all, and `canvas::paste_svg` is that same importer
reached from the clipboard. *Fix by striking the claim* from `finish_text_edit`'s delete arm and from
`empty_text_session_tests`' module doc; **the reachability argument does not rest on it** — the
clear-and-commit route above is the one a user actually takes.

⚠️ **The recovery is `Ctrl+Z` and the user has no reason to press it.** They typed nothing, the
selection is cleared, and the one line that could have told them says *"Removed empty text"* rather
than *"Deleted layer"* — an account of a thing they did not do.

**The comment on that arm stated the narrower rule the condition was reaching for**, which is how the
gap survived review: *"A text node that never received content is not a layer the user meant to create;
drop it instead of leaving an invisible one."* The node in the measurement **did** receive content. The
sentence was right and the predicate under it answered a different question.

**The fix carries freshness explicitly.** `preview::TextSession` gains a `created: bool`.
`canvas::open_text_session` sets it **true**, and that is the door every *create* path opens through —
all three of its callers have just minted the node they hand it: the Text tool's click (`begin_text`),
its drag, and its click on an outline (`begin_text_on_path`, D408). `canvas::begin_edit_text` sets it
**false**, being the door a *second* editing session comes through. The delete is gated on `created`,
and `original` goes back to serving only `TextSession::changed()`.

⚠️ **D170 is the entry that added `original`, and it says what the field is for**: *"a node created
empty must record an *empty* original, or closing it reads as a change and commits a second undo step
over the create."* That answers the **change-detection** question. It was being read to answer a
*freshness* question it cannot answer — a stated premise that is false rather than a silence in the
record, which is why D170 is amended here rather than merely cited.

Test `canvas::empty_text_session_tests::a_layer_emptied_in_an_earlier_session_is_not_deleted_by_opening_it`,
two sessions driven through the app's own verbs. **Two controls, because two different wrong fixes pass
without them**: session 1's own commit still happens (`undo_depth >= 1`, which is what says emptying a
layer is still an edit), and a node **created** by the test's own `begin_text` and left empty is still
removed, which is the rule §9.3 states. That second control asserts `session.created` before closing,
so the fixture is checked to be in the state it names.

⚠️ **The test's doc comment claims a *third* control and no assertion answers to it.** *"A node with
content still survives (the delete has not simply been removed)"* — but nothing anywhere closes a
session on a node that still holds content: `finish_text_edit` has exactly three call sites in tests,
all three in this module, and the first empties its node before closing. So the delete's **other**
conjunct, `content().is_empty()`, is pinned by nothing in the workspace. *Fix with one open-and-close of
the fixture before session 1 empties it*, or the comment is D318's shape again — a green test claiming
coverage it does not have, which is the one kind of prose no gate reads.

**Flip run**, `session.created` back to `session.original.0.is_empty()`: fails on *"the layer survives a
second session that typed nothing"* at `None` against `Some("")` — the predicted site, the node gone.

Distinct from the review's closed *"a text-tool click commits two transactions"*, which is about the
transaction **count** on the create path. This is about which nodes qualify for the delete. §9.3
amended, and D170 with it.

**D517 — A bare click through the hex field changes nothing. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — a
comparison at the field, on the bytes.***

`[S14.4-L1-04]`, Medium. `inspector::paint_hex_field` committed whatever `parse_hex` gave it back on
`resp.lost_focus()`, with **no comparison against what was already in the document**. Two defects
follow, and one comparison closes both.

**It quantised the colour by looking at it.** `text` is seeded from `ui::hex_of`, which rounds each
channel to 8 bits; `parse_hex` hands them back as `u8`; `Color::from_rgba8` re-expands. So a colour off
the 8-bit lattice — which is anything the picker's HSV plane produced — came back **changed** by a click
that typed nothing. Measured headless: `[0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 1.0]` → `[0.5019608, 0.2509804, 0.1254902,
1.0]`, `is_dirty()` true, and the saved bytes with it. That is `[S14.3-L1-04]`'s shape — a round trip
through a builder with no comparison — at a **second** site, and this one is measurably lossy rather
than merely a no-op.

⚠️ **The comparison is on the bytes, not the components**, and that is the whole of why it works: the
floats genuinely differ, so comparing them would have written every time. What has to match is what the
*field* can express — `parse_hex(&text) == parse_hex(&hex_of(current))`.

**And it spent an undo step on a click that changed nothing.** This field does **not** go through
`app::edit_valve`, so D316's engagement latch never reached it — and `edit_valve`'s own doc names
exactly this as the defect D316 fixed: *"A `DragValue` being typed into reports `changed()` on every
keystroke and `lost_focus()` on **two consecutive frames**"*. The same comparison closes that half,
because on the second frame `self.paint_hex` is `None`, so the text is `hex_of` of what the first frame
wrote and there is nothing left to do.

⚠️ **The finding measured `undo_depth 0 → 2` and the test in the tree measures 1.** Recorded rather than
rounded to the finding's number: the review's probe drove the real panel, and in this harness the two
`lost_focus` frames merge into one history run. **The claim the test makes is 1 against 0**, which is the
one it can prove — the step that should not have been spent at all.

⚠️ **G15 discipline, checked at review time and worth keeping in the entry.** D316's blast radius is a
*category* list — *"the colour picker, the guides, the stroke widths, the export fields, typography"* —
and it does not enumerate the hex field. Committing straight to `commit_edit` is the ordinary route for
an *instantaneous* control, and the reason on record for it is D312's — *"a button has no drag to
preview and no focus to lose"* — conditioned on exactly the fact that is false for a text field. So
this is a gap the record does not speak to rather than a rule that was broken, and what fell into it is
D315/D316's original symptom exactly.

`mixed` writes unconditionally: over a set that disagrees there is no one colour to compare against, and
setting all of them to one is exactly the edit being asked for. **D465's contrast is untouched by that** —
over a mixed row the buffer's own text is the word *"Mixed"*, `parse_hex` refuses it, and the write below
never happens. What this entry adds is the guard the **agreeing** case needed, which is the same shape as
D465's hazy-field rule reached from the other side; §9.4's *"the hex field beside it needs no such guard
and never did"* was true of the mixed case and read as a claim about the field, and is amended.

⚠️ **The stroke's comma-separated dash field is buffered on defocus the same way and is safe for a reason
of its own.** `inspector::strokes_tx` returns an **empty** transaction when the committed list already
says this, so its comparison sits downstream of the field rather than in it — §9.4 states that, and gives
the seven-fields-tabbed-through reason for it. Nothing downstream could do the same for a colour:
`slot_transaction` builds its `SetFills` unconditionally and the quantised one genuinely differs, so the
empty-transaction drop never sees it. That is D465's finding again — **the no-op family is the control
rather than the cure.**

⚠️ **`edit_valve` routing — the other half of the finding's fix sketch — was not done, and the reason is a
measurement rather than a shrug.** The sketch says to route the write through the valve *and* compare,
"which closes the quantisation half that the valve alone would not". The comparison turned out to close
**both** measured symptoms, so the valve would be belt-and-braces for a control with no drag to preview.
It is recorded as unclosed all the same, in `roadmap.md`: the argument for it is the *shape* rather than
a defect — §9.3 makes the valve the seam an inspector control's commit **timing** is decided at, and this
field decides its own. ⚠️ **It is not the only one, and the other has a stated reason where this has
none**: JPEG quality goes through neither shared committer and holds its in-flight value in
`export_quality_scrub`, because committing every frame would make the drag uncancellable (§9.4, D274).
That is the bar the routing question should be answered against — a control off the seam wants a
sentence saying why, and the hex field has never had one.

Test `panels::inspector::paint_hex_field_tests::a_bare_click_through_the_hex_field_changes_nothing`,
driving real pointer and key events through `RawInput` against `OndinApp::headless`. **The typed edit is
the control**, and it is what says the comparison did not simply turn the field off.

⚠️ **The test's first spelling shared one `egui::Context` across both halves and the control was silently
dead.** The context still carried the first field's focus and memory under the same widget id, so the
second half's click never took focus, `Event::Text` landed nowhere, and the control read as a fix that
had broken the field. **Measured by printing `app.paint_hex` after the text frame: `None`.** A fresh
context per run. This is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape — *the fixture never reached the state* —
arriving through the harness rather than through the data.

**Flip run**, the comparison removed: fails on *"a bare click does not change the colour"* at
`[0.5019608, 0.2509804, 0.1254902, 1.0]` against `[0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 1.0]` — the predicted site. With
that assertion disabled and the flip re-run, it fails on the undo step at 1 against 0, so both halves
have teeth.

🚨 **The *"nothing measured left to fix"* above was wrong, and D808 is what was left.** Nobody had
pressed `Escape` at this field. The routing question is answered there — with a sentence, which is the
half of `[S14.4-L1-04]` this entry left owing — and the defect found on the way is not the hex field's
alone.

**D808 — `Escape` committed a typed value at four chrome text fields. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19;
Keep — the rule is one function now, and the valve is still not the answer for the hex field.***

Measured on the real `inspector::paint_hex_field` with a `RawInput`-driven probe: click in, type
`336699` over a fill of `[0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 1.0]`, press `Escape` — the colour became
`[0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0]` and `undo_depth` went to 1. **egui does not revert a `TextEdit` on `Escape`**; it
hands back what was typed and merely surrenders focus, so a condition built from `resp.lost_focus()`
alone reads a cancel as a confirm. The key that cancels a gesture everywhere else in the app *applied*
the edit, and spent an undo step doing it.

**The rule already existed twice in the app and was broken at four sites beside it.**
`app::OndinApp::edit_valve` carries it for every *numeric* field — the `!key_pressed(Escape)` on the
falling edge of D316's engagement latch, put there by **D315** and ordered against the cancel by
**D317** — and `panels::dashboard`'s rename field carries it as an arm further up. The four that did
not: `inspector::paint_hex_field`, the inspector's layer-name field, `inspector::dash_list_field` and
`panels::export`'s prefix and suffix fields. `ui::defocus_commits(resp)` is
`resp.lost_focus() && !resp.ctx.input(|i| i.key_pressed(egui::Key::Escape))`, called at all four. The
buffer is still dropped on every way out; only the **write** is declined, or a half-typed name would
reappear on the next click into the field.

⚠️ **It reads the key rather than the focus, and those are not the same question.** `Escape` clears
egui's focus in `Memory::begin_pass`, so the frame a field reports `lost_focus()` is the frame the press
is still in `input` — which is D317's finding arriving from the other end. Asking `has_focus()`, or
looking at the next frame, answers nothing: by then the key is gone and the two ways out of a field are
indistinguishable.

**Why the valve is still not the answer for the hex field, which is the half `[S14.4-L1-04]` actually
asked for.** That finding wanted `paint_hex_field` routed through `edit_valve` *or* a sentence saying
why not, and the sentence is this: **a valve previews while the control is engaged, and a half-typed hex
is a colour.** `ui::parse_hex` accepts three digits, so `6D8CD9` passes through `6D8` — `#66DD88`, a
real green — and a valved field would put that on the canvas on the way to the blue. The buffer exists
precisely so that nothing between the first keystroke and the last is a value, which leaves the valve
with nothing to preview and exactly one sentence to lend. That sentence is `defocus_commits`, and it is
now shared rather than owed.

**Test `inspector::paint_hex_field_tests::escape_abandons_a_typed_hex_instead_of_committing_it`**,
sharing a driver with `a_bare_click_through_the_hex_field_changes_nothing`; the driver gained an `exit`
key parameter. ⚠️ **`Enter` is the control and it is not decoration.** The two keys leave the field by
the same door, so a fix reading *"did a key take the focus away"* would refuse both, and the only thing
that notices is an assertion that the ordinary way out still writes. Flip-checked by dropping the second
term from `defocus_commits`: red on the colour at `[0.20000002, 0.40000004, 0.6, 1.0]` against
`[0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 1.0]`, the predicted site, with the undo assertion under it good for the same catch
at 1 against 0. ⚠️ **One test covers all four callers because the rule is in the function and not at
them.** The three other sites have no `Escape` assertion and are **not** meant to grow one; what they
owe is to call this rather than to re-spell it.

⚠️ **§9.3's list of the five lines exempted from `valve_condition_gate` said a text field *"genuinely
does end on losing focus"*, and that is now half a truth**: it ends, and it does not necessarily
commit. Amended there, at the dash field's own exemption comment, and in §9.4's hex-field and
dash-list paragraphs. The gate itself is untouched and still right — the two terms it looks for sit in
two different conditions at each of these fields, which is a fact about where the buffer is stashed and
not about what commits.

🚨 **The probe written for this entry then turned up a second defect at the same seam (D821)**: the
key that no longer commits was still paying out a rung of the `Escape` ladder underneath the field.
Read the two together — this one stops the write, that one stops the press.

**D821 — `Escape` is spent on a chrome field that has just lost focus, and the rung goes *below*
`cancel_gesture`. *Found and fixed 2026-09-19; Keep.***

Measured with D808's probe: with a `TextEdit` focused, `input::resolve` answers `[Escape]`. egui
clears focus in `Memory::begin_pass`, so the press is still in `input` when the keymap runs — **D317**'s
own reading, and the thing that makes a *valved* field's cancel reach `cancel_gesture` at all.

**A plain `TextEdit` installs no preview, so the ladder fell straight through it.** Renaming a layer
in the inspector and pressing `Escape` abandoned the rename **and cleared the selection** — the
ladder's last rung — under the panel that was showing it. One press, two things, and the second was
not asked for. This is **D527**'s rule (*a press that dismisses a floating thing is spent on it*)
reaching the one family of control nobody had counted as floating.

A new rung in `OndinApp::escape` answers it, on `OndinApp::chrome_focus`.

🚨 **Below `cancel_gesture` and not above it, which is the whole of the placement.** A numeric
field's cancel has to go on reaching that function, because `cancel_gesture` is what sets
`gesture_cancelled` and stops the release committing after all (D317). Put the new rung above it and
every valved field silently starts committing what `Escape` was meant to abandon — the defect D315
and D317 exist to prevent, reintroduced by a fix for its neighbour. Because it sits below, the rung is
only ever taken when **nothing was in flight**, which is exactly the plain-text-field case.

**Nothing is undone at the rung.** The field has already abandoned its own edit through
`ui::defocus_commits` (**D808**); all this adds is that the key stops there.

⚠️ **`chrome_focus` is recorded rather than asked, because egui has no global question for it.**
`Memory::had_focus_last_frame` takes an `Id` and the ladder has none to give it, so the flag is
written at the **end** of each frame, after the `Tab` surrender — which matters, since a frame whose
`Tab` was ours ends with nothing focused (D123, D698).

⚠️ **"Anything focused", not "a text field", and that is deliberate.** It is
`egui_wants_keyboard_input`'s own definition — `focused().is_some()`, *anything*, a button reached by
`Tab` included (**D123**) — and narrowing it to text would make the rung disagree with the predicate
the rest of the keymap stands down for. Two spellings of "the chrome owns the keyboard" is the
duplication this app keeps finding in other places.

**Test** `app::library_wiring_tests::escape_out_of_a_chrome_field_does_not_also_clear_the_selection`,
flip-checked. `shortcuts.md` §11's ladder enumeration gains the rung.

**D516 — *Export all* really means every layer. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the ordering
without the outermost filter.***

`[S8.3-L1-02]`, Medium, and it settles `[A7-L8-01]`. `panels/export.rs · exportable_layers` walks the
whole tree and collects every node with a non-empty `exports()` — correctly — and then handed the
result to `build::in_document_order`, whose first line is `outermost(doc, ids)`. That filter drops any
id with an ancestor in the set.

**It is right for one door and wrong for the other.** `export_subjects` reads the **selection**, where
a group and something inside it both picked would plan the child twice — its own doc gives that reason
(D267). `exportable_layers` reads the set of layers **carrying export settings**, where a spec on a
nested layer is a deliberate instruction and exporting the group produces a **different file** from
exporting the child. A banner frame with an icon inside it, exported separately, is the workflow the
panel exists for.

Measured end to end on a `Group` set to export PNG 1× with a child `Rect` set to export PNG 1×:
`document_exports_anything()` answers `true`, so the row is live and its tooltip promises *"Every layer
with export settings, in one go"*; `exportable_layers()` answers **one** id; `export_plan` plans **one**
file. ⚠️ **Nothing reported the loss.** `write_export`'s `skipped` counter counts only layers with no
*bounds*, so the status line read *"Exported 1 file"* with no qualification while the rect's settings
sat in its own Export card producing nothing.

⚠️ **The documentation was the correct half, which is why this is a code fix rather than a doc fix.**
`exportable_layers`' own doc says *"Every layer in the document that is set up to export"*, the menu row
says *"Every layer with export settings, in one go"*, and `main.rs`'s `run_export_all` says *"the same
set and the same order the panel's Export all collects"*. All three describe what a user expects; only
`outermost` disagreed.

⚠️ **The CLI had the same defect through an independent copy of the walk**, so `ondin export --all`
dropped the same layer — **which is why nothing had noticed: the two front ends agreed about the wrong
answer.** Both now end in the same call.

`build::all_in_document_order` is the ordering without the filter, and `in_document_order` is that
composed with `outermost`, so the selection door is untouched **by construction rather than by care** —
the two spellings differ by the filter alone and neither can drift into the other's rule. A matched
member **is** descended into in the new function, for the same reason the filter is gone: another can
sit below it.

`panels::export::export_all_scope_tests::a_nested_layers_export_settings_are_not_dropped_by_export_all`.
The planned **filenames** are asserted rather than the count alone: two files colliding on a name is a
different failure from one file, and `plan` is where that would show. **Flip run**, `in_document_order`
restored: fails on *"both layers are collected"* at one id against two — the predicted site.

⚠️ **`[A7-L8-02]` is not closed by this.** `exportable_layers`' `.rev()` still carries a comment
claiming it is what produces document order, one line above the call that actually imposes it; the
ordering is imposed downstream either way, so that comment remains a thing to fix.

**D515 — A dotted spacing under the stroke's own width survives the tab row. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — `spacing.max(0.0)`, not `.max(unit)`.***

`[S14.3-L1-03]`, Medium; the test half is group **G9**. `inspector::pattern_for`'s `DashStyle::Dotted`
arm was `vec![0.0, spacing.max(unit)]` with `unit = s.width.max(1.0)`. **The stroke-width floor is the
fallback for a mode with nothing to inherit**, and applying it to the *inherited* value made the
function lose the number it exists to carry. Measured on a 4pt stroke, dotted, with a centre-to-centre
spacing of `2` — a state the dot-spacing field allows outright, its
`Scrub::whole(0.5).range(0.0..=ui::MAX_STROKE_WIDTH)` having no relation to the width:

```text
Dotted → Dashed → Dotted   [0.0, 2.0] → [12.0, 2.0] → [0.0, 4.0]
Dotted → Dotted            [0.0, 2.0] →               [0.0, 4.0]
```

⚠️ **One press does it**, which is the second line. `ui::segmented_enabled` records a click for any
*live* cell and the selected one is live, so the lit tab is a button and re-picking it re-derives the
pattern. The function's own doc is the indictment — *"Flipping Dotted → Dashed → Dotted has to come back
where it started, or the tabs are a way to lose a value by looking at it"* — and *by looking at it* is
exactly what re-clicking the lit tab is. §9.4 states the same guarantee almost verbatim, ending *"only a
mode with nothing to inherit falls back to multiples of the stroke width"*; the measurement is the
second half swallowing the first.

The arm is `spacing.max(0.0)` now, the same floor `Dashed` puts on both of its numbers. The
`DashStyle::Solid` **source** arm one block above already supplies the legible default
(`unit * 3.0, unit * 2.0`), which is where a mode with nothing to inherit gets its numbers — so the
floor on the way out was never the thing providing one.

⚠️ **No entry in this file and no passage in `architecture.md` clamps a dotted stroke's spacing to the
stroke width.** §5.3's bullet says the classification is *invariant under width*, and §6.3 and D69 are
about the zero-length dash's **cap** substitution rather than about spacing. The floor was undocumented
as well as wrong here.

⚠️ **The test written for this rule cannot fail on it**, which is the finding's other half.
`the_dash_modes_hand_their_numbers_to_each_other` uses `width: 2.0` and a spacing of `9.0`, so
`9.0.max(2.0)` is a no-op on every value it touches — and its own failure message is *"round trip lost
the spacing"*. Deleting `.max(unit)` outright left **975 of 975** production tests green, that test
included. `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape: the fixture never reaches the state the test names.

`a_dotted_spacing_under_the_stroke_width_survives_a_mode_round_trip` sits beside it and asserts the
one-click identity, the round trip, the identity for the other three modes — that being what the tab row
promises as a whole — and, as the control the clamp was actually for, that a mode reached *from* Solid
still opens on a legible multiple of the width.

⚠️ **The new test's first spelling was vacuous in the same way, which the same flip proved.** Its
identity loop built each stroke by calling `pattern_for`, so the clamp fired in the **setup** — 4 clamped
to 4 is 4 — and the loop passed under the defect; the flip skipped it and failed two assertions later on
the round trip. **An identity has to be asked of the value that entered, not of one the function under
test produced**, and having just written up why the *old* test was vacuous was no protection at all.
**Flip run** after the correction, `.max(unit)` restored: fails on *"re-picking the lit Dotted tab must
not move the spacing"* at `[0.0, 4.0]` against `[0.0, 2.0]`.

**D514 — A locked path refuses the verb its own second door let through. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — the lock on the fallback arm.***

`[S12.3-L2-02]`, Medium. `canvas::reverse_subpaths` has two doors. `canvas::edited_path` — the node
tool's path — carries D321's lock check and its comment says at length why the check lives there rather
than in `choose_tool`. The `or_else` fallback, for *a single selected `Path` outside point editing*,
asked `canvas::is_path`, which matches on the kind and nothing else.

So `Shift+D` — or the *Reverse subpath* row on the context menu, which dispatches the same action — on a
**locked, merely selected** path reversed its geometry and committed an undo step. Measured headless, on
a locked three-anchor path with `Tool::Select` and the selection set to it: `edited_path()` correctly
answers `None` in the same call, while `reverse_subpaths()` still changes the stored `BezPath` and takes
the undo depth from 1 to 2.

Nothing upstream re-added it. `app::dispatch`'s `Action::ReverseSubpaths` arm calls straight through,
with a comment saying it is deliberately *not* intercepted the way Delete and the arrows are, and
`menu.rs`'s `Row::new(Item::ReverseSubpaths)` carries no `dim_if` where its neighbour `Item::Join` does.
The locked layer reaches the selection in the first place through `panels/layers.rs`'s `select_from_row`
— the same route `edited_path`'s own comment names.

**The fallback itself is deliberate and documented** — *"It works on a selected path outside point
editing too, again as the radius does"* — so what was dropped is the lock, not the door.

⚠️ **The check went into that arm and not into `is_path`**, which the finding offered as the tidier
home. `is_path` is a question about the **kind** and has three other callers, every one of them reached
from a pick with its own interactability rule: `node_press` and its subject-switching arm both filter
`pick_leaf`, and `double_click_pick` is handed a picked leaf. Folding a lock into a kind predicate would
be a rule about one kind living in the code that knows about none, which is `edited_path`'s own argument
for where *its* check went.

⚠️ **This amends D321's enumeration the way D463 did.** D321 is a live *Keep* whose sentence is *"the
lock became one query the whole tree asks: text, points and the picture all refuse"* — exact about the
three **mode** doors it closed, and silent about a verb that has a door of its own. D321 is amended to
name this one, and §9.4's paragraph on the points guard with it.

`canvas::locked_path_verb_tests::a_locked_path_is_not_reversed_by_the_selection_door`. ⚠️ **The `Select`
tool is the fixture, not `Node`** — under `Node` the first door answers and has carried the lock since
D321, so the defect is reachable only through the fallback, which is the arm a user takes by selecting a
path in the layers panel and pressing the chord. The unlocked case is asserted first as the control, or
the assertion is about a verb that does nothing rather than about the lock, and `edited_path()` is
asserted `None` in the locked fixture so the test cannot pass through the wrong door. **Flip run**, the
check removed: fails on *"a locked path is not reversed"* at `"M40,30 L40,0 L0,0"` against
`"M0,0 L40,0 L40,30"` — the predicted site, the anchors coming back in the opposite order; the
undo-depth assertion behind it is checked second and the flip does not reach it.

**D513 — Release mask releases every mask the card beside it reports. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — the action carries a list.***

`[S14.2-L1-03]`, Medium, group **G17**. `inspector::mask_action`'s `Release` arm was
`node.children().iter().find(…)` — the **first** masked child — while `mask_card_targets` one row below
returned **all** of them, and `two_masks_in_one_group_are_both_targets` already said so. So *Release
mask* on a group holding two released one, the button **stayed lit**, its tooltip still read *"Release
mask — the layer draws again (Ctrl+Alt+M)"*, and the Mask card still reported **2**. Two presses and
two undo steps, with nothing on the first press saying so. Measured, after two `Ctrl+Alt+M` on single
children of a three-child group:

```text
round 0: lit=true   masks=[true,  false, true]   targets=2
round 1: lit=true   masks=[false, false, true]   targets=1
round 2: lit=false  masks=[false, false, false]  targets=0
```

**Three ordinary clicks reach it**: select one child of a group and press `Ctrl+Alt+M` — with a single
selection `build::mask` sets the flag *in place* rather than wrapping (D286) — then do the same to
another child.

⚠️ **The rule this broke is written on the function next door.** `mask_card_targets`' own doc: *"It is
a list because a group can hold two runs — a second mask among its children starts one — and the honest
answers there are to report 'Mixed' and to write to **both**, rather than to pick one and leave the
other reading as though it had been changed."* The identity row did the thing that sentence forbids,
one card above the card the sentence is about — and `inspector_mask`'s own doc claims the pair *"answer
it the same way"*.

`MaskAction::Release` carries a `Vec<NodeId>` now and takes it from `mask_card_targets`, which is the
query the card already uses and is already tested on. **One transaction over every target**, which is
also what makes it one undo step (invariant 5) — two presses cost two. The status line says *"2 masks
released"* for more than one.

⚠️ **Not a violated verdict but a gap, and G15's rule is why.** D286 defines the verb as reading *"one
selected layer that is a mask, or one selected container holding **one**"* — silent on two. D288 states
the report-Mixed-and-write-to-all principle **for the mode dropdown only**. A verdict's scope is what
it enumerates, so this is a gap D288's *reasoning* rules on rather than a rule that was broken. D286 is
amended to say what the arm now reads.

`releasing_a_mask_releases_every_one_the_card_reports`. ⚠️ **Asserted against `mask_card_targets`
rather than against the number two**, so the claim is *the two agree* and stays true if the fixture
grows a third mask; the undo is asserted too, because one step rather than two is the other half of
what the defect cost. **Flip run**, the arm back to the first target only: fails on *"the button
releases every mask the card reports"* at one id against two — the predicted site.

**D512 — An Alt-drag copy lands above its own original, whichever order the stack was picked in.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the indices, not a count of them.***

`[S12.2-L2-03]`, Medium. `canvas::clone_tx` corrected its insert index with a per-parent **count** of
copies already made. A count is only the right correction when every earlier insert landed at or below
this one — and **a selection is in pick order, not document order**: `Selection::ids` pushes as you
shift-click, and `build::outermost` preserves its input, which its own doc says in as many words.
Measured on two sibling rects `a` (index 0) and `b` (index 1):

```text
pick [a, b]  →  indices 1, 3  →  [a, a', b, b']   correct
pick [b, a]  →  indices 2, 2  →  [a, b, a', b']   both copies at the front, a' under b'
```

Shift-clicking front to back is the ordinary way anyone picks a stack, and which of the two you got
depended only on that, which nothing on screen reports. The result is precisely the behaviour this
document records as *the bug that was fixed* — *"Every copy lands one step above the thing it came
from, not on top of the whole parent"* (D40 for the Alt-drag, D42 for the preview that has to match
it) — and `clone_tx`'s own doc restates it. The ghost preview is built from this same transaction, so
it showed the wrong order honestly.

⚠️ **§9.4 states the mechanism as well as the rule, and had done since D100** — *"a flat count is right
only while the indices ascend, and they do not when the selection is walked top-down"* — so this is a
rule that was written down, obeyed by `insert_subtrees`, and quietly not obeyed by the one door that
does not go through it. The passage also claimed *"duplicate, paste and Alt-drag all agree on that
now"*, which was false for as long as the count stood; it is amended to say which of the three was the
exception, because the next reader of that sentence is somebody adding a fourth door.

⚠️ **The correct version was already written next door and its comment names this exact mistake.**
`build::insert_subtrees` keeps *"the indices this transaction has already inserted at, per parent — not
a count of them. See the note above on why the count was not enough"*, with
`shift = done.iter().filter(|i| **i <= base_index).count()`. `clone_tx`'s own comment claimed it
*"borrows the numbering rather than restating it"* — it borrowed `CopyNames` and **restated the index,
in the version already recorded as insufficient**. It keeps the indices now.

Not a rejection risk: `above + shift ≤ len` always held, so the transaction committed. It was silently
wrong, not refused.

`an_alt_drag_copy_lands_above_its_own_original_in_either_pick_order`, over both pick orders. ⚠️ **The
document-order case is the control and it passed throughout**, which is why this needed the reversed
order to see at all. **Flip run**, the count restored: fails on the reversed case at `[a, b, a', b']`,
the predicted site, with the ascending case still green.

**D511 — A declared size that is not a size is not one to either reader. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — one guarded reader for both.***

`[S7.1-L1-07]`, Medium. `svg_in::declared_size` guarded its `width`/`height` pair with
`w > 0.0 && h > 0.0` and fell through to the `viewBox`. `svg_in::view_transform`, ten lines below, read
the same two attributes through the same `parse_len` and divided by them **unchecked**. So the two
disagreed about which declaration they believed, and the transform lost. Measured, reading the root
`CreateNode`'s transform straight off the returned transaction, all against `viewBox="0 0 48 48"`:

```text
width="24"  height="0"    size 48×48   transform [0, 0, 0, 0, 12, 0]
width="-24" height="-24"  size 48×48   transform [-0.5, 0, 0, -0.5, 0, 0]
width="0"   height="0"    size 48×48   transform [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
width="24"  height="24"   size 24×24   transform [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, 0, 0]   (control)
```

⚠️ **Two of the three are singular**, and that is the half nothing recovers from: the whole pasted
subtree collapses to a point, and no scale gesture can undo it because every handle is in the same
place. The negative pair is a drawing rotated 180° through the origin, where a browser renders nothing
at all.

One guarded reader, `svg_in::declared_pair`, used by both. A non-positive declaration now means *no box
to fit into* — the arm `view_transform` already had for a missing `width`/`height` — so the drawing
pastes at its own units, which is what a browser's "render nothing" degrades to most gracefully.
`view_box` already checked its own numbers (`*w > 0.0 && *h > 0.0`), so this was the one of the
**three** sizing reads that did not.

`a_declared_size_that_is_not_a_size_leaves_the_drawing_at_its_own_units`. **Flip run**, the guard
dropped: fails on the *size* assertion at `24×0` against `48×48`. ⚠️ **The predicted site was the
geometry assertion and it was wrong — and that is the better result**: before the fix the two readers
disagreed, and one guarded reader makes them fail together. D394 amended, whose *"`viewBox` fitted onto
the declared `width`/`height`"* is the only account of import sizing either document carried; the
arithmetic itself is written down here for the first time.

**D510 — A segment's arc length is measured once per outline, not twice. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — performance, and the answer is unchanged.***

`[S4.2-L4-04]`, Medium, group **G10** — and this closes **part** of it. `geometry::round_run` calls
`fillet` per corner, and `fillet` measured each leg's `arclen` at the point of use. Every interior
segment borders two corners, so each was measured **twice** — once as the arriving leg of corner *i*,
once as the leaving leg of corner *i+1* — and a cubic's `arclen` is a numeric integration.
`geometry::local_path` runs on every painted node on **every frame** (`ondin-render/src/scene.rs`), so
this is per-frame work. The lengths are memoized now and `fillet` takes them as arguments.

**Lazy rather than a pre-pass**, which is the half that matters for the ordinary document:
`round_corners` takes this route as soon as *one* radius is non-zero, and a length is only ever needed
beside a corner that is actually rounded, so filling all of them up front would make one rounded corner
on a long path cost what rounding every corner costs. The `radius <= 0.0` check moved out of `fillet`
into the caller for the same reason.

⚠️ **It is worth about 7%, not the half `[S4.2-L4-04]` estimated, and only measuring said so.**
Release, a ring of cubics with every corner rounded: **11.68 → 10.64 ms** at 10,000 anchors,
**0.84 → 0.79** at 1,000. `inv_arclen` is a **root-find that calls `arclen` again per iteration** and
there are two of those per corner, so removing one of two *direct* calls is a small share of the work.
The redundancy was real and is gone; the projection was not. **Take a review's numbers as measurements
and its projections as guesses.**

**The finding's larger fix is declined** (§15 **D778**, 2026-09-15): **a new map on `Resolved`**
holding the rounded outline for a `Path` with any non-zero radius, filled and invalidated by the pass
that already fills `boolean`, so the walk is *handed* it — which is what `scene::Painted`'s own doc
says derived geometry must be. ⚠️ **It was open and `roadmap.md` carried it until that ruling**,
which struck the row; the per-frame rebuild is an accepted cost now rather than a queued repair, and
D778 has the trigger that would re-open it. ⚠️ **This said *"a fifth map"* until 2026-09-15 and D741 said *"a
fourth"* for a different one** (§15 D764): `Resolved` holds **six** — `world`, `world_bounds`,
`ink_bounds`, `inner_ink`, `text`, `boolean` — so both ordinals were wrong and the two entries read
as naming one slot. Deleted rather than corrected, a count in prose being a gate nobody built.

`geometry::tests::two_rounded_corners_on_a_short_edge_take_half_of_it_each` pins the one arithmetic
that reads a leg length: `t = (radius / tan(θ/2)).min(la/2).min(lb/2)`.

⚠️ **Its fixture had to be a 10 × 40 rectangle, and both halves of that are load-bearing — measured,
not reasoned.** On a 100-unit box with a radius of 10 the half-lengths never enter the answer at all.
And on a **square**, the two legs at a corner are equal, so the `min` has nothing to choose between and
only a leg that came back too *small* could ever be seen: on a 10 × 10 fixture, quadrupling one leg
left the test **green**. The rectangle gives each corner a short leg and a long one, and the same flip
then fails at **4.142 against 2.071**.

⚠️ **The obvious assertion was wrong and the run said so.** The first spelling expected `5`, the trim
distance, on the reasoning that the corner is cut back by half a side. It is — but the *arc* then
bulges back toward the corner, and what the fixture measures is the arc, at `t(√2 − 1)`.

**D509 — Moving a library keeps the names the files already had. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
the stem is kept where it is free.***

`[S1.3-L1-04]`, Medium. `library::relocate::relocate` re-derived every stem from
`entry.display_name()` — a **silent rename of every document in the library**, including files the user
named by hand.

⚠️ **What that destroyed is the sync-conflict mark, and that mark exists only in the filename.**
`scan::conflict_marker`'s own doc: *"Every pattern here is one `slug` cannot produce, which is what
makes the false-positive rate against this app's own files exactly zero"* — so re-slugging is the one
operation that can delete it. Measured: a library holding `landing-v4.ondin` and Dropbox's
`landing-v4 (1).ondin`. Before the move the copy is marked; after it, neither is, they are
`landing-v4.ondin` and `landing-v4-1.ondin`, and they **share one `meta.id`** — because a conflict copy
carries the *original's* metadata block, so both slug to `landing-v4` and the second takes `-1`. `-1`
is precisely the suffix `naming::unique_stem` gives this app's own collisions, so the pair became
indistinguishable from two documents somebody had simply named the same thing — except that any
legitimate pair has two ids and these had one.

Two entries under one id then collide on everything keyed by it: `.versions/<id>/`, `LocalIndex`'s star
and *Recent* row, and `cover::key` (`{id}-{modified}`, and `fs::rename` preserves the mtime, so the two
can produce the **same** cover key and the second card draws the first's picture). `recovery::pending`
resolves a snapshot with a `find` over that id — a `find` over a list that now has two matches, so a
crash recovery can offer to overwrite the wrong one of the pair.

`scan::Conflict`'s own note says why the mark matters: *"a conflict copy is a copy of the **file**"*,
carrying the original's name, project and id, so *"two cards, one name, one project dot, one cover, and
the only thing that differs is a filename the dashboard never shows. Marking one of the pair is not
decoration; it is the only signal there is."* (D375.)

The stem is kept where it is free at the destination; `naming::unique_stem` remains the fallback, which
is what merging two libraries needs and is what `Moved::paths`' doc — and D430's path map — is about.
`a_conflict_copy_keeps_its_mark_across_a_move`. ⚠️ **The mark is checked before the move as well** — a
fixture whose copy was never marked would pass the "still marked" assertion by never having been
unmarked, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape. **Flip run**, the stem re-derived
unconditionally: fails on *"the conflict copy keeps its filename"* at `["landing-v4-1", "landing-v4"]`,
the predicted site. §9.5 amended, whose *"`relocate` renames into a collision"* was a partial truth
while every stem was re-derived and is now exactly the rule.

**D508 — A number that is not a number never reaches the markup. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
the formatter floors, the region refuses.***

`[S8.1-L1-03]`, Medium. `ondin-export/src/svg.rs`'s `fmt` is the single formatter every number in the
SVG writer goes through — `svg_of`'s header, `path_d`, `matrix_attr` and `transform_attr` through it,
`opacity_attr`, `alpha_attr`, `stroke_attr`, `gradient_def`, `effect_def`, `shadow_graph`,
`adjust_def`, `image_def`, `with_image_clip`, and `emit_node`, `write_element` and `run_attrs` in the
walk itself. Both its arms printed a non-finite value verbatim: the fast path's `v.fract() == 0.0` is
false for `NaN` and `±inf`, and `format!("{v:.4}")` emits the literal strings `NaN` and `inf`. Neither
is a valid SVG `<number>`, so **one anywhere makes the whole file unparseable** — measured on an
imported `matrix(0,0,0,0,0,0)`: `<svg width="-inf" height="-inf" viewBox="-inf -inf -inf -inf">`.

**Two halves, and they answer differently on purpose.**

`fmt` **floors** a non-finite value to `"0"`. A wrong-but-drawable file beats an unopenable one — the
same choice the `-0` case already there makes, and the same direction D495 took in core. It is a floor
rather than a fix: the value was meaningless by the time it reached a formatter.

`effect_region` **refuses** a singular world transform. `world.inverse()` divides by the determinant,
so a node scaled flat — `Affine::scale_non_uniform(1.0, 0.0)`, which is a resize handle dragged onto
the opposite edge, and needs **no damaged document at all** — wrote
`x="NaN" y="NaN" width="NaN" height="NaN"` on its `<filter>`. `transform_rect_bbox` of a `NaN` affine
is a `Rect` of `NaN`s rather than `None`, so the def was collected, `defs.has` answered true and the
`<g filter>` wrapper was written. **Per the spec an unparseable filter region means the referencing
element is not rendered**, so one layer went silently missing from a file that was otherwise correct —
the worse of the two outcomes, because nothing about it looks wrong. It exports unfiltered now, which
is the fallback `ScenePainter::push_effect_layer`'s own doc argues for: *"it draws the artwork
unfiltered rather than dropping it, which is the failure mode worth having"*.

⚠️ **`fmt`'s floor alone would have written a region of `0`** — a filter region of no area, which is the
same silent drop with a parseable spelling. That is why both halves exist, and the test's two
assertions are each pinned by exactly one flip: the determinant guard removed fails on *"no filter is
written for a node with no area"* with the `NaN` assertion still **green**; both removed fails on the
`NaN` assertion at `x="NaN"`.

`a_flattened_node_with_an_effect_exports_a_file_with_no_nan_in_it` in `ondin-export/tests/svg.rs`.
⚠️ **The untouched sibling is not decoration**: with a normal layer beside it the `viewBox` is honest
and the file is plainly usable apart from the flattened node, which is what makes this finding's second
case the worse one.

For the record: `scene::effect_bounds` takes the same `world.inverse()`, so the canvas is not
*diverging* here — the difference is that a `NaN` rect handed to a backend allocator is a bad buffer
for one frame, while a `NaN` in markup is a permanent property of a file the user has already sent to
someone. §7 amended, whose model-completeness gate — *"everything the model expresses must round-trip
to valid SVG"* — was the passage this made false; nothing anywhere had claimed the writer may assume
finite input.

**D507 — A segment is rejected by its own hull before it is solved. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — performance, and the answer is unchanged.***

`[S4.1-L4-05]`, Medium, group **G10**. `query::outline_at` solved the exact nearest point on **every**
segment of every candidate, once per frame the Text or Pen tool is in hand — `PathSeg::nearest` is a
quintic root-find per cubic. The shape is G10's exactly: the *candidate* query is bounded,
`res.candidates_intersecting(area)` over a `slop`-sized box, so the bound is denominated in **nodes**
while the work is denominated in **segments**, and nothing bounded that. One imported path is enough.
`canvas::rail_at` asks this for the hover affordance and again for the click, so a frame can pay it
twice.

Re-measured in release on a ring of cubics, 50 calls each at `slop = 4`, before and after:

```text
segments      before     after
      10      0.0013     0.0007
     200      0.0142     0.0042
   2,000      0.1599     0.0408   ms/call
  10,000      0.7075     0.2041
```

**2,000 segments is the number to reason from** — an SVG-imported logo or map reaches it easily — and
there it is 0.160 ms/frame down to 0.041.

⚠️ **The control *hull*, not `PathSeg::bounding_box()`, and measuring is what chose it.** The tight box
is a root-find of its own — `ParamCurveExtrema` per axis — and gave back only **half**: 0.0685 against
0.0408 ms at 2,000 segments. The hull is four min/max pairs over points the segment already holds, and
it *contains* the curve, which is the property a reject needs: too generous costs a solve that was
going to be discarded, and too tight would change the answer. `query::seg_hull` is new and private, and
its doc carries that comparison so the next reader does not "simplify" it into the tight box.

The guard is a squared distance from the point to the box, **written out rather than
`inflate(slop, slop).contains(p)`**: `Rect::contains` is half-open, so a segment lying exactly on the
tolerance would be rejected. The threshold starts at `slop²` and narrows to the nearest distance found
so far, so once something is in hand the box test is against that rather than against the band.

`a_many_segment_outline_answers_the_same_with_the_segment_reject` in `tests/resolve.rs` is a 720-cubic
ring. **Two flips, and the pair is the point.** The reject with **no tolerance** — `> 0.0` for `> cap` —
fails on *"2 units off the outline at 1,0"*. ⚠️ **The probes are deliberately 2 units *off* the ink**,
inside a 4-unit allowance: a point lying exactly on the curve is inside its own segment's hull at
distance zero, so an on-the-outline probe cannot see that mistake at all. The reject **replacing** the
solve rather than guarding it — the box distance used as the answer — leaves the new test **green** and
fails the older `outline_at_finds_an_edge_where_hit_test_finds_an_interior` on *"an interior is not an
edge"*.

⚠️ **That second flip corrected what the new fixture was written believing.** Its draft doc claimed the
segment hulls *"cover the whole interior"*; they do not — 720 hulls round a ring are each under a unit
across and the centre is 100 units from all of them, so it is rejected trivially. The fixture where
hulls *do* swallow the interior is the **four**-segment ellipse in the older test, which already
existed. **A many-segment path and a coarse one are different risks, and only running both flips said
which fixture answers which.** §5.10 amended.

**D506 — The truncation ellipsis reaches the export as well as the canvas. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — appended to the last exported line's runs.***

`[S5.2-L1-03]`, Medium, group **G12**. `text::extract` appends an ellipsis run when
`shaped.truncated && parts.block.overflow == TextOverflow::Ellipsis`. `text::export_lines` — the
exporter's own walk of the *same* shaped layout — had **no ellipsis logic of any kind** and never read
`shaped.truncated`. So a truncated node exported as the clipped text with nothing to say it was
clipped: the canvas reading *"one two three four five …"* and the drawing beside it *"one two three
four five"*. The loss was not made up downstream either — there is no `TextOverflow` handling anywhere
in `ondin-export` — and no doc comment anywhere admitted it, so this is **not** on `[S8.1-L7-05]`'s
list of self-documented approximations.

**The two walks were built to agree, and one of them says so.** `ListMarkers`' own doc: *"a marker that
draws on the canvas and is missing from the export is exactly what a second path invites"* —
`ListMarkers` exists precisely so the two cannot disagree about markers. The ellipsis is the same class
of node-level ink and got no such treatment.

**Appended to the last line's runs rather than placed**, which is the one difference from `extract`'s
version and is the point: SVG `<tspan>`s flow, so the ellipsis lands after the text it follows without
this walk computing an `x` at all — and `ellipsis_run`'s clamp against the wrap width has no
counterpart here for the same reason, since flow cannot overshoot a measure it is not laying out
against. The style is the one at the last **visible** byte, exactly as D490 made `extract` take it,
with the same `rev().find(start < end)` rather than a containment test, because the last visible byte
can fall in a gap between two spans.

`an_ellipsized_node_exports_the_ellipsis_the_canvas_draws`. **`Clip` is the control and it is the one
that matters**: the ellipsis is conditional on the *overflow setting*, not on truncation, so a version
appending it whenever the node was truncated would pass a `truncated`-only assertion. ⚠️ **The
character count is asserted against the canvas's own glyph count** rather than against the literal
`"…"`, so the claim is *the two walks agree* rather than *this walk emits a character*.

**Flip run**, the append disabled: fails on *"the export ends in the ellipsis the canvas drew"* with
the text ending in `"five "` — the predicted site. §5.4 amended.

**D505 — One box-less member no longer takes the whole selection's chrome with it. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — and it amends D478.***

`[S12.5-L1-03]`, Medium. Delete a group's last child from the layers panel. `Document::op_delete`
removes the subtree and the parent's child entry and **nothing else**, so an empty `Group` is left in
the document — and an empty container has no local box at all: `geometry::local_bounds` is `None` for
`Group`, there is no boolean path, and the children union reduces over an empty iterator. Press
**Ctrl+A**. The whole selection then had **no transform box, no four corner handles and no size
badge**: it could not be resized, rotated or skewed, and nothing on screen said why. Every other member
is an ordinary rect.

The cause is one `?` in `canvas::selection_frame_extent`'s member loop. It now `continue`s past a
member with no box and answers `None` only when **nothing** contributed. An empty **Artboard** is safe
— it carries an authored `size` — which is why this went unnoticed.

⚠️ **This reverses what D478 decided, and the *consistency argument* is what reverses it rather than
being abandoned.** D478 wrote: *"A member with no box refuses the whole resize, where the old union
silently dropped it and scaled the rest. That is the stricter reading and it is the consistent one:
`selection_frame_box` already answers `None` in that state, so there are no handles to grab and the
gesture cannot start."* **That premise was the bug.** `[S12.5-L1-03]` measured the chrome refusing and
called it the defect. Once the chrome measures over the rest, the resize has to as well, or a grabbable
handle starts a gesture that refuses. Both readers go through `selection_frame_extent`, so they cannot
drift, and D478's paragraph is corrected in place in the source as well as in its entry here.

⚠️ **D494 widened the class rather than creating it**: a group whose only child is a mask now has no
box either, so the states that reach this are not only the empty-group one. Neither entry could have
said that alone.

The test is `canvas::headless_app_tests::an_empty_group_in_the_selection_is_skipped_rather_than_fatal`.
**The control is the same selection *without* the group, and the assertion is that the box is the same
box** — not merely `Some` — since a version answering with some other rectangle is a differently wrong
answer and that is the one shape separating them. `selection_handles` is asserted beside it because it
has its own legitimate way to answer `None` — a lone line — and its doc names exactly one such refusal:
a box-less member was a second, unstated one, and unlike the line it removed the chrome of every
*other* member. `select_all()` is driven at the end, because Ctrl+A is the door the user comes through.

**Flip run**, `continue` back to `?`: fails on *"the empty group is skipped, not fatal"* at `None`, the
predicted site. D478 amended; §9.4 amended with the rule the two readers now share — *a set's box is
the union of the members that have one, and is absent only when none does.*

**D504 — The pixel grid's two decision functions had no caller but the app. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the threshold is bracketed and the ruler inset gets its control. Test only.***

`[A5-L6-02]`, Medium, group **G9**. `grid.rs`'s two original tests are closed over the constant and
nothing else: `the_grid_threshold_is_the_zoom_readout_at_800_percent` re-derives
`(8.0 × 100).round() == 800`, and `a_cell_is_wide_enough_to_read_at_the_threshold` is literally
`assert!(8.0 >= 8.0)` — this project's second vacuity shape, a consequence every value ≥ 8 also
produces. Neither `OndinApp::grid_visible` nor `OndinApp::draw_pixel_grid` had a test caller anywhere
in the workspace: one production call site, zero test ones.

So all three of these stayed green. `zoom >= VISIBLE_AT_ZOOM` narrowed to `>` — the grid not appearing
at **exactly 800%**, which is the one number this module's whole doc is about. `self.show_grid &&`
widened to `||` — *View ▸ Show grid* no longer switching the lattice off above 8×. And the
`if self.rulers_on()` branch deleted, so the lattice runs under the ruler ticks, which is precisely
the outcome the code's own comment names: *"a lattice running under their ticks would make both
unreadable"*.

Two headless tests (`OndinApp::headless`, D303), reading `FullOutput::shapes` filtered by the grid's
own `INK` so nothing else emitted into the frame is counted as a grid line. The threshold is bracketed
at **7.99 / 8.0 / 8.01**, with `show_grid = false` asserted at each — the switch and the threshold are
separate reasons to be off, and only asserting both tells them apart. The lattice's leftmost vertical
is measured against `rect.left() + rulers::THICKNESS`, **with the rulers-off case as the control**:
deleting the inset leaves the line *count* roughly unchanged, so a test that counted lines would pass
it, and where the first line sits is the only thing that separates the two. ⚠️ **The fixture sets
`show_rulers` *and* `present`**, `rulers_on()` being `show_rulers && !present`, so a test setting only
the first would be asserting the inset on an app that might not have one.

**D484's own test already covers the half-pixel snap**, so the fourth mutation the finding lists is
not re-raised here; the finding predates that entry.

**Three flips run.** `>` fails at exactly 8.0, the predicted site. `||` fails one assertion **earlier**
than predicted — at 7.99 with the switch *on* rather than on the switched-off case, because
`true || …` is already wrong there. The inset deleted fails at **1.5 against 20**. §9.4 amended, which
said both halves of the threshold were pinned by the two tests above and neither of them ever called
into the grid.

**D503 — `group_chain`, the basis of every click-to-select decision, had no test at all. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-07; Fix — `query.rs` gets a test module. Test only, and half the finding was left
open — **closed by D805 on 2026-09-19**.***

`[A5-L6-06]`, Medium, group **G9**. `grep -rn "group_chain" crates/ --include=*.rs` returned **five**
lines: the `pub use` in `lib.rs`, the definition, and three production call sites in `canvas.rs`. No
test in the workspace named it, and `query.rs` carried **no test module at all** — its coverage figure
comes from `hit_test` and `local_box` being exercised through other suites. No gate could have helped:
it is a `pub` item in `ondin-core`, where `dead_code` never fires however many callers an item has.

Three tests now, each aimed at a mutation the review measured as green. **Outermost first, and the run
stops below the frame** — the order is not cosmetic, because the app reads the slice
positionally (`[_outermost, next, ..]`), in `pick_preview`'s own body until D805 lifted it into
`canvas::pick_from_chain`, so a reversed chain makes a plain click select the innermost
group and Ctrl+Alt the outermost, both gestures still doing *something*, which is why nothing
downstream would have said so. The frame stopping the run is asserted by the chain's **whole value**
rather than by the artboard's absence from it: that weaker assertion also passes a chain that stopped
one group early. **A boolean is a group as far as a click is concerned** — the `matches!(kind` arm
`CLAUDE.md` names as a `NodeKind`-sweep hazard beside `is_paintable`, `is_indexed` and the scene walk's
children loop, and the one member of that list with no test at all. Deleting
`| NodeKind::Boolean { .. }` makes a click select the operand, which `scene::paint_node` never draws:
the user selects something invisible and the boolean stops being draggable as a unit. **Stepping into a
group takes it and everything above it off the chain**, with the unrelated-`inside` case beside it —
that second one is the signal `pick_for_click` reads to *end* isolation, and it falls to a different
mutation, so both are needed.

**Two flips run, both at the predicted site.** The boolean arm deleted fails at `[]` against the
boolean's id. The isolation `break` moved below the `chain.push(c)` — Figma's isolation re-selecting,
on the very next click, the group you just stepped into — fails at `[outer, inner]` against `[inner]`,
with the unrelated-`inside` assertion still green, which is what says the two are independent rather
