than one written twice.

⚠️ **The finding's second half was deliberately not done here, and `[A5-L6-06]` was closed only for
`group_chain` until 2026-09-19.** Lifting `pick_preview`'s tail into a free
`fn pick_from_chain(ctrl, alt, chain, leaf)` per D269 and table-testing its five arms would cover the
three mutations left open — `ctrl && !alt` widened to `ctrl`, the `[_outermost, next, ..]` arm
collapsed, and `pick_for_click`'s `entered_group = None` guard — and it is a change to production code
rather than a test, which is not what this session was for. `roadmap.md` carried it, and **D805 below
did it exactly as written**: the lift, the table, all three mutations red, and the finding closed
whole. So what this paragraph now records is the *gap between* — a coverage entry that names the half
it did not reach is the reason that half did not become invisible.

⚠️ **One process note, because it is a new shape of `CLAUDE.md`'s editing hazard.** The test module had
to be written twice: a `git checkout` on `query.rs` to undo a flip discarded the **uncommitted tests
sitting in the same file**. The edit tools cannot truncate a file and a checkout can — **when the flip
and the new test live in one file, revert the flip with an edit, not with a checkout.**

**D805 — The click-to-select policy is a free function now, and `[A5-L6-06]`'s second half closes.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — the finding is closed whole.***

`pick_preview` read its two modifiers out of `ui.input` and decided in the same body, so reaching its
five arms meant driving egui five times rather than calling a function — which is why nobody had, and
why D503 above could close only the `group_chain` half of the finding. **D269's move, taken exactly as
`roadmap.md` prescribed it**: `pick_from_chain(ctrl, alt, chain, leaf)` is a free function in
`canvas.rs` and `pick_preview` is now the input read, the chain build and a call. The three mutations
the review measured as green — `ctrl && !alt` widened to `ctrl`, the `[_outermost, next, ..]` arm
collapsed, and `pick_for_click`'s `entered_group = None` guard — are all three red.

⚠️ **One real behaviour change, and it is not free.** The chain is built on the `Ctrl`-only path too,
where the early return used to skip it: `Ctrl` alone answers the leaf and reads no chain, so that
path now pays for a walk it does not use — one `group_chain` per hover frame, a shallow climb up
parents until it leaves the entered group or meets a kind it does not step into, plus a small `Vec`.
`pick_for_click` already does two of them on the click path and neither is measurable against the
scene walk beside it, which is the whole of the argument for accepting it. Named rather than glossed,
because a reader comparing the two bodies will find the early return gone and should not have to
wonder whether that was noticed.

**`pick_policy_tests::the_five_arms_of_the_click_policy` is the table, and its fixture is where the
vacuity was.** ⚠️ **`Ctrl` alone is asserted against a *deep* chain, not an empty one** — against `[]`
every arm answers the leaf, so a test that tried only the no-group case would pass against every
mutation in this entry, the first of the review's three included. The leaf's id is deliberately
distinct from every group's, so a wrong arm cannot coincide with the right answer.

⚠️ **The predicted failure site was wrong, and the reason is the useful part.** Widening
`ctrl && !alt` to `ctrl` is red on the **`Ctrl+Alt` two-group** assertion rather than on the
`Ctrl`-alone one: widening that arm makes `Ctrl` alone *more* often right, not less, and what it
swallows is `Ctrl+Alt`. Collapsing `(true, [_outermost, next, ..])` into `(true, _) => leaf` is red on
the same assertion, which is why the two-group and the single-group cases are asserted separately
rather than folded into one; `(false, [outermost, ..])` returning the leaf is red on the plain click.
⚠️ **The finding spells that second mutation the other way round** — `(true, [outermost, ..]) =>
*outermost*`, Ctrl+Alt becoming a plain click — and both spellings land on the same assertion, but
only because the fixture's three ids are distinct. The rule in the paragraph above earns its keep
twice over.

**The third mutation is a side effect on `self` and so stayed in `pick_for_click`**, which is why
`pick_policy_tests::a_click_outside_the_entered_group_leaves_it` drives a headless app through a real
`Ui` with the modifiers set on `RawInput` instead. ⚠️ **The guard runs before the chain is built** —
that is what makes the click that leaves isolation also select by the ordinary rule — so both halves
are asserted: the scope is gone *and* the pick is the outer group rather than the leaf, which a
version clearing the scope afterwards would fail. ⚠️ **The control is the click that stays inside.**
Without it, *"the scope was cleared"* passes against a guard that clears it unconditionally, which is
the mutation that breaks isolation mode outright. ⚠️ **This flip's predicted site was wrong too**:
deleting the guard is red on the **scope** assertion, `Some(g1)` against `None`. The reasoning that a
stale scope makes `group_chain` stop at a group the leaf is not inside and come back empty is sound,
but the scope assertion is written first and panics before the pick one is reached, so whether that
also fails is **reasoned and not measured**. The order is deliberate anyway — the scope is the cause
and the pick the consequence, so the failure a reader meets first is the one that explains the other.

🚨 **A doc-comment theft in a shape the neighbour grep cannot answer, repaired in the same change.**
`pick_from_chain` was inserted *inside* `frame_covering`'s doc run, between that function's summary
line and the rest of its prose: the summary came away as the head of the new function's doc, and
`frame_covering` was left with a doc opening *"**Area, not the centre point.**"* — still documented,
so *"did the item below lose its comment"* answers **no**, and the run-length ranking sees two
ordinary runs rather than one long one. The question that catches it is the mirror of the usual one:
**does the run above your own new item begin by describing your item?** `CLAUDE.md` keeps the tally
(D697); what belongs here is the shape.

**D502 — A duplicate is the same layer with different ids, and nothing said so. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the fixture carries a value in every field and the copy is compared field by field.
Test only.***

`[S2.1-L6-03]`, Medium, group **G9**. `capture_remap_insert_duplicates_a_subtree_with_fresh_ids`
asserted ids and shape and **nothing about content**, over a fixture that set none of the sixteen
fields `document::remap_subtree` copies by hand. So the test was satisfied by any implementation that
got the graph right, **including one that defaulted every payload**: changing
`exports: n.exports.clone()` to `Vec::new()` — a duplicated icon set up to write 1× and 2× PNGs coming
back writing nothing — left all 1,856 workspace tests green. Three of the sixteen carry a **documented
argument in `remap_subtree` itself** for being copied at all (`exports`, `effects`, `grids`), and all
three were enforced by nothing. That is this project's second vacuity shape — *an assertion the wrong
version also satisfies*.

The fixture now carries a non-default value in every field with an argument behind it: opacity, both
locks, a pivot, an effect, an export spec and a layout grid on the group; visibility, mask, mask mode,
name and a fill on one leaf; clip, fill rule, transform and a corner radius on the other. The copy is
compared **field by field** rather than as whole `Node`s, so a failure names what was dropped instead
of printing two trees. ⚠️ **The fixture's own non-defaultness is asserted too**, or the whole
comparison goes vacuous again the first time somebody simplifies the setup.

**Flip run**, `exports: Vec::new()`: fails on *"Grp: exports"*, naming the field, which is the
predicted site and the point of comparing one field at a time. It is also the only one of the three
the flip reaches, the loop hitting `exports` before `effects` and `grids`, so each would have to be
flipped separately to say the same of them.

**D501 — Nothing had ever fed a migration step the output of the step before it. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — one v1 file carrying all three legacy shapes. Test only.***

`[S1.1-L6-02]`, Medium, group **G9**. `migration_chain_upgrades_v0_to_current` builds its v0 file by
rewriting `schema_version` on a **current-shape** save, and concedes the consequence in its own
comment: every step past v0 is a no-op, so what it pins is that the chain *runs to the end*. The three
tests carrying real data — `migration_spreads_a_v1_corner_radius_over_four_corners`, the two v2 text
ones and `migration_moves_a_v3_frame_background_into_its_fill_list` — each rewind **one** version, from
their own step's immediate predecessor. So a `migrate_2_to_3` that depended on a v1→v2 artefact would
have been untestable to notice, because no fixture ever arrived at step 3 by way of step 2.

`a_v1_file_carrying_all_three_old_shapes_migrates_through_every_step` is one v1 file with a `Rect`
carrying a scalar `corner_radius`, a `Text` with a bare `line_height` multiplier and `align` inside
`style`, and an `Artboard` with a `background` brush — run through 1→2→3→4 with **each step's own
outcome** asserted rather than only the version number. The rewinds are the exact inverses taken from
the three single-step tests rather than written afresh, so this is a round trip through the shape the
old writers emitted rather than a guess at it, and the fixture asserts it holds one of each before
anything relies on it.

**This is coverage, not a bug**: the composition works today, and the four steps were read and are
total, all bump the version unconditionally, and none can panic. What it costs when that stops is
*"this old file will not open"* — data loss by a different road, landing on exactly the files that have
been around longest.

**Flip run**, the `2 => migrate_2_to_3` arm deleted: the load fails outright with
`UnsupportedVersion(2)`, the chain refusing loudly rather than silently losing the alignment, which is
the predicted site and the behaviour that makes a broken step loud.

**D500 — The height-limit half of `break_lines` was exercised by nothing. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — two tests with `Visible` as the control. Test only.***

`[S5.2-L6-04]`, Medium, group **G9**. `text::shape` sets `height_limit` to `Some` only for
`TextSizing::Fixed` paired with `TextOverflow::Clip | Ellipsis`, and **no test in the workspace built
that pair with overflowing content**. The only overflow-carrying test,
`ellipsis_adds_a_glyph_where_clip_does_not`, uses `AutoHeight(60.0)` and reaches truncation through
`max_lines`; the only other `Clip`/`Ellipsis` in a test is a serialization round trip of the field,
which lays nothing out. So `breaker.revert()`, the `truncated = true` that arms the ellipsis, and the
*"never revert the first line"* rule were asserted by nothing — `let too_tall = false && …` left the
whole workspace green.

Two tests beside `max_lines_stops_the_layout_and_says_so`, both with `TextOverflow::Visible` as the
control on the **same box and the same content**, so the assertion is about the limit rather than about
the fixture being small. `a_fixed_box_stops_at_the_line_that_would_overflow_it` is the limit itself;
`a_box_shorter_than_one_line_still_shows_that_line` is the `&& lines > 1` clause beside the revert,
whose own comment names what dropping it costs — *"an empty layout would lose the caret and the node's
identity with it"*, i.e. a node that cannot be selected back out of, guarded by one clause nothing
defended.

⚠️ **The short-box fixture's first spelling asserted nothing, and the test says so** rather than being
quietly corrected: the string fitted on one line at that measure, so the breaker never reached a second
line, never reverted, and reported `truncated` false. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s third vacuity shape — *the
fixture never reached the state* — met again.

**Flips.** `too_tall = false` fails on *"and `Clip` says it stopped"*: the predicted site was the line
count below it and was wrong, the flag being the earlier symptom because it is what arms the ellipsis.
**Both flips bite the short-box test at the same assertion from opposite sides** — 0 baselines with the
clause removed, 3 with the limit ignored, against 1 — which is what says that fixture is on the
boundary rather than merely near it. The `truncated` assertion beside it survives the first flip, a
layout that reverted its only line being truthfully truncated: **the flag is not the interesting half,
the surviving line is.**

**D499 — The arrangement API's whole `Axis::Y` half was executed by nothing. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — two existing tests widened rather than duplicated. Test only.***

`[S3.2-L6-02]`, Medium, group **G9**. An exhaustive census of every call to an arrangement builder in
`crates/` — tests *and* production — found **every one of them `Axis::X`, and every `align` call
`Edge::Min`**. So `along(Axis::Y, _)`, `lead(_, Axis::Y)`, `extent(_, Axis::Y)` and five of the six
arms of `align`'s `match (axis, edge)` table were run by nothing, while `input.rs` binds `(Y, Max)` and
vertical distribute to keys and `panels/inspector.rs` paints every Y cell of the align grid.

Two mutations the review measured as green against the whole suite: `build.rs · fn along`'s
`Axis::Y => Vec2::new(0.0, d)` rewritten as `Vec2::new(d, 0.0)`, which is *Distribute vertical* moving
layers **sideways**; and `(Axis::X, Edge::Max)`'s expression copied into the `(Axis::Y, Edge::Max)`
arm, which is *Align bottom* aligning **right**. A six-arm coordinate table written by symmetry is
exactly the shape where a copy-paste slip is invisible in review and obvious on screen.

The Y arms were read line by line and are **correct**: this is coverage, not a defect. The two existing
tests in `crates/ondin-core/tests/build.rs` were **widened rather than duplicated** —
`align_moves_world_bounds_to_the_target_edge` now loops all six cells, and
`distribute_equalises_the_gaps_and_leaves_the_ends_alone` runs both axes with the X fixture *turned*
rather than a second one written by hand. ⚠️ **The fixture has to differ on both axes**, or a Y align
is a no-op on a horizontal row and passes vacuously; the align fixture's two layers now differ in
position *and* in extent on both. Each case asserts the **cross** axis is untouched as well as the
aligned one, which is what catches an arm writing the wrong component of the `Vec2`.

**Two flips run, and both prediction lessons are worth keeping.** `(Y, Max)` given `(X, Max)`'s
expression fails on the *edge* assertion — the predicted site was the cross-axis one and was wrong;
both would fire, and the edge one is simply checked first. `along(Axis::Y, d) = Vec2::new(d, 0.0)`
fails on *"the middle layer did not move across the axis, 50 to 100"*, the predicted site — and then,
with **that assertion disabled and the flip re-run**, it fails at *"Y: 20 vs 120"*, so the gap
assertions behind it have teeth too. ⚠️ **Disabling the assertion in front is what shows whether the
rest of a test is load-bearing**, and a predicted site that fires first says nothing about the rest.

**D498 — The return half of the text-on-path door gets its first test. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — the round trip is asserted against the outline that went in. Test only.***

`[S3.1-L6-04]`, Medium, group **G9**. `build::detach_text_path` had **zero test callers**
workspace-wide: the definition, `menu.rs`'s `Item::DetachTextPath`, `inspector.rs`'s
`pub(crate) fn detach_text_path` and its call — not one of them a test. Its outbound twin
`text_on_new_path` has `clicking_an_outline_makes_a_railed_node_in_the_shapes_own_slot`, with four
stated claims and a ⚠️ on the one that fails quietly; the way back had nothing at all. Its only
production caller is a `&mut self` inspector method **no test can reach** (D269), so the builder was
the only testable seam and there was nothing on it.

`detaching_a_railed_node_gives_the_curve_back_above_the_text` sits beside the outbound test and reuses
its ellipse fixture. **The round trip is what makes it strong**: the rail that comes back is compared
against the outline that went *in*, not against a rebuilt one, so *"unchanged"* is the claim rather
than *"plausible"*. Four decisions ride on the builder and each is asserted — the rail comes back
byte-identical (`to_svg`); the new `Path` carries the **text node's** transform, because the rail was
stored in that node's space, where `Affine::IDENTITY` would put the curve somewhere the text has never
been, which is `text_on_new_path`'s own quiet failure arriving from the opposite direction; it lands at
`at + 1`, directly above the text; and **`on_path_offset` survives while `on_path` goes to `None`**,
inert today because nothing else can set `on_path` and worth pinning before something can — re-railing
a node that remembers where it used to start is a different picture from one that starts at the seam.

Both refusal arms are exercised, separately, because they answer the **same**
`OpError::WrongKindForOp` for different reasons: a node that is not text at all, and a text node
simply not on a rail.

**Two flips run.** `Some(Affine::IDENTITY)` in place of the node's transform fails on the transform
assertion and **only** that one — the rail's own `to_svg` is untouched by where the layer sits, which
is why the two are separate assertions rather than one. `index: at` in place of `at + 1` fails on the
sibling order at `[under, freed, made, over]`.

**D497 — The middle setting of a three-value control did the middle thing, and nothing said so.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the centre case is asserted through both callers. Test only.***

`[S5.2-L6-05]`, Medium, group **G9**. `text::justify_shift`'s `JustifyLast::Center => free / 2.0` arm
was executed by **no test in the workspace**, and it ships: the Type panel paints all three values
(`panels/typography.rs`, iterating `JustifyLast::ALL`) and writes the chosen one straight into a
`SetParagraphStyle`. The only other `Center` in the tree is a serialization round trip in
`tests/io.rs`, which lays nothing out. So replacing the arm with `Center => free` — a control whose
middle setting silently does what its right-hand one does — left the whole workspace green.

`centring_the_last_line_puts_it_halfway_between_the_other_two` asserts **an ordering plus a
midpoint**, which needs no magic number: `start < centre < end`, and `centre` within a point of
`(start + end) / 2`. The ordering alone would pass a `Center` arm returning `free * 0.9`, which is why
both halves are there.

**Asserted through both callers of `justify_shift`**, because there are two and a divergence between
them would be exactly as invisible as the gap was: `extract`, which is the canvas, and `export_lines`,
which is the SVG walk. They measure different things — a glyph's `x` against `ExportLine::x` — so the
assertion is made twice rather than shared.

**Flip run**, `Center => free`: fails on *"centre is short of end"* with the two numbers equal at
132.890625, the predicted site, in the canvas half — which is the first of the two, and why the export
half is asserted after rather than before.

**D496 — The closed-rail arm of the caret's normalisation was reachable by no test. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — a click past the wrap point is pinned. Test only.***

`[S5.1-L6-04]`, Medium, group **G9**. `text::PathWarp::shortest_way_round` — the whole of **D409** —
could be reduced to `pub fn shortest_way_round(&self, x: f64) -> f64 { x }` with **374 lib tests
green**. Every rail fixture in the workspace uses `fn straight(len)`, an **open** rail, where that
function is `x` by construction; `mod rail_session_tests`' three cases and the placement tests in
`mod tests` are open rails or zero offsets, and no test anywhere built a `TextEdit` on a closed rail.

What the flip re-arms is the reported bug D407 was written to fix — *"it keeps on editing the ghost of
the old position"*. Past the wrap point `PathWarp::nearest` legitimately answers a **negative** arc
length, around −705 where the text-local `x` is +49 on this fixture, because `nearest` deliberately
does not normalise: normalising there gave a half-way click an offset of −0.5, which is the other side
of D409's two-sided decision and is documented on the function. `Cursor::from_point` then clamps a
negative `x` to the start of the string, so clicking the ink of the later letters put the caret at
byte 0.

`clicking_bent_ink_on_a_closed_rail_lands_on_the_character_under_it` is a 120-radius circle with
`on_path_offset = 0.95` and `"ABCDEFGH"` at 20pt, clicking each glyph's own origin and asserting the
caret byte. A new `railed_at` helper takes the offset and `railed` delegates to it. ⚠️ **The non-zero
offset is load-bearing**: it is what moves the wrap point into the middle of the text, and at offset 0
the string begins at the rail's own seam with every letter on the near side of it.

**Flip run**: fails on `"D"`, caret **0** against **3** — five of the eight letters go to byte 0,
which reproduces the finding's own measurement exactly. §5.4 amended.

**D495 — A box that is not a number is no box at all. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — both bounds
functions answer `None` for a box nothing can measure.***

`[S4.2-L1-01]`, Medium, group **G1**. `geometry::world_bounds_of_parts` and
`geometry::world_bounds_of_path` each had exactly **one** `None` route — an empty `local_bounds`, or
an empty path — so a bad **transform** had none at all. `geometry::measurable` now guards both
returns.

**It tests two things, and either alone lets half the bad boxes through**; that asymmetry is the whole
of the entry. **Ordered**, because `f64::min` and `f64::max` return the operand that is *not* `NaN`,
so four `NaN` corners leave `transform_rect`'s seeds where it put them and the answer is
`Rect { x0: inf, y0: inf, x1: -inf, y1: -inf }` — inverted rather than empty. That half is a guard
that already existed next door: `resolve::clipped_to` is the one place in the model that rejected an
inverted rect. And **finite**, which ordering does not imply. `Affine::new([1e308, 0, 0, 1e308, 0,
0])` has **every coefficient finite**, so `build::affine_is_finite` — the guard D421 put on
`op_set_transform` — accepts it and is right to; the overflow happens in `transform_rect`'s corner
multiply and gives `Rect { x0: 0, y0: 0, x1: inf, y1: inf }`, correctly **ordered** and useless.
`transform="scale(1e308)"` in an imported SVG arrives as exactly that affine.

⚠️ **So this is not a hole in D421's guard.** It is a third shape of **G1**'s class, and the one that
matters for how G1 is tested: **a check on the operands cannot see what the derived value does**, so
G1's property test has to assert on derived bounds and not only on accepted operands.

The failure it prevents is the session's rather than one layer's. An infinite box unions all the way
up, so `world_bounds(root)` was infinite for the life of the session — and D334 names
`plan::raster_size` and `plan::raster_opts` as reading it — while the spatial index answered a query
5,000 units away from anything drawn. ⚠️ **`update` and `rebuild` agreed**, so `resolve.rs`'s
differential test was structurally blind to it.

**`None` rather than a clamp**, because both callers already answer `Option<Rect>` and every consumer
of theirs already handles the absence: a node with no bounds is out of the spatial index, out of the
cull and out of *zoom to selection*, which is the honest description of a layer whose extent is not a
number. A clamped box would put a click target on the artwork instead. `transform_rect` itself stays
total and its doc now says why — several of its callers have a `Rect` to return and nowhere to put the
absence.

Two tests. `geometry::tests::a_transform_that_cannot_be_measured_gives_no_bounds` takes four
transforms through both entry points with an identity control, and `tests/resolve.rs`'s
`a_layer_whose_box_overflows_is_left_out_rather_than_spread_up_the_tree` is the document-level one,
with the untouched sibling as an in-fixture control. **Two flips run**: `measurable` returning
`Some(r)` unconditionally fails on the `NaN` row, and `measurable` reduced to the **ordering** test
alone — the guard a reader would copy from `clipped_to` — gets past both `NaN` rows and fails on *"an
infinite translation"*. §4 invariant 8 and §5.9 amended.

**D494 — A mask lends its container the clip, not its own rectangle. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — a mask contributes nothing to the union.***

`[S4.1-L2-04]`, Medium. §5.9 states the rule in so many words — *"A masked layer keeps its own world
bounds; its container gets only what the mask lets through"* — and the code did the opposite whenever
the mask was **larger** than what it passed, because the mask child's own box was unioned into the
container un-narrowed. Measured: a group holding a 1000×1000 rect marked *Use as mask* with a 100×100
picture above it reported `world_bounds`, `ink_bounds` and `local_box` all at 1000×1000, where what
the group shows is the 100-unit square. *Zoom to selection* framed a square ten times the artwork, the
selection outline was drawn round emptiness, a marquee caught the group from 900 units away from
anything visible, and the inspector read W 1000 H 1000.

**Five arms of the same shape**, and there are five because two passes cross two kinds of bounds:
`resolve::recompute_bounds`' box union and, further down the same function, its ink union — both
`return b` after setting `mask_box` / `mask_ink`, both `return None` now; `resolve::resolve_subtree`'s
box and ink contributions, which were `match … { Some(m) if !is_mask => clipped, _ => cb }` where the
`_ => cb` fallthrough *was* the mask's own box, and which now open with an explicit
`_ if is_mask => None`; and `query::local_box`, the same `return b`, now `return None`.

⚠️ **This is not D460 and was not closed by it.** D460 corrected which box a mask *clips with* —
`mask_extent`, a mask group narrowing its own box with its own inner mask — where this is whether the
mask's extent enters the container's union **at all**. Every `mask_extent` call is untouched.

⚠️ **The existing fixture could not see it, and that is the interesting half.**
`tests/resolve.rs`'s `mask_fixture` builds a **50×50** mask under a **500×400** layer, so
`mask ∪ (layer ∩ mask)` is 50×50 either way and
`a_mask_bounds_its_container_and_not_the_layer_it_masks` passed whether or not the mask's own
rectangle was included. `a_mask_larger_than_what_it_passes_lends_its_container_nothing` turns the
fixture round. The old test is still correct after the fix and was left alone rather than widened —
widening a fixture three tests share is a different change.

⚠️ **One deliberate consequence, asserted rather than discovered**: a group whose only child is a mask
now has **no box at all**. It draws nothing — a mask is never painted — so *zoom to selection* and the
marquee have nothing to measure, which is the honest answer. The test asserts it so a later reader
meets it as a decision rather than as a surprise.

The ink arm is safe in the direction that union may not err, which the existing comment there states:
*"too small is the one error these bounds may not make"*. What is drawn is every other child's ink
intersected with the mask's, so dropping the mask's own contribution can only shrink the union to ink
that is actually painted.

**Five flips run, one per arm, and every predicted site was right.** `resolve_subtree`'s box → *"the
group is what the mask lets through"*, 1000×1000 against 100×100. Its ink → *"and so is the ink the
walk culls on"*. `recompute_bounds`' box and ink → **`rebuild` stays correct**, so both fail on the
`update` assertions; without those two assertions neither flip would have bitten at all.
`query::local_box` → *"and the local box"*. The `recompute_bounds` ink flip also showed that the
`update` ink assertion had **no message**, which it has been given. §5.9 amended.

**D477 — An image fill round-tripped into nothing, silently. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — one
flag, one walk-list entry, and a one-word repair written and taken back out. Entry reconstructed
2026-09-19.***

🚨 **This is a reconstruction, not a contemporaneous record.** The number was reserved and cited
during fix-phase session 4 and the entry was never written, so it has resolved to nothing since —
`CLAUDE.md`'s census read *"every one resolving except D476 and D477"*, and D806 says of the rule two
`svg_in.rs` comments cite this number for that *"D477 has no body entry"*. It is written from the
eight sites that cite it — `svg_in.rs`'s `patterns` report in `import`, its restatement of the
`skip`/`approximate` rule on D493's flag one call below, the `clipPath`/`mask` line of the
not-walked arm, `Gradients::patterns`' own doc, `resolve`'s `unpainted` predicate, `svg.rs`'s
`paint_attr` image arm, `an_image_fill_exports_as_a_pattern_over_the_encoded_original` and
`an_image_fill_is_reported_lost_rather_than_silently_blackened` — plus §7's two citations and D493's
closing paragraphs. **Everything below is quoted from one of those or read off the code at `HEAD`**;
the date comes from `review/findings.md`'s session-4 fix log, that session having written no block of
its own, and the sha beside it in that log resolves to nothing — see this file's header, which is
where the general form of that lives.

**`[A5-L6-01]`, High.** The writer emits an image fill as `<pattern><image href="data:…"/></pattern>`
and points the shape at it; the reader has **no `<pattern>` support at all** — `Gradients::collect`
keys `by_id` on `linearGradient`/`radialGradient` and `clips` on `clipPath`/`mask`, and `parse_paint`
has no arm for a pattern. So this app's own export, pasted back, lost its pictures, and lost them on
**neither report list**: 0 images in the document, nothing in `skipped`, nothing in `approximated`.
`svg_in`'s module header forbids exactly that — *"nothing is lost silently — a paste that quietly
loses half a drawing is worse than one that refuses"* — and the round-trip suite, which calls itself
*"the only thing that binds"* the writer and the reader, had no image case at all: each side had its
own green test on its own hand-written fixture and **nothing composed them**.

**Three parts.** `Gradients::patterns` is a `bool` set in the one `descendants()` pass and reported
once for the file as `skip("pattern (image fill)")`, which is the choice `Css::complex` and
`resampled` already made and for the same reason — *"some pictures could not be read"* is a fact a
reader can act on, where naming nine ids is a symptom they would have to trace back to it. ⚠️ **It is
set by the *presence* of a `<pattern>` element, not by a reference to one**, so a defined-and-unused
pattern still reports; named as a known bound rather than left to be discovered. Second,
`clipPath` and `mask` join `defs`/`symbol`/`style` on the silently-not-walked list, **because they are
definitions wherever they sit**: `Gradients::collect` registers both by id whatever their depth, and
the writer emits its artboard `<clipPath>` at top level, so the unknown-element arm was reporting
`skipped = ["clipPath"]` for a clip that had round-tripped perfectly. **A false positive on that list
is worse than a missing entry** — it is the one thing telling a user what a paste lost, and an item on
it that was not lost teaches them not to read it. Third, the round-trip test.

⚠️ **The test does not assert that the picture survives, because it does not.** Reading a `<pattern>`
back is a new paint-server kind in this reader and is left to whoever writes it, which is D411's
practice — *"recording the gap where the gap was so that closing it would be a failing test rather
than an act of memory."* **This is the report, not the feature.**

🚨 **The finding's headline symptom did not reproduce, and a one-word fix for it was written and taken
back out.** `[A5-L6-01]` read the re-imported rect as an *opaque black rectangle* and put it down to
an unresolvable `url(…)` falling back to the inherited `fill`, whose initial value is black — which
would make a ` none` fallback after the reference a one-word fix in `paint_attr`. **Neither half
reproduces.** `parse_paint` answers `None` for a `url(…)` it cannot resolve, so the shape comes back
*unpainted*; and measured in Chrome over HTTP, `<rect fill="url(#nope)"/>` and
`<rect fill="url(#nope) none"/>` paint the same **0** black pixels, which is SVG 2's rule and the one
browsers follow. The fallback was written, flipped, found to change nothing, and **reverted rather
than kept on "some other renderer might"** — the measurement is what allowed that call. The black the
finding saw is almost certainly the artboard `<clipPath>`'s own rect, which comes back as a **mask
node** carrying SVG's initial black because the writer gives it no `fill`; a mask paints nothing, so
it is harmless, and the first draft of the test failed by sweeping the whole tree for black and
finding it. The test looks the picture's rect up **by size** for that reason.

**`skip` rather than `approximate`** is the rule the two `svg_in.rs` comments cite this number for,
and it is D394's pair applied rather than a new one: *skipped* means missing, *approximated* means
there and slightly wrong, and a paint server this reader cannot read is **not there** — the shape
takes whatever fill it inherits, which for this app's own output is SVG's initial black. D493's
closing paragraphs carry that rule in prose for the fourth flag beside these, and §7 states it in as
many words; **this entry points rather than restating it**, and a reader who wants the rule with its
worked example should read D493.

⚠️ **The `url(` arm of D493's `unpainted` predicate is what stops this coming back, and the suite
proved it.** Written one step too broad — without that arm — the guard left the inherited paint
standing on a dead reference and an unresolvable image came back **opaque black**, which is precisely
the failure this entry is named for, reintroduced by a fix to something else.
`an_image_fill_is_reported_lost_rather_than_silently_blackened` went red. That is the load-bearing
detail here: the two
entries brace each other, and neither guard is safe to widen alone.

⚠️ **Two assertion messages in that test still describe the reverted fallback.** They read *"the
reference needs its `none` fallback"* and *"`none` means unpainted, not some other colour"*, with a
comment above them saying *"the reference carries `none` as its fallback"* — and the writer emits
` none` only on the arm where the def is **missing**, which a fill never reaches (`emit_missing`
diverts it to the placeholder) and which this fixture does not take. The assertions themselves are
right and their reason is not, which is the class nothing here can gate. *Fix by rewording the three
to the reader's behaviour — an unresolvable `url(…)` is unpainted on its own — when that file is next
open.*

**D493 — An unreadable paint destroyed the one it inherited. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the
parse guards the assignment, and the loss is reported.***

`[S7.1-L1-03]`, Medium. Two independent halves, either of which alone leaves a real defect.

**`!important` was handed to `parse_paint` verbatim.** `fill:#ff0000 !important` — what a stylesheet
with any priority in it writes — imported the shape with **zero** fills, invisible, with
`Import::skipped` and `Import::approximated` both empty. It is stripped in `declaration` now:
`!important` is a *specificity* input in real CSS, and this reader has no important-vs-normal ordering
to get wrong — its own `Css` doc says at length that it is a lookup and not a cascade engine — so the
only thing the marker could do here was make a perfectly good value unreadable.

**The two paint arms wrote the *result* of the parse into the style**, and `None` is `Style`'s
spelling for **unpainted**, so any value peniko refuses destroyed the inherited paint too.
`<g fill='#00ff00'><rect style='fill:var(--brand)'/></g>` came back with **no fill at all**, where CSS
drops the invalid declaration and the green stands. `var(--brand)` is what a design-tool or web export
writes. ⚠️ **Every other arm of `resolve` was already written the safe way** — `stroke-width`,
`stroke-dashoffset`, `stroke-miterlimit`, `fill-opacity`, `font-size` and the rest all read
`prop(…).and_then(parse_len)`, so a value they cannot read leaves the inherited one alone. `fill` and
`stroke` were the two that put the parse inside the assignment.

The loss is reported through `Gradients::unreadable_paint`, a **`Cell`** because `resolve` sees the
gradient table by shared reference and this is the only flag there set outside `collect`: the other
two — `patterns` (D477) and `resampled` (D459) — are facts about the *defs*, walked once up front,
and this is a fact about the *elements*, walked with the table already borrowed. A second walk to find
out would be a second cascade. A flag rather than a list of values, on the same argument
`Css::complex` and D477 make, and reported as `skip` rather than `approximate` on D477's rule: the
paint is not there in some other form, the shape simply takes whatever it inherits.

⚠️ **The guard was one step too broad, and this session's own suite caught it.** **Three meanings
share one `None`, and only the *text* tells them apart**: `none` and `transparent` legitimately mean
unpainted, and a `url(#…)` that does not resolve is a **valid declaration with a dead reference**
rather than an invalid one — D477 measured that case against Chrome and established that the shape
comes back *unpainted*, a ` none` fallback having been written for it and taken back out because both
spellings paint zero black pixels. Without the `url(` arm, leaving the inherited paint made an
unresolvable image reference come back **opaque black**, SVG's initial fill being black, which is
exactly the failure D477 is named for: `an_image_fill_is_reported_lost_rather_than_silently_blackened`
went red. *This is the shape session 3 recorded on `[S7.2-L5-01]` and had no name for — the finding's
own symptom is fixed and a second, quieter thing breaks.*

⚠️ **And the test was first inserted below, anchored on the next function's name, and took that
function's 58-line doc comment with it** — `CLAUDE.md`'s *anchor above, never below* trap, the
**ninth** recorded instance, committed by the session that had written up the eighth hours earlier.
`cargo` caught this one only because the displaced `#[test]` landed on a doc comment and became a
`duplicate_macro_attributes` warning; had the neighbour been an ordinary `fn`, or had the insertion
gone one line lower, every gate would have been green and 58 lines would have been describing the
wrong test. **`#[test]` is a coincidence, not a safety net.** Repaired, both docs verified back onto
their own functions with `grep -n -B2 "fn <the neighbour>"`, and the instance is written into the
test's own doc.

**Two flips run, one per half.** Removing the `!important` strip fails the first assertion at
`[0, 0, 0]` against `[255, 0, 0]` — **black, not empty**, because the other half now leaves the
inherited paint. Returning the `fill` arm to a plain assignment fails on *"the green survived"*.
Neither half masks the other; each fails its own assertion. §7 amended.

**D492 — An export scale that cannot be a size. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the operation
refuses one and the loader drops it.***

`[S8.2-L1-03]`, Medium. `op_set_exports` was six lines and bounded nothing — `nodes.get_mut`, a
`mem::replace`, a dirty mark. A `.ondin` carrying `"scale": {"Width": 0}` loaded, and
`ondin export --all` wrote **`Button@0w.png` at 1 × 1**: exit 0, no warning,
`PlannedFile::clamped == false`. The filename asserts a 0-pixel width, the panel row reads
`0w → 1×1`, and the asset is junk a build script will happily copy. `Times(-2.0)` is the same shape —
`factor` floors it to `1e-4` and the file is named `@-2x`.

⚠️ **Both other entry points already refused exactly this set and said why in their own comments.**
`ExportScale::from_label` filters `*px > 0` for `Width`/`Height` and `n.is_finite() && *n > 0.0` for
`Times`, documented as *"`None` … for a value that cannot be a size — zero, negative, and the
non-finite multipliers a `f32` parse will happily produce"*. And `main.rs`'s CLI parse rejects the
same set: *"Zero and negative are rejected here rather than left to `factor`'s floor, which exists to
keep the renderer safe and **would turn `--scale 0` into a one-pixel file nobody asked for**."*
**That is precisely the file this produced** — the comment describing the outcome sat on the two paths
that could not reach it, and the model was the only door without the guard.

**The two halves answer differently on purpose.** An *operation* is refused
(`OpError::BadExportSpec`), because the app should never author one: `quality_step` clamps to
`1..=100` and every seeded rung is one of `ExportScale::COMMON`'s own multipliers, so neither value
can come from this app's own UI, and what is left is a hand-edited file or another tool. A *file* has
its unusable specs **dropped** in `io::schema::into_document`, because refusing the whole document
over an export preset would lose the artwork to save the recipe — and `Width(0)` has no defensible
non-zero reading to repair it to, so it is not clamped either. That is §5.11's own asymmetry, the one
the out-of-range opacity clamp beside it already makes, rather than a new rule. `quality` is bounded
`1..=100`, which is what its own doc says it is and what the JPEG encoder takes; `0` is not "worst
quality", it is out of range.

`document::export_spec_is_usable` is the shared predicate, **written rather than reached for**:
`from_label` answers `Option<ExportScale>` from a *string* and this asks about a value that is already
one — the same rule, two questions — and duplicating three comparisons is cheaper than a conversion
that would have to invent a label.

The test's fixture is **hand-edited JSON, because the model now refuses to build one**: that is the
point of the two halves differing, and it is the only way to reach the loader's arm without a
test-only setter that would exist on `Document` solely to break it. Valid scales are asserted as the
control — the predicate is three comparisons, and getting one backwards would refuse every export in
the app with everything else green. **Both flips run**: the op guard made inert fails on `Width(0)`;
the loader filter removed fails on the surviving-row count, 2 against 1. §4 invariant 8, §5.7 and
§5.11 amended.

⚠️ **The same commit wrote the box assertion D490 had claimed and not made**, which is recorded at
D490 rather than here — including that the first attempt at writing it asserted `font_size <
box_height`, which ordinary type does not satisfy.

**D491 — A transaction that orphans a guide is refused. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — a
post-condition over every guide at the end of `apply`.***

`[S2.2-L2-05]`, Medium, group **G5** — and the class **D453** removed one caller from and said it
could not remove. `Document::check_guide_owner` states the rule — *"a guide may only be scoped to a
frame that is in the document"* — and enforced it on `AddGuide` and `SetGuideScope`, the two
operations that **name** an owner. There is a second way to break it, which is to remove the frame,
and `op_delete` never looked at `self.guides` at all. Measured through `Document::apply` alone, with
no hand-editing: the delete returned `Ok`, `doc.guides()` kept the orphan, and
`io::load(io::save(&doc))` refused the bytes **forever** — *"guide 51:4 is scoped to 51:2, which is
not a frame in this document"*. Autosave writes that file, and the in-memory session that could still
undo it is the only copy of the user's work. The loader rejects rather than repairs on purpose and
says so (§5.11): promoting the guide to global would move the line to a coordinate the user never
chose.

⚠️ **There was no live bug, and that is the reason this is a post-condition rather than a patch.**
Every production `DeleteNode` construction site was enumerated. `app::delete_selection` is the only
one that can name an `Artboard`, and it carries `build::guides_of`; the other six cannot name one at
all — `build::outline` refuses a frame through `can_outline`, `flatten_union` and `text_on_new_path`
refuse it by kind (D453), `ungroup` deletes a group, and the canvas's two delete a text node. What
existed was **an invariant enforced by a convention a fourth delete site would have to know about**,
in a class that had already produced three findings. So the check runs at the end of `apply`, over
every guide, where the document becomes real — and it catches the next operation that breaks the rule
as well as this one.

**After the loop and before `*self = working`, so a transaction stays all-or-nothing.** Checking per
op would refuse a transaction that ends up *correct*: `guides_of` puts the `RemoveGuide`s first and
the frame is still there when they run, so that order never holds an orphan at all — but the reverse
order, frame then guides, is legal, is what a caller might write, and passes **through** a state with
an orphan in it on its way to a valid document. `undoing_a_frame_delete_restores_its_guides` commits
exactly that transaction (it is that test's "wrong" order, wrong only for the undo), so a per-op check
would have turned an existing green test red for the wrong reason.

**`build::guides_of` is not demoted to an optimisation.** It is still how the Delete verb carries its
guides and how the inverse gets the order right, which is `undoing_a_frame_delete_restores_its_guides`
and §5.7's own paragraph. What changes is that a site which has not heard of it gets a refused edit
instead of an unopenable document.

**The assertion is the round trip, not the error type.** What the finding is about is a file that will
not load; asserting `Err(BadGuideOwner)` would pin the mechanism and let a future spelling that
corrupts differently through, so `deleting_a_frame_that_owns_a_guide_is_refused_or_still_loads` asks
for one or the other and takes either. The `guides_of` order is asserted beside it as **the control** —
a refusal that also refuses the correct spelling is worthless. Flip run, the post-condition made inert
with `let _ =`: fails on the round-trip assertion, the predicted site. D453 amended; §4 invariant 8,
§5.5 and §5.7 amended.

**D490 — An ellipsis was set in the type it replaced. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the style at
the last visible byte, and the colour line its sibling was already paying.***

`[S5.2-L1-02]`, Medium. `shaped.runs` is a range table in ascending byte order over the **whole**
content, so `.last()` answered with the style at the end of the *string* — which, on a truncated node,
is precisely the text that is not drawn. A character span anywhere in the invisible tail therefore
restyled the ellipsis. Measured: a `Size(40.0)` span over bytes past the one visible line put a **40pt
`…` in a 12.1-unit-tall box**, moved 16.5 units left, for a span the user set on text that is not on
screen.

**The information was already in hand and thrown away.** `last_line_end`'s third field carried
`runs.len()` and was read by nobody — the `_` in the pattern that destructured it was the tell, and a
tuple field nothing reads is a question somebody once meant to answer. It is the last **visible byte**
now, and the style is resolved at it. ⚠️ **`line.text_range()`, not `run.text_range()`**: a parley
*run* spans every line it was broken over, which is the trap `export_lines` documents and which this
would have walked straight into, the line being the thing that ends here. And the lookup is
`rev().find(start < visible_end)` rather than a containment test, because the last visible byte can
fall in a **gap** between two spans, and the run that begins before it is the one whose type the reader
last saw.

**Second half, and it is the guard-next-door shape.** `extract_flat` returns `color: None` deliberately
— its third caller is the font picker's family list, which draws in the chrome's own text colour and
must not have a document value leak into a control. `marker_run` corrects that for its caller with
`run.color = style.color` and a comment saying why. `ellipsis_run`, the sibling built the same way
three functions later, did not, so an ellipsis after a red run was **not** red: it fell through to the
node's fill stack. *Both of `extract_flat`'s other callers owe that line, and only one of them was
paying it.*

⚠️ **This region had exactly one assertion with teeth and it counts glyphs.** The review flipped the
style source to the node default — ignoring every span there is — and the whole workspace stayed green;
`ellipsis_adds_a_glyph_where_clip_does_not` passed because *"is there an ellipsis at all"* is the whole
of what it asks. **Nothing asserted what the ellipsis looks like or where it goes.**
`an_ellipsis_is_set_in_the_type_it_follows` is the assertion that does, with the same node and no span
as its control so that "unchanged" means unchanged rather than 10.0 by coincidence. Flip run, the
lookup back to `shaped.runs.last()`: fails on the font size at **40 against 10**, the predicted site.

⚠️ **Its sibling `[S5.2-L1-01]` is deliberately still open, and it is now the only part of this region
still wrong.** The ellipsis is drawn *on top of* the text it ends wherever the clamp pulls it back
inside the box — `x.min(w − advance)` keeps it in, and nothing shortens the visible string underneath
it. The honest fix is a visible change to every document already using the feature, so the review filed
it Bucket 2 and this session left it; `roadmap.md` carries it under *Now · Text*.

⚠️ **And the new test's own doc claimed an assertion it did not make**, which was recorded here rather
than quietly corrected, because a test's prose is the one thing in this project no gate reads (§15
D319): it said *"the box is asserted too"*, and the closure returned a `font_size` and nothing else.
**Written rather than struck on 2026-09-07** (with §15 D492), because the claim was worth making: the
closure returns the layout height beside the size, and the test requires it to be **the same in both
runs**. That is what makes the size assertion mean something visible — the box is measured from the
*drawn* line and does not move, so the 40pt ellipsis was not a large box with a large glyph in it.
⚠️ **The first attempt at writing it asserted `font_size < box_height`, which ordinary type does not
satisfy**: a 10pt font in a 10-unit line box fails it, correctly, an em not being a line box. Both the
omission and the wrong first form are in the test's own doc, since that is where the next reader of
the assertion will be.

**D489 — A one-glyph run on a rail was placed by its left edge. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
the advance scan runs over the flattened glyph sequence, not over one run at a time.***

`[S5.1-L1-03]`, Medium. `text::bend` places each glyph by its **own midpoint**, which is SVG's rule and
is worth the arithmetic because rotating about the left edge fans wide glyphs outward on a tight curve
— the error largest exactly where the feature is most visible. A midpoint needs an advance, and
`GlyphRun` carries positions and no advances, so the last glyph of a run borrowed its predecessor's.
**For a run of one there is no predecessor**: the scan took its seed, `0.0`. With `adv = 0` both terms
of the placement vanish — the sample point is no longer nudged half an advance along the rail, and the
origin is no longer pulled half an advance back along the tangent — and the glyph takes the tangent at
its **left edge**, which is exactly the placement the paragraph two lines above it rejects.

**Reached by an ordinary act.** Style one character of a railed node — one red letter, one bold letter,
anything that makes parley split a run — and that character rotates out of line while every neighbour
is placed properly. Measured on *"Wave along the rail"* at 40pt on a 120-radius circle: **0.149 rad,
8.56°, and 1.35 units** of position, on a character a span was supposed to recolour and nothing else.
It is also reached by any run parley splits for **font fallback** that happens to be one glyph long: an
emoji, a CJK character in Latin text.

**Runs are laid out in one flat coordinate space**, which is what makes the fix smaller than the bug.
The glyph after a run's last is the next run's first, so its advance is a real *measurement* rather
than an estimate, and only where there is no successor at all does a glyph still borrow. ⚠️ **The
same-line test is what makes that safe and must not be simplified to a comparison of `x`.** Across a
line break the next glyph's `x` returns to the line's start — but under a right or centre alignment it
can still be *greater* than the previous line's last `x`, so an `x` comparison alone would silently
accept an absurd advance at every line end. The guard is `n.x > this.x` **and** the two `y`s within
`1e-4`.

⚠️ **The test needed a curved rail and a metric-neutral span, and both of those are why this went
unseen.** `a_straight_rail_reproduces_flat_type` cannot see it: on a straight rail the tangent is
constant, so left edge and midpoint agree and only the position term survives. **Every rail fixture in
the module used a single unstyled run on a rail that hides the rotation**, which is why the review's
flip of the fallback line left all 374 tests green. And `CharAttr::Color` is chosen because it splits
the run while changing nothing parley measures — a `Size` or a `Weight` span would move the glyph
legitimately, and a difference would then be the span doing its job rather than the bug.

⚠️ **Flip run, the scan confined to its own run again.** Fails on the rotation assertion at **−0.0758
rad**, the predicted site, with the position assertion behind it. It is smaller than the review's
0.149 because that was a 40pt fixture and this is 20pt: the error is half the glyph's whole advance, so
it scales with the type. *An error that scales with the type is one a small fixture can hide.*

**D791 — The railed box is swept per segment at each segment's own curvature, and it is on trial
behind a toggle. *Committed 2026-09-15 and **not accepted**; on trial — promote or revert by deciding
the cost question below.***

`[S5.1-L4-02]`'s sketch, which asked for `text::bend`'s box sweep to be made cheaper. The sweep walks
the rail and unions the offset ribbon; it stepped uniformly at `warp.len / RAIL_STEP`,
`.clamp(1.0, 4096.0)`. It now samples **per segment**, at a step taken from that segment's own
curvature: the sagitta between two samples an arc `h` apart on curvature `κ` is about `κh²/8`, so
holding it under a new `BOX_SAG` gives `h = sqrt(8·BOX_SAG/κ)` — plus an offset-curvature correction,
because `place` maps across by up to the ribbon's reach and offsetting toward the centre of curvature
takes a radius `ρ` to `ρ − v`, so a step adequate for the **rail** is not adequate for the curve
actually being bounded.

**Separating the box's tolerance from `RAIL_STEP` is the substance of it.** That constant is justified
for `PathWarp::warp`, where every sample becomes a *drawn vertex* of a decoration ribbon and the
resolution is the point; the box sweep borrowed it for a computation whose entire output is **four
numbers**, so its density was denominated in rail units and its cost grew with the length of the rail
rather than with what the answer needed. ⚠️ **And the `clamp(…, 4096.0)` it replaces is an accuracy
*surrender*, not a safety bound** — past about r = 20,000 the uniform sweep stops honouring
`RAIL_STEP` at all — so a rule that keeps its promise asks for *more* there, not less.

**`BOX_SAG` is 0.005 and not the 0.05 it started at, and this account is inherited rather than
re-run**: the looser value is recorded as having broken
`tools::tests::dragging_railed_text_scales_its_rail`, the box feeding `resize_to_handle`'s solver
through `tools::railed_box`, so box noise becomes **artwork movement** — the rail crept 0.0087 on the
axis the drag was holding, against that test's `1e-3` tolerance, where the legitimate residual its own
comment records is 0.0002. The coupling is real whatever the number: *a twentieth of a unit is
invisible on screen and is not invisible to a solver.*

🚨 **The reason it is on trial is that `budget` is not a cap, and the shape of the floor is the whole
question.** Sample counts against the uniform sweep on the same rails: circle r=300 **944 → 583**,
r=3000 **4,097 → 1,747**, r=30000 **4,097 → 4,135**, and a 5,999-segment polyline
**1,922 → 17,998**. So the win is real at small and medium radius, it is **parity** at r=30000, and a
many-segment rail — a traced outline, an imported path, a pen drawing — costs **9.4× more** with
nothing to stop it.

⚠️ **That 17,998 was recorded as higher than the three-per-segment floor predicts and unexplained. It
is not: it is `3 × 5,999 + 1`, exactly.** A straight segment has zero curvature, so `h` is infinite,
`(slen / h).ceil()` is zero and `.max(1.0)` makes it one; `budget` then multiplies a `want` of 1 by
0.68 and `.ceil().max(1.0)` returns it to **1** again; and each segment adds its two end nudges. Three
per segment, plus the single closing `sample(warp.len)`. **So the cost is understood and is
`3n + 1`** — and the sharper statement of the open question is that the 4,096 allowance is *inert on
precisely the rail that costs most*, since scaling a `want` that is already at the floor buys nothing
back. The counts are `sample` invocations, which the uniform figures confirm: `ceil(1884.96/2) + 1`
is 944 and the clamp's `4096 + 1` is 4,097.

⚠️ **Two comments were struck as measurably false rather than committed**, and a sketch arriving with
both is the thing to expect from a sketch. A timing block — *"r=30000 3.399 → 1.443 ms"* — taken at
`BOX_SAG = 0.05` and never re-taken after the tightening, **contradicting a second block thirty lines
below it** that gave *"3.44 → 4.54"* for the same case, in the opposite direction, with nothing saying
which was current. **Two timings of one case is one timing too many**, and the deterministic half is
counted instead, a sample count being unable to go stale against a machine. And *"the same total
budget is kept"*, which the polyline falsifies outright.

**`const SKETCH: bool` selects between the two sweeps and stays until the cost question is answered.**
It is not decoration: the A/B is what answered the box-jumping report (identical boxes either way) and
the held-corner slide of **D789** (also identical, which is what said that one was pre-existing), and
it is what found **D792** — a defect whose only symptom is *a box five units too small* is not one
anybody finds by reading. ⚠️ **`[S5.1-L4-02]` stays open.** A cost that is not bounded is not yet a
decision, and this entry is the record of a trial rather than of an acceptance.

**D792 — A per-segment walk is traversal-dependent, and the flip read every segment's interval
backwards. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-15; Resolved — inside D791's sketch, which is still on trial.***

`PathWarp::at` maps `along` to `len − along` when `PathWarp::flip` is set (`on_path_flip`, §15
**D406**, whose *"every consumer follows without knowing the flag exists — the glyph rotations, the
second line, the decoration ribbons, the box sweep"* is the promise this broke). **D791's sampler
walks `warp.segs`, which is in rail order and knows nothing about that**, and treated each segment's
cumulative `s0` as an `along` value — so on a flipped rail it read **every segment's interval
backwards**. Its boundary samples landed mid-edge, and the end nudge that exists to ask a segment for
*its own* end normal landed in the **next** segment.

Measured on a closed 200×100 rectangle rail: the uniform sweep gives `x1 = 205.0` and the sketch gave
`x1 = 200.0` — the box sitting exactly on the rail, five units narrow on the right, with the type
hanging outside it. `flip = false` was byte-identical between the two, which is why nothing else saw
it. 🚨 **That is the same defect the sketch was written to remove** — the maintainer's *"17.46 units
narrow on the right"* — **surviving on the other traversal.** A per-segment sweep is the kind of
rewrite that has to be checked against both directions of the map it is sampling, because the map is
what makes a segment's interval an interval at all.

Two halves to the repair, and the second is what makes it robust: the interval start is
`warp.len - s0 - slen` when flipped, and the nudge goes **inward from both ends**, so that whichever
end `a0` turns out to be, the segment is asked for a normal a whisker inside each of its own two ends
rather than at a boundary `at` may resolve to the neighbour.
`text::tests::a_flipped_rails_box_clears_the_rail_on_every_side` asserts the clearance over the rail
is non-zero and equal on four sides, in both traversals and at two aspect ratios; flipped against the
original sampling it fails at *"a square-ish rectangle flip=true"* on the **right** clearance at
`0.0000`, the predicted side and the predicted number.

🚨 **The fixtures do not discriminate the two halves of the repair, and a green run here is not a
licence to delete the mirroring.** Reverting *only* the mirrored interval while keeping both end
nudges leaves every fixture green: straddling each mirrored boundary from both sides happens to leave
a sample inside every segment of a rectangle, at either aspect ratio, and a 20:1 rail did not break it
either. The mirroring is kept because reading a segment's interval backwards is **wrong in general**,
not because a test catches it. A rail that defeats the straddle exists on paper — a three-segment open
polyline at roughly 100 : 20 : 10, where the short middle segment owns an extreme — and **has not been
reduced to a fixture**. ⚠️ **Whoever reduces it should also settle a contradiction inside the test's
own prose**: its doc says the full original sampling fails at *"a square-ish rectangle"*, while the
inline comment over the fixture list says that rail *"passes against the defect"* and that *"the 20:1
rail is the one with teeth"* — which the 🚨 paragraph thirty lines above it denies for either ratio.
One of the two is wrong and only a re-run says which. *Fix.*

⚠️ **The contrast with `the_bent_box_holds_the_rail_itself` is the durable lesson.** That guard's own
note records the 17.46 bug escaping **four** fixtures — 341×172 and 62×40 rectangles, 20pt and 24pt,
default and cap-to-baseline trim, with and without a start offset — and being caught only by running
the maintainer's document through the two sweeps and diffing the boxes, because whether a lost offset
strands *ink* depends on the font, the string and where the glyphs fall against the corners. **The new
test asserts the ribbon rather than the ink**, so it needs none of that: the sweep covers the whole
rail whatever the text does, and a lost edge is a margin of exactly zero. *Where a defect's visible
symptom is document-dependent, assert the thing the defect is actually in.*

**D793 — The box sweep's reach is measured from the baseline, not from the text-local origin. *Fixed
2026-09-15; Resolved — and deliberately **untested**, see below.***

`PathWarp::place` offsets by `y - self.baseline`, so the reach D791's offset-curvature term wants is
`(top − baseline)` and `(bottom − baseline)`. It read `top.abs().max(bottom.abs())` — the distance
from the text-local **origin** — and the two agree only when the baseline sits at `y = 0`, which
parley does not do. Measured on this module's own rail fixtures: at 20pt `top = 0, bottom = 20,
baseline = 17`, so the old form said **20.000** against a true **17.000**; at 24pt under
`BoxTrim::CapToBaseline`, `top = 2.539, bottom = baseline = 20`, so **20.000** against **17.461**.

**It buys accuracy, not speed, and almost no speed at all.** `reach` enters only through the
offset-curvature term, where `κ·reach` is small unless the rail is tight, so the correction is a
per-cent or two of the step and the `ceil` eats it. Sample counts before → after at 20pt: **r=25
233 → 233** (the `.min(0.5)` clamp binds either way), **r=40 293 → 273**, **r=60 311 → 301**, **r=120
391 → 386**, **r≥300 unchanged**, as are the arch, the spike and the rectangle. Boxes move by at most
**0.005**, which is `BOX_SAG` — inside the tolerance that constant exists to declare.

**The argument is the *sign*.** The old frame over-estimated on every fixture tried, and an
over-estimate is the safe direction here — it only thickens the sampling. But nothing made that a
rule; it is what this frame happens to produce for these trims, and a reach that came out **short**
would thin the sampling on exactly the tight curves where the term is the only thing keeping the box
honest. *A wrong quantity that is currently conservative is still a wrong quantity.*

🚨 **Reverting this line leaves the whole suite green, and that is a fact about the suite rather than
about the change.** There is nothing for an outcome assertion to grip: by construction the two frames
differ only inside `BOX_SAG`, which is the tolerance every box test here is written against, and the
rest of the difference is a sample count nothing asserts. **So the line is guarded by its own
derivation and by no test** — `place` offsets by `y - baseline`, and that is the whole argument.
Change it only with that identity in hand, and do not read the green board as coverage.

⚠️ **The pre-fix comment was left standing in the same commit and has been removed since.** It sat on
the corrected line saying *"This is the wrong frame, and it is an open question rather than a fix"*,
ended mid-sentence on the word *"which"*, and carried a **third** pair of numbers — `top = 0,
bottom = 24, baseline = 19` labelled as 20pt — agreeing with neither measurement above. **A comment
that states the defect is the one a fix leaves standing**, its author reading it as the problem
statement rather than as a claim about the code; this is D784's `picker::ramp` two weeks later, and
nothing gates it.

**D488 — A layout grid's track count was bounded by nothing, and the guard beside it could not see a
count. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — `MAX_TRACKS`, clamped in `tracks`.***

`[S4.2-L1-02]`, Medium; **G1** crossed with **G10**. `layout::tracks` opens with a seven-clause guard,
and every clause of it asks whether the numbers **fit** — the extent, the gutter, the margin and the
track size, all denominated in units of the frame's own extent. What grows here is a **count of
allocations**, which is a different quantity, and the guard is structurally unable to see it: under
`Stretch` a track is `extent / n`, positive and finite for every `n` there is, and under
`Start`/`End`/`Center` it is the stored `size` and does not depend on `n` at all. So `u32::MAX` on a
400×200 frame gives a track of `9.31e-8` — greater than zero, finite, admitted — and then asks for
4,294,967,295 rects, which is **137 GB**. The allocation fails, `handle_alloc_error` **aborts**, and
nothing can catch it.

**Nothing bounded the field on the way in either.** `count` is a `u32`; `op_set_grids` is a
`mem::replace`; `schema.rs` is `grids: dto.grids`; and only the **panel** clamps, to 1000 — which is a
guard on the keyboard rather than on the document. A hand-edited `.ondin` carrying `u32::MAX`
round-trips through save and load unchanged. **And the file only has to be open**: `draw_layout_grids`
runs over every visible frame carrying grids, from the canvas paint, with no user action in it at all.
At 8,000,000 the app allocates and frees 256 MB **every frame** — 35 ms, a permanent 3 fps.

**A clamp rather than a refusal, because that is this field's own bargain.** `LayoutGrid::count`'s doc
already argues it: a field dragged through a silly number on its way somewhere else must not be an
error. That is `NodeKind::Polygon::sides`' rule — the outline builder clamps, the model does not — and
this had copied only its **lower** half, where zero draws nothing. `geometry::MAX_SIDES`' upper half
was left behind, and its stated reason transfers nearly verbatim: past a point the field stops being a
design control and becomes a way to make the app crawl. `MAX_TRACKS = 10_000` is deliberately well
above the panel's 1000, so a file written by some future build with a wider field is **drawn rather
than truncated**, and the panel's own maximum is asserted as the control for exactly that.

⚠️ **Flip run, and deliberately a bounded one.** Removing the `.min` outright does not fail the test —
it takes the runner down with the 137 GB allocation, which is the finding rather than a check on it.
The cap was raised to `2_000_000` instead: fails at 2000000 against 10000, the predicted site, which
proves the assertion reads the clamp rather than some incidental ceiling. *A flip whose honest form is
destructive still gets run, at a size the machine survives.*

**D487 — Distributing overlapping layers reordered them. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the span
is the greatest trailing edge, and a gap that would go negative spaces the leading edges instead.***

A background rect 800 wide at x = 0 with two 40-wide icons at 10 and 100 — the most ordinary
overlapping selection there is. Select all three, *Distribute horizontally*, and the leading edges go
`0 / 10 / 100` → `0 / 430 / 100`: the middle layer travels **420 units** and lands 330 to the **right**
of the layer that had been in front of it. One `SetTransform`, one undo step, no message. `[S3.2-L1-01]`.
The rule it breaks was stated in the code and, per the review's own check of the design, **nowhere
else** — `build::sorted_along`'s *"arranging a set never also reorders it: whatever is leftmost stays
leftmost"*. §9.2's arrangement passage carries it now, and §5.7a's listing says it beside the
signature, which is half the point of this entry: an invariant that lives only in the doc comment of a
private helper is one nothing outside that file is ever checked against.

**Two halves.** The span was `lead(last) + extent(last) − lead(first)`, and sorted by *lead* the last
box is not necessarily the one that reaches furthest: for that fixture it measured **140** for a set
occupying 800. It is `max(trailing) − min(leading)` now. And **with overlap you cannot have all three
of the things this function promises** — both extremes held still, equal gaps, and the order left
alone. Equal gaps were taken and the **order** was what gave.

**The order is the promise to keep.** A user watching two icons trade places has been handed something
they did not ask for, where a slightly uneven overlap is a compromise; so when the gap would go
negative the **leading edges** are spaced evenly instead, which holds the extremes too — the first and
last leads are exactly where they were, and only the interior moves. This is also what the old comment
claimed was already happening — *"the layers then tuck back under each other evenly, which is still the
even distribution of what space there is"* — and it was true for **equal extents and nothing else**.
Three 100-wide rects at 0/10/20 are a fixed point under both spellings, which is why the claim read as
true, and they are asserted beside the defect for exactly that reason.

⚠️ **Three flips, and the first two did not bite** — which is worth more than the fix. Restoring the
old `span` alone leaves the test green; restoring the gap-only loop alone leaves it green; **only both
together reproduce it**, at `[50, 60, 150]` → `[50, 480, 150]`, the middle layer landing past the one
that had been in front of it. So the two halves are not a fix and a refinement: **either one alone
closes this fixture**, which is what the review proposed and what had been read here as
belt-and-braces. They are kept together for different reasons — the span is a plain arithmetic error,
and the fallback is what makes the promise hold for a set the corrected span still cannot fit.

⚠️ **And the first assertion was vacuous.** It compared two sorted id lists; with the span corrected
the fixture comes out with two layers at the **same** lead, and a stable sort of a tie reports the
original order. **Ties are a compromise and a swap is the bug**, and only a pairwise non-inversion
test tells them apart — which is what `distributing_overlapping_layers_does_not_reorder_them` asserts,
over the three pairs.

⚠️ **Nothing else in the suite notices any of the three flips.** The two ends stay put and the gaps
still come out equal under every one of them, so a gap-equality assertion — which is exactly what
`distribute_equalises_the_gaps_and_leaves_the_ends_alone` is, over a set that happens not to overlap —
cannot see this defect at all. *The post-condition to assert of an arrangement is the thing it promises
about the set, not the coordinates it produces.*

**D486 — A guide stole the press the chrome had just promised. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
`OndinApp::chrome_claims` walks the same four rungs the press ladder does.***

`[S12.1-L1-02]`, Medium. `rulers::guide_input`'s only gate was `on_handle` — *"is the pointer on a box
handle"* — and `canvas::begin_select_drag`'s press ladder has **four** rungs above the artwork: the
pivot marker, a line's endpoints, the rail handle, then the box handles. `Handles::armed` knows about
corner handles, side bands and the rotate ring **and nothing else**, so **three of the four were
invisible to the gate**. Measured: a lone `Line` from (100,100) to (300,100) with a vertical guide at
x = 100 hovers `CursorIcon::Grab` over the endpoint, and the drag **moves the guide**. The same for the
pivot marker with a guide through it.

⚠️ **For a lone `Line` the gate was structurally false at every pixel**, not merely at the endpoint.
`selection_handles` opens with `lone_line` and returns `None` for one — a lone line gets no box, no
side bands, no skew and no rotate ring at all, which is D99's rule and D238's lift — so `handles` was
`None` and the test could not be true anywhere on screen.

⚠️ **And it is not a race, which is why nobody filed it as intermittent.** `guide_input` claims on
`primary_pressed` while `begin_select_drag` runs only on `drag_started`, so with a guide present
`self.drag` is already `Drag::Guide` before the pointer has travelled far enough for egui to call the
press a drag. The guide won every time.

⚠️ **The comment's own vocabulary was the tell.** The gate's comment excepted *"a selection handle the
guide happens to be lying across"*, and `begin_select_drag` says of the endpoints: *"A line's
endpoints, **which are its handles**."* Two passages of one file using one word for two different
sets, five hundred lines apart, and the narrower reading was the one the code asked.

**The point is a parameter because the two callers legitimately ask about different ones.**
`chrome_claims` is asked of the *hover* position, before any drag exists; `begin_select_drag` asks its
own ladder about `press_origin` — what the press was over rather than where the pointer has reached by
the time egui calls it a drag, which is D29's rule and that function's own long argument, and the
reason the two cannot share one fixed point.

⚠️ **A parallel ladder, not a lifted one, and the honest consequence is that the two can still drift.**
`begin_select_drag` needs the *identity* of the claim and this needs a bool, so what is shared is the
order and the membership rather than the code. A full lift is what the finding sketched and it is a
bigger change than this defect justifies — `guide_input` is also the ruler-bar door, which claims a
press from every tool. **The test is what binds them**:
`a_guide_does_not_steal_a_press_the_chrome_claims` sweeps 41 points along the line and asserts the two
agree at every one, with the endpoint as the defect and an empty-canvas point as the control — without
which a `chrome_claims` that simply returned `true` would pass everything above it. Flip run:
`chrome_claims` reduced to its old `handles.armed` term fails on the endpoint, the predicted site, and
the control stays green. *A fifth rung added to `begin_select_drag` owes `chrome_claims` a term, and
that sweep is the thing that will say so.*

**D485 — A file that is not ours came back as a document with no metadata. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — three arms answer `Inconclusive`, and the return defers to `root` so a second `meta`
can be seen at all.***

`[S1.1-L1-04]` and `[S1.1-L1-03]`, both Medium, one entry because both are
`io::probe::meta_in_prefix` answering `Absent` where the caller's full load is the thing entitled to
report the file.

**`Absent` and `Inconclusive` mean opposite things to the one caller that reads them.**
`library::scan::read_meta` maps `Absent` to a **healthy pre-library document** — default metadata,
`Entry::unread = false` — without opening the file, and only the `Inconclusive` arm reads the rest and
can report it unreadable. So a corrupt or foreign `.ondin` was told apart from a pre-library one
**purely by whether its first non-whitespace byte happened to be `{`**: a renamed PNG, a text file and
a JSON array were all listed as healthy documents that simply had no name. ⚠️ **The comment at that
very line already said the right thing** — *"this is a malformed file and the caller's full `load` is
the thing that should report it"*, which is `Inconclusive`'s contract written directly above a
`return MetaProbe::Absent`. Three arms corrected: the `!= Some(&b'{')` test, a stray byte where a key
or a close belongs, and a second `meta` key.

**The duplicate key is the same bug one level in, and it is the one with a consequence a user could
see.** `serde_json` keeps the **last** duplicate; the probe returned on the **first**. Both are legal
readings of the same bytes, and this module's whole contract is that the two agree — and they key
different things. The probe fills `Entry::meta`, and `library::cover::key` builds a cover-cache path
component out of `entry.meta.id`, while the recovery snapshot and the version history use the *loaded*
document's. **One file was listed, named and cover-cached as document A and opened, autosaved and
recovered as document B.**

**Refusing rather than matching serde's rule**, deliberately: a duplicate key is a malformed file, the
full load is authoritative anyway, and "keep the last" would still diverge for a second block sitting
past `root` or past the 4 KB prefix — so it would fix the fixture and not the class. Seeing a second
key at all means deferring the return until `root`, which costs nothing, `schema.rs` writing `root`
immediately after `meta`: the walk that rules out a duplicate is one key long.

⚠️ **The scan test named for this never reached the state it names.** `scan.rs`'s
`a_corrupt_document_is_listed_rather_than_hidden` asserts that a `.ondin` this build cannot parse is
listed and marked `unread`, and its fixture was `{ "schema_version": 3, "nod` — the one corrupt shape
whose first byte is `{`, and therefore the one that already landed on `Inconclusive`. It carries both
fixtures now, and they are not two examples of one case: **they are the two sides of the byte that
used to decide it.**

⚠️ **The `Absent` controls in the new probe test are the point of it.** An empty object, and a document
whose `meta` sits past `root`, still have to answer `Absent` — or the fix has traded a wrong answer for
a slow one, since `Inconclusive` sends the file through a whole `std::fs::read` plus `io::load`, which
is the cost `Absent` exists to avoid on a synced folder of unhydrated placeholders (D362). Flip run:
the brace arm back to `Absent` fails on the PNG, the first case and the predicted site, with both
