controls green under it.

⚠️ **That cost is now paid once per scan by every foreign file in the base folder**, and it is a real
trade rather than a free one: a renamed video with a `.ondin` extension used to be `Absent` for four
bytes and is now read whole. It is the right way round — the alternative is the dashboard asserting the
file is a healthy document — but note where it lands. The probe has one caller, `read_meta`, and
**`read_meta` has two**: `scan::collect` and `library::recovery::pending`. Nothing about a recovery
name changes (a snapshot that will not load is named from its stem either way), only the read.
*Revisit if a folder of foreign files ever makes a scan feel slow; the bound would be a size cap on the
fallback read, not a return to `Absent`.*

⚠️ **Still open, and deliberately not closed here: `Entry::unread` has no production consumer at all.**
The field is written by `scan::collect`, hardcoded `false` by `library/state.rs`, and read only by the
assertion above — a `PartialEq` derive on `Entry` being what keeps `dead_code` quiet about it. Giving
it one or deleting it belongs with the library-store pass; `roadmap.md` carries it.

**D484 — Two chrome numbers written in more than one place: the hover ground and the pixel grid's
snap. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep — one name and one call, and neither moves a pixel today.***

`[S18.2-L3-02]` and `[S16.5-L3-07]`, both Low, both group **G20** — the group D479 opened, which is
about one rule kept in several copies.

**The hover ground had no name.** `Color32::from_rgb(52, 52, 54)` is the ground every hovered control
in the app paints, and it was a literal at **four** production sites in three files and named at none:
`theme::install`'s `w.hovered.bg_fill` and `weak_bg_fill`, which is what **egui itself** paints for
every stock widget; `ui::icon_button_padded`, the tool rail and the top bar; `ui::button_face`, the
field-row family; and `inspector::template_cell`, the *Frame templates* cells. Four places that have to
agree, and a change to any one of them splits the hover into two greys with every gate green — the
stock half and the hand-rolled half being the two that would diverge, since nothing paints them side by
side to be compared. `theme::color::HOVER` now, read by all four; the same bytes, so nothing on screen
moves. The argument is `ui::SEGMENT_BORDER`'s, made about a smaller number — *"it is subtracted in one
place and painted in another, and those two have to agree"*. ⚠️ **`CARD_BORDER` is `(53, 53, 54)`**,
one level away and named, which is how close the omission was: a reader looking for the hover among the
chrome's colours found the wrong constant sitting exactly where the right one should have been.

**The pixel grid hand-inlined the guides' snap.** `grid::draw_pixel_grid` wrote `round() / ppp + half`
with the half **unconditional**, where `rulers::snap_across_axis` is sixteen lines of measured
reasoning — rewritten twice already, at D138 for the parity and at D479 for the shared predicate —
about when a hairline wants a pixel centre and when it wants a pixel edge. The copy agreed at every
scale measured, and **only because of a fact about the grid's own width that nothing in `grid.rs`
stated**: its line is
`1.0 / ppp` points, exactly one device pixel, so `floor(width × ppp)` is 1 at every scale and the odd
branch is the only one the copy ever reached. A 2pt grid line would have made it silently wrong.
`snap_across_axis` is `pub(crate)` and `grid.rs` calls it, once per axis, which makes `draw_pixel_grid`
its **second** production caller beside `rulers::draw_guide_inner` — so the base D479 parked for its own
decision now moves guide ink *and* grid ink, and `roadmap.md` says so.

⚠️ **The test was written over one width first and a flip proved it vacuous.** With only `1.0 / ppp` in
the loop, changing the width to `2.0 / ppp` left `a_pixel_grid_line_covers_whole_pixels_at_either_width`
**green** — because `snap_across_axis` handles the even case correctly, so the *right* implementation
passes at any width. What it was pinning was the callee's contract, which `rulers::guide_geometry_tests`
already pins, and it said nothing whatever about the merge. **Two widths are what make the difference
visible**: one device pixel wants a pixel centre, two want a pixel edge, and whole-pixel coverage is the
property that has to hold for both. Flipped on the corrected test by putting the unconditional
`+ 0.5 / ppp` back in place of the call: it passes at one device pixel — the branch it was accidentally
right on — and fails at two, spanning **99.5..101.5** in device space at `ppp = 1.0`, half a pixel over
at each end. *A copy that is right for a reason its own file does not state is not a copy anyone can
maintain, and a test over the one case that copy handled would not have said so. Where a merge replaces
a copy, the assertion has to cover the case the copy could not reach.*

**D483 — Text spent none of the picking allowance, and D115's own enumeration is where the omission
lived. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the arm inflates the box, and the case goes in the test that
claims "every kind".***

`geometry::contains_local`'s first line is `let tol = stroke_expansion(node.kind(), node.paint()) +
slop;` and the `NodeKind::Text` arm never read it. **D115 rewrote every arm to add the band**, and its
own enumeration of what it had rewritten — `Rect`/`Artboard`, `Ellipse`, `Polygon`/`Star`/`Path` —
never says `Text`, so the sweep skipped the kind users click most and nothing afterwards noticed.
§5.10's *"every kind spends it"* and the function's own *"every kind uses it now"* were both false
seventy lines above the arm that made them so. `[S4.2-L2-03]`.

**Two consequences, and the second is the sharper one because it is a disagreement rather than a
missing comfort margin.** The picking allowance did nothing there — a click a few units past a text
node hit nothing, which is the complaint D115 exists for — and a text node with a 40pt **outside**
stroke reported world bounds 40 units wider on every side than the region a click could reach, since
`stroke_expansion` gives an outside stroke its full width and `world_bounds_of_parts` inflates by it.
A band of the layer's own stated extent selected nothing, with the selection rectangle drawn across it.

The fix is `b.inflate(tol, tol).contains(p)` over `local_bounds` — the same shape `query.rs` already
writes for a boolean's **placeholder** cross, `b.inflate(slop, slop).contains(local_p)`, which is the
other box-shaped hit target in the tree. (Not the cached-outline arm beside it: that tests the derived
path under the node's fill rule and spends nothing, which is its own question.) ⚠️ **The case is added
to `a_picking_allowance_widens_every_kind_by_a_bounded_band` rather than to a test of its own**, and
deliberately: that is the test D115 *renamed* for exactly this rule, it had no `Text` case, and putting
the assertion anywhere else would leave "every kind" claimed in one place and asserted in another.
Three assertions, the same three the rect above them makes — 3 units past the box hits, 9 does not, and
a zero allowance still means the box. Flip run, the arm returned to the bare box: fails on *"3 units
past a text node's box is within a 4-unit allowance"*, the predicted site.

*The lesson is about the record rather than the code: **a sweep is only as complete as its own list**,
and D115's list is what a later reader — and this one — checked the code against. D115 is amended to
name `Text` and to say that it did not.*

**D482 — A run merged on the variant rather than on the field it writes, and a guide nudge could not
merge at all. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — `Operation::shape_key` is the merge key, and it is
deliberately not `overwrites`.***

`[S2.2-L2-02]` and `[S2.2-L2-03]`, both Medium, done together because both widen `History`'s `Shape`,
which is what the review asked for in each.

**A discriminant names the variant, not the fields.** `History::commit_into_run` keeps the older
inverse and drops the newer one, and its own doc says why that is sound: *"both edits to have
overwritten the **same** fields of the **same** nodes, which is what `Shape` checks"*. `Shape` was a
`(Discriminant<Operation>, NodeId)` per operation — which **is** the field set for 22 of the 23
overwriting operations, each of them writing a fixed group of fields, checked variant by variant — and
is not for `SetGeometry`, whose payload is itself a field selector with twelve arms. Measured through
core's public API on a 10×10 rect: `GeometryPatch::Size(20×20)` then `CornerRadius(5.0)` merged,
`undo_depth` came back **1**, and one undo restored the size and **stranded the radius at 5 with an
empty stack** — a state that was never committed, and nothing left on the stack to reach the real one.
Not reachable through the app today: none of `commit_run`'s four verbs — `nudge-layers`,
`resize-layers`, `nudge-points`, `nudge-guides` — ever puts two *different* patch variants on one node
in consecutive commits, each repeat of a burst building the same operations as the last. It is core's
public contract all the same, and the doc of the function that breaks it claims it is enforced.

**A guide nudge flooded history.** Hold `↓` on a selected guide and Windows auto-repeat puts about
**45** entries on the undo stack in two seconds, where the identical keystroke on a *layer* is one step
— §9.3's invariant is one gesture, one transaction, one undo step. `rulers::nudge_guides`' own doc
already claimed *"one press of `Ctrl+Z`"*, and it was true on the axis it was written about, across the
selected guides, while missing the repeat axis entirely. Coalescing was not declined here, it was
**unavailable by construction**: `Shape` was built from `Operation::overwrites`, which answers `None`
for every guide operation.

**One function answers both, and it is deliberately a second function.** `Operation::shape_key` is the
operation, the field inside it where there is one, and the subject; `History::Shape` is a vector of it,
and `nudge_guides` commits through `commit_run` under its own verb. ⚠️ **The finding's sketch was to
widen `overwrites` and that would have been wrong.** That function answers *"which node does this
operation overwrite a field of"*, and both its callers ask exactly that — `app.rs`'s `touched` count
behind *"Pasted properties onto n layers"*, and `inspector.rs`'s assertion that a recolour names no
frame. A `GuideId` wraps a `NodeId` (§5.2) so it makes a perfectly good merge key, but a guide is not a
node, and answering `Some` there would hand both callers a guide's underlying id as though it were a
layer's. **The ids do not collide** — guides and nodes are minted from one `IdSource`, which is
`GuideId`'s own doc — and neither caller is reachable with a guide operation today, so the cost is a
latent lie rather than a measured one. **Two questions that look like one**: the subject of an edit,
and the key a run merges on.

**Only `SetGuidePosition` is admitted.** `AddGuide` and `RemoveGuide` are structural, and nothing
repeats a colour or a scope, so admitting those would widen the merge for a gesture that does not
exist. ⚠️ **`op.rs`'s stale comment is corrected rather than left**: `overwrites` excused the guide arms
with *"a guide drag is one commit on release anyway, so nothing wants it yet"*, and `nudge_guides` is
the thing that wanted it — the excuse was about the *drag*, and the repeat is a different gesture.

**Both flips run, and the second is the one worth carrying.** `shape_key`'s `field` forced to `None`,
which is the key `Shape` had before: `two_geometry_patches_aimed_at_different_fields_do_not_merge`
fails on the depth assertion at **2 against 3** — the predicted site, the fixture's own `CreateNode`
sitting under the run — and the radius assertion behind it would have failed too. `shape_key`'s
`SetGuidePosition` arm removed, so it falls through to `overwrites()?`:
`a_run_of_guide_nudges_is_one_undo_step` fails on the depth assertion at **5 against 3** — the
predicted site, and *not* the predicted numbers, because the fixture commits a `CreateNode` and an
`AddGuide` before the run begins, so "three taps, three steps" reads as 5. Every other test in the
module stays green under both.

⚠️ **The guide half is asserted in `history.rs` and not in `rulers.rs`, because the obstruction was
core's.** The app arm is one line — `commit` to `commit_run` — and the line that made it possible is
the one in `shape_key`; `nudge_guides`' own call is covered by construction, one `commit_run` with
nothing between it and the transaction it built. *A new operation still has to choose, `shape_key`
enumerating rather than defaulting; what it now has to choose is two things, and a payload that selects
a field is the case to look at.*

**D481 — A resize refuses the member whose arithmetic overflows, not the whole selection. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the guard is on the product, and one of the three call sites spells out why it
is exempt.***

`[S13.1-L1-03]`, **G1**'s third guard shape — *all-finite operands whose product overflows* — and **G5**,
the app writing a document it cannot read.

**`MAX_SCALE` bounds the factor; the quantity that overflows is the product.** `tools::scale_along` caps
a single drag at `1e4`, which is a bound on what the *gesture* asks for and says nothing about what the
node already holds. A `Rect` storing `Affine::scale(1e308)` over a size of `1e-306` has every stored
coefficient finite, passes invariant 8 at `op_create`, and resolves to world bounds of an entirely
ordinary `(0,0)–(100,100)`. Select it with a plain 20×20 rect beside it, drag the selection's
bottom-right handle to `(200, 200)` — a factor of 2 — and `scaled_about` multiplies its basis to `inf`.
`split_geometry_scale` then calls `Basis::of`, where `a.hypot(b)` is `inf`, the `sx < DEGENERATE` early
return that exists for a *collapsed* node does not fire, `inf / inf` is `NaN`, and the transform that
comes back is `NaN` in all four basis coefficients — **pushed unconditionally**, because
`transform.as_coeffs() != node.transform().as_coeffs()` is true of `NaN`. Nor does it take a hand-edited
file: `svg_in::parse_transform` reads `transform="scale(1e308)"` verbatim, `1e308` being finite and so
surviving `numbers`' own `is_finite` filter (D421), so this is a document a paste can produce.

⚠️ **What the finding measured is no longer what happens, and the difference is why this is not another
Critical.** `[S13.1-L1-03]` recorded the `NaN` transform and an infinite width being *applied*, saved,
and the file never reloading. Since **D421** the op layer refuses a non-finite transform and
`Document::apply` is atomic, so what a user actually got was **the whole gesture silently doing
nothing**, every well-behaved layer in the selection included. Probed before anything was touched:
`apply = Err(NonFinite)`, four ops discarded, two of them perfectly good. D421 closed the
saved-and-unopenable half and left the half where nothing moves and nothing says why.

**Refusing per node rather than per gesture is the whole of the fix.** `tools::scaled_about` returns
`Option<Affine>` and answers `None` when any coefficient it produced is not finite — it is the one place
all three resize paths compute the scaled matrix, so the question is asked once rather than three times.
`resize_selection` and `scale_subtree` `continue` past a member that answers `None`, which leaves it
exactly where it was and lets the rest of the selection move. ⚠️ **`resize_geometry` spells the arm out
and returns an empty transaction rather than unwrapping**, and that is a decision rather than caution:
its operand is `Affine::IDENTITY`, whose coefficients are 0 and 1, so against a `MAX_SCALE`-capped factor
it cannot overflow — but the reason for that is about *the call site* and not about `scaled_about`, and
an `expect` there would be asserting something the function does not promise. §9.4 carries the rule and
invariant 8 the consequence that made it necessary: the op layer's refusal is per **transaction**, so a
producer that can overflow has to refuse per node upstream.

Two tests in a new `tools::overflow_tests`, on a fixture whose pathological member sits beside an
ordinary 20×20 rect. ⚠️ **That second rect is the control and it is load-bearing**: without it "one
member did not move" and "nothing moved at all" are the same observation, and a `scaled_about` that had
simply stopped working would pass. `one_overflowing_member_does_not_refuse_the_whole_resize` asserts the
three halves of "a no-op for that member only" — the ordinary rect is scaled, the pathological one is
byte-identical, and the transaction applies at all — behind a guard that the fixture's union really is
`(100, 100)`, since if the union is not ordinary the drag below is not one either.

⚠️ **The flip was run and it bit at the wrong place, which is the correction worth carrying forward.**
With the `then_some` replaced by an unconditional `Some(out)` the test fails on the **third** assertion
with `Err(NonFinite)`. The predicted site was the first, on the argument that the good member would fail
to move; it does fail to move, but the `apply` happens before any assertion reads the document, so what
the test meets is the atomicity rather than the arithmetic. **With an atomic transaction the failure a
test sees is never per node** — a prediction about which assertion bites has to account for the commit
standing in front of all of them.

⚠️ **`the_document_a_resize_leaves_behind_still_loads` passes with the fix removed, and is kept anyway.**
It is an `io::save`/`io::load` round trip, written that way rather than as an inspection of the ops
because *"the file never reloads"* is the failure the finding is named for and an op-shaped assertion
would be a proxy for it. Since D421 the refusal happens at the op layer, so no `NaN` reaches the document
either way: the test is the standing record that the two guards are separate, and the thing that notices
if the op guard ever narrows. Its doc says that rather than implying coverage it does not have.

**D480 — Three tests that could not fail, and running them found what the findings did not have.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the three assertions have teeth, and what each flip corrected is
recorded at the test.***

Group **G9**: `[S2.2-L6-04]` in `core::history`, `[S3.2-L6-04]` in `ondin-core`'s `tests/bulk.rs` and
`[S1.2-L6-05]` in `app::atomic`. One entry rather than three, because the coverage is the least
interesting thing about them — **each of the three turned up something its finding did not have**, and
the shape they share is at the end.

**Two lines that stop history corruption had no test with teeth anywhere in the workspace.** The
review deleted each in turn and `cargo test --workspace` was green both times. Without
`self.redo.clear()` in `History::commit`: commit A, undo it, commit B, press redo — the stack still
holds the transaction that redoes A, and it is applied to a document B has since changed. For a
`SetTransform` that silently re-writes a stale value **and pushes its own inverse onto the undo
stack**, so history ends up holding a step the user never made. Without `self.run = None` in
`History::undo`: commit C, open a run with A, undo, then commit B with A's shape — B folds into **C's**
step and its own inverse is discarded, so one undo reverts C *and* B in a single press and B is
unrecoverable. `a_new_commit_drops_the_redo_stack` and
`an_undo_ends_the_run_so_the_next_edit_is_its_own_step` are the pins; both flips were re-run and each
fails only its own test. `tests/spine.rs`'s `undo_redo_roundtrip…` is the near miss worth naming: it
walks the stack to empty without ever committing in between, so it cannot reach the state at all.

⚠️ **The second fixture had to be rebuilt, and only a failing run said so.** The first draft made C
another `SetTransform`, so A merged into C immediately and the undo two lines later took *both* back —
leaving nothing on the stack for B to fold into, and the flip would have been green for a reason with
nothing to do with the line under test. C is a `SetOpacity` now, a different `Shape` by construction,
and the opacity assertion is what says it survived.

⚠️ **The third copy of that line, in `redo`, is all but unreachable — and a flip established that
rather than an argument.** The obvious mirror of the test above left every test green: `run` is
*already* `None` at every redo that pops something, because the redo stack is non-empty only if
nothing has been committed since the last undo or redo (`commit` and `commit_into_run` both clear it),
and `undo` and `redo` both end the run. What is left is the empty-stack case, and it exists only
because **the line sits before the `pop`**: a redo press with *nothing to redo* ends the run in
progress, so the next edit of the same shape is a step of its own. That is *intended* — `History::run`'s
own doc lists a redo among the things that end a run — but it was a decision nothing recorded and
nothing could have caught being reversed. The test is named for what it actually pins,
`a_redo_that_does_nothing_still_ends_the_run`; the line now carries the argument; the flip fails it on
the depth assertion, 2 against 3.

**`a_frames_background_names_the_frame_as_its_layer` executed zero assertions, and D400 is why.** It
looped `build::colors_in`'s result skipping the child's `BLUE` and asserted on whatever was left, on
the premise stated in its own doc that *"the fixture's artboard has a background"*. That was true
while a frame's ground was a field on `NodeKind::Artboard`; **D400 moved it into the fill list**,
`op_create` gives every node an **empty** one, and the loop then ran on zero rows. So the rule the test
is named for went unpinned, and a census that walked a frame's *contents* into the frame's own row
would have been green. The fixture paints the artboard now, and the assertion demands the `GREEN` row
and panics when it is absent rather than filtering for it — **a loop over rows that might not exist is
the shape that made this vacuous.**

⚠️ **The control is the measurement, not the argument.** `build::census`'s `bump` was made to record
the painted node's *parent*: the new assertion fails on `nodes`, the predicted site, GREEN naming the
root rather than the artboard. The pre-fix body was then restored under that same flip and stayed
**green** — which is what says it was asserting nothing, where "it must have been vacuous, look at the
premise" is only a reading.

**`atomic.rs`'s headline promise was asserted by nothing.** Its module doc says that after
`atomic::write` returns, `path` holds either the complete new contents or the complete old ones. Both
existing tests exercise the success path, and the flip recorded in the first of them replaces the
`rename` with an `fs::copy`, which fails on the **leftover temp** — so the pair looks like it covers
the mechanism and covers the temp file rather than the destination. The regression that admits is the
one every reviewer of Windows code reaches for: *"`fs::rename` fails if the destination exists, so
remove it first."* `a_failed_write_leaves_the_old_file_intact` stages the refusal by making the
destination read-only — portable, one line, and measured against the alternative of holding the file
open with `share_mode(FILE_SHARE_READ)`, which produces the same `PermissionDenied` and needs
`std::os::windows` — and both existing tests stay green under the flip.

⚠️ **The flip's outcome is worse than the finding predicted, and that correction is worth more than
the prediction was.** The predicted failure was *"the file is gone"*. It is not gone — it is
**replaced**. On Windows `std::fs::remove_file` clears the read-only attribute and retries the delete,
so the flipped version defeats the very lock that stages the test: the rename then succeeds, `write`
returns `Ok`, and a document the read-only flag was protecting is silently overwritten with a success
report. *"Remove it first"* does not merely open a window in which the file does not exist; it walks
through a refusal.

⚠️ **And the assertions had to be reordered before the test would say that.** With `result.is_err()`
first, the flip failed on *"the fixture has to reach a failing rename"* — a **fixture guard**,
reporting that the setup was wrong when the setup was fine and the code had destroyed the file. **The
loss goes before the report**, and this is a new shape for that rule: the misleading assertion is a
*guard* rather than a mechanism, so the failure blames the harness rather than the subject.

Two platform facts are recorded at the test, measured rather than read out of documentation, so that
nobody re-derives them: `fs::rename` **does** replace an existing destination on Windows
(`MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`), so the instinct is wrong on its own terms as well as dangerous; and
`temp_for` appends to the whole destination path, so the temp always sits in the destination's own
directory and a cross-volume rename — the one case a plain `rename` genuinely cannot do — is
unreachable.

**Why these are one entry: three tests that could not fail, and not one of the three failures was
"somebody forgot".** One was a fixture that stopped reaching its state when an unrelated entry moved a
field out from under it. One was a rule asserted only where it happened to be true. One was a promise
whose *neighbouring* promise was tested, so the pair read as covered. What they have in common is that
**each looked like coverage from the outside** — which is exactly what a census of "does this function
have a test" reports, and is why G9 was found by flipping rather than by grepping. *Fix a suspicion
with a flip rather than with a count*: the question to ask of a green test is not whether it passes
but what would also pass it.

Three passages were brought in line with what these now pin: §5.8's `History` listing gains the `run`
field it did not have and the three things that end a run; §5.7a says which node a census row names;
and §9.5 gains `atomic::write`'s failure direction and the trap above it.

**D479 — A chrome hairline asked for a pixel centre whatever its device width was. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Keep — one predicate, two bases, and the fourth copy deliberately not merged.***

At `pixels_per_point = 2.0` — plain 200% Windows scaling — a 1pt chrome rule rasterised as
`[0.5, 1.0, 0.5]`: one whole device pixel with a half-covered one either side, which is the two-pixel
grey smear this arithmetic exists to prevent, arriving across three. Three sites carried the identical
expression `((rect.center().{x,y} * ppp).floor() + 0.5) / ppp` — `ui::rule`, the Align row's dividers;
`inspector::popup_rule`, the separator inside the boolean, mask-mode, stroke-align, stroke-sides,
stroke-cap and effect-kind dropdowns; and `settings::section`, beside every eyebrow on the Settings
screen. It asks for a pixel **centre** unconditionally, and a line whose *device* width is even wants a
pixel **edge**. `[S19.1-L1-04]` and `[S18.1-L3-03]`, group G20.

**The parity is what had no name.** `ui::hairline_on_pixel_centre(ppp, width)` is `floor(width × ppp)`
odd; `ui::hairline_in_column(centre, ppp, width)` is the snap that reads it — the nearest pixel centre
for an odd device width, the nearest pixel edge for an even one. The three sites are one call each.
**D46 is amended rather than overturned**: everything it says about *why* the snap is in device space
still holds, and the formula it prints as the fix is the unconditional one, right at every scale but
the even ones. The fractional scales do not move — 150%'s `[0.25, 1.0, 0.25]` is the best a
1.5-device-pixel line can do, since a fractional device width cannot put both edges on the grid — so
this changes 200% and 300% and nothing else.

**The review was wrong twice, and both corrections are the substance of this entry.**

⚠️ **`[S19.1-L1-04]` records `ui::rule` as *"pinned by nothing"*, and it was pinned by something
worse.** `ui::head_tests::a_rules_hairline_lands_on_a_pixel_inside_its_own_column` asserted a pixel
*centre* unconditionally. A 1pt line's device width is odd at 100%, 125%, 150% and 175% and even only
at 200%, so the assertion was right four times out of five and **wrong at exactly the case the code was
failing to draw** — a test that names a rule and asserts a special case of it, the **G19** shape,
sitting in the one place that would have caught the bug. Its device assertion is parity-dependent now
and its doc says what it missed.

⚠️ **G20's decision was wrong about the mechanism, and the group's fix shape changes with it.** T8
recorded S18.2's finding as *"the four mergeable `rule`/`snap_across_axis` copies all want the identical
contract, the only obstruction is a home"*, and `[S19.1-L1-04]`'s sketch proposed calling
`rulers::snap_across_axis` from `ui::rule`. **They share the parity and differ in the base, and the
difference is load-bearing.** Measured by sweeping the fractional part of a centre over
`ppp ∈ {1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2, 3}`: `floor + 0.5` is the nearest pixel *centre* and `round` the nearest
pixel *edge*, so each is nearest for its own parity and up to a **whole device pixel** out for the
other's — **1.0pt at 100%**, which puts a 1pt rule entirely outside the 1pt column it was allocated
between two galleys. That is precisely the failure D46 records (*"as much as 0.7pt right of centre and,
at 100%, mostly outside its own column"*, the second contributor to D44's uneven cluster) reached by a
second road. **So the shared thing is a predicate, not a formula**, and "one helper, four callers"
would have been a regression at two of them. `rulers::snap_across_axis` calls
`ui::hairline_on_pixel_centre` rather than re-deriving it, and keeps its own base.

⚠️ **A consequence recorded and deliberately not acted on.** `snap_across_axis` rounds for *both*
parities, so its odd case is a nearest *edge* with half a device pixel added — up to a whole device
pixel from where the user put the guide. Nothing has made that visible, because a guide has no column
to leave. It is not changed here: moving guide ink is a visible change to the one piece of this
arithmetic that *is* pinned by tests (`rulers::guide_geometry_tests`), and it wants its own decision
rather than being swept in behind a merge. Open in `roadmap.md` under *Later · Parked decisions*, so
that nobody "unifies" it later without deciding.

**Three tests in a new `ui::hairline_tests`, plus the corrected `head_tests` one, and three flips, all
run.** Forcing the parity `true` — the code before the fix — fails the coverage test at `ppp = 2.0`
with `[0.5, 1.0, 0.5]` against `[1.0, 1.0]` **and at no other scale**, which is why the sites looked
correct for as long as they did and is the argument for the parity being a named predicate rather than
a `+ 0.5`. Degrading the odd arm to `(round + 0.5)`, which is `snap_across_axis`'s exact spelling, fails
the drift test at `ppp = 1.0` at **1.0000pt** with the coverage test staying green — which is what says
the two tests are about different things. Degrading the even arm to `floor` fails drift at `ppp = 2.0`
at **0.4975pt** against a bound of 0.25.

⚠️ **That third flip did not bite at first, and the test was wrong rather than the flip.** The drift
bound had been written as a flat `0.5` **points**, which 0.4975 passes — so above 100% it was asserting
nothing at all. Half a *device* pixel is the quantity the doc always meant and the quantity `head_tests`
had used all along. **The flip that failed to bite is what found it**, which is this project's standing
claim about flip-checks arriving as a concrete instance rather than as a maxim.

⚠️ **Two of the three sites are pinned by construction and not by assertion**, and it is said here
rather than implied: only `ui::rule` is driven through `ctx.run_ui` and read back out of `.shapes`.
`inspector::popup_rule` and `settings::section` are each one call to `hairline_in_column` with nothing
between it and the painter, so what would catch a fourth copy appearing is a reader, not a gate.

**What is still open in G20 and untouched here.** `ui::menu_sep` paints `1.0 / ppp` **points** — one
device pixel — where its own doc says *"1pt"*, so at 200% a context menu's group separator is half the
weight of its own card's 1pt `MENU_BORDER` (`[S18.1-L3-04]`). Its *technique* is already crisp at every
scale; it is the width that is not the design's, and which of the two is right is a design question
rather than a defect — parked in `roadmap.md` beside the guide's base. ⚠️ **There was a fifth copy this
entry did not know about**, filed under a different section and closed by **D484**:
`grid::draw_pixel_grid` had `snap_across_axis` hand-inlined with the parity term unconditional, right
only because a one-device-pixel line never reaches the even branch. It calls the function now — so the
parked base has a second subject, and whichever answer it gets moves the pixel grid as well as the
guides. And `layers::snap_across`
quantises the **width** as well as the centre, taking the parity of `round(width × ppp)` and painting
that many device pixels: a different route to the right answer, self-consistent, recorded by the review
as clean, and not a member of this group.

**D478 — A turned set resized about a box its handles were not drawn on. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
D326's other half, closed. Keep.***

D326 gave a multi-selection an orientation that outlives the gesture that made it, and stopped there.
Its own closing ⚠️ said a set's **resize** was still measured on the upright union of world bounds and
still travelled along world axes, spelled the fix out in as many words — *"fix by giving the resize arm
the frame the chrome reads: `selection_frame_box` is the one answer"* — and carried **no verdict** for
that half. §9.4 repeated the warning. `roadmap.md` had nothing: `resize_axes`, `D326`,
`selection_frame_box` and *world union* all returned no match. So the only record of a known, described,
reproducible defect was a ⚠️ inside an entry headed *Fixed and tested*, for two weeks.

**Three sites answered one question and only two of them agreed.** `selection_handles`' `many` arm
placed every corner at `frame * (box corner)` on the oriented frame, which is D326's whole point.
`resize_axes` short-circuited `Target::Selection => Affine::IDENTITY`, so the **snap axes** a set's
handles were allowed to move the pointer along were the world's. And `resize_tx`'s `Target::Selection`
arm re-derived an upright union of `res.world_bounds` over `outermost` and handed it to
`tools::resize_selection`, whose `resize_factors` and `scaled_about` are world-axis-aligned. ⚠️ **Two
separate bugs, not one seen twice**: snapping the pointer onto the wrong axes happens before any box is
measured, and scaling about the wrong box happens after, so either could have been fixed alone and left
the other's symptom intact. Both had to go.

Measured. Two 100×100 rects at x=0 and x=200, selected together and turned 60° about the union centre
with the orientation left on the set (`Selection::set_frame`). Dragging the drawn TopLeft handle 40 units
along the set's **own** −x axis landed that corner **62.2243** units from the pointer, and moved the
anchored BottomRight corner — the one a resize exists to hold still — by **24.3782**. The unturned
control is **0.0000**. (The review finding `[S12.2-L2-01]` reported 62.04 and 24.27 for the same drag,
because it drove `finish_drag` and its pointer had been through `snapped_resize` first. Same defect, a
snapped pointer.)

**The fix, and the part of it a later reader would simplify away.** `tools::SelectionBox { frame: Affine,
extent: Rect }` replaces `resize_selection`'s `union: Rect` — one parameter rather than a seventh and an
eighth, which is D41's standing instruction about a parts struct arriving *before* the argument that
would need it — and `resize_selection` computes its factors and its anchor in `sel.frame`'s space
(`frame⁻¹ * pointer_world`), scaling each root there and mapping it back out: `frame · S · frame⁻¹ ·
world`. ⚠️ *Do not rewrite that as a world-space scale with the frame folded into the anchor.* It reads
as the same thing and is not: the scale would still run along the world's axes and only the anchor would
have moved, which is the half-fix that leaves the dragged corner off the pointer. ⚠️ **On an upright box
both maps are the identity, so it is bit-for-bit the arithmetic that was there before** — that is the
whole of what makes the callers below safe, and `SelectionBox::upright(rect)` is the name they ask for
it by.

`canvas::selection_resize_box` is `selection_frame_box`'s twin measured off the **committed** tree —
`ondin_core::local_box` plus `res.world_transform`, and the stored `selection.frame()` with no gesture
composed on it — which is the rule `resize_tx`'s arm already stated for itself: mid-drag the preview
already reflects this very gesture, and scaling relative to a box that is itself being scaled compounds
every frame. At the press the two answers are identical, and that is exactly the claim the fix rests on:
the box the arithmetic uses is the box the user grabbed a handle of. The stored frame is likewise the
right one and not an oversight — `Drag::selection_frame` answers `None` for a resize, so no reorienting
gesture is ever in flight here. The quad-union loop is shared through a new `canvas::selection_frame_extent`
rather than copied, because the rule it encodes is subtle enough to drift — quads, never bounding boxes,
since `AABB(G · ink) ≠ G · AABB(ink)` and an ink box would creep as the set turned (D326) — and
`canvas::selection_frame` is the one place the stored orientation and the in-flight one are combined,
now with three readers rather than one: the chrome, the snap axes and the arithmetic. `resize_axes` maps
`handle.outward()` through that same frame, which is exactly the shape the `Target::Layer` arm has used
all along.

**Two behaviour changes, recorded as consequences rather than as side effects.** The resize box measures
**geometry** where the union measured **ink**, so a stroked member's resize now moves by half a stroke
width per side; the handles have been on the geometry box since D326, which records that price for the
chrome, and this is the half of it that had not followed. And a selected member with no resolvable box
now refuses the **whole** resize, where the old `filter_map` union silently dropped it and scaled the
rest. That is the stricter reading and the consistent one: `selection_frame_box` already answers `None`
in that state, so there are no handles to grab — a resize that could run in a state the chrome refuses
to draw was the asymmetry, not this.

⚠️ **That second consequence was reversed on 2026-09-07 by D505, and the sentence above states the
premise that turned out to be the bug.** `selection_frame_box` answering `None` is not a state anybody
should be in: an empty `Group` — what `op_delete` leaves behind when its last child goes — has no local
box, so **Ctrl+A** over two rects and one empty group gave a selection with no transform box, no
handles and no size badge at all. `selection_frame_extent` skips a box-less member and answers `None`
only when *nothing* contributed, which is what both readers get, so the consistency argument this
paragraph makes still holds — it now runs the other way. Nothing else here changed: the shared
`selection_frame_extent`, the `SelectionBox`, the frame-space arithmetic and the three upright callers
are all as described.

**Three callers keep the upright union on purpose and each says why in place.** `app.rs`'s keyboard size
step, `inspector::scale_tx` and the inspector's W/H `MultiField` arm all pass `SelectionBox::upright`:
the box a typed W, H or % edits is the one the panel *reports* for a set, and a keyboard step is not a
corner drag and has no frame to be on. **The two boxes coincide until a turn or a lean outlives its
gesture**, which is why the split cost nothing for as long as D326 did not exist.

Two tests in `canvas.rs`'s `headless_app_tests`, one per bug.
`a_turned_set_resizes_about_the_box_its_handles_are_drawn_on` runs the turned case and the upright one
in a single loop over the *same* drag — 40 units along the set's own −x axis, which at rest is the
world's — with the upright pass as the control: it passed before the fix at `0.0000`, so the miss is the
orientation rather than the harness, and a fix that broke the upright case fails here instead of looking
like a success. `a_turned_sets_snap_axes_are_its_own` takes `Handle::Left`, whose outward direction is
`(−1, 0)`: on an upright set it travels on x alone, and at 60° on both. ⚠️ **Both flips were run.**
Restoring the upright union fails the first assertion at 62.2243 — the predicted site — with the upright
pass green; the anchored corner's 24.3782 had to be read by relaxing that first assertion for one run,
since it aborts before the second is reached. Restoring `Affine::IDENTITY` in `resize_axes` gives
`(true, false)` against `(true, true)` on the turned set, upright green.

⚠️ **The record's own failure is the half of this worth carrying forward.** D326 is not wrong about
anything; it simply put open work where the reader of a *Fixed and tested* heading does not look, and
nothing else in the project held it. *An entry that closes one half of a question and warns about the
other owes the other half a place that is read as open work* — a `roadmap.md` line, or its own entry
carrying a `*Fix.*` verdict. D326's ⚠️ is amended rather than deleted, in the past tense, for exactly
that reason.

**D475 — The typography panel gets its own test for the idle-frame clamp. *Tested 2026-09-07; Keep,
plus one opt-out that fixes nothing today.***

`[S6.2-L1-01]`: a text node whose letter spacing is `Em(3.0)` — 300%, against `Bounds::TRACKING`'s
200% cap — selected, one frame of the Type panel drawn with an **empty** `RawInput`, and it came back
`Em(2.0)` with `undo_depth 0 → 1` and `is_dirty()` true. At 16pt that is 48px of tracking silently
reflowed to 32px, with nobody touching anything.

⚠️ **The mechanism was already closed, and finding that out is most of this entry.**
`ui::value_field_f64` carries `.clamp_existing_to_range(false)` — one line for all 82 numeric fields —
and it landed in **D425**, for an imported blur radius rather than for this. In egui 0.35
`DragValue::clamp_existing_to_range` defaults to `true` and the clamp is unconditional and per-frame,
and `value_field_f64`'s `if nudged || *value != before { resp.mark_changed(); }` then reports the
widget's own rewrite to the caller as a **user change**. So the finding's headline no longer
reproduces. D425 carries the argument and this entry deliberately does not restate it.

**What was missing is a test on this panel**, which is the panel the finding measured and which
reaches the widget by **three different routes**: `length_char_field` through `char_valve`,
`type_line_height_field`, and `axis_field`, which discards `value_field`'s `Response` entirely and
writes through `write_axis`, whose only guard is `if value == current { return; }` — a guard the clamp
had just made false.

⚠️ **And this panel has no second guard.** `char_valve` is still the pre-D316 shape and deliberately
so, its own doc arguing the case: `resp.drag_stopped() || resp.lost_focus() || resp.changed()`, with
no engagement latch. The passing control one function away, `paragraph_length`, routes the paragraph
`Length` fields through `edit_valve`, whose latch (`let engaged = resp.dragged() || resp.has_focus();`)
means a clamp on an untouched field commits nothing. So **the widget's opt-out is the whole of what
stops a library default writing to the document here**, which is exactly why this panel wants a test
of its own rather than inheriting `ui.rs`'s.

`a_stored_tracking_outside_the_fields_range_is_not_rewritten_on_an_idle_frame` runs **two** idle
frames per case, because a widget's state is last frame's, and **the in-range control is what keeps it
honest**: without it, a field that had stopped reporting *any* change would pass. Flipped by restoring
`clamp_existing_to_range(true)`: it fails with `Em(2.0)` where `Em(3.0)` was — the finding's own
numbers — while the in-range control stays green.

⚠️ **Re-run on 2026-09-19, and those numbers are now measured here as well as carried** (§15 **D803**).
Removing `value_field_f64`'s opt-out fails this test with `Em(2.0)` where `Em(3.0)` was, the in-range
control staying green — the sentence above is this test's own result and not only `[S6.2-L1-01]`'s.
🚨 **The first re-run was spent on the wrong line and came back green**: `ui.rs` makes that call at
four production sites, `badge_field`'s is *byte-identical* to `value_field_f64`'s and is the **inert**
one, so removing it proves nothing and looks exactly like a flip with no teeth. **Name the mutation by
its function**; D803 carries the trap. What the re-run confirms with it is the clause above — *"the
widget's opt-out is the whole of what stops a library default writing to the document here"* — and
D803 names the arm the rewrite goes through, `char_valve`'s third, instrumented as the one that fires
on the failing run.

**One line that fixes nothing today.** `ui::badge_field` is the file's *other* numeric control and had
kept egui's default. Both its production callers pass an **unranged** `Scrub` (`Scrub::whole`'s range
is `NEG_INFINITY..=INFINITY`, and the pivot marker's own comment argues for that deliberately), so
there is nothing to clamp against and the opt-out is inert. It makes the same opt-out anyway, because
the day a caller gives that field a range is the day it silently acquires this behaviour with nothing
anywhere to say so. **Recorded as one decision made in both places rather than as a fix, and it is
unmeasured** — no test covers it, and none can while both callers are unranged.

⚠️ **The constants' own doc is now true and was false.** `MIN_LINE_HEIGHT_PCT`'s run reads *"Field
bounds. Caps on the **controls**, not on the model — any finite value is a legal attribute and **a file
may hold one**; what these bound is what can be typed or scrubbed."* Before the opt-out, a file holding
one was rewritten and committed on sight. Worth saying, because that sentence is the specification the
fix satisfies rather than an observation about it.

**This was a gap rather than a violation.** No §15 entry and no `architecture.md` passage governed the
Type panel's field bounds, or whether a control may rewrite an out-of-range stored value at all; the
nearest principle points the other way — §5.3's *"radii over half the shorter side are clamped where
the outline is built (`geometry::local_path`), **not on the way in**, so shrinking a shape and growing
it again does not lose the number the user typed."* D425 applied that to the widget; this adds the
panel-level test and the second opt-out.

⚠️ **What the finding is still right about is narrower than it was.** Its second half — one click on
the `px` chip turning `Px(50.0)` into `Em(3.125)`, a value the `%` end could not express — rested on
`Bounds::TRACKING` carrying `pct: -50.0..=200.0` beside a `px: -10_000.0..=10_000.0`, the two ends of
one control disagreeing by a factor of 312 at 16pt. **That is the pre-D425 tree.** `Bounds` has one
field today, `pct`, and `Bounds::px` derives the px face through `px_range_for(pct, font_size)`, so
the two ends cannot disagree and `Px(50.0)` at 16pt is out of range at *both* of them; `[S6.3-L1-03]`,
the root-cause finding for the bounds, closed with D425. What is genuinely left is one axis the fields
do not sit on, read in the code rather than taken from the brief: `text_chord`'s `TextChord::Tracking`
arm steps `0.01em` per `Alt+→` through `apply_char_attrs` with **no range check at all** — where the
`Size` arm in the same `match` says in a comment that `CharAttr::Size` clamps itself — and
`TextStyle::set` canonicalizes `letter_spacing` without bounding it. Held together those are a
question rather than a defect, since the model legitimately holds any finite value and the field now
shows it: *should a chord stop where the field stops?* Open in `roadmap.md` under *Now · Text*.

**D803 — A mutation named by the line it removes, in a file with four copies of that line and one
of them inert. *Measured 2026-09-19; Keep — D475's flip bites on `value_field_f64`'s own line, and
name a mutation by its function. It also names the only known user of `char_valve`'s third arm
(D802).***

**D475's flip sentence was quoted from the finding rather than measured at the test, so it was
re-run — and the re-run was spent on the wrong line.** That entry ends *"Flipped by restoring
`clamp_existing_to_range(true)`: it fails with `Em(2.0)` where `Em(3.0)` was — the finding's own
numbers — while the in-range control stays green"*, and
`typography::a_stored_tracking_outside_the_fields_range_is_not_rewritten_on_an_idle_frame` carried the
same pair in its doc under **Flip-check, run**. The first re-run removed `ui::badge_field`'s opt-out
and came back **green, both cases**, and was very nearly written up here as a flip with no teeth.
Removed from `ui::value_field_f64` instead, the test **fails with `Em(2.0)` where `Em(3.0)` was and
the in-range control stays green** — the flip note is correct in every particular, and those numbers
are now this test's measurement as well as `[S6.2-L1-01]`'s.

🚨 **A mutation named as *"removing `.clamp_existing_to_range(false)`"* does not identify a line.**
`ui.rs` makes that call at **four** production sites — `badge_field`, `plain_drag_value`,
`value_field_f64` and `bare_drag_value`, the last of them D552's — and two of the four are *byte for
byte* the same, `badge_field`'s and `value_field_f64`'s both being a twenty-space-indented chained
call with no semicolon. **The byte-identical pair is exactly the pair that was confused.** This is
`CLAUDE.md`'s *"name the mutation precisely enough to be re-run"* rule failing in a new way: the note
was perfectly precise about the *text*, and the text is what is ambiguous. **Naming the function is
what identifies it**, and the test's doc now does.

⚠️ **The failure mode runs in the dangerous direction.** `badge_field`'s opt-out is documented as
**inert** — both its production callers pass an unranged `Scrub`, so there is nothing to clamp against
— so removing it is a no-op, and a no-op is indistinguishable from a flip that does not bite. That
manufactures a **false negative**, which reads as *this test has no teeth* and invites deleting the
line the test exists to protect. The opposite slip announces itself: a flip that lands on a live line
and bites is its own evidence. ⚠️ **So an inert line is not only harmless documentation of a decision;
it is a decoy for anyone mutating the live one**, which is the cost D475 did not price when it made
the same opt-out in both places.

**The mechanism, traced when the result still disagreed with it and confirmed by the re-run.** This
path is ranged: `length_char_field` builds `Scrub::whole(0.5).range(Bounds::TRACKING.pct)` — `−50…200`
— and `value_field_f64` hands it straight to `.range(scrub.range.clone())` two lines above the
opt-out, so `Em(3.0)` is 300% of the range. `egui-0.35.0/src/widgets/drag_value.rs` clamps into its
local at the `if clamp_existing_to_range` block, then `if old_value != value { set(&mut
get_set_value, value); }` a few lines down, and marks the response changed at the bottom of `ui()` on
`get(&mut get_set_value) != old_value`; `value_field_f64`'s own `if nudged || *value != before {
resp.mark_changed(); }` is a second door to the same flag. Read end to end the rewrite reaches the
document, and it does.

🚨 **The failing run also answers D802's open question, and not in the comfortable direction.** All
three arms of `char_valve` instrumented on it: **the third arm is the one that fires** —
`resp.changed() && !resp.lost_focus()`, the arm D802 measured the picker's raw sensed regions cannot
reach. So the arm is **not dead**. An egui-initiated clamp rewrite is a `changed()` frame on a control
holding no focus, so it walks past `engaged` and `was_engaged` into `commit_edit` and
`text_session_restyled_after` — **the arm is the mechanism by which `[S6.2-L1-01]`'s clamp became a
committed document change and an undo step**, rather than a value redrawn and forgotten.
`clamp_existing_to_range(false)` is the whole of what keeps that user from existing in the shipped
tree. ⚠️ **Its only *known* user, not its only one**: `char_valve` has seven call sites and two are
measured now. What this changes for D802's ruling is its shape rather than its answer — *delete the
arm* is now a specific proposal with a reason, a **second** defence against the bug D425's line
already closes, and *keep it* means keeping a route whose only known user is a hazard something else
has to hold shut. **The ruling is the maintainer's and is not taken here.** 🚨 **It was taken the same
day and the arm is deleted (D812)** — on a read of the five unmeasured call sites rather than on a
third measurement, all seven being engagement-bearing with both `DragValue` helpers opted out
(D425, D552), so *"its only known user"* became *"no live user at all"*.

⚠️ **This entry was first written the other way round** — as a flip in doubt, on the premise that the
green run was real — and that premise was the wrong line. It is rewritten rather than left standing,
and the trap is recorded rather than quietly fixed, because the doubt had already reached D475 and
would have reached §9.2's one-line-for-82-fields argument next. **Nothing in the tree changed to
pre-empt anything**: the opt-out stays on D425's argument, `badge_field`'s stays on D475's, and the
only edit is the test's own doc, which now names the function the mutation belongs to and what the
instrumented run found.

**D812 — `char_valve`'s third arm is gone, and the asymmetry of the two failures is what decided it.
*Ruled by the maintainer, fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — D802's *Fix* and D803's hand-off
are both discharged.***

The arm was `else if resp.changed() && !resp.lost_focus()`, the one no other valve in this app has.
**D523** kept it for *"a control with no engagement to latch"* — specifically the picker's raw
sensed regions — on the reasoning that such a control has no focus to hold and, on a click that
never becomes a drag, nothing to latch, so a falling-edge-only valve *"would never commit it at
all"*.

**Both halves of that were falsified on 2026-09-19, hours apart.** D802 wrote the test D523 had
asked for and found the route does not exist: `picker::pointer_slot` answers a click through
`write_slot` and returns before it could reach `valve_slot`, so the hue slider and the alpha strip
never enter this valve on a click; a *drag* enters it as the engaged arm and its release as the
falling edge, which are the two arms every other valve has; and on the frames that route does enter
it, `changed()` is false. D803 then found the one thing that **did** reach it, and it is a hazard
rather than a feature: egui's per-frame clamp of a stored value outside a **ranged** field marks a
control holding no focus as `changed()`, so the arm walked past `engaged` and `was_engaged` into
`commit_edit`, committing an edit nobody made and spending an undo step. That is `[S6.2-L1-01]`,
and D425's one line was the whole of what kept it from happening in the shipped tree.

🚨 **What decided it is new since D803, and it is a read of the call sites rather than a third
measurement.** All seven are engagement-bearing — `ui::value_field`, `ui::bare_drag_value`, the axis
field and slider, the length fields — and **both** of the app's `DragValue` helpers opt out of
egui's clamp, `ui::value_field_f64` per **D425** and `ui::bare_drag_value` per **D552**. So the arm
had no live user at all, not merely no *wanted* one. D803's *"seven call sites, two measured"* is
seven **read**, which is the figure the ruling turns on.

**The argument is the asymmetry of the two failure modes, and it is what a future editor restoring
the arm has to answer.** An unmeasured caller that genuinely needed it fails **loudly** — *"this
control commits nothing"* is a bug report somebody files — where keeping it fails **silently**, as
*"a field nobody touched spent an undo step"*, which is a defect that reaches the document and the
autosave before anyone notices. Deleting it is therefore a second defence against the bug D425
already closes rather than tidying, and D425's line stops being the only thing standing between
that bug and the document.

**Test** `panels::typography::valve_arm_tests::a_changed_frame_with_no_engagement_commits_nothing`,
which builds the condition **by hand** with a ranged `DragValue` carrying egui's default. No
production control can reach that state now, which is exactly why the fixture has to: the test is
about the arm's predicate and not about any caller. Flipped by restoring the arm, it is red at *"no
undo step"* with 1 against 0.

⚠️ **The first draft of that test was about nothing, and only one habit caught it.** It used 999
against a `MAX_FONT_SIZE` of **1000**, so the value was in range, egui rewrote nothing, and the
fixture never reached the state it named — a green test asserting that an arm which had just been
deleted did not fire on a frame where nothing would have fired anyway. Asserting the fixture is in
the state the test is about is what found it, and nothing else here could have.

**D817 — A tracking chord stops where its field stops, and the bound is at the arm and deliberately
not in the model. *Ruled by the maintainer, fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved.***

`TextChord::Tracking` stepped `0.01em` per `Alt`+`→` through `apply_char_attrs` with **no range
check at all**, and `TextStyle::set` canonicalizes `letter_spacing` without bounding it — so a held
key walked tracking past `MAX_TRACKING_PCT` and out of what the field can be scrubbed to. The
`Size` arm four lines up is the other answer and says so in its own comment: `CharAttr::Size` clamps
itself to `MIN_FONT_SIZE..=MAX_FONT_SIZE`, so held keys stop at the ends without a second bound at
the chord.

**Nothing was being lost, which is why this was a question rather than a defect.** Since **D425**'s
opt-out — tested on this very panel by **D475** — the field *shows* an out-of-range stored value
instead of rewriting it, so a document holding 300% tracking keeps it and displays it. What the
absence of a bound cost is the two chords disagreeing about whether a held key has an end, which is
a thing the hand learns and then finds untrue one field over.

🚨 **The bound is at the arm and not at `TextStyle::set`, where `Size`'s is, so the two chords agree
about *behaviour* and deliberately not about where the bound is written.** These caps are on the
**controls**: any finite value is a legal `letter_spacing`, a file may hold one, and
`MIN_LINE_HEIGHT_PCT`'s own doc run says as much for the whole family. A bound in the model would
make D425's behaviour unreachable for this attribute — the panel refusing a document it is perfectly
able to display — and would be the one place in this app where a control's cap had leaked into the
format. *A reader tempted to "finish the job" by moving it down to `set` should read D475 first.*

**The px face is derived from the `%` face at the current font size**, through the same
`px_range_for` the field itself uses, so the chord and the scrub cannot come to disagree about the
cap in whichever unit the user happens to be in — which is the failure this would otherwise have
invited, the two faces being separate numbers with one meaning.

**Test** `panels::typography::valve_arm_tests::a_held_tracking_chord_stops_at_the_fields_cap`.
⚠️ **Two things the first draft got wrong, and the test records both because each would silently
halve it.** The stored default is **`Px(0.0)` and not `Em`**, so the em face needs a fixture of its
own or that half of the `match` is never exercised at all. And a probe reading `style.letter_spacing`
off the node measured `Px(0.0)` after four hundred presses: with a live session the write lands in
the **editor** rather than on the node, so the assertion reads through `TypeSubject` now — a test
that looks at the wrong side of a live session measures a value nobody is writing.

**D474 — The guide commit table gets its first test caller. *Tested 2026-09-07; Keep — the code is
unchanged.***

`[A5-L6-04]`. `grep -rn "finish_guide_drag\|update_guide_drag" crates/` returned **one** hit outside
the functions themselves, a comment in `canvas.rs`. The two tests that existed stop one call earlier —
`pressing_a_guide_inside_its_pick_band_does_not_move_it` and
`a_guide_pulled_from_the_ruler_lands_under_the_pointer` both drive `begin_guide_drag` and assert on the
drag's *opening* state — so **nothing in the workspace released a guide drag**, and the whole of the
decision that writes to the document, the six arms of `finish_guide_drag`'s `match (d.id,
d.discarding)`, was held up by its own comments.

`the_guide_commit_table_answers_each_of_its_arms` drives `begin → update → finish` on the existing
headless fixture and asserts against `session.doc.guide(id)` and the undo depth. **Three pairs, each a
gesture and the control that differs from it by one term** — an Alt-drag released over the ruler
against the same drag without Alt, a scope change against a second press with nothing left to change,
and a guide pulled out and put back against one dropped on the canvas — because the arms differ by one
term and either alone cannot say which term is in force.

⚠️ **Mutation 1 bites, and it is the one that loses the user's work.** Collapsing `(Some(_), true) if
d.copying => {}` into `(Some(id), true) => self.remove_guide(id)` — one character — makes
**Alt-dragging a copy and dropping it back on the ruler delete the original**. The arm's own comment
was the only thing enforcing it: *"not `remove_guide` — an Alt-drag was never asking to delete
anything, and the original has not moved."*

⚠️ **Mutation 3 bites**: dropping `|| g.owner != d.owner` loses a scope change silently. The test pins
it with **the line not moving at all** — drift asserted at exactly `0` — which is the boundary a test
of mutation 2 alone cannot see.

⚠️ **Mutation 2 does *not* bite, and that is a finding about the code rather than a failed
experiment.** `[A5-L6-04]` named `let moved = true;` as a mutation that would put an undo step in the
history for every selecting click. Run, it changes nothing: **D428**'s guard in
`EditorSession::commit_inner` already drops a transaction whose every operation writes back the value
that is already there, and a `SetGuideScope` to the same owner at the same position is exactly that —
`Operation::changes_nothing` has the arm. **The finding was written against a tree where D428 had
already landed**, and its stated consequence is refuted. What `moved` still buys is the op not being
built and the rule stated at the site that has it; its comment no longer claims to be what stops the
undo step, and that correction is the only code change in the commit.

⚠️ **And the obvious spelling of the no-op-press test does not test what it says.**
`OndinApp::headless` starts with an artboard and the fixture makes a guide with `owner: None`, so the
very **first** press over that frame is a legitimate scope change — it committed, and the assertion
failed for the right reason. Measured while writing it: `position` drift exactly `0`, `d.owner` the
default frame, `was.owner` `None`. The no-op press therefore has to come **second**, on a guide that
has already taken its scope, which is also the sequence a user performs — and is what makes mutations
2 and 3 one fixture rather than two.

**This discharges the other half of D35's standing instruction.** That entry closes with *"anyone who
finds a way to construct an `OndinApp` headlessly should pin this first"*; the way was found in
**D303**, and `guide_grab_tests` pinned the *teleport* half the same day. The commit half waited
because the harness was three calls short — `update_guide_drag` and `finish_guide_drag` are `&mut
self` and take no egui context, which is precisely the shape D303 made reachable. D35 is amended to
say so rather than reading as though its commit path is still unpinned.

⚠️ **One of the six arms still has no caller**: `(Some(id), false) if d.copying`, the Alt-drag released
over the *canvas*, where the copy is minted, selected and reported as *"Guide copied"*. The first
gesture in the test Alt-drags and drops on the **ruler**, so it exercises the discard and not the
landing, and §9.4's *"a copy released over the ruler is discarded … and the original is untouched"*
has a test where the sentence beside it does not. *Fix with a fourth pair* — the same Alt-drag ending
on the canvas, asserting one more guide, the copy selected, and the original where it was.

**D473 — `stack_escape` takes the union of the right quantities. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
the arithmetic follows §6.4 and nothing makes it keep following.***

`[S10.1-L2-02]`. `stack_escape`'s own doc said *"two effects both reaching 10px out do not reach 20px
out, they each reach 10."* That is true of two **shadows** and **false of anything §6.4 composes** —
and §6.4 composes two things. `render::effects::run` applies `Filters` and `LayerBlur` **sequentially
in list order** to the layer, keeps that as `graphic`, and casts every shadow from **it**. So a
`DropShadow`'s silhouette is the already-blurred layer, and two `LayerBlur`s convolve at
`σ = √(σ₁² + σ₂²)` rather than at `max(σ₁, σ₂)`.

Measured in release through the CPU backend, a 40×40 rect carrying
`[LayerBlur { radius: 12 }, DropShadow { offset: (0, 40), blur: 4 }]` — an everyday Figma stack. The
shadow's alpha down the centre column ran `… 87, 71, 54, 38, 0, 0, 0`: it **stopped dead at 38/255
with a hard edge**, exactly at `ink_bounds.y1 = 126`, losing roughly 18 device units — the whole faint
end of the gaussian — and leaving **a shadow with a ruled line across it**. The arithmetic predicted
the shortfall to the unit: claimed `max(18, reach(4) + 40) = 46`, true `18 + 6 + 40 = 64`.

⚠️ **Both single-effect controls were always clean**, which is what says this is the composition and
not the bound: the same shadow with no layer blur falls to `… 10, 3, 1, 0` and reaches zero exactly at
its own `ink_bounds.y1`, and the same layer blur alone ends at 0. A second instance of the same
mechanism: two `LayerBlur { radius: 12 }` cut at 5/255 where the single blur of the same composed
deviation fades to 0 with 7.5 units to spare.

⚠️ **The under-covered box is also the buffer**, which is why it cuts rather than merely mis-culls:
`grow_to_escape` ends `device_ink.intersect(grown)`, so the silhouette is read from a buffer that has
already lost the tail — **D342's mechanism one level up**. And §5.9's rule is that **too small is the
one error these bounds may not make**; `ink_bounds` is documented as deliberately over-covering and
was under-covered here.

**Per stage, and still a union.** Stage 1 is one isotropic reach from the convolved deviation of every
visible `LayerBlur` (`Filters` add nothing). Stage 2 is each shadow's own escape **grown by stage 1 on
every side**, since stage 1's output is its silhouette. The answer is the union of those — the same
rule the old comment states, applied to the quantities §6.4 actually produces. The composition is done
in **deviations** and turned back into a reach once, rather than squaring and rooting the reaches:
those agree today only because `BLUR_CUTOFF` is a constant, and would stop agreeing the day it is not.

⚠️ **An existing test was asserting the defect.** `a_stacks_reach_is_the_union_of_its_effects_not_the_sum`
pinned two `LayerBlur`s at **18**, the union, which is exactly the claim the finding refutes. It is
rewritten as `two_layer_blurs_convolve_rather_than_summing_or_taking_the_larger`, on a fixture chosen
so the three readings are three different numbers — **28 summed, 18 unioned, 20.5913 composed** —
because a fixture where two of them coincide cannot say which rule is in force.

**Flipped** by restoring the old body: fails at **46 against 64** and at **18 against 20.5913**, the
finding's own numbers. The new `InnerShadow` control stays green under it, because an inner shadow
escapes nothing whatever stage 1 does — which is what stops the fix being "grow everything by stage 1".

⚠️ **The finding warned *"the export goldens will move"* and they did not.** The golden document
carries no effect at all — `filter` appears 0 times in `every-kind.svg` — so that risk was
hypothetical here. Worth stating rather than reading the green run as proof the bound is unchanged:
**it is changed, and nothing outside `effect.rs`'s own tests was covering it.**

**D334 is the entry whose *"union, never a sum"* this narrows**, and its decision is right about the
case it was written for, two shadows; it is amended rather than left reading as the whole rule. *What
the verdict is for*: §6.4's two-stage composition is now written down twice, once as the pass and once
as the bound, with nothing that fails if the pass is reordered — **fix with one statement of the
composition order that both read**, and a fifth effect kind owes both in the meantime.

**D472 — Resizing a group carries a railed text with it. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the doors
carry the rail and the rule is written twice.***

`[S13.2-L1-02]`. `resize_to_handle` has had the rail arm since **D405** and `scale_geometry` did not,
so a drag through the **group** door reached a railed child as `scale_scalars` plus a bare
`SetTransform`. On a rail `TextSizing` is inert — the rail's length is the measure — so for `Auto`
`scaled_text_sizing` answers `None` and there was nothing left to write.

Measured on a group holding one railed `Auto` text plus an 80×40 rect, `Handle::BottomRight` to 2× on
both axes:

```text
group        161.88 x 170.77  ->  171.88 x 320.77   (asked 323.76 x 341.54)
railed text  158.59 x  30.75  ->  158.59 x  30.75   <-- unchanged
rect control  80.00 x  40.00  ->  160.00 x  80.00   <-- correct
```

The width is **47% short of the drag**, on the first frame, with no error and no report — because the
text's own ribbon pins the group's width, so the one child that did not move decided the container's
box.

**This is the round's recurring shape for the fourth time** — the guard next door whose doc explains
the very defect at the site without it (cf. `[S13.1-L2-01]`, `[S13.1-L2-02]`). `resize_to_handle`'s
rail arm says: *"it has to edit **something**: `TextSizing` is inert here, so the arm below would hand
back a patch the layout ignores and the handles would drag with nothing moving."*

**The two boxes come from the rail rather than from `Resolved`**, which is what makes this reachable
from `scale_geometry` at all: that function has no `Resolved`. `railed_box` — extracted from
`railed_resize`'s own correction loop, so there is one measurement rather than two — lays the current
rail out through the same path the canvas draws, and `want` is that box scaled by the residual factors
about its own origin, which is what `scale_subtree` means by handing them down.

⚠️ **The rect in the group is the control and it is load-bearing**: without it, *"the group did not
reach the box"* and *"nothing in the group moved"* are the same observation, and a `scale_subtree` that
had stopped working entirely would pass.

⚠️ **Nothing reached a rail through this door before.** `dragging_railed_text_scales_its_rail` is the
only rail test on any resize path in the tree and it calls `resize_to_handle` directly — which is how
an arm could be missing from the other door for as long as the feature has existed.

⚠️ **Four doors reach this arm and two of them were measured.** `resize_group` through `scale_subtree`
and `resize_selection` are the two the finding is about; `skew_to_handle` and `skew_selection` hand
`scale_geometry` the residual diagonal `split_geometry_scale` leaves after a lean, so a railed node
now re-solves its rail under a skew as well. Read rather than run.

**Flipped** by disabling the `on_path` arm: fails on the child assertion at
`158.5865013747961 -> 158.5865013747961`, unchanged to the ten-thousandth, while the rect control stays
green. Asserted loosely on the group and tightly on the child's growth, because `railed_resize` solves
its factor rather than taking it — the exact width is the solve's business and what is being pinned is
that the child moved *with* its sibling instead of standing still.

**D405 is the live entry for text on a path and addresses only the resize handle**, so this was a gap
in it rather than a violation; it is amended to say the group and selection doors carry it now. *What
the verdict is for*: the rule sits in **two arms of one file** that derive `drawn` and `want` two
different ways — `anchored_box` over `Resolved` in one, `railed_box` in the other — which is D293/D167's
shape. **Fix with one statement of it** before a third door needs a third copy.

**D471 — A drag with no button behind it paints nothing and lands nothing. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the paint and the drop are closed and the stranding is not.***

`[S17-L1-01]`. Pick a layer row up and, still holding the button, press the panel's own chord
(`Ctrl+Alt+\`, or `Ctrl+\` for present mode). `input::resolve` is *"a pure resolution of this frame's
events, with no state of its own"* and `dispatch` hands `ToggleView` straight to `set_view_switch` with
**no in-flight guard** — where the four actions that *do* have one (`Nudge`, `SizeStep`, `Delete`,
`Enter`) are intercepted in that same `match`. `resolve` runs before the panel is drawn, so the panel
is skipped on the very frame the chord lands, and `finish_layer_drag` runs inside `layers_tree`, which
is not drawn. **The release goes nowhere and `layer_drag` survives it.**

Bring the panel back and `drop_hint` read `pointer_interact_pos` **alone, with no test that a button
was down**. Measured end to end on a root → `e` / frame → group → `c1` fixture: the tree lit a drop
host, painted the blue drop line, and re-derived a target from wherever the pointer was *resting* — and
**the release of the next ordinary primary click committed it**: `undo_depth 0 → 1`, `c1.parent` root
where it had been the group, toast *"Moved layer"*, against a control at 0.

⚠️ **Guarded in `drop_hint` rather than at the view switch, because that closes the class.** Clearing
the drag in `set_view_switch` closes the one route; a drag stranded by any *future* route still paints
and still lands. It is also the recovery on the present-mode route, where `escape` cannot be one: its
first rung is `self.present = false`, which restores the panel with the phantom drag live, and only a
**second** Escape reaches `cancel_gesture`. `fold_layers_edge`'s own ⚠️ documents this exact class one
function away — *"this runs only while the panel is drawn … it stops being harmless the moment anything
outside `layers_panel` reads that field"* — and `layer_drag` **is** read outside `layers_panel`, at
`cancel_gesture`.

⚠️ **The guard broke six existing tests, and they were the ones that were wrong.** `pump` and `pump_at`
drove a `PointerMoved` and no press, so every drop-target test in that module was simulating a drag
**with the mouse button up** — the exact state the defect is about, asserted as if it were normal. Both
helpers press on the first pass now and let egui carry `primary_down`; repeating the press on all five
passes would work too and would be a hand on a key rather than a hand on a mouse.

⚠️ **The control asserts the *target* and not the line**, and the reason was measured while writing it:
the aim point is the middle of a container row, which is a drop *inside* it and lights the host's
ground rather than drawing a between-rows line — `Some(DropTarget { parent: frame, index: 2 })` with
**0** lines, correct, and it would have failed a careless `lines > 0`. The target is the load-bearing
half anyway: it is what a release commits.

**Flipped** by deleting the `primary_down` early return: fails on the first assertion, the panel
answering a drop target for a pointer merely resting on a row.
`layers::a_drag_with_no_button_behind_it_paints_nothing`.

**Nothing in §9.3 or §9.4 covered a view-switch chord fired mid-gesture**, and no §15 entry did either;
the adjacent one is **D31**, which establishes only that a `LayerDrag` *"has to be dropped here rather
than left to `finish_layer_drag`, since that runs on a release still to come"* and enumerates
right-click and Escape as the two ways out. So the design already knew this state can outlive its
normal completion path and had enumerated the exits — this is a route it did not have. *What the
verdict is for*: the phantom drag is now inert rather than absent, and `set_view_switch` still has no
idea a gesture is in flight. **Fix with one predicate every action that hides a panel asks**, in the
`match` that already intercepts four of them.

🚨 **Amended by D582 the next day, because the spelling above stopped every legitimate drop as well.**
A bare `return` on `!primary_down()` leaves the stranded drag *live* and merely unpainted, so it also
had to refuse the frame a real release arrives on — and `layers_tree` clears `target` at the top of
every frame while `drop_hint` is the only thing that re-derives it, so **the one frame that ends a
drag was the one frame that could not resolve one**. Releasing the primary over the tree landed
nothing for a day. The guard admits the release frame and **clears** the drag now, which is strictly
stronger: a stranded drag dies on the first ordinary frame instead of merely being ignored on all of
them. Everything above about *where* the guard belongs is unchanged, and
`a_drag_with_no_button_behind_it_paints_nothing` passes under both spellings — it never releases
anything, which is how the regression got in.

**D470 — A typed opacity digit lands on the layer it was typed against. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — the entry carries its subject and the rule behind it is still written out twice.***

`[S16.1-L1-02]`, and the one member of its group where the user touched **no control at all** on the
layer that changed. `OpacityEntry` held `first: u8` and `at: f64` and **no subject**, so
`fold_opacity_entry` re-read the live selection at deadline time, 600 ms after the keystroke. Measured
headless with `RawInput::time` driven, two rects at 1.0 with A selected and `4` typed:

| | A | B | undo | status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **control** — the selection stays on A | **0.4** | 1 | +1 | — |
| the selection moves to B inside the window | **1** | **0.4** | +1 | `"Opacity 40%"` |
| the selection is cleared inside the window | 1 | 1 | 0 | — |

The user typed a digit against A, watched A change, and B — which they merely selected — keeps the
value. One undo restores B; **A never gets what was asked for.**

⚠️ **The rule was already written two hundred lines above the type, in the same file.**
`OndinApp::session_scrub` — the sibling *"value in flight that `RenderOverrides` cannot preview"* —
says verbatim: *"the node is carried with the lists so a snapshot cannot be applied to a session that
has since moved to a different layer."* `OpacityEntry` is exactly that shape and did not carry it.

**Two halves, because the entry is read twice.** `fold_opacity_entry` commits against `entry.subject`,
and `set_opacity_pct_on` takes the ids as an argument rather than reading the selection itself. And
`opacity_step`'s pairing arm requires the subject to match: select A, press `4`, click B, press `5` —
that is not `45%` on anything, and reading the window alone made it `45%` on B. A moved subject starts
a new entry, which is what the second keystroke means.
