⚠️ **The empty-selection row was clean by accident and one level down**, at `set_opacity_pct_on`'s
`if tx.0.is_empty() { return; }` — where `opacity_digit`, the *other* reader of the same entry, has an
explicit guard. It is asserted anyway, because *"clean for a reason nobody wrote down"* is how the
moved case came to have no guard at all.

**Flipped at each half.** Committing against the live selection fails the moved row with `(1.0, 0.4)`,
the finding's numbers to the digit; dropping the subject comparison from the pairing arm fails with
`Land(45.0)` where `Wait(50.0, _)` is right. Both controls stay green. ⚠️ **The end-to-end test asserts
the undo *delta*, not the depth** — the fixture's own `CreateNode` is a step, so the finding's `0 → 1`
is `+1` from a document that already had its rects, and a test asserting the absolute depth would have
been measuring its own setup. The clock is driven through `RawInput::time`, which is why it is fast:
`OPACITY_DIGIT_WINDOW` is read against `InputState::time` rather than an `Instant`.

**D210 is the entry for this feature, and this was a gap in it rather than a violation.** It
enumerates the two ways the window shuts, the shared `opacity_window_open` boundary and the
`request_repaint_after` wake, and says nothing about the *subject* moving; `shortcuts.md` §2 likewise
enumerates the empty-selection case and not this one. Both are amended. *What the verdict is for*:
"a value in flight carries the node it is in flight for" is now spelled out on `OpacityEntry` and on
`session_scrub` with nothing joining them — **fix with one statement of it**, and a third deferred
edit owes it in the meantime.

**D469 — An occupied frame's name tag is a pick, and the menu door never asked. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — two of the three doors share one chain and the third carries a clause neither of
them has.***

`[S12.1-L2-01]`. `pick_leaf` **deliberately** skips an occupied frame so a marquee can be dragged
across its contents (D22), and the name tag is the only handle such a frame has left — so
`canvas_context_menu`, which asked `pick_leaf` alone, opened `Target::Canvas`, the **empty-canvas**
menu, at the very pixel a left-click selects the frame. Measured end to end on a 200×150 frame at
world (100, 100) with one layer in it, its tag drawn at screen (120.4, 88.5): `frame_label_at`
answered the frame, `pick_leaf` answered `None`, and the menu that opened was the canvas's.

**Its edge and its interior resolve through `pick_leaf` too**, so this was not merely the wrong menu
on the tag: **an occupied frame had no context menu reachable from the canvas at all**, the layers
panel's row being the only route.

`context-menus.md` §2 **C5** names the very function the door did not call — *"a frame is
right-clickable exactly where it is left-clickable. An occupied frame passes presses through so a
marquee can be dragged across its contents (`is_occupied_frame`), so its menu is reachable on its
**name tag** (`frame_label_at`), on its edge, or anywhere on it while it is empty. Nothing new is
needed for this; it falls out of C1."* — and **C1** is *"on canvas the menu's target is whatever a
left-click would have selected. Same query, same pixel."* Nothing in that file's §9 or in this section
accepts the difference, so it was a defect rather than a recorded deviation, and C5's closing sentence
is amended rather than left standing: the thing it says falls out of C1 is exactly the thing that did
not.

**One rule written twice with one copy missing a clause is D293/D167's shape, so the answer is one
function rather than a third copy.** `canvas::pick_at_pointer` — the name tag, then `pick_leaf` — is
that function, and the select-click arm and the menu door both call it.

⚠️ **`begin_select_drag` is a third door and is deliberately *not* folded in.** It carries a further
fallback, `selected_frame_at`, which is C5's *"or on its edge"* half — a widening neither of the other
two has, and one that wants an explicit decision rather than arriving as a side effect of sharing a
helper. Three doors, two of them now sharing one chain, and C5's edge clause answered by only one:
that is open work in `roadmap.md` rather than something settled here.

⚠️ **The flip broke only the new test — 1,002 others stayed green.** The clause was already in the
select-click arm and had been for as long as occupied frames have been unpickable, and nothing
anywhere asserted it, so the rule that *"the tag is the only handle an occupied frame has"* was one
comment and one line, in one of the two places that needed it. Flipped by replacing
`pick_at_pointer`'s body with `self.pick_leaf(world)`: it fails on the first assertion with `None`,
which is the finding itself, `None` being what sends the door to `Target::Canvas`. The **control** —
the same fixture with the frame emptied, where `pick_leaf` answers the frame on its own body — stays
green under that flip and is what says this is about the tag rather than about frames. Asserted on the
shared chain rather than by right-clicking the canvas, `canvas_context_menu` running behind
`resp.secondary_clicked()` and reaching it meaning driving the whole canvas panel; what makes the
assertion meaningful anyway is that the two doors now call the *same* function, which is the thing
that was wrong. `canvas::frame_menu_door_tests`.

⚠️ **This is where D22 reached code for the first time.** The census that evening gained eighteen
numbers, seventeen of them reserved for this round's own entries and the eighteenth D22 — an old entry
arriving in a comment when the code it is about is finally written down.

🚨 **The edge clause is answered as of 2026-09-19 (D816), and not by the widening this entry's last
paragraph and `roadmap.md` both pointed at.** Read D816 beside the paragraph above: folding
`selected_frame_at` into the shared chain would have made an already-selected frame's *interior* a
target, which is the half of C5 that has never been true.

**D816 — C5's *"or on its edge"* is answered, and widening the shared chain was the repair that was
declined. *Ruled by the maintainer, built and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved.***

`canvas::begin_select_drag` carried `selected_frame_at` and neither `pick_at_pointer` caller had
anything, so an occupied frame was reachable from the canvas by its **name tag alone** — where
`context-menus.md` §2's **C5** reads *"a frame is right-clickable exactly where it is left-clickable
… on its name tag, on its edge, or anywhere on it while it is empty"*. D469 closed the tag half and
left this in its own last paragraph.

🚨 **`roadmap.md` named the obvious repair — widen the shared chain with `selected_frame_at` — and it
is wrong, which is the most useful sentence here.** That function answers a frame's whole **box**, so
it would have made an already-selected frame's **interior** a right-click target. That is the half of
C5 that has never been true, and it is a half `pick_leaf` skips *on purpose*, so that a marquee can
be dragged across a frame's contents (**D22**). A one-`.or_else` fix would have bought the edge and
sold the marquee.

`canvas::frame_edge_at` answers an **occupied** frame whose border passes within `pick_slop()`
instead. **The same band every other pick in the app uses**, so it is the same width on screen at any
zoom and needs no constant of its own; and it is the **last** link of `pick_at_pointer`, after
`frame_label_at` and `pick_leaf`, so a layer sitting near its frame's border still wins the pixel —
which is what *"exactly where it is left-clickable"* has to mean when there is something to click.

⚠️ **A frame narrower than twice the slop is all edge**, having no interior left. That is the honest
answer at that size rather than a case worth a branch, and it is stated so nobody reads the function
as exact.

⚠️ **The box is the world *AABB*, so a rotated frame's band is its axis-aligned bounds and not its
drawn border.** This is the limitation `selected_frame_at` has had all along and the one **D36**
records for a rotated frame's ruler origin: nothing in `canvas.rs` resolves a rotated frame's edge,
and a click a little off the drawn line still lands in the band. Worth knowing before anybody builds
on it.

**Test** `canvas::frame_edge_tests::a_frames_edge_is_pickable_and_its_middle_is_not`. ⚠️ **One of its
two flips does not bite, and that is recorded in the test rather than tidied away**: dropping the
`is_occupied_frame` term leaves every assertion green, because the fixture's frame is occupied. That
term is about the **empty** case, which `pick_leaf` already answers on its own — so the flip is a
statement about where the teeth are not, which is the half of a flip-check worth writing down.

**D468 — Everything being transformed is excluded from the baselines, not just the node named. *Fixed
and tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the two sources agree and the exclusion is still asked once per source.***

`[S12.2-L2-02]`. `canvas::baseline_lines` filtered on `moving.contains(&id)` alone, with no ancestry
test, so a text node **inside** a moving group was still offered as a baseline. The baselines are read
off the **committed** `Resolved`, so the target did not move with the drag: the group was being pulled
back to where its own text used to be.

Measured on a group holding one two-line `Text`, dragging down:

| pointer moved (dy) | the group moves |
| --- | --- |
| 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | **0.0**, with a snap mark drawn every frame |
| 7 | 7.461 — breaks free |
| 12 **and** 20 | 17.461 (both) — eight units of travel mapped to one position |
| 30 | 30.461 |

The report shape is *"the group won't move"*, then *"it jumps"*. **The commonest gesture in the app, no
modifier, no unusual state.**

⚠️ **`snap::targets` had the whole rule and this had half of it.** Both are built side by side in
`canvas::snapping`, and on the same fixture `snap::targets(&[group])` returned **0 rects** where
`baseline_lines(&[group])` returned two baselines — the same question, asked in the same call, answered
opposite ways. `snapped_resize`'s own comment states the rule verbatim: *"everything being transformed
is excluded from the snap targets, not just the one node"*. `snap::is_inside_any` is `pub(crate)` now
and there is one spelling of it.

**It is not only the move.** Every gesture that reaches `snapping` drew from the same half-rule —
`snapped_move`, `snapped_resize`, `line_end_tx`, `pen_point`, `snapped_point` and `snapped_point_box`
— which is why the fix is in the source rather than in the drag that reported it. It bites wherever
the moving set can hold a **container**: `snapped_move` and `snapped_resize` pass the whole selection,
where the point-editing pair pass the one path they are editing and a path has no children to offer.

⚠️ **The three existing exclusions never exercised `moving` at all.** Every call in
`baseline_overlay_tests`' gathering test passes `&[]`, so the rotation, half-turn and hidden-node
skips were pinned and the argument that carries the fourth was not — which is how a missing exclusion
sat under a suite that read as covering that half. That test exists at all because `arch-scribe`
pointed out the three exclusions rested on reading (D355); the same observation now applies to the
argument nobody varied.

**Flipped** by deleting the ancestry clause: fails on the group assertion with the text's two
baselines. The `&[]` assertion beside it is what stops the test passing against a `baseline_lines`
that has simply stopped working, and the direct-node case is the control that was always right.
`canvas::a_moving_group_does_not_snap_to_the_baseline_of_the_text_inside_it`, which also asserts
`snapping(&[group]).baselines` is empty, the two having to agree being the whole point.

⚠️ **What the *Fix* is for: the exclusion is a property of each source rather than of `Snapping`.**
`snapping` has the moving set in hand and passes it to two of the three document-derived sources;
`guide_lines` takes no such argument at all, so whether a frame-scoped guide on a moving frame is this
same defect one source over is **unmeasured**. *Fix by asking the question once, where the set is
already known* — and a new source added to `Snapping` owes it in the meantime.

**D467 — Re-picking the family you are already in is a no-op, not a reset. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the one row is guarded and nothing stops a second caller inheriting it.***

`[S6.2-L1-02]`. Picking a family clears every variable-axis setting and every OpenType feature on the
layer, and the reasoning for that is sound and unchanged — *"a tag means something different in the
next typeface"*, `wdth 75` on a family with no width axis is silently nothing, `ss01` is a different
alternate everywhere. But it is written for a family **change** and it ran on a family **re-pick**.

So: a text layer in Inter with `wght 620`, `opsz 28`, `tnum 1` and `ss01 1`; open the dropdown to check
what family it is in, click the row the list draws as **selected**, and — measured headless —
`variations [opsz 28, wght 620] → []`, `features [ss01 1, tnum 1] → []`, `undo_depth 0 → 1`, the family
unchanged. No confirmation, and nothing on screen distinguishes that click from the no-op the user
meant it to be.

⚠️ **`apply_char_attrs`' equality guard cannot save it, and fires exactly as designed.**
`char_attrs_tx` reports a change because clearing two non-empty vectors *is* one. This is not the no-op
family (`[S14.1-L1-01]`) and no guard at the commit can see it: the write really does change something.

**`family_row` returns `clicked()` for any row and gates nothing** — `selected` decides only the ground
it paints — which is deliberate, since the list is drawn by hand for `show_rows` (§9.4). So the
decision has to live at the call site, and it was extracted into `family_actually_changed` so it could
be asserted directly.

**Three arguments rather than a bare `!=`, and the third is the case that gets it wrong.** `current` is
`attr!(subject, Family, Family)`, one member's family over a *mixed* selection — so re-picking **that**
family there is the real edit, the one that makes the selection agree, and the clearing is right for
every layer it moves. The row's own label reads the same `mixed` fact to print the word.

**Flipped both ways.** Returning `chosen` unfiltered fails the first assertion, `Some("Inter")` against
`None`. Dropping the `mixed` term — the obvious spelling — leaves the first three assertions green and
fails the fourth, which is what says that term carries its own case rather than decorating.

⚠️ **Asserted on the predicate rather than by clicking the row**, and the test says so: the family list
lives inside a `ComboBox` popup drawn by `show_rows`, so reaching a row means opening the popup and
hunting a coordinate inside a scroll area. The one call site is a single line and was read.

This reads with **D130**, the *Mixed* convention, and with **D465**, which is the same shape one panel
over: *a control that says "Mixed" is operating from one member of the set, and must not write that
member's value back on a gesture the user did not mean as an edit.*

**D466 — The top bar's buttons finish a text session before touching the document. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the damage is closed and the button still disagrees with its chord.***

`[S16.4-L1-02]`, the sibling of `[S16.4-L1-01]` — the round's only Tier 2 Critical — and it goes the
same way. `input::text_insert_mode` builds its action vector from `Action::TextStyle` alone: `Undo`,
`Redo`, `Save` and `Open` live only in `normal_mode`, and `top_bar` consults `self.mode` nowhere. So
with a live session `Ctrl+Z` did nothing and the Undo glyph 30 px away rewound the document beneath an
editor whose buffer was unchanged, and *Save* wrote **and pinned a version** from a `session.doc` that
did not hold the typed text.

⚠️ **The flip's symptom is worse than the finding described, and this is the sentence to keep.** With
nothing committed, the first undo step still on the stack is the **`CreateNode`** — so clicking Undo
mid-session **deletes the node you are typing into**, and the editor stays live over a node the
document no longer has. `[S16.4-L1-02]` measured `undo_depth 1 → 0` and read the consequence as
*"rewind the document beneath an editor whose buffer is unchanged"*; on this fixture the thing rewound
away is the subject itself. The save half fails on its own line, `"hello"` against `"TYPED"`.

**Finishing rather than dimming**, which is the choice this file had already made twice: `choose_tool`
for the tool rail's equally dead bare keys, and `go_to_dashboard` for the Critical. Both inlined the
same two lines; they are one named method now, `finish_text_first`, and the three top-bar arms — Save,
Redo, Undo — call it. Dimming would make the button agree with its chord and would also make a control
that visibly does nothing, which is what a person reports as broken.

⚠️ **What this does not settle, and the finding says so**: whether `Ctrl+Z` should be dead mid-session
at all. Nothing in the design answers either half — §9.3 records only that `TextInsert` is *"near
exclusive… no **bare** key resolves to an `Action` there"*, so the four dead chords fall out by
omission rather than by a decision with a reason. **The button and its chord still disagree**, which is
what the verdict is for; it is open work in `roadmap.md` under *Now · Keyboard* rather than settled
here.

⚠️ **Asserted at the seam rather than by clicking the glyph, and the test says so.** What is checked is
that each verb ends the session before touching the document; what is *not* checked is that the buttons
call them. `top_bar` is 200 lines of layout and a click into it is a coordinate sweep — which
`inspector::mixed_opacity_tests` had just shown to be its own hazard, its first aim landing on a
destructive neighbour (D465). The three call sites are one line each and were read.
`app::library_wiring_tests::the_top_bars_undo_and_save_commit_what_was_typed_first`.

**D815 — `Undo`, `Redo`, `Save` and `Open` resolve in `Mode::TextInsert`, and the finishing is at
`dispatch`. *Ruled by the maintainer, built and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — the question D466 left
open.***

The four chords were dead in a text session **by omission rather than by a decision**. §9.3 records
only that `TextInsert` is *near* exclusive — *"no **bare** key resolves to an `Action` there, because
a bare key in a session is a character"* — which is a rule about bare keys and was never about
chords at all, so the four simply fell out of `text_insert_mode` with nothing anywhere having
weighed them.

**Meanwhile the top bar's buttons for three of them were live the whole time**, and have finished
the session before acting since **D466**. So the button and its chord disagreed about the same verb
thirty pixels apart: clicking *Undo* rewound the document, `Ctrl+Z` did nothing. D466 closed the
damage — the button no longer deletes the node being typed into — and left this half open in its own
words.

`input::text_insert_mode` grows the four, with `normal_mode`'s guards **term for term**, every
`!m.shift` included. ⚠️ **They are written out rather than shared with `normal_mode`, and the two
modes' lists are different lengths on purpose**, so a future editor factoring them together would be
asserting an equality nobody has decided. `ctrl_shift_is_not_a_second_spelling_of_ctrl` sweeps
`normal_mode`'s arms and **not** these, so the new ones are swept separately.

🚨 **The finishing is at `OndinApp::dispatch` and deliberately not in the keymap, because it is a
fact about the *action* rather than about the key.** The buttons already spell it there; a guard in
`text_insert_mode` would be a second copy of one rule, and the next door onto `Undo` — a context-menu
row, a palette entry — would miss it exactly as the chord did. So `dispatch` calls
`finish_text_first` on the three arms that act on the document, and one seam serves every door.
`Open` needs nothing of its own: `go_to_dashboard` has finished the session since D466.

**Two tests, and they are two on purpose.** `input::text_insert_tests::the_four_document_chords_resolve_in_a_session`
covers the keymap; `app::library_wiring_tests::a_document_chord_in_a_session_finishes_it_first`
drives `dispatch` directly. `resolve` answering and `dispatch` finishing are independent claims, and
a single test that pressed a key would pass or fail for either reason. Both flip-checked.

🚨 **A doc-comment theft was found while reading for this and repaired in the same change.**
`OndinApp::finish_text_first` had been inserted directly above `OndinApp::top_bar` and anchored on
its `fn` line, so it took `top_bar`'s whole doc run as the head of its own — *"The top bar: brand
mark, breadcrumb, save state…"* followed by *"End a live text session before acting on the
document"* — and **`top_bar` had no doc at all**. That is **D805**'s shape exactly: the victim is
left *still documented*, by a run that opens by describing something else, so *"did the item below
lose its comment"* answers no. ⚠️ **The whole-tree length ranking cannot see it either** — the merged
run is 44 lines against a floor in the fifties. What found it was reading the run *above*
`finish_text_first` and asking whether its first line describes it, which is the only question that
catches this shape. The run is split and both items head-describe themselves.

**D465 — A *Mixed* opacity field the user has not moved writes nothing. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — the one field that called the valve unconditionally is guarded, and the guard compares a
number.***

`[S14.4-L1-01]`. `paint_row` seeds its `pct` from `Spread::base()` — the *first* paint in scope, one
member of the disagreeing set, which is exactly what the row has to hand its controls while it is
*saying* "Mixed" (§9.4's *says* / *operates from* rule; `mixed_row`'s own comment states it, and
`Spread::base` exists for nothing else). So a bare click into that field — nothing typed, nothing dragged —
committed that one layer's alpha onto every other. Measured headless on two rects at **1.0** and
**0.4**: the 0.4 became 1.0, `undo_depth` went 0 → 1, `is_dirty()` came back true, and the only thing
the user did was look at the field.

**The row already knew.** `hazy` is `mixed.is_some_and(|m| m.alpha)`, the same fact the formatter one
line above reads to print the word *"Mixed"*; it was used for the display and nothing downstream
re-read it. The guard is that a hazy field must **differ from what it was seeded with** before it may
write — which a drag or a typed number does and a click does not.

⚠️ **Nothing downstream can catch it, and the no-op family is the control rather than the cure.**
`build::edit_fills_all` filters **per node**, so over an *agreeing* selection the transaction is empty
and `commit_inner` drops it — which is why the agreeing pair was always clean and this was not. Over a
disagreeing one the write really does change something, so `[S14.1-L1-01]`'s
one-guard-at-`commit_inner` fix cannot see this, and `edit_valve` compares no value either.

⚠️ **Every other *Mixed* numeric field in the inspector was safe, and not one of them compares a
value.** The multi Appearance panel's opacity and radius, the mixed stroke row's weight and
`multi_number`'s six transform fields all build their transaction behind `interacting(&resp)` —
`dragged() || drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()` — which was written as a **cost** early
return, since each of those builds an operation per member of the selection every frame. It closes
this door as a side effect: with `edit_valve` never called on the frames the field merely holds focus,
its engagement latch never arms, so the `!engaged && was_engaged` transition a click produces never
happens. `paint_row`'s percentage is the one control that called the valve **unconditionally**, and
that is the whole difference. Read against the code rather than measured — but it means the family
question has an answer, and the answer is not *they all need this guard*: it is that a field which
stops routing through `interacting` inherits this defect with nothing anywhere to say so.

⚠️ **The survey above is right and its population is too narrow, which D534 found by walking into
the second instance.** The single-node Appearance panel's corner-radius field prints a **number** and
never the word — it shows `largest(corners)` when the four disagree — and it called `edit_valve`
unconditionally too, so a bare click flattened `(10, 0, 0, 0)` to `(10, 10, 10, 10)`. It took the
identical guard, `shared.is_some() || r != seed`. **What marks the family is being *seeded from one
member of a disagreeing set*, not saying `Mixed`**: the word is a symptom of the condition and not
the condition, so the question to ask of a numeric field is where its value came from rather than
what it prints. D534 has the measurement.

⚠️ **The hex field on the same row is inert for the opposite reason, and the contrast is the lesson.**
Its "Mixed" is the *buffer's actual contents*, so `parse_hex` rejects it and the write below simply
never happens — the field's own doc already says that is why it needs no special case. The opacity's
"Mixed" is a `custom_formatter` painted over a live `f32` the valve will happily commit. **A word
drawn by a formatter is not a value the code can refuse**, and any new mixed *numeric* field is on the
hex field's side of that line only if somebody puts it there (D130).

⚠️ **The first draft of the test flipped GREEN, and the reason belongs in the record.** It pressed,
released and asserted; nothing was written, with or without the guard. `edit_valve`'s `engaged` is
`dragged() || has_focus()` and it commits on the `!engaged && was_engaged` transition, so **a click
that leaves the field focused has not finished the gesture**. The report's *"press `Enter` (or click
away)"* is load-bearing rather than incidental: **a valve test that only presses and releases is
testing nothing**, and that generalises to every valved field in the inspector.

⚠️ **The aim point was found by sweeping x, and two of the field's neighbours are destructive.** In a
320-wide row the opacity field spans about **x = 200…255**, the `x` that clears every fill is
**260…285**, and the eye is **290…315**. The first aim was `320 − 28 − 20` and hit the `x`, which
emptied both layers' fill lists and failed the test on an index rather than on the claim. The test
asserts the fill count survived first, so a drifted aim cannot pass silently.

**Flipped** by dropping the `!hazy || moved` guard: fails on the first assertion, `(1.0, 1.0)` against
`(1.0, 0.4)`, with `undo_depth` at 1. The **control** — the same events over an agreeing selection —
stays green under the flip, which is what says this is not a test about clicking a field in general.
`inspector::mixed_opacity_tests` holds both.

⚠️ **Residue, and it is what the *Fix* is for.** The guard compares a number, so it cannot tell *not
touched* from *touched and brought back*: typing the base paint's own percentage into a mixed field —
which is how a user says *make them all this* about the number the field is already showing — writes
nothing, and neither does a drag that ends exactly where it started. And `hazy` is decided **as a
byte**, `mixed_row` rounding each alpha to `u8` before comparing because that is the precision the hex
field and the save format work in, so two alphas differing by under 1/255 are not hazy at all and a
bare click still flattens them. Both read rather than run. *Fix by latching whether the field was ever
dragged or typed into* — the thing `edit_valve` already keeps per widget id — *rather than by
comparing its value*.

**D464 — A modal owns the keyboard, and two of the three did not. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
the three arms are closed and "a modal is up" is still written out twice.***

`[S16.1-L2-01]`. The gate is one `if` / `else if` / `else` chain at the top of
`<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui`, and it had arms for the **context menu** and for **Settings** alone.
⚠️ **`input::resolve` is not a second guard**: it opens by asking `ctx.egui_wants_keyboard_input()`,
which is `focused().is_some()` rather than "a text field is taking characters" — and so **false** for
a modal holding three buttons and no text field. That `else if` was the whole of it.

Measured headless through `eframe::App::ui` with real `RawInput`, two passes per case:

| modal up | layer alive after `Delete` | undo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **none — the positive control** | **false** | 1 |
| `settings` — the one guarded arm | true | **0** |
| `confirming_close` | **false** | 1 |
| `recovery.pending` | **false** | 1 |

Under *Unsaved changes* the accidental deletion is what *Save and close* then writes to disk, which is
the one modal where walking away is not a way back. Under the crash-recovery card — drawn **above**
the view branch (D377), so it can be up over a freshly reopened document — the card blocks the
pointer, which makes the keyboard the only door, and it was open: `Ctrl+A` then `Delete` emptied a
document while the card was still asking about a *different* one's snapshot.

⚠️ **D330 is a live *Keep* whose body names this hole, issues no verdict for it, and whose stated
reason for leaving it alone was false.** Its keymap paragraph read *"the guard is in
`OndinApp::update`, which takes an `eframe::Frame` and is not reachable from a test even with
`OndinApp::headless` (D303, D269). The same hole exists in `close_confirmation` and is left alone
here."* Three things are wrong with that. There is **no `OndinApp::update`** — this workspace's
`impl eframe::App for OndinApp` has `fn ui` and nothing else. It **is** reachable from a test, by
`eframe::Frame::_new_kittest()` plus `ctx.run_ui`, which is exactly how
`escape_defers_a_recovery_and_never_deletes_it` already drove it, and **that test predates the
finding**. And the sentence names only one of the two uncovered modals: the recovery card is not in it
at all. D330's paragraph is amended in place and points here. *A verdict whose reason names a code
fact needs re-checking against the code* — the record's own claim of impossibility is what kept anyone
from writing the four-row test. ⚠️ **And the dead name had spread to four code comments**, none of
them about modals: `input.rs`'s and `canvas.rs`'s `took_tab` notes, `settings.rs`'s keymap note and
`dashboard.rs`'s `take_dropped_images` note all named `OndinApp::update` too. All four say
`<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui` as of 2026-09-07, corrected in the same commit as D468 — a method name
in prose is exactly the drift no gate reads (D319), and in D330's copy of it the name was doing the
arguing.

⚠️ **And the app's other key router already had all three.** §9.5 writes out `dashboard_keys`' guard
list (D374) and the recovery card is in it **by name**, with its own ⚠️ that `OndinApp::ui` draws that
card above the view branch and `dashboard.rs` knows nothing about it (D377). So the same question was
answered on the library screen and not on the editor's: `dashboard_keys` had to enumerate the modals
because it reads the context directly and knew it, while `OndinApp::ui` had `input::resolve` in front
of it and took the focus check for a guard it is not.

**The test carries both controls, and that is deliberate.** With **no** modal up the same harness must
*delete* the layer, or every green row is a harness that never delivered the key; and the `settings`
row is the arm that always worked, so what is left is a test about the two that did not. Two passes
per case, because egui resolves a modal against the stack the *previous* pass built. **Flipped** by
narrowing the arm back to `self.settings.is_some()`: fails on the `confirming_close` row, the layer
gone and `undo_depth` at 1. `app::library_wiring_tests::every_modal_owns_the_keyboard_not_only_settings`.

**What the *Fix* is for.** "A modal is up" is now written out twice — a three-term disjunction here
and a nine-modal one in `dashboard_keys`, the focus check beside it — and nothing makes a new modal
join either list. ⚠️ **There
is a third copy and it is already behind**: `shortcuts.md` §8a writes the dashboard's list out in
prose and names seven of the nine, missing *Edit project* and the recovery card — and §9.5's own copy
names eight, missing *Edit project*. *Fix with one predicate both routers ask*, which is the only
version of this that a prose copy cannot fall behind.

**D463 — A locked picture is neither croppable nor replaceable. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Fix —
two doors are shut and D321's own reason for leaving one of them open was false.***

`[S12.3-L2-01]` and `[S12.4-L2-01]`, and **the pair is the point.** D321 is a live *Keep* — *"a locked
group locks everything inside it, and the lock became one query the whole tree asks: text, points and
the picture all refuse"* — and its own list of what it closed is exact and stops at three **mode**
doors: `canvas::begin_edit_text`, `enter_action`'s `Path` arm, and `begin_image_edit`. So the app
refused to let you **crop** a locked picture through the menu and let you **replace it outright** with a
drop or `Ctrl+V`; and `edited_image`, which the crop *gesture* actually reads, refused nothing at all.

⚠️ **D321's stated reason for leaving `edited_image` unguarded is false**, and that is the record's half
of this. It says *"there is no analogous second door on image editing … `edited_image` needs no guard of
its own"*. The layers panel is that door **twice**: lock the row while image editing is armed —
`layers::RowHit::Lock` commits `SetLocked` with no mode check and nothing clears `self.tool`; or click a
**different**, locked picture's row — `select_from_row` calls `set_one` unconditionally and `choose_tool`
is not re-entered, which `app::image_tab`'s own doc states as a property (*"nothing has to clear this
when the selection changes"*). Neither route passes `begin_image_edit`, the one door that does check.
Measured headless: `edited_image` answered `Some((1:2, 0))` while `is_effectively_locked` answered
`true`, `crop_tx` built a 20-unit pan, `session.commit` returned `true`, and the fill landed at
`Crop, (0,0)–(0.75,1)`. Nothing refused and nothing said why.

**The drop needs no layers panel at all.** `toggle_locked` commits `SetLocked` and does **not** clear the
selection, so *select → lock → paste* is three ordinary acts. Measured headless on a locked rect: both
arms of `image_drop_target` answered `Some((1:2, 0))`, `SetFills` committed, `undo_depth` went 0 → 1,
and a solid fill became a picture — while `begin_edit_text`, the checking sibling door in the same file,
refused the identical node in the same probe. D183/D184 designed the drop/paste-replace mechanism in
detail and never mention the lock, so this is a door nobody exempted.

**Two guards, because neither closes the other**: a drop and a paste never enter image *editing*, so
they never ask `edited_image`'s question. Both sit on the **funnel** rather than on a door —
`edited_image` is the one query all readers of *"which image is being edited"* pass through, its
neighbour `edited_path` carrying its own guard twenty lines up for exactly that reason, and
`image_drop_target` is where both of `replace_image_fill`'s callers, `drop_images_at` and `paste_image`,
arrive. §5.5a's rule is what makes the first one obviously right: **a crop is a resize** —
`crop_resize_tx` writes through `tools::resize_layer` — so the lock reaches it exactly as it reaches its
neighbour.

**Flipped at each guard.** Removing `edited_image`'s fails on the crop assertion, with a `Some` for the
node it is supposed to refuse; removing `image_drop_target`'s fails on the drop assertion and leaves the
crop one green. The **control** — the same fixture unlocked, where both doors must answer `Some` — stays
green under both, which is what says these are guards and not a mode that stopped working.
`canvas::locked_picture_tests` holds all of it. `[S12.3-L2-01]` asked that nothing be found asserting a
locked layer's croppability before this landed; nothing does, and 998 `ondin-app` tests are green with
both guards in.

⚠️ **`edited_image`'s new comment names `edit_image_action` as "the one door that does check", and no
such function exists** — it is `app::begin_image_edit`, which is what D321 and §9.4 both name. A plain
`//` comment is precisely what no gate reads (D319 by a third road). *Fix the comment.*

**D462 — An inverted `Scrub` range is put the right way round rather than fatal. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the widget and its one document-fed caller are both closed.***

`[S18.1-L1-01]`. `f64::clamp`'s *"min > max, or either was NaN"* is an **unconditional** assert in
`core`, not a `debug_assert!`, and a panic inside `eframe`'s update closure takes the process down with
everything since the last `.recovery/` snapshot.

⚠️ **This is the only one of the forty-one `Scrub::range` call sites whose bound comes from the
document**, which is why an inverted range was reachable at all. `inspector.rs`'s *Scale* field for an
image fill in *Crop* built `floor..=10_000.0` from `ImageRef::cover_scale`, which is
`(fw / iw).max(fh / ih)` — frame world units over picture **pixels**, with no cap — so a **16×16 icon on
a 1920×1080 rectangle** gives a floor of 12 000 above a ceiling of 10 000. The `.max(0.01)` already on
that floor closes `clamp`'s NaN half and left the ordering half wide open. Measured twice in debug:
`settle` called directly, and end to end by driving a press and a 24 pt `PointerMoved` through
`ui::value_field`.

⚠️ **egui swaps where this app died**, which is why nothing upstream caught it:
`DragValue::clamp_value_to_range` opens by exchanging an inverted pair, so the widget rendered happily
and only this app's own re-clamp panicked. Two spellings of one rule, one of them fatal. Swapping in
`Scrub::range` makes the two agree.

**Both halves of `clamp`'s contract are closed, and the NaN half differently on purpose.** A `NaN` bound
**drops** the range rather than swapping it: `f64::min` answers the non-NaN operand, so swapping would
silently turn a single `NaN` bound into a both-ends-equal range and pin the field to one number. No
bound is the honest reading of a bound nobody can compare, and it is what the widget does with no
`.range(…)` at all.

**And the caller's half, which the finding left for a separate look.** The ceiling is `floor.max(10_000.0)`
now: cover is the floor **by design** — below it the crop would have to leave the source, where
`Extend::Pad` smears the edge row — so when cover is past 10 000% the honest ceiling is cover, not a
constant chosen for ordinary pictures. The widget must not panic; the panel must not ask for an empty
interval.

⚠️ **The finding's own suggested assertion contradicts its own fix sketch**, and following it would have
written a test the fix fails. It proposes *"`range(12_000.0..=10_000.0).settle(12_000.0)` asserting
`10_000.0`"* — which is what **clamping to the ceiling** would give — while the sketch beside it proposes
**swapping**, under which `12 000` is inside `10 000..=12 000` and stays. Swapping shipped, because it is
what egui does and the whole point is that the two agree.
`ui::scrub_tests::an_inverted_scrub_range_is_put_the_right_way_round_rather_than_fatal` therefore pins
the **interval** — floor, ceiling, and a value between — rather than one number that reads as either
answer.

**Flipped** by restoring `self.range = range`: panics inside `f64::clamp` with *"min > max, or either was
NaN. min = 12000, max = 10000"*. Driven end to end too, on both doors into `settle` — the prefix strip
and the `DragValue`.

**D461 — A nested boolean was previewed against its child's pre-drag outline. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the sort key is comparable between seeds now, and the fallback that hid it is
unchanged.***

`[S11.2-L1-02]`. `RenderOverrides::reevaluate_booleans` counted its sort key **upward from the seed**, so
a boolean nearer the root carried the *larger* number and `Reverse` evaluated the **outermost** first —
the opposite of the rule its own comment two lines above states (*"Deepest first: a nested boolean's
result is an operand of its parent's"*). Measured in release on `Subtract(Union(r1, r2), r3)`, dragging
`r2` — an operand of the **inner** union — 260 units right:

```text
outer committed BEFORE drag : x1 = 160
outer PREVIEWED during drag : x1 = 160     <- stale
inner PREVIEWED during drag : x1 = 360     <- correct
outer committed AFTER  drag : x1 = 360
```

The outer subtract sat at its pre-drag shape for the whole gesture and snapped into place on release.
**That is the exact report this function exists to answer**, quoted in its own doc — *"the boolean is
left behind and re-evaluates when I drop"* — still live one level of nesting up.

⚠️ **Silent, because the fallback is plausible.** With the outer evaluated first, `self.boolean` holds no
entry for the inner one yet, so the `nested:` closure falls through to `Resolved`'s **committed** cache —
a real path of the right shape, from before the gesture. §6.2's rule is that a missing preview is
recoverable and a lying one is not, and this is a lying one.

⚠️ **Reversing the old key alone would not have been the fix**, and this is the part worth recording. A
distance from *a* seed is not comparable **between** seeds: a multi-selection drag of two operands at
different tree depths ordered their booleans by an accident of which seed reached each first. The key is
the node's own **depth from the root** now — one scale for the whole document, so it composes — and the
`Reverse` sort is unchanged.

⚠️ **This function had no nested-boolean test at all, and the one that looks like it is not one.**
`a_ghost_evaluates_a_boolean_inside_a_boolean` seeds from `g.parent`, which is the root and not a
boolean, so `affected` comes back empty and what it exercises is `build_ghost`'s own children-first
recursion. Confirmed by breaking the sort and watching that test stay green.

**Flipped** by restoring the seed-relative key: fails inside `assert_preview_matches_commit` at the outer
boolean's path, the preview drawing **one merged subpath** where the commit draws two disjoint ones. The
**control** — dragging an operand of the *outer* boolean, where `affected` holds one entry and no
ordering decision is made — stays green under the flip, which is what says the ordering is the cause and
not the seeding. Both halves live in
`overrides::dragging_an_operand_of_a_nested_boolean_previews_the_outer_one_too`.

**D460 — A mask group's box is the box it clips with, and it was a tenth of it. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the readers agree now, and there are four hand-written copies of the rule they agree
about.***

`[S4.1-L2-01]`. `Resolved::mask_path`'s `Group | Root` arm skips a mask **inside** a mask group and
unions the rest **un-narrowed** — deliberately, and its own comment says why: the exact answer needs a
path *intersection*, and *"a clip that is too generous"* is the safe direction. All three bounds
computations did the opposite: they applied the inner mask. Measured in release on a group `M` marked
*Use as mask*, holding a 40×40 rect also marked *Use as mask* under a 400×400 one:

```text
mask_path(M).bbox = 0,0 .. 400,400   <- what actually clips, and what hit_test asks
world_bounds(M)   = 0,0 ..  40,40    <- what clipped the box of every sibling above it
```

⚠️ **The consequence is a layer that is on screen and clickable and is not painted.**
`scene::paint_node` sets `bounds_cover_subtree` for a `Group` and returns early when `ink_bounds`
misses the view, so the container's whole subtree was pruned on a box a tenth of the clip its own
children draw under. Driven through the real walk with a recording painter: **1** fill with the page
in view, **0** scrolled onto the artwork, **1** for the same group with no inner mask. Panning brings
it back, which is the shape of report this arrives as. Everything else reading the container's box was
wrong by the same 10× — *zoom to selection*, the selection outline, the marquee, the inspector's W/H,
and `ondin_export::plan`'s exported region.

**Two *Use as mask* commands on shapes assembled by hand.** `NodeKind::can_mask` names `Group`
explicitly and a mask built inside a group is the ordinary way to build one, so there is no import and
no hostile input anywhere near this.

**The fix is one function, `resolve::mask_extent`, called from every site that narrows a box by a
mask** — `recompute_bounds`' box scan and its ink twin, `resolve_subtree`'s loop for both maps, and
`query::local_box`, which works in the node's own space throughout and so has a local twin,
`mask_extent_local`, rather than an inverse per child. It is **arm for arm with `mask_path`**: a
`Group | Root` filters its mask children out and unions the rest, an invisible node answers `None`,
and every other kind is its own measured box. That is what makes it right rather than merely
different, and it is what stops the rule drifting from the clip again. It reads only child boxes that
are already fresh — in the full pass because the child's whole subtree has been resolved, in the
incremental one because a node outside the dirty set keeps a box that is still valid — and costs a
walk of the mask's subtree, once per mask. `Document::governing_mask`'s own instruction, *"fix a
disagreement by correcting the forward reader, not by routing it through here"*, is what this follows:
one of the two spellings of *what does a mask group clip with* had to give, and the clip is the one
three other readers already agree on (`scene::mask_geometry`, the SVG writer's `MaskMode::Shape` arm,
`hit_test`).

⚠️ **`incremental_update_equals_rebuild_over_random_ops` already generates `SetMask` and did not catch
this, because both passes were wrong in the same way.** It guards the change and was never going to
find the defect. Worth stating plainly, because the property reads like coverage of the rule: **a
differential between two implementations of one rule is silent about the rule.**

⚠️ **Flipped at each pass separately, and the predicted site was wrong.** The guess was that both
flips would fail on `world_bounds(G)`:

- **`resolve_subtree` reverted** — the full pass, which is all `rebuild` runs for a tree with no
  booleans in it: fails on `world_bounds(G)` at 40×40 against 400×400, **and** the render half fails
  at 0 fills against 1.
- **`recompute_bounds` reverted** — the incremental pass: `rebuild` is **still right**, so
  `world_bounds(G)` passes and the render half stays green. It fails only on the
  `update`-equals-`rebuild` assertion. **Without that assertion the flip would not have bitten at
  all**, and `update` would have silently disagreed with `rebuild` the first time anything inside the
  mask group was edited.

The two halves live in `resolve::a_mask_group_that_masks_internally_still_clips_with_its_whole_union`
and `render::a_group_masked_by_a_group_that_masks_internally_is_not_culled_away`, each with the same
control — the same tree with the inner mask flag off, which was never affected.

This reads with **D456**: both are *a second reader of the mask rule disagreeing with the clip*, that
one at the hit test and this one at the boxes. §5.9's *"a masked layer keeps its own world bounds; its
container gets only what the mask lets through"* is still true and is now true of the right box. **The
verdict is about what is left**: *what a mask group clips with* is spelled in four places that have to
be kept arm for arm, and a fifth reader will be written the way these four were — *fix with one
statement of it*.

**D459 — A gradient's payload is bounded, and it is the third quantity the importer bounds. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-07; Fix — the payload is bounded and the quadratic beneath it is not.***

`[S7.2-L5-02]`. Every shape naming a gradient got its **own** copy of the whole stop list — and not a
transient one: the copies are in the `Vec<Operation>` the paste applies, so they end up in the
`Document`, then in the JSON `io::save` writes. *S* stops × *K* shapes × 24 bytes, exactly quadratic,
and `size_of::<peniko::ColorStop>()` is 24, so that is a size rather than an estimate.

⚠️ **Neither existing bound sees it, and that is the point of the entry.** `roxmltree`'s `nodes_limit`
bounds the **XML** at 500,000 nodes: the finding's 452 KB fixture is 12,001 elements, 2.4% of its
budget, and the limit as written permits 250,000 × 250,000. D446's `MAX_SVG_NODES` bounds what is
**emitted**, which here is unremarkable — 6,001 emitted nodes against a budget of 50,000 leaves the
file entirely intact. **What explodes is the payload *per* node**, a third quantity, and
`MAX_GRADIENT_STOPS = 256` is its only bound.

**Resampled rather than truncated or refused.** Truncating keeps the first 256 and compresses the
whole ramp into the front of its range — a visibly different drawing; refusing loses the paint
entirely. An even spread keeps the ramp's shape, and at this cap a gradient has a stop every 0.4% of
its length, below what any renderer resolves — so a file that hits it is a generated one. **Reported
once for the file** as `approximated` — *there and slightly wrong*, which is `approximate`'s half of
the pair rather than `skip`'s — immediately after the existing `style (complex selector)` line, whose
comment already argues for reporting once about the file rather than once per element. That closes the
finding's G12 half.

**Measured before and after under the same flip**, timing `import` alone in release on the finding's
own *S* stops × *S* rects fixture, with a solid-fill control at the same shape count:

| S | source | import, before | after | control | stops held, before → after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 000 | 104 KB | 9.6 ms | 3.9 ms | 1.2 ms | 22 MB → 5 MB |
| 2 000 | 210 KB | 34.1 ms | 7.0 ms | 2.5 ms | 91 MB → 11 MB |
| 4 000 | 421 KB | 127 ms | 13.8 ms | 5.0 ms | 366 MB → 23 MB |
| 6 000 | 633 KB | **284 ms** | **20.9 ms** | 7.6 ms | **823 MB → 35 MB** |

The "before" column reproduces the finding's own numbers (9.4 / 35.0 / 133 / 288 ms), so the two
halves of the table are one machine's rather than two. **What changed is the shape**: ×4 per doubling
becomes ×2, matching the control.

⚠️ **And the fixture measured something else without meaning to.** Run through `Document::apply`
rather than `import` alone, the **solid-fill control** is itself quadratic: 53 / 206 / 826 / 1,869 ms
at the same four sizes, within 5% of the gradient case. That is the `Document::apply` Θ(n²) D446 named
as outranking both of its own halves — `op_create` resolving an unnamed node's name through
`child_names(parent, &[])`, a scan of every sibling — **confirmed here by a control that has no
gradient in it at all**. It is also why the test asserts stop *counts* rather than a wall clock: a
timing bound over the pair would be asserting on that instead. It remains unfixed, is open in
`roadmap.md`, and is the strongest candidate for a future session.

⚠️ **Flipped** by deleting the resample block: `a_gradients_stop_list_is_bounded_and_says_so` fails on
the stop-count assertion, 600 against 256. The control — a 64-stop gradient, kept exactly, with
nothing reported — stays green under the flip, which is what says the cap is a bound on generated
files rather than a tax on ordinary ones.

⚠️ **The finding's own sketch offered a second half, (b) share rather than copy** — an `Arc` behind the
importer's private `Style`/`Paint` — and it is recorded here as *not the fix*. It removes the
importer's three intermediate copies and leaves the final one per `Fill`, which is the one that
reaches the `Document` and the saved file. The quadratic is in the model, so only a cap bounds it.

⚠️ **Three of the comments this change added cite `MAX_SVG_NODES` as D447**, which is
`reset_transient_state` clearing `per_corner_radius`; the width bound is **D446** — the constant's own
doc, the resample block and the test's doc all say the wrong one. *Fix the comments.*

**D458 — An alpha mask's region is written in the space the mask is referenced in. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the element is closed and the class it belongs to is not.***

`[S8.1-L1-01]`. `<mask>` was emitted with `maskUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` and **no**
`x`/`y`/`width`/`height`. SVG's defaults for those four are `-10%`, `-10%`, `120%`, `120%`, and under
`userSpaceOnUse` a percentage is a fraction of the **viewport** read as a length in the *current* user
space — which for
a mask inside a transformed `<g>` is that group's local space, not the page. Everything outside the
region is mask value 0, i.e. erased.

Measured in Chrome over HTTP (`.claude/launch.json`'s `probe-static`), on a 400×400 artboard holding a
group with an alpha mask and a coincident red rectangle, which the canvas draws whole in every case:

| the group's transform | opaque to |
| --- | --- |
| identity | x = 399 |
| `scale(0.5)` | **x = 219** |
| `scale(0.1)` | **x = 43** |
| `translate(-1000)`, children at local `+1000` | **nothing at all** |

The three numbers are exactly `1.1 × 400 × scale`, which pins the mechanism rather than merely
observing a loss. **The last row costs everything**: a group whose children sit past 110% of the
viewport *in the group's own coordinates* loses its masked artwork entirely, at any scale — and the
file still opens, still validates, and still looks deliberate.

**The region is the mask's own ink box, mapped into this node's local space and inflated a tenth**
(`Resolved::ink_bounds` of the mask, through the inverse of the referencing node's world transform).
The mask's own box rather than the run's, and that is the load-bearing reasoning: outside it the mask
draws nothing, so its value is 0 there whatever the region says — an infinite region and this one give
the same picture, so the smaller one is free. Inflated by a tenth, which is SVG's own margin computed
in the space that was meant. A region too large is inert, and §5.9's rule about these bounds is that
too small is the one error they may not make. A mask with no ink at all keeps the **absent** region,
since it erases the run wherever it is evaluated and a degenerate region would only be a second way of
saying so.

**`<clipPath>` has no region, so `MaskMode::Shape` is untouched.** `<mask>` is the **third
region-bearing element this writer emits and was the only one written without one**: `effect_def`
writes `filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` with explicit `x`/`y`/`width`/`height` out of `effect_region`,
and `adjust_def` writes `x="0" y="0" width="1" height="1"` with a doc comment saying why. §7 of
`architecture.md` states the same `-10%,-10%,120%,120%` default verbatim for the filter case — *"which
crops any real shadow"* — which is the sentence `<mask>` needed and did not have. That is what the
verdict is about: the trap was written down for one element and nothing carried it to the second one
with the same default. *Fix with one place that computes a region for every element that takes one*,
or the fourth will be written without one too.

⚠️ **Confirmed in a real browser rather than only in markup**, which is D394's third amendment's whole
lesson — both sides of a hand-written fixture agree about what SVG looks like. Both writers' output for
the `translate(-1000)` fixture — a 400×400 red rect masked by a 300-diameter white ellipse — served
over `probe-static` and counted off a canvas in Chrome:

| writer | red pixels | rightmost red |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | **0** | — |
| after | 70 456 | x = 349 |

π·150² is 70 686 and the ellipse spans page x = 50…350, so both numbers are the drawing. **Zero is the
whole finding.**

**Flipped** by deleting the `region` interpolation from the `writeln!`, in
`an_alpha_masks_region_is_written_in_the_space_it_is_referenced_in`: it fails on the **absence** of a
`width` attribute rather than on a number, which is the state the finding measured. ⚠️ **The test asserts the region *contains the
mask's ink*, not a literal**, because a writer that produced the right numbers by coincidence in one
fixture would otherwise pass; its second assertion is that `x > 400`, since a region computed against
the viewport would sit near the origin and this one must sit near 1000. The `translate` row is the
fixture rather than one of the `scale` rows for the same reason — it is the case a *scale*-shaped fix
would miss.

**D457 — A thin concave boolean result is a shape, and it used to be deleted. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Resolved — this defect is closed, and so, since 2026-09-19, is the second one the control
turned up (D794).***

`[S10.1-L1-01]`. `representative_point` walked an **8×8 grid** over the subpath's own bounding box, so
a subpath thinner than about one eighth of that box fell through all 49 probes — and `from_flo` read
the resulting `None` as `else { continue; }`, i.e. *skip this subpath*. **The answer was not a bad
winding but a missing shape.** Measured in release against a sampled referee, on two fixtures neither
of which is contrived:

- a **crescent moon** — an r = 200 circle minus the same circle nudged 5 sideways, true area
  2 000.26 — came back **`None`**; the boolean drew nothing at all;
- a **bracket** — a 400×400 square minus a 10-unit L-shaped notch, true net area 156 100 — came back
  at **160 000**, the square's full area, the notch simply gone.

**Both silent.** Nothing panicked, so `failures()` did not move, `resolve::reevaluate_boolean` took the
`failures() == before` arm and cleared the node from `failed`, the layers row wore no mark and the
status bar said nothing (D298). That is exactly the mode D239's third amendment names: *"the boolean
draws, nothing is marked, `failures` does not move, and the shape is simply wrong."* The test asserts
`failures()` does not move, as the standing record of why the defect was invisible rather than as a
claim about the counter.

**Two changes, and they do different work.** `representative_point`'s fallback is now a **scan line**:
intersect a horizontal ray with every segment, sort the crossings, take the midpoint of the first span
that `contains` confirms. That is exact for a closed curve of any thickness, because the span it
returns is bounded by the subpath's own edges and so cannot be thinner than the shape is. Fifteen
heights rather than one, since a single line can hit a tangency or an hourglass's pinch; and `contains`
per span rather than trusting the parity of the crossing count, which a tangency (two roots at one x)
or a shared endpoint (one root from each of two segments) breaks. And `from_flo` now **keeps** a
subpath it cannot locate an interior point for instead of dropping it: losing the winding correction is
a hole that fills solid, losing the geometry is a shape that is not there, and the first is strictly
better.

⚠️ **A wider grid is not the fix, and the similarity sweep is what says so.** The grid was *relative*
to the bounding box, so the failure was scale-invariant: geometrically similar crescents (offset =
r/40) vanished at r = 10, 20, 40, 80 and 200 alike. That is also the control separating this from an
`ACCURACY` (0.01) tolerance problem, which would appear only at small radii. Any `STEPS` merely has a
thinner crescent, and a fix that raised it passes both area assertions and fails the sweep.

⚠️ **Flipped in all three combinations, and the predicted site was wrong once.**

- **Both reverted** — the state the finding measured: fails on the very first line,
  `expect("a crescent is a shape, not nothing")`.
- **Scan line reverted, the `else` branch kept**: the crescent **passes** — its geometry survives even
  with no interior point found — and the failure moves to the **notch**, at **163 900** against
  156 100. That is the winding half on its own: the hole is kept and not reversed, so under non-zero it
  fills solid. *The crescent assertion was the predicted site and it is not this one*; the notch is
  what separates "kept" from "kept and wound correctly".
- **`else` branch reverted, the scan line kept**: **every assertion green.** Not a failed experiment —
  it says the scan line is the load-bearing half today and the `else` branch is a belt with nothing
  currently behind it. Kept anyway, because *"I could not measure the nesting"* must never again mean
  *"delete this part of the shape"*, and because nothing in the module guarantees the scan line always
  succeeds.

The module's two existing guards — `a_hole_is_wound_against_the_outline_that_contains_it` and
`exclude_agrees_with_odd_coverage_at_every_sample_point` — both stay green, which is what says the
winding pass still means the same thing.

⚠️ **A separate defect turned up while writing the convex control, and it is not this one.** The
control is an `Intersect` producing a thin sliver *rect*, which was always right because a convex
subpath's bounding-box centre is inside it and the fallback never ran. Swept at four thicknesses in
release, `Intersect` of a 400-wide slot with a 400×200 rect:

| slot thickness | true area | `evaluate` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.01 | 4 | **2** |
| 0.1 | 40 | 40.0 |
| 1 | 400 | 400.0 |
| 10 | 4 000 | 4 000.0 |

So an `Intersect` result under about 0.1 units thick loses **half its area**, sharply rather than
gradually, in a shape with **no concavity and no hole** — which is neither `representative_point`'s
doing nor `from_flo`'s. `[S10.1-L1-01]` recorded that 2.0 as *"correctly, area 2.0"*, so **the
finding's own control was wrong about it**; the test's control moved to 0.1 so that it controls for
what it is meant to, which left nothing asserting the sliver at all. **Attributed and fixed on
2026-09-19 — a tolerance inside flo_curves that no argument reaches, D794** — and the control here
stays at 0.1 rather than being lowered back, because it is the *convex* case for this entry's
fallback and D794's own test is what covers the thin one.

**D794 — A thin `Intersect` lost exactly half its area to a tolerance no argument reaches, and the
fix is a scale as well as a tolerance. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — and `ACCURACY`'s own
doc is one of the things the fix had to contradict.***

D457's convex control turned this up as a by-product and could not attribute it: an `Intersect`
result thinner than about 0.1 world units comes back with **exactly half** the area it is owed,
sharply rather than gradually, in a shape with no concavity and no hole. It sat in `roadmap.md` from
2026-09-07 asserted by nothing, because the moment the control moved to a 0.1 slot — so that it
controlled for what it was meant to — the only case that exercised it was gone.

**The attribution is the entry.** flo_curves compiles in absolute tolerances of its own that no
argument reaches: `consts.rs` carries `CLOSE_DISTANCE = 0.01` and `SMALL_DISTANCE = 0.001`, and
`GraphPath` merges any two points closer than `CLOSE_DISTANCE` into one. A thin `Intersect` result's
two **short** ends are each exactly the result's thickness, so at or below a hundredth of a unit they
are not approximated — they are *erased*, which pinches the rectangle into a bow-tie, and a bow-tie is
two triangles, which is exactly half. Below `SMALL_DISTANCE` the whole result comes back `None`. The
element dump is the direct evidence rather than an inference from the area: the correct result has
**6** path elements — a move, four sides and a close — and the defective one has **4**, the two
collapsed ends leaving no edge behind at all.

**Neither lever works alone, which is the whole shape of the bug**, and the matrix was measured rather
than reasoned, on a 400-wide slot against a 400×200 rect:

| scale | handed to flo_curves | in world units | thin `Intersect` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.01 | 0.01 | **half** — the defect as found |
| 1 | 0.0001 | 0.0001 | **half**, bit-identical to the row above |
| 1000 | 10.0 | 0.01 | **half** |
| 1000 | 0.01 | 0.00001 | exact, down to a thickness of 10⁻⁴ |

The second row is the control that clears our own `ACCURACY`: taking it a hundred times finer changed
not one digit, because the constant doing the erasing is not one we pass. The third is the control
that clears scaling on its own: scale the geometry and scale the tolerance with it and nothing moves,
because the tolerance is once again the size of the feature. 🚨 **`roadmap.md`'s guess that
flo_curves' `ACCURACY` (0.01) was "the first place to look" was half right in the way that would have
stalled a reader there** — the tolerance is load-bearing, but only in combination, and the constant
actually deleting the edges cannot be reached from this crate at all.

**The fix is two constants and one seam.** `FLO_SCALE: f64 = 1000.0` is applied in `c()` and `k()`,
the only two coordinate-conversion functions in the module, so those two are the whole boundary —
⚠️ **a third conversion path, or any coordinate handed to flo_curves without going through them,
reintroduces this**, and nothing in the code can say so. `FLO_ACCURACY: f64 = 0.01` replaces
`ACCURACY` at the four flo_curves call sites in `combine()` — `path_add`, `path_sub`,
`path_intersect`, `path_full_intersect` — and is read in flo_curves' *scaled* space, so it is 10⁻⁵ of
a world unit.

🚨 **It contradicts a written rule, and the rule has been amended rather than left standing.**
`ACCURACY`'s doc opened *"Accuracy handed to every boolean, in world units"*, which is now false:
`FLO_ACCURACY` is what is handed. Its argument that 0.01 is *"finer than any pixel the canvas shows
below 100× zoom"* is true and is an argument about **rendering**, and this failure is not about
rendering — a tolerance the size of the feature does not draw it coarsely, it *deletes* it. What is
untouched is that doc's other half, the *"a constant, not a parameter"* reasoning: `FLO_SCALE` is a
fixed factor, not derived from the shapes or from the camera, so the same two shapes still combine to
the same path wherever they sit and at whatever zoom, which is the property that made the constant a
constant in the first place. §9.4 carried its own copy of the tolerance sentence and now states the
scaling seam instead.

**`ACCURACY` is now `#[cfg(test)]`.** No production line reads it, and making the compiler enforce
that was preferred to `#[allow(dead_code)]`, which is D672's direction — an allow-listed item is a
live root, and the claim worth having here is the one a gate can fail. It is kept rather than deleted
because three assertions in the module's own tests read it and because D457 and D614 both name it. The
cost is D319's and D699's: a production doc may no longer *link* a test-only item, so `FLO_SCALE` and
`FLO_ACCURACY` explain themselves by contrast with it in **plain backticks** with a sentence saying
why — a link the doc gate cannot resolve is a link it cannot check, and the gate exits 101 on one it
can see through.

**Cost: none measurable**, which mattered because a tolerance three orders finer could have bought
three orders more subdivision on exactly the path D614 is about. Timed in release against D614's own
fixture — N disjoint 20×20 rects folded as a `Union` — **0.37 / 1.00 / 2.61 / 7.33 ms** at N = 16, 64,
128, 256 against a baseline of **0.40 / 1.14 / 2.51 / 7.17**: inside the run-to-run spread at every
size, in both directions, with identical subpath counts.

`a_thin_intersect_keeps_its_area` sweeps thicknesses 1.0, 0.1, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001 and 0.0001,
asserting the area within 1%; asserts the result has **6** elements, because the bow-tie had 4 and an
area assertion alone would pass against any shape of the right size; and asserts `failures()` does not
move, since this loss is silent in D298's sense — exactly the mode D239's third amendment names, *"the
boolean draws, nothing is marked, `failures` does not move, and the shape is simply wrong"* — so the
counter cannot be what reports it.

⚠️ **Flipped both ways, and each flip alone reproduces the defect.** `FLO_SCALE` → 1.0 fails at
t = 0.01 with area 2 against 4. `FLO_ACCURACY` → `ACCURACY * FLO_SCALE`, i.e. 10.0 — the spelling that
*looks* obviously right, because it keeps the tolerance meaning a hundredth of a **world** unit —
fails at the same thickness with area 2.0000000208. 🚨 **That second flip is not hypothetical: the fix
was written that way first and this test is what caught it**, so it shipped for exactly one
`cargo test`. The predicted failing *site* was right and the prediction under it was wrong: every
thickness below 0.01 fails too, and 0.0001 fails at the `unwrap_or_else` as `None` rather than at the
area assertion — **a sweep that stopped at 0.005 would have reported a halving where the answer is an
erasure.**

⚠️ **The finding's control had the wrong expected value in it, and that is why this went unreported
for twelve days.** `[S10.1-L1-01]` wrote its convex control down as *"an `Intersect` producing a
400 × 0.01 sliver rect comes back correctly (area 2.0)"* — the true area is 4. The same finding argued,
correctly, that the crescent's scale-*invariance* ruled a tolerance problem out; the counter-example — an
absolute-scale defect that appears only below a hundredth of a unit — was in the very next bullet, with
its answer written in as correct. **A control is only as good as the number it expects**,
and nothing anywhere — not a gate, not a test, not a second reader — compares a finding's expected
value against arithmetic.

**D456 — A mask is not a rail, and neither is ink it has clipped away. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07;
Fix — three roles have reached this builder as ordinary kinds and there are three guards between
them.***

`[S4.1-L1-02]`. `query::outline_at` asked two of `hit_test`'s three questions and not the third, so the
**same two clicks answered differently through the two doors** — and the Text tool acts on this one.
Measured in release on the suite's own `mask_fixture`: an artboard holding a group whose children are,
bottom-first, a 50×50 rect marked *Use as mask* and a 500×400 rect.

Clicking the **mask's** edge, `hit_test` answered the artboard and `outline_at` answered the mask, so
the rail affordance lit up on a layer that paints nothing. `build::text_on_new_path` then **deleted**
it, the mask flag did **not** travel to the `Text` that replaced it, and the group's bounds went
`50×50` → `-11,-11..500,400` — the artwork it was hiding fully visible, with the status line saying
*"Type along the path; the shape became the rail"*. `Ctrl+Z` was the only way back and nothing said so.
Clicking the masked rect's edge out in the **clipped-away** region, where the canvas shows nothing at
all, `outline_at` answered the rect where `hit_test` answered the artboard.

**Two guards.** `outline_at` asks `masked_away` — the same function `hit_test` asks, whose own doc
already states both halves (*"a mask is never hit"*, *"masked content is hit only inside its mask"*) —
placed **behind** `is_effectively_interactable` and behind the kind and boolean-ancestor skips, because
it walks the ancestor chain and asks `mask_path`, the most expensive question in a loop that runs over
every candidate outline on every frame the Text or Pen tool is in hand. And `build::text_on_new_path`
refuses a node whose `mask` flag is set, the belt to those braces, for the MCP write surface and the
command line.

⚠️ **This is the sentence the entry is really for: D408's exclusion list is about *kinds*, and the
property that governs is a node's ROLE.** An operand, a mask, and ink a mask has clipped away are all
ordinary kinds that are not artwork on the page. A mask is an ordinary `Rect` — `resolve::is_indexed`
says so and `build_index` filters on nothing else — and it *must* be visible and unlocked to mask at
all, so `is_effectively_interactable` passes it too. Nothing in a kind-shaped rule could have caught
it. **This is the third role in a row to reach `text_on_new_path` as an ordinary kind** — D453's
boolean operand, D453's amendment's frame, and now the mask — and that is what the verdict is about:
three roles, three guards, and no single question asking whether the thing about to be consumed is
artwork on the page. *Fix with one such question*, asked at both doors, or the fourth role will be
found the way the first three were.

⚠️ **And D408's *"both doors agree"* is still not true in general.** The two doors agree about masks
and about clipped-away ink from here on; they deliberately **disagree** about a boolean's operands,
because `hit_test` is supposed to return one and resolve it through `group_chain` (D453). Both
`outline_at`'s prose and D408's own passage now read as two separate claims — D408's was amended
rather than left to be corrected from here, which is what D453 had to settle for.

**Flipped at each guard with the other in place.** Removing `outline_at`'s `masked_away` call: fails on
the first assertion, answering the mask. Removing `text_on_new_path`'s refusal: fails on the
`expect_err`, and what it prints is the defect in one line — `CreateNode { parent: <the group>, kind:
Text { … on_path: Some(the mask's own 50×50 outline) } }` followed by `DeleteNode { <the mask> }`, with
no mask flag anywhere on the node that replaces it. Both live in
`a_mask_is_not_a_rail_and_neither_is_ink_it_has_clipped_away`, with two controls that stay green under
either flip: the masked layer's own edge *inside* the mask is still offered, and with the flag off the
mask is an ordinary rect and an ordinary rail.

⚠️ **Worth recording as a fixture lesson.** The test's first draft aimed at the mask's *left* edge and
failed for the wrong reason, answering the masked rect — the mask's left and top edges lie exactly on
the 500×400 rect's, and that rect's edge *is* legitimately offered from inside the mask. A point that
asks two questions answers neither; the right edge asks one.

**D455 — A descending gradient ramp is not a wrong picture, it is no picture. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — both doors clamp and a document already on disk still exports the ramp it no longer
draws.***

`[S11.1-L1-02]`, and it settles the hand-off S7.2 made. That pass measured the **model** —
`<stop offset="0"/><stop offset="0.8"/><stop offset="0.2"/><stop offset="1"/>` imports as
`[0, 0.8, 0.2, 1]`, where SVG requires each offset to be clamped up to the running maximum — and could
not measure the picture. **The picture is a flat fill of the first stop's colour in all 100 columns**:
the ramp does not merely differ from what the file means, it disappears. Measured in release through
`VelloCpuRenderer` on a 100×20 rect, 100 of 100 columns wrong. **A descent of one part in ten million
does it** — `[0, 0.5, 0.4999999, 1]` is flat where `[0, 0.5, 0.5, 1]` is not — and *equal* offsets,
which is exactly what SVG's clamp produces, were always fine. That last fact is what makes the fix
safe: what it writes is the one shape this backend has never had trouble with.

**One rule, `ondin_core::image::make_stops_monotonic`, at two doors that do not cover each other.**
`svg_in::Gradients::collect` applies it so the **model** says what the file means — a re-export
round-trips, and the paint editor and the layers panel read the right ramp. `color::brush_to_backend`
applies it so a **hand-edited `.ondin`**, and every file imported before today, draws correctly; that
is the single conversion site the module's own doc already argues for, and neither backend normalises
(`gpu.rs` and `cpu.rs` both take the resolved brush verbatim), so it is the last place the rule can be
stated once for both. It is free there, the gradient having been cloned anyway.

**It is a clamp and not a sort, and `panels::paint::with_stops` keeps its `sort_by`.** Dragging a stop
handle past its neighbour means *"put it there"*; a file that says `0.2` after `0.8` is a file to be
read, not an intention to be guessed at. The two disagree on exactly this input — a clamp gives
`[0, 0.8, 0.8, 1]`, the third stop collapsing onto the second, and a sort gives `[0, 0.2, 0.8, 1]`, the
third stop moving — and **before this, the two rules plus the raw list gave one document three
renderings** depending on the route taken to it: import it, render it, or touch a colour and render it
again.

Two implementation details worth recording. The running maximum starts at **0**, not at the first
stop's own offset, because a ramp is defined on `0..=1` and both authoring doors already say so
(`svg_in::stop_of` clamps to `0.0..1.0`, `with_stops` clamps each stop it writes) — so a negative
offset reaches it only from a hand-edited file, where *"at the start"* is the honest reading. And `NaN`
is `max`ed away rather than propagated, `f32::max` answering the non-NaN operand, so a NaN offset takes
the running maximum; it should never arrive, since `build::brush_is_finite` refuses one at the op
boundary (D451), and the render path is not the place to find out.

**Flipped per door, and the pair of results is what says there are two.** Removing the render guard:
the pixel test (`ondin-export/tests/png.rs ·
a_gradient_with_descending_stops_draws_the_ramp_svg_says_it_means`) fails at **column 0**,
`(255, 0, 0)` against the ramp's `(253, 2, 0)` — column 0 rather than somewhere in the middle, which is
worth knowing: the flat fill is the *first stop's* colour, so it agrees with the correct ramp nowhere
at all, not even where the ramp starts. Removing the import guard: the model test
(`ondin-core/src/svg_in.rs · a_descending_stop_list_is_clamped_up_on_import`) fails on stop 2, `0.2`
against `0.8`, and
**the pixel test stays green**, because the render guard is downstream of it.

⚠️ **The *Fix* is for the document that is already on disk, and it is this entry's own "three
renderings" surviving in one place.** Nothing clamps on load, so a hand-edited `.ondin` — or any file
imported before today — keeps its descending list in the model. The canvas and a PNG export are right,
both going through `brush_to_backend`; `ondin-export::svg::gradient_def` wrote `g.stops` verbatim, so
an **SVG** export of that same document handed a browser the ramp the app had just drawn correctly and
the browser drew it flat. And `with_stops` sorts what it writes, so touching one colour of that
gradient commits the third picture. *Fix at the third door* — `io::load`, which is how such a document
reaches the model — or at the operation, where invariant 8's family put every other check of what a
brush may hold (D451). That is the same choice D448 and D451 had, and it is a decision rather than an
oversight.

⚠️ **The SVG door is shut, and the residue is narrower than the paragraph above describes.** Closed
2026-09-07 in the same commit as D458: `gradient_def` clamps a copy through `make_stops_monotonic`
before writing its `<stop>` list. **Clamped at the writer rather than at `io::load`**, because *what
does this file mean* is the writer's own question and the answer is SVG's, which is where the rule came
from — the model is untouched, and `an_svg_export_clamps_a_descending_ramp_the_model_still_holds`
asserts exactly that, a document not changing because it was exported. Its fixture has to bypass the
importer, writing the stops straight onto a `GradientBrush` and committing them with `SetFills`, or it
is testing the first door over again; flipped by writing `g.stops` again, it fails on the third offset,
`0.2` against `0.8`. **What survives is the load door alone**, and the *Fix* stands for it: nothing
clamps on the way in, so `panels::paint::with_stops`' sort still commits the third picture the moment a
user touches one colour of such a gradient, and the layers panel and the paint editor read the raw
list. That is one route rather than two, and the choice for closing it is the one the paragraph above
names.

Relate this to **D412**, the gradient transform `brush_to_backend` resolves in the same arm, and to
**D448**/**D451**, the finiteness family that reaches this same stop list from another direction. The
