group labels the review gave it are **G8**, the same decision in three places with the copies
disagreeing, and **G12**, both `Import` report lists coming back empty so nothing tells the user.

**D454 — An out-of-range blur is a wrong picture, not a hang and not a panic. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Fix — the render half is closed and the operation still accepts the number.***

`[S10.1-L1-03]` and `[S10.2-L1-03]`. The input is one SVG attribute. `<feDropShadow
stdDeviation="1e30">` imports with `Import::skipped` and `Import::approximated` **both empty**, lands
`Shadow { blur: 2e30 }` in the model, and `io::load(io::save(doc))` is `Ok`. So it is on disk, in the
library, and `library::cover::rasterize` renders every document in the base folder to draw the
dashboard — **one such file hangs the app at launch**, before anybody has opened anything.

**One defect with two unbounded sites, and they had to be fixed together.** `[S10.1-L1-03]`'s own fix
sketch was to cap the block factor; `[S10.2-L1-03]` refuted it — *"a cap on `k` alone leaves the
failure in place and only changes which line it happens on"*. Both halves of that refutation are
measured now rather than argued, which is the reason this entry carries numbers at all.

**`effect::MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK = 4096`.** `shadow_downscale`'s `k.ceil() as u32` **saturated**, so σ/k —
the one thing that function promises — went 24.0 → 46.6 → 2.33e20 above σ ≈ 1.03e11, the contract
broken by the cast that was meant to deliver it. `render::effects::coarsen` is Θ(k) regardless of the
surface it walks: measured in release on a 200×220 surface, 184 µs at k = 4096, 2.76 ms at 65 536,
44.3 ms at 1 048 576, and ≈180 s at `u32::MAX`, which is why the finding's two 100-second kills saw no
return. 🚨 **That is the loop D743 replaced, so the four figures above are historical from
2026-09-10**: both of `coarsen`'s loops stop at the **source** now, and the pass costs `w·h` however
large `k` is. What `MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK` still buys is the cast in the next sentence — above `i32::MAX`
it wraps negative and the GPU draws no shadow at all — so **the cost half of the argument for this cap
is D743's**, and this half is now about correctness. The degenerate arm was wrong in the other
direction as well: `if k.is_finite() && k >= 2.0 {
… } else { 1 }` answered `1` — *"blur it as authored"* — for σ = `inf`, the single input where no
downscale at all is certainly wrong. It answers the cap now; `NaN` and the negatives answer 1. And the
cap is what makes `fx_gpu`'s `Params { radius: k as i32 }` safe, where above `i32::MAX` (σ ≈ 5.2e10)
the cast wrapped **negative**, `fx.wgsl`'s `coarsen` ran neither of its loops, and the GPU drew **no
shadow at all** where the CPU drew a wrong one — the one arm of this that is silent rather than slow.

**`effect::MAX_KERNEL_RADIUS = 512`, applied in `render::effects::kernel_radius`.** That function had
no bound at all: **24 GB** of taps at σ = 1e9, and above σ ≈ 6.1e18 `(σ * 3).ceil() as usize`
saturates `usize::MAX`, so `kernel`'s `Vec::with_capacity(2 * r + 1)` is a capacity-overflow panic.
512 is **7.1× the radius `BLUR_SIGMA_BUDGET` produces**, so it cannot bite on a blur the design
considers reasonable, and it bounds a cost that is already linear in the radius: measured in release
on 200×220, a full-res `blur` is 9.3 ms at r = 72 and 239 ms at r = 3000, so the cap holds the
degenerate case to a small multiple of the ordinary worst case rather than to a hang or a panic. `NaN`
and the negatives answer 0 now rather than falling through the multiply.

**Placing that guard in `kernel_radius` is what closes the GPU, and it is the load-bearing choice
here.** It is the one function both backends' blurs go through, which is why it is there rather than
at either caller: the CPU reached the allocation *behind* `coarsen`'s Θ(k) walk — three minutes of
hang first — while the GPU issues coarsen as a **dispatch** and calls `effects::kernel` on the host
almost immediately. The same document therefore panicked one backend at once and hung the other, and
one guard in one function answers both. ⚠️ **D743 removed the CPU's three minutes and not the need for
the guard**: with `coarsen` bounded by the source both backends now reach the allocation at once, so
the asymmetry that made this placement *obvious* is gone while the reason for it — one function, both
blurs — is untouched.

**Both flips bite on the same line**, and it is the wall clock over the whole pass — asserted in
`an_out_of_range_blur_is_bounded_at_both_of_its_two_sites` *before* either mechanism, because what the
user loses is a frame that never comes back. Removing the `min` in `shadow_downscale` with the kernel
cap in place, release: **177.8 s**, printed by the failure, which is *"capping the kernel alone still
walks `coarsen` for three minutes"* measured rather than extrapolated. ⚠️ **That 177.8 s was against
the pre-D743 `coarsen` and is not expected to reproduce** — the loop is bounded by the source now, so
the flip walks `w·h` and the clock assertion should stay green. Re-run it before quoting it: what it
would stop demonstrating is the **cost** argument for this cap, not the cap. Removing the `min` in
`kernel_radius` with the `k` cap in place, debug: a panic *inside* `run`, at `kernel`'s `2 * r + 1` —
*"attempt to multiply with overflow"*, which in release is the `Vec::with_capacity` capacity overflow.
⚠️ **Neither flip reached a length assertion**, which is worth recording because the length assertions
look like the point of that test and are not: they pin the two contracts, and the clock is what says
the two contracts are the right ones. The clock is deliberately loose — 5 s against a measured
~0.2 ms — because it stands in for *"does not take three minutes"* and a tight bound on a shared
machine is a flake.

⚠️ **Explicitly not done: `op_set_effects` still accepts the payload**, so the absurd number still
reaches the model and the file. What changed is that it is now a wrong picture drawn instantly rather
than a refused edit. *Fix with the finding's sketch (b)* — reject a non-finite or absurd effect
payload at the op boundary, with `inspector.rs`'s `MAX_BLUR = 1_000.0` promoted out of the panel so
the panel and the operation share one constant. That is a shared `OpError` design and belongs with
`[S7.2-L5-01]`/`[A1-L2-01]`'s family rather than in this commit.

⚠️ **`buffer_downscale`, the layer-blur half, was not audited here.** `MAX_KERNEL_RADIUS` bounds the
kernel it eventually asks for, and nothing was measured about the buffer size it implies for an absurd
σ. Say so rather than reading this entry as covering both downscales.

This is the **render** half of the shape invariant 8's family keeps finding (D421, D448, D451, D452):
a number the document is allowed to hold that no downstream stage can survive. The difference is where
it lands. Those four end at `io::load`, refusing a file for ever; this one ends in the frame that never
finishes, and its input is *finite* — `2e30` is a perfectly good `f64` and every finiteness guard in
the workspace is right to pass it. It bounds the resample D403 introduced and shares its budget with
D395's `buffer_downscale`, which is why both caps are named in `effect.rs` beside `BLUR_SIGMA_BUDGET`
rather than in the renderer: a net for the number nobody has, sitting next to the budget the design
aims at.

**D453 — A boolean's operand is neither offered as a rail nor accepted as one. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07, both arms; Keep.***

`[S3.1-L1-02]`. Two 100×100 rects, the second overlapping the first from x=60, combined with
`Subtract`: the result is the strip 0..60, and its right-hand edge lies **exactly on the subtrahend's
left edge** — which is what a boolean *is*, so this is the ordinary geometry rather than a contrived
one. A Text-tool click on that edge picked the **operand**, and `build::text_on_new_path` consumes
what it is handed. Three things happened at once and none of them was announced: the operand was
**deleted**, so a two-operand subtract silently became its base; a `Text` node was installed
**inside** the `Boolean`, where `scene.rs` returns before the children loop and so never paints it;
and the status line said *"the shape became the rail"*. The caret was live over a blank page and
`Ctrl+Z` was the only way back, with nothing saying so.

**Two guards, and they fail separately, which is why the test asserts them separately.**
`build::text_on_new_path` refuses a path whose parent is a `Boolean` — the same refusal `mask`
already makes, in almost the same words and for the same reason: a boolean's children are operands
rather than artwork. It belongs at the builder because `can_parent(Boolean, Text)` is `true`, so
`Document::apply` has no reason of its own to say no, and because this is the door every caller comes
through — an MCP call or a future gesture arrives behind the pick rather than through it. And
`query::outline_at` skips any candidate with a `Boolean` ancestor, so the affordance never lights up
and nobody is offered a gesture that would be refused. Neither covers the other: without the builder
guard a non-canvas caller still consumes an operand; without the pick guard the rail cursor lives
over an edge that then does nothing.

**Where the pick guard sits is two decisions and both are load-bearing.** It is *before* the
`local_path` build and the nearest-point solve, so on a rejected candidate it saves that work rather
than adding to it — this loop runs over every candidate outline on every frame the tool is in hand.
And it is in `outline_at` rather than in `is_effectively_interactable`, which walks the same ancestor
chain and would be the tidier home: that function is shared with `hit_test`, which is **supposed** to
return operands and resolve them to their container through `group_chain` afterwards, so folding the
skip in there would make a boolean unclickable. ⚠️ **This deliberately makes the two doors disagree
about operands.** D408 closes its own paragraph on `outline_at` with *"both doors agree"*; that is
not the relationship here, and it should not be read as covering this — `[S4.1-L1-02]` reports the
same claim false in other respects too.

**Flipped per guard**, because one flip would have proved the pair. Removing the `outline_at` skip
fails on the pick assertion with the operand's own id and **leaves the builder assertion green**;
removing the builder refusal fails on `expect_err`, and the transaction it prints is the defect in
one line — `CreateNode { parent: <the Boolean> }` followed by `DeleteNode { <the operand> }`.

⚠️ **The control failed first and was right to.** It was aimed at the ellipse's *origin* rather than
at its outline, so `outline_at` answered `None` — and green, that control would have been asserting
that a plain shape is not a rail candidate either, i.e. that the feature does not work. It aims at
the leftmost point now, and the comment on it says where that is and why.

⚠️ **`[S3.1-L2-03]` is the same missing gate in the same function, and the refusal that shipped first
did not close it — a *second* guard, landed hours later, does.** That half is a **frame**:
`geometry::local_path` answers `Some` for an `Artboard` deliberately (D144), so `text_on_new_path`
took a frame as a rail, deleted it, and the guides scoped to it survived as dangling owners —
`io::save` succeeds and `io::load` on those bytes never will. The guard above is an *ancestry* test
and **could never reach this case**, a frame's parent being a frame or the root; what kept it out of
reach instead was `outline_at`'s **kind** skip of `Artboard` (D408: a frame is a page, and its edge is
a boundary rather than a drawn curve), one layer above the builder that needs it. So a kind test now
sits beside the ancestry one — `matches!(node.kind(), NodeKind::Artboard { .. } | NodeKind::Root)` —
and the two refuse for two different reasons.

**In core rather than left to the pick's kind skip, because unreachable is not refused.** The MCP
write surface, the command line and any second entrance added later all arrive at the builder
directly, behind whatever the canvas would or would not have offered. That is `build::mask`'s own
argument for its own refusal, quoted one guard up in the same function.

`a_frame_is_not_a_rail_and_taking_one_would_strand_its_guides`, in `crates/ondin-core/tests/build.rs`,
asserts **the loss before the mechanism**: it drives the builder and, if the builder is ever handed
back an `Ok` again, commits it, saves and reloads — so the flip prints `Integrity("guide guide b0a7:4
is scoped to b0a7:3, which is not a frame in this document")` rather than an error-code mismatch.
Flipped by deleting the `Artboard` arm: it fails exactly there, at the predicted site, with that
string. ⚠️ **The boolean test stays green under that flip and this one stays green under the boolean
flip**, which is what says these are two guards rather than one written twice.

**What the kind gate does not close is the class**, and ~~that half stays open: having `op_delete`
refuse a delete that orphans a guide, which is where this reads with `[S2.2-L2-05]`. The gate removes
*this* caller from the class; it does not remove the class.~~ **the class closed the same day, as
D491, and wider than this paragraph asked for**: the check is not an arm inside `op_delete` but a
post-condition over *every* guide at the end of `Document::apply`, so it holds for any operation that
can strand one rather than for the delete alone. This guard is still worth keeping — it refuses the
rail at the door with a reason of its own, where the post-condition can only report that a transaction
would leave the document unopenable.

~~⚠️ **Two comments the fix left behind.** The new guard cites *"the same refusal `mask` makes forty
lines up"* and that refusal is about six hundred lines up (`build.rs:496` against `:1139`) — far
enough that a reader will not find it, and the pointer is the whole value of the sentence. And
`outline_at`'s own doc comment still enumerates the exclusions — text, frames, and a boolean's own
outline — without the operand rule, which lives only in an inline comment inside the loop, where a
reader of the summary will not look. *Fix both comments.*~~ — **both fixed 2026-09-07.** The pointer
now names the sentence to grep for and records that it once said *"forty"*, and `outline_at`'s header
carries the operand rule as a fourth exclusion stated in its own right, distinct from the boolean's
own outline being a limitation.

**D452 — Every span guard in `image.rs` bounded the small end and none bounded the large one. *Fixed
and tested 2026-09-07; Keep.***

`[S9.1-L5-01]`. A `.ondin` whose image fill carries `"crop": {"x0":-1e308, "y0":-1e308, "x1":1e308,
"y1":1e308}` holds four **finite** numbers — so it is not the family D421 and D451 refuse — but
`x1 − x0` overflows to `inf`, and every degenerate-input guard in the module bounded only the small
end — eight of them spelled `<= 0.0`, which `inf` passes. Three consequences, measured from that one
document. `crop_clamped` divides `inf / inf`
and returns an all-`NaN` rectangle, and **one crop-pan drag commits that through `SetFills`**: the
file saves `"x0": null` and never opens again — D421's terminal failure reached with no non-finite
number anywhere in the input. `ImageRef::framing` returns a **singular** `Affine` with a `NaN`
translation, which is exactly what `Framing::identity` exists to give an answer instead of, and which
`degenerate_inputs_resolve_to_the_identity_framing` already documented as *"a backend question with
no good answer"*. And `ImageRef::picture_box` answers `Some(NaN…)` rather than `None`, whereupon
`tools::crop_resized` calls `f64::clamp(NaN, NaN)` and **panics** — on the UI thread, on a crop
resize.

The fix is `usable_span(x) = x > 0.0 && x.is_finite()`, spelled once and asked at every span test in
the module; `crop_clamped` returns `whole_crop()` for an unusable span exactly as it already did for
a non-positive one, so `crop_panned` cannot emit a `NaN`. §5.5a's rule — *"a zero-sized source, an
empty frame and a zero-area crop resolve to `Framing::identity`"* — was true of zero and not of
infinity, and reads *unusable* now.

⚠️ **The site count is the entry's most useful sentence.** The finding named **five** sites. A grep
for the `<= 0.0` shape found **eight**. `rust-mechanic`, propagating the change, found a **ninth**
(`missing_placeholder`) that the brief had not listed — and correctly refused to touch it, handing it
back rather than guessing, while pointing out that the helper's own doc claim *"every guard in this
module"* was thereby false. It also flagged a **tenth** in *positive* form: `ImageRef::crop_scale`'s
`span > 0.0`, which answers `Some(0.0)` for an `inf` span where the honest answer is `None`, and
which no grep for `<= 0.0` could ever have found. **Five, then eight, then ten.** The lesson is not
about this module: *a site count that came from one grep shape is a lower bound, and the shape you
did not grep for is the one that stays broken.* `ImageFit::Tile`'s arm already spelled the predicate
inline (`is_finite() && > 0.0`) and is left as the one place that had it right all along — worth
naming, because it is evidence the rule was known and not written down.

⚠️ **A gap in D451 that D451 could not have seen.** `brush_is_finite`'s `Brush::Image` arm read
`i.sampler.alpha` alone. `ImageBrush`'s own fields are peniko's; the **reference** hanging off it is
this crate's, and it carries the crop rectangle, `tile_scale` and seven adjustment sliders. So a
finiteness check written by reading `peniko::Brush` stops exactly one level short of the type the app
actually stores. `image_ref_is_finite` closes it. **Two guards now, and the test says which is
which**: `usable_span` stops the `NaN` being *manufactured*, `brush_is_finite` stops one *reaching
the document* if anything else ever makes one.

Flipped by restoring `w <= 0.0 || h <= 0.0` in `crop_clamped`:
`a_crop_whose_span_overflows_never_reaches_the_document` fails on its first assertion with all four
coordinates `NaN`, **and `degenerate_inputs_resolve_to_the_identity_framing` stays green** —
predicted there and observed there, which is what says the two guards are separate and neither covers
the other.

⚠️ **The residue is this entry's own headline with *origin* for *span*, and it was read rather than
run.** `usable_span` is asked of `r.width() * iw`; the Crop arm's third factor is
`Affine::translate((-r.x0 * iw, -r.y0 * ih))`, which weighs the crop's **origin**, and nothing weighs
that. A crop of `{"x0":-1e308, "y0":-1e308, "x1":-9.99e307, "y1":-9.99e307}` spans about `1e305` —
finite, positive, usable — while `1e308 * iw` overflows against any picture more than one pixel wide,
so `framing` answers a transform with an **infinite** translation. That is not *singular*, so it is
not literally the state §5.5a's rule names, but it is the same class of answer the rule exists to keep
away from a backend. It is not the document-killer this entry is about, and the two guards between
them are why: `crop_clamped` slides such a rectangle back inside `0..1` and collapses it to nothing,
and a crop that comes back `inf` through `crop_reframed` is refused at the operation by
`image_ref_is_finite`. What is left is an infinite brush transform painted for as long as the hostile
file is open. *Fix by asking `usable_span` of the mapped corners and not only of the span* — and
re-derive the overflow above first, because it comes from reading the arithmetic rather than from a
test that failed.

⚠️ **Two comments the fix left behind.** `OpError::NonFinite`'s doc, rewritten by D451 hours earlier,
enumerates what a paint can carry and stops at *"an image brush's alpha"* — the arm weighs the whole
`ImageRef` now, so the variant's own list is narrower than the check that returns it. And
`image_ref_is_finite`'s doc explains itself with *"`crop_clamped`'s guards test `<= 0.0`, which `inf`
passes"*, in the present tense, describing the state this entry fixed rather than the state it fixed
it to. Both are the drift D451's own closing note was about, one entry later. *Fix both comments.*

**D451 — Invariant 8's paint half. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep.***

This is the residue D448 recorded as open, and it turned out to be the larger half of it.
`OpError::NonFinite`'s own doc scopes itself to *"a node's geometry, its transform, or a guide's
position"*, and both paint operations stored whatever brush they were handed — `op_set_fills` checked
`is_paintable` and then `fills.to_vec()`, and `op_set_strokes` did the same. So §2's invariant 8, whose
whole claim is that the operation is *"the last place such a value can be refused while the user still
has their work"*, was **true of coordinates and not of paint**: a `NaN` reached the model,
`Document::apply` accepted it, `serde_json` wrote it as `null`, and the file answered *"invalid type:
null, expected f32"* the next time it was opened. D448 closed the SVG importer's route to that. This is
the door every **other** author of a gradient comes through — an MCP call, a future scrub, anything
that computes a stop offset rather than typing one.

**`brush_is_finite` covers everything a brush can carry, because the question is what `serde_json`
will refuse to write and not what looks like a coordinate.** A solid's four colour channels, a
gradient's kind geometry, every stop's offset *and* its colour, the gradient's own transform, and an
image brush's `sampler.alpha` — which turned out to be one level short of the `ImageRef` hanging off
that brush, closed the same day by D452. A colour channel is exactly as capable of being `NaN` as a radius is and
is written to the same file, so scoping the check to the things that read like geometry would have left
half the door open. `gradient_kind_is_finite` is **exhaustive over `GradientKind` with no wildcard**, so
a fourth kind in a future peniko stops the build rather than going silently unchecked — the argument
`Operation::changes_nothing` makes (D428). Strokes additionally check `width` and every `dashes` entry;
`stroke-dasharray="1e999 5"` was one of `[S7.2-L5-01]`'s five sinks and is closed at the importer, so
this is the same value arriving by the door the importer is not. Both checks run **before** the node
lookup, which is deliberate: the question is about the operation's payload, not about its target.

**The test was renamed, and the rename is the finding in miniature.**
`no_operation_may_write_a_coordinate_that_is_not_finite` became
`no_operation_may_write_a_number_that_is_not_finite`, because the rule was wider than the name and the
code was narrower than the rule. D421's entry above cited the old name and now cites the new one —
⚠️ **a test name in §15 prose is the kind of reference no gate checks**, which is D319's hole reached
from the documentation side rather than from `cargo doc`'s. Four arms were added to the refusal table:
a gradient stop offset, a gradient transform, a stroke width and a dash length. Flipped per term, and
**dropping only the `dashes` clause fails on *"SetStrokes (dashes)"* rather than on an earlier case**,
which is what says each arm carries its own weight rather than being answered by the one before it.

⚠️ ~~**`OpError::NonFinite`'s own doc and its `Display` string still say *coordinate***, in the variant's
doc comment and in `#[error("a coordinate is not finite")]`, so the widened rule is now refused under
the old name — and `brush_is_finite`'s own doc quotes that scoping in the present tense, as the state of
things rather than as the state it fixed. *Fix all three.*~~ **All three done the same day**: the
variant reads *"a number is not finite"* and its doc names paint, and the helper's own doc says *until
2026-09-07*. The table's arms cover the gradient offset,
the gradient transform, the width and the dashes; **the colour channels are checked and untested**,
which is the honest reading of the coverage rather than a gap worth a second entry.

⚠️ ~~**`op_create` now carries its four-line finiteness comment twice, verbatim** — `document.rs`, the
block beginning *"The check has to be here and not only at the loader"*. Harmless today and worth
deleting before somebody edits one copy and leaves the other, which is exactly how a comment comes to
contradict the code beside it.~~ **Deleted the same day**, one copy left.

**D450 — A font decoder's panic cost a worker for the session, not a face. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-07; Keep.***

`[S21-L5-01]` and `[S21-L1-02]`, closed together because they are one seam. A **53-byte** file — a
`wOF2` header declaring one table with `origLength = 1,000,000`, then a one-byte empty brotli stream —
panics `woff2-patched-0.4.0`'s `push_simple_table_record` with *"range end index 1000000 out of range
for slice of length 0"*: the table's source range is built from UIntBase128 values read out of the file
and never compared to the decompressed length. A second shape, three table entries of `0x7FFFFFFF`,
does the same. The dependency's `is_valid_header` checks the signature and its body is otherwise
literally `// TODO: Add other checks`, so there is no version of this that gets fixed upstream soon.
`load_face`'s `.ok()?` was written as though an `Err` were the only failure; `.ok()` turns an `Err`
into `None` and does nothing whatever about an unwind.

**What the panic cost is the finding, not the panic.** The worker loop is
`while let Some(job) = queue.pop()`, so the unwind leaves the loop entirely: the thread is gone for the
session, and — the half that makes it silent — the job's `FontMsg::Failed` is never sent, so `claimed`
keeps the key and `outstanding` never clears. That family reads as *loading* for ever and can never be
asked for again. `WORKERS` is 6 and `prefetch_popular` dispatches **fifty** jobs at the first poll
after the catalog lands, so this is the same ending D441 has by a second road, and §5.4a's *"a family
whose file the decoder cannot read falls back to the static cuts automatically"* was true of an `Err`
and false of a panic.

**Two guards, and they are not redundant.** `sfnt_from` wraps the decoder known to panic today;
`load_one_face` wraps the whole job, so `fontdb`, `std::fs::read` and the next decoder are covered
without anyone remembering to. `AssertUnwindSafe` for the reason `boolean::evaluate` gives (D239) —
nothing observable crosses the boundary, the agent and the spec being borrowed read-only and every
scrap of state a decoder builds being local to the call and dropped by the unwind. ⚠️ **Both are inert
under `panic = "abort"`, which is a build failure now rather than a comment asking for one (D445)** —
worth stating because two entries from this session now rest on that gate.

⚠️ **The half worth the most is that the first test was vacuous and the flip said so.** The hostile
bytes were written to a temp file and driven through `load_face` with a `FaceSource::File` — and it
passed *with the guard removed*, because **the `File` arm never decodes woff2**: the decode is on the
`Web` arm, behind `download`, so nothing headless could reach it. That is why a panic on a 53-byte
input survived a suite this size. `sfnt_from` was extracted so that the guard sits where the panic is
*and* a test can reach it; the flip now kills the test binary with the panic verbatim, which is the
shape of the production failure rather than a wrong value. **A guard behind a network call is a guard
no test covers**, and that generalises well past this one.

⚠️ ~~**The test's own doc comment says it asserts through `load_one_face` and flips by calling
`load_face`.** It calls `sfnt_from`, and `load_one_face` is unreachable from a test for exactly the
reason the paragraph above gives — so the prose describes a draft that could not have existed. *Fix the
comment*, and name the flip precisely: what bites is removing the `catch_unwind` inside `sfnt_from`.~~
**Done 2026-09-07**: the doc describes the test that exists, asserting through `sfnt_from` and
flipping by removing its `catch_unwind`.

**D449 — A picture's RGBA expansion is bounded in RGBA bytes. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep, with
the synchronous decode recorded as open.***

`[S9.2-L5-02]`. **Three caps were in play and not one of them was denominated in the decoded RGBA bytes
of a live image**, which is the whole finding. `image 0.25`'s `Limits::default().max_alloc` is 512 MiB
and bounds *the decoder's own buffer in the decoder's own format* — grayscale is one byte a pixel, so
it permits 536 M pixels and `into_rgba8` turns that into 2 GiB with nothing left to consult. `MAX_EDGE`
is denominated in **edge pixels**, so `60000×200` passes it and holds 48 MB. `DECODED_BYTES` is in the
right unit and weighs only **stale** entries, so a picture the document still refers to is never
measured against it at all — which is not an oversight but the design the module doc states and
`an_image_the_document_still_carries_is_never_evicted` asserts.

Reproduced in release, uniform grayscale PNG through `ImageStore::insert`, and **worse than the finding
filed**, because a uniform image compresses better than its fixture did: 1000² is 2.8 KB → 4 MB
(1,412×); 4000² is 24 KB → 64 MB (2,652×); **8000² is 76 KB → 256 MB in 433 ms (3,356×)**; 20000²
reaches 1.6 GB. `into_rgba8` allocates through `Vec`, so failing it is `handle_alloc_error` — an
**abort**, not something a `?` or an `.ok()?` anywhere on the path can see.

The cap is `MAX_DECODED_BYTES = DECODED_BYTES` (256 MiB), asked in `decode` **before** `into_rgba8`
rather than after, with its own `DecodeError::TooMuchPixelData` variant. Separate from `TooLarge`
because they are different questions with different answers: that one is a bound the renderer would
assert on, this one is how much memory the picture becomes, and a caller explaining itself to a user
wants to say which.

⚠️ **This does not fix the freeze, and half the reason for the entry is to say so.** A **50 MP camera
file is legitimate** — a Sony A7R V is 9504×6336, 240 MB of RGBA — and the pathological 8000² is the
same order of magnitude, so no cap that accepts the second can refuse the first. **The 8000² that was
measured is 256,000,000 bytes and passes the shipped cap**, which is the honest form of that sentence
and is worth knowing before anyone reads this entry as closing the 433 ms. What closes is the unbounded
tail — the 1.6 GB and 2 GB cases — and the abort. The 433 ms synchronous decode inside the dashboard's
egui pass (`library::cover::rasterize` → `export::png::png` → `prepare`, one document per pass, since
`Covers::get`'s 8 ms budget explicitly did not apply to the first render of a pass — its progress
guarantee, without which a library of slow documents would draw no covers ever) is a **threading**
problem. 🚨 **It was threaded on 2026-09-19 (D820), and the budget and the progress guarantee went
with it** — both were consequences of rendering *inside* the pass, and neither had anything left to
bound once it was not. The 433 ms is still 433 ms; it is simply no longer in a frame.

⚠️ **The test's control is the load-bearing half.** `a_pictures_rgba_expansion_is_bounded_in_rgba_bytes`
refuses a 9000² grayscale PNG of about 100 KB and then asserts the 9504×6336 camera file is
**accepted**, so a later tightening cannot quietly make the app refuse ordinary photographs — the cap
is a number somebody will want to lower, and the control is what says why it cannot go much below
where it is. Flipped against the plausible wrong version rather than against nothing: a cap on the
**file** bytes, which is the obvious reading of "refuse huge images", leaves the test green at 105 KB.
That is what says the *denomination* is the finding.

**D820 — A dashboard cover is rendered on a thread of its own, and the budget is deleted with what
it bounded. *Ruled by the maintainer, built and tested 2026-09-19; Resolved — D449's threading
problem, closed.***

`Covers::get` → `render` → `io::load` → `png::png` → `ImageStore::prepare` ran the whole
document→pixels path **inside the egui pass**, where D449 measured a picture's decode alone at
**433 ms** for an 8000² image. `roadmap.md` carried it with the remedy named and the *where*
undecided — *"which thread it goes on is undecided"*.

🚨 **It is a second worker of its own and deliberately not a job on `library::writer::Writer`'s
queue, and the reason is that module's own contract**: *"one background writer of anything, in
**FIFO** order"*, with the FIFO load-bearing twice — a `Forget` must not be overtaken by the
`Snapshot` it cancels, and a save must not be overtaken by anything. A cover render is hundreds of
milliseconds that **nothing is waiting on**. Putting one on that queue makes the feature which
protects the user's work wait behind the feature which decorates a card, and it does so precisely
when the library is large, which is when both matter most.

⚠️ **Nothing the renderer does is a record, which is what makes a second writer legitimate here.**
It may write a PNG into the cover cache, and `crate::atomic` **exempts** that cache as derived data —
a lost or half-written cover is regenerated from the document it came from. So this is not a second
writer of anything `writer.rs` protects.

🚨 **`FRAME_BUDGET` is deleted rather than retuned, and the entry should be read as a removal and not
a regression.** The 8 ms never bounded the felt cost, because the **progress guarantee** underneath
it rendered one document per pass *whatever the budget said* — without which a library of slow
documents would draw no covers ever. So the budget bought one stall per pass rather than none, and
the guarantee is what made that certain. Both were consequences of rendering **inside** the pass and
neither has anything left to bound. ⚠️ **`thumbs::ImageThumbs` keeps its 2 ms and is no longer the
same shape**: that decode really does happen in the frame, so its budget is still a budget. *A reader
generalising from one to the other would be reasoning from a similarity that has just stopped being
true.*

`Covers` gains three things. **`queued`**, so a card drawn on every frame it is on screen enqueues
**once** rather than sixty times a second — without it the queue grows faster than it drains and the
worker never reaches the second document. **`Renderer`**, spawned lazily on the first miss for
`Writer::spawn`'s reason (an app that never opens the dashboard, or a headless probe that never draws
a card, pays for no thread) and **joined** on drop rather than detached, so a `Covers` that goes away
with the base folder does not leave a thread rendering for a library nobody is looking at. And a
`#[cfg(test)] pub(crate) settle`.

⚠️ **`settle` is `cfg(test)` and not `pub`, which is D672's answer rather than D699's.** Nothing in
production waits for a cover, and `ondin-app` has no lib target, so `dead_code` *does* analyse a
`pub` item there — and it warned. The narrow `#[allow]` D699 argues for is the wrong tool here
because the precondition that forced it there is absent: no production doc names this method.

**Test** `library::cover::tests::covers_are_rendered_off_the_pass_and_all_of_them_arrive`, which
**replaces** `one_cover_a_pass_arrives_however_spent_the_budget_is`. The rule that one pinned is
**gone rather than changed**, which is why the test goes with it rather than being adjusted.
`a_document_with_no_cover_is_not_retried_every_pass` survives with a new tell: the budget was how it
measured a re-render, and the queue is now.

🚨 **The doc gate caught two dangling links this change created** — `` [`FRAME_BUDGET`] `` after the
constant was deleted, and `` [`Covers::settle`] `` after that method became `cfg(test)`. The second
is **D319**'s mechanism from the direction where a *production* doc may not name a test-only item, so
it is plain backticks and a sentence saying why. That gate is the one that reads doc comments, and
this is it working.

🚨 **The thread introduced a flake in another module's test, and finding it is the most useful thing
in this entry.** `panels::dashboard::tests::a_document_this_build_cannot_open_wears_the_mark_and_a_healthy_one_does_not`
asserts the red `UNREADABLE` chip, which `mark_of` reads through `Covers::unreadable` — and a cover
only learns a document is unloadable when it **renders** it. That test pumped one extra pass and
asserted on the next, and its own doc said those two passes were *"the cover cache's laziness rather
than a flake"*.

⚠️ **That sentence was accurate when it was written and this change made it exactly wrong.** The
laziness is still there; the **timing** it promised is gone. "The next pass" was a *fact* while the
render was inline and is a **race** once it is on a thread, decided by how loaded the machine is. It
is struck in place in the test's doc rather than deleted, because the stale half is the point — *a
comment can be made false by a change that never touches its file*. The fix is one line,
`app.covers.settle(&ctx)` before the assertion, which is what that method exists for; 25 paired runs
afterwards failed none.

🚨 **What found it was running the filter twenty times, and nothing else would have.** The whole
suite was green throughout, both full `--workspace` runs were green in debug *and* release, and a
verification run of the same two filters **three times each** came back clean. **2 of 20** paired
runs failed — `cargo test -p ondin-app library::cover` followed by `cargo test -p ondin-app
dashboard` — and only under a *filtered* run, which packs the related tests onto every core at once.
*Six clean runs is not evidence.* This is `CLAUDE.md`'s thirteenth gate hole and **D796**'s lesson
arriving from a second direction: there a shared OS resource, here a shared worker, and neither
visible to any gate in this project.

⚠️ **It is also what earns `settle` its `pub(crate)`.** The argument for the method was that the app
stays asynchronous and a probe asks for an answer, which `cover.rs`'s own tests already showed. This
is a **second module's** test needing it — the case that says it must not be private to `cover.rs`,
and the one a reader narrowing the visibility later has to answer.

**D448 — A gradient stop whose offset is `nan` cost the document, and the fix was one step too broad
the first time. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep, with the operation-side check recorded as open.***

`stop_of` in `svg_in.rs` is the **fifth sink** of `[S7.2-L5-01]`'s five-sink census and the only one
that survived the fix phase's first session. The other four — `feMorphology`'s radius,
`stroke-dasharray`, `parse_transform` (and so `gradientTransform`) and `view_box` — all reach
`numbers`, whose `.filter(|f| f.is_finite())` came in with **D421** — not D415, which is the text
editor's commit-on-leave and has nothing to do with it; each of the four was re-verified as already
closed rather than assumed. `stop_of` parses its own offset and relied on `f64::clamp` to bound it.

**`f64::clamp` propagates NaN by definition** — *"returns NaN if self is NaN"* — so
`<stop offset="nan"/>` reached `ColorStop { offset: NaN }`, `serde_json` wrote that as `null`, and
`io::load` of the saved file answered *"invalid type: null, expected f32"*. **The paste opens fine
and the document is dead the next time it is asked for**, which is the same class as the round's
Criticals reached from the clipboard rather than from a file the user chose. Rust's `f64` parser
accepts `nan`, `inf` and `infinity` case-insensitively, so the literal costs an attacker nothing to
write.

⚠️ **The half worth the entry is the fix that was wrong.** The first version filtered `is_finite`,
and the round-trip assertion **passed**. But `is_finite` also rejects the infinities, which the clamp
is *correct* about: `<stop offset="1e999"/>` means "at the end" and clamps to 1.0, and filtering it
drops the stop to the `unwrap_or(0.0)` — **moving that stop from one end of the ramp to the other**.
The predicate is `!is_nan()`. What caught it was the test's **control**, which asserts the two
infinities come through *clamped rather than dropped*, written to stop the test silently becoming a
test about `is_finite` rejecting everything. That is a shape the review has no name for: **a guard one
step too broad, where the finding's own symptom is fixed and a second, quieter thing breaks.** It is
the second time in this fix phase that writing a control found a defect the review did not have — the
first is `[S8.3-L1-01]`'s per-side texture limit, in session 2.

`a_gradient_stop_offset_of_nan_does_not_cost_the_document` drives the whole round trip — import →
`Document::apply` → `io::save` → `io::load` — because the loss is at the far end of it. Flipped by
removing the filter: fails at the `io::load` assertion with serde's wording verbatim. Asserting the
offset directly would have failed a line earlier on `NaN != 0.0`, which is the mechanism rather than
the loss.

⚠️ **Two comments still carry the first version's wording — fix them both**, and they are the same
mistake in its two shapes. `stop_of`'s doc credits `numbers`' filter to **D415**, which is the text
editor's commit-on-leave; it is D421. And the test's own flip note says it removes
*"`.filter(|f| f.is_finite())` from `stop_of`"*, naming the predicate that was replaced rather than
the one that is there — which, in an entry whose whole point is that those two predicates are not
interchangeable, is the one wrong word that would send the next reader back round the loop.

⚠️ **`view_box`'s `w > 0.0 && h > 0.0` guard is not the thing that was fixed**, and `[S7.2-L5-01]`
lists it as letting `+inf` through. It is unreachable by that route for a second-order reason worth
writing down rather than re-deriving: `numbers` drops the non-finite entry, so the list is length 3,
and the `[x, y, w, h]` slice pattern simply fails to match. The guard is doing nothing about
infinities and never has.

⚠️ **The residue is that this fix is at the importer, and §2's invariant 8 says the *operation* is
where finiteness is refused** — *"the last place such a value can be refused while the user still has
their work"*. `OpError::NonFinite`'s own doc scopes it to a **coordinate** — geometry, transform,
guide position — and `op_set_fills` checks nothing about the brush it stores, so the NaN offset went
through `Document::apply` untouched and only died at `io::load`; that is what the test's round trip
demonstrates. So the SVG route is closed and the operation route is not: anything else that ever
authors a gradient stop from a computed number — an MCP call, a future scrub — can still write a file
that never reopens. **Fix by validating paint at the operation**, which is where D421 put every other
non-finite value; until that lands, invariant 8's claim is true of coordinates and not of paint, and
this paragraph is the place that says so. **It landed the same day — D451**, which is the entry to read
for what the operation now weighs; this paragraph stands because identifying the residue was the larger
half of the finding.

**D447 — `reset_transient_state` clears `per_corner_radius`. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep.***

The Appearance panel's per-corner disclosure is a `HashSet<NodeId>` on `OndinApp`: a node goes in when
the user opens its four radius fields and comes out only when that same node's disclosure is closed
again. Three occurrences in the whole workspace, all in `panels::inspector`, and **no clear anywhere**
— so it accumulated for the life of the process, across every document opened, holding ids minted
from documents closed hours earlier.

`reset_transient_state` is the list it belonged on. Thirteen other fields on `OndinApp` hold `NodeId`s
from the outgoing document — `entered_group`, `points`, `renaming_layer`, `clones`,
`layers_range_anchor`, `effect_menu`, `pending_picker` and the five `*_synced_selection` vectors — and
most are cleared elsewhere on the way through an open. This one was cleared nowhere.

**Why no wrong pixel ever followed is the part worth recording, because it is why nobody noticed.**
`NodeId` is `(actor, seq)` with a random per-session actor (`ondin_core::id`), so an id from a
document that has been left **dangles rather than collides**: `doc.get(id)` answers `None` and the
entry is inert. The set simply grows. That is the same argument that keeps the other thirteen fields
harmless, which is why it is written down here rather than re-derived by the next person to read the
list — it makes this a hygiene rule rather than a correctness one, and it is the reason the test
asserts the **growth** (`opening_a_document_drops_the_previous_ones_corner_disclosures`) instead of
hunting for a wrong pixel there is no route to.

⚠️ **The defect is the list, not the field.** `reset_transient_state` is a hand-written run of
assignments with nothing checking that a field of its class is on it — `[A2-L7-02]`'s theme in a
second denomination. Flipped by removing the new `clear()`: fails on the emptiness assertion with the
stale id named, which is the predicted site because there is only one.

**D446 — SVG import is bounded in width as well as depth, and its child index is a map rather than a
scan. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep, with the real cost of a paste recorded as open.***

Two changes in one entry because they compound: the budget is what makes a hostile file stop, and the
index is what makes an honest one fast enough that the budget is the only thing stopping it.

**(a) `MAX_SVG_NODES = 50_000`.** `MAX_SVG_NESTING` bounds how *deep* the walk goes (§15 D416) and
nothing bounded how *wide* it goes, which is a different bomb with the same postage. A `<defs>` of L
groups each instantiating the next **twice**, plus one `<use>` at the root, expands 2^L from a file
growing ~50 bytes per level: **843 bytes was 16,384 shapes in 7.99 s**, and `use_depth`'s cap of 16
admits 65,536 — three `<use>` per level instead of two is 3^16 ≈ 43 million, a `Vec<Operation>` that
exhausts memory, and an allocation failure is `handle_alloc_error`, an **abort nothing can catch**.
Neither existing bound could do this job: `use_depth` counts *nesting*, so it is unchanged by how many
instances a level produces, and `import`'s `nodes_limit` bounds the XML nodes roxmltree *parses*,
where the whole 843-byte fixture is 47 elements.

It is asked by `out_of_budget()` at the top of `node_ignoring` — **the one choke point every emitted
node passes** — rather than at the six `CreateNode` pushes, so a refusal never stops mid-element with
a group created and its clip not, and the last thing built is whole. It counts **nodes, not shapes**,
and here the two are far apart: L=14 now stops at 9,997 shapes, because each `<use>` level also
creates a group and the groups spend most of the 50,000. That is the right denomination — a group
costs what a shape costs — but it means the number in `Import::shapes` after a refusal is not the
budget. 50,000 is chosen against real artwork rather than against the bomb, a traced illustration
running to tens of thousands of shapes and having to paste; **and the control is the half that
matters**, so L=10's 1,024 shapes are asserted to come through whole and unreported. A budget low
enough to stop the bomb and low enough to break real artwork would look identical from the bomb's side
alone.

**(b) `index_in` is a lookup.** It used to count matching `CreateNode`s in `ops` — always right, and
Θ(n²) over the import, because `ops` only grows and every created node scanned all of it. It reads an
`FxHashMap` bumped in a single `Builder::push` funnel that all **seventeen** append sites go through,
the root group's included. Measured in release, `import` alone: 4,000 shapes 11.9 → **4.9 ms**, 8,000
37.7 → **9.4**, 16,000 380 → **18.8**, 32,000 **1.81 s → 38.1 ms** — 47×, and linear at last, 2.0× per
2× of input. The branching bomb at L=14 went 7.99 s → 127 ms. ⚠️ **The funnel is a correctness
requirement and not a tidiness one**: a bare `ops.push` of a `CreateNode` makes `index_in` answer one
low for that parent from then on, and the symptom is a paste whose children arrive in the wrong order
— silent, and a long way from the line that caused it. For the same reason `index_in` must be read
*before* the `CreateNode` it indexes, `push` being what bumps the count.

**`[S7.1-L5-01]` needed no new guard, and it is asserted rather than assumed.** A self-referencing
`clip-path` aborted the process with `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` from a **218-byte** paste, and the
finding proposed a depth counter on `Builder`. That counter had already been written for a different
finding — `MAX_SVG_NESTING`, on `children`, which is the one choke point the clip recursion also
passes through — and closed this one on the way past. Both forms, the self-referencing and the mutual,
are covered by `a_clip_path_cycle_stops_rather_than_recursing_forever`, because *"the fix for A ought
to cover B"* is exactly the claim that deserves a test rather than a sentence. Flip: the cap raised to
100,000 and the binary dies with `0xc00000fd`, the reported symptom verbatim — which also means this
test can only ever fail by aborting, with no assertion message at all.

⚠️ **And the finding that outranks both halves: the real cost of pasting a large SVG is
`Document::apply`, not import.** `op_create` resolves an unnamed node's name through
`child_names(parent, &[])`, which walks every sibling into a fresh `FxHashSet` once per child created,
so applying *n* children to one parent is Θ(n²). Measured: 32,000 shapes is **38 ms of import and
62.6 s of apply**, on the egui UI thread — 1,600×. The review attributed the cost to `index_in`, and
it is not the binding term; no pass measured `apply` at all. **Not fixed**: the chokepoint is D127's
per-parent numbering, a deliberate rule rather than an oversight, so removing the scan is a design
decision about names and not a defect to close. Open, in `roadmap.md` under *Per-edit cost*.

**D445 — `panic = "unwind"` is enforced by the build, not requested by a comment. *Fixed and
flip-checked 2026-09-07; Keep.***

`boolean::guarded`'s `catch_unwind` is the only thing standing between a boolean over degenerate
geometry and the editor going down with the document open in it (§15 D239), and under
`panic = "abort"` it is inert: `catch_unwind` never returns. `Cargo.toml` carried a profile note to
keep the absence of that setting deliberate, and **the note argued the gate was impossible**, on two
claims that are both false. *"Nothing in the code can detect the setting or warn about it"* —
`#[cfg(panic = "abort")]` is a stable rustc cfg, measured with a two-line probe before anything was
written, `rustc -O` printing unwind and `rustc -O -C panic=abort` printing abort. And *"there is no
test that can fail if it stops being"* — `guarded`'s synthetic panic aborts its own test binary under
the setting, which cargo reports as a hard failure of the whole target, louder than an assertion
rather than quieter.

A `#[cfg(panic = "abort")] compile_error!` now sits beside the guard, naming D239 in its message and
pointing at the manifest note, which points back at it. Flip-checked with
`RUSTFLAGS="-C panic=abort" cargo check -p ondin-core`, which fails with that message.

⚠️ **This is a new shape for the gate-hole series and is worth naming as one.** The others on that
list are gates that do not cover what they claim — clippy without `--all-targets`, `cargo doc` without
`--document-private-items`, `deps_forbidden` pointed at a tree nothing builds (D302, D319, D427). This
is **a gate nobody wrote, because the documentation said not to bother**, and a note that exists to
keep an absence deliberate had been telling every reader the absence was undefendable. The rule to
carry is the mirror of the three-deep question asked of a gate that exists: *when the record says a
check is impossible, check.*

⚠️ **`evaluate`'s own doc still says the opposite**, in the paragraph immediately above the
`compile_error!` that detects it: *"under `panic = "abort"` the process would go down as before, and
nothing here can detect that"*. **Fix the comment** — it is the second copy of the very claim this
entry was written to retire, and it sits closer to the guard than the manifest note does.

**D444 — The layers panel's width bounds were derived from the header's gutter, not the tree's.
*Corrected 2026-09-07; 210 is Keep and the second reading behind it is open.***

`MIN_W` and `MAX_W` are derived rather than chosen — that is what `panel_width_tests` exists for — and
both derivations subtracted `2 * PAD_X`, the **header**'s 24pt of margin, where a row is narrowed by
the `ScrollArea`'s own inner frame. That frame is 6pt a side, 12 in total, and it had no name; it has
one now, `TREE_PAD_X`, and `app.rs`'s `Margin::symmetric` reads it, so the two cannot drift apart
again. Measured off a real `layers_panel` at `MIN_W`, a row runs `6.0..204.0` — **198pt**, where the
derivation said 186.

**Every width figure in both constants' prose was 12pt pessimistic**: a hovered top-level row's name
room at the minimum is **108.5** and not 96.5, the content width **198** and not 186, and a hovered
eight-deep row at `MAX_W` has **281.5** and not 269.5. `MAX_W`'s prose carries that row's other two
readings as well — the at-rest one with nothing on its right, and the at-rest one owing a `RowBadge`
its 4pt inset — and both moved by the same 12: **326** and not 314, **322** and not 310. All three
are corrected, because the reason the sentence beside them was already wrong once is that it had
picked the wrong one of the three; leaving two of them stale would have set that up again. Nothing on
screen changed, the error being entirely in the safe direction — 210 and 600 are both more generous
than they were argued to be.

⚠️ **What follows from the correction is a design question, and it is deliberately left open.**
`MIN_W`'s prose says *"210 is where two independent readings of it meet"*. Corrected, a four-deep row
stops drawing its name underneath the eye at **194.5**, not the 206.5 that sentence rested on — so
that reading would have allowed 195, and **the two readings no longer meet**. 210 is left exactly
where it is: the error was wholly in the safe direction, and a number that looks right on screen is
not a derivation's to overrule. But the argument for it is one reading now rather than two, and
whether to re-tighten it is the maintainer's call rather than this entry's. **It is open work, not a
verdict** — parked in `roadmap.md` under *Later · Parked decisions*, where a decision nobody has had
to make yet belongs; nothing on screen is wrong while it sits there.

**The band test failed on the correction, correctly.** Its lower bound was anchored on `MIN_W − 10`,
which was only ever a stand-in for the crossing, and the fix moved the crossing to the other side of
it; it is anchored on the measured 194.5 now. Asserting `hovered_name_room(MIN_W, 4) == 15.5` instead
would pin the *slack* rather than the property and would fail on any retune that kept the picture
right.

⚠️ **This is `panel_width_tests`' own `//!` inverted.** That module says *"a derivation nothing
re-runs is a number that stops being true the first time a row is retuned"*, and it was built to catch
a retuned row: every term in `hovered_name_room` is the constant the row walk itself draws with. What
it could not catch is a wrong **first** term. Before the fix, retuning the header's gutter moved three
assertions about the tree and retuning the tree's own gutter moved none of them — which is the module
measuring something no row is drawn from, with all of its arithmetic composed correctly.

**D443 — A span's attribute is canonicalized on the way in, and the *Mixed* symptom it was filed under
does not reproduce. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-07; Keep.***

`Length::canonical` rounds to four places so that span coalescing can use exact equality (§5.4), and
its doc comment said every constructor path went through it — *"the setters below, the scale tool, and
IO on load, so a hand-edited file cannot smuggle a value that defeats coalescing"*. **Nothing in `io/`
calls it.** `TextStyle` and `Spans<A>` are plain `#[derive(Deserialize)]`, so serde builds them field
by field and never calls a constructor, and a hand-edited
`"letter_spacing":{"Em":0.020000000000000004}` survived the load exactly as written.
`Spans::from_parts`'s doc made the same claim from the other side — *"IO's way in"* — and has no
caller outside its own file. Two comments describing a guard at two functions the loader never
touches.

**`Spans::clamped` is the seam, and it was already the right one.** It is the loader's single pass
over every span (`io::schema`), and `op_set_text` and `op_set_text_style` call it too, which is D422's
two-doors finding reused rather than rediscovered. It now puts every span's attribute through a new
free `canonical_attr`, which round-trips the value through `SpanAttr::set_on` into a clone of the
defaults and reads it back with `SpanAttr::from_defaults`. **That is the only way to canonicalize an
attribute without a per-variant list**, and it needs no maintenance: `set_on` is documented as
canonicalizing *"exactly as that scope's own setter does"* — because it **is** that setter — so a
variant added to `CharAttr` or `ParaAttr` is covered the moment its `set` arm is written.

⚠️ **The review's stated symptom does not reproduce, and the correction is the useful half.**
`[S6.1-L3-05]` filed this as the panel reporting **Mixed** for a node whose letter spacing is one
value to sixteen decimal places — `shared_in` answering `None`. It does not. `values_in` reads each
cut through `Spans::resolve`, which applies `set_on`, and `set_on` canonicalizes; so the *read* path
was always immune, and `shared_in` answers `Some(Em(0.02))` with the two spans still unmerged. What is
actually lost is `Spans`' own invariant (2) — *"two spans of the same `Kind` never overlap or touch
while carrying equal values"* — so the stored list fragments and every save writes two spans where the
document has one value. Smaller, and still real.

**The flip is how that was found.** Restoring `attr: s.attr.clone()` in `clamped`'s map bit on the
**span count**, `left: 2 right: 1`, and not on the `shared_in` assertion the predicted site named.
That assertion is kept in `a_hand_edited_span_value_is_canonicalized_on_the_way_in` deliberately: it
is the thing that stays green under the flip, and therefore the standing record that this bug is not
the *Mixed* bug.

**The residue, stated rather than assumed away:** the *defaults themselves* are not canonicalized.
Closing that needs a list of every `Kind`, which is the hand-maintained enumeration `canonical_attr`
exists to avoid, so a span whose canonical value equals such a default fails to elide. It cannot
produce the *Mixed* symptom either, that one coming from two spans rather than from a span and a
default.

⚠️ **`canonical_attr`'s own doc comment still states the symptom as fact** — *"the panel reported
**Mixed** for a node whose letter spacing is one value to sixteen decimal places"* — where the test's
doc carries the correction. **Fix the comment**: it is the paragraph a future reader will trust about
what this function is for, and it is a copy of the claim this entry exists to retire.

**D442 — A *Fix* verdict in §15.0 is restruck when the fix lands, not left asking. *Resolved for the
three; the convention is Keep.***

Three index lines were still asking for work that had been done for a fortnight — D334's for the three
readers measuring `world_bounds` where they wanted `ink_bounds`, D335's for a `snapshot_version` bump,
D336's for a recount — and in every case **the entry's own body already reported it done**. D334's
readers were swept on 2026-08-24, the day the entry was written. D335's bump landed the same day the
entry did, and by the time anyone read the index line the constant had gone two versions further under
D400, so the verdict was asking for a number that was history twice over. D336's count had gone nine →
ten → **eleven**.

**The mechanism is that a verdict is stored twice.** The body is what whoever does the work amends,
because it is what they were reading; the index line is a second copy of the same verdict a thousand
lines away, and nothing in this file connects the two — no gate reads either. So a *Fix* rots in
exactly one direction. It never becomes more urgent; it becomes a request for work that is finished,
which is worse than a stale fact, because it reads as a live instruction to the next person who opens
§15.0 looking for something to pick up.

**The convention: a *Fix* that has been fixed is restruck rather than deleted.** The line keeps the
deviation, states the date the fix landed, and says how long it stood open — because *"this asked for
work that was already done"* is itself the finding, and a deleted line takes the evidence away with
the error. D334's line is the model. The standing check is one command, now at the head of §15.0:
`grep -nE '^- \*\*D[0-9]{1,3}\*\*.*\*Fix\*' docs/decisions.md`, and for each hit **read the body
before believing the index**.

⚠️ **The sweep is for the *claim*, not for the entry, and that is the half the finding did not have.**
D334's stale verdict was mirrored in **four passages of `architecture.md`** — §5.9's bounds bullet,
both of §6.3's, and §7's `raster_size`/`raster_opts` paragraph — every one asserting that culling
reads `world_bounds`, two of them as an *open defect*, all of them for a fortnight after it had
stopped being true. The finding named two of the four. So restriking an index line closes the entry
and not the claim: grep the **sentence** the verdict was about, wherever it is written, because a
verdict quoted into the design document is a third and a fourth copy of the same rotting thing.

**D441 — Every font request has a deadline. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

`ureq::Agent::new_with_defaults()` sets **no timeout of any kind**. Read from `ureq-3.3.0`'s
`impl Default for Timeouts`: `global`, `per_call`, `resolve`, `connect`, `send_request`, `send_body`,
`recv_response` and `recv_body` are all `None`, and only `await_100` has a value. So a server or
middlebox that accepts the connection and then stops sending — a captive portal, a hung transparent
proxy, an idle-but-open socket — blocked `read_to_vec()` indefinitely. The worker never returned from
`load_face`, never popped another job, and was gone for the session.

**`WORKERS` is 6 and `prefetch_popular` dispatches fifty jobs at the first poll after the catalog
lands**, so six concurrent stalls at launch are one bad network away. From then on nothing loads at
all — the document's own fonts on the urgent lane included. Every family sits at `Pending` because
`outstanding > 0`, so §5.4a's missing-font warning never fires, the picker's loading dots pulse for
ever, and quitting is the only recovery. `fetch_catalog` goes through the same `download`, and a stall
there leaves `catalog_done` false for ever, which by `status_of`'s own precedence — `!sources_settled`
outranking everything below it — pins every family at `Pending` by a second route. The `.limit(64 MiB)`
on the body bounds **bytes**, which a stall never reaches; the only bound left was the OS connect
timeout, which covers a blackholed connect and not a stalled body.

**Four deadlines, and the global one is not redundant.** `timeout_connect` covers a blackholed SYN,
`timeout_recv_response` a peer that accepts and never answers, `timeout_recv_body` a body that stops
mid-stream — and `timeout_global` covers the shape none of them does, a peer dribbling one byte at a
time, which resets a per-read deadline for ever. It is end-to-end from the DNS lookup onward.

**Generous rather than tight (15 s / 30 s / 60 s / 120 s).** These are not latency budgets: a CJK
family's default subset is megabytes per weight, and a slow connection downloading a real file must not
be cut off. **The number that matters is that they are finite** — the failure being fixed is unbounded,
not slow — which is also why `every_request_deadline_is_finite` asserts `is_some()` rather than the
values, so tuning one does not break it.

⚠️ **`FontService::inert` built its own agent with `new_with_defaults` too**, which is the shape a
second construction always takes: a guard added at one site and missing at the other. Both go through
`fn agent` now, and the test asserts both.

Flip-check, run: `new_with_defaults()` in `agent()` fails at *"shared agent has no connect deadline:
None"* — naming which deadline is missing rather than only that one is.

**D440 — *Snap to grid* governs the five gestures that go through `snap_point`. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

Open the top bar's **Snap** menu, switch *everything* off — shapes, guides, baselines and grid — then
drag a resize handle, a line endpoint, a pen anchor, a path point or a path segment. Every one of them
still landed on a whole world unit. At 8× zoom that is a visible click onto a lattice the user has
turned off, and a fractional resize was unreachable by hand.

**Three of the four pixel-fallback sites consulted the toggle and one did not.** `snap_rect` writes
`if s.pixel && axes.0`, `snap_guide` writes `None if s.pixel =>`, `canvas::axial_corner` writes
`if self.snap_grid` — and `canvas::pen_point`'s own doc quotes that last guard verbatim,
*"`axial_corner` still rounds along the constrained direction **when the grid is on**"*. Meanwhile
`Snapping::pixel`'s own field doc calls it *"Whether an axis nothing else claimed falls to the
whole-pixel lattice — *Snap to grid*"*, and `canvas::snapping` fills it straight from the menu
(`pixel: self.snap_grid`). Creation's own rounding, `canvas::pixel_point`, asks as well. So the field
documented itself correctly, every other rounding site in the app honoured it, and the fourth reader
ignored it — §9.4's rule that the grid is the Snap menu's to switch off was right the whole time.

**One word each in two `else if`s**, because the arms are separate and a fix to one would look right in
a single-axis probe. Five production callers reach `snap_point`: `snapped_resize`, `line_end_tx`, and
the pen, point and segment drags.

⚠️ **`each_snap_source_can_be_switched_off_independently` names the three toggles and drives only
`snap_rect`.** That is how the switches came to read as pinned everywhere while one gesture in five
ignored one of them; `a_dragged_point_falls_to_the_grid_only_when_the_grid_is_on` is the same assertion
over the point path, and the grid-*on* case in it is the control — this is a toggle being honoured, not
a rounding being removed.

Flip-check, run per arm: dropping `s.pixel` from the **y** arm fails at the very first assertion,
`(102.4, 204.0)` against `(102.4, 203.6)`. ⚠️ **The predicted failure site was the single-axis
assertion further down and it never runs** — the first assertion compares both coordinates as a pair,
so it catches either arm, and the single-axis pair below it is there for the *locked*-axis rule rather
than as a second witness to this one.

**D439 — A container lands in the topmost member's slot, on all five verbs. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

Every container builder landed the new container in the **bottom-most** member's slot. Three siblings
`back`/`mid`/`front`, index 0 being the bottom of the stack: select `back` and `front`, leave `mid`
out, press Ctrl+G, and the parent's children came back `[NEW, mid]` where the design says `[mid, NEW]`.
So `front` — the topmost of the three — ended up inside a container painted **behind** `mid`, and a
layer the user did not select jumped in front of one they did. Measured on all five verbs: `group`,
`frame`, `boolean` and `flatten_union` each carried a literal copy of the same four lines, and `mask`
reaches them through `group`.

**The two rules differ only when the selection has a gap in it**, which is why this was never seen and
why both tests named for the rule are vacuous. `group_takes_the_z_position_of_its_topmost_member`
groups a *contiguous* pair that includes the top of the stack, and
`a_frame_takes_the_z_position_of_its_topmost_member` frames a *single* member — bottom-most and topmost
give the same answer in both. That is this project's own second vacuity shape, *an assertion the wrong
version also produces*.

**The design was never ambiguous**, which is what makes this a defect rather than a deviation. D286
states the rule where `build::mask` reuses `build::group` — *"the placement rule that lands the
container where the topmost member was"* — §9.4 states it for `build::flatten`'s two-or-more arm, and
**both function doc comments said it too** while the code under them did the opposite. There was
nothing to decide: the document was right and had been right all along.

⚠️ **The tell was dead code beside the bug.** `siblings[..first_pos].iter().filter(|c|
!unique.contains(c)).count()` can never drop an element under `position` — by the definition of
`position`, nothing in `siblings[..first]` is a member — so the filter could not do anything at all. It
is only meaningful against `rposition`, which is to say **the expression was written for the topmost
member and half of it was wrong**. All four copies carried the same dead filter, which is what four
copies do.

One `container_slot` function now rather than four literal copies of four lines, for the reason
`is_paintable` gives one file down: a rule spelled four times is a rule that gets fixed three times.

⚠️ **`frame`'s doc cited D249 for the placement rule and D249 does not contain it.** That entry is
about why `frame` is `group`'s sibling rather than a flag on it — the box, the parent predicate,
whether frames may be members — and says nothing about z-position. It cites D286 now. **The code was
wrong for exactly as long as the citation was**, which is worth a sentence: a citation that does not
resolve to the rule it is offered for is not a formatting defect, it is a reader left with no way to
check the code against anything.

Flip-check, run: `position` for `rposition` reports **all five** verbs in one failure, each
`got [front, mid], want [mid, front]`. ⚠️ **And the other 85 tests in `tests/build.rs` stay green under
that flip** — including `group_then_ungroup_round_trips_world_positions` and
`ungroup_splices_children_back_in_place`, the densest z-order users — which is the measurement that
says the coverage was vacuous rather than merely thin.
`a_container_takes_the_topmost_slot_even_when_the_selection_has_a_gap` collects all five results and
asserts once, deliberately: five separate `assert_eq!`s abort on the first, and "the other four" is the
whole reason the test names five verbs.

**D438 — The SVG `fill-rule` is written on both arms that write a fill. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06;
Keep.***

The rule was written on `emit_shape`'s single-element arm only. `emit_stacked` — the arm taken
whenever the paints do not fit one element, which means more than one fill, an alignment clip, or a
letterbox — built its fill attribute with `paint_attr` alone. So whether an even-odd shape exported as
even-odd depended on **how many paints it happened to have**, which is not a property anybody would
think to check.

**The reachable case is a `Boolean` with `BoolOp::Exclude`**, whose rule `Node::fill_rule` derives as
even-odd unconditionally (§15 D239). Give one an inside or an outside stroke — an ordinary thing to do
— and the shape leaves the plain arm, so the export read its outline as **non-zero, which for a
symmetric difference is a union**: every hole filled in, while the canvas drew it correctly. Same
document, two pictures, and nothing anywhere saying so. That is the one divergence §3 exists to
prevent, arriving through a condition that has nothing to do with the rule.

One spelling now, `with_fill_rule(fill, node)`, called by both arms, so there is no second place for
the attribute to be forgotten. ⚠️ **The suite's `an_exclusion_exports_the_even_odd_rule` exercised
only the arm that was already correct** — one fill, no stroke, and a negative half that is also the
plain arm — which is the shape of a test that names a rule and tests one of its two doors (review
group G19). It now covers a second fill **and** an aligned stroke, because those are *different*
conditions in `emit_shape`'s `plain` computation and a fix written inside one branch of that
computation would have satisfied only one of them. ⚠️ **The flip was re-run with the first new
assertion disabled**, because a test that aborts on its first case says nothing about its second: the
stroke case then fails on its own, which is what says both conditions really do reach `emit_stacked`.

**D437 — The CPU backend skips type it cannot paint instead of reusing the last paint. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

`apply_paint` answers `false` for "the brush resolved to nothing" — a fill whose image the store has
no pixels for — and its own doc says the caller skips the draw. `fill_path` and `stroke_path` beside
it both return on it; `draw_text` called it as a **statement** and dropped the answer. `vello_cpu`'s
paint is *context state*, so that did not draw the text in nothing: it drew the run in whatever the
last `set_paint` had left there, which is **the previous node's colour**. Measured as a word rendered
in the preceding rectangle's red, 3008 px of it, through `ondin export --png` — and since the CPU
backend is the reference, every golden agreed with it.

The GPU backend already had the guard, and its comment states the rule this one broke: type filled
with an unresolvable image draws nothing, exactly as a shape's stroke does (§15 D179, §6.3). So this
is **"a guard that exists next door and not here" twice over** — next door in the sibling method of
the same file, and next door in the sibling backend.

⚠️ **The test's assertion is the colour, not the pixel count.** "The text drew nothing" and "the text
drew in some other colour" are both plausible right answers to a count, and only *whose* red the
glyphs came out in says the paint leaked from the node before.

**D436 — A boolean carrying an effect pops the layer it pushed. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06;
Keep.***

`paint_node` pushes a node's effect layer near the top of the function and pops it at the very **end**
of it. The `Boolean` arm returns from the middle, because a boolean's children are operands rather
than artwork and the walk must not descend into them. That arm went through the `close` helper — which
unwinds the clip/opacity layer and ends any mask run — and carried a `debug_assert!(!outer_opacity,
…)` showing that the outer opacity layer had been audited too. **The effect layer is the fourth, and
it is the one that was missed.**

So a drop shadow on a boolean, an ordinary inspector action, made **the boolean and every layer
painted after it** disappear — from the canvas and from `ondin export --png` alike, because both share
the walk. Everything afterwards was drawn inside a layer whose bounds were the boolean's own ink box
and which was never composited. Measured at 11 200 px → 0 with an unrelated sibling at 2 304 px → 0;
the same effect on a `Rect` balances and draws, which is what makes this the early `return` rather
than `any_ink` or `effect_bounds`.

**Not moved into `close`.** That helper is called from three other places inside the children loop,
where the effect layer must stay open: it is the whole node's, not the run's, and folding it in would
close it at the first mask boundary.

⚠️ **`paint_ghost`'s identical arm leaks two layers and is unwound as well, though it cannot fire
today.** `geometry::local_path` answers `None` for `Boolean`, so `ghost_effects` is always `None`
there — which is a fact about a function two modules away rather than about this arm, and the day a
ghost boolean gets a path it would become the same bug in the preview. The unwind is written rather
than argued away.

⚠️ **The test asserts the sibling first.** A boolean that vanishes reads as "the effect is broken",
which is a guess a reader can make without any of this; a boolean that takes an unrelated rectangle
with it is a different bug and is the one that was happening.

**D435 — A font axis with a reversed or non-finite range is usable rather than fatal. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

A `.ttf` whose `fvar` `opsz` axis record carries `minValue > maxValue` registers cleanly. `skrifa`
returns the raw `AxisRecord` Fixed values with no validation of any kind, and fontique's own parse is
not a filter either — so the file goes in, and the **next `text::layout` of any text node** panicked
with *"min > max, or either was NaN. min = 200.0, max = 32.0"*. `f64::clamp` is an `assert!`, so this
fires in **release** as readily as in debug.

⚠️ **It is not hostile-only and it needs no unusual document.** The guard on that path is
`optical_size_is_auto`, which is the default, so every ordinary text node was armed the moment such a
family was registered; `register_fonts` is fed by the machine's own system fonts and by downloaded web
faces. And if the *document's* family is that font it fires at every launch, including through
`library::cover::rasterize`, which rebuilds every document the dashboard grid draws — the same seam
§15 D422 and D423 land on, reached without a click.

Two changes, and the second is the one that generalises. **`FontAxis::from_fvar` is now the one place
a `FontAxis` is built from a file.** There were two, `family_axes` and `family_axes_locked`, differing
only in where the axis name comes from — the divergence this project's own `is_paintable` comment
predicts — so a guard added to one would simply have been missing from the other. It orders the ends,
replaces a non-finite end with the other, and pulls the `default` inside the range: `fvar` does not
promise the default lies between the ends any more than it promises the ends are in order. And
**`FontAxis::clamp` replaces `f64::clamp` at both readers** — `text::axis_settings` and the typography
panel's `opsz` Manual switch — because the fields are `pub` and a later reader of `fvar` could skip
the constructor entirely.

⚠️ **Both halves of `ordered` are load-bearing and they are different failures.** A reversed pair
panics `clamp`; a `NaN` end panics it too, and `f64::min`/`f64::max` **return `NaN` for a pair of
them** rather than filtering it out — so ordering alone would have left the second case open while
looking complete. Both flips were run, and **both were mis-predicted in the same direction**: each
fails one line *earlier* than expected, inside `from_fvar` itself, with the finding's own panic
message verbatim, because the constructor is a second reader of its own range.

**D434 — A raster size the renderer can actually take, on every axis and after the pad. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

Three defects and one sentence: **an area cap cannot see a per-side limit, and the size that is capped
is not the size that is rendered.**

**The clamp handed the renderer the one number it panics at.** `MAX_RASTER_SIDE` was `u16::MAX`, which
is *exactly* the value `vello_common` documents as the viewport size it cannot take —
`snap_to_tile_coordinates` carries a comment saying so in as many words. So the clamp that exists to
prevent a panic caused one: `ondin export --png --width 65535` aborted, and so did a plain 1× export
of a document whose one rect is `1e30` wide — **no flag involved, only geometry a `.ondin` can
carry**, since `io::load` accepts it and `op_set_geometry` does not bound a size. `viewport_at`'s own
doc promised the opposite (*"the honest failure is a smaller file than was asked for rather than a
panic inside the renderer"*), so the promise was true of everything except the number it clamped to.
**This amends §15 D274**, whose §7 wording — *"the pixel count is capped at the CPU rasterizer's `u16`
per side"* — is now wrong, and §7 is corrected with it.
