The new value is `511 × 128 = 65408`, and **both factors are vello's**. `vello_cpu`'s depth buffer
holds one bucket per `DEPTH_BUCKET_WIDTH = 128` pixels and `bucket_span` computes a run's pixel span
as `index as u16 * DEPTH_BUCKET_WIDTH`, so the highest bucket index that cannot overflow a `u16` is
511 and the widest buffer that cannot produce a higher one is `511 × 128`. That also clears the second
site: `snap_to_tile_coordinates`'s `checked_next_multiple_of(Tile::WIDTH)` needs a side of at most
65532, and 65408 is already a multiple of 4. ⚠️ **Neither vello constant is public**, so the number
cannot be derived at compile time and a vello upgrade can silently invalidate it —
`a_raster_at_the_cap_renders_on_either_axis` renders at exactly this side on both axes and is the only
thing that would go red.

**The pad's own multiply overflowed, and release was the worse half.** `padded_square` computed `side
* side * 4` in **`u32`**, which overflows at `side == 32768`. A 4096×64 banner at 8× is a 32768×512
raster of 131 KB — an ordinary export set — and *Pad to square* on it killed the whole `--all` run
before a single file was written, because `run_export_all` renders everything before it writes
anything. In debug that was a multiply-overflow panic; in release the product wrapped to **exactly
0**, `vec![0u8; 0]` was allocated, and the copy ran off the end one line later with a slice message
naming neither the file nor the size. Every other size computation in the module widens first; this
was the one that did not, and it is now a named `square_bytes(side)` so the multiply can be asserted
against a number. ⚠️ **The result is still unbounded** — a square at `MAX_RASTER_SIDE` is 17 GB and
nothing refuses it — which is a *size* decision rather than an arithmetic one, is left to
`[S8.2-L5-05]`, and is stated in the code.

**The Export panel's row preview reached both panics**, because `MAX_PREVIEW_PX` is an area cap and
neither failure is about area: the ratios needed are only ~1074:1 and ~273:1. It squares the pair when
`pad_square` is on — the plan reports the *framed* size and `raster_of` pads *after* the guard, so the
guard never saw the number that overflowed — **and** tests each side against `ctx.input(|i|
i.max_texture_side)`. ⚠️ **That second test is a defect the review did not have, and it was found by
writing the first half's control and watching it crash**: a 32768×120 raster is 3.9 M pixels, under
the area cap, and `ctx.load_texture` panics outright — *"Texture "export-preview" has size 32768x120,
but the maximum texture side is 2048"*. The number is the **device's**, read off the context rather
than written down, since it is whatever wgpu reports on the machine the app is running on. All of this
runs inside `eframe::App::update`, where there is no `catch_unwind` anywhere in the app.

**D433 — The name search wraps at `u32::MAX` instead of panicking out of a duplicate. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

Rename a layer to `Rectangle 4294967295` and press `Ctrl+D`. `copy_name` starts the search at
`n.saturating_add(1)`, which at `u32::MAX` saturates to a number that is **already taken** — the
original's own name, which `CopyNames::rename` puts in `taken` because `child_names(parent, &[])`
excludes nothing. So `free_name` found it and ran `n += 1`: an **overflow panic out of core, on the UI
thread, during an ordinary duplicate**, taking whatever was unsaved with it. Release did not panic and
answered `"Rectangle 0"`, a name `numbered` documents as impossible and refuses to parse, so the copy
was mis-classified as hand-typed for the rest of its life. Both measured, in both profiles. A second
reachable spelling needs no `u32::MAX` in the *typed* name at all: `X 4294967294` beside a sibling
`X 4294967295`.

⚠️ **The doc comment's own bound argument was the drift, and it is why nobody looked.** *"A parent
would need four billion children to exhaust it"* is true of `created_name`, whose `from` is always 1,
and **false of `copy_name`**, whose `from` is parsed out of a string the user typed — the loop needs
one iteration. That paragraph is rewritten rather than deleted, because the reasoning it replaced is
the thing that has to stop being persuasive.

The search wraps to 1, which is `created_name`'s own rule and produces a name in the series: a copy
would rather sit just above its original, but at `u32::MAX` there is no "just above" to have, and the
next best answer is the one a fresh layer would get. The final line — reachable only if all four
billion names are taken, which no `taken` that fits in memory can be — answers a **duplicate**, which
is legal here (§5.7b, §15 D127: uniqueness is never load-bearing) rather than a name the parser
rejects.

Both flips run: `n += 1` fails in debug with *"attempt to add with overflow"* and in release at *"a
name the parser can read back: \"Rectangle 0\""*, which is why the parser assertion is not decoration.

**D432 — A read-only document's trash retention starts when it is deleted. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

The Windows read-only attribute refuses exactly **one** of the three steps a delete takes, and it is
the middle one. Measured rather than reasoned: `fs::rename` into `.trash` is allowed; `fs::remove_file`
is allowed too, Rust's implementation clearing the attribute and retrying; and the
`OpenOptions::write(true).open` inside `trash_stamp` is `PermissionDenied` — and *its* result was the
one being discarded. So the trashed copy kept the mtime of its last **edit**, the stamp being the
retention clock, and a document deleted after a year untouched was permanently removed by the very
next sweep while the Trash screen's own heading said *"kept for 30 days"*. Nothing was reported at any
point.

⚠️ **`trash`'s own comment argued the wrong way.** *"Errs towards purging it sooner — never towards
keeping something the user asked to go"* reads as a safe direction to fail in, and it is not: §9.5
calls the trash the library's **only** undo, so a document silently and permanently deleted is the one
outcome this feature exists to prevent. That comment is corrected in place rather than removed, since
the sentence is what made the discarded result look deliberate.

The attribute is cleared for the length of the touch and the **original `Permissions` object** is put
back — not `set_readonly(true)`. A document is marked read-only to protect it, and restoring one from
the trash must give back the file the user had, protection included; on Unix `set_readonly(true)`
would mean 0o444 and drop write permission from a group that had it. `owner_may_write` is cfg-split
for the mirror of that reason: `set_readonly(false)` means **0o666**, world-writable, on Unix whatever
the file's mode was, so the Unix arm sets `mode | 0o200` and only the Windows arm touches the single
bit. (clippy's `permissions_set_readonly_false` is what named this; it fired on the first draft.)
Setting permissions does not touch the mtime, so the stamp survives the restore call.

What is still discarded is the *unmeasured* remainder, and it is discarded deliberately: the delete
has already succeeded, and reporting it as a failure would be a lie about a file that has moved.

**D431 — A migration that cannot move a file renames it or says so. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06;
Keep.***

`merge_tree` had one collision rule — skip — and it was only ever argued for `.versions`, where a path
is `<document id>/<unix seconds>.ondin` and a collision really is the same document at the same
instant. The same line applied to `.trash` **strands a document**: `store::trash` uniquifies within
one folder and knows nothing about any other, so two libraries can each hold a `notes.ondin` that are
different documents. The source's was left in a folder the app no longer reads, **not counted in
`failed`**, under a status line saying *"Moved 2 file(s)"* — and `purge_trash` only ever reads the
current root, so it could not be swept either.

Three policies now, one per tree, with the argument for each written at its `Collision` variant rather
than at the loop:

- `.versions` → `Identical`. Skip, silently. Nothing is lost.
- `.trash` → `Rename`. The arrival takes a suffix through the same `naming::unique_stem` that
  `store::trash` and `store::file_document` already use within one folder.
- `.recovery` → `Stranded`. Left where it is and **counted in `failed`**, so the summary says so.

⚠️ **The renaming is what makes the third one different.** A snapshot's stem *is* the document id it
belongs to: `recovery::pending` matches on it, and `recovery::remove` refuses a stem that is not a
minted id — so a `<id>-1.ondin` would be offered to the user and then be **undiscardable**, which is
worse than being left behind and told about. A collision there needs two libraries holding one
document id, which is a hand-copied file rather than anything the app does.

⚠️ **The flip is the interesting half.** Setting `.trash` back to `Identical` fails at the file
assertion with the source document simply absent — and **`moved.failed` stays 0 under that flip**,
which is the silence the finding was actually about: the run that loses the file and the run that does
not are indistinguishable from the status line, so a test asserting only the counters would have been
green. The bodies are read as text so that a failure *names* what went missing.

**Fix, and it is not closed.** `scan::collect` skips any entry whose `file_name().to_str()` is `None`,
so a `.ondin` whose Windows filename is not valid Unicode is invisible to the migration too — the same
loss by a different door. That half of the finding was never reproduced, is not fixed, and is on the
roadmap rather than here. ⚠️ **It was reproduced on 2026-09-19 and it is fixed — see D809**, which
carries such a file across by its `OsStr` name and counts it when it cannot. This paragraph is the
statement of the defect and stands; its *"never reproduced"* and *"is not fixed"* clauses are spent.

**D809 — A `.ondin` whose filename is not valid Unicode: reproduced, and the migration carries it now.
*Reproduced, fixed and tested 2026-09-19; Keep — narrower than either fix the roadmap offered.***

D431 closed the `.trash` half of this shape and named the other in its own last paragraph.
`scan::collect` skipped any entry whose `file_name().to_str()` is `None`, so such a document was
invisible to the library **and to the migration**: *Change base folder* left it alone in a folder the app
no longer reads, **uncounted**, under a status line saying the move had succeeded. 🚨 **`roadmap.md`
carried it as *"never reproduced"*** — *"it is not established that a filename Windows accepts can fail
`to_str`"*, with the instruction *"reproduce first"*. **It has been.**

**The reproduction, on this machine, with a standalone probe.** A lone UTF-16 high surrogate is a legal
code unit and not a scalar value: `std::fs::write` on a path built from `OsString::from_wide(&[0xD800,
…])` **succeeds** on NTFS, and the entry `read_dir` hands back answers `None` to
`file_name().to_str()`. The same for a lone low surrogate and for a reversed pair. The controls — an
ASCII name and a well-formed astral pair — both answer `Some`. Nothing in this app can *create* such a
name; a sync client or another tool can.

**Neither of the two fixes the roadmap offered was taken, and the reason is the same in both
directions.** *Skip but count it* leaves the file alone in the folder the app has abandoned, which is
what `relocate::Collision::Stranded`'s own note calls the bad outcome. *Carry it by `OsStr` through
`scan::Entry`* would make `stem` an `OsString`, and **there is no honest label to draw for a name that
is not text**. What shipped is narrower than both: the document still stays out of the library's list,
and the **migration** carries it across verbatim.

`scan::collect` gained a second output and records a skipped entry when its extension is `ondin` —
compared as an `OsStr`, since the whole case here is a name with no `&str` to compare — and the entry is
a **file**, a directory called `<not unicode>.ondin` not being a document however unlikely. Everything
else about such an entry is unknowable from there: it is not read, so it is not known to *be* a
document, only to be shaped like one. `scan::unnameable(root)` runs the same `collect` and returns them
— **one walk and two outputs, by construction rather than by agreement** — so the two questions cannot
come to disagree about the two-level rule or about which dot-directories are skipped.

`library::relocate::relocate` moves each by its own `OsStr` name: no `naming::unique_stem` and no
re-derivation, there being no `&str` to derive from. ⚠️ **So a destination already holding that name is
a failure rather than a rename**, which is `Collision::Stranded`'s argument reached from a second
direction — one of these files cannot be told from another by looking, so the arrival is left where it
is and counted. ⚠️ **Moving it does not make it visible and deliberately does not try.** What the move
buys is that the file is where the user pointed their library, and that `Moved` says it went.

**Tests** `scan::tests::a_document_with_a_non_unicode_filename_is_not_listed_and_is_reported` and
`relocate::tests::a_document_with_a_non_unicode_filename_is_carried_across_and_counted`. The
platform-specific name is `scan::unnameable_doc_name`, `#[cfg(test)]` **beside** `unnameable` rather
than inside either test module, because two modules' tests need it and a platform fact spelled twice is
one that can come to disagree with itself. ⚠️ **The two arms are two different facts, not one fact
spelled twice**: on Windows a name is UTF-16 and the gap is an unpaired surrogate, on Unix it is bytes
and the gap is any byte that is not valid UTF-8. ⚠️ **The `#[cfg(unix)]` arm is compiled by nothing on
this machine** — the class `CLAUDE.md` lists four production functions in, with no gate for any of them
— so it is written to be read rather than trusted, and the measurement above is the Windows arm's.

§9.5's two-level scan paragraph carries the third rule now, and the bullet is struck from `roadmap.md`
with the clause in that section's table row.

**D430 — *Move my library* re-points the session through the path map, not a prefix swap. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.*** **The last of the codebase review's seven Criticals.**

`session.path` is absolute, so a migration left it naming a file in the folder the library had just
abandoned. The next save recreated the document *there* — while the new root already held the copy
`relocate` had carried across, with the same `meta.id`. Two files, one identity: the library listed
only the migrated copy, and every edit made after the move went to the one nothing lists.
`prefs.last_document` had the same problem one launch later, so *reopen last* would open the abandoned
file.

⚠️ **`relocate.rs`'s own module comment stated the opposite as settled fact.** *"A library moved
mid-session leaves the app writing into the new root on its next tick either way; what would be
stranded is a snapshot the user has not yet answered"* — which is true of the **snapshot**, since
`drop_recovery` re-reads `library.root` and the recovery key is the document id, and false of the
**document**, whose path is absolute and is re-read from nowhere.

⚠️ **A path map and not a prefix swap, and this is the part that is not obvious.** `relocate` renames
into a collision (`naming::unique_stem`), so `old/kestrel/notes.ondin` can arrive as
`new/kestrel/notes-1.ondin`; a caller re-joining the relative path under the new root would point the
session at a file that belongs to a **different document**. So `Moved` carries the `(from, to)` pairs,
`Moved::documents()` is *derived* from them rather than counted alongside — the status line and the
map cannot then disagree about which files went — and `Moved` loses `Copy`. Sidecars are deliberately
not in the map: nothing outside the module holds a path to a version file or a snapshot, both being
found by id.

Two flips run, each failing at an assertion the other leaves green. Deleting the re-point loop fails
at the session's path still naming the old root. Replacing the map lookup with
`strip_prefix(&old_root).join(&new_root)` fails with the two paths printed **identical** — a session
pointed at a stranger's file — which is why the test seeds a document of the same name at the
destination.

**D429 — The open document follows a library file that moves, in memory as well as on disk. *Fixed
and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

§15 D364 says *"renaming or deleting the open document moves the session with it"* and D379 says *"the
open document follows its folder exactly as it follows its file through a move"*. Both were half true.
Every one of these operations **edits the file**: `store::rename` writes a new `meta.name`,
`store::move_to_project` writes a new `meta.project`. The session's `Document` was never told, and it
is the session that the next save serializes — so re-pointing the path alone meant **the next save
undid the operation**, writing the old value back into the file the user had just moved. Measured on
*Move to project*: on disk `p-1` → `p-2` → `p-1`, after which the dashboard filed the card under the
project the user had moved it out of, **correctly**, because that is what the file said.

⚠️ **A second door, and a worse one.** `delete_project`'s follow was written `if session.path ==
Some(entry.path) && !keep_files { session.path = None }`, so on the **transfer** branch it did nothing
at all. The session went on naming a file in the deleted project's folder that no longer existed, the
next autosave recreated it there from a document still carrying the dead project id, and the library
then held **two files with one `meta.id`** — version history, the cover cache and `recovery::pending`'s
match are all keyed on that id, so all three began describing two files.

The fix is one helper, `OndinApp::open_document_follows`, rather than the two lines copied a third
time: the guard, the clone and the write-back are the part that must not diverge, and the patch is a
closure because only the field differs. Four call sites — `Act::MoveTo`, `commit_rename`,
`Act::Restore` and `delete_project`. ⚠️ **One of them, `Act::Restore`, is unreachable today and is
written anyway**: `trash_or_purge` sets `session.path = None` when it trashes the open document, so by
the time a restore runs there is no path left to match. That is a fact about a *different* function
twenty lines up, and the day it stops clearing the path that arm would silently become the rename bug
again. Checked, not assumed.

Both tests assert **the file after the next save** first and the in-memory metadata second, because
the loss is what the file says and the memory is only the mechanism. ⚠️ **The three existing transfer
tests were green throughout and always would be**: none of them opens a document, and everything about
the *files* was always right.

**D428 — A transaction that changes nothing is not an undo step. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06;
Keep.***

A completed interaction that turned out to change nothing committed a full undo step. Click into a
value field, type nothing, click away: undo depth 0→1, the document dirtied, autosave and the crash
snapshot fired, and `Ctrl+Z` appeared to do nothing and had to be pressed twice. A resize handle
pressed and released without moving does it. `commit_inner` dropped only *empty*
transactions, and a no-op transaction is not an empty one.

⚠️ **A third route was named here — *"a multi-row layers drop that lands rows where they already
are, which emits one net-zero `Reorder` per row"* — and this guard never covered it** (§15 D532).
The *net* is zero and the operations are not: each `Reorder` moves its row to an index it is not at
yet, so `changes_nothing` answers `false` for every one of them and is right to. The sentence was
wrong when it was written and §9.3 repeated it; the drop is guarded in `layers::plan_layer_move`
now, against the child lists that function already simulates. **A composition of real operations
that returns to where it started is a shape no per-operation test can see**, which is a limit on
this entry rather than a defect in it.

**Closed at one seam, not eleven.** The round that found this counted eleven broken sites across three
routes — click, type and drag — and three different per-door guards were proposed, none of them able
to cover the next door; there are of the order of a hundred doors. `Transaction::changes_nothing` is
asked once, at `commit_inner`, one line after the empty test.

The design of the guard:

- `Operation::changes_nothing(&self, doc: &Document) -> bool` is **exhaustively matched with no
  wildcard**, so a variant added later has to answer for itself rather than inherit a guess. `false`
  is the safe answer: a wrong `true` silently drops an edit, a wrong `false` only restores the
  behaviour the app already had.
- **An operation whose subject is missing answers `false`**, and so do the kind gates `apply`
  enforces — `SetFills`/`SetStrokes` on an unpaintable kind, `SetEffects` on the root. A commit that
  would have *failed* still fails and still reports; otherwise the guard would swallow the error
  instead of the edit.
- The four span-carrying arms compare **what `apply` would store**, not what the caller handed over.
  Every one of them clamps or re-states its list on the way in, so a `SetTextSpans` carrying a list
  the clamp brings back to the stored one is a no-op, and a `SetTextStyle { spans: None }` is a no-op
  when the stored list is already a fixed point of the re-statement.
- `SetGeometry` is asked of the **result** — `GeometryPatch::applied_to` compared against the node's
  kind — which makes one arm exact for all fourteen patch shapes and answers `false` for a patch that
  does not match the kind.
- ⚠️ **Equality is of the value written, not of the bytes stored.** `-0.0` and `0.0` compare equal,
  because nothing that reads the document can tell them apart; `NaN` compares equal to nothing, which
  is the useful direction, so a non-finite operation is never called a no-op and still reaches
  `OpError::NonFinite` (§15 D421).
- `Transaction::changes_nothing` is **all, not any**, and that is the whole specification. §9.4's
  *Hide* over a mixed selection emits a `SetVisible` per layer; the already-hidden ones are
  individually no-ops and the transaction as a whole hides something, so a per-op *filter* would break
  the case `set_switch`'s doc argues for at length. It is sound to test each operation against the
  document as it stands rather than against what its predecessors would leave, because if every
  predecessor changes nothing then the document it would see *is* this one. An **empty** transaction
  answers `false` — that is a different question, answered one line earlier at the commit seam.
- ⚠️ **The guard still calls `clear_gesture_preview`.** A no-op commit is the end of a gesture even
  though it is not an edit, and several callers rely on the commit to take a ghost off the canvas.
  Returning before that clear would trade an undo step for the stale-preview failure `commit_inner`
  is already annotated for (§15 D109, D316, D317), arriving by a new door.

⚠️ **It closed `[S23.1-L1-03]` and nothing said so for seven sessions.** That finding is the picker
ringing the palette chip whose colour is already in the slot — the ring means *"this is the one you
have"* — where a click measured `undo_depth 0 → 1` with the brush read back byte-identical. Its own
fix sketch named G16's single guard, which is this one, and this guard does absorb the door:
`Operation::changes_nothing`'s `SetFills` arm compares `n.paint().fills == *fills`, and the chip's
write is `paint::with_stops(brush, stops)` with an identical stop. It is **pinned** now by
`picker::grid_orphan_tests::a_palette_chip_already_in_the_slot_costs_no_undo_step`, driven at
`write_slot` — the single line the chip's click handler runs — rather than at a chip coordinate,
which would depend on how many distinct colours the fixture's palette happens to hold. Flipped by
disabling the guard at `commit_inner`: red at depth 1, with the control — a *different* colour
through the same door — green.

⚠️ **The general point is the price of this entry's own decision, and it is worth naming beside it.**
*A guard placed at a choke point closes doors nobody enumerates*, so the doors it closed are not
recorded anywhere and the next reader cannot tell a covered door from an uncovered one. That is how a
finding this guard had already answered sat open across seven sessions with a fix sketch pointing
straight at it. Closing at one seam rather than eleven is still right; what it costs is the
enumeration, and the only repair is a test at the door that names the entry.

Flip-checks run. `any` for `all` failed at the mixed-selection transaction assertion, as predicted.
⚠️ **The `Reorder` index "adjusted for the removal"** — `if index > old { index == old + 1 } else {
index == old }`, which is what somebody who has just read `op_reorder`'s remove-then-insert and
over-corrected writes — was predicted to fail on the *positive* half and failed on the **negative**
one: the over-correction does not break a row already where it is asked to be, it calls a real swap a
no-op, which is the worse failure of the two. Dropping `takes_paint` from the `SetFills` arm failed on
the root, as predicted. ⚠️ **And the app-side test first asserted `!can_undo`, which was vacuous** —
the fixture's own `add_rect` is an undo step, so the flip failed against the *fixture* rather than
against the guard; it now takes a depth before and compares after.

**D427 — `deps_forbidden` read a tree nothing builds, and `ondin-mcp` was never a subject at all.
*Fixed, widened and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

The test that enforces invariant 1 ran `cargo tree -p ondin-core`. Every gate that *compiles* core —
`build`, `test`, `clippy` — resolves the whole workspace, and with `resolver = "3"` feature
unification makes those two different closures of the same crate. Measured on core's own dependencies
rather than argued: `-p` reports `smallvec const_generics,const_new,serde` and `--workspace` reports
the same plus `union`, which `wgpu-hal` asks for and which reaches the build only through
`ondin-render`. So one member declaring `parley = { features = ["system"] }` would put a DirectWrite
binding into the closure core is compiled against and this test, reading core resolved alone, would
have stayed green. It walks `--workspace` now and cuts out the subtree under each subject node;
unification only ever *adds*, so the workspace closure is a superset and scanning it strictly
dominates. **One invocation and not two** — running cargo inside `cargo test` is the riskiest thing
the file does, and a second call is a second chance to contend for the package-cache lock.

**The prefix list was narrower than the rule it enforces, and it is matched by `starts_with`.** §3
says *"any GPU/windowing/UI crate"*; `"eframe".starts_with("egui")` is **false**, and so are `emath`,
`ecolor`, `epaint`, `epaint_default_fonts`, `glutin` and `raw-window-handle` — every one of them
really in the app's tree. `epaint` had a partial accidental backstop, pulling `vello_common`/`vello_cpu`
and so tripping the `vello` prefix, but that edge is version-contingent and the others had none at
all. The names are enumerated rather than inferred now.

⚠️ **`ondin-mcp` is the second subject, and §3 had always claimed about it the thing nothing
checked.** *"`ondin-mcp` contains no rendering or UI dependency"* was **false**: the crate declared
`ondin-export`, which reaches `ondin-render` and so vello, wgpu and naga. ⚠️ **That manifest line had
zero call sites**, as had `serde` and `serde_json` beside it — so deleting all three makes the
documented rule true at no cost, which is the option the review's own fix menu for that finding was
missing. **No gate in this workspace can see an unused dependency**: `unused_crate_dependencies` is a
rustc lint, allow-by-default, none of the five crate roots enables it, and clippy has no equivalent.
It cannot simply be switched on in that crate either — it fires per *target*, so a dependency used
only by a test or an example reads as unused, and this is an M0 scaffold whose `dead_code` is already
allowed. *Re-add a line to that manifest only with the `use` that needs it.*

**Flip-checked three ways, and the negative one is already standing.** Adding `"kurbo"` — a crate core
really depends on — fails with it named, so the subtree walk finds what is under a subject. Restoring
`ondin-export` to `ondin-mcp`'s manifest, the exact regression this now guards, fails with **sixteen**
crates named *(under ondin-mcp)*; two of them, `glutin_wgl_sys` and `raw-window-handle`, are ones the
original eight prefixes would have missed, which is the widening earning its keep on a real tree
rather than by argument. And **`"egui"` is in the list already** while `egui` is really in the
workspace tree under `ondin-app`, with the test green — so the walk excludes what is not under a
subject, and without that half the whole thing could have been scanning the workspace forest and
passing for the wrong reason. ⚠️ **An `unseen` assertion guards the parse**: a change to cargo's
`--prefix depth` format, a rename, or a `--workspace` that stopped including core would leave
`violations` empty and the assertion below it green.

**The right shape is an allowlist and it is not built.** §3 already enumerates what core *may* depend
on, so the test could assert the direct list is a subset of that and keep the prefixes for the
transitive tree. It was blocked on §3's own list being right — it omitted `roxmltree`, `skrifa`,
`read-fonts` and `flo_curves`, all really there — and baking a wrong allowlist in is worse than the
denylist it replaces. *Fix with the inversion: §3's list was corrected the same day this landed, so
the stated blocker is gone and the test's own doc comment still names it.*

**D426 — The library screen wrote 22 status messages and painted none of them. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

`EditorSession::status` is a single slot with a single production reader — `OndinApp::status_text`,
called from the *editor's* top bar, which sits below `OndinApp::ui`'s `View::Dashboard` return (§9.5).
So every failure `panels::dashboard` reported went nowhere: a *Delete project* that could not read
`projects.json` closed its confirmation, left the project in the sidebar and said nothing; a *Delete
files too* that failed to trash some members removed the row and left those documents on disk carrying
a project id nothing lists. ⚠️ **The message was not even cleared** — it surfaced later, out of
context, in the editor's top bar the next time a document was opened, which is worse than silence
because it attaches a library failure to a document.

**`app::status_label` is a free function and both top bars call it**, rather than the library
spelling its own. Two spellings would come to disagree about what a failure looks like, and there is
nothing about a status line that belongs to one screen. `max_w` is the only difference: the editor's
bar gives it whatever it needs, the library's has a search field painted across the middle of the same
46pt strip that a long message would otherwise run under. `truncate` rather than a wrap, the bar being
one line tall — a wrapped message is clipped mid-sentence with nothing to say it had been.

🚨 **That `max_w` is what D751 removed, and the two screens differ on purpose now.** Half the leftover
room beside a *painted* search field is a function of the **window** — 382pt at 1200, 22pt at 500,
zero at 436 — so the library's message shrank to an ellipsis and then to nothing. It draws
`app::status_dot` instead: a fixed box with the sentence on hover. What the paragraph above got right
is the part that survives, and it is the part worth keeping — *what a failure looks like* is one
statement, lifted into `app::status_color`, and only the surface forked.

⚠️ **This had to exist before D418's latches were worth having**, which is why the two landed
together: a `prefs.json` that cannot be read leaves the app running on defaults with `base_folder`
unset, i.e. an empty library, and without a sentence the user's obvious repair is to make a *second*
library beside the real one. The test drives both — a `fail`, then an `info`, then
`report_unreadable_records` — and asserts that an **empty** message returns the run count to the
control's, i.e. that the region is absent rather than present-and-blank, which is the version that
would pass a presence check while saying nothing.

🚨 **That test was re-aimed by D751 and the reason generalises: it read the sentinel out of
`galleys`, and a tooltip's ink never reaches `.shapes` at all.** With the library's surface a dot,
the assertion this entry is proudest of could no longer see the thing it was watching. It **splits**
rather than moving: `status_dot_color` says the screen is showing something and in which colour,
`session.status().text` says what the hover would read. ⚠️ **Asserting the text alone would be this
entry's own bug** — 22 messages went into a slot nothing drew for two months while a test on
`status().text` passed the whole time — so the dot assertion is what carries D426 forward, and the
empty control (a fresh session paints **no** dot) is what stops it being about nothing. **Both kinds
still, and it matters more now than it did**: the sentence is gone from that screen, so colour is the
only thing left on it separating a failure from a report.

**D425 — A `Length` field's px range is derived from its `%` range, and a range no longer rewrites the
document. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

Two field defects with one root — *a bound stated in the wrong place acts on the wrong thing* — and
they are one entry because the fix for each is a single line that reaches every field at once.

**There was exactly one px cap in the Type panel and nine fields used it.** `MAX_LINE_HEIGHT_PX =
10_000.0`, named for line height, bounded tracking, baseline shift, both decoration fields, the four
paragraph fields and line height — so **no field's two ends bounded the same quantity**, and the unit
chip that converts between them destroyed values. Measured: decoration thickness `Px(50)` at 16pt came
back as **32px**, letter spacing `Px(-100)` at 16pt as **−8px**, a **625×** disagreement at 8pt between
the two ends of one control. `Bounds` drops its `px` field entirely and `px_range_for(pct, font_size)`
derives it: `px = pct/100 × font_size` is exactly what `ondin_core::Length::in_unit` computes, so a
value legal at one end converts to a value legal at the other **by construction** rather than by two
constants happening to agree. The constant is deleted, not repaired — if a px cap is ever wanted that
is not the `%` cap in the other unit, it is a second quantity and wants naming as one. ⚠️ **The font
size is floored at 1**, because a multi-selection whose sizes disagree reports 0 and a range of
`0.0..=0.0` is a field that cannot be typed into at all, which reads as a broken control rather than as
a bound.

⚠️ **`both_ends_of_every_length_field_bound_the_same_quantity` was vacuous in its first draft and its
own flip said so.** With `Bounds::px` replaced by a hard-coded `±10_000`, every assertion stayed green:
the loop built its px face by calling `px_range_for` *directly* and never went through `Bounds` at all.
The first block now asserts that the `Bounds` faces **are** the shared derivation, which is what makes
the flip fail. It is driven through `Length::in_unit` rather than by comparing two ranges as numbers —
the arithmetic the field performs is the thing that has to land inside the bound — and over three font
sizes, because the disagreement is a function of font size and 16pt alone was only 62× apart, which
still reads as "large" rather than as "wrong". ⚠️ **Its honest scope**: it asserts the ranges are
coherent, not that every field asks for one, since `length_field`, `optional_length_field` and
`type_line_height_field` each call `px_range_for` inline and a `RangeInclusive` is a literal anyone can
write.

**The second half is egui's default, and it was rewriting documents.** `DragValue`'s
`clamp_existing_to_range` is `true` and applies on every frame, so a stored value outside a field's
range was silently pulled to the nearest end — and the `mark_changed` after it reported the widget's
own rewrite as a **user edit**, routing it through `edit_valve` into a transaction. An imported blur
radius of 1200 became 1000 on the frame the panel first drew it, with nobody touching anything.
`ui::value_field_f64` sets it `false`: **one line for all 82 numeric fields**, and none of them opts
out today (`grep clamp_existing_to_range` finds nothing outside egui), so this is where the decision is
made rather than a default any of them chose. It is §5.3's *"clamped where the outline is built … not
on the way in"* applied to the widget: a range bounds what a **gesture or a keystroke** can reach and
says nothing about what the document may hold.

⚠️ **Both of those clamps were on a *draft*, which is the third instance of the same shape and the one
that reached a user.** `NudgeStep::step` now clamps at the reader into `MIN..=MAX`, which is D349's own
ruling about this same file — *"a plain file that can be hand-edited, copied between machines or
written by a future version"* — made for the other ranged number in `prefs.json`. **The bad value is
not hypothetical: this build's predecessor wrote it.** The Settings field shipped as
`Scrub::fine(_, 2).range(0.01..=1000)` before somebody reported *"nudging by 0.1px is crazy"*, and
`Prefs` has no version field and no migration, so an upgraded install deserializes the stored `0.1`
verbatim. What the user then saw was the Settings field painting **1** — the modal clamps its draft —
over a document where an arrow key still moved 0.1px, and *Save changes* lit on a form nobody had
touched. Not clamped in `Prefs::load`, deliberately, for the same §5.3 reason as above.

**D424 — The canonicalizer manufactured the infinity it exists to prevent. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

`Length::canonical` rounds to `LENGTH_PLACES` decimals so that span coalescing can use exact equality
(§5.4). The obvious spelling of that, `(v × 10⁴).round() / 10⁴`, **turns a finite number into an
infinite one**: any `|v| > f64::MAX / 1e4 ≈ 1.7977e304` overflows in the multiply, and
`inf.round() / 1e4` is `inf`. Measured — `canonical(Px(1e304))` is finite, `canonical(Px(1e305))` is
`inf`. ⚠️ **The `is_finite` guard two lines above does not help, because it is asked of the *input*.**

That is a document that never opens again: `Px(inf)` is written by `serde_json` as `null` and refused
on the way back in. And it is reachable through the documented door — `Spans::set` routes every value
through the canonicalizer — which makes this the one position in the finiteness class (D421) where the
operation-level guard would be the **wrong** answer: it would report a refused letter-spacing edit for
a number the user is entitled to type. `round_to_places` returns such a magnitude unchanged, and that
is exact rather than approximate: at that size the gap between representable neighbours is
astronomically larger than `1e-4`, so there is no fractional part left to round. *The sanitizer that
produces the value it was written to exclude is the shape worth remembering; the guard was in the right
function and one statement too early.*

**D423 — `op_insert_subtree` refuses a set holding a node nobody lists as a child. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

The op walked *from each node to its listed children* — parent back-references, duplicates, kind rules
— and never asked the converse: whether every non-root node **is** somebody's child. `claimed` was
built and then thrown away. A node whose `parent` is in the set is not a root by the test at the top,
passes the single-root check, is inserted, and is listed by nobody: an orphan.

⚠️ **Reachable from the public API alone**, which is what makes it worth a line rather than a comment.
Two `capture_subtree` snapshots of the same node taken at different moments compose into exactly that
set — one of `P` before its child existed, one of the child `X` — with no `pub(crate)` access and no
hand-built `Node`. The state then panics `DeleteNode`, `Reparent` and `Reorder` at their three
`expect("child must be listed in its parent")` sites, and `io::save` succeeds onto a file whose `load`
fails with *"node(s) are not reachable from the root"*. **The loader has enforced this since it was
written** — check (5), the reachability walk — so the two doors into the tree were held to different
standards, which §5.11 says they must not be.

The fix is one comparison, `claimed.len() + 1 != nodes.len()`, and every production caller already
satisfies it: both `InsertSubtree` sites feed `remap_subtree` output from a single fresh capture. ⚠️
**That is also why the module's own premise was false rather than merely narrow** — its test doc calls
these "malformed subtrees the public API can never produce". What reaches this is anything that
*composes* captures: the MCP write surface, an importer, a multi-step builder, which is precisely the
traffic the model cannot vouch for. Flip: removing the guard leaves
`a_subtree_holding_an_orphan_is_refused` failing at the first assertion — `apply` returns `Ok` — and
the `DeleteNode` assertion below it then **panics** rather than failing, which is the invariant-8 half
and the more legible symptom of the two.

**D422 — A span is clamped onto character boundaries, not merely into the content. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

A `.ondin` with `content: "aéb"` and a span of `0..2` — byte 2 being *inside* the `é`, which occupies
bytes 1..3 — loaded with no complaint and then panicked on **every render**: `text::cased_text` slices
`content[range]` directly, and one line later parley's style builder does the same. Both are
`ondin-core`'s own runs, so the early return for `TextCase::Original` is not a guard; it only moves
which of the two fires.

**The blast radius is the dashboard.** `library::cover::rasterize` loads and rebuilds every document
the grid draws, synchronously inside the egui pass and with no `catch_unwind` anywhere on the path — so
one such file in the base folder crashes the app at every launch, and `Cover::Failed` never records it
because a panic does not get that far. That is D416's delivery route a second time, and by a different
defect.

⚠️ **`Spans::clamped` takes the *content* rather than its length, and that is the fix rather than a
convenience.** The magnitude clamp cannot *create* an off-boundary index — `len` is always a boundary —
but it could not repair one either. Snapped **outward** rather than dropped, which keeps §5.11's stated
posture (*"a stale range is a hand-edit or an older writer's rounding, not a corrupt tree"*) and keeps
the styling the file asked for over the whole character it half-named; a span that collapses is then
dropped by `normalize`, which already retains only `start < end`. ⚠️ **And this function is the only
correct site**: `op_set_text` and `op_set_text_style` call it too, so a repair placed at the loader
alone would have left the live-editing route open — the same two-doors finding as D423, in the one
subsystem where the second door is reached by typing.

**D421 — Finiteness is a validated property of the model, and the loader deliberately does not check
it. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

`NaN` and infinity had no refusal anywhere. A non-finite coordinate survives `apply`, survives `save`,
and kills `load` **permanently** — `serde_json` writes it as `null` and the reader has no arm for it —
so the file is lost through autosave and the crash snapshot as readily as through `Ctrl+S`. Invariant 8
is where the check belongs, because the operation is the last place the value can be rejected while the
user still has their work.

`OpError::NonFinite` is the new refusal; `NodeKind::geometry_is_finite`, `GeometryPatch::is_finite` and
`build::affine_is_finite` are the three predicates, and seven doors ask one of them — `op_create`,
`op_insert_subtree`, `apply_geometry_patch`, `op_set_transform`, and all three guide writers
(`op_add_guide`, `op_set_guide_position`, `op_set_guide_scope`), *not only the one the finding named*.
`GeometryPatch::is_finite` is matched **exhaustively on purpose**, so a variant added later has to
answer the question rather than defaulting to "fine". **Refused rather than repaired**, unlike an
out-of-range opacity on the load path: there is no defensible number to clamp a coordinate to — 0 moves
the shape, `f64::MAX` is not what was meant — and unlike a stale text span there is no repairable file
at stake yet, the value not having been written. `no_operation_may_write_a_number_that_is_not_finite`
drives all seven and asserts the document's **bytes** are unchanged after each refusal, since "returns
`Err`" and "changed nothing" are two claims and `apply` mutates a working copy as it goes. ⚠️ **It was
`…_a_coordinate_…` until 2026-09-07**, when D451 added `op_set_fills` and `op_set_strokes` to the seven
and the old name stopped describing the rule; the citation here is the kind no gate reads (D319).

**`svg_in` degrades rather than failing, which is the other half of the same change.** An import is one
transaction, so a single bad number would have cost a whole file; instead `numbers()` gains the
`.filter(|f| f.is_finite())` that `parse_len` already had — the asymmetry between those two is what let
`<path d="M 0 0 L 1e999 10 Z"/>` through while `<rect width="1e999">` was harmless and the module read
as guarded — and both `BezPath::from_svg` sites skip the shape and *report* it. Dropped rather than
clamped: there is no coordinate meaning "infinitely far". ⚠️ **A singular `transform` resolves to the
identity, and that is the reachable half.** `matrix(0,0,0,0,0,0)` is finite, so nothing refused it, and
the shape it produced was invisible on canvas but still selectable from the layers panel — and
`build::local_for_world` is `parent_world.inverse() * world`, so on a singular parent kurbo divides by a
zero determinant, every coefficient comes back `NaN`, and the next autosave writes the unopenable file.
The identity is the answer `image.rs` already gives for a singular brush transform, and it is honest: a
matrix collapsing space to a line draws nothing either way. The loader clamps `opacity` into
`build::valid_opacity`'s range for the matching reason — a hand-edited `"opacity": 5.0` used to load
into a state `op_set_opacity` and `op_insert_subtree` both refuse.

⚠️ **A matching refusal in `verify_integrity` was written and then removed as unreachable, and that
measurement is the part of this entry most worth keeping.** The plan was to *report* a damaged file by
node and field rather than let it die inside serde. It cannot be: **no JSON input can carry a
non-finite `f64` at all.** `serde_json` writes one as `null` and then refuses `null` where an `f64` is
wanted, and refuses an overflowing literal like `1e999` with *"number out of range"* — both at
`from_value`, one function above the integrity walk. So the whole of the protection is at the
operation, and §5.11's enumerated checks are complete without a sixth of this kind.
`a_file_already_holding_a_non_finite_number_is_reported_by_name` pins the **shape** of the refusal
(`IoError::Serde`) rather than serde's wording, and exists to stop the removed check being re-derived.
What is left over is the *message*, which names neither the node nor the field; improving it means a
custom deserializer for every float on the DTO, and is a decision rather than a fix. *Revisit only if
someone actually arrives with such a file.*

**D420 — A `Project::folder` is a single path component, and a Fontsource id is `[a-z0-9-]`. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

Two records read off disk and used as **filenames**, neither checked. They are one entry because the
rule is one rule: *a string that becomes a path component is validated where it is parsed, not where it
is joined.*

**`Project::folder`'s doc has always said "a stem, not a path" and nothing enforced it**, in a field
read straight out of a JSON file in a directory the design invites the user to share. With
`"folder": "../.."`, `Project::dir` returns a path outside the library, so every *New file* and
*Import* into that project is written somewhere nothing will ever scan again, and *Move to project*
`rename`s the existing document out of the library permanently. ⚠️ **`rename_folder` is worse than a
write**: it `fs::rename`s `root.join(old)` with `old` taken straight off the file, so
`"../../../Users/<you>/Documents"` moves that directory *into* the library under a slug — `unique_stem`
was applied to the destination and the **source** is what came from disk. ⚠️ **And the delivery route
needs no local attacker**: `relocate::merge_projects` adopts the source library's project records
wholesale when the user changes the base folder, so pointing *Change base folder* at a shared or
received directory is enough. `is_folder_stem` checks with `Path::components` rather than by looking
for `/` and `\`, which answers the Windows cases a substring search misses — a drive prefix, a UNC
root, and `.`/`..` in any position — and it is applied in `Projects::read`, the single reader, with
`rename_folder` asking again as the belt to that buckle. A bad value is **dropped rather than refusing
the file**, the trade `DocumentMeta::sanitized` makes for an id (D419): `None` is an ordinary state, so
the project still appears and nothing is hidden from the user, where refusing `projects.json` over one
record would empty the sidebar.

**The Fontsource catalog is the same shape at a different scale.** `static_face` builds
`{id}-{subset}-{weight}-{style}.ttf` and then `dir.join(&key)`, so an id of `"../../../../AppData/…"`
writes font bytes outside the cache and an absolute one discards the base; `weight` is a `u16` and
`style` comes from a fixed pair, so those two strings are the whole untrusted surface. The bytes must
pass `is_sfnt`, so the primitive is *write a valid font file to an arbitrary path* — bounded, and not
nothing — and it poisons the legitimate cache besides, since `"../fonts/inter"` collides two families
onto one file and `trim_font_cache` sweeps by directory listing, so an escaped file is never evicted.
⚠️ **Filtered at *both* parse sites, and the second is the one that outlives the network**: the catalog
is persisted, so without the filter in `read_catalog` one hostile response keeps working on every later
launch, after the server has been fixed. Rejected at the parse rather than sanitised at the join,
because the same string is used in two places and fixing one is how the other gets forgotten. `[a-z0-9-]`
is the shape Fontsource actually publishes, so a rejected entry means the response was not a Fontsource
catalog; it needs the API to be hostile or compromised — `ureq` runs with TLS verification on and the
download is capped — which is why it is a filter and not an error the user is shown. Flip: dropping the
filter from `read_catalog` fails on the length assertion at `"../../evil"`, and ⚠️ **the fetch side's
filter keeps that green**, which is exactly why both are there.

**D419 — A document's `meta.id` is 32 lowercase hex, checked at both readers. *Fixed and tested
2026-09-06; Keep.***

The id is joined as a **path component** by three writers — the crash snapshot, the version pin and the
cover cache — and nothing had ever checked its shape. A `.ondin` whose block reads
`"id": "../my-cool-design"` makes the snapshot writer build `root/.recovery/../my-cool-design.ondin`
and `atomic::write` rename attacker-chosen bytes over the user's real document, **every ten seconds,
silently**. On Windows an *absolute* id is worse: `Path::join` discards the base entirely.

⚠️ **The cover cache is the door that needs no click.** It renders every entry the dashboard's grid
draws, so merely opening the library on a base folder — a folder the design invites the user to point
Dropbox at — is enough; delivery does not require opening the file. That is what puts this and D416 and
D422 in the same family: *the landing screen reads every document in the folder before anybody chooses
one.*

`DocumentMeta::is_wellformed_id` is `ID_HEX_LEN` lowercase hex characters, which is what
`library::ids::mint` produces (16 bytes of `SystemRandom` as `{:02x}`, or a clock fallback of `f0` plus
30 hex digits) and the only shape anything has ever minted. **The validation has to be in core, where
loading happens, while the minting stays in the app** — the length is one number written twice for that
reason. `DocumentMeta::sanitized` drops a bad id rather than refusing the document: `None` is an
ordinary, fully supported state that every pre-library file is already in, and the library mints a
fresh id the next time it writes, where refusing the load turns a repairable file into one that cannot
be opened. ⚠️ **`name` and `project` are deliberately not touched** — a name is free text and
`library::naming::slug` stands between it and the filesystem; a project id is looked up in
`projects.json` rather than joined.

⚠️ **Applied at *two* boundaries, and the second was found by grepping the field rather than by reading
the load path.** `io::schema::into_document` is the door you have to walk through;
`io::probe::meta_in_prefix` is the **scan's** reader, which never loads the document at all and is what
feeds `library::cover::key` for every card on screen. A fix at the loader alone would have left the
whole dashboard uncovered. The three app writers additionally ask `library::ids::is_minted` before
joining — belt to core's braces, and not the same line of code twice: core closes the *class* at the
boundary where bytes become a document, and the app's predicate is what a fourth route into one of
those writers (a hand-built `Entry`, a future reader through neither `io::load` nor `io::probe`) meets
instead of an escape.

**D418 — Three records refuse to be overwritten by the defaults a failed read produced — and say so.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

`Library::projects_unreadable` had the latch; `prefs.json` and the per-machine `library.json` did not.
Both read an unparseable file as an empty one and then **wrote that emptiness back** at the first
ordinary write, and the doors are as ordinary as they get: every `open_path`, every star, every
duplicate, every search. So a single half-synced file cost every star on the machine at the first click
after launch.

⚠️ **`library.json` used to argue in its own module head that it needed no three-way read, and the
argument was wrong about which fields it holds.** `load`'s reasoning was *"this file is derived and
local; the worst an overwrite costs is a Recent list that has forgotten"* — fourteen lines below it,
`save_to` says *"nothing can reconstruct which documents this machine has opened, so a torn index
silently loses the Recent list **and every star**"*. The second is right, and the stars are exactly
what the first omits: they are user intent, not derived data, and nothing anywhere else records them.
*Two sentences in one file disagreeing about the same question, with the pessimistic one right.*
Reading the file as empty is still correct — the app has to run, and an empty Recent list is a
survivable frame; what was not survivable was writing that emptiness back, so the **write** is what
declines. The flag is `#[serde(skip)]` in both: it is a fact about *this* read and never a stored one.

⚠️ **A silent latch is worse than the loss it prevents, which is why
`OndinApp::report_unreadable_records` landed with it.** All three states look exactly like an ordinary
empty one from the screen — a library with nothing in it, a *Recent* list that has forgotten, no
projects — and the user's obvious repair for an empty library is to make a new one *beside* the real
one, which is the loss the latch was protecting them from, arriving by a different road. One sentence,
once, into the status line D426 built; `base_folder` is named in particular because it is the one
preference whose loss is not cosmetic and the others are habits. A `fail` and not a modal: all three
states are survivable and the app runs.

**Both records gained a `load_from`/`save_to` pair against an explicit path, and that is what makes the
failure testable at all.** `path()` reads `dirs::cache_dir()` with no injection point, so a probe
driving `load` would read — and one driving `save` would **overwrite** — the developer's own files,
which is why §15 D370 exists. **Each test does the whole round trip and reads the file back rather
than asserting a boolean is set**, and the `mark_opened`/`toggle_star` in between are what make the
flip bite *legibly*: removing `if self.unreadable { return; }` from `save_to` fails on the bytes
assertion — the predicted site — printing
`{"opened":{"doc-1":…},"starred":["doc-1"],…}` where `{not json` was, which is the loss itself rather
than an empty index. ⚠️ **Compared as text and not as `Vec<u8>`**, or the failure is two rows of
decimal numbers. The control is the other half: a **missing** file is a fresh install, and writing an
empty index over nothing is exactly right.

**D417 — A hex colour is guarded by character, not by byte length. *Fixed and tested 2026-09-06;
Keep.***

`dashboard::swatch` parses a project's `#rrggbb` out of `projects.json` and read `if h.len() != 6`
before slicing `&h[0..2]`. `str::len` counts **bytes**, so `"#€abc"` is six bytes and four characters:
it passed the guard and then panicked inside the `€`.

**That is a panic on the layout path of every frame of the library screen.** The sidebar draws one row
per active project unconditionally, and `reopen_last` is off by default, so the app opens on the screen
that crashes and there is no door back — the file must be hand-repaired before the app runs at all.
⚠️ **A *two*-byte character is harmless by luck** (`"éa0b1"` slices on the boundary and falls back as
intended), which is exactly why the mistake read as correct: **the first non-ASCII value anyone tries
is likely to behave.**

The guard asks `is_ascii_hexdigit` of every byte now, and the parse is one `from_str_radix` over the
whole string rather than three slices, so there is nothing left to slice. The `Err` arm is unreachable
behind the guard and is kept as the same fallback, so a future edit that loosens the guard cannot turn
this back into a panic. Falling back to the accent rather than to black or to a refusal is the file's
standing posture: `projects.json` is hand-editable and travels between machines, so a malformed value
is a thing that will happen, and a project drawn in the accent is a project the user can still click.

**D416 — The tree has a depth bound, at both doors, because a stack overflow is not a panic. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

§5.11's integrity checks bounded five *shapes* and never a **depth**, while the in-memory walks the
section delegates safety to — `subtree_ids`, `paint_path`, `resolve` — deliberately carry no visited
set and are recursive. A ~2,000-deep document of nested groups (about 900 KB, one line to generate, or
an imported SVG of nested `<g>`s) passed all five and then killed the process inside `Resolved::rebuild`:
measured at **1,000** levels in a debug build and **2,000** in release.

⚠️ **A stack overflow is not a panic.** `catch_unwind` cannot see it, no `Cover::Failed` memo records
it, and every unsaved edit in the session goes with the process. ⚠️ **And nothing is clicked to reach
it** — `library::cover::rasterize` loads and rebuilds *every* document the dashboard grid draws, and
the dashboard is the landing screen, so one such file in a synced base folder crashes the app at launch
with nothing on screen naming the file.

`io::MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 256` is **a stack bound and not a taste bound**, and the two numbers it sits
between are what chose it: two orders under the measured abort, and far past the handful of nested
groups anyone builds by hand. That generosity is the shape a refusal on the *load* path has to have,
since it can lock a user out of a real document. Check (6) **rides on the reachability walk that was
already there**, which is why it costs nothing: that loop visits every node once and the only new state
is a `usize` per stack entry — and it is an explicit stack rather than recursion, so *that* walk was
never the one at risk; the walks it certifies are.

**`svg_in` carries its own bound, 64, deliberately far tighter.** Two separate things go wrong past it:
the element recursion `children → node → node_ignoring → children` aborted a debug build at depth
**200**, and the *document* the walk builds must stay inside `MAX_TREE_DEPTH`, or an import would apply
cleanly, save cleanly and then refuse to reopen. In that module's own words, an SVG is "as untrusted as
input gets".

⚠️ **The flip on the importer does not fail — it takes the harness with it.** With `MAX_SVG_NESTING`
raised to 100,000, `cargo test -p ondin-core --lib` exits `0xc00000fd` on the 200-level fixture with no
assertion, no message and no stack trace, which is the whole argument for the bound. The loader's flip
is ordinary by comparison, and ⚠️ **the *interesting* flip there is raising the constant rather than
removing the check**: at 4,096 the refusal goes away and the process survives, because the test's 300
levels are nowhere near the abort. *That test proves the limit is enforced, not that it is low enough* —
the second half is arithmetic against the measured 1,000, and a test that reached the abort would take
the harness with it. Both suites assert the accepted half too (250 deep loads *and rebuilds*; 30 levels
import with their shape and no report at all), which is what would catch a fix that simply refused deep
files.

⚠️ **The operation layer does not enforce it**, and that is recorded rather than closed: a document
built by repeated `CreateNode` can still exceed what the loader will read back. Unlike the two doors
above, no measured route reaches it — nothing in the app nests without a user click per level. *Fix if
a builder, an importer or the MCP write surface ever nests without one.*

**D415 — Leaving the editor commits what was typed, and the window ✕ re-arms its own cancel. *Fixed and
tested 2026-09-06; Keep.***

Two ways out of the editor, each losing work, and they are one entry because the shape is the same:
*an exit is a thing with a list of participants, and both lists were short by one.*

**A text session commits nothing until `finish_text_edit` (§9.3).** `preview_session` only calls
`set_session_preview`, so the live editor is the only thing holding the content — and
`go_to_dashboard`'s save reads `session.doc`, which does not have it. So walking to the library
mid-sentence wrote the document *without* what had just been typed, and then dropped the crash snapshot
on the next line, because that save had made the session clean. The session itself survived the walk —
`go_to_dashboard` does not call `reset_transient_state` — and was thrown away by the
`reset_transient_state` the *next* `open_path` runs, so nothing anywhere held the text and nothing said
so. ⚠️ *`go_to_dashboard`'s own doc comment attributes that discard to `adopt_document`, which is an
`EditorSession` method and cannot see `OndinApp::text`; the test beside it names the right one.* `choose_tool` has carried this exact guard, for this exact reason: **a
button that leaves the editor is an exit, and every other exit commits.** ⚠️ *That sentence said
"since D294" until 2026-09-07, and **D294 is `Arming a creation tool clears the selection`**, which
says nothing about text sessions. The same wrong number was in `app::go_to_dashboard`'s doc comment,
where it came from; both drop it rather than replacing it, because a search of this section finds no
entry recording when `choose_tool` gained the guard. A citation that resolves and is wrong is
`[S18.2-L3-07]`'s class, and no gate can see either.* ⚠️ **The canvas's own
click-away rule cannot cover it** — `text_mode_input` ends the session on the *canvas's* `Response`,
and a click on a top-bar button is delivered to that button.

⚠️ **The test's predicted failure site was wrong, and the correction is the useful half.** As first
written it asserted `app.text.is_none()` before re-reading the file, and the flip bit there instead:
*"the session ended on the way out"*, which reports a mechanism rather than a loss. Both assertions
have teeth; the order decides which one a future reader is told about, so the **file** — the only thing
that survives the walk — is asserted first, and the flip now fails with `left: "hello" right: "TYPED"`,
the reported symptom in the failure message.

**The close request re-arms on every request, not only the first.** `handle_close_request` carried
`&& !self.confirming_close`, and the title bar is not covered by the in-app `egui::Modal` the flag
raises — so a second click on ✕, the ordinary reflex when a dialog appears, arrives while the flag is
already `true`, skipped the whole arm, and emitted no `CancelClose`. That command has **exactly one
emitter in the workspace**, so nothing cancelled the close and eframe took the window down with the
card still up and unanswered, unsaved work included. Cancelling again is free: the flag is idempotent
and the card is already drawn. Flip: putting the term back fails on the second frame's assertion — the
predicted site — while the clean-session control stays green, which is what proves the term was the
whole cause and that the probe can tell a cancel from no cancel at all.

**D414 — A `vello_cpu` bump moved every stroked pixel, and the setting D304 warned about did not
change its default: it changed struct. *Bumped, measured and tested 2026-09-03; Keep.***

The workspace pin went `vello_cpu = "=0.0.9"` → `"=0.2.0"`. It was picked up from D411's `cargo search`
pass — the roadmap's own note, since struck, that 0.2.0 was out and that the bump "is exactly the
moment a checked-in golden would move with **nothing in the diff naming the cause**". This is that
moment, taken deliberately so the warning could be *measured* instead of carried.

**It does not cascade into the save format, which is what made it safe to attempt**, and that was
checked in the published manifests **before** the pin was touched rather than discovered afterwards:
`vello_cpu` 0.2.0 → `vello_common` 0.2.0 → **`peniko` 0.6.1**, the same version the model is built on.
The model's `Brush`, `Gradient` and `Color` *are* peniko types and they are the on-disk format
(§5.11), so a bump wanting peniko 0.7 would have been a document-format migration wearing a
dependency bump's clothes — a different decision, with a different price, and the right answer to it
would have been to leave the pin alone. The order matters: the manifest read is thirty seconds and it
is the only thing that tells the two apart before the work is done.

**The mechanical half.** `RenderContext::render_to_pixmap(&mut resources, &mut pixmap)` is gone; it is
`render(target, resources)` and `render_with(target, resources, settings)` now, with the arguments in
the other order. Four call sites in `cpu.rs` — the export walk, the effect-layer flush, the font
picker's preview strips, and one test.

⚠️ **The interesting half is that `RenderMode` moved out of `RenderSettings` into a new
`RasterizerSettings`, and that is the shape the warning did not name.** D304 recorded `RenderMode` and
`num_threads` as *defaults rather than pins*, and the roadmap's parked *PNG goldens* entry said the
difference "only shows up at a version bump, which is the one moment a golden most needs to be
trusted" — imagining a changed default. The default did not change. The **struct** changed:
`export_settings`'s `..Default::default()` went on compiling and went on meaning something different,
because the field it was defaulting is no longer in the struct at all. *A `..Default::default()` is a
claim about a set of fields, and nothing checks that the set is the one you meant.* Neither `cargo
check` nor `clippy` nor `cargo doc` has an opinion about a field that left.

**`RasterizerSettings` also brought three live knobs nobody had named** — `composite_mode`,
`pixel_format` and `offset`, each of which changes what lands in the pixmap, and all three arriving on
defaults through `render()`. So the fix is not to re-spell `render_mode` where it now lives but to
stop defaulting: `cpu::raster_settings()` names **all four** fields and is passed to `render_with` at
every one of the four call sites. The values are today's defaults, chosen rather than inherited —
`RenderMode::OptimizeSpeed`, which is inert here (⚠️ the speed/quality `match` in
`dispatch::single_threaded` is behind `cfg(all(u8_pipeline, f32_pipeline))` and only `u8_pipeline` is
on, so **D304's "`RenderMode` is inert in this build" finding was re-checked against 0.2.0 rather than
renumbered, and it still holds**); `CompositeMode::Replace`, because every target this hands to is a
fresh `Pixmap`; `PixelFormat::Rgba8`, which is **load-bearing rather than nominal**, since
`color::straight_rgba8_from_premul` reads the buffer as premultiplied RGBA8 immediately afterwards;
and a zero `offset`, the context and the pixmap always being built at the same size. Default features
are unchanged across the two versions (`std, png, text, u8_pipeline`), which was checked and not
assumed, because that feature set is what makes the first of those four inert.

**All 31 suites and 1856 tests passed on the bump with no change, and that proves less than it looks.**
Every pixel assertion in the workspace is a threshold — `red > 128`, `alpha == 0` — and the goldens
that exist are SVG and JSON, so **nothing here byte-compares raster output at all**. A green suite is
therefore consistent with the raster having moved, which is precisely the state D304 said a PNG golden
would end. So the comparison was made by hand: §11's `golden_document` at 840×680, rendered under both
versions to **raw straight-alpha RGBA** — not PNG, because two encoders can emit different byte
streams for identical pixels and the question is about pixels.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| bytes differing | **162** of 2,284,800 (0.0071%) |
| pixels differing | **78** of 571,200 |
| worst channel delta | **1** (mean 1) |
| channels moving | R on all 78; G and B on 42 each |
| alpha channel | **does not move at all** |

⚠️ **Alpha is identical, so coverage is identical and only colour rounds differently** — the same
signature D304 found across SIMD levels, and the reason the two pictures are indistinguishable by eye.
The differing pixels form **four tight clusters**, each about seven rows tall, mirror-symmetric about
both axes of one shape.

**Attributed rather than assumed**, which is this file's own rule for a residual. The fixture's
hexagon carries a `width: 3.0`, `Join::Miter`, `StrokeAlign::Outside` stroke; hiding **that one
stroke** and re-rendering under both versions makes the two buffers **byte-identical**. So the whole
difference is that stroke and the four clusters are its joins. The fills, the gradient, the blend
layers, the glyph runs, the boolean, the path, the `Line`'s own 3.0-wide centred stroke and the rect's
2.5-wide dashed one are all unmoved.

**That is D304 arriving by a second road, and it is the sentence worth keeping.** D304 measured across
*SIMD levels* and found the stroked path the only level-variant primitive; this measures across
*library versions* and finds it the only version-variant one. Two unrelated variables, the same
primitive — which makes it a fact about **stroke expansion arithmetic** rather than a fact about
either variable, and the thing to suspect first the next time a raster moves for no reason anyone can
see.

**The consequence for §11 is a third axis on a PNG golden.** It was already per-architecture, because
`Level::baseline()` is target-derived (D304); it is now per-architecture **and** per-`vello_cpu`. That
does not block the goldens the way the architecture does — a pinned dependency *is* a pin, unlike a
CPU that is detected — but the regeneration note had to say it, or the first person to bump this crate
would read a diff on every stroked shape as a regression and go looking for the exporter change that
caused it. **It says it, written the same day**: `ondin-export/tests/goldens.rs`'s module header now
carries the axis, the measurement, and the instruction — regenerate, and **check the residual is
confined to strokes with a worst delta of 1**. ⚠️ **That last clause is what turns this measurement
into an acceptance criterion rather than a fact about one bump**: two runs agreed that strokes are the
whole of it, so *a residual anywhere else is the finding*, and the next bumper has a test to apply
instead of a judgement to make.

⚠️ **A cost worth recording: the tree now carries two `vello_cpu`s and two `vello_common`s**, because
`epaint` 0.35 itself depends on `vello_cpu` 0.0.9 (`cargo tree -i vello_cpu@0.0.9` names
`epaint → egui → eframe`). Nothing crosses between them — our backend uses 0.2.0, epaint's internals
use their own, and `peniko` unifies at 0.6.1 — so it is duplicate compilation and duplicate binary
rather than a correctness problem, and it resolves only when the egui trio is bumped. `fearless_simd`
**did** unify, at one copy of 0.4.1, which matters beyond tidiness:
`export_pins_the_simd_level_rather_than_detecting_it`'s doc rests on there being exactly one, and the
count was re-taken in `Cargo.lock` at the bump rather than carried forward.

**Four doc comments the bump made stale, all fixed** — and the class is worth naming, because not one
of them would have failed a gate. `color.rs`'s header said "VERIFIED against the pinned vello/vello_cpu
0.9/0.0.9"; `cpu.rs`'s pin test named the `=0.0.9` pin and the `fearless_simd` count; `effects.rs`'s
header said "`vello_cpu` 0.0.9 implements only two of the four we need". ⚠️ **That last one was
re-checked rather than renumbered, and it holds**: 0.2.0's `filter/` module gained `flood`, `offset`
and `shift`, and neither `ColorMatrix` nor `Composite` is among them, so the argument for owning our
own effect passes stands for exactly the reason it did — a renumbered version in a claim nobody
re-measured is how a comment comes to assert something that was true of a different release. And
`export_settings`'s own doc, whose "the other two fields" sentence named a field that is no longer in
the struct: the same mistake as the `..Default::default()` above, in prose instead of code, and with
the same amount of tooling able to see it.

⚠️ **And the entry's own lesson happened while the entry was being written.** Sweeping the documents
for `0.0.9` turned up an older §15 claim — that `vello_cpu` has `Mask::new_luminance` and that
`push_layer` takes `mask: Option<Mask>` — and it was left at the old number rather than renumbered,
because nobody had re-measured it and *a version number that travels without the measurement it stands
for is the whole of what this entry is about*. It was then measured against the 0.2.0 source and both
halves held (`Mask::new_luminance` is still in `vello_common`'s `mask.rs`, and `push_layer` is now
`(clip_path, blend_mode, opacity, mask, filter)` — the fifth argument `cpu.rs` passes `None` is the
new `filter`), so the sentence carries `0.2.0` and a note saying it was re-checked. **The two
version-named claims in this session came apart**: one needed a real correction and one was simply
still true, and **nothing about either sentence said which it would be in advance.** That is the
argument for measuring rather than renumbering, made from the case where measuring found nothing —
which is the case that tempts everyone to skip it.

*Keep.* The bump is taken, the settings are pinned rather than defaulted, and the difference it made
is measured and attributed. *Revisit at the next `vello_cpu` bump*: re-run the same raw-RGBA
comparison over `golden_document` before believing a green suite, and read `RasterizerSettings`'s
field list against `raster_settings()` — the field-set claim is the thing that failed silently this
time and will fail silently again.

**D413 — Moving a radial gradient's centre translates its focal point; it used to collapse onto it.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-03; Keep.***

**A radial gradient is two circles and this control names only one of them.** `peniko`'s
`start_center`/`start_radius` is SVG's **focal** circle — `fx`/`fy`, the point the ramp radiates
*from*, which is what makes a sphere read as lit from one side rather than as a flat target — and
`end_center`/`end_radius` is the outer circle, which is the one `paint::radial_centre` reports and the
one `with_radial_centre` is named for. That function wrote the requested point into **both**:

```rust
start_center: centre,
start_radius: pos.start_radius,
end_center: centre,
end_radius: pos.end_radius,
```

So the offset between the two circles was destroyed, and an imported highlight snapped to dead centre
the first time anyone nudged the control — the chip's drag handle or either of the CX/CY fields, all
three of which route through this one function (`picker::radial_controls`).

**The fix is that the move is a translation of the pair rather than an assignment to each.** `let
focal = pos.start_center - pos.end_center;` and then `start_center: centre + focal`. The focal offset
is a property of the gradient's *shape*, exactly like its radius — which this function's own summary
line already promised to keep, for the other circle, since before there was a second one. Both terms
are in the brush's own space, so a gradient carrying D412's squash keeps the offset it draws with
rather than the one it was authored with.

⚠️ **No gradient this app authors could ever have shown it, which is this entry's real subject.**
`Gradient::new_radial` puts both centres on the same point, so the focal offset is zero for everything
`paint::default_brush` makes, and every fixture in the panel's own tests is built by `default_brush`.
The pre-existing `radial_centre_round_trips_as_a_fraction_of_the_box` **stays green through the flip
that restores the bug**, because its fixture agrees with the buggy version and the correct one alike.
*A test cannot see a field its fixture leaves at the default.* The fixture had to come from the other
direction — a gradient that has a focal point, which in practice means an import — and building one by
hand is what makes the case reachable at all. **That is the fifth time in this run that a rule needed a
fixture chosen to reach it**, after D407's decoration band at `y = 0`, D409's offset-free rail, D410's
`Start`-aligned node and D412's off-centre squash.

⚠️ **And nothing in the workspace asserted the focal point *anywhere*** — not in the panel, not in the
writer, not in the round trip. A grep for `start_center` and `fx=` across every test in `crates/` came
back empty. That is the same shape as D411's finding about the round-trip suite having no effect
coverage: a path that works, that both sides implement correctly, and that no assertion would notice
losing. So a second test went in with the fix,
`a_radial_gradients_focal_point_round_trips_where_it_sits` in `ondin-export/tests/svg_roundtrip.rs`.

**The pre-existing writer and reader were both already right**, which is worth stating so nobody goes
looking for a second half of this bug: `svg::gradient_def` emits `fx`/`fy` from `start_center`,
`svg_in` reads them defaulting to `cx`/`cy` — SVG's own default, and the concentric case the model
draws — and `transform_gradient` maps both centres. The loss was in the panel alone. ⚠️
