**`start_radius` is a separate matter and is *consistently* unsupported rather than lost**: neither
side handles SVG 2's `fr`, so an imported focal radius is always 0 and the writer has none to drop, and
nothing here authors a non-zero one. Worth a clause so a reader does not mistake the symmetry for a
second gap.

**Two flips, and they catch different mistakes.** The fix flipped back — `start_center: centre` —
fails the new panel test's last assertion with `Vec2 { 0.0, 0.0 }` against `-10, -5`, the collapse
itself named in the failure message. The round trip flipped against the plausible wrong *writer* —
`fx`/`fy` emitted from `end_center`, which is a copy-paste away and is also what someone would write
believing the focal point defaults to the centre — fails on the offset assertion. ⚠️ **That test's own
`fx=`/`fy=` presence check cannot catch the second one**: the attributes are still there, carrying the
wrong point. Both halves are needed.

**Both new tests assert the offset relative to the centre rather than as a coordinate**, and that is
load-bearing rather than a style. What a focal point means is "ten left and five up from the centre",
so a test pinning it to a coordinate would pass a version that moved the pair by the wrong amount in
the same direction — and in the round trip's case would also fail spuriously, the writer framing its
output on a `viewBox` computed from world bounds.

**It matters more now than it did last week, which is D412's doing.** Before that change an imported
ellipse was already being approximated to a circle and *reported*, so a lost focal point was one
distortion among two on the same path. Now that the geometry survives, the panel discarding the focal
point would have been the only remaining place an imported radial gradient was quietly made into
something else. ⚠️ **The focal point is carried but has no control of its own** — the picker draws one
handle, on the outer centre, and there is no canvas gizmo for gradients at all — so an import is the
only thing that authors one and this function is the only thing that could destroy one. *Revisit if a
focal-point handle is ever added*: at that point the offset stops being invisible geometry and the
panel needs to say it is there.

**D412 — An elliptical radial gradient is a circular one under a squash, and the wall was a missing
field. *Built and tested 2026-09-03; Keep.***

The roadmap's *Now · SVG import* section carried this behind a reason: ***"An elliptical radial
gradient, which `peniko` cannot hold — the model's are circles."*** The ask was real, the reason was
wrong, and D411's audit of the same section re-scoped it the day before this was built. What that
re-scope was worth is the whole of this entry.

**It is this file's *"a `cannot` whose reason names a specific helper"* shape**, which is the part
worth recording. The sentence is *true of* `peniko::RadialGradientPosition` — two circles, and nothing
in a pair of circles can say "ellipse" — and irrelevant to the problem, because an ellipse **is** a
circle under a non-uniform transform. Meanwhile **both backends already had the mechanism, and had
been using it for every image in the app**: `ondin_render::cpu::apply_paint` set a paint transform for
an image's framing and then explicitly `reset_paint_transform()`ed before every gradient, and
`gpu::resolve` returned a brush transform for an image and `None` for everything else. Nothing was
waiting on an upstream release. What was missing was a place in the **model** to put the affine.

**The field, and the second generic parameter that made it small.** `Brush` was
`peniko::Brush<peniko::ImageBrush<ImageRef>>` and is now
`peniko::Brush<peniko::ImageBrush<ImageRef>, GradientBrush>`, where `GradientBrush` is a
`peniko::Gradient` and a `kurbo::Affine` carrying it from the space it was authored in onto the
shape's own. `peniko::Brush<I, G>` is generic over *both* payloads, and D176 is the long argument for
why substituting the first one meant the save format did not move for images. This is the same door,
used a second time, for a reason nobody had in mind when it was chosen — and it is why an elliptical
gradient cost a field rather than a brush enum of our own.

**On the brush rather than on `Fill`**, which is what makes it one change instead of two: a `Stroke`
carries a `Brush` as well, and a gradient-stroked shape wants the same treatment for the same reason.
A field on `Fill` would have needed a twin on `Stroke` and a rule about which of the two a shared
helper meant. (The roadmap's own re-scope said `Fill`; it was wrong about that too, in the harmless
direction.)

⚠️ **Wire-compatible by `#[serde(flatten)]`, and the half that would rot quietly is
`skip_serializing_if`.** A gradient written before the field existed is a JSON object of peniko's own
keys, so flattening puts `transform` beside them rather than nesting the gradient a level down: those
files load unchanged, and a new file gains the key only when the transform is not the identity.
Nesting would have been a schema break for every gradient ever saved, in order to add a field almost
none of them use. The *second* half is the one nothing would report: a `transform` key on every
gradient would still **load** everywhere, so no test would go red — what it would cost is invariant 9,
since every document containing a gradient would rewrite on its next save and the git diff this format
exists to keep readable would become noise. `a_gradient_written_before_the_transform_existed_still_reads`
is the only thing that says so, and it asserts both halves.

⚠️ **The old bytes in that test are the old *type*, serialized — not a JSON literal.** The payload
before this change was a bare `peniko::Gradient`, so serializing one is exactly what a pre-2026-09-03
file contains, and it cannot drift when peniko adds a field. Worth stating why rather than leaving it
as a style: the first draft *was* a literal and was wrong on its first run, having guessed
`"interpolation_alpha_space":"Separate"`, a variant that does not exist. **A hand-written fixture for
a foreign type is a guess about someone else's schema.**

**`svg_in` bakes where baking is exact and carries where it is not.** `Paint::brush` used to fold the
whole `gradientUnits`/`gradientTransform` mapping into the gradient's geometry through
`transform_gradient`, and reported *"elliptical radial gradient (drawn round)"* wherever
`Paint::squashed_radial` said the mapping was not a similarity. Now a linear gradient's two points
take any affine and a radial's two circles take a similarity and no more, so **only a squash survives
as a transform** and everything else still bakes. Two consequences, and the second is the one to keep:
`Import::approximated` no longer carries that string at all, and the geometry of every other gradient
stays in the shape's own space — **which is the space the paint panel reads and writes stops in**.

⚠️ **The deadband under that predicate was the last thing on this path still wrong with nothing
saying so, and it went the same day.** `Paint::squashed_radial`'s threshold was `1.05`, and five
percent was the *right* number while it chose between *approximating and saying so* and *approximating
silently*: under it nobody can see the error, and reporting one on every ordinary file would be noise.
The deadband's own behaviour never changed here — a 2% squash was baked and reported nothing before
this change as well — but **what it was choosing against did**, and once the alternative is *exact*
there is nothing left to trade. It is `1.000_001`, which is what makes the module head's *"nothing on
this path is approximated"* true rather than nearly true.

⚠️ **And that threshold's flip came out the opposite way from the prediction.**
`a_squash_under_the_old_deadband_is_carried_and_a_similarity_is_not` asserts both halves — a
`scale(1, 1.02)` carries a transform, a `rotate(37) scale(3)` does not — and restoring `1.05` fails
the first, which is the change's own point. Dropping the threshold to `1.0`, no deadband at all, was
predicted to fail the **second** and does not. That is a finding about the arithmetic rather than a
weak test: for a similarity the two singular values come out *bit-identical*, so the ratio is exactly
`1.0` and no margin is needed to keep it out. Tried twice — first `matrix(0, 3, -3, 0, 0, 0)`,
dismissed as too exact since every operand is a small integer, then `rotate(37) scale(3)`, where the
relative error still lands below the f64 epsilon *at* `1.0` and rounds away. **So `1e-6` is insurance
against a mapping composed through more arithmetic than any fixture here builds, not a working part**
— the first draft of that doc comment said it was needed for noise, which was overstated and is
corrected in place. The control keeps its place for a different reason than the one it was written
for: it pins that a similarity is **baked**, which the feature depends on however the threshold is
spelled, since otherwise every rotated gradient grows a field it does not need and rewrites its
document on the next save (invariant 9 again).

**The render boundary was one slot that already existed.** `color::brush_to_backend` has returned a
`(Brush, Affine)` pair since D186, and its gradient arm answered `Affine::IDENTITY`; it answers
`g.transform` now. `cpu::apply_paint` no longer clears the paint transform before the match and sets
it from the answer in both arms instead, which *keeps* that function's own "set on every call" rule
without a second arm having to remember it, since a solid answers the identity. `gpu::resolve`'s
`matches!(backend, Image(_))` became a `match` with a gradient arm, passing `None` for an identity
because vello takes an `Option` there and an identity brush transform is what "no brush transform"
means. ⚠️ **The pair's second element now means a different thing per variant** — `to_source` for an
image, the whole transform for a gradient, nothing for a solid — and that is stated on
`brush_to_backend` rather than fixed by splitting the function, on the grounds that the alternative is
three call sites each remembering which of two compositions their variant wants.

**The SVG writer had never emitted `gradientTransform` at all.** `gradient_def` takes a
`GradientBrush` now and writes `gradientTransform="matrix(a b c d e f)"` on all three emitters — the
linear one, the radial one and the sweep-as-radial approximation — omitting it at the identity, which
is the attribute's own default, so no existing file's markup moves. ⚠️ **Before this, a gradient that
had somehow acquired a squash would have gone out round with nothing said**, where the import
direction at least *reported* its loss. That asymmetry is why the new assertion is
`an_elliptical_gradient_round_trips_as_the_same_ellipse` rather than a writer test: only a round trip
can fail on the silent half.

**The panel speaks the shape's space, and the brush may not.** Four accessors read or write a
gradient's geometry — `paint::linear_angle`, `with_linear_angle`, `radial_centre`,
`with_radial_centre` — and the rule is uniform rather than per-control: **a reader maps forward
through the transform and a writer maps back through its inverse**, so what the panel shows is what is
on the canvas and what the user types is where it lands. Ignoring it would report the wrong angle and
centre for an imported gradient and then write a value that missed by the same amount — invisible on
every gradient the app itself authors, which is every gradient in every test that existed before this.
⚠️ **Clearing the transform instead would have been cheaper and is worse**: it turns an imported
ellipse round the first time anyone nudges its centre. Changing the *kind* still discards it —
`default_brush` builds every gradient with the identity through `From<Gradient>` — which is the one
gesture that means "throw this geometry away", and is therefore how a user deliberately makes an
imported ellipse circular again. `with_stops` clones the brush, so the transform rides along untouched
while colours are edited; that is invisible in the code and is stated on it. The inverse is safe
because `squashed_radial` only stores a transform whose smaller singular value exceeds `1e-9`, so the
determinant is bounded away from zero.

**`PaintSummary::Gradient` deliberately does not carry it.** The MCP summary is a kind and a ramp with
no geometry at all — no start, no end, no centre — so a squash would be the only piece of a gradient's
placement an agent could see, which is worse than seeing none of it. It goes in when the geometry
does, which is a decision nobody has taken; `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` is unmoved because the output is.

⚠️ **The one assertion that can say the feature works is pixels, and its fixture had to be chosen to
reach the rule.** `a_squashed_radial_gradient_paints_an_ellipse_rather_than_a_circle` in
`ondin-export/tests/png.rs` puts a circle of radius 20 at `(50, 50)` under a squash **centred on that
same point**, renders it through the CPU backend, measures the half-ramp distance along each axis and
asserts the **ratio** — exactly 2 by construction — rather than either distance, since the absolute
numbers depend on the ramp's interpolation and on where vello puts the boundary texel. The first
fixture was a bare `scale(1, 2)` over a circle at `(50, 25)`, where the transform *moves* the gradient
as well as shaping it: flipping `brush_to_backend` back to `IDENTITY` then failed the test's **guard**
— "0 across, 0 down", nothing reddish anywhere near the centre — rather than its ratio assertion. A
true failure about the wrong thing, and one that would have passed a backend applying the translation
and dropping the scale. Centred, the same flip fails where it should, at `ratio 1.000`. **This is the
fourth time in three days that a rule needed a fixture chosen to reach it** — after D407's decoration
band at `y = 0`, D409's offset-free rail and D410's `Start`-aligned node — and the first where the
wrong fixture failed *loudly*, which is precisely why it was nearly kept.

`a_squashed_radial_gradient_is_reported_rather_than_drawn_silently` **asserted the opposite until
today** and is now `a_squashed_radial_gradient_is_exact_rather_than_drawn_round`, asserting both
halves as a pair: the circle is unmapped (`end_radius` is 10, where baking would have made it 60, or
24.5 area-preserved) *and* the squash is on the brush. The existing SVG golden is byte-identical,
which is the invariant-9 claim confirmed by a gate rather than by argument — that fixture's gradient
has an identity transform, so nothing was written.

**D411 — A `<filter>` comes back as an effect stack, and the entry that covered the gap was false in
both halves. *Built and tested 2026-09-03; Keep.***

The roadmap's *Now · SVG import* section carried this as the first of five open items: ***"Filters. No
answer in the model at all, and the only one of the original list that is a feature rather than a
mapping."*** Both halves are false. `EffectKind::DropShadow(Shadow)`,
`EffectKind::InnerShadow(Shadow)` and `EffectKind::LayerBlur { radius }` are **exact** counterparts
for the three things a `<filter>` is usually written to say, so reading one is a *mapping* and always
was. It is this file's own **list** tell (the roadmap's *an entry's premise rots faster than its ask*)
in its second shape: "no answer in the model at all" is a claim about the set of `EffectKind`s, and
nothing recompiles when that set grows — the entry was right that something was open and wrong about
what and why, and *the wrong reason is what kept anyone from picking it up.*

**What it was covering is the part worth the entry.** `ondin_export::svg::effect_def` emits a whole
multi-primitive `<filter>` for **every** effect stack (§7, D333), and the reader accepted a `<filter>`
that was exactly one `<feGaussianBlur>` and nothing else — `blur_of`, which is as far as D394's fourth
amendment needed to go for a drawing whose fifty-six filters were all Inkscape blurs. So **every
effect this app exported was lost on re-import**. It was reported as `skipped: ["filter"]`, so nothing
was lost *silently* and the module's contract held; but the *Copy as SVG* round trip did not close for
a single shadow, and the entry that should have sent someone to look said the model had nowhere to put
one.

⚠️ **Nothing said so, and one thing should have.** `ondin-export/tests/svg_roundtrip.rs` opens by
calling itself *"the only thing that binds"* the writer and the reader, on the argument that neither
crate's own tests can see the drift. It had **zero** effect coverage: not one test wrote an effect and
read it back. The gap sat in the one suite built to catch exactly this class of bug, which is why
`an_effect_stack_round_trips_as_the_same_stack` is the first thing this change added.

**What is read.** `struct Blur` / `blur_of` are now `struct FilterRead` / `effects_of`, which reads a
`<filter>` as a whole **effect stack** in five shapes: a lone `<feGaussianBlur>`, unchanged, which is
Inkscape's *Blur* slider; a lone `<feDropShadow>`, one primitive saying the whole thing, at the spec's
defaults — `dx`/`dy` of 2, `stdDeviation` of 2, opaque black — and ⚠️ **with no spread, so the model's
is zero rather than approximated**, nothing having been lost in the reading; the **shadow chain**, a
silhouette (an alpha-only `feColorMatrix`, or any primitive reading `in="SourceAlpha"`), an optional
`feComponentTransfer` inverting alpha (`tableValues="1 0"`), which is what makes it an *inner* shadow,
an optional `feMorphology` for the spread, an `feOffset` and an `feGaussianBlur`, then `feFlood` and
`feComposite operator="in"`, plus a second confining composite for an inner shadow; a bare
`<feOffset/>`, the writer's identity primitive for a stack that resolved to "unchanged" (§7), read as
an **empty** stack rather than as an effect or a skip; and `<feMerge>`, which is assembly and carries
no effect of its own.

**Document order is stack order**, and the walk is linear rather than a graph traversal for that
reason: a filter graph is a DAG in principle, wired by `result` and `in` names, but the writer emits
stage one in list order and then the shadow chains in list order, so the markup already says what the
stack was. ⚠️ **The `feMerge` at the end is the trap**, because it lists the results *differently* —
behind, layer, in front — so reading the assembly for the stack order swaps an inner shadow written
before a drop shadow. The cost of the linear walk is a file that names its results out of order, which
is legal and which this refuses rather than misreads.

⚠️ **The dilation's sign depends on which shadow it is.** `shadow_graph` picks the operator as
`(spread > 0) != inner`, because growing the hole an inner shadow casts from is *shrinking* the
shadow — so a reader that takes `dilate` to mean "positive" negates the spread on every inner shadow
in the file and on nothing else. The flip is `if dilate != inner` → `if dilate`, the reading anyone
writes first, and it fails at the **third** of four combinations (`true dilate`, 3.0 against −3.0):
the first two are the ones both readings agree on, which is why the test asserts all four rather than
the two obvious ones.

⚠️ **The offset and the blur are accepted in either order, and that is not laxity.** A shift commutes
with a convolution, so blurring an offset silhouette and offsetting a blurred one are the same
picture; this app offsets first and every pre-`feDropShadow` hand-written file blurs first
(`feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha"`, then `feOffset`). Insisting on one order would read half the files
that mean this. Flipped — requiring the offset first — the failure lands on `out.skipped` rather than
on a wrong shadow: the chain refuses **whole**, which is the right failure and is the rule below.

**All or nothing per `<filter>`**, which preserves
`a_filter_this_cannot_hold_is_skipped_rather_than_half_read`'s rule from D394 through a much larger
reader. One unrecognised primitive refuses the element rather than reading the rest, because a
half-read filter is a drawing that is wrong with nothing reporting it, where a skipped one is at least
counted. Flipped — the final `return None` becomes `i += 1`, walk past what you do not know — it
imports a layer blur for a filter that also displaces the drawing.

**`flood-color` and `flood-opacity` are read through `property`**, not through `attribute`, which is
D394's fourth-amendment rule and is not theoretical here: they are presentation attributes, and a file
that writes its filter primitives through `style=""` would otherwise give every shadow the default
opaque black and say nothing. The colour is split across the two — SVG has no place for a colour with
alpha in it here — so dropping the `with_alpha` is the difference between a shadow and a black shape.
That flip fails in **four** places, including the new round-trip test; two were predicted. *The alpha
is read by every door into this*, which is the argument for `flood_color` being one function rather
than a line in each arm.

⚠️ **The one thing this app writes and cannot read back is `EffectKind::Filters`, and it is a reason
rather than a gap.** `ondin_render::effects::filter_matrix` folds brightness, contrast, saturation and
hue into a 20-value `feColorMatrix`, and **it is not invertible**: brightness and contrast are both a
scale on the same channels, so their product is one matrix that any number of pairs produce. The
matrix does not determine the four numbers that made it, and a reader that guessed would round-trip a
value the user never typed — which is worse than a reported loss, because it looks like a success.
Such a stack is skipped whole and reported, and `FilterRead`'s doc comment says so where the next
person to add a primitive will read it.

⚠️ **The round-trip test asserts *which node* carries the effect, not that the shape does.** The
writer wraps a filtered node in `<g filter="url(#…)">` rather than putting the attribute on the
element — a stack applies to a container exactly as it does to a shape, and one spelling serves both —
so the effect comes back on a **group** and the tree gains a level. That is the same shape as the
`<polygon>`-becomes-`Path` asymmetry this suite's head already records, and it is deliberate on both
sides: the picture round-trips and the structure does not, and asserting the shape's own stack would
demand a collapse the reader has no business doing.

**D410 — A handle on the rail, dragged to slide the type along it.
*Built and tested 2026-09-02; **reviewed and accepted on screen** the same day — "pretty
good, let's call it closed". Keep.***

The last thing D409 left open — *"if we add the option to drag it along the rail, we're done with
it"* — and the thing that turns `on_path_offset` from a value the click writes once into one a
designer can adjust.

**A filled dot where the type starts**, drawn on the rail that D408 already puts on screen. *Round
where every transform handle is square, and filled where they are hollow*, and both differences are
load-bearing: a square handle resizes the box it is a corner of, and two marks that looked alike
would be a promise this drag does not keep (§15 D14's argument for there being no mid-edge squares);
hollow exists so a transform handle does not paint over the corner the designer is aiming at, and
there is nothing under this one but chrome of ours.

⚠️ **Measured, not eyeballed: the handle is `0.1` screen units from the first glyph's own origin,
across four offsets round a ring.** It is not merely *near* the text — `bend` places a glyph by its
midpoint and steps back half an advance along the tangent, so the origin lands back on the rail at
flat `x = 0`, which is exactly what `PathWarp::start_point` returns. The test allowed **25** units
first, on the reasoning that the two were half an advance apart. They are not, and a tolerance that
loose would have passed a handle sitting a whole letter off its own text.

**`Drag::RailOffset` carries nothing but the node**, and the first version carried the offset the
press began at. Dropping it is the better shape and the reason is a fact about this codebase worth
stating: `set_preview` writes `RenderOverrides` and leaves `Resolved` alone, so the **committed**
offset stands still for the whole gesture and can simply be read each frame. A carried copy is one
invariant worse — it has to agree with the node's, and a stale one drifts in silence.

**The arithmetic is one addition, and that is the return on `nearest` measuring from where the text
begins**: the warp's start already carries both the alignment and the committed offset, so the
pointer's distance *from that start* is exactly the change being asked for. `committed + nearest /
len`.

⚠️ **An offset on a closed rail is kept inside one lap, and the reason is not cosmetic.** Both
readings draw identically — `PathWarp` wraps — so nothing on screen says which was stored. What the
number reaches is the SVG writer, as `startOffset`, where a viewer is under **no obligation to wrap a
negative percentage**. An open rail is left alone: past its end is a real place there.

⚠️ **Three flips, and the first two did not bite — each for a different reason, and both were about
the fixture rather than the code.** Dropping `shortest_way_round` changed nothing because the
distances in play were under half a lap. Dropping the lap normalisation changed nothing because the
fixture was **`Start`-aligned**, where the warp's start is exactly `offset × len` and the sum reduces
to `along / len`, in `0..1` by construction — the normalisation is *unreachable* there. It becomes
reachable only when alignment contributes a term of its own, and on a **centred** node the same flip
fails at `−0.445`. That is the third time in this feature that a rule needed a fixture chosen to
reach it, after D407's decoration band at `y = 0` and D409's offset-free open rail.

⚠️ **A fourth fixture was simply impossible, and the test that used it failed honestly.** The
round-trip case handed the arithmetic a starting offset of `0.25` while the node still said `0.0` — a
state the gesture cannot produce, since the offset and the warp are read from the same node. Fixed by
committing the offset the case is about. **A fixture has to be in a state the code can actually be
in**, which is the same lesson from the other end: the previous three could not *reach* the state, and
this one could not *exist*.

**Right-click cancel needs nothing new.** The gesture previews through `set_preview`, so
`has_gesture_preview` sees it and `cancel_gesture` clears `Drag` and the preview by the path every
other drag takes — the fourth "scrub that previews through something other than `RenderOverrides`"
this file warns about is still three.

**D409 — The menu row goes, and the type starts where you clicked.
*Built and tested 2026-09-02; **reviewed and accepted on screen** the same day (D405). Keep.***

Two asks in one message, after living with D408 for an afternoon. *"We don't even need the Text on
path menu when selecting a text and a path. It's redundant and the click-on-path affordance is what
people know."* And: *"It always starts the text at a specific point — with a triangle, I click on the
base, and it always starts the text on the right edge, at the top."*

**The row is deleted rather than kept as a quieter door.** `build::text_on_path`,
`build::text_on_path_pair`, `Item::TextOnPath`, `Context::on_path_pair` and the app verb behind them
are gone; *Detach from path* and *Flip to other side* stay, because those act on a node that is
already railed and have no gesture of their own. **Four steps became one**, and the two in the middle
— select the text, then shift-select the shape — were the ones nobody guesses.

⚠️ **Two stale doc comments survived the deletion with every gate green, and a third was caught by the
one gate that reads prose.** `grep`ping the removed names found `canvas.rs` and `query.rs` still
naming `build::text_on_path` in comments — the case CLAUDE.md's "after deleting anything `pub` in
core, grep the name" exists for — and `cargo doc` then failed on two `[`text_on_path`]` *links*, in
`build.rs` and `inspector.rs`. **The grep and the doc gate caught different instances of the same
mistake**, which is the argument for running both.

⚠️ **The citation count did not go down, and it could have.** This is the refactor case that file
warns about — a `D`-number can vanish with the code it sat on and nothing would say so — and the
set-difference is what says it did not: 292 → 293, gaining D409, losing nothing, because D405 is
cited from several other places besides the function that was deleted.

**`on_path_offset` is a fraction of the rail's length.** Not a distance: a resize handle scales the
rail (D405), and an absolute offset would slide the type toward the start as the curve grew under it.
It is also the unit `startOffset` already spoke, so the writer composes the two — a node centred a
quarter of the way along writes `75%` with `text-anchor="middle"` — and ⚠️ **the anchor is not folded
in**, because the two say different things: the anchor is how the text sits *about* a point and the
offset is *which* point, and an absolute start with `text-anchor="start"` would give up the one
robustness the percentage buys. The reader keeps it now instead of reporting it as approximate; a
`startOffset` in **user units** is still reported, because converting it means measuring the curve,
which is what `PathWarp` exists for and not what a reader should duplicate.

**A closed rail wraps, and that is not a nicety.** Once a click decides where the text begins,
starting it just *before* the path's own first point leaves almost no room on a shape that plainly has
a whole circumference of it — so the offset feature would be broken on exactly the shapes it is most
for. `PathWarp::closed` is the last element being a `ClosePath`, and it changes which question
`fits` asks: an open rail bounds the *arc length reached*, a closed one bounds only how far the
**text** has run, since a loop has no end to fall off.

⚠️ **The control for that wrap was vacuous, and the flip is what said so.** "Every rail wraps" left
`an_open_rail_still_runs_out` green, because with no offset the rail's `start` is zero and the two
conditions — *the arc length reached is inside the rail* and *the text has not run longer than the
rail* — are **the same inequality**. The fixture now carries an offset, which is the only way the two
come apart. **Two rules that coincide at the origin need a fixture away from it**, and that is the
fourth "its fixture never reached the state" in this feature.

⚠️ **`nearest` had to stop normalising, and the reason is that two callers want opposite answers.** A
caret wants the result in the lap the text is on — `−0.9 × len` and `+0.1 × len` are the same point on
a loop, and handing the first to `Cursor::from_point` clamps the caret to the start of the string. An
*offset* being measured for a fresh node wants the plain distance round: normalising there gave a
click at the half-way mark an offset of **−0.5**, the same place written as a negative, which the SVG
writer would then emit as `−50%`. `shortest_way_round` is the caret's, applied in `to_layout`.

⚠️ **The click is mapped through the node's *world* transform, not `node.transform()`.** The point
arrives in world space and the rail lives in the path node's own; the node's own transform is
local-to-parent, so using it is out by every ancestor — correct at the root and wrong inside any
frame, which is where every real drawing is. **The flip fails with a plausible number rather than an
error**: 0.204 instead of 0.5, which is a place on the ellipse, just not the one clicked.

**Verified by rendering, four clicks on one triangle**: with no offset the type starts at the apex and
runs down the right edge, which is the report exactly; clicked on the base, the left edge and the
right edge, the first glyph lands **on the click point** in each. ⚠️ **Text clicked onto the base
reads upside down and backwards, and that is correct rather than a bug** — the base is traversed
right-to-left by the shape's own winding — which is what *Flip to other side* is for. Auto-flipping on
the tangent's direction was considered and declined: it is right for a triangle's base and wrong for
type running round the bottom of a circle, which is the case the feature is most used for.

**Not built, stated:** there is still no way to *move* type along its rail after the fact. The field
and `GeometryPatch::TextPathOffset` are the door a drag would come through — the patch exists so such
a gesture would preview and undo like every other — and the gesture itself is unwritten. Raised in the
same message and explicitly not pressed: *"the latter could be complex, so it's not a big deal."*

**D407 — The warp speaks text-local space, in both directions, and the caret goes through it.
*Fixed and tested 2026-09-02; **reviewed and accepted on screen** the same day — "yes, much
better". Keep.***

Reported from use, one symptom: *"when editing a text on path, the cursor shows on the original
position of the text, before it was set to follow the path — it keeps on editing the ghost of the old
position."* **Three bugs, one root**, and only one of the three was the reported one.

**`PathWarp::place` took *baseline-relative* `y` and two of its three callers had no baseline.** It
took that convention because the glyph loop in `bend` happened to have one to hand and subtracted it
there; the render boundary handed it a `DecorationInk::band`, whose coordinates are ordinary
text-local ones, and `warp_rect` would have done the same. **On 20pt Inter an underline drew at 21.94
below its rail where it belongs 2.94 below — one whole baseline**, plainly visible, and asserted by
nothing. The baseline moved *into* the warp, so `place` now speaks the space every caller already has.

⚠️ **The existing warp test could not catch it, and the reason generalises.** It built a band at
`y = 0` — the one coordinate that means the same thing in both conventions. **A fixture on the single
value where two spellings agree cannot tell them apart**, which is why the replacement takes its band
off a real layout and asserts the fixture separates the two before asserting anything else.

**The caret was the reported half and it is the same shape of mistake one level up.** D405's own doc
comment on `TextRef::on_path` claimed that carrying the rail there bends "the renderer, the hit test,
`geometry::local_bounds`, the SVG writer, the live edit session" without being told to. True of the
first four. **A `TextEdit` bends its *box* and nothing else**: every caret rectangle, every selection
rectangle and every pointer question is computed against parley's own flat layout, which the bend is
applied on top of rather than inside. So the session drew its caret and read its clicks in a space the
ink had left — a whole baseline out across the rail, and on a centred node **209 units** along it.

**`TextEdit` caches its own warp, built by the same function `extract` uses.** `warp_for(parts,
shaped)` is one door: a second construction would be a second copy of the alignment rule, and a caret
one alignment-offset from its own ink is precisely what was being fixed. It is cached rather than read
off `TextLayout::warp`, which holds the identical value — getting it means `extract`, which rebuilds
every glyph run, and a caret is asked for on every frame of a blink with a drag asking a pointer
question on top.

**Both directions, and they are different mechanisms.** Out: `caret_quads` and `selection_quads`
replace the rectangle-shaped API, because a caret on a rail is a short segment *across* a curve and a
selection band is a ribbon along one. ⚠️ **Several convex quads rather than one polygon** — a band on
a curve is concave, and `egui::Shape::convex_polygon` draws a concave polygon wrongly rather than
refusing it. Flat type comes back as exactly one quad, the corners of the rect this used to be, and
`quad(KRect, …)` was deleted because the caret was its only caller. In: `PathWarp::nearest` is
`place`'s inverse, and `TextEdit::to_layout` — the single funnel every pointer question already went
through — un-bends *before* `YMap`'s own inverse runs, because paragraph spacing, trim and vertical
alignment are flat offsets the bend was applied on top of.

⚠️ **`subsegment(0..t).arclen()`, not `t × len`.** A Bézier's parameter is not its arc length, and the
difference is a whole letter on a curved segment while being exactly zero on a straight one — so a
version using the parameter passes every straight fixture. `nearest_inverts_place` round-trips on a
quarter circle for that reason.

**Three flips, each aimed at a different half.** Restoring the baseline confusion fails the decoration
test at the underline's own position and takes three other rail tests with it. Making `warped` return
the flat rectangle fails both session tests, and its message *is* the report — caret at 158.9 against
ink at 368.3. Removing the inverse from `to_layout` fails only the click test, which is what says the
two halves are independently pinned.

**D408 — The Text tool writes along an outline you hover, and a rail is drawn.
*Built and tested 2026-09-02; **reviewed and accepted on screen** the same day — "the
click-on-path affordance is what people know". Keep.***

Both asked for from Affinity, and the second is why the first is worth having. Setting type on a curve
was reachable only by making a text layer, selecting it *with* the shape, and finding *Text on path*
in a context menu that is already long — four steps, the middle two of which nobody guesses. Affinity
makes it a cursor: hover an edge with the type tool and the pointer says you may write there.

**`query::outline_at` is `hit_test`'s complement, not a variant of it.** One asks what the pointer is
*over*, the other what it is *on the edge of* — and a curve is its edge. The difference shows at a
shape's **middle**: `hit_test` reports the shape, this reports nothing, so a click in the centre of a
circle plants an ordinary text node and a click on its rim writes along it. ⚠️ **The first reading of
why it was needed was wrong and a test caught it**: the claim was that an unfilled shape has no
interior to hit, so `hit_test` would miss its edge — but this app's hit test does not consult the fill
at all, and an unfilled ellipse is clickable anywhere inside it. The assertion failed, the doc was
wrong, and both were rewritten to the reason that survives.

**Nearest wins, where `hit_test` is deliberately topmost-first.** Two outlines can both be inside the
tolerance — concentric circles, one shape crossing another — and the one the pointer is tracing is the
one meant. **Text and frames are excluded, each for its own reason**: a text node's outline must not
shadow *edit that text*, which is the same tool's other answer to the same click, and a frame is a
page whose edge is a boundary rather than a drawn curve. A **boolean** is excluded as a limitation
rather than a decision — its outline is derived into `Resolved` — and `build::text_on_path_pair`
refuses one for the same reason, so both doors agree.

⚠️ **Amended 2026-09-07: *"both doors agree"* is two claims and only one of them holds.** They agree
about the boolean itself, which is what this paragraph was about — the refusal survives the verb's
deletion, `build::text_on_new_path` reaching it through `local_path` answering `None` (D409 deleted
`text_on_path_pair` with the context-menu row). They agree about a **mask** and about ink a mask has
clipped away only from D456 on, `outline_at` having asked two of `hit_test`'s three questions and not
the third. And they **deliberately disagree** about a boolean's **operands**, because `hit_test` is
supposed to return one and resolve it to its container through `group_chain` (D453). The list of
exclusions above is about *kinds*, and what governs is a node's **role**: D456 is where that is
written down.

⚠️ **The cursor arm and the press resolve the same three answers in the same order, and that order is
the contract.** Existing text, then an outline, then bare canvas. Get it wrong and the pointer
promises one thing while the click does another — clicking a text layer sitting on a shape's edge
would consume the shape.

**`build::text_on_new_path` is `text_on_path`'s sibling and is simpler in the one place that matters**:
the text node is *created* in the space the curve is already in, so the rail needs no rebasing and
there is no inverse to get wrong. It lands in the consumed layer's own z-slot, because a rail is
usually part of an arrangement and sending the result to the front would reorder the drawing as a side
effect of typing on it. `TextSizing::Auto` whatever the defaults say — the sizing is inert on a rail,
and a stored wrap width nothing reads would come back the moment the type was detached.

**The pointer is drawn rather than a glyph, and is the only cursor here that composes two ideas**: an
I-beam, which is what the platform already means by "text goes here", over an arc, which says *which*
text and where. No icon in the set says both, and the stock `CursorIcon::Text` is what it must not be
confused with, since that one is in use eight lines away for "click to edit the text under the
pointer". ⚠️ **Two mistakes in the first drawing, both found by dumping it as ASCII and neither
visible in the source.** The arc was centred on the texel *index* `w / 2` where the figure's own
centre is the half-texel `w / 2.0`, so its right end sat a whole row below its left. And it was the
I-beam's own width, which reads as a bowl the letters sit *in* rather than a path they stand on — it
is wider than the beam now, with its apex under the stem, so the type stands *on* the curve. Both are
kept as assertions on symmetry and on which row is widest.

**The rail is drawn while a railed node is selected or being edited** — the second ask, and the one
that makes the first usable. *Text on path* consumes the layer the curve came from, so afterwards
nothing on screen says where the curve *goes*, only where the letters currently sit, which is a
fraction of it. ⚠️ **The outline only, deliberately no anchor points**, which is where this departs
from the app it was taken from: handles are an affordance and this curve has none — the rail is a
field on the text node, not a layer, and nothing edits it in place. Drawing the points would offer an
edit that does not exist. Solid rather than dashed, because a dash means *notional* and a rail is
authored geometry that decides where every glyph goes.

**D406 — The flip is one bool on the warp, and `<textPath>` comes back in.
*Built and tested 2026-09-01; **reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-09-02** (D405). Keep.***

Both halves of D405's own "what is not built" list, asked for together the same day. They are one
entry because the flip is what forced the writer to decide *how* it says which side, and that
decision is the reader's problem too.

**Flipping reverses the direction and changes the side, and those are not two settings.** Traversing
the rail backwards negates the tangent; the normal is the tangent turned a quarter, so it negates
with it. One sign, `PathWarp::flip`, and every consumer follows without knowing the flag exists — the
glyph rotations, the second line, the decoration ribbons, the box sweep. **That is also what a
designer means by "the other side"**: type around the bottom of a badge has to read left-to-right,
which it only does if the direction flips too. ⚠️ **The flip that would catch a half-implementation
is not "turn the feature off"** — it is negating the tangent and *not* letting the normal follow,
which is the version somebody writing this by hand would produce, and it leaves the direction
assertion green while failing the side one. Run, and it fails exactly there.

**`on_path_flip` is a field beside `on_path`, not a payload inside it**, which is `Node::mask_mode`
beside `Node::mask` for the same reason D225 gives: a flip kept inside the `Option` has nowhere to
live while the rail is off, so *Detach from path* would silently discard it and putting the text back
on a curve would come back the wrong way round. `GeometryPatch::TextPathFlip` is its own patch for the
matching reason — a patch carrying both would make *Detach*, which sends `TextPath(None)`, say
something about the flip as well, and the obvious something is `false`. **The destructive toggle
spelled as an operation.** `the_flip_outlives_the_rail` is the test.

**The row is checkable rather than a pair**, the shape `ClipContent` already has: it is one state with
two values, and a pair of rows would have to *name* the two sides — which depends on which way the
user happened to draw the curve, so neither name would be true of every rail. It is *Flip to other
side* and not *Reverse direction*, though it is both: the side is what a designer is looking at, the
direction is the mechanism. ⚠️ **The tick is asserted as `Some(false)`, not as "not `Some(true)`"** —
`checked` is an `Option` and `None` is a row that is not checkable at all, which is a plausible slip
that draws no tick in either state and passes any assertion phrased as an inequality.

**The writer says "flipped" by reversing the rail, not with SVG 2's `side="right"`.** Two reasons and
the second decides it: `side` is SVG 2 and unevenly implemented, where a reversed `d` is SVG 1.1 and
cannot be got wrong by anybody; and it is **not an approximation**, because our own flip *is*
traversing the rail backwards, so the reversed path is the identical drawing rather than a stand-in.
The `startOffset` percentages go on meaning what they meant, measured from the text's own start.
⚠️ **The cost is that the round trip loses which of two spellings the flip was in, not the flip** —
`svg_in` reads it back as a reversed rail with the flag clear, drawing identically. So
`a_flipped_rail_round_trips_as_the_same_drawing` asserts on the *ink*, and its doc says in as many
words that asserting on the flag is the mistake to avoid. Checked in a browser beside our own CPU
render: both put "OVER" reversed and inverted at the same place on the arch.

**The reader is the writer's inverse and needed no new collection to be one.** `Gradients::ids` is
already *every* element carrying an id — what `<use>` needs — so resolving `<textPath href>` is that
lookup plus `BezPath::from_svg`, the same `d` grammar every shape goes through. What moved is that the
runs live inside the `<textPath>` child rather than under the `<text>`, so the loop reads the child's
children and everything else about `Builder::text` is unchanged: a `<tspan>` inside a `<textPath>` is
a `<tspan>`. ⚠️ **`text-anchor` parts company with itself here**, and it is the one place the two
readings differ: flat text has a box, so `middle` is the box shifted half its width and nothing is
left over (D394); railed text has no `x` to shift *from*, so the anchor is the whole of where along
the curve the type sits and becomes `ParagraphStyle::align`. ⚠️ **The referenced path's own
`transform` is ignored, per SVG, which is the opposite of what `<use>` does** — a `<textPath>` takes
the target's *geometry* into its own user space — and is reported rather than applied. Everything else
unreadable is reported too: no `href`, an `href` that resolves to nothing, a target with no `d`, a
second `<textPath>` on one element, and a `startOffset` that the anchor does not already explain.
**None of it comes back as straight text**, which is the plausible-looking wrong answer.

⚠️ **The round-trip test passed for the wrong reason first, and the flip is what said so.** With the
reader's rail ignored entirely it failed correctly — the layer comes back as *nothing*, since a
`<text>` whose content is inside a `<textPath>` has no text of its own. But the second flip, leaving
the flat baseline translate on top of a rail, **did not bite**: the fixture's rail ran through
`(0, 0)`, which puts the first glyph's baseline at `y ≈ 0` — exactly what the flat arithmetic reads as
the ascent — so the bug moved the layer by 1.0 units and the tolerance swallowed it. Moving the rail
to start at `(10, 60)` makes the same flip fail by an ascent. **A fixture that does not reach the
failure is the commonest way a round-trip test passes for the wrong reason**, and it is the third
instance of that shape in this file after D394's `<tspan>` case and D405's alignment gate. The test's
doc now says why the rail is where it is.

⚠️ **Two broken doc links were caught by the gate rather than by review**, both `[`NodeKind::Text::…`]`
written in `text.rs`, where `NodeKind` is not in scope. That is the flag added on 2026-09-01
(`--document-private-items`) earning its keep on the first change after it landed — every one of those
links is on a private item.

**D256 — *Join* as a command, because the gesture cannot be aimed at two ends already where they
belong. *Built and tested; the coincident ends are the one thing here worth a look on the machine.***
§6.5's last row, and §9.2 was right that it needed an entry point of its own. Joining has existed for
as long as the pen has, but only in one shape — draw *into* an open endpoint — and that cannot be
asked of two ends already sitting where they should be, which is exactly what an import or a flattened
boolean leaves behind. So the subject here is the **point selection** rather than the pointer. Both
doors go through `tools::join_runs`, which is what stops them coming to orient a splice differently;
that function's own doc comment records why its orientation is the opposite of the pen's resume.

Two new free functions beside it: `joinable_ends` says what a selection names and `join_ends` performs
it, with `OndinApp::join_subject` and `join_points` as the app wiring. The row's gate is
`menu_context`'s `can_join = join_subject().is_some()` — **the builder's own precondition rather than
a rule restated at the row**, which is D87 and D230's rule, so a live row cannot reach a `join_ends`
that then declines.

**Two shapes under one row, which is Illustrator's *Join*.** Both ends of **one** run close it:
`closed = true`, no anchor added, no subpath removed. Ends of **two** runs splice into one open run,
which takes the **lower** of the two subpath indices so the runs nobody touched are not renumbered,
and the higher entry goes. The join then **selects the segment it made** (`PointSet::set_segment`)
rather than clearing — the same answer `insert_point` gives and for the same reason, that the edit
renumbers the run and a set kept across it would light the wrong anchors (`PointSet::retain_valid`);
the only difference is that one names the anchor it inserted and this names the segment it created.
The seam is named by the anchor the new segment *leaves*, which is `geometry::anchor_runs`' numbering
— the head's last anchor for a splice, the run's last anchor for a close.

**Three refusals, and the third is the one reading would not have found.** A closed run has no ends.
An anchor in the middle of a run is not an end. And **the two ends of a two-anchor run cannot be
closed**: a `closed` flag there adds a second segment retracing the only one — a shape with no
interior, out of an edit that looks on screen exactly like the no-op it very nearly is. Splicing that
same two-anchor run onto a *different* run is fine and is not refused.

**Nothing is merged, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.** Two ends that happen to sit on
the same point become two anchors with a zero-length segment between them, exactly as
`canvas::pen_join` leaves them. Merging would need a tolerance and a rule about whose handles survive,
and consistency with the gesture was judged worth more than either. Recorded so it is not re-argued —
and *this* is the corner worth one look on the machine, since a zero-length segment is invisible and
is what the selection lands on.

**A dim reason that is slightly wrong in one corner, recorded rather than hidden.** The row says
"Select two open ends of this path to join", which for the two-ends-of-a-two-anchor-run case reads as
though they are not open ends when the real reason is that closing them produces nothing. One `bool`
and one sentence was judged better than a second `Context` field for a corner of a corner. *Fix with
that second field if the sentence is ever reported as confusing.*

Four tests in `tools::tests`, each flipped against the version somebody would actually have written:
`join_takes_two_open_ends_and_refuses_everything_else` (drop the two-anchor guard; and ask `closed` of
only the first of the pair, which passes the closed-run case half the time, depending which way round
the selection was made), `a_splice_reads_end_to_end_through_the_seam` (reverse the head on the wrong
end — half the four-case table is what catches it),
`a_splice_keeps_the_lower_slot_whichever_end_was_grabbed_first` (write the joined run to `a.0` instead
of `min(a.0, b.0)`), and `closing_a_run_adds_no_anchors_and_names_the_closing_segment` (name the
closing segment `(sub, 0)` instead of `(sub, last)` — plausible, because the close joins the last
anchor back to the first, and wrong, because a segment is named by the anchor it leaves). Neither row
is reachable from the keyboard and neither is an `Action`; the `OndinApp` wiring above these functions
is read rather than tested (D35).

**D257 — *Copy properties* / *Paste properties*, and what the payload leaves out is most of the
decision. *Built and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** The last row of `context-menus.md` §9.2
and both of `shortcuts.md` §7's `Ctrl`+`Alt` rows, which are one pair seen from two files. §7 had
deferred four rows behind one blocker; D248 showed the blocker bound only these two, and building them
discharges it outright — that section now has no deferred row left in it.

**Three fields, and what is *not* in them is the decision.** `build::Properties` carries fills,
strokes and opacity — the appearance, and nothing else. Position, size, rotation, the name, the pivot
and the lock are excluded because the verb is "make this look like that" and every one of those is
about *which layer this is* rather than about how it is drawn; Figma draws the same line. **Geometry
is excluded for a second reason on top of that**, and it is the one that would otherwise be revisited:
a corner radius lives in `NodeKind`, so it means nothing carried from a rect to a star, and carrying
it would be a per-kind bridge rather than a field. Not in v1. §7 asked the question outright — "which
properties? fills, strokes, opacity, radius, type?" — so this is the answer, and the question is
struck along with the rows. The fills come off `fills_seen_as`, so a frame's background arrives as a
one-entry list and can be handed to a rectangle.

**A text node's per-run colours are neither lifted nor overwritten**, which is worth stating because
the row is offered on text and looks broken there. Character spans beat the node's paint, so pasting
an appearance onto text whose runs carry their own colours changes what is underneath them and nothing
visible moves.

**`properties_of` refuses a group rather than answering with an empty appearance**, which is the
distinction `paint_targets` already draws — a group is organisation, a frame is a thing — and the
failure it prevents is not a panic. `Properties { fills: [], strokes: [], opacity }` is a
*well-formed* payload, and it **clears** whatever it lands on: copy from a group, paste onto a
rectangle, and the rectangle loses its fill and stroke to an edit that looked like it should do
nothing. The group's opacity is real and is deliberately not a reason to allow it — one field is not
an appearance, and the Transform card already has that number.
`a_group_has_no_properties_to_copy_and_a_frame_does` pins both halves; the flip is `properties_of`
without the refusal, which is the shape somebody arrives at by reading the struct rather than the
verb.

**`paste_properties` is three existing verbs composed, not a fourth walk**, and that is what makes the
row's scope answerable rather than a new rule to learn: `set_fills_all` (through a group, stopping at
a frame), `set_strokes_all`, and `set_opacity_all` (**outermost only**, because opacity composes down
the tree and setting it twice lands at the square). The two scopes differ, and they differ here
exactly as they already differ everywhere else in the app.
`pasting_properties_paints_through_a_group_and_fades_only_the_group` is aimed at precisely that, and
its flip is the plausible wrong version: one walk over `paint_targets` for all three properties. The
*rendered* result of that is the same, so only the document says which of the two happened — which is
why the assertion is on the operation list rather than on pixels. Free consequence of the composition:
each of the three drops the targets that already agree, so pasting an appearance a layer already has
is an empty transaction and no undo step
(`pasting_the_properties_a_layer_already_has_is_not_an_edit`).

**The source is the key layer, else a lone selected layer.** D113's key layer is already this app's
answer to "which of these is the reference", so a multi-selection is not ambiguous here the way it is
in Figma, which simply refuses one. Without a key it *is* ambiguous and the row dims — taking the
first in z-order would be a rule with nothing behind it. So *Copy properties* has **two** refusals and
the row's sentence picks between them on the selection's size: "Make one of these the key layer to
copy from it" for several, "This layer has no fill or stroke of its own" for one.
`the_property_rows_dim_on_two_different_questions` flips against collapsing those into one sentence,
which passes every other assertion in the test, and against hanging *Paste properties* on
`can_copy_props` instead of `has_props` — the copy-paste slip the pair invites, and which would leave
the paste row live over an empty clipboard.

**A third clipboard slot, and it is deliberately *not* kept exclusive with the other two.**
`clipboard` and `guide_clipboard` clear each other because they are two spellings of one clipboard and
`Ctrl`+`V` has to be unambiguous about which it means (§9.4). This is a different clipboard with a
different chord and a different verb, so holding an appearance *and* a set of layers at once means
exactly what it says: `Ctrl`+`V` pastes the layers and `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`V` paints them. Clearing one from
the other would make copying a layer silently forget an appearance the user is halfway through
applying. It needs no `clipboard_stamp` receipt either: nothing about it reaches the system clipboard,
so there is nothing for it to go stale against.

***Copy properties* stays live on a locked layer and *Paste properties* dims.** Reading a locked layer
is not editing it, and a lock that stopped you sampling a colour would make the layer useless as the
reference it is most likely to be — the same argument D225 made for *Export original…*. The partner
writes, so it dims, and it dims with the **lock's** sentence rather than the clipboard's because that
is the refusal to act on first. That ordering is load-bearing and invisible: `Row::dim_if` overwrites,
so the last one wins, and swapping the two lines silently changes which sentence a locked layer with
an empty property clipboard shows. Both rows wear the same glyph (`SLIDERS_HORIZONTAL`) and the
accelerator column is what tells the pair apart.

**`Group::Properties` took the built primitive menu from 18 rows to 20**, which is what
`context-menus.md` §3 has counted by hand all along — the group has been third in that table since the
file was written and empty in the code until now, so this number moving *up* is the two converging
rather than drifting. It sits between Clipboard and Structure because that is what it is: a second
clipboard, carrying an appearance rather than a layer.

**The `!m.alt` guard on the clipboard event loop is a branch now, and the three events go three
different ways.** The guard existed because `is_cut_command` never looks at Alt, so `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`X`
arrived as an `Event::Cut` and **deleted** the selection where Exclude was asked for (D204,
`shortcuts.md` §L2). Alt now selects a *row* rather than dropping the event: `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`C` is
`Action::CopyProperties`, `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`V` is silenced here, and `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`X` is **still nothing**,
because it belongs to Exclude's release arm and emitting anything for it would put the destructive cut
straight back. That is the whole of why the two rows had to be one job. Alt is tested **before** Shift
on the `Paste` arms, so a hand still on Shift cannot make `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`Shift`+`V` resolve to both
rows.

**`Ctrl`+`Alt`+`V` is read from the key *release*, not from `Event::Paste`, and this is the finding.**
`egui_winit` pushes `Event::Paste` only when the clipboard yields non-empty **text** (D183), and a
property paste has nothing to do with the OS clipboard. Read from the event, the chord would work
whenever a sentence happened to be copied in another application and do nothing the rest of the time —
an intermittent bug from the chair, and **a test driving a synthetic `Event::Paste` would have called
it fixed**, which is D219's vacuous shape arriving from the other direction. So it is read at the same
seam Exclude is: `egui_winit`'s swallow sits inside `if pressed`, and the release falls past it.
`a_property_paste_does_not_need_the_os_clipboard_to_hold_anything` is the pin, and its flip is
`Event::Paste(_) if m.alt => push(PasteProperties)` — whose first assertion passes, because the
synthetic event is always there, and whose empty-clipboard assertion fails, which is the real case.
`alt_turns_the_clipboard_events_into_the_property_rows_except_the_cut` flips against
`Event::Cut if m.alt => push(Action::Cut)`, and `a_property_paste_is_not_also_a_paste_in_place`
against testing Shift before Alt.

**A prediction that turned out to be already answered, corrected rather than deleted.**
`shortcuts.md` §7 warned that the release arm would need the same discrimination "or `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`V`
pastes a picture as an ordinary paste". It does not: `cmd_only` is `command && !alt`, so
`Ctrl`+`Alt`+`V` never reached `Action::PasteRelease` in the first place. The fear was written against
the image-paste work (D183, D204) and the guard it feared had been written there.

**One residual exposure, shared with Exclude and not introduced here.** The modifiers are read on the
*release* frame, so lifting Alt before V makes `cmd_only` true again and the release resolves as an
ordinary paste; the same is true of `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`X` and Exclude. It is the established shape of every
release-read chord in this keymap, and closing it would need `resolve` to remember which modifiers
were down when the key went *in* — state that function deliberately does not have. *Recorded as a
known seam. Revisit only if it is reported from the machine, and then for both chords at once.*

**D258 — A scoped SVG export applied the origin's own transform twice, and the test over it never read
a number. *Resolved.*** `svg(doc, res, Some(id))` handed `res.world_transform(origin)` to `emit_node`
as its `outer`, and `emit_node` composes `outer * node.transform()` — so the origin's *local*
transform went on twice, while the viewBox beside it was written from `world_bounds`, which applies it
once. On the export fixture, whose board sits at `translate(10, 10)`, the header said
`viewBox="10 10 400 300"` and the group came out at `matrix(1 0 0 1 20 20)`: a tenth of the artboard
hanging off the right and bottom edges, a blank strip at the top left, and every child of it carried
along.

The fix is to ask for the origin's **parent's** world transform, which is what `outer` has meant all
along. One expression rather than a branch on which caller this is, because the whole-document case is
the same statement — the root has no parent, so it answers identity — and a `match` there would be a
second place for the two cases to drift apart.

**The part worth recording is why nobody had seen it.** `single_artboard_export_is_scoped_and_valid`
covered exactly this path and asserted that a `<rect>` and an `<ellipse` were *present*. It read no
number at all, so it was green for as long as the path had been wrong. It is
`single_artboard_export_lands_inside_its_own_view_box` now, and it asserts the **pair**: the viewBox
comes from one query and the transform from another, and what makes the picture right is that the two
agree — checking the transform alone would pass against a viewBox written from the wrong corner.
Flipped by putting `res.world_transform(origin)` back, where it fails.

**And nothing in the app called this path.** `main.rs`'s `ondin export` passes `None`, so the only
caller was that test; D259 is what gave the code a real consumer, and that is how the bug surfaced at
all. The general shape is the thing to carry away — *a path with no production caller and a
presence-only test over it is not covered, it only looks covered* — and what it buys is that the CLI's
own `--artboard`-style scoping, if anyone adds one, is safe on arrival rather than broken on arrival.

**D259 — *Copy as SVG* and *Copy as PNG*, and the receipt neither of them writes. *Built and tested; not
yet reviewed on screen.*** `context-menus.md` §3's ninth group, which has been in that table since the file
was written and had never held a built row: `Item::CopyAsSvg`, `Group::Export`, one row on every layer
menu through both doors, `icon::SHARE_NETWORK`, and no chord — `shortcuts.md` binds none, and a chord
invented at a row is one that file does not know about. Never dim, either: the menu is open on a layer,
so there is always something to write, and reading a **locked** layer is not editing it (D225, D257).
It is *half* of §9.3's *Copy as SVG / PNG*; the other half was scoped out below rather than deferred,
and arrived on 2026-08-22 on the terms that scoping set.

**Why it is worth having before the export UI.** It was, for the few hours until *Export as…* landed
the same day (D264), the only way artwork left this app without
the CLI. §9.4's two *Export* rows want a file dialog, a format picker and a scale and are blocked on
all three; this wants a clipboard. And it goes out through the **semantic** writer, so what lands in
the other application is editable groups and shapes rather than a picture of them.

**New in `ondin-export`: `svg_of(doc, res, origins: &[NodeId]) -> String`, of which `svg` is now one
call.** What a *set* adds over the single origin that existed is a selection — a viewBox over the union
of the origins' world bounds, and each subtree emitted under its **own parent's** transform, so several
layers picked out of different frames land where they sit relative to one another rather than stacked
at a shared corner. Two properties of it are load-bearing and easy to tidy away. **Order is the
caller's and is kept**, because the output has to be byte-stable (invariant 9) *and* because SVG has no
z-index — the last element painted is on top — so a caller handing over a selection owes it in document
order or the copy arrives restacked. And **nothing is deduplicated here**: a caller passing both a group
and something inside it would emit that child twice, and the filter for that is `build::outermost` at
the call site, because this function has no way to know whether the repetition was meant.

**`OndinApp::copy_as_svg` reads the committed document and `Resolved`** — the same pair `ondin export`
renders from — so what is copied is what a save would write and a gesture halfway through a drag cannot
leak an uncommitted position into another application. `outermost` for `copy_selection`'s reason.

**No `clipboard_stamp`, and that is the decision rather than an omission.** The stamp is the receipt
saying "the in-app payload still describes what the OS clipboard holds" (D218); this writes real,
complete text that stands on its own and has no in-app payload behind it. Leaving the stamp alone is
therefore not a gap but the correct answer: `owns_the_clipboard` says *no* afterwards, so `Ctrl`+`V`
stops offering layers the user has since replaced with an SVG.

**A consequence worth naming rather than hiding.** With SVG text on the clipboard, `Ctrl`+`V` pasted it
as a **text layer** — the SVG source as literal characters (D218, D221). That was exactly what the
existing rules said and what `roadmap.md`'s "can't paste SVG in" meant; it was recorded
here so that whoever built SVG *import* would know this is the one place the two rules meet, and that
closing the round trip is a change to the paste path rather than to this row.

✅ **Built 2026-08-31 (D394), and this paragraph is why it went where it did.** The importer sits in
`paste`, `paste_in_place` and `paste_at`, between the app's own payload and the text-layer fallback;
this row is unchanged. *A note left for a future reader was read by one*, which is the argument for
writing them — and the prediction it made about the **site** was the part that saved the work.

**~~No *Copy as PNG* beside it, and that is §3's own answer rather than a deferral.~~ The other half,
built 2026-08-22.** It was scoped out here rather than deferred, and the objection was mechanical:
`png(doc, res, &Viewport)` is **viewport**-scoped — a `view` rect and a pixel size — with no way to say
"only these layers", so a PNG of the selection would quietly have included whatever else overlapped its
box, and building it meant either render overrides hiding everything else or a second entry point into
the raster path. **It was the second entry point, and D264 built it for another row the same day**:
`scene::build_of` walks a set of origins and `raster_of` frames them. What was left was the scoping
proper, which was never mechanical — §3's Export group listed two rows and a PNG was not one of them —
and under it one question, whether the clipboard wants a *picture* of the artwork beside the editable
copy at all. It was put and answered **yes**; `context-menus.md` §3's table lists three rows now,
amended to the code rather than the code trimmed to the table. **No new D-number, deliberately**: this
is not a second decision but this one's scoped-out half arriving on the terms it set — with the cost
stated, which is what the struck sentence asked for.

**`raster_of`, not `png_of`, and that is the part worth recording.** `arboard::ImageData` takes raw
straight-alpha RGBA; `png_of` returns an *encoded file*, and handing that over is not an error — the
clipboard reads the bytes as pixels and the paste is noise. **The wrong version compiles**, the width
and height coming honestly from `extent`, so nothing but a test stands between it and shipping. That is
why the two lines are lifted out into `OndinApp::png_for_the_clipboard`, an associated function taking
no `self`: `copy_as_png` itself ends in the OS clipboard, and a test of *that* would write to the
user's.

**One resolution and no submenu.** `RasterOpts::default()` is the whole specification — scale 1.0, no
background, no trim, no padding. Figma was **tested on the machine** on 2026-08-22 and offers a single
*Copy as PNG* with no 1×/2×/3×; it had been assumed the other way first, and that is recorded as a
measurement rather than a preference because otherwise the submenu gets re-proposed by the next reader.
A multiplier belongs to the inspector's Export panel (D274), where a *repeatable* export is the thing
that keeps settings, and this row keeps none for the same reason *Export as…* kept none. **That
reason outlived the row it was borrowed from**: *Export as…* was removed hours later (D264), leaving
the Export group the two clipboard rows and nothing that writes a file, so the argument has to stand
on its own — and it does, more simply. A clipboard write is a one-off by construction and has nowhere
to keep a setting even if it wanted one.

**`arboard` directly, not egui.** `ctx.copy_text` is a *text* clipboard, which is why the SVG row above
can use it and this one cannot; `arboard` is already a direct dependency of `ondin-app` with
`features = ["image-data"]`, and already opened in `paste_image` to read a picture **in** (D183). Same
door, opposite direction. **No `clipboard_stamp`** either, inherited deliberately from the row above and
for a sharper reason than it has: of every row that writes to that clipboard this is the one whose
content cannot be turned back into layers at all, so `owns_the_clipboard` must go on answering *no* and
`Ctrl`+`V` must stop offering layers the user has since replaced. `build::in_document_order` for
`copy_as_svg`'s two reasons (D267) — `raster_of` keeps the caller's order and cannot check it, exactly
as `svg_of` cannot.

**The PNG half's tests**, the SVG row's being the paragraph below.
`the_clipboard_picture_is_raw_pixels_at_one_to_one` asserts the fixture's extent first, a
raster of the wrong subject satisfying the shape assertions on its own, then that the picture is 100×60
and that the byte count is `w × h × 4`. Flipped twice, and the two assertions catch different mistakes:
the `png_of` shape **passes the size assertion** and fails on the count alone, 216 encoded bytes against
24,000, while `RasterOpts { scale: 2.0, .. }` fails on the size instead, 200×120. Neither assertion
alone would have caught both. `nothing_selected_is_no_picture_rather_than_an_empty_one` is the refusal.
The primitive menu is a row longer for this, and the test that counts it is renamed with it —
`a_primitives_menu_is_twenty_four_rows_in_canonical_group_order`, which the paragraph below still names
by the number it carried the day this entry was written.

**Tests.** `a_set_of_layers_exports_without_its_neighbours_and_keeps_world_positions` asserts two things
that fail in opposite directions: **scope** — exactly one `<rect>`, which is the count rather than the
presence because the artboard's own background is a `<rect>` too, and no `<ellipse`, `<line` or
`clipPath` — and **placement**, the rect at `matrix(1 0 0 1 30 30)`, 20 inside a board at 10. The flip
is emitting under the identity, which is the obvious spelling given the subtree is being lifted out of
its parent, and under which every scope assertion still passes and only the transform fails.
`a_primitives_menu_is_twenty_one_rows_in_canonical_group_order` and
`a_booleans_menu_is_the_long_end_of_the_range` are the two ends of §3's length range, which this row
moved to **21–27**.

**The PNG half is not yet reviewed on screen either, and two things specifically want looking at.**
Whether **transparency survives the paste** into a real application: this puts a picture on transparency
by construction, and Windows clipboard alpha handling is inconsistent between receiving applications, so
what happens to it is not knowable from here. And whether `FILE_IMAGE` beside `SHARE_NETWORK` reads as a
**pair** or as two unrelated rows — the glyphs were chosen to say *raster writer* and *semantic writer*,
and that distinction has to survive being seen at 16pt in a menu. *Both open.*

**D260 — *Convert to path*, and a scoring that names a dependency goes stale when something else grows
it. *Built and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** `context-menus.md` §5.6's third row sat in §9.3
as a **feature**, on the grounds that "glyph outlines have to come out of `skrifa` and through
`geometry`". **By the time anyone came to build it they already had.**
`ondin_core::text::outline(&TextLayout) -> BezPath` has existed since outside-aligned type strokes did
(D145) and does exactly this job: it walks the layout's runs, pulls each glyph's contours out of
`skrifa` at the run's own size and variable instance, and places them at the glyph's own coordinates.
So the *feature* was wiring plus one refusal.

**That is the shape worth recording, rather than the row.** A scoring that names a **dependency** is a
claim about the rest of the codebase, and it stops being true the moment something else needs the same
dependency — silently, because nothing recompiles when it does. It is the failure `roadmap.md`'s own
opening warns about ("a premise that is a list") arriving in a second shape: a premise that is a
*missing part*. What is left unbuilt in this ledger is scored the same way — *Mask* on the model having
no mask in it, the two *Export* rows on there being no export UI — so re-derive both from `crates/`
before estimating either.

**A third verb, not an arm of `outline`.** `build::outline_text(doc, res, ids, id)`, with
`build::can_outline_text(res, id)` beside it. The split is the one `can_outline` already drew when it
refused text: every other kind's outline is a pure function of its own geometry, and a text node's is a
**shaped** thing. So this is the one of the three conversions that needs a `Resolved`, exactly as
`flatten` does and `outline` does not. It shares `replace_with_path` with `outline`, so the slot, the
name, the transform, the paint, the opacity and the moved pivot survive by construction (D230).

**The glyph coordinates are already node-local** — the same ones the render walk hands a backend — so
there is nothing to transform on the way out. That is the whole risk in this verb and it is silent: a
path is still a path wherever it lands. So
`converting_text_to_a_path_keeps_its_slot_and_puts_the_ink_where_it_was` asserts the result's **world**
bounds sit inside the box the text occupied, with a tenth of the em of slack, which admits a round
letter's optical overshoot and nothing like a whole-box offset. Flipped against
`path.apply_affine(node.transform())` before the replace — the plausible mistake, since the glyphs
*look* like they need placing — where the ink lands a full (70, 50) away.

**`can_outline_text` asks `text::outline` rather than counting glyphs, and the flip proved that
necessary rather than merely tidy.** A text node whose every character is a space has glyphs and **no
contours**, so the cheap proxy calls it convertible and the verb then answers `EmptyGeometry` after the
click — `context-menus.md` §3's one prohibition on a row. Under the flip the empty-content case still
passed and only the spaces case failed, which is the half a proxy hides;
`converting_refuses_a_non_text_kind_and_text_with_no_contours` covers both. Empty content is refused
rather than converted, for the same reason: a `Path` holding nothing draws nothing and could never be
picked on the canvas again.

**Cost forced the gate to be a snapshot.** `ContextMenu` gains `text_outlineable`, taken once at open,
because asking the question *builds the outlines* — about a microsecond a glyph (D145), which is why
the render walk gates the same construction on there being a visible stroke to use it. A paragraph is a
millisecond, every frame, for as long as the menu is up. That files it beside `system_text` and
`system_image` as a snapshot field but for a different reason: those are about a shared OS resource,
this is about arithmetic.

**It lands in `Group::Structure`, not the text head**, even though §5.6's table lists it as a text row.
§3 groups by what a verb *does*, and this one replaces the layer; it shares the slot with *Outline
shape*, and the two are mutually exclusive by kind, so no menu shows both.
`convert_to_path_is_texts_row_and_never_beside_outline_shape` holds that, flipped against filing it in
the head and against dropping the dim.

**Its label is *Convert to path*, not *Outline text*, and the wording is load-bearing.** This is a
one-way door — the string is gone from the model and no amount of anchor editing brings it back — and
"convert" says a thing became another thing where "outline" reads as a decoration you could take off
again. No confirmation dialog: undo is the way back, which is what Illustrator, Affinity and Figma all
rely on for the same conversion. **The status line names it** — "Converted to a path — the text is
