gone; Ctrl+Z to undo" — because a layer that still *looks* like a word is exactly the one whose loss is
invisible.

**D261 — The three text-sizing rows, and the panel's control lifted into a method so both doors are one
verb. *Built and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** *Auto width* / *Auto height* / *Fixed size* as
three checkable rows in the text head, directly under *Edit text* where `context-menus.md` §5.6's table
puts them, carrying the panel's own cell index as `Item::TextSizing(u8)`.

**They were invisible to that file's ledger in both directions, which is worth fixing rather than only
noting.** §5.6 scored them *wiring* and §9.1 — the wiring list — never named them, so §9.5's "Landed:
all of §9.1" was true and said nothing about these, and the "not landed" line did not name them either.
An unbuilt row that appears in no bucket cannot be counted from either end. §9.1 names them now.

**A deliberate duplicate of the Type panel's segmented control**, and the one place this registry
repeats a control rather than reaching a verb nothing else offers. §5.6's reason stands: *Auto width* is
the most reached-for text command in Figma, and right-click is where a Figma hand goes for it.

**So the panel's body was lifted into `OndinApp::set_text_sizing(id, cell)`** (`panels/typography.rs`),
which is §8's rule — a row and the control it duplicates must be the same verb — and is the half of
this change with any risk in it. What the method carries, and what a second call site would otherwise
have had to remember: the switch **adopts the shaped size**, so changing mode does not move the text;
it goes through `text_session_restyled`, so a live editor re-shapes rather than drawing to the old
width; and it reads the **preview** layout rather than the committed one, because during a live session
the size being adopted is the one on screen and adopting the committed size would snap the box back to
what it measured before the last keystroke. The tick is read off the **display** node for the same
reason, so the state the row reports and the state the verb reads are the same side of the preview.

**Offered only over a *single* text layer, and §3's head rule is not strict enough on its own.** "Every
member qualifies" is satisfied by a pair of text layers — both *are* text — but the tick is a fact about
one node, and two layers in different states have no honest answer to put there. It is spelled
`LayerState::text_sizing: Option<u8>` rather than an index plus a separate "is it text", so the state
with no answer cannot be spelled at all: a default of `0` would tick *Auto width* on a rectangle.
`the_three_sizing_rows_tick_one_and_only_over_a_single_text_layer` is the test, flipped against a
constant tick and against pushing the rows on the kind alone.

**The labels are the menu's own, not `TextSizing::LABELS`.** Those read "Auto W" / "Auto H" / "Fixed"
because three cells of a segmented control have no room; a menu row has a whole line, and an
abbreviation there is a panel's constraint leaking into a surface that does not share it. Three
different glyphs too — a box growing sideways, one growing downwards, one that does neither — because
the same icon three times over three labels reads as generated.

**D262 — A label ran under its own accelerator, and a floor cannot compact anything on its own. *Built
and tested; not yet reviewed on screen.*** Two chrome reports from the machine on 2026-08-20, in one
message, and they belong in one entry because the second is why the first was measurable: compacting
every menu meant reading `ui::menu_row`'s anchors, and the anchors are the whole of the first fault.

**A label that is too long does not clip, wrap or reflow — it *overlaps*.** *Reverse subpath direction*
ran under `Shift+D` in the screenshot, and the row was not special in any way: `ui::menu_row` paints
the label and the accelerator as **two `Painter::text` calls at fixed anchors**, the label left of
`8 + 15 + 9` and the accelerator right of `width − 8`. There is no layout between the two, so nothing
can give. Measured, the old label ended at **173.8pt** where `Shift+D` began at **155.2** — an overlap
of 18.6 — and the new label, *Reverse subpath*, clears by 32. The rename was the report's own
suggestion and it loses nothing: a subpath has one property you can reverse.

**The reason this survived every menu test is that no test had ever measured a string.** `menu.rs`'s
suite asserts about rows, groups, order and gating, and a fault that shows only on the one row whose
label is too long is invisible to all of it. `menu::tests::no_menu_label_runs_into_its_accelerator`
closes that: it lays every `Item::ALL` label at
11.5pt and every accelerator at 10.5pt against `menu_row`'s own anchors and demands **4pt** of
clearance. The bound is measured rather than round — *Copy properties* and *Paste properties* already
sit within 20pt of the accelerator column, so a looser bound would not have caught the reported row and
a tighter one fails on the next reasonable label. (The tightest row in the registry is *Make this the
base operand* at 9.1pt, and it has no accelerator to run into.) Flipped by putting the long label back.

**A clipping guard in `menu_row` was considered and not built**, and that is a decision rather than an
oversight. It is the general fix, but every current label clears after the rename, and a test at the
*source* — the registry — catches the next one without changing what any row draws. *Revisit if a
label ever has to be data rather than a literal; a truncated row is better than an overlapped one only
once the string stops being ours to choose.*

**The other half: two points off every menu row.** Reported as "the layer menus have gotten a bit too
tall… this will be global for all menus". `ui::MENU_ROW_H` goes **24 → 22** for the dropdowns, and the
menus that allocate their rows exactly get a constant of their own, `ui::MENU_ITEM_H` at **24**,
**replacing three separate copies of `26.0`** — `menu::ROW_H` and *two* `const ITEM_H` in `app.rs`, one
in `zoom_control` and one in `view_and_snap_menus`. The triplication is the point: "compact every menu
by two points" is exactly the edit that finds two of three and leaves the third behind, and a top-bar
menu two points taller than the context menu beside it is §8's "two menus read as two apps" fault
arriving by omission. The two-point gap **between** the two constants is preserved deliberately: an
exact-allocated row carries a glyph column *and* an accelerator column where a dropdown row carries a
glyph and a label, and what was asked for was the same amount off everything, not a new relationship
between the two surfaces. Measured over `menu::height` with a throwaway probe, since removed: a
primitive's menu (21 rows in 8 groups) 646 → 604, text (25 rows) 764 → 714, a boolean (27) 818 → 764 —
42 to 54pt, about 6.5%.

**The finding is that a floor cannot compact anything on its own, and it nearly shipped as a constant
that changed nothing.** `ui::menu_rows` sets `interact_size.y`, which is a **minimum**: a
`selectable_label`'s natural height is its 15pt row plus `button_padding.y` twice, so at the theme's
padding of 4 it is **23**, and a floor of 22 against a natural 23 is ignored outright. It works only
because every dropdown's own scope has already brought that padding down to **0** (the control's scope)
or **2** (a line spelled beside `menu_rows` at six sites), putting the natural height at 15 or 19. All
four combinations were measured before the number was chosen. *A new dropdown that leaves the theme's
padding alone gets a 23pt row and no error.*

**The wrong fix was built first and then removed**, which is the part worth keeping. `menu_rows` was
given `button_padding.y = 3.0` so that one helper would own both numbers. It is unnecessary — every
caller is already at 0 or 2 — and worse than unnecessary, because the sites that spell the padding do
it **after** `menu_rows` runs and would silently override it: a fourth number living in a shared helper
and applying nowhere. *The tripwire for the 23pt row is the test, not the helper.*

**And the test that guarded this had to change, because its old form was the trap.**
`inspector::stroke_row_tests::a_menu_rows_height_does_not_depend_on_its_state` asserted `first >= 23.0`
— "the floor has to clear the tallest natural row" — which was true of the old numbers and says nothing
about whether the floor is *deciding*. It asserts that the painted height **is** `ui::MENU_ROW_H` now,
which fails when a future compaction lowers the constant past the natural height and the rows do not
move. Its fixture had to grow with it: it set `button_padding.y = 0.0` and only 0, so the first flip
did not bite at all — at padding 0 the natural row is 15 and the floor decides whatever it is. It runs
over **both** ambient paddings in use, and the flip fails on the `pad = 2` case, which is the one the
old fixture could not see. *A fixture that pins one of two real ambient values is a test about one of
them.*

**Nothing about the separators changed, and they are the next lever.** `ui::menu_sep` was still a 1pt
rule with 4pt of air either side, and `menu::SEP_H` still 9 — so the primitive's eight groups spent
**63pt** on seven hairlines, more than two and a half of the rows the compaction just shortened. Named
here rather than left to be rediscovered: *if the menus still read long on screen, take it out of the
air around the rules before taking another point off the rows*, which are already inside the export's
26. **Asked for and done the same day — §15 D263**, which also says how that 63pt over-sells the case:
seven separators losing 2pt each is 14, against the 42 the rows had already given up.

**D811 — A menu row's height is either an argument or a floor, and the warning that said "any new
dropdown" could not be applied without reading the callee. *Record-only; recorded 2026-09-19;
Resolved — nothing was defective and nothing was repaired, and what moved is where a rule is written
down.***

`roadmap.md`'s *Now · Inspector* carried the menu-row border as a bullet from 2026-08-31 — egui 0.35's
per-state frame arithmetic, the 21-against-23 at the panels' zero padding, the two points on the other
axis, the floor that only ever *raises* — and none of it was ever work. **Every sentence of it was
already in the code twice over.** `ui::menu_rows`' own doc carries the arithmetic, the measurement and
*"so the border goes"*, with the argument that zeroing `bg_stroke` on all four states is a stronger
guarantee than clearing a floor because it does not depend on where the natural height happens to
fall; `ui::MENU_ROW_H`'s carries the floor rule, the 22-since-2026-08-20 (**D262**) and the tripwire —
*a new caller that leaves the theme's padding alone gets a 23pt row and no error*, which
`a_menu_rows_height_does_not_depend_on_its_state` asserts against at both of the paddings in use. A
standing trap is a doc comment's job, and `roadmap.md` holds open work only.

**One sentence of the bullet was in neither, and it is the one that makes the warning usable.** The
sub-bullet's finding was that *"any new dropdown owes `ui::menu_rows` and that padding"* is **too
wide**: there are two *families* of menu row, and the warning is true of one of them. A row built from
an egui widget is sized by `button_padding` and `interact_size.y`, so `MENU_ROW_H` is a **floor**
under it and the ambient padding decides whether the floor decides anything at all. `ui::menu_row` and
`ui::menu_item` take the height as an **argument** and `allocate_exact_size` it, so `button_padding`
cannot reach them and the floor is not what holds them still. *The tell for which family a row is in
is whether its height is an argument.*

**The Export panel's own menu is the caller that proves it.** `panels::export`'s `export-menu`
popover calls `ui::menu_rows`, sets no padding after it, and is **correct**: every row in it is a
`ui::menu_item` or a `ui::menu_row` with the height passed in — `inspector::menu_action`'s dimmable
rows included, that helper being `menu_item` under a `scope` — so there is nothing for a padding to
reach. A warning phrased about dropdowns in general scores that menu as the failure case. 🚨 **And it
passes `MENU_ROW_H`**, the *dropdown* constant, to functions of the other family, so the constant a
row names does not say which family it is in either; only whether the height is an argument does.

**It is filed on `ui::MENU_ITEM_H` rather than on `MENU_ROW_H` because a warning belongs where a
reader meets the exception.** Somebody adding a menu reaches for a height constant first, and the one
they reach for is the one that has to tell them which rule they are under. Beside `MENU_ROW_H` the
paragraph is a caveat on a rule the reader has already decided applies to them; beside `MENU_ITEM_H`
it is the answer to the question that constant's reader is actually asking, and it links
`MENU_ROW_H`, `menu_row`, `menu_item` and `menu_rows` so that either door reaches the other.

⚠️ **The shape worth keeping is that a warning which cannot be applied without reading the callee is
half a warning**, and this one had been half a warning since the day it was written: a reader
following it would have "fixed" a correct caller by adding a padding line to a menu whose rows cannot
see one. That is the same failure as a citation resolving to the wrong entry — it names the right
neighbourhood and is wrong about the rule — and nothing here can gate it, a comment's *advice*
compiling as readily as its facts.

*(Recorded 2026-09-19; **Resolved — record-only.** No production line changed and none is proposed.
**The citation is planted by hand** on `MENU_ITEM_H`, a record-only entry being invisible to the
citation census until somebody does (D741's fix for D735's shape) and that constant being the one
place a reader meets the question *which rule is my row under*. The *Now · Inspector* menu-row bullet
and its ⚠️ sub-bullet are **struck from `roadmap.md`** with a clause saying where they went, and that
section's table row goes from *"Two items"* to one — `char_valve`'s third arm, the ruling **D802** and
**D803** left — since a count of items is exactly what goes wrong when one of them is a note.
⚠️ **§6's `menu_rows` paragraph named the wrong callers while this stood**: *"Eleven popups call it —
five in `inspector.rs`, six in `typography.rs`"*, where the measurement on 2026-09-19 is **seventeen
call sites — six in `inspector.rs`, six in `typography.rs`, four in `export.rs` and one in
`dashboard.rs`** — so its enumeration omitted the very caller this entry turns on, and the file that
caller lives in. Amended there, with *"six of the eleven"* setting the padding themselves becoming
eleven of the seventeen and the export popover named as the one call site none of the arithmetic
reaches. 🚨 **The same stale six is in `a_menu_rows_height_does_not_depend_on_its_state`'s own doc
twice and is left standing**, along with that test's *"Every call site sets 0 (the control's own
scope) or 2"*, which the export popover does not and does not need to; reported to the maintainer
rather than corrected here, `inspector.rs` being under edit while this was written.)*

**D263 — Three points of air, and a border the height never counted. *Built and tested; not yet
reviewed on screen.*** The second half of D262's compaction, from the same report on the same day: the
maintainer asked for the separators too after seeing what the row change did. `ui::menu_sep` drew a 1pt
rule with 4pt of air either side and now draws it with **3**, so a separator costs **7** where it cost
9. **The rule itself did not move.** A hairline is the thing being seen and the air is only what it
costs, so a separator that has to read as a *group* boundary wants to stay visible rather than stay
surrounded.

**The number stopped being written twice, which is the part that was actually load-bearing.**
`menu_sep` allocated `1.0 + AIR * 2.0` and `menu::SEP_H` was a hand-copied `9.0` in another file — two
numbers obliged to agree with nothing keeping them in step, and **no symptom if they drifted** except a
menu opened near a viewport edge landing in the wrong place, which is the one state nobody exercises on
purpose. There is `ui::MENU_SEP_H` now, with a private `SEP_AIR` beside it; `menu_sep` allocates it and
`menu::SEP_H` reads it.

Measured over `menu::height` with a throwaway probe, since removed — original → after D262's rows →
after this: a primitive's menu (21 rows, 7 separators) 646 → 604 → **592**, text (25 rows, 8
separators) 764 → 714 → **700**, a boolean (27 rows, 8) 818 → 764 → **750**. So 54 to 68 points off the
whole compaction, about 8%. **The separators were the smaller half**, and D262's prediction that "the
hairlines were 63pt, more than two and a half rows" over-sold them: what is available from a separator
is the 2pt of air, so seven of them give 14 where 21 rows at 2pt each gave 42. *A term's total size is
not the size of the cut it can stand.*

**And building it uncovered a placement bug older than any of it: `menu::height` never counted the
frame's border, so `menu_place` clamped every menu against a box two points short on both axes.**
`ui::menu_frame` carries `.stroke(Stroke::new(1.0, …))`, and a `Frame`'s stroke **grows its outer
rect** — so a menu paints `2 × 1pt` wider and taller than its content plus its inner margin, and
`height` returned content and margins only. `menu_place` flips and clamps against a size it is handed
*before* the `Area` is shown, which is the whole reason the number is computed rather than measured, so
a menu opened near the bottom or right edge overhung by two points. Silent, small, and only in the
state `menu_place` exists to prevent. Fixed by naming the border: `ui::MENU_BORDER = 1.0` is what
`menu_frame` strokes with, `height` adds `MENU_BORDER * 2.0` **inside the function** rather than at the
call site — its contract is "the height a menu will paint at" and a menu is always in `menu_frame` —
and the call site hands `menu_place` `MENU_W + MENU_BORDER * 2.0` for the width. **No ink moved**;
`menu_place` only ever decides a position.

**How it was found is the general point.** `menu::tests::a_menus_computed_height_is_the_height_it_paints`
builds a real `menu_frame` with real `menu_row`s and `menu_sep`s over five shapes and compares the
painted rect against what `height` returns. It failed on the *first* shape — one row, no separator — at
**34 computed against 36 painted**, which has nothing to do with separators. The existing test,
`a_menus_height_is_its_rows_its_separators_and_its_gaps`, could never have caught it: it was written
from the same arithmetic it checks, so it agreed with the function about a term neither of them had. *A
test that restates a formula cannot find a term missing from it; only one that measures the drawing
can.* **Both are kept, and neither replaces the other** — the new one proves the total against reality,
the old one says which term is which, and a total-only test passes happily with two terms wrong in
opposite directions. The shapes are `[1]`, `[3]`, `[1,1]`, `[5,1,4]` and `[2,3,1,6]`, because one group
exercises no separator and one row exercises no gap, which are the two terms most likely to be wrong.
Flipped by giving `SEP_H` back its own `9.0` while `menu_sep` draws 7: it fails from `[1,1]` on and the
`[1]` case still passes, which is exactly the drift the shared constant now prevents.

**One thing is left undone and it is a call to make on screen: the card paints 212 wide where
`context-menus.md` §8 says 210.** Same cause — the border is outside `MENU_W`, which is used as the
*content* width (`ui.set_width(MENU_W - MENU_PAD * 2.0)`). The **placement** on x is fixed without
touching the drawn width, because narrowing every menu by two points is a visual change nobody asked
for. Making the card 210 outer means `set_width(MENU_W - MENU_PAD * 2.0 - MENU_BORDER * 2.0)`, which
takes 2pt off the label column and wants `no_menu_label_runs_into_its_accelerator`'s `inner` moved with
it — every label still clears, the tightest row carrying an accelerator by about 20pt. Recorded as an
open difference in `context-menus.md` §9.6 rather than left as a silent two points. *Keep the air, the
shared constant and the border; decide the card's width on the machine.* **Decided on 2026-08-23 and
the sketch above is what was built — §15 D307**, at every call site in the app rather than at this
one, since the divergence was never the context menu's. The width half of the fix above went with it: the call site
hands `menu_place` a plain `MENU_W` now. *The height half of this entry is unchanged*, because a height
is summed from its rows rather than named by the design, so `menu::height` still adds the border itself.

**D307 — A card's named width is the width it paints. *Fixed and tested at all eight call sites; the
eighth was found by reading, not by failing.*** D263 left this as "a call to make on the machine", and
it was made the other way round from how it was scoped: not "should the context menu come in by two
points" but "why does any card in
the app paint a width nobody named". `ui::menu_frame(pad)` puts a `MENU_BORDER`-wide stroke on an
`egui::Frame`, a `Frame`'s stroke **grows its outer rect**, and every call site wrote
`ui.set_width(W - MENU_PAD * 2.0)` — the padding subtracted, the border forgotten. (There are **eight**
of them; the pass that fixed it counted seven, which is the last paragraph here.) Measured with a
throwaway probe over the four `(width, pad)` pairs the app opens a card at: the context menu named 210
and painted **212**, zoom 150 → **152**, view/snap 160 → **162**, every `POPOVER_W` card 272 → **274**.
The design's numbers, read off `design/Editor.dc.html`, are the **outer** card; the app's were the
content box, and the two had been read as the same number since the first menu.

**The fix is one `const fn` in `ui.rs`** — `menu_inner_w(card, pad) = card - pad * 2.0 - MENU_BORDER *
2.0` — threaded through `app.rs`'s `dropdown` helper (which covers both top-bar menus), `menu.rs`'s
context menu, **both** of `export.rs`'s popovers, two popovers in `inspector.rs`,
`typography::MENU_INNER` and four test-side reconstructions of the same number. `const fn` because
`MENU_INNER` is a `const` initialised from it. **A function rather than eight corrected subtractions**
is the whole point: the same arithmetic written eight times was wrong eight times in the same
direction, and nothing in the suite could see it.

**Three things fell out without being touched, and each is a correction rather than a restatement.**
`menu.rs` was handing `menu_place` a size of `MENU_W + MENU_BORDER * 2.0`, correcting by hand for the
mismatch; that is a plain `MENU_W` now, so the placer and the drawing are one number instead of two kept
two apart. `OndinApp::popover_left` computes its lane clearance as `inspector_column.left() - width -
GAP` with `GAP = 10.0`, and being handed the *content* width made the real gap **8** — it is 10. The zoom
menu's anchor right-aligns as `head.rect.right() - MENU_W`, so the card overhung its own head by two
points; it is exact. Each of those is a placer reading a width that the ink did not agree with, which is
what makes "the design's number is the outer box" a rule about more than the drawing.

**The height half, the same day.** `typography::body_max_h` — the scroll budget for the type popup's tab
body — subtracted `SCREEN_MARGIN * 2.0` and `MENU_PAD * 2.0` but not the border, so the tallest Character
tab could stand two points past the margin it was computed to respect. It subtracts
`ui::MENU_BORDER * 2.0` as well now, **spelled out rather than routed through `menu_inner_w`**: that
helper is about a width the design *names*, and this is a height taken from what the screen has left. A
`Frame`'s stroke grows its outer rect on both axes, and only the width axis had ever been looked at.

**What was measured before the change, because a 2pt narrowing is exactly the size of thing that flips
an assertion nobody re-ran.** D263's own note and `roadmap.md`'s entry both warned that
`no_menu_label_runs_into_its_accelerator` — a headroom assertion over all of `Item::ALL`, with the label
and the accelerator painted at fixed anchors and the accelerator's at `inner - 8` — could genuinely tip.
Over all 36 accelerator-carrying rows: at inner 200 the tightest is *Paste properties* at **19.69pt**, at
inner 198 it is the same row at **17.69pt**, against a bound of 4. It did not flip, and the check was
worth doing rather than assuming. That test's `⚠️` flip note moved with the anchor — *Reverse subpath
direction*'s `Shift+D` begins at 153.2 rather than 155.2 now, an overlap of 20.6 and a miss of 24.6. The
other width-reading test, `the_settings_popup_fits_four_tabs_and_a_close_button`, goes from a 54.0pt tab
cell to 53.5 against a floor of 44.

**One test broke, and it is the reason this entry exists.**
`the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height` selected painted rects by a literal `250.0` — the old
inner width — and failed with *an empty list* rather than with a number: "the fixture painted 0
full-width rects". It reads `menu_inner_w` now, as do two further tests that had reconstructed the inner
width as `POPOVER_W - 22.0` with the padding inlined and were silently measuring a card that no longer
exists. **A fixture selector written as a literal fails by matching nothing, which is the failure mode
that reads as a broken test rather than as a moved number.**

**The kept assertion is `ui::context_menu_chrome_tests::a_menu_card_paints_the_width_it_is_named`**: all
four `(width, pad)` pairs through a real `menu_frame`, asserting the painted outer rect equals the named
width. Flip-checked against the version every call site actually contained — `w - pad * 2.0` — and
it fails with the reported symptom in the message, "the context menu card is named 210 and paints 212".
Four pairs rather than one because the bug was invisible at every one of them for the same reason.
**When the helper was flipped, exactly one test failed out of 661.** Nothing in the suite had ever pinned
any card's painted width: each number was only ever compared against another copy of itself, and both
copies were the content box. That is how this survived from the first menu, and it is the general lesson
— *a constant checked only against a restatement of itself is unchecked.*

**There were eight call sites, not seven, and the eighth is the lesson above in its second form.**
`export::export_settings_popup` still had `POP_INNER = POP_W - POP_PAD * 2.0` after the other seven were
converted — the export **settings** popover, not the export **menu** popover beside it, which was
threaded; two popovers hang off the one panel and only one of them was counted. It was found by *reading
the sweep*, and nothing failed when it was wrong, because **the assertion drives `menu_frame` directly:
it pins the helper's arithmetic and cannot see a call site that does its own subtraction.** `POP_INNER`
reads `ui::menu_inner_w(POP_W, POP_PAD)` now and carries that history in its doc comment, so
`architecture.md` §9.4's "272 wide, the shell every other card here uses" is true of every popover
without exception.

⚠️ **The honest limit of the guard: no test can catch a *ninth* popover that computes its own inner
width.** `a_menu_card_paints_the_width_it_is_named` would pass beside it, exactly as it passed beside the
eighth. What is verified is that nothing computes an inner width by hand today — `grep -A 2 "menu_frame("`
over the workspace, eight call sites and two test-side reconstructions, all of them through the helper —
and a grep is a fact about a moment. The shape that would make the mistake **unrepresentable** is a
`ui::menu_card(ui, width, pad, body)` owning both the frame and the `set_width`, so that a call site never
names an inner width at all. *Not built, and offered rather than done unasked; build it the next time a
popover is added, which is the moment the risk is real.*

**D264 — *Export as…*, and "blocked on an export UI" was blocked on a raster walk — then the verb was
removed and the walk stayed. *Built 2026-08-20; removed 2026-08-22. The `scene::build_of` half is
load-bearing and is not going anywhere.*** `context-menus.md` §4 and `roadmap.md` both carried both *Export* rows as
waiting on "an export UI nobody has designed", and that is **D260's shape exactly** — a premise that
names a *dependency* rots when something else grows it, and nothing recompiles when it does. Re-derived
against `crates/` on 2026-08-20, the sentence was false in three directions at once: `svg_of(doc, res,
&[NodeId])` had arrived with *Copy as SVG* the same day (D259), `rfd::FileDialog` was already open in
**five** places in `app.rs` — *Save as*, *Open*, *Place image*, *Replace…*, *Export original…* — and
`png(doc, res, &Viewport)` had been there since M0. What the rows wanted was named as "a dialog, a
format and a scale"; two of those three were sitting in the tree.

**What was genuinely missing is not a UI at all.** It was written down in `Item::CopyAsSvg`'s own doc
comment, which scoped *Copy as PNG* out on the grounds that "the raster path is viewport-scoped with no
way to say 'only these layers', so a PNG of the selection would quietly include whatever else overlapped
its box". ⚠️ **That comment no longer says it** — the row was built on 2026-08-22 and the comment
rewritten to record that the ground had gone (D259), so the quotation above is history and is kept as
evidence of what the blocker actually was. The objection was correct and is a *renderer* gap: `scene::build` starts at `doc.root()`, so the only
way to aim it is a box, and a box round a selection is not the selection. **`scene::build_of` is the
answer** — the walk over a set of origins, each painted under its **parent's** world transform, which is
`svg_of`'s emitter written in the other renderer. It is deliberately written to *look* like `svg_of`,
because the transform is where the mirror can go wrong: handing `paint_node` the node's own world
instead of its parent's applies the local twice, which is the slippage D258 records against the SVG
writer. `build` is now one call of `build_of` with the root on its own, so there is still one spelling
of the walk, and `render_to_rgba` likewise wraps `render_subtrees_to_rgba` rather than growing an
argument its two dozen test call sites would all have to pass.

**Two properties fall out of scoping and are worth stating rather than discovering.** Ancestor clipping
does not travel — a layer inside a clipping frame, exported alone, is not cut by that frame, because the
walk *starts* at the layer; `svg_of` already behaved this way, so the two writers agree and "export this
layer" means the whole layer. And **nothing behind is painted**, artboard background included, which is
what puts a selection export on transparency without anyone asking for it. `ondin-export/tests/png.rs`'s
`a_subtree_export_paints_neither_its_neighbours_nor_the_ground` pins both, and they needed **two**
assertions rather than one: the fixture puts a green rect *over* the red ellipse and an opaque blue
ground *behind* it, so a walk that fixed only one of the two would pass half the test. Flipped against
the plausible wrong version — frame a viewport on the bounds and render the whole page — where the first
assertion reports the sibling's exact green and the second the ground's exact blue.

**The PNG is 1:1 and takes no scale argument, which is a decision and not a deferral of one.** World
units are px by implication everywhere else in the app (`roadmap.md` *Units*), so one device pixel per
world unit is the only framing that needs nothing decided: the file comes out exactly the pixel size the
inspector's W and H report. A 2×/3× multiplier is a real want, and it is a **control** — it needs
somewhere to live before it needs a parameter, and a `scale: f64` that both callers pass `1.0` to would
be the decoy D2 exists to warn about. ~~*That multiplier is the one piece of these rows still open.*~~
**It got its home on 2026-08-21** (D274) and the parameter is real, on `RasterOpts`; `png_of` stays the
1:1 shortcut. The reasoning above is why the shortcut is still the right shape and is not a leftover.

**The dialog was the format picker**, so there was no second widget asking the same question in the
same box: `svg` was offered first and seeded the name, `png` second, and the chosen extension decided
the writer. `wants_raster` was lifted to a **free function** and pinned, on this file's standing
pattern — the decision is the testable part and `export_subtrees` was an `OndinApp` method, which
cannot be built headlessly. **SVG was the fallback rather than an equal branch**: a path with no
extension is reachable through the dialog's *All files* filter, one of the two writers had to take it,
and a file that turns out to be markup announces itself in any text editor where a mis-named PNG does
not. Flipped against `ends_with("png")` — the obvious spelling — which takes `logo.notpng` as raster
and `logo.PNG` as vector while the two happy-path assertions still pass. **All of this went on
2026-08-22 with the row**, `wants_raster` and `written_name` with it and
`the_export_extension_picks_the_writer_and_svg_takes_everything_else` with them; the paragraph is kept
because the *shape* is reusable — an extension is a format picker only where a dialog is the last
thing standing between a decision and a file, and the Export panel picks its format from a control,
so there is nothing left here to interpret.

***Export frame as…* is subsumed, not deferred.** `context-menus.md` §5.1 specified it as a Frame head
row, and building it now would put two rows that run the same code over the same subject on one menu:
`svg(doc, res, Some(ab))` **is** `svg_of(doc, res, &[ab])`, and §3's Export group is on every layer's
menu — so with a frame right-clicked, the frame *is* the selection and *Export as…* already is it. The
§5.1 row was written before §3's Export group had any built row and before the writer took a set; it is
a decided non-goal now rather than an open item, which is what stops it being re-argued. The one thing
it could have meant that the general row does not — "export the frame this layer is *in*", from a
child's menu — is not what §5.1 says, and is a different row if anyone ever wants it. **The subsumer
changed on 2026-08-22 and the non-goal did not.** *Export as…* is gone and the Export panel is what
subsumes §5.1's row now — which is the stronger form of the same argument, since the panel is exactly
what made the general row redundant: a one-off file export that is not worth a row on every layer's
menu is not worth a narrower one on a frame's. Reinstating it would be reinstating the withdrawn verb
one kind at a time, and that is the thing to say to whoever proposes it.

**The label is *Export as…* where §3 says *Export selection…*, and the card decided that rather than
taste.** D262's `no_menu_label_runs_into_its_accelerator` caught it on the row's **first run**: the
specified wording ends at **129.7pt** against a `Ctrl+Shift+E` starting at **131.8**, clearing by 2.1
where the test wants 4. `Ctrl+Shift+E` is a wide accelerator and the label column is what pays. The
wording shipped ends at **93.1**, clearing by 38.7, and it is not merely the short one that fit: it
reads as a pair with *Copy as SVG* under it — both "the same artwork, in another form" — and no other
row in this menu names the selection either, it being *Cut* and not *Cut selection*. Worth recording as
D262 paying for itself twice inside a day: the test was written for a reported overlap and has now
stopped one being written. **The divergence this created is gone with the row** — `context-menus.md`
§9.6 listed it as its eighth item and now lists eight items again — but the *measurement* is not
spent: it is the standing evidence that the label column has about 2pt of slack against a wide
accelerator, which is what §9.6's item 7 has to weigh before narrowing the card.

**`Ctrl+Shift+E`, and the guard that matters is on the other chord.** `shortcuts.md` §8 reserved it
(Figma's) and it was free. Plain `Ctrl+E` is *Flatten*, and the risk was never that Shift fails to
reach the export — it is that a *Flatten* written without `!m.shift` would fire **as well**, dissolving
the selection into a path behind a modal file dialog where the user cannot see it happen until the
dialog closes. `Flatten` already had the guard, and
`export_and_flatten_are_distinguished_by_shift` kept it, its load-bearing assertion being the
**absence** of `Flatten` from the shifted chord's answer rather than the presence of the export.

**That guard is now the whole of the hazard, and it reads like a redundant one.** With the export gone
`Ctrl+Shift+E` is **unbound but not free**: nothing answers it, and the only reason nothing answers it
is the `!m.shift` that was written to keep two verbs apart. A future editor tidying a condition that
excludes a chord which no longer exists would give the hand still reaching for the old export chord a
dissolved selection instead — over a boolean or two or more layers, which is exactly where *Flatten*
does something, and exactly where a designer would be reaching to export. The test is rewritten as
`a_stray_shift_on_ctrl_e_does_nothing_rather_than_flattening`, asserting that `Ctrl+Shift+E` resolves
to `vec![]`, and it is flip-checked by deleting `!m.shift`: the first assertion — plain `Ctrl+E` gives
`[Flatten]` — still passes, and the second fails with `[Flatten]`, which is the whole point of keeping
both in one test. **"Unbound but not free" is a distinction worth a sentence wherever this keymap is
described**, and `shortcuts.md` §8 carries it on the row.

**Found on the way and fixed, because it is the damaging kind.** `png.rs`'s module doc said "text glyph
rendering is deferred with the rest of shaping". `cpu.rs` has filled glyphs through `vello_cpu` for long
enough that `png.rs`'s own `text_rasterizes_ink_pixels` exists to assert it, and that test was written
for this exact claim. One site, corrected. The shape is worth keeping: **a doc comment naming something
as *not built* rots silently**, because nothing recompiles when the thing arrives — which is the same
sentence this entry opens with, one layer down.

**What was not pinned.** `export_selection` and `export_subtrees` were `OndinApp` methods, so the wiring
— that the row reached the verb, that the dialog's answer reached the writer — was read rather than
tested, the same wgpu seam `resize_tx` and `canvas::autopan` sit behind. The three pieces that *could*
be free functions were (`wants_raster`, `png_of`, `scene::build_of`), and were. Both methods and
`wants_raster` are gone; the other two are not.

**The verb was removed on 2026-08-22, and the reason is that it had become the slower of two doors onto
the same file.** *Export as…* asked where, what format and at what size on every single use and
remembered none of it. The inspector's Export panel (D274) answers all three from the layer — it builds
a button reading `"Export {name}"` for one layer or `"Export {n} layers"` and clicking it calls
`run_export` — so the one-off was not a second door onto a *different* thing, which is what usually
earns one, but a longer route to the same file. Gone with it: `Item::ExportSelection` (the variant, its
`Item::ALL` row, its `spec()` arm with the *"Export as…"* label, `icon::EXPORT` and `Ctrl+Shift+E`, its
row push and its dispatch arm), `Action::ExportSelection` and its chord, `OndinApp::export_selection`
and `export_subtrees`, and the two free functions the compiler then found dead, `wants_raster` and
`written_name`.

**Removed as a whole verb rather than as a row, and that was the decision rather than the tidying.** The
cheaper change was to drop the menu row and leave the chord, which keeps the capability for whoever
knows it is there. That is precisely the reachability failure `context-menus.md` §5 argues the head
exists to repair — a verb reachable only by a gesture nothing announces — wearing different clothes,
and it would have left a chord whose only documentation was a keymap file. Either the verb is worth a
row or it is not worth a chord.

**What did *not* go, and this is the trap in the diff.** D264 built two things and only one is removed:
`scene::build_of` is the walk over a set of origins that the removed row paid for, and it is now the
**only** spelling of the scene walk in the workspace — `scene::build` is one call of it with the root
on its own, and `VelloCpuRenderer::render_to_rgba` one call of `render_subtrees_to_rgba` — so the
canvas, `png::raster_of`, *Copy as PNG* (D259), the inspector's Export panel, the JPEG path and the
CLI all run through it. Nothing about this entry's second and third paragraphs is history.

⚠️ **`png_of` is a different matter and is the one thing to watch**: it
had exactly one production caller and that caller was *Export as…*, so the workspace now reaches it
only from `ondin-export/tests/png.rs`. `ondin-export` is a library and `png_of` is `pub`, so
`dead_code` will never say so and every gate stays green — the shape CLAUDE.md warns about. It is kept
deliberately, as `raster_of`'s 1:1 shortcut with the framing argument above attached to it, and its
doc comment names *Export as…* among "the callers that genuinely mean 1:1", which is now false.

*Fix the `png_of` doc comment's caller list. Then leave the function: a shortcut whose reasoning is
written down is worth more than one call site.*

**D265 — *Export original…* dimmed in one door and not the other, and the file said it dimmed in both.
*Fixed and tested at the time; history since 2026-08-23, when both doors were removed (D305). Read
the rule, not the row.*** Found the same day as D264 and by the same method —
reading `context-menus.md` against the code rather than picking an item off it. §5.7's entry for the row
has said since it was built that "it dims only for a *linked* picture, whose bytes the document does not
hold". The **inspector's** door does exactly that: `menu_action(ui, exportable, …)` with a `why` that
says the document does not hold the bytes, on `doc.image(&id).is_some_and(|e| e.bytes().is_some())`
(D225). The **menu's** door carried no gate at all — `rows.push(Row::new(Item::ExportOriginal))` — so it
offered a live row and refused *after* the click, with a status line.

**Two doors onto one verb giving opposite answers is D261's failure**, and this is its quieter shape: not
two verbs that disagree, but one verb whose availability is decided in one place and not in the other.
The fix is the predicate, not a second reading of it — `LayerState::picture_linked`, set from the same
`ImageEntry::bytes` question, and the row's `why` is the inspector's sentence.

**The field is named for the exceptional state, and that is what makes it safe.** `LayerState` derives
`Default`, so `false` has to mean "the row is live"; an `embedded: bool` spelling would default to
dimming, and the four fixtures in `menu.rs` that set `has_picture` and say nothing about bytes would all
have started reading as linked. The test flips **both** ways for that reason — dropping the `dim_if`
fails the second and third assertions while the first passes, and the `embedded` spelling fails the
first instead.

**Unreachable today and pinned anyway.** Nothing in the app can author a linked picture (`roadmap.md`
*Images*), so no user can reach either door's answer. That is the argument *for* the test rather than
against it: the day linking lands is the day nobody will be looking at this row, and the two doors will
already agree. It is also worth noting what the gap cost while it existed, which is nothing — and that
this is precisely why it survived: a row that is present in both states looks identical in a screenshot,
and the difference only shows after a click nobody can make yet.

⚠️ **The subject of this entry no longer exists.** *Export original…* was removed from both doors on
2026-08-23 (D305), so `LayerState::picture_linked` — which had already become `picture_refusal` under
D280 — is gone, the test is gone, and there are no two doors left to agree. **What survives is the
finding, and it is the more useful half**: a verb whose availability is decided in one door and not
in the other is D261's failure in its quiet shape, and the fix is always the shared *predicate*
rather than a second reading of it. The paragraph above about naming a `Default`-derived flag for
its exceptional state is a general rule about `LayerState` and applies to the next field added to it.
*Keep as history; do not read the mechanism as live.*

**Found beside it, in `build::boolean`'s doc comment.** "A boolean's operands are outlines, and a text
node has none until its glyphs are converted — **a feature that does not exist yet**." That last clause
was true when written and stopped being true on 2026-08-20, when `build::outline_text` landed with
*Convert to path* (D260). The **refusal is unchanged and deliberate** — `operand_path` still answers
`None` for text, and converting silently on the user's behalf would take a one-way door for them — but
the comment implied there was no route at all, when the route is now a menu row. Same class as D264's
`png.rs` finding, one crate over: a comment naming something as not-built rots silently.

**D266 — A lone line's chrome hung off one answer in name and three questions in fact. *Built; two of
the three readers asserted since D303, the third's guard unobservable by construction — Keep, with the
blind spot named rather than queued.*** D238 lifted `canvas::lone_line` to a free function and
pinned it, and both `roadmap.md` and the function's own doc comment then said the same thing: it is
"the single answer" the corner handles, the side bands, the skew, the rotate ring and the size badge
all hang off. **That was a premise that is a list, and the list was right while the mechanism was
not.** Three sites ask the question. Only `selection_handles` asked `lone_line`; the **box outline**
and the **size badge** asked `line_ends`, which is `lone_line` with a `preview_world_transform` lookup
in front of it.

**The failure mode is the one `selection_handles` had already written down.** Its own doc says it is
"refused on `lone_line` rather than on `line_ends`… The rule is about the kind, so it should not be
able to fail open" — and the other two sites were the fail-open spelling, unchanged when that one was
fixed. A lone line whose world transform did not resolve fell past both: the `None` arm of the outline
match drew `selection_quad` for it, which is the four-cornered box the whole feature removes, and
`draw_size_badge` quoted the "142 × 0" its own comment names as the thing not to say. All three ask
`lone_line` now, and the outline arm asks the kind *separately* from the placement, because it
genuinely needs the two endpoint positions and the kind question is not about them.

**Honest about what this is: a latent inconsistency, not a reproduced bug.** Nothing shows
`preview_world_transform` answering `None` for a node that `lone_line` has just read out of the same
session, so this may never have drawn a wrong frame. It is worth the change anyway on the argument the
older comment already makes — a rule about a kind that can be defeated by a lookup is one bad frame
away from a bug report, and the user catches single frames. **Two of the three readers are asserted, and
the third turns out not to be a missing test at all.** D303 made both writable and D318 wrote them:
`a_lone_line_gets_no_selection_chrome_but_a_line_in_a_set_does` drives `selection_handles`, which was
the reader that was *already* correct, and `a_lone_line_gets_no_size_badge_and_a_rect_does` drives
`draw_size_badge` — flip-checked by deleting its `lone_line` guard, which turns the lone-line case
`Some`. Its observable is the returned `Option`, because the guard fires *before* `badge_placement` is
computed; reading the painted shapes would only add a way to be wrong about which pill was which.

⚠️ **The box outline's guard is unobservable by construction, and a test of it would be vacuous.**
`draw_canvas` matches on `line_ends` **first**, so a lone line with a resolvable transform takes the
`Some` arm and draws its segment; the `None if chrome && !lone` arm is reachable only when `lone_line`
answers `Some` and `preview_world_transform` answers `None` — a node in the selection and in the
document but absent from `Resolved`, which is exactly the fail-open state this entry fixed and which
nothing in the app produces. So "no box round a lone line" **passes with `&& !lone` deleted**, which is
the vacuous assertion this project's own rule is aimed at: *what would also pass this.* Writing it would
be worse than leaving it read. *Pin it by authoring the missing `Resolved` entry, or leave it read* —
but do not file it as a gap, because it is not one.

*Worth keeping as a shape, because it is the third of its kind in one day: a doc's claim can be true
about the **outcome** and false about the **mechanism**, and only the mechanism tells you what breaks.*

**D267 — An exported selection came out restacked, because a selection is in the order you clicked it.
*Fixed and tested.*** A live bug in shipped code, found by checking D264's own new row against the
contract its writer states rather than by anyone seeing it. `svg_of`'s doc is explicit — "Order is the
caller's and is kept… a caller handing over a selection owes it in **document order** or the copy comes
back with its stacking rearranged" — and **no caller was meeting it**. `Selection::ids` is *pick* order
(`push`, on every shift-click) and `build::outermost` is documented as preserving "input order", so
selecting the front shape and then the one behind it handed the writer a reversed stack. SVG has no
z-index: the last element emitted is the one on top, and nothing downstream could have corrected it.

**It shipped with *Copy as SVG* (D259) and D264 inherited it**, which is the part worth noticing —
the second door was written by reading the first, so it copied the fault along with the reasoning. The
contract was stated correctly in the writer's own doc comment the whole time. *A rule that lives only
in the callee's documentation is a rule every new caller has to re-read, and the second one did not.*

**`build::in_document_order` is the fix, and it is `outermost` plus one pre-order walk** — a member
emitted when the walk reaches it, children pushed in reverse so they pop in document order
(`subtree_nodes`' rule), and a matched member not descended into, since `outermost` has already
guaranteed no member sits inside another. **Not `outermost` doing it itself**: that function is on
every bulk *edit* path, where the input order is either irrelevant or is the user's own — the key
layer, the z-order verbs — and sorting underneath those would change code with nothing to do with
export. Both export doors go through the new one.

**The test asserts its own fixture first**, which is what makes it about anything: it checks that
`outermost` on a back-to-front pick really does come back reversed, or the comparison would be document
order against document order and would pass against no implementation at all. Flipped against
`outermost` alone — the shipped behaviour — where it reports the exact reversed triple. A third case
covers a member nested in a group, because the plausible wrong version that descends into a matched
member passes the first two and only that one distinguishes it.

**D268 — Image editing replaces the crop tool: the bounding box *is* the crop rectangle.
*Built and tested; run on the machine the same day and accepted — "works exactly as I imagined it".
The one thing missing from that look is D269's, and it turned out to be older than this entry.***
Reported after living with the feature, and the
report contains the diagnosis: *"if I select a Crop mode, I expect resizing the bounding box to
actually crop and it doesn't."* Everything a picture could be told to do lived on the Fill row — a
four-cell mode strip and two popover buttons — and cropping lived in a rail tool beside them, so the
one control named *Crop* was the one control that did not crop.

**This reverses D181's central argument, and the reversal is worth stating rather than quietly
performing.** D181 answered D118's mode rule — *a mode entered only by double-click is the failure to
avoid* — by giving cropping a rail slot, the letter `C` and chrome of its own, and argued cropping
needed all three **more** than point editing does, "because cropping is otherwise indistinguishable
from resizing: both are a drag on a picture with a box round it, and only the chrome says which one
is about to happen." That sentence was right about the ambiguity and wrong about the cure. Chrome
cannot fix two gestures that mean different things; **making them one gesture can**. A rail button
also arms a mode with no subject, which is the state D118 was really warning about — and the mode
strip, sitting outside any of it, went on offering a *Crop* whose whole job was to change nothing.

**What answers D118 now is that the mode cannot be entered without a picture to enter, and that
entering it puts a 272pt card on the panel and an outline round the whole photograph.** It announces
itself by being impossible to be in by accident, which a rail button is precisely not. Two doors:
double-click, and `Enter` on a selected picture. **Four now** — the *Edit image* row below, and since
2026-08-23 a click on the fill row's swatch or its *Image* label, which is the shape the gradient row
beside it already had (D305). `C` is unbound and goes back to the comment tool
that will want it (`shortcuts.md`). It stays a `Tool` variant — renamed `Tool::ImageEdit` — because
the input routing, the cursor, `chrome_hidden`, the `Escape` ladder and `Enter`'s toggle are all
keyed off `self.tool`, and a parallel `editing_image` field would be a second answer to "what is the
canvas doing", free to disagree with the first. The subject stays derived: `canvas::edited_image`,
`edited_path`'s rule.

**The geometry.** Outside the mode a handle resizes the layer and the picture scales with it; inside,
a handle moves one edge of the box with the picture nailed down in world space, and a drag on the
picture slides it under a box that is nailed down. Neither can scale the photograph, deliberately —
scaling is what resizing does outside the mode, which is the division the user stated
(*"Out of editing mode, the image always resizes. Within editing mode you resize and move the crop
area"*). So `crop_zoomed` and `crop_zoom_factor` are **deleted** rather than left as `pub` items with
no caller, and side handles are live where the crop tool had none: with a *moving* box there is no
stretching degree of freedom to protect against, which was the whole reason D181 refused them.

Three pieces, each testable alone. `ImageRef::picture_box` reads the whole photograph's rectangle off
the very transform the backends paint with — a second copy of the four modes' arithmetic would be a
fifth opinion about one drawing. `tools::crop_resized` moves the grabbed edge bounded by that
rectangle, so the drawn outline is a real limit rather than a decoration. `image::crop_reframed`
re-reads the old mapping at the new box's corners, which is the one answer that leaves the picture
still; it is deliberately unclamped, because a crop that left the source would be a *frame* that had
grown past the picture and the caller is the one holding the frame to stop that with. `crop_resize_tx`
then aims `tools::resize_layer` at the corner `crop_resized` returned and emits **one** transaction
carrying the geometry and the `SetFills` together.

**Two tests found real faults, and both were the kind a green suite hides.** The first asserted that
the box written is the box the crop was computed against, and failed immediately — on the *test*: a
`Rect`'s geometry starts at its own local origin, so `resize_to_handle` writes the size and translates
the transform to meet it, and the two rectangles agree in **world** space, not local. Worth recording,
because "they agree by construction" was written in two doc comments before it was checked in either
space. The second fault was real: **a handle dragged past its held edge mirrored the window**, which
is right for a resize and wrong for a crop — and it swapped which corner had moved, so the aim landed
on the held edge and the layer collapsed to a point. `crop_resized` now holds each handle on its own
side. The weaker assertion that would have been written instead — "not inverted" — passes against the
mirroring version, since it merely swaps which edge is which; the exact rectangle is what
distinguishes them. `a_crop_drag_leaves_the_photograph_exactly_where_it_was` asserts the whole
composition at the reported symptom, the brush transform in world space, and was flipped against
leaving the crop alone — the very behaviour complained about.

**The offcut is drawn, and it is real ink rather than a scrim.** `canvas::image_ghost` builds a
`RenderOverrides` **chrome ghost** — a `Rect` at `picture_box` filled with the same picture uncropped,
orientation and adjustments along with it, at `GHOST_ALPHA` times the layer's own opacity, at the
layer's own index so it draws *under* it. `whole_crop` on that rectangle is the identity by
construction, the mapping `picture_box` was read off being its inverse, so the ghost cannot land
anywhere but exactly around the window whatever the orientation. **It is a `Ghost` but not a
preview**: `is_empty` is how the app asks "is a gesture in flight", so counting it would have
`cancel_gesture` unwinding a drag nobody started on every right-click — hence a field of its own that
`ghosts_of` chains, which gets the z-ordered draw and the anti-cull for free. It is re-installed
**every frame from one place**, the top of `draw_canvas`, which is downstream of every way the state
can change; the alternative is the second call at every `set_preview` call site that `preview_guide`
pays for, and a call site that will one day not make it.

**The card is one `Area` with two tabs, and the mode owns it.** *Framing* and *Adjustments* were two
cards behind two buttons (D190); with the buttons gone there is one card to place, so it carries a
tab strip instead of competing with its twin for an anchor. What D190 got right survives the move —
the two are different jobs done at different times and stacking them makes a card too tall — and the
split is now one click rather than two. It has **no close button and no click-away rule**: it is not
a popover somebody opened, so a click on the canvas (very often the next crop drag) must leave it
standing, and `Escape` already means something one rung up. That is an absence of a rule rather than
a fifth copy of `dismissed_by_click`. `OndinApp::image_menu` collapses to `image_tab: ImageCard`,
which deletes three pieces of housekeeping — the reset on a selection change, the remap through a
paint reorder, the drop on a row drag — because a stale value can no longer exist.

**The mode strip moved into Settings and changed meaning.** It is no longer the way into cropping; it
is the way out. Pick Fill, Fit or Tile and the picture is re-framed inside the box the crop left and
the ghost goes with it, the rectangle surviving untouched so returning to Crop brings both back. The
old `IMAGE_STRIP_CELL` trap moved with it and had to be re-derived: `ui::segmented` pads two either
side, the card's controls are 26, so both tracks take `CELL - 4`. `an_image_rows_two_lines_share_their_edges`
had nothing left to measure and is replaced by `the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height`,
flipped against a bare `CELL` painting 30 — the mistake the image row made in both directions across
two revisions (D180, D190).

**One thing was taken away without a replacement, and it is named here so it is a decision. It came
back on 2026-08-22.** The `context-menus.md` §5.7 head lost *Edit crop…*, which left image editing
the one "one level in" verb with no menu repair — the very repair §5 of that file argues the head
exists to provide. Naming it as a decision is what made it re-askable, and living with it answered
it the other way round: ***Edit image*** now heads that table, first of five rows, and the whole
argument for putting it there is the one written above. **First of two since 2026-08-23**, three of
the five having gone to the Settings tab or out of the app entirely (D305); being first is what makes
it a repair, so the order assertion is worth as much against one neighbour as it was against four.

**Named for the mode, and without the ellipsis this entry gave it.** *Edit image…* was the spelling
in the design and in the paragraph above; the ellipsis was inherited from *Edit crop…*, which earned
it back when it opened something. This row steps into a mode exactly as *Edit text* and *Edit points*
do and neither of those carries one, so the row is *Edit image*, `icon::CROP` and no accel — matching
*Edit text*, which `Enter` also opens. **The estimate was wrong too**: not one registry entry and one
arm but five sites — the `Item` variant, its row in the `cfg(test)` `Item::ALL` table that §10's
completeness test reads, the `spec()` arm, the row push and the dispatch arm — counted in
`roadmap.md` the day before, and six counting the `Item::EditPoints` doc comment that asserted the
absence was deliberate and had to be rewritten to say it was reversed.

**The row cannot drift from the mode, because it is not a second reading of the same rule.**
`LayerState::has_picture` is `tools::croppable_fill(node.paint()).is_some()`, and `croppable_fill` is
the *same function* the `Enter` arm and the double-click arm gate on, so a picture the row is offered
over is one the mode will take. That is what `context-menus.md` §5.7's opening sentence had claimed
since before this row existed; it is now load-bearing rather than descriptive.

**It took no `dim_if(locked)`, and that was a match rather than an exemption. ⚠️ Reversed on
2026-08-23 — the row dims now (D320).** The reasoning is kept because it is the shape of the mistake
rather than the mistake itself. Neither of the other
two doors looked at `Node::locked`, and neither did `canvas::image_edit_input` or
`inspector::write_slot`, so a locked picture could already be entered and cropped. Dimming this one row
would have made the menu the only door that refuses — D261's two-doors-disagree failure, arrived at
by tidying rather than by drift. All of that was true, and it was true *of a path that read no lock at
all*: matching a gap is not agreement. D320 closed the gap in `begin_image_edit` and let this row
follow, which is the only order in which it may dim. **Only one of those two doors was genuinely
reachable on a locked
layer**, and it is worth knowing which: `query::hit_test` skips a node that is hidden or locked at
any depth, so the double-click never arrives, and the arm's silence about the lock is incidental. The
live one was `Enter` on a layer selected from the layers panel — which is also the door this row
travels beside, C4 putting a locked layer's menu in the panel. So the agreement being preserved was
with `Enter`, not with three doors evenly. ⚠️ **There were two live ones from 2026-08-23**: the
fourth door is a click on the inspector's fill row, and the inspector's paint rows are deliberately
live on a locked layer — a lock stops a layer being dragged about, not recoloured
(`select_by_color`'s own note) — so the count in this paragraph was out by one and the conclusion was
not (D305). Both are shut now, in the one place they share. The pin is
`a_lock_dims_both_of_the_picture_rows`, which is its **fourth** name: it was
`a_locked_picture_can_still_be_exported_and_nothing_else_about_it_can_be_touched`, then
`a_lock_dims_the_three_picture_rows_that_write_from_the_menu_and_neither_of_the_other_two` when a
second undimmed row made that false, then `a_lock_dims_original_size_and_leaves_edit_image_alone`
when the head came down
to two rows (D305), and renamed once more the same day when this row started dimming (D320). **The
plausible wrong version inverted with the head, and then again with the verdict**: with three dimmed
rows
under one live one, the mistake to guard against was a `dim_if(locked)` typed on everything; with one
of each, it was a hand making the pair agree in either direction, so the test was flipped both ways and
neither flip disturbed the other; with **both** dimmed the pair agrees by construction, so what guards
this test is no longer inside it. That guard is
`app::image_edit_lock_tests::a_locked_picture_refuses_every_door`, and the relationship was checked
rather than assumed — delete the guard in `begin_image_edit` and this menu test still passes (D320).
**The two live rows
were live for opposite reasons** and the distinction is worth keeping even though neither row carries
it now: *Export original…* because
locking protects a layer from being *changed* and reading its bytes changes nothing, *Edit image*
because the other doors did not check — which is precisely why it is the one that stopped being live.

The dispatch arm is `canvas.rs`'s double-click arm written out again — `selection.set_one(id)`,
`choose_tool(Tool::ImageEdit)`, the same status line. The string is **duplicated on purpose**: it is
the mode's onboarding, a door that stayed silent would be the one door that does not explain itself,
and if it ever earns a constant all three want it at once. **It earned one on 2026-08-23**, when a
fourth door landed on the fill row and three copies would have become four: the arm is
`OndinApp::begin_image_edit(id)` now, and all four doors are that call (D305).


**D269 — The crop chrome had never drawn once, the dashed window that replaced it, and the card's one
pitch. *Fixed and tested; the retuned dash not yet reviewed on screen.*** Reported the moment D268 was run:
*"the only thing we're missing is a bounding box on the image while in editing mode"*, with a Figma
screenshot of a dotted one beside a screenshot of ours with no box at all. Two separate things, and
only one of them was the thing asked for.

**The box was not missing a treatment — it was never drawn.** `draw_crop_box` was called from inside
`draw_points`, whose first line is `let Some(id) = self.edited_path() else { return }`, and
`edited_path` requires `Tool::Node`. So the call could only run in a state that by construction has
no crop in it. Meanwhile `chrome_hidden` was faithfully suppressing the *selection*'s box on the
grounds that this one replaced it — so the crop tool shipped with **no box and no handles at all**,
and that is how it shipped for as long as it existed. It predates D268 by a long way: the misplaced
call is in the commit that introduced the function.

**D181 recorded the chrome as "reviewed on screen and accepted".** It was not, and could not have
been; what was reviewed was a picture panning under the pointer, which works and needs no box to
prove it. The lesson is narrow and worth having: *"reviewed and accepted" is a claim about what was
looked at, and a drawing that is absent is exactly the thing a review does not notice* — nobody
misses a box they have never seen. The comment on `chrome_hidden` was the tell, and it was the wrong
way round: it explained at length why the selection's box is taken away, which reads as evidence that
something replaces it.

**Nothing could look at it, which is why it stayed.** `OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState` and is
not constructible headlessly (D35), so no test in this crate can say where a `&mut self` method is
called from. The response is the one the origin fields already took: the shapes are lifted into a
free `crop_chrome(window, picture)` and pinned — all four sides dashed, four hollow handles, the
picture's outline only when there is a crop. The placement of the call is still unpinnable and still
the user's eye. **`an_unclosed_quad_leaves_one_side_bare` is the flip run as its own test**, because
`Shape::dashed_line` takes a polyline: hand it a quad's four points and it draws three sides. The
main test asserts **per side** rather than counting segments, since three sides' worth of dashes is
still plenty of segments and a count passes against the bug.

**Retuned twice on the machine: 1pt at 3/3 → 2pt at 4/4 → 3pt at 6/6** — *"a bit thicker and even
slightly coarser, just so it's a different enough affordance to the normal bounding box"*, and then
the same again. The first version borrowed the guide extension's dash wholesale, which put the crop
window at the same weight as the selection box it stands in for and at a pitch fine enough that the
two read as one rectangle from any distance. The dash is the *whole* of what says this box crops
rather than resizes, so it has to be legible as a dash before it can carry that: 1/3/3 was a hairline
that happened to have gaps in it, 2/4/4 was better and still close to the 1.2pt selection hairline,
and 3/6/6 is a mark of its own. **Two rounds is the tell that the first number was reasoned rather
than seen** — borrowing an existing constant is a good instinct and was the wrong one here, because
the thing being borrowed was chosen to *recede* and this has to assert. `CROP_DASH_PX`, `CROP_GAP_PX` and
`CROP_STROKE_PX` are module-level so the test reads them instead of copying their values —
`IMAGE_STRIP_CELL`'s lesson — and the segment count is asserted against the constants rather than
against the number they happened to produce.

**Dashed rather than solid, at the guide extension's dash.** Figma dashes its crop rectangle and the
reason it works there is the reason it works here: a dashed edge reads as *provisional*, a line you
are still moving, where a solid one reads as the edge of a thing — which is exactly the difference
between the crop window and the photograph's own outline behind it. The dash is the app's existing
"the same thing, carried on past where it stops mattering" vocabulary (a guide's extension, a text
node's line box) rather than a third spec.

**The handles went back to hollow with it**, asked for as "the same bounding box we use for any other
layer". They were filled, on D181's argument that with two identical rectangles in the same place the
shape of the corner is the only thing saying which gesture is armed. The dash says it now, and says
it along the whole perimeter instead of at four points — which frees the corners to obey D14 again: a
filled handle paints over the very corner it is there to place, and in this mode a handle really does
place the layer's corner.

**The seven adjustment rows lost their own pitch, in the same report.** They sat at 4 where every
other control in the card sits one `IMAGE_CARD_GAP` apart, and seven of them stacked that close read
as a table rather than as seven controls. The yardstick came with the report — *"the same vertical
spacing as any other field rows, for example between Horizontal/Vertical and tile repeat in the
Settings tab"* — which is the card's own `item_spacing`. So the fix is the **absence** of a number
rather than a bigger one: the override is deleted and the rows inherit, because the claim being made
is "the same as the rest of the card" and a second literal is a second thing to retune. The pitch
became `IMAGE_CARD_GAP` at module scope for the test to read.

**That test caught itself being vacuous, which is the finding worth keeping.** The first version put
the fixture's scoped field inside a `ui.scope` — the adjustment rows' own structure — and asserted
the gap above it. It passed with the scope set back to the reported 4, because **the gap above a
scope is the parent's**: a pitch set inside one is only visible *between* items inside it, and a
scope wrapping a single row shows nothing at all. Two rows in the scope is what makes the fixture
about anything, and the flip then reports the exact symptom ("two rows inside one scope sits 4 apart,
not the card's 10"). *The question to ask of a green test is not "does this pass" but "what would
also pass this" — and here the answer was "the bug".*

**D270 — Image editing had no way out with the mouse. *Built and accepted on screen — "Done works" —
with one correction.*** Reported
straight after D269: *"we can only exit with enter/esc or pressing a tool button. Maybe a light blue
'Exit' or 'Save' below the bounding box, like the size pill?"*

**It shipped setting `CursorIcon::PointingHand`, which the chrome does not do** (§9.2, D63): a web
page uses the hand to mean "this is a link", a design tool's chrome is all controls, and a cursor
that changes on every one of them says nothing and flickers. Caught on the machine — *"I think we
have a rule for that already"* — and the rule was right there. Worth noticing *why* it was broken:
this is the first thing on the **canvas** that is a plain button, and the canvas is where cursors do
change (`cursor.rs`), so the habit of the surrounding file won out over the policy. The pill answers
the pointer with its own ground instead, which is what the hover wash is for.

⚠️ **Three call sites in `panels/typography.rs` still set it**, all on the *Show all features* reveal,
which is a `Label` acting as a button and has a test asserting the hand
(`the_features_reveal_asks_for_a_pointer_and_a_bare_label_asks_for_an_i_beam`). §9.2 names two
surviving exceptions and that is not one of them, so either the policy has a third exception or that
control does not. Not touched here; it is a decision rather than a slip to sweep. The *other* half of
that row's cursor handling — the `.selectable(false)` beside the hand, which was this project's first
answer to a label claiming the I-beam — has since been settled app-wide at the style instead; see
D277, which the row's own comment now points at.

**The gap is the mirror of D268's own argument.** That entry took the crop tool off the rail and
answered D118's mode rule by making the mode impossible to enter by accident — a double-click on a
picture, or `Enter`. What it did not notice is that it had removed the *exit* at the same time: the
rail button had been a way out as well as a way in, and what was left was two keys and "pick a
different tool", none of which a pointer can reach. A mode that announces itself loudly and can only
be dismissed from the keyboard is still a mode somebody can get stuck in.

**The size badge's slot, and not merely something like it.** `color::BADGE` *is* `color::SELECT`, so
"a light blue pill under the box" is a description of the badge that already exists — same ground,
same `BADGE_INK`, same 4pt radius, same `HANDLE_PICK_PX` gap below the box, placed through the same
`badge_placement`/`badge_frame` pair. The slot is free by construction rather than by arrangement:
`chrome_hidden` is true throughout image editing and both the badge and the origin fields are drawn
inside that guard, so there is still exactly one thing hanging under the box at a time — W × H, or
the origin's two fields, or the way out. Upright, where the badge turns with the shape: an egui
widget cannot be rotated, which is the same constraint the origin fields hit (D253).

***Done*, not *Exit* or *Save*, and the report offered both.** Every drag in this mode commits on
release (§9.3), so there is nothing unsaved for *Save* to name and no work for *Exit* to be
discarding — either word describes a step that does not exist, and *Exit* in particular would suggest
the crop is about to be thrown away. *Done* is what the button does and what `Enter` already does,
and it goes through `choose_tool` for that reason: a third way out that unwound different state would
be a third answer to one question.

**An `Area` at `Foreground`, which is D252's mechanism reused rather than a second one.** egui
resolves the press to the topmost layer by itself, so the canvas needs no gate and its hand-rolled
hit testing goes on working around the pill — pinned by `overlay_claim`, which this inherits whole.
It also inherits D254's consequence: an area shields the layer beneath it *indiscriminately*, so the
wheel goes nowhere with the pointer parked on it. `wheel_input`'s exemption now names two layers
instead of one. The pill is the smaller target of the two and hangs directly under a picture, which
is exactly where somebody zooming to judge a crop puts the pointer, so it needed the exemption more
than the fields did.

**A real allocated widget inside the area, not the area's own response**, which is a placeholder over
the rect and never reports a hover — the trap `inspector::menu_action` exists for, arriving on a
button instead of a row. Hover is a white wash over the ground rather than a darker blue: the ground
*is* the accent, so there is no tier to reach for, and a button that does not answer the pointer
reads as a label.

**Read, not tested** (D35), and the same seam D269 was caught on: `OndinApp` holds a wgpu
`RenderState`, so nothing here can say that `crop_exit_pill` is *called*, only what it would draw if
it were. What is checked is that the call sits at the top level of `draw_canvas` with no early return
above it — which is exactly the inspection that failed for `draw_crop_box`, so it is worth saying that
it was made deliberately this time rather than assumed.

**D271 — A *Scale* field beside *Tile*: the zoom the crop gesture deliberately cannot do.
*Built and tested; the pair took glyphs after a look on screen, and the scrub was retuned under
D273.*** The last thing missing from image editing, and the
report named the shape it should take: *"a percentage text field next to the tile field; so same row,
divided in 2 by the 2 textfields"*.

**It is the other half of D268's split, arriving late because the split created it.** That entry made
a handle drag move the *window* with the picture nailed down, and a pan slide the *picture* under a
window that is nailed down — precisely so that a crop and a resize stopped being the same gesture.
What both of those hold constant is how big the picture is, and the old corner-zoom that used to
change it was the thing being removed. So the zoom had to come back somewhere, and a field is the
right somewhere: it is the one parameter of the three that is a *number* rather than a place.

**Local units per the picture's own pixels, which is what `tile_scale` already means** — `1.0` is one
unit per source pixel. That is why the two sit on one row: the same measurement, read by one mode
each, with exactly one of them ever live. The pair is now also the clearest statement the card makes
about which mode is running.

**The floor is `cover_scale`, and that answers the question the report asked.** *"Figma only does
scale up, which feels limiting, but there may be a reason for that I'm not thinking of."* There is,
and it is geometry rather than a choice: under `Crop` the rectangle maps onto the frame **exactly**,
so there is no letterboxing for a smaller picture to sit in — zoom out far enough and the crop must
leave the source, where `Extend::Pad` smears the edge row. The bottom is the rectangle at which the
picture just covers the window, which is `Fill`'s. **Any editor whose crop maps a region exactly onto
a frame has that floor**, so it is a good guess at Figma's reason — but it is a guess, and it is
written here as one rather than as a fact about their implementation.
**But "only up" is a misreading of what that bound is**: cover is not 100%. On a layer smaller than
its picture the floor is well under one unit per pixel, so the field runs from *there* upwards and
scaling down is available for the whole of that range. `Scrub::range` is clamped to it rather than to
a number chosen for the widget, so the value cannot walk away from the picture.

**`crop_scaled` is `crop_zoomed` back under a new name and a fixed anchor**, which D268 deleted along
