with the gesture. The *gesture* has not returned. Uniform about the window's centre: uniform so it
can neither introduce a stretch nor remove one the layer's own resize put there, and about the centre
because the window is not moving, so zooming about a corner would slide the subject out of it.
`ImageRef::crop_scale` reads **one axis** for the same reason — reading x and writing a uniform
factor round-trips exactly, where recomputing each axis from the frame would silently un-stretch a
picture nobody asked to change. `the_crop_scale_round_trips_and_bottoms_out_at_cover` uses a 2:1
source in a 1:2 frame so that a symmetric fixture cannot hide either fault.

**The dimmed readout is seeded, not stored.** A picture nobody has cropped carries `whole_crop`, a
sentinel that stretches when mapped onto a frame of another aspect — so reading its scale would put a
number in the dimmed field that switching to Crop would immediately contradict. It is read off
`cover_crop` instead, the same seed `paint::with_fit` and the canvas gesture both use, so all three
agree about what entering Crop shows.

**The pair went in as words and came back as glyphs** — `icon::RESIZE` for a picture being made
bigger, `icon::GRID_FOUR` for one being repeated, each with a tooltip that now opens with the name.
The words were the seven adjustments' rule applied one control too far: no icon set has seven
tone-adjustment glyphs anyone can tell apart, which is why *those* are labelled, but two is not
seven and these two are as far apart as glyphs get. It also buys the number the room the words were
taking.

**Halving the row put it back in D253's territory**, and that fault is worth restating: the origin
pill shipped clipping `31.25%` by less than a point. Measured here rather than estimated — the widest
reachable string is `9999.99%` (not `10000%`, since `ui::number(2)` trims trailing zeros), and it
ends at 113 in a 122pt half, leaving 9 against the 10 on the left. **The first version of that test
was aimed at the wrong failure**: written on the assumption that a `value_field` puts its value flush
right, it asserted the number cleared the label — which two left-aligned runs always do, at every
width, including the ones that clip. The value is laid out *after* the prefix, so the failure is ink
past the field's own edge, and the flip at 90pt is what says the test can tell a fit from a clip.

**D272 — The crop offcut slid a pixel against its own picture. *Fixed and tested.*** Reported as
*"when resizing the crop area, there is a little movement on the ghost… like a 1–2px shift to the
right and back while I resize"*, with the picture inside the window sitting still — which is the
whole diagnosis, because it says the two are being *rounded* apart rather than *computed* apart.

**`snapped_box_world` rounds an axis-aligned box's edges to whole device pixels and then rebuilds its
scale from the rounded span.** Two rectangles of different sizes therefore round differently, and the
offcut is a continuation of the layer drawn as a separate and much larger rectangle. Worse than a
translation: the rebuilt *scale* is a proportional error, so a half-pixel miss over a 120pt window is
a whole pixel out at the ghost's far edge, several window-widths away. That is the 1–2px, and it
changes as the window is dragged because the rounding does.

**Both opt out, rather than the ghost being made to round like the layer.** Making them *equal* is
the requirement, and the layer's rounding is computed deep in the walk from the device base, so the
only place the two can be made to agree is by neither rounding. `RenderOverrides::unsnapped` answers
for exactly two ids and derives them from the chrome ghost itself — the ghost, and the layer it is
glued to, which `set_chrome_ghost` now takes as a pair. Derived rather than kept in a set of its own
so the two cannot come apart: one place says which boxes have to agree, and it is the place that
creates the second one.

What that costs is the seam mitigation `SNAP_BOXES_TO_DEVICE_PIXELS` buys, on one layer, while
somebody is looking at its crop. That constant's own doc describes the trade in the other direction —
snapping makes edges *step rather than glide* — and a stepping edge is precisely what was reported.

**Found by writing the assertion first, and it took two attempts to aim.** The test composes each
picture's brush transform with the transform it is painted under and requires the two to map a source
pixel to the same place. Its first metric compared the transforms' **coefficients** and reported a
quarter of a pixel — under the threshold, and wrong: coefficients weigh translation and scale alike,
and the scale is the term that hurts. Measuring at the *source's own corners* reported the full pixel.
It also sweeps twelve sub-pixel frame widths rather than checking one, because at a single width the
two can agree by luck and the complaint was that it drifts *as you drag*.

⚠️ **A first fix halved it and was not the fix.** Exempting only the ghost took 2.5 units to 1.25,
which is the shape of "much less than before, but still there" — a second cause, not a mis-tuned
first. The residual was the *layer's* own rounding, and no amount of adjusting the ghost could have
reached it.

**D273 — A multiplicative value scrubbed in whole units lurches at the bottom of its range.
*Fixed and tested.*** Reported as the Scale field being *"a bit glitchy/jumpy when scrubbing… it tends
to jump in the canvas rather than be a smooth scale. Especially around the 85–120% (for my exact case
85% is the min scale). Up from there it tends to be smooth."* The band and its upper edge are the
diagnosis handed over: a fault that fades as a number grows is a fault measured against that number.

**A crop scale is multiplicative and was being scrubbed additively.** What the eye reads is the
*relative* change: a feature `d` from the centre of the window moves by `d · Δs / s`. One whole
percentage point is 1/85 of the picture at the floor and a third of that at 300%, so the same
keystroke lurches three times as far at the bottom — which is the reported band, and why it stops.
`Scrub::fine(0.5, 2)` makes the step a hundredth of a point, and the field beside it keeps whole
units on purpose: a tile scale changes how big one repeat is, and a repeat has no centre for a step
to swing a distant corner around.

**The probe had to be re-aimed, and the first reading is worth keeping.** Measuring how far the
*picture's* edge moves reported the same number at every scale — correctly, and uselessly: the
picture's width is `s · iw`, so its edges travel at a constant rate per unit of `s`. The thing that
moves faster at the bottom is the content inside a window that is standing still. The test takes the
source pixel under the window's corner and asks where it lands afterwards, flips against the whole-
unit step it shipped with, and asserts the *ratio* between the floor and three times up — because
"a small number is small" would pass against the bug.

*A step size is a claim about the derivative of what the user is looking at, not about the number in
the field.*

**D274 — Exports became repeatable: settings on the layer, saved with the document, and readable
by the CLI. *Built and tested; five rounds of on-machine feedback folded back in — the passes
below.*** Reported as a comparison rather than a
bug: *"Our Export As in the menu is fine, but has nowhere near that degree of flexibility. More
importantly, exports are not repeatable."* Figma keeps a layer's export settings on the layer, so the
same asset can be produced again without re-answering anything; *Export as…* asked the format, the
place and the name every time and remembered none of it (D264).

**And on 2026-08-22 this panel became the only door to a one-off export file.** *Export as…* was
removed outright, on the grounds this entry establishes: a card that answers where, what format and at
what size from the layer, with a button that runs the export, leaves a menu row asking the same three
questions as the slower route to the same file. That raises the stakes on everything below. **The
panel is no longer the *repeatable* half of a pair** — it is the whole of "get this artwork out as a
file", the CLI aside, and the two-doors framing that several passages here lean on has one door in it
now. Concretely: a regression in `run_export`, in `plan`, or in the card's ability to seed a spec is
no longer a regression with a fallback behind it, and the cost of the removal is a real one — the
menu row wanted no setup at all where the panel wants a spec on the layer first, so the cheapest
possible export is a click or two dearer than it was. That was the trade, taken knowingly.

**The multiplier had been waiting for this, and said so.** `png_of`'s doc comment and §7 both carried
the same sentence — a 2×/3× scale *"needs somewhere to live before it needs a parameter, and a
parameter every caller passes `1.0` to would be a decoy standing in for a decision nobody has
taken"* — and `roadmap.md` repeated it as the one piece of the two Export rows still open. The panel
is that somewhere. This is the shape the roadmap's own warning is about, in the other direction: a
premise that was *right* when written and stops being right the moment the thing it waited for
arrives.

**The settings are document state, and that is the feature rather than an implementation choice.**
`Node::exports: Vec<ExportSpec>` — format, scale, prefix, suffix, background, JPEG quality, trim, pad —
written through one `Operation::SetExports` and saved by `NodeDto` under `skip_serializing_if`, so a
document nobody has set up to export writes exactly the bytes it wrote before the field existed
(invariant 9, and `export_settings_round_trip_and_cost_nothing_when_empty` asserts it against the
byte-for-byte file). Three consequences follow and all three were the point: the list survives a
reload, it undoes like anything else, and **the CLI can read it** — `ondin export doc.ondin --all`
runs the whole set with no window and no GPU, which makes a `.ondin` file a build input rather than a
place assets are copied out of by hand. Figma needs a plugin and a token for that.

**One interpreter, three callers.** `ondin_export::plan` is the only place a spec becomes numbers:
`Width(512)` into a multiplier against *this* layer's box, `Background::Frame` into a colour by
walking up to the enclosing artboard, a layer's name into a filename nothing else in the set has. The
panel's button, the CLI and the zip all go through it, so a file exported by clicking and the same
file exported by a build script are the same bytes under the same name. The alternative — each door
reading the spec its own way — is how a 2× from one of them comes out a pixel wider than a 2× from
the other.

**Three findings the tests produced that reading would not have.** The pixel cap was being applied
*per axis*, so a `512w` on a 100×50 came back a 65535 square: the same picture at the wrong aspect
ratio, which is a worse answer than a smaller one and one nobody would read as "too big". Capping the
*scale* until both sides fit is the fix, and `an_impossible_size_is_clamped_and_reported` is what
found it. The three finishing steps also have an order that is the whole of their meaning — trim
reads alpha, so a background composited first leaves nothing transparent to trim, and a pad applied
before a trim has its own padding trimmed off — and `trim_runs_before_pad` tells the two orders apart
by the size that comes out. And the scale test was flipped against the *plausible* wrong version
rather than against nothing: scaling the viewport's `view` alongside its `pixel_size` produces a
buffer of exactly the right size with the artwork in a quarter of it, which no assertion about
dimensions can catch.

**Where it departs from Figma, and why each time.** Figma zips anything past one file; this offers
both, because *"a lot of the time I just wish to export all the files at once in a folder instead of
having a zip, unzip it into a folder, cut into another folder."* So the destination follows the file
count — one file gets a save dialog with a name in it, several get a folder — and *Export as ZIP* is
a second button that appears exactly when there is more than one file to put in one. Figma also
stores the settings and still asks where on every single export; *Export all* (`Ctrl+Alt+E`, and a
row on the page menu) remembers the folder and asks nothing after the first time, which is the half
of "repeatable" that Figma leaves on the table. JPEG is new here — the `image` crate's encoder was
already in the lock through `ondin-render` — and its lack of an alpha channel is answered by the
background control rather than by a matte field only it reads: the stored value stays `Transparent`
and what it *means* for a format with no alpha is white, which the row says out loud rather than
rewriting the setting behind the user's back.

**PDF is deliberately not in the format list.** The cheapest honest route is our own SVG through
`svg2pdf`, and it is a reasonable one — §7 already asserts SVG as the model-completeness gate, so PDF
would inherit that gate instead of needing a third per-kind writer. What stops it being free is a
`usvg` dependency tree, text arriving as outlines rather than as text, and SVG filters going
unsupported, which is exactly what an adjusted image fill emits (D186). A dropdown entry that
half-works is worse than one that is not there, so the enum has three variants and the reasoning sits
on it.

**The costs worth knowing.** The panel is the only place in the inspector that renders and encodes
the artwork, and it does so only in the *Preview* section, only while that section is open — which is
why it starts collapsed — and only once per edit, keyed on a new `EditorSession::revision` counter
beside the layer and the spec. A preview keyed on less would be a confident picture of something that
is no longer there. Two new crates enter the lock, `zip` and its `typed-path`, with
`default-features = false` and the one deflate backend that uses the `flate2` already there.

**A design pass followed on 2026-08-21 and changed three things, one of them semantic.** `design/`
was regenerated with the note that *"field spacing, margins, popup style and positioning are all used
extensively everywhere else"* — so this panel is not a place to invent, and what it had invented was
taken back out. The per-row settings became a **popover** rather than an inline block: the block was
`stroke_sides_row`'s call and the wrong one here, because four labelled sections pushed the export
button and every row below it down the column, which is exactly what `stroke_menu_popup` cites for
going the other way. The row became the design's `74px 1fr 28px 28px` at a 7pt pitch — 74 being the
first width that clears the combo measurement the old 62 failed — and gave up its pixel-size cell,
which now hangs off the settings button as a tooltip: a number that can be five characters or eleven
has no fixed cell it can honestly live in, and `3840×21…` is wrong rather than abbreviated. The
explicit `add_space` calls went with it; `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` was already that distance, and a
hand-rolled copy of a shared number is how a card comes to disagree with its neighbours by a point
(D180).

**The semantic one: the density marker became automatic.** Figma's typed field is a suffix because it
is what keeps `Button.png` and `Button@2x.png` apart — so it has to be typed on every second row and
is `@2x` almost every time it is used. Deriving that from the scale makes the collision impossible by
construction, and a vector spec carries no marker at all whatever its scale says, because
`Button@2x.svg` would be a name asserting a resolution the file does not have. The typed field became
a **prefix** — `hero/`, which with the folder switch on is where the files go. *(The suffix came back
beside it the same day, and the derivation survived as its default; see the second-pass list below.)*

**Two widgets came out of it and belong to everything, not to this panel**: `ui::action_button` (a
wide button with a glyph and a word, centred as a pair) and `ui::toggle_row` (a full-width switch
with a tick or a dash pinned right), both on the same `button_face` as the square icon buttons, so a
switch in a popover is tonally the same material as a button in the card behind it. **What did not
come out of it is the shell**: the export popover is the *third* copy of 272/11/26/9.5pt beside
`typography.rs` and `stroke_menu_popup`, and the three did not agree on the section gap — 11 here, 15
there, 10 in the stroke card, each with a reason recorded. Promoting the shell into `ui.rs` would
have to pick one, which is a decision about two other panels and did not belong inside a change to
this one. **It was picked the same day and by the person the three cards are for** — D275 — which is
the answer to a disagreement that had been left standing because each side of it was locally right.

**A second pass on 2026-08-21 after living with it, and six of its eight items were mine to have got
right.** Worth listing as a set, because the shape repeats: every one is a place where the panel
either invented something the rest of the app already answers, or answered a question with its own
reasoning where the neighbours had a rule.

- **The card stayed open on a layer that exports nothing.** Fill and Stroke close when empty
  (`sync_paint_collapse`) and the `+` in the header opens them; this did neither, so the resting
  inspector grew a card whose whole body was the words "No exports". The mechanism was already there
  and shared — what it needed was a second synced-selection field, because
  `paint_subject_changed` **consumes** the edge and two callers in one frame lose it for one of them.
- **The background row read "White (no alpha)" when Transparent was picked.** Meant as honesty about
  what a JPEG will actually do; lands as a control disagreeing with the list it was picked from. The
  substitution is real and is now in the tooltip, where it explains instead of contradicting. *A
  control states its setting; a tooltip states its consequence.*
- **JPEG quality scrubbed twice as fast as anything else in the panel** — `Scrub::whole(1.0)` against
  the 0.5 both opacity fields ask for, reported as "0 to 100 in about 250px". Not a judgement about
  quality: a rate chosen rather than taken from the neighbours. **It settled at 0.25**, half the
  consistent answer, and that is the interesting part: matching opacity was still too fast, because a
  quality is not a percentage of anything on screen — nothing moves as you drag it, so the useful
  band is 60 to 95 rather than the whole range, and it wants to fall under a hand's width. *A scrub
  rate is set by what the number does, not by what the number is.*
- **And a right-click did not put it back**, which is the more interesting half — and the fix for it
  was wrong too, in the opposite direction, which is what makes the pair worth writing down.
  `cancel_gesture` undoes a scrub by *dropping the preview*; the field committed every frame through
  `commit_run`, so there was no preview to drop and the value the pointer happened to be over stood.
  Moving it to `edit_valve` fixed that and broke the field outright — **"JPEG Quality doesn't
  scrub"** — because the valve *is* a preview and `RenderOverrides` absorbs a `SetExports` as a
  no-op, so every frame of the drag re-read the committed number and the field never moved. Neither
  shared committer can serve a control whose edit has nothing to preview: one gives up cancellation,
  the other gives up the live value. The answer is the third shape the app already has for exactly
  this — `session_scrub`'s — an in-flight value held by the panel (`export_quality_scrub`), read
  while the pointer is down, committed once on the release, dropped on a cancel. Its decision is
  `quality_step`, a free function, because it is now the piece with the worst record in the panel and
  `OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly to test the method (§15 D35). **A cancellable gesture is one
  whose intermediate states were never committed, and a live one is one whose intermediate states are
  visible — a control that can preview gets both from the valve, and a control that cannot has to
  hold them itself.**
- **The suffix came back beside the prefix**, and the two now coexist: a suffix left empty derives
  itself from the scale (`effective_suffix`), and typing one replaces the derived value rather than
  joining it. That keeps what removing the field bought — the collision is impossible without anyone
  typing `@2x` — while restoring what it cost, which is `-dark`. The field's *hint* is the derived
  marker, so an untouched field says what the file will actually be called.
- **The asset size came back, on a line under the row rather than in a cell.** It had been dropped to
  a tooltip because a number that is five characters or eleven has no fixed cell it can honestly live
  in; a second line has no such limit, and the answer to "why is my icon 47 pixels" is worth reading
  without hovering.
- **The Preview moved inside the Export card**, as a `section_head` rather than a `panel` — a preview
  belongs to the export set it is a preview *of*, and a second floating card under it read as a
  second feature. Its caret still does the one thing the separate card was for: opening it is what
  turns the render on. It gained the design's checkerboard ground, which is the only way a
  transparent export can be told from a white one.
- The eighth was a nice-to-have declined for now: *Colour* in the background dropdown reads as a
  promise of a picker, and there is nowhere to put one — the picker targets a paint slot on a node
  and an export background is neither. It says **White**, which is the value that was wanted.

**A third pass the same day, and all four of its items were spacing or the scrub.** The scrub is
above; the three spacings are worth one note between them, because they are the same mistake. A row
and its size line were 6 apart and one row sat 15 from the next — neither number was chosen, both
fell out of a `ui.scope` with an `item_spacing` set on it, and the 15 in particular is `paint_unit`'s
documented trap: **egui advances past a widget by the spacing in effect when that widget is placed**,
so a pitch set for the two lines is also spent after the last of them. Written as `paint_unit` writes
it — zero inside, both gaps allocated — the numbers become sayable: 8 within an export, 18 between
one and the next, which is the distance two stroke entries already have and was asked for in those
words. **They then came down on the machine, over three passes, to 3 and 6** — which is worth
recording as a correction to the rule rather than as a tweak. `paint_unit` doubles the card's pitch,
and its 18 is sized for an entry of two *controls*; an export row is a control and the caption
belonging to it, so what has to be legible is not "these are two entries" but "this caption goes with
the row above it". That is carried by the **relationship** between the two gaps — the inner one being
the tighter — and a relationship survives at 3 against 6 where a doubling does not describe it at
all. The doubling was the wrong rule to borrow, not the wrong number.

**Which of the pair moved last is the part that names the rule.** Asked for 6 between exports and
then, rather than opening that up again, for the *caption* to come in: at 6 two rows sit the ordinary
field-to-field distance apart, the same as any two stacked controls elsewhere in the inspector, so
that number is the one with a reason outside this panel and the annotation is what has to earn its
place inside it. *When two gaps are being balanced, move the one that is not already a number
something else uses.*

**And the last step needed a structural change, which is the part worth knowing.** 6 is *below*
`CARD_ROW_GAP`, and a scope can add to an inherited spacing but not subtract from one — so as long as
the row units were children of the card they could never sit closer than 9, whatever was allocated
between them. They are now a region of their own with the pitch taken to zero and the whole gap
allocated, which also makes the trailing leak zero and so leaves the button below the list at the
card's ordinary 9. *A spacing you can only add to is a floor, and a design that goes under it needs a
new region rather than a smaller number.*

**And they were still wrong on screen, by exactly ten points, with both numbers correct in the
source.** Reported as *"the spacing between row and dimensions went crazy… now they're like
double"* — a compaction and a small increase asked for, and both gaps grown instead.
`Ui::horizontal` takes `spacing.interact_size.y` as a **minimum row height**, and `theme::install`
sets it to 24; the size line's ink is about 13, so its row came out 24 tall with the number centred
in it — five points of nothing at each end, landing on top of the gaps either side. The row *above*
it was never affected, because its controls are 28 and the minimum never bit, which is why the fault
looked like it belonged to the gaps rather than to the line. Zeroing `interact_size.y` for that one
scope is the fix.

**The test that now holds it has three assertions and the useful one is not either of the gaps.**
Measured between rects, the broken layout *passes* both: the line's rect did begin 8 below the row
and end 18 above the next, and only the ink inside it had moved. So the load-bearing assertion is
that the line is **its own height** — under 20 rather than 24 — because that is what makes a rect gap
and a seen gap the same measurement. Written the obvious way, this test would have been green against
the bug it exists for. *When a spacing is right in the source and wrong on the glass, the thing to
measure is not the spacing.* The fourth was the two switches in the settings card, which had a tighter gap of their own on
the reasoning that two switches are one section; they carry no shared label, so nothing on screen
said they were, and the pair read as crowded against an otherwise even card. *A gap nobody chose is a
gap that will be reported.*

**A fourth pass on 2026-08-21, and two of its three items take back an answer this entry argued
for.** Both came from using the panel rather than from reading it, and both are decided.

- **The `+` over a disagreeing selection overrides rather than appends.** Appending to each layer's
  own list is what was built, and `append_exports` carried the argument in its doc comment: the one
  edit that is meaningful over a disagreement, and therefore the reason the header's `+` stays live
  where Fill's goes inert. Lived with, it is not a wrong answer but a dead end — thirty layers that
  disagreed still disagree after the click, so the card says the same sentence back at you with one
  more file per layer to show for it, and nothing inside the card resolves the state. The click now
  goes through `write_exports`, replacing every subject's list with the one seeded export in a single
  transaction, so one press leaves a selection that agrees and rows to edit. The destruction the
  careful reading was avoiding is real and is what Undo is for. The `+` is still live over a
  disagreement; what changed is the reason, and any prose repeating the old one is wrong rather than
  merely dated (§9.4 was). The card's two faint lines became one — *"Mixed exports. Add to
  override."* — because with the verb in the sentence the second line had nothing left to say, and
  the header's tooltip went three-way so the destructive click announces itself before it happens
  instead of in the card afterwards. **Fill's `+` stays inert over a disagreement**, and that remains
  the opposite answer for a reason other than symmetry: a disagreeing paint selection already has a
  way out of the state, since the stand-in row edits every paint in scope and its `x` clears them,
  where the mixed-export card offered nothing but the sentence (§9.4). *An edit that is well defined
  and leaves the state it was reached from unchanged is not a way out of it.*
- **`next_export_spec` seeds 1×, always.** It used to hand out the first `ExportScale::COMMON`
  multiplier not already spoken for — 1×, then 2×, then 3× — on the reasoning that a row identical to
  the one above it is a row you have to change before it is any use. On the machine that reads as the
  panel guessing: the second click on a card of icons produces a 2× nobody asked for, and the sizes
  are the setting a designer changes first anyway. A duplicate row is a visible, one-click-to-fix
  state; a wrong multiplier is a file that comes out at twice the size it should be. Duplicates were
  already safe on disk — `de_collide` gives the second one ` (2)` before the extension — so the
  ladder was buying something that had been bought elsewhere. The **format** is still inherited from
  the last existing row, and PNG when there is nothing to inherit from, a disagreeing selection
  included, because a list that is all JPEG is a decision about the whole list rather than about one
  entry. *Seed the setting that cannot be wrong in preference to the one that saves a click.*
  **Corrected the same day and only halfway — see the fifth pass below: the ladder is back, and what
  survives from this bullet is the *first* row, which is now 1× by construction rather than by
  luck.**
- **A row that draws no size line sits 9 from the next, not 6** — `ROW_UNIT_GAP + ROW_LINE_GAP`,
  spelled as this list's own two numbers. That is every row over a multi-selection, where
  `export_size_label` is deliberately blank because one number would be true of at most one of thirty
  differently-shaped layers, and it is also a single layer's SVG row, which has no pixel size either.
  The correction falls out of the reason 6 exists: it sits *below* the card's own pitch because a
  unit is a row plus the caption belonging to it and needs the contrast to read as one thing — strip
  the caption and there is no unit left to hold together, so six points between two bare 28pt
  controls is crowding rather than grouping. The sum happens to equal `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` and is
  written out rather than borrowed from it: that they land on the same number is corroboration, not
  derivation, and a future editor who replaces the sum with the constant has tied this list to a
  number decided about something else. The last row still allocates nothing, so what separates the
  list from the *Export n layers* button is unchanged. *A tightened gap is an argument about what is
  inside it, and it stops applying when the contents do.*

**A fifth pass the same day put the ladder back, and it is not a revert.** *"The `+` should climb the
multiplier again — 1×, 2×, 3×, then 4× for ever."* The fourth pass above read the complaint as being
about the ladder and it was about the **first rung**: the seed a fresh layer gets has to be 1×, and
the rows after it should still climb, which is what the panel had appeared to do and had never
actually been doing. The old rule picked the first `ExportScale::COMMON` multiplier **not already
used** by a row of the same format, and that answers a different question — one about which
multipliers are free rather than about how many rows there are — so it got both ends wrong. A fresh
layer took 1× only because nothing had claimed it yet, and a list that already held a 1×, however it
got there, was handed 3× for its *second* row. Counting rows is what was described and is now what
happens: `ladder_scale(rows) -> ExportScale::Times(rows.min(3) as f32 + 1.0)`, called by
`next_export_spec` with `shared_exports(…).unwrap_or_default().len()`. **The cap at 4× is a decision,
not a fallback** — past 3× the list stops being a density ladder, and climbing further would be the
panel inventing sizes rather than following one. Every rung is in `ExportScale::COMMON`, so a seeded
row can be read back off the combo it sits in instead of looking like a typed one, and the format is
still inherited from the last row with PNG when there is nothing to inherit from. `ladder_scale` is a
free function for the reason `quality_step` is: it is the whole of the rule, and `OndinApp` cannot be
built headlessly (§15 D35), so a ladder left inside the method is a ladder nothing can check.
`the_add_button_climbs_one_two_three_and_then_stays_at_four` asserts the six-element ladder and that
every rung is one of the dropdown's; it was flip-checked against an uncapped `1 + n`, which passes
the first three rungs and then walks off. *A complaint about a sequence can be a complaint about its
first term.*

*A panel that answers a question the app has already answered is a panel that will answer it
differently.*

*A setting that lives in a dialog is a setting the user re-enters; the same setting on the layer is a
file another program can run.*

**D275 — Five popovers carried four different section gaps, each with a reason about its own card.
*Built; a reversal of a number that had been asked for.*** Reported as one line: *"section gap on the
popovers should be 10 on all of them: export settings, export menu, stroke settings, typography
settings, color picker."*

They were 15 (the type popup), 11 (export settings), and 10 (the stroke card and the colour picker) —
and the export *menu* already comes to exactly 10, because `popup_rule` spends 5 above its hairline
and 4 below it. So the change is two numbers, and what makes it worth an entry is that **both were
argued for, one of them by the same person.** The type popup's 15 is recorded a few entries up: at 10
against an in-section gap of 5 the ratio is 2:1, which read as one long list rather than as sections,
*"a bit too tight"*, with 5 more asked for by name. The export card's 11 was the design's own number
for a four-section card, defended here as "the same argument written twice" — a difference in section
count rather than a difference in style.

**Both arguments are about one card, and the complaint is about five.** The popovers are the same
width, the same padding, the same 26pt controls, and they open into the same lane one after another;
read that way a gap that changes between them is not a distinction, it is a wobble — which is exactly
what `typography::COL_GAP` already says about a *one-point* horizontal difference between a popup and
the card it hangs from. Consistency across the set outranks the ratio inside one member of it, which
is this project's usual answer and the one it did not reach on its own here.

`ui::POPOVER_SECTION_GAP` is the one number, and the three sites that had literals now name it. The
type popup keeps a `SECTION_GAP` alias rather than being rewritten, so what the Character tab spends
is still readable as a decision that was made about *it* — and the history of the 15 stays on it,
because a reversal with the reasoning deleted is how the 15 comes back.

*A number defended by a reason about one card is undefended against a complaint about five.*

**D276 — A layer's name on a button painted straight out of the card, because `Painter::text` clips
against nothing. *Fixed and tested.*** `ui::action_button` came out of the Export panel and belongs
to everything rather than to that panel (D274) — and the Export panel is also where it meets the one
thing it was not written for. The button under the list reads `Export {name}`, so its label is not a
phrase this module chose and there is no length a layer's name cannot be: `Export Ellipse 11312312
3123123132` ran out of both ends of the card. Nothing about that is visible in the source. The button
lays its own text out and paints it with a `Painter`, which clips against nothing and has no wrapping
to fall back on, so a label that does not fit is simply drawn where it would have gone.

The fit therefore has to be asked for at layout time: the label is a `LayoutJob` under
`TextWrapping::truncate_at_width(rect.width() − PAD * 2 − GLYPH_PT − GAP)` and is painted as a
galley. `PAD` is new and is 10 — what the pair keeps clear of the button's own corners, so an elided
name ends in a `…` with air after it rather than against the rounding. **The pair is then centred by
the *elided* width**, which is the load-bearing half: `action_button` measures before it places
because a glyph and a word are centred as one thing, and measuring the untruncated label would push
the pair off the button it had just been made to fit.

`ui::tests::a_long_action_button_label_is_elided_inside_the_button` asserts both halves over two
names, because either alone passes for the wrong reason — a galley that is `elided` can still be
centred by the full width and hang off the left, and ink inside the rect proves nothing about a label
that happened to be short. Flipped against `truncate_at_width(f32::INFINITY)`, the version somebody
would actually have written, the two names fail differently, which is why there are two: the reported
name lays out at 220.9pt in a 221pt button, so it is the **padding** that catches it and the
containment check alone would let it through by a twentieth of a point; the longer name overflows
47pt off the *left*, which is the centring rather than the width.

*A widget whose label its caller supplies has no maximum length, whatever every call site in the tree
happens to pass today.*

**D277 — Chrome wore the I-beam: every panel header and the layer name said "text" over a control.
*Fixed and tested; the second report of the same complaint. The layer-name half was reversed on sight
the same day (2026-08-21) and that field keeps its I-beam — the paragraph on the layer name below is
the reversal.*** Reported as the inspector's eyebrows —
*Appearance*, *Fill*, *Stroke*, and the rest — and the layer name at the top of the panel all showing
a text cursor. Two mechanisms underneath, and only one of them has a switch.

**The headers are egui's own default, and nothing of ours said otherwise.** A `Label` is selectable
unless told not to be, and `LabelSelectionState::on_label` sets `CursorIcon::Text` for as long as a
selectable label is hovered. Nothing in `ui::section_head` mentions selection, or could — which is
why the fix is `style.interaction.selectable_labels = false` in `theme::install_style_into` rather
than a `.selectable(false)` on the header's own label. **Off at the style, because the alternative is
a rule some two hundred `ui.label` calls have to remember**, and the one that forgets is the one the
eye lands on. It costs nothing that was in use: the only production call to `Label::selectable` in
the workspace is the typography row's, and it already passes `false` (the other is inside that row's
own test); `selectable` and `sense` are separate fields, so
labels that act as buttons keep their `Sense::click()` unaffected; and text *fields* are untouched,
because a `TextEdit` sets its own cursor and should. The headers are where it was loudest for a
reason worth keeping — that row is also the click target that opens the card, so the pointer was
saying "text" over something that behaves like a button.

**This is the second report of it, which is the part that says where the answer belonged.** The
typography panel's *Show all features* row drew the same complaint first and was answered at the call
site, with `.selectable(false)` and an `on_hover_cursor(PointingHand)` over it — D270 records the
hand half, which is still a third exception to §9.2 that has not been argued. The local
`.selectable(false)` is now redundant and is kept on purpose, as a statement that the row is not
text whatever the style says; the measurement recorded beside it is the useful part, because
`selectable(false)` alone reports `Default` and so was never the fix for *that* row's cursor — the
hover cursor was, and it wins either way. *An answer written at the call site that reported it will
be reported again from the next one.*

**The layer name was a different mechanism a style flag cannot reach, and that half is reversed.**
The identity card's first row is a frameless `egui::TextEdit`, and a `TextEdit` sets
`CursorIcon::Text` itself whenever it is hovered and interactive, so the call site wrote over it
*afterwards* — `if resp.hovered() && !resp.has_focus() { ui.ctx().set_cursor_icon(CursorIcon::Default)
}`, carved out while focused because once the caret is in the field the thing under the pointer *is*
text. This entry recorded the cost of that in the same breath as accepting it: the field is
frameless, so the I-beam was its only affordance that the heading is editable at all. It was not
acceptable once seen. Minutes after it landed — *"Name should have the I-beam. I forgot it's
editable. Let's bring it back."* — **the override was removed entirely**, focused carve-out and all,
and the row's own comment now says the I-beam is left alone on purpose and that the arrow was tried
for a session and taken back. **The eyebrows are not the same case however alike the two look from
the pointer's side**: they are labels, and there is nothing under them to edit. So the surviving rule
is narrower than the fix that produced it — chrome takes the arrow, and a *field* keeps whatever
cursor says what it is, which for a frameless one is the only thing saying it at all. *A cost
recorded as knowingly accepted is still a cost, and "knowingly" only lasts until somebody sees it.*

**Both tests read the icon over a real widget, and the surviving pair no longer say the same thing.**
`ui::head_tests::a_card_eyebrow_takes_the_arrow_rather_than_the_i_beam` drives a pointer onto an
actual `section_head`'s word and reads `platform_output.cursor_icon`; its second half turns
`selectable_labels` back on and asserts `Text`, so the arrow in the first half is a *result* and not
a pointer that missed — the failure mode of every cursor assertion.
`inspector::identity_row_tests::the_inspector_name_takes_the_arrow_until_it_is_focused` is gone with
the override it pinned, and
`inspector::identity_row_tests::the_inspector_name_still_offers_the_i_beam_it_is_editable_with`
stands in its place with a single arm: hover the field, three passes for the frame-behind
interaction state, assert `Text`. It asserts an *absence* — that nothing writes over the widget's own
cursor — and is worth a test rather than a comment precisely because the case for the arrow is still
there to be made again by anyone who looks at that row sitting beside the eyebrows.

**D278 — The panels scroll without a bar, and the popovers keep theirs. *Intentional; this is the
code catching up with the design rather than a departure from it.*** Both `egui::ScrollArea`s in
`app.rs` — the layers tree's and the inspector column's — now pass
`ScrollBarVisibility::AlwaysHidden`; the tree's was egui's default `VisibleWhenNeeded` and the
column's an explicit one. It is recorded here rather than only in §9.2 because the **boundary** is
the decision, and a future editor who finds two hidden bars and a visible one will read that as an
oversight and tidy it.

**The design already says it, in two different ways.** `design/Editor.dc.html` gives the inspector
column `overflow-y:auto;scrollbar-width:none` — scrollable, no bar — while the lists inside the
popup cards carry a `data-otscroll` attribute whose stylesheet draws a 6px rounded thumb at 22% of
the text colour. The mockup distinguishes the two cases deliberately, and the code had the column on
the wrong side of it. The layers tree is the one place the design is silent: its container declares
no `overflow` at all, because nothing in the mockup overflows it. Extending the rule there is the
maintainer's call, and the tree is where the bar showed most — a document of any size overflows it,
so the bar was a near-permanent second edge sitting just inside the panel's own.

**The reason is that the cards have no container.** §9.2 records that the inspector is an `Area` of
cards floating on the artwork with no backdrop pane, so a bar down their side reads as the edge of a
box that is not there — and it appears and vanishes as panels open and close under it. A popover is
the opposite case: a list you page through, where the bar is the only thing saying how far down it
you are. D104 draws the same line one level in, giving the axis and feature lists a permanent gutter
and the card around them an overlay.

**Hidden, not disabled.** The wheel, the trackpad, drag-to-scroll and any programmatic `scroll_to`
still work; the value feeds nothing but `show_bars` and `show_scroll_this_frame`. The layers tree's
drag-to-edge scroll while a row is dragged (§9.4, `ui::edge_scroll_speed`, the same curve as
`canvas::autopan`) lives *inside* that scroll area and is untouched.

**Nothing moved, and that is worth stating because it is not obvious.** egui's default `ScrollStyle`
is the *floating* one, and `ScrollStyle::allocated_width()` returns `floating_allocated_width` for a
floating bar, which `floating()` sets to 0 — so the bar was already painted over the content rather
than beside it, and hiding it reclaims no width. That default is what is in force, because
`theme::install_style_into` never touches `spacing.scroll`: it sets `item_spacing`, `button_padding`,
`interact_size`, `icon_width`, `icon_width_inner`, `menu_margin` and `indent`, and nothing else.
*Anyone giving the app a solid or thin scroll style later should know that `AlwaysHidden` zeroes
`current_bar_use` whatever the style says, so these two areas would then be the only ones not
reserving a gutter — and their contents are laid out to the full column width.*

**No test, on purpose.** The change is one enum value; a floating bar only paints while the pointer
is inside the area, so a probe would have to drive the pointer in to observe the absence it was
asserting; and "no rect was drawn in this lane" is a test about egui's drawing rather than about a
decision of ours. What pins this instead is the design file and the comment on each of the two
`ScrollArea`s.

*Resolved for the headers; resolved the other way for the field. A cursor is whatever was set last in
the pass before the frame ends — that is what let an override at a call site beat the widget it
followed, and it is a fact about egui rather than a description of anything in the app now, since
nothing overrides a widget's cursor any more. A rule about cursors still has to say where it is
written as well as what it says.*

**D279 — Vertical writing mode is a non-goal, and it had been one for months with no record outside a
code comment. *Intentional; recorded, not decided — the decision was already in force and already
deciding things.*** Found by the 2026-08-21 pass over `roadmap.md`, which was looking for premises that
had rotted and turned up the opposite failure: a decision that was working correctly and could not be
cited. `roadmap.md` §0's non-goal list did not name it, nothing here did, and `architecture.md` §5.4
does not mention it either. The only statement of it in the tree is a doc comment on
`panels/typography.rs`'s `REGISTRY`.

**It is not an unstarted feature; it is a rule that withholds ten controls.** The OpenType list offers
a tag when the registry's own UI suggestion says a user may choose it (D157), and four sets depart from
that answer. One of the four is this: `vert`, `vrt2`, `vrtr`, `valt`, `vhal`, `vpal`, `vchw`, `vkrn`,
`vapk` and `vkna` are all "active by default in vertical writing mode", **and this app has no vertical
writing mode**, so a switch on one of them cannot do what its label says — it substitutes rotated or
re-spaced glyphs into horizontal text. That is the `init`/`medi` argument one axis over: a switch that
is a lie rather than a mechanic. The table marks all ten `offered: false`, which puts them behind *Show
all features* rather than deleting them, so a font that carries one can still be inspected.

**The model has no expression for it and that is the deliberate half.** `ParagraphStyle::direction` is
a `TextDirection` of `Auto | Ltr | Rtl` — the **bidi** base direction, which is what parley takes when
nothing overrides it — and not a writing mode. Adding one is not a field: it is a second axis for every
box, every trim, every caret, every hit test and both export writers, all of which are written across
the inline axis and down the block axis with those two fixed. Nothing about that is cheap and nothing
about it is nearly done.

**The trap this is written to stop.** The ten withheld tags read as an oversight to anyone completing
the registry against the OpenType feature list — they are real tags, the app knows their names, and
`offered: false` looks like a gap in a table rather than an argument. Flipping them costs nothing to
type and produces the failure nobody would connect to the change: a designer switches on *Vertical
kerning* and their horizontal line re-spaces. **The tag table is not the place that decision is
allowed to be re-taken.** *Revisit only if the model grows a writing mode — at which point all ten
become offerable in one edit, which is the shape the table was left in on purpose.*

**D280 — A picture copied into another document arrived as the missing-picture placeholder, and the
panel then blamed a feature the app cannot author. *Fixed and tested.*** Copy an image layer, open a
second document, paste: the layer came across and the photograph did not, and *Export original…* went
dim saying *"This picture is linked, so the document does not hold its bytes"* — which was false twice
over, since nothing in the app can author a link (§5.5a, and the *Asset* rows in `roadmap.md` are
blocked on exactly that).

**Three links, none of them wrong on its own.** A node holds an image *key* and the bytes live in a
table on the `Document` (§5.5a), so `capture_subtree`, which clones nodes, hands back half a picture;
the layer-paste path went through `build::insert_subtrees`, which emits no `AddImage`; and
`app::reset_transient_state` clears `alt_clone` — whose ids are minted from the old document's stream
and cannot outlive it — but deliberately leaves `self.clipboard` alone. **That last one is a feature,
which is what decides the fix**: a clipboard that survives an open is the only way to move work between
documents, so the answer is to carry the bytes, not to drop the payload on open.

**`build::image_ids_in` and `build::missing_image_ops` are the two halves, and they are in core.**
§8.4's reason: MCP write tools and the CLI need the identical answer, and a second copy in the app
would drift. `image_ids_in` walks every fill and stroke brush and returns sorted unique ids
**including hidden fills** — the visibility flag says whether to draw the brush, not whether the
document needs the bytes, and dropping a hidden picture would make the eye a destructive control that
reveals what it destroyed one paste later. `missing_image_ops` emits `AddImage` only for what the
target lacks, which is `Document::has_image` doing the job it already does for a second placement of
the same file, so pasting back into the document a copy came from produces nothing and the ordinary
case is unchanged. Ids are content hashes, so an id from another document is the same key for the same
bytes and nothing has to be remapped on arrival.

**The ops go first in the transaction**, which is `tools::place_image`'s rule and its reason: one paste
is one undo step, and `apply` inverts by reversing, so the inverse has to take the table entry out
*after* the layers that were using it. `insert_all` prepends them; the duplicate path passes `&[]`,
being unable to leave the document it reads from.

**The clipboard became a struct rather than a second slot.** `OndinApp::clipboard` is now
`Option<Clip>` with `subtrees` and `images` in one payload, specifically so the two cannot come apart —
drift between two halves of one copy is the failure this bug is an instance of, and `guide_clipboard`
beside it is already a pair kept exclusive by hand (§9.4). The entries are taken in `copy_selection`,
at **copy** time, which is `clipboard_from`'s moment and the same shape of reason (D251): that box is
recorded then because a cut deletes the layers it measures, and these are recorded then because the
document holding the bytes is certainly the one on screen only until the next open.

**The message needed three states, not two.** Both doors asked `bytes().is_some()` —
`inspector::exportable` and `menu.rs`'s `picture_linked` — and that is equally false for a linked
picture and for an id the table does not hold, so the second was told it was the first.
`tools::original_refusal(doc, id) -> Option<&'static str>` became the one predicate both doors read
(D261's rule: two doors onto one verb that disagree is the thing that rule exists to stop), and
`LayerState::picture_linked: bool` became `picture_refusal: Option<&'static str>`, carrying the
*reason* rather than a flag so a third state costs nothing — all of which went with the rows on
2026-08-23, per the ⚠️ below. **The dangling case stays reachable after
the fix** and is not a leftover: a foreign or hand-written `.ondin` may carry a reference its table
does not hold — §5.5a says that is a state and not an error — and a copy taken out of such a document
brings it along, because `image_ids_in` can only carry entries that exist.

**The lesson is the `pub`-with-no-callers rot, and here it cost behaviour rather than a stale comment.**
`ImageEntry::is_linked` sat `pub` in core with **zero callers** — `dead_code` never fires on a `pub`
item in a library, which is CLAUDE.md's warning — while both doors hand-rolled `bytes().is_some()`, a
predicate that cannot tell apart the one state neither of them had thought about. The thing that would
have found it was already written and simply never reached.

⚠️ **And it is back in that state, which is worth a sentence rather than a footnote.** *Export
original…* was removed from both doors on 2026-08-23 (D305); `original_refusal` was the only caller
of `is_linked`, so deleting it returned that predicate to **zero callers** for the second time — with
every gate green, for the same reason as the first time. Nothing regressed, because nothing can
author a link. What is at risk is the *reasoning*, so it was written down where the code was: a
comment where `original_refusal` stood in `tools/mod.rs`, and `is_linked`'s own doc in core, both
naming the three states and both saying explicitly that inferring "linked" from absent bytes is the
bug this entry is about. **That pair is the spec to rebuild from the day linking is authored** —
rebuild, do not re-derive, because re-deriving is what produced the two-state version. A
`refusal_tests` module was written mid-change to keep the assertion alive and deleted an hour later
when the second door went too: a test of a deleted function is not a test, and a comment marks where
it was.

**It had its caller, and the middle arm asked rather than assumed.** `original_refusal` matched
`Some(e) if e.bytes().is_some()` → `None`, then `Some(e) if e.is_linked()` → the linked sentence, then
`Some(_) | None` → the missing one. Spelling that middle arm as a bare `Some(_)` would be correct only
while `ImageSource` has exactly two variants; asking the predicate is what makes a third variant fall
into the arm that names no mechanism instead of being silently called linked. *Do not collapse the two
guards back into one — the shorter match is the same bug this entry is about, one variant later.*

**The test is `ondin-core/tests/build.rs::a_copied_picture_arrives_in_a_document_that_never_had_it`**,
which builds a document with an embedded picture, captures the subtree, carries the entries into a
*second* document, and asserts the picture arrives and that a second carry adds nothing. ⚠️ **The flip
is kept in the test rather than run by hand**: inserting the same subtrees *without* the ops reproduces
the reported bug, so a change that made `missing_image_ops` return nothing fails here instead of
passing quietly. That test is live and unaffected — the paste half of this entry is what still runs.
The menu side **was**
`export_original_dims_for_a_linked_picture_and_says_something_else_for_a_missing_one`, deleted with
the rows on 2026-08-23 (D305); it is described here because how it was written is the part worth
rebuilding. **Neither
sentence was retyped in it**: both were *provoked* out of `original_refusal` — read once from a
document holding nothing under the key, then again after an `AddImage` carrying an
`ImageSource::Linked` entry — and the test asserted the two differ and that each row carried its own.
A row that had drifted from the
shared predicate fails; a test that spelled the strings itself would not, which is the drift D261 is
about.

**One editing hazard, recorded because it is the second instance of it.** `original_refusal` was
inserted *below* `croppable_fill`'s doc comment rather than above it, which silently reassigned six
lines of documentation to the new function and left `croppable_fill` with none. Every gate stayed
green, and `empty_line_after_doc_comment` — the lint that catches the neighbouring mistake — cannot
fire, because there is no blank line to see. Both are repaired. *Anchor an insertion on the line above
it, never on the item below: nothing in the toolchain reports a doc comment that has changed owner.*

**D281 — An exported SVG broke its underlines around every descender, because the file never said it
should not. *Fixed and tested.*** `svg::run_attrs` writes decorations as the CSS `text-decoration*`
presentation attributes and wrote nothing about skip-ink — whose CSS **initial value is `auto`**, which
browsers implement as interrupting an underline around every glyph the band passes through. The canvas
does the opposite, deliberately: `scene.rs` draws the band after the glyphs, "so an opaque underline
sits on top of a descender rather than under it. There is no skip-ink". Neither renderer was wrong.
What was missing was the file *saying* which of the two pictures it meant, so one document had two. The
fix is one attribute — `text-decoration-skip-ink="none"`, written when `style.underline.is_some()`.

**It is the one property in that writer whose *absence* is a statement**, and that is the thing not to
tidy. Every other `text-decoration-*` there is dropped when it has nothing to add: `agreed` drops the
colour and the thickness when two decorations on one run disagree, and the style is dropped when it is
`solid` *precisely because* that is CSS's initial value (D112). This one cannot follow that rule,
because the value we want is not the initial value — silence is what produced the bug. A future editor
generalising "skip whatever the consumer would infer anyway" across the four will put it straight back.

**Underline only.** css-text-decor-4 applies skipping to underlines and overlines and not to
`line-through`, which has no descenders to miss, so a run carrying a strikethrough alone would be
stating a property that decides nothing. A run carrying *both* still writes it, for its underline —
which makes this a different question from `text-underline-offset`'s beside it, not the same one. That
one is dropped when a run has both, because CSS has no way to say two offsets (D159); this one is not.

**It sits outside the shorthand-order argument** (D112), with `text-underline-offset` and for that
property's reason: skip-ink is not a sub-property of `text-decoration`, so the shorthand does not reset
it and its position among the longhands decides nothing. ⚠️ **If a consumer ignores it, it is already
ignoring its three neighbours.** Whether the `text-decoration-*` family is honoured as SVG
*presentation attributes* is one question for all four, so this adds no failure mode the colour, the
thickness and the style do not already carry. *If that answer ever turns out to be no, all four move
into a `style` attribute together — not this one on its own.*

**The test is `ondin-export/tests/svg.rs::an_exported_underline_says_it_does_not_skip_ink`**, in three
arms: underline alone writes the attribute, underline *plus* strikethrough still writes it,
strikethrough alone does not. The third arm also asserts that its fixture emitted
`text-decoration="line-through"`, because otherwise the negative passes by drawing nothing — an
undecorated run contains no `skip-ink` either. ⚠️ Flip-checked by writing the attribute
unconditionally, which fails the third arm.

**Nothing carried this before it was found**: not `roadmap.md`, not this file, not a code comment. It
is the second defect out of the 2026-08-21 verification pass to be fixed the same day (D280 was the
first), and it was found by asking what a *consumer* does with what we write rather than by reading our
own code — which is not a question that pass was built to ask, and is where the two renderers agreeing
with each other stops being evidence. *Revisit if canvas skip-ink is ever built* — the roadmap entry
scoping that work is still open, and the day it lands this attribute becomes a lie in the other
direction rather than a thing that quietly still holds.

**That day was 2026-08-25 and the attribute is gone (D356).** The canvas skips now, so CSS's initial
value is the behaviour and the writer states nothing — which makes this entry the record of *why* the
silence was wrong for four days rather than a description of the code. The three-arm test went red on
schedule, which is the whole reason it was written this way; the ⚠️ note above about the
`text-decoration-*` family being one question for all four is still live, minus the fourth.

**One editing note, as evidence for a rule that already exists.** Re-applying one edit to `svg.rs` with
a scripted read-modify-write, to run the flip check, produced a **whole-file diff** — CLAUDE.md's
warning that a scripted rewrite on Windows silently re-decides the line endings, demonstrated rather
than argued. `git checkout` restored it and the edit went back in through the editor; the committed
diff is 28 lines.

**D282 — Masks are built, and D191's verdict on them is reversed. *Built and tested; asked for, and
not yet reviewed on screen.*** `Node::mask: bool`, and a node carrying it paints nothing: its outline
clips the **run of siblings drawn above it** in the same parent, up to the next mask or the end of the
child list. Figma's rule. (Everything below describes what is now `MaskMode::Shape` — D288 added a
second mode where the mask's *alpha* decides instead of its outline, and says which of these statements
it changes.) D191 kept them out of v1 on the argument that the fill model covers "image in
a circle" — which it does, and which is why they could wait — and the user asked for them on
2026-08-21, so the *reasoning* there survives and the verdict does not. The two cases D191 named as
uncovered, a picture masked by **text** and one masked by a **group**, are exactly and only the two
arms this grew.

**It is node-level like `clip` and it is not the same switch**, which is the confusion to keep out of
this codebase: `clip` cuts a container's *children* to its own frame, `mask` cuts its *siblings* to its
own outline. `NodeKind::can_mask()` is spelled beside `clips_children` and is `takes_paint() || Group`,
so **Root and Artboard are the exclusions**. Root is not a layer and has no siblings. A frame is a page
that already carries `clips_children`, and a page that *also* cut the pages after it down to its own
box is not a thing anyone means to ask for — two switches on one layer looking like a pair. Figma
allows it; the layers panel is what settled it here, a frame's row already spending its one badge slot
on `800 × 600`.

**`Document::governing_mask` states the run rule** — the nearest *preceding* sibling with the flag, and
`None` for a node that is itself a mask. That second half is what makes a second mask **end** the
first's run rather than nest inside it: a mask *begins* a run, and a run cannot begin inside itself;
without it a stack of two would clip the second by the first and everything above by both. A third arm
says **nothing masks inside a `Boolean`**: its children are operands rather than artwork, so there is
no run there to clip. That one does not fall out — the walk stops at the container and never notices,
while the hit test reaches the operands through the spatial index, so without it a mask pasted or
reordered into a boolean makes part of that boolean unclickable while changing nothing about how it
draws (`resolve.rs::a_mask_among_a_booleans_operands_does_not_clip_them`, which is a *hit-test*
assertion for exactly that reason).

**The rule is stated once and read twice, and that is deliberate.** `governing_mask` has exactly **one**
production caller, `query::masked_away`, which asks it *backwards*, node by node. The other three
readers — `scene::paint_node`, the SVG writer's child loop and the two bounds passes in `resolve` —
carry the same rule *forwards*, holding the current mask as they iterate (`MaskRun`, `mask_box`),
because that is the natural spelling mid-iteration: a backwards scan per child, of a list you are
already holding, would make the walk worse rather than better. So **fix a disagreement by correcting
the forward reader, not by routing it through the function** — which is what the function's own doc
comment now says, having briefly claimed four callers instead.

**What holds the two spellings honest is that they are asserted against the same arrangement of
siblings**: `ops::a_mask_governs_up_to_the_next_one_and_is_never_masked_itself` pins the backwards one
and `render::a_second_mask_ends_the_first_ones_run_instead_of_nesting` pins the forward one, so a
change to the rule that touches one and not the other fails the other. *Keep the two fixtures the same
shape.* That pair is the whole reason this is a duplication worth having rather than a trap.

**`Operation::SetMask` is refused on a kind that cannot be one** (`WrongKindForOp`), where `op_set_clip`
lets an inert flag sit. The difference is what the flag does: an inert `clip` is a switch nothing
reads, while a mask that "cannot be one" would still have to be *drawn* somehow, the walk having to
decide whether the layer paints — so a state with no answer must not get into the tree. It dirties the
node's subtree only, being masked being a fact about where a sibling *sits*; what changes for the
layers above is the parent's box, which `Resolved::update` already walks up from here to recompute.

**`Resolved::mask_path` answers in the parent's space**, the space the siblings are drawn in, so it can
go straight to `push_layer` under the parent's world transform or into a `<clipPath>` beside the
parent's `<g>`. Its arms are `boolean::operand_of`'s plus the text one, with every remaining kind sent
through `Resolved::local_path` rather than re-split here — that function already knows a boolean's
outline comes from the cache and everything else's from its kind.

**A group's arm is a `Union`, not a concatenation, and the reason is narrower than `operand_of`'s.**
This clip fills non-zero, under which two *same-wound* members appended do merge — so the careless
version passes a careless test. What breaks is two members wound **against** each other: their overlap
sums to zero and comes out as a hole exactly where the shapes cross. A user's own paths carry whatever
winding they were drawn in, so that is the ordinary case rather than a contrived one, and
`a_group_masks_with_the_union_of_its_contents` is built out of it for that reason. ⚠️ *A test built
from two same-wound rectangles would prove nothing here.* It is also the one arm that costs real
arithmetic, bounded by what is inside the group.

**`None` means *masks nothing*, never "clip everything
away"**: a hidden mask, an empty text node, an empty group and a cancelled boolean all answer it, and
every caller reads it as no clip. The other reading would make hiding a mask look like deleting the
artwork. And the fill rule the group arm leans on is not a choice either: **non-zero** is what the same
outline is filled with when the layer paints normally, so what a mask keeps is exactly the ink it would
have laid down.

**One conservatism is written into the code and belongs here too.** A mask *inside* a mask group is
skipped from the union — it paints nothing, so unioning its outline in would make the group keep ink it
does not draw — while its own siblings are unioned in **whole**, so such a group offers slightly more
outline than it shows. Both readings err the same way, towards a clip that is too generous; the exact
answer needs a path *intersection*, which is a second boolean per mask per frame for a case nobody has
asked for. *Fix with an intersection if someone builds a mask inside a mask group and reports the
difference.*

**There are two derivations of that outline and that is deliberate**: `scene::mask_geometry` is the
override-aware mirror, the same relationship `build_of` has with `svg_of`, so a mask being dragged
clips where the pointer is rather than where the last commit left it. What holds them honest is
`overrides.rs::a_mask_previews_the_clip_that_committing_would_draw`, and the guard was **strengthened
for this**: `Call::Push` now records the clip **path**, not merely whether there was one, because
otherwise the two derivations could disagree about the *shape* and still pass. The fixture masks with a
group, the recursive arm being the one easiest to get subtly wrong. Ghosts carry the flag too
(`GhostNode::mask`, `ghost_mask_geometry`), so an Alt-drag copy of a masked group previews masked.
`RenderOverrides::absorb` **refuses** `SetMask` beside `SetClip`, which costs nothing: a mask changes
which *other* nodes are clipped where an override is a patch on one node, and nothing sets it
mid-gesture.

**`scene::MaskRun` is a layer of its own, nested inside whatever the parent already pushed.** It cannot
fold into the parent's clip — a parent has one clip for all its children, a mask has one for a *run* of
them, so a frame with two masks needs three clips over three stretches of one child list — and it
closes and reopens with the parent's layer for `escape_clip`'s reason, in step with it, mask first out
and mask last in or the pops unwind in the wrong order. `render.rs`'s `max_depth` assertion is what
says "nested, not beside", which is invisible in a fixture holding only one of the two clips. (It
carries a `RunKind` since D288: this paragraph is the `Clip` arm, and the `Alpha` arm is a layer with
no clip plus a composite at the end of the run.)

**SVG emits a `<clipPath id="mask-{id}">` and a `<g clip-path="url(#mask-…)">` over the run, and no
element for the mask itself** — it is not artwork. No transform on either: `clipPath` is
`userSpaceOnUse` by default and the space at the reference is the parent's, which is the space
`mask_path` answers in. No `clip-rule`, SVG's default being non-zero, which is what the canvas fills.
(An **alpha** mask exports as a `<mask>` holding the layer's own markup instead, and *does* emit the
mask's drawing — D288, which is also where the `mask-type:alpha` trap is.)
The save format is `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "is_false")]` and **defaults off** where
`clip` defaults on: a file written before masks existed had none, so **no existing file's bytes
changed** (invariant 9), pinned by `io.rs::the_mask_flag_is_absent_from_a_document_that_has_none`. It
is kept inert on kinds that cannot be one at load (`dto.mask && dto.kind.can_mask()`), as `clip` is,
which guards a hand-edited or future file rather than our own default.
**`build::replace_with_path` carries the flag across**, so *Outline shape* and *Flatten* on a mask do
not silently release it and shove the artwork above back to full size — the loss the pivot note there
records, one step louder. `build::flatten_union` deliberately does not: it makes a genuinely new layer
out of several and inherits only paint.

**The MCP snapshot gained `mask` beside `clip`, and `snapshot_version` went to 6** (§7.3). It was
`pivot`'s precedent that made "no bump" arguable — an additive write-only field needs none — and the
decision went the other way on **5's own argument**, applied honestly: a reader that has never heard of
masks gets *two* statements wrong about one page, describing the mask as a shape sitting there in
whatever fill it carries when nothing of it is drawn, and describing every layer above it as whole when
each is cut to that shape. 5 bumped for one such misreading of one layer; this is two, and the second
is about **layers the flag does not appear on**, which is the part no field-by-field reading of the
schema would turn up.

⚠️ **It is also the first bump where an untouched document's snapshot changes bytes**, and that is
worth knowing before someone treats it as a regression. `adjust` is absent when nothing is adjusted, so
5 left an untouched picture byte-identical to 4; `mask` is **not** skipped when false, sitting beside
`clip`, which has always been reported for every node because the model carries it there. That was
taken as a reason for the number to move rather than an argument against reporting the field — a
consumer diffing snapshots reads the version first. *The full reasoning is the doc comment on
`SNAPSHOT_VERSION`; keep the two in step.*

**Tested in `ondin-core/tests/{ops,io,resolve,build}.rs`, `ondin-render/tests/{render,overrides}.rs`
and `ondin-export/tests/{png,svg}.rs`.** The one that covers the sideways dependency is
`incremental_update_equals_rebuild_over_random_ops`, whose op mix now includes `SetMask`: it is the
only op in that mix whose effect on a box travels to a *sibling's* container, so the incremental pass
(children before parents) and the full one (the child list in order) reach the same union by different
routes. *Keep it in the mix.*

**D283 — A masked layer keeps its own bounds; its container gets only what the mask lets through.
*Keep, with the marquee gap stated.*** `roadmap.md` named this as one of two decisions nobody had
taken. It is a split rather than one answer, because the two ends want opposite things.

`Resolved::world_bounds` is **not reduced by any clip, a mask included** — the same answer the frame
clip has given its children since frames clipped. Two things follow. It is *conservative*: a clip only
ever removes ink, so a box that ignores clips is never too small, which is what culling and the spatial
index need of it. And it is the box of the thing you are **editing** — dragging a photograph about
under a mask is the whole gesture, and a selection outline that shrank to the visible sliver would
leave nothing to aim at.

A **container** is the other way round: each masked child's *contribution* to the parent's union is
clipped to the governing mask's box, so zooming to a mask group frames the picture you can see rather
than the whole photograph behind it. It is implemented in both `resolve_subtree` and
`Resolved::recompute_bounds`, and **mirrored in `query::local_box`** — which it has to be, that being
the box the selection outline and the resize handles are drawn from, so a container whose world box
stopped at its mask and whose local box did not would draw handles in one place and snap to another.
Order-safe in both passes: a mask is a *sibling*, so by the time a container is measured every child's
box is fresh — the incremental pass measures children before parents, and the full one walks the list
in order, where a mask precedes everything it masks.

**What it costs, plainly: a marquee or a snap can still find ink a mask clipped away.** That is a real
gap and it is not a new one — it is the same gap the frame clip has always had — and the reason to say
so here rather than to fix it quietly is that *whatever closes it should close both*. `resolve.rs`'s
`a_mask_bounds_its_container_and_not_the_layer_it_masks` pins the split at both ends, including the
local box.

**D284 — A mask is never hit, and what it masks is hit only inside it. *Keep.*** The other decision
`roadmap.md` was holding. `query::masked_away` filters `hit_test`, and it is two things at once that
are the same fact read from either end.

**A mask is never hit.** It paints nothing, so there is nothing on the canvas to aim at, and a click
where a mask sits belongs to whatever it is letting through. It stays selectable from the layers panel
and a marquee still catches it — both of those go through bounds rather than through here, which is
D283's split doing useful work.

**Masked content is hit only inside its mask.** Without it the clipped-away half of a photograph is
still clickable, which is the exact complaint that makes an invisible layer feel like a bug: a click on
empty canvas selects a picture that is not there.

Two details are load-bearing. **Every ancestor is asked**, not just the node's own parent, because a
mask two levels up clips this layer just as surely — the run it governs is a run of *groups*, and what
is inside them travels with them. And the point is put into the **parent's** space, never the mask's,
or the mask's own local transform is applied twice. A mask with no geometry falls through to the next
ancestor rather than out of the walk, `None` meaning "masks nothing" here as everywhere else.
`a_mask_is_unclickable_and_what_it_masks_is_clickable_only_inside_it` asserts both ends, and it is two
assertions rather than one because two different pieces of code answer them and each passes the
other's case.

**D285 — The identity row's Mask is a toggle, and the layers badge is how you find one. *Built; read
rather than tested (D35), and not yet reviewed on screen.*** The slot §9.4 had been holding since the identity
row was built is wired. It is the only one of the three 28×28 actions that is a **state** rather than
an event: Group and Ungroup happen and are over, where a mask is something a layer *is*, so the button
lights `active` while the layer it points at is one and clicking it again releases it. That matters
more than it sounds — it was for a day the **only** way to release a mask, the layer drawing nothing
for the canvas to offer a handle on, and it is still one of only two (D286 added the chord and the
menu row, which reach this same verb).

`Inspector::mask_action` — `mask_target` until D286 widened it — returns what the click would *do*, or
the sentence saying why the button is dim. It picks the **bottom-most layer of the selection**, which is Figma's rule and the
only one that reads off the canvas — a mask clips what is drawn *above* it, so the mask is the one
underneath — and it asks the *parent's* child list rather than the selection's, which is in click
order. (Both halves have since moved: D286 gave the default an override — an `Alt+Shift` key layer wins
where one is designated — and D287 narrowed the default itself to the bottom-most member that is **not
a picture**, and lifted the whole rule into `build::mask_target`, which the control and the builder now
both call. ⚠️ That is a *different* function from the `Inspector::mask_target` named above, which no
longer exists; the names are one letter apart in meaning and a search finds both.) The rest of the selection **was**
never written to, which D286 also changed — two or more members are now wrapped in a group. It requires
**one parent** across the selection, because two layers in different groups have no stacking order a
mask could mean and the answer would be "the bottom-most of these" for a value of *bottom* nobody can
see. A `Result` rather than an `Option`, because each refusal has a different thing to fix and a
disabled control that cannot say which is the failure the row's tooltips exist to avoid.

**One refusal lives here and could not live anywhere else**: a layer whose parent is a `Boolean`. The
*kind* is maskable, so `op_set_mask` would take it and the flag would sit there doing nothing —
`governing_mask` answers `None` inside a boolean (D282), there being no run of artwork to clip. The op
