layer cannot refuse it without deciding that a *parent* makes a kind unmaskable, so the gate is the
button's, and the tooltip says why. It is the one case where the control is stricter than the
operation, and that asymmetry is deliberate: a button that lights up and changes nothing on screen is
worse than one that explains itself.

**The layers row is the other half, and it is not decoration.** A mask draws nothing, so its row is the
only place in the app that says the layer is still there; `ph-circle-half` therefore takes the
right-hand badge slot **ahead of** the frame's size badge and the `Subtract` base mark (D244). No row
can want two — a frame cannot be a mask (`can_mask`), and a boolean's operands are consumed rather than
painted, so a mask among them would clip nothing.

**This shipped with no chord and no context-menu row, and both were added the next day** (D286): the
one open item it left was which key to spend, and `context-menus.md`'s non-row had a *reason* that had
already expired. What survives here is the identity row itself. ⚠️ Not testable: an `OndinApp` needs a
wgpu render state to construct, so the row's gating is read rather than asserted (D35), which is
`group_actions`' situation exactly.

**D286 — Masking wraps the layers in a group, takes the key layer, and has a chord and a row.
*Built and tested; the user's own four asks after living with D282–D285.*** Four changes from one
review, and the substantive one is the third.

**`Ctrl+Alt+M`, Figma's chord, which D285 left as the one open question.** `M` was **completely
unspent** — not one binding in `input.rs` or `shortcuts.md` used the key in any combination — so this
is the rare chord that cost nothing and had no collision to argue about. Alt-modified like
`Ctrl+Alt+U`/`S`/`I`/`X`, which is the company it now keeps: those four make or change a container, and
with the wrapping arm below, so does this. `input.rs::masking_is_a_chord_and_the_bare_letter_is_still_unspent`
asserts the chord **and** that plain `M` and `Ctrl+M` stay empty. ⚠️ *The second half is the one that
matters*: the risk is not a collision today but someone later giving `M` a tool, and a keymap only
notices that if something is asserting the emptiness.

**A context-menu row, *Use as mask*, which reverses `context-menus.md`'s non-row.** That entry refused
it because nothing in the model expressed a mask; the reason expired when the model did. It sits in
`Group::Structure` **after the group verbs and before the four booleans** — after *Ungroup* where that
row is present and after *Frame selection* on a shape, where it is not — because with the wrapping arm
it is one of the container-making verbs rather than a property. **Checkable like *Clip content*, not
like the booleans**: a toggle whose off-state is worth showing, against four alternatives of which one
is current. It ticks off a new `LayerState::masked`, true when the layer **is** a mask *or* is a
container holding one — both halves, because the second is the state the verb itself leaves behind, and
a tick that knew only the first would go out the instant the operation finished. **Absent, not dimmed,
where the verb has no answer**: a selection containing a frame (a frame can neither be a mask nor be
grouped — the same pair of reasons *Group selection* is absent for) and inside a boolean.

**The row moved the counts, and that is worth stating because `context-menus.md` §3 hand-counts them.**
A primitive's canvas menu went **22 → 23**, a boolean's **28 → 29**, the Structure group **6 → 7**;
the pinned test was renamed with it, to `a_primitives_menu_is_twenty_three_rows_in_canonical_group_order`
— `..._twenty_four_...` since *Copy as PNG* (D259), which is also what took text's 27 to 28. §3's *tail*
of 19 is untouched, Structure not being part of it. ⚠️ **This is the first row to lengthen those menus
by a decision rather than by an implementation**, so §3's "nothing outstanding can lengthen these
menus" has been amended rather than left: it was a true statement about the open ledger and was never a
ceiling. The file and the code are converging here as they were at 22 — a verb listed as a deliberate
non-row becoming a real one — but for a different reason, and the difference is the interesting part.
Text's 27 is **read rather than re-measured** and stays unpinned.

**Masking two or more layers wraps them in a group** (`build::mask`), and this is the user's own
reasoning rather than tidiness: *"Since layers are still independent after masking, I still have to
manually select 2+ layers to move them around. The group solves that, and it makes it obvious who's the
mask layer and who's not."* Both halves are the feature — one thing to drag, and a container whose
contents are exactly the mask and its subjects. It calls **`build::group`** rather than repeating it,
so the no-frame/no-root admission test and the placement rule that lands the container where the
topmost member was are stated once and cannot drift between the two verbs; then the chosen layer is
reordered to index 0 and flagged, all in **one transaction and one undo step**.

**One member is the exception and takes no group**, and the reason is not economy. There is nothing to
wrap it *with*: `group` itself refuses a group of one, and wrapping would change **which layers it
masks**, a group being a new parent — the lone layer would stop masking the siblings the run rule gives
it (D282). *Do not "simplify" the two arms into one.* Two refusals `mask` owns rather than inherits: a
kind that fails `can_mask`, and **any parent that is a `Boolean`**, so the chord — which does not pass
through the inspector's own gate — cannot reach the silent no-op D285's button refuses.
`build.rs::masking_a_pair_wraps_them_in_a_group_with_the_mask_at_the_bottom` carries a third layer that
must not be swept in and asserts the single undo; `masking_a_lone_layer_flags_it_where_it_stands` and
`mask_refuses_a_frame_and_a_booleans_operands` cover the rest.

**`Alt+Shift` designates which layer becomes the mask**, asked for by analogy with what the key layer
already does: *"We use that to key on align and boolean (subtract applies, no effect on the rest). So
if I select 2+ layers, I key a specific layer and that becomes the mask. Without a key, it uses the
same automatic logic as now."* Implemented exactly as `build::boolean` does it for a `Subtract`'s base
operand, and doing the same thing to the order: the chosen layer moves to index 0 of the new group and
everything else keeps its **relative** z-order. A mask clips what is drawn *above* it, so "the mask"
and "the bottom of the stack" are one position — which is why designating one is a **reorder** rather
than a flag on the selection, and why the rearrangement must be the smallest one and not a sort.
`the_key_layer_becomes_the_mask_and_the_rest_keep_their_order` keys the **top** layer deliberately,
that being the case the default answers differently. (The default it overrides is no longer plain
bottom-most — D287 made it the bottom-most member that is not a *picture* — and the override is
unchanged: the key still wins, including over a photograph.) A `key` not among the members is ignored rather
than refused, as `boolean`'s is: it belongs to some other selection. That makes **three** consumers of
the one designation — align, subtract, mask — which `context-menus.md`'s *Make this the key layer* row
now says.

**And one consequence of the toggle, stated rather than left to be discovered.**
`Inspector::mask_action` answers `Make { members, key }` or `Release(id)`, and **Release is read from
either end**: one selected layer that is a mask, *or* one selected container holding one. The second
arm is not a convenience — the make-arm leaves the **group** selected, so without it the operation
could not be undone from the selection it produces. ⚠️ **"Holding one" was the whole of what this
paragraph enumerated, and a group can hold two** (§15 D513): the arm was `.find(…)`, the *first* masked
child, while the Mask card one row below already returned all of them, so *Release mask* on a group
holding two released one and left the button lit. It is `Release(Vec<NodeId>)` now, taken from
`mask_card_targets` and written in one transaction, which is D288's report-Mixed-and-write-to-all rule
applied one card up. ⚠️ **The trade is that a selected mask-group
answers *Release*, so the button and the chord cannot turn that group into a mask of *its* siblings**;
nested mask-groups are reachable only by other means. That was judged worth far less than the release
path, which is the difference between a verb you can take back where you are standing and one you
cannot. *Revisit if nesting mask-groups turns out to be something anyone does* — the fix would be a
modifier or a second row, not a change to which arm wins by default.

**D287 — A shape beats a picture as the mask, the group step comes first, and a stale comment nearly
bought a redundant badge. *Fixed and tested, except the double-click, which is read; the user's report
after using masks.***

**Start with the correction, because it cost the most.** Asked what shows which layer is keyed, this
project's own maintainer-facing comment answered "nothing on screen currently announces either", and
the answer offered on that basis was a new layers-panel badge. It was false. **`canvas::draw_key_outline`
has traced the keyed layer's exact outline at 3px in `color::KEY` since D113** — the user settled it
with a screenshot of a thick magenta border round the keyed rectangle — and a `Subtract`'s base operand
additionally wears the layers panel's stack badge (D244). Both designations are announced, and have
been. The comment beside the *Make this the key layer* row is corrected, and so is
`context-menus.md` §5.8's row, which carried the same sentence: the half that is still true is that
`Alt+Shift`+click is the only way **in**. ⚠️ *A stale "nothing shows this" is the most expensive shape
of rotted comment there is*, because it does not read as a doubtful claim — it reads as a gap, and the
work it invites is work nobody needed. Suspect every one of them; there is one left in `menu.rs`, on
`Item::MakeBaseOperand`'s own doc.

**A shape beats a picture as the mask.** `build::mask_target(doc, members, key)` is now the only
spelling of which member becomes one — the **key** if one is designated among them, else the
**bottom-most member that is not a picture**, else the bottom-most — and both `build::mask` and
`Inspector::mask_action` call it rather than each deciding. The user's words: *"If I select an image
and a shape, the shape should always be the mask."* The plain bottom-most rule (D286) got that wrong
the *ordinary* way round, which is why it was worth changing rather than explaining: an image-filled
layer is in this model a **shape with a photograph in it**, so its outline is a rectangle, and the
normal way to build the picture — drop the photo, draw a shape over it, mask — leaves the photo
underneath. So the photo became the mask and cropped everything above it to its own box.

*Recorded while in there, because it is easy to read as redundant and is not:* `mask_action` also
**dry-runs `build::mask`** on a throwaway `IdSource` before answering `Make`, the way the boolean
dropdown tests its own predicate. The named refusals above it are chosen for what they can *say*; the
dry run closes the class — whatever `build::mask` inherits from `build::group` and the list has not
thought of, which today is a selection with a frame in it. Without it the control is live and the click
reports a failure, which is the state the identity row's tooltips exist to prevent.

**The key still overrides it, and the alternative was offered and declined.** The user said outright
that *"not respecting the key for images as masks is also defensible"*; the other side was taken and
the reasoning belongs here. Masking with a photograph is a real thing to want — you get its box —
`Alt+Shift` is how the user says they meant it, and it is the same gesture that already overrides
z-order for a `Subtract`'s base operand. Refusing an image outright would make the gesture **silently
do nothing** on the one selection where the user had been most explicit, which is worse than an
unusual result they asked for. It falls back to bottom-most when *every* member is a picture: no
better answer exists there, and one photograph cropping another is evidently what was asked for.
`a_shape_is_preferred_over_a_picture_however_they_are_stacked` puts the picture in the **bottom** slot
deliberately — ⚠️ *with the shape at the bottom both rules agree and the test proves nothing* — beside
`keying_the_picture_makes_it_the_mask_anyway` and `two_pictures_fall_back_to_the_bottom_most`.

**`Paint::image_fill` moved into core, and the timing is the point.** "Is this layer a picture, and
which fill is it" was `tools::croppable_fill` with sixteen app-side call sites; `mask_target` made it a
question the **model** asks. It is `ondin_core::Paint::image_fill` now and `croppable_fill` is one line
onto it, so the sixteen sites keep the name that reads right where they are and there is still one
rule. That is D261's lesson — two doors onto one verb must not be two answers — applied *before* the
drift rather than after it, which is the only time it is cheap.

**The group step now comes before the content step** (`canvas::double_click_pick`). Reported as: *"once
a group has an image… if I double click on the image to select it, it goes into image editing. I should
be able to double click to select first, then double click to edit."* The kind arms were asked first,
justified by a comment saying "an image-filled shape is a leaf, so there is no group step it could be
stealing" — true of a leaf on the artboard, false of the same leaf inside a group, which is exactly
where it was stealing one. The order is now: descend while there is a group to descend into, then open
the content; `entered_group` remembers how far in you are, so the third double-click on a nested
picture is the one that crops. **It changes text and paths too**, which had the identical fault with
nobody reporting it — the consistent rule, "one level means one", is what fixes all three, and it is
Figma's behaviour. ⚠️ **This rests on reading, not on a green assertion**: `OndinApp` holds a wgpu
`RenderState` and is not constructible headlessly, so `double_click_pick` has no test (D35). Said
plainly here rather than implied away.

**What was deliberately left.** The user reports that masked layers are now easy to tell apart thanks
to the group, and that it wants long-term use before deciding whether anything more is wanted. That is
a decision to wait, not an open gap, and it is recorded here rather than in `roadmap.md` precisely so
it does not become a task nobody asked for — which is the same failure the key-layer badge above very
nearly was. *Revisit when the user has lived with it and says what is missing.*

**D288 — Alpha masking, and why luminance is not here. *Built and tested; the GPU half is read, not
rasterized — see the warning.*** `MaskMode { Shape, Alpha }`: the outline clips, hard-edged, or the
mask's own **alpha** decides per pixel how much survives. `Shape` is the default and is what every mask
made before this meant. The user was offered three scopings and picked **"alpha now, luminance
recorded"**, which is why this entry carries the absent mode as well as the built one.

**Luminance is missing on a *dependency*, and the limit was measured rather than assumed.**
`vello_cpu` 0.2.0 has `Mask::new_luminance` and its `push_layer` takes `mask: Option<Mask>` (⚠️ **both
halves re-checked against the 0.2.0 source at the `=0.0.9` bump rather than renumbered** — the mask
constructor is still in `vello_common`'s `mask.rs` and the signature is now
`(clip_path, blend_mode, opacity, mask, filter)`, the new fifth argument being one `cpu.rs` passes
`None`; §15 D414); **vello 0.9's GPU `push_layer` takes no mask at all**, and no Porter-Duff `Compose` or `Mix` moves colour into
alpha — the conversion is not expressible in the compositor. Symmetry would therefore mean rasterizing
the mask subtree offscreen and converting luminance→alpha on the GPU path too, per frame, which is the
class of divergence §3 exists to prevent. Shipping the CPU-only version would make the canvas and the
export disagree, silently, on documents that look right until they are exported. *Re-check when
vello's `push_layer` grows a mask parameter* — that is the day this closes, and **nothing about the
design has to change when it does**: `MaskMode` gains a third variant and the walk gains a third arm.
⚠️ This is deferred with a blocker, not a non-goal and not open work; it is here rather than in
`roadmap.md` precisely so it is not re-argued from first principles by someone who has not measured it.

**The mode is a field beside the flag, not a payload inside it, and the reason is a gesture.** Set a
mask to Alpha, release it to look underneath, put it back. An `Option<MaskMode>` has nowhere to keep
*Alpha* while the mask is off, so the release quietly discards it and the toggle turns out to have been
destructive — a data loss with no error and no undo entry of its own to notice. So `Node::mask_mode`
sits next to `Node::mask`, is inert-but-remembered while the flag is false, and **`SetMaskMode` is its
own operation** rather than an argument of `SetMask`. `ops::the_mask_mode_survives_the_mask_being_released`
pins it, including that the mode is writable on a layer that is not a mask at all. Its `changes_ink()`
is **true even then**, where it changes nothing on screen: the honest reading of that question is about
the operation and not about the state it lands in, which is the answer `SetGeometry` on a shape already
that size already gives. `RenderOverrides::absorb` refuses it beside `SetClip` and `SetMask` (D282).

**One mechanism, both backends.** `ScenePainter::push_mask_layer` is
`BlendMode::new(Mix::Normal, Compose::DestIn)` — what is already in the enclosing layer survives in
proportion to the alpha drawn inside this one, and the colour drawn inside is discarded. Both backends
take it as an ordinary blend on their own `push_layer`, so the GPU path needs nothing vello does not
already do, and there is no second implementation to drift. It is **a method of its own rather than a
fifth parameter** on `push_layer` because it takes none of that function's other decisions: no clip,
no fill rule, no opacity. `cpu.rs::dest_in_composites_a_soft_alpha_mask_and_ignores_its_colour` is the
dependency-behaviour assertion the whole feature rests on, kept from the probe that produced it —
*keep it; it is what will notice when vello_cpu's compose changes under us.*

**`MaskRun` carries a `RunKind`, because the two modes are two layer arrangements.**
`Clip(BezPath)` is a shape mask — one layer, the mask never drawn. `Alpha(NodeId)` carries **the node,
not geometry**: an alpha mask is not geometry, what matters is the ink it lays down — its fills, its
gradients, a photograph's own alpha channel — so the only way to ask for it is to *draw* it. That is
also why it arrives at the **end** of the run: the mask composites over what it masks, so what it masks
has to be there first. ⚠️ **The alpha arm's run layer carries no clip on purpose** — it is an isolation
group, and without it the composite reaches past the run and erases the page behind it. A future editor
tidying "why does this layer have no clip when the other one does" will break exactly that.

**Two asymmetries worth stating, because each looks like a bug.** A shape mask with no geometry masks
*nothing* (the `mask_path` `None` reading, D282), while an **alpha mask with no ink legitimately erases
the run** — that is the mode being honest about what it was asked, not a case to guard. And **neither
mode reads the mask node's own `opacity`**: for a shape mask the outline says which pixels survive and
nothing about how much of them does, and for an alpha mask the opacity is already part of the ink by
the time the mask is drawn, so folding it in here as well would apply it twice. Ghosts carry
`GhostNode::mask_mode`, so an Alt-drag copy of an alpha-masked group previews in its own mode.

**Save format and snapshot.** `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "is_shape_mask")]`, so a document
whose masks are all shape masks — every document written before the mode existed — changes no bytes
(invariant 9); loaded **without** gating on `mask`, deliberately, since the mode is remembered while
the mask is off. `io::the_mask_mode_is_absent_until_something_is_not_a_shape_mask` asserts both
directions. The MCP snapshot reports `mask_mode` as a **string** (`"Shape"`/`"Alpha"`) on §7.3's
`line_height` precedent — a name survives a mode being added where an integer discriminant silently
shifts meaning — and `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` goes **6 → 7**, the same class as 6's argument one step on: a
reader on 6 knows the layer is a mask and describes a soft-edged alpha mask as a hard clip, which is
wrong about every pixel along its edge.

**SVG keeps the two modes apart, and one attribute is doing the work.** A shape mask stays a
`<clipPath>`; an alpha mask becomes `<mask id maskUnits="userSpaceOnUse" style="mask-type:alpha">`
holding the layer's own markup, with `<g mask="url(#…)">` over the run. ⚠️ **`mask-type: alpha` is
load-bearing**: SVG's `<mask>` defaults to *luminance*, so without it every alpha mask exported would
silently become the one mode this app does not have — and would look right whenever the mask happened
to be white, which is the failure that survives a casual check. It is the CSS property rather than the
presentation attribute of the same name, which has the poorer support of the two spellings.
`svg::an_alpha_mask_exports_as_a_mask_element_typed_alpha` covers it.

**The inspector's Mask card** is the user's own asked-for shape: directly under the identity card, one
full-width dropdown, present only when there is a mask to describe. Present-or-absent rather than
always-there-and-inert, because a card that is usually dead is noise a disabled *button* is worth
paying for and a whole card is not. A third mode drops into the same dropdown with nothing else moving.

**It follows a mask *group*, and that reverses what this entry said first.** It shipped reading the
selected node's own flag only, on the reasoning that `mask_action` answers `Release` for a *group
holding* a mask too and the group is not the thing with a mode. The group is still not the thing with a
mode — but it is the thing the **user has in front of them**, because `build::mask` leaves the group
selected (D286). So the card vanished at the instant the operation finished, and the mode was reachable
only by opening the group and picking the layer inside, while the identity row's button one card above
went on reporting that this very selection was masked. Two controls, one question, answering it
differently; the reasoning above was the inconsistent one and the reversal is the user's, who asked for
it in as many words. ⚠️ **That is the second thing in this feature settled by "the two controls must
answer one question the same way"** — the first was `MaskAction::Release` reading from either end
(D286). *Treat a third occurrence as the rule rather than the coincidence it now looks like.*

**`inspector::mask_card_targets` is the rule, and it is a free function on purpose.** `OndinApp` holds
a wgpu `RenderState` and cannot be built headlessly (D35), so a decision left on the method is a
decision no test can reach — and this is the rule the user asked about *by name*, which makes it
exactly the kind that should be answerable by something other than my reading of it. It answers: the
selected layer if it is a mask, otherwise its **direct** mask children. Three properties, each with a
test in `inspector.rs::mask_card_tests`:

- **Its own flag wins.** A group that is itself a mask *and* holds one describes itself, or selecting
  it would edit a mode belonging to something a level down and not to the layer in front of you.
- **Direct children only, which is what makes nesting safe** — the case the user flagged as the one
  they expected trouble from. A mask group nested inside another group leaves the outer one alone: the
  outer's children include a *group*, and a group is not a mask. So the card describes one level and
  never reaches through, and there is no arrangement where selecting an ancestor silently rewrites a
  mode several levels down. `a_mask_two_levels_down_is_not_reached_from_the_top` pins it and was
  flip-checked against the plausible wrong version, which is recursing instead of stopping.
- **A group can hold two runs, so the target is a list.** A second mask among the children starts one,
  reachable by dragging a mask in or by masking twice inside one group. They report **"Mixed"** on
  `mixed_stroke_properties`' convention — Mixed is a report, never an entry in the list, and nothing is
  lit while they disagree — and a pick writes to every target that *would change*, in one transaction,
  so picking the mode both already share adds no undo step. Answering with one of them would leave the
  other reading as though it had been changed.

**There is no "mask group" flag, and the user proposed one.** Being a mask group is derived from the
children every time it is asked, which is D113's rule and D244's precedent: the `Subtract` base operand
is derived from the tree rather than stored, so dragging the operand up one row stops it being the
base. The same property buys the same thing here — drag the mask out of the group and the group stops
being a mask group, with nothing to go stale and nothing to keep in step. *That is why the offer was
declined; a later reader will otherwise wonder.*

**The test to name is `png::an_alpha_mask_fades_what_it_masks_and_reads_only_its_alpha`**: the shape-mask
raster fixture with one operation added, so the difference in the pixels is the mode and nothing else.
Content survives at **alpha 128** — not 255, not 0 — and stays **red** under a half-transparent **blue**
mask. Those two numbers are what separate alpha from both of the other answers: a clip would leave 255,
and the luminance mode we do not have would have read the blue as a brightness and produced a third
number again. ⚠️ Flip-checked by treating `Alpha` as `Shape`, which fails at 255. Beside it,
`render::an_alpha_mask_paints_its_ink_into_a_composite_layer_after_the_run` asserts the arrangement —
two fills, one `push_mask_layer`, the isolation layer carrying no clip, `max_depth` 3 — and the
preview/commit drift guard now runs its three gestures in **both** modes.

⚠️ **The GPU backend's alpha mask is unverified.** The mechanism is the same `BlendMode` on vello's own
`push_layer` and the scene builds, but there is no headless GPU rasterization in this workspace, so
"both backends agree" rests on **reading** for the GPU half — the CPU numbers above do not cover it,
and the user has not seen it on screen either. *Say so rather than letting the pixel test above imply
two backends.* It is the first place to look if an alpha mask ever draws differently on canvas than in
an exported PNG.

**D289 — Alt draws from the centre, and `Alt`+`Shift` reaches the resize handles. *Built and tested;
the gesture routing is read (D35). **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22** — "confirmed, each
one landed".*** Two annoyances reported together, and they turn out to be
the same shape: a modifier that works on one gesture and silently does nothing on its twin.

**Alt while *drawing* was never read.** `create_corner` took `shift` and nothing else, so the create
drag ran corner to corner however the hand was loaded — while a resize had answered Alt with
`tools::Resize::symmetric` since the beginning. The user's example is the one that makes it obvious:
an ellipse is placed by its *centre*, so the gesture wanted is click the middle, hold `Alt`+`Shift`,
pull a circle out around it. Figma, Illustrator and Photoshop all read Alt this way. `create_box`
wraps `create_corner` and mirrors the near end through the press point when Alt is down; a line takes
the same arm, since its two ends are not a box but are the same two points.

**Constrain first, mirror second, and the order is not the obvious one.** The grid's order is round
*then* square (D47); this one is square *then* mirror, and both are load-bearing for different reasons.
Squaring from the press gives equal extents out of the centre, so doubling them leaves a square
centred where the hand pressed. Mirroring first and squaring after also yields a genuine square, of a
plausible size — it measures the constraint across a box the pointer is only half of — and centres it
somewhere the hand never pointed: a 30 × 20 drag from `(100, 100)` lands centred at `(100, 110)`. That
number is measured, not argued: the flip check was run. The pixel grid survives either way, since
`start` is on it and `2·start − corner` therefore is too.

**Both tests assert the *centre*, never the size, and that is the whole of what makes them worth
having.** The plausible wrong version of the feature — keep `start` as the near corner and push the far
one out to twice the drag — produces a box of exactly the right extent in exactly the wrong place, and
so does the wrong composition order. A size assertion passes against both. `centred_ends` is a free
function for the reason `squared_corner` is (D35): `create_box` is an `OndinApp` method and no test can
reach one. `alt_grows_the_drawn_box_out_from_the_press_point` and
`alt_and_shift_centre_the_square_on_the_press_rather_than_near_it` are the two, and both were
flip-checked against both wrong versions.

**`Alt`+`Shift` on a handle did nothing, and the user's diagnosis of why was right.** `drag_started`
gated the whole select drag on `!(alt && shift)` to protect the key-layer chord (D40, §9.4): Alt alone
means drag-a-copy, the copy commits on any release that moved, so a designation that slipped past
egui's drag threshold would leave a duplicate behind. Refusing the drag makes the slip do nothing
instead. Correct on the artwork, and meaningless on the box's own chrome — a designation is a click
*on a layer*, so no slip off a handle can designate anything, and none of the chrome gestures
duplicates. The guard moved inside `begin_select_drag`, below the pivot, line-end and handle arms.

**It read as a dead spot rather than as a refusal, which is the part worth remembering.**
`select_cursor` answers from `Handles::armed`, which never saw the chord, so the cursor promised a
resize for the whole press and then nothing happened — the failure mode a *visible* refusal would not
have had. Worth suspecting wherever a gesture is gated somewhere its cursor is not.

⚠️ **The arithmetic was already tested and still shipped broken.**
`tools::alt_and_shift_resize_proportionally_about_the_centre` has passed the whole time; `resize_opts`
took both modifiers correctly and was never reached. The gate was two functions above it, in the code
that decides whether a gesture starts at all, and no test in this workspace can reach that — `OndinApp`
is not constructible headlessly (D35). *A green test on the maths says nothing about whether the
gesture arrives*, and this pairing — tested transform, untestable routing — is where to look first
when a modifier is reported inert.

**Left alone deliberately:** `MIN_CREATE_PX` still measures the pointer's travel rather than the
resulting shape, so under Alt a 3px drag makes a 6px shape and is still discarded as a stray click.
That threshold exists to tell a click from a drag, and the gesture is what it should be reading.

**D290 — A value field was two or three tab stops, and two of them painted nothing. *Fixed and
tested, with real Tab events. **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22**.*** Reported on the
Transform panel, where the fields are used in pairs:
from X, one Tab put the focus somewhere invisible and a second Tab reached Y. The user's reading —
"probably focusing something I don't see" — was exactly right.

**`Sense::click()` is `CLICK | FOCUSABLE` and `Sense::click_and_drag()` is `CLICK | DRAG | FOCUSABLE`.**
That is the whole bug. A `value_field` is three interactive rects — the prefix scrub strip (D75), the
`DragValue`, and a clickable unit at the far end — and only the middle one has a keyboard face. The
other two were built with the named constructors, so both were focusable, and focus on either landed
on something that draws no focus ring, no caret and no selection. A plain field was two stops and a
suffixed one was three. The fix is to spell the flags: `Sense::CLICK | Sense::DRAG` and `Sense::CLICK`.
The canvas size badge's label strip (D253) is the same widget shape and got the same change.

**Measured before it was touched, and the measurement is what named it.** A throwaway probe drove real
`Key::Tab` events at a two-field row and printed `Memory::focused()` after each, resolving unknown ids
through `Context::read_response` to a rect and a `Sense`. The answer came back as
`[[10.0 1.0] - [26.0 27.0]] Sense { click drag focusable }` — 16 × 26 pixels at the left edge of the
field, which is the prefix strip and is not a thing anyone would have found by reading. *A focus bug is
a `Sense` bug about a third of the time and never looks like one in the source.*

**The kept test asserts a *set*, not a step count.** `tabbing_a_row_of_fields_steps_from_digits_to_digits`
sweeps six Tabs and fails if any focused id is not one of the two fields' digits. A count would pin the
reported bug and nothing else; the set catches a fourth rect acquiring `FOCUSABLE` later, which is the
same bug by another route. The second field in the fixture is deliberately the **suffixed** variant —
flip-checked both ways, and a row of two plain fields goes green with the unit's half still broken,
which is precisely the vacuous test CLAUDE.md's "what would also pass this" is asking about.

⚠️ **A comment asserted the opposite and had done since the suffix landed**: the unit's `interact` was
introduced with "the field keeps the rest of the row, which is what leaves one focus target for typing".
The arrangement was right and the conclusion was false, because `Sense::click()` does not mean what its
name suggests. Corrected in place.

**One behaviour change beyond the tab order, stated because it is not obviously wanted.** Clicking a
prefix strip no longer takes focus from whatever had it, so scrubbing X while Y is open for typing
leaves Y open. That reads as an improvement and was not asked for. *If it turns out to be wrong, the
answer is to focus the **digits** from the strip rather than to give the strip its focusability back* —
the strip has nothing to do with focus.

**D291 — A click with a shape tool created nothing, and now it creates one at 100 × 100. *Built and
tested; the routing read (D35). **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22**.*** The user's spec,
implemented as given: 100 × 100 rect, 100-diameter
oval, 100 × 100 triangle, 100 × 100 star. The two counts were already right —
`POLYGON_DEFAULT_SIDES` is 3 and `STAR_DEFAULT_POINTS` is 5 — so only the box was missing.

**It did nothing, and not by a decision that was ever made.** `MIN_CREATE_PX` carries the comment "so a
stray click with a shape tool creates nothing", which reads as the click being handled and refused. It
is not: egui reports a still press as `clicked()` and **never** as a drag, which `text_gesture`
measured for D170, so `drag_started` never fired, `Drag::Create` never began, and that arm was never
reached. The only gesture it discards is the out-and-back drag. The comment has been corrected — *it is
the kind that makes a gap look like a policy, which is worse than no comment.*

**The click synthesizes the gesture instead of duplicating it.** `click_create` calls `begin_create`
— which picks the parent frame by containment, mints the id and seeds the tool's side count — takes
two points from `click_box`, and hands them to `commit_create`. That tail is new only in being
extracted: the drag's release now calls it too, so "a text box opens for typing, an image spends
itself, a shape is handed back to Select" exists once rather than twice. Writing the box out by hand
here would have been a second creation path, and D167's lesson is that a second path silently loses
whatever the first one earns next.

**Alt centres the default box and does not resize it**, which is the single point where Alt reads
differently from a drag's (D289). A drag's Alt doubles the extent because the extent is what the hand
is authoring; a click authors none, so doubling would answer an unasked question with a 200-unit shape.
Both halves are asserted, and each kills a different wrong version: reusing the drag rule wholesale
gives a correctly centred 200 × 200 (fails the size), and ignoring Alt gives a correct 100 × 100 in the
wrong place (fails the centre). Both were run. Shift is silent here — the default box is already
square, so the constraint is already satisfied and a second reading would have to be invented.

**Frame and Line are excluded, each for its own reason rather than by oversight.** A frame is a
container, so a default-sized one guesses at a layout rather than at a shape — Figma answers a frame
click with a size *menu*. A line has no box: the box arm would give it a diagonal nobody asked for, and
a horizontal default would be a rule invented here. Both are one arm away.
`four_tools_answer_a_click_with_a_default_box_and_all_of_them_drag_one_too` pins the membership as a
list rather than a count, and pins the containment — a tool that answered a click but not a drag would
be a shape tool with no way to size what it makes.

**D292 — A shape being drawn had no size pill, and the two pills are now one painter. *Built; the
placement is tested, the routing read (D35). **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22** — "the
pill follows the shape now".*** Reported plainly: "when creating a shape, it doesn't show the size pill
below it, the same one we show when a layer is selected."

**The cause is one line and it is the same shape as D291's.** `draw_size_badge` reads
`selection.ids()`, and a shape being drawn is not selected until it commits — so there was never a
selection for it to hang off. Not a decision, just a gesture that had no entry into the slot.

**The pill is the *same* pill, and that is the requirement rather than a nicety.** The drag's readout
becomes the selection's readout in a single frame on release, so the two have to be indistinguishable:
`paint_size_pill` is now the one painter, and `size_label` the one rounding. Two pills that differed by
a point of padding or a decimal would show as a twitch at precisely the moment the eye is on the
number. Drawn upright and unlocked for a create — a shape is drawn axis-aligned, and nothing has had a
chance to lock it.

**A shape being drawn takes the badge slot ahead of both other claimants**, which is the block's
existing "one readout at a time" rule (D252) extended by one arm. It is not cosmetic: `choose_tool`
does **not** clear the selection, so arming the Rect tool with something already picked leaves that
layer's chrome on the canvas — without this arm a create drag would show a second pill, in a different
place, quoting a layer the user is not looking at.

**The outline and the pill quote one box.** `create_outline_box` wraps `create_box`, and both readers
go through it — the same argument D51 made for the outline against the transaction, one axis further
along. The Line tool answers `None` there, so it gets neither: its drag runs corner to corner, and both
a box round it and a `W × H` under it describe a shape it is not making, which is the same reasoning
that keeps the badge off a lone *selected* line.

**What is tested is the placement, and it closes a real gap rather than restating one.**
`the_size_pill_hangs_clear_of_the_bottom_handles_grab_radius` paints through the shared function and
asserts the pill's top is at least `HANDLE_PICK_PX` below the box — the **relationship** the gap exists
to satisfy, since a closer pill covers the bottom handle's grab area on a narrow shape and that handle
stops being reachable. The neighbouring `badge_frame` test pins the arithmetic against the design's
*hypothetical* 11px and therefore never touched the number the app passes. Flip-checked at a 2px gap,
which fails with "pill top is 2 below the box, which does not clear the 9px handle grab". Whether the
create drag *reaches* the painter is routing inside `OndinApp` and is read, not tested (D35).

**D293 — Space+click fell through to the tool, because the pan guard was written three times and
carried twice. *Fixed; the routing is read (D35), and the user reproduced both the fault and the fix.
**Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22** — "space + click does nothing now", a general
confirmation rather than a walk through each of the three arms.*** Found while building D291 — the new shape-tool click arm was given `!panning_armed` and the
two arms beside it were not — reported back rather than fixed on the spot, and then confirmed from the
app: "hard to hit, since panning is usually space+drag, but worth fixing."

**Space+drag pans, so a Space+click is that same gesture having not travelled.** It must do nothing.
Instead it reached the tool: with Text it planted a caret, and with Select it changed the selection —
or, on empty canvas, cleared it *and* dropped the group scope, which is the destructive one and the
one nobody had noticed. The drag arm below had the guard from the beginning, and so do `guide_input`,
the pen, the node tool and image editing, each spelling it out for itself.

**The fix is the binding, not the condition.** `let clicked = resp.clicked() && !panning_armed;`, read
by all three click arms. Adding a fourth `!panning_armed` would have fixed the reported case and left
the shape of the bug intact — one rule, one copy per arm, and nothing to notice when the next arm is
written without it. *This is the second time in three days that a per-arm repetition of a gesture rule
turned out to have a gap in it* (D289's `Alt`+`Shift` guard was the first, gating the whole gesture
where it belonged on one branch). **Treat a guard that appears once per arm as a guard that is already
wrong somewhere.**

**Only Space actually changes.** `panning_armed` is `space || tool == Hand || middle-button drag`, and
the other two cannot reach a click arm anyway: Hand has no click arm, and a middle-button drag is not
a primary click. Stated so a later reader does not go looking for behaviour that was never there.

⚠️ **Nothing here is testable and that is not a shrug.** All three arms live in
`normal_mode_input`, and `OndinApp` cannot be built headlessly (D35). What *is* pinned is the premise
underneath — `text_gesture` measures that egui reports a still press as `clicked()` and never as a
drag, which is why a click arm exists at all and why it needed its own guard rather than inheriting the
drag arm's.

**D294 — Arming a creation tool clears the selection. *Built; the tool set is tested, the clear
itself read (D35). **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22**.*** Asked for directly, off an observation left at the end of D292: `choose_tool`
did not clear, so arming the Rect tool with a layer picked left that layer's outline, handles and size
pill on the canvas underneath the box being dragged out. You are about to draw something; there is
nothing to be selected. Figma's behaviour.

**On `drags_a_box`, which is the existing name for exactly this set** — Frame, Rect, Ellipse, Polygon,
Star, Line, Text and Image, the tools whose whole verb is *create*. A second list would be one more
thing to keep in step, and there is no member of that set the reason fails to cover: Text is about to
draw a text box, Image about to place a picture, and neither reads the selection for anything (Text
works off a hit test, Image off `pending_images`).

**Four deliberate non-members, and two of them are sharp.** Select and Scale operate on the selection,
so clearing it is the one thing they must never do. Hand pans, and losing a selection to a pan is
D293's mistake one gesture over. **Node and ImageEdit are *entered from* a selected layer** — a
double-click switches to them with the layer picked, and `edited_path` reads that very selection to
know what it is editing, so a wrong answer here would empty the tool at the instant it opened. The
**Pen** looks like it belongs and does not: reached from inside a path edit it carries that edit on,
and the `pen_bias` arm returns before the clear could fire — but the exclusion is deliberate rather
than incidental, because a pen armed on empty canvas has no chrome problem to solve. It places anchors
one click at a time and never drags a box over anything.

⚠️ **It fires on the tool *switch*, so `place_image_action` clears too** — `Ctrl+Shift+K` and the
rail's image button arm `Tool::Image` from an action rather than from a tool pick. Right for the same
reason, and recorded because it is the one member of the set a reader will not have pictured.

**Checked before writing it, because "who calls this and how often" is never in the text of the
function.** A `choose_tool` called once per frame would clear the selection every frame and make
drawing impossible. Both entry points are edge-triggered — the rail's arm is inside `resp.clicked()`,
and the keymap's is `i.key_pressed(key)` — and the create flow is safe by ordering: `commit_create`
sets the new layer's selection and *then* switches to Select, which is not in the set, while an Image
placement with more files queued does not switch tools at all.

**The predicate now has two consumers with different failure modes, which changes what its test is
for.** `drags_a_box` used to answer only "does a drag draw a box"; a wrong *exclusion* was harmless.
Now a wrong exclusion silently deletes a selection, and `Tool::ImageEdit` turned out never to have
been asserted against the predicate at all. It is in the exclusion loop now.
*When a predicate gains a second consumer, its negative members stop being decoration — re-read the
list rather than the definition.*

**D295 — The Image tool's click did nothing, and a doc comment of mine said it did. *Fixed and
tested. **Reviewed and accepted on screen 2026-08-22** — "image placing works good, tested with
multiple images too", which exercises the queue arm as well as the single placement.*** Reported from
the app while trying `Ctrl+Shift+K`: "once I've selected a picture, I can
only click and drag it in the canvas. I can't do a single click and it automatically is placed at its
native resolution and ratio — which is what I usually go for."

**The gesture was written, correct, and unreachable.** `place_image_at` → `create_image` →
`fitted_image_size` is exactly the rule asked for: the picture's intrinsic size, aspect kept, shrunk
*only* if it exceeds the frame or viewport (D177). Its only caller was `finish_drag`'s short-drag arm,
which carries the comment "**the click gesture, and the primary one for this tool**" — and a still
press is reported by egui as `clicked()` and **never** as a drag (`text_gesture`, D170), so
`Drag::Create` never began and that arm was reachable only by dragging out past 6px and coming back.
The primary gesture of the tool, unreachable by its own name.

⚠️ **This is D291's own doc comment being wrong, and it is worth naming as mine.**
`clicks_out_a_default_box` justified excluding Text and Image like this: *"every member of that set now
answers a click with something — Text plants an auto-width node, Image places its picture at the fitted
size — but those two answers are their own and are handled before this one."* Text's was. Image's did
not exist. I asserted a routing table in prose, in the very comment whose job was to explain which
tools the table covered, and nothing anywhere could contradict it. **A prose claim about a routing
table is a claim nothing checks.**

**So the fix is the table, not the arm.** `Tool::click_makes() -> Option<ClickCreate>` is an exhaustive
`match` over `Tool` with **no wildcard**, and `canvas::normal_mode_input` has one creation-click arm
dispatching on it instead of three separate `if`s. Three answers rather than a boolean, because what a
click has to decide when it is given no box is where the *size* comes from: a constant
(`DefaultBox`), the file (`FittedImage`), or what gets typed (`TextNode`). A new `Tool` variant now
fails to compile here until somebody says which it is.

**Both halves are needed and neither is redundant.** The `match` makes a *missing* arm a build error;
`every_tool_answers_a_click_with_exactly_what_it_should` makes a *wrong* arm a test failure, listing
all fourteen tools rather than spot-checking, since the list is precisely what prose got wrong. It also
asserts the containment — anything answering a click drags a box too, or it would be a creation tool
with only one way to be given a size. Flip-checked against the bug exactly as shipped (`Tool::Image =>
None`), which fails with `left: None, right: Some(FittedImage)`.

**`Sense`-style naming trap, one level up.** `clicks_out_a_default_box` was an honest name for what it
returned and a misleading one for what it was *used* for — the click routing — and the gap between
those two is where the missing arm hid. The replacement is named for the question the routing asks.

**D296 — `cargo doc` is a gate now, and it is the only one that reads the doc comments. *Built; 52
warnings cleared and the gate flip-checked.*** Asked for after D295, where a doc comment of mine
asserted a routing arm that did not exist: nothing in the workspace could have contradicted it, and
`cargo doc` — which nothing ran — was already reporting fifteen of its siblings.

**The gate lives in the source, not in an environment variable.** Each crate root carries
`#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links, rustdoc::invalid_html_tags)]`, so plain
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` exits **101** rather than printing warnings nobody reads, and it
does so from any shell — `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings"` would have been a gate that only worked in the
one place somebody remembered to type it. Flip-checked with a deliberately dead link: `error:
unresolved link`, exit 101.

**`private_intra_doc_links` is allowed on purpose, and that is a decision rather than a shortcut.** It
accounted for 25 of the 52 and fires on links that are *entirely correct* — they name a real item that
merely cannot be rendered as a hyperlink in **published** docs. These are not published docs; they are
read in the source, where "go and look at `from_flo`" is worth saying about a private item. It cannot
hide staleness either, which is the only thing that would make the allow dishonest: a name that does
not exist at all is a `broken` link, never a `private` one.

**What the 52 were.** Twenty unresolved names, twenty-five private-item links, four ambiguous
(`[plan]` meaning the module beside a function of the same name; `[png]` likewise beside the crate),
and three unclosed HTML tags — which were not prose at all but `ondin export <file>` in the binary's
usage block, where rustdoc reads `<file>` as a tag and `[gui]` as a link. That block is fenced now.

**Two of the twenty were stale docs rather than stale paths, which is the whole point of the gate:**

- **`ui::SWITCH_SIZE` and `switch_row` both described "a [`switch`]"**, and there is no `switch`. The
  function is `paint_switch` and has been for long enough that nothing remembered.
- **`panels::export::export_menu_popup` asserted a contrast that had stopped existing.** It read "a
  popover rather than rows in the card, which is the opposite of the call `Self::export_settings_block`
  makes", and *both halves* were wrong: there is no `export_settings_block`, and the inline block it
  meant became a popover itself — a change recorded in that function's own doc ("a popover, and it
  replaced an inline block") and never propagated to the paragraph pointing at it. Two doc comments
  about the same pair of functions, disagreeing, with every other gate green. Rewritten to say what is
  actually true: both are popovers and the difference is what each holds.

*A rename updates the code the compiler can see and leaves every sentence about it standing.* That is
the class this gate exists for, and it is the same class as the `pub`-item-with-no-callers trap in
CLAUDE.md's clippy note — the tooling is silent precisely where the prose is load-bearing. **And it is
silent across one whole region of that prose**: this gate cannot see inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module,
because `cargo doc` builds without the `test` cfg, nor into any file under `crates/…/tests/`, because
there is no `--tests` flag to point it at a test target — both measured under **D319**, which is where
the practice that has to stand in for them lives. "The only gate that reads the doc comments" is still true and is
narrower than it sounds.

**D297 — Two of Text's three sizing modes had no numeric door, and the door the third had wrote the
wrong mode. *Built; the rule is tested both ways and the box width flip-checked, the row itself read.***
The roadmap carried this as D242's list rotting again one kind over, and the premise held this time:
`inspector_single`'s `size0` answered `Some` for `TextSizing::Fixed` and `None` for `Auto` and
`AutoHeight` alike, while `tools::resizable_size` handed the handles `Size::ZERO` and `(w, 0)`. So the
canvas would widen an auto-height label and convert an auto one, and no field in the panel could do
either — *something a handle can do that no field can*, which is the sentence D242 exists to make
false.

**`AutoHeight` is the worse half and it is the reason this was not cosmetic.** Its width is not derived
from anything: it is the number the user dragged, authored state exactly as much as a `Fixed` box's
width is, and the panel showed no field for it at all. `Auto`'s two numbers are emergent — but so are a
`Path`'s, a `Boolean`'s and a `Group`'s, and D98 and D242 already settled that *a derived box is still a
box* when the handles resize it.

**The row reads `local_box`, not the field.** One arm — `NodeKind::Text { .. } =>
preview_local_box(id).map(|b| b.size())` — covering all three modes, because that is the box the handles
are drawn on and a panel disagreeing with the handles about how wide something is was the whole
complaint. `text::box_of` answers the shaped extent for `Auto`, the **authored** width with the shaped
height for `AutoHeight`, and for `Fixed` the very `size` the old arm returned, so nothing changed for the
mode that already worked. Unlike an empty `Group`, there is no case where it vanishes: `local_bounds`
falls back to `text::measure` when no layout is cached.

⚠️ **The second half was the bug, and it was invisible while the first half hid it.** `size_tx` wrote
`GeometryPatch::TextSizing(TextSizing::Fixed(…))` for any text node, unconditionally. That was harmless
only for as long as the row refused to appear for anything but `Fixed` — the moment it names an auto box,
an unconditional `Fixed` turns *typing a width* into a mode change nobody asked for, and would have
undone D148's whole point one control over. **Extending the display arm without this would have shipped a
worse bug than the gap it closed.**

**So the rule is spelled once, in `tools::resized_text_sizing`, and both callers go through it.** It
takes the new size and one boolean — `authors_height` — and is the panel's spelling of
`Handle::anchored`'s `holds_y`: an auto mode survives a width and becomes `Fixed` on a height, and an
already-`Fixed` box stays fixed either way, because the question is *height authorship* rather than which
number moved. `resize_to_handle` now calls it with `holds_y.is_some()` where it used to inline the
condition. The mapping the panel makes is the finding worth stating: **W is the side handle, H is the
bottom one, and the proportion lock turns W into a corner** — with the lock on, W drives H as well, and a
corner is precisely the handle that fixes a text box. That fell out of the existing pairing code rather
than needing a case.

**What is tested.** The drag half already had four cases (`dragging_a_side_of_auto_text_gives_auto_height`
and its siblings) and they now exercise the extracted function, so the refactor is covered by tests
written before it. What was **not** covered anywhere is the fact the new `W` field's honesty rests on:
that an auto-height box reports the width the user authored rather than the width of the ink.
`an_auto_height_box_is_as_wide_as_it_was_authored` asserts it at 400, where the box is wider than the
text, *and* at 30, where it is narrower than a single word — one sample cannot tell an authored width
from a shaped one — with the `Auto` mode beside it as a control, so the test is about the mode rather
than about `measure` handing its own input back. Flipped by making `box_of`'s `AutoHeight` arm answer
`content_width`, which is what the arm one line above it does and therefore the wrong version somebody
would actually write: `auto-height authored at 400 measured 153.18`.

**Not tested, and said plainly: that the row appears, and that W maps to `authors_height: false`.** Both
live in an `OndinApp` method and `OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState` — the same seam D242 and D229
record. What is pinned is the verb the field writes through.

**D175 — A document opened before the catalog landed never fetched its own fonts. *Resolved.*** Found by
asking whether the missing-font warning §5.4a promises would tell the truth if it were built: it would
not, and the reason is a bug rather than a wording.

`ensure_document_fonts` walks the tree once, at `open`. `ensure_loaded` queues nothing for a family it
cannot resolve, and `faces_of` resolves against two things that arrive on background threads — the system
scan and the web catalog. On a cold start with no disk-cached catalog neither has landed. Nothing asked
again, so the document's text sat in the Inter fallback for the rest of the session, with the family name
showing correctly in the panel the whole time.

The retry is the one the previews already had, keyed on `families_changed` — which fires exactly when the
system scan or the catalog merges, the two events that can turn an unresolvable family into a resolvable
one. `ensure` skips a face already claimed, so re-walking is idempotent.

**Read, not tested** (D35); what is testable — that `ensure_loaded` is a no-op for an unresolvable family
— is already true and is not the part that was wrong.

**D160 — The picker's two unbounded costs: a frame's worth of rasterizing, and a cache counting the wrong
unit. *Resolved.*** Both are the same mistake twice — a bound on something that is not what actually
grows.

**The preview raster is on the UI thread, and it stays there.** The *bytes* are off it, but
`FontPreviews::paint` rasterized on a cache miss synchronously in the frame, so a flung scrollbar could do
a screenful of those in one frame. Moving it is not available: `text::family_preview` goes through core's
thread-local shaping engine, so a worker would build its own font collection instead of sharing the
registered one. What is bounded instead is **how much of a frame the misses may take**, and a deferred row
draws its name in the UI font — the fallback `paint` already had.

**A time budget rather than a count of strips, and the measurement is the reason.** One warm strip costs
0.022 ms in release and 0.80 ms in debug at 100% scale — 0.031 against 1.25 at 200%. A **40× spread**: a
count tuned to the debug cost would leave the release build doing a fortieth of the work it could afford.
`FRAME_BUDGET` is 2 ms. Two things are stated in the code rather than left to be rediscovered: the first
strip of a frame draws **whatever the budget says**, or a slow enough machine never shows a preview at
all; and a deferral calls `request_repaint`, this eframe being reactive. *The measurement is a floor, not
the cost*: it re-rasterized one family, so parley's family lookup was warm.

**`PREVIEW_CAP` bounded a count of families, and its own comment gave the reason that is wrong**: a face
is tens of KB for a Latin subset and megabytes for a CJK one. It is now `PREVIEW_BYTES`, 48 MB, chosen so
the Latin case is untouched — 240 families at ~150 KB is about 36 MB — while a CJK browse settles around
twenty families instead of 240. `FamilyState::bytes` is summed as each face arrives, the only moment the
size is known.

**`PREVIEW_FLOOR` is a floor, not a second cap, and it is small on purpose.** A byte budget alone evicts
families that are still *on screen* as soon as a few heavy ones fill it, and the picker then re-fetches
them next frame. 24 is just above the twenty rows the list shows. At 48 it would have been the binding
constraint for exactly the case the byte budget exists for — a generous floor is a weaker cap in disguise.

`families_over_budget` is split out of `trim_previews` for the reason `tools::resized_box` is split out of
`resize_to_handle`. Three tests pin it, and
`a_strip_past_the_frames_budget_is_deferred_and_the_budget_resets_next_frame` asserts the distinction that
matters: a deferred family leaves **no** cache entry, where an un-previewable one is remembered as `None`.
Its own first version proved nothing — it called `run_ui` once per row, and the budget is per *pass*, so
it reset between them.

**D161 — `cargo build --release` did not compile, and no gate said so. *Resolved.*** `theme::install` set
`style.debug.warn_if_rect_changes_id = false` (D65), and egui puts `DebugOptions` behind
`#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` — so in a release build the field does not exist and the line is not a no-op,
it is a type error.

**Worth more than the one-line fix is why nothing caught it.** `cargo check`, `cargo test` and `cargo
clippy` all run the debug cfg, so the workspace's whole gate is blind to a release-only error; the release
build was run for the first time to measure D160's per-strip cost. **A gate now covers it**: `cargo check
--release -p ondin-app` was added on 2026-08-18 to `CLAUDE.md`'s build block and to the `rust-verify`
agent's gate list.

**D157 — The OpenType list was the raw `GSUB`/`GPOS` table; it is now three tiers of authority.
*Resolved.*** Behind the raw list were two live gaps of our own: `feature_name` hardcoded `ss01`–`ss10`,
so `ss11`–`ss20` and every one of bundled Inter's **fourteen** `cvXX` fell through to a raw tag; and
`feature_rank`'s `t.starts_with("ss")` arm caught `ssty` — math script-style alternates, a mechanic.

**Three problems wearing one coat, and each has a different authority.**

1. **`ss01`–`ss20` and `cv01`–`cv99` are the registry's two font-defined ranges, and the font names them
   itself.** `text::family_features` returns `FaceFeature { tag, name, tooltip, values }`, read through
   `FeatureRecord::feature` → `feature_params` → `StylisticSetParams::ui_name_id` or
   `CharacterVariantParams`. The generic "Stylistic set 7" stays as a **fallback**: plenty of faces
   document their `cvXX` on a web page and leave the table NULL in the binary.
2. **Every other registered tag means what the registry says it means**, so a static table is
   *completable* rather than a guess. `REGISTRY` carries all **124** individually registered tags of
   OpenType 1.9.1.
3. **Anything else is a private tag**: the four letters, no invented prose, and withheld.

**The curation is the registry's, not ours**: a tag is withheld when its own *UI suggestion* says control
"should not generally be exposed to the user". Four departures, each because a switch would be a lie
rather than a mechanic: the **vertical-writing** features, in an app with no vertical writing mode;
**`aalt`**, whose suggestion describes a glyph palette; **`ital`**, which the panel's italic control
already applies; and **`size`**, which carries a tracking curve rather than a state. *Show all features*
reveals the withheld rows, so nothing is unreachable.

**Dropping `GPOS` wholesale was considered and declined.** It is where the mechanics are — but it also
holds `kern` and the CJK width features a user genuinely chooses, and the tag's own registry entry already
answers the question. Two answers to one question is how they come to disagree.

**Two traps, both of which would have shipped silently.** read-fonts picks which `FeatureParams` table to
parse from the **first two bytes of the tag**, so `ssty` is read as a stylistic set and hands back
whatever sits at that offset; the gate is `typography::stylistic_set`, which asks for a *number*. And a
**NULL `name` id is `0`, which is the copyright notice**. `feature_string` bounds ids to the spec's
256..=32767; confirmed by removing the bound, which puts "Copyright 2016 The Inter Project Authors" on the
hover of all fourteen `cvXX` rows.

`inter_labels_its_own_stylistic_sets_and_character_variants` pins the whole read — the strings arrive,
**no other tag carries one**, and every tooltip stays `None`.
`the_feature_registry_is_the_whole_registry_and_says_each_tag_once` pins completeness, load-bearing rather
than tidy: a missing row is reported as a private tag, so an omission is a wrong answer and not a gap.

**The last piece — `numNamedParameters > 1` means a 1..n choice rather than a switch — is now built
(2026-08-16), and what unblocked it was finding a face.** A probe over 315 local files found **zero**
`cvXX` naming a single value. Monaspace is the failure mode tier 1 predicts: it documents named `cv` values
on its website and declares **no** params table. Three SIL faces on Google Fonts do declare them, and **the
only way to see one is to install the full face and restart** — this entry first said they arrive through
the app's own web-font cache; that was tried and is false, because what the cache holds is a Latin subset
with every `cvXX` gone (D192). Across those three faces, 106 `cvXX` features name a value at all, **97 of
them exactly one** against 9 naming more, so the switch stays the overwhelmingly common row.

**A count could not survive the read, so `FaceFeature::values` is the names themselves** —
`Vec<Option<String>>`, index `k` being value `k + 1`, so a count and a list cannot disagree.
`named_values` reads the **consecutive** `ParamUILabelNameID` range and leans on `feature_string`'s
existing bound for both hazards rather than adding a second rule.

**The control is a dropdown under the name, and arithmetic chose it rather than taste.** The list is
**240** wide, and the widest real pairing wants **240.1** on one line with the label in its own column.
Three faces is the whole evidence base and the next face's names are bounded by nothing, so one line was
rejected on a tenth of a pixel. A dropdown rather than a segmented track by the wrap controls' own
criterion: a track is for a handful of one- or two-word options. **"Off" is an item in the list rather
than a switch beside it**, because `FeatureSetting::value` is one number for both questions and two
controls writing one field have eventually disagreed everywhere else in this app; a value past the end
shows as "Value 7" rather than being clamped, so a document written against another face is not silently
misreported. `features_section`'s `toggled: Option<Tag>` became `written: Option<(Tag, u16)>` covering
both kinds of row — two `Option`s would be two `apply_char_attrs` calls off one `set` clone, dropping the
first.

**Its two halves have to sit closer to each other than to their neighbours, and the first version did
not.** The row took `LABEL_GAP`'s 5 as its own `item_spacing.y`, which *reads* as 5 inside against the
list's **1** between rows — but that 5 was spent under the dropdown as well as above it, so what reached
the screen was 5 against 6. Reported from use: "hard to understand where the row ends."

**A spacing cannot express that rule, which is why both gaps are allocated by hand.** A widget banks its
trailing spacing at the moment it is *placed* (D195), so the combo is followed by whatever spacing was in
effect for it and zeroing it afterwards is too late. Sweeping the row's spacing through 2, 5 and 10 moved
the gap *below* the dropdown to **13, 16 and 21** — the two ends move together, so no value of it is
tighter inside than outside. `feature_choice_row` therefore sets `item_spacing.y = 0.0` for its whole
scope and allocates both gaps explicitly: `CHOICE_LABEL_GAP` (2) and `CHOICE_ROW_TAIL` (6). Measured off
the painted ink, the version reported as bad is **9 inside against 10 below**, and the shipped one is **6
against 11**.

**That one point between 9 and 10 is why `a_choice_row_groups_its_label_with_its_control` asserts `below
>= inside * 1.5`** rather than the obvious "outside is bigger than inside": the obvious version was
written first and *passed against the spacing that had been reported as unreadable*. It sets the list's
1px `item_spacing` itself, because the row is only ever drawn inside that list. What it does **not** catch
is the double payment itself: the banked-spacing version measures 6 against 13 and passes the ratio
comfortably (D195).

**Two things are not pinned, and both matter.** Core's `ParamUILabelNameID` read has no permanent test
against a real font — the specimens are not vendored, and a face installed on one machine is not a
fixture. And the layout is **seen but not accepted**: the full Andika was installed on 2026-08-16 and the
row drew, which took an installed face and a restart exactly as predicted. What came back was the one
defect, the spacing, fixed above. *The rest has been on screen once and drawn no comment either way, which
is not the same as reviewed. Ask when a multi-value `cvXX` face is next on the machine.*

**D158 — An auto-sized label's left edge widened it rightward from the origin. *Resolved.*** An `Auto`
text node's handles are drawn on its **measured** box, while `resizable_size` reports `Size::ZERO` —
honestly, since an auto node has no size field. So the edge a resize gesture holds still was the local
origin, which is where the *left* handle is.

`tools::anchored_size` is the fix and the split it makes is worth the second function: `resizable_size`
answers "is there a size field to replace" and every other caller wants exactly that, where a *gesture*
also needs the box the handles were drawn on. It is keyed on the sizing mode rather than on which extents
happen to be zero, so it states the same rule `TextSizing` does.

`dragging_an_auto_labels_left_edge_holds_its_right_edge` asserts the **held** edge, the only reading that
separates the two behaviours: both produce the same new origin. It also caught that
`dragging_a_side_of_auto_text_gives_auto_height` was *encoding* the bug — it expected 80 for a left drag
as well as a right one, which is only true when the anchor is wrongly at the origin.

**Trim was left open here and is closed in D162** — where the diagnosis in this paragraph turned out to be
half wrong, worth keeping rather than quietly correcting. It said the mismatch applied "for a `Fixed` box
as much as an auto one". It does not: only an **auto** box is offset, because that one *is* the visible
extent and carries the top inset as its origin.

**D159 — A run with an underline and nothing else can now export its offset. *Resolved.*** It stays a real
limit for the run carrying an underline *and* a strikethrough: `text-underline-offset` is underline-only
and one element cannot say two offsets. What D81's `<tspan>` per run changed is that the *other* case is
now unambiguous — and since the panel's decoration control is exclusive, it is also the ordinary one.

**The sign flips, and that is the whole of the care this needs.** Ours is parley's: `Decoration::offset`
is measured from the baseline with positive **up**. CSS measures with positive **under** —
css-text-decor-4, the zero position being the alphabetic baseline. So the exported number is the negation
of the stored one, and getting it backwards puts the line the same distance on the wrong side of the
baseline with nothing to error on. It sits outside the shorthand-ordering argument the other three
properties share, because the spec puts it outside: `text-underline-offset` is explicitly *not* a
sub-property of `text-decoration`.

`an_underlines_offset_is_exported_negated_unless_a_strikethrough_shares_the_run` covers all four readings.
Confirmed against both mistakes: dropping the strikethrough guard and dropping the negation each fail it.

**D155 — Four things found by running it, one of them D154's own regression. *Resolved.***

**Styling a selection deselected it**, and the consequence is what made it worth reporting: you do not
notice, so the *next* property lands on the whole node. `TextEdit::reshape` rebuilds the selection with
`Selection::from_byte_index`, which is a **collapsed caret** — right after an edit, where the selected
text is gone, and wrong after a *restyle*, where every byte is still there.
`reshape_keeping_selection` rebuilds both ends, and both restyle callers take it.
`styling_a_selection_keeps_it_selected` fails on the old helper with `11..11` against `0..11`.

**The Text tool could not enter an existing text layer** — it planted a new node wherever it was clicked,
which made it write-only in the one place you most want it. It routes through `text_layer_at` (which is
`pick_leaf` filtered to text, so locking, hidden layers and z-order need no second set of rules).
`draw_hover_outline` follows it: the tool outlines what it can *enter* and nothing else, since over a
rectangle the click still plants a node.

**The cursor stayed an arrow while text was being edited.** Entering a node by double-clicking with Select
leaves the tool on Select — the one posture where the arrow is plainly wrong. A live session now owns the
cursor over its own layer whatever tool opened it (`over_edited_text`, against the node's *local* box so a
rotated layer answers about its own rectangle). `dragged()` holds it through a selection that overshoots.

**And the colour picker stopped committing on a plain click, which D154 broke.** D154's `Preview` verb put
the colour in the render override on the press frame — and `TypeSubject::of` reads through `display_node`,
so on the release frame `apply_char_attrs` compared the new colour against *its own preview*. That is
D109's shape **arriving by a new route**. Reported as "I have to click and drag for it to register a
colour" — so the stated cause named the half that was already fixed.

**The first fix for it was worse than the bug, and that is the part worth keeping.** Clearing the preview
before building the subject looks like the obvious way to read committed truth, and it made the wheel and
the opacity strip *completely* dead: `Session::clear_preview` also drops `preview_holds_session`, and a
preview may belong to a **live text session** — so every press threw the uncommitted text off the canvas.
`Session::committed_node` and `TypeSubject::committed` are the narrow answer.

*The rule, since two bugs in a row came from it: **a preview is not one thing.** A gesture's preview is
stale the moment anything commits; a session's stands for content that has not been committed yet. Code
that wants to ignore a preview must read past it, never clear it.*

**Then the picker did nothing at all over a text *selection*.** Two gates conspired, neither introduced
here: `CharWrite::Preview` **declined** a partial subject, so the press showed nothing; and the fallback,
`char_valve`'s partial branch, gates on `resp.changed()` — which a `DragValue` reports and a **raw sensed
region never does**. The picker's wheel and opacity strip are `Sense::click_and_drag()` regions, so press,
drag *and* release all fell through.

**For a live selection the three verbs are one write**, and saying so is the fix: nothing a session styles
reaches history until the session ends (§9.3), so there is no undo step for a repeat to leave behind.
`char_valve` is deliberately untouched — its `changed()` gate is right for the popup's own fields.

*The general shape: **a gate written for widgets does not hold for raw sensed regions.** `changed()`,
`lost_focus()` and friends are `Widget` conveniences; any valve reached from a raw region has to gate on
the pointer instead.*

**And collapsing the verbs dropped the gate, which looked identical from outside.** Widening the test was
right; writing *unconditionally* was not. Several of the picker's controls call `valve_slot` **every
frame**, so each stamped its own frame-start value into the editor every frame, overwriting whatever the
control actually under the pointer had just written. Still "frozen", for a third distinct reason.

Settled by instrumenting rather than by a fourth guess — a trace showed **two `Valve` calls per frame plus
eleven with no `pointer_slot` at all**, which named the unconditional callers immediately.

*Worth keeping about the method as much as the bug: three fixes in a row were wrong because each was
reasoned from the code alone, and the frame-by-frame call pattern is not in the code. **A valve reached
from more than one control cannot be verified by reading it** — the question is who calls it and how
often, which only a trace answers.*

**D156 — The picker's handle jumped sideways near black, and the picker now remembers the HSV it wrote.
*Resolved.*** The handle's position is re-derived from the **stored colour** every frame, so it is only as
stable as HSV↔RGB is invertible, and near black it is not. Over the 218×104 plane, at `v = 0.02` the
*entire* saturation range maps to **nine** distinct 8-bit colours; recovering `s` from one of them moved
the handle up to **36pt** sideways while the pointer moved smoothly. In f32 the same round trip is exact,
and the *value* axis is fine throughout. So it is saturation, and it is the quantization.

Which is why the picker already carried the **hue**: a grey has no hue in its RGB, so dragging value to
zero and back came out red — the same problem seen once, in the one place it is total rather than merely
coarse. `Picker::intent` now carries the whole `Hsv` **and the 8-bit colour it produced**, and `hsv_for`
returns it while the slot still holds that colour. Keyed rather than threshold-gated, so an edit from
anywhere else changes the key and falls straight back to deriving.

The text colour feels it worse than a fill does, and that is D154's doing: `canonical_color` quantizes
`CharAttr::Color` to 8 bits on every write. The canonicalization stays — it is what lets spans coalesce at
all — and this fixes the control instead, which is where the fault was: the *stored* colour was always
right.

*The general shape: **a control that derives its position from the value it wrote needs the value, not the
position.** Any lossy round trip through the document turns a smooth gesture into a jumping one, and the
loss is worst exactly where the gamut is thinnest.*

*The three canvas fixes rest on reading rather than tests (D35). Only the selection collapse, which lives
in core, is pinned.*

**D154 — Per-run colour, end to end. *Built.***
Planned in a `per-run-color.md` that has since been deleted, all six of its steps built — so this entry is
the whole record. Its three recommendations were all taken, and the reasoning for each is kept here
because each rules out a *bigger* design that would otherwise look like the obvious next step.

**Solid only, not a `Brush` per run.** A gradient has to answer what its geometry is relative to — the
run's box, the line, or the node — and every answer is wrong for some case; the run's box also reflows as
you type, so a gradient anchored to it would move while you typed into it.

**The node keeps `Paint.fills` as the default**, and `TextStyle::color` is `Option<Color>` where `None`
