means that stack. So there is **no migration**: every existing document deserializes to `None` and draws
exactly as it did. Moving paint wholesale into the attribute model was the alternative and would have
broken the Paint panel's shared path, Group Colors, `colors_in`, and the save format for every text node.

**One colour per run, not a list.** A run with a colour draws once in it; a run without one draws the
node's whole stack. The asymmetry is deliberate — a node can carry two stacked translucent fills and a
run cannot — because a per-run `Vec<Fill>` needs a coalescing story for visibility flags, which is where
this stops being tractable. It is the same trade `Decoration::color` already makes.

Three things fell out that the plan did not have to guess at:

- **`CharAttrKind::Color` is appended**, because that order *is* the `(attribute, start)` sort a file is
  written in (§5.11, invariant 9): inserted anywhere else it reorders the spans of every document already
  on disk. `colour_sorts_after_every_other_attribute` states it as a test, because the failure is a diff
  nobody would look for.
  🚨 **Both sentences of that bullet were amended by D598 and the second was simply wrong.** The test
  it names no longer exists — it compared `Color > kind` against a hand-written list of the other
  fourteen, and every one of those comparisons survives *any* permutation of the fourteen, so the
  guard this entry named as its enforcement enforced nothing (`[S6.1-L6-02]`, measured: `Family` and
  `Size` exchanged left 1,479 tests green). It is `CharAttrKind::ALL` and
  `char_attribute_kinds_keep_the_order_a_saved_file_is_written_in` now. And the *reason* above is a
  proxy: a kind that **arrives** reorders nothing — the fourteen keep their relative order whatever
  index a newcomer takes, and `CharAttr` serializes under its variant *name* rather than its position
  — so what churns is a kind that **moves**, and then only the documents holding spans of **both** of
  the kinds it moved past. Appending is still the rule because it is
  the one edit that cannot move an existing variant. See **D598**.
- **Colour is canonicalized to 8 bits per channel, alpha included** (`canonical_color`) —
  `Length::canonical`'s lesson in another type, since `Color` is `[f32; 4]` and float equality would
  fragment the span list forever. This also **fixed a pre-existing bug**: `canonical_decoration`
  canonicalized its two `Length`s from the start and left its *colour* raw, so a decoration recoloured by
  a drag already fragmented. `a_typed_colour_and_a_picked_one_coalesce` and
  `a_decorations_colour_is_canonicalized_too` cover both.
- **The walk inverted to `for run { for ink }`**, which is the entirety of the render change: `TextRun`
  was already per-run and both backends already honoured its brush, so what was node-level was the loop.
  It changes paint order *across* runs — before, every run in fill 1 then every run in fill 2; after, run
  1 in fills 1..n then run 2 — which is identical wherever glyphs do not overlap, and visible only where
  glyphs from adjacent runs overlap *and* the fills are translucent. Stated rather than fixed.

**A decoration under a coloured run takes that run's colour**, resolved in `decoration_ink` where all
three levels are in scope: its own colour if set, else the run's, else the node's stack. "Absence means
the text's own colour" has always been the promise, and it stopped being true the moment a *run* could
have one.

SVG carries it: a coloured run's `<tspan>` gets a `fill` (and `fill-opacity` through the same
`alpha_attr` every other paint uses), and an uncoloured one gets no attribute at all, so absence inherits
the `<text>` element's — the same meaning the model gives it.

**The MCP snapshot does not carry it, and that is a note rather than work.** `snapshot.rs` emits
node-level paint, so a run colour is invisible to it until it emits spans; MCP is parked (§8), and this is
the second thing waiting on that (the missing-font warning §5.4a promises is the other).

**The surface is one row, not two, and the hoist is what made that true.** A `PaintSlot::TextColor`
joins `TextDecoration` as the second **character-scoped** slot — the ones whose write is a character
attribute rather than a transaction — and `PaintSlot::char_scoped` is now the single predicate all three
verbs branch on, routing to one `OndinApp::write_char_slot`. With one such slot that had been a diverting
`if` in `write_slot`, another in `valve_slot`, and a bare `return false` in `preview_slot`: three places
to keep in step, and the third was simply wrong.

So **D129's press-preview gap closed as a side effect**, exactly as the plan predicted it would. A
colour picked on the picker's plane used to do nothing until the pointer moved, because the press frame
previewed nothing and the valve has no frame of its own before a drag starts. `CharWrite` names the three
verbs (`Commit`, `Valve(&Response)`, `Preview`) and the third sets a render override without committing.
It still declines for a **live selection**, whose route is the editor's own spans rather than an override
(§9.3) — writing those is an edit, not a preview — and the caller falls back to the valve there as it
always did. Deliberately *not* routed through `char_valve`: that clears its own preview by committing on
release, and a press-and-release that never becomes a drag has no such frame, so reusing it would have
left a stale preview on every one of the popup's other valved controls. That is why the gap was recorded
rather than papered over.

The row itself is shared: `char_color_row(ui, subject, slot)` drives both, because a decoration's colour
row and the text's colour row are the same four controls over the same `Option<Color>`. What differs is
one sentence — a decoration inherits *the text's* ink, the text inherits *the layer's fill*, and
"inherited from the text" on the text's own row would be circular — so `CharSlot::swatch_tooltip` and
`reset_tip` carry the wording and nothing else forks. `char_color_attr` is the one builder every write
goes through, so the row, the picker and the three verbs cannot disagree about what setting a colour
means, and `None` is the inherited state rather than a missing value. The hex buffer had to become
`char_hex: Option<(CharSlot, String)>`: two of these rows are on screen at once, and one shared buffer put
the digits being typed into one row into the other.

The section is **first in the Character tab**, above Case and Decoration, which both describe ink that
inherits from it.

*`OndinApp` holds a wgpu `RenderState` and is not constructible headlessly, so the three verbs' routing
is not unit-testable and this rests on reading. What is pinned instead are the free functions the hoist
depends on: `every_character_scoped_slot_round_trips_and_no_other_claims_to_be_one` — the guard the
three-branch shape could not have had — and `the_colour_builder_covers_both_slots_and_the_inherited_state`.*

**D153 — An inheriting run claimed to be style run 0, so a span on the first character leaked onto the
whole node. *Resolved.*** Found while building D81's export seam, and it reached the **canvas**, not just
the export.

`shape` pushes the node's defaults with a run index and then each style run with its own, and the brush
parley carries is that index. But it also **skips** pushing any style run whose style equals the defaults,
so those bytes keep the defaults' brush. With the defaults on `0`, an inheriting run was
indistinguishable from *style run 0*.

That is harmless exactly when style run 0 *is* the defaults — which it is whenever the user styled
anything but the first character, so the wrong answer was accidentally the right one. Style the **first**
character and every inheriting run took that span's baseline shift and decoration. In the case that
caught it, parley never split at all — a baseline shift is ours rather than a parley property, so with the
brush collapsing too there was nothing left to split on, and a shift on "a" lifted the whole of "abc".

The fix is a sentinel: `DEFAULT_RUN = RunIndex::MAX`, so out of range means "the defaults", and brush `0`
unambiguously means style run 0. Resolving by *location* instead was the other candidate and cannot work
— a `GlyphRun` has no byte range of its own to locate.

`a_baseline_shift_on_the_first_run_does_not_move_the_rest` is the assertion, and the shape of the bug is
worth keeping: **a sentinel-free "index or default" encoding is ambiguous at index zero**, and the
ambiguity hides wherever index zero happens to be the default.

**D82 — The typography popup dismissed itself on the click that opened it. *Resolved.*** A click-away
dismissal has to forgive two things, and the popup forgave only one. The click that *opens* a popup
happens on the frame **before** the popup exists, so from the popup's own first frame it is by definition
a click outside itself. `stroke_menu_popup` had this right from the start — it takes the opening button's
`Response` as `head` — and the typography popup was written without that term because it anchored itself
off the *panel's* rect and so never had the button to hand.

Three changes, none of them the missing `&&` on its own:

- `type_alignment_row` now **returns the button's rect**, carried out of `panel`'s closure as a plain
  local (the closure is handed `&mut Self` and nothing else).
- The rect is the popup's **anchor** as well as its exemption, so the popover is placed from the control
  that opened it. One value, two uses, no second thing to keep in step.
- `head` is **not** optional at the popup: a collapsed Type panel draws no button, and `type_menu_popup`
  closes itself rather than floating on. A popover with no opener is a panel quietly editing something the
  card no longer shows.

**The decision is a named function with a table behind it**, `dismissed_by_click(ClickAway { .. })`,
because the interesting cases are the exemptions and they are what a dismiss test forgets to write.
`the_click_that_opens_the_popup_does_not_dismiss_it` was checked to fail with the term removed.
`the_alignment_row_hands_back_the_rect_the_popup_anchors_to` covers what the table cannot — that a rect
reaches the popup at all, since `on_head` computed from nothing would pass every case above.

*Any new click-away popover owes both exemptions: the overlay check for its own combo lists (D74) and the
opener's rect for the click that summoned it. The two misses look identical on screen — a popup that will
not stay open — and have nothing in common underneath. A third was added in D188: a release outside is
only a click away if the **press** was outside too, which the terms here cannot see because they all read
where the pointer is now. A fourth in D214, where **both** exemptions miss at once: a context menu has no
head to be forgiven and `any_click()` counts the secondary button, so the release that opens one is the
click that dismisses it, and the answer there is a flag on the menu rather than a fifth term.*

**D222 — A thin line was almost impossible to click. *Resolved.*** *(Written as D103, which was already
taken by the `ParagraphStyle::each_line` entry; renumbered here on 2026-08-19, the same way D124 became
D126. The paragraph entry kept 103 because `typography.rs` cites it and nothing in `crates/` cited this
one.)* A 2pt hairline is a one-point band each side of the segment, which at 100% is about two pixels of
target.

`query::hit_test` and `geometry::contains_local` take a `slop` in **world** units. It is the caller's
number because only the caller knows the zoom: `canvas::pick_slop` is `PICK_SLOP_PX / camera.zoom`.
`PICK_SLOP_PX` is 4, against a corner handle's 9 — a handle is chrome the user aims at deliberately, while
a line sits *among* other artwork. **Only an open shape spent it**: the `Line` arm was `stroke_expansion
+ slop`, added rather than maxed so a heavy stroke stays grabbable across its whole width *and* keeps the
comfort margin. **D115 reversed that half** on a second report and gave the `Line` arm's formula to every
kind. Tests pass `0.0` when they mean exactly.

**The second change is the interesting one: the allowance had to widen the R-tree candidate query as
well.** A horizontal line's cached world bounds are a zero-height rectangle, so a point even slightly off
it did not intersect them and the line never reached the exact filter — the first version of the test
failed on precisely that. `hit_test` queries a `slop`-inflated rect about the point now. Widening a
candidate query only ever *adds* candidates, each of which still has to pass its own geometry, so
exactness is untouched. *Any future tolerance owes the same second look: a hit test does not start at the
exact test.*

`a_picking_allowance_widens_every_kind_by_a_bounded_band` covers both halves and both negatives — past the
endpoint is a miss, because the distance is to the *segment*, and 9 units off the side is a miss because
the band is bounded.

Two limits were read off the code here rather than chosen, and one is gone. The number is a world distance
*used* in the node's local space, so a line under a scaled or leaning ancestor gets a band scaled with it;
the camera zoom is not in that matrix and a rotation preserves distances, so the ordinary case is exact.
The second was that an **unfilled `Path` still got nothing** — deferred here to editable paths, and fixed
by D115 in the hit test, which is where it turned out to live.

**D102 — A handle dragged past its anchor would not flip a path or a boolean. *Resolved.*** Every caller
of `tools::resize_factors` had it, a `Group` included; only `Rect` and its relatives escaped, because they
go through `resized_box`, which reflects the box across the anchor instead of scaling it.

**Two separate places threw the sign away, and fixing the first alone was not enough** — which is the kind
of thing this list is for, because a fix that only makes the symptom smaller is how one of these survives
a round (D96 is the other example, in this same round). `tools::scale_along` did `(wanted /
current).clamp(MIN_EXTENT, MAX_SCALE)`, turning every negative factor into `1e-6`: instead of turning
inside out the shape collapsed to a thousandth of a unit and then grew again on the *same* side. It is
`factor.signum() * factor.abs().clamp(…)` now. And `resize_factors` took `.abs()` of the pointer's
distance from the anchor, so the sign never reached `scale_along` at all — removed on all three branches,
including the `keep_ratio` pair, where the shared magnitude is `copysign`'d per axis so a proportional
drag can still flip **one** axis only.

Handing a negative factor on is safe precisely because `split_geometry_scale` knows what to do with one:
`Basis::of` peels the reflection into `Orientation::mirror` and the geometry still gets a positive scale,
which is §5.6's rule. `dragging_a_handle_past_the_opposite_corner_flips_a_path` asserts the world-space
box lands on the far side of the held corner **at its original size**, the clamp's signature having been a
collapse rather than merely a wrong position.

**D101 — X and Y reported the transform's translation, not the box's corner. *Resolved.*** Reported as
boolean coordinates resetting to 0,0 while "shapes within the boolean group report correct x/y" — and that
second clause is the diagnosis. For everything with an authored size the two points are the same one,
which is why `inspector_transform` reading `world[4]`/`world[5]` was right for years. `build::boolean`
gives its container **no transform of its own**, so the translation is the *parent's* origin however far
across the page the artwork sits. A pen `Path` has the same gap, and so does a `Group`.

The field shows `world · local_box.min_corner` now — the corner the selection outline is drawn round — and
the *edit* is a **world-space nudge**, `place_at(id, translate(typed − shown) · world)`, rather than the
old rebuild from the stripped basis. The nudge is exact for the identity edit and correct for any basis;
the rebuild could only ever land the *origin* on the typed number.

**Trimmed text is in scope of this, deliberately.** `BoxTrim` moves a text node's box off its local origin
without moving the ink, so the field reports the trimmed corner. Toggling trim therefore changes the
number in the field and nothing in the saved file, and that is the invariant the rule protects.

`a_booleans_box_corner_is_not_its_transforms_origin` pins the *cause* rather than the panel, which needs a
GPU context (D35), and one of the operands is asserted to have a local box starting at (0, 0) — the case
that made the old reading look correct, kept in the test so a reader can see why the two points are ever
confusable. *Anything else that reports a node's position owes the same question — is this the box, or the
matrix.*

**D100 — Several copies out of one parent landed in the wrong slot. *Resolved.*** Found by reading
`build::insert_subtrees` against the new placement rule (D40), not reported. It keeps a per-parent count
of how many subtrees this transaction has already added and adds it to each placement's index — exactly
right while the indices ascend, and wrong when they do not: children `[x, y]` with both copied and the
selection made **top-down** gives placements at 2 and 1, the shift turns the second into 2, and the
inserts land `[x, y, x', y']`. Copied bottom-up the same document comes out `[x, x', y, y']`, the intent.

Fixed the way `layers::plan_layer_move` plans a multi-row reorder (D54) — simulate as you go, rather than
sort the placements, which would have fixed this case and left the mechanism still assuming something
about its input. `added` now holds the *indices* already inserted at per parent, and each placement is
advanced past only those that landed **at or below** it.

`several_copies_land_above_their_own_originals_in_either_order` asserts both orders, and needs both — the
bottom-up one passes with the flat count in place, which is exactly how this survived.

**D99 — A `Line` had a bounding box that did nothing useful. *Resolved.*** Asked for as one handle on the
start point, one on the end, and a blue line along it. `canvas::line_ends`, `preview::LineEnd` and
`Drag::LineEnd`, with `tools::move_line_end` doing the geometry and `tools::line_ends_world` stating the
model fact both the chrome and the Shift constraint read.

**The suppression is one refusal, not a kind test in every gesture.** `canvas::selection_handles` answers
`None` for a lone line — since 2026-08-19 on `canvas::lone_line` rather than on `line_ends`, which was the
same question with a transform lookup in front of it (D238) — and the corner handles, the four side
bands, the `Ctrl`-skew, the rotate ring and all of their cursors hang off that one answer.
`draw_size_badge` returns early on the same condition, because the number it would quote is the bounding
box's: "142 × 0" for a horizontal line.
A line has one measurement worth reporting and it is its length; until something shows that, saying
nothing is the honest answer. *Keep the suppression in `selection_handles` rather than spreading it: a
per-gesture `matches!(kind, Line)` is five places to forget one.*

**The two ends are not symmetric, because the model stores only one of them** (§5.3). Moving the end is a
single `LineEnd` patch. Moving the start is a transform edit — **translation replaced, basis kept** — plus
a re-expressed `end`, so the far point stays where it is instead of travelling with the origin.
`moving_an_end_of_a_rotated_line_keeps_its_basis` was verified to fail when the basis is dropped.

Shift constrains to eighths of a turn about the *other* end, via the same `canvas::axial_corner` the line
tool uses while drawing; snapping is the **unshifted case only**, because a point snapped to a guide and
then forced to 45° is on neither.

*The transaction geometry lives in `tools/` so that it can be tested at all (D35), and the consequence was
a stated gap: the chrome suppression itself was **not covered by a test**. Half of that closed on
2026-08-19 — the rule is now the free function `canvas::lone_line` and it is pinned (D238) — and what is
still only on screen is the drawing that follows from it.*

**D98 — A lone `Line` and a lone `Path` had dead resize handles. *Resolved.*** The handles drew, they
armed, they showed the right directional cursor, and nothing moved. `canvas::resize_tx` had two paths — an
authored `size` went to `resize_to_handle`, anything else to `resize_group`, whose whole body iterates
**children**. A line and a pen path have neither, so the transaction came out empty. Measured before
fixing: `resize_group` on a lone line, 0 operations.

`tools::scale_geometry` could always do the work — which is exactly why dragging one of these *inside* a
selection of two always worked, and why the gap survived. What was missing is the anchor arithmetic:
geometry scales about the node's **origin**, and a path's box is usually nowhere near its origin, so the
node's transform takes the correction `anchor·(1 − S)`. **The routing is structural, not a fourth list of
kinds**: no authored size *and* no children scales its own geometry. `a_lone_line_and_path_scale_from_a_handle`
uses a path whose box is deliberately off its origin — the case the correction exists for, and one that
passes by accident when the box happens to start at zero.

One thing to know before reading the routing as the whole story: **a lone `Line` does not reach
`resize_geometry` from either surface.** D99 gives a single selected line two endpoint handles instead of
a box, and the inspector's W/H fields miss a `Line` because `size0` reports no box for the kind. So the
`Line` arm here is exercised by its own test and by nothing else today. *Do not delete it on the strength
of no caller reaching it — a numeric length for a line would want exactly this.*

*Owed, and now paid:* the inspector shows **W and H for a `Path` and a `Boolean`**, falling back to
`preview_local_box(id).size()`, with the write through `tools::resize_box_to` — a synthesized
bottom-right handle drag rather than a second copy of the anchor arithmetic. Routing through the handle's
own path is the better answer: a `Path`'s width has no field to assign, so the gesture is the only
definition of it there is.

**D97 — An outside stroke's clip was padded by the shape and not by the ink. *Resolved.*** Reported
against a 241pt outside stroke on a 142pt boolean. Most of what that shows **is** mathematically right,
and the answer to the question as asked is "mostly not a bug": at the SVG default mitre limit of 4 a
corner throws a spike four times further than the flat of the stroke reaches.

One part of it was a real bug, and a silently wrong drawing rather than a coarse one. The complement
rectangle an outside stroke is clipped against (§6.3) was padded by the shape's bounding box's width plus
its height **and nothing else** — no allowance for the stroke at all. Generous for a hairline and
*narrower than the ink* once a stroke got wide: the complement's outer edge sat inside the stroke and cut
straight rectangular bites out of it. The reported numbers: a 142×142 outline gets 284 of padding while a
241pt stroke reaches 964 at a mitre.

`scene::outer_bounds` takes a `reach` now, and `scene::miter_reach(width, limit) = width ·
limit.max(1.0)` is where the rule is stated. `svg::align_clip` got the same allowance, because the two
must agree or an export differs from the canvas. Both tests were verified to fail with the old padding,
and the failure message quotes the report's own numbers.

*A boolean is where this shows first, and that is not coincidence: its outline has sharp vertices wherever
two operands' edges cross, so it throws the longest mitres of any shape. Any future padding that is a
function of the path alone owes the same question — how far can the ink go, not how big is the shape.*

***The `miter_reach` term is unobservable in pixels today, and that was established by flipping it rather
than assumed.*** Added 2026-08-19 with the pixel tests of D93:
`an_outside_stroke_on_a_boolean_is_the_complement_mitre_and_all` samples the corner bisector of a 6-wide
outside stroke on an 80×80 ring, where a 90° corner throws its mitre tip 6√2 ≈ 8.5 from the vertex — so
there is ink at (5, 5) and clear air at (2, 2), which is the first time the mitre has been seen in pixels
at all. It still does not pin this entry's arithmetic. `outer_bounds` pads by `(width + height).max(1.0) +
reach`, which on that ring is **160 before `reach` contributes its 24** (`miter_reach(6, 4)`, the default
limit); fold `miter_reach` to zero at the `complement` call site and nothing observable changes — the
corner probe stays `Stroke` and every flat-edge probe stays right. What the corner probe genuinely holds
is that the complement covers the whole plane outside the shape, corners included, and the test's own doc
comment says so rather than reading as the stronger claim.

What does watch the term, precisely, because the two unit tests in `scene.rs` are easy to over-read.
`the_mitre_allowance_is_the_limit_times_the_width` pins the **formula**, against literal constants.
`an_outside_clip_clears_the_widest_mitre_it_could_have_to` pins that `outer_bounds` **spends** `reach` at
all — it fails with the old shape-only padding at its two wide rows (241 at limit 4, 600 at 8), where the
reach exceeds the shape-derived pad, and passes regardless at the narrow ones. It does not check
`miter_reach`'s value, since it computes the ink it expects from that same function: shrink the formula
and both sides of the assertion shrink together. *Revisit if that pad is ever tightened — it is a rule of
thumb rather than a bound, so it is the obvious tidy-up, and the moment it stops dwarfing the ink
allowance this entry's arithmetic becomes load-bearing with nothing at the pixel level behind it.*

**D96 — A dropdown's rows changed height when the pointer crossed them. *Resolved.*** Reported with the
user's own theory — the border on the active item — which was right about the mechanism.

egui 0.35 resolves a `Button`'s frame **per widget state** and computes its inner margin as
`button_padding − bg_stroke.width`; a resting row then drops the stroke from the layout while a hovered
*or selected* one keeps it. The panels set `button_padding.y = 0`, so that margin is −1, and measured: a
resting row wants 21pt and a hovered or selected one 23. The old floor of 22 sat *between* them — so the
selected row in every dropdown was permanently a pixel taller than its neighbours, and the rows below
whichever row was hovered moved down by one.

`ui::menu_rows(ui)` and `ui::MENU_ROW_H` (24) are the fix, called by all eight dropdown popups. 24 clears
both natural heights.

**That was half a fix, and this entry said so in the wrong direction** — it recorded that removing the
border was deliberately *not* the answer. Reported again: "there's still a little shift on hover, much
less than before". The state-dependent margin is short on **x** as well — 8 − 1 — so a hovered row wants
two points more *width* than a resting one and the popup grows to its widest row, re-laying out every row
in it. A floor cannot fix an axis that has no floor on it. So `menu_rows` now also zeroes `bg_stroke` on
`inactive`, `hovered`, `active` and `open`, which makes the two branches geometrically identical on
**both** axes. The fill is the hover cue on its own, which is what a menu row conventionally uses.
*Restoring a border to a menu row puts the shift back.*

`a_menu_rows_height_does_not_depend_on_its_state` asserts **width** as well as height, across the states
and at four scales. The height half was verified to fail at a floor of 22, the width half with the stroke
restored — 69.22 against 71.22, exactly the 2pt. It needs no synthetic hover, because a *selected* row is
framed too. The font-family dropdown never had either problem because it paints its rows by hand (D84).

*The general lesson: a widget's size can depend on its interaction state, so a row floor has to clear the
tallest state rather than the resting one. The sharper form is what the second round paid for —
**equalising the states beats clearing a floor**, because a floor only exists on one axis and a
state-dependent margin need not.*

**D95 — Grouping inside a boolean re-parenthesises the operation. *Intentional.*** Noticed as a possible
slip: enter a boolean, select two of its operands, press `Ctrl+G`, and the group really is made. It is a
feature. `boolean::operand_of` gives a `Group` the *union* of its contents, so a group inside a boolean is
one operand: brackets in what is otherwise a flat left-to-right fold. A nested boolean set to Union says the
same thing, and grouping is the gesture the hand already knows. Figma allows it for the same reason.

Measured, because the claim is only worth anything if the answer changes. Three 100-wide bands over the same
100-tall strip, at x = 0, 50 and 80, under `Exclude`: ungrouped the fold is `((a ⊻ b) ⊻ c)` and comes to 100
wide, and with the last two grouped it is `a ⊻ (b ∪ c)` and comes to 130. `Subtract` would have hidden the
difference entirely, since `a − b − c` and `a − (b ∪ c)` are the same set, which is exactly why
`a_group_inside_a_boolean_is_a_single_operand` uses Exclude. *Do not "fix" this by refusing `Ctrl+G` inside a
boolean: it makes a shape the user asked for, and that test is what says the answer changes at all.*

**D94 — The Alt-drag copy of a boolean previewed its operands, not the boolean. *Resolved.*** Reported as
"alt+drag shows a copy of the original shapes on the draggable clone, instead of the boolean preview" —
sharper than the note carried as "a ghost boolean previews as empty", and the difference mattered, because
it was two faults rather than one.

The ghost walk had **no derived outline to draw**: a captured subtree has no `Resolved` behind it and
`GhostNode` carried nothing but the kind. `GhostNode::path` is that outline, filled in `build_ghost` —
children-first, threading a map so a boolean inside a boolean is read rather than evaluated twice — so the
arithmetic runs once per gesture and never in the scene walk. It is also what pushed `boolean::Operands`
into losing its `&Document`: the ghost is the third view (§9.4), and it walks the captured `Node`s
directly, so there stays one reading of what an operand contributes.

And `scene::paint_ghost` **did not stop at a `Boolean`** the way `paint_node` has since D88, so it went on
to draw the operands over a result that was not there. That is the half that was visible.

Both halves were checked to fail independently.
`a_ghost_boolean_previews_its_own_result_and_not_its_operands` is differential — the preview must draw
what the commit draws, since a ghost drawing *nothing* is also wrong and only the comparison says which of
the three states it is in — and `a_ghost_evaluates_a_boolean_inside_a_boolean` pins the children-first
order, which a walk that built the parent first would get silently wrong by combining against nothing.

**The mirror case was found by probing the adjacent path rather than reported**: Alt-dragging a copy of a
layer that is *inside* a boolean. `ClonedSubtree` parents the copy to its source's parent, which for an
operand is the boolean, so the release changes the shape. Measured before fixing: 150 wide previewed
against 270 committed. Two different mistakes, worth keeping apart:

- **The seed.** `reevaluate_booleans` walked up from each *moved* node's parent, which is right for a move
  and wrong for a ghost: a moved node reshapes every boolean above it, a ghost reshapes the one it is
  parented *to*. The seed set is `moved`-parents chained with the ghost parents.
- **The lookups.** `operand_children` returns the committed children **plus** any ghost parented to that
  node; `operand_visible` is the matching branch, `nested` falls back to a ghost's own `GhostNode::path`,
  and `transform_of` now checks **ghosts first**: it used to answer `Affine::IDENTITY` for a ghost id,
  because `absorb` writes a `SetTransform` aimed at a ghost into the ghost itself. Nothing drew wrong from
  that — the ghost walk reads `GhostNode::transform` directly — and it only mattered once a boolean began
  evaluating over a ghost operand.

So the honest summary is that a preview **can** add artwork a boolean consumes, while still being unable
to reparent, reorder or delete: `absorb`'s comment stays true, and `children_of` is the one lookup that is
no longer purely the document's. Pinned by `a_ghost_operand_widens_the_boolean_it_is_dropped_into`, which
asserts the widened outline *and* runs the preview-equals-commit comparison.

**D93 — A boolean's stroke alignment was measured through an outline it cannot build. *Resolved.***
`geometry::stroke_align_applies` was `local_path(kind).is_some_and(is_closed)`, and `local_path` returns
`None` for a `Boolean` on purpose (§9.4) — so a boolean answered "not closed", the one answer its outline
is never. Two consequences, both silent: the alignment dropdown was absent from a boolean's Stroke panel,
and both the walk's `closed` gate and the SVG writer drew an inside or outside stroke **centred** while
`Resolved` had already sized the node as though the ink were where the model said. The predicate
special-cases the kind now rather than measuring it, which is sound because `boolean::from_flo` closes
every subpath and normalizes each one's winding: a derived outline is closed by construction.

The exporter had the same fault twice more, out of the same call — `svg::align_clip` and
`svg::resolved_dashes` both built from `geometry::local_path(node.kind())`. There is one
`svg::outline(node, derived)` now. `an_aligned_stroke_on_a_boolean_exports_with_its_clip` asserts the
`clipPath` rather than the width, because the clip *is* the construction: no clip means no alignment,
whatever width was written.

*The general shape: a predicate that measures derived geometry has to be told which kinds derive theirs.
Any new `is_…(kind)` reading `local_path` owes a `Boolean` arm.*

*Measured in **pixels** as well, added 2026-08-19 in `ondin-export/tests/boolean.rs`:
`an_inside_stroke_on_a_boolean_lands_inside_both_of_its_edges` renders the ring the hole test uses —
`Subtract` of an 80×80 at (10, 10) and a 40×40 at (30, 30), filled red and stroked blue at 6 — through
`VelloCpuRenderer` at 100×100 and classifies probes along one scanline as nothing, stroke or fill. The
`clipPath` assertion above is the **markup**, and markup cannot see the raster backend doing something
else: `scene.rs` builds the same intent out of different code, clipping to the outline itself with
`ClipRule::NonZero` for Inside and to an "everything but the shape" complement with `ClipRule::EvenOdd`
for Outside.*

*The **hole** is what makes it worth the pixels. "Inside" means inside the filled region, so on a ring the
band on the outer edge runs inward while the band on the hole's edge runs **outward from the hole**, into
the ring; both are asserted, and so is a fill band surviving between them — without which "the stroke is
inside" would pass over a ring painted stroke-colour edge to edge, which is exactly what a doubled width
with no clip gives. The centred alignment is asserted at the two probes the inside one leaves empty, so
neither of those passes by the stroke simply being absent. All three alignments were scanned before
anything was asserted, and all three are right: at width 6 inside puts its bands at 10..16 and 24..30,
centre at 7..13 and 27..33, outside at 4..10 and 30..36 — every probe therefore sits at least 1.5px clear
of a boundary, which keeps the antialiased edge out of the assertions. **The two flips fail in different
places**, which is why both edges are in the test: dropping `NodeKind::Boolean` from
`stroke_align_applies` — this entry's own bug — re-centres the whole stroke and shows just outside the
outline, while clipping to `outer_bounds(shape, 0.0)` instead of the outline in `scene.rs`'s `push_layer`
call paints the band straight across the hole and leaves both outer-edge probes exactly right. A test
that sampled only the outer edge would have called that second version correct.*

*`an_outside_stroke_on_a_boolean_is_the_complement_mitre_and_all` is the other half, same ring, same
scanline, added the same day. **Outside is not the mirror of Inside in the code**: the walk cannot clip
to the shape, so it builds "everything but the shape" — `outer_bounds` with the outline appended, taken
even-odd — and `scene.rs`'s own comment justifies the even-odd rule by saying the hole **is** outside.
That is a claim about pixels and now has one: with the bands at 4..10 and 30..36, the stroke sits outside
the outer edge and paints **into the hole**, where the inside one painted away from it, with fill
surviving at 12 and at 26. The flip is that construction losing its second half — clip to `outer_bounds`
without appending the shape and even-odd keeps the interior too, so the just-inside probe at 12 comes
back `Stroke`. Two further probes on the corner bisector, ink at (5, 5) and clear air at (2, 2), put the
mitre in pixels for the first time; what they do **not** do is pin D97's `miter_reach`, and that finding
is recorded there rather than here.*

**D92 — The paintable-kinds list was written a *third* time, in the inspector. *Resolved.*** Reported
after living with the feature: "adding fills and strokes — which now don't show at all in the inspector".
`inspector_single` chose its panels from its own hand-written list of kinds, and it had drifted exactly
the way D87 predicted: the op layer and the bulk-edit walk both knew that a boolean paints, and the panel
did not. So the builder could hand a new boolean the bottom operand's paint and there was then no way to
change it. The panel asks `node.kind().takes_paint()` now.

*The lesson is D87's sequel rather than D87 again: fixing a rule that is written twice means finding
**every** copy, and that fix removed one and left one standing. `takes_paint` is the list — nothing else
may spell it out.*

**D91 — Exclude behaved as Union, and holes filled solid. *Resolved.*** Reported as "exclude doesn't
really work — it just unions", then narrowed by the user in the same breath: "it does work, but very
specifically… I moved the oval 1px and it triggered the exclusion". That second observation is what made
it findable, and it was pointing at two separate faults that looked like one.

**`Exclude` was composed wrongly.** `sub(add(a,b), intersect(a,b))` is the textbook identity and does not
survive contact with a graph-traversal boolean: the intersection's boundary consists *entirely* of pieces
of the operands' own edges, so `path_sub` is handed the same edge graph as `a ∪ b` and re-assembles `a`
and `b` as two separate loops. Measured rather than reasoned about — a throwaway probe dumped each
result's subpaths and their signed areas, and Exclude's were the two original shapes, untouched, to the
last decimal. It is now `path_full_intersect`'s two exterior paths from one cut.

**And the winding convention was wrong**, which is the part the 1px observation was really about.
flo_curves reads a path set even-odd, so it returns a hole as a subpath wound the *same* way as its
container; Ondin fills non-zero, which paints that solid. Nudging an operand until the overlap reached an
edge turned the hole into a notch — one subpath, no winding question — and the operation appeared to start
working. `from_flo` now alternates each subpath's direction with its nesting depth.

*Two things worth keeping from how this was fixed.* The winding normalization's first version was itself
wrong, and its own test caught it: a ring's bounding-box centre lies inside the hole, so each subpath
looked nested inside the other and neither was reversed. Depth now needs the enclosing subpath to be
strictly *larger*, sound because boolean output has no crossing subpaths. And both tests were checked to
fail with their fix reverted, each reporting the user's symptom in its message.

*Both faults now have a **pixel** assertion as well, added 2026-08-19 in
`ondin-export/tests/boolean.rs` — the gap `roadmap.md` held open, since a geometry test cannot see a
backend fill an inner subpath solid. And the pair confirms that "two faults that looked like one" is
literally true at that level too: losing the winding correction leaves the **exclude** test green, and
replacing the exclude arm with `path_add` leaves the **subtract** test green. A hole from a reversed
nested subpath and a hole from two disjoint ones cannot be caught by the same assertion.*

**D90 — Resizing a boolean previewed the operands moving but not resizing. *Resolved.*** The preview's
evaluator overrode **transforms only** and read each operand's *kind* from the committed document. A
resize is partly a `SetGeometry`, so every operand got its new position and kept its old size: the circle
moved, the rectangle did not grow, and the box stayed whatever the un-grown rectangle spanned.

The lookups are now a named struct (`boolean::Operands`) rather than loose closures, so a caller has to
answer all of them; `RenderOverrides` supplies `current_kind`. The test asserts the previewed box
*doubles* rather than merely *changes* — "the outline changed" was already true of the broken version.

**D89 — A boolean was measured by its operands, not by its result. *Resolved.*** `query::local_box`
answers containers by unioning their children through their transforms, which for a boolean measures
exactly the shapes the operation *consumed*. It now reads the cached outline first, and
`session::preview_local_box` reads the *previewed* outline first.

**The third symptom in the same report had the same cause**, which is worth recording because it did not
look related: "transforms on booleans act like transforming a multi-selection". A boolean already took the
*group* resize path. What was wrong was the box that path is given: with a reference rectangle larger than
the artwork, the handles sit off the shape and a drag maps to a scale factor the eye does not expect. One
fix, three symptoms.

**D88 — Booleans drew their operands on top of their own result. *Resolved.*** `scene::paint_node`
painted the container's outline and then recursed into its children, so every boolean drew its result
*and* its inputs over the top. It made the feature look unimplemented rather than buggy, and each
operation failed differently, which is why it read as three separate faults:

- **Subtract / Intersect / Exclude appeared to do nothing** — their results are *smaller*, so the operands
  covered them completely.
- **Union appeared to work**, until an operand moved, when the still-drawn child was the thing that
  visibly moved.
- **The operands kept their own fills**, so three fills were on screen where the model says one.

Two further gaps fell out of the same root, both "the container is not really a shape yet": `Boolean` was
missing from `resolve::is_indexed`, so a boolean could be selected from the layers tree but not clicked;
and `query::group_chain` did not treat it as a group, so a click that *did* land went to an operand.

Separately, the preview was a frame behind: `Resolved`'s cache refreshes on commit. `RenderOverrides` now
carries its own boolean cache, and the evaluation is one parameterized recursion
(`boolean::evaluate_node`) shared by both.

*The lesson is about what "the model is right" is worth: every one of these was in the architecture text
as an intention — "the container paints one path and its children do not paint independently" was written
down before it was true. Prose is not a test.*

**D87 — `is_paintable` was a second copy of `takes_paint`, and adding a kind split them. *Resolved.***
`takes_paint`'s own doc comment said it was spelled there so that "two lists of kinds would drift the
first time a kind was added" — and `document::is_paintable` was that second list all along. Adding
`Boolean` to the first left `SetFills` rejecting the very transaction `build::boolean` emits, with
`WrongKindForOp` and nothing pointing at where the two disagreed. Found by a test asserting the new
boolean inherits its bottom operand's paint, which is the only reason it was not found by a user seeing an
invisible shape.

*The general lesson is the one the comment already drew: a rule about kinds that is written twice will be
updated once. Both copies were three lines and obviously equivalent, which is exactly why nobody looked.*
There was a **third** copy, in the inspector, and this fix did not go looking for it — D92.

**D86 — A layer dragged out of a frame stayed clipped by it until release. *Resolved.*** Found while
testing the canvas auto-scroll, and the two are related: auto-scroll makes it *easy* to drag something a
long way out of a frame. The clip was correct about the tree and wrong about the gesture — the dragged
child is still a child until the transaction commits. `RenderOverrides::escape_clip` takes it out, and the
walk closes and reopens the parent's clip layer around it.

**Two attempts, and the first one was wrong in two ways** — both caught by the user, and both the tempting
implementation:

- It drew the escaping layer **last, on top of its siblings**, which is what a deferred second pass gets
  you for free. Figma does not: z-order is information the user is steering by. Hence the
  close-and-reopen, which keeps the child in its own place.
- It escaped the clip **for the whole drag**, from the first pixel. That removes the only signal for what
  the release will do. The escape is now bound to `move_destination` — the very function the release calls
  — so the picture and the drop cannot disagree.

Two more things worth keeping straight. It is set from the **gesture**, not inferred from the overrides,
because a resize also rewrites a child's transform and a box growing past its frame's edge *should* stay
clipped. And the **Alt-drag copy needed the same switch** (`escape_clip_ghosts`).

Pinned by three tests in `overrides.rs`, each asserting the buggy state as well as the fixed one — the
fixture's *other* children are clipped either way, so "is anything clipped" would have passed for the
wrong reason (it did, on the first attempt). One asserts the z-position explicitly, since that is the half
that was wrong and looked right.

**D85 — The Type panel had three control heights in one card. *Resolved.*** Measured by the user as 24px
for the family dropdown, 26px for the variant, 28px for every field beside them. Both wrong numbers came
from the same fact stated two different ways, and neither is visible in the source:

- **A `ComboBox` paints exactly `interact_size.y`** (plus `button_padding.y`, which these rows zero). Say
  nothing and it takes the theme's 24. The family dropdown said nothing.
- **Its border is stroked *inside* its own rect**, so `FIELD_BORDER_H` must not come off its height. That
  subtraction is right for content inside a `field_row` and wrong here, giving 26.

The same trap D45 already recorded one dimension over. Now stated whole in all four places, and pinned by
`combo_height_tests`, which asserts all three numbers — 28 asked for, 26 from the subtraction, 24 from
silence — so the test names the symptom rather than just the fix.

*The panel's fields are 28px and the popover's are 26px on purpose (`CELL`'s own comment: a nine-row
popover should not tower over the card it belongs to). Uniform means "matches its neighbours", not one
number everywhere.*

**D83 — The Google Fonts catalog is fetched and disk-cached, not shipped with the build. *Deviation,
kept.*** §5.4a called for "a catalog of family metadata [that] ships with the app (regenerated each
release from Google's metadata; refreshed online when available)". There is no build-time generation
step, so what shipped is the other half only: `FontService` fetches the Fontsource list and
variable-axis endpoints, writes the result to `catalog.json` in the OS cache dir, and reads that copy
*first* on every later launch while a refresh runs behind it.

That has the same two properties the shipped catalog was for — the picker is populated on the frame it
first opens, and it works offline — from the second launch onwards. The gap is the **first** launch
with no network: the picker then lists system fonts alone. **D352 narrowed what that costs everywhere
else**: one successful online session warms fifty families' regular faces onto disk, so every offline
session after it has faces to draw with and not only names whose downloads never arrive. It cannot be
narrowed past the first run, and that is arithmetic rather than a limitation — `warm` asks `faces_of`
for each of the fifty, `faces_of` has no `CatalogEntry` to build a `FaceSpec` from, and a machine that
has never reached the network has nothing to prefetch *from*. A generated catalog would close it at the
cost of a release step and ~1 MB in the binary for data that goes stale between releases anyway.
*Kept; revisit if first-run-offline turns out to matter, in which case ship a trimmed catalog (family
names and ids, no unicode ranges) rather than the whole document.*

**D84 — The picker's family list was rebuilt in full every frame it was open. *Resolved.*** Reported
as "opening the font family dropdown is slow, it takes about a second". It was not I/O: nothing is
fetched by opening the list. `ScrollArea::show` clips *painting*, not widget code, so all ~1900
families were laid out, id-hashed and glyph-rasterized to show twenty rows. Virtualized with
`show_rows` (§9.2), which is why the row height is now a constant and the rows are painted by hand.

The second half of the same report — "applying a font takes several seconds" — was I/O, and three
things compounded: `ureq`'s free functions build a use-once agent (a fresh DNS lookup, TCP connect and
TLS handshake per file), the faces were fetched one after another, and `defSubset` for a CJK family is
megabytes per weight (`noto-sans-jp`'s Japanese subset is 2.4 MB). Now: one shared agent, a bounded
pool, the regular upright dispatched first and registered on its own so the canvas swaps at the first
file rather than the last, and a variable file where the family has one, which turns nine downloads
into one (§5.4a).
